column46: Revesby, 9 February 1717. Yesterday I was sent for in all hast by your steward Wright to speak to him before he dyed, but I found him much better than I expected, and I think in no apparent danger. He has not yett received Michaelmas rents but will, he says, do it and return it you as soon as he get out. I believe the man is safe enough, but in all things very slow. He desired me to send you his humble service etc., but att present can't write himself. I took effectual care about your boards, but their is few of em but what are in use, viz. 70 in the doors, stairs and the best chamber floor att Sandoms house, and the most of the rest are fitted for the 3 floors cornish etc. in the new building, one floor of which will be now saved by a plaster floor. The whole was 200 and not 240 as you mention. I have heard nothing from the surveyor since he left me. We agreed he should send you the survey to London. As to Lord Harborough's estate, by what I can find it will improve something, and since it lies so convenient for you I would advise to buy it. I wish you all health and success in your designed purchase of £1200 per annum . Tic a prodigious thing and must be very cheap to pay both taxes and interest. I beg your pardon for this freedom, but I suppose you must borrow unless you sell some part of Lincolnshire as well as Nottshire Yorks and Derby. The country are fully satisfied about the improvements youve made here, and tic impossible, I believe, ever to think of getting one penny abated, tho Isle try all ways to do it. I thank God my stock of all kinds does very well. My sheep make great improvement, so that against another year I design to stock more with them. My horses are in good order and my beasts likewise. I told the Pad as you call it to cess you one guinea loss, so that considering the work I lost little by it. You may depend upon my coach mares as and when you please to command em. I wonder you should in the least dispute it, they are and shall be kept in very good order. I shall observe your directions in not fixing for Derby. I am infinitely obliged to you for the trouble you about a place Our duty and love attend you all. I am your most dutiful son and servant, J. Banks. The woodman goes on very well. The old ones were discharged at his first coming. I have not seen a right horse for your weight since I came into these parts. I can't as yett dispose of your 2 corn farms as you desire, nor I doubt I can't, so pray your orders how to proceed. I can't find Mr. Hatson's bill; I wish your get me another, and Isle order his monies.

Boston, 20 February 1717. I had yours and was at Reavsby last week and understand Mr. Banks and Lady is going a journey, and if you please we will stay till their return before we begin the work again. The sashes is ready for the three windows and will out of hand make the two you've ordered, and as I said before they shall be as cheap as from London. I beg you'll please to give order for the other three that they may be put in when the scaffaling is ready. I need not tell you the house will look oddly without 'em, and as for the old windows and glass (if you've not occasion for 'em) I will give the worth for 'em. In my next you shall have particulars, and am, with duty, your honor's humble servant, Jno Sherlock.

column39: The Letters and Papers of the Banks Family of Revesby Abbey. 1704-1760. Ed. by J. W. F. Hill. The Publications of the Lincoln Record Society, 45. Hereford. 1952.
column46: 23 February 1717. I have yours, and am content you sash all the 5 front chambers, but am much afraid you have not seen the newest fashioned ones and the scanshons of the wood, therefore if you'll send me a most critically exact measure l'le get you one made here with or without a frame and send it down per next ships. If you please I'll only send you the guts, but send me a most exact measure. I'll also find all pullys and cords from hence. I wish the best chamber was done window high, I mean wainscoted, and then the rest we might when I come down. I would have the 5 sashes come up to the or at most not above an inch of brick arch appear. If you'll order this matter I leave to my son and you.

Revesby, 24 February . I'm not a little concerned that you should think that I'm negligent either in ordering your affairs or answering your letters nicely. I'm sure I do both to the very utmost of my capacity, and as for Mr. Wright I'm very sure I've had more trouble with him than it would have been to me to've received and returned you all your rents, and for what I can see I've no reason to alter my character that I've all along given you of him. However Ladiday is not yett passed, and he says that the rents are never thought much att if they pay but one 1/2 year before another come due. Mr. Wright has never yett paid Ralph Kirkham the monies. He returned my Mother to London, so that I've been obliged to let Ralp have sometimes £30 or £40 or more to trade with all. I only mention this to show you his slowness. Since my letter is gone to my father H it would disoblige him beyond measure not to come, but if you think proper to command me in any service at Scofton, I can easily from thence step on to the Assizes, and will if you please. I do not doubt but by the blessing of God we shall perform our journey safe. We have so ordered our house as to housekeeping and business when I come back that if I did not go now I can't go till June. I'm very sensible of the great charge that building or altering is, and would endeavour to contrive to put you to as little as may be. Your great generosity to me in that particular affair needs no spinning on, therefore I've made a little draft in this paper which I'll explain on the other side, which, when corrected by your hand, will perfectly satisfy both me and my wife, and greater additions may be made to it, when ever you think fit. I should be mighty glad if you approve of it. As for the pheasants I do not design to keep 'em up att all, but let 'em run about in the yard if they please. Perchance some of em may stay home in the yard. I can't here of a drover, therefore must beg you'll order 'em to be packed safe and sent by the Lowth carrier, to be left for me att Horncastle. I thank you for the votes. Our Tory rogues won't believe theirs anything in the invasion, and say its all a plot to get 4s. in the pound. I've rattled 'em up. I am, Sir, your most dutiful son and obliged servant, J. Banks. (Plan) Imprimis a garden to the south 35 yards by 25 up which a gravel walk into the Hall (which I propose to be the little parlour and vestible), which is the grace of every house. Second, the dining room as at present, but a drawing room where the two larders now are, only I would take of it a screed as in the draft, one part for a bottle house, the other to keep salting tubs, flower tubs etc., the sellers may be settled I find by the sough, then I would make the present hall into a common sitting parlour, only a passage cut of with rail and banister att the top to give light. This will make our sitting parlour better by being nearer our business, and keep the best end of our house always clean, and make the offices no worse. I would have two half doors to run into the .... that would go out of the hall to the best stair case. Dick Sandom's old doors were too low to use again, most of 'em very bad, and they made mortar boards but I'll take the 2 good ones for some use.

Boston, 25 February 1717. This day I received yours and am sorry we've gon on so fast for the sashes is ready for the other two windows. The reason is the men that makes 'em is stayed for in another place hear. I've sent the mould of both the inside and outside; please to take some workman's opinions. You know there's 12 squares in a window, they're 17 inches and 1/4 and 11 inches and 1/4. I pray you send some to see they be stright and please to send more than the just number. As for pullys, they're all in as good as any is made. I've some from London but I've better from Lincoln as I will show you the difference, Please to send lines and I think putty for you'll get it cheaper and better then the glayser you've from Spilsby, and theirs a worse from Horncastle offers his service to your son that did work for Mr. Whelpdaile (and badly too). He put glass into 9 little window where I was concerned and charged 50 li. of putty at 12d. per. Please to send brass pins to fasen the squares in the rabbits and screws to make fast the sashes. Ther's some that has keys to 'em but are offen out of order; the other I think the best. You may have these at Mr. J. Child's, ironmonger, at Temple bare. I don't know the man, but have had such things from him, and is very willing to mend or change anything that is a mis. I understand you would have the best chamber done first. Please to give your order about the particulars following whither you'll have the games splad or window shuts or a pear glass or glass over the mantle or wood or stone chimney piece or panel hanging or a pice painting over the chimney. I had rather take my work but in this I can't tell how it can be done. If you please I'll send you men that is as honest and good workmen as any is and will have no more wages for 'em then at Boston. Mr. Banks may take account of 'em. If there be the least objection against 'em they shall be removed, and for my own journeys and assistance I'll refer to your honour. I know you'll want deals I told Mr. Banks so, and there's none to be had but at one place, a young carlos merchants. We was both in a mind to secure 'em and I have done so. They're fit for business and cheap. Your humble servant, Jno Sherlock.

column39: The Letters and Papers of the Banks Family of Revesby Abbey. 1704-1760. Ed. by J. W. F. Hill. The Publications of the Lincoln Record Society, 45. Hereford. 1952.
column46: 28 February 1717. I like this pattern of sashe guts with the alterations by the props very well, and what you have made will doe, but let the rest be made thus. I have wrote fully to my son that Isle allow 2s. 6d. per yard and you'll find all, or Isle find deals and pay 14d., so if workmanship or stuff come to more he to bear it so you must settle it with him. In that great room the windows in the end are to be made up and only 2 in front and my son may have shuts and ends splayed or let them alone, but the place betwixt the windows must be for a great glass. He knows best whether heel have a chimney glass or not. I would have the chimney .... as they are and a large panal over the chimney and the rest of the room window sole high, and a small cornish to nail the hangings to. You may make sashes for the 5 windows in the chamber. Be sure they reach to the cornish or within an inch. When you are working there let Potter be ordered to rectify his base work in the parlour chimney windows and floor. Desire my son force him to doe it then. I am in hast. Your faithful servant, J. Banks. Pray keep this pattern. I desire your further directions about the glass sash cord, how much and how much putty. I never trouble Gazer to put in the glass, but my joiners always doe it.

Boston, 30 March 1717. The last I se your son he said we should begin with the next month, and not hearing anything on it I made bold to send this. I've reserved some of my best men for you and as I said before I can't tell how to take the work for it will be mixed as it was before. I'll have no more wages then we've at home, and for my journeys I'll refer to your Honour. The measure of work that is done comes to more than day wages but I desire no more then as above, and likewise no more for the sashes then you can have 'em from London, which I desire you'll please to let me know and I'll make you a bill of all that is done. The sashes is all ready and coloured on the outside and fit for putting in. They're as good as can be made on the heart edge of the plank. Workmen that does their business well will tell you not above half a plank is fit to make sashes. The frames is made of oak with an archetrave. Please to favour me with a line, and twill oblige, Sir, your most humble servant, Jno Sherlock.

column39: The Letters and Papers of the Banks Family of Revesby Abbey. 1704-1760. Ed. by J. W. F. Hill. The Publications of the Lincoln Record Society, 45. Hereford. 1952.
column46: 2 April 1717. I am favoured with yours, and in my son's absence would advice to begin to put up the sashes and wainscott the great chambers and floor daughter's dressing room and wainscott and finish it, and the servants room below, for wee shall come down very early of the year, and he will not have room for us. The glass, sash coards and pulley are all put up, and shall be sent directed to you per next ships. As to the price of sashes here I profess to you I have them offered according to the patterns here of my own windows, which are of the best kind: the sashes are about 7 foot high, only 6 lights in a sash, to wit 12 in a window, and my glass here are 19 inches by 12. I say the woodwork Essay the wood work with pullys but without coards and weights, at 20s. a window they reckon the 12 lights at 12d. a light and the frames at 8s., but I'll freely give you a guiney. Since deals are dear I would have my sons great chamber only wainscoted window sole height, and the sashes put up to the outside cornish or within an inch, and a cornish round and as much left for hangings as conveniently can. A door must be made where the way is designed into the intended new wing. Let it be contrived to save deals as much as you can, and no .... but the stiles stuck with beads. As I wrote my son word, I'll pay by measure, but let him make out for his own conveniences and jobbing. I will order my son let you have moneys what you want, who am your affectionate friend and servant, J. Banks. This letter should have come of Wedensday but was forgot by mistake.

column39: The Letters and Papers of the Banks Family of Revesby Abbey. 1704-1760. Ed. by J. W. F. Hill. The Publications of the Lincoln Record Society, 45. Hereford. 1952.
column46: Overtone, 5 April 1717. I am very glad you've sold Scofton etc. to your satisfaction. Theirs no doubt but the monies will yield you twice the profitt that place did. My wife joins with me in returning you our most hearty thanks for your repeated kind offer, of what we shall have occasion for, att Scofton, and particularly for reserveing the 2 marble chimney pieces, too which I've bought one here 4 foot high and 5 foot long and a slab for the hearth of 5 foot by 20 inches. I rejoiced very much to see by my mother's last and kind letter that she was very easy as to the selling of Scofton, so that I hope every one is pleased with it. She added that you had some thoughts of furnishing up Shirtliffe Hall. If so you'll want I reckon all your household goods that Mr. Sutton does not buy. My wife desires you'd not part with any of the pieces of tapstery and if you do not use them else where your self, would be extremely glad your let 2 of 'em be putt up in our best lodging room, which she thinks would make it very handsome. I reckon their is their a little tumbrel cart which I desire to have, if not otherways disposed of. I suppose nothing will be done about the goods till you come down, and then if you please I'll wait of you over, but att present I cant see my going would of any advantage. I hope this affair will bring you down very soon into the country, which we shall be extremely glad of, and will hasten the fitting up of the house as soon as we return, which will be of Easter Monday. As to the orders youve given Mr. Sherlock if you please to give me leave I'll tell you my thoughts, after which you may either continue or alter your orders as you think proper. The floor in the best parlour is so very bad that it shames the room so I would have those boards used in my wife's dressing room, and the parlour all new floored and the vestible laid to it. Potter shall lay down the old floor according to promise, so the charge will be no more, this peace of work I would have first gone about. 2d to take down the partition between the hall and great stair case and put up the prop that the mason may lay the floor, then the sashes put in the chamber. My wife has a great many things litterd in the great lodging room and the key locked up so that to go into that room as youve ordered would be highly inconvenient. If you please to alter Mr. Shirlock's orders as soon as I get home I'll fetch up Ketton stone and plaster for the 2 floors in the new building, and all shall be done with dispatch. Pray Sir do you design the garden walls to be built as soon as brick and lime ready as we agreed before. If so I will not bestow any charge of fitting up the little court. I'll send you Shirlock's letter next post and will take the best care I can as soon as I return about Coap's farm etc. I'm glad youve sent R. K. tobacco. I dare say he'll earn it if you please to employ him. You almost surprise me in telling me, Hagnaby is so soon exposed to sale. I got a promise att the assizes that our cause about How Briggs should be diferd so hope shall have your assistance in it. I'm surprised Mr. Wright should not make you return. The man grows worse and worse. All here join in most affectionate duty and service as due to yourself our mother and sister. I am, your most dutiful son and obliged humble servant, J. Banks. My wife continues by fits very much indisposed with the headache. Pray be so kind as to send me either by the post or carrier the lease I left with you from old Booth to J. Milns. I suppose you could do nothing with Oldfeild. Pray, dear Sir, is my settlement executed by yourself and the trustees. If not, I beg you'd please to get it executed before you come down, and bring it to me. My father H. desires me to acquaint you that it is his opinion still to lay the declaration in Derbyshire, and Mr. Marples will prove the debt, and his evidence corroborate Alsops account, tho not duly subscribed. He presumes he ownd the debt to you, and promised you part of the monies.

column39: The Letters and Papers of the Banks Family of Revesby Abbey. 1704-1760. Ed. by J. W. F. Hill. The Publications of the Lincoln Record Society, 45. Hereford. 1952.
column46: Revesby, 27 April 1717. We called at Scofton and staid 2 nights according to your desire, in which time I viewed both all the household goods, and quick stock, an exact catalogue of which I've taken, a copy of which is annexed to the catalogue of goods pitched on by me of the other side, and this day I've sent a drover to assist in bringing what goods they do not buy home hither, to put in the fenn. My drover likewise brings me a few sheep out of Derbyshire, which I bought when there, purposeing the convenience of getting them home, so your cattle shall be taken good care of. I cant say the sheep or beasts are in so bad order as was represented, 2 carthorse and 2 or 3 beast are miserably poor, but all the rest in pretty good order. I ordered Mr. Langley not to be run down in the price, for since tic against summer I do not doubt but we shall make out a good price by putting them into the fenn, barring accidents. We ordered Alice to make up all the beds, and let down the curtains against Mr. Sutton's coming, but to put all up again after he was gone. Both she and Will, as well as my honest neighbour Langley, promise their best assistance to the last. Every body seems mighty loath to part with you and your family, and as sorry they are to have such a neighbour, who is the most unacceptable couple that you could have sold it to. I'm the sorriest for poor Mr. Calton. I wish you could some way procure him a lease. I see in a letter to Mr. Langley, you promise to take care of him, which can be done no other way. In short you know his violence against Papists in every sermon, which will turn him out a course, so by that means he'll not only lose the farm, but the monies he's laid out to improve it, which I'm told is above forty pounds. I humbly beg your pardon for this digression, but I only tell you this that if possible before the executeing the conveyance you may take care of the poor man, which would be a credit both to you and us all, in the county, and the contrary I doubt a great reflection. As for the goods pitched on, I only desire what you think convenient, part, all, or more, as you please. I've got a boat, which I'll send when you please. I've had a letter from Sherlock that they cant come till Monday, but then will fall on, pell mell. I've sent for the windows etc. I think to get the hall floor laid and that particon taken down immediately. The hall floor cant be settled unless all windows altered, so pray your full orders per next. We viewed Tumby since we came home. I like it better and better every time I see it. Our humble duty attend your self and dear mother and sister. I hope we shall get all things in tolerable order against Midsummer, the time you apoint for your coming down. I am, dear Sir, your most dutiful son and obedient humble servant, J. Banks. I've got you an horse which I believe will fit you very well. Otherways when you see him we can sell him again.

Revesby, 30 April 1717. Yesterday Mr. Banks wrote about the best chamber, and hope shall have your answer. The chimney in the dining room won't be in the middle. With advice of Mr. Banks and lady (if you please to admit on it) to make a drawing room over the cellar, this chimney will fit it and there is a convenient place on the wing of the chimney to make one for the dining room. And when you please to build another wing to answer the last it may be a bedchamber below and dressing room and closett above. This will be a very good house without any further adishon. If we've good success in taking down this wall (which I don't fear) we've another project which I think you'll like, that is to take down the other wall in the hall and build a place without the house to remove the stairs whole into, which will make the hall a large room. And I'm, with all duty, your honor's humble servant, Jno Sherlock.

Revesby, 15 May . I humbly thank for your kind offer of one of the best beds (we should have been very well content with the old bed as in last), so my wife pitches of the kalomanco bed, but shall want some little stuff thats near of the colour to hang out the room, the quantity of which I'll send to you as soon as I have measured it. We shall want one feather bed and the chairs you mention, but pray have regard to the paper of things we pitched on about 5 or 6 posts agon, being mostly such things as would be useful to us and sell but for little. Pray remember cabinets and chest of drawers for your own use. I likewise thank you for the marble harth, and desire you'd buy me one stove grate with one fender and set of utensils as poker tongs fireshovell and belows, and pack them in the half hogsheads, and if you please the spices in another, that I send a catalogue of in my next. I never had my deeds for the Door estate from you. They are, I believe, in your iron chest at Scofton. Pray push R. Clay on, if he can sell it for its worth. Pray leave no stone unturnd in this affair of Howbrigs. We'll spare for no charges to do our selves justice, which I'm sensible has not been done us hitherto. The lime and bricks are going about with all expedition. I cannot hear of my friend (since my return) who manages Coap's farm. He's taken a ramble to see some relation, but I'll watch his return. I have got the £50 from Soresby. Many thanks to you are due. I sent of Monday for the Tax Act but could not hear of it, have sent an especial messenger to day, and Mr. Short is by appointment to be with me to day to read it together. Yesterday I went to Mr. Wright, who said he was sending you a pretty good return just then. Since you design to be down so soon, I think will respitt that affair, for it must run in another channel, unavoidably. Eager of Moreby gave Mr. Wright no notice of leaving his farm till the day before Martinmas day, so that we're of opinion we can force him to hold it another year. I'm in no want of either hay or corn, and you may depend upon it all things shall be provided for your reception. I'll get the barn done and trust to your generosity. I'll take care of lime and of Cope too. Our attorney for How Briggs never could get a copy of the indictment tho he demanded it twice, which we take to be another reason why they should not give judgment against us; so without further order I will not ask for a copy of the indictment, fearing it may prejudice us. Mr. Sherlock and I have just been talking over the model in yours of the 5th, and since we've not time to do anything but finish our present undertaking, so we can take more time to consider of it, only desire your positive answer whether the chimney shall be removed or stand as it does, and have 2 wainscott pillors put up as in your last. The enclosed is the wages which I think more than Mr. Sherlock talked of or writ, one of the 2, but I can't find the letter. I've spoke to him. He says they never have less. I can't say but they are diligent understanding men and work from 5 to 7. Pray your thoughts of it, and send me back the bill. Our humble duty attend you, dear Mother, and sister. My mother I'll send her affectionate service as due. I am, your most dutiful son and obedient servant, J. Banks. Pray what becomes of Cuss: Hancock? I wish you could do something for him.

column39: The Letters and Papers of the Banks Family of Revesby Abbey. 1704-1760. Ed. by J. W. F. Hill. The Publications of the Lincoln Record Society, 45. Hereford. 1952.
column46: Revesby, 19 May 1717. Upon peruseing the Land Tax, we found it quite altered to what it was before, and if you look page 214 you'll find their is time given till the 29 September, so that we shall have time enough to consider of this after you come down and my neighbour Short retourns home, and the Act is so very exact that we shall have occasion to lay all our heads together. As to Parson Cope I've been with him, and he seems very civil, told me he had not his writings in his own hands, but would send for the lease and show it me in a little time. I discharged the milner from workeing up the wood, but it went against my conscience, for I never saw a milne so much out of repair. In short twil cost as much to repair as to build it from the ground. I desire to have a pair of fine wasted hoes the same of the cloth. Pray order your servant to write 2 lines to Waddell himself. I delivered the silver hilt to the wagoner himself, gave him sixpence and he promised to deliver it to you himself. The 10 inches of wall shall be put up again, 'twil be as soon done as spoke of. It was part taken down before your letter came. I'm very sorry you should seem so very angry at so small a transgression. I'll assure you your orders shall be observed as nearly as may be for the future, for I am far from contradicting your orders in these affairs, that was it not for your goodness and generosity I should never alter anything. I design to take a butler that is a gardiner, so if you please should be very thankful if your engage me Tom, Mr. Jaqueline's nephew, who is now gardiner att Scofton, I shall be obliged to you. If you please send him the enclosed letter and add what you seem convenient to it, I've forgot his surname. Your tenant Clarke grows so very infirm with the continual pains of the stone that he desires to resign his farm, and young Tom James will hold it if you think fit. They have both been with me. I believe he'll be a very good tenant. We rejoice to hear my mother is so much better, pray God continue it. Our most affectionate duty, love and service attend you, dear Mother and sister, as due, I am, honoured Sir, your most dutiful son and affectionate servant, J. Banks. Enclosed is the list of the groceries etc. which we desire you'll please to buy for us, and send in an half hogshead.

According to your order I've sent the bearer and by him a small token of oysters which I desire you'll accept. I've thought what you said in making the new wing an apartment which will be very good and may bring the bed chamber to the stair head and have the dressing room and dark closett at the other end. I had forgot to speak about the old windows, I could a disposed of 'em in summer and may be I can the next, but desire to know the price. I think you'll have occasion for most on 'em your self. You said it was your desire to have the old account set stright. Please to leave order by your son, and if you find anything in it that is not fair make what abatement you please. It may be you'll think my assistance too much, but I've not set down half my journeys. The sashes I got nothing by and Mr. Banks can tell you what I got by my men. However I'm willing to serve you as I have done. Sir, her's two bills, one as my book is, the other cost a guiney. Your direction about it shall be observed and acknowledged a great favour done to your honor's humble servant, Jno Sherlock.

5 June . If the proposal for dear sisters M-h be pleasing to you and agreeable to her, we shall be extremely glad and most heartily wish success to it. Enclosed is the copy of our indictment. I could not possibly get it before. I am surprised att what Marshall wrote to you. He told me the ladies were his relations. Isle write to him again myself, and will endeavour to find out who Cope pays rent to. We kept no copy of the note for groceries but will guess att it, viz consider as we did before what we want . I was yesterday with Mr. Wright who is trifles, but yet I do not think fit to quarrel right with him. Iv spoke to Kirkham to pay you £60 next Friday seven-night which he says he'll do if his man has not .... of retourns in his way to London, and Mr. Wright has promised me the monies and says he will send you all he has, but he's nothing but shuffle, and theirs no dependence on his word, but since you are to be down so shortly, I would not have any bustle made, for then you may take your accounts and your affairs out of his hands. Michael will manage the receiving of the rents very well, but I can't spare him any further att all, for he manages all business att home and never stirs out except to wait of his mistress when she dines with a neighbour or so; so that I doubt you can have little use of him in any other capacity, for now hay time and harvest is coming on that he'll be continually engaged but att meal times. was here yesterday and has turned his to me, so that now their wages are pretty reasonable, so that I shall not change them. They now have one shilling, 3d. a peace less then before. We have finished the best chamber and all that alteration except laying the floor and a little matter of the wainscott in the new dining room, so that I hope we shall have things in tolerable readiness by Midsummer or a week after. The boat man that was to've brought my goods from Scofton has sent me word their is not passing Fossdyke, and Iv sent thither and find it too true, so that I must fetch my goods by land carriage, which I think I can do pretty reasonably, only I cant bring the malt, so desire it may be either kept for me till a boat will come, or else sell it their. But pray in your next be pleased to tell me what goods I may bring from Scofton for I think either to go or send Michael to see them packed up, and I think to get them brought by that carries wool to Wakefield, weeks time. I've put my coach cart mares in pretty good order. I never have them very poor. You talk as if corn was cheap with you, tic far otherwise here, oats are the lowest 12s. per quarter and wheat £2 3s. 0d. per quarter. I am glad youve sold your stock to the Brigadier for our fen is but very indiferent, and I'm afraid their'l be great loss. One of your mares was very near dying but, we've recovered her, but I've one fallen ill myself that I doubt will dye. The brick goas forward apace, and I hope will prove very good. Our most affectionate duty love and service attend yourself, dear momma, and sister. I am, dear Sir, your most dutiful son and servant, J. Banks.

column39: The Letters and Papers of the Banks Family of Revesby Abbey. 1704-1760. Ed. by J. W. F. Hill. The Publications of the Lincoln Record Society, 45. Hereford. 1952.
column46: Revesby, 29 June 1717. Enclosed is an exact account of what I've brought from Scofton, which I hope will be agreeable to your commands. I fancy when the cabinets drawers etc. are brought twill be the safest and best way to bring them all along by land carriage. The best great bell I've brought away, and you may certainly take away the other, for they are no ways fastened to the freehold. I've likewise ordered the bowls to be set by for your use, tho the Brigadier said he was to have them, but I do not find that by the articles. We've cleared Mother closett as you ordered for Mrs. Sutton, and return you a 1000 thanks for all these great favours. My neighbour Campsall came to speak to me about driveing the sheep. I doubt he's a villain, and the rest not much better by his talk, for he says Will kept a cow or 2 all winter of your hay, and that he can tell of other misdemeanours. When knaves fall out honest folk will come to their right. Mr. Stevens met me here last night just as I came home and is going about his business. I'll take care of the writ of error as you direct. I know not what to say about Joseph. I doubt he's but a drunken carlos fellow, and for his abilities in looking after horses I know nothing, tho he's very tractable and willing. Our most humble duty and affectionate service attends you dear mother and sister, and I am, dear Sir, your most dutiful son and obliged servant, J. Banks. I've bought no yett ewes, for had bought in my full quantity before I received your letter. You've one score of sheep very fat, which I advised Mr. Langley to sell, and the rest will be fat in 6 weeks time.

Kirkby on Been, 4 July 1717. I would gladly have waited upon you at Reavesby, but I am not able to go or ride so far by reason of my great weakness and many infirmities and old age. Sir, I understand that there is great need of more timber to finish the repairs of Tumby mills; and if you please out of your own generosity will order some timber to complete the work, no man shall be more thankful to you for it then myself. By the late owners that I farmed it of I was to have all timber found me, but what your covenants are about it I neither doe desire to know nor to make any question of it, but you will doe what is just. I should be very desirous to see you at Kirkby; if not I would endeavour to waite of you at Tumby if I can possibly get so far, who am your most humble servant and tenant whilst, Jose: Cope.

column39: The Letters and Papers of the Banks Family of Revesby Abbey. 1704-1760. Ed. by J. W. F. Hill. The Publications of the Lincoln Record Society, 45. Hereford. 1952.
column46: 6 July 1717. I see by yours of the 27 June which is the last I received that you thought I had marked too many things as you well might, But I dare say you scarce thought so when you saw the inventory of what I brought away. The reason of my markeing so many things in the inventory was, that I thought by some of your former letters you seemed to think you would live att Revesby the most of the time you will be in the country, except some little time att Hurne which place I fancied you'd have had furnished in such manner as to have been in a tolerable condition to have received you, but as I hope that I've taken nothing away att present but what you will like of, so will pursue your further directions for what you would have done. Pray what do you do about Lord Harborough's estate? It will vex you if it be bought out of our hands. I can't yett find out who Cope pays his rent too for the Ladies farm in Revesby, the enclosed I received from him of Thursday which you must pray give an answer too by the return of the post. I scarce know how to advise you for the milne takes as much repairing as if it was to be built new, the goits, dams, soles and wheels and everything being made new. I go now and then to see they do what they do do, substantially, but if you can force him to repair with his own wood, I would have you doubtless to do it, otherways you better let him have a little wood then let the milne be unfinished. My wife joins with me in humble duty to yourself, dear mother, and affectionate love to dear sister. Pray how goes on her match? We should be glad to hear, heartily wishing it may be to all our satisfactions. I am, dear Sir, your most dutiful son and obedient humble servant, J. Banks. My wife will write to my mother next post. Your monies comes in but slowly, but however I've laid wait for returns and will pay them the monies as I get it. You must order that affair positively when you come down.

I had yours this day seven night that you left for me when you went from Reavsby. I'm sorry you should complain of my bill. Mr. Banks knows what I got by my men. He did say there wages was thought to be unreasonable, so I desired him to get other hands as soon as he could. I would not have the work stopped and told him he might pay these as I did (till then), but he got none and I lost there summer for I wanted 'em at home where our wages is paid without abatement. The removing the stairs you was not charged with. The modilion cornice you agreed it should be put about the end, but it was such an od thing we did not know what to do. All was done by your consent and if you think fit to make abatement for this and the alteration of the summer tree do as you please: as to the wast about the colour know nothing on it only a little Wm Green brought that was valued at 18d.: as to the work coming to more by day then square I can't help. You may please to remember I often wrote and told you such alterations and jobs could not be taken. I know I gave rates of new work and you set 'em down and the sash windows at 30s. a piece, but you sent me London rates and I charged you the same. I acknowledge a mistake in my bills for the 13 of May. I did not set down my men's time for that week, and when that and for my time is added I believe they'll be right. I did not set down half the times I was there, and if you don't think I deserve so much give me what you please. I beg our accounts may be set stright. The next sashes will pay for the old transoms. I desire to know the price. I can justly say if you pay the whole bill I don't get one farding by it neither do I desire it for what is past nor for what is to come, for it may be in your power to do me kindnesses and in particular something I have in hand about the breach at Dagenham. I think you know it has runt several years and has been offen attempted and all has miscarried as well as Capt Perry the last year (experance has taught me I can stop it). I've wrote to him that I will give him proposals to his satisfaction. I believe he will give me answer. I don't do it to lessen him in any respect. I shall make bold to let you how the matter goes, and am with duty your honor's most humble servant, Jno Sherlock.

column39: The Letters and Papers of the Banks Family of Revesby Abbey. 1704-1760. Ed. by J. W. F. Hill. The Publications of the Lincoln Record Society, 45. Hereford. 1952.
column46: Revesby, 24 January 1718. I enquired of Mr. Wright what became of the windfalls. He says their was but one ash worth anything, and we had it sawne into joists for Sandam's house. I'll sell but few ashes this year, but will try both ways, viz whether it be better to sell them standing or worked up, so by that means I shall know better against another year. I would gladly have your advice before we sell many, for it will disfigure the grounds mightily. By the enclosed note you'll see what I've done with Parson Whelpdale, so I shall take care to let his farm to advantage for the ensuing year, and you must set your reckoning straight when you come down into these parts. He seems very civil, and says he'll submit all to you when you come down. I've appointed your tenants to pay me their rents of Tuesday and Wedensday next, tho I am afraid they will not all pay. However, I've ordered Mr. Stevens to pay you on my account 15£ and I've ordered 50 or 60£ more to come to you speedily out of Derbyshire, and I've laid wait for retourns here, which are exceeding scarce. However, I'll always take care to send you monies as soon as it comes to my hands, and will make up and send you your accounts as soon as this half year is pretty nigh got in, and anything more you please to command me. Here is about 40 or 50£ per annum upon sale in East Kirkby, but the title is upon the same hold with Parson West's estate there. They ask 20 years purchase. I fancy I could buy it for 19. It's some little to be improved, but not much, but for the title you are the best judge. You must give me speedy orders about it, for I've but time till I hear from you before they will publicly offer it to the best bidder, tho perhaps chapman will not be plenty full on account of the title. Poor Widow Lamin wants to take administration to her husband's effects. Pray have not you a power as successor to the Abott to grant administrations, or must she apply to Doctors' Commons? I beg you'd be so kind as to buy me livery cloth lineing and buttons for 2 men's liveries and let it be sent down by the carrier. If there be half a yard to spare I should have use for it, hat lace and buttons for 2 hats if you please. Pray tell Mr. Chapman I'm ashamed sent his monies. My illness has prevented me, but the first bill I can get I'll return it him. Pray my kind service to him. Pray what hopes of the loins? Is not Lord S-d married? What says Lord Molesworth? Sure faith has left the earth, and in time we shall all be dogs chopping in the baskett for our own bellies. I am, dear Sir, your most dutiful son and obedient humble servant, J. Banks. Tom Henley is run his country having got 7 or 8 in people's debt both here and at Maram. He went the day before Xmas but we expected his return till last week, so I must be forced to set some one else on. He only finished the staircase and best parlour shutters.

column39: The Letters and Papers of the Banks Family of Revesby Abbey. 1704-1760. Ed. by J. W. F. Hill. The Publications of the Lincoln Record Society, 45. Hereford. 1952.
column46: 28 January 1718. I am surprised at what you write of my letter coming so late to you. Surely it was occasioned by my son's illness, to whom I have wrote this post, to make an end of it with you, for its now all out of my hands, not having your bills nor my own remarks, but this I can remember, the wainscott and every thing else came to double the usual prices allowing for jobs and alterations, so you had need be kind in it. I'll serve you about Dagenham or any thing else in my power, being your real friend and servant, J. Banks. You never told me how you liked my observations on the papers you sent me.

Kirkby on Been, 11 November 1718. I give your worship my humble and hearty thanks for your kind letter you sent me the other day, which I take for a true kindness, and if I had bin able I would have answered it the next day. Mr. Gelsthorpe hath bin with me the other day, and I gave him full satisfaction upon all accounts wherein I was concerned with his lords and masters, to whom he promised me to write to let them know everything how it was. As for the great wast mentioned in the wood, I doe not know that I had the least stick of it to my own use, neither root nor branch; and if you doe not already know I could easily inform you if I saw you. The wood was employed at the mill, and two gartrees of mine I bought and payed for, and ten pounds in dale boards, and another tree that cost me five pounds for a fulling mill stock, besides abundance of iron work and nails, and hundreds of days for workman's wages, whom I had for 6 pence a day and some meat; and you discharged me for working any longer for a good space of time; and afterwards when you was pleased they should work again I was forced to give them 12 pence, 18 pence a day, and two shillings and more; besides the fulling mill cost me above 3 score pounds building, and it and the tenters and hot press and plate and the mill tools were sold for little or nothing. So if I can get nothing of Gelsthorpe I shall loose 500 pounds by the mill, and I have bin as hardly and harshly dealt (with) all as I had bin the greatest knave upon earth; and you have discharged some for paying me any tithes, which I can make it appear to you that you are of it; and whenever I dye my Lord Chancellor will put in a minister tithes and a great deal more, which I can and will make it plain see you. In the meantime I pray God to bless you and all yours and prosperity, which is all at present from your weak and very humble ilst, Jose: Cope. I have ngs to inform you of but I am not able at present.

column39: The Letters and Papers of the Banks Family of Revesby Abbey. 1704-1760. Ed. by J. W. F. Hill. The Publications of the Lincoln Record Society, 45. Hereford. 1952.
column46: Revesby, 16 January 1720. I communicated yours to W. B. and considered matters with him before I sent for Mr. James, and what's underwritt is the best terms I can get him too, so W. B. is as capable to follow your directions as if I myself was here, and Mr. James desires an answer by the return of the post. He will take all Tupholm's farm att 70£ a year, and only insist of having the house and particularly the roof repaired well att your charge, which will be no great matter when your here to direct it. He will keep the high field lands, and his father's 18£ a year att the present rent, and the upper part of Tom Clerk's farm att 50£. So what he will part from is his 13£ a year, late Dr. Loves, Clamp Close and Abbey ground, which he pays dear enough for, and his homestead with all below it att 30£ a year. But as to his Rowborrows he's unwilling to part from it on any terms, and says he pays you at least 12£ a year for it, if you consider what his plowd marlins abated the rent of the whole, and that Tom Clark was charged 11£ for it in Lord Barkshire's time. This is the state of this matter, and now you'll expect me to say something. My opinion is that as you have high lands enough to spare about St. Sides, you'll not be in such need of Rowborough as you seem to fear; but then I can't flatter you with hopes of any great matters of rise from his low farm, tho doubt not but it will advance perhaps 6 or 7£ a year, which I know is nothing of what you'll expect may be raised in his farm, but you must consider, he keeps near 2 3rds of his old farm att least att an equal proportion of rent to the rest. W. B. perfectly understands what I write to you, and has a copy of it, and will pursue your directions, which he begs may be very plain, for he is not scholar enough to understand so great a calculation by way of value per acres etc. as the nature of so great a farm requires, and I shall not be here to advise him. Of Thursday last we had our wood sale, where we had but a very small appearance to what I have seen, nor could I in any manner answer your expectation in selling the wood (which I feared before you left Revesby), so after about 5 hours talking with the company, we parted without selling them any but 5 or 6 pieces in Sherwood att about 18d. per pol which tho it be as good as the sale in general is, nay better by 3d. per pol, is, I doubt, far short of your expectation. The country generally complain they lost by the wood they bought of me the last year, and that there are great quantities now before hand, and likewise that there was so dry a season this last summer, that great quantities of fen fuel were got, which hinders the sale of kidwood. And now give me leave to tell you that I never viewed wood more exactly then I did these two sales (having so fatigued myself 2 days together as I will not tell you), and truly find Fulsby sale much worse then I ever saw it, so that I fear 10£ an acre will stretch it when ever it is sold, and 12£ an acre for Sherwood the like. I'm sorry I can't give you a more satisfactory account of this affair, and assure you I've not been wanting in what in my power; so please to consider and order what you think convenient on the whole, and if I can be serviceable to you, shall be very ready to make another journey over. I can't get the bricklayer near me, but have given Wm such instructions that he can't mistake me about his drawing. And as to the brickmakers I agree with you that they are a pack of rogues, tho both Dickinson and the Bilingay men promise me to go on with there work, but the Bilingay men shut have some monies when they have turned the clay, else can't subsist. I will let Holden's farm before I go away if he gives me not good security. I've given full directions about the planting, and likewise to buy you oats. I fancy they will scarce be cheaper then they are now. I've made it my business to talk with all your tenants and neighbours about plowing your closes, but find 'em all engaged in there own affairs for the spring, so that I fear Wm will be pushed. I've been with old Smith and several fen men, but find thatch so dear, it is not proper to lay in a quantity. I this day finished receiving rents. The total of rents and arrears amounts to £231 13s. 0d. The copy of my receipts encloses a copy of your rental directed by Wm. The tenants that are now behind say they can't possibly pay before 18 or 20th of March. I've received the sum above exclusive of the taxes, so you may reckon on above 30£ more received. Tho even then it will be but a poor business to what you expected. I will take care for your bacon. I have bottled your 2 hogsheads of Bawtry beer, it run seven dozen of the large quarts and 9 pints. I expected some more pints, but the vessel was reasonably full when spiled. Its good beer, but att present very flatt. I hear Mr. Stevens can return your monies, tho in these parts I could not get any, so have order Wm to go of Monday morning with the monies to him and hope you'll get it soon. My most humble duty and affectionate love attend you, my dear mother, brother and sister. I heartily wish you all health and happiness. I am, dear Sir, your most dutiful son and obedient servant, J. Banks. P.S. Poor Lattice has been very ill since I came hither, but Mrs. Tupholme sends me word she is better. Here is the greatest mortality that ever was known in these parts, but much greater in the fens. Leak and Leverton have buried half of there inhabitants, as reported. I thank you for your news of prosecution to be within a year, etc. The 2 Agers of Moorby are about selling there farms to Mr. Hamerton off Horncastle, att 195£ each, but have a month's time to redeem them, and will let me have them att 200£ each, tho att the most improved value they are but let att £9 each, the landlord pays land tax, which is as dear as an egg a penny. So if you've a mind to purchase one or both of 'em please to signify it in a post or 2 to me for fear the time of redeeming be lost. Mr. Hamerton buys whatever he can in Moorby or Enderby, tho never so dear. He know nothing that I am on the scent of it.

column39: The Letters and Papers of the Banks Family of Revesby Abbey. 1704-1760. Ed. by J. W. F. Hill. The Publications of the Lincoln Record Society, 45. Hereford. 1952.
column46: Revesby, 19 February 1720. Yours of the 9th instant I received in course, and am very sorry poor Jo still continues ill. Thank God my wife was better when I left her, and Lattice is got very well, as I hope this will find you, and all my good friends in Boswell Court, on whom my affectionate duty and love attend. Considering the posture of your affairs here I judged it requisite for me to come over to see how all matters went on, and in the first place I took a view of Sir John Hales estate att Bollinbroke, which if it can be bought to your mind, will give you an entire principality in these parts, Sir John being chief lord of many neighbouring towns appurtenance to his manor of Bollinbrooke, which att this time they are endeavouring gradually to excuse. Likewise all the touls taken in all these parts are belonging to it, so that if you was possessed of it, I am persuaded you would do great things with it. I would have viewed every particular of the land but could not get it shown, the tenants being all sick or from home. They generally complain tic very dear, tho the neighbours say tic a handsome peniworth, and that there is one farm in the tenure of Mr. Hereby the attorney that will improve. If Jarvis Scroope be in Town he will manage this affair so as for Sir John to offer it you, but I fear he's left London so if I find him att Lincoln will get him to write forthwith to Sir John. The wood by Will Wests and another called Hall Hill near Earsby, much larger, belong to this estate. I have bought George Agar's estate att Moorby cheaper then I expected, tho tic dear enough in reason: enclosed is the article. The other brother will not sell for a deal more, and the division was perfectly equal. The lands are mortgaged to Mr. Hamerton of Horncastle, so he must be consulted when he will have his monies paid in, which I will do, and endeavour to get him stay till Lamas; if not, he must have it att Ladiday. On second thoughts it had much better be att Lamas, then you might draw the conveyance and see your title. I have got a seemingly honest fellow and a good workman of a bricklayer from Spilsby. He has been 2 days att work with me here, and will come and finish the rest of Monday 3 weeks, against which time we will have lime burnt for him. I have given the fellow full instructions. I have warned your rent day with some threats, and have got some returns, and will lay out for more. I've order 170£ to be paid you in 14 days or thereabouts. Your tenant Smedley is dead, and I have seized of what he had, and wish it will pay you. It shall do as far as it can. I will leave orders with Wm how to proceed. All the world stand amazed att S. S. Stock. I'm sorry for your misfortune as well as my own; dare say F. H. has got well by it. Fancy .... is as you write. I'm sorry you give yourself any trouble about him. My servant directs you a copy of the wood sale, which I fear you'll not approve; however, assure you no more could have been made. I think it proper for W. B. to sell what remains standing as well as he can; am sure you'll lose by it if it either stands or you work it up. I wish you have sail for your kids and polls (before rotten) that you worked up last year. There has been so much of this sort of wood cut lately. Mr. Wright never sold such a sale or anything like it. Sherwood I'm of opinion is sold dear enough. The three Not. men whom I met would not budge above 11£ per acre. The viewed our firths but can find no land fit for hops att all. It is now time to order your brewing 2 or 3 hogsheads of ale or 7 of small beer, it would be the better to brew soon. They must set it in the outward seller. Direct Wm in that point. Your brickmaking goes on very slowly. They Bilingay men are quite run off and Holden is very sick and fallen to the parish, tho Dickinson and he promise fair. W. B. says you once offered him to let him Smedley's farm and build him a room. He desires me to acquaint you that if you be of that mind now, and will lay him the 2 closes now Flater's to it, and continue his salary to look after your woods, he will settle in this country and look no further. I have nothing farther to add but that I am your most dutiful son and obedient servant, J. Banks.

Lincoln, 8th March 1721. Honoured Sir, John got. safe to Revesby on Saturday night and every thing very well, but the bay mares back is a little bruised. He went over to Donabys with her, but he was not at home, but William Banks promised to go over with her and send us word what Donaby said of her. The bill of charges for his coming down. Sir, we came here yesterday and found every thing very well. Both misses are very well but Miss Lattice heal is a little sore yet. Sir, this is Mary's bill for the twelve shilling. Mary Brinkley left when she came to Revesby. She cannot remember the day of the month when you had these things. Sir, there is 21 quarters of oats come into the chamber but we have not measured them yet, but will send you an exact account next post. Sir, there was one came here last week to summons you to be upon the grand jury. He spoke to Will but he doth not know the man's name that came. The bill for the gin left Mary. Sir, Mrs. Ann saith that all the things is lock that was in the work drawer so there is nothing to make Miss Lattices nor Miss Bettys caps on. Mrs. Heseltine saith that bibs and aprons is worn and not frocks now there in morning so if you please to give her leve she make some of that holland you send down. Miss wants some black stockings and gloves and we can get none here. No more at present from your most humble servant. Wm. Burbidge.

15th March 1721. Honoured Sir, Mr. Royal will get the windows done as speedily as he can. Willaby came here to work on Monday last and began to take the window down in the passage, but it is so rotten that it will do no good, so haith left it there and is mending the side of the house next the garden as you ordered. Sir, he thinks it will be a great hazard to pull down that window in the passage to make a door there, for he saith the house is so cract it will be in great danger of falling. Sir, Robert Brakenbury and the other men came here on Monday night last, but Mr. Brackenbury could not but in the trial until this morning about nine o'clock, but you have got it. It hardly held an argement it was so plain. Sir, Robert Brakenbury did not bring the note, so have not paid him, from your most humble servant, Wm. Burbidge.

18 March 1721. Honoured Sir, I spoke to Prigon to brue a hogshead and half of strong beer, but he said he could not promise me to come until today, so went down last night to know when he could come, but as he said he brewed all for Mrs. Sandby at the White hart and she had now almost 20 quarters to brew to go to Boston, so desired you to excuse him for it was impossible for to do it now. Sir, William is now brewing 6 strike for 3 hogsheads of small beer. Please to see the bill of disburstments from March the 12th to the 18th 1720-21. Sir, the strong waters that is set down in the bill was for the old man that came for a witness that morning he was going he would have six pence in his pocket and his bottle of brandy or he would not go out of the house. Sir, John desired me to let you know straw is very reasonable now and if you stay in Lincoln you would not have to serve you until new came again so if you think fit to buy a load or two more. Sir, Miss Lattice and Miss Betty is very well and gives their duties. Nancy desires to know whether you will send some cambric and holland for Misses mobs for you locked all the holand up. The workman's names and days they have worked here this week. from your most humble servant, Wm. Burbidge.

1 April 1721. Mr. Potter hath not done the pails yet, but promises they shall be done and nailed up by the next Saturday without fail. Sir, there was no ordinary briks to be got, so Willaby spoke for a load of square ones such as the kitchen is paved with. He saith they are the cheapest for ware, so he on this day will pave it. Sir, Mrs. Haseledine hath hired two maids. Sir, the gardiner came here yesterday and saith the bay mares back is a great deal worse but when we came away John told me there was no danger but it would be well in two or three days. The disburstments from March the 27th to April the 1, 1721. Sir, we have had a missfortain with which I thought fit to acquaint you with. The last night the mare Cate got loose and run a bit of wood under her shoulder, but I hope it will be well in a short time, from your most humble servant, Wm. Burbidge.

I beg pardon I did not write before now, but did not come out of Derbyshire till Saturday, and before I had got the letter write the post was gone out. Sir, in your last you write that you would have Mr. Dickinson to take the close of your hands. John protests that he never hard word of it until your letter came. Sir, Mr. Dickinson doth not desire any thing for the dressing the close but saith it was not in his bargain, but will not be .... to the cleaning the close and repairing the hedges. Sir, the bay mare's back was not so very ill when we came away from Revesby. I wrote word as John told me, and so did Donaby's man say it would soon be well. Sir, I could say no more then they told me. To be sure you had more judgment in those matters then I or at least should have. I wrote to Revesby but have had no answer as yet. Thank God Cate mends very fast. Sir, I am sorry I should make such a mistake in the strong beer, but thought you would know what it meant. Sir, Joseph Hodgkinson desired me to send you word that he had got the moneys ready, and hoped you would be there to receive it, for it would be hard for him to pay interest in boath places. Sir, Mr. Hodgkinson bid me send word how long since Susana Bunting's father died for I suppose the Hackleas lease was taken that year he died. She saith it was fourteen years the 7th day of this month. Sir, if you please to put in to me, for I think it will go sooner from you then from here if you please to give your self that trouble. Sir, I inquired about a man, but could hear of none, but Godfery Hodgkinson he would very fine come, and doth not doubt but he could please you. I told him his business was not only for shooting but must do several other things, but he said he did not doubt but he should please, and for wage he would not differ if he had nothing, so did not bid him anything until I had a letter from you. They are all very well in Derbyshire. The disburstments from Monday the 3th of April to the 10th 1721. Potter hath done the pales. The prowler is come and we have taken the old frame and but it to the new .... Honoured Sir, from your most humble servant, Wm. Burbidge.

1 May 1721. We have got a henn to sit the eggs when they come but must pay 2s. 6d. for her sitting. We went all up and down but could not get one under that price. Sir, Thomas Aspen hath one half of the glases and the other is on cucumbers for selves. Sir, the pantry is finished all but the cubard that you purpose to be done when you come down and the windows which the glass is not put in yet. The parlour harth is done and the door and garden door that goes into the yard. The pails are done but the door is not hung yet. The windows in the best room are done. I do not know of any thing else to do except you please to have the harth in the kitchen mended. Mary was saying you talked something of that when you was down. Sir, Miss Lattice face is mended. The old scarr is a great deal better than when you went, but the other is as ill as ever but no running. Sir, there is very little of the baccon flitches cut of. John hath not been well so had a mind of a bit of baccon. I think there was about 1/2 a pound cut of. Sir, we here hare that my Mrs. is ill but hope it is not true but a great many comes to inquire how she doth. Sir, Miss Lattice wants a hoop ever ill. This is so bad she hath she can scarce ware it. Sir, you desired to know what clerks was at Horcastle. There was Mr. Boughwright's clark and Mr. Grantham's. Mr. Boughwright's clark had the share that I had, but the other had £5. 4s. There was a 11 in all. My share at Gainsborough and here was £4. 18s. Honoured Sir, from your most humble servant, Wm. Burbidge. Mrs. Jinkinson is something better than she was but very wake.

Lincoln, 18 June . The garden sith is so bad it is impossible to use it in mowing the close. Sir, I am sure you had better hire a man to mow the close then set Will to it he knows nothing of mowing he would leave more grass uncut then would pay a man his hire. If you would please to ask John he can satisfy you. Sir, I believe the close at Bracebridge will want mowing in a short time if the whether would take up. Sir, it was not Prigon that brewed strong beer, it was John Cumpton. I paid him as soon as he brewed the brewing. If you please to look over the letter I sent about the 29 of March you will find it therein. Sir, both misses are very well, from your most humble servant Wm Burbidge.

column46: Revesby, 12 February 1722. My wife and self were very much surprised last night with the melancholy news of my dear mother's death, and most heartily condole with you thereupon. I've this day sent a servant to Lincoln to fetch me your letters both of yesterday and to-morrow, and if I receive them soon enough will give you an answer by this post, if not of Wedensday. My wife and I have considered of your desiring me in Town, and since this fatal accident has happened, it must remove all suspicion about my coming to Town; so if you please to give leave both my wife and self will wait of you the week after the next, for fancy our being together after such a misfortune will be agreeable to us all. If you think our coming proper we shall bring no maid servant and only one man, and so keep house till we be fitted with mourning etc., and my wife will endeavour to get a maid in Town, for we have given Nany Brinkley notice to leave us. If on the contrary you do not approve this our design, I beg Mr. Harry will order our mourning, and that it may be sent us hither by the Louth carrier as soon as ready, and we will stay here till we get them. I beg pardon for the freedom above, but shall be perfectly pleased to do just as you please. We do not propose to bring any horses if we come. Wm. Banks having let all the lands has nothing material to write so omits this week. My wife joins with me in humble duty to you, with affectionate love to our brother and sister, heartily wishing you all health, and am, dear Sir, your most dutiful son and obedient humble servant, J. Banks.

column39: The Letters and Papers of the Banks Family of Revesby Abbey. 1704-1760. Ed. by J. W. F. Hill. The Publications of the Lincoln Record Society, 45. Hereford. 1952.
column46: Revesby, 8 February 1724. Enclosed comes your measures about the rooms, and also an affidavit which Mr. Robertson tells me you know the affair and desires you will assist him, for that Mr. Manby very much oppresses the country by this chicanery. Doubleday's men go on very well, and we can't possibly get the ditch under 2s. an acre so big as you would have it, and it will be dear earnd. It's all hard chalk. We have had a very poor receipt. In all with what oddments William received before I came £90. 12. 4 and near fifty of it disbursed. You shall have the particulars as soon as I get home to make them out. The cry of want of moneys is grevious, and tho perhaps you'll think much that I get no more, I have the worst of it in hearing their complaints. I have taken what precaution I can that you loose nothing in the end, and have sharpened them up as much as I can, and will be with 'em again the latter end of the month. I have settled and received the rents of most of the leaders, but I assure you they grumble heavily, and whether I can get 'em to lead any more I know not. However, they'll not meddle att the present tho I've offered to pay them as they bring each load in. The parson Mr. Alexander has been with me again. I like him very well. He says now he does shoot, but durst not since he came of this side. He will be shortly in London, where I've ordered him wait of you. He seems to me very likely to fit you. I have had a chapman or 2 for half or a 4th of the old stack, but no body yett will buy the outsides tho I've offered to cut 2 yards deep. They offer us six pound for half the stack and that's all. But methinks if it was mine I would get another pair of bullocks and give them all the worst of the outside and the wood close hay (which no body has yett offered to buy) and so lead all home myself. If you come soon you'll want a good .... for yourself. The leading all the stulps rails and pales take 2 horses every other day and sometimes every day, and have done as long as they can without hay, that I believe what I advise will be the only way. There's no such thing as a draught's going to Boston, as I have wrote twice to Mr. Palfreman, tho I never could get an answer from him, and its but reasonable. He brings 'em down to the fenn side down the dichch to Cow Bridge. Since he has kept 'em so long pray write sharply to him to that purpose. Your plaster is not comed tho the boats are returned. The Trent was so much out that they could not find the plaster and fish it up. I can't as yett get a brickmaker under 5s. per 1000, 5 score to the hundred, to take the clay as it is, but am trying what I can do, but shall conclude with him in a week if I can't get it under or be not country ordered by you. Pray what quantity do you depend on from J. Rogers? What can be done with P. James is done both by Mr. Short and William, but he will stay att home. The other affair about Newcomen I am doing what I can in. I hear Whelpdale's giving out great words that he's come here again, but I've order William, no parson but Alexander comes into the church, who I have ordered at present to attend the cure. Your brewing and bottling I will take care of. I have now given the vessels out to be mended and we will go briskly on when I come over the end of this month. We have sold about 14 or 15 pieces of the wood unsold, so if he get 6 or 8 more in about 10 days sold we will have another sale. I am, dear Sir, your most dutiful son and obedient servant, J. Banks. I hear matters in the election go on very well of this side all over, but am now in the dark for the other parts.

Boston, 9 February 1725. I received yours and return you thanks for your favour towards me in speaking to Mr. Viner. As to Nordike bridge, I have the stone ready to begin it as soon as your honour comes down, for I think the weather is not proper to begin it at present. In taking down the old church and rebuilding it your honour desires to know the lowest price what I will take by the square yard or rood 7 yards long and a yard high to the rood, the lowest I can doe it for is 6s. six shilling per yard, you finding stone brick and lime and all other materials. As to the windows and doors I have included them, for we find more trouble in those things then in solid work. If your honour don't like the above proposal I am willing to do the job for you by the day as you and I can agree, and will make the stone hold out as far as I can, but am afraid there will be a want. I am, your honor's most obedient humble servant, John Blackbone.

Hooton Roberts, 30 August 1726. I had sooner sent you my hearty congratulations, as I now do, for your recovery from your late indisposition, but that I have been in daily expectation, for a considerable time, of giving you an account of my wife getting into the straw; and though she has far outgone her reckoning, yet I thank God is at last safely delivered of a boy, and both in a hopeful way of doing well. Here is likely to be a great contest betwixt the two candidates who offer themselves for this county, viz.: Sir John Kay and Mr. Turner. Sir Thomas Wentworth (from whom and his late worthy father I received many favours) has sent to me to desire my vote for the latter, whom I would willingly oblige if you think it proper; besides I hear His Grace the Archbishop of York favours that interest, so that it may be a step, some time or other, towards preferment, but I shall act entirely in favour of your determination. Mrs. Rayner, my mother's sister, and old Mr. Steer are lately dead. My mother seems very hearty and presents you with her most affectionate humble service, and my spouse with your godson join with me in humble duty, and in hearty love and service to good cousins as you see them, and I am, honoured Sir, your most dutiful nephew and obliged humble servant, Jo: Banks. My little house fills apace, so that I am about sending out my eldest son to school, as soon as I hear of a good master and cheap board. The master in this town teaches no further than grammar, besides writing, and the first 4 rules in arithmetic, which my boy has gone throe: it will straiten me pretty much, but I am resolved to do what I can for him, being a sprightly youth, and of a promising genius. My new enclosure cleared about £16 this year, thanks to you for your kind assistance towards it.
