column46: Porto Novo, the 14th May 1687. Mr. Davis, Honoured Sir, Since my letter which I wrote this morning I understand that this night came a letter to the Subidar and Avaldar from Nulla Buckoor Marcar who is at Trimlevass who advises them that they have done very ill in Imprisoning me; and that by your assistance it may bring a great deal of trouble on them and also advises them that I am not in fault; the Slaves which went on my ship not being mine and therefore no reason I should pay the Custom and several other arguments hee uses to them to clear me but the Avaldar having taken a fee hee prosecuts the Chulea Amid Marcars revenge on me to the Except they would murder me I understand these things from one of the Avaldar's Servants who is always near him I having bribed him to acquaint me with Passages; but I hope in God I shall have a time to have my satisfacson for Amid Marcar for his making me wear Irons &ca. Sir, Your Most humble Servant in Affliction Thomas Bowry.

London, the 3d August 1704. Capt. Thomas Bowery: Sir, Mr. Stark and I wrote you last night, to which I Refer you. I suppose to Morrow wee shall hear if she should be stopped. I Cannot believe they will meddle with her. If Such News should Come I will dispatch my man to you that Wee may have your Company on Saturday. I am Offered 2 letters to Lye Ready if Occasion should be, one to Duke Hamilton the other to the Attorney General. Pray your advice if shall send them to my friend on Saturdays post. Last night I Omitted giving you an Account what they would Write upon her from thence to London, because Could get no price made and it is the same again to day, the Insurers being down in the Mouth, or at least out of Policy pretend so to be from an alarm Come this day of 13 sail of ships and St. Helena being taken by the French. I suppose Capt. Tolsen will give you the Particulars of it, to whose Letter I Referr you, being in haste. I am Now favoured with yours of Yesterdays date, and observe the Contents, and so soon I have the Cargo, will send it to you. Capt. Tolsen told me what you Write to him about Enquiering after £1000 Stock. Mr. Peter Albert, who is one of the Concerned in the Arabella , Came to me upon Exchange and Enquired where you Weere and if Wee had our Stock . I told him we had. Then, says he, "I should be glad to meet with you and Capt. Bowery to putt in with you £500 Stock I have of this Year." I told him when you Came to Town we would meet him. You say you doubt I have the Capt. to too small a Some. He Wrote for no Credit, but I thought it Necessary to send him some Credit, not knowing what might happen. My Service to your self and Lady is all at present from Sir, Your humble Servant, Tho: Hammond. To Capt. Those. Bowrey att Waggons Coffe house att Tunbridge Wells, In Kent.

August the 3th 1704, 5 Clock affternoon. Sir, According to your order in your Letter dated the First off August, I engaged Mr: Johnson to go to Mr: Stileman For that Business mentioned in your Letter, and his answer Was that he did not Know att what price permission Was att presentt, butt about a month ago hee had 30 gines Pr Centt proffered, butt hee did believe he should not obtain it now; butt being going outt off town this Morning, he desired him to meett him att Robins Coffey house on Wedonsday Next, and hee Would give him his Result att What price he would dispose off it. So that, according to your order, you may assure your Selff I will use my utmost Indivers to Serve you. Their is this day by a Letter Com to Mr. Loide, as it appears to bee a Letter that hath bean Enclosed in a Letter to a Friend. It First saith that he was Master off a small Ship bound from Compoetchy to England, but that his Ship was very Leaky and a French Frigate Came up With him and took him off, which he Was glad , For otherwise his Ship and hee and all the Rest had perished in her. now on board the French Ship. The Lewtivetenent Was an Englishman Who infformed him that on the 26 off April Last that Ship with 9 more took St. Helena, and beffore hee Came from thence, the 16 off May, they had taken these Ships as Follows, Viz: the said and (1) Dudly , (2) Orenzeb , (3) Robert and Nathaniall , (4) Legorn galy , (5) Gloster , (6) Colchester , (7) Chamber Frigate , (8) the Cathern , (9) Holland Frigate , (10) Haliffax , (11) Samuel and Ann , (12) Mary and two Ships Names Not Known. Hee had the opportunity to Send the Letter by a Dutch Ship that Was affter taken by the Said French Ship, and the Master having Ransomed his Ship, he desired him to take this Letter and put it in the Nearest place in England to London. I hope the accountt is deffecttive, First by Reason I do believe that Such a off Ships would Not be att St. Helena So early; thirdly hee doth not Mention the Name off his own Ship; thirdly there is None that owns the Sending this Letter Which Came by the penny post to Mr. Loyde and dated From Bantrybay, and Several other Supisious deffects in it So that I hope it will prove butt a trick by the Stock Jobers or the Like. I have ordered the Casks For the Coals to be Ready to Morrow morning, a Fleett being Come into the River. I have Not Spook with Mr. Hale as yett. I have Sentt him a Letter, butt have Received No answer so that I have not paid him as yett. Both Madam Garners desired to be Remembered to you and Madam Bowrey. Wishing you all the pleasure and Sattisffaction you hope For, So with my humble Service and my Wives, I Restt, Sir, Your humble Servantt, Jose: Tolson. This For Capt. Those: Bowrey att Tun Bridge with : Tun Bridge.

August the 9th 1704. Sir, I received yours dated August the 7th, all in which I will, you may assure your Selff, Indeiver to accomplish. Mr. Weles Seems Very Wiling to oblige you in any thing as I have asked off him as yett, butt I have not Spook to him about the Lineing off the Yards as yett; but I Spook to Mr. Carby and hee hath promised to have it done in 2 or 3 days. My Johnson Wentt this day to meett Mr. Stileman, according to his appointment, butt he did not Come, nor has not been there this day, So I Suppose he is not Come outt off the Country. Mr. Johnson would have gone to his house, butt I thought it more Convenient to Wait an opportunity to Meett him axidently on purpose then to Show much Forwardness, So my brother Johnson hath promised me to Waitt to morrow att Robins Coffee house For him and I will know in the morning Whether he is in town or Not, off which I shall be Impatient to give you account off his answer. I have not as yett heard off a Cheaff mate that I believe may be to your Satisffaction, to which End I will use all diligence that in me Lies. Mr. Hamon is outt off town, butt is expected to morrow and then I will sertiffie him off What your Letter pasiffis Concerning Captain Juniffer, and then I intend to get him to be bound For the Letter off Mart, according to your order, if I can. We have had 4 Males this affternoon, by which the Malecontent in Hungary have broke off the accommodation. The Camisars are Masters off the Feald. Marchall de Talard hath joined the Baveriens and Prince Eugene is within 2 Leagues off the grand army. The Dutch East India Fleett is arrived att the Texell, butt the printed news gives no accountt of the Resolution . Your Humble Servantt, Jose: Tolson. I was att Mr. Hamon and See a Large Letter directed to you Which they told me was about the Woster , Which I hope you have Received. I forgot the Gentlmans name that you spoke to me to Enquire about the Wosters Insurance, For which I have been troubled For my Negligence to Neclectt any opportunity to serve you. For Capt. Bowrey att Tunbridge Wells. With love.

August the 11th 1704. Sir, According to your order, Mr. Johnson hath Waited on Mr. Stileman and his answer is that he will not dispose off the Licence off that £1000 under 30 gines per Cent att present, and his Reason is that he hath given Commission to a certain Gentleman to dispose off it for him, who hee hath not Seen Since Mr. Johnson First spook to him. So hee hath ordered Mr. Johnson to meet him on Wednesday Next att the East India Coffee house. Betwixt this and then hee shall see the gentleman beffore mentioned and then hee will give him a Forther Result of the Matter. I have been some what Indisposed these 2 days, butt I thank god I am Now Very well. If not, I should have had the Letter of mart or now. I rest, Your Humble Servant, Joseph Tolson. Mr. Stark Justt now brought News to the Garter that Separate Stock was Felon 15 per Centt, the Event off which I shall Inquire and give you Noteis theroff. For Capt. Bowrey, att Tunbridg: with Care.

London the 16th August 1704. Captain Thomas Bowery, Sir, I am favoured with yours 14th Instant. For Answer, Mr. Stark has secured two Warehouses at Brewers Key and Mr. Dupuy hath One in Mincing lane which we Can have. Mr. White Recommended Mr. Stark to them. It will save Cartidge, &c., which would be Chargeable, and I suppose Wee shall not keep long before wee sell. I have not yett speak with Mr. Albert about his stock, nor will not till hear further from you. I saw Captain Tolson at 3 of the Clock and then he had not an Answer from his Friend. No News from the ship since my last. When I have any you shall not fail hearing from me. I am sorry you are disappointed of the Enjoyment you went down to Tunbridge for; hope it will soon blow over. Wee launched the Betty Gally last Monday and are fitting as fast as possible. When I have any News from the ship you may depend of it the same post. I am Sir, Your Most humble Servant, Those. Hammond. To Capt. Thomas Bowrey, att Tunbridge wells In Kent.

August the 17the 1704. Sir, I omitted Writing Last night by Reason that I expected you In town upon the unwelcome news of Mr. Turners death, For which I am heartly Sorry to See the house so much discomposed, and Likewise for your Indisposission Which I understand Rather Increases then decreases. Mr. Johnson Waited For Mr. Stileman 4 hours, but he did not Come according to his appointment, so according to your order, I shall be willing to act with the utmost diligence that Lies in me. This day I have got the Letter off Mart and protection For my men. Mr. Hamon and Mr. Stark was bound For me, the Charge off that and the protection and My Charge and all will amountt to 11 pound or thereabouts. So I Rest In hopes and wishing to hear off your health and Welfare with my Servis to madam Bowery, Your Humble Servant, Joseph Tolson. I writ this att Mr. Hamons who gives his Servis to you and there is No Forther news off the Woster then that the purser, Mr. Loveday, is dead. This For Capt. Bowry, att Tunbridge.

column46: Clifton in Essex, October the 19th 1704. Captain Tolson, Mr. Dupuy and Mr. Griffin. As far as I did observe or can be informed, the ship sailed and worked better coming down to Gravesend when she was upon an Even Keel then she did afterwards when brought by the Stern. Therefore tic my advise to try first at 4 Inches by the Stern, and from that to an Even Keel, and so to 12 Inches by the Stern, in which Compass will undoubtedly be her Trim. I hope Mr. Grist will not reach you. If not, would have you sell all things he has aboard in India and put the produce thereof to the Ships Account. I was telling you of Mr. Grist making a demand for an Allowance when ashore in India. I doe absolutely forbid the allowing him any thing or your Selves any such Expenses on any account whatever, without a very good reason set down in writing in your Journal for every days Expense; and in such Case not to allow above two Shillings a day, but hope you will wholly avoid all such Expenses, for they will be a great prejudice to our small Stock. Captain Tolson is obliged to find his Table with all things but the Common Provision of the Ship. In respect to which I must needs take notice of the taking a whole Sheep and a Shoulder of Veale at Gravesend, and by Agreement with the Butcher set it down as Beef, and that too with a great Deal of Ill husbandry in giving 3d a Pound for a whole Sheep, when could buy any Single Joint for 2 1/2d a li . I hope we shall have no more such doings of setting down one thing in the Name of another. It is not warrantable, and what I shall find out and will never allow. I would have you Buy the Steward a Book for him to keep a Daily account of the Expense of all sort of Stores under his Charge and of all fresh Provisions received and how Expended, which account would have brought in to you and Examined weekly,and signed by all in Commission as Supra Cargoes, which account to be delivered to the Owners at your return to England. Captain Tolson has a verbal leave to provide a Bowl of Punch of a Quart of Arrack every day for himself and those at his Table, which would not have Exceeded, for if wee have not a great deal of good Husbandry (which hope every one of you will contribute too), wee can never propose to make a profitable Voyage with so small a Stock. I hope this will find you so far as the Downs, where hope you will make no Stay, but proceed on your Voyage, with or without Convoy, according to your Instructions, and Pray God direct you and send you a good Voyage is the desires of Your affectionate Friend Those. Bowrey. I direct this to Mr. Dupuy and desire an Answer by the first Conveyance to Wellclose Square, and would have every one of you Copy this into your Book of Instructions. To Mr. Joseph Dupuy, Merchant on board the Mary Gally , Capt. Tolson, for East India. In the Downs; if gone, to be returned to Mr. Alias Dupuy, Merchant In Mincing Lane.

column46: October 20th 1704. Captain Tolson, Mr. Dupuy and Mr. Griffin. I wrote you yesterday, which hope came to hand, directed to Mr. Dupuy. I then wrote you about the Ships trim for Sailing, since which, discoursing Mr. Charlton, it is his Opinion that the Ship Sailed and Worked much better coming down to Gravesend then she did afterwards, which he attributed to her being brought more by the Sterne and Staying the Mast too far forward after came to Gravesend. Therefore tic my advice to bring the Ship to Swim on an Even Keel or an Inch or Two Inches by the Stern, and to Stay all the Masts to hang a little aft, whereas they all now hang forward. All your safety depending on the Ships Sailing, hope you will neglect nothing relating thereto. I am, Your affectionate Friend, Tho: Bowrey To Captain Joseph Tolson, Commander of the Mary Gally , in the Downs.

Portsmouth, October 26th 1704. Sir, I sentt a Letter Yesterday wherein I mentioned that I Intended to Saill in the affternoon From Spethead, but it proved Little wind, and I heard that the Litchffeald , a Fourth Ratte, was bound to the Westward. So I went on board her and the Commander told me that hee must Sail to morrow if he turned all the way down the Channel, and that hee was to go to Cape de Word Islands, So that I thought, the Saffty off going with him, worth my while to Stay 1 day or 2, without your postive order to the Contrary. So that I Expect to Saill to morrow a Long with the Litchffeald , the Commander having promised me his utmost Care in Convoying me Sofa to the Westward, and I shall take his Instructions in writing to Night. The wind is now att S.E. b S. The Reason off my Coming in hear, I inserted in my Last, which was, that affter having been Chased by a Ship off I believe about 30 guns, whom I outt Sailed, all though She seemed very clean and her Consort a Snow which was to windward. She Fired 3 Shot att me, butt none off them hit me; and after that I discovered 3 saill S.W. b S., 2 off which Stood to the Northward, in order, I thought, to Cut me off to the Westward. I Stood with Dunoze pointt till I see the First 2 Spook off boar S.W. 1/2 W., and att the same time I See 2 Small Snows W.S.W. From me, and then I Sprung my Loffe to go in to Spitthead. One off the Snows was so as to Row within a Mill off Benbridge point, in order to Cut me off. Butt affter I fired att him, and I believe hit him, hee Rode as Fastt as he Could back again. I Find my Ship to Saill So that I Fear none, if I have butt Sea Rome. I Rowed her 2 Knots in a calm, So that I hope my ours will Stand me in good Stead, For I see the French make great use off their ours. So I Restt all your humble Servants, Jose: Tolson These For Mr. Thomas Hamon , a Merchant, London, with care.

Spitthead, Mary Gally , October 27: 1704. Sir, I have sentt 2 Letters Mr. Hamon, supposing you not to be att home, wherein I sertiffied him off the Reason I putt into this place which was as Follows. That in order to my Instructions, on Monday att 5 in the Evening I sailed outt off the Downs with the wind att N. b Et., and att break off day wee see 2 Saill, the one W.S.With., the No. Wee ware then about 5 Leagues to the Westward off Beachey head, and steering away West For Dunowz , the Southernmost point off the Isle of wight. The Westermost sprung his Loffe and stood short our Fore Foot. Then I bore away and hee tacked. Then I sprung my Loffe and Found that I Could go so Fore to windward as to bee all most out off gun shot. When hee Came upon my quarters, hee tacked and Fired 2 Shot att me under dutch Colours, butt I did not intend to trust him. So hee gave us Chase and I Farly out sailed her. Hee Seeing that, Fired 1 Shot att me, which Fell Close by our Side, and in a Little time Lefft his Chase; and his Concarte , which wee deserned to be a Snow, Bore down to him, hee Lieing by For him. He appeared to be a ship off 30 guns and very Clean. She appeared to be French belt to me, having no galeryes, only a badge. Two hours affter I discovered 3 Saill S.W. b So. Southerly, 2 off which Stood to the Northward, the wind att N.Et. I stood on my way till they bore S.W. b With., and then I discovered 2 Snows W.S.With., so that I see it Impossible to Stand on and avoid Speeking with them. So I sprung my Loffe and Stood in For this place. One off the Snows Rowed in with me, thinking to have Cut me off att benbridge pointt. It Falling Calm, I got outt my ours and Rowed, and when She Came pretty nigh me, I Fired att her 3 Shot; and she, Fearing wee should be hard For her, and her Consorts Cold not get to her Releiffe, she turned tale and Rowed away with all Expedission. We Rowed our Ship 2 knots in a Calm. The Litchffeald , a 4 Rate, came Yesterday outt off the harbour and I heard that he was bound to the westward. So I went to the Commander and desired to have his Convoy. Hee told me that hee Should Saill this day in the Affternoon and that hee was bound For Capdevard Islands, and that hee would take all the Care hee Could off me to see me sofa outt off danger off these seas. So, Except your order to the Contrary, I intend to Embrace the opportunity off his Convoy. I have drawn a bill upon you For Five pounds by Captain Reed, Commander off the Colchester , East India merchant Ship, which is all att Present From your Humble Servant, Jose: Tolson I hired a deall boatt the day I came From the downs to Fill my Water. My puttick plates; some gave way, So that I have made new ones at this place. For Captain Thomas Bowrey, Living in Well Close Square, London.

column46: London October the 28th 1704. Capt. Tolson, Mr. Dupuy and Mr. Griffin. Sirs, Captain Tolsons of the 26th Instant to Mr. Hammond is received, by which I am Informed of your escape from the French and of the ships good sailing, both which is very acceptable News and doe very well approve of your staying to go in Company with the Litchfeild man of War. God send you a safe passage and would have you try (when have opportunity) the ships sailing by staying her Masts aft, Looseing the wedges, shifting her more by the Head or Stern &ca., as your discretion will direct you. I desire Mr. Dupuy and Mr. Griffin to be very secret with what they are particularly trusted with and not to discover it to any one in the ship or any other Person in India or Elsewhere. As Mr. Grist is excluded the Commission, so he is not to be privy to any of your Orders nor to sign any Letters you send us, which is to be signed by all three of you and which you are to direct as ordered in your Instructions, and would have you write us by the Litchfeild , when part from her, all proper about the ships sailing, on which depends our greatest safety. I came to Town today and Mr. Hammond Just gone out of Town, so did not see him nor any other of the Concerned. I wish you a good Voyage and all of you a safe return to Your affectionate Friend, T. B. My Love to my Cozen Toms. Studds. I received his Letter. To Captain Jose. Tolson commander of the Mary Gally at Spithead. If gone, to be returned to Mrs. Gardiner in Well Close Square, London.

column46: London, November 4: 1704. Capt. J. Tolson, Mr. Dupuy and Mr. Griffin. Sirs, I received Caption Tolsons of the 30th past, when under sail from Spithead. Wee having had the Winds Westerly, doubt you have bin obliged to putt into Port. I wrote you to the Downs directed to Mr. Dupuy and to Portsmouth directed to Captain Tolson, which know not if you received. Therefore please to advise per next if you received those Letters and give a full account of your Ships Sailing with the Men of War you went out with, who sailed best, and what difference, &ca. What is entrusted in particular to the two persons you know of, I desire them to keep as a great Secret, not letting any one in the Ship, or in India, or Elsewhere know any thing of it. I am in doubt of Letters being Intercepted by the East India Company, therefore both you and wee must be very cautious of what we write. The two Letters I sent you were directed to be returned if you were gone. Therefore, if you have not received them they are Intercepted; but therein is nothing to our prejudice. I hope you will lose no opportunity of Sailing, for it will grow late for your reaching the West Coast in due time, so hope you will not touch any where till reach the West Coast. I am, Your affectionate Friend, T: B. My Love to my Cozen Toms. Studs. To Captain Joseph Tolson Commander of the Mary Gally , In Plimouth. If gone, to be returned to Mrs. Gardiner In Well Close Square, London. Sent a Copy to Falmouth.

column46: London the 7th November 1704. Captain Jose. Tolson, Mr. Dupuy and Mr. Griffin. Sirs, Fearing you may be put into Port, this serves to advise you that wee are informed that had you staid longer at Spithead there was Orders from the East India Company to search your Ship. Therefore, if this finds you in Port, wee advise you to set Sail with the first opportunity of Wind, either with Convoy or without, least any such Orders may reach where you are, and that you may be stopped on any Vexatious pretence of said Company. Wee desire you to give us a particular account of the Ships sailing with the Men of War you Sailed with &ca., and hope you will use all endeavours to find her Trim, thereon depending the greatest of our Safety. As it now grows late for your reaching the West Coast in due time, so hope you will touch no where till you reach said Coast. What is particularly entrusted to Mr. Dupuy and Mr. Griffin wee would have them keep a great Secret and to doe what relates thereto at the West Coast or Batavia among the Dutch or Chinese, at any rate as well as they can, and not to let any English at any Place in India know any thing of that Concern, nor none of the Ships Company, if possible to be prevented and order all your Ships Company not to discourse with any English or others in India any thing relating to your Cargo out or home. Wee would have Mr. Grist admitted to act in relation to the Cargo, telling him we doubted of his going in the ship when at Gravesend and for that reason gave the Instructions to Mr. Griffin, but hope his future diligence will make amends for his Neglect here; for as hee is concerned with us, wee have reason to hope that his own Interest and future Preferment will be an obligation to his Industry and secrecy in all our Affairs. Show him this Letter and all else relating to our affairs. So wishing you a good Voyage and safe return &c., Your affectionate Friend, T. B. Capt. Jose. Tolson: Sent 2 Copies one to Plimouth (returned) and one to Falmouth under Cover to Mr. Hammonds Friends.

column46: London, September the 13th 1704. Mr. Charles Sherer: Sir, This comes by the Mary Gally . Your advises or other favours to the Captain of said ship in his Buying, selling, &ca. will be a great favour to me and shall be acknowledged in due time. Here is arrived this season the Worcester , in whom I was Chiefly concerned, in whose voyage we suffer much by the Impudence of Mr. Callant, the Supra Cargo, who had opportunity of making us a very great voyage had he pursued his Instructions. As it is we shall clear about per Cent profit. He is dead, so Captain Matthews the London will clear about profitt. As to Public News. The Chief actions this sumer has bin in Bavaria where the Duke of Malborough marched to the assistance of the Emperor with about 45,000 English and other Nations in the English Pay, and has in Conjunction with the German Army gained two signal Victories over the French and Bavarians. In the first the Enemy were beat from strong entrenchments and lost about men killed and taken prisoners, among which Marshal Tallard, a General, 16 other General Officers, 1200 Officers and soldiers and the whole Country of Bavaria reduced to the Emperors obedience. In Savoy the French have taken one Considerable town. By Sea the French are not able to meet us with a Grand Fleet so endeavours chiefly to Protect the Trade of the Spanish West Indies and to destroy the Merchant Shipping English and Dutch, which is too often effected, more throe our own negligence then their own power. If you please to favour me with any thing material of the Transactions of any part of India, it will be very acceptable. This with mine and Wives service to your self and Lady, I conclude, and am Your Humble Servant, .

column46: London, Oct. the 13: 1704. Mr. Robert Leslie: This comes by the Mary Gally , Joseph Tolson Captain and Supra Cargo. She is a Separate Stock Ship and so is Entitled to the Protection of the united Company in all Privileges they enjoy in India, in which ship I am concerned. Any Assistance or kindness you shall doe for said ship will be taken as done for me. I wrote you by the Rising Sun , Captain T. , desiring your assistance to him. I hope he has bin in Bengal. I forbear mentioning any thing of your relations here, I having delivered to Captain Tolson Letters from your Grandmother and Aunt. I doubt not but you received the Books I sent you and hope by this time you are in a good way of getting a Living, for the and Ingenuity you are endowed with (provided you lead a Godly and virtuous life) can scarce fail of raising your fortunes in India. If you have bin at Maldiva, I desire you to inform Captain Tolson of the Navigation thither and the Method of Trade there, the Price of Cowries for Rice, what sort of Rice or other goods proper to carry thither and any other matters useful to him. Or if you have not bin there, that you would make such enquirys of any English or Moors who have bin there and inform Captain Tolson, and to procure him if possible a servant to go with him who is acquainted there. As to Public News. I have wrote Mr. Sherer, and Captain Tolson has the News Papers which you may peruse. If any thing material happens in any part of India, your advising me thereof will be very acceptable. This, with mine and Wives Love and service, is what offers from Your Loving Friend to serve you, .

column46: London, the 7 October 1704. Mr. John Beard: Sir, I wrote you of the 23d November 1703 per ship Rising Sun , Captain , recommending him to your favour, which ship hope may have bin with you and enjoyed your favourable assistance, which I am still a solicitor for in behalf of the Mary Gally , whereof is and , by whom this comes. She is a separate stock ship, so Entitled to the Protection of the United Company, which hope they will not refuse to act herein as the Law requires, and for which we pay them 5 per Cent on the Gross sales at the Ships return to England. Dr. Evans, Bishop of Bangor, is now in Wales. I advised him of this ship going for Bengal. He wrote me he would send Letters, but have not received them. This, with all due respects, is what offers from Sir, Your most Humble Servant, .

column46: London, the 11th October 1704. To Captain Pitts: Honble. Sir, This comes by the Mary Gally whereof is Captain and , wherein I am chiefly concerned. She is a Separate stock ship and has the Certificate to show, so hope shall enjoy all due Protection from the Company at all places in India. The Concerned designing said ship to Stop at Fort St. George, I am in Duty bound to address your Honour, desiring your Favours in all matters relating to said Ship and Cargo and shall much esteem all Kindnesses showed. The ship is bound from Fort St. George to Bengal and the Captain has orders to carry Letters or doe any service you please to Command thither. Supposing this ship may arrive with you before the Companies ships, have sent your Honour the Printed news of the sumer past, which hope may be acceptable. I hope your Honour will pardon this presumtion, having never had the Honour of your acquaintance, but presume you are not a stranger to my name which is well known to Mr. Aflack and any others who were at Fort St. George when I lived there. I conclude, with all due respects, and am Your Honours Most Humble Servant, .

Cape bon Esperance. Sir, Being willing to make use of all Opportunities, that any way might appear to present, to give you an Account of our proceedings, according to my last dated the 31 of October, Set Sail from Spit head under the Convoy of the Litchfield with the Wind at N, Et. We Sailed through the Needles at 4 a Clock in the Evening. I quickly found that my Ship did not sail so well Large as I expected, the Litchfield sailing some small matter better then I did, all which Advantage the Captain, Contrary to his promise, made use of, although in 48 hours he did not gain above 4 Miles of me. On the 2d of November, upon the break of the day, I saw a sail somewhat near me, and perceiving her to be a french ship, I fired at her, after which he Endeavoured to Enlarge his Distance and made the best of his way from me. In a Small time after, I see the Litchfield take the forementioned his Consort, being both from the West Indies and bound for St. Mallo, and the Same time I saw a Sail to the South Eastward who Immediately gave me Chase. And he thereon Sent 6 men unto the prise and made the best of his way. I Came up with the Prise and asked him what his Captain took those Ships to be, and he told me his Captain took them to be french Men of War or Privateers. I asked if Intended to shorten Sail for me. To which he answered he believed not. I kept on after him till 11 a Clock, and when See that he did not Intend to shorten Sail for me, and my Chasers nearer me then before, Endeavouring to get to Windward of Me, I Clapped upon a Wind, and I soon found my Ship to mend her Pace from 4 l/2 knots to 9 knots, the Wind at WNWt. I stood away With. and the Easternmost Ship bearing Et. b No., I found them to drap a Stern a great Pace. After I Clapped upon a Wind, I slackt my Rigging, so that by 2 hours Computation I had gained 5 Miles upon them, and they left their Chase. I believing the Ship to be somewhat by the head, I unstowed my Anchors and stowed them again at the Mainmast. In the Night we fell unto a fleet, amongst we discerned was a Light. I Immediately altered my Course, and it falling Calm, I got out my Oars, which I find very useful to me upon such Occasions; so I believe they did not see me. The next Day wee had a Storm of at S.With. We were then in the Latitude of 48d. No. We splitt our Mainsail and lay under a Reef Mison. The next Day I resolved to make Sail to the Westward, apprehending less Danger in standing away With. and With. b No., then lying a trying. The Weather Continued 4 Days, in which time I had very good Observations, and the Course I steered Carried Clear of any part of Ireland, and the Ship being tight, made no Water. We kept on till the Wind veered about. The 6 Day of November att Noon I spied a french Snow lying a trying. He see but our topsail abroad and run past him at such a Rate he never gave us Chase, we then having the Wind att No.E. b No. and steering away S.With. We run 10 knots. I see none afterwards that seemed to be Desirous of seeing me or speaking with me. I made Cape de Word Islands and went of the Eastward of them in order to shorten my Way. I met with very Contrary Winds and Calms hath very much defrayed my Passage, for I find my Ship to Sail very well. The 10 of December I had the Misfortune of Carieng away in the latitude of 4d. South, though I had secured my Mast with out Lickers and what I Could in order to Carry Sail; for not being able to Cross the Line so far to the Eastward as I Intended, I was Obliged to Carry sail in order to Carry Clear of the Coast of Brazil, which I feared. I made Tristan de Cuna the first of January , since which I met with Contrary Winds. I Arrived in this Place the 19 Inst. , where I found Captain Engeldu in the Suzanne from Surratt, and Captain Jacob Wright in the Legorne frigate, both bound for England, by both which you may Expect Letters. The Wind hath blown very hard 2 Days, I having given my Ship a pair of boot topps. And with the Consent of Mr. Dupuy and Mr. Griffin, we thought it might be for the Good of the Voyage to buy for the Cargo Six Leagers of Wine, for which we gave 45 Dollars per Leaguer, of the money Received for Beer, according as you ordered I might, of which I have sent a small Cask by the Suzanne , Captain Engeldue, and I have left this with a Deanes ship and 2 more, that is, One with Captain Engeldue and one with Captain Wright, the Deanes Captain having promised me to take a Particular to Send it to England. All which being true Copies of this. I Am now unmoared in order to sail on my Voyage. So we rest as before Your humble Servant, The Cass qt. 12 Gallons marked MG.

Cape, Janry. the 26th, 1704/5. Honoured Father and Mother: Wee having Arrived here the 19 Instant and Having an Opportunity of writing to you by the Leghorne Frigate, I made bold to trouble you with a line or two to tell you of my health and all our Ships Company, and of our safe Arrival att this place, wee touching here only for Water. But since my being here I have been in Company with a Gentleman , which is a Liver att this place, which Came from the ship Abbington from Carver, he being Carried by Misfortune from this place by the Josiah , Captain Pie, And after a short stay on board the Josiah , took Passage with Captain Goodfellow for the Coast of Mallabar and went to Carrwar, a factory , to Lade Pepper on the Coast, But his Description of the Voyage it has been Very unfortunate, for as he Verifies it for truth that Captain Goodfellow is Dead and Mr. Gun Drowned. The fifth Mate, one Davis, is att present Commander and Mr. Watts Chief mate. But as for Mr. Newport, the Men has Made Objections against it, and he has Left the ship for Not succeeding his birthwright to be Commander. But as for my brother , he is in very good health and a brisk sailor and Minds his business very well, and is very well respected be every body. And by the same Information, Captain Pies men was going to Run a Way with both Ships, had it not been discovered, and Eight Confessed designing to Kill Captain Goodfellow and Captain Pie, but some made Objections Against Killing Captain Goodfellow, saying "his good by Name and good by Nature." Being in Conclusion of the Matter What to doe, was Over heard by one Tag, and he discovered the Matter; and so it was prevented. Likewise I will give you some men's names as I hear was Living when this man Left her (being 7 Months since) on the Other side, but since this Misfortune on board the Abington . Captain Lashley, Commander of the Neptune , has Lost his ship a going down the Coast Just within Cape Comrine , and it is Reported that he was sent for to Command the Abbington , but am Not Certain, but by all Proprability it will be so, for the Abbington is gone for Bumbay and he has been sent for thither; therefore it is Believed to be for the same account. If not, I hear a Very good Carrectter of the said Davise, now Commander. So no more Concerning our Neigbours, but must think a Little of my self. Wee are now att the Cape, as I wrought before, and all in General in health, and are in fare Prospect of Making a Very good Voyage for our Owners by all people as wee Can Learn of, and am Very well satisfied in my Voyage, ship and Commander. So no more, but Conclude in Health, wishing the same to Your self and Mother, Likewise to my Brother and Sisters, Giving my Duty to your self and Mother. Love to Brother and Sisters and all friends in General. I remain till Death, Your Dutiful Son, Richard Griffin. Pray tell Madam Humfrey that William Crouch is in good health, he being a Cousin of theres. Likewise give my service to her and the Captain, if at home. Likewise to Captain Wells. Mr. Grist and Mr. Dungey desires to be remembered to there friends. The Gentleman that has gave this Report arrived here but two days before us and Designs for England this fleet, his name being Mr. John Vande Burgen, but must first go for Holland. Living on board the Abbington as I am Informed Mr. Davise, Commander now Mr. Watts, Mate Wm. Crouch, Midshipman Griffin, Do. Tho: Monday, Do. Giles Loan, Do. Jno. Packer, Purser Mr. Collins, Carpenter Mr. Dungey, Do. Mate These being all I knew, made no further Enquiry Concerning Strangers. Robed. Watson, Drowned. To Mr. Nicholas Griffin, Living a Little be Low Ratclif Cross near London: Per Leaghorne Frigate.

Calcutta December the 12. 1705. Sirs, Having this Good opportunity by Captain Wibridge, I am willing to Give you A full Account of the passages, Conveniences and Inconveniences that hath Attended our Voyage to this Place. The 31st of October 1704 I passed the Neadles under a Convoy of Captain Thomas Billingsly in her Majesties Ship the Litchfeild , who served me as you see in the Copy of my Letter from the Cape of Good Hope, which Gives you An Account of our departure from thence and what had passed in our Passage to that Place. I departed from the Cape the 26th of January and the 26th of February I Lost my fore topmast Again. The 5th of April wee where in the Latitude of 4d. 50m. S. and 66 Degrees to the Eastward of Cape Bone Esperance , having had a very tedious Passage, and where I Exspected to have met with the Westerly Monsones, I met with Little Else but Calms. The 19th of April wee made the South end of the Island Nassaw which was my Design to fall in withal, Although I hoped to have made it sooner, but by great Calms and Westerly Currents I Could not Accomplish my desire sooner. In Council wee Resolved to go for Bencolen, where wee Arrived the 24th, and by the Government very civilly Received. My men was something Inclineing to the Scurvy. I would have Proceeded According to your Order, but having a Relation by 2 ships from Battavia that Europe Liquor being a Very Dead Commodity, After having Endeavoured to Oblige his Honour and Council if Possible to Engage in A Contract According to Instructions, which I could not Accomplish, Although I Proffered Cheaper then Ordered, wee Resolved to go to Padding in Order to Dispose of some, if not All our Cargo. In this time my men began to be very sickly. My Second mate there desired his Cleareance, which I had no great Reason to Deny him, Although to my thinking I had used him as A Brother for his farthers sake. Att that time 2/3 of my men was sick, therefore think him very Ungrateful according to my Judgment. I shiped another there att the same Wages, who was no Artisst, butt my want of men Obliged me to have some , Although Mr. Hancock, who I have now made my second mate, by All Appearance was more Capable then hee. I Cleared Mr. Dungey the 8th May 1705, who hath behaved him self so that hee is now going home from this Place A Midshipman with Captain Lane for Europe. I set sail from Bencolen the 17th of May in the Morning. The Contracts made there I have sent here Enclosed, and Likewise att Bantall, att Pollosinck, &c. Att Padding I had but small success, finding the Places as the Relation in my Last from Battavia, whereof you have here Enclosed A Copy. To my Great dissatisfaction, then, I made the Best of my way for Battavia. I had trusted the Chief of Bantall to the Value of 800 Spanish Dollars, and Although I had from under his hand and the Seconds Likewise, I was detarded Eight Days att Bencolin before I could get the Principal without Demoareidge , According to Contract. The 10th of July I Arrived Att Battavia, Where I found Mr. Hinmars, who was very willing to give me all the Advice he Could to my Interest. But he departed from Battavia the Next day after I came hither, Mr. Vancaster, as in the Copy of my Battavia Letter, being Dead before I Could speak to him. I found my ship to be in Great Dainger of the Worm, and my Maine Mast Proving very bad, I found my Self Obliged, for the security of the ship, to Dispose of my Cargo, being much touched with the Worm. I had Carpenters and Colkers , days Work, 118, Att A Rupee a Day, my Colker being sick and Deyed 7 Days after I bungun the Work. I had 200 Take boards att 18 Dollars per Hundred, 4 Pecoll of Nails att 12 dollars per pecoll; for a Great boat to Putt my Lumber in, 3 Dollars per day; 6 Ducats to the Subanders Boateswaine as A fee to not to take notice of what buisness I did, for I could not Get A free Liberty to Lay her Ashore. And for Oacom , Dimmer , Oil, the Hire of English men and Cooleys, the Whole Cost of the sheathing and Cheking the Maine Mast and the Making the tops will Amount to 450 Rex Dollars, as by my Books will Appear, besides the Loss of time. So that I advise you, never Propose to send out Another ship unsheathed, nor to take the Advice off that Old Knave, Ketch to send ships to India, Where the Long Passage Oblidges the Carrying of sail, to not Allow security for the Masts, for which hee hath had my Wishes that he had Perished in the Coal Lighter where the Waterman Left him, for I doe Asure you that it was a Great Prolonging of my outward bound Passage. These fitteagues, and the Indispossion of my Assistance by sickness and my stock being small and Waisteing Daily, made me to Comply with the Articles hear enclosed. I Departed from Battavia the 2d of September very Deep Laden. I met with a very Long Passage and Very Hard weather. The 10th of November I Arrived in Ballasore Road. Mr. Grist was Left att Battavia. Likewise Att the same Place I met with Mr. Webber and two other of the Prosperouses Men, the One the Great Villon, the Chief Actor in the Running Away with her. I would Gladly have sent him to Justice, but upon Consideration, 1st that my Own Officers in whom I could trust being Indisposed by sickness, and feareing that if I Demanded Justice of the Government they would have delivered them into my Hands; and believe my men to be very Honest and did not Care to have them Corrupted by Villons. Mr. Webber I gave A Passage to Bengal, he being very Poor, but behaved himself very civilly on board my ship; and what ever he hath been formerly, I believe hee will make a Good Man. I shiped him by Recommendation Chief Mate on board the Mary Ann , Captain Godwin, A separate stock ship, and he is gone to Batavia, and as I understand, bound for England from thence, in which Employ I hope hee will doe very Well. My second Mate I Shiped at Bencolen I cleared hear for some Certain Reasons of Negktlecting my buisness to disadvantage of yours and my Interest. I Paid him his Wages and maid Mr. Hancock my second mate, who hath behaved himself very well and in my Eye is most deserveing of That post. Att Battavia I had Considerable Loss by bear being sour, and 7 Chests of bear that Came on board Last, att the Opening of them at Padding, Appeared Like unto the Dunghill, in so much that wee saved but 34 Dozen, being filled up one with another, much of which proved Bad afterwards and turned to Little Account. The strong bear burst several of the Cask. The Chease I sold Last att Battavia, having disposed of but Little before. I sold them 1 Dollar 3/4 per Chese, one with the Other. Att Battavia I Lost my best bower Anchor, and the Reason my Cable Parted, I Judge it to be Cut by Anchor flukes; and having no buoy, and the Anchor sunk in the Mud, Could not get him, the Want of which I Cannot Excuse, by not being of my Necklect, by no other way then my buisness Lieing heavy upon me and my People sick, I was forced to Let things be some times Contrary to my Inclinations and Judgment. That Night I Arrived in Ballasore I took A Dutch Piolett and Gave 100 secar Rupees to Carry me up to Calcutta, but he having not so Good Exsperiance as hee ought to have, Run us Upon A sand the Next Reach below Jangerall Point, the 16th of November, Where I Lay 2 tides. The 1st Tide I Exspected every Minute to have seen her go all to Pieces, Lieing Right Thawrte the Tide, which Run Like the Currant under London Bridge. I had shored her, that she stood upwright, and as Pleased God, Contrary to All Human Reasons, she did not make any More water then useally, which is butt very Little. The Next tide I Got out the best bower Anchor Again which wee hove home the Tide before, or Else wee had Got her of, and by the Help of the Wind and All my sails set I Got her of before Any Assistance Came. Captain Hurl sent me two boats, his Long boat and Yawle and the Bucksees , Mr. Prattle, two tow Boats and A sloop. Hear I received your Letters, but as yett I doe not find any Reason to believe that I shall have any Evil treatement from the Government. Wee have sold our Cargo, Most of it to his Honour Shelldon, so that he being my friend I doe not fear any Examination of my Affairs. I have had some proposals with his Honour to Come hear Again, which Believe I shall, and then, without your orders to the Contrary, God willing, I will Return for Europe. I hope to bee in A Condition by that time to Purchase a Cargo of 40,000 Rupees, and if the best of our Judgment may be safe to follow your Instructions in our Return to Europe, I shall give All due Respect to them; but if any way more safe, you may Depend that I will use my Endeavours to Come safe. And I hope to make all the Gentlemen Concerned Gainers by the Voyage, so that I hope none will be forward in Insureing, for I doe Value the safe Return of the Ship Equal with my Life, and will as soon Loose one as the Other. My Intent is to Come home with the Dutch fleet, so that I hope to Depart this Place 12 Months hence. I am very Likely to Come by A very bad market for the Glass ware, it being A Very dead Commodity. Wee have 12 Rupees for 75 li. of Pepper and for Arrack 90 Rupees per Leaguer. I have made a Cable of Koyer, my small bower Cable proving not Trustworthy, for att Bantall it Gave way in fair weather and no strain. The buoy Rope broke and I lost the Anckor, but being in search After it, I found Another About 2 cwt. Less, which I Always find will hold more then I am Willing to trust to that Cable. I sold the Yaule att Battavia for 40 Dollars, finding one boat to be sufficient for my Compliment of men. As for Opium, the Price it bears now att Battavia and the Price in Bengal I find it no Commodoty, and the Gentlemen with whom I made these Articles is the Cheafe trader in Battavia for Opium, and they will not have any Opium in the ship, for hear it is att 300 Rupees per Chest, and Att Battavia by Reason of the War, it is but 190 Rex Dollars per Chest; so that I think not to take any on the ships Account, but Rather take the Privilege in the Articles mentiond in Other Goods. I will send you An Account more Att Large by the Fleate frigate, Captain Newton, of my Affairs here, but shall be Always Cautious of Interceptions, for as for the Letter sent for the Downs, I neaver Received it, Dated the 19th of October, but the Letter dated the 28th of Do. I did receive, when the ship was Under sail and after I had sent mine away, Dated the 30th 1704. As for Mr. Wells, I doe not find but that hee hath done you Just part of a Man in All Respects Relating to the Ship, for if she Had not been stronger then it Might have been Exspected one of her built , she never had Come whole, having such a Large Quantity of Coper, Toothanegg and tinn as I had. The Maine mast I hope will doe very Well, but it was far from as Good as it should have been. The Gilded Knives I have had most Part by me till I Came here, and the Glass ware, all the shales. I can get no more then 4 Rupees a peace for them, and before I Came to this Place I neaver Could have the Proffer of Any money for them. The Spanish Rashes I Left att Battavia in order to bee disposed off in the Merchants hands I have dealt with. I have had one Hogshead of Wine Leaked out. I bought Koyer for 4 1/2 Rupees per maund, and Captain Hurl took some exceptions because I would not give him six, and so he sent me 3 Leaguers off Arrack back, Complaineing off the Goodness, although hee had his Mate on board to see it Good and in Good Condition delivered. The Dutch men I brought from Batavia, being 3, is all Run away hear, having had A Months Pay advance att Battavia. Archiballd Whittman Hath been A Very Diligent servant to the ship and a very sober Good man, and I have Respected him, and hee hath Acted as Boateswaine this 6 Months, the Boateswaine having been Indisposed by sickness so Long, and I am dubious of his Recovery. If he Recovers I will make the Aforementioned my Gunner, and I hope you will Consider and Gratify the Diligent, all which I shall give you a true Relation. If God should Call me aside, I hope I have those to that will use their Endeavours to guard their Own Reputation and your Interest, Although I praise God I am and have been in Perfect Bodeyly health, so that with Gods Assistance I can foresee no Aspect that you may not have a Good Voyage. Neither have I any reason to speak ill of those who it should Please God should bee my successors, so that I hope none will be forward in Insureing. The Cargo I brought hear Amounts to 50,000 Rupees and upwards, all which and more is to go back in my ship, according to our Contracts with his Honour Sheldon and others, so that my security neaver goes out of my Hands, and you may Depend never shall. I ordered a Case of Arrack to bee sent from Battavia, of the best that Could be Procured, which I hope will Come to your Hands in order to drink to our safe Arrival to yours and our satisfaction, to which I Pray God Assist our Endeavours, which shall not be wanting, so far as Life and Health permit. Joseph Ford and William Smith (the man I had in the rome of James Jones) Run Away Att Bencolen the 15th May 1705. Mr. Sheldon has promised to Dispatch me from Calcutta by the 25th of January next. Att our Coming the shore of Batavia, the Day before I took my Leave thereof, I Gave Notice to All that belonged to me that I would sail att 2 in the Morning. Mr. Grist went on shore that Afternoon and I told him that I should sail by 2 in the Morning. The Gentlemen with whom I Dealt Came off in Order thereto and I set sail att 4 in the Morning, and att 11 I see a boat following me and Mr. Grist to be in her, I sent the Gentlemen's Paunch along to fetch him, but by some misfortune the boat Lost us and did not Come to us to the Place appointed, which was off Bantam Point, in order to Take in the Gentleman. I doe believe Mr. Grist was in the boat, for att his Coming into the Paunchalong, the Other boat returned. The Gentleman I put on board the Panther , Captain John Camel Commander, bound for Betavia. Mr. Grist had behaved himself very well, so that I am positive he had no design to Leave the ship, nor I any Reason to Leave him but by misfortune. So wee Conclude and remain, your most Humble and faithful servants, Joseph Tolson Joseph Dupuy Richard Griffin

Bancolen the 20 Juin 1705. Sir, Since our last we have not being favoured with any, from the which shall cause brievity. This shall only be to Inform you that in Settling the Accounts that the weights of the Spanish Ps. 8/8 did not agree. We made by our Weight but 814 Ounces and 942 ps. by tale. I cannot tell where the error Should be. You delivered them to Mr. Griffin all Sealed, and he kept them unto his Custody till they were Delivered to Capt. Tolson. There was one of the bags which was burst in Mr. Chest which, has he says, had received Damage by Saltwater. I have no more att present only Referr my Self to the General Letter and So Remain Sir: Your most Humble Servant, Joseph Dupuy. To Captn. Thomas Bowrey, in Well Close Square, London.

Batavia, January the 17th 1705/6. Capt. Bowrey, Sir, I thought it proper to Inform You that our Ship Going for Bengal in the Service of Mr. Jno. Moor, Merchant here (Leaving me behind, through an Unlucky Accident), here were some Letters for you and some other of the Owners left in the abovesaid Merchants hands by Capt. Tolson, with a small matter of Tea, Lacquer and China Ware, which he Thought might be acceptable to your Lady, to be Sent home by the first Opportunity. And in Order thereto, upon the Arrival of the Dover here, Mr. Moor spoke to Capt. Garraway about it, but Received an Unexpected Answer, Vizt. , that he would neither take or Suffer to be Taken on board, either Letters, or any other Individual matter, wherein he might Seem to serve Capt. Tolson. The Occasion of his Aversion I am sensible of, so cannot Impute it to any Brutishness in his Temper. However, I being Sensible of this, and well knowing the Import of the Letters, went to the Merchants and had the Letters delivered to me and Clapping a Direction to Mr. Hammond over the Direction to you, delivered them to a private person (by name Mr. Jones) as my Letters, which he promised to putt into the Post Office, as Soon as arrived in England. Sir, I have nothing to Inform you of more, save that the Merchant Expects the Ship here in next March. What ever must doe then God knows, for our Stock's produce, with the rest of our Treasure, will not purchase a Cargo here to Answer your Expectation. However, hoping for the best, I Conclude with all due Respects, Sir, Your most humble Servant, Alias Grist. Sir, pray Give my Service to Mr. Hammond, &c. To Capt. Tho: Bowrey, Att his house in Well Close Square, Near Rattcliffhighway, London.

Batavia the 5th September 1705. Sirs, I send you these lines, begging your pardon that att present I cannot give you a more full Account of our proceedings. I have here enclosed his honour Watts Account Curant and Mr. Bugdens Chief at Bantal. I found in my Outward bound passage a great unconvenience by the Want of tops and Riging to secure my topmast. I carried away 2 topmasts outward bound, and for want of riging to secure them, I never was able to Carry what Sail was Convenient to gain a passage, which together with the Contrary Winds I met with, made my passage very tedious. The 24 of April I Anchored in Sillybar road (where I found the Dover , Captain Garway), which is about 16 Miles from Bencola. The Governor sent horses for us the next day. In that place my people begun to be very sickly. I had some dealings with the Governor as you see by the Relation that I had. We thought it the best to proceed to the Northward, although our time in our Instructions was out. In so doing I found my Self in a great error, for Padding, it is not the place it is represented for the taking of Europe Goods, it being small and a place of little Consumation, there being not above 8 or 10 people of note. I could have had 400 pecull of Benjamin, but the price being high, did not deall with them. I did not sell above 500 dollars worth of Goods, which made me heartily repent my Coming there. I toke Gould which I sold for 23 per Cent. at Batavia, where finding my bear to sower, I made all the Expedition to sell, which I did, strong and small together, for 40 dollars per but; the lead att 4 1/8 dr. per pecull, the Guns and Anchors 6d per 112 li. as marked. Here I found my Ship to be in great danger of the Worm, which made me make all the haste I could to get her Sheathed, and her mainmast being Sprung in the head I was forced to get it out and Check it. It hath not proved good, Several pluges Starting out of it which he had Cut in the fitteag. I have had here, you may Judge, no little trouble, having not had above 3 people besides my Self well in the height of my buysines. In the night I went on Shore and in the day on board to Stow my Ship, both of my Mates being Sick and Mr. Dupuy having the Ague. Mr. Vankester whom I had a letter for and a box and hamper, from whom I expected Assistance, died Coming on shore in the boat, after the Receipt of the letter. These disappointments made me Except of the Articles Enclosed of which money I have paid in 7191. 2. 1., and I have left on Shore with him 7 hogshead of Cape wine, 22 bags of Shot the bail of Spanish Rushes to dispose on for us and to be Accounted att our Return. And I have on board all the Glass ware, 10 leagers Arrack, 50 pecull of Pepper. On the Ships Account I paid 5/8 of a dollar for Carpenters and Corkers per day. I Sheathed her all with teek board. All which Account I, God willing, will give you in my next, and I hope you will pardon my Shortness and Consider my trouble and hast and not Impute it to be any Neglect. In great haste we Conclude, hoping in Short time to give you a account Jose. Tolson Joseph Dupuy Richd. Griffin Mr. Grist is Left att Batavia. We have Sent you a Case of the best Arrack. To Capt. Thomas Bowrey in Well Close Square near London.

London the 12th Nov. 1705. Capt. Jose: Tolson, Mr. Jose: Dupuy & Mr. Richd. Griffin, Sirs, Wee received yours from the Cape, when Outward bound, and hope this will meet you there in your Voyage homeward where, if you are soon enough, we would have you come in Company with the Dutch Ships for Rotterdam, and if not, we would have you follow the directions already given for your Voyage homeward in your Instructions. Capt. Green and his Chief Mate and Gunner is hanged in Scotland, very unjustly, and we have lost the Worcester and Cargo there. Therefore, avoid Scotland. Saltpetre and most Sorts of India Goods is rather dearer then when you went out. Wee apprehend wee have had some Letters Intercepted by the East India Company, therefore would not have you write us of any Transactions of your Voyage, but when have opportunity, to write us only where you are and to send an account of what goods then aboard for our Accounts, and at the first Port you come to in Holland, England or Ireland, to send Mr. Grist and Mr. Dupuy up to us to give us an account of all matters of the Voyage. We hope a happy meeting here and are Your Loving Friends Those. Bowrey Those. Hammond El. Dupuy Goo: Jackson To Capt. Jose. Tolson Commander of the Mary Gally from India to be left at the Cape of Good Hope with the Dutch Wine Merchant. per Mr. Jno. Rogers Q.D.G. in the Liampo and per in the Windsor Gally per Mr. G. Hond: Sir, I Send you these Lines to Inform You that, to my Great Dissatisfaction, I Remain in this Port still. In my last I Gave you an Account of our Intent to Go for Benjar, but not being able to procure Spanish Money and the Exchange going so high as 33 per Cent, that is 133 Rex Dollars For 100 Spanish Dollars, me alter my Resolution, and I made a Verbal Contract with the same Gentleman as I Dealt with before for 2000 Pecoll of Sugar att 4 Dollars and 1/4 Rr. per Pecoll, to be putt on board by the 10 of June, and 100 pecoll of Benjamin att 35 Rex Dollars per Pecoll. The Rest of my Money I Reserved to Invest in other Goods fit for Suratt, For which Place I Designed the Cargo, but the Strickness of the Government's Inspecting into the Trade of the English has been such that I have not yett on board above 500 pecoll of Sugar and 200 pecoll of Sugar Candy and 105 pecoll of Benjamin. The Gentleman that made the Contract with me has been very Dilatory to my Great Discomfort, next to the Point of Despair. He promises to Dispatch me in a very short Time, and for some Reasons believe he will perform it. I have on board about 8 pecoll of Spice, 100 pecoll of long pepper, 25 pecoll of Long Turmeric and Some Round Pepper, and I hope in a Short Time to Give you a farther Account of our proceedings, and with the help of God to make the best of our way for England. Mr. Dupuy has been very unserviceable and pernicious to the Ships Interest, as will by his Actions appear, to my Great Dissatisfaction, that I can no longer hide his base and Ridiculous Actions, as will herein appear. Att my arrival at Bencola he refused to proceed any farther with me, and Gave me under his hand the Enclosed papers. Att my Return from Padding to Bencola he had by his unbecoming Behaviour and Extravagancys made himself odious to the Governor and Gentlemen of the place, and by Sickness did appear like a Ghost, and in Reputation like a Vagabond, which made my heart bleed to see him in such a Condition, so that att his Request and For his Father's Sake, I received him on board, For which he hath given me a great deal of Reason to Repent it. Att my Arrival att Batavia, most of my men being Sick, and Business laying heavy upon me, my Mates and Mr. Grist being likewise Sick, he pretending to be Indisposed, he went to the Gentleman I dealt with and took 25 Dollars, as he pretended, For my Use. I ordered the Gentleman to Let him have no more, but he, under pretence of a bill Drawn that would be accepted In Bengal, Got 330 Dollars of the said Gentleman; and in Bengal, as I Suppose, he sold the said bill, if he had such a bill. When I was ready to Sail he came to me, being followed by a Sergeant and a File of Musqueeters, and told me he was sent For by the Chief . Att which I answered, "What have you done?" And he Told me, "Nothing." I asked him if he owed any body any money, and he said, "No." So I went to the Chief with him, and all the Punch houses in Town came in with their bills upon him, to the Value of 300 and odd Rupees, besides all other Debts to other Gentlemen, which he had with Lying and Weedling Got of them, in which faculty he is become as perfect a Master in as any Kidnapper in London. The Chief in Bengal made me Give them a Bond for the Money, of which I doe not Question but you have an Account before this time. And here he hath made himself so ridiculous that there is not One Gentleman nor Sailor of whom he could borrow money or moneys worth, that he hath not used all Deceitful ways imaginable to Accomplish his End; and hath Gone on board of other Ships and bought Chests of Wine. But as it happened, I had notice of it and they stopped them. This and the like has occasioned me a great deal of Trouble, and the Subander has sent me one Bill of one of the Public houses, with order to pay it, and I expect the rest, so that I cannot Forbear making you acquainted I have appointed to meet the Gentleman this day, in order to Give him a Bond for the 330 Dollars, and I hope that you will take Care that his Father shall discharge the same, as it was your pleasure to send him with me as my Second, and I for the good of the Voyage Engage my Self in such Cases, that I must either pay or Engage For it, and if I pay, it must be out of the Ship's Stock. And it is hard to pay Permission For money to Trade and such young Fellows drink and whore with the Principal. I never knew of this money he borrowed till he came Bantam Point For Bengal. My Ship is in a very good Condition, and my men in health. Archibald Whiteman is dead, and I have made John Mitchell Boatswain in his Room. John Painter is dangerously sick. I have my Complement: all English Except 2. My Mates, purser, Doctor, Carpenter and Thomas Studds are well. For these Reasons abovementioned wee have thought Fit in Council to Exclude him From any farther acting in that Station, as the Enclosed will make it appear, For Fear of Mortality any Farther Damage should Ensue. I hope to Give you a farther Account in my next. Since what wrote before, have met the Gentleman about the 330 Dollars, but find him Deaf to any Thing of Bonds, so that after all means and persuasions used, I may assure you I shall be Obliged to pay the Money and 30 Per Cent. for the Use of it. After our humble Service to you all, Wee Conclude and Rest, Sirs, Your humble Servants, Jose: Tolson Richard Griffin Alias Grist Batavia, Mary Gally , July 28, 1706. The Enclosed papers, save one, are Copies of them signed Per Mr. Dupuy, which now I have on board to produce hereafter, if Occasion For it. To Capt. Thomas Bowrey, These.

London the 31/30th May 1706/1707 Capt. Jose: Tolson, Mr. Jose: Dupuy & Mr. Rich: Griffin & Mr. El: Grist: Sirs, Expecting your Arrival in Holland, this is to advise you that so soon as you arrive there, we would have Mr. Dupuy and Mr. Grist to come for London by the first Conveyance to give us an Account of all Matters, with an Invoice of the Quantity and Quality of the Cargo then aboard. Give us no Account of Transactions of the Voyage by Letters, for we have reason to think the East India Company Intercepts them, and give a Charge to whoever you dispatch for London not to give any person but ourselves an Account of any Transactions of the Voyage. Wee doe strictly Charge you not to sell or suffer to be sold any thing out of the Ship, considering the Bonds we are Engaged in to the Contrary. We would have you come with the first Convoy that offers from Holland for the River of Thames where God send you safe to Your Loving Friends, Those. Bowrey Those. Hammond Goo. Jackson Alias Dupuy Sent one Copy under Cover to Mr. Sam Moors at Amsterdam and one delivered to Mr. Dupuy to send to Rotterdam.

Dunckirk, September the 1th 1707. Captain Bowrey, Sir, though I am not ambitious of being the Messenger of bad News, yett I think it proper to Inform you of the Loss of Ship Mary Gally , and to let You know our Misfortune may in Great part be attributed to your Order to the Commander of not putting into any part of Scotland, as your Letter left att Cape Bone Esperance will show, although Mr. Dupuy nor self was made acquainted with nothing of the Matter till wee had lost Company with the Dutch Fleet, which is now about 5 weeks ago. After which, having used Endeavours to find them again and all Hopes of it Frustrated, though a fair wind presented for putting in to Norroway, yet no Argument could prevail with Captain Tolson, though wee Gave him our Opinions in Writing, which though might differ in some small Matters, yett all Concurred for making the best of our way for the Nearest Port, where wee might harbour the Ship with Safety, which was some part in Norroway, wee then being Per Account off not above 25 Legs, and the Wind fair and fresh Gale. Now after wee had neglected that Opportunity through the Commanders Obstinacy, who was Absolute in his Resolutions, after much blowing foggy Weather and the Wind either Contrary, or little or too much of it, it pleased God to Send us a fresh Topsaill Gale att NNW., so to the NU. and WNW., with which wee might have fetched in to any part of Scotland, and though Hee had made many specious Pretences to us before of Getting into any part of Scotland, rather then Risque Ship and Cargo longer, yett then, contrary to Expectation, no Port must serve his Turn butt Newcastle, where, about 15 Legs Distant, were Chac't the Coast by French Privateers, and as soon as Got clear of One, through favour of the Foggy Weather, always fell in with Another. In Short, after wee had carried away our Mayntopmast and found the Ship that Chac't us come up with us att a Great Rate, wee brought too, and made the Ship Clear for Engaging. When he was alongside us, he plied us very hot with his small Shot, wounding 9, and killing one in an Instant, and had not God Almighty been att the Expense of a Miracle, had Taken us, for our small Arms were of as much use as a Bartholome fair Bow and Arrow. And for your Great Guns, they Jumped out of the Carriages att first firing, so that with our Height in the Wast and these Implements of War, we were finely fitted. After wee Got away from her, wee Shaped a Course for Norroway, and just as saw the Land, fell in with 2 Sail of Menn of War, who took us and brought us in here. I have much more to Say, but shall Defer till Arrived in England, Where shall Expect to be informed what part of the Sum of £4080 is remaining behind, in order to receive my Dividend. We came out in the Dark and have made a Dark Voyage of it. The Injustice Done me relating to the Commission, although as the Case now stands, is of no prejudice to my Interest. You may think I am a little blunt with you, but Sir, Loosing Gamesters have Liberty of Speaking. Had I my Effects Insured, I should have been Your very Easy humble Servant, Alias Grist. What above written attested to be true Per Richard Griffin John Elliot To Captain Thomas Bowrey, Marine Square, London, England.

October the 13th 1707. Sir, I Received your Letter in which you desire me to get an affidavit off the manner off my being Superated From the Fleet and off my being taken, and what Cargo was on board on the owners proper account, all which I hope to Sertyffye you by the Next post. For yesterday, being beffore the Judge to make my declaration, he promised to take my affidavit when I had got it made and Ready by a Note Republike . I asked Mr. Griffin to Sign with me, butt hee Reffused, Saying hee would have his wages First. Butt you need not wounder att his ingratitude, in which he hath so offen and Clearly showed him Selff guilty off, both to you and me, together with his incelentt behaviour and Ignorant acting when I was incapable, to your Lose and my Ruin. I pray God be my Comfforte, who hitherto his been my Support From Sinking under So greatt afflictions and Miserable Condission as I have under gone and had no other comffortt then that hee will Never Leave nor Forsake them that put their trustt in him. I am very weak in my Knee, butt I Find it to grow stronger by degrees. There hath Several Splinters off the bones come outt, butt I hope it is cured now. It hath broke outt Several times, both where the Shot went in and where it came outt, and one small bone worked out. The Ship is not Sold as yett, as the Judge Sertiffied in yesterday. The board is on, For that I Feared the tching off the Worm beffore I cold get it putt on. Her Riging is very much Shot and damaged both Standing and Running. Her Cables - the Sheet Cable is good; the best boar much wore, and there is about 50 Fathom off kire . She appears Some what Strained Ever since the pillett Laid her aground going up Bengal River. There is 4 anchors, 10 Guns and about 16 tun off Casks in her when I was taken, 2 Suits off Sail, 1 half wore, the other 2/3; one I made on board outt off 2 Dutch Main Sails I bought att Batavia. The Judge hath promised me to take my affidavit, So that, as Soon as the Note Republike hath done it, who hath now my Copy, I will dispatch it away, according to your directions, and a copy theroff, which I hope shall be the Next post, and I do not Fear it. I have Sent you 3 Letters beffore this. As For the Ships book and any papers, I Fear they cannot be Recovered, For the officers having plundered very much, Feared that books or papers should discover it, they made away with all off them, save the invoice off some purchased in Bengal, which the Judge told me was gone to Paris, and that they would not discover any other papers, alleging that the people had hove them over board. The Captain is gone from hence some time ago, that took us. There is 3 off my wounded men dead off their wounds, and the 4th not Like to Live. In my Letter that I sentt giving an account off the Cargo, I Forgot 30 Maund off bowrax or tinsel, purchased on the owners account. Dear Sir, if any thing lies in your to the advancement off my Enlargement, I Humbly desire you will not omit it, which will bee the Greatest obligation that you can Lay upon your distressed and Humble Servant, Jose: Tolson. October the 13: 1707: Dunkirk hospital. The Reason off this Letter coming 4 days Loiter then it is datted is that I cold not get it sent to the post house, So that with it I have sent the affidavit as you wrote For, and a copy theroff I gave to have it made by. I had the affidavit the day Mr. Griffin and Mr. Greece and the doctor and Mr. Dupuy Reffused to sign, alleging that they would have their wages First, and as I understand, they have sentt you a Letter to that porpose. I very seldom see them. Mr. Dupuy took up off the Merchant I dealt 330 Rex dolor, and with his other bills off Extravigance he Run outt there 589 Rex dolers, all which I was Forced to pay outt off the Ships Stock. Mr. Grist toke up 190 off the Merchant I dealt with in the time I was upon my voyge From Batavia to Bengal, all which time hee Lay att Battavia, being left by his Idleness and Negligence, For he went on Shore about no business. I hope Sir, that when I come in England, that you will doe me , that I shall not be brought in trouble about the months pay in Six, which I am very much thretoned by several off them, who aledgeth their is noon paid, For God knows, though my Wounds hath Not proved mortle by them, I am reduced to a poor condisson. For if it had pleased God that I had been capable , your ship had never come to France, nor I have lost my voyage, which both I valued Equal with my Liffe, as I shall very well Sattisffie you when it pleases God to permit me to see you, till which time I Rest, your distressed Serventt, Jose: Tolson. October the 17th 1707.

Dunkirque, the 15th off November, 1707. Sir, I Received yours dated the 22th off October, in which was one incloased to Thomas Studes, which I delivered, and have in the Cover Sentt you an answer thereto from him to his Mother. I got the affidavit Made according to your desire, and Sentt it, which desire you will give me an accountt if you have Received them, I mean the affidavit and the copy, and there you will Find in my Letter to you the Reason why I cold get none off the Rest to Sign with me. I have had greatt trouble to get baill and it hath cost me above 50 Shilings to procure Friend to keep me outt off the Common prison, which hath been the occasion that I coulld not answer your desire in the Letter, For that I cold not go about to get what accountt you desire. Butt by the Next post I will Send you the Nearest account that I can make up off what men and what money paid them. I have taken No money upon the bottom off Mr. Sheldon, nor any other, save 1000 Rupees off Sir Edward Littleton, which Engages or Enlarges the Ships Cargo. is other bounds , the Condissions off which will sertyffye you when it please God that I shall Return For England. I am Some thing indisposed att present and very week in my knee still. I had 24 Men and boys when Engaged and 23 when taken, 14 off them outt off England and 10 Shipped and bought in the Country ; 2 off the last, being the cook and boy, was the owners slaves. The boy the Captain off the man off war gave me to tend upon me, butt if I can Save him hee shall be att the owners pleasure att my Return. I have drawn a bill of Exchange For ten pound upon Mr. Dupuy by Reason off Mr. Puoarte being gone to Paris, and I have Received butt ten pounds off him, which I desire you to advise Mr. Dupuy off, and that you will be so Kind as to See it Excepted. So I Restt, Your distressed Servant in bonds, Jose: Tolson. For Mr. Bowry Merchant, Living in Maroon Square, London.

May the 15th 1708. Sirs, I send you these according to your order att the Union Coffye house. On the 24 off July Last, about 4 in the affternoon, being then in company with 14 Saill off Dutch and 2 English homeward bound East India Ships, it happened to prove a very thick Fog, and toward the morning Came on a Storm of wind, which brought the whole Fleett under a main Saill, the Wind att N. Et. Att 2 in the affternoon I see one Dutch Ship and the Frederick bear up and Lay their heads to the Southward, which I did Likewise and berthed our Selves to Leewards off them both. A little time affter the Frederickes main tack gave way and I see her beat up and brought to on our Lee quarter. In the evening I perceived them to Fall to Leeward apace, and designeing to bear down to them, I Found it to blow So hard that I durst not venture to Meddle with any Saill For Fear off carrying all away or Foundering. The next morning I boar down, having watched a Slatch off weather (I believe 3 Leagus), butt cold not decern any Ships, the weather having continued very thick all the time. So I brought to again. The Storm abateing on the 30 off July I Surveyed our watter and provisions and found in good Condission: 2 Months of all Sorts, according to Computation, and theirupon Consulted with all my officers what was best to be done. Wee concluded that in the Courses Steered they designed to go to the Northward off the Islands off Fairo , So in hopes that wee might meett with them their, I spent 9 days, butt Finding all in vain, I Resolved to make the best off our way For the First port that I cold get in Saffty to in England or Scotland. But when I came near the Ferth the wind blew very hard So that I cold not cary my topsails with less then both Reeffes in, the wind at W. b So. to With. So I Resolved to make the best of my way For Newcastle. Butt on the 14 off August in the morning see 2 Ships ahead off me. So I tacked and Stood to the Northward. They gave me Chase all that day, and although wee careyed away our maintopmast, wee bore away and Steered Such courses as wee Lost them. On the 15th in the morning, having got up another topmast, butt the Riging not Set Fast, when I see that a priviteer that had given us Chase 2 hours, I see would inffallably Speak with us. I Resolved, as God is my witness, to deffend my Charge with the Last Drop off my blood, and so caled all my people together and prepared our Selves to him. He came under our Lee quarter, in order, as I believe, to board us, butt Finding warm a Receipt, hee Shared off and Lay under our Lee bow, and their plied us with a very warm Fire, most From Small arms. For, I believe, an hour and a halff beffore I Received that wound that disabled me. And then, by the help of Mr. Dupuy, I was Corryed down and ordered the Rest to go to Close quarters, which was perfformed and prepared For with the best provision I cold make, having 6 powder Chests upon the quarter deck and 16 quarter Shells, and upon the Forecasle 2 powder Chests, and my Small arms in the best Condission I cold Keep them. Indead, the behaviour off my mate Griffin I cannot Commend, For beffore I was wounded in the Knee, hee had Lefft his quarters above a quarter off an hour, and taken with him all who was Givein him to take care off, telling them, as I understand since, that I had ordered them to Close quarters. And when Thomas Studes would have come up, hearing me and the rest upon the deck busy in Entertaining and Returning the Enemies Fire, hee would not Let him, and when the Priviteer putt off, all that I cold persuade him to go up and incorage the people, he Refused, telling me that it was Impossible to Stand upon the quarter deck. So Mr. Dupuy Looking down, as I Remember, I beged off him to help me up , and Mr. Griffin helped him to get me up, butt Sit and Served outt the powder him Selff Some time affter, till the Enemy was quite outt off muscat Shot and making the best off his way.
