So having sit till I was cold, my wounds become very painffull, and then they carried me down and putt me to bed, and I ordered Mr. Griffin to make the best of their way For Noraway, the wind being Westerly, with which there was no hopes of gaining the coast off England or Scotland. Butt the Management that was used affter I was down, I pray God Let never any honest man be a specktater off. For as I was infformed by the Carpenter Next morning, hee went to his Cabin and did not so much as inform them what course to Steer. And Sum time affter hee was going S.Et., when his Course was Et. And when I asked him what hee mooned by that Course, hee went to his drafft and told me hee would bear away, For hee had not minded beffore the wind then being at S.S.With. And when She came beffore the wind, She Shiped Sum watter. And presently I heard such distraction and Swaring that wee Should all be drowned, as if the Ship had been going to the bottom. I asked the matter, and hee told me She shiped watter over the gunell, att which I ordered him to go N. b W. with the wind upon that quarter till hee came in the Latitude off 57 30' N. and then to go away E.N.Et. In all this Time I beged off him to get up the maintop Saill, but cold not persuade him to do it. The day beffore wee ware taken he told me hee was in the Latitude I had ordered. So I ordered him to Steer away E.N.Et., and att 8 o'clock Caled him and told him that I did not think it sofa For him to Stand till 12, and that I would have him bring to att 10. Butt being so drunk that I could Scarce get him to Speak, hee told me one watch cold not doe it, and So, Contrary to my order, Fell asleep, as I was infformed, and stood till 12. In the breek off Day they told me that wee where within 2 miles off the Shore off Uteland , to my great Mortyffication, praiseing God that so many Soulls had Escaped So Eminent a danger. Some time affter they told me they See 3 Saill off hagboatts, which in hope to have got a pilett outt off them, I ordered them to endeavour to Speak with them. Butt they whithered us and would not bear down. So being, by the Manidgment as I had seen, without a better pilett, the Next Night would produce a grave For all off us, I ordered him to Spread the Ensign in the maintop mast shrouds to See if any off them would bear down to us. But they would not. Then hee cam and told me that they see 2 Ships to Leeward off us. I asked him what them Looked Like. Hee told me hee believed them to be 2 off the Dutch Fleatt, and asked me if hee should bear down to them. And I told him to do what hee would, and thinking that if they ware an Enemy and to Leeward, they would unavoidably Speak with us, wee having No main top Saill. So God Almighty knows and be my Record whether my Liffe or the Ship I had in my Charge was most dear to me. For while I am on this side the grave, the Lose off her hath taken away that which may be Imputed the Enjoyment off the Liffe in me. And as For Those dimentts , I only desire you to consider whether if I had had them all and Free off a bad consequence, whether they would have Surmounted my Intrests in the Ship or no, whereas I took but one off the three parcels into my Custody, the prime cost off which, according to the bill off Laideing, is about 600 pagodus; and whether that cold make me satisffaction or not, I Lieve you to be Judge off what Interest I had in the Ships Saffty what is hear Inserted. When you pleass to order me to wait upon you and the party their, which did not appear yesterday, I shall be Ready. Your humble Servant, Jose: Tolson. To Capt. Bowry and the Rest off the owners off Mary Gally .

March 15th 1707/8. Captn. Bowrey, Sir, The Bearer hereof desired me to Inform you he was not indebted any matter in the Ship's Book, to which I can swear too. His Circumstances being very poor and mean, I suppose You will not deny paying him part of his Wages, considering he was a Person that behaved himself very bravely in the Engagement with the French Privateer, when Mr. Tolson and his Rascally Mate Griffin left the Deck, and consequently, in their belief, Gave up the Ship Mary Gally , the former having a wound in his Excuse, the latter not only keeping between Decks in the time of Engaging, but hindering those that were Quartered with him from coming up to assist those that kept the Deck, as your Kinsman Thomas Studds and others that were with him informed me after the Engagement was over. I am Sir, Your humble Servant, Alias Grist. Attested to per ... John Eliot. To Captn. Thomas Bowrey, Present.

May the 19th 1708. Captain Bowrey, Sir, I am informed Captain Tolson avouches to you and the other Owners that the 190 Rex Dollars paid Mr. Moor for my accountt was not to run upon the Bottom of the Ship and the premium, or advance upon it, to be left to the Discretion of the Owners att the safe arrival of the Ship. I wonder he should affirm so known an Untruth, when in Mr. Griffins Hearing and also in Mr. Dupuys, more then once or twice, this was the verbal agreement, that in case of the Loss of the Ship, that Debt to be null and void. And when we first discoursed concerning that Debt, Griffin was by, and offered to pay Mr. Moor the money for my account, in case the Captain was not free to pay it. Also was paid out of the Ships stock near double the Sum for the account of Mr. Dupuy, on the very same Terms. And consequently the Owners may, with the same Equity, make a Demand of the money from Mr. Dupuy, as stop any part of my Wages or Ships Debts upon that account. And again, Sir, att the juncture when this money was paid, how inconsistent must it be with your Interest, nay with common Reason, to lessen the Ships Stock upon any other Terms then the Bottom of the Ship, especially considering the smallness of it, and that there was no necessity for it, because I could be supplied by another Hand. And if the money was Lent upon any other Terms (as it was not), then the premium would have made but a small amount to the Debt. When I saw Captain Tolson last, I showed him the Terms wee agreed on in Refference to that money. All his answer was, he could not remember it. But I find he can remember and forget as suits best his Convenience. And, Sir, as to that Objection about paying my part of wages Due to the Ships Company, that does concern me Solely. Some of them are more indebted to me then my Share amounts too, and if any of them, for favours shown them in the voyage and out of Consideration to my present Circumstances, should be easy as to that matter, none of the Owners will suffer on that Account. Therefore, I crave the favour of you, Sir, to Get in my money as soon as possible. As to that matter concerning the 592 Rex Dollars said to be twice Charged in Mr. Moors Account Current, all I can say to the matter I wrote after a Copy, and as Captain Tolson Dictated, the account was delivered to him, and he only Received the Balance. And if Mr. Moors paid that Sum less then his Due, it is my Belief it was not with Desine, because that after he took his Account from me, in order to know the Balance Due from him, he came the next morning and said he was not satisfied with that account, because Captain Tolson had not Gave him Creditt for One half of some Charge he was att in Getting his Goods ashore, it being, as he affirmed, agreed so between them, and brought an Account that he made up, affirming the Balance came Short of the Captains Demand. Now the Querie lays, if he was sensible of his Advantage, why would he not rather be Quiet and set down the Gainer, rather then occasion the overlooking the Account again, which must have found out the mistake, unless it must be allowed him to be a very honest Gentleman, as most that ever dealt with him avouch. But as to Captain Tolson's Character of him, I don't wonder att it, for I never Knew him speak well of any man, besides Captain Jones. And as to that other business, concerning the Sharing the 500 Dollars that Mr. Moor allowed for Demorage, if I was to appear before the Tribunal of God to morrow, I could with Safety Swear the minute before that (to the best of my memory) on Monday Evening, Captain Tolson, Mr. Griffin and my Self being att Mr. Vanderbegs att Batavia, he spoke to us to come with him into his Chamber, and having Shut to the Door, made to us the following proposition, Vizt. , that in order for sharing the 500 Dollars, he would first take out 1/6 part, as being 1/6 part Owner; that I should have 1/24 part out for the same reason, and then the remainder should be divided in fifths, he taking two fifths, and the remaining 3/5 to be equally divided between Mr. Griffin and me. Tic well for him Dupuy is absent and Griffin and I at variance. Otherways this part of the world would be too Hot to hold him. I am informed, Sir, that my Name is signed to several of Captain Tolsons papers. I am sensible to some that Mr. Griffin and Mr. Dupuy signed too, I signed also, but I am fully assured to none of any vast importance in the latter part of the voyage. I beg pardon, Sir, for being so tedious, and am, Sir, Your Humble Servant, E. Grist To Capt: Tho: Bowrey, In Marine Square, near Rattcliff Highway: Present.

August 9th 1708 Sir, I received your Note, but withal desire you to consider the Debts due from the Ships Company to me. As your Business could not be well performed by several on board the Ship without my assisting them with Clothes, &c. (which was by the Captains Order), it is very hard if I must have no allowance for so necessary supply. Your answer heretofore was, I must have my Recourse to Captain Tolson, who Gave me Order for Serving the men; but if he be put past a possibility of paying me, I know not to whom to apply besides your Self and the rest of the Owners. What I have all ready Given Oath too, I am, and ever shall be, ready to attest too, though upon my Death Bed. But there can be no policy in Serving you farther to my Cost, which will follow if Captain Tolson recover no part of his wages. I desire, Sir, that Equity May have its Course. Then, I am well asshur'd, I shall be Considered. I was chiefly accessory to saving the Ship once (which without vanity I may avouch), but never lent a helping hand to the loss of her. I am, Sir, Your humble Servant, Alias Grist To Captain Thomas Bowrey, att his House in Marine Square, near Rattcliff Highway; Present.

June the 15th 1708. Sir, The Severty off your persecution is such that I cannot Apprehend your Intention to bee Less then that you Intend to drive me off the Stage, off which my Sad circomstances off the Loss off my Limes and all that I had in the world makes me weary off; and you cannot be more desirous off it then I am Free to make you a Sacriffice off it. The great God be Judge off the Reason I have given you (For I know none) to proceed against me in this Nature. Your deserning eye is able to pentrate into the unjustness off those False accusations which the devil and malis hath Invented against me, off which God alone can be Judge, Since I Find nothing will Stick with them to make their False Stories plausible, So that if they can butt invent, they can affirm. So that I can not pretend to compose any matters till I know what they are, and as you told me that their Memory might not bee good att a time when they might make their affidavit, So that I Find if they have not Invented enough, they Intend to do it. I only desire you to Consider the Case and do by me as you would doe by your Selff, and you would Never incorage Such insolent villines, which plainly doth appear none in my Circomstance was Capable off keeping under Government without some Roger, For which their malis hath Invented those Stories, Finding you Ready to Incorage and give Ear to their ungrateffull and False using me. My not deserning your perffections early hath proved my utter Ruin, For I always did Suppose Captain Bowryes virtues to have been Equally composed with those pirffections off wisdom I Deserned in him, butt to my greatt disatisffaction, I Find these perffections may be Saperatte, and honour goes no Forther then Interest can cary it. So that my want of Fore Knowledge hath made my Liffe a pray to a merciless Enemy, to whom, God is my Record, I have given no Just ocation, Neither Do I know when you can Expectt butt my Liffe, Except you would have me be your Slave, which I would willingly bee, if you could turn my Skin From White to black, if that would apeass you. But you cannot Expectt that I can make any Such Sacryffice with my Known Vizogminy ; and according to what I can Fore See, you can have no other End then one off those, my misffortins having made my Condition Reather to be pitied than Envied, being Reduced to become a pensioner to the Charty off those which is pleased to admit me to their table and to assist me in the time off my Conffinement, to whom I am engaged even for the meett I eatt and the Cloths I ware, Even For more then I can tell which way to repay or am worth in the World. So that my condition being Such, I hope to Let you have your Ends Shortly, butt not till I can Leave that behind me that shall make appear your Crewltty. And although I never intend to survive the off any Secrets Committed to me, I shall not Faill to Leave that behind me that shall. If you please to answer these, I desire you to send it to the Jameco Coffy house or To the Union Coffy house, For the difference that is betwixt us is a Secret to my wife, and I desire you would not disclose it. Yours, Jose: Tolson To Captain Bowry, Living in Mereen Square, Merchant, London.

July the 6. 1708. Sir, I send you these, desiring your Answer, that I may make Demands as Easy and Reasonable and short as I can. As concerning the note to Mr. Finch att the , I desire you to take a right consideration off the matter, wherein you See even made you criditure For a passenger att my own table, which you know I can with Justice demand, and I cannot see any Reason it can be Reffused, and Likewise Several others off the men that Received money off me att the , which will, I do not Question, be allowed me. But it will contain a Long and tedious Consideration to an arbitrator. So that if you are willing to pay that note to Mr. Finch, I am willing to Let all such tedious demands pas by. And as I have made you creditor For all, I cannot Forbore complaining when you Reffuse so small a matter. So I desire you will Let me know your Resoltt in the matter in a Line to me directed to Mr. Johnsons. Your Servant, Jose. Tolson To Captain Bowry, Living in Maroon Square, London

June 29: 1708. Sir, I understand by Mr. Hamon that you have Reported that I was flouted outt off the court in the Late Trial betwixt Mr. Wright and John Eliot. And as I doe believe you are Imposed upon by mallishous persons Infformation, I hope, as it is a thing that has to bee proved, that you will doe me the Justice as to make a due Inquirey into the matter and give a just Report thereof to those whom you have, in my opinion, undiscreetly made bold to Scandlies me with. In this I hope you will not Faill, since it is a thing that Honour and Justice binds every body to that is misled by False infformation. As For several other Lies that you have been infformed in, I blame the and not you. Butt, this being a thing that is very easy to be proved, I think you doe me unjustice if you doe not make me Reparation in it. I cannot even my selff with saffty to come and speak with you, understanding that their is an action out against me by Capt. Bapty For his 2 servants wages, and I am unwilling to lie in a prison and doth not Know where to get baill. So I desire that you will speak to him and see what may be done in the matter without Rigour. For the other matters in queston, I am willing to Reffare it to 2 Comanders off ships, you chuseing one and I another, if you will give me your promise that att our meeting you will not endeavour me being arrested. Butt things may, with the best off our Indivers, be accommodated For the beneffitt off my Selffe, you, and the rest of the owners, which will perhaps not Fall out so, if Rigorous meenes be used and things put out off the Channel they aught to run in. So I desire you will come with my Johnson to me, that wee may consult who to leive the matter to; and if you are not inclined to leive it to arbitration, that wee may consult other meens to bring it to a speedy trial, which will be the Costliest way off arbitration, and I believe not to our advantage. I do not abscond For any thing that you have to say against me, but will appear att your somence att any time. Your servant, Jose: Tolson P.S. Mr. Johnson will waitt on you att change time and I shall not be Fore off. To Capt. Bowry.

Messrs Willing & Morris Bristol 28 July 1774 Gentlemen I had the pleasure of writing you the 6 Inst offering you my Services at this port, Since which I have had a Letter from Mr Elliot of London, advising me that he expected two Cargoes of Wheat from Maryland, and that you was so obliging as to recommend him to me in case our market afforded Encouragement; as that was the Case, I wrote in pursuance of his Orders to Falmouth to direct the first Cargo to proceed directly to this port. Hereunder you have an Account of all the Wheat & Flour imported this year into this Port, of the former there is not a Bushel unsold, (except one Cargo from New York which turns out of very ordinary Quality) the price 6/6, & that price might be had with the greatest Ease for a considerable Quantity, indeed I have no doubt of making more for that Cargo of Mr Elliots on its arrival. the Flour also goes off readily at 45/ per Sack of 2 1/2 cwt. or 18/ per cwt Firsts, and 41/3 or 16/6 per cwt Seconds and as the dry Weather sets in will increase in Sale. The extreme bad Weather we have had for some time past very much affects the Corn in the Ground, and it is most probable the Crop will be short; in consequence there will be Encouragement for American Wheat, the prices of which will without Doubt be supported. In Spain the fine appearance has had an Effect on the prices, which are much sunk, as in Italy, the declension of Prices at Leghorn to £15/4 by the quantities of American Wheat and also Levant Wheat arrived there (and since indeed still lower) have made the foreign Markets very critical but if the same Appearances continue of the Crops at home there will be room for Speculation, and notwithstanding they may have an Effect on your Market, yet the advises from Italy, & Spain must more than counterbalance the Amounts from hence, and keep your markets moderate. When our very good friends Messrs Herries & Co did me the favour to write to you first on my offering my Services to you through the Channels of their House, I did not think it necessary to write at the same time, hoping to be favoured with hearing from you, which as I did not I was fearful you had engaged yourselves, but on their letting me know, you wondered I had not wrote you, made me give you a general Letter of offers of Service, and your since advising Mr Elliot to apply to me, demands my Acknowledgments, which I have also requested our friends Messrs Herries & Co (with whom I have many years had the pleasure of corresponding) to do the same to you for me I shall continue to advise you of the Occurrences of our market, or any other Method you will be obliging to point out to me, and I sincerely hope that this Correspondence may prove mutually agreeable. I shall on my part be happy to convince you of the Respect and Esteem with which I am Gentlemen Your most obedt Served Rich Champion PS. 1 Augt I have by this post advice from Leghorn that the Harvest in Italy has turned out but middling in Lombardy very scarce In Tuscany worse & in Sicily & Naples moderately that it is much questioned if Export will be granted the prices of best soft wheat had rose to £18 & £20 & were expected higher.

Messrs Willing Morris & Co. Bristol 25 August 1774 Gentlemen My Last was 28 Ulto . Since I have none of your favours. The Friendship Capt Young arrived here the 21st in the Evening, & the next morning I reported her. From the first appearances I was in great hopes that the Cargo would have turned out in very good order, which made me decline fixing a price, as several people agreed to buy largely, if they like the Quality, & though it appeared light at first, yet it is a common law that the lightest gets to the top, and I had sold on these Conditions full half when the price was fixed, which I intended to do at 6/9 per Bushel; but when we had begun to discharge, as we came to the bottom of the 'tween Decks, we found it heated, & on opening the hold, it was extremely hot, we go down as fast as possible, & the heat now begins somewhat to abate, however it has stopped the Sale for the present, which I had on these appearances declared at 6/6 per Bushel, the lightness still continuing, not weighing more than 57lb per Bushel, and the latter Sales have been 60 lb per Bushel, and some lighter have been made up that weight. I must confess I was sanguine enough to hope to render you a pleasing Sales at 6/9 per Bushel, but the quality will not admit it, however I hope to get 6/6 which will be a good price, greatly superior to any in this kingdom. You may depend that no pains of mine shall be wanting, as I shall have great pleasure in convincing you of the Regard I pay to the pleasure of executing your Business in this place. Flour governs at 18/- per cwt superfine and 16/6 per cwt commonfine, & a ready Sale. I have subjoined to this the Imports since my last. I shall follow Mr Ringgold's directions about the Vessel, & get what freight & Servants I can, but I fear they will not be in either Case so favourable as I could wish, for as the Vessel is confined to Maryland there is but little freight, had she been permitted to go to New York, I could have got a tolerable one. The Captain has taken a great deal of Care of every thing belonging to her Our Harvest is now setting in, & upon the Hills near us it will prove good, which will somewhat flatten this market, & indeed has already in some degree, there not being the briskness there was a fortnight ago, however I do not think there will be any material alteration for these two months to come. The Harvest in the Southern part of the Kingdom as I last wrote you, is not so good as near us, which is a more hilly country. Most of the Cargo, indeed all which I had sold was for the Country, which will show you how much Service the Importation of American Wheat has been. I really most anxiously wished that your Cargo had turned out cool, & a heavier grain, (for it was tolerably clean) as in this first transaction I had great hopes of rendering you the best Sales furnished this year from England, however in this Case you must take the Intention for the Act, & depend upon my Care in the present Situation of it, in doing everything for your Interest. I shall detain this Letter to the last moment of the Vessel's departure, to let you know what further passes. I have taken the Liberty to send you a few Books which were writ by Doctor Priestly concerning America. There is a great deal of Justice in his Sentiments. I most heartily wish an End to the unhappy disputes with America, but at the same time I most sensibly feel the very great Injustice with which America has been treated by Great Britain. May the latter become sensible of her unjust Behaviour, is my sincere Wish! I shall be always happy in convincing you of the great Esteem with which I am Gentlemen Your most obedt Served Rich Champion PS 26 August. This Vessel takes her dispatches today. We have gone down lower in the hold & find the heat to abate very much, so that we are now employed in shifting the Cargo, and taking out all the wheat that is hot, & putting it in warehouses to cool. This will be an additional Expense, but is necessary. I have no doubt of obtaining 6/6 per Bushel, but it stagnates the Sale at present. The Heat appears to arise from Mr. Ringgold's filling the Vessel too close.

Messrs Willing Morris & Co Bristol 5 Sepr. 1774 Gentlemen I had the pleasure of writing you by the Concord, and Ann. I have now the Satisfaction of telling you, that I have completed the Sale of the Friendship's Cargo, not only what remains in the Ship, but also what was heated, and put in warehouse at 6/6 per Bushel, and I shall deliver it as fast as possible. the last week was very wet, and assisted me much in the Sale, for I found no small difficulty, as the Character given the wheat hurt it much, and the weight proving light (now only 58lb per Bushel indeed not quite that in what is cool) did not help me; however I paid all possible I attention to it and I am happy my Endeavours were crowned with Success which I hope will meet with your Approbation, a Circumstance which will give me the greatest pleasure. The price is a good one, indeed superior to any market in Europe, however I have no doubt of obtaining 6/9 for another Cargo, if the quality turns out good, & it is delivered in good order. Mr Elliot tells me he shall send the Hopewell to my address, but cannot let me know the quantity of Wheat and Indian Corn in her. Our Harvest will turn out very middling, therefore I think there is little doubt of prices being supported; indeed I rather expect they will advance, if there is any decline it will be about Christmas, and rise directly; however even that I hardly think will be the Case, for the weather having been lately wet, & now again with every appearance of continuing so (for our last few days have been fine) the Corn will be so late got in as to give the farmers full employment for some time to thrash out for sowing, so that I really believe this will continue to be one of the very best Markets for American wheat; if not (as it is now) the best. It bears every appearance of it. I sold of this Cargo 6000 Bushels to one Man in that Country from whence we usually have supplies. I shall continue to keep you advised, and shall be glad to receive your Commands for I am with great Truth Gentlemen Your most obedt Served Rich Champion PS. Mr Ringgold's orders are so close to the Captain, that I could not ask for some freight to Baltimore which I might have got, & I can get none for Chester, therefore I shall send the Salt, & what Servants I can get which I have little Encouragement for. I have wrote this in great Haste the wind having this morning shifted to the Eastward & I send this to the Vessel which is in the Road

Messrs Willing Morris & Co Bristol 30 Sepr 1774 Gentlemen Since I had the pleasure of writing you 25.26 & 31 Ulto. & 5 Inst. I have entirely discharged the Friendship, and tomorrow she will be ready for the Sea. Contrary to my Expectations, the Wheat at the bottom continued very light, and I had no less than 2500 Bushels returned to me for its lightness, weighing no more than 56 lbs per Bushel; however the wet Weather continuing, I resold at the same price. I have not yet delivered the Wheat from the warehouse; however as it must be satisfactory to you to receive the Sales I have made it up making some allowance for loss of measure and if any difference should arise, which can be but trifling, the Ascot Current may be charged with it. The ships Accounts I have transmitted to Mr Ringgold together with some Cordage and Canvas for the future as he desired the Ship might have sufficient for the 2d & 3rd Voyages. Capt Young who has paid great Attention to his Vessel, & has been extremely frugal, seemed rather uneasy at this additional Expense; but Mr Ringgold writing particularly for it, & a non Importation being expected, I thought it most prudent to send rather a full Quantity than a short one. Since I last wrote you the Weather has been extremely wet. This has very much delayed the dispatch of Cn Young, but to the Harvest it has done incredible damage. I herewith give you the Importations since my last. Wheat rose to 6/9 a fine Cargo of Baltimore Wheat fetched 7/- weighing near 60 lb per Bushel, & now the price is 7/3- Flour super 18/6 common 17/ per cwt. These prices must continue if not advance & if you can get Wheat upon moderate Terms it must answer very well. If you favour me with your Commands, I am sure I can render you good Sales and whatever you send this way I shall be happy in the Execution of your Orders. You have I understand sent Flour to the market. I know that many Gentlemen for the sake of the Commission have offered a Concern. I must confess for my part, that however I might wish to execute Commissions only, & which a Man does most Justice to his Employers, yet I would not refuse to gratify the Wishes of any Gentleman of your Consequence. I have not yet had the pleasure of hearing from you that I hope soon, when if you will do me the favour to let me know your Inclinations, I shall be happy to conform as much in my power to them as possible. I have the pleasure of calling Mr. Robert Kirkpatrick (of the House of Kirkpatricks & Ascot) my intimate Friend. He is well known to you. The House of Herries & Co I have long corresponded with, and as I have Connexions with almost all the ports in Spain & the Mediterranean though your Connexions are so extensive, there yet as some times chance may make me useful, I only wish for Employment. This market has been the best in Europe, and is likely to continue so. We impatiently expect News from America. Your fate now depends upon your firmness, but that firmness will be, I hope, tempered with Moderation. A Non Importation will I suppose take place. It becomes your Interest, from the very great Stock of Goods in the Country, which must otherwise become a Burden - but a non Exportation should be the last Resource. It is a Measure big with Danger, and like a violent Medicine administered in the last stage of a fever, the Chance of Life or Death is equal. The Arrangement of Affairs made by the late Mr Grenville was both impolitic and unjust, widely different from that of Sir Robert Walpole a minister who was a thorough Judge of Manners and of Men. When applied to tax America he gave this Reply; he would leave that, to such of his Successors, who were less friends to Commerce than himself. On the contrary he encouraged their Trade, convinced that the more profit the Americans made, the greater would be the gain at home, and that in a method more agreeable to their and our Constitution. Mr. Grenville forgot the Connexion between the two Countries, - he tyrannised over America by oppressive Acts destroyed a lucrative Trade which brought Riches into Great Britain, and specie into America, and at the same time imposed Taxes, to be paid only in that Specie of which he had deprived them. However just the Sentiments of Lord Chatham generally were, respecting America, his distinctions of internal and external Taxations are, as Mr Grenville justly observed Distinctions without difference. They are too much blended to admit a Limit to each. The Question of Taxation arises from a higher principle, - the general privilege of every Subject of Britain to pay no Taxes but by consent of himself or his Representative. Every Charter granted by the Crown, which bears the least opposition to this principle, is an infringement of the Laws of the Kingdom, and must be null and void. Two Constitutions in one Empire are absurd, and this would be the Case, if America without representation is subject to the Authority of a British parliament. Britain would be a free, America a despotic Government. If the British parliament has a sovereign Authority over the whole Empire, why does it not lay Taxes on Ireland, which is chiefly inhabited by Colonists from hence. It has been said by many, that America is as much represented as Birmingham or Manchester, who send no Representatives to Parliament, and it is most absurdly said, for not to mention that many of its Inhabitants are represented by the County Members, what equity is there in a Comparison between a British Parliament laying Taxes, in which every Member must bear a part, and assuming the same power in America, where they have no property to tax. An Englishman not represented knows, that he cannot suffer but with the Legislators themselves - an American not represented lies wholly at the mercy of those who cannot feel with himself. It is with more Truth that the Advocates for Taxation claim the privilege of Prescription for what they have done, since it is an indisputable fact that in many Instances, America has submitted to British Laws - but how will this poor plea avail? Just so far as an Infant, unable to help himself, receives food and raiment from one of more advanced Years. Till he grows into Man he cannot resist, whether the Treatment be just or unjust; but when that period comes, he has full Liberty to judge for himself, and make use of the Understanding which God has given him, without any other Constraints than those of civil Society. This is a parallel Case with America When her Colonies were first planted, they were few in number, and met with difficulties. They made such Establishments as their Situation would afford. The Parliament formed many useful Laws, which the Americans received with Gratitude, and found the salutary Effects of in their Governments. In this State they grew up, and are now become numerous and powerful. They feel a Gratitude to the Mother Country for its protection, but amiable as that passion is, it does not preclude every other duty. It does not, I say, preclude the higher duty of Love to our Country, and that Love cannot be more shown than by a constant Attention to its Rights and Privileges which the Parliament have in their persons infringed. Affairs are now in such a critical Situation, that one Party must recede. If equity prevails every Law of the British Parliament, which claims a sovereign Authority to tax the Colonies, must be repealed. And as the two Countries are in mutual Interest inseparably connected, an Act of Parliament declaratory of the Rights and Privileges of America, as British Subjects after the manner of the Great Charter, and Bill of Rights must be formed, and this must be done by a free Conference between the two Powers. I am not so sanguine as to expect this from the present Ministry, their Principles do not sufficiently lead to Liberty to expect it from them. Indeed it is a melancholy Truth, that the Actions of many of those who call themselves friends to it, have so much run into Licentiousness, as to be the unhappy Cause of a great defection to a spirited and formidable Opposition. Many cool and judicious men were disgusted at such violence, however their Numbers are still great. In this Contest they will appear to support you. So violent are the Passions of the English that what first strikes, takes deep root, - and such was their Anger against Boston, when the Bills passed, that it entirely precluded Reason. At this Period, I well remember that to open one's Lips for America, which I often ventured to do the torrent was so great, that it was difficult to stand singly, as I almost generally did, against it, but now one may declare one's Sentiments without Clamour, and be at least heard; though even at this time, the violence of Boston has not lost its effect - However the excessive heat is abated, and as they get still cooler, they will see the Injustice of Parliament, and be most probably hurried to the contrary Passion. One Extreme generally produces another. Pardon this long Intrusion. My Zeal for an oppressed Country caused it. As a British Individual, and the ensuing Election will give me some Opportunity, I shall be happy in contributing my Mite. I am with the greatest assurances of every respect and Esteem to yourselves Gentlemen Your much obliged & most obedient Servant Rich Champion PS. Octr. The Parliament is dissolved - the general Supposition for this unexpected Event is, the Minister dreads the News from America, & is fearful the People at home would be so inflamed as to elect a Parliament not answerable to his Wishes, & he thinks them now more cool - There will be an opposition here but I fear not a powerful one. I was in hopes Mr Burke would have appeared - though that is not now quite over. If this Vessel is detained you shall hear more.

Messrs. Willing Morris & Co. Bristol 24 November 1774 Gentlemen. My last was 22 Octr. Since I have your favours 5th Sepr & 3rd Ulto . I should not have suffered any Vessel to have sailed without writing you myself, had not my time been so fully taken up at our late Election as to render me incapable for above four Weeks of doing other business. Three Candidates first started, Lord Clare Mr. Brickdale & Mr. Cruger. Mr. Brickdale being an unpopular man, must have lost it & the two other Gentlemen elected; but Lord Clare having declined to favour Mr. Brickdales Interest after the Election had began, & all parties had polled men, Mr. Edmund Burke was nominated; a Gentleman whose excellence of private Character does not fall short of his very great abilities in public. Bristol has acquired unusual honour by her choice; the more so as this Gentleman was not personally known to six people in the town, had no previous Canvas made for him, did not arrive till near the week after the poll began, & had the personal weight of Lord Clare with all the Government Interest against him. The Election which began without party, men more than measures being the object, did not terminate so. The different parties contending with warmth for Mr. Burke & Mr. Brickdale, between whom the contest lay, Mr. Cruger very early had secured his Election having made a previous Interest long before & having a great superiority in the popular esteem over Mr. Brickdale Mr. Brickdale threatens to petition, declaring he can make it a void Election, but you may take it for as near a certainty as the strongest probability can make it, that he can do nothing & if he could, this I am sure of, that Mr. Burke has gained so many friends since the Election that there would be no doubt of his Election for Bristol. I look upon him to be now for life. His Character is such that he has gained greatly the affections of the Citizens. I have already given you my sentiments on the subject of American grain, the present price is now 7/6 per Bushel a price which is far beyond any other market in Europe; it is uncertain if this price will keep up about Christmas; it may fall to 7/- but there is the greatest probability of its rising in the Spring, so that if the Friendship returns here I have very little doubt of making a great sale. Indian Corn is now 3/9 We are attempting to get the duty off that Article & have great hopes of success. the event you shall know. I have already given you my sentiments about Concerns in Cargoes; the Honour and pleasure attending the execution of your Commands will make me willingly follow your Inclinations. the same terms therefore that your other Correspondents have proposed to you of concerns, I will cheerfully acquiesce in. Your bills as you propose for nearly the value of the whole shall be duly honoured. You will be so kind only as to make them at as long a date as you can. Mr. Burke intends moving the House to have the duty taken off Indian Corn which will be a great service to that Article many benefits may arise to you. I am very certain of & make no doubt of its passing - a few of us applied to him here & met with his cheerful acquiescence and in commercial affairs you know his abilities. The prospect of Wheat is very great for the ensuing Year as your prices are moderate & ours must be high. I need not therefore add any thing more on this subject. I enclose you the Accounts of the Friendship the whole of which is settled with Mr. Elliot except the damaged Wheat which is not yet quite sold & the delivery of the heated however I did not choose to keep open the Accounts longer as the Election totally stopped all business here. I shall therefore render an after account but it will be but a trifling one. My warmest wishes are for the happy Reconciliation of Great Britain & America, but I dread the wickedness of administration in obstinately pursuing their destructive plan; the Mother Country has been cruelly unjust. may she repent of that Injustice and once more assume the tenderness of a parent. You will much oblige me by your public news your letter of the 3rd Octr. being without any - I have great pleasure in the assurances of being with the most perfect Esteem and Regard Gentlemen Your most obedt Served Rich Champion

Mess Willing Morris & Co Bristol 17 Jany 1775 Gentlemen I have your favours 3 Oct & 25 Novr since I had the pleasure of writing you the 28 Decr. Wheat is now fixed at 7/ pr Bushel & if any alteration it will be for the better. Flour 17/ 19/- Indian Corn 3/9. Messrs Herries & Co wrote me that they expected a Cargo very soon from you, & I gave them our prices. I suppose I shall have her here, as the best American Wheat sells there from 50/ to 51/- & our prices are equal to 56/. Mr Elliot writes me that the Hopewell is at last arrived in London withed. touching at Falmouth, the Cargo in bad order though better than expected. I find by the Lists that the Friendship Young is arrived at Maryland I shall therefore be expecting to hear her Destination. The Duty being taken off Indian Corn will be an advantage to you in the sale of the Hopewell's Cargo. I am glad that the first Service of Mr Burke to his friends here should be of the first Advantage to your House. I hope the Bills you mention to draw on account of the Friendship if she comes here will not be at a short sight, but you will take care to make them agreeable in that particular. I shall pay due Honour to them. Your Exchange is fallen amazingly. I mentioned the prices of Wheat, but did not that the demand is brisk, & a prospect of advance towards the Spring. We have had little or no frost, & remarkable mild weather. In general these Winters do not produce good Corn harvests in the succeeding Seasons. The Ministry keep their resolves very secret about American affairs. London has petitioned, so has this place. Several Gentlemen were very active in promoting a petition here, though not without a good deal of opposition from the other party (for even party Spirit reigns though in a matter of Trade of such consequence.) Mr. Burke's friends in particular have forwarded this Business, indeed that Gentleman the more he is known the more he must be admired. I send you by this Conveyance a Speech of his on the American Bills last Spring, a most masterly one indeed it must be so or it could not be Mr Burke's. The Ministry have acted a weak & a wicked part in their political System towards America which will be remembered long by this & heavily felt by both Countries. In any thing that occurs I shall write you for I truly am Gentlemen Your obliged & most obedt Served Rich Champion

Messrs Willing Morris & Co. Bristol 31 Jany 1775 Gentlemen I wrote you a few Lines to give you the melancholy News of the designs of Ministry to persist in their foolish and wicked Attempts against America; the Wind having ever since detained the Vessel I am enabled to acknowledge the receipts of your favours of 10.21 & 21 Decr. the Insurance was made agreeable to your orders. The Friendship does not yet appear. I shall pay due Honour to your Bill to Messrs Sergeant Chambers & Co £981.15 - . When you draw payable in London you will please to draw at a longer date than here, as the difference of time is from twenty to thirty days owing to a provision being necessary to be made there in time. Notwithstanding the Arrival of several Cargoes Wheat continues at 7/. & will be supported though the Sale will be slower than common however I am happy in being able to render you in all probability if the Vessel arrives safe, & the Cargo in good order a good Sales. I never was so much at a loss what to think of the approaching Period, as I am at present. The Country is in want of grain, & had it not been for these Supplies, we should have been in great distress. Many Cargoes arriving together, though they occasion the sale's being now slow yet the prices do not, & will not fall below 7/. but how this will be when the Manufacturers are discharged from Employment and a scene of riot & confusion ensues is impossible to foresee. If the Populace should rise for they must be in a Starving State, Granaries generally become the first sacrifices & Corn must be sold out cheap to satisfy them. These Disorders are to be expected. I should therefore think it most prudent by no means to venture at this market at a higher price than what the friendship's cost, & at the exchange you quote; even this is too high in my opinion to balance the hazard which may accrue from the expected disturbance in England. I am of opinion that the months of July & August will not be the worst for prices, as the Season this Winter has been so very mild, as to make us expect the Spring to be very backward, & consequently the Summer to be unfavourable to the Harvest a Circumstance which often happens. Besides in this Country there are some complaints of the Corn from the extreme wet, which may in the End prove of bad consequence. These are now Conjectures which Time only can determine but they appear to me to be founded on some probability so much so, that I will be concerned one third in two or three Cargoes of fine Wheat of the prices you mention as not exceeding the prices of Six Shillings per Bushel or even on board of Six Shillings & Sixpence; higher I have given you my reasons why I think it imprudent, & this is beyond what I think Wheat will be at with you, when the demand is a little abated. You will please to let your motions be governed by the quantities you know are destined for our market, which by your extensive Correspondence you will be able to learn. I shall keep you constantly advised. The Champion belonging to me I have if not loaded at Carolina ordered to Philadelphia. if he does not get a good freight at Carolina, he is to come to Philadelphia, when if you can load him at these limits please to do it, if not get him the best freight here you can. Your Bills shall meet due Honour for what you draw on my Account, & on yours also, which I shall be obliged to you to do at as long a date as you can, & after the Vessels are sailed if convenient, as it will make the advance easier, & I should be glad to give every assistance in my power to you. I am going to London on the business of a very frivolous Petition presented against the sitting Members by the unsuccessful Candidate When I am there I shall advise you every thing I can collect respecting America bad News it must be as the Ministers are determined upon pursuing their foolish & wicked Measures. The Merchants they have treated with great Contempt - We petitioned here but all to no purpose. Mr Burke which you will see by the public prints has exerted himself in behalf of America, but a corrupt Majority in Parliament oversets every honest Attempt. You will excuse my further enlarging now. I shall only add that in every part of your Business here I shall exert myself in showing how much I am Gentlemen Your most obedt Served Rich Champion

Messrs Willing Morris & Co. Bristol 6 March 1775 Gentlemen My Last was 24 Ulto Since I have none of your favours. The News from New York, since strengthened by the Testimony of the Quakers in your Province, leave no doubt with most people (of which I confess myself to be one of the number) of the Submission of all America to the present System of Government in this Kingdom. It is a pity, that these Circumstances had not been duly considered, before the Americans determined upon meeting in Congress, the resolutions of which by being broke through, only confirms the opinion already adopted, of the weakness of the American Counsels. I am still of the same opinion, whatever may be the Event, that these Laws of Taxation were impolitic and illegal, that they are subversive of the constitutional Liberty of the Subject, and will in the end be destructive of the present Constitution. And I am still further of opinion, that had the Colonies been united in a firm compact to resist these Laws, it was not in the power of the Mother Country to have compelled her. It is a fact that since America has been in a State of Resistance, great Confusion has reigned in the Counsels of the Ministry. When the violent and oppressive Acts passed against Boston last May, the Ministry placed the strongest dependence upon the other Colonies not supporting her, and when he found that they had determined upon a Congress, he laughed at it & looked upon an Union as a thing absurd and impossible In this Situation the new Parliament met, when the Kings Speech was couched in warm terms against America. But no sooner was the resolution of the Congress known, & the union with which their determination was made, than the Minister was really frightened, & expressed himself to that purpose in the House before the Adjournment. However there being a little time to breathe before the Parliament met, the most violent of the Ministry declared themselves openly against America the danger being distant. Again the News from Virginia threw them into Confusion, & produced a delusive but apparently conciliatory motion from the Minister, but with such a variety of Opinion were his Colleagues & his Superiors, that they had nearly quarrelled. Now the News from York has raised their Spirits, & they talk of a Bill to shut up the Ports of Virginia & Carolina. The Act to restrain the Fisheries or in other words to starve the four New England Provinces still goes on. But if there is any wisdom in the Ministry, they will now as some Provinces have receded, & others must, adopt moderate Measures, in order to produce some degree of reconciliation and fix their revenue System on a settled basis. The Advocates for America of which there are able ones in the House, though few in number, receive now in a pretty extensive degree, the Epithets of factious, and ridiculous. To suppose there was Virtue enough left in America to produce any firmness, they are styled ridiculous and for the Resistance which America has made, they are stiled factious as having caused it. Our Representative Mr Burke has indeed exerted himself in the Cause of the Colonies with a warmth, which becomes the dignity of his public, & the honesty of his private Character, and however wanting any of the Americans may have been in support of their own Cause, Every Man who appeared in their defence here, was supporting in their persons the Liberties of the whole Empire, which cannot be constitutionally taxed without the Consent of the people or their Representatives, & if a Revenue is formed in America, will only be used to strengthen the enormous power of the Crown by adding to the List of Placemen and Pensioners. As for us poor Traders who have dared to express our Sentiments in favour of the Colonies, we have the Comfort not only of being called factious, but also of being called fools for our Interference with a Business, which did not belong to us, for that the Business of a Merchant is his Interest only, which he ought to prefer to every other Consideration, & which we were by our Encouragement to America evidently injuring, by an Interruption of our Commerce. Indeed I am convinced, that Interest is the Soul of Traders in general, & that this will put an end to the resistance of America upon public and virtuous principles. However I shall ever be happy to have an Opportunity of saying that a House in Philadelphia, the greatest perhaps in Europe led the way, by an entire Sacrifice of its private Interest, to the public Advantage, and founded an Opposition which had it been strictly adhered to, would have saved Posterity from the miseries of an arbitrary Government, which this Nation is hastening apace to, and for which the Introduction of a Revenue System in America, will prove a certain groundwork. I have not made much progress in the Sale of the Friendship's Cargo of Wheat. It is clean and good white Wheat, but this quality is not so much liked here being light, & not producing the quantity of Flour. Indeed our Consumption in this part of the Country is almost wholly of red Wheat, as they are much heavier and produce more flour. So that these Sorts of Wheat will have the preference. However I do as others do here engage the weight to be 60 pounds per Bushel & will not go under 6/9 per Bushel. I have no doubt of finishing the Sale at that price only I must wait a little patiently Some of the Blackprince's Cargo have been sold at 6/7. warranted 60 lbs per Bushel which somewhat affected the market However I shall not lower. I am determined if there is the least possibility of supporting the price, which I am sure may be done with great Ease, for there was no manner of occasion for lowering the prices from 7/. as the demand would have been the same. As a proof of it, of the great Quantity imported the greatest part is sold by far, notwithstanding the floods & bad weather which impeded the Country Navigation. The Weather is extremely bad, & there is no doubt of the Corn's being greatly injured, & indeed every prospect of a middling Harvest, so that this Country must be in want of Grain. I have given you my Sentiments fully on that Article, which I confirm with respect to want of it here. Had not the Supplies we have had, arrived, Wheat must have been 12/ per Bushel at the least. With respect to Export in future you will know best, but by the appearances of things I suppose it will now be open. The Manufacturers are fuller of work here than I would have thought, especially at Norwich Manchester & in Yorkshire, & even at Birmingham there is a good Trade, nor are the Clothing Countries yet affected. The principal Distress lies with the Nail, Duffield & Serge Manufacturers who are already great Sufferers. I shall advise you what further occurs for I am with great Truth Gentlemen Your most obedt Served Rich Champion

Bristol 26 March 1775 Gentlemen On the other side is Copy of my last. I sent you also a few Lines by Cn Clark via New York enclosing Copy of the Resolutions moved for by Mr. Burke last Wensday but with the usual Success. The Ministry carrying it against him by a great Majority. How they could put a negative upon Resolutions which are in themselves incontestable, how they could say that the Colonies did not raise subsidies at the requisition of a Secretary of State, and had not the thanks of Parliament, when it appeared on their Journals, is astonishing. These Resolutions are couched in the true Spirit of the Constitution of this Country, & far superior to the conciliatory Bill of Lord Chatham, which abounds with numerous difficulties. When the Colonies refuse to raise Subsidies at the requisition of a Secretary of State, then & then only can they be complained of. I hope the next Congress will determine with Wisdom, & whatever Errors they have perceived in their last determination, will be rectified in this, but above all to conciliate the affections of the people at home I think essentially necessary for the good of the whole. I go on selling Wheat at 6/9. I have sold more than half the Cargo, though have delivered but few. Several Cargoes of heavy Wheat dropping in prevents my selling this Wheat which is lighter so fast as I could wish. The Weather is somewhat mended which makes this Article & flour rather dull at present. I am always with great Truth Gentlemen Your most obedt Served Rich Champion PS. The new England fishery Bill was read a third time in the Lords & an amendment made by Some of the Ministerial Lords. It was sent back to the Commons when one of the Amendments has been received the other rejected even by the Ministry themselves Many think the Bill will be

Messrs Willing Morris & Co. Bristol 15 April 1775 Gentlemen My Last was 26 Ultimo Since I have your favour 22 Feby. Your Opinion about the Quantities of Wheat and Flour sent here is just, & the price has been supported tolerably, though it might have been kept up at 7/. however considering the variety of hands it was in, it was better than expected, especially as many were eager to sell, & some was actually sold at 6/7; however the steadiness of the other Holders supported the price. You may judge how great our Wants were when we have already imported 181,852 Bushels Wheat & 18,711 Barrels flour & yet the price kept up. You are right in one respect about the Friendship's Cargo being of good Quality. It was a clean good grain, but white, consequently light, & not so much admired here as the heavier grain which though not so white is preferred greatly & will produce a much larger quantity of Flour. This made it a difficulty with me to support the price at 6/9 when there were so many Cargoes of heavy wheat at market a preferable grain however as nothing could induce me to lower the price I only lost a quicker Sale as I have now nearly sold the whole, though I have not delivered a great deal the purchasers being very slow in taking it away. The Weather has been favourable of late, but it is not too late to give up all fear of bad before the Summer comes on. I shall keep you constantly advised, but let it be a good Harvest Wheat will not be under 6/9 till November. No news in politics. The restraining Bills have both passed you will easily discover the mood of Government which prevails here. We shall be anxiously expecting to hear from America. I am with great Truth Gentlemen Your most obedt Served Rich Champion I have given a Letter of Introduction to you to a Mr Darety a Frenchman who is going to America. He is a very ingenious Man & is master of many different kinds of Manufactures any ways connected with Chemistry - The Culture of Silk in particular. He may perhaps be found especially by some of your ingenious people, an useful Man.

Messrs Willing Morris & Co. Bristol 7 June 1775 Gentlemen My Last was 15 April Since I have your favours 30 March & 11 April. I was in hopes to have been able to have rendered your Sales & Acct Current of the Wheat, but the quantities on hand there prevented the people taking away, so that the Warehouses are not yet cleared, which is the occasion of my not being able to settle the Account. They promise me it will be cleared soon. Wheat, owing to the Quantity imported, the very dry weather which has stopped most of the Mills, and the very promising appearance of the new Wheat, has declined to 6/6. The Importations into the Kingdom have been immense, & without them Wheat would have been very high. How to advise you in future I know not. If the Weather continues favourable Wheat will not be dearer, & I fear will fall, but if there should be wet sufficient to endanger the Harvest, it must keep up & rise; at present the quantities are large in the Kingdom for sale, but then they must go off gradually, as there is very little English Corn. Superfine flour 17/6 common 15/6 16/ Indian Corn 3/3. The latter Article will I think increase in demand, but the Summer not so much so; The Duty being taken off is greatly in its favour. Mr Burke our Representative daily rises in the Esteem of the true friends to his Country. His last Speech, which I do not send you, as it is gone out from London, as soon as published, & I was from home when it came out, shows him to be a true friend to the Constitution of the whole Empire, & a perfect Master of its Interests. I have heard nothing about the Champion, & therefore am uncertain whether she will come to you, if she does you will in course follow my orders, but in the present state of the market, I should not think it prudent to make any Concerns now, as the Harvest is so very promising, nor can I recommend any to be sent here after the receipt of this Letter. You shall however be further advised. The late Disturbances at Boston have various Effects here some believe, others disbelieve the Story. I think it for my part too clear an Account to admit of the least doubt. What the Ministry will now do it is impossible to say, give way at last they must. I am with great Truth Gentlemen Your most obedt Served Rich Champion

26 August 1775 Gentlemen I wish it was in my power to convey News to you, which might give you hopes of conciliatory measures being pursued in this Country, but I am sorry to say, there is no appearance of it. The recruiting Parties are very busy; great preparations making at the Board of Ordnance, and every movement indicating War. The Troops at Boston to be reinforced with 6000 Men. General Gage is expected home, and General Burgoyne, it is said, has leave of absence. The Congress Petition was delivered by Mr Penn & Mr Lee. There was certainly an impropriety in the mode of address to the Agents. In the first place it should not have been addressed to Agents, who cannot act in their official Capacities without the order of their Assemblies, but who would cheerfully have undertaken it in their own. Nor did the Congress leave any option of Conduct, for by the simple direction to the Agents & Mr Penn, without any address, it lost a part of that respect which was due to it. Mr Penn imagined that there had been Instructions contained in it. It is a pity that discretionary orders had not been given to that Gentleman. I do not mean by this, that many are of opinion, the Petition would have had an Effect, but it would most certainly have been treated in a manner more suitable to its dignity. The Government have actually hired Transports to carry some Hanoverian & Hessian Troops to Gibraltar & Mahon, to replace the British Regiments there, who are to return home. You may know by the Proclamation what the designs of Government are, & I much fear that the Parliament will meet in the same temper. It will most probably be convened early. Another shilling in the pound land Tax is expected to be raised. This, with the Surplus of the sinking fund, & a vote of Credit, will enable the Ministry to go through the Expenses of next year, without additional Taxes. Their View appears to be the plunging this Country into an unnatural War by degrees, till we are so far engaged, as to be unable to retreat, & if the people are not roused this winter, it will, I fear, be the Case; for if they can manage their money matters, without additional Taxes, & only a tolerable Trade is kept up, which even such a War as this will assist, I am apprehensive the people will not be brought to speak out. Trade in general is tolerably good, which, considering the entire Stop put to the American Trade, is somewhat surprising, but two Causes have operated this year, which has been in a great measure its Support. The one is an amazing Trade carried on with Poland & Russia, which has taken off great quantities of our Manufactures; the other is, the Spanish Flota now fitting out. These two Causes have been the great Support of our manufactures this year, and have made up for the deficiency of the American Export. How long this will last, cannot easily be foreseen, perhaps not through the Winter but it still continues, and though many Branches of the coarse woollen, & heavy Iron Manufactures are materially injured, yet there is sufficient Employment to make it tolerable to the Sufferers at present, though the winter will I think try several manufactures now employed. After all I cannot think, (though the People should be quiet) that this unnatural War can be pursued, many circumstances concur to render it by no means popular. Not a few, even of those who are Enemies to America, do not approve the Measures of Ministry, but think that their attempts to get the better of the Colonies, have been weak and blundering, and that a revenue purchased on the terms of Conquest, may be bought too dear. In the present convulsed State of affairs, it is impossible to form a Judgment of Events, and though I do not despair of a change in the people, I dare not flatter myself it will soon be the Case. However, America is not destitute of friends. She has some in this City, who will exert themselves in her behalf, and who, at the same time that they glory in possessing the name and privileges of Britons, admire those who so nobly protect them. I did hope, that all those who are closely connected with the Colonies, by commercial Ties, would equally join in her defence, but it is a Truth, though a melancholy one, that the generality of the American Merchants are not your best friends. We shall make an attempt to procure the repeal of the Acts, God grant us Success, & put an end to these unhappy Disputes. If we fail, our Inclinations to you will be the same, and we have only to wish our powers were equal. We can depend upon the hearty assistance of one of our Members, whose great abilities are only equalled by the goodness of his Heart. His Efforts for Peace have hitherto indeed failed, but still let us not give up Hope, or lose the sight of that wished for Event. I ever am Gentn Y most obedt Sert RS I send this by Mr Wake a Gentleman of your Province. You'll excuse hurry, as I am pressed for time

Bristol Novemr 1775 Gentlemen I enclose you a Copy of the Bill which Mr Burke intended to have introduced into the House, as a ground of reconciliation. I also send you an imperfect abstract of what he said, and even not yet concluded, but you will see the ground which the Friends of America have taken by it. I wish it had been more perfect, but such is the dislike the present Ministry have to their Debates being heard, that in all probability one of the best, and most judicious Speeches ever made, will be lost. Mr Burke was more than three hours speaking. The Propositions were supported by 105, and if Mr Burke had not been obliged to defer it for a Week, they would have been by 150, for so many are the friends to America at this time. Its Enemies are so much diminished, as not to exceed the 210 who voted against them. The rest, though disposed to Ministry, are tired of the Expense and uncertainty of the American War, and are not fond of acting. The Number of Lords favourable to America is very considerable for fortune and Influence, but above all, for their great Character. The Minority in both Houses are almost wholly composed of those who adhere to Lord Rockingham, who is at the head of the remains of the Whig Party, and have been ever steady friends to America, as you may judge by the Votes and Protests they have signed from the beginning of these Troubles, as well as by their Conduct when in Administration. Many Persons have endeavoured to alienate the minds of the Americans from them, who alone are able and willing to serve them, by putting them out of Humour with the declaratory Act; but those who know this Country are sensible, that the declaratory Act was the price paid to the prejudices of the Country for the Relief then given to America; and which if it had been in temperate hands, like those who first made it, and repealed the Stamp Act at the same time, might have proved not only safe to America, but useful to her, and the whole Empire: but the new Arrangements which Lord Chatham unfortunately made upon their Ruins, which turned out the Whigs, and put the Tories into place, have enabled the Latter to domineer in this Country ever since, and to revive the old Scheme of making America submit to Taxation, and to pursue it with unremitting Rancour. The Whigs in England are the only body which the Whigs in America have to trust to, if they do not mean Independence; for if they have any such Views, the Whigs in England must equally be her Enemies with the Tories who are now in Power. Though they love the Liberty of America upon Principle, because they would have all Men possess Liberty as well as themselves, yet they have a strong predilection, even a stronger to the Interest of their own Country than the Tories, and never will abandon or give it up. They are willing to make Concessions as you see by the Bill, and trust for a grateful Return to the Duty and Affection of America. They are willing to give the strongest public assurances, which in the Nature of things can be given for the Liberty of America in the one great and essential point, but must require that America should on her side abandon, or at least not insist on some Claims that tend to weaken or rather take away the rest of the general, superintending legislative Authority. When Men are inclined to reconciliation, and the great point is secured, they will not be embarrassed, it is to be hoped, upon matters of less moment, and which perhaps may be of no moment at all, when the fundamental point of Liberty, relative to Taxation, is secured. What has strengthened Administration, and weakened the Hands of the Whigs in this Country more than can be conceived is this, that it is represented here, that America is adverse to every Set of Men among us, and urged as a Proof of their aiming at Independence. This is continually urged by Lord Mansfield in the House of Lords, and the Declaration & Resolutions of the Congress, which make no sort of distinction between that Administration, which resigned every thing for their Relief, (and in attempting it, ruined their Interest at Court, and has kept them out of Power ever since), and the subsequent Administrations, which have uniformly acted against America upon System, have given but too much Countenance to this Opinion. It is inconceivable how much the Whigs have suffered in the public Opinion from these Proceedings. Lord Chatham is now so ill that it is impossible, taking his advanced Age and extreme Infirmity together that he can live long, and he is now, as he has been for some past utterly incapable of all Business. When he did come out, he did not act in concert with the Whigs. which, considering his great Name and Talents, is much to be lamented. The Propositions which he made in the House of Lords were made without any consultation whatsoever with them, and were in several respects contrary to their Sentiments, and were supported by them in the House of Lords only that the Ministry might not derive any appearance of triumph from any Disunion among them. The Plan to which Lord Rockingham and the Body of the Whigs adhered is that expressed in the Bill, which I send you, and which in substance were the resolutions moved for by Mr Burke last Session. You are to judge, which of these two Plans you like best, but to one of those two you ought to give Countenance, or you cannot expect friends in this Country. The Duke of Grafton, and his friends, as well as several other Gentlemen have returned to the Whig Cause, from which they have been unhappily separated, and I believe, will tenaciously adhere to it. I repeat it again, and I had it from authority, that the Whig Party which is composed of Men of the first Rank reputation and knowledge in this Country is the only reliance of America, supposing she means honestly and sincerely to be dependant on Great Britain. The Individuals here, who act in opposition from their private purposes, or the clamours of the Mob, which may be easily raised, and as easily silenced, she must pay no Regard to. But then America, instead of discrediting the Whig Party, must give them Credit and support by showing that it is of a bad System that they complain, and not of the whole Country. The Quarrel between a party here and all America may be decided in favour of America, without prejudice to this Country; but a Quarrel between the whole body of the two Countries must be injurious to both, and it is hard to say to which of them in the greatest I am ever with the most sincere regard Gentlemen Your most obedient Served R Champion. This News may be depended upon. The Government do not intend to make their grand Armament at Boston. They will only reinforce the Army, there, so as to enable them to maintain their ground, if the Provincials do not carry the place this winter. The whole force is to be 26000 men including those now in America and three Regiments of Scotch Dutch, who are to come over in the Spring from Holland, and be sent to Scotland to recruit, & from thence to go to America. No other foreign Troops are to be had nor would the Dutch have given them but they were paid a most extravagant Price for them. They are now about 2000 though nominally 3000 which Number they are to be made. This whole force is to be divided in America, and sent to New York Virginia and So. Carolina, so that there will be no very considerable Army, though strong bodies of perhaps 8, 6 & 4000 men to these places, but the numbers are not ascertained though they will be strong bodies. All Commerce is prohibited with America, but Commissioners are certainly going out, but their Names not yet mentioned. The Scotch Factions prevail at Court. The Bedford Party are a good deal divided some having joined the opposition. Lord Chatham will never again appear out. The Minority is considerably strengthened. Lord Rockingham is the head of a formidable party indeed almost all the Minority are immediately attached to him. The Strength however is greatly inferior to the Ministry, and will be except the rest of the Bedfords, which are the strongest part of that party and the support of Ministry leave them. It is impossible to say what may happen. 9 decr. 1775

Messrs Willing Morris & Co. Bristol 5 Decr. 1776. Gentlemen The various Conveyances by which I wrote you with Accounts &c arrived, I hope safe, though I have not had the pleasure of hearing from you. I have the greater hopes of it, because they were sent, before this unnatural War had arisen to the height which wholly has separated this Country from yours, and deprived us of an Empire, which was our Glory and our Boast. May God grant that the Authors of this War, whose tyrannical Behaviour have driven a brave People, jealous of their Rights, to the necessity of throwing off a Government, which had first deprived them of its Protection, meet with their just deserts! This is poor Satisfaction for the melancholy Scenes, which attend a civil War, but is, I fear, all that this Country can receive. It is a melancholy Consideration, that all the Connexion we can now have with each other, is to solicit good offices in behalf of those who have the Misfortune to be taken Prisoners in this unhappy War. I have to entreat that in favour of Capt Isaac Pocock, who commands a Vessel belonging to me called the Marquis of Rockingham, if he should have the Misfortune to be taken. She is bound to the West Indies. As she could not be in time for the Convoy, and it will be a very great Inconvenience to me, not to have her in the West Indies to bring home my remittances, I put a few Guns on board her, as a means of defence only, for I can never, consistent with the principles I have always possessed, act offensively against a People supporting their Rights, and therefore can by no means think of taking a Letter of Marquee. I solicit your friendship to procure the release of Capt Pocock and permit him to depart with the first Ships for Statia or any port of the West Indies, he may want to go to. Any little Supplies of money you will be so good as to let him have, and I will repay it in the manner you shall choose, in the West Indies I apprehend most convenient to you. If he is carried into any port of New England, he will send this to you, and you will still be so good as to grant him your good offices. If Capt Wm Innes Pocock of my Snow Champion, laden with Herrings from Gottenburgh to Statia, should have been also taken I beg the same Indulgence to him. I shall be always happy in having it in my power to render you Services for I truly am Gentlemen Your most obedt Served Rich Champion
