column46: London. May 15th, 1708. Sir, Nothing but the indisposition I have been in could have prevented my returning you thanks for the favour of yours, but since the receiving your Letter I have been confined to my bed a great part of the week, by a rash which now thank God is almost gone; Jacky came to town of Thursday and our friends in Lincoln Inn Fields took a whim to go lye one night in Hertfordshire, and were but to return late the night my boy came. However I sent to forbid his coming here least he might get any disorder which young creatures are subject to; however my Sister brought him with her to see me yesterday morning. He's very well but I find is not yet reconciled to Eaton. He told me he had writ to you the first Saturday of the month, and begged I would from him tell you something about his gold he left behind him; to which I replied yes, but did not understand what he meant; if it be of consequence I shall hear of it again. So will you I make no doubt. His wig becomes him very well, and he's pleased with his watch. This now time to wish you joy of the Election. I am glad the Lord is sensible. Theare are whiggs enough in the County to make one member of . But had it not been for shame I could have been in a prodigious ill humour that Mr. M- interest was not so good as the D-ke . Had those Copes but lost the making off their bosom snake for a representative I should never had ailed anything but old age, though by that I should have lost a great deal of sweet conversation I now have the prospect to enjoy next winter att the of . Thomy was so fond of the conquest he'd made that immediately he franked a letter to town not considering it could not go and was putt out again att the post house. Yet methinks I am concerned to find so good a commander as Sir dirst not stay to attack (though but with a few men) those who pretend to no skill in war though often to judge of battles; if Lord Terawly should hear that he retires to his castle for security upon the approach of the enemy without making the least defence, he might justly say it was not so when we were att Port St. Marries, but it shows the Court had reason to putt him in disgrace. But I will leave these worthless folks and proceed to the Keelmen. You, I thought, had made a plain story, and I had joined with you in opinion, but since I see a letter from a of the town to excuse that and lay the thing upon the fitters, for now that rabble were gone to work; att this I was a little surprised, and could not forbear asking if they rowed the Keels to the barr and back again for diversion, being all the ships were gone to load att Sunderland. This, with the late proceeding of that corporation to the troops from Ostend, are contradicted and the story only raised by some enemies to town. But what is the greatest jest to me, the noble Earl's friends say you all of you mistook him that day he invited you to dinner; he never designed to let up Lord Lumley "O," quoth I, "that's a pretty air. Now he's showed his teeth. But how could so many mistake the same story, and Mr. Carr engage himself, if it never was mentioned". "No," they said, "he named some such thing without design to vex our neighbour, and he being jealous took what he said in jest to be earnest". "That may be," says my Aunt, "but I will be the one as soon as the other." And perhaps all was jest for Nany made an inquiry after the commission that was passing and it proved one for no body till he spoke ever heard it mentioned. So I don't wonder after all this that they endeavour underhand to ruin the instert of the person who so rudely refused a first vote. Lord Halifax dos not understand the opposing of a good vote when he might have opposed a Ticker. I hear little news. Sir Bucknal and Colonel Plumer design to petition against Freeman and Halsey, which pleased my Sister. Last night I was told that Lord Griffin would this day be called to know why sentence might not pass upon him, and that Lord Duke Hamilton would be made a Peer of Great Britain, being he has changed his principle as one might see by his bail supported by four great gromelsotions whiggs, who are angry not to be more regarded. I approve of the thing but would have Lord Belhaven made one also for then he and Lord will make the house spend many a pleasant hour. Colonel M- is to be Lord Dover and ell's well. If you have seen the female Grenadier and the ballad made of that man's wife to the tune of the Dame of Honour, you must have been diverted. This now time to conclude and assure you Sir, I am your most humble servant A. Clavering. I beg my service to your spouse. I can't find out the second that went in procession with the monks when some walked for a show. The clergy will hang me if they can but I shall always keep out of there clutches. Just now I have had a visit from Frank , but he came not in. My Aunt's your servant. My Uncle's out of town.

column46: London. May 29th, 1708. Sir, Yours came safe to hand of Monday last, and had I not been prevented should sooner have returned you thanks for it, as also for the concern you are pleased to express for my indisposition. I thank God I am perfectly recovered of it after keeping house 15 days. I have att the request you made sent you both ballads; the latter, with some verses made by Mr. Walsh (before his death) upon the same occasion, were given by the of to some ladies since the reconciliation betwixt her and bed-chamber woman; which convinces me it is a politic part only they play. The Queen has got the gout in her foot, which misfortune has prevented Mrs. Temple's marriage this week; it not being proper to ask the consent of the Queen now, but next week it will certainly be. I cannot agree with the town to think it a good match, but she has prospects, att a great distance, for an estate, but the Gentleman's own estate is but small. How Segnior Carnaro will bear this I can't judge; when, for her refusing to live in Italy with him, he kept his bed three days. By the concern that others show upon the same account we ought to look upon as a jest, for Mr. Windam has already off the death of his beautiful mistress. Lord Longville's sister come in for maid of honour in Mrs. Temple's room. Last night I heard of the removal of Lord Chief Justice to be made a Baron, and that Sir Jekyll was to succeed him in office of ; Sir James Montague to be Chief Justice of Chester, Sir Thomas Parker Attorney General, and Mr. Airs Solicitor . This is to employ the minds and heads of idle people, and I look upon it all as spoke without grounds, for Lady Holt has not personal interest enough att Court to make this alteration, and till then I believe her Lord will be continued in his place. They have also turned out Lord Little Chamberlain, but this they always doe upon all occasions. After this groundless news I fear it is true to tell you that Lord Windsor, having got himself and Shipen chose for , and being himself chose elsewhere, designs in the last place to bring in the great and valiant Caesar, who I hoped might have retired this winter for the sake of his health. The election of Rutlandshire is carried as wished, and the of has turned off all his tenants, and putt out of offices all who were suspected to be for Mr. Sherrard. I am glad Sir Arthur Kay lost his att York. Lord is upon peace and behaviour. I wish you Wednesday well over. A certain Lord I perceive is mightily caressed amongst your magistrates. Has he got a lease of the lives of some that he's bustling 3 years before hands?. My Lord and Sister I hope will return tonight. Jacky and his niece are both well. I showed him what you said and unfortunately, as he was att breakfast with us yesterday, in came Mr. Freak, but Jack never moved from my elbow the time he staid, nor could not be prevailed upon to give his consent to the match, though I told him he was the first proposer of it. I am called of to the Park therefore can only beg a humble service to my Cousin and return you my uncle and aunt's, who give you many thanks for your repeated assurances to assist them in their affairs and subscribe myself Sir, ... A.C. I should be undone had I seealed this, and not from the above said, wish our neighbour and all you his friends success of Wednesday. To James Clavering Esq. of Lamesley near Newcastle upon Tine.

column46: London. June 10th, 1708. Sir, I hope here this you have received a letter from little John who left us last Friday and returned to Eaton in the coach with Mr. Brag. I gave him a strict charge to remember the first Saturday of the month. The day seven-night he dined with Lord and, as he told me att his return, my Lord him if he was not his tenant in a lead mine, to which the child said, "Yes". "Then," replied my Lord, "If we can but agree Master, I hope we may be landlord and tenant as long as both live". "Indeed," says Jacky, "Sister, I carried myself very well. I did not laugh, but drunk the healths of my Lord, Lady, Mrs. Vane, and Mr. Wm. Vane, but not the mad-man's, though he was the eldest son". I am not in the least surprised that the magistrates should treat my neighbour so rudely. It was what I expected. There letter makes out what is said in town upon that score, that they could never forgive Mr. making himself governor of the Hoastmen's compagny, that there (in the letter) they plainly point att. I have vanity enough to think I could return an answer to it, to Mr. Car's advantage, but to vex the souls of the rest. They certainly lye under great obligations to him, but there was no occasion in espousing his interest to affront the other. However, I am glad it was not in their power to turn him out. After all the proffers they made several letters were writ to the high sheriff of Durham to beg of him to oppose Sir and, as I hear, the like to Mr. Davison of Beamish, but both declined. Lord Wm. was plain with more than one person. He, we say, gave J.O. the lye, which is not usual from one gentleman to another. "So," says I, "but my Lord considered him as an attorney and consequently a- and as the piper's son of Berwick". In the Print Sir had the pre-eminence. The magistrates doe me a great deal of honour in telling of my good judgement in the matter of elections. I did not know I had any interest in that town, but suspicion is sometimes as bad as fackt, and as they are a parcel of worthless fellows I despise what they can say and shall continue my old opinion to let them talk of me till they are wary and then they of course will quit the subject. Who is your sheriff and representative that did not sign the epistle? My neighbour will treat with respect those who never deserved it from him. I have scarce any news. Mrs. Hales comes in maid of honour upon pretence that Mrs. Yelverton is too young. The Queen still has the gout and dos not go to Windsor till next week. Sister Cowper has been out of order these 3 or 4 days. Of Tuesday I governed and sent for Dr. Morly, but he not being att home then, she never would speak with him since, she being better. Therefore you know means was not proper. It was violent pain in her head that came att a certain hour so violently that by the screams she gave one would have thought her upon the rack. She was much better last night and spoke of coming abroad, which I could not consent to. I thank you for your letter and am Sir ... I beg my service to my Cousin. My aunt's your servant. My uncle left us to go a horse hunting. To James Clavering Esq., of Lamesley. To be left att the Post House in Durham.

column46: London. June 26th, 1708. Sir, Yours of the 18th instant came safe 2 post ago, for which my thanks are due. My sister, I thank God, is now perfectly well, and give me leave to tell you that you misinterpreted my meaning about her, and when she denies anything of that sort I am apt to believe she speaks truth. She's really a slow hussif, and, I fear, designs, before she has another little one, to spoil this girl, for that I think is often the fate of the first child. I dined in Lincoln-Inn Fields of Thursday (it being my Lord's birthday) and then spoke to her about the putting some friends into the Commission of Peace joined with the Ma-t's as you mentioned. I understood her she had writ to you about it to tell you she feared it was not in my Lord's power but that she would inquire after it, and see what was to be done, that she might not be unjustly blamed by them a second time. The revolutions which attends the brains of those men are not a little surprising. Can they, after all the abuse putt upon my neighbour, ever think of treating him? Is it out of respect to him, or to have the world say that they are true and zealous friends to the Government, and as my Lord of dos, take this way of convincing unbelievers they Drink the Protestant Succession? We still in this part of Great Brittian complain of Lord who we say gave himself to much Liberty of Speech when amongst you, and carried the jest so far as to call the Mayor a Blockhead or some such like thing. Methinks the quarrel att Durham has but an ugly aspect. Some are so kind to that velvet head to say it was policy in him to get the useless General to dispatch his for the advantage of his spouse. I have charity enough yet to look upon that as malice, but at the same time the ground of this quarrel must be laid at his door. How can any man have so mean a soul as to make himself a mere tool to the high-Church? With my consent, if Nicholson should drop, both the Sir and Brother ought to swing that there may be no more Jack Halls. Did the General's second ever see or understand the use of a sword in such like cases? Would he not be of more use to him with a good oak stick? However if this quarrel is to have no end Sir should be advised rather to fight with sword and pistol upon one of the breed of the horses the Lord Lieutenant has had ever since the revolution; being he thinks it is honourable to fight upon such foolish reasons. The character which has been given of your pupil ever since his return to Eaton, must make up for his diffects whilst in town. The discipline of the school I perceive keeps the young man in awe, and in my thoughts the resolution you took of his remaining there some time without coming to London will be no small advantage to him. Cousin Smithson seems inclined to have me go next week with her to make him a visit. If so in my next can give you a fuller account. Doll leaves us of Monday next for Newcastle. I do not hear she yet has disposed of her liberty, though I fear will soon, so you'll first have the opportunity to wish her joy. We have no news in town but a parcel of weddings which have long been on the stocks. A Ball there was last Tuesday given by Lord Dorset to his admired Collier; a handsome entertainment, a great deal of good humour and gaiety was amongst the whole compayny. My uncle and aunt are your servants and bid me return you many thanks for your concern in there affairs, and that if you think it convenient should be glad you would let Mr. Poyen accompayny you to Durham when you go to speak to and if they can be any way serviceable to you in town begs of you to be so free as to command them. I beg my service to my Cousin and am Sir ... Pardon me if I give you the trouble of returning my service to my neighbour and thanks for putting his name on the direction of your letter.

London. July 27, Sir, Pardon me that I have not sooner given you joy of your nephew, but the sudden journey my Lord and sister took into Kent (from whence they returned last Sunday) made me differ writing sooner, being desirous to inquire into the affair you mention. If by the copy of the abstract there is the power wee hope for, you need no longer doubt of seeing a great alteration, and the sooner that can be done and the better. Had you not formerly given me a hint of a designed invitation I should have been under a great surprise. Was his partner present? You also mention the high Church's deserting a velvet head has Sir stiles him, and that he seems desirous of coming unto the name of an honest man by joining with those of good principle, but since the loss of him is no great shock to that party you ought to have some great proof of his repentance here you admit him. The news here has a very low ebb. The weddings in the Devonshire family has occasioned some discourse. Lord James has a fair prospect to be unhappy. We impatient ourselves for news from Flanders, but I am one of those who thinks that the damned Duke of has been an ugly thorn to us by his counsel to perplexed Vandome; but time will let us see more clearly into that affair. I therefore can only daily pray for a second success upon them, for such another slight skirmishes as the Jacks call it, would send the children into France. However what has been done has not a little set the brains of witty men to work in making ballads and ridiculing the Princes of the Blood; but as they all do, I must not quit this subject without praising our young Electoral Prince who has done that which has not imprinted a mean thought of him in the heart of the English. My uncle Manson left us last week and went into Yorkshire. In 14 days time I believe my aunt gos to Bath; and after the thanksgiving I shall take a turn into Hertfordshire, my Lord, sister and family go tomorrow. This high time now methinks to conclude, considering this will take you from more agreeable conversation being as I doubt not att Durham. My aunt's your servant. So am I to your spouse and give me leave to assure you Sir ... I find I must wait the sitting of the Parlmt for the explination of your new title. Don't you know your kinsman Sir Thornton is a prisoner to the French? That is often the fate of travelers.

Hertingfordberry. Sept. 23d, Since I have an opportunity of sending my letters by the Sealours , I can't let it pass without returning you thanks for yours dated of the 10th, as also to assure you I am heartily concerned to hear your spouse has had so great an indisposition especially att this time. I live in hopes your next will give me an account of her perfect recovery (and that she's in no danger of parting so soon with her little one) which I sincerely wish her. Doll write me she spent some days with you. How do you approve of our new Kinsman? I am a perfect stranger to him For her sake I wish he may prove better than was expected; when one has foolishly parted with their liberty one has need of all the comforts one can, and in that state I fancy all are often too few. I expect the above said lady in town soon. I suppose her stay att York will not be long. It is well if she comes safe up from thence. I hear that robbing is come fashion. She will there meet with the news of the long expected match betwixt Mr. Bourchier and Mrs. Bellwood, a dapper couple. I have sent my play fellow the willow ribbon upon that account. I hope it will come safe to his hands. You have surely heard of the match Lady Key's friend and companion made now in less than a month time att Bath. He pretends to an estate. That is he formerly had one. His children are in this country with their mother's relations and to her, poor woman, though a vast fortune, he was the most ill natured beast in the creation. He's a great liar. I remember him when I was there. Perhaps upon second thoughts that may have first been occasioned by his poetry, for that dos often require lofty flights and expressions. But what is still more amazing is that the lady she's with had no hand in making the hopeful union. You tell me that when my neighbour comes to town he will have the original charter perused (which I shall have related over a pot of tea. I am obliged to you for acquainting me therewith and do assure I will for the future be more civil than when he pursuit his Godson). I see no cause of fear in that respect. All I hope will go well and it is what all honest men will approve of. I heard some whig Lords lamenting the loss of the place. I am told the young senator I am for promoting has got a rival. I won't say who because my author is not very good. Indeed he's no poet, no ill-natured beau, but an attender att the Senate in the Tory corner, where the great Hercules with his club will be introduced. Sure should that happen and some farces again played in the House it should be the marriage-hater match and he play the part of Solon and Tom Titt that of Bias. I hear he has built fine stables and coach-house what he dos design. It is now to late for what he projected, for I am of opinion that when the troops went northwards upon the sham invasion, he design baking for the whole army and those outhouses were to keep his firing dry. My imagination dos not much stand towards him. I am out of humour and so shall be till I know the fate of Lille. This post, that Earl's troops have took with the defeat that Cadogan gave La Motte, has given some small hopes, but how long that will continue I almost fear to know. I can but fancy Bouffleurs fears the surrender least the same fate should attend him as did att Namur. Therefore if a Prisoner he will be one on honourable terms, but some extraordinary things suppose he thinks out to be the last action of a man's life. I dare answer if we fail in this siege it will breed ill blood among us and give occasion to cry the battle of Oudenarde was no complete victory, nor Earl's descent no great hurt to the French, for which I have often wished I had had the hoisting of the beast, tide in ropes, from the one ship to the other, and then I could have assured him he should never have undertook an affair again where his worthless person should have been exposed. He may say, let those who love fighting have enough of it for my part I don't. However this putts me in mind of Wager. Are you not a great admirer of his since he has took the commission from his two captains, Windsor and Bridges? I dare say they two were brought up under Sir George Rook, and after all we in great mercy when they come into England shall make them Griffin I fear. Did it not show to much barbarity in my temper I could wish for less mercy and more justice. The Queen comes to Kensington of Tuesday which will occasion this family to remove to town for a few days. If I go up with them I think they shall drop me that may get myself settled against my Aunt returns from Bath. Your pupil is well though he never writes to anybody, but I don't doubt but when Christmas draws nigh I shall be made a staking horse of to get him a release, which I assure you I shall and doe oppose. My sister and Lord are your servants. I beg my service to my cousin, and am Sir ... What is your neighbour Mrs. Johnson a doing she dos not get a husband as well as other Kiblesworth ladies? Pardon all faults in this for our good lady and servants are att family talk by me and I am almost deft with them.

column46: London. Oct 16th, 1708. Sir, Yours of the second from Richmond had not laid unanswered so long (especially when I was almost in town a forthnight without my aunt) had I not been desirous of having you att home here I ventured to write, which by this time I hope you are, though you made no mention how long a time you would spend abroad. I heartily rejoice to hear your spouse has her health so well. When she has occasions for things useful for one in her condition I hope you will lay your commands upon my sister and self who will both use our utmost endeavours to serve you, as I hope we shall doe cousin Little soon. Our friends in Lincolns Inn Fields came of Wednesday and are all well. If you would not judge me very partial I could tell you my niece is one of the finest girls I ever saw, and since we left Hertfordshire has got 3 teeth. My sister writes this night to Jacky to lay her commands upon him to write to you, if that will have any effect. I could wish he were not so great a humourest but I fear it is not without cause Mr. Brag makes those complaints; for by what I hear from other hands the whole school are weary of him. I write to my two sisters att Greencroft this last week. I hope they have received my letters. You seem to desire the name of Lady Key's compagnion att Bath. It was Mrs. Ann Beaumont a person of £300 fortune, who married one Rudgers, a piece of a poet as to lampoons, panegyrics &c., as also poverty, for that part of his estate, which is not settled upon his first wife's eldest son, is mortgaged to John, Duke of Malborough. That name makes me think of the siege. What say you now? These delays I hope make you sensible I did not see more difficulties than were real though it then made you intertain ill thoughts of me. However I am resolved to hope the best and don't doubt but Prince Eugene will do his best to redeem his last year's fault though some will not allow that. If any misfortune is yet to happen att that place I shall go almost melancholy mad, for the loss of poor Monsr. D'Auverquerque has not a little seized upon me; he was a truly valuable person and one who will be genarly lamented by all honest people, as well as his family, though the town are malicious enough to say that when the news came to his lady she bore it with Christian patience and said she ought not to regret att anything the Lord does; but I can't give creditt to this story, or, if true, so far from thinking his death is but a month to soon (for that also is laid to her charge) that I could wish he could have spent the years over again; but since that can't be we must content ourselves in deploring this death (as he set us the example) for a faithful friend. I see some compagny yesterday who regretting the want of news from my neighbour. The last letters from thence having given an account of some indisposition he was under. The country I fear grows to cold for him and though the Parliament is putt of to a longer time yet he ought to consider the weather and ways will be daily worse, which can make travelling no pleasanter. However let him putt of those thoughts as long as he will. The Speaker I desire may not be chose without him. That affair lies dorment yet to see how the world wags, but I'm told if Sir Onslow be baffeld there he will be made a baron and I perceive there yet remains one difficulty; that is, if the Whigs will turn as they did last year and not keep firm one to the other or rather all to the Court, they will indangour a Tory ministry. It is late so I quit this subject and all other least I loose my supper and shall only beg you will pardon the faults of this (for my aunt and I are both writing upon table which is loose and consequently plays prettily) and give me leave to present my service to my cousin and assure you I am ... My aunt A. is your servant. I had almost forgot to beg you will secretly tell your sister Nancy I have the 3 books of Grand Cirrus, by aunt Ward's leave, to read and that I will take great care of them, as also that I am her servant.

column46: London. 20th, 1708. Sir, Yours of the 26 of October now lies before me which I am really ashamed to look upon and should be att a great nonplus to answer were not my excuses just. When I received yours my aunt was then very ill and under my care, my uncle was in Yorkshire, and Dr. Ratcliff out of town. It is certain the bath did not agree with her as usual, and this last indisposition of hers was the Colic. She kept her chamber about ten days, and when she began to get downstairs then went our Lord High Admiral and since his death I have been buying mourning and shaping as much, I am sure, as any other shop-keeper. So much I am positive I have cut out that I have not time to cut my own linen out and what's worse I am weary of the employment. The old saying, I may vouch, is true, to spur a free horse to death. My sister has this moment sent to tell me she's received a commission from your spouse and if I will go and assist her she will call of me. So I must leave of and prepare to get ready against she comes. Adieu. Sir, att my return home att two a clock, I met yours which my neighbour had send me. I am sorry I am so great a stranger to your spouse as that she should believe I can think it any trouble to serve my friends. You see by the former part of this I did not stand upon ceremony. Your affairs are bespoke. I think are handsome and are what I hope you will like and not think dear. If you both approve of them we shall be extremely satisfied. I wish my cousin a happy moment and I hope she will use these affairs often. My neighbour came to town of Saturday last. You say his indisposition made you part with him uneasily. He yet has some remains of his cold but looks well and is very cheerful. I see him of Monday and then I told him by his stay in the North I began to fear the Speaker would have been chose without him. But he answered imedaitly that though he was ill he durst stay no longer for he was sure, if he had, to have met with a reprofe from this family, and, as he suggested, so it was, for in a civil way my aunt reproved him for his visit to Lord . This has so far made an impression on him that hearing my aunt's cold was no better when I was abroad, he came and insinuated himself so much into favour as to undertake to cure her if she would throw of her nurses (which were my uncle and self). You shall be judge. Is this fair proceedings? Have I not reason to complain for I design it loudly att our next meeting? Mr. I hope will answer the character his friends give. I have desired my neighbour to advise and protect him, but it was before he used me thus ill. As to public affairs I heart none good. It is by the generality of people believed the French will sit down before Brussels. However I keep to my former resolution. Whenever the citadel of Lille is took I will have a bone-fire. Have we had any loss by the late promotion think you? I can but say I am pleased when I think and hope our new Lord President had his head preserved to make the other party ones more smart. His advancement is a dreadful thing. The other two the torrys would have submitted to if he had been but dropped. Yet methinks altogether it looks well, as also that her Grace of is coming again into favour. I should if I had'd power chose an impeached Earl for the Lord High Admiral, but, as it is, I must be content though he is not so himself. We talk of an Irish baronet that's almost mad for Mrs. Hails, the maid of honour. He proffers her to stay in England, to have a thousand pound a year jointure, and desires nothing but her person. Don't this look well? Yet it is to be feared in prosess of time he will agree with the opinion of her old lover, Mr. Ash. My paper will let me add no more save my best service to your spouse and once more assure you I am ... This night I write to the Esq. att Eaton. I forgot to tell you I hear Lord Little Chamberlain is to have a blue garter and the marquess of Dorchester to have his place.

column46: London. Dec. 9th, 1708. I give you many thanks for your kind offer of being mediator betwixt my neighbour and me. The difference was easly adjusted by reason of a good sermon I heard the bishop of Serum preach upon this subject and his discourses out of the pulpit have always a great influence upon me; and so that day it had upon Mr. Freeman of Hertfordshire, who never in his life made sister Cowper a bow but then. I have - seen my neighbour about the business of the of the Charter which has so long been He told me it was promised him as yesterday, so I expect he will soon let me have it. I wish that, and whatever else is for the establishing of his interest in that vile corporation, was done, though now there's no election he seems to be looked upon with civility by some. I have rejoiced as much as you could att our late good news of Saturday. I had my bonefire, which alarmed the whole square, and I may venture to say gave as much uneasiness to my neighbours as either yours or the healths you drunk to your kind friends; but as the light my fire made was extinguishing, a gentleman, who lives not many door , light his, which I was glad to see, and shall never be easy till I am of his acquaintance, though he's a married man. What a reprimand shall I have from our ghostly father (who, with his Dolly, came to town last night) when I see him, for Mr. Forster spent that same evening with us, and declared Lady Inn's care of Prince Eugene's glory should be printed and sent over to him. Also he would tell it all his acquaintance in town. If my Lord should once break silence upon that subject our discourse I dare say would be diverting. The Queen comes to chapel of Sunday and of Monday, sees compagny for the first day, and so will continue the week. For one hour in the evening she's to lye upon the bed with one curtain open, to have 2 candles in the room, and two sticks upon the fire. The new opera is to be of Tuesday and new Italian has indeed a most glorious voice. I heard him of Tuesday last in Lincolns' Inn Fields, where he was brought by Lord , and Lord President was amongst us. I find that same person a great thorn to the High Church, though they endeavour to carry things fare, for the morning after he was declared several people came to his levy, who had never made him one civil visit since he had been Chancellor. The Pope and Emperor, I find, are about an acomodation but as the Germans, in my thoughts, are always making ridiculous agreements so they doe in this. But what will you say if it be true Prince Ragotky has took a flight into Poland to join the Crown General and oppose Stanislaus? That, may be hoped, prove a means to continue the war between the Czar and King of Sweden. This is all the news I have to relate save one alteration I heard of att St. James, which is a new bed-chamber woman. Poor Mrs. not been well, so not capable to serve, and in her place comes in one who is to marry Dr. Moore, Lord Droigheda's son and cousin to one of the clerks of the closett, as also a crony of It is now high time to bid you adieu when I have returned the services of this family to yourself, and beged mine to cousin, and leave to assure you both I am ... Xmas draws nigh I have often letters from Eaton. Your spouse's affairs will set forward next Monday I hope.

column46: Dec. 25th, 1708. Sir, My sister Cowper here she left the town desired I would ones be her Secretary, and beg of you and your good spouse to excuse her not writing. She has really never been well since that fright. However I hope that may not be altogether the occasion of her indisposition (though she'd have my head if she knew I said so much), and I am to say a world for her not giving you an account about the box, which was directed to Mrs. Mitford, but as compliments were always out of my rode I beg you will spare me the trouble, and imigane all that any one could say on that subject I should say. Now must proceed to tell you Jacky is left in town during their stay in the country. He's so much improved in all respect that it would have been barbarous to have sent him down again, and I hope for the future we shall hear no more complaints concerning him. This day he's wholly spent with my neighbour. They have not been gone from hence above an hour, and had I had any paper then you should have had a frank. Mr. Gowland's agent has never been with my good neighbour. It is late. I must hasten when I have wished you joy of the surrender of Ghent, the evacuating Bruges, and the bringing in two whiggs into the House last Tuesday, att which I know you will rejoice. I wish we may always have the like occasion to congratulate one another. Jacky charged me with duty to you and my Cousin whose servant I am, as also to yourself ...

column39: The Correspondence of Sir James Clavering. Ed. by H.T. Dickinson. Gateshead: Surtees Society. 1967. Surtees Society Publications Vol CLXXVIII.
column46: Feb. 19, Though I have a letter to Ireland now before, about half writ, I am resolved it shall waite another opportunity to be finished that I may have time to return my thanks for the favour of yours of the 11th and 19, which came both safe to my hands; and to assure the Vaudois I am concern for his cough and cold. I doubt not but the creeping so into the sick wife's warm room has tendered you to much for the dreadful cold weather we have had of late, and in which I hope my cousin will see great alteration here she gos out of doors. Whilst I think on, let me return you my uncle and aunt thanks for your kind wishes. It is an alteration everybody is pleased with, save the family who has lost the place, who thereby are ruined. The young Eatoner is well. I had a letter lately with some apologys for his silence, which he excuses by his exercises. In return to which, I told him I always was glad to hear from him, but I would upon no score have him forget his book, for without some learning he'd make but an indifferent figure in the world, and att last gave him a charge to write and give you joy of your son. Has he performed it? The family in Lincoln's Inn Fields are I hope well again and the big belly gos on again by providence and no care of the good woman's. When you hear from her she will then I suppose tell you what cousin Liddell's spinett cost, for she made me no answer. Yesterday I gave her the lead mine lease, to communicate to her Lord. When I hear his opinion concerning the matter shall not fail by the first post to acquaint you. All we thank God have had a sensible proof of Mr. Dixon's esteem for us, which, in a short time now, I hope will be known to more than ourselves. It was Wednesday seven-night I was swore to the answer of your Bill and then Mr. Sanderson told me the day following he would not fail to write to your Governor and proceed with all speed. Since then he made the same fair promises to my neighbour with the assurance he'd have the Bill and answer heard of Monday or Tuesday last, and then come and acquaint me (who was still angry). But now it is and no news of Mr. Sanderson, which will fall heavy upon my poor neighbour, for I shall certainly ferrit him about again upon this his honest cosen's way of proceeding. My neighbour I long to see, I own, to laugh att him for the Tuesday He, that morning, told me the Tory petitioner had been heard and had so fowl a cause he must be reject'd, but the jest of the Town upon it pleases me mightily for they say the rich rogues, the Whigs, were busy lending their money to the Government, whilst the poor rogues, the Tory, (who for a long time have deserved no bribes) having none to lend stuck to the and brought in the Tory. Our friend was att the House to see fair play, which I am concerned att. It will make people believe he's disaffected. However what a noise abroad shall we make. To have so great a subscription so soon full, that above a million was reject'd; but when all come to be asked, after the Books were shut, when it want'd six hundred thousand pound of being full, to give our High Allies the States of Holland leave to join with us. By a letter or two to your Governor and my Steward you will find I am turning stock-jobber, and yesterday the new subscription was rise 5 per cent which advantage I must be content with in case you cannot supply me with money. The story of our chief made my neighbour and self very merry; I wish I could return it to you, but what one hears is so false that when you have told a thing you've nothing more to do than to contradict it; which putts me in mind of doing it to a former letter of mine wherein I told you the had ask the Queen's consent to marry Mrs. Hales. She now, by the permission of her friends, is treating a match with Sir Maud, a teague, but the most people believe she married privately to Colonel Sidney. I wish the former disappointed or a pair of horns on his head. He's dealt rudely with an agreeable young woman in this neighbourhood. Lord second , the Town says, certainly marries Mr. Gore a citticen who has £5000 per annum . Your seal was safe. Madam had not been in the office nor was I to hear any blockhead preach of the 31th nor of the 17th, and had I been in I shoud have given the vicar my room att church. One sermon (upon Divinity) a week serves me, but some reviews I would see oftener. I love truth. It is well high time to conclude when I've desire you to return my best service to your spouse, and my namesake, and tell her that Mrs. Betty Rich has sent to desire her books for which I give her many thanks. I am, though I have filled my paper, in haste to go visiting, therefore adieu, and believe me the Vaudois' most humble servant.

column46: April 14th, 1709. By this last post came to my neighbour a very mild petition from the keelmen to the Queen. 3 affidavits took by Mr. Ellison, one of Johnson's, one of his man's, in which he says most of his men had protections, whereas had it been inserted that some were, and the others refuse, the effect was the same, and then leave had been given to have took it in the worset sense, which would have been to us no disadvantage. But what I am most surprise att is that this justice should allow a man (Jackson) to take an oath upon belief when he had no further to go to be certain than to Mrs. Binks, and two several hands to the affidavits. It is pots worse than that he sent formerly undated, which was took notice of, as I doe believe this will. Well I have an inclination to shame him and putt myself into the Commission of Peace and come and sit amongst you. What we expect by the next post may, I hope, prove more effectual than what is already come, for I've yet exorted you to nothing but what Lord ordered. No poor man ever fretted more than he's done att your slow proceedings, and I dare be bold to say if this miscarries, by your not making out what he promised to Lord , he'll concern himself no more for us (nor can I ever ask him). Sir Harry's interest depends upon it, and I must freely tell you that had I forseen the nice consciences of the northern people I should have plead'd hard for the Governor to have accept'd of the trouble, which would have done him less harm than rubbing his inflamed legs with Hungary water. Well he is a considerate man and throwing it into his head and stomach was the best way in the world to deliver him soon of a burdensome life. His slow amendment is a full proof of his good conceits. By my last you'll see I was not a little peevish, and should still have been so had not Mr. Barnes letter divert'd my spleen, by saying, if the tools prove sufficient I doubt not but the Lady Ann will apply them dexterously. No letter from Johnson. I wish you joy of the Mayor's good graces and am ... This family salutes you. So do I yours. I'd forgot Lord who was by Sir attended yesterday on our pupil's account. He did not sign the agreement, but inferred that one good turn deserved another, and that we should forgive Gibson his debt (what is it?). The particular I reffer you to my neighbour. It is so late I can scarce see. Adieu.

column46: London. June 2d, 1709. Had I not last post had as many letters of ceremony as I could answer I had then writ to you to tell you that, of this day seven-night, Sister Cowper then told me she'd showed yours to her spouse, and his answer was that he did not know what advice to give you in that matter. "That's well sister," said I, "for it is now 2 post to late to send any directions." What my neighbour did in this affair I don't know, but I perceive we lye a little thereby under your reproof. As to my own part for the future I assure you I shall not depend on the above mentioned person, but always ferret her about till I receive some answer. My neighbour came last night and delivered yours (for which my sincere thanks are due) and I would have had him read it, but some chimera took him att that very instant that he could not read it, but he would have it home with him. I fancy with a design to get it by heart for he's not yet returned it. However att night I will send for it, that tomorrow I may deliver it to my sister (who went into the country yesterday and returns today). Something you mention of a parson. Those are animals I have an advertion too, but as they are such as we must dispense with I will use my endeavours to procure him this preferment, if not already bespoke. Next post you shall hear more. Is not this Lord a sort of a Plague of Egypt to us. I desire nothing more than ones to have an end with him, and for ever to add him in the Church litany. Mr. Sanderson came to me of Tuesday for that his Lordship calls the article betwixt us, which I desired might be entirely reject'd till Sir Harry had received an answer from him of a letter he that post sent, which we may reasonably suppose will be near midsummer, so that of course this product of Sir J. Tillie's brain must be invalid. Sanderson also promised to writ this post to the Governor of further instructions as to our accounts. Lord laughs at me and calls me lazy and I don't know what, that I have never been with our Master yet, nor heard of walking Chancery Lane in my pattens with a green bag. And pray where lies the fault that I proceed no faster? Our young squire is come to town and extremely down in the mouth. Whatever is the matter? I can judge nothing but the resentment of not coming up att Easter or not approving that my Lord and sister were gone out of town when he came. He was yesterday with his sisters, and run away from hence this day to go with them to see my namesake and Mrs. Mitford, whilst I went up for some money, though I did, when I went down, design to have sent him, which he prevented. Travelling agreed extremely with the young woman. Poor Betty of Sunday went out with my sister to air, as far as Kensington, without a hood, which gave her cold. She had a sore throat, a cough, a violent diffluction of rheum and some uneasiness in her breathing, and today, thank God, she's better. Peg's a strong runt, which doe you call my favourite. They are both fine girls. The latter tells me she likes the family mightily where she is, but cannot reconcile herself to schooling. But whilst I remember let me not forget to give the Vaudois many thanks for the trouble of my Bill. This Bank is resolved to have all our money before any peace can be concluded, which now I see no great signs of. Twill for a while please those Hell Hounds who stile themselves church-men, but I hope they may live to see that tyrant consent to by force to things not thought of when an accommodation was set a foot in a friendly manner. I hear no other news spoke of save that Abigall is more and more in esteem, and, from good hands I believe, I heard the former favourite never appeared but when sent for. She's played her cards well, but I care not. It is Johny not she I think we ought to esteem. My paper will scarce let me add my best service to your good spouse and assure the Vaudois I am ... This family salutes you. This day I have ended my baby cloths. The news of the indisposition from the little last night I doe believe given his Papa To James Clavering Esq., of Lamesley. To be sent by the Post Master of Durham.

column46: London. June 9th, 1709. Though it is very late yet I know the Vaudois will expect I shoud be as good as my word, and tell how far we have transacted towards the parson. This morning my neighbour was with me when my sister came to call me out, so I desired him to make Madam a compliment for the letter he'd sent her concerning this man; which he did. She told us she did believe my Lord was not spoke to by any for it, but that the Court of Chancery, Council, and Causeroom last night had so fatigued him that he yet had not seen the letters, but this day he shoud, and accordingly after diner, much compagny being with us, she, though she could not speak to my Lord, yet when she found some parsons wanted him, sent and bid Mr. Oaker let Sir Allen know that there was a person recommended to that living in case any spoke for it, and that when my Lord and she went out to air she'd acquaint him with it. The result you may expect by the next post. I had made a sort of a forfeiture of my word now had not my Lord surprised me this day with a letter from your mayor, signed by 8 other aldermen, to request his Lordship's favour in procuring the Queen's approbation, to serve by a deputy as town clerk. This is so unexpected a turn I could not omit acquainting you therewith. Nothing more humble could come from a vasal that theirs was, but, to make the obligation greater, he's found out that they and Sir don't agree as to the power given by the Charter, for which reason, with the former concerning the parson, I shall tomorrow take the liberty to send my neighbour to wate on his good friend that he may be seen solicit his own affairs. Time will not let me add more, but that for your diversion, now the peace is off, I have sent you the Royal Shuffler. Adieu. I salute your good spouse and remain ... My namesake dined with us in Lincoln's Inn Fields this day. She's very well. My sister will next post second you concerning your petition in her behalf.

column46: London. July 28th 1709. Sir, Yours of the 16th is now before me and shoud sooner have acknowledged the favour thereof had I not waited to know your motion by a letter from your Mama to our girls yesterday. I perceive you are for Richmond, where I hope this will meet you and your good spouse safely arrived. You surprise me att the constant attendance of our prelate and his compliments to my cousin . That was, I believe, like the drinking of the protestant succession, more out of fear than liking. That gent, I hear, has him in awe, and when under that sort of hatch he has a constant set of speechs. Your neighbours are all so much for the defence of the Church that I can easily believe those poor Palatins will have no great help nor encouragement for you. The generality here grumble much att them, as foreigners come to eat the bread out of the mouths of our own poor. I shall be sure to observe those hints you give me of what you found in the accounts of 1708. I am impatient till it is arrived, for here we keep without business. I have not yet said anything to himself, but I shall, I believe, here we part. For one thing I have remarked he speaks well of none, save sometimes of had two post ago a letter from the Governor in relation to my aunt Newton and the next post I think to write to her about it; being he says this scruple was never raised till her son-in-law came, and that you were willing to reffer it to Goo. Ledgard, but however if she would pay according to her own reckoning you would leave to a reference the matter in dispute. In my last I think I told you she's willing to pay now £40 and find security for the rest. What say you? I have not one word of news for you. My sister is still on foot, which I am very angry att, for of Tuesday she was so much out of order that I putt of that post writing to you, in hopes of an opportunity to tell you she was in bed, but I now see no signs of it. Adieu. I find fixing my eyes long now I am a cold-bath patient dos not agree with me. Therefore excuse haste in the Vaudois ... This family salute you; so do I my cousin. I shoud make an apology for my paper but I've not a scrap more in the house. I had almost forgot to ask what goods yet remained unsold of the girls for I believe sister Cowper may yet be a chapman for part of the plate when she knows what there is. To James Clavering Esq. att Richmond near Borrowbridge.

column46: Augt. 25th, 1709. My last was writ in so great hast that I've forgot whether I made any answer therein to yours dated from Greencroft and Lamesley or only gave you the account our good Lady was delivered. As I am still a sojourner with her it is but just she shoud be the first subject in my letter. Therefore I shall proceed to tell you that for near the 1st week she recovered so very well one would have been surprised. Since then the quite reverse, though now I hope I may venture to say she is, we hope, like to doe well. My Godson thrives most purely. My aunt and self talk of quiting this solitude next week for dear London, a place I begging to like as much as if I were deprived of living there. But 3 weeks is time little enough for us to remove houses in. From the Governor you would receive an account that Hall returned home by Leeds to set matters right with Atkinson, who I plainly see is a steward. It is most notorious to pay so much out of so small an estate and not to have anything to show for the certainty thereof. I've in the foregoing project, I think, verified the old saying. Hall could give me no account of what goods yet remained unsold in any kind, only that those sold to Phil. Hodshon was to cost our poor girls a law-suit this assizes. As to Lord I see no way we can deal with him if he consents not to the method Lord Chancellor proposed. By the decree the trustees are to treat with him, and the master to make the report to my Lord, so that when his honour comes amongst you, you are to doe as seems most agreeable to you for I join with the decree and leave it to you. I hope Mr. anger against me will daily increase. I give him leave if I get but my boy's money again and twill go hard if I do not. I suppose he's to be swore as well as you to the accounts which diverts me that you shoud scarce look them over and yet be putt to your oaths. I'd a visit from my Beau Master here I left and am ready att a sumance, whenever he commands me, to return that usual compliment. I've heard no complaint of you. Yours was the last letter I received from the north, but what doe you mean by setting your foot on somewhat you say was erroneous? Our surprise was equal att my aunt Ward's return into England. I hope she's not come to spoil the good design I hear Mrs. Mitford said (when in town) was undertook to send your two younger daughters to their sisters next spring. It is a vast expense they are att to have no education thereby. These poor things must, for there ages, meet with great difficulties in their learnings. Saturday I was alarmed with a return of poor Betty's illness, and that very moment by order of my sister I set pen to paper to beg of my neighbour to recomend her as a patient to Colebatch, if in town, if not to Sir Blackmore; for as we remember that was your request as to Johny when you left him. If you approve of any else let me know. We skipped for his negligence. If I hear she's worse or the has an ill opinion of her I shall imedaitly troop to town to look after her. I've no news to send you. I hear nothing spoke of but the Czar's generosity to the Swedish prisoners, save Count Piper, who most believe will be retaliated on for poor Patkull. The Czar's peculiar mark of esteem to Rensfield is what was not expect'd; that att his own table, the day he got the battle, he shoud ask him, why the King of Sweden could be so unadvised to enter so far into an enemy's country to fight so great a body of men with his handful. He shoud answer, it was against the consent of him, and the army, but that the King my master was resolved thereon and we have learnt to obey and love him so well to follow him even to destruction. If so, replied the Czar, give every man his sword, and you take mine (which he then took from his side) and wear it for my sake as a proof of my esteem to you for your fidelity to your master; and you shall all know the Moscovite have learned to be civilized as well as the art of war. What a turn is this to have the young hero swim over a river with 300 horses to save himself; and Piper stay to deliver himself prisoner of war. My paper will let me add no more in praise of the Czar, so can only give the services I am command'd from family, and assure you I am to you and your spouse a real humble servant. If you've any receipt of your pupil's they will be expected. I've this moment got a letter from my neighbour and one from Mrs. Caverley and Betty is now very well though she's been in great danger. It is a convulsive asmat, Colebatch calls it.

column46: London. Sept. 3d, 1709. Yours by last post deserves the quickest return of thanks I can possibly give so this post I won't omit assuring the Vaudois his last was very acceptable. I left the country of Wednesday and then all were in good plight; and so I found our little ones here. Poor Betty still looks pale and ill, but so much mended that one could scarce believe it. She and Meg were here all the day yesterday, the latter as wild and headless as ever, the former in love with her French and wishes to be mistress of it. She told me what care my neighbour took of her when she was ill. Good man, he's always ready to serve his friends. I am glad to hear thy 2 sisters are well and such fine girls. I own I daily wish them here with these 2. Their expenses are large to receive no advantage. I long to hear the success of your diner. Is the world in earnest run mad? Can anybody think of decoying people to do an absurd thing when it is plain all their other actions tend to the good and welfare of the infants? You've resolved on a good answer, I think, and stick to your points for I am ambitous to hear the world say that ours are the happiest orphans in the world. I've foreseen this project ever since the motion Mrs. Ellison made, yet was surprised as I writ her Mrs. W. of the journey and rout northwards. See how we mistake ourselves when she can think to make this pass on us as accidental. One or two letters I've had from her since her arrival, but all such matters I are to be kept from me as a person who they are sure will never consent to any such demands. Your conversation with Mr. is to me very diverting. I doubt not but if it was in his power he would set our youth att work with us, but we may say, as Mary in the scripture, we have chose the better and will not go from it. I expect next week the account for the master about winning the new colierly. All the journals and vouchers I sent Sanderson when I went out of town, that they might be laid before the master, who was to give Mr. a sumons to answer about his money. Then I'm sure he'll persist that we are in a wrong method, but his cousin Ann he knows was always mischievous. Had we had more of our money in his hands 'twoud a been a greater charge to Jacky than bringing his accounts into Chancery. As to the house-goods, if I knew what plate there was, perhaps I could help you to a chap-man for part if not all. What other stuff is left, in my thoughts, ought to be disposed of. It can be of no use to them. So if you find any fault in that article let me know. The bill of particulars I took from Hall and gave it amongst the rest. I never thought that affair well managed and so told Hall, both then and now when here. My neighbour's my witness and he denied he'd more to do with it than to receive the money, though I said in that case as you doe. I join with you. A reformation in our servants would be of great use. Why doe you not begging? If you allege faults and want a word of command you may receive it. I care not what they say of me. Twill be the old again, "now Madam Ann is come in we shall have no quiet". This bring to my thoughts a matter I've yet not mentioned to you or my steward, which is that I observed, what of our coals, which are vented by other fitters, are brought to account? But no notice ever took that I hear of, of what coals ours vend for other owners, which as I am informed ought to be done. Another equerry is, pray, after so many disputes how comes Milly to have the part of Bink's ship? There's £17 profitt set down to her. I've once more entered into the discourse with our council about Lord from whom I received no encouragement, though I told what a rare thing it was these two last years. If my Lord will take, as I formerly writ you, a yearly part of the mine by way of rent then perhaps we shoud have leave for that; but he can let no lease, take no fine, nor can we give any, were his terms more moderate than he att present mentions. They say an infant's money ought not to be hazarded. The Court can't justly answer it, and if they could, this may prove ill, then begings the young heir to rangle, if it is well, the thanks are, they were obliged to do so for their own credits. It is the answer I received, but you may sound my Lord when you see him. I told Lord of the joy my very good Lord of Durham expressed, that he, the best and civilised of all the fellows, had got a son. He says he believes his joy unfeigned, and so do I, when I consider he loves all those who have him in awe. Well I've now answered everything in your letter so I proceed to tell you that the best return I can make you for it is to come to the agreeable surprise we'd yesterday, by Mr. Mackey's son, postmaster of Ostend; which was that after both armies had for 2 days cannonaded each other, and that we were joined with that part of ours from Tourney, the Prince of Orange and the Duke of Argile entered the woods betwixts us and them, and after great resistance made them retire where they could draw up in order of battle; and that they had after that this further advice that we had defeated them, though Bouffleurs came to serve as Villars' aid-de-camp . I am impatient to the last degree for further particulars, which I hope will be good, for I comfort myself with remembering that this very man sent us the news of Web's actions with La Motte 2 or 3 days before the express came. This may, for ought I know, be as great a cordial to the sick Governor as any the physicians can prescribe him. He love good news from Flandres and this will revenge poor Count Mercy's defeat, which I yet mourn for, as I doe all accidents that befall our Elector's army. As to domestic news nothing is spoke of but Lord Shaftsbury's wedding, which was of Monday, to a relation of his own with a £3,000 fortune, which is so small for his estate that his friend Sir Cropley has got the vapours upon it because he first see her att his house. The covetiousness of mankind! But why say I so of him, that could oblige his sister to marry that beast Sir James Ash, because of his estate? It is plain he thinks of nothing but money so may be allowed to grieve that his friend, who needed no fortune, shoud marry to please himself. However this wedding is a surprise to the world, that so splenetic a man shoud marry. This therefore renders it evident that neither that, nor vapours, nor any other melancholy, can secure one from thinking of that word matrimony. We see, one time or other, all folks are caught in that snare. I'm also told the great looses ground daily. That all is done that possibly can to make her throw up her key, which the world says is designed for Lady Hide. A proper thing for her, who then may keep the councell-room door closer than last year. In the meantime whose hands think you we are most in? Pride and covetousness has been the ruin of that lady and would soon be seen were it not for her husband. The town also talks that the Duke and of Ormond are come together again, and that he's discharged Lady Mary. Were it not for lengthing this letter, which is already to long, diverse excuse ought to be made for it. As it is I will conclude with my best service to your spouse and assure you, I am ... This family salute you. Pray send some money for your girls as soon as you can.

column46: London. Sept. 15th, 1709. I am surprised your guest shoud be thus long of breaking there minds upon so material a point, especially after so many fair opportunities offered. It is, I am satisfied, no chimera of your author or myself. Some such weighty afair as the care of one's own brother's children must have drawn one from the kindest friend in the world. Well I've turned this over and over and amongst our bairns and them I can't raise £300 per annum . This can never maintain them in meat, drink, close , lodging, learning &c. So of consequence, were it as desired, Johny could not improve att so great a school. Wherefore to take him to his sister's and have a tutor for him at home were the best. Perhaps charges, his trustees think high. To salve which att fourteen choose a new guardian. Why not He's been a good friend to the family. Then of nessecity must the bringing the accounts into Chancery be of no effect; but as you are resolved to grant no quarter I've rested easy on that subject. But the baseness of that man will always reign uppermost in my thoughts. I durst venture to swear he's been Wethearley's chief councellor in his knavery. I'm not surprised att the account you give for this last seven or 8 years I've hated him as Old Nick dos the colier, though he's been thought so honest. I wish you success in your counter-design against him. Whenever you've an inclination Mrs. Guardian shoud raise herself she's att your service. Till then like fire I will conceal myself, to break forth with the more vehemence. I dare say 3 of us only wish to have matters acted with justice and honesty to our pupil, that he and we may both be safe from all back friends. I hear the fitters have signed so that point I hope will be easy to you all for the future. I've order £40 of the money you've returned to be paid Mrs. Caverley, and when our country friends come we shall know what more they've occasion for. I see the girls today. They are both hearty and send you their duty. What did you with 2 different set of people in the house att once? I pitied you on that score. If they are with you, I'm their servant. Matt. Smithson is in my debt 2 letters. Did you make your chief rejoice for the good news? How do you approve of particulars? We are here grown weary of so good a subject to. It was candid with lies and scandal in many thing to make it keep the better. The Duchess of Beauford is dead in childbed and I meet with none that can answer my query concerning the Duke so I must apply to Mr. Bickerstaff of the Tattler to know whether his Grace shoud drink down his sorrow or refrain excess for some few days. We are here in confusion pulling down everything in order to remove into Bedford Row. I am called on again and again. My aunt has been ill ever since her return from the country. Yesterday was the first of her getting abroad. I've not time to read what I've writ and hardly as much as will give me leave to assure you this family are your servants, and that I am to your spouse and the Vaudois ... I made no bonefire because our sovereign ordered the guns to fire the first time since we wore black for the Prince of Denmark.

column46: London. Sept. 24th 1709. I've now a quarter of an hour to spare before we remove into Bedford Row, which house we are to be in next Thursday; so I can't do better than thank the Vaudois for both his letters. The first thing that presents itself is the interpretation you putt on the narrative (as I remember) I gave you of Lord Shaftsburry's wedding. I never forswore entering into that state of life but am no nearer changing my condition that I know of than when I was seven years old. But in case I were, if I but once reflect'd on Mr. Bickerstaff's Tattler of the Civil Husband, I am sure it would break all resolution I could make to change my way of life. That is so good an account of the married state that it ought not to be forgot. But I will leave this happy or miserable subject, being not so fit for letters, and proceed to tell you I'm glad you've changed hands in your suit. Since that gentleman gives over accting for us I hope our servants make no more of those needless journeys to Durham, for besides the charge they've been dear journeys to us. I always understood that the lead was sold only in your name and that of my steward's. If so the cheat is upon the free-men, but in case is concerned then undoubtedly you pay toll, as much as if it were in the name of the infant. As to Lord I always thought you or your Governor had been told that when he went to Lord to satisfy him about the refusal, he carried with him a new drawn copy of a settlement whereing he was only tenant in the mine for life, and deprived of taking a fine of renewal when our time was expired. This occasioned our good Lord to tell him, as I've formerly hinted, that he might let it by taking a yearly rent of part of the mine, but that for the fine his demands were so high, and a mine so uncertain, that his opinion was the Court would never consent to grant it for an infant. The reversion is lodged in one of the sons. I've forgot which, but that's no matter. The elder one can't deal with and the younger is so like the father that one would have nothing to do with him. This is all that requires an answer in your first and as to the second I sincerely rejoice the ladies are afraid to break their minds to you. Women ought not sure to ask the question first, but if love or despair forces them to go beyond the rules of decency for an example to others they ought to receive a denial. I durst not so much as name the girls in the letter I writ. I expect my Lord and sister in town tonight. He drops her as he goes to Windsor and calls of her in his return. I shall acquaint him with what you mention, but let me tell you that last year we resolved on cousin Strother of Foberry for high sheriff the election year, but if the torrys are to name them doubtless they will then leave all honest men out. In my next you shall hear more on this head, and before I conclude a word to councellor Douglas. It is the return I always thought my neighbour would have. I doe assure you no tutor ever took more pains to make his young charge polite than I have done to make my neighbour lay aside part of his civility to those monsters. I often coat him the civil reprimand his friend Coatsworth gave on that subject. But what will all this signify? He's took a tour where the beau monte is and will certainly return with ten time the complaisance he used . Some time longer he must stay (not to perfect that accomplishment in him, but that will give him a greater habit, which we shall find difficult to break in this necessary point) for his room were yesterday but begun to be painted, and a little dry here he returns is but fit. Nay I expect he'll be full of complaints for the smell of paint may do his head no service. But who would not be nice whatever one personally suffers. Att his return I shall call for Hall's inventory. I see our girls today. They are well. I paid them 40 pound of Jack's money. They write for their things att Greencroft so I've decided they may be sent to Johnson, who I desire you will order to let them be sent to misses att their arrival, with a note of the charge and they shall pay those who deliver them for the boxs Waters sent Lord 2 months, because they'd nobody to send after the master. Don't fail when Mons is took to please your parson and beautiful daughter with a blaze. You whigs make great illuminations. May we often have those happy occasions and then let the parsons say their worst. To do worse than other men is their daily practice. Hang Dyer. Monsr Bouffleur's letter, copied from grand Cirrus, make our victory more glorious than we ourselves do. I've not time to enlarge though I can talk of it hours together and never be weary, but time dos only allow me to beg of you to pardon the faults of this which I can't look over, and to beg my best service to your good spouse, and to assure this family salute you and that I am to the Vaudois ... Your next direct into Bedford Row. Cousin Little is return their from Morelack.

column46: London. Nov. 8th, 1709. Yours last night I received, and must not only tell you I'm concerned for poor Jenny, but that I am now turned nurse to dear Betty, who was well and with me when yours came to hand, but this morning I was concerned for she'd took one of her fits of her ashma and sent for the Dr., but before either he or I could come she was well again so he ordered her a vomitt. She continued well till above 4 a clock this afternoon, and since then has had little or no respitt. I again sumon'd the Dr., who, upon seeing her, laid aside the vomitt and had her blooded, which he hopes will be of more use. Some other things he's ordered her to take, which I hope may relieve, but my sentiments are she'll not be cured. I am impatient to hear of poor Jenny and shall till the worst day is over and when, please God, she's recovered and got strength I beg you will command her to be well physicked. I read my neighbour your excuses and I can tell you Dr. Colebatch is angry att him. He's got cold. Last night it lay much in his head, which I did not like, but his oracle says it is nothing but a cold and that, methinks, is bad enough. I've had one this month and for these last ten days I've kept house, but for an elopement I made the fifth to give thanks for the Revolution. Was I to blame in that when I'd my riding hood on? But in my return home I met our neighbour, who chid me and bid me get home and sit in my hood by the fire-side; it was fitter for me. May I not return this compliment, think you, when he came abroad? My cough continues, and to appease Lord who for near a year and 1/2 has fancied me in a consumption; and now a cough has so confirmed him in this opinion that I'm come to asses' milk; and last week I was whimsical enough to be of the same thoughts, but though I am no better for his perscription yet I've argued myself out of my last week's folly. Other particulars of your last I reffer for another post. You've read, I doubt not, the Saturday's Gazette , and consider how early your intelligence comes. The corporation has been nab'd. It is so late I can add nothing but your girls duty to you and my cousin, and believe I am to you both ... I'd a letter half wrote to my steward when I was sent for and now has not time to end it.
