column46: London. Nov. 26th, 1709. I thought to have writ to the Vaudois last post, but just as I got my paper ready the learned, bold and pious Mr. Sacheverel's sermon came about so that I could not forbear laying out that two pence and sit down and read it, but I've got no further than what I might have bought for three farthings. This is the real cause I writ not sooner to tell you Sanderson made me a promise this day seven-night, that of Tuesday att the furthest, he would attack your Trustee, that we might know more of his sentiments concerning this foolish proceeding of ours in Chancery. Be you good boys now Madam Guardian is begun. I fear will pretend to be from home, and be as dilatory in an answer as possible. I've three letters of yours before me for which accept of my best thanks, and that I may not mistake I will answer them in order. I'm glad poor Jenny is so well recovered. I wish Milly as well over that disease. Ours here are now in perfect health. From our pupil I never hear, so believe him well. If you recommended the account of the Quarantian to Johnson, he kept it as a secret for I never heard one word of the matter from him, nor anyone else. The plague was a desirable evil would it only have swept away the thirteen heads and their adherents, but that alone could not be. The Town Clerk shall hear I take his bawling to myself as he desired my interest with Lord Chancellor to procure his son the place. If I'm not aimed att, perhaps half wits, to convince me, may name boldly. However I'll try. The coiners made a loud clamour here in town. The report is spread with zeal against you whigs. I am not a little pleased to find you bear their threats and aspertions so bravely. You shoud turn Governor for I plainly see that he, who bears that name, will not only make his Doctor's directions to him of no effect, but he'll worry my neighbour into the same misfortune. Can nothing one can say convince him he has not erred; his power is not shooks by this action; his judgement not called in question by any of reason and justice? What then would he be att when he regards the malicious aspersion of Belzebub's creatures, before the praises of honest men? The slander is so gross as will not bare. None of you who are living, nor my poor dear Papa, who is dead, will suffer in the least by it. Had none of you shown resentments in the report before this, one might have laid hold of some who had given themselves an air in saying it, and though it is now a hard frost I'd with pleasure undertake a journey of 400 miles to see an or any of the Corporation pilloried. Why dos Sir Wm. Bowes' memory escape? He was a friend to Baker, and as they give convincing arguments to prove what they say, why leave out this? I shall laugh to see the scales turn. Baker, Hunter, Hall of , Pots, nay even my tenant Squintavego, I'd part with, for a day of justice and to prove my sincerity, if I thought the latter had coined in the paper mill, I'd come and blow it up. However, good Vaudois, endeavour to bring your friends to themselves, for the teasing my neighbour with this att a time when he's uneasy about carrying public affairs, and when Bowman is walked of, so much in his debt, in lieu of being supported; under this every letter must give new cause for the spleen. If it continues I'll write to Mr. Bickerstaff to forbid the correspondence for some time, or else my neighbour, who justly may be said to be of the living, in a short time may be interred by the compagny of upholsters. I hear Tho. Gibson, it is to be feared, is come a fool's errant. This day or tomorrow he's to be introduced to Lord . If his designs prove abortive I shall be concerned, for by his avertions one would swear he was of my education. But what further regards him I reffer you to better hands and shall come to your second letter. I wished you joy of your black habitt, it is true, in hopes it might make affairs easier. I believe he was a kind husband and in affliction one's words are not to be regarded. I still hope the change will be for the better. Give me leave to desire a particular account of Lord and Wheately for I must be convinced that that matter is so concluded that our pupil can find no fault therewith. He, you know, has a notion that he was tricked of that lease by my neighbour. Therefore we must be cautious. As to the silver spoons I can't be , but I am to the tankard and in the servatore in the parlour lay the account of the plate and the weigh writ by or his order. Let Hall show you that for he shall not cheat my girls of their tankard. As for your bachelor friend I think he's not returned, but, however, I shall speak to my sister to prevent any accident. And as for the second, as I remember from what I've heard on the like occasion, there's nothing to be done; but in case I make a mistake the father has putt it in the best method, for if ever any of those things bear they are given as marks of favour to Members of Parliament; but if this happens as you wish, if my speaking of the person you think will be service, in obedience to your request I will not faill to doe it. Your last is in favour of Mr. Nelson, our pupil's master, for a living in Northamptonshire, which is not yet vacant. I'm sorry his friends have putt him upon so foolish a project. No livings in Lord gift are ever promised before the death of the incumbent, and, further, those in that part of great Britain have generally three, four or five several people about them, so are nab'd as soon as the deceased can be cold. If in the north anything fell in his gift, by timely notice and your recomendation I doubt not but he might succeed, for I will answer that not being in favour with the Cathedral of Durham shall be any hindrance. What remains more is to tell I suppose the rejoicing putt out all thoughts of money with the Governor for we've had none from him. I hope you'd a merry meeting of Tuesday. Had I room I'd send you no politics, but wedding news. I've some which I must refer, and now conclude with assuring the Vaudois I am to himself and spouse ... Did you tell your Mama concerning my nursery? My uncle and aunt salute you. Lord of Durham is come. I'm going to ask him how he dos.

column46: London. Dec. 3rd, 1709. By this time I hope your Durham visitant is returned to consult with her spouse about a proper answer to be given Sanderson, who has done as he promised in relation to that affair. By a letter from my steward I perceive you have had a demand from Duke for £300 on a note of my papa's, which dos not a little surprise me. Having occasion to write to my lady this post I have took notice thereof in the following manner: that if it is a book debt to Mrs. Malabar, I can give a good prove for the clearing all when he left her shop; if to old Sir James, he would not let him run in arrear; and if to Sir , which I could not comprehend, I thought as all debts had been paid a more early demand might have been made of this. That I was now my guardian and could allow my Trustees to pay no further than the Court would indemifye us in, for men who acted with so much justice, honour, and honesty ought to be preserved from after calumnies. The law was pretty strict in our case and by it we are governed. All debt were required to be asked in a limited time. That I was sorry to find things of so long a date revived for the consequence of it (though not dangerous) might be troublesome to us all. Have I done right or no? Tell me and upon what grounds this thing is up. It may be thought impertinent in me to take notice thereof, but I will speak 300 words before I part with that sum. Last night I'd letter. Nothing of great consequence, though it is a confirmation of the goodness of the . But as matters are ordered the doing this contrary to the proclamation can't be punished. It was not made treason (though the Custom House officers might for not doing their duties), which I know will fret the Vaudois. I hear you're about taking my aunt Newton's part of the colliery. I wish we were quit of her. I've never seen Madam Ward but once, though often att one another doors. When you see my steward, my service, and let him know I got the bill, and in a few post shall answer his. My neighbour told me he'd some thoughts of a tour to Raby. I am sure if my Lord says as many fine things to himself as to his papa, upon his account, he can make no justifiable excuse for staying away. You won't accompagny him I dare say. In my last I said I had not time to give account of the fine weddings, and, as I believe in your next you will demand it, I've set pen to paper this day to satisfy your curiosity in relation to that affair. The first bride was Mrs. Ann Savile in Golden Square, aunt to Sir . She's now in her sixty-nine year, is married to Sir Forbes, a Scotch man with five children and a pension as maintenance. He's fifty. He went for a great estate and two girls and said he hoped for a heir from her. She went for twelve thousand pound and has not two. This lady had the courage and resolution to deny the dying lover three times and, had he not supported himself att the pails of the door, he must have expired with that, the last nay say. She, seeing that, had compassion, and resolved to ease his grief. The marriage was a little retarded about the settlements on younger children, but that being concluded the happy day was fixed. When he and she, with numbers as much as filled five coaches, went to Pal's and were there joined, she so out of countenance to mumble a few words before the parson (that she winked when she was given and said she can't tell who was her father) had she not some reason when she reflected it was the first of her saying obey att 69 when she was only fit for her grave. However the paint of her face cracked so that her real skin was seen. The next day she see compagny in a great gown and, because found fault with by some friends, she bought a grave manto of cherry colour, which she now weres. She's breeding, but I'm of opinion won't go to her full time. They are a loving couple and she declares she would not be 15, to live so long unmarried, for the world. Thus much for them. I come in the second place to the great fortune, Mrs. Reeves. She's long had a and Garth for physician, who, for her illness, advised her to marry. She asked if he was in earnest. He vowed yes. She told him she'd follow his advice, upon which he proposed young Colonel Sidney. They ware married by the Bishop of Ely in his chapel. Lord Delawarr gave her and spectators were the two above-said, young Egerton and two men more, Lady Sidney and Lady Catherine, Lady and Lady Brown. The bride and bridegroom they went out of town for three or four days and then returned to receive visits. Of the Thanksgiving Day some compagny was there when Lady Betty was saying, "How shall I get home for squibs this night." "O", says the bride, "you shall lye with me". "What, then," cries Lady Betty, "will you doe with my brother?" "O", says the bride, "we'll putt him to bed to his tutor". This exasperates the young man, who now thought he'd a right to govern, so told his sister she shoud go home (which she did). He sat in the visiting room all the week, where many of these speatches were made. Of Sunday they went to church in their wedding garments. He looked babies in her eyes all the time, and in the evening went to kiss the Queen's hand, but the lady-in-waiting turned them back, not being in mourning. She'd all close to borrow before she could dress and go. Her fortune is better than £30,000. He a place in the Guards and a vast deal in debt. Lord and Mrs. Collier retired as soon as the big belly was discovered. When I've said all this perhaps you've had it already from better hands, but I meet in compagny with nothing more new. It is late and you have reason to complain of the length of my letters. Therefore adieu Vaudois. Believe me ... I beg my best service to your spouse. This family salute you. Do you remember the keelmen? Xmas draws nigh. We twice spoke about them. Sister Cowper has got your £50 bill. Jack comes to town of Thursday seven-night. I never hear from him.

column46: London. Jan. 19th, Had I not had so great a weakness in my eyes since my illness that I've been incapable of anything (but playing att cards and three times a week reading the Tattler by stealth) I shoud not thus long have differed given you thanks for your many and frequent inquirys after me. My complaints, thank God, are now very few. I've been once abroad, but as the weather is so extremely sharp I shall move but like a snail. This is the first time of my setting pen to paper since I writ my name in a letter to you. Your of Christmas Eve now lies before me, since which I've received a copy of the account betwixt Sir James and my papa. I find seven years rent due for the Westerhaugh Close farm of £60 p. annum , ending 1701. This I suppose to be the farm my gave up att Sir own request after my death. The balance of this account comes to £258. 13. 6., which my Lady Clavering says is writ by old Sir James and signed by my father. If what I suspect of this being the same farm be just, I can't comprehend that seven years shoud be due for it and my after that pay the rent whilst she had it. Has Tom Lowry ever been asked concerning it, for that was his affair, or dos know of any account that passt betwixt those two, Sir and my dada? For as the master (and not me) must be satisfied in this I desire a particular account concerning it, that he may have no opportunity to call either your judgements or that of the Court in question by choosing so ignorant a . I will say no more as to that letter. This been the material point my good secretary told me he left unanswered. As to the rest I will in right to my self be silent when I consider they are he has already touched upon. So shall proceed to yours from Greencroft. I condole with you in your disappointment of the 4th instant. I was in great expectations to hear of your success, having had so many assurances of the sincerity of the new friendship with the . Though att the same time I can but own I thought it impossible for men to putt of their natures. But, good Vaudois, do not fret to much. I've just been a sufferer by it myself, for fretting I am sure did me no service and perhaps helped on my illness. Rest you satisfied. My neighbour, honest man, comforts himself a little with the thoughts the Whigs will make a glorious campaign against Sacheverell. Particulars I leave to him. So now I come to our pupil. I must be not well now and then to try the of my friends. My girls cried and fretted so that I had , as if they were mad. Johny asked after me, which was more than he did to his own sisters; and of Sunday last my aunt had her first admittance into the house he was in. He came to her, how I did and immediately asked his sisters leave to come to see me. was in an excellent humour and we talked politics till ten a clock. This you must own a favour not usual, which encourages me to pursue his affairs with more pleasure. You mistake me as to . The question I asked was not to part with him. You had formerly given me some reasons for not dowing it and this was only to satisfy some little inquietudes in my mind. I long to know what has said to you. No answer yet to Charles Sanderson. What is this business with widow Acherley? I do not rightly comprehend it. As to Monsr. Poyen, I will observe your commands. Your girls are very well and I believe return this night. I've now answered both yours. I must give you a word or two of what you seemed so much to desire, viz. the Mr. Tong and Mrs. Stote. I doubt not but every particular has reached you here this, so will not trouble you with a repetition. But when att her age, with all her charms, she was stole, and by a clergyman, I can but be amazed to think what this world will come to. If he sues her for her fortune, she will prosecute him for his life in stealing a hairess. Twill be a sweet trial. I'll hear it, for it must be new to be stole with one's consent by her order. He got the license. She kept the ring 14 days, set the wedding day, which was on my Lord Mayor's show, was married in her Christening mantle. Nay more, the did not know how to perform his office and gave the rong hand. She told him so, pulled of her other glove and gave the other. Yet was stole! 'Ent this pretty? After this she made a modest request that the shoud not be ownd till May and that he was not to own her till then. He set her home that night and att the door they parted and it was convenient, it being a secret they could not lodge together for my lady is her bedfellow. In fine she's affront'd and I fear it is att his modesty and vows never to own him. She will be tore in pieces by wild horses before she will live with him and here I must leave them for my eyes begging to be very sore. So can only assure you of the best wishes of this family and to assure I am to your spouse and to the Vaudois himself ... If you see your Governor my service. In a post or two I shall answer his. Pardon faults for every moment one or other has come to ask me questions.

column46: Jan. 31st, 1709/10. These shoud have been with you last post, but whilst I was writing my aunt came and talked, putt me quite out, and made me write nonsense. It was then ten a clock so I was forced to differ it to this post. Mr. Poyen write to Mr. of Saturday and bid him show it and desired I would do the same in one to you, which is the occasion of the cover. I was forced, when the matter was argued, to be in a passion to keep me from laughing. All will doe well I hope, for here they have took the alarm and I've promised to be as impertinent as Mrs. and expect to have my follies as calmly bore with. I can't, nor will I, hear of any more civil proceedings to . My patience is flown. The master must make his report. has heard nothing of Acherly's widow. All this exasperates me and me a more adversary. Let pretend what ignorance he will, those receipts for the rent of that farm I must have produced. So tell him, for I will take no excuses nor pretences. And as for , what are you doing with him? You've hurried me to death to give you a handle to turn him of, and yet you complain of his neglect. When you see him next, ask him from me if I did not declare to him that whichever of Jacky's servants pretended to refuse to obey your or the orders att all times, and upon all accounts, I would discharge. I'm generally a person of my word. Let him persist and try. For out he must go. An example must be made, that's plain. My nurse, I find by both yours, continues to make complaints. Sure he's the troublesomest man alive. He tells you stories, things and would have me worry myself into the country when I am as fat as ever on my face and have a fair clear complexion like a lady. This I affirm for three days ago I was told that in a room full of . It was said that if ever Mrs. Clavering was handsome it was since she'd the meazells, which has given me so great an opinion of myself, that I dare not go into the City least I be forced into Pal's for my beauty, as Mrs. Tong was for her money. The orders of the Court has been twice posted on her door. If she gos not home to him before tomorrow night he'll have my Lord Justice's warrant to fetch her. Poor wretch, what will then become of her when she now vows the sight of him will kill her? Nay, were they to continue separate she shoud doubtless dye the moment she hears he has seized on the estate. My neighbour is just come in so adieu. I'm ... You see my sent me not gilt paper though I was to write to an alderman or for him to see. This family salutes you. You find in the cover I desire this to be delivered to your spouse to prevent the suspicion may have by the mark when you show it, which you must doe.

column46: London. Feb. 22th, When I'd got a frank last post and putt myself in a writing posture and all materials ready, Sister Cowper sent that moment for me and kept me till 11 att night, which prevented my thanking the good Vaudois for the favour of his letter and telling him that I rejoice att his being so well recovered as to be able to get a hunting. As you make no complaints I judge you got no harm, though I by my last night's visit have got so great a cold in my head I can scarce see. I find by woeful experience I'm fit for nothing but a wanded chair in the chimney corner. I am sorry our affairs give you so much trouble. I desire you make take what assistance you think necessary on this occasion. I fear we must struggle with many difficulties before we shall come to be tolerable easy. To be perfectly quiet I'm convinced is beyond the reach of a collier. The devil has possessed our men I believe. I wish when you see Lowry next you'd ask from me the reason of this change, that as soon as his master was dead he shoud loose his honesty, for being fully convinced of the truth of this, by concealed mismanagements, I fully resolve nobody, that has a horse in our waggon way, shall take the way off us. So let them be att rest. I'd, if I could, have every servant of ours born with a mortal aversion to each other. That's the only thing can secure one from being great sufferers. I doubt not but the good character Hall has given me has increased this pertness in them. Therefore this, with the other misdemeanours, I'm resolved he shall change hands and I desire you will advice Mr. Barnes, who is an honest , to recomend that fellow no more. I send you the enclosed open, for you and the to read, that Hall may father no more lies on me. I heartily pity you in this juncture when I look upon you as loosing your Guide and . The resolution my neighbour has took, to have my steward up, who has so long laid dormant on the account of his indisposition, I hope will be seconded by you, who must be an eye-wittness of his sufferings. Perpahs as our affairs now stand you could be pleased with his stay. Yet you are to consider to what a height his illness is grown, and, by longer neglect, we may loose him for good and all. What then would the Trustee and Madam Guardian do in relation to Johny's affairs. Therefore press him to leave you that he may putt himself under his doctor's care, whose has hopes, when under his eye, to relieve him. I look upon him as in a deplorable way wherefore he ought to shorten his present stay amongst you. I see my neighbour this day. He looks better than I've seen him this month. I'm forced to writ this over night that I may not be prevent'd again. I've not yet seen Sanderson though I've writ to him, and my neighbour went and left word att his house that I want'd him and all this won't doe. I begging to fear I'm as far versed in Chancery proceeding as I shall ever arrive att. This evening I passt att Cousin , where I spoke of J. civil return to those who had got his son that place. He condoms I hear, said I , those who stopped the proceedings in Council, which I take to be aimed att my , by the application made to him after; or me, perhaps, he suspects to have given notice. When the son, by you , spoke to me, I gave my advice as a friend, from which they met with no ill success. This then deserved a more grateful return. My Lord is beyond his reach, and will, as long as possible, keep out of his clutches, having made this resolution, that I never will submit to anything within the walls of , but when necessity obliges me. If the thing has been rong represented to me, I've took care to do it to my Lord, for when I make any request to him for others I always tell how it is received. This I hope will bring a confession, which, if a true guess, you shall know. I suspect you to be concerned. I come in the next place to the affairs of the Portuguese Ball. Nothing was ever seen so sumptuous and fine; 39 ladies he invited to supper and the came after att 11 and the mockers att one. There was all sorts of dresses amongst those people, even to a Dr. Sacheverell, who was half our parson and half Spanish friar, which some of his compagny obliged so far as to desire an unmasked lady to take the Doctor out to dance. The supper was magnificent and in wast order, all sorts of fruits as melons, grapes, &c., so naturally done in ice that nobody could tell them from real. But, what was to me the worst part of the ceremony, he'd got the gout, which had put of this entertainment a week, but that he might no longer disappoint the ladies he ordered his physicians to strike his disease out of his limbs into his head or stomach for he valued not death after that night. And the next day when he, in the morning, sent his body squire after the ladies invited to supper, and in the afternoon went himself. It is late. Adieu. I am ... I beg my service to your spouse. This family salute you. Feb. 23. has been here and brought me a letter has honoured me with, and the things relating to Acherly's widow. Next week we are to look over all the accounts, for now makes himself debtor only £392; a good deduckment. Did he ever pay for Jacky's board when att Howton? I hear this moment the boy's not well att Eaton, but my sister said nothing of it this morning, though she'd a letter. Worthley, this night, burries his eldest daughter, who died of grief for the follies and imprudences of the younger sister. Adieu.

column46: London. March 23, 1709/10. This is to condole with the good Vaudois the loss we've so lately sustained. A thing so surprising that the whole universe must have us in horror for it, were it not for the money with which we supply our own troops and those we hier. Of Monday to have a majority of 17 votes and of Tuesday loose the small punishment designed but by one, and that voice that - . I will say nothing but the absented Lord the day before. The of Somerset, one whom the Queen of the Friday had, in civil terms, asked a vote, and yet drunk waters the Monday and cast us of Tuesday. You know I'm Truth, as is said in the play. I never go to a Court and therefore understand not Court politics. Lord was not well of Tuesday. No appeared that day but (except Oxford, but of that I'm not certain). The punishment desired, by the Lords we esteem, was this, a silence for five years and during that time to be incapable of any benefice. And had they asked but one year, it had been denied. The silence is now 3 years; the sermoned burnt att the Royal , the Lord mayor and sheriffs being present; the text cut of, because that's scripture. Well Vaudois, happy are those who were a black robe, when the doctrine they preach is to be disavowed and yet not suffered to be punished. I shoud advice all house breakers, &c., to were that habitt. Now I'm convinced it is the sanctuary of all villainy. Be not surprised att the rejoicings made on this occasion, when here we'd bonfires, eluminations, &c., of Tuesday. The , thus insulted, is insupportable and to be overlooked. It is true the English never know when they are well. A Church Ministry we now want and shall have, as soon as Johny can decently be thrown aside, I doubt not. May those who love to be priest-govern'd have enough and obey passively there superiors. I abhor that doctrine and am to espouse that of resistance, when it is lawful, but in that I'll be my own judge. Keep up your heart. I warrant you God is above the devil. We have not seen the end of this yet, and, for my part, I wish we may not feel a heavier blow. In the meantime learn to bully your adversaries, as they do us. After all this I must tell you I've some favourites amongst the clergy and none more so than the Dean of Windsor, who has been sent for to St. James. I know not what for, but he told a lady I see last night, "Madam the of passive is so far from being the of Our Saviour, that 't has been putt into men's heads by the devil". To cheer your drowping spirits I must conclude with a story of the of and a mis-coted text of Harry Mordant to the Commons yesterday. The 1st was this. The of told her Duke he was to vote for the Doctor and speak as his did. To which end, of Monday, she him up and bid the servants tell the of , he was gone out. (Fearing him), the Duke comes. The servants obey the Dutchess's commands. His Grace, not satisfied, lights out of his coach, run over the house, meets with one room locked, calls and was answered, "I'm here, but can't get out. My wife's locked me up". To which the Duke says, "I'll release you". Away he runs, fetchs a ladder, set it to the window, the Duke out, and putt him in his coach and bids him say in the House as he did, for he'd speak loud, which, I can witness, was observed. The former part I don't aver. However it is a good story; and in that of I shall be short. He, yesterday, bantered the Lords on the punishment, by representing how dear this had made that insignificant creature to his party, and begged leave to conclude with a miss-conster'd text of scripture as the reverend divine had set the example. His words, , were these. "It is the Lords doings, but not mervalous in our eyes". God send this well over. I like it not. But adieu. I'm for the opera, it being the first time I've been a play-house these 13 months. I salute your spouse and am ...

column46: . April 1st, 1710. Thanks to the Vaudois for his 2 last letters, which I read with concern, to see so zealous a Whig have so little power to defend himself from the insults of such a turbulent faction. It is what has been allowed here, and so rest content. Be satisfied the sermon is burnt, the doctrine censured, the Oxford Decree burnt, though the rights of the Christian Church went along with them. Praise the clemency of the Whig ministry, otherwise called by the Torrys the Comon-wealth ministry. It is that is aimd att, and not the succession. Dr was a true Churchman, a pious soul, an angel sent from God to exort us to follow the right way. How then can you be angry att rejoicings when no guile was found in this man? Sure you interpret his words in a rong sense and fancy he talks against the dissenters, and favours papist. Good creature, he meant no such thing. He was only doing his duty and preserving the rights of the Church. This is mostly the cant of that set of people you hate. The mob was also who were doubtless weary of the Toleration. Though the parsons are not of thundering out there anathemas for a young Oxonian last Sunday att the Temple said, no Prince on earth had power to call God's vicegerents (for so he stiled the parsons) to account on any score. Their power was from a more supreme being &c. So went on. Att last says this Moses for meekness, the primitive moderation was allowable, but for this modern moderation, if I understand my business, it is a damnable sin. I've this consolation yet from this doctrine that now they've rope enough they'll hang themselves. I suppose you've heard how our neighbour of Hedley-fell has carried himself. The Duke of , I hear, plays him a good trick. He's to sumonce the Kitt-Katt to meet, to make inquiry after one of the society who has made an elopement with Robin the Trickster. A very good whim I think. It is of a giddy person. Now I must tell you I was lately myself insulted. On this occasion I went to make a visit where the picture of the perjured priest was, which putt Lady Ann into a raving fit. I left nothing unsaid that could, I thought provoke. Att last I was told in derision, "If you are so warm and fiery you'll never get a husband". "O Madam", says I, "you mistake that matter. I despise all Torrys, were their estates never so large, and yet don't despair for I am sure the Whigs like me better for being true to my party". And so we parted. The perjured priest read prayers att his own church, of Sunday morning, where there were such members of the mob, that those near him kissed his hand. Others touched his garments and were blessed. Yet I do not hear that all this has produced thanks to the Gloucester Address. Dare you venture to give my service to the minister of Gateshead and tell him I am sorry he has so publicly distinguished himself on this occasion? I fear he neither get by it in the time of this Bishop nor in any other, betwixt you and I. But here I must quit the parsons. I am weary of them. I thought I shoud have had some business to have sent you, but the , I believe, told you all last post, which was that we had ordered a view to be took of Hedley-fell for to try what we could do there. So can set no till some end is made of this project. Your has been a house-keeper ever since he came to town and till today has, I assure you, given his doctor great uneasiness, he being much worse than his own accounts represented him, which made the other give little or no hopes of his duration here. I see his doctor this day, and he says his legs are better, and, if they continue, he shall hope well for him. However it be, sure he's now in a deplorable condition. Patience is counted a virtue but in him 't has been a fault to an unpardonable degree. Adieu. This family salute you. So do I your good spouse and am to the Vaudois ...

column46: April the 20th, 1710. I should sooner have congratulated the Vaudois on the late piece of good fortune, that befell him by the exit his kind aunt has made, had you not in your last told me that you were for diverting yourself on the moors a week. I won't say I envied your pleasure when of this day 7 night we had the agreeable news that our army had made themselves masters of the French lines by their practising our Church doctrine of non-resistance. But his news was soon allayed by a new Lord Chamberlain, who has crept into the cabinet, a province not belonging to his office. That was a surprise on the world and what no Whigg can digest. More changes were immediately spoke of and nothing but a thorough reformation in both church and state was to be looked for. Then I wished my self out of the hearing of everything and could but think you happy in a place not troubled with politic designs. This neighbourhood of Saturday were so peevish on this subject that I, who had appointed Mr. Sanderson to come to me to look over affairs, (and by that means forced to look amongst the vouchers), was so modelled that all my papers I thought were signed by Sheus ... However we set ourselves right and was to write last post to desire him to pay us in his balance to the account speedily, by which means he might hope for better usage in the objections we make to the accounts. As soon as my brains are settled I will look in the for that money you mentioned that Hall (has rong booked) paid Mr. Silvertop and that of the fitters, but the journals of every year are in my master's hands. But I must return again to our new officer the defence of the Church - . His having but one eyes speaks his praise as much as his meek and gentle carriage did att the trial. He has allotted the management of the Playhouse to her Grace, which made her of Monday night so far forget herself as to undertake the shouldring out of the lady in waiting and playcing herself there, which gave her athority to marshall all the ladies as she pleased and to entertain the Queen with the news of my Lord Mayor of York's going to travel, which made all people laughed. She'll soon, I believe, aquire the title of the Queen Church Warden. This has putt the Torys into an airy temper, insomuch that our Bishop, who I dined with of Monday, could not contain himself but chatter'd like a mag-pye. He then was in hopes of delivering, or introducing, the Durham address, but as the Queen will here no more of those papers read of, no side, his honour gos away with a flea in his ear, which dos a little divert me. You will by this post have a letter from Red Lyon Street so I will say nothing of them. The can give the best account of himself and of the world. So referr you to him and shall conclude when I've assured you the news att Whitehouse relating to sister Cowper was not false. I salute my cousin and am to the Vaudois ... Betty has got her cough again for which I've ordered her some linseed oil. I durst not omit this post writing least you shoud say I was grown great and lazy and employed a secretary.

column46: London. May 27th, 1710. You will say that you made but a seasonable complaint of Harry's manner of leaving his farm when I tell you my sister Cowper, who returned from Hertfordshire last night, this days has made me a load of complaints on this account, viz. , that the old back parlour was the tippling room; that the best of the guests were entertained in our room above stairs; that Harry laid his corn in the best parlour till the floor is mildued; the butter firkens were in the little parlour and the brian that run out of them had spoilt the boards; that he has took away the great pot in the furnace att the end of the kitchen-grate and says his gave it him. He lies. It was sold when the kantin was att Chopwell, but not to him. He's also got one of the bars in the kitchin-grate away. That one of the dressers in the was always 3 dressers, and the pan out of the stove there is gone likewise. Out of the garden house is gone all the shelves, the glass of all the windows, and what glass frames there was for the cocomber beds. The windows of the house are all out of repair. The fires made so seldom that the sealing of the rooms is dropping. That that of the porch wants mending. That Ralph and he quarrelled about this affair, but his answer was, he was putt in trust of the house by his late and he shoud do as seemed him best. What is worse he has not laid any manner on the ground, but carried it of with him. This has made a great cry in Inn Fields and what you must see . He must either restore or pay for what he's took away. It is not being Weatherly's friend shall make me favour him. Well Vaudois, what say you? Is it necessary by this representation to allow 40 fother of coals for fires when there was none made? No, no, that trick will not pass on chancery folks. Nay, Ralph is not clear. There's a great crack in the wall betwixt the pantry and the stable, which are his apartments. That the buttery, the two rooms that were nursery's were for Ralph. The new painted room as it was called, the kitchen, still-house, and the old parlour, where Duke Lauderdale used to lye, were for Harry. The rest of the house reserved, only the hall on Christening days. Pray look and see how the brewing vessels are in the brew-house and if the blew and gold leather is in one of above stairs. The bid me to tell you he's got your knifes and forks, but Lord Pawlett, and Sir Harry have agreed that the set could not be complete without spoons; that the blame is to lye on them and so the and Segnior, att a venture, have bespoke them. Your cradle and baskett I go about of Monday and 't shall be sent with speed. As to other materials of your letter I refer them to another post when I can have more leisure to treat of them. Only before I conclude must advice you not to fear Dyer's threats. The Ministry, att this bout, won't be altered. A stop is putt att present to that scheme. Adieu. I am to the Vaudois ... This family salute you. So doe I my cousin. I'd forgot to tell you Dr. has great hopes of your , though he's often uneasy.

column46: June 13th, 1710. By searching my pockets I fear I find two of the Vaudois' letters uninsured. The one of a long date and what I ought to make a long apology for had it not been caused by a mistake of your 's, who, when he writ to you, was to have inserted that we agree with you in letting that part of Chopwell you mention. Fires doubtless will be of great service, yet was pleased to make a forget thereof. Suppose, as the pot in the kitchen belonged to the girls, I take a fit to make Mr. Hayhurst return it me and set it in the right place. I shoud but serve him as he deserves. I am glad our coals prove so good, thought we have no vendor. I shall now proceed to the most material part of your last, which ought to have been answered last post, durst I have ventured to have given of my own head. The same I must now return you, which is, that att this time, you can have no opportunity to proceed against your prelate. The proragations are to short. The uproar amongst you are surprising. What are we to do? Vindicate ourselves before the Council, and what then? I rejoice poor Dan has escaped their furry. I hope to see a revenge, but this subject has given me the spleen so much I dare not enlarge, least I convince you of it. Therefore adieu. Believe me ... I salute my cousin, whose cradle will be ready in few days.

London. June 17th . It is well for you I was not in a writing mood last post or you had had a double trouble, for my spleen and resentment went then so high I must have communicated some of it to you. The turning out of glorious Lord Sunderland gave me some uneasiness affairs had an ill prospect and I almost apprehend that might add to the necessity of my loosing some of my giddy blood this morning, for a pain in my side; but those fears are a little vanished since the Whiggs have been so brave and daring, all to let know that no money was to be had, for they could not advance for the army when a Tory Ministry was to succeed, for all securities then were nought, which alarmed all and, by the help of present Councilours, the head Whiggs of the City sent for, and assurance given from the Queen's own mouth of no further change. This did not sufice, for yesterday all foreign ministers were sent to, the like assurance given them and, as I hear, a promise not to dissolve the Parliament. So they are now beaten and a stop putt to there present insolence. The next thing in view is our girls, who the has writ about to you some time ago and proposed their coming up with his widow, who by a letter to him, I perceive, is willing to undertake the trouble on the road, but sending to Mrs. Mitford's in your absence to let them know when she shoud be beginning the journey. By the message returned it seemed as if it was a surprise the children were to be removed. As she is willing to take the trouble I think, with submission to the Vaudois, we ought not to slip this opportunity. If Milly's weakness requires the cold bath she shall go in with me. And as to any other pretence of not having close &c., for the journey twill be better to provide here. These girls were made so little and straight that they were almost useless, but to your directions I leave them. Their sisters are till they see them, and, by former assurances from you, I give them hopes twill not be long here they meet. Sure your kind indulgence to their aunt, in granting them so long a stay with her, dos not make her mistake your kindness and look on them as inheritance. They are now old enough to receive education. Jacky was never so good as this time in town. In his days received praise and thanks of his friends for his courteous behaviour. I shoud enlarge, but my hand you know is tied up so must conclude when I've assured you, I am to the Vaudois and his spouse ...

column46: . Aug. 8th, 1710. By yesterday's post I your kind reproof for my silence. I own it was the second letter I was indebted to you, but had you not two of mine before I yours of the 22d of July, which I shall first return thanks for and beg of you to make my compliments to my cousin for the favour of hers, which came enclosed in it. By the account you give you've had glorious doings since the Holy Prelate came amongst you. How many more knaves and fools are there in the county than I thought of. But upon reflecting sure they have been the worst enemies that ever the had, that putt him upon this public entry. Can this have been the best of his actions for many years, that she shoud thus be applauded? He spoke not for the Doctor, which his of Bath and Wells did. I heard indeed of one good effect, which was that his Lordship now knows what party he would be of. For 76 years consideration he professed himself a Tory, a thing suitable to his genius, for all and are of that faction. But I will quit him to tell you of a glorious young rogue, Lord Ashburnham, who, by the of Paulet, was as good as closeted, to endeavour to persuade him he ought to resent Lord 's being preferred to Lord Troop of Guards before him, who was major in the Troop; a man of quality and fortune, who might command an interest wherever he came; and that he hoped his Lordship would not enter into the schemes of some men, but would always be a zealous server of his country and join with the Queen and her Party. The youth, with patience, heard him a full hour, then told him, "My Lord, I am not sensible of any injury done me in my Lord 's prefferment. Methinks it is an honour done the nation to have the Guards commanded by one of his quality &c., and I think it an honour to serve under him, for which reason I will keep my commission. Indeed had that empty-headed, ridiculous &c., of been preferred I should have took it for an affront and have thrown up the next day. As to the other part of your discourse it tends to a vote, I will deal with you as an honest man. I design you none and, to prove myself sincere, may my estate sink under ground, my tenants be ruined, my family perish, and myself 'd if ever I give you a vote". Is not this a tight Whig? Thank God his brother made room for him. Lord did as well. He writ word he heard the Duke of or Lord had a mind to his Troop. If so, they shoud have it att their own terms, but if the of or his Party, he would not sell. They might take it from him, but he woud't part, in that manner, from a present of his masters. This is all the news I've for you so shall proceed to yours by the last post. I am sorry to hear poor Milly is ill and of so ugly a distemper, for it is a devilish corrupter of the blood. I know by experience, you cast not the ill effects of that disease of some years. I am glad she was amongst you. This putt me in mind of asking your pardon if, in a letter, I some time ago writ to you, about their coming up, I said anything you could take amiss. I designed not to give you any uneasiness. You know you last year told me they shoud come up att my sumonce and I thought no time could be more proper than when my steward was in town, whose actions are justly approved by all. Though this, perhaps, may meet with a little sencure being a request of Lady Inn's who sure never merited a good word from any northern body, having never had any. Nor can she say she is ambitious of it from any inhabitant save the Vaudois, who has proved himself so sincere a friend to the family. From all hands I hear Madam &c., makes loud complaints of the remove. I expect'd it, and, as I always feared a brush on this occasion, the sooner it is over the longer time we shall all have to forget it; and I can but say, I hope it is not in the power of any to make a difference betwixt 2, who are using their utmost efforts to preserve a poor family from ruin. Adieu. I salute my cousin and am to the Vaudois ... You are desired to give an account of what happens to Mr. Baker att the Assizes.

Kind Friend, I think Lady Ann has given you measure and may serve for answer to two (you say) she was in your debt. However here is room enough left for the invalid to let you know, that he yours of the 28th ultim: , as well as that of the 4th, for which his thanks are due. By the first, you discover an anxiety more than ordinary the management of public affairs, which perhaps may in a great measure deserve it, but you have painted to yourself a cloud much blacker than I hope it is in reality, which is of no other use than to plague yourself and dispiritt the well-wishers. I remember when in the utmost extremity of my illness my Dr. always gave me hopes, though perhaps he had but small himself. Yet it had a good effect. It raised my drooping and sunk spirits. You, in another capacity, are the Dr. You are one of the chief supports of our cause, and, when the hangs down his head, very well may the common soldier, that fights under his banner, despair of success. The fate of the is not yet determined, so everybody hopes as he wishes. Neither your to Lady Ann, nor self, mentions a word of Lord 's resolution, which was to be you att your assizes by Mr. Forth, but I guess it, having seen a letter under his own hand 2 posts ago, wherein he discovers his inclination to the fashionable doctrine of passive obedience, by this expression, it is folly att this time of day to strive against the stream . No news abroad, but Johny Mann's intelligence says Bethune will be in our hands by the 12 inst. att furthest. Mrs. commission to Mr. Richardson shall be executed tomorrow without fail. My man shall take his receipt. I heartily thank you for your congratulation. design for the Bath middle next week. My dadd will be with you almost as soon as this. salutes you, and we are both much concerned att the irreparable misfortune befallen your table. The man shall not want a severe reproof, but that is no satisfaction to you. Certainly the breach must have bin made on ship board. My devoirs to your dowey. I am in reality honest Jamie, thy faithful friend. .

column46: London. Sept 2d, 1710. I was of Thursday obliged to go wish joy to Sir Franklin's daughter, who this week was married to young Mr. Worstley of Ovingham, or you then, as you expect, had your chide. Be not displeased, good Vaudois, att a few reasons I give for not joining in your late proposal. You first say the disburstments from Christmas to May-day out-strip the and brings the balance to six hundred and odd , for which you take a mortgage of 30 p. ann. att 5 p. cent., with the son's and son's son bond and judgement, and give your receipt for so much ready cash. My own sentiments on this is that you cannot doe it. You are not safe. There may be a prior mortgage. If not, consider we are in Chancery and, without leave, this can't be done. But as my lawyer will be this night in town, I will inform myself and send you word next post. Next, consider, if we accept here of this security, we shall be obliged to doe the same to , where I must have ready money; and that, if you engage alone in this affair, you putt it out of my power to serve you for the future in getting the court to discharge that trustee, by desiring the money and disbursed may be yours and my steward's joint order. Consider with your neighbour, if you see him, of this till you hear again me. And had he used us as he ought this must have putt a stop thereto, but as he has daily repeated his insolences and I've so just a reason to resent it, don't, good Vaudois, involve yourself, for that villain. Confinement has a little terrified the cousin and may doe the same by this. Are we to suffer him to sell land and turn the money to another use than paying our debt and then take what security he will give? No! No! Then we must doe the same by all other abusive servants. Say what you will to him till next post, but my own thoughts are rigour. And, after the letter I writ him, to think himself above writing and acknowledging his faults! It shall make him sensible the law is in my hand and that, from a friend, I can become an enemy. For may I never find mercy, nor justice, from mankind if I bate that £600 or one farthing. Your kindness in this as well as other affairs my pupil and self must ever acknowledge. Our gaudy Chancery days are att end. We must walk wearily and tread sure. I wish my aunt would keep her promise. She's much in arrear. I am sorry that Mill's illness increased. Her sisters are by me and very well. are all your servants. They have been 4 days att this week, which they are all delighted with. They send you their duties. for the old subject; the account of the Durham exploit in entertaining the Beaus. and are valiant men. Could they so courageously take a boy of 9 years old prisoner, what would they doe in a field of battle? Had I such sons, they shoud not stay att home now the common enemy threatens us. I hope the Querrys, that I hear are dispersed over the nation, have retch you. They are very shrewd. I see one of each and hear Mr. and the of had sent them. You don't, I hope, despair of your namesake's election. His mama, I hear, will spend freely. God send him success. You, by my 's letter, would hear of a lady under examination. I can, on that head, only add she is discharged, and the writs for a new parliament, I hear, will bear date the 20th instant; that Lord is to be Lord , Lord president and some seem to think Lord will command your fleet. Sir Jenings, they say, will keep in. Both parties love him so, that they join in choosing him att his borough, and yet both own him a tight Whig. If I hear more in the evening, shall add a P.S. In the meantime will only desire you to inform me if Sir Delaval is in the country and how his letters are direct'd. Ask no question to me. I must own business must not be neglect'd, and the thing has long depended. Adieu. I salute your spouse. When lies she in? This family are your servants and so am I to your mama and sister Alice, but more particularly the Vaudois' ... Cousin Smithson writ to me to desire her spouse might be in our affairs, had we any. What say you?

column46: London. Sept. 5, 1710. As the contents of your last required consideration, so it is travelled into Hertfordshire and you must wate its return for an answer. As this has happened I once hoped I might have given the Vaudois a letter of only congratulation on the birth of his son, which I sincerely wish him, and the mama, joy of; as also her a good and speedy recovery; but my well designed compliment was spoiled by two visitors I had this morning, viz. Mr. Oldner and Linskell, with a loud complaint of our coals, which are so bad and small that they won't go of. told me as he'd loaded att Stella always he wished to continue it, but now the coal-burn mixture was so great, and the coals withal wrought so small, that they would not go of here; that besides they were mixed with a few of Bensham or Team, if not Wm. Cotesworth's, what he had often complaind, but in vain; that he, the next voyage, would up to Lowry, and, if the coals proved no better, he and several customers must leave us, but here they went of he'd tell me and beg I'd use my authority with the servants, for Johnson's answer was, he was by you commanded to obey Cotesworth's orders and that was the thing. I told him I was heartily sorry to hear this . That the coals this voyage all over might be worse, I doubted not, for the coals we had been forced to work during the time they played the fool and laid idle in town, must be sold and they must blame themselves for that. That we were forced to work to keep the pittmen free of the keelmen, they had spirited up to rebellion, and the fitters with them. I know all your tricks though I come not to the Gate. I will assure you I will use my endeavours to have you pleased next voyage, but I can't promise. Though I'm the commander of the Master's affairs, every servant thinks himself above observing my orders, and no body more so than your friend , who has never, like other fitters, given me a line since the rebellion, though he may justly believe I know it. But when he was wanted was always gone to his country house. I observe this the more, because formerly I knew of him how things went. But the last letter I writ att Mr. Oldner's request was as to a servant, which I took not myself to be. That, as to Cotesworth, I had appointed him over the servants that I might have some intelligence and know how things were; that Johnson and he were so great enemies I was sure he would sell none of his coals, and if we mixed with or Team I wondered they sold not better. That I feared mixed elsewhere or he'd give an account, as other servants did, of what ships loaded and with what coals, which he would not comply to. That masters, I supposed, cried out too, but he could mixed with his own. "And so", said I, "My friend, if thou coudst but tell what a life I've amongst them, you'd pity me, but your cry is loud now you have no gift and the fitters a constant salary". "I", said Mr. , "Madam you really have hit the thing, but I must join with my friend. Your coals were never so bad since I knew them". "Mrs. Anne", says , "Thou must govern or the squire is ruined". "I play", says I, "The devil att this distance and you see it won't do. I think, I must come play it amongst them. However, I will do what I can for you now". Good Vaudois, as this is like to be the last voyage this year, I beg we may go of with what credit we can, in hopes next year of success. Recomend it to Mr. Cotesworth from ... I salute your family.

column46: Sept. 28th, 1710. I am uneasy not to have heard of the Vaudois for sometime. I, one time, fear the illness of his spouse prevents his writing. Att others, I fear thy letters, which are opened, are lost. However it is, I take the first opportunity of acquainting you I the bill of £62-12s-3d and shall pay it to my sister for Jacky's use. Pray send no more. I'll live on creditt till I can say your letters are not opened and you see my old seal, unbroke, come to your hands. I should be concerned att this usage, did I not reflect it was for the improvement of the ignorant. For a free air is now amongst us, and that so often complaind of nicety of the English, laid aside, for a more familiar correspondence. Pardon this digression. (Now I've to submit passively to fate and let the Church doe what it will, but touch my lands) and tell Harry Waters, Mr. Dove never had notice the bill was drawn on him, though he's paid it. All here are well. Our little one will receive a name this week. I wish good news from you and as much as you please of our own affairs, but no politics, I charge the Vaudois, whose friends here live att ease and now, I may say, enjoy themselves. The family salute you and spouse. So dos ... I wish my godson success. I have not time to write a larger letter. The mail stays. Therefore can only thank you for yours, which I since this was writ and that I wish my cousin a speedy recovery and that my service may be returned my godson whose loss I . This family salute you once more. I'll over Wm. Cotesworth. Yours came unopend.

column39: The Correspondence of Sir James Clavering. Ed. by H.T. Dickinson. Gateshead: Surtees Society. 1967. Surtees Society Publications Vol CLXXVIII.
column46: London. Oct. 31st, 1710. My hurry has been so great since I went back into the country and returned to town that I have now an opportunity of thanking you for two letters. I had writ last post had not sister Cowper sent for me to her, before she left the town. I am heartily concerned to hear your spouse is still so weak. She has my best wishes for a speedy and perfect recovery. I begging this in the morning before I can give you the sentiments of my steward in regard to our pupil's affairs, so shall begging with my own. I am sorry you could not send me a copy of my own and I fear you will have no opportunity. It must only be handed amongst the Torys. I have, sometime ago, raised that set of liars southwards, as I've intimated to the lady by this post; but you are not quite in the secret I find. It is Tom and , who first said it was a reflection upon the prelate and lady, but as yet could not be made out. I find the other raised. The lady and Duke have quarrelled about the Duke's warmth, so I've thanked her and told Sir that ingratitude to my memory may be worse to him than all the services that those 2 men can do for him. Let us comfort one another, good Vaudois. Mine can't be made scandal magnatum so I keep up my whigish philosophical resolution and the courage of Robin Walpoole, who is the person I copy after. Capt. Jumper's letter, writ by Lord Orford's command, the Post-Boy printed. If mine have the same fate, I shall take it for a great honour to succeed so great a man. Yet you and I are in better circumstances than Mr. Tong, who I'm told is to be suspended for calling Sir lady, att the election, " ". If the priest have that liberty, sure the liberty, laity, that depend not on them, may take it. But I abhor that name and I can't tell you the takes it not to herself nor so meant, and as for copies there was one att the High sometime ago. Innuendoes and forced constructions are the only means left them; and I only desire you will give my service to my godson, whose indispositions I am sorry for and whom I desire this may not be a matter of concern. Were I not once in 4 or 5 years to do something extraordinary, I should not be remembered amongst that set of vipers. I shoud be glad to see you, but not on the account you mentiond. My sister come this night to town to look a house. They met not with one when last in town. Lord Keeper comes into theirs. Your friend, young Hetherington, is advanced to be Deputy Purse Bearer in the room of Roberts, who sometime since caned the Boy. I can only, on that subject, add that that new lord is resolved to follow the steps the other trod. The Chancery is to be kept in the same manner. Mr. Cowper is the 2d man, without the bar, called of, which the Torys . Now to my pupil. The reproof you've given Lowry and Allen are just. But permit me to tell you, as I have leave from my steward, so I must beg you will order and command the waggon-men, who run their over the staith or who were the cause of their neighbours misfortunes, to be discharged without any delay. For, shoud we once pardon this petty treason against us, we shoud always have them plotting our ruin. Wholesome severitys the Torys will allow, because it is doctrine, and let us begging here. As soon as I can get your letter of account from sister Cowper I will personaly wait on my master. Under that pretence, for the following reason, Sanderson has often told me that we could hope for no better security from than the remainder of a mortgage your has of Mr. Widdrington, which I like not. Therefore to prevent any mistakes I will discourse him myself and not trust it to Sanderson.

column46: London. Dec. 12th, 1710. I readily lay hold this opportunity of writing, though it be to trouble the Vaudois, that I may convince him my late silence was no disrespect. Know then, that amongst all the proposals has made to repay us, none seems so fair as that assigning over to us his part of the Duke's lease, wherein your Papa is concerned, for a security that in 6 months he shall pay in the money, in case the master approve of it. Sanderson has therefore writ to Mr. Gowland this post, to desire of him to go to your Papa, to inquire and look into those deeds, and, with your Papa's permission, to send us copy's of what will be neccessary, which I hope you may venture to intercede for, on our behalfs, that we come to some conclusion with that worthy . I have no news for you. Therefore I will get this franked as the only way I have to excuse the trouble given by the Vaudois' most humble servant ... I beg a humble service to your spouse.
Honest Jamie, pray thee do me the same and believe me to be your friend, . I hope Madame Governance has recovered the fright the Alderman putt her in.

column46: London. December 21st, 1710. Since my silence fills the Vaudois' brains with chimeras, I will for the future take what care I can to prevent it, (att least till the Parliament has doubled the price of letters as it is at present talked of). You taxs me with owing a thing I assure you I am ignorant of. So soon may the innocent be thought guilty! Why do you give creditt to all our foolish northern reports, especially to one the world ought to have been weary of some years since. However I have many thinks to return the good Vaudois for his kind wishes. Therefore will not disown that my head these 2 or 3 last years has run much after a lady's, but the person, whom my inclination lead me to think of, was a North . This year he's forfeited my warm heart by voting for the new Lords returned to and now I've fixed it on a Whig bully in hopes of better success, though his wife is yet living, being I can neither speed with widowers nor bachelors. That part of your last, that relates to business, I will reffer to another opportunity. That's after I have discoursed my steward. So will fill this with the transactions of the British as I hear them. I will first begin with good Lord Wm. , who in the committee carried his Election, though his council did what they could to give him up and my good cousin Grizill said he hoped in God the House would root him, when it was reported to them. Lord had near 50 votes the majority, therefore you can't say his namesake was a little partial. The next day the late Chancellor, late Chief and the two secretaries were roasted on account of the Bewdley Charter, which argued in before Sir Holt, the Queen and Council, before it was granted, and, after that, confirmed by the last Parliament, by which Comodore Cornwall sat the last . I need only say that Mr. Lechmere was returned by the new charter and Mr. Winninton by the old. Mr. Freeman of opened the cause and all the rhetoric that could be mustard, was, on this occasion. Att last Mrs. Stotes' Mr Shippen said, it was arbitary and illegal and tended to the distroyeing the constitutions of Parliaments, that an humble address shoud be presented to her to repeal the Charter. This was carried 213 against 53, with leaving out the first word, though one certain considerable man shoud say it was the most arbitary and illegal proceeding ever heard of, save the business of Edmunds, for which Dr. Harris and poor Piershouse lost their places. The condemned the Charter, spoke much to the memory of Sir Holt, never mentioned Lord Cowper, though he made him . Sir was glad to see the face of a British Parliament, the former one looking like military ones. This reminds me of a pleasant whims of your Richmond representative , who, it is said, came into the house and aloud said, "I much go into the Court of Request to try if I can meet a face I know, for by God I know not one here". The Whigs pleaded hard and home on the behalf of their late friends, Sir Jekyll, Mr. , &c., and honest Walpole, who, when he'd said all he could, told them, if they past that vote, it was branding the memory of one great man, endeavouring to blott the character of the greatest living and it was to him - , and so made a low bow and sat down. I am glad to hear my girls are well and, when I've seen my steward, I will answer your proposal. Betty, poor girl, had last Sunday, two violent fits of her astmah, but is now well again, by the help of the apothecary only. Jacky is come and proves a bully on the Whig side. Give me leave to trouble with a story relating to him. Att Eaton the school is divided and . Jacky was one day engaged fighting a Tory boy and Lady Oglethorp came and bid him give over. Jacky pursued his quarrel so she called him names, and told him she'd box him if he gave not over. came up, but mist her blow. This, you may believe, fired Johny, who turned and gave her a severe blow on the face and bid her a Popish hussy, putt her child in the warming-pan and carry it the Queen and make the nation believe it was hers. I've scarce left room (to tell you I write to Lady this post about Mr. Wright's advice) nor to give the services of this family to you, to whom I am ...
Pray send to Goo. or Tom Hall and either will settle my account with you. I have not my books so can't inform further than that I am indebted to the concern only £5 this last year.
