column46: London. Dec. 30th, 1710. This is the first week of our having a coach to visit withal (my uncle being but just returned out of Yorkshire), which business has these 2 post prevented my writing to the Vaudois. And, though I'm invited out to dinner, in order to spend the whole day, I will spare some small time to tell you, that if you continue your thoughts of the manner proposed to send our girls, tic was is approved of here; and whatever agreement you make with the servant shall be punctually performed; and whenever you think it convenient to send 'em we shall be glad to receive them. As to the purchase you mention, if it is what you think convenient, we must acquaint the master. For the court, you know, is to direct us how the money is to be disposed of. now works himself into what is of no use to him. He's angry I am not content, nor don't approve of his management, and wish the rest of the money may be as well account'd of. thinks it a great , after his services to the family, that I shoud scruple his anuity or charge him more than he likes. I vow I think by his expressions his troubles some time confound his thoughts. As soon as Mr. Gowland give the account of that lease, we shall proceed as far as possible. I have no news to send you. The disgarded officers and the is all the talk. Some say a conformity bill will be brought in soon, but time must prove that. Consider I am to dress, therefore excuse hast in ... This family salute you. So do I, my cousin. I am to tell you from my steward that he spends this day upon a dull whisk invitation, with the gentlemen at the end of the row, if he can get.

column39: The Correspondence of Sir James Clavering. Ed. by H.T. Dickinson. Gateshead: Surtees Society. 1967. Surtees Society Publications Vol CLXXVIII.
column46: London. Jan. 16th, As I have always been famous for contradiction it will be no surprise to the Vaudois to tell him my Christmas rambles begun, when Christmas was ended. I had Turkey feast to attend and a whig play, which occasiond my not sooner thanking the Vaudois for his good wishes and New Year's Day letter, but the telling him also I rejoice Milly, and now Jenny, are so well got over those 2 dreadful diseases, small pox and measells. You take me, I perceive, to be a new acquaintance of a worthless, I shoud say worthy, divine. Pass not so hard a sensure on me, I desire. I knew so many more of that robes than's good, that I avoid them now as much as possible, but would sooner go to hear their doctrines than follow their practice. News, I know, you will expect. I know nothing of Commons. My mind runs after Lords and great men. You must have heard Lord is gone to Vienna with the thanks of the Lords for his great services in Spain, and Lord Gallaway, Lord Terlawly, and poor Stanhope sensured, without leave to produce a paper by way of defence. This is not all the surprising scene. The Lords of the Council are in the same manner, for the advice by which Spain was lost, and consequently Toulon. A majority of 20 against them and when called on to deffend themselves their mouth were tied, and, without the leave, they could not divulge the councils. Upon which the white staffs were detached to know her pleasure, who graciously gave them leave to discover all. The was then a cabinet man, and generously sensured himself. Mr. Harley was then Secretary, and it was then a mixed ministry. Lord Lindsay came to the Whigs, when he see the speed the others made. The Bishop of Winchester is with the distressed. Lord Ossulston, the of Litchfield, the of , Lord Pembroke, and that glorious honest youth, Lord Lincoln, who has nothing but a pension to depend on, and vote for his country. I've heard a bird whisper he would not loose thereby. Pray God it may be true. Now the managers of this are, as I hear a-visiting, Duke , Duke , Lord Scarsdale, Lord North, &c.; men of worth, who are indefatigable in the service of there country. Shoud I now be sensure, I should value myself so much, that I shoud scarce know how to behave myself. Friend, I wish you joy of your idle life. Be of good cheer. What has been, may be, the Torys and papists say. Who knows who may be sensured and who thanked? But I must conclude. Compagny to pass the evening are come in. Adieu. My best wishes attends your spouse, and believe me ... My uncle and aunt salute you. Duke , I fear, is a time server. He voted against Lord Gallaway.

column39: The Correspondence of Sir James Clavering. Ed. by H.T. Dickinson. Gateshead: Surtees Society. 1967. Surtees Society Publications Vol CLXXVIII.
column46: London. Feb. 13, 1711. When I've scearcht my pocket and find a letter of the good Vaudois from Richmond, yet unanswerd, I wish for my own sake I had not been so exact in looking to the dates of those letters that lye by me. However I will pass it by in silence (as there's nothing material in it) and come to that dated of the 30th , in which you complain of want of health. But could I believe you so much Tory, to passively submit to the peal, you mention, when you returned from killing a brace of hares, my compassion for you would seas. Yet, as you have renounced politics and talk so passively, I don't well know what judgement to make. You may, for all that, resist and be for the Church. Though this may seem an objection, yet to show you I believe you still Whig, (though you may be raised out of the of Peace) and so moderate in your censure and revenge, that, as you desire, I may join with you in taking some on my steward. Let me know what you propose and I will, if I can, assist you therein. I am concerned to hear you are so perplexed as to threaten some with the Peace. Your reports I think I shall contradict at the end of this letter, and, whenever I do change my name, I shall not disown it. Till then, believe not what you hear. I, perhaps, can guess why all this and why my friend Vaudois is so teased. Nothing of that kind, I can assure you, has prevented my not writing sooner. I have been out of order and can't now say I am perfectly well, and holding down my head is troublesome. I hear Lady Clavering gives Doll up for author of her news. How comes Doll by the secret, whom I've not seen her, I don't know the day when, though I must att the same time own I'm the faulty person? This may serve to convince you, who are a reasonable man, of the little creditt is to be given to the world, who are always making and breaking matches. I'm of opinion, as long as the world marries me, I shall never change my state of life. Nay, I don't know but I was as near it of my Christening day as I am now. Charles Sanderson tells me by my steward, for he won't come near me, that he's yet had no account of Mr. about that lease I writ so long ago of to you. Now the first, I fears, a canary bird, so wish you could spur up the last, that I might see the and come to some end of our affairs. They fret me and plague me to death, for I believe we shall never get farther. So those parts of your letters must yet remain unanswerd. I am glad the girls are coming, by which I shall be free of the troublesome questions of those here. As to Mr. Bourchier's gold, it is only the peace that lapped up and writ on for him. As you've renounced politics for once, I once take you att your word and so will conclude in assuring you I am ... I salute my cousin. I've lately received a letter from Mr. Poyen, who desires Mr. Bernardeau and he may be chapman for some lead, which my sister and I agree to. They will speak to you of it.

column39: The Correspondence of Sir James Clavering. Ed. by H.T. Dickinson. Gateshead: Surtees Society. 1967. Surtees Society Publications Vol CLXXVIII.
column46: London. Feb. 20th, I had resolved before the Vaudois' came to hand, to give him the trouble of a letter by this post, to acquaint him that of Friday last my steward received a letter from George Hall to desire an enlargement of the time for paying in the money; that if he sold the estate now it would be to great loss, and as he had ever behaved himself with the utmost respect to us all, he hoped we shoud consider his poor family, and stuff to this effect, which did not a little surprise me. Now, good Vaudois, consider it was att your intercession I so long forbore, and I now demand of you a hearing. It is not with the consent of the master we have proceeded in this affair. Therefore, as the time of payment is come and the money no nearer to us than formerly, I will neither let you nor myself be laid liable to inconveniences that may attend us on this occasion, and therefore request you to proceed against the said Hall in the most vigorous manner the nature of the affair permits, for shoud we grant six months longer we shoud have the same request att the end of that time, and so to the world's end. But , in case when this is read to Hall, he desires a forbearance till he receives Mr. Liddell's answer, this is all he's like to have, for the has been a house-keeper near a week and is to ill still to answer any letter. So you must excuse him to that person of so excellent behaviour that must move our compassion, but I will leave him to you, in hopes you'll do us all justice, and tell you, I sent yours to the sick, who, in return, desire his service and to tell you it is 10 days ago since he gave you notice your mares were set forwards and before this reaches you he hopes they are safe in your custody. I heard a week ago they were got well to Stamford. As to other matters you'll give me leave to be silent till I can see and trouble my steward with them; save the girls, which will be heartily welcome and hope come perfectly safe, and prevent the going forward of some people's discourse. Your other directions shall be observed. Had I any news I'd send none to one who stiles himself a Tremor. But will undertake to chide one for never naming wife nor bairns when they write. Adieu. I to your spouse and self ... is now a merry divided town. Their inferior representative had att supper lately the great Dr. and six other parsons. Their only wanted the old woman to make it fit for a Gunpowder plot.

column39: The Correspondence of Sir James Clavering. Ed. by H.T. Dickinson. Gateshead: Surtees Society. 1967. Surtees Society Publications Vol CLXXVIII.
column46: Feb. 24th, Whether I am my own or your 's secretary I leave to the Vaudois to determine. I am first therefore to tell you, from that gentleman, your cloths are bespoke. But, as you lately have assumed the title of Tremor, he's took you att your word and made your new habitt of the Church nor Republican colour, but betwixt the two. Now, Sir, I am farther to tell you, if you expect this suite complete you must send up by the return of the post the measure of your head, for that, your vows, he brought it not out of the north with him. I come now to my pupil's affairs, therefore shall range the objections in order. As to the fitting out ships, we have parts in, my steward tells me it is unavoidable or we must dispose of them. However, I think you'd doe well to call on Mr. Johnson for an account of those ships, we have parts in, and desire att the end of every year he would bring to account, who we have profitt of and who not. 2dly, it is looked on here to be the only way to dispose of our keels. The article of repairs, I observe, runs very high. The properest way therefore to dispose of them is to send for a carpenter to purchase them of us and, if he will advance us anything in the price, we shall oblige ourselves to take them of him, for such a number of years as you think fit, att the common price of keels, and so take out our debt, if he can't pay the money down. Wm. Cotesworth will assist you in this affair. 3dly, I can but commend the Vaudois for the just objections he made to the negotiating bills. The salary is now so good I shoud have thought that article might have been omitted. But supposing that for the future he will make good the master's notes, we shall allow it. But if he insists upon it, that it is what's allowed to other fitters, we must comply rather than quarrel, which I think a hard sentence. Lastly, as for the premium to masters, as our coals were bad this year I fear we must allow it. However, you may cavil a little on that score, but not break and assure them that for the future, as this new seam is so hopeful, no such thing shall be allowed of hereafter. For the agreement att the Gate, nothing can be done for us there till that affair of the last year is settled with 'em. It would get air and turn to our disadvantage, so we must be dormant and wait with patience till a fit opportunity. You are desired to be, and advice you to be, cautious of what is said concerning the coal trade. As you will perceive, by the 's to the , things have already took air that may lead us into trouble, and if Mr. come up, as projected, it must be given out he comes upon his own business. It is so late I can only see to add my best service to your spouse, and assure you I am ... My steward charges me with his services to you and family. Mr. send word our security is to be Mr word, that all the money shall be paid before May day.

London. March 3d, As I had nothing material to impart to the Vaudois I differed writing till I could give him an account our girls were safely arrived and in very good plight. had as good a journey as the season would permit, and from York had my uncle Allanson's , who has been kind beyond expression. I've left the 4 sisters together and Mrs. Caverley has took a lodging for Mrs. Milly near her so that my servant or one of theirs shall always be with her. I must return you thanks for your dispatch to Mr. . In my last I told you the word of a gentleman was to be our security. Since then, till this afternoon, could not set face of Sanderson and I have rung him such a peal that I believe he won't be fond of coming again. He denied neglecting us, either now or att any other time, and he'd write to Mr. and and demand further security or take him up upon contempt of the court. I would neither hear nor answer, and we parted in a huff. For here I take a resolution on this head I must advise with your , who I apprehend will give over writing, in case anybody will ease him. His papa is out of order, therefore your letter is dispatcht to me, that I may tell you the measure of the child's head was not enclosed in the letter as you mention and that caps or hats are chiefly used, but he will waite your further orders as to this commission. I am also commanded from the same hand to tell you that ought to be gently used in this affair. If it be a thing of moment and worth prosecuting, then doe it, but, if it is a trifle, he will take snuff at it and make it a handle to leave the concern. And where are we then? And in regard to Hall, we both agree that if Mr. Headword will give us security, that he takes the debt upon him, and he shall have 1/2 a year time to pay it in. This is the resolution here, if you agree thereto. I can't conclude without telling you I was yesterday surprised with a made to me, to contribute something to bury Dr. Durant withal, who dyed merely of want of necessaries, unknown to his wife or any friend. She was to come up to him this summer, believing he got a good living in town. But this is to melancholy a subject to enlarge upon and therefore shall only add my best to your spouse and assure you I am ...

column39: The Correspondence of Sir James Clavering. Ed. by H.T. Dickinson. Gateshead: Surtees Society. 1967. Surtees Society Publications Vol CLXXVIII.
column46: . April 3d, 1711. I was prevented last post by compagny from returning the just thanks that are due to the Vaudois for his good salmon. I affirm it to be good for I've lived upon it ever since and treated my neighbours, who are whigs, with it also. Your health and family's we drink daily. How sister will prove I know not. She run away and left it and stays some short time in the country. So you must yet waite with a little patience. Pray, good Vaudois, why will you chide me for not giving you an account of Sir health? During his indisposition I believe a litre went to and every post; at least to the one place so I could not fancy you could continue a stranger to his indisposition or recovery. All I can say is that he kept house to receive visits. We friends in this row went to breakfast and he looked so well then, I thought might venture out, but he confined himself to be visited, as he was , by all the ladies of his acquaintance; and some few days ago ventured out, to return some of them. So now you may depend he is on the mending hand. The other contents of yours must not answer till I see my steward in the evening. In regard to the coal trade, Mr. is to be sent to the Gate and the result you shall have from either him or your . But, consider, this is a time of great difficulty. In your affair I will engage no further. I avoid it as you do politics. Next am to tell you Mr. is to write to somebody, his name I know not, to press the payment of that money of Lord before he leaves the country; and if Gibson do not perform covenants we must try if anybody can hold him. As to the map, we readily agree to your proposition and the thinks it, as I perceive by him, the cheaper way. The management of Farm is left to you to do as you think fit; which answers all the material parts of your letter, so adieu. The Bell is going about, and can only add the service of this family to yourself and spouse, and to I am ... The is both your servants. A lottery there will be, but nothing is yet come to a resolution concerning it. I inquired.

column39: The Correspondence of Sir James Clavering. Ed. by H.T. Dickinson. Gateshead: Surtees Society. 1967. Surtees Society Publications Vol CLXXVIII.
column46: London. April 10th, 1711. Being alone I begin my letter, though I can make it but a confused thing till I've seen my sister about the State Lottery, and Mr. Wright, who I expect att 7 a clock. Therefore in the meantime shall return the Vaudois thanks for his kind letter by yesterday's post. I need not, I hope, tell him how much I pity him with the masters and fitters. The of them perfectly crack my skull, but the word Patience is ever and anon whispered in my ears as if 't could have an effect where the signification of it was never understood. But as they fitters are far behond my comprehendtion, as viewing a staith when there's a flood and the like, well may they then saw for a mixture of better coal elsewhere. You are therefore desired to propose to Capt. Little, that our fitters take part of Team top coal and mixed with ours so, and all go by the name of Stella. That if the mixture shoud not give content Sir would be no sufferer, if otherwise, both parties will thereby receive an advantage, their woarse coals going of with our good ones. His answer to this, return to me, as I doe to you the enclosed Bill, which will not be paid, and am ordered to beg of you to see it deducted from the Governor's account, who last post had a complaining letter from both and Waters. Sister is just gone and bids me tell you that all their money is on the Land Tax att 9 or 10 p. cent. For the lottery scheme, her master has not seen it, but as soon as he dos she will send me his opinion of it and, though he's a disbanded courtier, his sentiments shall be transmitted to you. He dos not perfectly sink the creditt, for what money he has the Government makes use of it, and I hope he now receives as great a salary, all things then considerd (that then attended his place and now the double interest), as he did then, and has his liberty into the bargain. True it is my selling out of the Bank made as much noise here than amongst Torrys, as 'thas done with you; but I met several there and advised them to buy in, for I'd sold, not liking the hands we were falling into. Are you, good Vaudois, weary of an ignorant life that you desire news. Since it is your own request I will tell you. The town says Mr. Harley is to be Earl of March and Lord Treasurer, Earl Powlett, Master of the Horse, and the other Comissioners turned to grass for the summer. Lord Dartmouth is to be Master in Sir Franklin's room and Lord Mar marries Mrs. Hill and is to succeed in the Secretary's place; and after the rising of the all that ever bore the odious name of Whig must turn out. How I shall laugh then, to see the mungrells, time servers &c., scratting their knavish sow's crown. Revenge is really sweet. Yesterday I see a letter from , £100 more was to be paid Mr. Gowland as last Saturday, £100 in a few days, and the rest att Whitsuntide when he received the money for his estate att Shinkley . I wait to hear the first confirmed by next post or I'll proceed for his contempt of the court. Give yourself no uneasiness about the monster of mankind as you call him. The Holy Father has been pressed to receive him into his Church, but as he'd done a public benefit so he ought to have a public reward, and refused all that spoke in the fool's behalf. Mr. Wright has been here and showed me the original paper betwixt Sir and my papa. I told him I perceived there was an account of some coals that Sir refused to pay, and, till that was ended, I could not order the payment. I made my story a little confused, but told him as soon as that was agreed shoud order the money, but must beg the original to be shown the Master. He told me whenever I pleased to command he would waite on him with it, and so we parted. My papa kept him in money always. What allowance your made I know not. You are to Mr. Poyen about the coal bill and our mixture , which was read a second time his day and committed to a private committee. I can see to add no more than my service to your spouse and assure you I am ... The salutes you all. He was informed by Mr. , who said he had from good hands heard that you, Mr. Ellison, Mr. Spearman and himself were turned out of the Commission of Peace.

column39: The Correspondence of Sir James Clavering. Ed. by H.T. Dickinson. Gateshead: Surtees Society. 1967. Surtees Society Publications Vol CLXXVIII.
column46: London. April 26th, 1711. This I send to your own habitation not knowing which way you design to steer, though you say south-west first. In that I resemble our kinsman, who when he was showed and south never knew the other 2 points. However, I hope this may come safe to the Vaudois' hands, that he may know how heartily concerned all here were att the account Mr. gave of your indisposition (and he as much rejoiced to hear of your recovery). Without asking leave of your spouse I must chide you when you could be so foolish to catch cold with physic. (The next time you undergo that operation I hope your spouse will lock you in your room). What had become of us had you had the ill fortune you've had so fair a chance for? In a just regard to your own young family, as well as your friends , and those abroad, you ought to have a particular care of your health. And by way of punishment for this I will pronounce neither maids, wives, nor widows, you merited a visit of condolence from, as our had in his long indisposition. He was in your case since and sent us word one day he was very full of pain by the jolting of a hackney coach, and that attending the coal committee would undo him. I sent him word by signeur, that in his last illness I pitied him, but could not doe so now. Since a hackney coach did not agree with him, he might have kept his own horses and not have sold them, at least till the Committee had ruined the coal-owners. Upon that subject I am to add att night. Therefore shall only tell you the fatigue agrees well with Sir Harry. Of Sunday he seemed to be very cheerful and well. This account I give you because you say can hear seldom of others. The Bill I received, and your has given it to Peter, who has had a letter from concerning it. Now, Vaudois, in regard to our pupil. I remember in one of your letters you tell me that half micksture is as much as you can allow and some masters are honest enough to own the coals very good, were it not for the outcry att the Gate and I conjecture assisted by the fitters, for in the last fleet some of our own were loaded att Team. Some part that, part ours and the remainder Sir , which I understand not. The , you say, refuses us coals, and Sir Harry, of Sunday, seemed to resent a little that sent some of his keels to be loaded att his staith when the had forbid because he had no coals, and a promise made no keels shoud be sent and yet the next day they went. I could not help saying, Sir, you've no cause of resentment, for, after all, everyone must own that he's a good paymaster, which some of your fitters are not. The anger shoud be from me, whose hired servant he is, and without whose leave he gos to other staiths. However as Sir seems to agree with the by taking no farther notice of the proposal, I hope, as we can't be serviceable to one another in that colliery, it may be soon in our powers to obey Lord pleasure in not mixing coals with anybody. And for Bensham I have a reason to have an avertion too and therefore must inquire what we doe att that staith. The Bill is the devil. It is cooked and cooked till I see coal-burnes are cooked out of the markett for they are to come singly; that's, I say, not to be sold att all , if other clauses dos not throw it out the Bill. Adieu. When he's 14 he shall choose another Madam Guardian, for the complaint to prevent mixtures was made by the Oldners against coalburns and the clause inserted. I'm so mad I care not what's done, so shall reffer till the next post saying any more on that head, save that the fitters are mauld, in case the account passes. I salute your spouse and am ... My story is imperfect, but I'll mend it soon, when I hope may say the Bill is thrown out.

column39: The Correspondence of Sir James Clavering. Ed. by H.T. Dickinson. Gateshead: Surtees Society. 1967. Surtees Society Publications Vol CLXXVIII.
column46: London. April 28th, 1711. I was in so devilish an humour last post I believe you could not make anything of what I writ. Therefore must not omit this post explaining my meaning, which is this, the lightermen complained of coalburn-coales as what they had been great sufferers by; and the mixing of them, as well as others, was an injury to the public. Therefore desired a clause to prevent the mixtures att staiths, for the future, which was granted. The good name given us by this must of necessity, I see, fall very heavy on Jacky and provoked me not a little, knowing how indifferent that colliery is for the markett. But though the Commons shoud pass that act as it is, I hope we shall make friends that either the masters and lightermen shall be also included or that rejected in favour of the owners, by the Lords, which has given me some quiet of mind for the present. But take no notice of this, I beg. Of Thursday your and I were att daggers drawing about Jack's trade, on the account above mentiond. I told him I now see since our fitters found the sweat of coming to his father's staiths, so low in the river, and good coals, they were att Team come nearer (if not up) to proportion, and we short. That since we could have no coals att Team, where Sir was soly concerned, I had my reason to object to Bensham and I was of opinion that Jacky must work his Leadgate so as to make his colliery go singly of, as long as it could, and then do as well as possible. The wagon-way would be saved so far. And in fine I was so weary, that I'd keep my trust no longer than Jacky was 14, to choose some other. The same I repeated to Sir this day, only with this addition, that I would sooner serve him than any in the river, but must serve myself first; that I see a small encouragement would bring my fitters to his service; that when the was concerned for both, I never made any inquiry, I believed him equally just; that now it was the business to promote his only advantage and, therefore, as we were on another foot, I was obliged to be more cautious in those affairs; that since the thought it not feasible to take from Team, I looked upon it as a denial and the more so since he was pleased to be silent on the opinion since it was 1st mentioned. But without his answer I was not satisfied. "I shoud expect the same Sir," said I, "by any who came to Stella". However we parted without a further answer or resolution, till which I really think our fitters must be forbid Team. I always forget to beg of you to keep the account separate of the expense and profitt of the colliery won, so it must go into Chancery, that by that they may judge of the reasonableness of our petition and upon what ground they grant us any other. This I shall mention to Peter. Can you tell me how that £40 dispute on coals is betwixt us and Sir John, and what more we have to deduct, that we may end that account? I received a letter from , wherein he says he has paid Mr. Gowland £350 already and had Johnson's hand for paying the 50 in dispute, with the interest, and the other money shoud be paid in May when he the money for Shinkley estate, if I'd forbear him so long. I've ordered Mr. Sanderson to waite on the Master to know his answer, and that shall be returned him, for I won't make myself liable to the debt indeed. Adieu. The is by us. He and this family salute you and your spouse. I am to you both ...

column39: The Correspondence of Sir James Clavering. Ed. by H.T. Dickinson. Gateshead: Surtees Society. 1967. Surtees Society Publications Vol CLXXVIII.
column46: London. May 11th, 1711. The last post would acquaint you I'd writ as civil a letter to Lady as she did to me, in your regard of your worship, and wherein I told her you shoud conclude the account, that you att once might right Jacky and yourself in matters now depending, which will I fancy grate them, and not a little, and, as soon as I receive my master's order, you shall have it communicated. As I'm engaged tomorrow I begging this the day before, that I may bring it so near a conclusion that my apointement may not prevent my returning you sincere thanks for the favour of your last letter and saying somewhat of the posture of my pupil's affairs, in regard to the well cooked up Bill att present in the Commons house. The advantage of it, the world must plainly see, was only to a few, and as the Oldners did us the honour to name our coals as base mixtures before the Committee, I can't be so much imposed on, but to think this must be of pernicious consequences to us. Though, thanks be, the clause is so worded everybody will be sufferers thereby. I'm a true collier and must rejoice when the shoes pinches any of the trade; and, give me leave to say, as good a lawyer in my own affairs as one you lately conversed with, as to what were distinct collieries, and who, to you, was against that mixing clause, though to others of the trade, whose letters I've seen, could object against nothing but the enacting clause. This I call blowing hot and blowing cold and must form my judgement of him as I've received the several copies of his. Not having practised the law I can't penetrate further into the merits of one I'm not acquainted with. Nor dos hearsay affect me on his score. He seems to think he knows my Lady Ann and has every since protection time. But I leave him for one we are more concerned with. Mr. , I doubt not, you look on as a sincere friend and the public happy in his services, but Mr. Cotesworth I admire of all mankind. Since he came to town have seen him but one half hour, and since the Bill. He was never the person that came to ask if I liket or disliket it, or any part, or to say, "Madam, you must look about. Your coals were made the foundation for that clause. I am in general and therefore must not show myself in the interest of a particular person, but some care ought to be took". No, I'm a female and consequently not capable of understanding further than that some one day, betwixt this and Monday , he leaves the Town. must receive him and, with some turn, he shall give his thread of discourse. I shoud fancy we have vast obligations, but I've made my silent observations and am entirely of what I formerly surmised; so much that my eye shall never be of him and, for his sake, att Xmas next I shall begging, that as we pay punctually, so shall all do to us and then everyone pay the balance of their account (by which means I shall, I hope, leave you in a good state, though you are pleased to make me a great and undeserved compliment on that score). To what I've said will be alleged the spoke. It is true, he did it att &c., but could any one believe he was to press the thing farther. No, Sir Harry had the prospect then of receiving too great an advantage, for his son, in duty, to appear against it or to espouse warmly the cause of the opposers. I can see traps laid and lying, to swallow undeserving persons in. But I believed your so just, when steward to both familys, that now he's out of the one's service nobody shall be able to allege against him, that by his eagerness to serve his pupil, one may conjecture he's been too negligent of the other. I know few of his honesty in the world, but to prevent what may be said, I desire to manage for my son a little; and a virago I know I shall be called, but I care not. I am conceited this London spoils us and fancy I could understand my trade as well as many coal-owners Mr. has been with. But as the Bill, they tell me, will be lost, that putt an end to all disputes. Saturday. This morning Mr. Sanderson came and, as my presence was not absolutely necessary att the Master's, I gave him his papers and full instructions, upon which this resolution was took. As the writes me, Mr. has writ a on the back of the account for Sir John so sign, which gos down this post, and fittage money is to be deducted, as also money I've out for my lady. But take your £100 and pay the balance, I say, and from me tell her I've no interest att the Gate. So I beg the favour of her to return me a bill of £165, to pay of the upholdsterer, as soon as she can, that I may discharge that debt here I go into Yorkshire and next post she shall hear from me. I've not time to add more, save my service to your spouse, who am the Vaudois' ...

. Nov. 25th, . I was the last post day prevented returning you my thanks for your long letter by endeavouring to get advice for you to ease your concience and I hope effected my design. I met with our old friend, who came to town for three or four days. I laid forth your grievances and received the following private answer. As to , that what he has done won't prejudice the Trustees, for the objections to his account may still be made, and will be allowed by law, notwithstanding the part he has acted. The rest I give, as you desire, for the good of those employed. However you may use roguery as see fit to check him. I had yesterday from Mr. Ord the copies of Newton estate, and shall proceed in that affair. I met one we always consulted in the matter, who tells me that Atkinson putting himself into gaol, with a design to defraud us, will avail him nothing; that for his villainous actions he advised the severest prosecution of the law and that without delay; not only as he deserves it, but as it is absolutely necessary in our case, to convince all employed under us that we are not in jest and neither mean to cheat the infant, nor see him cheated. Johnson's late management has not a little surprised me, but if my friend understands the law, that loophole will not prevent Jacky's having justice done him by the law. Now I am upon this topic, let Piety send me a true estimate of affair, and, if it is overcome, let us proceed to something else. I have not yet received the accounts for the last two years and this is the third year wanting att Xmas. I perceive by you Mr. account are yet unbrought in, which I've often desired you to solicit. If he's not a good , let Piety help him. I spoke to Mr. Sanderson to mention this to him some time ago, but Vaudois, you can best judge of the delay. Only this I will affirm to you, had you complied to what Lord advised you, when in town, this difficulty had been over. He proposed an estimate of all debts owing to Jacky, by whom and upon what score and of how long standing, and beg the direction of the court in suing the several parties, or if the time ellaps, you and my pay the debts to Jacky when att age, for the law will not suffer him to loose it. You best know the reason why you comply not with his advice, but this I will affirm, if you press not the passing of the accounts and the redress of the complaints, if you dye your family is ruined, and if you live 7 years longer you are so yourself. And as you, in kindness to my papa's memory, undertook this, I can't help being concerned to see you act such a prejiduciall part to your young family as well as yourself. If this spur you not, the Guardian must sew the Trustees. I debated this to Mr. Cotesworth when in town, which he may remember. I wish you well settled in your new house since you removed, but I liked the other better. My salutes you, &c. I read him yours and as he only neglected answering the part of the Bill, I fancy I may say, it is come safe or he would have spoke. I am to you and yours a most faithful servant . I will not be excluded serving you upon this remove. I know no more of what you mention than the child unborn and can receive no more prejudice by stirring than Mrs. Smith, for my illness was a cold I got by returning late from my aunt's when she was ill and the Dr. thinks madam too consumptive to bear a cough. That's all.

column46: London. Dec. 16th, 1712. I have been prevented two post of writing to you by the hurry I have been in upon the removal of your girls to Cousin Waite's, which I accomplished last Saturday, much to their (and I hope their friends) satisfaction. I shall proceed to tell you Dan. got well up after a very ill journey. The particulars you will have from himself, I dare say, so will not mention them and only run on to acquaint you with the cause of my spleen a few post ago. I had been to solicit Jacky coming to town this Xmas and though my answer was ambiguous yet I perceived he had committed some great fault and that if they took him, which was uncertain , he was to have no followers, but the bent rather run upon changing his abode when in town. To this I answered, the child, and those concerned for him, vary. I was confident sensible of the obligations they lay under to them upon that score, but if his being longer there was inconvenient, those concerned for him must think of some other place for him; and only desired to know the cause of his disgrace, which was a letter he forged, I fear , last Whitsuntide to excuse his task; but since, as I judge by talk, he's this Xmas to come there, but not to stay so long, which I own I approve, of this I was to say nothing and therefore you must not. As to the accounts, we agree in the abilities of one person employed, but how those merits can be of use, when the accounts are so long refused, is the question. I've often asked my lawyer that, and, it is on this score chiefly, he recomends you to the Chancery. For when arguments, says he, won't prevail, then the fear of a suit from the court will spur him on to the delivery of them and prevent the inconvenience for the future. What remains further to be added is, Vaudois, I am no longer guardian and therefore incapable of serving you. Charles has so long buss'd it about, it can be no secret and, for my part, I resolve to lay all aside. You must not be surprised when I tell you that seeing the great regard my master has for , I've never made mention of his name near twelve months, and I can but suspect it is upon his score my advice to pass the accounts is of so little weight. Besides I've sent so many times to our lawyer to ask that question concerning accounts, that I've met with jesting reproofs, which I believe bear earnest with them; and all won't do; that to make all easy I must give over meddling. I see I've so much fire and quickness for your solicitor, which is a great fault. He'd keep you in his hands and I would have you out. He has a great influence over my , as I could demonstrate were you here (but it is too much for letter). In the business of Atkinson, which I've been by Lord Cowper in, for my won't speak good nor bad to it, so it becomes my particular province and that I believe must see finished for you. As to all others am as ignorant as the child unborn. I am concerned for you and your family, for as you are not in court, if the accounts pass not, you are in worse circumstances than if you'd never desired their protection. My best service to madam, whose comissions shall execute with pleasure and am to yourself ... My salutes you both. This letter to yourself. To James Clavering Esq., att Newcastle upon Tine.

Midsummerday. It is three post att least since I promised my sister Cowper to intercede with you, in her name and that of your daughter Jane, to let poor nurse Wear have her house repaired now this dry weather (and so give no denial). But your Governor's resolution of going down has so fretted me that I am, as to my own health, where I started, though, thank God, I now begging to be easy and I hope in some measure prepared for whatever news I may receive concerning him when in the country. For to be plain with you, Vaudois, I know he is so little his own master, that after the journey and the welcomes succeed, I expect not to see him more, or at least in so miserable a state that death were better. But by reflecting I find your letters have more force than my concern (for I never heard him mention it but once) and that it is you that, as I hear say, occasions this journey. I hope you then will from time to time give me a true state of his condition. I omit the word health because I'm confident he can enjoy none. As I shall always be in expectation of the worst there will be no need of dissimulation in this as you did when you told me you feared such a journey would be of the worst consequence to him. And as soon as you arrive, send for him. What can have happened to make this sudden change when you were expected here again att Michaelmas? Let what will, be the event, you will ever justly comdem yourself if you stick not to Lord Cowper's advice, for that only will govern Mr. Freak. I wish I had the girls' accounts for I want to pay some things for them before I may leave the town. Adieu. I salute your spouse and am Vaudois' ... Madam, from Sir I hear, gos this day, but takes not leave of Lady Ann. You may tell your spouse. To James Clavering Esq., at Lamesley, near Durham.

column46: July 20th, 1714. I was in hopes to have met our friend to have enabled me, as you desired, to give you some advice, but all attempts of that sort have hitherto been vain. This day is dedicated to Mr. Kemp and orders, if he comes, to come for me for I want his opinion on Caverley Pinkney's letter also, to communicate to you. What you say in your last I easily give credit to, for after I have chid you I did not look on you as the sole occasion. I could but observe (though I was not allowed it) that a more secret reason induced, and if you value a character, and if my information be right, you must produce in court all the authorities you have, upon which you ground your aspersion. For, Vaudois, without you can make out you have not defrauded the , your pupil, you'll not have a release speedily. And as you have acted justly I would have you now publicly show it, whatever threats, &c., are used, as you mention, to you. As you ask my opinion I freely give it you, and, as I heard in Street, you, in your last but one, say something of extraordinary thinks you've received from a certain person. Pray what were they for? I'm yet a stranger thereto. The knowledge thereof may be of use to you. I am glad you've disposed of Lowrey's place to Richard Allen. It was always designed him upon the like occasion for many years before my poor father died and what I shoud have solicited for him had I known it sooner. This week your two girls and I go into the country to breath a little fresh air, and where I propose to recover a crazy constitution as far as can be done by one, who every day expects to hear the northern people have welcomed your Governor to the grave or near it. But this to yourself, for my complaints shall not reach one whose joy upon the intended ramble was not to be expressed. Direct yours hereafter to the Maurice Ashley's house in Row and then I shall have them that night or next morning. Adieu. My best wishes attend your spouse from ... Sir or Mr. Gen. will perhaps intertain you with news of Mrs. Smith, therefore I shall be silent.

column46: Augt. 14th, 1714. I've many thanks to return the Vaudois for his kindness to my master and for his diligence in giving me an account of his health. I am glad to find that by experience, the advice of using exercise and living regular, he's sensible conduce to his recovery, or his father and all friends, as well as Doctor, surgeon, and , have so great an esteem for him they would not have pressed anything but what reason convinced them must greatly turn to his advantage. In the terms they did this advice. Pray settle your accounts and come both away, not only to make an end of that troublesome affair, but to intertain yourselves with the coronation of the greatest prince in merit, the universe can boast of. I shoud say somewhat to you upon the late accident of your family, but I'm so lost in the satisfaction of this new government I can think of nothing else. Jamie Crags returned yesterday with the King's thanks to his Parliament and the Regents, and that he and the Prince set forwards next and of Saturday propose to be att the Hague. The Princess is with child and will follow. Robin Walpole moved yesterday to have the troops paid, upon which Speaker declared the motion past with a Latin sentence and then all the vile Whigs laughed. They've also enabled the to pay out of the first aids the £100,000 for the Pretender's head, and are to enact it. This I hope will please you as 'thas us all, and my girls say they only want the Supply Bill you promised them to perfect their joy. I'd a letter from Dan. since I'd yours, full of the accounts I sent and some errors I've committed, but no money nor mention thereof. That I may always write such news is the sincere wish of, Vaudois, ... All round me salute you. So do I your spouse. To James Clavering Esq., at Stow-House.

column46: Augt. 31st, 1714. Your two letters I this moment as I was setting pen to paper to acquaint your spouse, I got Mrs. Ashley to send her, by Robed. Pilin yesterday's the 30 of Augt. carrier, a box directed for Mr. Ralph Mitford, in which is a white popling gown and petticoat linend with a black and white sarcenett, a black and white satin gown for your son Jack. But, as master Tom's vest and tunic was not then come, these first things went in one box, which was no sooner gone than master's things came and were sent in a box by the same carrier and directed as the former. I hope you'll all like them. Calimanco and camblett, I feared, would be too hot for the children, but if you'd have the two hats follow, you must send me word. I'm heartily concerned your spouse is so much out of order. God send her safe in her bed. As to the other particulars of yours I'll return an answer as soon as Mr. Freak comes up, if that will do for you. I'm glad you've begun to meet with some of the errors, and hope this next term will settle all matters to all your satisfactions, for assure yourself it can never be in your power, for the future, to run yourselves into the like inconvenience. When this is once ended you will find yourself entirely att ease. The 21st Mr. York paid me 60 guineas for the use of your three daughters, equally divided, so place it in their accounts. I shall in a little time call upon your for this last small bill of yours. All here att home and next door salute you and your spouse. I'm to both, good Vaudois, ... Our good and glorious king set out but yesterday from Hanover. I can just add Lord office was this day sealed up by the Regency, but he's not turned out. To James Clavering Esq., at Greencroft.

column46: London. August 2d, 1722. Sir, My thanks are greatly due for the favour of yours dated the 27th July and shall heartily rejoice when an opportunity offers to return you the congratulations. I can easily judge, by the vexations such a delay occasioned myself, how anxious it must be to you to continue under the same circumstance. And were it in my power to serve you I shoud readily embrace it, for I had said as much to Mr. Sanderson as I was capable. Elsewhere I've no interest. I bless God I've paid the outmost farthing. Yet shall rejoice to hear, and see, our late pupil meets with greater advantages his new friends. The services, we've done, are past. I can therefore only advice, as I wish the prosperity of you and your family, that you would conclude. I fear you are to expect no quarter; and he's now beginning with the Cole-Ch. Therefore consider if more vexation may not be raised to you thence. I shall rejoice to hear your spouse is in a safe way. The window curtains for the wrought bed were not bespoke. Your other bed is ready and your instructions Mr. Cox will observe as to your chairs, &c. I thank you for your prints and rejoice to hear our good is well approved. My papa has made himself worse by fretting that he could not . I hope he now begings to mend, though very slowly. God preverse his life, so neccessary to his family. I am Sir, ... I'm my cosen's servant.

column46: London. 24th, 1726. Sir, Your obliging letter of the 18th lies before me, with the continuance of your kind wishes for me, which deserve my best thanks. I wish as you doe, am yet a stranger to all but what you mention. am heartily concerned you've met so many vexations and uneasiness. Pray, what provision can the Baronet make for his lady? When he left us, female talk was, that he would have enough for her and the sisterhood, and I ask no questions for conscience sake. Nor shall I dare to name to our friend that's reported our pupil is to be more nearly related to her. The discharge of Wheately surprises me, who after doing so much and being so able a steward, shoud quit. Am heartily glad Alderman Ridley is recovered and the same for our Tom., though I never refflect upon his education with common patience. Yet two lives are better than one. Sir picture is drawn and some say designed for his mama. If my former news was true concerning him, Lady death is a great misfortune. Your commands are always executed with pleasure, to the best of my poor capacity, but I can't allow you have any occasion for what you mention. And let me beg you not to vex so to give you any return of your old complaint. Am not forgetful of my promise on that occasion, as soon as I can get to see the lady. My service attend my cousin and your young folks and believe me ... I thank you for your kind wishes for Isabel. I've just got her out of her chamber to mine.

column46: Oct. 1st, 1726. Sir, I was prevented last post from returning you thanks for the of yours by dining that day out of town. I am heartily concerned for the difficulties you meet with and the uneasiness the treatment, yours mentions, gives you. I hope you know me too well to believe me capable of doing anything to prejudice my friend at any time; and much more after a caution. The same I doubt not may affirm for Doll, if she has not already for herself. Nay, further, am confident are too well known to be applied to on that account. Nor, when the warmth of words are over, I believe the worst part. am infinitely obliged to Mr. York for his discourse to the one brother in presence of the other, who is as extraordinary in his way. My service attends him and my cousin. Two pieces of news two different papers furnish me with this day. The one is journal with the match of Esq. and Mrs. Bright, niece to Col. Little, and one with Sir son and one of Miss Claverings. The other a statute of bankrupt for one Dick, hoastman and fitter, and the persons concerned according to the statute are to apply to Airy. Your thoughts on this will oblige ...

column46: Oct. 13th, 1726. Sir, Am favoured with yours of the 8th and am concerned you shoud return out of order from the sessions. I hope for a better account of you in your next. The came to town on Friday. My Lady, Mrs. Waite, and self, met him at Stevenage according to promise at parting. The world might justly condemn any person that did not defend their legal right, but what title has Mr. Bows to stop our kinsman? I apprehended the coals went through no other grounds than were my old uncle's, which could be let to others, but no way-leave required on the other side. It is nothing new to have weddings in a widow head, but at this time to clear myself must tell you I dined that day out of town and that paragraph was read at table, and none else. At the same time some present said Mr. Bows had shown resentment, when in town, to the spreading the report. My adversaries have got an order on Michealmas-day, that their cause may be heard with mine and depositions, took on one side, serve for the other. Dos this look like accommodation? I understand so little the affairs of your neighbouring corporation that I don't know whether this late choice of a mayor is better or worse for Mr Ridley. am sorry he's so long confined. I wish yours, and the Long Newton family, joy of this little fellow. You won't own it, but our talk still continues yours is increasing. You've told me news, I rejoice at, about my Lord of Landaff's family. I am, Sir, ...
