column46: London. Nov. 29th, 1726. Sir, By this time I fear you've ranked me in the same class with my female neighbour, though I now assure you have been prevented returning the thanks due to you, for your letter from Long Newton, by my winter friend, my cough, which has occasioned my making a perpetual noise in the ears of my friends this three weeks or more. Yet am unwilling to suffer Small to cut my throat least that shoud feed me, for, thank God, I am become so considerable I think myself fitter for a cart than a horse were I to be conveyed any way; and at the same time have had employ in another kind, to be ready for Lord when called for (which sort of business you know my giddy head must be clearer at) for they supenead me to the passing judgement, which roll, I must own, was sent by clerk, to whom I observed, all rebukes were not lost on his master. My female neighbour has been much out of order in a cold and sends me word, in great concern, expecting next post to bring news of her niece Hauxley's death. I can't greatly lament any that are took from so great an uncertainty in fortune. Living upon dependence is to me great misery. In a letter from the country they write me that you look as well and brisk as ever, which I assure you I rejoice to hear, though am sorry I am so bad an accountant as you seem to prove me. Our town is dull. Italian plays are all the mode and I don't understand one word of the language so content myself with a twelve-penny amusement, now and then, at the Oratory. Though, I must remark, am no schismatic for I only go on lecture days. If you have not yet read two volumes of ficktitious voyages of fairies, giants, flying islands, &c, said to be Dean Swift's and have had a great run here, you may peruse them at leisure, for now the fashion of praising them is almost over. My natural stupidity, which could not be moved by education, could not penetrate the deep design of the author, save to ridicule the depraved taste of mankind in general. Once is an age my fashion dress come in vogue, though here no hopes of success. No, no more than of the number of rabbits set forth in the newspapers, and of which a book is printing, with a plate of the 17 rabbits, whole and piecemeal, they say, which must make money to the author, being entirely news. These at present are visiting topicks. As to what you and I have oftener heard of, give me leave to ask what colliery Mrs. can gain out of Sir estate? This is common chatt. As is, I fear, Lady bringing up her daughters, and the offer there from our pupil, who I hear is looking out a house in George Street. The post-bells calls. Adieu. My service attends my cousin and believe me, Sir, ...

London. 11 April, 1717. Dear Brother, I am to give answer to your favour of 2 instant, att the first reading of which I could scarce believe my own eyes and, if I was as disposed to quarrel as you seem to be, you have laid a sufficient foundation to ground a breach upon; but I must tell you that my friendship and affection is so deeply rooted that it will be difficult to shake it, and, if yours were established on as firm a basis, you could never raise such diffidence and jealousy and make such insinuations against me, who never deserved the least from you. Notwithstanding you say you do not suspect me imposing on you in the seeds, what can you mean by keeping the dispute on foot, and though I have in several letters declared I charged no more then I paid, and that probably you might be misinformed, for Goo. Waylett, the seedsman att the Wheatesheafe in Leaden Hall Street, over against St. Mary's church, of whom I them, who I complained to on your first letter, solemnly protested to me that I paid no more then others for the same quality att that time, which I believed, because he is a man of fair repute, and I did not think he would cheat me in so trivial a matter. Nay, moreover, he showed me his book, that he made everybody that then bought of him pay the same, and though you have mentioned this affair in so many letters, and cannot forbear touching on it, (which, unless I was quite stupid), discovers your mistrust of me, and, because I defend myself, you pretend to carry it with an air of authority and resentment. To justify myself still more I have given you the name of the seedsman, and where he lives, and do now send you his bill, with his receipt on the back of it, which you may compare with the account I sent you, to see whether I have pocketed; but I desire you'll return me the bill, which I must keep as a voucher, and, though I could not before satisfy you of my innocence, yett I hope this will, that so may hear no more of this grand dispute of the seeds; and though I shall be always glad to serve you, yett if you, suspecting my integrity, think fit to honour anybody else with your commissions, I shall be no looser thereby and shall not regrett it. am sorry you have provoked me to declare myself in this manner. I make no doubt but you'll be able to give good reason for your conduct as to politics, but you ought not to take amiss if I term Sir , and , persons disaffected, for I believe I may charge my memory with remembering that you, yourself, have bestowed those high and mighty titles on them. I never will presume to dictate to you what company is fitting for you to keep, such a magisterial air would ill become me, but must say am sorry that you shoud pronounce yourself unanimous in the sentiments with those gentlemen aforenamed. As for making a second visit to the you desire, if it were to do you service, I would readily do it, but to make her another visit, without any prospect of doing any good for you, will look like making pretensions for myself, and may give the world a subject for discourse, which would be very ungrateful. So I hope you'll not expect it from me. According to your order in your former you have your account currant; the due to me £5. 14. 3; which I hope you'll find without error. I fear my mother will be great a looser by not accepting your proposal, that was last made, for a rent charge, and when she stated to me that she would not comply with it, because she would not consent to have the entail cut of, on my account, I thanked her for the consideration she had for me, but begged of her not to forego so great an advantage, as the rent charge would be, on my account, and that, for my part, I did not in the least mistrust my doing anything unfair by me, as my mother herself can tell you. Who that person is you hint att, that finds his interest in the unnatural divisions between them, you know best. I, att this distance, am ignorant, and, as I am conscious to myself of innocence, I cannot impute your insinuation to myself, whatever you may do, for I guess, as you have made me a rogue in your own thinking in one thing, you take it for granted I am so in everything else. But, whatever you may believe of me, I have laboured to pacify and compose matters as much as lay in my power, and, though have not been successful, yett shall persevere in my endeavours. I hope you will not revive these paper wars that have of late been between us. I, for my part, offer to bury all in oblivion and to continue that love and affection as inviolably as ever, which never was in the least lessened to you by what has past, nor ever shall by any bone of contention that may be thrown between us hereafter. I am dear Brother, your most affectionate and faithful humble servant Thomas York. To James Clavering Esq., att Stowhouse, near Durham.

. 4 May, 1717. Dear Brother, I am with your favour of the 28 past. I am as willing as you are that the paper war, we have had for some time, may cease, what has passed be buried in oblivion, and, according to the saying, of the falling out of lovers is the renewing of love. Let us enter into the strictest ties of love and friendship and endeavour to make the knot so strong, not to be slackened by any accident for the future. Though to clear myself of what you cast on me, of being jealous without reason, I must beg leave for the last time to add a few words upon this ungrateful subject, which has given me great disquiet. You did more then insinuate in very plain words, which to my poor sense could bear but two meanings, and that, either I was so careless in your affair, to let myself be imposed on, or did impose on you; and though att the very first I told you, I did for you my best, and beleivd you paid no more then the just price, and that it was not impossible but you might be misinformed or that there might be some mistake in it. Yett you, not content with this but letter after letter, I think it is been ever since Xmas, could not forbear your reprimands and expressing your mistrust of me, though the most it could be for would not amount to above a few . Thus I desire this odious subject may have an end and I can assure you, though what has happened might have made some impression on an unsteady mind, it has not in the least on mine, and the respect and value for you is as great as ever, which I will demonstrate whenever have occasion of serving you, which, I protest to you, was and always will be with the same goodwill and zeal for you as for myself. As for the topic of politics, whether the complaints, you with too much reason make, can be laid more justly on those that are turned out or those that are kept in, I will not determine. However I may venture to assert, that the grievances and mismanagement, you intimate, was not the reason of that change and that the present gentlemen will not redress those egregious faults and that such blunders have been committed by this new set, as sufficiently bespeak them unequal to their business and to carry on the grand affairs in hand. If you and I must not speak well of a ministry, because we have not what we ask, though we have both perhaps good pretensions; you, by your faithful services and venturing and exposing your person att your proper charge, and I, by my father's steady adherence to the present government, who desired nothing for himself if they would only give me a small place of £2 or £300. I say, if we must not commend a ministry till they give us each a place, I fear they must never have our good word. I never knew any ministry without faults and I believe the late had their share. I am glad we agree in the characters of some of your neighbours you associate with, though, if I can understand your former of 2 past, you would not allow them that denomination you do now. Do not let the present have the merit, if 12,000 men are disbanded, because that proposition was made by Mr. , and to let what was saved thereby go towards the £250,000; but then it was violently opposed by your patriots, and he branded as an enemy, and now in a few days, truly it is become so good an expedient to be putt in practise, as it's said. So things change. I could mention many more instances, but I'll say no more. The distraction that reigns in our family is very melancholy to reflect on and I fear there will be no avoiding the sad consequences that must ensue, unless my mother consents to leave the matter to be decided by arbitration, which I have earnestly recommended to her, that I wish it does not putt me out of her books, though it is plain that method will be most for interest. For if, as my brother asserts, he has had the best advice about this case, that her personal estate is his, then, if they go to law, it will all be given from my mother, with costs, besides a vast expense in defending her cause, with the plague and vexation that attends law-suits always. Whereas, if it is put to refference, she may perhaps be awarded to pay only part. And, as I can safely say I have not given any other then healing advice and tending to compose their differences, I am resolved to continue to act the same neutral part. Yett, rather then hear of their animosity and unnatural proceedings, which is very shocking to me, if I could have the least encouragement of going anywhere abroad, I profess I would instantly retire out of England, let it be where it would, for no other reason then that I might be out of the way, and the hearing, of these fatal discords. I repeat to you, the love and friendship I bear you is very sincere, as will appear upon all occasions from, dear brother, ...

. 30 May, 1717. Dear Brother, By an accident I did not get your letter, of the 24 instant, time enough before what I wrote you, the last post was sent to the post, and, as ill luck would have it, we have had three holidays together; the King's birthday, the , and today Ascension Day, on which all businesses is att a stand. And this fine weather drawing people out of town, I am informed Mr. Hutton is in the country, so that I could not proceed with that expedition in your affairs as I shoud have desired. However, I have been with Mr. Moore, who will send to him to meet us on Saturday morning, so you may expect to have a more particular account in my next, of the answer Mr. Hutton gives. My mother has been prevailed on to employ Mr. Waits in drawing up her case, in order to have Mr. Vernon's opinion on several points, and to be further assisting to her in his profession, which, I think, is one great point gained, that she has an honest attorney, that will not hurry her into vexatious lawsuits out of any self-interest; and we take all opportunities to incline her to a pacifist disposition. I am dear ...

. 4 June, 1717. Dear Brother, Mr. Moore and self were to meet Mr. Hutton on Saturday last, but he disappointed us, which made me not keep my word of writing you last post. I have since had the good fortune to see Mr. Hutton, who told me that he had an interview with Mr. Moore, before he begun his journey, who he fully discoursed on the matter, and who made an affidavit to some matters he required of him. As Mr. Moore is on his journey home he will probably give you a better account then I can. Mr. Hutton told me that he had wrote att large to Mr. Dixon without having any answer. He seemed dubious, when the matter came to a hearing, how the court would take it. As I am a novice in affairs of this nature and little acquainted with the particular circumstances of your case, I could only talk to him on generals and recommend your interest to him in as strong terms as I possibly could. To which he answered me, that everything shoud be done by him in his power to promote your advantage and, as I remember, he said this affair would come on on Thursday and he seemed to think it would not be against you if the depositions in the hands were delivered into court; which I thought would not answer the end, but he overruled me with reasons I could not reply to. I wish he may make good his professions of sincerity to you and that this affair may end to your satisfaction. I am, dear brother, ...

London. 9 July, 1717. Dear Brother, I am with your favour of the 2 instant, with an enclosed bill of £110 on Claude Jamineau, to which I shall procure the needful and, when in cash, follow your orders in taking Mr. Waite with me to Mr. Freak and paying him £100 on account of John Clavering Esq. A suite of gray cloth for 2d. mourning is now in hand by Mr. Turnbull, who has promised to send it to you by the first carrier. He assured me he has your measure still by him and doubts not of fitting you. If the rancour and malice of your ill-natured enemies prompts them to attempt more mischief against you, may they receive the just reward, that is, be disappointed in all their designs and projects, and be obliged to make submission and pay the costs and charges you may be att. I believe my mother has but little encouragement from her lawyers, that she has been with for advice about her monies. As to all differences I do not find but they stand just in statue quo . On Sunday last my mother invited my , Mr. Weddell, and myself, to dine with her, and made a proposal to my , to give him £500 if he would give her a discharge for his claim to her personal estate, which he refused and insisted on £800, but that was not agreed to and so nothing was concluded on. Yett I hope a lawsuit may be prevented. Neither of them seem now very fond of entering the lists, and both of them concur, seemingly, not to meet att Richmond together, which I hope may prevent fresh differences. As the Parliament will rise in four or five days I suppose my brother designs for the country, not that I have any other grounds but my own bare conjecture, and my mother talks of taking a turn to Bath, if the doctor says it will do my sister Betty good, and after that, if one can judge by her discourse, she does not think of seeing the country very speedily. I am grown so indifferent as to politics that I never inquire or trouble myself about them, for I think I am so inconsidered, that neither anything I can do, or wish, can have any more influence then my endeavouring to stop the tide att Gravesend with my finger. To what purpose, then, is it to vex oneself. And, as to Ministers, I have one opinion of them all, and, as long as I hear that King George and that family is secure on the throne and that there is no fear of the Pretender coming amongst us, I am easy, and am, dear brother, ...

London. 6 Augst., 1717. Dear Brother, I cannot let slip one post without giving answer to your favour of the first instant. I doubt not but you have received your suite of cloths, the taylor having assured me that they were sent, as wrote you in my former. Your bill of £110 was punctually paid and I was no less punctual in the payment of the £100 to Mrs. Little, who I went to, along with Mr. Waite, the very morning the bill was due. You'll have perhaps heard that Mr. Freak is dead. I wish with all my heart that all further quarrels and differences between my mother and brother may be prevented, but I much dread the contrary. I am glad you have again disappointed the designs of your enemies and I hope you'll do the same as often as they renew their attempts against you. You wrote me in a former, that the father and mother took part with you against the adversary. I am now sorry to see they have so far altered as to show such uncommon civilities to your greatest enemy. As to politics I am of the same opinion I was, that it is trifling for a private person, as I am, to be solicitous who is in the Ministry, for neither my wishes or inclinations will avail one way or other; and I am glad you begin to come into my sentiments. I am, dear brother, ...

. 5 Augt., 1718. Dear Brother, I am with your favour of the 31 past, with 2 bills for £235, of which I shall take proper care as to acceptance and payment; but I wonder that Mr. Bernardeau, who professes kindness for you, shoud make his bill of £210 att 40 days date, when he knows that you want to have the money soon, in cash here, to pay it in. Mr. Waite began his journey for the north last Friday. Before he went I was in consultation with him about making the first payment, but since that I am informed, that Mr. Hiccocks, the Master in Chancery, who is appointed by the court to receive the monies &c., relating to this trust, is gone to France and will not return before the term begins, so that I shall be glad to receive your order how to comport myself; whether you would have it paid into Sanderson's hands, the solicitor, who I suppose may be trusted with the monies; but then whether interest will be allowed from the date he receives it. Pray think of this and let me have your directions. Likewise, if you think Mr. Waite's opinion needful, I doubt not you know how to write to him, and you may desire him to give me his sentiments hereupon, to prevent loss of time. I note you are making all the dispatch you can to send up the of the money you propose to pay into court. I am sorry that the young gentleman shoud so misbehave himself to loose his reputation and to follow the steps of his sister in what is so obnoxious. I fear you are to expect no favour from that quarter. If you have strict justice done you, without the trouble and expense of law, you come of well. It is the part of everyone of us, that wishes sister Betty well, to give a helping hand to what will conduce so much to her happiness. By what my mother wrote me I concluded the matter had gone further then I find from you it has. If my sister has no objection to his person, I wish with all my heart it may be accomplished. What I mentioned in my former was expressly by my directions, and I hope she may be prevailed on to make an addition, to promote my sister's welfare. I make no doubt but you'll do all in your power to bring it to bear, and I dare say you'll proceed with that caution, prudence and secrecy, that if it shoud not go on, to do neither party any prejudice. I mean, if it shoud be made public or take air, and afterwards break of, Betty may not be blown upon. And, I fancy you'll agree with me, the best method, to prevent that, will be to learn the utmost limits of the of one, and the offers of the other, before a formal courtship begins, by which you may guess if any probability of success. But this I know is needless to mention to you, because you know much better than I how to proceed in an affair of this kind. My service attends the women and I am, dear brother, ...

. 23 1718. Dear Brother, I am without any from you to answer and so am now to acquaint you that I have used my utmost endeavours to procure payment to the two bills hereunder specified, but all to no purpose, and I begin to despair that they ever will be paid, particularly the note of John Hartley, who says he has no money, and cannot pay it, and I may arrest him if I please, for in short it is out of his power. So I desire your orders what to do with it. I believe the best way for me will be to return it to you, that you may recover that money of the person you took it of, who I hope is an able man. Langley does not give so plain an answer, but I fear it is not better with him for my goldsmith has a bill on him that he has denied for this 2 or 3 months. I am, dear brother, ... John Hartley's promissory note, in date 21 July att 30/d date, payed to Wm. Kitchingman, due since 23 Augt. Wm. Langley's promissory note, in date Augt. att 30/d date, payed to Simon de Landifield, due since 3 instant.

Richmond. 1st. June, 1722. Brother, Hoping to see you either here or att Greencroft before my return I will defer answering yours, which I just before I left London, till I can do it by word of mouth. I reached this place on Wednesday afternoon under the greatest concern for the sad occasion that called me down, and, as an additional trouble to me, I find new differences and troubles arose here, which I want skill to compose. I wish my abilities were equal to my inclinations. I will not add further then my respect and service to your spouse. I am, ... To James Clavering Esq., att Greencroft, near Durham.

London. 28 June, 1722. Dear Brother, I left Richmond last Sunday evening and arrived here safe on Tuesday afternoon, full of a due sense for the very kind reception I met with att Greencroft, for which I return you my hearty thanks. I could wish that I could tell you I had left our friends att Richmond in a disposition to promote their own peace and happiness. My mother had been told more then once that she could not maintain her right to the £500, and I hope time will induce her to resign up her pretensions to that, and then I hope the maine difficulty is conquered and there can be no difference of moment about anything else. I hope you'll continue to cultivate a good understanding, to which end I endeavoured to contribute all I could by removing some groundless mistrusts. The coldness between my and me was much heightened before we parted. He set me to Bedale and in my way thither took upon him to catechise me and demanded of me to know everything my mother had said to me, nay, what she had given me, and, because I could not be so particular as he expected, I we shoud have parted in downright anger. What he means by this I cannot imagine. I am sure I never did him any ill in my life. He takes no care to cultivate an understanding and if you and I follow his steps, for ought I know, we may stand on as bad a footing and have as little expectations. I plainly told him, as I was not a man of ambition, I was very well content with my present way of living, which I could just support with the assistance I have from my mother, but, if he was desirous of regaining her favour, I would desist from my application and would turn my thoughts of making my fortune some other way, and, as I have health I hope I shoud find friends to send me abroad, for I would not submit to starve att home and cast any disgrace on him and the family. How he'll proceed gives me no great pain. The most welcome news you can send me will be the happy delivery of your spouse, and am with great truth, ...

London. 4 July, 1723. Dear Brother, You telling me in yours of 7 past, that you intended the week after for Scarborough, made me send my answer on the 13th. directed thither. But, not hearing since from you, I am doubtful whether it has reached you, so this is designed to find you att your own house. I went out of town Friday last, the 28 past, and was detained by a friend that was with me that I did not return till yesterday, the 3 , and found att my lodgings a letter from Mr. Gowland, in date 29 past, telling me you had disappointed him of monies for the fine for your assault on the Gray; that your motion would come on the 2 ; desiring my attendance with the monies to pay such fine as the court ordered. I guess if you had desired this of me you would not have much of the trouble of writing me about it and much doubt your having failed in having made the necessary provision in Mr. Gowland's hands. However, can assure you I have your welfare so much att heart if I had been in town I would not only have given my attendance, but, as I am very low in cash, I would att least have endeavoured to raise the monies on my credit, which being very indifferent. If had not succeeded I hope you will take the will as kind as doing the deed itself. But am glad to find that Mr. Gowland has, by his dexterity, got a reprieve till next term so that you have now time enough before you. It will be very good news to me to hear you, as well as spouse, are well, and am ...

London. 20 July, 1723. Dear Brother, The receipt of your of 12 removed many gloomy apprehensions occasioned by not hearing from you so long, and, though you do not think me worthy to be advised of the illness, nor anything else that passes, yet I can assure you I take no small pleasure in the account you give of your recovery, heartily congratulating you thereupon and wishing you a long of health and happiness. I am extremely concerned to find your spouse labours under so bad health. As she has my sincere wishes for her recovery, I cannot doubt that either advice, or anything else, will be neglected. I shall impatiently long for good tidings of you both. I am glad you have so good hopes of defeating the malice of your enemies. It runs in my head that I had send you some of the receipts for the money I paid Little, but I find I have those for the large sums I paid to Mr. Hiccocks. I cannot imagine what is meant by those irregular and unwarrantable proceedings att the late election of sheriffs unless the enemies of our government are forming designs to embroil us in new troubles and so are resolved to have sheriffs att any rate that will serve their turn, but I hope, as the administration is aware of them, they will be baffled. We have had fine rains of late, which I hope has recovered your often grass and done no harm to your corn, and am ...

London. Augt., 1723. Dear Brother, I am with the of 26 past and do sincerely congratulate you and your spouse on your recoveries and offer up my hearty wishes that you both may grow sensibly better every day till you are perfectly restored to your health. I am att a loss to guess att the motive of the excuse you make for denying me the favour of informing me of your health. I hope you have no hidden reasons for resuming that thread of correspondence, which was carried on between us some time since, which, however agreeable to you, can assure you was not so to me. I am far from being inquisitive and neither do expect nor desire to be informed of anything that is a secret or not fit for me to know and all that I am desirous of knowing is relating to the welfare of yourself and family and, for the rest, it will be time enough for me to hear what relates not to yourself nor the family when it is made public in the world. I will make a strict search after the receipts for the monies I paid on your account and give you the particulars in my hands, att the foot. I wish you may be able to overcome the wiles of your adversaries and shall be glad I could contribute anything to it by answering interrogatories relating to any discourse I had with Sanderson and will recollect what passed in conversation the best I can, but, as I am to be upon oath and my memory not the best. I doubt not but you will be content with the best recollection I can make. I am glad the good Bishop met with a reception, so much beyond his opponent, from , who, must loose his interest by making use of such popular arts, especially when they do not succeed. I am sorry for the accident befallen your son and heir and but hope no arteries and sinews may be touched, and am ... I wish when you go to Newcastle you would be so good to inquire of Dr. Brady, who is heir and to Mr. ... Eyons deceased, there being a small sum in the hands of a friend of mine, belonging to the deceased, who would be glad to part with it to any person he can safely pay it to and that will give a legal discharge.

London. 29 Augt., 1723. Dear Brother, In answer to your favour of 16 , though I am never better pleased then when I hear from you, yett when business or the absence from home deprives me of that pleasure, I must submit to it with patience, without putting you to frame an excuse, which piece of formality is better laid aside between us. As I never look upon anything a trouble to serve you, I do now send you, according to your desires, copies of the receipts for the several payments I made, by your order and on your account, for the executorship of your kinsman Clavering. As no man can be supposed to spy out mistakes in himself, so soon as a standerby, I am persuaded you'll not take it ill if I discharge the office of a true friend, in offering to you my sentiments upon your resolution of making the utmost defense you can in order to expose him. I wish some subtle lawyer has not buoyed you up with hopes of success, to encourage you to enter the lists for selfish ends of his own. I doubt not, because you say so, that you may have it in your power to show that they have been very malicious and base in their proceedings against you, but you forget that you have also laid yourself open by having such a large sum of money in your hands belonging to your trust and, when was called upon to pay it in, was not ready with it, which occasioned their applying to Chancery. Whereupon the court made an order for you to pay so much half yearly in discharge of principal and interest, and, in my weak judgement, if you bring this matter before the court again, they will, in their turn, throw dirt att you, unravel all your accounts over again, and, if they can make objections to some articles, put you to a great charge, expense and trouble, besides costs of suite, and confirm the former decree of paying interest. You may be assured I shall be very willing to serve you, in recollecting anything that will be of advantage to you. Be pleased to send me up the letters themselves, that relates to any conversation I had with Sanderson relating to you, for without them the chief, I remember, that passed between us, was his professing a great friendship to you and his excusing you from any dishonest views in running out the infant's money, because you so readily came in to make over your estates as a security. The sum belonging to the late Mr. Eyons is £4. 19. 5, was paid into my hands by Mr. Weddell before he went into the country, which I am ready to pay your lawful heir, upon a legal discharge of receiving so much from Mr. Weddell by my hands. It is no small concern to me that you cannot give better news of your own, nor your wife's, health. I hope you do not let spleen add to your distemper. I cannot doubt the taking all proper care of yourself as well as her. You have my heart's wishes for your recovery, and I beg to hear of you. I wish the putting yourself to the charge of entertaining the may answer your . I fear all great men are alike. I am, with sincerity, ...

London. 28 , 1723. Dear Brother, You, having been so dilatory in favouring me with an answer to my last, putt me under melancholy apprehensions, which your favour of 15 instant has now dissipated, and I heartily rejoice with you that you have att last subdued your troublesome indisposition, and, I hope, without the fears of a relapse. I wish you could have given me as good an account of your spouse. The gout is a very irksome and disagreeable remedy, but it may perhaps be better to undergo some present pains, which are not immediately dangerous, then to languish under a worse illness that foreboded instant and imminent hazard. She has my best wishes for her speedy recovery. I cannot help hoping that both you and your kinsman may incline to make an end of all differences in a peaceable way. Pushing matters to extremity will not answer his purpose, but sure I am, it will not yours in the long. And, this being my real opinion, I could never forgive myself if I did not impart it to you, though I know I lay myself open to your censure for taking this freedom upon me. I am highly pleased to find there is a disposition to accommodate the affair in peace and quietness. You'll not want your share of applause for the part you have acted to bring it about, and I am persuaded you have too much goodness to use the power, you say have, of making retaliation, otherwise then very gently. It is a further confirmation to me that you are eased of your pains, because you are disposed to show the wit and mirth. It is very surprising you had not your intelligence earlier and that you shoud be so late in your congratulation. I had however rather be the object of your merriment then your malice and ill-will. You will, I doubt not, acquaint with the needful the first opportunity. I am ...

London. 11 January, 1723/4. Dear Brother, In answer to your favour of 24 past I am to thank you for the bill of £10 you send me for mourning, which I have . I make no manner of doubt of your being every day more and more sensible of your great loss, for she certainly was a most affectionate and faithful wife and a most tender and provident mother to her children and, as that weight of care does now evolve on you, I dare say you'll discharge yourself as a prudent and kind father. I am very glad to hear you gave so favourable an account of your health, and I hope you'll continue to recover sensibly every day, which I heartily wish. Since you inveigh so loudly against the late swearing act you'll find there is a bill bringing in to explain and amend it, which I hope will pacifiy all reasonable men, though it is impossible it shoud all that join in the outcries against it. It seems to be confessed the act was passed in a hurry and was not so well considered as it ought. Humanum est error , but for a set of men to clamour att any severe laws that themselves, by their restless endeavours to disturb our peace, have putt the Legislature under a necessity of making for our safety, is very unreasonable; but I think no well-wishers to our constitution shoud chime in with them in their groundless and false invectives. That you may enjoy all health, happiness and prosperity in this and very many ensuing years is heartily wished by ...

Richmond. 8 March, 1723/4. Dear Brother, Since my coming hither 4 or 5 days ago your favour of 27 past has been transmitted to me. I can easily believe, without your assurances , the great loss not only you, but the poor children have sustained, never to be repaired, for she undoubtedly was a most affectionate, loving wife, a frugal, careful manager of your family affairs, and had an indulgent, tender regard for her children. If I was given to be opinionated of myself perhaps self-conceit might so far blind me as to take to myself that purity of thought, which you, to be sure, very seriously would ascribe to me; but if I would do you justice I ought to celebrate your sublime way of thinking, which does indeed far surpass my poor understanding for I never knew before that vices could interfere to moderate grief. I do not pretend to be so pure and undefiled as to be free from faults, but I thank my God, as I am not high-minded and have not those incitements to avarice and self-love, the ambition of living in a grand way above my circumstances, I have not that call to an immoderate desire of wealth, further then in common with all mankind, to take a proper care, as far as is consistent with strict honesty, to support the way of life I am in, without running out my fortune or putting myself to the inconvenience of borrowing of others. I know by some quotations you formerly made out of Tillotson, that you are well read in good books, but in my low opinion you are as wrong in your application of this borrowed sentence as you was in the other before. He must be more than man to know the motives that directs men's actions and, besides, it is not so very Christian to assign ill causes, why any man does good. But let us state this quotation and then see in what light it appears. As to your services to the government, I will concur with you, they have been great and conspicuous, and I wish with all my heart, they may be rewarded suitable to the merit of them. I wonder why my wishes and desires, that you make an end with your Chopwell relation, without going to law, shoud stun you. I am sure it is not the first time, by many, I have said so, and I give you joy and sincerely rejoice with you, that you have obtained an order to your liking, and are now disentangled of that vexatious affair. As I am a great lover of peace and concord, and can lay my hand on my heart and safely say I never did delight fishing in troubled waters, never did sow the seeds of strife and contention, never endeavoured to set one relation against another by raising groundless mistrusts of each other, nor ever made use of indirect underhand practises for selfish ends of my own, so let the consequence be what it will, I will inviolably adhere to the same pacific measures, that the world shall have no cause to censure me justly, nor I have reason to reproach myself; and if you are disposed for any hidden reasons, to commence a new paper war with me, you shall carry it on by yourself. If I had not had it explained to me since I came here I should not have known what you meant by going to Newcastle to be cut. I am truly concerned for the occasion and heartily wish success in the operation, a good recovery, and long health and prosperity. The short time I propose staying here will not permit me paying you a visit, for I must return in 10 days. I am ...

column46: London. 20th February Dear Brother, I am duly with your favour bearing date the 13 instant and dare say we do not differ the least relating the administration affair. As I would be glad to put our case on a good foot we cannot complain of being denied an inventory. What then? We must allege a sufficient cause to lay a good foundation for our proceeding, to show we are in earnest and determined to have justice. For my part, am the worst in the world representing this case to counsel and do wish your presence here to put matters in agitation or, if you'll get our complaints stated, I will then consult Mr. Copper. But I think, as brother intends a visit so soon to Richmond, it will be better to rest it till his return, to see if reasonable things will be offered. Though I declare it's my opinion, nothing will make her comply except filing a bill, I submit everything to your consideration and better judgement, and shall concur in anything you transmitt to me. Mother has wrote me two letters in an affectionate manner but nothing relating the administration. In her last she desires me to write to Mr. Rut, that he would employ some attorney to procure her the £100 she lent Mr. Owen, which I shall decline, having had nothing to do with that affair from the beginning, and put it upon my brother. I am sorry your kinsman runs matters to so great a violence, and wish Lady Cowper's death may make any alteration. I hear Mrs. Little made her appearance abroad soon after her death without the least regard or common decency of dress. I suppose she had no mourning given her. I sent the enclosed to Mr. Gowland, with my request to expedite your affair, who returned me for answer, that his best endeavours shoud be employed and that he would come to see me. I always intended making Mr. Rut a present of his Majesty's approbation, but I did not apprehend the charge would have been so great. I have only time left to reprimand you for the unaccountable negligence of your own welfare; that I am surprised you continue in that lethargic humour to be deaf to all advice of your friends, besides physicians, and I wish you have not suffered already to prevent a cure in time. Your enclosed to Mrs. Waite was carefully delivered and your letters have come without any remarks from the post office. When you hear of any good French wine I desire your remembrance of me. I am dear brother, yours very affectionately, J. York. To James Clavering Esq., att Greencroft, near Durham.

column46: Richmond. Jan. 16th, Dear Brother, Your favours of 7 and 11 date accompanied me yesterday att 4 in the afternoon and, according to your request, take the first opportunity of returning thanks. I perceive your son remains yet with Mr. Scaife and except you know him to be neglected, I fancy, though Mr. Scaife has left of a public school, yet surely capable and not wanting to instruct Jamie. Otherwise he would have certainly sent him to his son. Therefore I hope there is no occasion for any uneasiness and in my thoughts it would be better to have the spring a little more advanced before you place him to any school about London. However I shall be ready to do everything in my power, that you may think for the boy's interest, but I cannot possibly call att Cambridge or should I venture him to ride post with me. Though when att London he may come in the stage coach and I will take care of his arrival and conduct him to my lodgings, and where you please to order him afterwards. I shall endeavour to follow your directions in every particular and desire you'll join a friend with me, for perhaps I may be att a loss how to act for the best. However I pray let your directions be full in all respects. Mr. Recorder and nephew are not yet arrived. It's now past 9 in the evening and no tidings of the post so I commit this to my neighbour's care, to darling son. column46: London. 24 February, Dear Brother, In answer to your favour, which I could not answer sooner, I take the first opportunity to congratulate you on the pleasures and happiness of a married state, and as I have a very great respect for the Lady I heartily wish equal and mutual satisfaction, long to live and enjoy each other, and desire the tender of my particular respects in the best manner. I hear no tidings yet of your son. Mrs. Little has wrote to his master to know the terms of the school, where att leisure times, I perceive, they learn dancing, French, &c. So desire to know your thoughts, whether you would have him initiated so soon in these accomplishments. We had last Tuesday an election controverted att the bar betwixt Mr. Collier and Mr. Waller. The petitioner only prayed a void election, and the sitting member after some debates gave it up to save his friends from the censure of the house. I am ... I am very sorry for the misfortune of our friend att Long Newton, though am glad the worst is past and hope he will recover soon. I am just going to the House and, if any novels arise, will give you a further trouble. This day the King came to the house of Peers and gave the royal assent to the land tax bill, the lottery bill for a million, and the bill for punishing mutiny and desertion.

column46: London. 3 March, Dear Brother, Upon receipt of your favour waited on Mrs. Little with the enclosed, and, when your son James arrives, I shall be sure to consult her in all respects as I think she will prove an excellent governess to us both. Mrs. Waite is a great rambler, that I have not yet met with her att home to pay my devoirs. What Mrs. Little thinks necessary, in equipment or otherwise, for your son, I shall readily order matters accordingly. Yesterday we had a pretty extraordinary petition from Mr. Hampton, setting forth his inability to pay his debts due to the Crown, when he was Treasurer of the Navy, desiring a composition to pay 10s per round, which was referred to a committee of the whole house. column46: London. 15 March, Dear Brother, Mrs. Little prevented my writing the last post, who then gave you an account of your son, , as I think now, is in a hopeful way of doing well, having no ill symptoms, that I hope in a week's time to attend him to school. His master was with us this morning in East street, with whom I had some little discourse, and, on the first appearance, your son approves of his as well as myself, and he likes him the better because he's not in orders; and I please myself that all the lost time will be regained by the master's careful eye and due observance, provided the boy settle well att first and willing in his endeavours. The master signified that whenever a lad proves so refractory to be incorrigible, and continues so, he always desires his parents to remove him, least his other boys shoud be spoiled. As he certainly is in the right, Jem shall want no instructions or advice from me and it will be a great pleasure that he answers the end of your care and charge in his education, for now is the very time of making a good groundwork, to enable him for better proficiencys on his appearing in the world. suppose you have already the charge and method of the school and you may be assured I shall act in everything as Mrs. Little directs or advises. column46: London. 22 March, Dear Brother, I am favoured with yours and a bill for thirty pounds, which I hope will be duly honoured when due. Since Mrs. Little writing you last post your son is better. The fever is now intermitting, that Jesuits' bark is now applied and do not question in a few days to conquer the fever, though I have my concern that something worse will be hard to avoid, which is a consumption as the Drs. apprehend. Yet under all events you may be assured no care will be wanting to do everything to restore his health, which time alone must direct to inform you more. I presented your letter to Mrs. Little yesterday and then, as well as often before, made your compliments upon the unexpected trouble of poor Jem. We have been under expectation these two days of a message from his Majesty; prevented, as I suppose, by a great minister's Lady falling ill of the small pox; which we shall have next Thursday. column46: London. 29 March, 1726. Dear Brother, In answer to yours, the lingering indisposition of your son, who in times is better and worse, has given me great uneasiness, that this morning I consulted Mrs. Little to have a physician in time, to know the true state of his case. So, on her recomendation of Dr. Hulse, I met him this evening att 6, who apprehends an impostumation on his lungs, and, if it ripens kindly, to throw up all that nauseous matter by spitting in a plentiful manner, he hopes the poor boy will do well. Otherwise in a gradual manner is afraid will overcome his strength. This being the true state in the Dr.'s judgement. He has prescribed some powder and asses' milk, Bristol water for drinking, pudding and fish for his diet, and prohibited all manner of flesh. Under these rules I have taken some pains to desire his obedience without reluctance, whom I left well satisfied to take everything prescribed. I can only repeat my good wishes and assurances, that no care will be wanting in us to restore health. I do not apprehend imediate danger, but, I fear, if he does not begin to pick up crumbs soon, we must submit to the Divine pleasure; and all will be owing to the irregular life at Hisson, which the poor boy owns, and confesses many of the pranks he committed there to weaken him, and has had complaints this half year. I met with Mrs. Waite this evening in East street, who, being not easily found att home, paid her five guineys by your order. Mrs. Little writes you this post. My love and respect attend all with you and I am ...

London. 2 April, 1725 Dear Brother, I am with your favour, and take care of the enclosed, and sorry that I can give no better account of your son, who, I fear, daily wastes and except the vomica shoud naturally take place to throw up the ulcerous humour, which is so nauseous that when he throws up anything it is past enduring the room, so that I really despair rearing him up. Under these circumstances he may continue some time, but the doctor disheartens me from any hopes of recovery, and all that can be done att present is to ease him in his pain and cold; and besides he's so refractory taking what is proper for him, that I believe Mrs. Little has a hard task to govern him. The Dr. has ordered him to be blooded this evening and waits on him tomorrow morning, where I shall attend and you may depend hearing further the next post either from Mrs. Little or self, who am ... is safe returned to Town, but I hear no novels from him. I shall in a short time think of moving northwards, except my staying could be of any real service to your son's recovery, and I hope may have your leave.

column46: London. 7 April, 1726. Dear Brother, We are adjourned this day to next Wednesday, which will give me so much idle time to settle my affairs in order to return home, the session drawing near to an end, and if you have any commands I shall be glad to receive them by first opportunity. Since my last your son is much in statue quo , appears brisker, though gains no ground, that I am afraid he insensibly decays. As all who are consulted have little hopes of his recovery so that Mrs. Little could wish you to see him and bring up your son Tom to school and carry down poor Jem if he's able to travel, for the Dr. does say their is little to be expected, except his own country air will restore him. I cannot advise anything myself, not knowing how your affairs may suite such a journey, so submit Mrs. advice to your own government. In the meantime shall continue due attendance on the poor child and shall be glad to receive any further directions, wherein I can serve you. I am ... My respects and service attend all with you.

column46: London. 12 April, 1726. Dear Brother, In answer to yours, if Mrs. Liddell's and my letters are come safe to your hand must imagine you on the road or preparing for a London journey to see your son, who languishes daily; and his own impatience to see you, and return home, makes him fret and very uneasy, as he was this morning, which provoked a violent fit of coughing, and the matter he throws up as nauseous as possible, which he has voided plentifully these two days; and it's the general opinion that nothing is so likely to restore him as such a vacuation, which is so corrupt that he can scarce bear the stench himself. For my part wish him att home or that any way could be contrived without hazard, for I am sure he will be under no government except you are with him. Therefore Mrs. Little thinks it absolutely necessary, if can order your affairs att home, to loose no time as well on your son's account as Sir James Clavering, who is thought to be in as dangerous a way. I can only remark that, as the poor boy complains of the uneasiness in a coach, as he takes the air sometimes, I am afraid he will scarce be able to undergo a long journey especially in the stage coach and, besides, no passenger will be able to endure his coughing, &c. I am ... My respects and service wait on sister and the lads.

column46: London. 15 April, 1726. Dear Brother, Not hearing from you last post I continue writing to Greencroft, though I could wish you here upon many accounts, as now I am afraid your son will not survive many days. I found an alteration this day att noon. in great pain, working inwardly, and very low spirited, inclinable to slumber, and said little. So we sent for the doctor, who prescribed something to ease him, but has not the least hopes and says, that the first warm weather will go hard with him. Attended this evening att 7 to use my persuasion to take what the Dr. ordered. I found him something better, but would by no means submit to a glister to cool his body, not having had a stool these three or four days. Till at length, after an hour's entreaty, on condition that I would buy him "Robinson Crusoe", he would suffer it. Upon which he grew very outrageous and would not keep the glister two minutes so it could not have had the full desired effect. Yet he found some benefit immediately. Mrs. Little, as well as myself, have had no little trouble and concern, on this refractory disposition, to do himself good. I have little more to add except to prepare you to submit to the divine pleasure, which must be all our fate's sooner or later. If it shoud please God to preserve life till you see him it would be a great satisfaction and pleasure to us all. Otherwise, for want of directions, I shall consult Mrs. Little in everything for the best and I beg leave to conclude with true concern ...

column46: London. 19 April, 1726. Dear Brother, In answer to yours shoud be very glad to give you a more agreeable account of your son's state and circumstances, in which an unexpected turn has happened since my last, which gives great relief and made him abundantly better; that is a humour fallen down to his foot, which the doctor says this morning is the gout, and proceeds entirely from his irregular vicious life att school. It may do great service if it can be prevented from returning to his body, provided he will be governable and leave of his outrageous fits. I wish this humour would grow and swell more to a head and then burst, as there is no hopes left without an extraordinary evacuation somewhere. It's certain he's much eased att present, more lively and brisk, but continues very weak, besides his lameness that he cannot point the ground. I consulted the doctor, for his returning home, who gives no encouragement to endure the journey with safety, though says he can do him as much service att Greencroft as here, in corresponding about his case from time to time. There is no immediate danger att present, but God knows how soon it may happen. Therefore if you could continue to undertake a journey hither it would give equal satisfaction. I am sure to yourself as well as your friends as I hope you'll make no longer delay. I hear mother threatens much after the session is up, that the decree is not served and obeyed. So something or other shoud be done. If no accommodation is to be met with, we must submit to everything or I shall join with you in any measure you think proper. I am afraid nothing is to be expected from brother. I believe the best way is to instruct Mr. Rut to form a mediation and desire him to make a purpose visit, that matters may not depend in this manner, to be liable to any advantage of the law against us. I pray you duly to consider as you do not know how she may be hurried on, and I believe Mr. Rut may bring matters to an accommodation and I will abide everything agreed on amongst you. I am ... I beg my humble service to sister and all yours. I shall wait your answer and then think of returning homewards. Shoud not Coppers be demanded and paid of, who has not yet returned me my settlement?

column46: London. 3 May, 1726. Dear Brother, I have yours of the 29 instant and do assure you am now heartily weary of this Town and nothing but the love and respect I bear to you and yours could have detained me thus long, though God knows att this juncture every day appears more melancholy when I see poor Jem in such piteous and languishing a condition. Nothing that he has taken these 3 days stays with him, and is now in the weakest state to live that ever poor boy was, and the sooner God is pleased to take him the happier, for he has endured more than can be possibly imagined. What relates Mrs. Liddell's servants, if I have no particular order from you, I shall desire to consult Mrs. Waite and, as far as my cash reaches, I shall freely employ it to discharge all demands on this unhappy occasion and I hope the account will show that nothing has been unnecessarily expended, though we are unfortunate in our best endeavours. I am going this evening to take my last farewell and I believe Mrs. Little writes this post, to whom I refer more perticulary. I have been twice att Mr. Copper's for his account, as I was this day, which yet wants to be drawn out. I gave him a cover to write you this post. Whatever you and Mr. Rut agree on I shall readily concur and am of opinion that its none of our interests, since the proceeding begun, to have it lie dormant in this manner. An unactive suit often brings the greater charge att last and do not know what advantage mother may receive from it, either by attachments or extents against me, for I would not willingly be in her power or agents to be under any difficulty (notwithstanding I know my privilege). Yet nobody knows how indiscreet the master may be in his abounding wisdom and I am apt to believe do not stand well in his good graces. I am ...

column46: London. 7 May, 1726. Dear Brother, Yours came duly to hand yesterday and I believe that some or one of your friends have been constant writing to you every post. However, if your female correspondents performed what they promised or intended, may safely say for this last month we have not omitted one post, so probably miscarriages has happened some way. I am surprised you could entertain the least hopes of your son's recovery or long continuance, who lingered on beyond everybody's expectation, as you had the melancholy account from me last post. Also the funeral intended for tomorrow att nine in the evening, which I hope will be performed in every respect, to have your approbation. On which occasion can add no further particulars to my last, except that Mr. Richardson refuses to take his fees, and, calling to mind the family's constant civility and respect to you and yours, so we think proper to compliment the doctor, son and daughter, with scarves. I had a letter from brother in answer to mine, giving some hopes of his attendance. Yesterday Mr. Copper visited me when I had company that we could have no private discourse, that I desired, if he had brought his bill to leave it with me, which he did, though little unwillingly. I find he has separated the charges. He acknowledges to have received on your account £25-5s, and the bill charged to you amounts in the whole to £44-3s-9d. The bill charged to me in the whole is £15-14s-2d so that your £25 being deducted from the whole brings it to £18-18-9d, which I will discharge if you please, though I think it very extravagant and many articles superfluous to aggrandise it. I shall call in all demands next week and do my utmost to discharge everything, but I hope by that time you may send bills. I shall certainly wait your answer to this by return of the post and do my utmost to show you that I am with sincerity ... As to mother, what you think proper to do I shall most heartily concur in, only that things may not sleep in this manner.

column46: London. 12 May, 1726. Dear Brother, In answer to yours I have little to say since my last, to which refer you, as everything was performed on Sunday, that decency and respect required, and I hope nothing can be deemed amiss, when I have the satisfaction of seeing you. Indeed I owe great obligations to the two ladies for their kind assistance on all occasions, especially to Mrs. Little, who had it more in her power to be serviceable; and friendship when tried, to find it real, is an inestimable jewel. Upon your letter to Mrs. Waite, she consulted me what to give Mrs. Liddell's servants, in which case I own myself no judge, but she thought guineys a piece would do well. So I gave her three guineys, desiring her to distribute it. I have now discharged all demands upon poor Jam's account except Mr. Small, who to me declined making any demand or bill, but would leave it to myself. So truly I was afraid trusting myself in giving more than what he deserved. On this consideration have prevailed with Mrs. Little to undertake him, who I doubt not will manage for the best. When I have your answer shall make provision and discharge Mr. Copper's bills. I propose, God willing, on Wednesday next to leave this dusty town, either in the Stamford coach, which goes in one day, or take post att hand, and hope to lie in my own bed the latter end of next week, where I shall be glad to hear a good account of your welfare, being concerned for your present indisposition. I think never yet mentioned my correspondence with Sir Wm. Louder, on your late servant's account, who has put me of from time to time in hopes of the money, and yesterday told me that he had discharged the man and did not care what became of him. He's married and lives somewhere in the neighbourhood about Swillington. I am, dear brother, ... My respects and best wishes attends you and yours.

column46: Richmond. 20 May, 1726. Dear Brother, On receipt of your favour I was in some hurry preparing for my journey the next day, which performed very well to this place yesterday in the afternoon though the heat was violent and the dust troublesome to bear. I hope Mrs. Little would plead for me, which shortens my apology. I am truly concerned for the continuance of your ill state yet I am of opinion that moderate exercise on horseback is the best physic and I advise you not to neglect such gentle means in time. As to your omission of the rings I found there was no hair saved, and indeed my time so short, that I could not have them done before leaving the Town. Besides, you did not mention whether male or female, for your two friends in the country, so that your direction was a little lame to have acted upon such an occasion. As to myself, desire you'll not think to be att any charge and I think it unnessary and believe it not expected from you to the family by London Wall, whom I waited on before I left the Town, but found only the Dr. att home. paid my compliments and returned all due accknowledgements upon your account. You may send other things what the country affords, which, in my thoughts, will be more acceptable, as he hinted some obligations to you in that way. Mrs. Waite, when I consulted her about the rings, she advised that Mrs. Little might have a ring of £5 or £6 value, if you thought proper, and refused any such thing for herself. I promised to communicate her thoughts to you on this subject and submit it to your animadversion, for there is no haste required. My neighbour's come in to visit me so I must hasten and can only add that I answered all demands on your account, by bill or otherwise. likewise paid Copper's unreasonable bill and shall be glad to receive any further commands, wherein I can serve you. My respects and service waits on sister and the lads, who I hope keeps well. concludes me ... expect you att our races.

column46: Richmond. 27 May, 1726. Dear Brother, I have your favour and thank you for the kind inquiry, which my letter this day 7 night would give some satisfaction. So far is it from my thoughts to put any inconvenience upon you to straiten your affairs, that I propose this expedient, if it's approved of, to make up the debt a hundred pounds, into your own pocket, and to account with you till matters are accommodated or ended in Chancery amongst us. If you please to give your bond or note for this purpose, I will order the remainder sum into your hands when you please, though I beg your early answer, that I may provide accordingly. I am truly concerned for the continuance of your ill state of health, which makes me very uneasy till I have a better account. I wish you would try change of air and let me see you, which I promise myself will not be long. However I do engage you att our horse races. column46: Richmond. 18 Dec., 1730. Dear Brother, Att the time of my writing last to you (notwithstanding the little regard shown to you) I thought proper to give you the earliest intelligence of mother's circumstances and how affairs stood, by my neighbour Wilson's going to Newcastle, who dropped my letter att the Red Lyon, which did not require so immediate an answer as I must accknowledge your favour this day by the post, and, since my last account, do not think mother much altered in appearance, but doubtless much weaker though she has a strong appetite and will eat what she pleases. sometimes very restless and uneasy and cannot lie in bed and dozes in the chair. This afternoon, with much difficulty, we prevailed to send for Dr. Johnson of York, but I cannot conceive any hopes of her recovery; that the least disorder must carry her of, as she will not be governed and would have nobody in time but poor Nan Dike, who does her best. I am happy att present, being restored to mother's favour by her blessing and I could wish, before her departure, she would be in peace with all the world and not make such reflections about her funeral. These two days she has said little about it. Brother has been with me since Sunday at bed and board and I think it would be hard to quarrel with me, when everything goes according to his own desire, and I hope he will be easy upon all accounts. column46: London. 27 Feb., Dear Brother, I have yours dated the 18, which came to hand the 25 instant and believe am not mistaken in what Mr. Booth told me. Though I am far from blaming you accepting of these terms, for peace sake, rather than run the uncertain fate of the determination, attended with unknown charge and inconvenience, but I think may venture to say the judge has not proved your friend as he promised. Yesterday you send me to an ale-house, where I met with the scarlett oak acorns. I found them extravagantly dear and not very fresh, that I only purchased a hundred att 5s., which I send in a little box by Monday's carrier, directed to Mr. Gates in Newcastle. I shoud advise you to steep them in water the night before you set them. As to the true pitch tree and as you say some ceries of a fur unknown, suppose you mean species, were all sold and gone. The Lords have put of the pension bill to next Tuesday, when it is said Lord will demonstrate that the bill, intended to prevent bribery and corruption, will effectually establish it. So there is little hopes of success. By letters, yesterday from Richmond, give me a melancholy account of mother; that they dispaird her surviving two or three days, which set Brother forward (as he intended before) this morning of his own horses, but I fear she will be gone before his arrival. I am no further informed of her will than when I wrote you from Richmond. We have been told lately from a great man that we shall soon be put on a new foot both at home and abroad, so I hope our trade and manufacturers will revive and flourish att home and abroad, and establishd'd upon a lasting foundation. column46: London. 20 April, 1731. Dear Brother, I am obliged with your favour yesterday, dated the 15, and return you my thanks for your care of me, which, if the clarett proves really good and strong, without art shall desire a third part and wish you would send it to Richmond the first opportunity, before the warm weather advances, well packed in strong short-neck'd bottles. By brother's account yesterday, mother is in very deplorable, melancholy circumstances. She has now Dr. Metcalfe joined to Nan Dike, who has prevailed to consent to have some issues put on her back, which no doubt will give great relief and prolong her time. Brother presses me to return home, to which have answered, if mother desires and my presence is acceptable. I propose to pay my duty &c., the first week in May, having taken place already in the York coach for Monday the 3 of May. to accompany a young lady, who is going to spend the sumer with her sister, Mrs. King, att Bewerly. So if you have any further commands you know the time of my residence here. I think do not want a gardiner att present, but I am told now the secret of my old gardiner leaving me, having got one of my maids with child. That, I believe, made him uneasy to scamper in time, which I guessed att was the case why he gave me such short warning and left me, as he pretended, upon account of more wages, when I was sure he never would have the same given him. But this is the fate of bringing youths up to buisiness. column46: Richmond. 22 October, 1731. Dear Brother, Since the 13th past I have been att Bewerley Court keeping, &c., and returned home yesterday. Otherwise shoud have acknowledged sooner your favour of the 12, for which now please to accept my best thanks as I am very glad to have your good thoughts and concurrence of the present treaty on foot (having had the lady long in my mind, to renew my former addresses), which I heartily wish may be so happy to effect, that it may be a greater inducement to see you and yours oftener att Richmond. column46: Richmond. 9 Nov., 1731. Dear Brother, I have your favour this day and am very sensible of your good wishes to me, as I am very glad my choice meets with your approbation. hoping to succeed att last with the lady I have long admired and coveted, but I am not so fortunate yet to know the time for my happiness. must see London first and depend upon the favours already received. I am expediting everything, by the assistance of Mr. Rut, to clear the way, and I hope before the end of the approaching session to give you a good account and salute you with a new sister. I am sorry to hear the ill news of loosing any of my friends or acquaintance, but we must all pay that debt to nature sooner or later. I perceive the colliers are become very uneasy and troublesome. I wish we have not reason to complain of the farmers before Mayday. Though I have no apprehensions on my own account I am very unwilling to leave the country without seeing you, and if I could for one night, I would gladly undergo the journey, but in case I am disappointed beg you'll excuse and accept of my good wishes and inclinations to you and yours. There is an account betwixt us. If convenient to you, please to make it up and enclose it and draw on me for the balance att London, which shall meet with due honour. I am, with true love and good wishes to you and family, ... It is agreed to leave this place on Monday 7 night.

column46: London. 7 December, 1731. Dear Brother, I hope my affair in hand will plead sufficient excuse for not accknowledging sooner your favour of the 19 of last month. For though I move my gradual paces, yet I presume they will prove sure and successful in a little time. Yet impatient for my approaching happiness. I had a most agreeable pleasant journey, the weather and roads very favourable, and, by God's providence, landed the ladies safe in this town last Wedensday; who are both well after their journey and begin now to be ready to take wing, and, when my fair one is fully satisfied with the diversions of this Town, I hope she will think and give me leave to take her by the hand and receive the usual blessing. I shall be glad to hear that peace is settled amongst the colliers; as I wish likewise justice to be duly administered, that might may not overcome right in having a proper regard to trade in general, that your neighbours may receive some benefits from your impartial determinations and agreements. I shall be very ready to observe your commission in what you want in this Town, and when I have the proper dimensions of the chimney pieces shall immediately order them; and please to give me full directions to prevent any mistakes. column46: 15 February, Dear Brother, I am not sure whether I am debtor to yours of the 31 and, having but little leisure on my hands, am determined however not to loose the present opportunity of returning my due accknowledgements. So happy times are approaching; but in lieu of this the duty of salt is revived which I fear is to continue and prove a very heavy burden, besides the ill consequences that may attend. This day the committee, appointed to enquire into the abuses and notorious villainy of the charitable corporation, moved for several of their officers to be taken into custody, for fear that they shoud escape examination as some of them already are gone into parts beyond the sea; also that they might have power to examine evidences in the most solemn manner. column46: London. 6 March, Dear Brother, Your favour of the first instant came duly to hand and am glad you give so good an account of yourself and wish you may perform your journey well and that I may hear a good account of you att Richmond, where I am sure you'll find one, who posseses me entirely, to make you welcome and will take care of you. The late inundations will prove very chargeable to me in many places and it is very well we have only one shilling upon land and no new fund or tax to affect us this year. There is a great debt upon the navy, but I do not know how that will be supplied. We shall have a full house next week when the new excise laws will be communicated, which has occasioned so much clamour. Then the world will be judge of the monster as it is called. I know nothing of the Were bill miscarrying. shall make some enquiry and find out the true reasons. I rejoice my nephew continues well and good, which must afford you great comfort and satisfaction. column46: London. 20 March, Dear Brother, I am obliged with your favour of the 11, and though we have had variety and uncertain sort of weather yet no covering of snow, which must do good. The justice has no reason to complain of me, having paid him the last visit, and I shoud be sorry to loose the friendship of my good neighbour. I hope it is no crime for man and wife to possess each other and the more entire, in my thoughts, greater is the happiness, which I please myself will always continue a blessing to me, and I heartily wish the same to all my friends and acquaintance. I recommended Lady Darcy to your horses and I perceive she's determined to have them at your own price. My wife tells me how kind you was by return of her servant, for which my thanks. Last Wedensday was a very fatiguing day when the scheme for preventing frauds in tobacco, by way of excise was opened and fully debated; divided yeas 265, noes 204. I got not to bed till 4 that morning and upon the report of Friday we had another laborious day and detained as late, and divided to agree with the committee yeas 249, noes 189; so that a bill is ordered to be brought in according to the resolutions, and, if the regulation of wine comes on to cure those frauds, I see no end of this session. I perceive the River Were bill is thought convenient to be dropped on account of the City of Durham petitioning to have the navigation lengthened to Durham, which alarmed the coal owners, who do not like it or their aldermen to be made trustees, &c. column46: London. 7 April, 1733. Dear Brother, I am obliged with your favour of the first of this month, hoping now your health is perfectly reestablished. Last Wedensday we had a very long day upon the first reading of the Tobacco bill and divided whether it shoud be read a second time, yeas 236 noes 200; so that it is a nice point att present to judge what will be the fate of it. The budget of the wine affair is put off to Friday next, that some think it will be further adjourned. column46: Richmond. 6 Nov., 1733. Dear Brother, I have your favour of the 30th of last month to accknowledge with my thanks, and rejoice to hear the welfare of the lads, whom I wish well placed. Eaton and Westminster you do not like so cannot recomend any to you. I am sorry for Alderman Rudstone and the misfortunes attending, but I hope you will be no sufferer. I am extremely obliged for your care in providing some claret for me, never had bad from you and wish for your company to taste the last cargo before it is all gone, for which I am your debtor, and desire to know how accounts stand. War is now proclaimed for this County against the ensuing election. Sir Savile declines; Sir Miles Stapylton, att the late meeting att York, was put up by the Tories and Sir Rowland Win by the whigs, and both have declared by sending circular letters. Only the latter joins interest with Mr. Turner, which I hope will make the former drop his pretensions att this time. My wife joins with me in due respects, and I am ... By a letter this post and sister with their little girl, after an agreeable journey, are safe arrived in town.

Dear Brother, I have your favour of the 13th and am sorry for your congratulation, as I fear Sir will be hurried on by party rage without any probability of success. I do not hear Mr. has lost any interest upon his conjunction except your friend , who will he remembered if he persists att your county-Election when opposition happens. I wish the times do not put all tenants to their shifts, but some endeavour to take all advantages without a cause, which may be your case, as certainly are not desirable and better parted with, without loss, when opportunity serves. The fine weather continues yet, that I will not be without hopes of seeing you. I am concerned for the ill news from Sedgefield. I heard Mr. Fletcher intended to start from London last Wedensday. column46: Richmond. 21 December, 1733. Dear Brother, Having been abroad for a week past I hope will plead my excuse not answering your favour of the 14 sooner. The six pound of tea, &c., is charged att three pounds fifteen shilling and sixpence, which I please myself will rectify and set the account upon a true balance; and if you had not given me hopes of seeing you here, from time to time, I had certainly visited Greencroft, though now must despair of that pleasure till my return from Parliament. Our Recorder gave us great satisfaction. How bravely your constitution holds out in the service of your country. I wish we were to be as quite as I find you are likely . I shall be very ready to do my best service to the memory of my old friend, when called upon. Am sorry to hear that he left his circumstances so bad, which perhaps shortened his days. Sir Miles Stapylton came to Town this evening and intends tomorrow, being Saturday, to try the affections of the good people here, who I believe are all pre-engag'd, except seven or eight. wish it may give a check to his future proceedings and stop in time to save his pocket and trouble, for I cannot conceive the least hope of his succeeding, but I fear party rage is too predominant in him. I thank you for the favour to be a partaker of your wine. When it is bottled desire your notice to send for it, if it cannot be brought hither by the carrier.
