column46: Richmond. 29 January, Dear Brother, In answer to your favour of the 24, I am now preparing for my journey to Parliament, hoping I shall be excused upon the call of the House, this day ordered, as I intend, God willing, to set forward next Thursday; and shall be glad to receive your commands directed to Mr. Williamson's, stationer by Gray's Inn Gate, Holborn. For my part am not so deep in politics to judge of peace or war, but I can scarce think we shall enter upon the latter, contrary to the interest of the nation. I am this moment interrupted by Mr. Wharton, a noted Attorney of Newcastle, who is playing the same game here, upon the of Richmond account, as was done in my father's time, and I hear he's a very proper person to stir up such dead controversies. I have ordered Furnis to send you six stone of soap, and when I hear of any chaps shall recomend your coach geldings. column46: Richmond. 21 June, 1734. Dear Brother, I am favoured with yours of the 17 and fear the late rendezvous att Newcastle was thin, that the History of the 4 Kings was not regarded, or that cash runs low. Saturday proved a day of rain here, without intermission, and made great floods, which saluted my walk without doing the least damage, except leaving a little wreck behind. I am sorry your neighbourhood has suffered so much. do not hear of the like damages here. I believe Mr. Clennell is not much lamented. I had such a misfortune lately in a visit returning from Mr. Metcalfe's of Nap. My horse fell with me and laid upon my foot, who crushed and bruised it severely, which keeps me att present under confinement, but I hope to be att liberty to take a journey next Wednesday to Bewerley, where I shall stay two or three days. I have a letter from Brother this day, who tells me will be att Helperby with his little child latter end of next week proposes to spend one day here and then returns cross the country to his wife and girl att Worcester, and, about the latter end of next month or beginning of August, brings them to these parts to breathe Yorkshire air. I please myself with the thoughts of paying my respects att Greencroft sometime next month, but, when you can transmitt the account betwixt us, you'll oblige ... My wife sends you her best repasts.

Dear Brother, I must now return my accknowledgements for your favour of the 21 of last month, and, as you expect no wine this year, I shall provide elsewhere and wait till I can partake with you. The thoughts of reducing national interest from 4 to 3 has cause a great run upon the Bank by artful men, which is now over. Happy for us that there is a law to prevent stock-jobbing, otherwise people's properties would have suffered greatly att this critical juncture, though it's believed, upon the first reading of the three bill, engines will be set att work again. I pity the female world, if the bill takes effect, to be reduced of a quarter part of their income, wherein there are many hard cases. column46: Richmond. 6 August, 1736. Dear Brother, I have your favour of the 30th last past and congratulate your safe arrival att Greencroft, as I am glad your expedition proved so pleasant and agreeable. The melancholy account you give of the great destruction and scarcity of game, I fear, is become too general in all places, that the species must certainly be lost if timely care is not taken. I have now an indictment depending att the present assize against a notorious offender, which I wish may deter others from the like idle and pernicious practices. I was the first day att York races, where I found a thin appearance and the worst meeting since the establishment. I despair now seeing you till your assizes are over and your usual diversion with your friend Bootle. I could wish the time fixed to be att home, having promised to make Mr. Fletcher a visit att Hutton, and, if you'll make one of the party, I believe it will be the beginning of next month. column46: Richmond. 5 Dec., 1736. Dear Brother, I am obliged with your favour of the 2d ultimo and sorry to be deprived so long of your company. I have no thoughts yet of a journey to Town, which I shall defer as long as I can. column46: Richmond. 17 May, 1737. Dear Brother, I got well hither on Saturday last, and this day brings me your favour of the 12. As I am sorry to find you continue yet uncertain in favouring us with your company here, which wish may be soon for fear shall be upon the ramble next month, in making visits to stay from home. I have bought you half a dozen turn overs and two of Spanish snuff, which I wish may please, and shall be glad to know how to convey them. I have been under apprehensions some time for my kinsman, who, I fear, will not be a man long in this world. I am concerned for poor George. Though he wants the doctor's advice, my love and best wishes attend him and his brother; and I am glad you was so well diverted att races. I am ...

27, 1713. Honoured Sir, I have taken a view of the Leadmiln and compute she will take about £8 to putt her into order. As she is, will not be fit for no busness. So I would not do anything about her till I advise you of the charge; and as you direct I shall observe. I think we shall get as much profitt by smelting the slags as will double answer the charge. Then she will be ready for any other business that falls out. The trials att Whitefeild-Moorgate and the falls all offer pretty fair att present for good cole. But if your worship design to give five to the score, I think we must defer working them and take worse. I heartily wish you and yours good health and am Your worships most humble and most faithful servant Weatherley. The bearer is our schoulemaster. I have telled him what you ordered and if you approve of him. I fancy he will accept your offer. Vale. To James Clavering Esq., att his house in West Gate, Newcastle.

Leadgate. Oct. 26, 1714. 'd Sir, According to your order I have reduced Coleburn pitts to 2 1/2 tenns a week for each pitt till the pay. Then, God willing, shall bring them to 2 tenns a week and no lower they can be brought. The bearers pitt is a very troublesome pitt and more charges lys on his then the other two. So if your worship please to allow him 3 tenns a week, it would doe well. If it cannot be allowed I fancy he will not cary his on, so leaves it to your worship's pleasure. I understand by young , that he would take 14s p. tenn and thank you too. I a letter from Caleb, by which I understand the bargain I let, when last up, proves very well, gets both in sinking and driveing, and he greatly hopes it will turn to account. I have also a letter from Martin Furnace and he says they get very good oar and hopes they will get as much of it as will defray the charge. So I hope the disbursing of the other £50 will bring us in what we have disbursed from first to last, which I shall be very glad to see. If your worship have a letter from your brother York touching my Lord Pawlet's business, I beg the favour to know the contents. I think your worship did tell me this day seven night that you were for Yorkshire shortly. If you be, pray let me know sometime before, and I will send for the man that gave me the account of White's leadmine. If his report be true it will be worth our while to look after it and therefore would have you to here what this man can say, before you go. I am with all sincerity ... Weatherley. To James Clavering Esq., att Stowhouse.

London. Jan. 16, 1717/8. Honoured Sir, I bless God I got safe to London Tuesday gon fourteen days. Yester night wee had a meeting att my master's lodgings touching Mr. Johnson's account. Mr. Bernadeau in his objection says that Mr. Johnson was not to have the 1/2 p. cent after the increase of his sollery. He says the advance was not for quiting the 1/2 p.c. chalder but for the answering of bad debts and the returning of the bills into cash. So my master desires you to let him know upon what score the advance was given, and likewise if you received £22 0d money of him for the by vend of my Lady Clavering's coals. I heartily wish you and all yours a good New Year and many of them. My service attends you and am with all sincerity your worship's most obedient servant. Weatherley. My master gives his service to you and family.

Jan. 27, 1718. Dear Sir, I received both yours and have seen one from Mr. Gowland to Mr. Lee of Chancery Lane, in which he proposes that this dispute shoud at last be left to Mr. Rut and himself. What my Lord will think fit to do, I know not, for I fancy the Mowbrays are now preparing him for the engagement; and a cruel disappointment to them it will be if this trial at law should be prevented. But I must confess I extremely admire at your appointment of a Reference for determining betwixt you and the other freeholders. When I had made such proposals as must have been more advantageous to them (and with good authority too, notwithstanding all that Mr. Mowbray can say to the contrary) then the two New Referees I am sure could make. The time now for applying healing methods is almost elapsed, and therefore I will make this only one proposal more and if it is rejected, I will never concern myself farther in the matter. You insist upon having your boundaries enlarged to Redwells which will never be agreed to. I daresay it never will. Now if you will be satisfied to make a division of the moor or common that lies betwixt Salter's Sick (the first boundary) and the Redwells, and take the half of it by way of addition to your first boundary, I hope my Lord and the freeholders may be brought to acquiesce in it. I have no more to say but that I wish you may not stretch your demands 'till you loose your opportunity, for I am truly persuaded a fair trial at law will leave you far short of what is now offered. I am sure I would not upon any account wrong you of one pile of grass that I could believe of right belonged to you. I have been extremely ill of a cold, which has brought a fit of the gout upon me, of which I have been confined almost a fortnight. My wife joins with me in respects to your good Lady and believe me, I am Sir most faithfully and affectionately yours J. Eden. I am sorry to hear you go on so violently against the Waltons, for I find all the neighbourhood have high resentments of that matter.

Nov. 11, 1718. Dear Sir, I have wrote to my Lord Crewe by this post to know his Lordship's disposition in your affair. I shall also write to Mr. Baker and Mr. Stevenson, &c., to know what it is they insist upon, that, if possible, wee may prevent any further expenses and make a good agreement amongst you (if possibly it can be done) when I get into the country again. Therefore I desire you'll stay your hand a little till I hear from them, and be assured no body will be more glad and ready to serve you, then, Sir ... J. Eden. Wee have after a long debate voted a war with Spain. My wife sends her service to yours.

Nov. 22, 1718. Dear Sir, I shoud not forgive my self in hast, if by advising you to stay your hand, I shoud lead you into an error that might have such ill consequences, but I am apt to think the proposals I design to make will appear very fair and desirable to all the parties concerned. Suppose then to make peace betwixt my Lord and you, that wee allow your claim to a manor; will you be pleased with a boundary from Chapman's Well to Stanley burn head, thence to Salter's Seek and from somewhere thereabouts directly over to the Loud house, joining upon the wall of your own enclosure? It is true, this is something less than what Sir Williamson insisted upon, but I would fain hope you'll be contended with it; and if my Lord can be prevailed upon to give leave to the other freeholders to divide and enclose the rest (or some part) of the Commons adjoining to your boundary, I would hope that might satisfy them to all intents and purposes, and upon so good a footing, I might have the pleasure to see a lasting good agreement and friendly correspondence once more established amongst you. If this shoud take effect, I shoud think it but reasonable that the freeholders, who have leave given to enclose, shoud pay a little matter for each acre, yearly, towards the improvement of the living of Lanchester, and my Lord will have no other consideration for parting with the Commons, but the patronage of Lanchester Church. If this scheme meets with the general approbation of all the parties concerned, I will hasten it as much as I possibly can, that it may without the least loss of time, be finished. I desire you will consult your friends and neighbours concerned and let me have your Answer as soon as conveniently you can. I will write to Mr. Baker by this post to the same purpose and I hope you'll have a meeting upon it and send me your resolutions upon it. My spouse joins with me in respects to your good Lady. To her and you, Sir, I am ... J. Eden. I would have this proposal kept as much as can be from taking air, 'till wee know how your freeholders will receive it. You must discourse upon it with them freely, there's no avoiding of it, but to others - silence.

Dear Sir, I received yours by the last Saturday's post, which I must confess gave me but little satisfaction. You could not be more pleased to have your desire in this affair then I should be in contributing my best wishes and endeavours towards it, but it happens at this time that I cannot gratify the friendship I have for you, and do justice to the trust reposed in me. If the bounders, which I proposed, will not please, I believe some farther concessions may be obtained, if reasonable ones will content you, which may be referred to the commissioners to be appointed by the Act of Parliament, which must be had, if the division goes forwards. Or if you had rather have it so, the present referees may determine that point this next spring or early in the summer. But unless your demands are very much contracted I cannot hope to see any other end put to this troublesome affair, but what an expensive suit of law must give; and it is very probable (whatever you may hope for from a trial) you may be obliged to sit down with a much less share then is now offered to you. I can tell you too, your neighbours seem better inclined to an accommodation then you think (as appears by your last letter), though they are far from apprehensions of being worsted by you, in case it comes to a trial, but you may be sure, they will insist upon it, that after a boundary is consented to, and settled, that you shall not afterwards make any new pretensions to any farther share of the Commons, upon any claim whatever. I cannot forbear taking notice to you, that I hear you give it out that I had positive orders from my Lord of Durham to put an end to this matter at the Reference upon any terms, which I do assure you is very false for I neither had message, nor letter, from his Lordship relating to my conduct in that affair before I got to London; and it is very absurd to imagine any such orders could be given to predetermine my judgement in the matter. I can only say farther, that if his Lordship makes any concessions, it is not from any diffidence of his cause or of his success if he can have justice, but merely for peace sake. I shall be glad, if what I have proposed in this, has your approbation; I shoud think myself very happy in being instrumental to restore peace and good neighbourhood amongst you, which is so valuable, that a great many acres upon the barren commons can never be a sufficient recompense for the loss of it; and, give me leave to add, from the sincere friendship I have for you, that I wish you had rather pardoned generously the Walton's for a fact committed so long ago, then prosecuted them with so much severity. I think, it would have been much better upon more accounts than one . Pardon my honest freedom; let me hear from you, and putt me if you can into a way to serve you and rid you of this troublesome affair, which will be more acceptable to no man living then to, Sir, ... J. Eden. My spouse joins with me in respects to your good Lady and yourself.

Dec. 20th, 1718. Dear Sir, I received yours by the last Wednesday's post, and am sorry that I cannot, at present, give you the satisfaction you desire, it being impossible to make any right judgement of what farther concessions can be made, without a map; but if you expect any great matters more, you'll certainly be disappointed. I wish you would not think too well of your own pretensions, which may prevent all endeavours to end this affair in an amicable way, and prove a fatal error to you at last. You seem to think I have a commission to make an end with you upon any terms, which I do assure you is a grand mistake. My Lord may make some small concessions for peace sake, but take my word for it, he'll stand another trial if you putt him anything hard to it. I could give you a convincing proof of it, if it were not improper to trust it in a letter. If boundaries can be fixed to please you, you may expect all that can be done to make you safe in your possession of it. But till the first point is settled, it is to no purpose to trouble ourselves about the other. I will only say, that excepting my Lord's death (which I hope is yet a great many years distant), you need not have any apprehensions of being made uneasy, or of being disappointed, by staying till I get into the country. I'll write more in a post or two, and at present have only time to give my wife's respects and my own to your good Lady and to assure you that I am, with great sincerity ... J. Eden.

Dec. 25, 1718. Dear Sir, You must either have more patience or I doubt it will be impossible to give you that effectual security which you so earnestly press for, in so hasty a manner. My Lord's death, if it shoud happen soon, may be very inconvenient to you, take what method you please in this affair, either by trial or reference. Can you propose any method yourself for your own security? Or will you refer it to Mr. Gowland to draw up an agreement in the strongest terms that can be conceived, to bind the Bishop, yourself, and the freeholders, which when approved by Mr. Spearman on behalf of his friends, may be sent to my Lord for his approbation? Your boundary must be particularly set forth in it, as consented to, by my Lord, and when you have all set your hands and seals to this agreement, it may be a foundation for an Act of Parliament, which must be had for dividing the Commons. Now when you have my Lord's and the freeholders' hands and seals to such an agreement, you may wait with less uneasiness for an Act of Parliament. For though such an instrument may not bind my Lord's successor yet surely it will bear a very great weight with him and incline him very strongly to approve of what has been done, and to suffer it, to be perfected according to that design. I will write to Mr. Rut about the farther concessions to be made, for I think he will understand me, though I have forgot the names of the boundary marks, and, since you are so hasty, let him try to adjust that matter twixt the freeholders and you. I must only put you in mind, that you are to be concluded by this agreement from making any farther claim in respect of the pretended manor of Iveton. If by Mr. Gowland's assistance you can invent any ties strong enough for the and his successor, I hope you will let us have them and make your self and your neighbours easy, which I heartily wish may be speediy affected; and it will not be more to your satisfaction then to the pleasure of ... J. Eden.

Feb. 28, 1718/9. Dear Sir, I am heartily sorry to find that there is so little hope of accomodating this difference betwixt the Bishop and you. I thought the last proposal so much to your advantage, that upon my word, I was more apprehensive of meeting with objections on my Lord's part then on yours. I was so desirous to bring you to an agreement, that I ventured to make a bold push, and acquainted my Lord with it afterwards, and to tell you the truth, (though I doubt not but he would have confirmed it, because he had given me authority) he seemed to me not very much to approve it. And since you have refused it, I give you fair notice, that if you should take a fancy to accept it, I will not undertake to make it good. You mistook me in the mention made of the referees - I meant not that you had taken any new ones in the case twixt my Lord and you; but in that betwixt you and the freeholders - and I thought the kind and beneficial offers made to them from my Lord, by me, were better then could be made by any other hand without my Lord's authority. I grant too, that you never in your letters may have mentioned your consent to contract your boundaries to Redwells, but it was what was offered by Sir Wm. Williamson at the reference, and Mr. Rut, I think, has hinted something of that kind since, in a letter to me and I thought they might have had your consent to doe it. I lately saw a scotch of a bill, for determining this dispute by to be appointed by the Parliament. It was to be sent into the north to be jointly considered by Mr. Rut and Mr. Gowland to see what they could make of it. Pray let me know if you have heard any account of it. The noise has been made about the Pretender's being taken proves to have been groundless. But there is a Bill to be brought into the of Lords on Monday next, which is of an extraordinary nature. It is concerning the estate of the peerage of Britain; and by it, they say, twenty five Scotch Peers are to have the privilege for them and their families of sitting in Parliament, and all the other Scotch peers to be excluded, and be disabled from ever serving as peers there. The King will have power to make six English peers more but after that, to create none 'till the number of them is below two hundred, which they are not afterwards to exceed. My wife joins with me in hearty respects to your good Lady and pray believe that I am with great sincerity ... J. Eden.

Sept. 28th, 1719. Dear Sir, I have seen the articles with your amendments, to which, I find, the Freeholders not in the least disposed to consent. They are surprised, (and not without reason) that you shoud think of having two acres in lieu of those you leave open to the Ivesteners; since though, taken from your Greencroft manor, they will be added to that of Iveston. You have forgot, I believe, the first articles of agreement, when you demanded an allotment for Burnhouse for you were to provide for that and Whinny Garths and Nunshouse upon condition of having 80 acres, which was agreed to. Then you proposed to take twenty acres (instead of 80) if they would take care of Nuns House which was agreed to. Thus the case stood and therefore you cannot in honour insist upon that point. And your having your allotment made by the in the first place , is what they refuse to comply with, insisting upon the general division altogether. I wish to see you at Whitworth, where I shall stay till Thursday morning to accommodate these differences, which I think not very material. I had almost forgot the 2d acre, which the Ivestoners are resolved never to agree to, and truly Mr. Rut and all of us, wee think it too hard that you should have both the 20th acre, and 2d new Tons too; I am sorry these new difficulties shoud be started and perhaps there are some others which I do not now think on. I am ... J. Eden.

Jan. 4th, 1719/20. Dear Sir, I should make some apology for not having answered your obliging letter sooner, but I am confident your friendship will doe it better for me then I can for myself. I am surprised the Waltons should stand off with so much obstinacy, and whether they mislead, or are themselves misled, the difficulty of making them accede will be equally troublesome, yet I am not without hopes, that when I get into the North they may by proper methods be persuaded to hearken to reason. My Lord Wm. Pawlet has been often with me, to desire my assistance in fixing his boundary, and when that is done, there will, I think, remain no pretence for them, to give you any farther disturbance. The conclusion of your letter has something of the riddle in it where you tell me if I follow not a laudable example in coming down, &c. , you know who will be blameable. I fancy you will not think me blameable for keeping to my post in my country's service, when for ought I know, my attendance may be more necessary then ever. Deserters may plead some merit with the enemies of their country; but never surely with those whom they have forsaken. If you have a dissolution in your thoughts, I can tell you, wee have almost given over thinking on it here, and I would not alarm my friends in vain. People are everywhere making different conjectures upon what my Lord Stanhope's journey will produce. It is said, there is a peace upon the anvil twixt France and Spain, by which all those valuable advantages in trade which were lately in our possession will be given to France, and wee shall have so many months given us to consider on it, if we'll come into 't or not. I can't yet guess how long this session may last but if wee are to enquire into the state of the fleet and some other matters it may perhaps be a long one. I am told there will be a call on Thursday sonnet, and no favour to deserters. I have the satisfaction of Mr. Shafto's and my 's company, which makes me easier then I shoud otherwise be from home, and my good . We often remember you and your fireside. My respects to your good Lady and pray believe me ... J. Eden. I wish you all many happy new years. I hope you have taken care of the highway for which my word is engaged to Mr. Stephenson.

Durham. 4 March, . Sir, This afternoon Mr. Spearman, Mr. Hunter, Mr. Stevenson junr., and Mr. Whittingham sent for me to the post-house, and there showed me a letter from Mr. Denton, the solicitor, and also a letter from you touching the about the Commons; and after some introductory discourse they told me that most of their adherents had now deserted them or at least so far as to refuse payment of any proportion or share of expenses; and that Mr. Bowlby might be sent up to prove the signing of the agreement. Therefore, to discharge that and also the fees in both Houses, it was necessary to raise £120: in this manner - the said £80, and you £40: or otherwise the whole affair must consequentially cease. I told them this seemed to me an unequal contribution and no way conformable to the agreement, which was to raise the expenses rateably according to the value of your estates in the Book of Rates. To which they replied that all but them refusing and you receiving the greatest share of the Common. They thought the above method was just enough. Thereupon I took leave, informeing them that I would (as they requested it) give you an account thereof, which Mr. Spearman also promised to doe this post. Your servant called this morning and told us your Lady's family at Stow house were well. We are mere strangers to the of your . My father is and so I am, Sir ... Gowland.

Durham. 13 March, 1720. Sir, I a letter last post from your son giving an account that his Bill had past the House of Lords, but he was now under a great uneasiness for Mr. Ord's son's taking from Mr. Pit's counsel (as he said by your order) the Tanfield writings, which hath so provoked that gentleman and given him such jealousy of unfair dealing that he's for declaring void the bargain, which will be the greatest in kindness that any can propose to doe to the family and the poor children must think as well as he, who are innocent and unconcerned in the family prejudices. I must tell you that I cannot believe this to be by your order; nor shall believe it; until I have it from yourself. If you have any reason to give I wish that you had first writ it to me and I should certainly have mediated the matter to your mutual satisfaction. If this bargain be obstructed by any evil counsellors they will not be able to answer to God or man the miseries that may attend his family, which I beg of you to prevent. It is in your power and have not that to answer for. I am so concerned that you must excuse my expressions, which are the of true love for your family. I can't think that Mr. Grey gave any such advice, but I doubt you are into other hands, that I should never desire to be advised by. I beg of you write without fail tomorrow to alter this hindrance and to carry the writings where they were. Otherwise give me a good reason against it that I may not alter the good opinion I always have of your integrity and uprightness. My service to Mr. Grey and his lady and Madam Anne, and am Sir ... R.G.

Durham. 14 March, 1720. Sir, Yesterday morning I went to wait upon Mr. Spearman touching the money to be raised for carrying through the bill about the Commons and discoursed him upon the proportions; the result whereof was this, that many had unhinged departed from the agreement and all refused to pay their contributions but 4 persons vizt. Mr. Spearman, Mr. Stevenson, Mr. Hunter and Mr. Whittingham and that they proposed that you should advance £40 and they £20 apiece, but after a little reasoning he thought it an unreasonable imposition for you to pay double and therefore he would agree to £20. However, in his usual obscure way he said, if it was not done the bill must drop for they would doe no otherwise. Just as I am writing this Mr. Spearman's clerk is come to tell me that he hath this post a letter from you and that Mr. Hunter and Mr. Whittingham will be in town in the afternoon and desires I may meet them at the post-house, which I shall doe accordingly, and so write underneath what passes. Above you have a copy of my father's letter sent this morning to your father. If we receive any answer it shall be imparted to you. I am just come from Mr. Spearman and Mr. Bowlby, who were but the other gentlemen expected did not come; therefore Mr. Spearman the matter thus - that you should be bound with the four gentlemen, above named, for the sum to be advanced, and that the same shall be raised out of the moneys collected and to be collected by virtue of the agreement, and in case of less the obligors are to contribute equally. Mr. Spearman will send for those four gents. to be here on Thursday and I shall send for the Lords to be here the same day and then endeavour to reconcile the difference and if he be satisfied I think your bill will be in no danger. Mr. Bowlby proposes to go in the coach on Friday if he can take a place for that day; but on horseback he dared not venture because he is much afflicted with the gravel. My father is, and so am I, Sir, your very humble servant ... Ra: Gowland jnr. Mr. Hopper being from home I could not search the office for the recovery with which I acquainted Mr. Wilkinson, who told me he had no letter about that affair nor heard nothing thereof since you went to London. I congratulate you on your bill passing the House of Lords, but doe not find it in the votes this as I expected.

Durham. 25th April, 1721. Dear Sir, This day Mr. Carr of Cocken and the Lady Margaret Paxton (the beauty) were married. I knew nothing of it till near 9 in the morning. I yours and know not where to lay the superlative fault of not looking into your title. Could any man imagine but that had been known before you entitled? Ralph desired of Mr. Grey an abstract of the deeds, which he refused him. That Mr. Pit hath made Ord his solicitor must be plain; that he's what I writ to your father that his advisor was. That letter makes me out of favour with old and young of them. The packet will be sent when post horses comes from Northumberland. I am sorry for your ill usage, nay barbarous, and advise you to bear under the oppression with an humble submission to the will of God and despond not. Why are you angry with my son? If the other side will not employ us would you not have us before for those that will? You know my principal and practise and so it follows, to act for our clients with more zeal than for ourselves and not to betray them and surely then wee lay no foundation for reflection that can be called just. I think he doth what he ought to doe and what I shall encourage him in to act vigoursly for his client. You dropped him in your bill and got another, and in this he's not, nor was, any way concerned for you or any of those who are for the division bill. What your friends or others without just cause reflects on him, will neither hurt him nor me, and if he or I was concerned for you and not in the house of Lords surely he may be there for those that never opposed you; but will readily agree that you have what is allotted to you. If Jack Hunter had not been what he is and refused the men their known right, they had never opposed it. Why should not openly appear and how can the miscarriage of that bill reflect on him? He hath reasonable sent him from my clients this post, which ought to be embraced if not. Then wee cannot be blamed. Enclosed you have Row's bond. The charges are of three; judgements, and £91. 5s. 10d. besides what the sheriffs and gaolers' fees and entering satisfaction on the judgements. His wife was here to know if I your order to discharge him. I am very weary yet am Sir ... Ra. Gowland.

Durham. 25th April, 1721. Sir, I can add that I have done the utmost in my power for service and had not I been more active therein than some others I can tell the length it would have gone. I have been an instrument as much as possible to mitigate and lessen Hunter's demands and brought him to this proposal for peace sake, whereof no advantage is to be taken if not complied with, vizt. , that he shall have a quantity of the wast in proportion to the book of Rates in respect of his freehold and other lands and tenements, and the like quantity to be laid continuous thereto in respect of his manor and for his consent also and the mines under both the allotments and if this is secured to him by an additional clause he will agree thereto. I am heartily concerned for the obstructions you meet with and think you have been abominably dealt with and wish you speedily extricated from all difficulties and am ... Ra. Gowland jnr. N.B. All treaties or proposals were rejected here by Mr. and Mr. .

Durham. 5 May, 1721. Kind Sir, I thank you for your congratulation. I shall rejoice to hear that the counsel agree with you and Pitts. I am much concerned at your uneasiness. When you and the Moor Hunter and the others had come to an agreement and you had all signed, and your boundary set out therein, in the bill before the house, and all agreed to the sole conduct of Spearman and Hunter and sent to the Tory solicitor above, and wee all laid aside, surely wee might be for the two lords; and you know, when here, that wee were so concerned, if you had then desired wee would not, I should have sit still for anything but a great trouble that I shall get by it or my sons either, for I doe not take them to be generous and considerate clients. But having undertaken it and when readily agree to your what can wee now doe? I did not suppose that doth appear for any but the Lords, for the solicitor for those that carry in the bill solicits for the whole bill to pass and not for their parts exclusive of yours, and, if so, if that bill pass it is for the whole and sure in that you are included, and if so then doth not solicit for you and the Lords too. That would be inconsistent, if you oppose them, though they will agree for your allotment to stand unimpeacht by them, but then that, I doubt, must be on a new bill and not this joint bill. Assure yourself John is the sole that occasions their appearance. He owns them Lords of the Manor, but that the manor doth not extend beyond the dike stakes. Then the moor can no way belong to the tenants as appurtenance to their several enclosures; for if the moors be the common appurtenance to their in grounds, then they are parcel of the manor, and to talk otherwise is greatest absurdity. I know is their great advisor and was present when kept their last Court. Whether I or any of my sons had been concerned or not wee should not have valued for anything that wee shall get by it. What was written to you was so reasonable as none but John Hunter would oppose, he having the 's lease. He would extend that to the cole mines on Medomsly fell, and so extend the 's bounder further then it ought, and if the have the mines there, he must be Lord of the Manor, not the Hunters. I doe not know what you mean by - biding you look to yourself - I cannot see and could wish that any can use the least argument to show our being for the Hunters is dishonourable. If I apprehended it so, I would soon give it up. If they come about Row's matter I'll pursue your directions. You must setle the account for principal interest and costs and send me down, that I may know what to take the security for. I think our justices acted with prudence like good protestants and friends to King George, not to be governed by Tories, though the City Conyers hath prevailed on, they being wonderful ingenious, considerate and well affected. Sir Wm. Williamson and his side offered to address the King by congratulation on the birth of the prince and then petition him for justice on those miscreants. But to address the Commons was imitating '41, to set the King and people by the ear. They were for hanging the robbers, if it could be by law, and I think I gave you my judgement before you went hence, that they should be hanged if it could be and all their estates forfeited and added to the South Sea stock; and that wee are all for. I understand not-quiting the seven millions - nor doth any of the papers explain it. I am weary yet always would approve myself to be ... Ra. Gowland.

Durham. 7 Jan'y, Worthy Sir, The resolution taken at our last meeting, not being putt in execution, occasions you the trouble of this to remind you thereof (least you should impute it to my neglect) I have enclosed sent the form of a summons usual in those cases (as I'm informed), which I submit to your correction you being the properest judge thereof. If you and Mr. Stevenson think fit to sign it, or to get it signed by any other you think proper and sent forthwith to be served on the party before the Sessions that in case he refuses to appear thereon wee may then meet and come to further resolutions about our business. I take it the summons is to be sent by the Justices themselves otherwise would have saved you that trouble but since the charge is to be bore by the public I hope you'll excuse ... Rob. Spearman.

Durham. 26 January, Worthy Sir, I had the favour of yours, for which, and the news it brings, I return you due thanks; and when you and Mr. Wright have agreed of a day to meet here, if you please to let me know your day I'll attend you and in the meantime I think it may not be amiss to give Mr. Hunter and such other of the freeholders as you judge notice of the day and place of meeting that they may bee present (which may take away objections which may be raised) and give an opportunity (when together) to forward matters which I take to be a necessary point, which is wholly submitted to your prudent management by Sir ... Rob. Spearman. Since the receipt of yours I had a letter from Mr. Eden, which says my Lord Pawlet is very pressing to have a copy of the agreement betwixt my Lord of Durham, you and the freeholders, of which your thoughts are desired if to be done.

Durham. 7 February 1720. Worthy Sir, I had the favour of two letters from you, which I deferred answering till now, in hopes of hearing from Mr. Eden, but he being silent I conclude nothing is to be done with my Lord. I therefore wrote to Mr. Eden by last post, to let him know that it was the opinion of those here not to attempt the bringing in of the Bill without my Lord's consent, so that we are wholly at a stand at present and I find nothing can be done unless Mr. Eden and you can prevail with my Lord to join with us, which be pleased to try again that we may once more have peace and quietness in the parish, which is what's desired by ... Rob. Spearman. To James Clavering Esq., at a Painter's in Bedford Street, near Bedford Row, London.

Durham. 25 February, 1720. Worthy Sir, I doubt not but you mine by last post, which would give you an account of what happened at our last meeting. This day Mr. Stephenson was with me and brought the enclosed (which has no weight in it) and he has to endeavour to get me a copy of the made by Mr. J. Hunter of Billingside and the other freeholders. He tells me that Major Nicholls, Mr. Sandford and several others of the substantial freeholders are for opposing the Bill, and that their chief objections are the want of a comon-quarrey in that quarter, and that they have no better allowance for working the colemines and wayleaves in their grounds, and for making, keepeing and repaireing of gates, so that I doubt we shall have a sore struggle to get forward, unless my Lord Wm. espouse it heartily. I have got a letter from Mr. Cotesworth to tell me that he had the copy of but had not time to it, so as to send it, by last post. Therefore he only told me my Lord he had it and named the £200 charges which he left to his Lordship to explain. I am Sir ... Rob. Spearman. To James Clavering Esq., att Stowhouse.

Durham. May 14, 1720. Sir, In answer to yours by the bearer, the Bill is perfected and sent away to be filed and I expect the spas down in a post or two, and, as soon as they come, shall get them served. For dispatch of the business in hand I take it is necessary for you to give instructions for your answers that they may be got drawn and sent up in time. The copy of the Bill is by me which you may see when you please, and your presence will be absolutely necessary here to make application to those concerned for the Bishop in order to have his answer drawn and filed, and, to that end, if you please to appoint a time when you can be over I hope to be able to attend you and in the mean time am Sir ... Rob. Spearman.

Durham. 4 June, 1720. 4 a clock. Sir, I have just now received a letter by a special messenger from Mr. Eden to acquaint you that his affairs are such abroad, that he cannot possibly meet on Monday (as he designed). Therefore I send this to give you an account thereof to prevent your journey that day. I have desired Mr. Eden to appoint another day (as soon as conveniently he can) and give me notice thereof in time that I may let you know the same. I am Sir ... Rob. Spearman. Upon receipt of Mr. Eden's letter I wrote this in hopes of getting it sent by your servant (who I sent to enquire after) but he being gone I sent the bearer on purpose herewith. You are to pay the bearer nothing, for that I will discharge.

Durham. 24 Dec., 1720. Worthy Sir, I shall observe your directions relating to the Petition. I had no letter from Mr. Eden (which I am very much surprised at). I was to waite on Mr. Cotesworth, who told me, that, in case my Lord laid his commands on him, he would still be ready to doe the best service he could. I enquired of my Lord had answered his last letter, which he said he had not, but to let me hear from him when he did; and so we parted. I heartily wish you a good journey ... Rob. Spearman.

Durham. 26 Dec., 1720. Worthy Sir, By last post I had the favour of a letter from Mr. Eden, which is to the effect following - That my Lord Wm. and he should have met last Wednesday night (by my Lord's appointment) but the house sat so late that he desired another day so that he fancied on Thursday they would have a trial of skill. But my Lord says he will not retreat from any of his demands and Mr. Eden tells him he cannot comply with them and thinks my Lord seems unwilling that it should be broke off. Please let me know how I may direct a letter to you at London least I should have occasion to write. I wish you a happy Christmas and many ... Rob. Spearman.

Durham. 28 March, 1721. Worthy Sir, I can only tell you that our partners came here yesterday and signed the bond. I have by this post sent Mr. Denton a bill for £80. As to the objections you make to the notes you signed, I doe not find but you'll be made easy in it and if we can but keep together as I hope we shall I doubt not but we shall gain our point, if the Parliament continue sitting any reasonable time, which is what I most doubt ... Rob. Spearman. Since the sealeing of my letters to Sir J. Eden and Mr. Denton to whom I have wrote by this post. I have an account from Mr. Bowlby from Ferry-Bridge by letter from thence dated last night that the waters are so out that he will not reach London till Saturday next. To James Clavering Esq. at a painter's in Bedford Street near Bedford Row, London.

Durham. 5 May, 1721. Sir, Yours of the 25th past came to hand with one enclosed to Johnson, which I sealed and dispatched to him, and I had an account by Mr. Hunter that it came to his hand, but cannot hear that he took the least notice of it to his neighbours. I have had another letter from Mr. Denton for more money, wherewith I acquainted our partners (and that it may not be awanting at this juncture). We applied to Mr. Wilkinson, who got us £100 of Mr. Wm. Norton for which we have given our bond, wherein your first named, and is to sign (as we and I doe not in the least doubt, but you'll doe it, but to satisfy the other concerned I have by this post sent a note or memorand to Mr. Denton, which will inform you more fully of the matter and which your desired to sign before him and Mr. Hunter; and when done to return it and I shall get the rest to sign it. The last note you signed, relating to the money got of Mr. Randolph, is yet in Mr. Gowland's hands and must be delivered up to you when you return though signed. You see Mr. Burton is come in, which will ease us; and to satisfy him we have undertaken the said memorand shall be signed by you and the rest. Please therefore dispatch it. I returned by last post £80 more to Mr. Denton and the remainder of the £100 went to discharge our debt to Mr. Wilkinson and at the post-house. The expense above is thought to be very great, so that it's desired you'll be as frugal as you can, for I find it will be a difficult matter to raise more money here unless we have good success upon hearing the petition already preferred (to prove which Mr. Didsbury went post from house last Tuesday). I am informed that when Lord Hunter's petition was preferred we had not one in the house to speak for us, and that in case any had opposed it, it had been thrown out as irregular, which news I was surprised to hear. I hope better care will be taken the petition be heard or we throw our money away and shall be laughed at. I had by last post a copy of Lord Hunter's petition, upon which I have made some observations which I have by this post sent to Mr. Denton. I heartily wish you good success upon your hearing for all here will think it long until they have an account thereof. I am with all due respect ... Rob. Spearman.

Durham. 9 , 1721. Worthy Sir, I send this to remind you that the money borrowed of Mr. Randoph will be due the 18th instant, so that a meeting some day next week is absolutely necessary, that it may be got raised against the time, for by what I can find, their will be no overplus of the money returned to London and therefore Mr. Randolph's principal and interest must be made up amongst us. Please appoint a day latter end of next week and let me have notice thereof in time that I may get notice to our partners. I am Sir ... Rob. Spearman. To James Clavering Esq., att Stowhouse.

Lamesly the 3 of Dec. My Dearist, I can't possible express the satisfaction I take in the receipt of your oblidging letters which makes me not dar to omit a post returning answer, thoy mine be of little Consequence, for fear of discouridging so great a kindness, nothing being of pleasure to me with out them. At this time is my only divertion, Sister Nancy is all my Company. Uncle Harry went of friday to and I imagine is gon to Richmond to day. A mane is Come hear on purpose to let him know that the Election is of thursday, so I think I must pay him because it is upon your account. I am exstreamly glad you meet with so maney good friends and espesholly amongst the bishops, where I the most feared. I hope you need be in no manner of dispute in the matter of succsess. Your obligations is very much to the Lady Wood for so great sevillitis, and mine no less for her noble present. Pray tell me if you think it reqesit that I should send her thanks. I asure you it will be very acceptable to me. I wounder to here Lady Clavering is so stirring Lady. I never took her to be a stickler upon any account. I think she will get no great credit by following the Lords to the house you mention. It may be matter of concern to all Sir James' friends to here he gos on in such a course. I heartily wish you may be victorious in your pursuit and soune at home again. The latter, I fear, I wish much more sincerely than you doo; you that meets with so maney diversions and good friends is no wounder if they take your heart. For my part hath nothing to diverte my thoughts from you. You write me exstrodnary news about the queen and her parliament, which we have all reason rejoice at. I wish for the lunge continuance of it. I thank you for the print you sent me. Charles say he hath not occasion for any beans of any sort. If you have a mind for flowers he will write what sorts. For my wants am unwilling to trouble you with further than I have occasion, knowing London is very expensive. Pardon my nonsense and give my duty and servis were due, wishing you good health and succsess Dearist Yours intirly Affectionate wife Ca. Clavering would think it not amiss to buy some. I send this day to Hebbron for the wine it being of. Cousin Ellison is very ill. For James Clavering.

Lamesley the 6 of Dec. My Dear, I would not have you be uneasy upon my account for I'm now pretey well again and am concerned you should take advis of the doctor at London. It is only so much money thrown away. However must return you my best thanks for your great care and kindness over me. I am really taking what Mr. Heslop prescribed, which, with my being blooded in the arm, I don't fear but may do me good for the present. For the sack you was so very kind to order me to take, I fulfilled very faithfully till my bleeding begun and then I asked Mr. Heslope whether it was fit for me and he said "No". You might be assured I would pursue your request in drinking it, thoy I thought it much too good for me. I rejoice exstreamly that you keep your health in the perpetual hurry you are in. I shall lunge for some news of your business, that may give me hopes of seeing my Dearist, for whom I so much desire the company of. I have not yet heard of the money Mr. Pinkney was to bring me which hinders me paying Mr. Dubleday's rent. I beg you'll buy me a paer of worsted stockings of about 6 or 7 sh. a paer and bring them with you, and be pleased to send me down in a post letter half an ounce of french quiltin cotton, which trouble I hope you will pardon and believe me Dearist ... My obligations is very much to Mrs. Hebburns and I'm in a very great dispute with myself what to make her a requital of; whether to send her something or to desire you to make her present of a guiney. I should be glad of your information of. Your moire that was ill is very well again and all the rest of your horses and doges.

Lamely the 8 of Dec. My Dearist, I dare not but pursue your commands thoy you give me no manner of incouridgment to it by your example. A larger epistle from you would have been much more exceptable to me than all the doctor's prescribshons, which I nor sister can read won word of, so must rest satisfied without the enterpretetion of till seas you. It is french to hus. I live in hopes you wont keep hus long under that ignorance by the sight of my Dearist Jewel. Which news will be pleasantest thing to me you can possible send me. You say you had not a letter from me in your last. If you had given me the satisfaction of answering won, you had certainly been troubled with my nonsense. I am sorry to perceive by my Brother of Sir William Blackitt's Death. I have greatly of compassion for the mallingcoly lady, without dout is so. Uncle Harry is not yet come from Richmond but we are in expectations of him. Mr. Davison and Lady was here yesterday to make a visit. I lunge for the time that may bring hus some news of your business which my good wishes attends a lunge with your welfare am ... Sisters gives their servis.

Lamesly the 10 My Dear, Since the receipt of your last, hath been in so extreme concern for to find your anger so violent against me, that makes me scarce know what I either say or do. What ever reason I have given, I'm certain death it self would have been much more acceptable then that unwelcome letter, and I don't know to what purpose I should make any endeavours to preserve life or health for won that valuys them at so mean a rate as I do, since I am so wretshed a creator in your thoughts. My grieve is insupportable. I can only say I beg your pardon, and as for the occasion that ofends you, was my desire of hearing from you, which I shall never name more I asure you. Let my ill-natur be what it will, you are the first that ever accused me of it. I don't know what you would have me dow in gratification. I think I an't been wanteing in my thankfulness where due, to the best of my poor to any of your relations. I am suer I would dow it much more to them then to my own. For my wants, what you think fit to bestow upon me shall be very acceptable, be what it will. You are very wrong informed in my negleckting writing to my mother. I'm certain was indebted to her won letter. My Uncle Harry came from Richmond of Saturday. Mr Shifty declines standing at Newcastle. Pray let it be my request to you, if you have any regard to my happiness and satisfaction in your absence, that I may your esteem and favour. It is the only thing I desire in the world, and if that may not be granted me, it shall be my petitions a silent grave, which I been pretty nigh one since I see you, thoy I have so little pity from you in your last. Pray give my duty to father, whom I am very much obliged for his kind letter and believe me ... Father is here to night and gos away to morrow. Sir Harry Little summoned him and Uncle Harry to meet him at Newcastle today. We are invited to dine with the parson tomorrow, and Uncle Harry is invited to Lord Catchisside's funeral.

Lamesley the 17 My Dearist, If that I did not desire to aquit my self of what you continually charge me with, would not give you the trouble of my epistle this post, as sister Alice writes. Your daily accusing me is a concern that I can not lay any thing of but you call it reprimanding you, which I know nothing of, nor I hope ever shall. It's fit you should be your own master and take your liberty for me and from henceforth will never name your writing in any kind, since it is such a crime. It is my part to write as oblidgingly to you as I am capable, and I think have don it to the best of my poor . Indeed mine is not in so good a still as I could wish but I hope they may be accepted as coming from an affectionate sincere heart as the more refined. So I beg it of you may have no more angry words and I promise shall have no reason I can prevent. For the latter part of your last letter, I wounder why you should imagine it to be a pleasure to me, since I never gave you reason to accuse me of imodisty of all faults. If you had seen me read it might have observed a great maney blushes, which it provoked exstreamly, without any great satisfaction. shall now relief you from my nonsense, believing me ... Cousin Pell is come tonight for news. Refers you to sister Alice, who is better at giving you it than myself.

Lamesley ye 20 of My Dear, Pursuyant to your commands will take all your reproves and reflections upon me with patiens, and without naming it further, hoping the same from you. Thoy I asure you it is no little concern to me, and I need nothing to be an adition, for my mallingcolly is suffictionat, being quite abandoned of all company except master. He and I is like two forlorn people these long nights and ill whether. We desine not to endure it lunge next week. The latter end of it, will go to Greencroft, it being the soonest cane be ready, Master having to aquiep of new Cloths. I dare not stay for your orders in them so hath chose a drukitt for him, being advised to it for the winter. Must have another at easter. Hise wants is from top to toy, which I shall supply as well as I can. For your buying him anything at London, we think it needles for a growing boy and you know his way of wearing them. What he wants may be got as good here. He is very well and ollso good, but hath lost his reading most exstreamly. I make him read one a day. Can't read one verse without miscalling his letters and putting in words of his own, nor can turn to a Chapter. A great deal of pains must be taken with him to come to it right. I tell him must write to you. I beg you'll get me some thread, a quarter of a pound of 6d an ounce and the same of the rest, 12d an ounce, and 10d, and 8d an ounce, and 2 ounce of 2s, and 3s, and 4s, and a hundredth of needles, small one. I write yesterday to Mr Hall for the money. I have Charles to pay out of it which makes me fear can not pay little master's master what you ordered. I shall lunge to here of your hearing of your business that may give me hopes of seeing you. Wishing you success in it and a merry Xmais and happey new year; in hast am ... Our clothes wife dyed yesterday of four days illness. You may direct your next to me here.

Lamesley the 22 of May My Dearist, I received your most charming and affectionate letter with all the joy imaginable and I wish I was capable of returning it as deserves. I can assure you I thought it the most delightful thing I have seen since parteing with my Dear, for whose absence nothing can diverte but your kind letters. Your last hath revifed my mallingcolly drooping spirits, which for want of company gave me constant opertuniteys to think and lamment being deprived so lunge of my greatist happiness in world, my dearist Jewel, whose company alone I pref before all the pleasure upon earth, and am glad to find yours is not much less and shall promise you nothing shall be wanteing in my part that may purchus those great blessings ever so much desired by hus both. Knowing it to be a dissatisfaction to you, hath accationed me meney an uneasy hours upon that account, which you have not suspected. I would willingly lie my life done to procure won of those comforts that woude be happiness to you. I did not imagine Dr. Colbatch his prescribtion had been any way tending to my better health in that perticiller, or otherwise should not have been so backward in taking them, but now will be no longer an enemy to myself in it, for I will resolve to pursue it, and since you are so kind to say will get them for me, I chonce much rather to have them therir than here, so will give you trouble of the enclosed. I find you are much the better fichisshon than I am, for I never thought my illness had been so fatal against children as you say. For the other part of the letter, I hope you will excuse me in disobeying you in not naming what you request. shall be more obedient at meeting, for your little son is very well. He's my bedfellow. I have got him part of his nessarys. He gives his duty to you. He calls me "Mamay". I have got my box with all my things which I like exstreamly, and mighty cheap every thing, and much sooner than I expected all things. I must beg you'll pay her and will give you an account what it is. Mrs. Hebburn says my father hath payed the old score. I desire to send her something by sea. Last night with my letters I had won came directed for Mrs. York at Newcastle, franked by my Father. I thinking it for me, opened it and found it from Bro. thanking for her present and had send her a barrel of oysters. I sealed it and send it enclosed. Pray don't mention that I opened it. I was this day informed that cousin Ellison payse for his wine now at Xmais and that your part comes to £5 6s. and shall I send the money Hebbron or what must I do? I fear coming short of money and their is non to be had to spare. My time being now expired for sending the letters must bid my dearist adieu ... Uncle is just come and gives his servis. I have been in expectation of him this 2 days and hearing nothing from Greencroft was just a sensing to know how they did. Pray pardon all mistakes for I'm just started of cowld.

Greencroft 29 My Dear, I received your last at Greencroft. I came last night and I have no opportunity of answering yours by the next post so I hope you'll excuse this not coming sooner. I am very much grieved to find myself so unfortunate to have disobliged you again by not wateing of sister's home. If I had known your mind, I desired, should certainly have don it, thoy never so inconvenient to myself, for I never am better pleased than when I have your abriabation in all things. As I have often towld you it is my wholle endeavour to do what is most exceptable to you and chief care to make you as happey as lys in my poor. I came of horseback behind uncle Harry, who was very careful. You might been assured I should have paid Chas. as you ordered me if I'd had moneys from Mr. Pinpney, which I towl'd you before have not, thoy you accuse me of not doing it, which makes me fear have committed a misdeamener. I am straited in it for I have paid Cousin Ellison. The advise here, as we both desired Cousin Mitford's care of the things that comes by sea, the better way to go to Newcastle. Sir William Blackitt's corpse is buried today as they say. Jack Leabon has a new coffin cow that he would be glad to give any body the use of till Mayday, and we being in sad want of milk, with your leave and aproveing, would take her till that time. I hear since the begineing of thise that Cousin Mitford is very ill. The Dr. say it is an ague. I wish you well of your cowld and maney happey new years and that we may see you soon, which is the constant wishis of ... I am come to a lose, hath lost won of the buckles you bought me. must desire you to get me another of the same sort and then will give you no further trouble with my wants. I have given Sir Harry Little my watch to carry up to get cleaned. Poor mane, I am mighty sorry to see him so much out of order. All here remembers to you. My little spark gives his duty. He is very good boy. I hope he will write by the next post. Pray my duty to father.

Greencroft. 3 My Dearist, I'm sorry to find you surprised with my enclosed. I hope you will pardon it. You gave me so great incouridgment to send the Doctor's note, if I was willing, that I thought it needles to delay time. I am always very backward in endeavouring my own health further then what conduces to the procureing that wished for happiness by hus both, being ignorant that the use of those things was for that intends or otherwais should have immediately got them interpreted and put in execution, never imagineing my bleeding did me any prejudice that way. The reason I was so hasty in paying Cousin Ellison I was informed that he was to pay for the hogshead of wine this Xmais and knowing I should not have so good an opportunity while here to send it. I am now quite of taking Jack Leabon's cow, being poor and not worth the keeping. I am very glad to here you was so diverted the holidays and entertained and should rejoice you could tell me was perfickly well. I never here anything from father. Pray tell me how he dus. This enclosed I believe will aford you a good diversion as it hath don me. Master Landlord's soon came to see him, so master maid him inditer, which is very comical and I was unwilling to give him the trouble to write another. He is a very good boy; I think improves in his reading, wants nothing but pracktis and being minded. His master never hearse him but one a week read and scans that he says. He and his sisters entertained hus with being dressed in boys close and him in girls. Molly desires you'll receive for 2 geanes of won Mr. Slinger, who will come and pay you for it, which is all from ... Will. bids tell you he hopes you'll remember the Dutch mastiff for his cotch pox . Father was at Sir Harry Liddle's Election; imagining sister Alice giving you an account of it, will not give you the trouble of any more nonsense, which I hope you will pardon.

Greencroft the 10 of My Dearist, Yours is ever very acceptable to me and I think it my chiefest happiness now in your absence to be obliged with hearing from you so frequently, which deserves my best thanks as ollso for your care you are pleased to express over me in my journey hear. I beg your pardon sincerely if I interpreted your words to a wrong sense, as I think I did only in answer to yours. You are very diverting with your mane George. It seems he is of value in his own eyes. I wish he had behaved himselve so as might have been serviceable to you. Any way of coming down is too for him. For your lining I took a note of them before we what you have increased. I hope you remember your orders that precious spark shall perform. When I named a buckle to you I imagined you had not forgot the buckles you bought me which I lost won of, to my concern. Sir Harry Little left Newton for his London journey to day, as we believe. He, not being certain himself, leaves both his sons in the country and takes stage coach at York if he cane. My little sweet heart went to scooll of tusday to his great grieve. Would gladly go to New:castle scooll and come home every night. He had not got his task, and, with out a good wiepping now, will never get it. All the arguments could use was in vane. I did not pay either his master or landlord, having not money. The last account had of cousin Midford that she was better since Saturday. That day was very ill. When I came hear I sent a box with a couse pie and some bounges in it, to go by seay for M. Hebron, whom I might requite some way for all the trouble I give her in buying my things. I can not expect she should dow it with out a gratuity. All people that is employed is gratified some way or other. This being what I thought for the charge. I fear it will have the same fate of my Mother's, because believe it goes in the same ship I here you are concerned for , so begs you'll take the same care of mine. Shall enclose the with the name of ship and master. This night hath heard a peace of very ill news which is a trouble to me now in your absence and feareing it will be so to you makes me unwilling to name it. Nancy the cotch maer dyed last night. Will., having carried her to New:castle that day to bring home some otes, not observing her ill before Codding was laid upon her and then laid her self down several times and expired that night, which is all the account I can give of her illness. Pray be not concerned at it. If you prosper in your business will balance that, which I heartily wish you may and that you may continue your health is the sincere prayers of dearist ... Pray my , let me entreat thee to take it with potions and courage what way ever fortune gives the cause.

Greencroft the 11th My Dearist, My great joy and pleasure is to here from yourself, that you keep well with all the hurry and fiteek you have had since we parted. God continue it till our meeting again, which I feed my self with hopes will not be lunge now to that happey minet we shall meet. You don't tell me what I must dow with George when arrives for your lining note I have in my clositt at home, and can't tell how to come by it. Milley I gave leave when I came here to go see her Father and Mother and is not yet come back. I think it will be the same thing when you come down to compare notes. I have thoughts of going home of tusday senite. Stay to hear either good news or bad. We are betwixt hope and despair. I wish it may succseed well, or otherwais fears you will be mightily discouridg'd after so much pans and charge you have bestowed. I am glad you tell me Father and sisters is well. You was very kind in going along with the latter to make that visit, which I desired they would dow. I here Uncle Rogers is lame and keeps his room and his mane, Bony, they think wont live. They say Cousin Midford is better but very weak. Their in hopes will recover. In peruseing your letter again I find we shall not be honoured with the sight of George, so when goes home will send you the note of your linings. All here presents you with what is due and desires the acceptance of my duty to father and your dear self, who is nameless in mine, believing me dearist ...

Greencroft the 15 My Dearist, Thoy you tell me I need not write, yet can not forbear, knowing it will come to you in time before you leave London, which rejoice me very much to perceive by yours to me, that I was in some liklehood soon to see you, but where quickly vanquished by the sight of Harry's letter, which gives very little hopes either for your soon coming down, or the cause. If we be so fortunate to here good news next post from you, shall assuredly perform your orders. I was in great hopes the latter end of the mounth would bring you home, and I think you kinder to my relations at Newbey than they deserve, abundantly. can come so often by hus and never call. I can't say but poor sister Betty is rather worse. She hath a mighty desire for some Scarbrouhe watter. Father sent Tick for some, but is not come back. I heartily wish it may dow her good. If you write to me by next Saterday's post, pray direct it hear, for I think shall not be gon this day senit. Being in hast, can only wish you health and a good journey, if comes next week, and am the enclosed your note of lining. Dearist ...

Lamesley the 25 My Dearest, Will, with yours, was the most welcome sight I have seen since you left me, after so long a parting without hearing from you, which was a great mortification to me. I write to you by friday's post in hopes it would come to your hand being directed to the Black Swan, but I find it has not, which I am sorry for. I'm mightily concerned to here your journey hath dealt so ill with you. Indeed what I feared that it would return your pains for we had fevear whether here last week. I think it's much to be feared, with the great fateags you have had, it has brought what won't easley be cast of. I beg of you to take care of yourself and to make it your chief business to preserve your own health, which will be my pleasure. Since you have not got mine must endeavour to call to mind the business in it. Cousin Midford I prevalled upon to stay till Wednesday, who, as she went home, called to see the Ladies at Ravensworth and they, that night, came here to make a quarter of an hour's visit, and of Sunday in Church time see Mrs. Art and send for me their and Cousin me to go to Mrs. Johnson the next day, which I did. But sister never inquired nor went to Cousin Collior's thoy Cousin Ellison was with hus, who is so kind to stay with me. Sister Carry's mighty nise; never takes any notis of me, but I find it is the same to all people. I perceive they was to go of Wednesday to Hebbron, but I cante whether they kept their resolution, having not seen any of them since, nor the gentlemen since they came from Durham. Upon counteing my money since you went I find but £10 besides the debts you paid me. I understood by you it was £20. Pray let me know which it was. I desire to put up master's lining in a box and send it by Saterday's carrier and directed it as the other was and put some tins in it, if it will howl any, for tea. Since you went the fessond henn is dead. Was found tralled to a sink and half eaten with some fermine. Your button is found. I suppose you lost it in coming from Greencroft on Giblesworth lane. A boy found it their that Saturday and he brought it to me the other day. Since the begineing of this, Mr. and Mr. Beach and several others came here. The latter being for London I give him the trouble of Master's lineing, which saves me the sending of a box. Our duch cow is just colfen and I desire to know how the colfe must be disposed of. I hope you wont forget to buy candles this week and me a pair of worsted stokinn. I fance by this you are suffishontly wheryed and am suer I am very sleepy myself, being late and can't think of any thing more. Hoping this will find you have arrived at London, with my best wishis for your and servis to Master and my brother. Duty to Father. Pray pardon all my nonsense ...

Lamesley. 29 My Dearist, Since you are not so kind to write to me yet I can't forbear dowing it to you, to inquire how you have preformed your journey this desined day, for mine proves so very rainy that I have deferred it till tomorrow, in hopes it may be more fortunate, and my missing the post tomorrow put me upon writing to day, being desirous of constant hearing from you. Pray let me know in your next how my father is for I have not long. I don't find that John the groom has any business, so if you pleased to order him he might help the gardiner. They came to me for the fees and window money, which I have paid. Sister Little is gon to Hebron. It is reported she desires to come to Ravensworth again to stay the next week, not to return to Greencroft. Pray my duty to father and servis to my brother and entreat your care of yourself. Having no news must conclude myself ...

Richmond the 2 My Dearist, I am glad you have got well to your journey's end and am sorry you reprove me so sharply for desiring your care of your self and ollso that I am so very ridicullas and foolish for being civil to your relations. I hope I did nothing that made me appear so or that exposed me. should be very sorry if I knew it. Out of kindness to you is my inducement to make me carrey as oblidging as I cane to all your relations, which I should hope might not be ungrateful to you. I would do nothing that where so, I'm suer. I go here of Wednesday, sadly wheryed after a seveare journey of two days. My sisters gives their servis and desires you'll remember your promise to prevall with my Father to buy them close. I'm concerned my Father is so unfit for his journey. I have pleased my self with the hopes of your coming down with him, which you don't mention. That makes me not know what to think. The fans is non of mine as I remember. They belong to Greencroft. Pray give my duty to my Father and thanks for his last, with servis to my brother and sister and am to your dear self etc ... I am very sorry Master's lining cloth did not prove right. My mother gives her servis. To James Clavering Esq., att Lamesley, near Durham.

Richmond the 6 I am mightily concerned and surprised to find my Dearist dus not come down with my Father, which I always expected, being it is the longest time you pleased me with that you would stay. I thought my sister would be ready against your time, because she has had so long a warneing, but I shall never believe your promises more. It is you I fear that's loath to leave London as you're free of poor me. I would have my cloths send to Lamesley and for coffey and tea you know my wants. I was in hopes you would have taken care for that. If you please if coffey be reasonable three pt of each. I'm glad to here you keep well. I beg you'll let me here from you every post, which I have been deprived of more than I desired. Pray give my duty to father and servis to sister and brother and I am ...

Richmond the 8 My Dearist, To morrow being the horserace day makes me write to day, to tell you of my great lose, which I'm in great afliction for, having lost my pritey pug. By an accident was killed, and without your help must mourn for it. So I must beg of you to supply me with a another if you cane. Get a pretey little won, other wais let it alone. Pray be so kind to endeavour to grant my petition and you will oblige me mightily. If cane get won before my brother comes down pray send it by him. I know you will arayn and conteme me of carlessness, but first know the matter of faked. Pray pardon thise trouble. You don't let us know whether Mr. Partridge be dead or no. If you see Mrs. Heburn before my peteycot be don tell her the lenth of my peteycote is yard 1/4 and naill. I wont detain you longer from your diversions, than to give my duty to my father and servis to friends. I am, my mother and sisters is your servants. Pray remember the latter's close. I have just got yours and have not time for more than to tell you I got it open without a seal upon it ...

Richmond the 11 My Dearist, You are not so kind to keep your promise with me in writing every post, which I towld you would be the greatest pleasure I could have in your absence. I fance Thursday is some busy day with you. I am glad you will have so good company to come down with you, as Sir Little, but I am in great fears he won't keep to the time you mention, for he is seldom in haste to leave London. I must satisfy my self without seeing my dearist thise lunge time, which is a great mortification to me. Will. tells me he desires the hind wheells may be an inch hyer than these. My sisters gives you their servis, and join with me in thanks for your petition to my father, which I beg you will still continue, with my duty to him and servis to my brother and sister, wishing you all the pleasure and devertion that London cane aforde and am ... I had a letter last night from Mrs. Ann N., who is mighty angry and fas that my mother towld her, that I said, that Mrs. Millmankes had enticed Grace away. Pray remember to seall your next letter to me. Mr. Place won the horse race plate. I thank my for his last letter to me and I wish him a good journey.

Richmond the 16 My Dearist, Yours puts me into a mighty consternation what to think, being you name your sudden coming down, but I don't perceive it is before the time you proposed with Sir Harry Little, nor the reason that puts you in so much hast, that I am perfectly in a mist. Neither can I tell why you should give me such a hint as rash judging, and I am sorry to be unfortunate in only having a sight of you after so long a absence, but if it be your mind, must submit to it with all the resignation I can. You never towld me any thing of Master's illness, which I am sorry to here. The cotch wheells I write you word of last post. I desire you'll get me three bottles, won of Hungery watter and another orinch flower and honey watter, and ollso to send me down in a post letter, a knott of this, to string my pearl nekless, of the smallest that is to be had, and a pearl needle, which must be both got at the jeweller's. If these things be not tow much trouble shall be thankful, and should have thought it an obligation it would have been so kind to a got me squirrel, but can't expect it now since you are such a hurry. I heartily wish you a good journey, whenever you take it and to where, with my duty to father and servis to my brother and sister and conclude me ...

Lamesley. 15th Jan. My Dearist, It was with pleasure I received yours to here you got well to Richmond. I have lived my old retired live since you left me till Sunday I had cousin Tailor's company at dinner and she has invited your son Jemey and myself to dine with her of their birthday. I am much concerned to here of poor C. Blackitt's death. I wish it may give my sister Nancy warning not to be her own destroyer, which I am much afraid of since you give so ill an account of her. My calfe was sowl'd for 12sh. of Thursday and Will. went with the cows of Friday to Kills and went to Greencroft, but I had no sparaygrass worth sending.
