Dear Sister I received yours dated Novr 6th and should, as you say, have known better how to have answered it before now, had you kept off the first half sheet of it, as the second contains all that I have not heard many times before and as you say what I wrote last was so very disagreeable. I should expect you would have dropped this kind of Paper war, without which it is almost impossible we should be better friends - It has been about some Idle trifling differences in opinion in Religious matters that were the cause of the greatest mischiefs and cruelties that ever were committed - but I shall never be convinced to the contrary of what I now think, by you, unless you learn to mend your Orthography or spell better; because No person on earth I am very certain can understand the true meaning of what they read unless they read it right and unless they understand its true meaning it is impossible their Ideas of things can be rightly formed, and if not rightly formed, it is, of consequence that they cannot be sufficient judges of any thing of consequence: Now you surely do not understand the true definition and derivation of the words Lutheran, Calvinist, Methodist, &c, otherwise you could not spell them wrong - your Quotations from the Scriptures are the same; and a great many people liking to be thought of a religion that has a pretty sounding name without understanding its meaning, is just the same as people here buying old Shop worn goods because the Shopkeepers stick them up in their Windows and call them Duncans greys; Duncans, hats Caps &c &c - I also see that you quite misunderstood some parts of my letter. I think also you talk very absurdly when you say we must not act according as our reason directs us; and that our reason may lead us astray; if we are not to act according to reason, what were our reasoning faculties given us for? Reason points out to us that there must be a supreme being; Reason tells us that if we do to our fellow creatures as we would be done by were we in his place must be pleasing and agreeable to the Deity if we can for a moment suppose him to be all goodness and merciful, as I think we ought or if he has any superintendence over us or any thing to do with us it must be pleasing to him to see us do well. It is by acting contrary to our reason that all the mischief which happens to mankind do arise and for which we shall be deservedly punished. Again If God calls any particular men to become preachers he would most undoubtedly call those who are not entirely void of Sense and abilities, as some I know. They are preachers of their own appointment they they have called themselves. God would not appoint men and boys as preachers who could not read a Chapter in the Bible or a paragraph in a Newspaper as it ought, and some who are hardly able to Spell their own Name. It is very easy to pick up enough of true Methodical cant by constantly attending Meetings 5 or 6 times in a week to enable any man to be able repeat the same - A Man may have attended Medical or Surgical Lectures for many years and yet remain a Bungler in his profession all his life unless he has good sense, and takes reason to his Aid in every thing he does; and the same thing must apply to a preacher who only preaches what he has learnt by Rote and a Parrot may therefore be called an Orator or a preacher with the same propriety. I again say that God might find men of as acute judgement and sound argument among the middle Class as among the rich and great; for in general the rich and great have but very little else than their riches to recommend them - but these you say are secluded from divine knowledge - and only gave it to those who could not understand it; but if as you say, God sent poor men, as the Apostles were, yet you will see by their writings that they were men of common sense, whether the tenets they upheld were right or wrong; I hope therefore you do not intend to put the Missionaries on a footing with the Apostles. Many of them left a real comfortable home and peaceful habitation for to gain an Ideal one, and engage in a thing they did not know its end; while the Missionaries all of them left theirs for the sake of being better clothed and fed, and to lead a Lazy indolent life. We are not to employ our reason - again you say, Search the Scriptures and hold fast that which is good - now I will maintain that reason is necessary, and with it some more sense than many preachers I have heard harangue to a gaping audience to select the right from the wrong, as you allow with every body else that some part of it is wrong, or else we might hold fast the whole - You must also have heard, or you have heard very little, that there have been men who have died in support of principles which are now exploded and thought absurd and ridiculous all over the world; and I will still suppose that there are some good - of every persuasion however they differ in opinion from you or me. Dear Sister I have stretched this letter to an abominable length and hope this will be the last of the sort we shall send one another. I have not heard any thing of Brother Robert since I heard from you. I hear the St George has come into the River Midway which is near Chatham about 60 Miles from here I shall write to him whether he is there or no. I believe they are not yet paid off and I suppose they will not pay them off till they are turned over into other Ships for fear if they let them ashore they would not get them again - The Brittania which came home in company with the St George is at Portsmouth and is not yet paid off. I had a letter from Brother John since I wrote to you last and he was very well then but had been very poorly as usual - I have not heard from Joanna lately. Brother Thomas is very well and desires his kind love to you as I told him I was going to write to you - I Show him those of your letters which I thought I might - If you write to him I suppose the post may find him direct to him No 15 Moors Yard - St Martins Lane London or you send it to my care and then direct as usual to me. I have nothing very particular to write respecting myself but that I am very well (I hope you will not be offended because I have nothing particular to write as you were at Linkinhorn) I wish I had but there is nothing doing at present concerning the Collection as the governors have too much to do with the Moneys at present to think of us. Mrs Hr was down at Teignmouth in Devonshire last summer and Mr & Mrs Gilbert came up from Priory and staid with her a few weeks but went back again as Mr G. was taken very poorly; our family staid there some months, it is the lowest watering place on the Coast. I expect we shall see Mr John H home again soon as he was at Lisbon with his Regt but all our Troops there have been ordered home, that is, they have been ordered to leave that place, by the Queen of Portugal, of which Lisbon is the Capital, as London is of England. I shall expect to hear from you soon and hope I shall find you in a good humour - Please to remember me kindly to every one I know & you see and I remain your affectionate Brother William Cleft London 13 Castle Street Lr Square Janry 9th 1798. You should always leave a space for the Seal or wafer as I have done which prevents any of the words being tore out. and fold your letter as this is Done.

Dear Brother, As I have not heard from you since your favour of the 23rd of Janry I have again taken Pen to enquire after your health & welfare as it is the greatest Happiness I enjoy at present to hear from you so often as convenient, I cannot think the reason I have not yet heard from Brother Robed yet I expectd to have heard from him long before now if he had been in England as I were Informed, may God protect him be where he will - please to let me know in your next if you have heard from him - I writ to Sister Betty at the same time I did you last but have recd no ansr I suppose she is displeased with me as well as you but I suppose it is not Suitable to their religion to forgive small faults as perhaps she may have seen some in me which puts me in mind of Mr Rundle's words Viz Men have many faults, Women have but two That's nothing good they'll say nor nothing good they do Mr & Mrs Gilbert I hear are gone to Bath in the road to London Wm Tabb desires me to give his kind love to you he is still Footman to Lady Dowager Molesworth but his wife keeps a public house near the house where he lives which is at the Revd Mr Molesworths St Brook near wadebridge I dare say before now you have heard of the death of my good and worthy Master Sir Wm Molesworth - he died the 22 of Febry in the 40th year of his age - his death will make great alterations in the family the Steward is now in town I find Settling matters, he hath discharged four of the Servts I find which is Mary Edwards house maid & a Laundry maid Likewise my worthy friend the Coachman & Jose Netting the Groom & we expect to know who goes & who rems at Pencarrow in the course of a few days - we have Just recd a letter from the Coachman in which he says he left his place last Saturday but (I suppose throug haste) forgot to mention where to direct to him for which reason his wife would esteem it a great favour if you would be so good to enquire where he is and be so good to let me know as soon as possible - as he is desirous for her to come to London, but as he is out of place and it being very uncertain how long before he may get one worth notice she says she would much rather for him to come down into Cornwall please to give my love to him and let him know that we are all well & desirous to see him, his wife would not wish you to say any thing to any of the Servts only to ask where you migt see him please to say his wife hath called on Geach but I believe of no use at present if you see any of the Servts please to give my love to them - I have for some time past been taking up the weekly Numbers of the Encyclopaedia Londinensis or Dictionary of arts & Sciences I see in the Anatomical parts there are Many of the copperplate prints representing the different parts of the Human Body Dissected by Dr Hunter which I suppose was your Master and also please to Give me your advice on the Subject whether I had best continue them or not I have 27 or 26 Numbers some parts of the work I like very much but there is a D-d parcel of Algebra Anatomy & a deal of useless and am not so far as B-- yet - so that I th almost Endless work - so I must conclude with my best wishes for your Health & prosperity & ever remain your most affectionate Brother John Cleft Pencarrow April 6th 98

Plymouth July the 1 99 Dear Brother I once more take my pen to writ you a few lines which I hop will find you in Good health as like wis my Brother Those and to let you know that I am livin in Plymouth I Came hear to Christmas I should have wrote to you as soon as I Came hear if things had answered my Expectation but far from it Every thing seemed to be a against me but I hop it is all for the best Joanna sent to me time after time to Come to Plymouth to Live she sent me three letters to desire me to Come to live at Mr Lines with her her Master an Mistress desire her to send for me and they would Pay my Expense and Give me five Guineas a year an they would wait for me till such times as I Could Come and Every thing should be made a Greabel but when I Came I found it otherwise their maid was Married to Thomas williamson and they had a another in her Place so I might due as I would for they I Got a Place in two days after I Came hear but I had a fortnight to wait for it an if I had known what a Place it was I would have waited till this time be fore I would have Gone to such a Place I did not stay but a month and that was long a nough to almost kilt me I Goot such a vilant Cold I have not been well since I was three wickes then before I Could Geet a Place so I was Pretty well off by this time what it Cost me in Come hear and my lost time and what it Cost me hear while I was out of a Place it was near fifty shilings an they never Gave me a farthing which I think the Least they Could have dun after takin me out of my Place was to have Paid my Expense up but I bless the Lord for it I have a better Pace now then theirs is tho I have but four Pound a year I have been in this Place since 27 of Febry and in this time they have Changed their Citchin maid four times and the fifth Gave warning last Sunday an Joanna hath warned her self off twice she sais she will stay no longer with them she desires her cind love to you and to Brother Thomas she desired me to ask you if ou thought well of her Come to london and if you think she might due better their than hear and if she was to Come which way you think would be best fore her to Come Dear Brother I should be Glad to know what is be Come of my unfortunate Brother Robert if I had seen him or had known any thing of his misfourtin I should have wrote to you I saw Brother John at Christmas shout me the Letter you sent him which all most Broke my heart to think what my Brother had brought on him self Brother John was very well then he had Partly wrote a Letter to you which he said he was Going to send to you in a few days I saw John ford last wick he lives a Dock he desired to be rememberd to you and to Brother Thomas an he told me that Mr Gilbert famly had been at London an ware returned so you knew I ware at Plymouth by them Give my Cind love to Brother Thomas and tell him I should be much obliged to him if he would send me a Pear of shoes as they are very dear hear and money is very scarce with me at Preasent he knows something what travling is I was told a Stuarday By one of Bodmin that Thomas arther was sent to Exeter Jail the day before with several others for tring to Geet some of the french men out of Prison and that he was the ring leader and tic thought that nothing will save his life he was living at Dock he is but Just out of his time I hope you will be so Cind as to writ me afew lines as soon as you receive this to let me know how you are an how you Go on now and if their is any altration a I have not hard from you since your time was Expired Mrs Gilbert told me that you was Learning something in the surgery Line which she hoped would be better for you if you Pleas to direct for me at Mr Hamblens upaset the Guildhall Plymouth I still remain your Ever Loving and affectnot Sister till death E Cleft

London July 12th 1799 Dear Sister I received your kind letter yesterday and according to your desire I have not been long answering it. I have often been thinking of writing yet I did not know whether I had better do it or not because I could not find any satisfactory reason for your not writing to me for so long a time as I wrote to you since I had received any answer, and thought from the kind of jangling way of correspondence we had fallen into that I had better wait to see when you would write & then I should see what sort of humour you were in - as I thought of course you was too much affronted or too proud to write. I always thought all along since I saw Mrs Gilberts people that you was very comfortably settled in the same house with Joanna or else I should have sent at any rate before this time to know what you were doing & how. I cannot give you any particulars concerning Brother Robert as I have not heard any thing whatever of him since I sent to John & which you say you saw. I should suppose he is onboard the Echo Sloop of War, as that was the Ship he belonged to and to which he said he was to be sent as soon as it came back from a Cruise He promised very faithfully to write to me when I saw him wherever he should be but he has never done it. The Echo comes to Plymouth occasionally and if it should come there you may probably be able to enquire if he is onboard or not - I shall make all the enquiry I can against I write next. The letter you tell me John intended writing to me has not been finished yet, or at least has not come to hand. The last time I heard from him was when Sir Wm Molesworth died and he wanted me to find out the coachman as he had left his place, that his wife might know where to write to him I heard by Mrs Gilbert that he is still at Pencarrow - I should like that Joanna and you would keep near each other till you both could be provided for in any better way than you are at present - I believe good places here are not always to be met with any more than in the Country and I see that in many places they are great slaves. I do not know of any thing at present by which I could advise either you or Joanna for the better tho I am very sorry to find you so ill off - but I shall probably have it in my power shortly if you could find a Place where you could make yourself more comfortable, and I will endeavour to make up the difference of wages between what you might expect in London, from Plymouth, as I find that at last our collection is likely to be shortly settled and at present I see nothing against my being settled at the same time - Government has at last agreed to take it and most probably in the Course of Six months every thing will be settled and I shall then know whether I am settled for life or whether I am to begin the world again. However time will let us know all these things - and as long as I keep my health & hands I am not afraid of living whether or no. I have not had an opportunity of seeing Brother Thomas since I recd your letter as I have not seen him for above a fortnight and he then told me that he was then looking out for a lodging as the Landlord of the house where he lodged was leaving it, and all the lodgers were obliged to move. He was to let me know where to find him but I have not seen him since, however I may expect he is very well or I should have heard. I may suppose that you have been told that he got married about 15 months ago or some such time. I think he might do much better now than when single for I always used to find her hard at work when I went to their lodgings - and I believe they live very comfortable, at least as far as I see and they seem to agree very well She was an old Bristol sweetheart I believe, and I suppose it was the principal reason of her coming to London. She was sent for by an old Mistress of hers who had come to London some time before, and when she came they did not use her so well as she expected or else she wanted to get married or something but so it was that they got married a good while before I knew any thing of the matter - She is one of Somersetshire and appears to be much about his own age. I suppose a pair of Shoes would cost as much sending as they are worth and perhaps you would want them a good while before he would find time to make them for when I used to bespeak any of him I often had to buy a pair from a Shop & wear them out before I got the others - besides I found that he got more by making shoes only - than buying the leather & cutting them out &c and would have been out of pocket by selling them at the price I could get them at at a shop so that for some time he has not made me any. You will see I have sent you two guineas which will buy a pair of Shoes & any thing else you have most need of and if you get this without any trouble as I hope you will it will not be a great while before I shall have it in my power to send again As I must take this letter to the post office to pay the money I do not know whether they give me an order to put in the letter or write upon this same paper but you will see that when you open it. I expect Joanna is not in want of any such remittance because she is too proud to write to me however I expect to hear from her soon, when I hope her & you will let me know, and I shall send her something to buy a new gown as soon as convenient after I have received an answer from you to let me know if you get this & whether you have any thing to pay at the office or not, but I hope not as I pay for sending it at this General Post office I shall expect to hear from you soon and having nothing more particular at present to write - but remember me to all enquiring friends I remain your affectionate Brother William Cleft Direct as before Late John Hunters Esqre 13 Castle Street Leicester Square London July 12th 1799.

My Dear Brother I received your Cind Letter and order the 16 & the next day I went to the Post office they told me the order was for Plymouth Dock I told my Master I must Go to Docks and he was very willing I should Go he told Mistress that I Must Go to Dock but said I should not Go till such time as I had Put away the Clothes for it was our washing wick we wash once in three wicks so I finished a thursday Eving by six oclock an then I went over to Dock Poost office I showed them the order they asked if my name was Elizth Cleft I said it was they told me to sine the order so I did and they Gave me the two Guineas so I had no troubel to geet it nor any thing to Pay and I had a Pleasant walk I was back to Plymouth by Eight oclock my Dear Brother I return you my sincere thanks for this favour and I hope you have not straitened your self to send to me I hop I shall recover this a Gain if the Lord is Pleased to send me my health I have been hear all most five months and I hope I shall see this year out for I cannot bear Changin Placesis if I Can help it an their may be Greet altrations by that time for I little thought this time twelves months to be in Plymouth at this time we are But a small famly only Master Mistress and my self I have a Great deal of Confinment I seldom Go out side the door from one end of the wick to the other It is very seldom I see sister Joanna Except when I go to church then I run in to see her they live Just by new chruch Mr an Mrs Lyne seem very glad to see me and all wise speak very Cind to me when I go in she hath asked me down many times to drink tea with my sister I am sorry that Joanna is Come Off tho they did not use me well he is a very quick tempered man and Sister is very quick to an I am afraid she will not Geet a better Place she is Coming off next wick I believe she is very well an Gives her Cind Love to you and she will writ to you as soon as she is setteld dear Brother if you should Geet any account of Brother Robert I hope you will let me know if he should Come in hear I should suppose he would let us know as he knows Joanna is living hear if I should Geet any a count of him I will let you know I hard from Brother John since I wrote to you a woman he desired to Call on us at Mr Lines he was very thin he is to Contune at Pencarrow to look after the house and to Ceep it in repare what he Can and the old Mr Rundel an one man more there is no fire to be let in the Great house for one year An Brother John said at the time I was their he thought it would be Great Part of it down it Looked very wished then all the Plastering in the frunt was falling down then - if I was to remember Every one to you that desired to be when I was at Bodmin I might fill this Paper with that only Mr and Mrs Eyre deseird to be Rememberd to you an Frances an Joseph an John Mr and Mrs Eyre was very Cind to me whin I was at Bodmin they would scarce Let me Go out of there house to Eat or drink if they Could help it - it was very lat at Night whin I Came at Bodmin Every Person ws Gone to bead so that I scarce knew whir to Geet a bead I went up at Jacob hockens an nocked an Jenny asked who was their I spook she knew my voice an nancy run down Nacked to let me in which was very Cind an said I should be welcome to sleep their as long as I staid in town but in the morning when I Came down to Mrs Eyres she was very angry that I did not Come their and Neck them up she said if it had been two oclock in the morning she would have Come down and let me in she ordered the maid to make a bead for me in one of the best rooms an saw me to bead her self an tuckt me up for fear I should tack Could an would not let me sleep any other Place while I was in town an desired when Ever I Came home I would all wise Come there an the Poor Children ware over joid to see me they thought I was Come there to live a Gain I drank tea twice at Priory I suppose wm an betty told you that I was down to see them they told me that wm was Goin to be married to Jenny that lives at Mr Flamicks Those Arther took his trial last wick at Exeter sizes he is imprisoned 6 month an find £20 Pound Dear Brother when you writ me a Gain I should be Glad to know if you saw Brother Robert after he was Confined if you Please to Give Joanna Cind love and mine to Brother Thomas and his wife an tell him he might have left us know he was married wm Roberts an his wife an Catty Row desired to be rememberd to you time will not Premit me to writ any more at Preasent But I Remain your Ever Loving and affectnot Sister Eliz Cleft At Mr Hamblens opposite the Guild hall Plymouth Sunday Eving July 21 1799

Ford Augt 11 99 Dear Brother, I suppose long before this time you must think I have entirely forgot you but believe me my love for you is just the same, though so long since you had a Specimen of my rememrance I shall not set about finding excuses but own my fault, & hope you will forgive my neglect in time past, I have deferred writing so long I am almost ashamed to write at all but it (I hope) never shall be the case again, I did not know of Mr Gilberts going to London till Just as they returned I happened to be at Bodmin when William returned at Mrs Tabbs I were Just got in to the house speaking to Mrs Tab when the Coach stopped at the door, I went out to see who the Passengers were as I thought it might be some person or persons I knew I met a young man at the Door who took me by the hand and asked me how I did (it being very dark I did not know him at first but on entering the house he was soon Surrounded there was Mr T Pearce desirous to hear from his son Those who I find is in London myself in great hopes of having a Letter from you, Mrs Tabb & Daughters to Enquere after Sally & Mrs Williams (formerly Arthur) to enquire about her husband who I find is in London with Miss Hannah Beard his Housekeeper - I were happy to have so Satisfactory an acct of you by W Williams but I thought I shoud have had a Letter by him though I had not writ you so long, I recd a letter from Richd Branch (Lady Molesworths Footman a few days ago who (I am happy to say) speaks highly in your favour - he says I met or saw your Brother the other day who is Quite a Gentleman behaved young man I like his Solid manner very much - I am really sorry for Brother Roberts misfortunes, I shoud be very happy if I could hear the same Character of him as the above - please to let me know when you write whether you know where he is my love to Brother Those & let him know I shall Trouble him with a Letter soon, please to let me know whether he is married or not & how he goes on I am still at Pencarrow as usual but shoud be much happier if the family were here as usual, when I lost Sir Wm I lost a good Master & a True friend but its vain to rapine - I hope I shall do very well if please God to bless me with health - Sister Betty called on me at Christmas as she returned from Penzance she Slept at our house at Mrs Jefferys - one night I would have had her stay longer but she wanted to be at Plymouth as soon as possible, I went as far as Bodmin with her, I slept in Town one night & returned the next morning I expected she would have staid 3 or 4 days at Mr Eyres they were very kind to her & desired her to stay for a week I promised her to come again to Bodmin before she went but before the time appointed she was gone & I have not heard from her since There is a Camp on Bodmin Race Ground in which is the Artillery, the Stafford, Militia the Radnor Do & Cornish Supplementary Do it is the first of the kind I ever saw I think its a very pretty sight, Wm Tabb always enquires for you & desires to be rememberd to you, I hope shall hear from you soon so I must conclude with my best wishes for your Health & prosperity and am with great respect your Afeitionate Brother Jno Cleft shoud wish to know if you shoud like to venture in ye Lottery as I shoud wish to buy a Sixteenth share of a Ticket shoud you pr chance see Mr Branch or any of the family please to give my love to them

Plymouth Never the 10 My dear Brother I have once more took the Liberty of writing to you which I hope will find you in good health as thank god this Leaves Sister and my self at present I should have wrote you Long before now but I have for some months past been rather unsettled in service not that I have been out of a place at the same time I thot of Leaving my Last place for 2 months before I did and now I have been where I now am for Just those 3 months and I don't Like it very well but shall If possible make it doe for the winter It tic so very disagreeable in Living as a single sernt which I have under took for with an Adml and his family and I have scarce time allowed to Eat drink or sleep therefore I humbly hope you'll Excuse this my very bad writing and as for poor Sisters place if possible ten times worse then mines for which I am really sorry for My dear billy I hope to hear from you as soon as possible and hope never to be so Long without hearing from you again as I have since I receieved your Last and I should be hapy to hear peticularly how you're going on and in what manner as I have not had a Letter for so Long a time you will please to give my Kind Love to Brother Those Likewise to my new Sistr tho unknown time will permit me to say no more at present I Conclude your Ever Affectionate Sistr Joanna Cleft you'll direct for me at Adm'l valiants georges Street Plymouth

Plymouth the 1799 My dear Brother I Can nolonger with patience wait the return of an answer to the Letter I sent you 3 weeks since and this morning my Mrs told me the dreadful news of the plague being in London and if so My dear brother I shall be miserable to think of my shameful neglect in not writing to you since I received your Last Letter I must therefore desire you my dear billy to answer this by return of the post and Let me know Every thing peticular you Can as I shall be very unhappy till I hear from you, and poor Brother Those and his wife and desire him to write me as I should be happy to hear from him I hope you'll Excuse this sad scroll of writing as my heart is ready break while I write to you fearing this may be the Last I may be permitted to send you as I am sure all Letters will be stopped imeadently if this dreadful news is true tho I hope and trust in god tic not so poor sister is Just distracted Likewise about your welfare she desires her Love to you and Brother most Affectionately My dear i desired you in my Last to direct for me at Adml valiants where i have been only 3 months and this week I think to Leave them again to return to my Last place at Mr Lines as they gently desire me to Come back again nor should I have Left them at first had I Left my Mrs know the real Cause of my Leaving her which was no'other then that of my Fellow servants daily threatening to poison me on account of a young mans paying more atenshion to me then she Could wish so I undertook as a single servant with an adml and his family where I thot have Continud but to oblige Mr and Mrs Lyne I must disobledge them where I am at present time will permit me to say no more at present I Conclude your Affectionate Sister Joanna Cleft My dear write as soon as possible and direct as usal at Mr Lines new Church Lane

column46: Oxford. Aug. 18 1732. Dear Brother, I am ashamed that you have not heard from me since my flight to Oxford with Mr Atwell, but as I can make no tolerable excuse I shall say no more than to satisfy you that it was idleness and not forgetfulness. ... Mr Atwell and I were fit persons to be left housekeepers in your absence and then to run away from our charge: desertions of less importance have been punished with death. Mr Atwell believes you think him executed already by his not having heard from you, but won't take the pains any more to convince you of the contrary. I hope Lady Cowper has received benefit from the waters that the next time we meet our Laughters may be incessant, not being interrupted by any sickness except - you know. Pray my humble service to her with Mr Atwell's. To The Right Honble Earl Cowper att Tunbridge Wells.

column46: Exeter College. July 31 1738. I should not have neglected to have returned an answer to your kind Letter by the same Post if it had come time enough, however I hope this will not come too late to convince you that I am very sensible of the obligation I lye under towards you for your good offices, and shall be very sorry when you will the same disagreeable Task on my Account, however I own (so good an opinion I have of your Master's sincerity) I shall now take the Gown with more satisfaction, indeed if you had not been so good to have taken that trouble I don't think I could with prudence have entered into the Profession. The Conversation I had with Mrs Points was owing to one she had with you at Lady Sarah's the subject of which, such as it was, was myself. You agreed there that it was not feasible to get any place from the Court of any Value without having a Seat in Parliament which at the best would be very precarious and depend upon behaviour in the House, and that a patent Place for Life was impossible to have granted, and the former being upon behaviour might be taken from me at a Time of Life I c'd least spare it, and so leave me worse than it found me. I was thoroughly convinced of the Strength of these Arguments, and therefore said to Mrs Points I must take the Gown. Indeed I had Objections to it and have still, but what in time may wear off. The disrepute the profession is in at present, the fear of not being looked on in the same light by our own friends, which is the unavoidable Consequence of the former, the difficulty of behaving so as not to give offence to those of the same order who make it their business to scan every word and action, nay misrepresent both if they can have any prospect of jockying you out of your expected Preferment, these are all Objections, but the Principal remains behind. The great difficulty I shall have to bring myself to preach, indeed I think it is insurmountable. The Nonsense I hear weekly at St Mary's convinces me that Talent of talking sense is given but to very few, and I have not vanity enough to think I should be an exception where the exceptions are so few, and not Courage enough to undertake what I have so small a prospect of succeeding in. But there are Preferments that do not require it as Prebends and Canonrys which would be more suitable Preferment for me till I am better qualified or more used to the business of Preaching (if ever I do use myself to it) than any Parish Living. Being in your Neighbourhood would make me infinitely happy, but make me shut up my Lips for ever, for you are the last Person I cd expose myself before, but if you c'd content yourself with the saving doctrine of such a one as Squires, and not insist on the venturing to hear worse, it would be the thing of all others I would choose, and whether Ldy Cowper or Lt Grantham succeed or no my Obligation to them is the same. I hope there is not the necessity for my being one of the Chaplains as you apprehend. My Lt James Beauclerk they have provided for without, and I shed be loath to turn Courtier when a Parson, who refused it as a Layman. I hope this one example will have some weight with my friends, but I hope to hear your further thoughts upon . I am afraid I shall have tired you, and Little Caroline find more fault with her Uncle than her Pappa.

column46: Heinz Hill. July 10 1739. Mr Colleton has a Gardiner who is afflicted with a distemper which puzzles the most knowing Physicians and Surgeons to tell what it is. Some say it is a Calculous disorder which requires Oleaginous Medicines, each have hard words enough at command to show their Ignorance. The Fellow is a very fearful poor wretch, applies to every body, and holds to nobody long, that no day passes over without a fresh Doctor, for each of which he has a fresh Symptom, this not only puzzles them, but sets them by the Ears. Mr Colleton therefore desires that you would, if you can conveniently get him into Hide Park Infirmary, which by putting him into more able hands may be a means of reliving the poor fellow, and at the same time of restoring the peace of Reading.

column46: Bond Street. Feb. 13 1744. You desired I with send you all the news I cd pick up. I can hear of none but what relates to the fleet which at present gives this disturbance, nor of that, any thing of certainty. The report yesterday morning was, that this fleet lay off at the Goodwin's, but in the evening, in Ormond Street, Mr Townshend, who was just come from the Chancellor's, said that it most certainly was all got into Dunkirk. This again at night was contradicted at St James's, and that only some few were gone into Dunkirk to take the Transports aboard, and that the main part of it still remained off the Goodwins, and this still remains uncontradicted, so the most likely to be true. A Messenger this Morning from Spithead gave notice that the whole Squadron under Norris's Command with be sailed by Six or Seven at furthest, so they expected news of it every hour. Orders are sent as far as Preston for the Regiments quartered there to be immediately on the March for Kent, although most likely they will come too late to be useful; the Militia in the Tower Hamlets are ordered out, and for the safety of the great cannon at Dover Castle, T. Hales was sent away immediately with orders not to stay any where 'till he came there. The Buoys in the Nor are all taken up, that the French may have some chance of being drove on the Sands. These are all the particulars I c'd pick up to day at Court and I have almost put them together in the same disjointed manner I heard them. I think all their precautions discover more fear, than is reasonable, unless they are mistrustful of People at home. If Norris's Squadron shed fail very possibly we shed soon see who and who are together, but 'till then I fancy they will have too much wit to countenance an invasion, however they may wish it. I am going to St James's, where possibly I may learn more, which if I do, you shall have. Your Master this Morning I thought looked down, and very ill, which I was sorry to see. I hope it is nothing but fretting, and that he will recover his good looks with the first good news. No further news to day, but that the Breast Squadron is certainly in Dunkirk. Mr Points says that it is without doubt that an invasion was intended, and that their orders were to land in the first place they c'd conveniently. This is denied by the Ministry at Versailles....

column46: Moat. Dec. 8 1745. I am sorry to find by your Letter that affairs are in so bad a situation, it is very different from what I cd have imagined with two such fine Armies it was possible to have happened, however I have still great Confidence in the Vigilance and activity of the Duke, and that he will be able yet by the interposition of his forces to save us all from this impending danger. If he once is able to bring them to a battle, I hardly am anxious of the event, and if that succeeds to my hopes, my fears of any Invasion will vanish. Indeed one at this time may be of fatal Consequence, yet I think it hardly practicable whilst our Coast is so well guarded, that on the whole though I think we are in a very precarious condition, yet I am far from looking on it as desperate. We have a good Fleet, three very fine armies, each one much superior to the Enemies, and the body of the People, excepting the Papists, on our sides, and ready as I hear in London to join the King's Standard whenever it shall be set up. These are all promising Circumstances, and such as must in human probability be more than a match for our Enemies, either at home or abroad, unless our day of retribution is come, when we are to be deprived of those blessings, we have either slighted or abused. I think you are very much in the right of securing whatever is valuable in the best manner you can, and that it is the Duty now of every Nobleman and Man of Fortune to follow the Fortunes of the King, and to hazard every thing in the defense of his Country, but I still hope, that there will be no necessity for your undergoing the Trial. Shed there be, and you are called upon to hazard your Life in its defense, you don't think I hope, that I can stay unconcerned here at Canterbury, and wait the Issue of the Event. In that case, wherever you are, I must be. I shall at least by it lose the misery of anxiety, and so serve myself, though I may be useless to the common cause. Could I be of real Service any where, I shd be glad, perhaps sometimes I might, if those who heard me were as much convinced of my sincerity as I am myself, but that is seldom the case. At this time however, good Service consists more in action than talk, and that I think we are not so famous for, though no good man wed shelter himself under a black Gown when it became an immediate Duty to lay it aside, which I take to be the case in times of very imminent danger, or at least to act so in it as to show he does not wear it as a Cloak to Cowardice, otherwise his exhortations to steadiness and Courage will only expose him. But I have rambled excessively from my first purpose, which was not to say what I could or ought to do for the Service of my Country, but what my own peace and contentment of mind wed oblige me to do in case that you were necessitated to put your resolutions in practise, and to beg in the mean time that you with not give way to any Melancholy Apprehensions which our present ill situation may suggest, but apply what I call my Sovereign Cordial in all difficulties and distresses, which (pardon the Preacher) is this reflection; "That every Man must be finely happy, if he has not by his folly and ill conduct forfeited all title to be so; or otherwise no one can be finely miserable, whilst it is consistent with infinite goodness to make him otherwise." Excuse this scrap of my Pulpit Eloquence, and believe me.

column23: brothers (younger brother to older brother), close
column39: Letters of Spencer Cowper, Dean of Durham 1747-74. Ed. by Edward Hughes. Andrews & Co. and Bernard Quaritch: Durham and London. 1956.
column46: Durham. Oct. 16 1746. I began my last letter so late that I was obliged if I intended to send it by the post to make it a very short one. I have now time to make amends for it, if it is really a fault, though very little pretence from the little this place can send you worth your notice. I recd but two from Kensington, since your accident, so whatever number you favoured me above it, are lost to me. In regard to myself, I think my disorder is whimsical as you possibly can; but very vexatious at the same time, the shape it has lately appeared in, is an indigestion, which perpetually makes me, as Sancho says, eruct , this I can but attribute to the Spa water, which though good for my other complaints is allowed by my Dr to disagree and turn sour upon some stomachs, and what almost confirms me in this is, that 'till I began the Spa water I had no complaint in my stomach that I observed, and since then, never continued it for 3 days without having it to a great degree. Though I suspected this for some time I have often been willing to make further trials, as I found it benefit my head, and revive my spirits very much. Now I am resolved 'till my stomach has recovered its tone to discontinue it, and content myself with the Assa foetida and other nasty things the Dr has prescribed me. What makes it more whimsical it comes without any warning. Yesterday morning I was in full health and spirits, eat my breakfast of chocolate and drank my Spa water after it, went out in the coach, the most summerlike warm morning I ever saw or felt this time of year, turning in at the College-Gate in our return a sudden jolt gave a turn to my stomach, brought on my indigestion and hysteric chillnesses which lost me my dinner, and hung upon me the whole day. Today I have omitted the Spa water and am much mended, took my airing in the coach as usual, and have since ate a good dinner, and with an appetite. You will pardon these little punctualities, the distance between us makes them satisfactory, and what you might judge me worse than I am, were I to omit. A little to explain my lunacy; it has been an observation of Dr. Askew's in all disorders of the body which proceed from a fullness of blood, the strongest symptoms always appear towards the changes of the moon, and this he says a practice of 30 or 40 years have confirmed to him, and the changes in great measure of my case occasioning that fullness upon the weakened vessels in my head, and consequently the occasion of the hysteric disorder being then more violent, for which reason he desires always abt that time, 'till I am perfectly recovered to live a little lower than at other times. I, from looking back to my worst bouts, find great reason to think him right in this particular, and so intend as much as possible to adhere in that regulation of diet at the time he proposes. I find myself rambling again backward to my own case, and wasting my time on paper as if I was writing to an Apothecary for advice. I will correct myself, and only add this one thing, that, thank God, since you are recovered the hurt you received, and are escaped so great a danger, I know of nothing that can give me an hour's uneasiness, but great reason in that and other things to be thankful and happy with my present lot. Was my health equal to my present ease of mind I should have no complaints to trouble my friends with. That, I think greatly on the mending hand, and hope soon to have "men's sana in corpora sano" ; which is all one can reasonably wish and more than, considering the danger I escaped, I had reason to expect or hope for. I hope L. Car. is recovered of her cold and shall soon see it under her own hand. A few weeks I take it will lodge her in Albemarle Street, in the meantime I think the less she sees of her poor Mama the better. I would give you, since she is so bad, the same advice, and approve much of your London scheme this winter. You will find it difficult and troublesome if the war continues to go abroad, and for my own sake I can hardly wish any obstacle to it removed. If I could hope this place could be made agreeable to you to spend your summer in, if you want to be at a distance from your misfortunes, it would make me very happy to attend you here; sometime of it I don't doubt but you will, and if all would be so to you, I am sure it would be to me. I should be much pleased was the issue of Lady Cathcart's quarrel with her Irishman to be the letting of that house for any term of years. I should be glad to leave Muffetts on so good an account, which to be sure has the misfortune of being too far distant from Colegreen, and though the situation of Jewin Water is not so good, yet the country makes amends sufficiently for that. I thank you for what you call your selfishness, and pursuing of selfinterest, which, though, as it sounds a little worldly, I must not indulge you in it, and therefore must desire you to give it its righter name, partiality to me, and then I shall not have so little of self love has not to set the value upon it it deserves. "Rust to a point and fix at last". Poor Win! I hope whatever change he makes in his life it will be for the better, and whoever he brings to Bedwell will make it still more agreeable to him. I thought that affair had been all over as lately I had not heard anything of it; but by his discourse with you, it is certainly concluded on; for being wearied with one kind of life is a proper prologue to the breaking one's intention of altering it, as it carries an apology (though a very unnecessary one) along with it. I am surprised that the Tar water should occasion a return of his asthma, as it generally allowed, and he has experienced in other people to have been a sovereign remedy for it. If that medicine ever does good, it must have the same fair play all other medicines have of a regulated diet, and one conformable to it, otherwise the mischief it does is not fairly to be put to its account. As few who take it regard this, unless they are in very ill health I wonder it has not done more mischief than it has: and think that people's taking it in so irregular a manner as most do with so little apparent prejudice is a good proof that it really has not that heating quality that is objected to it. Was not my nervous complaint to go off as I hope it will under my present regimen, I should be tempted to try its efficacy, as in most disorders of that sort it has succeeded, but I believe I shall find no occasion soon for it or any other medicine, so much I rely on the course I am now in. Lady Sarah in her letters complained much of her rheumatism, but the wholesome air of Pall Mall has now removed all complaints, and she calls herself well. This Mrs. Cowper's attachment to London makes her believe, which I put her out of humour by laughing at. She, thank God, holds well, is gone to a Ball tonight after having entertained half a score city ladies at dinner. My residence, to my great joy, ends on Sunday, and afterwards I hope ('till the approaching Chapter) to have a few weeks quiet, which will go a good way towards making me better. My greatest plague is to find conversation every day for 2 or 3 visitors whose names I hardly know; but I grow more hardend to it than I used, as I now look upon it as a thing of course. Our joint loves to yourself and little ones. I should trespass the other way should I say more than that I am My Dearest Br Ire Aff, and most faithful Br and Served. Sp. Cowper Friday 17 I have, this afternoon, another obliging letter to thank you for. Pray tell friend Coote that Mrs. Cowper joins with me in congratulations upon his succeeding to a stall at Peterborough. We only regret, since he has set his face northward, he has not as good a call to Durham. Unless he is obliged to you for this preferment, I don't recollect on whose interest he can have had this little piece of good fortune. You have heard certainly of Mrs. Madan's fall down stairs. Surely we Cowpers are all in a tottering way. I am sorry she has not escaped so well as we!

column46: Durham. Nov. 1 1747. I flatter myself that my last found you safe and well at your Journey's end. I had the pleasure to hear you were so as far as Hains-Hill, and I hope the rest of your Journey was as successful. No doubt you found Bath in high spirits on our success at sea. All that wish well here were much so. The news of it came very opportunely to us, while Town and Country were assembled at the Deanery to drink the King's health. I feasted that day to the number of 66 or 67, besides serv'ts, and though at first the numbers a little discomposed me, I found myself at the end less fatigued than I could expect, which I attribute to riding out that morning. Our evening might have concluded with rejoicings in the Town, but our Mayor, being neither a Glazier nor a Tallow Chandler, he ordered a Bell to go round the Town to forbid Illuminations and Bonfires; so all the Loyalty was within doors, and at the Assembly Room, where there was a sumptuous Ball. The worthy Harry Vane, who came to my feast, was my guest that week for two or three days. They are now returned, and I have the pleasure of knowing my public life is over for this year, and that now I can enjoy my fireside in comfort, while I stay. Lady Anne, I hear, has taken a house in Albemarle Street and will be there in a few days. What stay I shall make in Town this winter I must be obliged to you for a dwelling for, if it won't be inconvenient for I shall grudge any new expenses 'till I have got clear of all my debts, which with good economy will be some time about . You don't expect news from this corner of the World, and I hear none, that you cannot know sooner from other people. I have at last got Clavering's old Schoolmaster his wish, a Living in this County: that I hope will show Uncle I have not quite forgot him. It is at a place on the East Coast, called Shieles, and is worth ab't 90£ a year. The situation bad, amongst salt pans, and exposed to very cold breezes from the sea, but it is the very thing the old man pitched upon when it was before vacant, so I have no reason to think he will refuse it. I got the present Incumbent removed to another Living purely to make room for him. Mrs. C. joins in Love to you, Our Compl'ts, to Cos. Spencer. I am glad to hear he is with you. I believe he wants repairs, and hope when the waters have put him into a good one, he will take better care both of his Mansion and its Inhabitant.

column23: brothers (younger brother to older brother), close

column46: Durham. Sept. 1 1748. I came safe to this place, thank God, last Tuesday, after as pleasant a journey as heat and dust wed suffer, but as I travelled the common road met with no variety that can be entertaining. Yesterday I went to Newcastle and returned thence this Evening. My call there was to attend the meeting of the Sons of the Clergy, when there is a collection of the same nature, though very different value of that in London, and where my great presence was though necessary to give it some countenance. This was my first excursion to Newcastle and unless I have the same call, or some business, don't care whether it is my last; for so filthy, so dirty a disagreeable place I never saw. It has indeed the riches and trade of London in some degree, but with it the nastiness and filth of Edinburgh, the inhabitants of the poorer sort seem to vie with one another in dirt, and was Mr. Coulson ever inclined to entertain you with a beastly instance of it, he has one cut and dried which with match anyone of that sort you ever heard. I believe it will make him value cleanliness as long as he lives, and look upon it as a invaluable blessing. I don't in him any inclination for Scotland, though by his late ramble his friends at Hertford will think him ripe for any freak. I have great comfort in finding my house fit for ire Reception, the new part of it is as well aired as if it had been finished last year and the old so cleaned and smugged up by the diligence and care of Maud, that it is a wholesome at least though not a cheerful or elegant habitation. She is in high Spirits at having got the better of all the filth and dirt of the place, though the setting ab't it cost her some tears, I daresay of regret for the exchange she made for Colegreen. I now grow impatient to see you, so I hope as Mr. Points is obliged to spend this Month in Town with his Master you will anticipate ire kind visit and partake of the sport of this Country sooner than you at first proposed.

column46: Durham. Oct. 15 1749. I hope I make up by the frequency of my Letters what they want in size and proportion, for I would not willingly fail in every Circumstance of a good Correspondent. I am glad to hear that M'Uncle and Aunt are reconciled, I take it for granted, though you leave me to guess at that, that it has been brought about by your good offices. I need not ask what share Madam Jane had in this reconciliation, but shoud be glad to know how she bears it, and whether she can look her sister in the face after her ill usage? for I think no assurance can go through so much. Ire. two last accounts of Lady Anne gives us all great pleasure, and I am still in hopes that you may by degrees persuade her to alter her hours. Pray tell her we congratulate her upon her new purchase in Albemarle Street, I don't doubt her present amendment to be owing to it. The accounts we have had lately from Midgham has undone all that Air and Exercise had been doing for the female side of my house, in short, Mrs. Cowper's spirits have suffered by them exceedingly, and Emily has been more like a Mope than a sensible creature for these last 3 days, but better news today has revived them, and I believe if Tuesday does not contradict todays favourable account of Mrs. Points they may soon return to their right reasons. They have kept in close quarters all the time, and poor Lady Caroline these last two days has been forced to head my Residence Table, which she very kindly undertook, and goes through as if she had been born and bred at the Deanery. To add to Ma'am Cowper's misfortunes she has had an exceeding bad Cough, which still hangs about her, but is not quite so troublesome. I have my Complaints too, but of a very late date, stooping down in the Library today before dinner I gave myself one of those wrenches in the back I complained of at Muffets some years ago, what is the strangest is, it was neither by a sudden twist or stooping low, but by a very gentle motion. At present it pains me a good deal, and almost makes me a cripple, but as I know a few days will set all right I am not uneasy at it. I am sorry to hear that you have had a return of your Diabetes, I hope next summer you will pay another Journey to the Hot Well, and in the meantime use much of that water.

column23: brothers (younger brother to older brother), close

column46: Durham. Aug. 30 1750. This is for the same purpose as the former, to give you satisfaction as to ourselves, by letting you know our journey ended last Tuesday by a safe Arrival at Durham. Good weather and fine roads made the rest of our way as agreeable as possible: but at York we met with difficulties: it was the last Day of the Races, and every tolerable Room but one at the Inn was taken by the idle people there of all sorts. This with the dirtiness of the house, smell of charcoal, tobacco, and kitchen grease, almost put Lady Sarah besides her patience, or to use Lady Cowper's phrase, made her cloven , the worst was that Sunday intervening, we were obliged to spend near two days there, though the dispersing of the Company made the last more tolerable. The first news I heard there was that Chitty St. Quentin had been long ill of a Fever, and as yet not able to leave his room. I paid him a visit, found him pretty cheerful, but not yet quite recovered of his illness. He inquired much after you, expressed great Love and kindness for you, which, knowing you both, I dare say was sincere. I gave your Complts to him. I was not very sorry to have York prove so disagreeable as I thought it with turn out to the advantage of this place. In this I am not quite disappointed, for Ma'am Sall seems well enough satisfied with it. The Prison Gates and the popt-out heads had, its true, some effect on the Lady, but I believe more by the Lively picture you drew of them one day at dinner. But in general both the Town and Country far exceeds her expectations. I wait with some impatience for tomorrow, as I hope for a Letter from you. It is an intolerable thing that the Post must carry our Letters round by London. I believe it makes a difference of 3 days in the carriage, which fling us at a much greater distance than we really are, which God knows there is no occasion for. I shd have been more satisfied if we had left Lady Cowper perfectly well, but she seemed, though out of danger, far from it, when we parted, and I know the nature of that Complaint too well to be perfectly easy till it is wholly removed. We are still without Bishop: the Conge` d'elire is not yet issued from the office, we shall be ready, when it does, like good subjects to elect his Majtys. choice: were we left to our own it with, I fear be a matter of greater difficulty. There with be at least 13 Candidates, and I shd put my negative on all but one . But, as it is to proceed in a less contentious way, and our only interest lies in unanimity, there will be no delay of our side, whenever our Powers come. Next week is talked of for it. I have had a letter from Butler: he speaks doubtfuly of the time, but believes it won't be later. The Bp of Gloucester, it is thought, will be his Proxy at the inthronization. Our Choir looks dismal, surrounded with Black Cloth and Scutcheons, but as it is the only sign of Sorrow in the place it is more bearable. Dr. Mangy is in perfect good health.

column23: brothers (younger brother to older brother), close

column46: Durham. Aug. 23 1751. I am this moment almost come to this place, too late and too much tired to say much, and very willing however to give you the satisfaction I know it will, of hearing that Mrs Cowper, myself etc, are well and safe at the journey's end. I was in hopes to have found a Letter here from you to tell me you are safe and well arrived from Bristol. The weather at present promises to be so good that I hardly doubt of your undertaking your Norfolk expedition, if you do, I hope it will be a pleasant one, and conduce to my Lady's and all your health. Spen. Madden won't let me finish this Letter without joining his Complts to Mrs Cowper's Love and mine to you and yrs. He at present is wild about the beauties of this place, I intend to lower his imaginations tomorrow, by sending him into the Town in high Market to regale himself with what is filthy and nasty, for I believe at present he wed be as immovable from it, as Old St Cuthbert's body was formerly.

column46: Durham. Sept. 24 1752. Many thanks to you for ire kind Letter. I am glad to find by it that you are well, and have some hopes, as Lady Cowper has not yet miscarried, that though she is the Opprobrium of the Physicians she will now go on her time safely, and at the end bring you a little William that you may have your Bow well secured by its double string. I find by a Letter from Newland Hall that Will. Cowper's wife has a Daughter, it will be no advantage to them to increase their stock, but I wish yrs was, for though I cannot possibly live to see it, I should regret dying with the certainty of the Estate's going into that family. As for what becomes of the Deanery at that time, whether Chapman or Orator Henly has it, it concerns me very little. The Ministers may dispose of that as they think fit, the only spite I shall exert towards them on this occasion will be to keep it from their disposal as long as I possibly can. I am just returned from our Abbey, where the Old Baronet gave us a funeral oration on our late good Friend, not quite in the Henlyan stile, but as agreeable full as if it was. It was a very short, but very affecting sermon, so much so that short as it was I thought I must have gone out before it was over. The Text "he being dead, yet speaks". I had an intention somewhat of the same kind, not knowing his, or suspecting he would venture on preaching at all, but I am glad for many reasons he undertook it. I doubt whether since even hearing affected me so much I could have decently delivered any thing on this subject, and I have not the vanity to suppose that the audience are not bettered by the Exchange. I have often wished Henly's Bones broke for his Impudence, but never so much as now. The worthy E.P.R. who is supposed to give this Lampoon, is one Edwd. Pickering Rich once Curate at Cheltenham-Wells, whom the Bishop silenced and turned out of his Curacy for Preaching Treason, or rather praying Treason, for he had learned from his associate Henly to turn his prayer into sin, by making it an Abusive Libel against the King and Royal Family. What the scoundrel means by the Bp's not being reconciled to him on his death bed I can't conceive. I do not suppose that the approach of death would make him in love with blasphemy or Treason, or at all more engage him to them who were Professors in it. I have the charity to hope and believe, that even these two Wretches will look upon either in another light when they come to die, and be as little at peace or in reconcilement with themselves for the impious use they have made of their Function, as the Bishop could possibly have been in the height of his Resentment. I should be glad to know however the meaning of the last lines of the libel ...who shed a Tear? Why B for Interest, and St P. for fear! for here he is so dark that his scurrility has quite lost its weight, by being unintelligible. Your account of poor Lt Fordwiche's mistake has made us laugh heartily; he will look extremely silly when he sees my Lady next, or his Uncle Elliot, whom, I suppose, received the other Letter. If poor Diamond should not get a Master I don't know what must be his fate. I am loath to pronounce sentence upon him, as I think he is not yet uncomfortable to himself. I have very little reason for my own sake to care about my wall-fruit, but am sorry for my Lady's and ire own, that it don't turn out well. There is something I hope to be allowed for the wetness of the year, which as affected all the Fruit. I'll remember you to Mr Little.

column46: Durham. Aug. 31 1753 You will expect to hear I have finished my journey. It was ended thank God, last Wednesday, and with as little uneasiness to a sore part as I could expect. We took Sr W. Milners in our way, and rested there four days, this was a great ease to me, though one day there I was alarmed with a slight return, but living low and cool carried it off. The day I came here, our good Bishop retired to Auckland, and intends to stay there 3 or 4 weeks, so I have not yet seen him. He left however a very obliging Message behind with Dr Bland, which in some measure has relieved a suspicion his sudden retreat had raised in me, that the same college was not to hold us both. I intend next Monday to follow him to Aukland and see there whether it is practicable or not to be on good Terms with him; for I reckon my reception there will determine it. One bad symptom I think is, his strict Connexion with Lt Bernard, whom I hear directs him in all things, and with whom I am in disgrace for detecting his insincerity in relation to Ashley. This good Peer rages against the Memory of poor Bishop Butler, and t'other day in a public Company called him an Old Rogue and Hypocrite. Hypocrisy I think is one Vice L'p is not so accountable for as many others, so he was in the right to make that the subject of his invective, though few will think that the Bp is hurt in the charge, but enough of these. Our poor friend, Sr John is revived miraculously, and I think, if he continues to gather strength as he has done for this last fortnight, may bid fair for weath'ring the Winter. His Neighbour, Dr Leslie grows more illustrious, he is setting out for Ireland; but by his Conversation one would imagine he was just returned from it. He has lately purchased two Coach-horses which completes his set, and somebody asking him whether he would not appear on the Raceground with his six horses, he made answer: "No my Dear now! not till I get to my own Country of Ireland: for was I to drive six here they would call me proud Scot !" This and his tying up his Weather Cock to the East to secure a fair wind are our great topics at present of mirth. Another piece of drollery has happened which will serve to fill up my Paper. Our Bishop the other day received an anonymous letter full of bitter complaints against a Clergyman of this Diocese; charging him with many immoralities, false doctrine, and corrupting and altering the Liturgy, besides the reading it in an irreverent manner: one instance of which was that in the Litany instead of "all Bishops , Priests and Deacons" he read "all vicious Priests and Deacons". I have just had ire very kind Letter. Mr Crow who came in this Evening, desires with Compl'ts that I would tell you he thinks it Best for the Dogs themselves, as well as to avoid the hazard of Carriers, that they should stay 'till I return, when he answers for putting them into ire hands as staunch Dogs as ever was broke.

column46: Durham. Sept. 1 1754. My promising to write today is my only inducement as I have nothing to add to my last, but particulars of my journey from Norwich to this place. I left the good Bp's Palace the Friday after I wrote from thence and with no small reluctance. To make the Pill go down the better he went with us that day to Mrs Townshend's of Hunningham. Its a pretty place altogether, its situation something like Lady Cathcart's as well as the House. The Grounds about it very Park-like and pleasant, but they are surrounded almost by a barren Heath and the Sands very deep. From hence I went on the Monday to dine with Horace Walpole at Wolterton. The House, which he built, is an extraordinary good one, very elegantly finished and furnished, and particularly as to Tapestry, which is the best I ever saw. His Plantations are very fine, in the midst of which, opposite to his House lies a handsome piece of Water, inferior, but very much resembling Lt Cornwallis's at Culford. I found the Old Gentleman in perfect good health, and so stout upon his Legs (I wish you were so) that he ran with me into every creek and cranny of his House above and below, and afterwards walked me over all his Grounds and Plantations near home. He was very kind and civil, but I cannot say so much of Madam my Aunt, who entertained us with scolding her Servants all the while we were there. The next day we took our leave of Mrs T. and spent it at Rainham. Lt T. very grumpy to Mrs Cowper, but very complaisant and flattering to me. The House is one of the most comfortable houses to live in I ever saw, and yet it is full stately enough even for a Townshend . The furnishing, which was done by the late Lord, who refitted it entirely, is in a better taste than that of Houghton as it is not so tawdry, and the furniture he put in is very handsome, the rest being I believe the same age with the House, which I take to be one of the first of Inigo Jones's works in England. But the Beauty of the place lies, or rather did lie , out of doors, for this good Lt has managed matters so as nearly to destroy all that it excelled other places in. For he has felled the finest Trees in the great wood near the House, by which means the rest are so injured that they wont long survive the loss of their Brethren, and the lake is so neglected that it begins rather to have the appearance of a Marsh overflowed than what it is, and this only to save the expense of keeping up its head, which would not have stood him in ten pound a year. Poor Mrs C. was sadly mortified to see her favourite Spot, which used to be her boast, so sadly changed since she lived there with her Father, but she had the prudence to stifle it 'till she had turned her back upon it. It certainly is in sad ruin, but yet it has enough beauty left to be thought the finest place in Norfolk, I mean by those who prefer natural beauties to the modern artificial ones of Pagodas and Chinese Baby Houses. His good L'p took us out in the Evening to show me, as he called it, the Place , but it ended in the sight of two or three filly-foles at the bottom of the Park: and when on his ordering the Chaise to turn about, as I promised myself to view something that was extraordinarily worth taking notice of, it was to show us a large Dunghill , which he assured me was of his own making, and the best improvement there. Enough of him and his ill humours. We staid only that Night, and the next Morning went with Mrs. Townshend whom we again picked up on the road to Holkham. The Body of the house is coverd in, but I saw no part of it finished but the Statue Gallery, and Eating Room, which are fine Rooms and proportionable to the greatness of the Plan, the Egyptian-Hall is as yet an empty shell so I can say nothing of it. The Plantations are rather grown, but I fear it can never be hoped they will be considerable. The Sea Breeze is so strong, that not only the Trees but the walls of the house seem corroded with its salts. From hence the day following I kept on my Journey towards the Fens by Swaffham and Downham, and saw Houghton in the way. The Collecting all the best pieces into the Gallery has a fine effect, though it makes the rest of the house less worth seeing, both they and the furniture are well preserved, but the outside of the house and about it betrays the want of an inhabitant. My Paper is so near an end that did my remaining Journal afford anything more worth writing I shd not have room.

column46: Durham. Oct. 2 1756. I am sorry to find ire Letter of the 26th in my Pocket unanswered, but Residence must excuse all. Things go on here at their old Rate. Mrs C. sometimes well, sometimes ill, and ire humble Served at this time neither well or ill. We have had a most dreadful Hurricane here, exceeding that you may remember some years ago at this place many degrees. It happened on Wednesday night last about 3 o'Clock. I have only lost a chimney, but the B'ps damages won't be made good for two hundred pound. The worst to me is, that it has torn all the Wood on the Banks of the River to pieces, and left that pretty place quite desolate. It looks as if an high-land Army had passed through, and done all the mischief they could. I hope you have escaped in Hertfordshire. I dread much the consequence, as to our Shipping, particularly Boscawen's Squadron off Breast. I don't know how to flatter myself that ire Letter will succeed, if you don't, thank God it is not a favr you stand in any need of. I am more troubled about the ill success Heavisides has had in removing ire Palpitation. I cannot but think it to be Nervous and that Valerian and those kind of things together with Exercise will carry it off, was it any serious complaint you with not have intermissions, so don't alarm yrself about it, for that will only serve to increase the Malady. As to Brown's sauciness, I believe you have nothing to combat it with but Patience. These are Hamlet's days, when the "Foot of Peasant comes so near the heel of the Courtier that he galls his Kibe." Lt Darlington, for what end I don't understand, has all at once taken it into his head to return to his former Civility to me. He has been here twice within this Week, and promises another in his own Person or Lady's next Saturday. Are not we very happy? The horrid stories that go about of his Daughter &c lessens much I think the reputation of this Lordly Intimacy, and makes me very shy of encouraging it, and wish he would select any other of my Brethren to bestow the honour upon. Yet I don't know well how to avoid it here, except I do as you recommend for L'Hirondell, give him one of Johnny Keel's broad hints, and as he is our Lt Lieutenant I don't know how becoming that may be. Talking of L'Hirondell, I had a Letter from him in Hertfordshire, but I left it unanswered as I shall all he writes to me, and I think you would do right to take the same resolution. There is no end of him. My Brethren are as tired of him, and with as much reason as myself, particularly Dr Bland, whom, knowing our Intimacy, he plagues Post after Post, so on the whole I fancy he can promise himself no good from us.

column46: Durham. Sept. 11 1757. The Sequel of my unfinished Letter, though not much to the purpose, shall now follow, and I recollect all my anecdotes of Raby were not quite exhausted. Our Lt Lieutnt chooses, as every one observes, to sleep in a whole skin, let it be ever so dirty, for there has, as yet, been no meetings, either for making out Lists, or any other the necessary steps for forming the Militia, and I believe that Prudence will prevent his now taking any measures for putting the late Act in Execution for the Riots it has occasioned in Bedfordshire and other places are enough to deter stouter hearts than his from meddling. I am glad to hear that you and the Gentry you had called together were suffered the other day to go so quietly to ire own homes, for since I heard of poor Sr Rog. Burgoyne's Hair-breadth escape at Biggleswade I shall be apprehensive for every one you shall have for the future. Our Bishop now blesses himself that the Lieutenancy did not fall to his Lot, but I think the less he says of that the better. It is certain that if he had had it, and acted with the same Remissness, the outcry from the Quarter that Power is lodged in would have been grievous, and all charged to the ill Consequences of that being continued in the Hands of an Ecclesiastic. I thank you much for the News in ire Sect Letter. People have observed our good Bishop look blue (I don't mean true Blue) but they don't know the Cause, for they have not heard of Peggy Bank's Marriage. Some say that she with have had him since he came to the Palatinate, and his Brother's fortune, and that he has refused in his turn. I shall dine with him to morrow, along with Mrs Cowper and Mrs Dolben, and women are such curious observers, that I don't doubt that mine will find out with what kind of Temper he takes Piggy's Match. My Br George writes me word to day that the Fleet was sailed. It is very possible that in some degree the delay might be owing to Domestic Dissensions, but in a much greater, I hear, in having no stores or Ordonance ready to put aboard, and that all was to seek when the Expedition was determined on. If so they have been obliged to the contrary winds for covering their shameful neglect. I think ire proposal to Amphlett not only kind, but beneficial, if he has stock enough to set out on, but don't know enough of farming or of his affairs to know whether he has sufficient, so can only hope that he will determine on what is best for himself. I am sorry to find you so low-spirited at the Conclusion of ire first Letter, but hope it was only a transient fit of low spirits which ire Dogs and Pointers have already removed. You'll think me as bad as a chronological Table at the End of an Almanac when I tell you that I remembered Lt Fordwiche's Birth-Day on the 6th. Ire best Concerts happen generally after I have left Hertfordshire, and I have nothing yet to supply their place, but the little meetings of the Choir-Men at my house, and even they have ceased since Mrs Shirley went. Nine Violins is a strong Reinforcement, and what I shd not have expected at a Hartford Concert. When the Mesh's Geese are put to the Spit, our Concerts begin. I believe one more Winter leaves us Masters of the field, for the Gentlemen-subscribers are heartily sick of the Expense of theirs, and the chief Manager has left this Town and Country for good and all.
