The other day he spent at the Denoyer's; Maize Je no crois pas, qui'l ait intention de se Noyer . He will be more likely to Sally forth, and gain possession of the Castle. His affairs are, I think, en bon train , but don't tell him I say so." Poor Mrs. Thrale and Fanny have both been pretty Ill together - Dr. Richard Jebb constantly attending them; he won't take a Fee on Fanny's acct. though ever so earnestly pressed; he so greatly admires her, as he declares. I had a Letter from her the 2nd of this month; she intends to spend some time here, when both she and her affectionate Hostess are both better - at present she, by Dr. Jebb's orders (besides being 2ce blooded) refrains even from Asses Milk and Potatoes, as too nourishing; and at that time, actually lived wholly on Turnips , with a very little dry bread, and what Fruit she liked; but nothing else of any sort. Drink, Barley Water; and Rennet Whey. As to myself, I am in the old way, neither better; nor worse. Lovely weather; Roads better than in the Midst of Summer; but we are dreadfully off for Water - our Ponds and Pumps Dry, and but for Polly Hubbard's Well, we must go without Tea, Coffee and Water for Dinner. Mr. Woodhatch's Cart, with an empty Wine Pipe fetches Water from Ruxley River (a mile and a half off) for his own Family and ours for Washing, Brewing and even for our horse and Cow. Good bye. Love to M. L. Ham and Kate send much of Do and are quite impatient for You to come. Kate says she owes You a letter, and will write soon. I don't at all hate you. Lem. Ches., Oct. 16, 1781.

Chesington, Dec. 29, 1781. Dear Sop, - I put off my answer to your two letters, till I could give you some intelligence about Electrification, which I here enclose. I think the account sent, gives You ample encouragement to come to Town; if you can possibly bear the Journey - bring your Maid with You, and when you have been sufficiently shockified (though you see, they pretend to produce the Effect without Shock) come and stay the Summer round at poor deserted Ches. I have near 30 Doz. of Port, old and sound, as yet not began upon and has now been in bottle about three months; it is about 5 years old, and will be in high order when You come; as a further inducement, you will see by this letter, that Susan and that gallant and agreeable Young Fellow (who very, very soon will be united to her) are likely to become your housemates here; and I think you will be highly pleased with him - an open, unaffected, manly, intelligent Creature, as ever I know; let all these Accounts put together have due weight with you. I don't know what to say about placing out your Money - there will be time enough before You receive it, to consider, and weigh the matter duly; We shall then see more what aspect things wear - at present the prospect is dreadful; and I am convinced Many People will do, as my Friend Mr. Wright did in the time of the last Rebellion, when I was with him at his Country house at Sunbury for several months till the news of the decisive Victory at Culloden, and the total defeat of the Rebels; and in a Week after he pulled out a small Box he had hid, and opening it, showed me six Bags with 500 Guineas in each, which an hour afterwards, he and I in the Chaise with him, carried to Child's, the Bankers; in times of such horrible Danger hardly anything but hard Gold seems secure, and the growing Interest seems scarcely an Equivalent for the Risk of the Principal; besides, at such times, it is frequently impracticable to get one's Interest on the best Mortgages, and to redeem them impossible; at present therefore let matters rest, and make no application to Mr. Stephens. Mr. Allen tells me he has wrote to You about little Sam. Thank you for Venison, which was dressed for Dinner on the Sunday. Cooke's Voyage published is not the Authentic one but put out by some of the Ships Company of an inferior Rank, merely to get a penny by starting before the true one can appear. At last, the Affair of that worthless Wretch C.- is decided - the Bp of London absolutely refused to ordain him; and advising him, at the same time, with Mildness, to think of some other plan of Life through Regard for - whose - He plainly told him that not only he could not Ordain him, but that he was under a necessity of certifying to the Archbishop his refusal, and requesting him to enter a Caveat, in the Prerogative Court, against his being ordained at all. I am really glad of it, though they are all greatly afflicted at this Disgrace. I understand - will try to send him abroad somewhere. Lord North's Brother, the Bishop of Winchester, and his Lady are grown most violently fond of the Burney Family - there is a whole heap of them now with them at Farnham for the Xmas Holidays; and several more are going there. I hope it will turn out advantageously for them; particularly for Charles and Hetty. I am glad to hear young Jack goes on so well, now he is come to his Estate, and consequently that will exhibit a comfortable neighbour, in the room of (I was going to say ) - but I will say . Pray remember me kindly to Molly Leigh, and Mrs. Frodsham, when you see them. I am very glad the latter is got up so well again. I heartily wish her Captain, and my Captain Gem may speedily bring home good fat Prizes and a Peace; and then let the Sea rumble and tumble its Bellyful; while they, instead of swinging in a Hammock luxuriously sink in a down Bed with each of them their Girl by their Side. I think, I wish neither the Gentlemen, nor the ladies any harm; as to my own crazy self, I am not well - indigestion and sleepless nights seem to be settled on me, as an Annuity for my Life. Ham and Kate pretty comfortable; they both send you much kindness and many good wishes; and are in great hopes of seeing You in Consequence of Electrification. I have no Franks to my self; but that don't signify; wish away for dear Nation. Yours sincerely, Lem. I began this letter two days ago, but this is New Year's Day.

Dear Sop, - Burn You, Why don't you answer my last letter? Are your Rheumatics so bad you can't? I enclose a letter from Fanny, where at the bottom you will find Mrs. Byron, (who has had so much Experience of electrification) thinks you and your Maid may manage the affair to great advantage - in truth, I suspected Dr. Graham's declaration, was selfish; and that he wished to draw People to Town, for his own Advantage; so that if You have a mind to try at home, I think it is well worth while to be at the Expense of Six Guineas for a Machine; therefore let me know your resolution, and I will try to procure one for You, if you approve it - send me ample directions what Days Your Burford Carrier sets out, what is his Name, and where he lives; that no time may be lost, if you will have one. My hand Shakes, as You may may see, and I am otherwise not well; Sleepless, fluttering inside and Indigestion. Don't communicate to any one a single word about Fanny's Book, which in a few months I suppose will come out. You see how triumphantly she goes on. If she can coin gold at such a Rate, as to sit by a warm Fire, and in 3 or 4 months (for the real time she has stuck to it closely, putting it all together, will not amount to more, though there have been long Intervals, between) gain £250 by scribbling the Inventions of her own Brain - only putting down in black and white whatever comes into her own head, without labour drawing singly from her own Fountain, she need not want money. She has been from hence above a month, on occasion of Suzette's wedding (who with her Lord is now here) and since She has been in Town, I find She is Courted, Caressed, and sought after by the Wits of the Great Folk, it would be enough to turn her brain if it were not a pretty strong one. Suzette's Husband, Captain Phillips, is a noble, Brave, open, agreeable Fellow but 26; and I really believe, now he is married and settled (apparently in a high degree to his own liking) he will prove Economical, for which he naturally has a Turn - when not led away by high Spirits of Company. They both make us very comfortable here; but I fear their stay will not be long, as he is under Recruiting orders, to go to Ipswich; however he has applied to his Colonel to change that place for Kingston, Epsom and their Environs, and if he succeeds they will probably be here a good while - wherever he goes, or stays, she is to be with him. Good bye! Kate tells me she has a letter to go in this only Frank. She, Ham and Suzette desire Love, &c. I don't hate You. Lem. Ches., Jan. 25, 1782.

Dear Sop, - I should have wrote sooner, but waited for intelligence about the proper method of applying the Electrical machine for the Rheumatics. I believe there is no mystery in the matter, and the plain, simple, and only way is to electrify the parts affected; but to do any good, it must be followed up constantly, assiduously and for a good while together every day; however, begin gently, and try how You can bear it - it is a new discovery, and you must feel your way in the Dark; if you have any encouragement from your Trials with Hunt's Machine, make no hesitation about procuring one of ire own directly, to have it always at Command. As to Suzette and her Man, they have left us almost three weeks, to the great Sorrow of Us all; but there was no Remedy; he was ordered off by his General, on a recruiting party to Ipswich; and there they are together; for Susan and he have agreed the matter, that wherever he is sent, She is to pack up her bundles, and trudge along with him, except he should be commanded abroad; and in that case (which is by no means, I find, unlikely) she acquaints Kit, she should like to be with Us. He seems perfectly to adore her, which She returns very properly. He is a most ingenious Creature; and such a Gentleman mechanic I believe is not in the Kingdom; he has presented the Museum with Models of a vast Variety of Vessels, Utensils, Arms, &c., &c., &c., executed with his own hand alone with a degree of neatness and accuracy that cannot be surpassed; for which he has reced a letter of thanks and acknowledgement in form from the Governors of the Museum; and a Ticket of Admission for ever for himself, and Company with him to visit every part of it whenever he pleases. These Models are of the many uncommon things he met with in going round the World. He is now but Six and twenty - a fine made, tall, stout, active, manly-looking young fellow as you shall see. I think Susan has great luck. I have reced a letter from her from Ipswich, full of Content, which I have not yet answered. As to my own Carcass, I find little alteration; otherways than that, since I have totally left off Tea, and constantly breakfast on Coffee, my Stomach and inside don't feel so relaxed, and washy as before. Cider (of which I have now got a pretty good Stock, and in tolerable drinking order) I find, agrees with me better than Wine or any other Liquor. My knuckles feel very Rheumatic or Gouty - I don't know which - weak however to a great degree. According to your Success in Electricks perhaps I may be tempted to try. As to Politics, and money matters, I think things look but gloomy - those few that have any money are and must be anxious what to do with it. Surrounded with danger and difficulty on every side the new loan, it is true, fills as fast as they please to call for more and more - why? - because Government pays a most monstrous Interest for the present - on calculation not so little as 7 P. Cent. The money Jobbers, English, Dutch, French even French - (in a word every where) that supply this loan, do it evidently to make a market of it; not to keep it for themselves, but to sell it out again to advantage, as fast as they can to the Dupes that think of nothing but high present Interest, inattentive to the principal; and as to that the Devil take the hindmost, the funds fall and must fall every day - the Consols this time two years were at 61 and 61 1/2 - Now they fluctuate between 54 and 55-7 P. Cent. fall in 2 years - but to go on paying the Interest only for any length of time (without thinking of Principal) of the Public Debt, is as impossible, as for me to lift up St. Pal's. One thing I like well enough just now. Mr. Shaw, who owes you on his mortgage £1,400, and who, you know, had Notice to pay it off, as in April next, has writ me a letter, asking me if I would consent that he should pay off £700 only at that time, and let the other half remain on the mortgage security another Year or perhaps less - to which I have for you consented - for the mortgage is a most ample Security for the £700, and himself a wealthy man. I wish all ire money was out as well; if he had a mind to continue it on, longer when the time comes, I should not object myself. Of the I have heard nothing of late. I am not sure they may not be a little up, at my declining to go there on account of ill-health, &c., but really is too much - but then, I might indeed have but the same I am very glad the Hammonds are so Comfortable in their Banishment. As to I think you are well off to be rid of his most tiresome Correspondence. I fancy Mr. Allen will hear no more of him. He is a worthless Character, I think - selfish and unfeeling. My Will, (which I told you, I meant to alter and join Mr. Edison with you in the Executorship) has been done a long while, and to him I have a good while ago transmitted a duplicate; and I have several times intended, but forgot, just at the time I was writing to acquaint you of it. Acquaint me what opportunity I can have of sending it to you, and I will do it. Having just got a few franks I enclose 2 of Fanny's last letters, which with the others you may return when you have a good opportunity. You see it has got wind that she is soon bringing out a new Work; so you will judge what you may communicate. My Franks are so small, I don't know whether I can enclose one to myself. Good bye. I don't hate you. Lem. My love to Molly Leigh and Mrs. Frodsham when you see them. Do. to M. L. Send me a Burford Journal and how You all go on there. Ham and Kate well and send much love to You. Ches, Feb. 26, 1782.

Dear Sop, - I find our letters crossed each other - however somebody must acknow: So, here goes - first as to Stock; I did on receipt of yours, write immediately to Mr. Medias, recommending (if he approved) the Consols; which by his answer, I find he did in part, but said he took time to look about him a little; what he has done since, I don't know; though by this time I suppose you do; probably in Do 3 P. Ct Consols, as I don't see how he could do better. My opinion of Stock is the same it has been of a long time, viz. that they never can be a Solid and permanent Security; as I think it impossible in our irretrievable Condition that this ruined Nation can hold on paying the National Interest on the Debt already incurred; how then must it be, when that Debt is, and must be increasing every hour in so frightful a Degree? Notwithstanding all this, we can do no better. We shall sink together; the Stocks at present pay 5 P. Ct and perhaps may hold on, or at least pay something, while You and I live; and when we are gone, those after us must look to themselves. Indeed, nothing but Land, good Farms, are to be depended on; and even then, when the great Crash comes, will be miserably low - but let me turn away from this horrible prospect. Since I wrote last Mr. Allen has been here, and according to his word brought down a Cargo of letters to him; and a long verbal Account of him he gave me into the Bargain - such a one I hardly ever heard of anybody; he thinks him (and so do I) at least half, if not whole mad. In one letter, he showed me, he says, he has an ample Subsistence, good health, in no bad repute, and yet is miserable! He gave Mr. Allen a particular of his Income, which is a clear £316 a year; of which he does not spend quite half; he torments him by letters, and visits ten times a Week, giving for ever fresh instructions for his Will; and every time new Alterations, after Allen has drawn it up according to his last Orders - many of these directions are such; so wild, and even contradictory, that Allen says, if he were to follow them, he himself would be deemed a Madman; and his reputation suffer in the World. He seems to proceed upon this Hypothesis. First, that all the World are Rogues and Villains; next, that they are all in a Combination to cheat him - he is continually turning away his maids, and taking new Ones, on that Supposition - he is, it seems, at present in great distress on that account. He tells Allen he is convinced the present one Robs him, and yet does not know how to turn her away, as she was recommended to him by a family he is mightily connected with, and who had and have I would sooner be a Toad, and live upon the Vapour of a Dungeon (as Othello says) than continue to exist in such a State of mind. So much for him. By your own account of yourself your Electrifying Scheme seems to be at an End; and not without reason. You had better Success a pretty deal by the Jumble of travelling; have you forgot the surprising effect of your Rapid Journeys, the first Season you came hither? You seemed new-made. Change the scene therefore as soon as possible - dispatch your beastly papers; get out of your abominable Hermitage next ire dreary, dismal Garden; and bring hither yourself, your Maid, and those few papers you reserve for my sight. As to my own Carcass, it is a Scoundrel one, much out of repair, can hardly be propped up, and hardly worth that. Sleepless night and indigestion, &c., &c. The new Ministry have just given honest Gem a fine 50 Gun Man of War; so now he must be a Post-Captain. I had a letter from him yesterday from Plymouth, where he is now extremely busy in fitting her out; though she won't be ready to Sail in less than Six weeks, he is in the highest Spirits and Jollity on the occasion. Hetty and her Eldest Girl, I expect here for 4 Days next Saturday. Fanny's Book can't be got out before the Birth-Day - great Expectations are raised about it! Mr. Payne told me (I forget whether I did not tell You this before) that he and his Partner (Mrs. Cadell) in this Publication, did not intend to limit their generosity to the bare price stipulated (£250) if the work answered, as they imagined; but that they intended (privately) to present her with a handsome pair of Gloves over and above - this he whispered to me in Confidence as a secret - this I guess will be t'other £50 - a pretty Spill (£300) for a young girl in a few months to get by sitting still in her Chamber by a good Fire! She is to come here after she is perfectly delivered of this new and promising Babe, and her month is up, and set about brooding and hatching another; and I believe her Stay will not be a very short one, so that if you are not shocked at the Idea of being under the same Roof with her (She, I can tell you has the highest opinion and regard for you), I think the Intelligence might be an additional motive to induce and to hasten You to come this way. Old it seems has been pretty ill, of late; and the rest were all for it seems, She is grown more sour than ever; but, Hold a Bit! She has made good her own Words - that nothing but a Cannon Ball will do for her. She should cry out, with the Devil in Milton, when he first viewed the happy pair in Paradise, Evil, be thou my Good! and I have treasonable Correspondence about her. I must transcribe a short Paragraph in her last, to make you smile "As to Precious (her nick-name) I really think she is just now more intolerable than ever; good Success galls her most bitterly; or else it is, that instead of being tamed, (as other wild beasts are) by going without meat, for her health, it has made her more fierce and savage. Nothing is said that she does not fly in a Passion at and Contradict! Whatever is, is Wrong! that's her Maxim. I think she ought to be indicted for Living : for she is a Nuisance to Society: She is 'an unworthy member of Society'"! Pretty well this, for but she deserves it all, and more poor the best natured, inoffensive of beings, is the object of her extremest hatred. Good bye. Ham and Kate send all kinds of good wishes, and long to have You come - so Come and be hanged directly . I don't hate You. Witness my hand, Lem Ches., May 23, 1782.

Dear Sop, - I am out of all Patience at these cross Accidents happening just at such a time as this. I was in full expectation of seeing you at this place before now; and only waited thus long in hopes of telling you the Coast was clear and summoning you to come away. I had wrote likewise to Mrs. Graeme to the same purpose and acquainting her with your intention to come hither, was contriving that you should both meet here. I believe, nay, I am sure, I sometime ago mentioned the Burneys being here - the Dr., his wife, and Mrs. Young (her old Friend) came on Saturday 3 weeks, with design to return on the Tuesday. Madam in the meantime was taken so ill, she could not go back; and since that time she has grown so much worse, that it was thought to be a desperate Case, insomuch that the famous Dr. Warren, the King's favourite Physician, was sent for hither from London, who when he came gave but little hopes. She has ever since lain struggling between Life and Death, and has been thought actually dying more than once: particularly a week ago Mr. Hemming saw her, and said she would not live till morning; for that the Death Sweats were upon her. How it will end, God knows. She still lives, but without sleep, and almost without food. There is a little Tent Bed made up in her chamber, in which Kate and her Friend, Mrs. Young, by turns lye in every night alternately to attend her, as she is decid'd too bad to be left to a Nurse. I suppose Kate will be knocked up, and the other, too, as they are obliged to be up every now and then, through the night. Her son was sent for up out of Norfolk and is gone again this morning. It is absolutely impossible for her to be moved, it seems; as Hemming says she would dye upon the Road; so that we are in for it to some purpose. The Dr. lies up in Kite's Cabin in the Garret. She has an ass here, and her milk seems to be her chief nourishment, for she is allowed nothing of animal food, not even the weakest Broth, and is indeed become a mere Shadow. They say for the two last days she has not been quite so bad; though this last night it seems was a bad one, almost wholly without sleep (it was Kite's night), of which she procures none without opiates, and hardly any with them. One would think this could not hold long; but Hemming says now he does not foresee any immediate change, but thinks it will prove a lingering affair. How provoking! The moment the business is decided, either by her recovery and removal home, or (which I think more likely) by her removal out of this World, You shall hear; and then don't delay a moment, but come directly. Now for business. What has been done with Gabriel Medias? Have you had your Account? is your balance of Cash, Bonds, &c., &c., remaining in the late worthy good man's hands, yet laid out in Consols? Have you reced from Allen a form of an Order to Mr. Medias to deliver ire Mortgage Deeds into Mr. Allen's hands? The 18th of this month there was another £100 of Nosh's Mortgage to be paid off by Mr. Tyler to You. What has been done in that affair? Pray send me a particular detail of all these matters as soon as you can. Mr. Allen has been so busy and perplexed that he has hardly had time to write, so that I have heard little from him of late. I have seen in the papers an Account of the Capture of Capt. Frodsham's ship, and his own Imprisonment, for which I am much concerned on his Wife's Account. If You have any intelligence concerning him and his Situation since his arrival at Breast, put it in your letter. Send me word how You hold out Yourself, and be sure to keep stout enough to make your Journey hither as soon as I can give you the Notice I wish for. As to myself, my Digestion and Sleep are wretched. At times, I feel as if I had no inside; but as I am in my 75th year, I cannot expect great matters in my favour. Therefore Patience! Ham and Kate continue, in spite of trouble and watching, comfortably well and send much love. Adieu. Sick or Well, I don't hate you. Lem. Chesington, July 29, 1782.

Durham 1st October 1784 Mr Gill had so much to say about his tour into the west that I could not get from him last night. He has a nephew a son of Joseph, not of Arramathea but Shildon that he wants to put to us, to work and learn farming, we to find him victuals only, Mr Gill clothes, I told him I could say nothing as I had no house, and was rather cold about it, and said he would see you at the fair. But I have been thinking, as he is a smartish boy, writes a good hand and understands accounts he may be useful, however you may think of it, and will see him at the fair, and can talk to Mr Gill about him. May turn him over to me at Whitsuntide, as I suppose Mr Leadbetter will go with you. Pray think William Atkinson on about examining the ewe lambs tails and tups old and young and ewes and gimmals for yellow ones. A young butcher was dressing a sheep in Chester , and I asked him if they got 4d per lb? Yes replied he smartly for good ones such as yours. I thanked him and rode on. I promised Jack Embleton and Richy Moffat a lot of your Peels sheep when you begin to sell, and I would advise to sell for decent profit at all times, and I am of opinion that mutton will be dear very soon. You will see G. Holmes and Mr Sharp &c at Newcastle fair, join with them to handle a part of Gregsons ewes, when they please at 4d per lb, 21 groats is 7s, 4 times 7 is 28 and 6s offal makes 34s but be content with less money, you know it is very easy to reckon upon paper. It strikes me that you should not sell fat cattle cowardly, why sell fat and buy lean at a fat price. Jack Embleton declared to me that the west country cows were sold at Morpeth on Wednesday at 4/3d per stone. Let James Culley go to Morpeth market some day perhaps he can take it on his road to or from Yarm, and see Redhouse. I give you joy of the good weather. Corn is no worse here and people all leading. Do not neglect to sow the horse close &c when fit, get seed wheat ready and make preparation. I sent a letter by Adam Cummins last night from Newcastle. I have just seen Gilly Starforth and always behold him with fresh astonishment, but everything astonishes about this factory and these people. Old Mr Starforth is still by the seaside but much better. Both Gilly and George declare they have sent 3 sheets to Morpeth directed for James Crosbe, but no direction where to be left, pray tell Crosbe to enquire for them of all the carriers. Gilly says they are coming north in a week or 2, but it may be I suppose 2 or 3 more weeks first. Grange. Dined with Mr Robson, young Ralph is a fine boy, Mr Crawford and his son in law fond of him you may be sure. James has 6 stots rising 3. I bid him 7s 6 for 4 they go to Yarm fair on the Monday. If James Culley be for Yarm, he must not attend Wooler, therefore a day or 2 can make no difference, and he may look at these steers. I only name this, do as seems good. Tell Mr Forty I saw his brother and sister all are well. I then went to speak to Mr Dobson, and met with Crosier and George Surtees, Mr Hodgson of Alwent &c &c. George Surtees like drunk at ten o'clock in the morning, Crosier fat, very civil all. But let me return to the honest though greasy butcher, Mr Matt. You know what I am going to say, we get more by these greasy butchers than the fat Surtees's. Mr Dobson says he sells mutton at 4d that good mutton and beef are both scarce and is of opinion that there is a probability of mutton and small beef being scarcer between and Candlemas than in spring because the consumption is so small poor people can't afford to buy, is not this likely reasoning, and may teach you and us to sell for profit all along. He says he does not kill half the large sheep he used to at this season and his neigbours the same. Bought the other day of the Cook &c near 400 small sheep and near 30 cattle. I think you must buy Mr John Robsons wethers, and may enquire about Mr Wilsons of Islington. I now think dear as sheep are they will pay till Christmas, but am not fond of keeping all till spring, your own dinmonds &c must be kept. Barmton. Mr Collings prize tup is not very capital to handle, but rather catchy to look at. It looks like Mr Wastles judgement weakening Mr Collings says he has let one to George Lax &c better than him but not so pleasing to look at, he was gone so did not see him, let at 9 guineas also, Mr Colling will not be a mar trade. He is clear for letting at good prices or none. Mr Colling has some promising lambs, which I am glad off. Wheat a better crop here than I expected, oats a bad one, beans good and barley good, this last grain I am inclined to think has a chance to get a fall people have got that idea upon their tongues end, therefore perhaps you had better sell a part. So much cider and the crop universally good in England. Yarm 2 October. Found my cousins as well as could be expected and my sister and Nelly well thank God. Tell James and my sister at Eastfield I pray that she must not come to the fair as room is not to be had, upon which account my sister and Nelly set of for the north next week, that they may not crowd them at the fair. I need not remind you of paying attention to Matt. Make my best respects and wishes to my sister and James, accept same yourself and believe me at all times ire truly offed Goo Culley PS As my sister has seen me, she and her niece propose setting forward in the beginning of next week, but as they may stop a day or 2 at Newcastle, you are not to expect them until they come. I was at Burton, Mr Wastle poorly, Mrs Wastle very well. Mr Wastle says beef must be 2s 8d before March. Northallerton a pretty good show of cattle, and not quite so high as have been. I send this by your friend Mr John Mason to Alnwick fair. Bob got here with the tups all well by 6 o'clock but I have not seen them. Mr Wastle says Mr Charge sent bad quays into Russia. Tell Nanny Brown I saw her brother Jack, who desired his love, and his wife is still poorly.

Northallerton 6th October 1784 Dear Matty I left Barmton this morning Mr Colling in company, saw 6 very good 4 years old oxen of John Laxes, and at Smeeton saw a famous cow bought of James Brown Oldborough at 26£ out of pocket. They are bought by a steward of Sir George Stricklands and its supposed for a gentleman near Bristol who married Sir George's daughter, several more bought but not arrived. The tups were gone when I got here. Nothing but single horse carts here, most drive 2 and many 3. I passed 9 drove by a man and 2 boys, I asked how they did upon passing waggons &c. He says 'Wayey if we turn yan o them out od way they all follow' but I must observe Mr Matt that these are broad and good smooth roads. However they will soon come up to the Irish. I have met with some gentlemen receiving taxes who advised me to write to you to enter a horse form and say that if I ride 90 horses I need only pay for one, but Matthew Galloway must pay they say, that is, every person must pay for But if William Brown &c rides upon a young horse on breaking, or making up for sail &c he is not taxable. 7th Birdforth. We are to have 2 stots of Richmond 13£ very little I shall get Richmond to send them to Mr Collings (Barmton) before Yarm fair, so James may take them up, and I will get Mr Colling to pay him for them. His tup pleasing but not very fat, an admiral. Billy Walker sold most of Mr James Ewes at Allerton at 21s 6 per . I have a notion they would do him good, but I wont say they that bought them will profit much. Firkins 33s the highest for dairies. Weather keeps very good and mild. Mr Brough has arrived. James should pay him for the 2 steers at Yarm, and he will allow for the tup 2£ 2 only, as he had only 18 lambs got by him. Saturday 9th Milton. I am determined to show the large tup on Monday though I believe I shall meet with some rubbers. Mr Sails tups are come, also Clevers &c skin still their object. Coaching horses I am told are scarce and were sold at Howden though others could not, it appears to me absurd in our way to breed any other than strong horses. Wheat good in this market sold for 6 to 7s per bushel oats 18d per quarter, barley 27, turnips pretty good and bought from 2£ to 2 15 per acre. Mutton 4d to 4 1/2, beef 4d. Mr Cleaver has insisted upon having 10 ewes tupped of J. Taylor by big tup. I am to dine with him tomorrow. I saw him and he is bright, pleased with the tup, and like a man acknowledges ours are the best sheep in England save Dishley. Mr Cleaver behaves like a gentleman and was always candid. I saw the tups and indeed they are strange ones, shin with a witness and no more I beg pardon heads and bones. Farewell in haste Goo Culley

Sawton 10th October 1784 Dear Matty I sent you a letter from Milton yesterday. Afterwards we took a look at the tups which were comed to the fair against Monday, my friend B. Sails make only a middling figure. He was not come himself. A Mr Lees of Lackenby much worse, this young man has been thorough Lincolnshire and hired a tup of Mr Chapling a rare skinned one he says, such a one as will please the Wolds people. Surpassing strange! These people do not see thorough their delusion, no wonder my brother James lost his useful sheep by breeding to the tastes of these mistaken folks. I am very sure you cannot conceive how bad these sheep are. I would not have missed coming this road upon any account, when they will awaken from their delirium I know not. I asked young Lee if the tup he had hired of Mr Chaplin was fat, he candidly confessed he was not, but a deal of bone, and skin thats the thing Mr Matt. The fattest sheep he saw were at Mr Codds of Bakewells kind, but said they were little waddling toads . Everybody are running upon big ones, I assure you Mr Matt therefore if you want to pursue the tup trade, you must have some large ones. I have made a mistake in sending the little tup here, they say hes only fit for a fallow field. What a charming country this is? How hospitable the farmers? No wonder the poor Scots never wish to return from it. You must not wonder if I stay among them, they are so fond of me. We like far too well. 11th Monday. A good show of oxen and very high sold from 22 to 28£ a pair. Straw oxen they call them but fit for turnips. A strange show of tups. Mr Sail let 11 out of 12 and not one good one, but they were next best to ours, which was looked on with astonishment, indeed he made a famous figure amongst these thick skiels and skins, we had much credit, and it is not impossible but we may have some visitors from this quarter. Our tup was so much handled that I was afraid it might hurt him. Mr Taylor talks of keeping him another year, but will write to us. One of the (John) Wreinghams sent his compliments to James and talks of being over between and Candlemass. I could have let a few tups tolerably well I think, though they are not fond of going above 5 guineas. Mr Sail let some at no more than 3 and Messrs C and Kendal from 1/2 to 3 guineas, sold many very low I dare say, it is amazing to me that they do not try to get better, because they confess they are wrong, and many of the Wolds people are or seem to be convinced of their mistake, and they must necessarily change the sort. I am of opinion they are ashamed to come to us, because they were in our country, though Mr Cleaver is to have 10 ewes tupped by our tup and he candidly owns, and has said to many people, John Taylor one, that ours were best in England except Mr Bakewells and he thought ours as good. We went from Milton past Howden and crossed the Ouse a Dutch river or done into Marsland as they call it equal I suppose to the banks of Nile and where they improve land worth almost nothing to near a £ an acre, by letting on the tides and warping it they can cover it with this warp or sleech and mud in very little time to one or even 2 foot thick but the thicker the longer of drying and being fit for tillage, it then brings most plentiful crops of grain &c in short the improvement is beyond conception. All this country is a moss below, and thousands of trees are dug up wherever they make their cuts &c or dig peats, in the moors which are an amazing tract of land laying behind the good land, which good land has been indisputably made by these rivers before the drainage took place. Lord Percy has a fine estate here and highly improvable. This mode of improvement had been used some time ago but laid aside and now renewed with fresh vigour and not likely to be lost until all be lost as my friend Ben Sail says. We were at a Mr Empsons looking at some large oxen but not capital old and corking about a hundred. Mr Sail has a desire for your quays and best oxen, but is not determined to go over yet, if he goes for Carlisle he will probably take road by Fenton. Thursday morning 14th . We arrived here yesterday. Old Rumps very fresh and clever, I think indeed full as young as last year, this is very good to like and very fat, he has worn better than any of his brothers I know of and has been hard used. I own I am pleased with him. 2 tolerable ewes comed with him to be tupped. I met here with your letter of the 3rd inst for which I thank you most heartily, hearing from ones friends is to me like a drink to the thirsty or rest to the weary. I am happy to hear all are well, my best wishes attend you all and beg my compliments to your two female guests. I forgot to tell you Mr Bates joined me at Milton in the fair morning and is very well. Mr Colling did not come though he promised but I had a letter from him to this place along with yours to enquire about Milton tup show &c. He bids fair to drive out Mr Sail &c from that market if he chooses for I think every requisite is cantered in Mr Colling necessary to form a capital tup breeder. I hope sister and Nelly are arrived and I flatter myself your corn is mostly in by this, if your weather has been equal to ours. Be not afraid of your old wheat, new wheat its true is better all the way as I go south but like last year its all or mostly ill fed, not perfected, and all corn seems as though it would not be low. Barley 28 to 30s here I think oats are as dear with you as anywhere I have been. I am glad Mr Wilson takes the Old Thing the price of his 3 are 30 guineas then if I remember right. It's a great price for Mr Gregsons ewes 25s per but to be kept until March is a long while and if good perhaps should Mr Edison came from Wakefield here last night says not so good quite as it was but good enough, and expects an advance by Christmas or sooner. But one thing frightens me respecting mutton, viz. the immense quantities off fruit everywhere, it is utterly impossible for you to form any idea of the quantities 200 waggon and cart loads are said to go every week to Leeds market of apples &c. You may rest assured we have rare times amongst them, consequently poor people will and do live much upon apple pies &c and very lucky it is for the butchers all say mutton would not have been met with if the demand had been as usual. Still I think mutton must be 4d and I would advise to sell always for profit. We shall leave this place in 2 or 3 days. I hope to meet with letters at Dishley. My horse stands his journey well but continues to sweat immoderately. Have you heard from Richard? Or did you not see him at Alnwick. Has Bill Pickering hired a tup? Has G. Logan never seen the dinmonds yet? Let me know all about Wooler fair? Excuse this scrawl and believe me yours always Goo Culley I am glad Matt behaves well, tell him his father often thinks of him and will love him if he is a good boy. Did you buy Joe's steers?

Monday morning. Dear Sisters. I send you Goose last letter. Be so good as return yours in 2 or 3 days. Shall be glad to see Nelly over to day as the ladies go away tomorrow. Shall be glad to hear of little Nelly being better. Everyone sends best respects with ire offed brother Matt Culley

Wentbridge 15th October (Friday) 1784 Dear Matty I sent you a letter yesterday and propose going south tomorrow. I think if G. Logan has not sold those lambs of the Lord of Hilton you should buy them. Lambs were sold from 14 to 16 per at Darlington, large but bad, and at 12 to 14 upon the Wolds. Mr Sail goes on briskly in the tup trade, let 11 at Milton and 2 since we came home. I think we stand a chance for his custom afterwards, he talks of looking at the dinmond tup at Mr Collings. I would gladly have him to come your way to Carlisle to look at our cattle for winterers, but I am afraid he will not. I have told him of Mr Thompsons 2 heifers and the best ox (Walkers) also Purvis's steer and he would probably pick out 2 or 3 from Mrs Comptons oxen. Its possible he may come, but would have me write to you to send up the 4 I first mentioned, but I said I would not as I would gladly have him go, so he says he will write to you himself. He wants 7 head of cattle, so I said we had 8 clever bullocks bought of Mrs Compton, from which he might pick 2, 3 or 4, but he still replies he cannot go, and that you know better than he what he wants, so whether he comes or not I know not. If he does not pray do to the best of your knowledge, and you can meet with the cattle upon the road and he and I can settle the price please God as I return. If he should come show him your tups, what you use, and the dinmonds as well as you can, but show Blewcap &c and some of the best dinmonds by themselves at last. If you send him the cattle unseen give me your opinion of the weights and what you think they should be by stone before they come away. And on second thoughts had you not better send one of your own drivers all the way for fear of worst by being ill drove? (suppose Lisle Johnson William Atkinsons best man.) Sheep continue very high in all markets fat and lean. Mutton everywhere 4d per lb but that high price I think is much against the consumption. Friday afternoon. This moment Mr Sail received 2 letters one from Arnold with Mr Bakewells compliments to Mr Sail and self, that Mr Bakewell was gone to Caistor fair but will be glad to see us after Monday. The other from Mr Bakewell himself, wishing to see Mr Sail and me after Monday as he was on his road to Caistor. If it had come in the morning I believe we should all have gone to Caistor to have met this old gentleman amongst the Lincolnshire geniuses, but only observe how he concludes 'I will only say that as brother Chips Mr Sail and Mr Culley will not have any objection to being informed the tup season is likely to finish well, for since Monday the 4th some have been let at 20, some at 30, 1 at 40 and one at 100 guineas'. Yrs &c R. Bakewell. Mr Popplewell offered to buy me a boar and sow of the right Berkshire kind but we have not fixed how to get them to Fenton yet. Mr Sail thinks it best to have a cart for one horse made here to take home scythes sickles &c and can load her out with nails &c would one put the pigs in? Sow is to be with pigs. Rotheram Monday 18th . Mr Sail came with us to this place last night. This the week market, the fortnight days are best which as the same week as Wakefield, then what remains unsold goes forward to Wakefield this market is held upon a very dry clever piece of ground with oblong square pens for sheep like Morpeth only these are fixed, as well as those for cattle. Which last are high raised as you may suppose and very convenient indeed the pens for the cattle are open at one end. Cattle sold rather below 4s mostly long horns or half breed, and consequently steerish and not very fat, sheep 4 1/2 sink very indifferent ones in general, except one lot with light skins, totally different from all the rest which were in general from Lincolnshire, but the few I mention I traced to Meadow place poor Mr Algoods I mean, the tup that got them came from that neighbourhood, no good ones Mr Matty but what may be traced to Dishley. Mr Sails sheep are at turnips near this town, and a middling lot only I think, will take some making fat. Mansfield 22 miles from Rotherham. We have just dined here upon good beef stake, and intend for Redhills tonight. Barley 32 per quarter, amazing quantities of malt made here, our landlord says 30000 quarters is carried by land to Chesterfield, Buxton and even Manchester. 3000 people employed in making common white thread and hosiery. We parted with honest Ben and his agreeable nonsense at Rotheram. I still think he will see you in his road from Carlisle though he says not. I have given him orders for 6 doz. scythes and 30 doz. sickles and to load out with nails of different sizes. Suppose you were to order some table knives and forks &c or anything else that can be had from that quarter, that my sisters or you and James may think of, in the spring will be soon enough for the cart to go down, but Ben will write if he does not come and then you and William Brown &c can order what scythes and sickles &c &c &c you please. Redhill evening. We here met with one of the great London horse dealers, who had come with Charles Hodgkinson from Harborough fair. This Spencer furnishes with horses 3 of the regiments of light horse. I bid Charles tell you that we were so far well. He will probably see you at Newcastle fair for which place he sets of in a few days. Charles said good horses will be dear at Newcastle though Spencer says the tax will hurt. I find this horse fair goes badly down, and people are at a loss what to enter. Dishley Tuesday 19 . Disappointed at not receiving a letter from you. Mr Bakewell not come home, and if he does not come to night, shall go to Mr Stubbins's tomorrow. We have had a walk thorough Dishley stock, in part with honest Breedon, the best tups all gone, but what are left exceed what ever we have seen, farther than ever. Such ewes as strike me with fresh wonder, he leads and ever will as long as he lives. I find the tup Mr Bakewell has let the other day for 100 guineas is the other brother to him that was let at 80 to near Spilsby and 20 ewes served, what do you think of your shearings now Mr Matt, they are brothers. You may tell Mr Logan this is the sheep Mr Bakewell wrote to him about after his return home and offered at 60 guineas. Mr Bakewell is just come so must give over at present and finish in the morning. Mr and Mrs Bakewell desire compliments, Miss Smith desires hers to Matt and Nelly. Wednesday morning. Just 3 weeks since I left you and no letters by this mornings post so shall finish this and send you, for your not writing is no excuse to me. Mr Bakewell says Mr North is to be here on Thursday to wait on your humble servant you see what respect I have found in this enlightened country Mr Matt. Enough to swell a man of less vanity than that of brother George. Mr Thomas Bates and I go for Mr Stubbins today, and return to Loughborough market tomorrow and where then I know not. Mr Bakewell talks of going to a fair at Horncastle ever we attend, and may be out some days, but I may do Dishley, as I can think of no other place at present and sh easy if I do not hear now and then from you. Mr Bakewell says as the entering of one horse apiece sufficient, supposes the Act can mean no more, and that you have no occasion to pay for your servant riding about among the work people. Mr Bakewell seems to have the ball at his foot now, and you may be sure he will play it to advantage, he refused 50 guineas for the tupping of 20 ewes from a Mr Green in Lincolnshire the other day, same as had Rumps, and thinks Mr Green would give 100 for 40, which Mr Bakewell calls only half a rode, what will the matter come to think you? He says there will be some sport another year, those that live to see it. The matter is not to overdo it, but they have drove of several customers, and Mr Breedon has catched them, but not made the most of them Mr Bakewell thinks. Its lucky for us 2 hand folks that they do them so high here, we must live under their feet at any rate and be thankful, but one thing is clear to me, always to do a few well rather than many badly. I am with very sincere regard to everybody ire ever aff Goo Culley PS Perhaps you will not be plagued with such long letters in future as we shall now be much engaged with Mr Bakewell.

Dishley 24th October 1784 (Sunday) Dear Matty I have this morning received your long, kind, and friendly letter, for which I beg you will accept my best thanks. I was very anxious to hear from you indeed! All this kind family, with my worthy companion join me in respectful compliments. The weather has been most favourable indeed, seems now to be changing, as we have had a coarse night last night and a little snow fallen though no quantity of wet yet, the ground is so dry in this quarter that people cannot sow wheat. You have done very well in the tup letting way, I am vastly pleased with what you have done only I think if Mr G. Logan would give 30 guineas for the 3 dinmonds it might do very well, but I would not abate one shilling of that. Mr Gregsons ewes may do, keeping considered, though it is a very high price. I hope Mr Robsons ewes and wedders are better bought. I am glad you have sent a part to Mr Sharps turnips and recommend to take a fair profit at any time. These ladies have made a short stay with my sister. Bill Gill is the properest man I know of to buy or hire a good horse. Am glad your corn markets keep so good, and I think it right to be doing in part though most people think that corn will be well sold, yet they expect barley to lower a little. You do not mean that Bartholomew Brown sells oats at 18s per 6 bushels? If so it is the highest price I have heard of. I am glad that you have dealt with Mr William Bates. A Mr Gibson who manages the brewery near Hexham has a brother at or near Lichfield who has bought 20 ewes of Mr Paget for his brother in the north at 3 guineas per and a tup at Mr Pagets are good sheep, very different from anything they have had I dare say, what can these people mean by going so deep. Am happy your tups keep improving pray pay attention to them and the tup lambs, if you are not 2d you are far forward. By Mr Bakewells own confession, we are 3d in his alphabet, viz we have been longest in the Dishley blood except Mr Stubbins. I am glad Crosbe has sold so many cattle, it will help to pay your debts for you must owe a deal. I hope Mr Bates is right in the tup Mr Embleton should have had. I suppose Tommy Embletons ewes cheap. I hope Mr Sail has been with you ere now and bought your best cattle? I care not how few you winter, you can pay the more attention to sheep and tups &c. You did well to quit your bad dinmonds, did you not sell the bad gimmals? Sheep must have been high at Wooler fair and are so everywhere if a check do not come before spring. Have you sown the horse close? We have been at Mr Stubbins and saw Cambrels the 100 guineas tup, a good tup but not good enough everywhere at the price, but he can let at his own price now Mr Breedon and Bettison have him between them. Mr Bakewell has refused 50 guineas for tupping 20 ewes since by a tup Mr Princeps used last season, he has faults too, but the people here are all infected with that kind of enthusiasm which perhaps its lucky we were inocculated with long ago. Poor Mr Walkers aged father has had a stroke of the palsy and lies dangerously ill, so we are not likely to see his son suddenly. We have had Deverel, Buckley, and many other geniuses, indeed they pay me too much respect. We were to have gone to Horncastle fair but are now for Burton, but may change again, the old boy has much to do and often changes, Mr Smith of Birmingham and a son and daughter here, also a young Russian, a fine boy, has been here near a year. One of the Wildboars stays here constantly too. Mr Bakewells cabbages planted in April very good, and those in the latter end of May very well. Carrots thick but not long, owing perhaps to the carrots being prevented from getting lower for the sods that are first turned down before the soil is ploughed upon them, what you call double spitting. I find the rape stood the last winter well, and they prefer it to stubble turnips or anything else. Breedon says they would scarce get better of it in April and May. Mr Buckley says the same. Mr Bakewell is very fond of saving land in winter, I mean pasturage, what ever he can. Pray keep Matt with you if not inconvenient to my sister (your wife) but if he disturbs her let him go. Be sure you examine your ewe lambs for yellowness, and all your tups and tup lambs, there can be no harm in it and it is of much importance for us to be clear of every malady we can, it will hurt Will Marshall much I think. Mr Thompson had wrote to Mr Bakewell for his last years tup at 20 guineas but Mr Bakewell let him at home for 30, I think we have a much better chance from Mr Bakewell letting at such extravagant prices, none but tupmen can come to Dishley, none else can afford it, and we can do very well with less prices. Mr Bakewell let a tup to Mr Buckley at 40 and bid him 20 guineas to be of, and had a customer at 80, but Buckley would not. A nice sheep with wool or pelt and extreme small bones, it is unaccountable what prices they have got to. Mr Bakewell says there will be sport next season they that live to see it. Mr Logan will probably come, but if he be for a good one will be high taxed, therefore think he is wrong in putting of a year, besides 100 is too much for him to give in his present situation, but he must judge for himself. A capital one will not be had at Dishley another year under 100. You may put down Mr John Taylors 2 tups at 21£. I suppose Cheviot will be well covered as the Forest hills are white this morning. The Revd Sir Horace Trelawny from ditto in Cornwall bought 4 heifers of Mr Bakewell last Thursday but I have not learned price. Mr Bakewell talks of our going to see him but perhaps we shall not as the season is cooled. Monday 25 (Burton upon Trent). We are just got here to a fair, horses very high, 2 year old colts 25£ per many of them. Mr Walker of Woolsthorpe came to Dishley last night. His father has had a stroke of the palsy lately but is better though not out of danger. We are to visit Mr Walker after this jaunt. Mr Walker says the London market has been very bad for fat lately, and from present appearances there seems to be a dammback at present in many parts of the south, this may be from turnips failing &c but I am of an opinion it would not effect you, as such numbers of goods have come south. I do not find that any sheep have let for above 30 guineas Dishley excepted, and not many at that, this is obvious from Dishley being the fountain head of the fashionable stock. Lichfield 28th . Laid here all night and had Mr Gibson a linen draper, whose brother manages for the company of the Hexham brewery, he has bought more than 50 ewes, from different people, 20 from Mr Paget at 3 guineas and 1/2 guinea for tupping, these are to be feared Mr Matt but he has luckily bought a few gimmals and a tup of Jack Raby, and which tup I hope they will be so kind as cross Mr Pagets ewes with afterwards and that will I think do their job. You need not take any notice of this Sir, but I would have been as pleased if they had kept from Mr Paget or the Dishley tribe. We had also your friend Whitfield, very civil poor man but I am afraid does not fall into much business and is not very popular. Mutton 4 1/2 here. But at Tamworth fair last Monday sheep were heavily sold and were said to drop 1/2 per lb, however they were all sold, some say 10000 sheep (fat) some shearings sold at 32s per, is not very low, but turnips being a bad crop in general and the consumption of butchers meat less on account of its high price and plenty of apples, may make this flatness upon fat stock, but most people think, fat must be high. The London markets have been very bad some weeks from same cause perhaps. Corn markets much the same all the way from the middle of Yorkshire viz. wheat 6 to 6/4 barley 3/6 to 3/9 but everybody think the latter must drop from the very great crop. Oatmeal advances in the west and that grain is said to yield badly. 29th Birmingham. Dined here and once more beheld this busy place with fresh pleasure, went to Hornby a small town with a fair for cattle, horses, hops and onions. Hops 5£ per cwt. Cattle rather flat. Stratford upon Avon stands in a fine country then to Shipstone in Worcestershire wheat 36 quarter worth 8s, barley 30s. Next day 30th to Mr Fowlers, where we saw the best horned cattle I ever saw, but descended from Dishley. Mr Fowler a steady sensible Quaker has a tup from Mr Bakewell at 40 which he has hired again at 60, and only a clumsy sheep in my opinion. Mr Fowler went with me to Mrs Rayns (J. Surtees). She cried for joy. 31st to Warrick, where we saw 3 capital long horned oxen of Lord Warricks. November 1st Coventry fair. Fat cattle better sold and sheep sharp, but London market is got up again, was exceedingly bad. 2d. Shelton Mr Huskisson in good spirits, and Jack. Miss at Ashby with her sister who is under Dr Thicklands care and in a poor way by accounts. Mr Huskisson has bought me a filly and a colt which we shall take down in our hands if we get no more, but if we buy any more shall write to you to send a man up, as it is very uncertain when we shall return if all keep well want some money and not very little if we buy 1/2 a dozen horses and stay long, but will let you know more of that in another letter. These good people will part with cash at present. Still amazing dry weather, sometimes a little hazy but no wind. Dishley Wednesday 3rd . Just returned from our 10 days tour, where I received 2 letters from you and one from Mr Sail. I am sorry for Mr Sail but mistakes will happen, I never promised Mr Wastle, I only said they would have made good ones in his hands, but he's a deep one and can turn anything to his own liking. Pray tell me if you think I should take any more from him on my return. I spoke to Mr Stubbins about wood and he is to make enquiry. I am a little surprised about B. Tulip and Bill Hunter, but wonders never cease. Mr Brown's failure shows how cautious people should be in trusting people with mortgages &c. You must continue writing to Dishley though we may be often from home, and you may depend upon hearing from me from every quarter of the kingdom be where I will. About the 15th we talk of going south either to Mr Youngs or to return by him, undetermined yet. If we go a long journey I fancy we shall both have to borrow, as money goes apace I assure you. Mr Thomas joins in good wishes with ire offed Goo Culley

Dishley 4th November 1784 Dear Matty On our arrival here last night I finished a long letter and sent you, in answer to 3 I have had since I wrote, for which accept my best thanks. I met with the 2 last both last night, one begun the 22nd the other 25th ult . I am extremely obliged to you for my attention to my child, the Almighty will reward you and my sister for it, I cannot do it equal to my wishes. If you could see Mr of Belford any time, I would wish him to go to school another summer certainly. I hope my sister keeps pretty well as you say nothing in your two last, may she have a happy moment and all go well. Mr Bakewell talks of going into the west and my friend Thomas is afraid of the expense and talks of returning soon. I should be glad of his company but would be sorry to lead him into unnecessary expenses. Indeed money goes like dike water, but my brother my kind brother never said I spent too much, but if you wish us not to go I will return with Mr T. Bates whenever you please, it is my duty and was always a pleasure to me to return to such kind friends and I hope ever will. Be sure you tell William Brown that I often think of him, and all our connections. Upon my word T. Tulip is a manager if he has brought about a union with his sister and Scot. I do not understand that story of my aunt Hunters, it is unpleasant. I am glad Ralph Reid &c is alive. I am glad that so many sheep and cattle have come south from you, if turnips are cheap do not finish your own stock of all kinds, Mr Bakewell is clear for eating turnips, cabbages, and carrots &c early, his reasons are they never do stock so much good as in the autumn, nor never go so far, stock as it were become naturalised to them before the bad weather comes on, and if they eat turnips &c they save the grass, which keeps always better than turnips, and the more grass you save until spring the better, and the first saved is always best, and he is more an advocate than ever for leading turnips off, says if Mr Collingwood was properly talked to, he would allow leading of, as the taking from. A must improve B in proportion, and it cannot be supposed you want to take them on to another persons premises, besides the truer turnips are eat the more passes thorough the animal machine, consequently the more valuable manure which is the case when led off, but when eaten many tops shells &c are wasted which cant do the same good as when it passes through the animal, but I am afraid John Trumble and Master are too narrow to properly consider these philosophic principles. I do not recollect that we were to take Mr William Walker of Beals stock. I am glad you have got your stock all to turnips, the weather is so favourable they must do well, and by all means I would recommend to sell for a reasonable profit, you can always either buy more or keep your store stock better which is highly important. My father Atkinson is elderly and I am afraid does not always live so regularly as he ought. Its pleasing to hear that the daughters and grandchildren of fat Crops are so pleasing, if you can properly mix or blend the valuable qualities of fat Crops and Blewcap you will almost rival Dishley, for I confess though we are nearly equal (situation and keeping considered) to most of his neighbours yet we are a good deal short of Mr Bakewell still, but be thankful that you are in his best blood, and let us make the most of it. What Dishley will come to I know not, nor what they have made this season I know not for they decline speaking, but I have a notion more than 1000 of tups a good deal and I shall not be surprised if he makes 500 of 5 sheep next season for you see they have made 100 each of 2 this year, and have had 60 bred by Mr Codd for 1/2 the rode of his tup for next season, he pays 60 for his whole use this year, and I was by when Mr Bakewell let Mr Fowler a middling sheep for 60 next year for which he pays 40 this, that whatever Mr Logan does, we and many people will be shut out and I think my friend George will be gravelled a little, if they come to ask him 100 or 120 for his favourite next season and I rather think that may be the case. Sir William Erskine is very genteel and I approve of your answer to him. I am sorry you sold no horses at Newcastle, the mare you bought must I think be cheap perhaps I am doing wrong in procuring young horses in this country. I dare say James has bought these heifers cheap of Mr Purvis. Many people are unable to sow wheat in the vale and in all the clay country, it is so dry a time for the snow only fell upon the high country and to the westward. Mr Walker of Woolsthorpes father died yesterday week. I find Mr John Bates (who I am sorry to say was robbed poor man) and I were wrong in not buying all the Hilton sheep you had offered, but I think times have held out better with you than in the south for in parts here the store sheep have dropped a little. By a letter from Mr Sail last night he scolds me, but expresses his satisfaction at your anxiety and wish to serve him. I have told him in my answer today that it was his own fault in writing to Denton and asking so many foolish questions, were we going to send him or recommend any cattle to him but what were nice ones, he should have gone to Fenton. What way have you commissioned your oil cakes? They are not to be had in this country under 6£ or 7£ per ton, they say they can sell them for 6£ per ton ground down for manure. You are right beef cannot drop this winter now especially as London market is up again though Mr Sail says Wakefield was very bad on Wednesday, but that must have been owing to the Lincolnshire men sending too much stock to Wakefield in consequence of the London markets being so bad but I hope that will change again soon. It matters not if Mr Browns business was 2000 per annum if he did not look after his affairs, the larger the concern always the more danger Mr Matt, therefore it behoves us to be vigilant attentive circumspect &c. You remember Mr Peas at Darlington, and I blame Mr G. Logan and everyone that meddles with so many different kinds of business. I have always thought it best to pursue that line that we have been most conversant with. I am glad you have been able to pay your credit, keep that up if you borrow of a bank. I am sorry to ask you Mr Matt: at this dead time for money but as we have bought 2 young horses at 20£ and may buy more and half our cash is already near expended, I believe if you can make it convenient, you must be so kind as get our friend Capt. Ralph Forster of Berwick to give you a bill upon London at 30 or 40 days (if your pinched Mr Forster will give you a little time for the money) for 50£. You must observe to enclose the bill in a cover directed to Mr Bakewell Loughborough, then if Mr Bakewell and I happen to be from Dishley, Arnold will open it, and give you immediate advice of the receiving of it. You may at same time write to me another letter which will when I come to Dishley again acquaint me with the bill or it is possible the bill and your letter may reach this place before we go south as our departure is very uncertain, and you will be sure to do this job as soon as you conveniently can. I asked Mr Bakewell if a draft upon Surtees and Burton would do and he says it could not be negotiated here or else I have stamps but I should have got leave of that bank to have drawn on their bankers London. I am in haste yours affectly Goo Culley Loughborough one of the clock. I have been thinking if 50£ is too much for you to spare send me a 40£ bill. Is it not amazing that this extraordinary genius should be able to electrify so many people with the same or nearly the same degree of enthusiasm, and as it were to draw them all to one focus or point, for in fact he has convinced the unbelievers of the truth of his sheepish doctrine. I was shown some letters from Lincolnshire where they candidly confess their errors and mistaken opinions, and as that is the case, what may he not be able to accomplish, for Lincolnshire is a large field that has got more to do than any other country almost that I am acquainted with and Warrickshire from being so near akin to Lincoln has got a good deal also to do, that it would seem now as though he would have a chance to do a deal at strange unheard of prices.

Dishley 10th November 1784 Dear Brother I hope you have not forgot to gather a quantity of haws to raise quicks? I sent you 2 letters near together and in the last requested a 40 or 50£ bill. We have been at Mr Pagets and have seen the ewes bought for Mr Donkin, they are no better than I expected, not very good handlers, though I am certain better than any they have ever had, and tupped by a pretty good sheep. Which sheep Mr Paget has made 40 guineas of this season, besides what ewes he has served of his own. Mr Paget is very clever, has got well forward, but is far short of Dishley. We are now going to visit Mr Walker of Woolsthorpe, and to be back at Loughborough fair on Saturday. Mr Jones of Horton is to go with us. My friend T. Bates was talking of leaving me, but is now determined to stay as long as I stay, from an indulgent letter received today from his honest brother. We have been down at Mr Walkers, who I still think is a clever youth, his sheep pretty good, the vale is a fine country, Belvoir a small castle but wonderful situation, and prospect truly astonishing. My honest friend Mr Jones went with us, we came back to Loughborough fair, which was dear for cattle and horses also foals. We went to Dishley all night where we had Mr Walker who came home with us, Mr Paget, Mr Knowles, &c &c, a rare deal of talk upon tups, bulls, &c &c. Next day Sunday went and dined with Mr Jones and next morning Mr Walton brought me your last letter dated 8 of October instead of November I fancy, but notwithstanding that mistake Mr Matt I was happy to receive it, pleasing intelligence to hear of you all keeping well, and of my children behaving well, may you all keep well and their behaviour continue, I pray God and may we return to you in health and safety. Wheat rather drops in these markets, but everybody are of opinion that it will be dear in future as wheat yields badly in general, barley rises now 28 to 30s and people begin to think it will stand price though a very large crop. Oats 16 to 18s and likely to hold price. Many say that wheat must be dear another year as little has been yet sown in these midland counties, owing to the very dry time which has continued until yesterday when we had a wet day, but this 16th day of November is a very fine morning. We are now at Holme, the Stubbins all well and desire along with Mr Walker their best respcts. Mr Watt has neglected to enquire about wood, but on enquiring of a carpenter of Grantham who Mr Walker employs he says he cannot sell spikes under 4s per gang, 25 to the gang sets felloes 9s per dozen, axle trees 3 shafts per pair 3s 6. 16 . We are much obliged to you Sir, for your kindness in promising to remit us some money 40£ will do very well I believe as I shall now buy no more horses, and perhaps have done wrong in buying these, though they promise to be useful but I confess high priced 20£ for 2 yearlings besides &cs. It is a little surprising that horses should be so exceeding dear in this country and cheap at Newcastle but they are different kinds of horses, and I know of no horses which pay so much for their keeping and breeding as the blacks, and they are of a much worse kind than they were I think, that valuable kind from Blaze is quite lost and will not be readily recovered, though everyone now almost are growing fond of good middles, light ends, and less bones than they were, the hairy fleshy legs, large buttocks, &c &c are going out of fashion, and well they may, for I still think them most useless animals. I am glad you are going to quit a part of those ewes I bought, I think it always right to sell for a fair profit and to good hands especially, 31s 6d is a great price, but I suppose Crosbe has given Mr Singleton a choice. Pray how do you stand with him? I am always and shall be I think cautious after T. Matthews, for I look upon that money as mostly lost, and Lowry though he has given famous prices and good profits for those cows, should be kept short in hand, as well as our friend Richmond. There can be no crime in attending honestly to ones interests and too much credit often injures both seller and buyer. I am very glad that James Crosbe has sold the 4 cows he bought of Buckley for so much profit. As to Starforth he has and ever will be an inconsistent being, but if his money is safe I can forgive the rest though very unpleasant, however you are right to write to him in severe terms he can bear it all, and money he must pay against your rent. I am afraid Mr Anderson will not take bills upon him, though Surtees and Burton would negotiate them and you can draw them at a short date. I am glad your markets keep so good. Beef is scarce 4s here except nice, mutton indeed holds 4d per lb. tallow same as with you and shins 3 to 3s 6d per which I suppose exceeds Newcastle &c. I know Mr Sail blames me, but the blame rests with himself in part, but mostly with Mr Wastle. Mr Wastle is a surprising man to be a dying, however the price pays you very well. I will remember to give Mr Sail 10s 6d I think. I am very surprised how you come to think that oxen would not drive to Mr Sails? Well you have made an excellent end of the sheep you have sold hitherto which shows you can do as well without me as with me. You do well to to let me know that you have sown so much wheat, think you not that I am interested in all you do? How surprisingly late you harvest, I mean the ruff close &c and Mr Thompson is compared with everything here? I advise to sow all the wheat you can with propriety, many people tire of sowing wheat in this country, because it runs the land wild after oats &c, but that is a reason why you should sow more. You rejoice me with saying your turnips are so good, God be thanked. They are very indifferent here in general but they sow with dung in common. You have worked up T. Clark and R. Mills to better prices than I could have expected at so late season. Mr Bakewell lets as low as 4 guineas to neighbours who are no tupmen. I think I shall not quarrel with Mr Wastell, but I shall certainly talk a little to him. Mr Sail should have come to Fenton. Pray tell Mr Leadbetter that I am highly obliged to him for his behaviour to my son, and pray tell Matt that his father will love him for being a good lad. Do you ever examine his pockets? I hope my sister and you are sensible of my gratitude for your kindness to my poor boy, I pray God reward you all. I include all my friends and do not think a weakness to acknowledge that my heart feels when I am upon this subject. I am glad to know that Dr Kerr is to be his master. I have no fear of the doctor making a bad use of it. Be sure you remember me to all my friends and acquaintances. I am really sorry at Mr Pickering's behaviour, it is ill usage to both us and his son William and I think you had better not be too severe until you can see him or see Billy Pickering, as I think Bill has a good deal of honour and honesty. Your brother Bates is gone with Mr Walker to Woolsthorpe this morning, and they meet me at Loughborough on Thursday. Mr Bates desires his warmest thanks to you, and is now determined to go with us and I fancy we shall go south west the latter end of this or beginning of next week, nor can I tell where you can write to but Dishley, and the oftener the better. I dine with Mr Deverel today, stay all night and to Mr Thackers tomorrow to settle that account, so to Dishley again. You need not hurry about this bill until you be at Mark fair if this be with you before you send one. I wish E. Tulip happy and am with every good wish yours always Goo Culley PS This family joins with Mr Walker in compliments. PS I am to have some more information respecting the price of wood. You have certainly made a good end so far of your fat cattle and sheep both store and fat, these Yorkshire men do well in drawing so much money from the north

Dishley Thursday 18th November 1784 Dear Brother On Monday last I received a letter from you promising a bill soon of 40 or 50£ which letter I answered and sent from Nottingham on the Tuesday. Since then have been at Mr Deverels and Mr Thackers who paid me the ball 4£ 11s 6d so you may settle that account. The full ball was 4£ 11s 8d. Mr Thacker is a most respectable character, highly esteemed in his own neighbourhood, and said to be enlarging his fortune by a successful train of business. He can grind 100 quarter per week, but does 50 upon an average, is concerned in a cotton mill at the same place, which I was favoured with a sight of (I forgot to tell you that my friend T. Bates is gone to Woolsthorpe but we expect him and Mr Walker again today). This is an amazing piece of machinery totally inexplicable by me, but I can conceive it would have been a great feast to you Mr Matt: they employ above 50 children of both sexes and of different ages, who have one man to manage them in every room, the whole is an astonishing proof of mans inventive powers. The whole apparatus cost about 4000£. I am happy to tell you that there is one erected at Tedbury in Staffordshire, which is principally employed in spinning wool which though more difficult to spin than cotton, these gentlemen tell me there is not to doubt but in a few years there may be many employed in spinning wool. There is also a forge mill for rolling iron plates for tinning, much in the same stile as Mr Kendles above Warkworth, which gentleman I find is a native of Staffordshire and was concerned in the same manner, in that populous country, may probably have connections with his brothers who carry on similar works in Staffordshire. A woollen or fulling mill is also in this busy place, all upon the Derwent 8 miles from Derby 8 from Cavendish Bridge, a most eligible situation, because the canal that brings wheat &c to Mr Thackers mill, communicates with the Trent, Mersey, Severn and Thames and consequently with every sea that surrounds this wonderful island. Mr Thacker bought some of your kind of spring wheat while I was with him at 2 guineas per quarter. Wheat is dropping at present but Mr Thacker is so candid as to say, that he is quite of opinion that wheat will be higher sold in the spring and summer, from its being a much worse crop than people at first thought: it yields ill both to the flail and flour. If you please Sir you may consider this information as coming from a respectable quarter. Barley he is not so clear about but is sure it will not be low, thinks it very likely to hold if not advance in price. Oats are sure to advance he says. We have had a succession of wet for many days, 8 at the least, and is very like to continue if we may judge from appearance, and if so we may retard if not quite stop our western tour. You may tell Mr Thompson of Lilburn, that I have not forgot him, that on asking Mr Bakewell he abruptly said he would sell none (bulls) and I have seen few besides that please me except for Mr Fowlers who will not sell a good one. Good long horns are in fewer hands than sheep, and they are not in many hands. Its amazing how fashions change, not many years ago nothing would do but short carcases and short legs, now they must be long carcased and stand high or they will not do at all, thin necked, straight topped, flat topped, and wide, in short light in the useless parts, and thick in the useful parts. I am talking of sheep Mr Matt, most people fond of size, hence you may trace the taste for the Durham sheep. Mr Deverels look sadly, but may answer for a few very large sheep. He has let his Durham tup for more than he cost. The very high prices Mr Bakewell has and may let at stagger all their neighbours, and what it will come to I know not but the higher he lets the better for those that have of the same family, and the higher the sheep will stand in credit. Mr Bakewell is gathering a vast quantity of haws, so I hope you will not neglect. He says people are tired of growing quicks, and probably will not be so keen again. Unavoidable delays always attend matters of consequence. Mr Bakewell cannot go until another week on account of some particular business, so I think we shall turn and be coming home unexpected. Had we thought of it, some of the sheep drivers coming to York might have come up for my two yearlings, for they will hinder us much on our return, as they cannot travel above 20 miles per day. I now repent that I allowed Mr Huskisson to buy them, indeed he would have kept them, but I could not do that with propriety. One good will attend it, the slow rate of travelling will suit our horses, not but they have stood the work well. Your horse still sweats, but not so much as he did, and keeps his condition well.
