We have had a very severe frost now for 2 days, after a great wet. 20th . You have not told me but I hope you have examined all your tups and breeding sheep for yellowness? Mr Bakewell lost his credit entirely, he says, in one part of the south not to be retrieved, by a tup of his proving yellow, and getting yellow ones. It is of high import to attend to every outlet now. Old Rumps's sons are in higher credit than any others out of Mr Bakewells hands now, therefore I hope you will attend to them. Mr Walker says cabbage is the best to teach tup lambs to eat green food in the winter, they generally sink or lose condition before they take to eat turnips properly. Tell William Atkinson to be sure all your sheep are well kept. In this country, they now do not keep their store ewes so well as they used to do in the autumn, but keep them better as they get heavier with lamb, as many have been lost in this country with many being in too great condition when lambing time came, but that is a complaint that ours have not the same chance to be lost by. 21 . Mr Bates is in high favour with Mr Bakewell in consequence of his fondness for watering ground. Mr Bakewell always calls him Brother Bates . Wool I am told lowers in price in this part which I am sorry for. Mr Bakewells cabages are very good this year and his turnips tolerable. Lord Winchilsea was here yeaterday, a pleasing young nobleman, who talks of having some stock from Mr Bakewell. He has a seat in the southern part of this county. Have you sown any wheat at Cornhill? Has Brother James sown much? I hope you do not neglect to give your work oxen turnips along with their straw, remember how well they did with it last winter, and it is much cheaper feed than hay and I believe better for working or growing cattle. Do give all your young cattle a few turnips or shells with the straw. The Dishley people give cabbages, turnips, or carrots to all their cattle with straw sufficient to keep them open in the bodies. I see I have acted very foolishly in permitting Mr Huskisson to buy us those 2 yearlings, not only in being too high priced, but their inability to travel so far, when so young, and at so late a season, besides their staying at meat so long with Mr Bakewell is what I do not like on reflection, because it may be 6 weeks or more before we return, in short I am in ill humour with myself about these said horses, and yet for you to send a person on purpose for them will add still more to the price. However I shall leave this to you and William Browns consideration. Would old John Wright and his ass be able to fetch them? If anything should happen the poor old man by the way I should repent still the more, so I know not what to do, had it been summer it would have been no great matter, but now they must have hay &c. Pray help me to contrive some way to relieve me in this, in many respects seeming difficulty, I would think nothing of the trouble of taking them down in my hand only the eating Mr Bakewells hay &c. You see us two and 4 horses so long together is terrible and not easy kept. As to myself, I grow shamefully fat and cant help it without I should starve myself altogether. I am sure you would not know me? If a man comes for these 2 yearlings he should either have Jock Galloway or if he could be trusted to walk it would be better, but if he rides upon either, he will kill them. They will travel 20 or 24 miles per day and any man may well walk that. He may lead one and the other will follow like a foal. They are shod before and he may have them done behind. We have been at Mr Huskissons again, Lord Wentworth, Mr Knowles's, Mr Creswells, Mr Salisburys (Goo), &c &c. And on our return this 24th November received a letter from my sister Jane, and finished by James, pray tell them I am particularly obliged and will as soon as possible answer them. In answer to yours Mr Matt I am glad the distillery is to go again, it will make a difference to the price of barley I have no doubt, and you will see by a part of this letter that barley rather mends in price in this country, it will also compel the factors to comply with the resolution respecting boll and score, in truth it makes little difference upon the whole, but I have not time to enlarge upon it now, Mr G. Logan will find it rather difficult to hire a good sheep at Dishley next season according to present appearances. I had rather Bill Gill has come here for a horse. The 2 Jameses have sold the 100 ewes well. I am sorry Mr Atkinson has missed the mountain. It is not enough that your lambs are clear of yellowness, you must examine your tups and tup lambs and breeding ewes &c &c. I am pleased with your hiring James Kerr and James Hewitt and I would not have you miss Andrew Laidlaw. We talk of going south on Friday first but would wish the bill here in the mean time. You will see what I have said about the horses above, and would have you do as seems best. If Lisle comes at all, he may as well come to Dishley, perhaps John Breedon will show him a little of the stock, let him have a letter from you to Breedon requesting a sight of such things as are agreeable to themselves, and as Mr Bakewell and we would probably be out Breedon will then rather show him things. Let him call at Wentbridge as I may possibly send them thither. I think May or in the spring better for Matt going to Mr Armstrong than now, but would wish you to speak to Mr Armstrong about it and take Matt with you if weather permit, you have all my thanks, and the Almighty will reward you for your attention to my children. I am exceedingly happy that Dr Kerr manages him so well. Pray God continue them good health and his Almighty Grace. As Matt thrives so well, he need have no bark, or I was thinking it might be right to give him a little bark and red port or the latter now and then may be better. Why does Nelly grow so thin? I hope she is allowed milk enough &c and puddings. Is not ripe fruit wholesome, I wish you and them had as many good apples and pears &c as we met with everywhere in this land of plenty. By a letter this day from Mr Stubbins I find Mr Pickering (William) has wrote to him lately and was so kind as to desire him to tell me, all was well with you. My thanks pray when you see him and compliments. You may depend on my calling at Denton on my return and lending every assistance in my power to Messrs Hardcastle and Peacock. John Todd is in luck. I am sorry you were disappointed in not receiving my answer to your last but am sure it would not be far from Wooler at the time you mention, as I wrote immediately on receipt of yours and shall write as often as possible when out though you can only write here unless to Mr Bells London that married Nanny Atkinson, as I shall be there if we be in London, which we shall certainly be which ever way we go. But more of that in my next as I shall send this immediately. Mr Bates and everybody join in due respects with your ever offed Goo Culley PS I like the idea of Lisles coming for the 2 yearlings best because he will see the country and is able and I hope will be willing to walk with them 20 or 24 miles per day, but he must be charged not to ride upon any account as they cant bear it, but if he leads one the other will follow like a foal in a day or 2.

Dishley Thursday 25th November 1784 My kind friend and brother Though I sent you a letter last night in answer to one from you, and one from Jenny and James, I must not omit acquainting you that I have this moment received Messrs Surtees and Burden draft on London at 40 days for 50£ for which you have my best thanks. Its money makes the mare to go Mr Matt: there is only one evil will attend the matter, like all children Master Thomas and I will be playing tricks when we get to London, and not get so soon home again as we ought to do. Mr Huskisson is luckily here this moment and I believe rather scant of cash, so I hope to get cash for my bill today and pay him for the horses. Mr Huskisson advises me to buy a stone horse, which his brother Sam has and which horse Sam bought in the mares belly at Dishley sale, says he will suit us to cover our own mares, and work, is the sort Mr Huskisson likes, and what we like, and supposes he will be bought for 30 guineas is well bred, and out of as good a mare as any that ever was at Dishley and got by G horse, but is almost blind. Now you must consult with Jenny, William and Bartholomew Brown on the matter, the quere with me is whether it is right to breed horses or not? If it is whether strong or light? Reason says strong ones in our situation are best, and indeed they pay the most in all situations I believe. I hate stone horses to use as stallions in travelling the country &c but querie whether it is not right to have one for our own use? if it be right to breed at all, because it is clearly better to breed good or useful horses than unuseful, and it will prevent us from being plagued with other stone horses and their keepers coming about us. And perhaps the best farmers horses are bred from a black stallion (if not too clumsy) and country mares. You may be sure I shall not buy this horse or any other without the approbation of my friends nor until I see the horse and if I should buy him or any other before my return, it should make no difference in your sending Lisle or any other for the two yearlings because he would not bring the stallion with them for the stallion must I apprehend be led by himself. I am glad the Stones fair proved so good, and also that your receipts were good, as well as payments . The latter are always certain. Beef cattle are scarcely sold here at 4s per but mutton keeps 4d and tallow is 5d. I am with true regards Yrs Goo Culley Loughborough corn markets much the same. PS Buy Matt strong shoes or clogs, only I am afraid clogs would hurt his ankles. Mr Thacker has promised to give me cash for the bill. NB I believe we shall go south tomorrow if all be well, therefore if you hear nothing to the contrary may send a letter to Mr Bells that married Nanny Atkinson, my sister can give you a direction. I mean a letter directed to me at Mr Bells, as I shall be anxious to hear of you all. And if we once set forward it may be some weeks before we return.

Dishley 26th November 1784 Dear Matty Mr Bakewell advises me, to have you direct to me thus (Mr Culley at Mr Honeyborns No 10 Throgmorton Street London) until you have advice to the contrary. Mr Honeyborn is his nephew, that we pronounce improperly Huniball, and says we shall stay in that part of London near Mr Honeyborns, and that he will send any letters after us, which may come to his hand, in case we should travel further south or west. By my writing you so many letters just now, you are not to expect Mr Matt: that you are to be plagued with so many every day or every week, no: I fancy when we once set forward we shall be so taken up with business or the contrary that we cannot write so often as you and we would wish, however you may be sure I will write as often as I conveniently can. Pray tell Mr Thompson of Lilburn that Mr Bakewell has a bull, which he would recomend to Mr Thompson as a particular good ox and heifer getter, is of as good a sort as any they have, but I cannot prevail upon Mr Bakewell to take less than 15£ per season for 2 seasons, and not even so little as that except Mr Thompson will be at the expense of both fetching and taking back to Dishley. I believe this is the lowest that he will take, therefore Mr Thompson must judge for himself. I will endeavour to describe the bull. He is rather larger than the generality of the Dishley bulls, with very little coarse about him except his neck which is very leathery and coarse indeed, his rumps, hips, sides, and top all very good in my opinion, that is not so exceedingly wide, as kind to handle, very mellow in the touch indeed, and better flesh upon him than most bulls, perhaps as good as many oxen, his colour light red, and bone fine, in short if we were not too far from Mr Thompson, I should have no objection to join him in the hire, but perhaps Mr Thompson may get some of his neighbours to join him though B. Marshall may not, though I fancy Mr Marshall would like this better than the one they had from Dishley before. Yet he is far from catching except you feel, and then I think he will please a judge. But after all this recomending a stallion is only an unthankful office, and I would not have ventured to have said this much, if not to a Mr Thompson, or such like reasonable person, who would believe that I would not wilfully mislead them, I may err thorough ignorance but not intention. It appears strange and awkward to me, after being already 8 weeks from home, to set out upon a fresh journey, that may employ us almost 8 weeks more. But my friends have always been kind to me, and when I reflect that we were glad to spend a few days or weeks with this extraordinary man when we could scarce afford it, makes me scruple less to spend a little time and not a little money with this genius, now we can the better afford it. Besides he is so much more communicative now than in Ashworths administration, indeed there is nothing now scarce that he will not give a straight answer to. One thing though is not so well we are seldom trusted without a guard only I have the honour to be guarded in general by the old General himself, in short he will scarce let me be out of his sight. As to my friend Thomas he rises in his esteem every day, so that you see we are a kind of prisoners. But we are not to complain of this because everybody else are treated in much the same manner that come to this place, and few days without some company lords or peasants . This kind of management hinders us from gaining that information from the servants to which we dare not so well ask the superiors, and a shilling will often purchase a good deal from a domestic. Nor are we to blame this conduct when we are given to understand that his servants are not unfrequently inveigled away by people that come about Dishley. Even your friend Trigger is going to leave Mr Bakewell and its believed that some have enticed him away and you must not be surprised, if Fenton people fall under some suspicion, not from Mr Bakewell but some others. However I cleared up that matter by asking Trigger, who declared he never heard of it before. I believe it had its origin from some nonsense Ned has talked after he returned to Dishley with the stallion from Fenton. If Lisle is not come away for the yearlings before this come to hand, could he not bring the tup cart with him to Mr Collings and take the 2 tups home, viz Dr Edwards and his, he could leave the cart and horse at Mr Collings till he return. I offer this for your consideration. Mr Tailor of Salton will keep his another season I fancy though you had not time to write to him and I am afraid he has not wrote to you, perhaps I may call on him as we return. Newark on Trent 27th . We left Dishley this morning, viz Mr Knowles of Nelson who is going with us into Lincolnshire, Mr Bates and self. Mr Bakewell was to meet us here as some business detained him an hour or 2, but he is not come and now 8 o'clock at night, but I suppose he will reach us tmorrow at Wragby. We propose going thorough Lincolnshire and Norfolk to Mr Youngs in Suffolk and so to London. The weather is most delightful, after 10 days rain and 3 sharp frosts. Mr Bakewell is much mortified at not being able to find my M.S. in Dishley house, suppposes it has been lent but not to some of his neighbours and not remembered who. However he is more vexed at it I believe than I almost ever saw him. So we cannot show it to Mr Young, but its perhaps as well. Pray Mr Matt if I can be of any service to any of our connections in London let me know, not that I suppose we shall stay many days there until we visit the famous Mr Ducats. Some people say Mr Bakewell will not be rich still, without he make 2000 per annum of the letting scheme and his stock in feeding &c and 500 of corn, because they say the riding expenses is 500 at least with sending out tups, housekeeping 500 I believe labour 500 at least I suppose more and rent 500, therefore without he makes more than 2000 he can save nothing. However if he don't save now he never will I think, because its unlikely that these times can hold long, and what a shocking thing it would be for him to fail a 2nd time, but I understand they are paying of and doing well and I hope he will do. You see Mr Matt I send but little waste paper though I have little to write about but in writing to a friend I have no notion of pinching. God bless you all says Goo Culley

Wragby Lincolnshire 29 November 1784 Mr Matt We were going to breakfast with Mr Codd, but Brother alias Professor Bates as Mr Bakewell calls him had hurt a toe a little which is subject to inflame in frosty weather, and as he has had it to plaster with beeswax and butter it has stopped us half an hour, which time I have stole to write. We left Dishley on Saturday and at Newark that night I put a letter in to the post for you. On Sunday at Lincoln viewing Minster and at church. Monday a fair at Lincoln with large show of cattle of every kind but one like Mr Sails sheep, and came here last night. Louth 1st December. Yesterday morning we breakfasted at Mr Codds from thence to a Mr Joshua Walesbys a tupman who has a very good shearling of Mr Walkers of Woolsthorpe, got by a Dishley tup, and a very large tup of Mr Chaplins, as different from Mr Walkers as two sheep well can be. We went next to Mr Chaplins but were only allowed to see the cattle. Mr Chaplin was not at home nor son but the servants no doubt had their orders, indeed Mr Bakewell and Codd are very odious to this country breeders, and especially to Mr Chaplin who is at the head of them and whose stock is diametrically opposite to Mr Bakewells and that sort. Mr Chaplins dinner bell rang while there but we were not asked to dine so went to this place and put dinner and supper into one. I tire though of this sauntering about we shall be long of prosecuting our journey at this rate, to be sure Mr Bakewell moves slow and days are short, but expenses run high, for we live all on the public at the rate of no less than 10s per day. When shall I repay this Mr Matt? Mr Bakewell hires all his principal servants for 3, 4 or more years at once, says then that they are then more interested in your behalf than from year to year &c. I wish you would make some water roads, you can do that in soft wet weather, down by the ladies close side, all you have to do is make the water run as thin and as level and equal as you can, down the middle of the old road, the stuff thrown to both sides, make a good walk or riding path in particular times, you have many other places in Fenton which will answer well in this way, wherever the fall is not too rapid. I beg you may make some trials upon a small scale at first when the places cut much a few stones can be put in but do not that too hastily as time will teach you and the sand washing in often does the job. A wash road must be quite contrary to a raised one, because the washed one must be hollow and troughed. The weather is rather wet again but fresh and good upon the whole. 2 December. This night at Swinhop Mr Walesbys a tupman where we also saw a rabit fold taken. They go at 8 at nights, they close the fold on the side next the burrows, the nets having been set on 3 sides before, then the warrener and some assistants attend all night or else the rabbits eat their way thorough the nets, as soon as light in the morning all hands and dogs to work, when the poor rabbits are hunted down or into false holes where they afterwards take them out, from 100 to 500 couple are taken at different times. A snow has fallen in the night prevented the rabbits from resting so that few were taken. December 3. All night at Mr Richard Codds who lives at Wikeham a good house and 300 per annum belongs to your friend Mr Harrison of Walworth. Mr Codd says it is dear, was valued by Butler. Torrington is the other estate belonging to Mr Harrison, which Mr Codd tells me is better land than this. Some good ground here but as I have not yet seen it, I cannot say what it is in general. Mr Codd takes it upon account of the house as he is a very independent man, married Mr John Codds sister who was a widow and has no children by him. As your brother and my friend Mr Thomas Bates is not much better of his toe, though no worse, yet can't prosecute his journey with that pleasure he would wish, so has determined all at once to return north, consequently I have not leisure to say all I could wish at present. It is totally uncertain when we get to London, or when I return, we get very slowly forward indeed, days so short, and people so kind. I do assure you we live well only too well Mr Matt. All the care I can take I can't keep from getting too fat. God bless you all my best respects to all and believe me ire affty Goo Culley PS I shall leave this open for Mr Bates to fill up as I have no secrets.

Hilton December 13th 1784 Dear Brother Mr George was so kind to leave this letter for me to fill up and send from Newcastle, but being so anxious to get home I forgot the letter having a very sore toe or chilblain which I am very subject to in winter, which was the cause of my return northward so soon, which I submitted to with great reluctance from the very agreeableness of my journey with so good and intelligent company. I am apt to think would not have minded if I had continued my journey from the different manner of living that I am accustomed too, I am greatly obliged to you for the great respect you payed me in your brothers letters, and only wish that I may always merit your respect please to remember me to my dear sister and I should be happy to be under her care as surgeon. My mother was speaking about coming to Fenton but from a slight cold she has got and the inclemency of the season she thinks it may be some time first, we are quite blown up with snow the roads impossible in may places so that the tups cannot come according to appointment but I hope to hear from you soon when you will fix another time, and when you send would be obliged to you for a few cuttings of your tree willow. My mother and brother joins me in complements to the whole family and am dear Sir with great respect yours sincerely Thomas Bates NB I purpose being at Fenton as soon as I can bear a boot upon my foot if it had been any way tolerable perhaps might have been the bearer of this letter.

Manby Mr Codds 4 December Dear Matty Our friend Thomas left me at Mr R. Codds yesterday morning, and I sent a half finished letter by him. We meet with uncommon civility, among these hospitable gentleman breeders who to be men of so much good sense, its truly amazing that they should be so ignorant of good stock, and that they should have so long stuck to such useless stock, but the batle is now over they now give up to better judgement, this truly great and indefatigable man Mr Bakewell convinces in general wherever he goes, how much does his country owe him! But his merit will never be truly known, until he be dead I have often said. 5th December Tunby Swan - an od house, but a very good inn I assure you, fish beef and apple pie &c with nuts and apples after dinner are comfortable things on a bad snowy day. Mr Codd and I parted with Mr Bakewell yesterday, and went to a fen farm of his where we saw his tup hogs large and fat indeed going among cole or rape in this flat wet country by the Within which is made navigable between Gainsborough and Boston. We staid last night at Billinghay a large village upon the fen, and then this morning early went to Thickby Mr Fishers where we saw an ox heavier and perhaps still be made heavier than Mr Hills, a milk white, both sire and dam came from Teesside but Mr Fisher had forgot the mans name, he is I think the heaviest ox I ever saw, and very good points in general bones small, but not so very complete as Mr Hills was. We saw several good short horned cattle in this quarter, bred from Teeswater cattle. We crossed the Within again by Tattershall, a fine flat country to this place Mr Fishers is near Sleaford another market town. I am to meet Mr Bakewell in the morning at Spilsby. I was witness to Mr Codd hiring the tup he has this season at 60, for 100 the next to tup 80 ewes only for Mr Codd, and 20 for Mr Bakewell before he leaves Dishley. What do you think of such work Mr Matt. I rejoice at it for my part and wish the old boy his health to play these pranks for years to come, it will be better for us and those near akin to him beside it will keep Mr Logan or at any rate he must pay a great price, if he comes another year and will have a good one, or anybody else, as for us I think its prudent to feel how we are a while before we give 100 guineas. 7th A very snowy morning and much wet had fallen in the night, so that the fen country is much of it covered with water. Breakfasted with Mr Stevenson steward to Sir Joseph Banks, who was abroad with Capt. Cook, lives at Reesby in this neighbourhood and is president of the Royal Society. From hence to Spilsby with a market today. Monday Here I met with Mr Bakewell again and parted with Mr Codd. Met with a London drover who came on to London on Friday and says the market is bad 4s per stone sunk and 4 sink for sheep. Tuesday 8 . Another wet morning, it has now rained and snowed most of 3 day days and nights. Waters are very much out and increasing, they talk of some of the banks having given way, a thing noways uncommon in these fenny countries, and does great damage when that happens, however we are in safe and good quarters at Mr Wrights Spilsby, and I assure you will not stir until we can do it with propriety. Mr Wright is a young man of a pretty fortune, natural son to a Mr Wright who is dead. His mother lives with him, and is much fatter than Mrs Moody. This is the Mr Wright who hired the tup called Shoulders which sheep Mr Logan bid 60 guineas for, he is a very nice sheep indeed, little but firm proportions light shin and pelt like paper, is now I may say rather very fat after serving 7 score ewes and being sunk in condition by being put in a poor pasture from the 20th of July to the time he was put to the ewes. Mr Bakewell says Mr G. Logan shall not have him under 120 guineas for his ride next season so Mr Logan may expect to be well done over if he comes to Dishley. Give me leave to explain Mr Bakewells mode now it is in my head in the tup way. He shows his tups (at least those fit to be seen) as soon as they come home from their rodes, to the 1st of June, then they clip and show none for 8 days, then on the 8th of June they exhibit them stripped and show the let and unlet sheep until the 20th of July when they show the unlet ones no more but put them into a poor pasture until they go to the ewes, by this mode they are better able to do business, and peoples thoughts are not taken of the unlet ones by seeing the let ones. These methods strike at the roots of the Lincolnshire breeders, for theirs are never fit to be shown until near Michaelmas. But the battle is over in Lincoln and they have nothing to say now against Mr Bakewells sort only the wool, and that is now confessedly better than Lincolnshire in quality not 2 lb a fleece less weight in short the wool buyers prefer the Leicestershire and Mr Bakewell and his kind have a fine field before them indeed. I almost wish to be fixed in this fertile country. Mr Codd let 150 tups last season and made 930£ of them this is from his own mouth. Its like a new creation nay I am of an opinion that a Lincolnshire breeder would sooner come at his point by breeding from honest ewes than from their own, for I think no country can show such bad ones. This is the same Mr Wright that has Mr John Charges bull, is now 9 years old and in my opinion exceeds the bull John Lax has in some particulars, indeed this young man has it in his power to make a great figure in the breeding line. You must remember Mr Matt that the said tup Mr Wright has is brother to your shearing tups, as well as Cambrells, and of a most valuable sort I think, therefore pray proper attention to them and your tup lambs, for they are worth attending to they are now in fashion and will not soon go out I think for the principles are founded upon reason and true judgement it is like building a house upon a rock. God bless you all says ire offed brother Goo Culley PS You may be sure I long to hear from you, but must wait till we get to London. We make way very slowly as the sailors say. Mr Wright is to go with us for a few days, perhaps to London. I hope my friend T. Bates is near home by this, I gave him a letter to fill up and put into the post at Newcastle as he passed there. Mr Burns shepherd bought a tup at Leicester of the Dishley folk during the interregnum at 60 guineas and all the best sheep Mr Bakewell has are got by him, so much for Dishley blood, this information from Mr Wright, who hired of them from Mr Bourn before he knew Dishley.

Spilsby 8th December 1784 Mr Matt I sent you a letter from this place this day, and as we are confined here with bad weather, I cannot do better than employ a part of my time in writing to you believing that you will be willing to pay postage for my nonsense mixed with some perhaps useful intelligence. 9th At Boston last night, where we sent for poor old Raynor formerly a tupman that used to bring tups to Milton, has fallen very poor, lost an eye and teaches school 2 miles from hence, and I am sure Mr Matt that you will not be angry at my giving him 1/2 a guinea and Mr Bakewell the same. We made the poor old man happy and felt pleased ourselves. This an amazing rich country I now have seen the land that carries nay makes fat an ox and 4 or 5 sheep per acre it is rich indeed, and when we consider the very bad kind of sheep it makes it more wonderful. However Mr Bakewell is like to reap a rich harvest in this country, and indeed they are coming over faster than one would imagine. Pray Brother keep these confused letters of mine together for my satisfaction and use, as I am unable to write a journal and letters to you must take care of these I beg. We are now at Holbeach a small market town outside the Wash or lost dike Wash, a small disagreeable place indeed, a road I shall not venture again I think, our guide rode with a long pole to grope or feel the road for fear of inlets or seeks where horses are sometimes lost and rider in imminent danger. Very lately a man lost his horse and escaped himself with some difficulty. This country fitter for geese and ducks than people and indeed we are not to wonder at its being so thin peopled though amazing full of stock they say unless they stock very hard they spoil the ground and that the land at Long Sutton is much worse since old Wallets time for want of stocking harder. They say sheep will not do upon old dead grass or what they call fog. At Boston they have bored 340 feet without meeting with water and are determined to persevere a little longer as fresh water is a blessing unknown here except what is catched from rain. Sutton 10th . A heavy snow having fallen last night, has prevented our viewing the richness of the land of this first grazing country perhaps in this island, where the famous Wallet made so much noise his descendants are likely to come to beggary. 'Sic transit gloria mundi'. Mr Wileman a very spirited clever man who now lives where Mr Wallet did live has 2 rams from Mr Bakewell this year. Mr Wileman tells me that a considerable quantity of wheat has lately been bought here to go abroad, but where to he knows not, so high as 50s per quarter some say to Ostend, but that is conjecture. This price for wheat is the more remarkable as it is higher than in the inland counties, for at Loughborough it was only 45s. I can form no idea of these prices standing, but shall tell you more when I hear of it respecting corn, oats 8s per comb, no barley grown here. Course of crops in general beans and wheat alternately without fallow. The spring wheat is taking place, they sow their beans broadcast. 11th Long Sutton. It has been a most astonishing frost indeed but I have no doubt of you and William Brown and all the Privy Council doing to the best of your knowledge. I hope you have sold more of your ewes and other sheep, it is always generally right to sell for a fair profit, I am very happy you sold your cattle so near, I never think wintering cattle pay like sheep. I hope your oil cakes are arrived safe they are not to be bought under 5£ 15s and 6£ here. It is said barley is much dipped at Lynn and to the south: I do not understand this, when wheat is advancing. The wheat I mentioned is going to America (Nova Scotia) I believe. Sunday 12th December Wisbeach. This is a considerable town much corn comes down the Nen, and is principally bought by a Mr Baker of Lynn whose clark Mr Donkin is a Morpeth man and he and I got acquainted. They do a deal of business to Leith and up the Firth to Mr Steins and know all our corn merchants &c. Indeed this is a most fertile country all the Isle of Ely is I am told, some land keeps from 5 to 10 sheep per acre in the summer and near a beast per acre to keep it down, also generally a horse in every piece of 7 or 8 acres which they think does little harm. The graziers and farmers are a genteel sensible intelligent sort of men, drink wine like water, very expensive I assure you, seem to have read much, and in general well bred. They tell me that Mr Mewburn has realized 800 per annum . Planting wheat costs 10s per acre 5 pecks per acre do not hand hoe, only dibbled upon clover lees what they call flag, put it in about 2 or 2 1/2 inches deep, 2 rows upon a flag or furrow 9 inches wide and as flat as possible, they plow 4 inches deep. This information from a Mr Saffray who prefers Gilsthorps plows to the wheelplow, says nothing but custom can authorise the wheelplows. Lynn Regis 13th . We are just arrived here, and as Mr Bakewell had ordered his London letters to meet him at this place, I was in hopes of a letter also, but I could hardly expect it there has not been time, but I hope to be gratified with a letter when we reach London which I fancy will be this week about Sunday. We have been all last night with a Mr Thistleton at Walpole a village in Marshland 5 miles on this side Wisbeach. We have been 3 days in travelling 19 miles indeed the weather has been very winterish. Marshland properly so called, consists of 7 towns or parishes, all very rich land except the fen part which is untrained, and produces only reeds and other aquatic weeds with which they thatch their houses uncommonly neat thorough all this rich flat country, which in all probability has all been got from the sea at different periods, prodigious quantities of wild ducks, teals and other fowls are decoyed or shot in these fens and sent to London also many eels and tench and pike caught. They have a common here called Marshland Smee said to be preferable to Sutton common, carries in summer, I am credibly informed 10 of the large long wooled Lincolnshire sheep per acre, besides many young cattle and horses, indeed we have rode over a tract of country from a little on this side of Spilsby to Lynn of near 40 miles extent besides it extends along the Lincolnshire coast northward, and up to Peterborough westward, and southward into Cambridgeshire Huntingtonshire and some say thorough Essex to the Thames, which is so flat that I suppose a few feet of water would cover the greatest part of it and so rich as is not easily conceived, those parts excepted which lye so low that the water is not or cannot well be got of and are called fens or lows from 4 to 10 sheep per acre beside cattle in summer and 1 1/2 sheep per acre in winter. But thorough all this tract of county the sheep and cattle are in general (I mean the country breed) of the very worst quality and worth the least per lb of any other part of the kingdom that I know of. At crossing a place called Germans Bridge 4 miles from this town over the river that comes to Lynn the stock immediately change, from Lincolnshire sheep and cattle you come at once to Norfolkers, from the longest wool to near the shortest and in many other respects very different. Now they cannot both be right for the same kind of land, it's a quere with me if either are right. Mr Donkin is of opinion that barley and other grain, wheat excepted will drop in price, barley I understand has fallen most rapidly within these last 10 days in the southern part of this island, therefore perhaps you had better sell what barley you have thrashed or in hand, though one does not know, if they come to export much it may make a material difference in a few weeks. Mr Bakewell desires to join in good wishes with your ever offed Goo Culley PS I forgot to tell you that turnips are a very good crop in this country I am told, but will be able to tell you more of this in my next. Fat cattle fell in price at Boston fair last Saturday and at some other fairs lately, London market bad, indeed I should not wonder if this weather putting in so severely does not hasten many people to market that would have put of a few weeks, some people are afraid of turnips going with the frost, but I hope you have more snow to cover yours.

Lynn 13th December 1784 I sent you a letter from hence last night, and this is a very coarse day indeed. Business is done here in the corn buying way in the readiest and most methodical manner I ever saw, the factor takes his stand, and the farmers present their samples in paper bags, he bids always within 5s per last (all combs and lasts here) generally only bids once, except the sample is of good quality, if the farmer accepts the offer, the buyer takes it and bag, and puts into his pocket but first, sets down with a pencil the quantity in lasts and combs, the price per last and sellers name, but what I was most pleased with, was a little poor boy or girl standing by every buyer with a spread apron to catch the corn that fell from the merchants hand as he was viewing the samples, so that nothing is lost and in the numerous samples that here are exhibited, more is saved than you would imagine. Astonishing quantities of barley, and a good deal of wheat are shown in this busy market, several white peas and some rye. They begin about 12 o'clock and at one the bell rings and everybody go to dinner. The barley is ill coloured and thin this year sold from 11 to 12£ per last, wheat from 21 to 24£ per , white peas 15 to 17£, oats 7 to 8£ 8s per last, 21 combs are allowed for 20 always and in all grain. The oats very bad in quality and few shown, they are called short smalls very improperly, for they are long smalls, I know not what kind they are, but suppose them a bad kind of Dutch oats, wheat and barley the great exports. I am told that more corn is exported from Yarmouth, however a very great deal is shipped from hence, more than from any port I am acquainted with. The market place is a fine square, on the north side the cross and shambles form a crescent, behind them stand cattle and pigs and a Dr Yeldall a quack doctor before upon forms stand first, the Marshland butter, eggs, poultry &c in 2 rows then the Norfolk butter &c then in the open area stands the factors and farmers. Except the market place this town consists of narrow streets like most ports, but covers a large space and has been fortified by a mote and wall. (15 Wednesday). Still frosty and likely to continue, we are now at Castle Rising an ancient borough, 4 miles to the left of Lynn, near the sea. We have altered our rout for the present, and if the weather hold shall not go to London now because our motive was to visit Mr Ducats, but if this frost continues we cannot see Mr Ducats management, however you may still write to London until you have my orders to the contrary, because we may go to London nevertheless if the weather change, after we have visited Norwich &c which is our present plan. A Mr Faucet who is mayor of this old borough has 2 tups of Mr Bakewell this season and where we now are. (Thursday 16th ). We left Mr Faucets hospitable mansion thorough Dessingham and Tring to Somerfield a very excellent farm a Mr Curtis's who Mr Young mentions in his Tour. This gentleman has excellent conveniences and plows 1000 acres. barley, wheat and turnips with clover is the common practice, but it is amazing how few cattle they winter here, upon straw in short the straw is in a great measure wasted. This country is in general poor land and appears to be tiring of the plow, many heaths in the days ride. From Mr Curtis's to Mr Wrights where we saw some Norfolk sheep, a very middling sort to me. We now passed through Burnham to Holkham, but unfortunately Mr Coke is from home. The general practice of feeding turnips I find is by pulling the turnips around the hedges and making lanes or roads thorough the piece, which are taken either to cattle in the folds or in grass fields to plow next spring, the remainder they eat with sheep upon the ground, then always plow 3 times and sow 3 bushels of barley with 10 or 12 or some 16 lb clover and only 1/2 a peck rye grass but is very careful to have good seed and pure rye grass, a little trefoil and white clover also when meant for pasture. They plow in both wheat and barley, the wheat mostly in stitches or 2 plow bouts, mow barley and reap the rest. It is truly astonishing to see almost a whole country under the plow and in general well done, they generally plow 2 and 3 acres in summer all use wheel plows here and say they cannot plow so much with any other plows. I was mistaken in thinking they soiled horses in the summer, but I think they are wrong in not doing it. They chain their horses in the stable by the forefoot to the manger posts instead of tying by the head, an odd way this I think. Friday 17th . We this morning after viewing the elegant house and sumptuous furniture of Mr Cokes at Holkham, his horned and polled sheep, with the idea of imparking 10 miles circuit of ground, the richest service of plate they say in this island and the bed where the Prince of Wales slept a few nights ago, passed through a well cultivated country to Fakenham, a small market town, and 1/2 a mile further at the Kings Head Hampton dined (an ordinary inn) and just by the famous Hampton Green where the Scotsmen annually sell many thousands of Galloway and West Highland cattle. The fair begins the 22nd of November and continues until all are sold, many are now unsold especially one Moffat from the border of Airshire who sells vast numbers. The weather setting in so severe is against my countrymen but they die hard, and sell their cattle very high indeed. An old genius called John Stone who has kept the market 43 years knew me by being once in my company along with Mr Thorne, who tells me Mr Thorne died last March. From here to Dereham a pretty market town 14 miles a woodland country ill cultivated most of the way. This country like many others seems only well cultivated in particular places, indeed I have not so very high an opinion of this promontory as I had. Their great is the plow, but they have the worst way of converting that straw into manure I have anywhere seen, and as to stock of most kinds, they are totally ignorant, they use their sheep only as carriers of manure from one field to another. We propose for Norwich in the morning from whence I intend to send this, and would have you write no more to London as I think we shall turn to the north again from Norwich to Bury where we have ordered our letters to meet us from London, for it means nothing going to the metropolis or Mr Ducats this season, this season when we cannot view the country for snow. If the weather should change we may still change our minds and go further south, but of that you should have notice if we go. You may still write to Dishley because though I shall not stop much there yet it will be a while before I reach that place I suppose as we travel very slow, Mr Bakewell being unable to make much sail. Bumps I mean my horse has a good time of it which will enable him I hope to stand work better after, his legs swell a little at nights but nothing to signify. I hope you will let me know how my friend T. Bates is, Professor as Mr Bakewell says, I am very anxious to hear of you I confess, having heard nothing now of some weeks, but I hope the best. I beg you will tell my sister Jane Culley that I am sorry I have not found time to compose her and James letters but I am sure you will excuse me, when I assure her that I have not leisure, for we are so engaged in conversation &c &c that I have barely time to scrawl these letters to you, and I hope you let all my friends see these letters that choose, as I have no secrets nor wish for none. It's a long time to be absent from my children but I consider them in the best of hands, who with them have my prayers and I trust will ever have my grateful thanks. We have in this country 4 or 5 inches of snow but when we were near the sea at Holkham we had no snow. At this place we have met with our quack doctor again, brother in law to Dr Green. 18th . We arrived at this populous place to breakfast, and a view of the market, an amazing quantity of provisions, astonishing number of people, but the corn market is smugled, and not done openly and methodically like Lynn, the streets narrow and very close built, said to contain 40000 people, the manufactory flat in what they call Norfolk stuffs. This day and last night soft and inclined to rain, but as the wind keeps easterly I think it will draw to frost again. As the post goes out in an hour or less and we are just going to dine must conclude by wishing the compliments of the season and every other good wish to all the Culleys and connections and am yrs &c Goo Culley

Norwich Sunday Dear Jenny I was much obliged to you, for your kind attention in writing me a few lines. I hope you will accept my sincere thanks for the indulgence you and Matty have given me, it will be my duty to make a proper return. I wrote to Fenton yesterday, which letter I expect all my friends to see for I have no secrets. I am glad you have got so well forward in business, and have sold so many of your fat stock &c. Markets have been long overloaded and this weather will make them more so yet. Mutton is sold everywhere that we have been at 4 and 4 1/2d per lb. For particulars I refer to my letter to Matty yesterday and am with true regard to my sister and the Nellys your ever offed Goo Culley PS I feel for you in this hard weather but am glad to hear that you have so much snow as it will save turnips &c. As soon as we reach Bury shall turn north. Except the weather turn frosts and I may be tempted to go see Mr Ducats management but much will depend on the letters from Matty, however I would not have Matty write any more to London until he hears from me again, but to Dishley.

Norwich 19th December 1784 Dear Brother I sent you a letter on Saturday from this place, and one to my sister yesterday. We dined with the famous Watson, who formerly lived at Ellerton near Catterick in Yorkshire, and now practises farriery in this large city. He is vain but clever, and reprobates the gambling life, in short he is an odd compound, and succeeded to a Mr Clover who was most eminent in his profession, and has retired from business with 10000£. There are 34 parish churches, besides a French one, and many meetings of various sects. The river Yare runs though the midst of the town, and is navigable for small craft from Yarmouth which is 20 miles from it. A very large market indeed, and the farmers, and farmers wives come in market carts, many hundreds of them, and bring not only poultry, and butter and eggs, but veal, pork, and mutton, killed by them and retailed here. A man last night robbed 3 or 4 of these carts as they returned home, at last a rough farmer comes up and said D-n you Sir I'll lose my life before my neighbour shall be robbed, he immediately seized the fellow, though he had a brace of pistols, tied him put him into his cart, and brought him back to Norwich in triumph, where he now lies in irons. Stratton 12 miles south of Norwich Monday 20th . We are now bound for Ipswich, as Mr Bakewell would see the famous Suffolk Punch horses. We have had 2 days softish but no thaw, for the country is covered with snow as soon as you leave this city. They pay 8d in the £ poor cess, and this once flourishing manufactory is now said to be on the decline, in short we are told that Yorkshire and Lancashire are stealing the trade from both the west and east of England. The cattle in this country are polled duns in general and I conceive them to be bred from the Galloway cattle as they are very small but not as true made as the latter. The country on both sides this city is divided into small enclosures, which appears to have been done many years as the trees are old pollards in the hedgerows, the management the same as in every part of Norfolk, the plow is their , stock they seem totally ignorant of, and it is amazing that in a country where so much straw is grown that they should not breed more cattle. I suppose they buy more Scots into this country than any other in England, they firkin butter but sell it at only 26s per firkin. We saw Mr Coke of Holkham at Norwich, a very agreeable man, but lost his election for the county by being a Foxite. Mr Bakewell gives his ewes and other sheep barley straw in hecks, on turnips, when hay is scarce, and always recomends hay to hogs at turnips, or other sheep, or some dry meat. Scale End. We this day left Harlestone a few miles to the east of us, another great fair for Scotch cattle, which they call the finishing fair, it was removed from Hoxam a few years ago. Woolpit is in Suffolk and I had always been led to believe that it was in Essex. We are now among the Suffolk chestnut horses, a very useful kind I think, though their legs are round and fleshy, but no hair, backs not wide, but a deal of belly, and horses with a belly are often hard and of a good constitution. We saw a stallion near 16 hands, cost 76£ yet not so good as some geldings and mares which we have seen. This inn is 20 miles from Norwich, 23 from Ipswich, 23 from Bury, 23 from Thetford and 20 from Beccles, a very good house indeed. Stoneham pie in the vale 1/2 mile, we cross a small river by a wooden bridge into Suffolk and a little further by mistake we get to Eye a small market town, but soon get right again and about 6 o'clock arrived at this inn, a very cold frosty night. Stonhampie 21st . We slept all night with the Revd Mr Philip Toosey who is going to Canada by the appointment of Government, with his family and servants. I am to write by him to William Cleghorn. We have seen several Suffolk horses, they are sorrels with white faces in general, shoulders too forward thin girth thick bellied, short quartered, and round legged, yet they said to be good drawers and hardy, which may be for thick or deep bellied horses are often of a good constitution. They soil many of their horses in this country. Many cabbages are grown here but of a much inferior sort to Mr Bakewells. I wish I may remember to buy some cabbage seed before I return from Dishley. We passed thorough Stowmarket and Woolpit where the great fair is for short horned cattle in the latter end of September and is in this county though I always imagined it was in Essex. Still quite an enclosed country with many oak trees, and the most pollards I ever saw. Bury 22nd . Came here this morning in a very heavy snow. Market day, some cattle (Suffolks) and very shabby. Barley 20 to 22s per quarter rather a better price for good than had been of 2 weeks. This is a very large clean town, much long wool brought here from Lincolnshire, combed and spun, and sent in yarn to Norwich and London while most of their own wool goes to Yorkshire, this seems very odd but so it is. Was very happy to receive a letter from you here by way of London being the first of near a month. However I am happy, very happy to hear you are all well, as to the weather never mind as long as you have no hay down that is we must be content always with what pleases God to send us, it is same for you as other people, not but I long much to be with you, to lend you my feeble aid, it is now 3 months this day since I left Fenton, and when I get back I know not, we travel so slow I am quite tired, but I cannot help it as I cannot leave Mr Bakewell until we get to Dishley, which I hope will now be in 6 or 8 days, as we turn north tomorrow after seeing Mr Young. I am glad you have got so much wheat sown, Mr Alder is rather light but perhaps he dare not act otherwise. I forgot to tell you Mr Young like others is no prophet in his own country, and its said he is going to drop his monthly publication I believe you are right Mr Matt short thick carcases are best, thick on the top. I am glad you have gathered some haws, and also that you are going to plant cabbages and turnips for seed, but I am afraid the snow has catched you. I am glad you keep sending to Crosbe better sell for little profit than be left for turnips. Snow is a blessing in that light to save your turnips. You say nothing of oil cakes, I am afraid they wont come. Pox on Mr Walkers dinmonds they are unlucky, but never mind do the best to your knowledge and all will go right. When lambs lose their lies as Rumps's did last spring they seldom or never recover it therefore cannot look well. I am afraid the remittances from America will be uncertain by all accounts but how have you paid your March rents if you have got no money from Starforth. Its certainly right to give your work oxen and all your young cattle a few turnips along with straw for a thousand obvious reasons. I am happy very happy surely to hear of my childrens welfare, and I am particularly obliged to you for your attention to my boy and his clogs I wish my sister would allow Nelly more liberty, but I hope she will as I wrote to her about my girl from Norwich. Children and all young animals are fond of liberty, plain wholesome food and plain whole clothes are clearly right to me. Mr Matt keep Matt whole and as plain as you will, make up some more of my old clothes for him when he wants for they will be of no use to me. I wish much to be at home to live poorly for we live so well and do so little it is impossible but to grow fat. T. Bates got fat well my off. I blame you not for Alex Weightman going away, only stick to the Browns, and you will do for the rest. R. Davison may do very well. It was a fortunate event that Crosbe &c sold all his cows, and that you have so few fat cattle for wintering, I think nothing of sheep compared to cattle, and I find most people say that cattle pay less in general for wintering upon turnips than sheep, as to wintering a few for summer grazing upon straw and a few turnips a different affair. The quantity of Irish cattle that are come over and may make a difference in the spring, as to prices, the Scots are hard with the Galloway cattle now in hand in this country, and will lose by them I am told. We saw the terrible accounts of the loss by sea newspapers, it is very odd by the papers, the snow has fallen on almost every part of this island but where we have been, for 4 or 5 inches deep here and no drifts, very decent riding, only we walk. I do not remember that I said much to Mr Barugh about from done it for the best poor man, and we especially I must be care matters, indulgent brothers hurt me I believe. As the post goes shall conclude with every good wish your offed Goo Culley PS I am afraid the weather would catch my friend T. Bates you say nothing of him.

Bury 23 December 1784 Mr Matt I sent you a letter yesterday from this place after receiving yours of the 4th and 7th inst. I also wrote to you from Norwich and to my sister, from Lynn, from Spilsby or Boston I forget which, and from Newark, and Dishley, and have only received yours of yesterday. But I am content and happy as I had a good account. I only now fret that I am unable to assist you, in this critical season, and when I shall reach you I know not, for we move slow indeed. We breakfasted yesterday with Mr Young, who wishes much to have the sending of my manuscript into the world, but his own writings and deeds are in such bad repute that Mr Bakewell will not allow me to trust it to him, saying that everything that comes through Mr Youngs hands will appear to disadvantage, such bad credit are his writings in his own country. And indeed when we consider it is not to be wondered at, people that devote their time to writing cannot act or execute. His sheep are scabbed, his cattle ill chose and worse managed, in short he exhibits a sad picture of mismanagement. We viewed Sir Charles Davers's flock, they are rather better than the general run, but they never can be right with narrow sharp tops, and thin sides. I have had quite enough of this. We dined at a Mr Simons, along with 3 French men one a count, 3 courses with candlelight, sad work, only plenty of apples by good luck. 24 . Mr Young came to us to breakfast at the Bell this morning and took us to a Mr Pricks where we saw 11 rams, then to Mr Wrights who has very nice conveniences, and a number of cattle feeding upon turnips. We now turned to the left to Barrow where Mr Macro made us very welcome to an excellent dinner &c &c. A fine fellow this lives like a prince, he farms 1200 acres. We saw 12 tups here measured the horns of one 36 inches long, and 9 1/2 round at the root, takes in cattle to straw at 6 per week. We staid all night, Mr Young with us, and breakfasted next morning Xmas day at Mr Mures a Scotsmen who made a fortune with the famous Atkinson in the contracts upon rum &c in Lord North's administration. However Mr Mure of Saxham is much of a gentleman, is retired from business and feeds 120 cattle of all nations upon turnips and cabbages tied up, has a machine to weigh them alive, which he does when put up and when intended to be sold. Here Mr Young left us, a man of the quickest conception I ever remember meeting with, but perhaps too precipitate, have you taken his Annals? Mr Macro conducted us to Dallam to Mr Houghtons who bought a horse of Mr Toosey bred by Mr Bakewell middling only. We dined and parted with the hospitable Macro, who I hope we have converted, at least he intends to visit Mr Bakewell along with Mr Young in March. Much is to be done in these horned countries but when I know not, the change is so very great that people cannot easily reconcile their ideas to a long wooled sheep with a thick carcase, who have been used to their deer kind of sheep, the more they approach to deer, the more lean flesh and less fat in proportion but more gravy of the claret kind Mr Matt. Mr Bakewell and I have recommended this consequently gentlemen's mutton and the manufacturers mutton are of two kinds, the one lean with gravy, the other fat with oil, the gravy meat open greened and porous, the fat meat fine greened and close. A Norfolk man says a sheeps horns should come out forward and turn in such a measure as you shall see the ears through or behind the horns. A Wiltshire breeder says on the contrary that a sheeps horns shall come out backwards so that the ears may be seen before the horns, but a Sussex man says they are both wrong, for a sheep ought to have no horns. I forgot to observe that the Norfolk man is for a black face and legs, a Wiltshire white face and legs and Roman nosed, and a South Downs or Sussex breeder no horns and grey face. (We are charged 3s 6 for a fowl and 6d more for toasted cheese, and 6d for fire, but we are at Newmarket Sir.) It's a Suffolk man who says a sheeps face should be speckled. Sunday 26 . This morning we left Newmarket and breakfasted at Cambridge, where we paid 1s a piece and 3d per horse hay, this the highest I was ever charged, a dear country indeed, though a very fruitful one. From hence we turned aside to St Eves, as the market and show of cattle is tomorrow, only a small place in a flat country full of willows, the river Ouse brings up coals from Lynn and is navigable to Bedford I believe. Monday 27 . Saw St Eves market about 200 sheep and 80 cattle, none good, but I am told this is one of their smaller markets and so it might being the first after Christmas. 7 miles to Huntington famous for Cromwells birth. We passed Godmanchester, and 1/2 a mile from Huntington is Hinchinbrook seat of Lord Sandwichs, his Lordship very civil, gave some beef, ale and wine. 12 1/2 miles to Stilton where we stop for this night. I forgot to tell you that 2 miles on yon side Cambridge is a single house called Sturbidge where the famous fair is held, its said a single peddler happened to set down his pack in harvest and they thronged so about him that the following year many more came which was the beginning of this fair, which is now like most others of that kind much declined. (28 ). Breakfasted at Wansford in England an excellent house indeed, from thence to Stamford, one part in Lincolnshire and rest in Northamptonshire. We now left the great road, to Oakham in Rutlandshire, where we slept. Just by this place stands Burleigh, a well situated seat of Lord Winchilsea's, who was gone to the metropolis or we should waited on his Lordship. Thursday 30th . From Oakham we breakfasted with Mr North, from whom Culley Harrison had gone on Monday for home. Mr North tells me Mr Harrison is to be married to Mrs Warcop and to live near Lemon Lane on an estate of the late Mr Warcops. We got to Dishley last night, where I found Lisle Johnson had set of with the young horses on Monday last, but was grievously disappointed that there was no letter for me, but concluded you had wrote to London but when Mr Bakewell received his letters from Mr Honeyborn this morning behold no letter for poor me . News in suspense is torturing' says Shake. I pray God send me good news. As I have had no letter I shall most likely leave this place in 2 or 3 days (if weather permit for a quantity of snow is fallen this morning), shall stop a couple of days at Mr Sails, and so to Mr Colling where I hope to meet with a letter. We wanted much to know Mr T. Bates is, among other things. Last Monday market London was exceeding good for cattle and pretty good for sheep, previous to that very bad. Corn markets much same every where, but now expected to advance, at least not to fall lower. This weather has all the appearance of continuance but whether or not its always right to act with prudence. I should advise to use turnips and straw in every case you can, and save hay, because turnips are always to be feared in such severe frosty winters, but hay will keep and may be wanted, besides oats will advance in course I apprehend. I hope you have had a cheerful Christmas may you have a happy new year and many is the sincere wish of your much obliged and ever offed Goo Culley PS This family all join in compliments where due and wish to know of Mr Bates's health.

Dishley 1st January 1784 Dear Brother How it has happened I know not but I have received no letters from you since that I received at Bury by the way of London of the 4th and 7th ult . You may believe I am anxious, but it is best to hope the best. I wrote to you from this place on Thursday, we arrived from our southern tour the day before, and this day I am determined to turn my face south north, as there seems no likelihood of a change. Monday 3rd Doncaster. Mr Bakewell and I set out from Dishley on Saturday 1st and got to Nottingham market, and meeting with many acquaintances, amongst the rest Mr Deverel, Mr Bettison, Mr Breedon &c we spent the evening and staid all night at the White Lyon, where Mr Bakewell begun the new year (strange to tell) by letting Mr Breedon for 3 seasons to come the tupping of 40 ewes only, with any one tup Mr Bakewell has, Mr Breedon to choose what tup, at 100 guineas each year, Mr Bakewell reserving the rest of the rode for his own use, or to dispose of, as he thinks best. This is making more than 200 of one tup, what will they come to? Mr Breedon seemed happy at the offer made and was not long of making the bargain. At the same time Mr Bettison bid 120 guineas for the use of Cambrels, but Mr Bakewell would only let half his rode, and on the same terms as Mr Breedon had dealt. Mr Bettison and Deverel are to go to Dishley some day this week, and I do believe Mr Bettison (whatever Deverel may I know not) will do business, and I am clear Mr Bakewell will only let the half rodes of his best sheep at present, and of these for no less than 100 guineas for 40 ewes from one breeder only. For we had this talked over, and determined upon, on our way to Nottingham. It is very clear that he will do his sheep of character at strange prices. He says and I agree to it, that a customer will give no less but more for a tup, that you insist upon 20 or 30 ewes done by, it stamps a kind of value upon him, and a man will also give 100 for the tupping of 40 of his best ewes, by a capital tup, rather than hire one that is not tried at one third of the money. He considers all these matters over in every point of view, and then determines on a fixed price for the day, but alterable another day, if he sees right, but never the day he fixes the price. He says he finds much advantage, and trouble saved by these resolutions. I own that things never would have been so high, under any other administration as Mr Bakewells but he has now diffused such a spirit thorough this island, and the breeding is fixed upon such sound principles, that without we should lose our liberties or some other serious matter, this sort can never go out of fashion, nor this spirit subside. It snowed all the day yesterday as I came from Nottingham to this place, and wets a little this morning, but not a true thaw I think, the storm has upon the whole been a very mild one in the part of the country where we have been. Wentbridge 3rd January 1785. I had some faint hopes of a letter at this place, but am again disappointed, what can be the matter that I have had no letter of so long a time, the old saying is that No News is good News' pray God send it good when I get it. I am determined to send you this today that you may still have time to write to me to Mr Collings at Shirningham which I shall make my head quarters, until I leave the county of Durham, pray Mr Matt if you have not leisure to write, get Dr Kerr to write how you all are. By a letter I had from Mr R. Colling, I am told Mr Wastle does not like Mr Thompsons little heifer, says she gets no weight, if they do not pay well, my friend Sail is as well without them. If I was not so anxious to hear you all are this new year, I would go to Wakefield market as it is on Wednesday however I fancy I shall still go because I would like to feel and see how things are going and like to go in this 2nd market in England, as much depends on that market to us and the north. Mr and Mrs Sail join in best wishes with your ever offed Goo Culley PS I never sent so short a letter before. Pray tell me how my friend Thomas Bates is, Lisle Johnson told them at Dishley that he was robbed as he went home, but I hope it was his brother he meant of.

Wentbridge 6th January 1785 Dear Brother I sent you a letter from hence the other day, and did intend to have seen Wakefield market, but the weather was so wet we could not go. The snow all went here, and the waters much out, but a severe frost again this morning. I only wait N. Edisons arrival to tell us how the the market was, and then I steer north. Whitwell 7th . Edison did not come so I turned for York, and at this place all night. I thought now I was here that I might as well see John Taylors tups, and Richard Barugh, and pay Richard for his pigs. An extreme frost, I begin to fear turnips, though there is no wind. William Walker of York says fat will be very scarce in this neighbourhood after a while, only the storm hastened many things to market, they sell best mutton and best prices beef at 4d per lb. Mr Sail sends his compliments to you and James. Salton 7th . I look upon this to be the happiest corner in this island, here is all the ancient English Christmas plenty and hospitality, all that rural festivity and honest simplicity of manners that characterizes a people above want yet untutored in the vices of the age. I let my friend John Taylor and his brother in law Hay the best sheep for next season again at same price 15 guineas. They paid me for last season, but John Taylor has not settled for the other, but will pay me at next meeting and if he cannot let him to somebody at 5 guineas more, will keep him again at 4 guineas. He says we shall have more customers from Milton side next year, and I hope we shall. I breakfasted this morning (Saturday 8th ) at master Kendals, who said nothing, then I called on Mr Cleaver, who says he will have one of our best tups next season. Mr Cleaver is rather precipitate, therefore I will not be sure of this coming, however I may say as Mr Bakewell used to say of Lincolnshire 'these people must either come to me or somebody else'. This day a little more snow fell. I am now got to my old friend Mr Boroughs, but he is gone to Easingwold. However I stay all night, and it suits very well, for I have both breeches and boots to mend, and no wonder, I believe want of clothes will drive me home if nothing else will. Whitby butchers have been buying beasts for the shipping, give 30s per cwt, Messrs Cleaver and Kendal &c say that fat will be scarce. Sunday 9th . Arrived at Mr Collings, where I saw a letter from James Culley acquainting Mr Colling that Morpeth market was only indifferent &c &c. (Monday 10th ) I came to Darlington where I met with a letter from you, which had been at Dishley and which acquainted me of a letter sent by you to Mr Bells at London that I had no chance to receive. But I am glad to hear that my friend T. Bates is arrived safe. I am glad that you have sold so many ewes &c and that you have bought Lowry Gibsons turnips, it is certainly right rather than be fast, James poor fellow has all the trouble, but I hope to be with you soon to partake of the trouble, indeed its more than time. I propose if all be well to be at Morpeth on Tuesday come a week at the Phoenix where I shall be glad to see James &c. It will be Tuesday the 18th inst in the evening before the market. I sincerely wish my sister and Mrs Forty a happy time both. I think the two Jameses sold their sheep very well at Morpeth. I wish Sir Francis Blake &c good luck. I dined and Bob Colling with me at Mr Hills, and paid him for his bull calf I bespoke as I went south, it is a promising calf I think. I also bought and paid 9£ for a cow for a nurse for it. Mr Hill and Colling both think it best to send a single horse cart for it after a while, of that we must consider when I get home. I got to Denton this evening, and by Mr Peacocks advisement met M. Turner at John Woods where he made a tender of his rent provided I would allow him 3 interest for the times he has paid you his rent before due as he calls it saying he was only to pay his rent at Candlemass &c, but the truth is he wants to quarrel and does not how. I told him I only acted as agent for you and that I had no right to allow interest without your leave, so he put up the money again. I shall speak to Mr Hardcastle about this matter before I leave this country. We had agreed, I mean Mr Peacock and I to send for Mr Dixon and get the article forwarded. I say article because on my calling on Mr Hardcastle this morning he told me an article would be sufficiently binding upon stamps. But as Mick Turner is so obstinate I know not what to do. However I think we will send for Mr Dixon and talk to him about this matter, as you are certainly bound to give Dixon legal possession of Denton farm at the term next ensuing. He Turner is certainly the most brutal animal living, he would gladly have quarrelled with Mr Peacock and me if we would have differed with him. It is past 11 o'clock at night and I am sleepy, and you may be sure we will act to the best of our knowledge. So God bless you all. Goo Culley PS Tell James I shall be at Morpeth on Tuesday the 18th at the Phoenix.
