column46: Decr. 9 1749 Dear Sir I Yesterday received a Letter from Dr. Akinside, & as you seem particularly to desire his Opinion I will give it you in his own Words. "Pray make my Compliments to Mr Cooper & thank him in my Name for his Present. I think his Design extremely good; his Book in general just in point of Sentiment; well adorned with Learning, & that pertinent: only the Style seems too much raised, & too full of Compound Words." I have the Pleasure to tell you that the Sale has been so brisk that I have none left, but am pushing on the Printer with great Expedition that I may not balk the Demand, & you will see a new Edition advertised I hope in ten days time. I am Dr. Sir Your most obedt R. Dodsley

Decr. 19 Dear Sir I heartily beg your Pardon for not giving you an Account of ye Expenses & Profits of this First Edition of ye Life of Socrates, which I should never have done had not You reminded me of our Conditions which had totally slipped my Memory till you recalled it, but which I am very ready to comply with whenever you please to send your Orders. I printed 500, but there are but small Profits arising from this Edition, occasioned by ye Expense of ye Cuts & the high Price of ye Paper. The Profits will be considerably higher in the second Edition as ye Cuts are paid for, & as I was obliged to make use of a cheaper paper (though a very good one) none of the former sort being in the Market. It is not yet proper to advertise the 2d Edition as the first, though all out of my hands, is not yet out of ye hands of the Wholesale men, who would complain if a 2d Ed was advertised before they had sold the First. But I dare say they are very near gone, & ye 2d Ed will be ready this Week. However as the Town will be empty I should think it better to defer advertising till after ye Holidays, but will be directed by You. The Words Second Edition are in ye Title Page, & the Errata in the First are corrected in This. But two of ye Errata you last sent were too late to be corrected, a new Errata will therefore be made for them. I have heard nothing of Mr. Warburton, nor any Criticisms worth mentioning, except what I think I mentioned before viz that several people when they came to ask for it expected a larger Work. I send you enclosed that part of the Monthly review that contains ye Account of Socrates which I suppose is all you want. The Account is on the other side, & whatever Books You please to order I will punctually send. I am Dear Sir Your most obliged humble Served. R Dodsley You will observe that ye Acct of Socrates is not concluded in this Number.

Leicester Decr. the 23d 1749 Dear Sr. Send me down as soon as you can get 'em, the Amsterdam Edition of Diodorus Siculus in two Vols in Folio, of 1745. & Gale's edition of Herodotus. - I must confess that I expected you had disposed of double the number of books you mention, by the repeated & complimentary accounts I have received from my acquaintance in London of the Success of my performance, however to put a Stop to any difference betwixt us in regard to the second Edition, if you will allow me 18 pounds in Classical or other Books, the whole Copy is your own to do what you please with; I mean 18£ including the Clear profits of the first edition, which you know by your own account is 4 already. - if you agree to this I shall from time to time send for such Books as will come to the money, if more I will pay you the balance. - as to what you mention about the advertisement I leave it entirely to you. let me have one Copy of the second Edition neatly bound, together with the Review for the Month of December, (wherein I find an account of Socrates is to be continued) by the Nottingham Stage Coach, which sets out on Monday Jany. the 1st, but if the Review shd not be published till that day, then send both on Tuesday the 2d by the Leicester Carrier. I am, dear Sr, Your most humble Served. J. C. Cooper/ Junr.

Decr 26 Dear Sir I am extremely sorry that you seem not quite satisfied about the Number printed of the Life of Socrates. It gives me a pain that I have not been used to feel. I wish I could give you any stronger Satisfaction than assuring You that I scorn to impose upon any man, much less upon You whom I have reason to think my Friend. But to put an end to all this, I agree to your Proposal & will send you down the Books ordered by the first opportunity, I will send you one of ye 2d Edition as soon as I can get one bound & also one to Mr. Franklin. I will send the Review when out. I rec'd a Letter from one Mr. Bolton Simpson a Clergyman who says you are mistaken in saying that Plato & Xenophon avoid mentioning each other in their Writings, for that in Book 3 Chap 6 Sect 1 of ye Memorabilia Plato is expressly mentioned. I am Dr Sr Your most obedt &c R Dodsley

Leicester Dear Sr I received your Bill & the Pamphlet, the balance of the former I will send to town the first opportunity. - pray send me down, as soon as ever it comes out, Mr Warburton's Book about the Miracle which defeated poor Julian's irreligious attempt to rebuild the Temple of Jerusalem; I see it is advertised to be published the beginning of March, therefore perhaps, Knapton could let you have one immediately in Sheets, which if he can, be so good to send it by the very first Nottingham Stage Coach or Leicester Waggon only Sewed together. - at the same time send me one of your Memorandum Books. - pray don't fail of sending to Knapton the moment you receive this, for if you can procure me One of these death doing Books to Infidelity directly it will oblige, Dear Sr Your most Obedt. Humle Served. J.G. Cooper Junr. Mr Jackson, who is going to publish his long expected Book about Chronology, desired me to acquaint you the next time I wrote, that he proposes to have Subscriptions for his Book taken in at your Shop among others, & desired to know whether he might put in your Name. I should be glad to have your answer, but suppose it is a thing in course. - I have not a frank, therefore place this beside other letters You receive from me unfrank'd to my account. I see my Book has not yet been advertise'd again. let me know how your Subscription for ye Prints goes on To Mr Dodsley / Bookseller / at Tully's Head / in Pall Mall / London

Leicester October the 22d 1750 Dear Sr I am very sorry you are necessitated to put a list of any Errata at all to a Third Edition, which might have been prevented if you had let me known that the Public had been so favourable to my Performance as to require this fresh demand. it is true I was six weeks this year at my own house in Nottinghamshire fitting it up & buying furniture against I go there, but I cannot conceive how that could raise a report that I had left this place which I never proposed to do till next Spring, neither am I altogether so obscure but that a letter directed to me here would have been sent safe to any place I remov'd to; however if the success of the sale should so far exceed my expectations, as to occasion a fourth edition (which you may be enabled to judge of by the latter end of next Month) let me know in time that I may send you a small Appendix, if you think it worth having. - the Subject I am now upon you shall be acquainted with before any body else, but at present it is known to no one but myself, & considering I'm a modern Author that's a great deal to say too. my little Library is not yet complete & till it is so I shall write for Books, for considering the little encouragement Learning meets with, I don't think it justice to my Family to purchase the Tools, and afterwards shall think any Character too dearly bought that is to be paid for at the expense of my ease; therefore you see I have very good reasons to work in the literary Shop just to such a time & no longer, but whilst I do so, you may rely upon having the refusal of my Wares. - when do you begin to publish your historical prints? I would go through with 'em as I have already Subscribed, therefore constantly send 'em as they come out, & place the usual expense to my account. - let me have by the return of the Post the Midwife's Magazine if any such Pamphlet is really published, & when The Gout, Business, & your Customers of Quality will afford you leisure I should be glad to have a short answer to the above particulars, in the mean time I am, with sincere wishes that you may live free at present from the first of those three, & hereafter from the two latter, Dear Sr, Your most humble Served & Sincere Friend J G Cooper/ Junr. My compts. to Mrs Dodsley, & if she is not utterly averse to being four & twenty hours out of the sweet Smoke of St Jame's, I should be very glad to have the pleasure of her & your company for a week or a fortnight the next Time you come into Nottinghamshire at Thurgarton in that County, for I shall be quite Settled there, (please God my wife & I live!) next Summer.

Dear Sir I sent you last week by Thatcher's Barge all your Parcels, in which were included two Epping Cheeses which Mrs. Dodsley desires Mrs. Spence will be so good as to accept. I hope you have before now recd all the cargo safe . exct ye Gr H. I have this day sent the Pope's Works (which came from Mr Warburton ); down to Hungerford, to go by the same Conveyance. I am afraid my design on the Banks of the Thames will not proceed to Execution, the Landlord and I not having yet agreed. As the idle time of the Year is now come on, I have begun it with the most idle of all Productions, a Love Song: I intend it for Mr Tier's, to be sung at Vauxhall. Pray tell me whether it is good for ought or not. I wrote it, alas! not from any present feelings or sensations, but by recalling past Ideas to my Mind; and therefore it may possibly want that passionate Tenderness requisite to the Subject: however I think it so much too young for me at present that I shall not let Mr Tiers or any body else know that it is mine.

Thurgarton August the 26th. 1751. Dear Sr I recd about three days ago a letter from an unknown hand, which was directed & franked by you, containing several handsome & undeserved compliments on my Life of Socrates, & informing me too at the same time of a thing which I did not know before, that Mr Warburton had made a trifling & insolent reply to some of my notes in his new commentary on Mr Pope's Essay on Criticism P: 151. the same Person exhorts me to make a reply. I should take it therefore as a favour if you would send me down that Volume of the nine which contains his commentary, (for you must know it is a wipe inserted only in this very last copy of the whole Works & not in the detached piece published a year ago) & I will consider what is to be done. pray send it by the very first Nottingham Coach directed to be left for me at Mr Chappel's linen draper in that Town. you may rely upon it that I will neither blot or abuse the Book, but I promise you if any unforseen accident should happen I will take the whole Set. if you know who the Author of this anonymous letter is be so good to favour me with the knowledge of his name, by the return of the Post, directing your letters always to me at Thurgarton near Newark in Notts. if you should have a hurry of business & can't favour me with an answer yourself to this, pray let your Brother give me a Single line. I am, Sr, Your Sincere Friend & humble Served. John Gilbert Cooper I expected to see you this Summer with Mrs. Dodsley in Nottinghamshire

Leicester Jany the 19. Dear Sr. The Death of my poor dear Wife having drove me from the family Seat in Nottinghamshire which I newly fitted up & furnished last year, I shall advertise it to be let in the London Evening Papers next week. therefore should take it as a favour if you would permit me to refer the inquirers to you for farther Particulars than what can be inserted in an advertisement; which farther particulars I have herein enclosed for you to show any Body who comes to you about the Business. I received Julia but no Bill as I desired in my last , therefore desire you would let me know the first leisure hour you have what I am indebted to you & I will send you an order for the money. What success has my Pamphlet had? what of Warburton? my compts. to Mrs Dodsley. I am, Dear Sr your most humble Served. & well wisher J. G. Cooper Junr

Winchester Jan. 16. 1753. Sr. Instead of informing you that my Book is ready for you, as you might by this time reasonably expect, I can only tell you of the delays & disappointments I have met with. Last Month my Affairs were entirely at a stand for three weeks: My Composer was crippled with the Rheumatism, my Corrector taken ill of the Small pox, & my principal agent forced to fly from it. They are hard at work now, & promise me to finish with all possible expedition: every thing is printed off, but the Outworks, Contents, Index &c.; & I believe I may depend upon being ready to publish early next Month. I find my Expenses will rise higher than I imagined; & they tell me at Oxford that I cannot afford to sell under 12s. unbound; I suppose you will allow me 10s. I will order them to be sent according to your directions. I have lately received from Italy, An Account of the Protestants in the Valleys of Piedmont: it is drawn up in the form of a Letter by a Friend of mine at my request, as I knew he had peculiar opportunities & advantages in informing himself: and he gives me leave to publish it. The Subject is interesting & curious: & my Friend's Acct. will I think give satisfaction. It consists of 12 pages rather larger than this Paper, written very close in a very small hand; & I suppose will at least make a sixpenny Pamphlet. As he is still in the Country & has spoken his mind freely, he does not choose to put his Name to it: but it need be no secret that I am the Publisher. Let me know what you think of this design, & perhaps I may send it to you soon. I saw tother day in a Letter from Mr. Garrick, that Mr. Spence acknowledges himself to be the Author of ye. Gamester , a Dramatic piece now in rehearsal at Drury Lane. Pray explain this to me if you can. I left in your hands my receipt for Dr. Newton's Milton: pray send it to me hither, together with the New Volume, neatly bound. Believe me, Dear Sr. Your most faithful Humble Served. Robed. Lowth.

Winchester 1753. Sr. I have received Newton's Milton, & Sets of Mr. Warton's Virgil; but no letter, or any intimation for whom these Other are designed. I believe my Book will be sent to you & Mr. Millar the beginning of the week: I have ordered 200 to you, & 100 to him. I have forgot whether you did not order 200: if this should be a mistake, you can easily rectify it by writing to Mr. Clements at Oxford. I enclose a List of Persons to be Presented, with all necessary directions about it. You must order the Book Binder not to beat the Title, Inscription & 6 last Sheets: the rest will bear well. I leave the business of Advertising to You: R. Clements is the Bookseller concerned at Oxford. I send you likewise the Account of the Vaudois. As to the manner of Printing all I can say is, that I would have it done very neatly, & as correctly as possible. The Author, I suppose, will want some Copies for his Friends; I have not yet directions about it; but shall order immediately a Dozen to a Relation of his. I suppose you will allow us as many as he will want. I send you his Manuscript in which. by his desire I have corrected all inaccuracies of Expression that occur to me. You will observe that the line drawn sometimes at the bottom of the page is, not for Italicks , but to separate the references from the text. In page is a Reference in my hand, which. I have added for the Readers' satisfaction, and have marked for Italicks , as it is an addition. In the same page I have taken the liberty of striking out a Line, which. seems to me inconsistent, or false, or at least obscure: you may, if you please, insert in its place the following words: "who had as little compassion & generosity, as zeal for the Protestant cause," - but it will do very well without any supplement. Pray let me know what you propose to do in this business, & how my is like to go on & when we are to publish. I had pretty well made out Spence's secret before you told it me, how does the plot succeed? Believe me, Dear Sr. Your most faithful Humble Served. R. Lowth.

Winchester March. 15. . Dear Sr. I received by the last Post another letter from the Author of the Account , in which., he directs me to send some of them to his Friends; which. as I suppose it is already Published by this time, I must beg you to do immediately, as follows: To Mr. Hayward in Throgmorton Street 12, more One Copy to The Arch Bp. of Canterbury Bps. of Bristol Gloucester Durham Exeter Salisbury St. Asaph Rochester The Duke of Bolton Lt. George Cavendish Lt. Frederick Cavendish Lt. Grantham Lt. Pulteney Augustus Schutz Esqr. ( in Brook Street Sr. Wm. Young Baronet. These to be sent without any mention of the Author's name: but if any of them make any enquirys after him of you, you may tell them if you please from me, that it is Mr. Devisme Chaplain to Lt. Rochford at Turin. Send one if you please from me to the Bp. Norwich. To the same Mr. Hayward pray send two more of my Books bound directed likewise to Lt. Rochford at Turin as before, & in the same parcel put up Leland's Answer to Lt. Bolingbroke's Letters, & any other Answers to the same that are in ye. best esteem. My friend orders me 12 Copies of the Account ; I have no demand for them here: but if you will please to give half a dozen to Mr. Spence judiciously perhaps want more Copies yet; he does not know what number you will allow him, but is ready to pay for those yt. exceed it Page. 25. for Seal read Seat . I am, Dear Sr. Your most faithful humble Served. R. Lowth If Mr. Hayward should want any more of the pamphlets, pray let him have them, accounted to the Author. To Mr. Dodsley / in Pall Mall / London

column39: The Correspondence of Robert Dodsley 1733-1764. Ed. by James E. Tierney. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 1988.
column46: Pallmall Novr. 10th. 1753. Dear Sir I received and read with great pleasure your little poetical Packet, for which I think my self very much obliged to You, and shall wait with much impatience for your second. However, it will come time enough if it comes with in a month or five Weeks. I don't know how I came to think your next Town was Stratford, unless it was because I used to direct to Lady Luxborough so, and I thought the Leasows and Barrels had been very near each other. I like extremely what you have sent, but if you think proper I will show them either to Sir George, or Mr. Wm. Lyttelton. Most of those which compose the three first Volumes, were shown to Sir George before they were inserted. I am much obliged to You for your readiness to contribute on this occasion, & shall endeavour all I can that ye Fourth Volume may not disgrace the three former. I am going to publish a Poem on English Agriculture, & in a Week or ten days will beg your acceptance of one, which I will direct for You to be left with Mr Baskerville at Birmingham, as I don't know how other ways to convey it to You. I am Sir Your most obliged humble Served. R Dodsley To Wm. Shenstone Esqr. / to be left at the Post Office / in Birmingham / Warwickshire

Pallmall Jan 12 Dear Sir I have recd two more Paquets from You for which I am very much obliged to You; but I think there is very little of your own in either of them, so that I am in hopes of another Paquet from you, especially as I have not yet received the corrected Copy of the Pastoral Ballad you mentioned. I believe I shall not print the Volume this Winter, as it will be a Season in which scarce any thing will be thought of except Elections. I sent a month or six Weeks ago to Mr Baskerville one of my Poem on Agriculture, together with one directed to You which I hope you have received, though I am afraid you will not be much entertained with it. I have been laid up with the Gout these 5 Weeks, or you would have heard from me sooner. Wishing you all the Compliments of the season I remain Dr Sir Your most obliged & obedt. Served. R Dodsley To Wm. Shenstone Esqr. / at the Leasows near Birmingham

Thurgarton Sepr. the 21st. 1754 Dear Sr. I have now finished my letters concerning Taste , & have transcribed a great part of 'em for the press. they will all make up a volume as large as my Life of Socrates printed in the same letter upon the same paper. as I propose to lay out some money in books at Docr. Mead's Sale, I shall expect five & twenty Guineas & the Ruins of Palmyra for the copy. if this suits you let me have a line by the return of the Post, & I will send up what papers are transcribe'd for your examination by the next Stage Coach; which if approved of, you may put into the press immediately, & I will send you afterwards a design for a little Title Page Frontispiece I don't propose to put my name to the first edition therefore enjoin you Secrecy. - as I know you are so fond of accuracy, I have taken uncommon Pains & have polished these trifles as much as I was able. my best compts to Mrs Dodsley. I was extremely sorry I was so unfortunate not to see you when you was in Nottinghamshire, which was occasioned by an engagement I was under to go to the Duke of Rutlands the very week you was at Mansfield, however I staid at my Bror wett's four days longer than I intended on purpose to see you. I am, Dear Sr, Your sincere Friend &c J:G:Cooper Junr. direct to me at Thurgarton near Nottingham.

Leicester October the 7th 1754 Dear Sr I recd. the favour of your letter dated October the 1st, and am very ready to comply with your request to print 750 copies of the first Edition, nor do I desire any gratuity at all for the second Edition, except it be the ruins of Palmyra, & that too only provided it runs briskly off; nay more, I will very readily relinquish any part of what you propose for the first if the sale should not be successful, or the whole, rather than you should be one shilling out of pocket, for I would sooner give up the harmless Vanity of saying hereafter to my Child, "this shelf of Books was my own acquisition", than have the mortifying reflection that it was at the expense of another Man, especially of one too whom I have some reason to regard. - I shall return again to Thurgarton tomorrow whither I shd be glad if you could send this week a sketch of the copper plate in a letter, that I may correct it if there is any thing therein that does not answer my expectations. I have sent my Papers this day by my Sister Gardiner, who will reach my Father's house in Hertfordshire next Thursday, & will forward 'em to you the day after. they are sealed up in a brown Paper with my arms upon it. as soon as the first Sheet is printed off, send it down in a Frank, which I will correct & send back by the return of the Post; & so continue to do sheet after sheet till I can come up to Town, which will be the 12th of November. - I was necessitated by the nature of my Subject to take the little essay on the polite Arts , which I wrote in the Museum, as you will observe. all your Friends are well at Mansfield & desire to be remembered to you. Nelly Wright will send your Testament by me. my compts. to Mrs Dodsley. I am, Sr, your Sincere Friend & humble Servant J G Cooper Junr. direct to me at Thurgarton. don't let the Print be less than that the Life of Socrates was published in, in short I would have as many Pages as there is in the Manuscript if possible, or at least very near.

Thurgarton Monday October the 14th. 1754 Sr. I hope you received my Papers safe the latter end of last week which if you did I expect to receive the first sheet from the Press next Saturday at the farthest, together with the design delineated, for as the Parliament meets the 14th of next Month there is no time to be lost. I am very sorry Mrs Dodsley is obliged to go to Bath on account of her health, but if they stay any time there I shall have the pleasure of seeing 'em proposing to be there myself the latter end of next Month. direct to me for the future at Nottingham, or at Thurgarton near Nottingham, & not near Newark, for the former is the Post town I always send to. I am, Sr., Your most humble Served. J G Cooper. Junr. I have enclosed four franks and will send more when wanted.

Claverton near Bath 26 October. 1754. Sr. As I have the highest opinion of Mr Shenstone's judgment, I should have no reason to doubt that those little pieces of mine, which he has thought proper to transmit to you, deserved a place in your collection - If I could be certain that he was entirely unbiased by his regard for the Author - They are now however in the hands of a gentleman, whose judgment, I am convinced, is not inferior, & who is under the strictest Obligations to Sincerity - Please therefore to use your discretion Sr with regard to the insertion or omission of any or all of them - & to fix my name, if you think proper, to "The Cabinet" though it is a name so little known out of the University (& by this time almost forgotten there) that, I am sure, it will rather borrow from, than add any lustre to ire Miscellany - The Cabinet, (or Verses on Roman Medals) is a subject that will please the Virtuosi - & though nobly treated by the greatest of our modern Poets - yet your Epicures (such are men of Taste) love the same Dish cooked different ways -& I have descended to some minutenesses which will please a true Medallist - better evan than Pope's - especially as he has mixed some Satirical Raillery in his Poem - As to the Fable of the Pepper-box & Salt-Seller - though Mr Shenstone was so highly pleased with it, as to induce me to inscribe it to him - & to tack some Lines to the End for that purpose - yet he now thinks it rather too ludicrous for ire Collection & more proper to be joined with some Collection of Tales to insert it in ire Miscellany - his Name & The moral at the End - after "And to the Sideboard still confined" should by all means be omitted - The Panacea, or Verses on Fishing, may help to make a Variety through ye uncommonness of ye Subject - And the Doctrine I seriously think of importance - as I am convinced most of our Maladies owing to Plethoras & what is called Living Well - The Heroines occasioned by the Publication of Con. Philips's Mrs Pilkington's & Lady V-ne's infamous adventures in Per. Pickle - have been applauded by my Acquaintance - & if you don't think the Subject too particular, I believe they are the best of my Contribution - The Stanzas on Parting , are favourites of Mr Shenstone's, - but I'm afraid are rather too Tender for the Public Ear - otherwise I should be glad to have them inserted - For you must know Sr. that I left a Fellowship of All-Souls Coll. for a handsome Wife - & should take some pleasure in letting my Friends see that I was not disappointed in my expectation of happiness - The adding "Written some years after marriage" - will disinguish them from a common Love-Song - But I submit this & every thing that I send you to your Judgment - & am Sr ire humb Sert. Ric: Greaves. P.S. Mr Shenstone has promised to send his Pastoral Ballad by the Way of Bath - but I am surprised at his Delay - If it comes into my hands I will forward it to you the next Post -

Pall Mall Octr 29 Dear Sir I do not wonder at the perpetual Interruption which You complain of; the Possessors of such Beauties as you enjoy, must expect to pay some tax for their Pleasures. And how happy are You, that the very tax it self is frequently an additional Pleasure! I am very much obliged to You for the trouble you have taken, & will punctually follow your directions. I shall be glad now to have your Pastoral Ballad & whatever else You may think proper to send as soon as possible. May I not prefix to Lady Luxborrough's Lines the Words - Written by a Lady ? I recd. Mr. Groove's Pieces by Yesterday's Post. I am sorry I was so circumstanced that I could not possibly pay my respects to Sir George Lyttelton. I am Dear Sir Your most obliged &c R Dodsley To Wm. Shenstone Esqr / at the Leasows near Birmingham

Saturday night. Dear Sir I received your final Packet, and am much obliged to you, for all the trouble you have so kindly taken on this occasion. I have spent this whole day amongst your Papers & those of your friends, & have put them as nearly in the order you desire as I can. I hope to send you proofed sheets of the whole of them before next week is out, which I beg you will correct & send back by the return of the Post. I have impertinently attempted to alter one Stanza of Lady Luxborough's, which pray restore to it's original reading if you like it better. The Ballad in ye scottish Taste I have omitted. And one of the Songs which you would have kept out (ye Lady's Visit) I have put in. But you will order that as you please. Nancy of ye Vale you never sent. I am Dear Sir Your most obedt. Served. R Dodsley To William Shenstone Esq. / at the Leasows near / Birmingham

column46: Pall mall Janry 18th. 1755 Dear Sir I recd your Specimen of an Essay on the Genius of Pope. I dare say you will contrive in your Animadversions to allow him all his due praise; and where you differ from him will do it in such a manner as to render it no impropriety in me to be the Publisher of it. I like your specimen of Paper & Print, & think you should work off 750. But this I leave you to determine. An air of Dogmaticalness I know you will in general avoid, yet in ye beginning of ye 2d paragraph is there not a little the appearance of it? Might it not run thus? - "It is somewhat strange, that in the Pastorals of a young Poet there should not appear a single rural image that is new: yet this I am afraid is ye case &c.". My 4th. Volume will come out the beginning of February. I was in hopes of seeing you in Town before now, when will you come? I think you are right in concealing your self as the Author; and you may be assured I will not divulge it. I will write to your brother to night. I hope Mrs. Warton is well. I endeavour to be as well as I can, and therefore will not attempt to say any thing on my loss. I am ever Affectionately Yours R. Dodsley PS I have drawn a line you see under ye words I would have you change. You will laugh at me perhaps for changing something for somewhat , but don't you think there is some difference? In ye 3d Page should not explode precede extirpate ? Do complaints of immoderate heat totally lose their consistency in a British Shepherd, in ye midst of Sum~er?

column39: The Correspondence of Robert Dodsley 1733-1764. Ed. by James E. Tierney. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 1988.
column46: Pall mall Febry. 15th. 1755 Dear Sir I am afraid You have thought me long in giving my thanks for all your kindness, and for all the trouble you have taken on my account. I am in some pain for those different readings which You left so imprudently to my determination: but I have done as well as I could, & have generally thought it the best way to follow where you seemed to point. The concluding Stanza in Mr. Whistler's Poem I wish You may like. Pray direct me how I must send you the Volume. I hope to be able to send it in about a week. The Three Vols are at present out of print, but I think they will be ready in about a Month, when I purpose to send you a complete Set. Would Lady L- think it impertinent if I sent her a Set? Pray give me your opinion. I purpose also a Set for Mr. Graves, and Mr. Hylton, but know not how I can send them. Mr. Jago is in Town & has told me how to send his. I am in a perpetual hurry & scarce know what I write. I am ever most faithfully & truly Yours R Dodsley I send Lady L's Letter enclosed; from which I think it plain she had no objection to my saying - By a Lady of Quality .

The Leasows, March 4:th. 1755. Dear Sir, I return you many thanks for the Compliment you make my Friends & Me in the offer of a set of miscellanies x I dare say Ldy. Luxborough will take it well to be included in it. My Expectation of seeing the last volume advertised, was the reason I have not made you this acknowledgment before. The Delay has given me some Pain; not through the least Impatience of seeing my Trifles made public; for I am really fearful of the appearance, & could wish a longer time to adjust the state of my contributions. But this very Wish makes me reflect upon the time that has elapsed since I wrote to you; & of which, I trust, I could have availed myself to your satisfaction & my own. I suppose that the Impression must now be taken off; if otherwise, & that for any particular Reason you have chosen it should be deferd I should be glad that you would afford me ye earliest Intelligence. I am ever faithfully & affectionately yours Will: Shenstone My Lord Dudley will accept my respectful Compliments & pardon my Freedom in requesting yt he would frank me these few Covers. We are told here yt my Lt. has lately taken a House in Town, which seems to t

Newport Pagnel Thursday night March ye 20 1755 Dear Sr. I recd. the favour of your letter this day at Northampton, & am got to this place with my Children in my way to London. Surely you'll be able to sell the small number you mention in two or three days. therefore entreat you not to balk the sale but to keep the types still standing (as it is a small thing) that we may strike off a second impression without loss of time, in case there should be a demand, as I make no question but there will be. have courage, advertise well, you shall have all profits, & I will indemnify you by standing to all loss if there should be any. if the Printer has taken down the types & you find there is a quick demand on Friday, I beg you would make him fall to work to compose afresh that night, make him work all Saturday & have a second impression ready for sale early on Monday morning. I shall be with you on Saturday night. do all you can, for you know I dote upon the words Second Edition in a News Paper. adieu. yours in haste Most Sincerely & affetely J G Cooper Junr.

The Leasows, March the 23d 1755. Dear Sir I had the Pleasure of receiving the fourth volume of your miscellanies, which arrived as I remember last thursday was seven-night. I am obliged to you for the care you took to forward it, when printed, as well as for all that Trouble I occasioned you, before . Some Improvements may be made in a subsequent Impression; & whenever this is proposed I dare say you will give me notice. In general, you have done all that I could expect from a Person of Genius and a Friend. It remains for me to wish that the Book may fully recompense you, I will not only say, for the Pains you have taken, but for the Discernment you have shown. It contains many excellent pieces, that are entirely new to me: & if others that are no less excellent have been printed before, it cannot reasonably be objected by such as consider your first Design. Is it impertinent to ask the Names of those Persons who have not inserted them? If so, I drop my enquiry. The Pages, where their lines occur, are, 73. 114. 119. 170. 200. 202. 227. 228. 233. 250. 253. 265. 267. 305. 307. Should the parliament sit till June, I have some thoughts of printing my ode upon Rural elegance; together with some such other Pieces as may make a 12 penny pamphlet. - But if my Purpose continues you will hear from me again soon, & I shall send you up a copy, about half-correct, for your Opinion. I hope Mr. Baskerville meets in London with the encouragement he deserves. I long to hear from you upon all accounts, am, your most affectionate & most obedient Servant Will. Shenstone

column39: The Correspondence of Robert Dodsley 1733-1764. Ed. by James E. Tierney. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 1988.
column46: Pall mall March 25th. 1755 Dear Sir It is with pleasure I inform You that your Poems in my 4th Volume are very much approved of by several people, particularly by Dr. Akinside, who, desired that I would give you his Complimts and thanks for the pleasure you had given him in reading them. I shall be very glad to hear how you like the rest of the Volume: it is here in general well approved of. I sent you by ye Carrier last week carriage paid, four sets, one of which. I beg You will accept for your self, one for Lady Luxborough, one for Mr. Greaves, & one for Mr. Hylton. I hope the sending them will not give You much trouble, as I am ashamed, and ought to apologize for what I have already given, instead of adding to it. A set for Mr Jago I have sent by his direction to a relation of his in town, who will forward it to him. And if you have any other friends that you would choose to make presents to, I beg you will without the least scrupple send me your com~ands. I am very glad to find that my favourite, the Pastoral Ballad, is universally admired. I wish I had had the Lass of the Vale, whom you once mentioned; I dare say she is a beautiful and accomplished, though rural, Girl; and I therefore wonder how you can be so cruel to lock her up from the World. But I will take care to get it insinuated to her that I intend to fit up another Apartment, where I hope she will prevail with you to permit her with some of her companions to pay me a visit. I am Dear Sir Your most obliged & obedt. Served. R Dodsley To William Shenstone Esqr / at the Leasows near Birmingham

Pall mall Augst. 28th. Dear Sir It is a common saying, that Home is home, be it ever so homely . The Morality of the Maxim I will not dispute; but after having experienced so much Ease and Politeness, after having been so agreeably entertained, and in so elegant a Place as the Leasows, I cannot help thinking and saying to my self, Home is but homely at best . This small alteration in the Axiom with regard to Tully's Head, I hope however you will try to disprove next Winter upon the spot: and indeed your Company here will go as far towards it as possible. As an inducement to which, in lieu of the shining falls of your translucent Cascades, Pallmall shall roll over its Pavement a string of gilt Coaches and Chariots, in brilliant succession. In lieu of your Larks and your Nightingales, our tuneful Savoyards, from their musical Coffee-mills, shall grind you as much Melody as your heart can desire. Then as to your Nymphs and your Naiads, your Dryads and your Hamadriades, are they more fair, more kind, or more com~on than those which shine with us in every Street, making Night beauteous? Besides, those Ladies of yours in the Winter creep into their Oaks, or shrink down to the bottom of their Lakes, and you can have no enjoyment of them: (which by the bye is doubtless the cause of your low spirits at that time) whereas ours, in the midst of frost and snow, shine bright as the stars of Heaven; and are always obligingly ready to entertain you, even in the coldest season, with a very warm reception. And is not this a comfortable Consideration? Much more might be urged in favour of this precious Town; but I hope what hath been said will have sufficient weight, with a well-dispos'd mind, to induce You to undertake the Journey. If not, I will change the manner of my attack next time, and bring down upon you such a force of Artillery as shall soon compel you to capitulate, if not to surrender at Discretion. In my return to London I called at Barrels, and dined with Lady Luxborough. Her Place is very pretty, and She received me with great Condescension: but She complains of your Laziness in returning her Visit, says You have not been there this Twelvemonth, and I think seems a little angry upon that account. I could have told Her, by way of softening matters, that You had treated with more neglect a much greater Personage than her Ladyship; but as you was not there to answer for your self, I kept silence even from ill words. The Person I mean is no less than the Goddess of Fame; who, I heard you say (indeed you did not name the Lady) had waited at your door five Years in expectation of certain Elegies which you had promised her: and methinks I see her at this instant standing on tiptoe on the top of your Cupola, waiting with great impatience to snatch and bear them to Tully's Head, from whence she intends to distribute them to ye admiring World. I send you enclosed the Parody on Dryden's Ode, in which there is a deficiency that I hope you will try to fill up. I have sent also Swift's musical Burlesque, and the World. I hope it will not be long before you give me an opportunity of sending one of your own. I had this day the pleasure of Mr Hylton's company, and of drinking your health. He talks of staying in Town about a fortnight, and I hope to see him often. I am much obliged to Mrs. Mary, and beg my compliments to her; but I think you are not at all so, for her wishing you a humdrum Companion who have nothing upon earth to recommend me but the sincerity and truth with which I am Dear Sir Your most obliged and obedient Servant R. Dodsley

column46: Pall mall Febry. 9th. 1756 Dear Sir And must I then give up all hopes of printing your Elegies this Winter? Does the cruel and voracious Monster Mr. Pixel told me of devour your whole time, and eat up all your thoughts? Would to God you were writing an Elegy on the Death of your Law-suit! That would be, as some Author has it in the Title page of his Play , a lamentable Tragedy mixed full of pleasant Mirth. Upon my word, Sir, if You do not bring me up these mourning Muses, nothing elegant will come from Tully's Head this season, I shall loose the Fame of being the Muse's Midwife, & my hand for want of practice will forget its obstetric faculties. Consider too, if these Ladies, from that antiquated sterile Precept of Horace, should get a trick of going pregnant nine years instead of nine months, who the devil will be able to get a livelihood by being employed as their Mid wife? Besides, Sir, you exchange the Pleasure of begetting nine children, which might easily be done in that time, for ye plague of nursing one little Embryo: and will the Ladies, think you, have any objection to nine times the pleasure which that old fellow Horace would allow them? No, no; I shall have them all on my side to a Girl! They are doubtless for a quick Conception, and an easy Delivery; and so am I. In the Name of all the Muses then, and if You value your Reputation as a Man amongst them, I beg you will make no longer delay. If You do, take notice - I will sit down in Vengeance, and write an Elegy on the Barrenness of your Muse, on the decay of your own Abilities, or on some other scandalous Subject, that shall blast your Character as an able Poet for ever. But in hopes you will think seriously on these things, I will at present suspend my Wrath, and subscribe my self. Dear Sir sincerely and affectionately Yours R Dodsley P.S. I beg my Compliments to Mr. Hylton and all Friends. I had the pleasure of enquiring after your Health the other day of my Lord Stamford, but not the satisfaction of hearing that you intend to Visit to London this Winter: however, after the dreadful Denunciations above, I hope You will tremble and obey.

column39: The Correspondence of Robert Dodsley 1733-1764. Ed. by James E. Tierney. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 1988.
column46: June 28th. 1756 Dear Sir I hope, and it is a hope which gives me great pleasure, that I shall be with You about the 14th. or 15th. of July, as I set out for Oxford on the 9th or 10th. where I shall stay two or three days. I long to see the new Edition of your Place, which, from what You say, will I suppose by that time be completed: but, were it not that I can despair of nothing, from your Taste in Rural Elegance , I should think it impossible that you will be able to make any addition to its last year's Beauties. Your politeness in saying that I shall contribute any way to your Enjoyment of these Delights, I am afraid I shall prove to be merely a Compliment, as I bring in my hand, according to your request, an unfortunate melancholy creature, whom you will find so perverse in her Disposition, that she will take pleasure in nothing so much as in causing your tears. However, You shall have as little of her Company as you please, and if we find her in the least disagreeable, we'll lock her up, and banish her from our walks. I hope indeed to be much better entertained with the tender Conversation of certain Ladies of your acquaintance, to whom I flatter my self I shall once more have the pleasure of being introduced. But take care of me, for though I am a grave man, and from my age may perhaps be unsuspected, yet I feel such sparks of Passion lurking in my breast, from the remembrance of their beauties, that I shall certainly be tempted to run away with some of them. I beg my Compliments to Mr. Hylton, whom I shall be very glad to see; and though I think him at present most virtuously inclined shall hope so far to inveigle him, as to engage his assistance in all my attempts, whether of Rapes or Robberies. I am Dear Sir most sincerely Yours R Dodsley

Pall mall Augst. 28th. Dear Sir As you know how difficult it is to prevail with. ones self to sit down to write, I hope You will pardon my long silence, and not believe me at all the less sensible of those pleasures I received at the Leasows, for this delay in acknowledging them. Cleone also makes her Compliments, thanks you for the Improvements she received under your correction, seems to hold up her head mightily upon some little Commendations which You were pleased to flatter her with, and is vain and silly enough, poor creature, to fancy you might possibly be in earnest. I had the pleasure of meeting with Mr Graves, am much obliged to You for his acquaintance, & was very sorry I could have no more time with him. However, he very obligingly made the most of what we had, read over the Piece, & pointed out to me several little Inaccuracies, which I doubt not will turn to my advantage. I have made many Alterations since I came home, and some considerable ones. Have You thought of an Epilogue? I could wish, if You are so kind, that I might be favoured as soon as is convenient. I have enclosed the other three parts of your Pastoral, set by Mr Earn, and he says, as well set as any thing he has done. He desires his Compliments. I wish I knew in what You are just now employed. Are You busy with your Architects in the Wing of your House? Or wandering in little Tempe projecting new beauties? Are You teaching honest Thomas how to bend your Stream in the most natural meanders? Or are You listening with a deep regard to his more sage directions? I expect to hear, when he finishes his mortal course, that he is transformed into a River God, and hath taken up his station, reclined upon an Urn, at the top of Your great Cascade; or rather perhaps on that beautiful spot where your River breaks out in the before mentioned Vale. After all, methinks I do not heartily wish to find you employed in any of these ways; but rather (provided the Epilogue be finished) in correcting & marshaling Your Elegies, or in designing Your Ornaments for them. Not in contriving beauties that may detain you at home, but in projecting such as may invite You up to Town: where I will flatter my self with a sure and certain hope that I shall not fail to have the pleasure of seeing You this Winter. I am Dear Sir affectionately Yours R. Dodsley

Dear Sr I am obliged to Mr Shenstone for many opportunities of Enjoyment but for none more than what he has lately furnished me with - by favouring me with a Visit pray. I am only afraid, that the Credit of my acquaintance with men of his Genius will gain me a Character for Criticism & Learning which, I am conscious, I cannot support - As he knew our Interview would be very Short, he desired me to be acquainted at first Sight - which however I found a superfluous Request with regard to a person of your benevolent ingenuous appearance - The Consequence I believe, was, That I appeared to you in the same Dishabille of Conversation - in which Mr Shenstone always indulges me - I am sure at least I took the same freedom with your Play - that I do with his works - which I cannot expect to know without some Confusion - since I find by Mr Warton (whose Part in a 4. day Excursion to the Helicon Camp) what great hands it has before passed through - However Sr. you will easily see what a small value I lay upon my Hesitations - As to the Epilogue, I am ashamed that I did not write to him so soon as I ought to have done - But if he has done anything I dare say, it is superior to any Hints I could have given him - All I could observe upon the Occasion, was. That the Epilogues wh have been popular , were those that were formed upon a Satirical Contrast between the Romantic Behaviour of some of the chief Characters in your Play - and the degenerate Behaviour of ye moderns - at least this trite method was what occurred to me - & I hinted to him something of this kind in regard to Cleone's conduct. But as I know him very dilatory - & also suspect it is a way of writing which he has not been used to - I have scribbled a few flippant Lines to this same purpose - which may serve as a plan for some better hand to improve upon. Though I have observed that such vulgar Jokes go down better upon such occasions than those things which require more deep attention - We shall never come to London without returning ire Visit in Pall mall Mrs Graves is quite vexed with me for not bringing her acquainted with Cleone. She has a Turn for affecting Tales - & I think an incomparable Natural Taste I hope to read it to her after it has been upon the Stage - She joins me in best Respects - I am Sr ire obit hum Sert Ric Graves P.S. The Reason this has not passed throe Mr Shenstone's hands is because I would not forestall any thing he may have for the Anvil - R G To / Mr Dodsley / at his house in Pall-mall / A single sheet London

Lapel House 16th: Sepr: 1756 Dear Sir, How I shall be able to answer your obliging Letter, or at your request to obviate all Mr. Shenstone's ifs that may retard our journey to London, I cannot foresee; when my Ideas will scarce serve to furnish out the One, or my power be of Force enough to complete the latter: however I have too much Interest at Heart to refuse my Services where it may possibly be attended with so much pleasure to myself. Much I hope; but More I fear that I shall not be able to shut Mr. Shenstone up with myself in a post Chaize; if I should be so happy, depend upon it that none of the generation of Nimshs shall excel us in driving. The Reason why I did not write sooner was upon Account of the Books. The 21st. of last Month Lord Dudley received his set of Poems & Mr: Wilmott's also from Mr. Male's - All the enquiries that I can make will give me no light concerning mine: Mr. Male's people declare they never received any parcel directed for me; and his Nephew who would be the most likely to know how Lt: Dudley's parcel came, is now out upon a journey, so that I cannot find out the Carrier. - Ire: people probably may remember who they were sent by, so that you may be at no Loss concerning them. If the Parcel should still be at the Inn; I should be glad if you could add to it 2 or 3 Quires of the same paper your letter is wrote upon, & of which I have enclosed a little Bit - otherwise you may send it any time hereafter, directed for me here, to be left at Mr: Male's Ironmonger near the New Church Birmingham. Mr: Shenstone received a Letter from Mr: Graves, wherein he speaks of the great pleasure your Visit gave him; I hope your whole Tour was agreeable to yourself, and that Cleone has not any reason to repent she left London in Company with Mr: Dodsley if wishes could avail, you would easily command the best of mine, or my Pen either, could it serve you as well as Mr: Shenstones. alas! I dare not tell you how idle he is - He's ordered me when I wrote to avoid all mention how he was, or had been employed. I hope Cleone will not suffer for it - There has been & is continually parties of company at the Leasows, the attending upon many of them, may in some measure excuse Mr: Shenstone's indolence; when Winter approaches I shall open my Entrenchments and endeavour to take him either by Sap or Storm : However I succeed be assured that I am at all times Dr: Sir Ire: most Obliged Hble Servant John Scott Hylton Please to make my Compliments to your Brother. To / Mr: Dodsley

column46: Sept. 28th. 1756 Madam About a fortnight ago Dr Mounsey acquainted me with the honour your Grace did me in desiring to see my attempt at a Tragedy. I had then no Copy but what was so blotted as to render it scarce legible; and being too well acquainted with its many natural Weaknesses and Imperfections, I was not willing to add to its faults by suffering it to appear before your Grace in so unadvantageous and disrespectful a Dishabille. I transcribed it therefore, and You may now read it with somewhat more ease, but whether with any satisfaction, I am very doubtful. I wish I could flatter my self that it hath merit enough to prevent your Grace from repenting your Curiosity: but indeed I lay it before You with real diffidence: should it however be so fortunate as in the least to engage your attention, I shall look upon it as a happy Omen of its future Success. I am &c When your Grace hath perused it, You will be pleased to return it, as I have no other perfect Copy.

Claverton, 30 Sept 1756 Dear Sr I received both ire kind Letters in due time - The former of which (though I forget a particular acknowledgment) gave occasion to my own Attempt at an Epilogue - as I was apprehensive of Mr Shenstone's dilatory temper & as I knew that kind of ludicrous Performance was as much beneath the Dignity of a Tragic Writer - as it would be for Rubens or Guido to locker a Frame - for one of their Sublimest History-Pieces - As you only object to the Conclusion of my Epilogue, I am inclined to believe that it has some degree of Merit - but hope however you will be furnished with a better by some of your Friends - & beg that mine may be considered, as a mere Nothing - What induced me to conclude it, as I have done - was the Consideration of the Effrontery of the present Age - in keeping Mistresses upon Principle - which made the last Line appear emphatical enough to me - But upon reviewing it - I find it, as you observe, a very abrupt Conclusion - I have been very much engaged this last week with Company which our Race on Claverton Down has brought us - or I should have answered yrs sooner. I have now but just sketched out 2 or 3 additional Couplets - which I must leave you to complete - I don't know whether I am not too rude to the Fair Sex - But by all accounts (& even by what I see at Bath) the Ladies in high life preserve appearances less in this Age - than they were ever known to do - & deserve some pretty bold Rebukes from the Stage (which they still frequent) - though they will not give us an opportunity of showing them their transgressions frm ye Pulpit - I write this Post to Mr Shenstone from whom I have not heard since I saw you - I am with Mrs Graves's Complts Sr. Ire affect. humb Sert Ric: Graves I hope to get some Franks wn. our Season comes in - To Mr. Dodsley / at his house in Pall Mall / London

Thursday Sir I am told, that You have complained of my giving Orders to the Doorkeepers to refuse You admittance into our Theatre - Since I have been Manager, Every Author, from ye highest to ye lowest, who has wrote for our Stage, has had, & Shall have, the Liberty of the house - It is their Right & not to be taken away at ye Caprice of a Manager; therefore You may Enjoy it freely without being obliged to Me; a Circumstance which. will give You no little pleasure, as You have lately boasted with. some warmth that you never was obliged to Me - But why would You make ire. Complaints & spread a false report, till You had been convinced of ye Truth of ire. Suspicion? Because an Old Office Keeper at ye Boxes (where you seldom go) was ignorant Enough not to know Mr. Dodsley as an Author, Mr. Garrick the Manager is immediately to be taxed with. low, impotent Revenge - were You denied admittance into ye Pit, ire. usual place ? or Behind the Scenes, which. indeed is a Matter of Favour? - no - had You suspected that particular orders had been given by Me about You, why did you not write to ye Managers to know the Reason of those orders ? had you done this, the Mistake had been cleared, & You had not been guilty of so much Injustice to Me. I must desire You to retract the wrong You have done Me in censuring Me too hastily, & I must assure You when any ill usage calls forth my resentments, I take care never to let 'Em carry me into Mean~ess or Injustice - I am Sr. Yrs. D. Garrick

Octr. 18th. Sir When I was refused admittance into your Theater, by a Box keeper who declared he knew me, but that my Name was not in the list of those who had the freedom of ye House; and when I desired Mr Verney who was with me to assure him that I was free and Mr Verney refused to give him that assurance; what had I to suppose but that You had given orders I should not be admitted? In this supposition I met two of your friends, to whom I mentioned what had happened and my suspicion that you was concerned in it on purpose that it might come to your ear, and give You an opportunity of setting me right if I was mistaken. A day or two afterwards I mentioned it to another of your friends, for the same purpose, and to no one else have I opened my lips about it: and when I received an assurance from you by this last Gentleman, that you had given no orders of that kind; my answer was, that I could easily believe you had not, and that your denial of it entirely convinced me the fault was only in ye Door-keepers. Here I thought an end had been put to this trifling affair: but it seems this straw was to be caught at, in order to give You an opportunity of showing the continuance of your unaccountable resentment. But I pass over in silence ye harsh and indelicate Expressions in your present and former Letter. I cannot yet bring my self to return them; but have still endeavoured to remember though you forget, we once were friends. And if ever I should be obliged to appeal to the Public on the treatment I have received, be assured, though I may be as you insinuate, the lowest Author of the Stage, you shall have nothing to fear either from my Meanness or Injustice ; as I trust I shall always preserve my Character as clear from such imputations, as that of Mr Garrick. I am &c

Pallmall Dec 13th. Dear Sir I am much obliged to the accident, whatever it was, that furnished the Mystery of the Blank Cover, as it has produced me, saving the too friendly partiality of it, a very agreeable letter. Nor shall I easily be persuaded that the said blank cover, as You are pleased to call it, was not a very extraordinary Performance; more faultless, and less to be condemned than any thing I ever put out of my hands. I cannot take it kindly therefore, that you should endeavour to depreciate my Talents, by pretending that ye very Work I least accused my self for, has nothing at all in it. I beg You will answer me seriously. If there was nothing in it, how could you possibly bring so much Wit & Humour out of it? Should a Highwayman rob You of a thousand Guineas, count them out before you, and then pretend he found your pockets quite empty; would you not think him a very audacious Rogue, and immediately ask him how he came by the money? I would not be understood to insinuate here, that You have no Wit and Humour but what you stole out of my blank Cover; that might be carrying matters too far: Your Poets I have heard, are in some Language or other emphatically styled Makers , and so you may pretend perhaps that you make Wit and Humour, as God made the World, out of Nothing. This may be so for ought I know; appearances are indeed against me: but I am a strict Reasoner, and having learnt it as a Maxim in Philosophy, that Nothing can give that which it hath not its self, I cannot but conclude that ye aforesaid Cover was amply replenished with Wit and Humour. Now as ye said Wit and Humour was entirely my own, was all I ever pretended to, and my whole stock, to endeavour to sink it upon me, & pretend there was nothing under this extraordinary Cover, is very cruel; and in You a mere wanton Cruelty, as it plainly appears You have enough of your own. "It not enriches You (as Shakspear says) "And makes me poor indeed." But I have played this Battery methinks till my feeble fire begins to fail. Let me try from another quarter. I cannot help admiring the ingenuity of your paradoxical Compliments; they are certainly true Wit, which has been said to consist in bringing things together which have seemingly no resemblance: but should an arch and judicious Critic happen to change your civil and yet into a severe and therefore , what would become of all your Paradoxes and Compliments? I fear they must all vanish, like false appearances of old at the touch of Ithuriel's Spear; and, to my great mortification, nothing but plain reasoning and naked Truth would remain in their stead. But enough of this - Your Letter found me confined with the Gout, & to this I hope You will attribute my idleheadedness in scribbling so much stuff. I must now be more serious, as I find I am not to expect the favour of seeing you in London this Winter. This really gives me great chagrin, as I had promised my self much pleasure in your company. I hope however you will send up your Elegies by Mr Hylton, as I shall have a convenient opportunity by him of returning You the money for them. As to correcting ye press, the proof sheets may be sent You down by the post. Be so good also as to send me the Ode on Rural Elegance, and what other pieces you think of favouring me with for the Miscellany, as I shall put to press early in the spring, and yours must be the very first things I begin with. Dr. Akenside also forbears to give me any thing to begin the 6th. Vol till he sees how You begin the 5th. You may perceive by this how much depends upon your kindness, and upon the speediness of it. As to my Tragedy, Mr. Garrick has absolutely refused it, and therefore any alterations or improvements I may have made since You saw it, are I suppose to very little purpose. However, I still continue to file and polish now and then, and have made also some small alterations in the conduct. I have strengthened Glanville's Motives to his Villainy, and made him not proceed so far in his attempt upon Cleone. I have altered the scene in the 3d Act which You objected to, where her murder was attempted; and believe I may have added here & there some touches to the pathetic. I shall be much obliged to You for Mr. Graves's Epilogue with your Improvements. I have had the pleasure of seeing your friend & Neighbour Mr. Perry two or three times, who intimated to me your intended favour of a Chine and Turkey. He has somewhat to communicate to You in which I shall be very glad if I can be serviceable to him. I write this whole letter in a hurry in hopes that you may favour me with an answer to the most material parts of it when you write concerning him. I beg my compliments to Mr Hylton, the hopes of seeing him soon gives me much pleasure. I intend to direct a Hamper with a Barrel of Oysters and some Porter for the Leasows against Christmas. I am ever Dear Sir Affectionately Yours. R. Dodsley

Claverton Jan-7-1757- Dear Sr Though it is a great pleasure to me to hear from you some times yet I am sorry you should consider yrself as under any obligation of ceremony - to answer every Letter which I may have occasion to trouble you with - I know you are generally much better employed - As to Mr Shenstone's delay in sending you an improved Copy of the Epilogue - I must take part of the Blame upon myself - I received his Alterations as long since, as the 21st of Decembr. and to my Shame, I own, have not returned my hyper-critical Remarks upon his Criticisms - till this last Post - I don't know how it is - but I generally find a greater want of leisure upon these festival Occasions - than at any other time - The truth of the case, I believe, is, That from considering it as a Season of Indulgence - I sink into down-right Idleness - which I think is distinguished from Laziness - as the latter implies doing nothing - and the former doing nothing to ye purpose : The being employed - but not about our proper business - which at that time was the finishing our Epilogue - In short, I think you have so much reason to be disgusted with me and my friend in this affair, That you would serve us right - to throw yourself into better hands - & deprive us of the Honour of serving even as Pages in the Train of your Cleone - For I hope Sr you do not look upon us, as such tame Critics - as to give up our Opinions of that Lady to a mere Superficial Hero of the Stage - or think that we cannot distinguish between Merit & Success - The latter, you know, It is not in the power of Mortals to command , - but, I am sure, you have done more - you have deserved it - I know enough of the Theatre from Report - to be convinced, that Delicacy of Sentiment - Beauty of Diction - Moral Reflections & the other Perfections of Composition are of little moment when the M-n-g-r is not Complimented with a shining Character - to display his Personal Merit to the best advantage - Well; but to return to the Business in hand. Mr Shenstone has so well unravelled & Connected my Sentiments - and added 3 or 4 Lines towards the end - which so happily apply those last Lines of mine to ye Subject of the Play - that I begin to look upon what I only sent to keep a place (like a footman in the Boxes - till its arch-type should appear -) as not entirely undeserving your Notice - at least I think it is as much corrected as it is capable of being - I have sent him 4 Lines alluding to the profane Employments of our modern Ladies on Sunday Nights. Which I think might be introduced instead of ye present after " ne'er dreamt of Happiness abroad " - because though he has taken some pains to connect the present Lines - yet I think it ye most exceptionable part of the Epilogue - I only want to have him make it worthy of his Adoption - as I imagine his Name is respectable - & mine cannot appear - As to my Panegyric upon the Master of the Tully's Head - I own - it would be a fulsome Compliment to any modern Author - to pick out one of the celebrated Ancients - & without any other Reason but a Similitude of their Studies, to form a comparison between them in favour of the modern - But I must insist upon the propriety of my taking an occasion from a particular Circumstance - to lament - That a Person of true Genius & real Learning should be forced to make a mercenary Use of the Honour paid to a Brother-Genius - ; who, if he had lived in happier times - would probably have received the same Honour himself - Tully indeed was but an unsuccessful Poet - yet the circumstance alluded to - will be an excuse for comparing you to him rather than to Virgil or Horace or any other Writers of the Augustine Age - Mr Shenstone has omitted the Name of Augustas to avoid the clashing of ss - but he has certainly made me sacrifice sense to Sound in this instance - because Caesar always means Julius unless restrained by some additional Name or Circumstance. I did not know of his inserting it in the Birmingham Journal - till he sent me word himself - I have put him in mind of publishing his Elegies - but he makes no Reply - Mrs Graves joins with me in best Respects & complts for ye year 57. I am Sr. ire affect: humb Sert Ric: Graves To / Mr Dodsley / at Tully's head / in Pall Mall / London

Lapall-House near Hales-Owen Birmingham 20 Janry. 1757 Dear Sir, I am both sorry and ashamed to think that I have been more than 3 months regardless of your Letter, which I ought to have answered the next post, had it been only to have informed you that I received the Books, which have considerably shortened some of the winter Evenings, and added greatly to my Amusement. - Although I am now set down to my Bureau in order to furnish out a Letter which may in some measure compensate for my long silence, I fear my magazine of intelligence will appear rather like the unconnected narratives of an old woman, than like a regular Epistle. - However, I will begin with Mr: Shenstone, who all the Summer since your departure from hence, has been principally occupied in laying out his Valley of Tempe, and attending the Nymphs and Swains who came to visit it; exclusive of this, he has been obliged to transact a good many (though not a many good) Things in regard to the Law-suit he has been for some time engaged in with his perverse Cousin; which to one of his Disposition, with: give infinitely more Pain, than to those of a less delicate Turn of Mind: But I hope an amicable reference, which is now on Foot, will terminate all these disagreeable Occurrences, and establish his Peace. No wonder that the Muses have been neglected: yet I will not hold him altogether blameless, for he might have devoted some time to them; and I often threaten to inform against him to Mr: Dodsley. That, that - . I do not know what name bad enough to call it by - that lazy procrastination , has infected his whole Habit both of Body and of Mind, and as the Disease is desperate, palliatives will work no good - What a pity it is, that some nay many fine Things which he has wrote must be buried in obscurity? like the alterations he has made in ire: Epilogue, but believe he has not quite finished it. - Surely Mr: Garrick is the most absolute Monarch that ever governed the Stage, and I am almost ready to question his judgement after rejecting your Cleone; but as you have now an opportunity of adding to her Beauty & Merit, I hope she will some time hence shine forth with redoubled Charms. - I see very little of the World here, and learn very little News, and since Mr: Shenstone has left off taking in the News, I neither see the World or the News-mongers of it. But not to pun - I have not seen one of ire: papers called the World these three Months or more, and Mr: Shenstone as well as myself cannot conceive what goes with them. - As touching my journey to London I will not say (in excuse for my Laziness) there is a Lion in the way - but really it is now become precarious. My Lawyer has not my Business in readiness which I was to transact; and I have got a rogue of a Tenant who is playing the Devil with one of my best Farms, and unless I watch him close up to Lady-Day, I shall be a great sufferer by him: however I hope to be in London this Spring, and want no incentives to enjoy the Pleasure I should have in your Company: I wish I could be of service to you when I come for I greatly pity your Sufferings, and I am sorry to hear of them. The Gout is the approbium Medicine , and past the Art of Me, or My Brethren, to eradicate; but I hope you are at Liberty to walk about, & enjoy Life again. - It will be a mere Compliment, to say, that I have laid out for a Hare this month past, for you, and cannot find one; however if I do, no Friend that I have should be more welcome to it than yourself. Mr: Baskerville & Docr: Ash have had a great quarrel; the latter aspersed the Character of the former most vilely touching his Wife, which: Mr: Baskerville resented, and wrote a very sensible and smart Letter in vindication of himself, which is shown about privately. Will your two Vols: of poems come out, to complete the Set? this Winter, or not? if it must depend in some measure upon Mr: Shenstone's Contributions, give me a Commission, and I will persecute him so, that He shall take up Pen and Ink in mere Despair, & self Defence. I hope ire: Bror: is well, please to make my Compliments to him; & if I have tired your Patience by the length of my Letter, I hope you will impute it to the desire I have of testifying by any means that I am ever Dr: Sir Ire: most Obliged & Obdt: Hble Servant John Scott Hylton

Pallmall Febry. 17th. Dear Sir You must think me a most absurd fellow, that at the very time I am waiting with great impatience for some of your Pieces to begin the 5th. Volume of my Miscellany, I should think of troubling You with a trifle of my own. But I shall be glad if You will just favour me with a few moments to read over the enclosed, and should you happen to think it capable of being made fit for the Public, I should be very glad it might receive your corrections. I know I ought not to trouble You on this account, but as I intend in case it be published to lie quite concealed, I do not choose to show it to any one here. I send another copy of it by to night's post to Mr. Graves. I have sate in a chair near three months & cannot yet set either foot to the ground. I flatter my self with hopes that you are preparing to enable me to put my 5th. Volume to press, which I shall be glad to do as early in the spring as possible. I send you enclosed a small collection of Poems just published by Mr. Whitehead. I was to have had two Odes by Mr. Gray, but they are not yet sent me. I was to have had too a collection of Elegies, but ah! - I am ever Dear Sir affectionately Yours R. Dodsley

Claverton, 22, Feb. - 1757 Dear Sr I have read ire Melpomene with great pleasure - & am sure it will require but little Correction to make it fit for ye public - How far it is qualified to please the gross Taste of that fickle Lady - you are a better Judge than I can be - who have had but a very slender acquaintance with her. I take the first vacant moments to answer yours; Because I think there is little Room for any Verbal Criticism (which is the height of my Aim) - & therefore I will refer to your own Revisal, what occurs to me (on the first Perusal) to be capable of Improvement in a higher Sphere - In the Region of Terror I would have you consider whether another Source of that Passion is not to be sought after in Superstition - or that Propensity which, I think, is natural to us, to be afraid of Ghosts & Apparitions - especially as you profess to follow Shakespeare to his hidden Recesses - who has certainly made a fine Use of it - I know it is ye Fashion of this enlightened age utterly to reject every notion of this kind - But, if something of it is not natural to us, how can we account for ye Prevalence of those apprehensions, through all ye ages of ye world - The greek word for Superstition - Deisi-Daimony - signifies properly ye fear of Ghosts or Demons - either good or bad - And the Appearance of Brutus's Genius - which (according to true History) appeared with circumstances of Terror - and another Story in Pliny's Epist. - quite in ye modern Taste of Apparitions - proves these Fears to be natural at least not ye Invention of ye Monkish Ages, as is commonly said - For my part, I have still so much of ye Nursery about me - That I never see Hamlet's or Banquo's Ghosts but my Blood runs Chill - & fills me with a surprising Terror - But I only hint this - & would have you try to introduce a Ghost after ye Image of murder - Stanza 9 - "But whence that murmering Noise! The Earth opens - & a horrid Spectre rises - & beckoning stalks amid visionary Tombs & Charnels to where his mangled Corpse is deposited without ye Rites of Sepulture - &c - in ye usual Style - & ye Effects of raising the Hair, like Quills on ye fretful Porcupine - but you are acquainted with Shakespear's Language & will find no difficulty in executing such a Stanza - if perhaps you have not already rejected it as improper - St. 7 Stran - inverted - Encircled - 9 - As to ye Language it is very elegant - & I can see nothing that needs correction. except ye Rhymes - in one or two Stanzas - which return too near together - There is rise & his - St. 3 - eyes & dies St. 5 - Eyes & Ties St. 7 - arise Blasphemies - St. 9 - & arise Sighs St. 10 - rise eyes St. 11 - Sighs Eyes St. 13 - one alteration however in Stanza 10 - I think will be enough as all the rest are at a sufficient Space - between these - The three Epithets - St. 3 - express ye thing vastly well - But Milton having used The Vast Profound , as a substantive - makes it sound ambiguous - qv - St. 5 - "Powers of Manhood" - sounds to me as relative only to ye male Sex in opposition to ye female - qv. whether Powers of Nature would do - St. 7. - disowns all Human Types - hardly strong enough - ? - St. 9. - Despair used as a Person L.1. & as a Passion L.7. - "A Reprobate to Heaven the Caitiff dies " "with Execrations, Groans & horrid Blasphemies" - q - St. 10 - I cannot assist you - but think the two last Rhymes should be altered - appear - & Fear - q - To melt ire feeling heart - with Fear St-11-12-13-14 - & - all very beautiful & ire Instances finely chosen & Picturesque - St-14 - "What is so sweet as Friendship" - How sweet ire Charms of Friendship?" qv - St. 20 - " And art thow skilled in raising the Passions? - whether this is not the very thing - which he desires to be instructed in? - If so however it will be easily altered - But I believe you are right. He desires to be instructed in Shakespear's art of pleasing - She bids him study Nature & ye wit of raising ye Passions. You see Sr I take the freedom of - deliberating & proposing my most unreasonable Samples in your Company - I depend upon Mr Shenstone's Decision - who is generally infallible in his Criticisms - But sometimes lays too great stress upon Trifles - Mrs Graves & myself are at present under ye greatest ax~iety - on acct of our Children - whom we have banished from our care - to be inoculated - She joins in best respects with Sr ire affect - humb Sert Ric: Graves

Febry. 24th Dear Madam You judged (as indeed you always do) very rightly, when you imagined that ye flavour of the Hare would be improved to my taste by its coming from Your fair hands: I will not therefore thank your father for it, being much more obliged to him that he has thus given me an opportunity of thanking You . I hope it will not be long however before I see him in Town, & am glad to hear his confinement has been owing to a sprain only, as I had heard before it was the gout, and very sincerely sympathised with him, having not been able myself to set a foot to the ground these three months . Your friend Mr. Cooper is just come in upon me & thinks himself very happy in having an opportunity of sending you his Compliments. I beg You will make mine to every friend in Mansfield who may happen to enquire after me: I cannot help feeling a kind partiality in favour of the place, but fear I am growing too infirm to entertain the hope of ever seeing it again, which to confess the truth is a reflection by no means agreeable to me. I have no news to send you except that it is now generally believed Admiral Binge will suffer on monday next, all ye solicitations of his friends to procure a pardon having proved in vain. I am sorry to hear Mrs Wright was so ill when you wrote, I beg my compliments to her, and hope this will find her better. My good Lord Radnor I am afraid will scarce get over this winter, in whom you will lose an Admirer, who often used to enquire after your health; and I a friend for whom I had a very great regard. Thus our friends drop from us one after another, leaving us at last alone, joyless, comfortless, unconnected; but thereby kindly disposing us to rejoice in the hope of following them. But methinks I hear You cry out, Good Lord! how grave the man is? One might have heard a sermon in ones own parish church. It is very true, as you say, & I don't know how it has happened; but believe I am low spirited, which I never used to be you know, and so for fear I should preach you quite asleep, I will put an end to my letter & my moralising together. I am &c
