column46: Pallmall March 11th 1757 Dear Sir I cannot help feeling awkwardly to my self in sitting down to write this Letter, being sensible that any modest man who had asked a friend's opinion of his piece, and received no answer, ought to take that silence not only as the civilised, but the tenderest kind of Disapprobation. To confess the truth, from any body but You I should certainly have so construed it; but, not to mention the partiality of your friendship which I flatter my self with, I know I have such a chance of its being in You mere Indolence, that, notwithstanding the imperfections of the Poem, & the probability that your silence proceeds from the polite motives hinted at above, I will just venture once more to put you in mind of it. After this, it would be quite tearing & impertinent to say a word of your long-expected Elegies - Epilogue - Poems for the Miscellany - or any such things. I will therefore pass them over at present in silence - though I could be very glad to read the Elegies in print, to see the Epilogue as you have now corrected it, & to put ye 5th & 6th Volumes of the Miscellany to press as soon as You please, that I might have ye Summer before me to print them in the best manner. Is not Mr Hylton coming to Town? May I not expect a packet by him? Or, why cannot You accompany him? Methinks I could start up on my feet with great alacrity, to see You come in; which is more than I have been able to do these four months; having been so long confined by the Gout, which still continues its tyranny over me, and chains me down to my chair. In this wretched situation, for Charity's sake have some pity upon me; send from your Pharmacopoeia of Wit some cordial drops to cheer my spirits, et eris mihi magnus Apollo . I am Dear Sir very truly & affectionately Yours R. Dodsley To William Shenstone Esqr / at the Leasows / near / Birmingham

Pallmall April 11th Dear Sir After the pains you have so kindly & so effectually taken with my Ode, I can never with any face accuse you again of Indolence. I have adopted, as You will see, most of your Alterations; and as I had made several others since You saw it, I was desirous of letting You see it again as soon as possible, that it may receive the benefit of another revisal, which You have so generously promised to bestow upon it. I must own I could wish it might appear soon, if it can be made tolerable: but am afraid of being too troublesome to You. I write in such a hurry that I shall not remember half of what I have to say. I thank You and Mr. Graves however most heartily for ye Epilogue. It has no fault but too much length, which is easily mended. Must I put your name to it, or Mr Graves's? I thank You also for Mr Perry's Poem, and for what I hope is but the beginnings of your own. All the doubtful readings in the enclosed I beg You will determine. If I should think of another Stanza I will send it to You. I wish this may be either sense or english, but I cannot read it at present being quite pressed for time. I am ever Dear Sir Your most obliged & office. Served. R. Dodsley

column46: Pallmall Ap. 21st. 1757 Dear Mr. Shenstone I have already so much obligation to You for the pains you have taken with my Ode, & for your improvements in it, that I am ashamed to give You any farther trouble, being apprehensive your Goodnature may be quite wearied out with my Impertinence. But having made some small alterations since I sent you the last copy, I cannot forbear submitting them to your consideration. O dire effect! His changing &c. I hope you have altered ye last lines of this stanza. I cannot please myself. Is that expression allowable? I had thought of a new stanza to be introduced here, but I don't like it. I will transcribe it however, as you may possibly strike out something from it, or supply its place with somewhat better. I think this image wrong, as it is difficult to imagine a King should become a Beggar. I once thought of making it suit Belisarius; but that would be historical, and all the rest is visionary. In short, I submit the whole Ode to your Judgment; and shall be very glad, if you think it at all fit for the public, that I may receive your last corrections as soon as is convenient, as I would willingly publish it before the Town grows empty, which will now be very soon. Mr. Spence meditates a visit to my Lord Wentworth in Leicestershire in about two months, when he intends to persuade my Lord to come with him to see the Leasows, having a great desire to be acquainted with You. I need say nothing on this occasion. Two persons of tempers so congenial, as they must certainly like each other, will easily become acquainted. I beg my Compts. to Mr Hylton, whom I was in hopes to have seen in Pall mall long before now. I suppose You are not content with hating London your self, but will persuade all your neighbours to hate it. I wish however You would come see it, if it was but even for a week. I am ever Dear Sir affectionately & sincerely Your obliged humble Served. R. Dodsley

May 3d. Dear Miss I hope your good father got well home, & did not increase his cold that night at Drury Lane, where we parted. For my own part I waited there, tell him, above half an hour before I could meet with a chair, so that getting a cold which again reduced me to my flannels, I am now practising Philosophy upon crutches: & you cannot conceive what a complacency & respect I grow to have for my self, on the contemplation of my own virtues of Patience & Resignation. I heartily thank you for your kind invitation to Mansfield: ye single consideration of being so charmingly nursed, would be a strong temptation let me tell you. But God bless your Charity, & send you better employment with a man than to wrap his legs in flannel. He must be an impudent fellow that could think of subjecting You to such a task! You, who have had no benefits from the Creature! Let those who have known what he is good for, take care of him when he is good for nothing. But it is of a piece with the rest of your Character; your virtues are not of ye selfish kind, but pure & disinterested; & I wish I could flatter my self with the hopes of being able to get down, that I might give you an opportunity of exercising them in my behalf.

June 17 Sir Having made very numerous, & some considerable alterations in my Play since You saw it; & having been informed that You are not unwilling to give it second reading in company with some of our common friends, I take the Liberty of letting you know that I am very ready to submit it to such a perusal. But as I flatter my self you may possibly find most of your former objections now removed would it not be more agreeable to You to give it another reading first alone? If it would, I will send it to You whenever you find your self at leisure.

Sedgefield near Durham Aug. 9. 1757. Dear Sr. I have been obliged to publish a Sermon preached at ye. meeting on occasion of the Public Infirmary at Newcastle. It is printed there & I have taken the liberty of putting Yours & Mr. Millar's name in the Title-page I have ordered 150 to be sent to You, of which. be so good as to send a part to Mr. Millar with my humble Service & request that he would be so kind as to assist in ye. sale. It is published for the Benefit of the Infirmary, & if it produces any gain, it will so far do some good. I must further beg the favour of you to send a few Presents of them for me, which. I will give you a List enclosed The Life of William of Wykeham is finish'd; & ready for the Press. I beg you to confer with Mr. Millar about the Publication of it, & give me your joint advice upon ye. matter. As far as I can guess, it will make a pretty large Octavo, without swelling it in the printing; though I would have it printed well & decently. It will not be a Book for Common Readers; it will not have much either in the matter or the manner that will be entertaining to the generality: it is chiefly calculated for those that have some relation to the Subject of it, & may merit the attention of a few others that see something more curious than ordinary in Antiquities & History. So that it will not safely admit of a large Impression. The Title is to be "The Life of Wm. of Wm. " are all the circumstances I can think of to direct you in forming a Judgement upon it. And when I have told you, that I would not part with the property of ye. Copy & shall want a number (about 60 or ) for Presents, you may easily determine upon your Proposals, & I shall as easily agree to them. - If you choose to print now, ready to publish early in ye. winter, I can send it as soon as you please. I have nothing to add but a Preface, giving an account of my Materials for which. the Book itself need not wait. Believe me, Dear Sr. Your most obedient humble Served. Robed. Lowth P.S. The Sermons for Oxford

Augst. 30th. Dear Miss When your kind Invitation came to Pall mall I was set out for Birmingham, where I have been for five weeks. My brother sent your Letter to me thither, and I should have answered it sooner, but that I fully intended to have stolen a week from my business there, and slipped away in a Post-chaise to Mansfield. But this I found it impossible to accomplish; though it was very much in my wishes. However, if I should be so happy as to escape the Gout this Winter, I may probably be bold enough to make an attempt at seeing Mansfield next Sum~er. At present I am very lame, & though I have been so long from home, I am not yet able to walk but with great difficulty. I am much afraid, if I should have another attack this winter, that the use of my legs will be quite taken from me. Poor Lord Radnor is gone. He died a day or two after his birth day, having rounded seventy years. He left me a hundred pounds, which I would very gladly have stayed for some years longer. I beg my compliments to all friends, and am &c

Wm. of Wykeham sets out this day from Durham to wait of you. He travels slowly, & will not arrive in Town till this day fortnight. If he does not come to your hands soon after that, be so good as to enquire after him, at the Newcastle Carrier's at the White Horse in Cripplegate. I have no objection to your Proposals; & if upon looking over & examining it you shall think proper to alter your design in any particular, I shall as readily agree to any alterations you shall propose. Though you'll find, as I told you, that it will not be a Book of amusement for common Readers, yet the number of persons that bear some relation to Wm. & his Colleges, to satisfy whose Curiosity it is chiefly designed, is pretty considerable. This is a circumstance yt. shd. enter into the account: the chief hopes you advise dwelling upon it to enlarge your sale I leave yt. entirely to your judgement. I am very much for your being of the cautious side, & with. rather have you under than above the mark. I must beg of you to get a careful & intelligence Corrector. There will be no particular difficulties in the Book itself; the References & Notes will require the chief care: the Appendix, though better written, will be more troublesome especially in the old French in one part, & in abbreviations of the Latin. You might send me by the Post any particular sheets where there are the chief difficulties: if you do, remember to send ye. Ms. too, for I have no Copy. You'll think it proper to print the Appendix on a different & smaller Letter; & I suppose, put it to press together with the Book. In the beginning of the Appendix you'll find two loose Papers; one a Contents; the other a genealogical Table. The latter is to go at the end of appenx. & I have made inquiries about ye. drawing of Wm'.s Monument in Winchester Cathedral for a Frontispiece; & have some hopes of having it tolerably done by one now in that neighbourhood. But if you should chance to know of any Artist going that way, that could do it well, pray send him to the Dean of Winchester. I should be glad to see your first sheet by way of specimen; perhaps you won't care to stay for my opinion upon it: however, send it me to satisfy my curiosity. But before you send the Book to the press, I must beg the favour of you to take the trouble of rea: :ding it over carefilly yourself: & not only to alter any mistakes in writing, spelling, &c. but to give me your observations, & objections to any passages; & mark all improprieties of expression, obscurity, &c. for all which. I shall be much obliged to you. Mr. Spence is returned to Byfleet: he has seen part of it; but if you can catch him, make him look it over again. The Preface is done; & you shall have it & communicate this to him. I forgot to desire you to send a Sermon to ye. D. of Newcastle. Send one now: his Grace will not think of its being too late, if he thinks about I find they are over weight for the Post; so those out of Town wait till you have an opportunity: & pray add to the List, Lord Wentworth. This has put me in mind to look over my former List of Presents; & I find I cannot reduce it to under Fourscore for Wykeham. What you saw in the Papers is true. I shall be very glad of your Company at The Chaplain's Table; but don't yet know when I am to be in Waiting. My Wife presents her humble service; & You will believe me to be, Dear Sr. Your most Affectionate Humble Served. R. Lowth P.S. / Wm. of Wm. Section 1. page. 1. before ye. word (inquisitive) insert, (idly.)

column46: Sepbr. 15th. 1757. Sir. I have kept the Tragedy a Week longer than I should have done, that I might thoroughly consider it at different Readings, & be the better Enabled to give my Opinion of it - where ye. particular Alterations have been made I cannot positively point out, but I really think, that ye Play is the better for them - Yet notwithstanding these Amendments, and ye other Passages of Merit, it is still my Opinion that ire. foundation of ye Whole is defective, & that ye Schemes that are formed & the Circumstances that arise in ye Course of ye. Fable are too bloody, shocking & improbable - If you please to remember these were partly my Objections to the Plan before You had written a Line of ire Tragedy - If you will do me the Justice to believe that this Judgment of mine is sincere & unprejudiced, I will very readily agree that it may be Erroneous; & I hope that it will prove so, whenever Your Master, & Mine, the Public, shall determine the Question. I am Sr. Your most humle Served. D: Garrick.

Pall mall Sept. 20th. Dear Sir I have delayed thanking you for all the Civilities, the Kindness, and the pleasures I received at ye Leasows, that I might send you at the same time a proof of your Poems and of your Grove; and that I might give you the time for filing and polishing which you desired. I think the Design is executed very neatly, & hope you will like it; Mr. Giles went to Grignion & gave him some useful directions. I have interleaved the Proofs, that you may insert any alterations you think proper. You will see I have omitted the Evergreen, and Candour, which You seemed most afraid of, & intend to insert them without a name. I beg my Compliments to Mr. Hylton: pray what becomes of his meditated Pastoral? I enquired about a Green Chagrin Pocket-book, but as I am told it will come to two guineas exclusive of the Clasp, I deferred buying it, till I have your farther orders: in the mean time have sent You the Morocco one mended. When you shall have corrected the four Sheets I have sent, which I hope will be in about a month or six weeks at most, you may send them up in the four franks I have enclosed for that purpose: I hope by that time to have finished both the volumes. The Printer says he shall be able to keep the press standing of these four sheets, till you can send them back, which is a great convenience to me, as it permits me to go on with the rest. As You have so much time, I have sent no proof to Mr Graves, because I thought you might possibly make some corrections, & would rather choose to send your own proofs to him. I have showed Dr. Akenside your Elegy; he is prodigiously struck with it, & hopes you will some time or other before it is long, let the public enjoy the pleasure of the whole Collection. I have sent you one of my Ode, & one for Mr Hylton: I have also sent by the Penny post one to Lt Lyttelton's House in Town, whether they will send it to him, in the Country I know not; but if they should, and You should happen to see him, pray don't say whose it is, as I would by no means be known. Mr Garrick has finally rejected Cleone; so instead of dying of Grief, she may now go hang her self in Despair. Or rather truly, ought not the Authur to be hanged, for wasting so much time to so little purpose? But he is penitent, and will do so no more. I beg my Compliments to Molly, and thank her for all her care of me: and pray let her give my love to the Cows for their delicious suppers. I am Dear Sir Your mostd affectionate & obliged humble Servant R. Dodsley

Claverton 10 October. 1757 - Dear Sr I ought sooner to have acknowledged the Receipt of your Poem - which I have perused again & again with fresh pleasure: And, to speak like a Critic, will venture to pronounce it an excellent Composition! It is finely imagined & (now at least) vastly correct - I suppose Mr Shenstone put you upon re-considering & methodizing it - and altering several particulars - which neither my self nor, I am sure, any common reader would have suspected Capable of any improvement - This Ode must necessarily do you Credit with every Reader of Taste & Delicacy - I only wish you had prefixed your Name to engage the Curiosity of those, who may not have Judgment enough at first Sight to fathom its Beauties - or may over-look it amidst the daily Productions of the Press - I hope this Performance is only prepatory to ye printing - if not ye acting of ire Tragedy - I am (with Mrs Graves's Respects) Sr ire obliged humb Sert Ric: Graves. I have waited a Post or two for a Frank - but was unwilling to defer my Acknowledgements any longer - To / Mr Dodsley / at his house in Pall-Mall London

Sedgefield Octr. 17. 1757. Dear Sr. What can be become of our friend Mr. Spence? When a man of his punctuality does not keep to his time, one is always in pain about him. He said he was to be in town the first week of this month; & therefore I had troubled him with a small Commission which. otherwise I shd. have mentioned to you in my last. I am now afraid of deferring ye. matter any longer lest I should interrupt your proceedings. It was to send me back again one page of my Wm. of Wm. in which. I wanted to make some alteration, as I had forgot to do it before I sent it to you & cannot recollect it sufficiently to do it otherwise. In the Sixth Section towards the middle you will find a Paragraph beginning with these words, The Original Drawings - Be so good as to cut out the next leaf after that, & send it to me; I will return it to you in a Post or two after. I want to know about what time you will want the Preface & Dedication; because with regard to the latter I must make some preparations, which. I would not do till all is near ready. Once more I beg you with. get a Corrector for all the Latin part, or our Book will certainly be disgraced. Believe me, Dear Sr. Your most Affectionate R. Lowth

Sedgefield Novr. 3d. 1757. Dear Sr. I return your proof-sheet, as soon as I go from hence. I shall be able to do it one day or other, when I get to Durham. In the mean time observe that what you send me by your Tuesday nights Post will probably be still a post longer in getting back again; for I have no regular method of getting my Letters from Durham yt. come by that Post. Send me no more Copy: I can do well enough without it, if you will but compose the pages & other figures in the references, & see that they are right. I believe there is a Copper Plate of Wm's. Crosier, which. is preserved at New Coll., engraving at Oxford by Green: You may perhaps hear something about it from Mr. Those. Warton. When you receive the Monument from Taylor, pray send it on to me. If I don't like it, I believe I shall employ Green to go & take it at Winchester, & engrave it. Observe, that I spell Bull always with an e at the end, as being more regular & agreeable to the geniology, & also to distinguish it from that other word of the same sound which. has been the source of so many puns upon this. You will tell me that practice & customs are against me, & make an appeal to Johnson's Dictionary, &c. Regardless, I think I am right, & believe I could give authorities: but if you contest ye. matter, I submit. I am sorry you have let into ye. secret of Melpomene. I had intended to have made some inquiries of you about it. I should have desired you to inform me who was the Author; for that I had read it several times, & could not guess at him, not knowing any one that was capable of writing it. I observe that ye. prevailing fashion of Odes at present is to be dressed out in abundance of fine imagery & fine words, which do not permit the reader to come at the sense that may be at the bottom, but at the expense of the Tenth reading & hard study into the bargain: here I found a Noble Plan invented, disposed, & excecuted, with great spirit, sublimity, & force of imagination; at ye. same time clear & perspicuous throughout, connexions, descriptions, & ye. whole expressions which. excels in an unaffected simplicity and warmth: - this & more I should have said to you; but since I find I am informed of the Author, I have nothing further now to say; however there is one word in it to which. I have an objection & the greater, because it is the last Be pleased to consider, whether to fly away & to fly , or to go swiftly away, are not two distinct words; whether flew , the past time of ye. former expresses more than was upon the wing , with out any intimation of to or from , coming or going ; & whether to express what you mean, you should not have said, fled , or flew away . I mention this, because I am willing to suppose yt. ye. Public have taste enough to call for a new Edition of Melpomene soon; when, if you approve of my remark, you may easily alter it: and I expect that you repay me my Criticism in kind & with interest. I should have thought that this Prologue might have easily introduced Cleone: but perhaps it may be an objection against Melpomene in the Ode too, that she deals too much in the strong, the simple, & the intelligible. If such is the case I enter my Protest aged. ye. public sentiment, & heartily thank you for the unusual pleasure it has given me. I have finished the leaves which. I wanted to revise and will return ym. by the next Packet. Warton may perhaps send you from Oxford a drawing of Wm's. Arms for ye. Pedigree: if not, I shall send you a small print of ym. to use for direction, as soon as I hear from him. Believe me ever, Dear Sr. Your most Affectionate humble Served. R. Lowth.

Sir I have at last, though with some reluctance, determined to publish the following Scenes, which. it may be presumption to call a Tragedy, as You have not thought them worthy of being represented as such at the Theater in Drury Lane. It is now between two & three Years since you first favoured me with a perusal of this Piece, which I then told You I should not have ventured to offer to ye public had I not been encouraged to it by the favourable opinions of several of the best Judges amongst my Acquaintance. I forbear to mention Names, for though the list would do me Honour, it might carry an air of ostentation & vanity which I should choose to conceal. I will ingenuously confess however, I have kept ye Piece by me thus long, in expectation that from the concurrence of these opinions, with those of several others of your own friends, very eminent in the republic of Letters, you might possibly have been induced to honour it with the indulgence of a Trial. But no intimation of change in your sentiments appearing, I have now relinquished the vain hope of seeing it on the Stage, (ye only point of view in which a Dramatic Performance can be seen to an advantage) and must content my self with setting it before the public in ye dim light of a printed Pamphlet. How much of its Terror & Passion will be lost in this imperfect view, may be easily conceived; for it is not who reads it, that will be able to supply his Imagination the striking Graces of Action, & expressive Feelings, with which I have sometimes flattered my self, You & Mrs Cibber might have animated some of the Scenes. Let me not be betrayed into saying any thing which may look like self-approbation: it is extremely disagreeable to me to speak at all on this Subject; and nothing but the mortification of being obliged to publish a reject'd Play could have induced me so far to differ with a person of your judgement as still to suppose to say but if I have not been more flattered than it can be well imagined a person of my small consequence would be, the Piece not quite destitute of some degree of theatrical Merit. I am sensible the Play has many defects, & I will only apologize for them by confessing that I could make it no better; I had not the vanity to think of producing a perfect Tragedy, as I never remember to have seen that way so. but if I have not been more flattered than it can well be imagined a person of my small consequence would be, it might probably have passed with pardon, if not with applause. I will not venture to say more in its behalf; I am afraid this is full as much as it deserves: besides, it is now before the Public, and must tell its own story as well as it can; they will not be biased in its favour by any thing I could say, were I ever so much disposed to defend it, which however I am by no means inclined to attempt. After all, tic very possible I may be more obliged to You for refusing it, though it might somewhat chagrin me at first, than to any of those Friends whose sentiments (perhaps too partial in its favour) might have betrayed me into dangers, from which I am now Sir happily preferred by your more kind severity. For though I have endeavoured and at ye expense of some time and pains, in ye production of this piece, to form a Fable on one single striking Action though I have attempted to draw and enforce from this Fable an important Moral, have laboured that ye conduct of the Piece should be easy and unembarrassed, & the Passions strong and various; though I have aimed at nature and simplicity in the Language, at propriety in the Sentiments, and that the circumstances and incidents should be interesting and affecting, yet I am very sensible how probable it is I may have failed of success in the execution of some or all of these things: only give me leave once more to observe that if I have so entirely failed as You seem to think I have several persons of the best and most acknowledged taste and Judgment have either been mistaken themselves, or have unaccountably concurred in flattering and deceiving me. But whatever may be the case, for I will seek no farther into your reasons for rejecting it, I assure you all animosity and resentment have long subsided in my breast; I now submit it to yours and to ye Public view with perfect tranquillity and resignation, & if you should ever so far change your opinion as to think it worthy of a trial on your Stage, I hereby give up all claim to any profits which might possibly arise from the author's nights in case of its success, and if such faint shadow of advantage is worth acceptance, transfer & assign them, to the use of the Society for ye Encouragement of Arts, Manufactures & Commerce. I am &c

Pall mall Decr 3d. Dear Sir I have received both Sheet B and D, but by the alterations you have made, there will want about three pages to fill up Sheet C, which. I hope you will take care to supply from your hidden stores. I filled up Sheet D with your verses on Riddles, & with Mr Whistler's two small pieces, which I put in between Mr Graves's & yours. I think ye Speech of Nancy of the Vale had better be marked as it is, than printed in Italics. I cannot like - Paradise's - Nor do I think there is the least occasion for a Note to explain the other reading. I have not been able to find a better word than moldering in The Ode to Health but I will keep the sheet unwork'd for a week, that you may have time to find a better, but I think it will be difficult. What think you of the word blame instead of tax , in the Winter's Visit? Surely You have much improved ye Ode after Sickness. Suppose the 3d Line of it should be And wandered forth alone; I have taken care to indent the Lines in this Ode as You directed, and the whole of it comes into this sheet, so that there will want at least three pages to fill up Sheet C. I am extremely sorry to hear you are not well, & on that account am really both afraid and ashamed to press you about the other two Sheets; if therefore you can let me have them any time before Christmas, it will do very well. I am just upon the point of concluding both the Volumes, and if any farther touches are to be given to the plate, pray let me have your directions. I beg my compliments to Mr. Hylton & to Molly, and am Dear Sir most affectionately yours R. Dodsley

Lapall-House, Hales-Owen near Birmingham 6th: Decr: 1757. Dear Mr: Dodsley, I am ashamed, and almost afraid to take up the pen to write to you, considering of how little importance my letter is likely to prove, and how much less my pretentions are to expect any further Indulgence from you, in point of time I mean, wherein I may be able to finish my Eclogue. I have wrote about 60 lines, which will be the better half of my production, but Mr: Shenstone tells me I shall now be too late, and I have small encouragement to proceed, for he is too much embarrassed with his own pieces to attend to mine; add to this I have now a great deal of Tenants business upon my Hands and other unforeseen and unavoidable Avocations, that exclude Poetry, and every other Amusement. - What can I do, how long will it be before you print off, will it be 3 weeks? If the day of Grace be not past, I will repent me of my Idleness and double my endeavours to complete my peace as well as I am able. - I have been often with Mr: Shenstone, and he is now busy in correcting the remainder of the Sheets, he has not been either in good Health or good Spirits to attend to any Thing, and it has caused him no small degree of uneasiness that the attention requisite to his own Affairs should prove prejudicial to the execution of yours. - I have a Box of papers and Writings that my Attorney will send down to me by the Coach next Monday, and should be obliged to you if you would send the following Books for me in two parcels to Mr: Edwd: Inge Attorney at Law in great Brook Street near Hanover Square. - West on the Resurrection, & Lt Lyttelton's Letter annexed to it, and the Preceptor. - any time this week. I am much obliged to you for your Ode, which you were so kind as to send me, & think it an exceeding good one: Mr: Shenstone with. have your Name affixed to it; and I do not see why it should not. - I wish I could come to Town, I would but can not, then should I know all that I have to hope or fear, and if there is no prospect of my completing my Eclogue time enough, I hope you will forgive me for so vain an Attempt to shine in an Undertaking superior to my Genius. I am Dear Sir Ire: most obliged & obedient, Hble Servant, John Scott Hylton P.S. I beg my compliments to your Bror: who I hope is well. Lord Dudley's death has put an end to all Franks, with me. To / Mr: Dodsley / in / Pall-Mall / London

Decr 19th. My Lord The Consequences of Good-nature are too frequently troublesome. Relieve a beggar at your gate, and you are sure to find him there again. Your Lordship's favourable opinion of Cleone, has encouraged me to solicit a boon in her behalf, which if it be not improper for your Lordship to grant, will certainly be of great service to me. As Mr Rich has at last engaged Mr. Barry and Miss Bellamy at his house, I have determined to offer my Tragedy to him; but am advised to strengthen my application with a line from some great person whose opinion would have weight & consequence with him. Your Lordship's favourable sentiments signified by a Line for me to take to Mr. Rich, as it would do me great honour, I am convinced would also give me so much credit with Him, that he would at least be favourably disposed towards receiving it. I would not have presumed to trouble your Lordship with a letter on this occasion, intending to have waited for your return to Town, but am advised to be as expeditious as may be in my application, as it is expected some thing else will be offered him. I am &c

Tuesday Decr. 21. 1757. Dear Sir, I received your Letter this morning to my no small Confusion - Yet blame I no One beside myself ; or rather that Incapacity I feel for Criticism , which makes me wish, in any sort, desire to delay your publication. When I sent my last Packet, I purposed by ye. next post to explain the uses for which it was intended - I have not done so - have not been able to do so - & now am surprised to find yt. another Sheet is gone to the Press - for According to ye. Construction I put upon ire. last Letter, I thought it might be not altogether too late , if I regulated ye. whole by Xtmas. I hope ye. Elegy is not yet begun in Sheet B.; & even thus, if it were not inconvenient to stop ye. press a little, I would rather it were Too many of my Pieces are entirely t done, in. otherwise - I think to write again, & have reserved my only Frank, for tomorrow - Mean time I give you my Thoughts in regard to ye. Compositions your Letter mentions . In ye. Ode to Health, I could propose no better word in. falling instead of moldering ; & if you happen to prefer ye. Latter , I will by no means disagree with you. In regard to the Song "I told my nymph" I desire yt. you would follow all ye. readings you propose / The same, as to "ye Compliment 1743. / As to ye. Ode 1739, I am neither wholly satisfied with ire. reading or my own. However; does not Aid in ye. first Line run better in. Charms? Love's imperial power was known is flat, & Love here is a Person , tho a Passion in ye. 5th. Line / But I leave you to penetrate my reasons, why I propose ye. following alterations, for ire. Choice . I think ye. second preferable; as " insidious " suits better with " betrayed " in ye. next Line, & not ill with "was known" in this . The " betrayed " used in ye. next stanza may be exchangd for revealed , or some word of equal Import - I don't know why I prefer "Lips at once & Eyes" &c: so very probably you are in ye. right - Quick Lightnings doesn't run so well as " the Lightnings &c: but is is perhaps preferable on another score - As to the rest, please to follow your own readings in regard to this Ode - The Plate will require but very trifling alterations, if any; & may be sent at a Minutes warning. I have but a mean Opinion of two or three amongst ye. songs; & was thinking, (with this last ode Lysander & some few other Pieces in my manuscript) yt. I could have supplied their Place to advantage. Do you remember ye. Verses on ye. Kid? - but I will write again to-morrow, & speak more Explicitly on the Occasion - Do you think Mr. H. Walpole would oblige me with. a Copy of ye. Travels he has lately printed? (Hentznerus, I think is ye. Name -) I do not mean any otherwise then through your Mediation. You judge rightly of me in thinking how much it pains me to print precipitately - My gratitude suffers equally in subjecting you to Inconvenience. I am therefore truly under much anxiety - but with. abundance of good-will, Dear Mr. Dodsley Yrs. very affectionately W. Shenstone Pray write. To Mr. Dodsley / at Tully's head, in / Pall-mall London

column46: Pall mall Janry. 5th. 1758 Dear Sir I begin now to wait with great impatience for Sheet A and C, as much time will be taken up (the Impression being 6 Vols) in gathering and making them fit for the binder, and in binding a pretty large number before I must venture to publish. You will therefore be so good as to send them me with all convenient dispatch, as I am desirous of giving them as much of this season to spread in as possible. I was disappointed last Monday of Mr. Walpole's book, there being none to be had; I therefore did not send the Tea; but will endeavour to procure one by some means or other & send them together. Mr Walpole made me a present of one, which I have lent to a Gentleman in the Country; if I can get no other I will send You that as soon I can get it. I am ever most sincerely & affectionately Yours R. Dodsley

column46: Jan 5 1758 My Lord I have delayed my acknowledgments of ye Honour your Lordship did me in giving your Opinion of Cleone, till I could obtain a definitive answer from Mr. Rich, which. I have not been able to do till yesterday. He tells me his Engagements will not permit him to perform it this season, but promises it shall be done if I think proper the beginning of the next. To this I have acquiesced, provided Mr. Barry & Miss Bellamy continue with him; but if they leave him I can by no means think of venturing it at his house. I am extremely obliged to your Lordship for your favourable interposition, and hope you will pardon my having presumed to request it. I am with real Gratitude & great respect, My Lord, &c

Pall mall Janry 21st. Dear Sir I have just received a letter from You which I perceive was written before You received my last. I find you have enabled me to fill Sheet C without the help of Jazzy, but I hope what I said in my last, will induce You to revoke her doom. I could add to those reasons many others. I really look upon it as the most striking Poem in the whole Collection. I think it will do You more credit than any other of your Pieces. It will certainly do no disservice to ye Collection of Elegies, but may be inserted amongst them, whenever they appear and will in the meantime most strongly recommend them to ye Curiosity of the Public. Besides, so many of the best Judges have seen it, so many more have heard of it, and in short such an expectation has been raised about it, that to be disappointed of it will be very mortifying, and may do mischief. Many more reasons might urged for her present appearance, all to whom I have mentioned it cry out against you for the thought of suppressing it: so pray by the next post give us the satisfaction of hearing that she is to appear. I have a thousand things to say, but am seized with the Gout hand and foot & write in great pain. I can put Mr. Hylton's Tale into a leaf which I have been obliged to cancel. The Sentiment I had printed before with ye Evergreen & another without your Name. Pray send the Rural Elegance, & let me finish, for I shall now be in great trouble & anxiety which accompanied with pain is too much. The Season is wasting, and I have between 6 and 7 hundred pound buried in the Paper & print of this Edition, which I want to pay and cannot till I publish. I fear it is impossible You should read or understand what I have writ. I am ever most affectionately Yours R. Dodsley

Claverton, 3. Feb. 1758 Dear Sr I am obliged to you for a kind Letter of the 25th. of October. last - which perhaps I ought to have acknowledged before this time - But when I consider the importance of your engagements - & your connections with all the great Genii of the Age, I cannot but look upon my Correspondence, as beneath your Consideration - After almost half-a-years Silence however I am favoured with a Letter from Mr Shenstone - who laments (as, I, &, I believe, you, have reason to do) his dilatory temper - yet hopes at least that I correspond with his friend Dodsley - Who, he informs me, is endeavouring to rescue more of my Rhymes from utter Oblivion - Now, as the mere admission amongst your eminent Hands has, I find, raised me to some degree of Consequence with many People - I should be sorry to forfeit it again, by exposing any more of my Levities - as I expect to be pardoned for once - by insinuations - that those Trifles crept into Print - through the partiality of my Friends - But should think myself inexcusable to be repeating those Follies at my Age - & amidst the Avocations of a serious Profession - by Mr Shenstone's account however, matters are advanced too far for my Remonstrances - & I know I am safe in the Hands of a Person of your Judgment & Character. But should be glad to know, in one Line, what particular Piece or Pieces of mine, you have honoured with ire approbation - I dare say, that which I gave you upon my own place is not one - as it appears excessively insipid to me - after four years - and it would be ridiculous - even to have made such a place ye subject of any Meditation - However I have made one or two alterations in those Stanzas - which to me, appear of as much Importance as the Thing itself - The most material Article of my last Letter to Mr Shenstone - was a Request to him to publish his Elegies - upon which head, I think I used some forcible arguments - But he vouchsafes me no answer - as, I believe, he is at a Loss - What Answer to make - Though perhaps a Person that is capable of writing with so much Delicacy - may see many nice Objections - which are invisible to my grosser Perception - Mr Shenstone agrees with me, that you ought to have affixed your Name to ire Melpomene - not only for the Sale of it - but, as I am certain, your Name would have been a proper Introduction of it to the Notice of all People of Taste - You greatly surprise me, by what you hint about my being engaged in an Entertainment for ye Public as I communicated something of such a Scheme to Mr Shenstone under ye Seal of inviolable Secrecy - and could have forgiven him for whispering it to any one, rather than to you - As I should be sorry to have you think, that I would publish any thing which I should be ashamed to submit to ire Inspection - Something of that kind however I must now own, that I have bestowed (at different times) perhaps two months Labour upon. But a number of disagreeable domestic Concerns - have put, I believe, a final Period to my Labours - You will not suspect that there was any thing immoral in my undertaking - for I intended the Reverse - But the Species of writing was of the lowest kind - & my many Interruptions - would have prevented my executing it with any degree of Perfection - It was begun in a Pique - & continued from the amusement I found in it - & if I had ever published it, I own it would have been with a View - of getting about as much money - as with. have purchased 2 or 3 Folio's of ye ornamental kind - which out of regard to my family, I could not prudently do - But I have at present no prospect of Leisure to complete it - before the Date of its Popularity will probably be expired - I am Sr ire obligd humb Sert Ric: Graves To / Mr Dodsley / at Tully's head in / Pall-Mall London

The Leasows 4 Febry: - 1758. Dear Sir, As it is now near Eight o'Clock, I shall not have time to write you any long Letter, but I am desired by Mr: Shenstone who has really been extremely ill, ever since he has wrote to you, to acquaint you that he purposes if he have a tolerable Day tomorrow to return your proof Sheet. He could not possibly do so to night, upon account of the time at which he received it. Upon just casting an Eye over it, he thinks the transpositions of Stanzas will occasion the first Line of the 23d: Stanza to be (as it now stands) not altogether intelligeable. But he hopes when he returns the Sheet to fix all necessary alterations. The kind Letter you was so obliging to favour me with, I will answer soon. Mr. Shenstone joins with me in the Compliments with which I am Dear Sir Ire: most Obliged & Obedt: Hble Servant John Scott Hylton To / Mr. Dodsley / in Pall-mall / London

The Leasows. Sunday Night 8 o'clock. 9th: Febry: - 1758. Dear Mr: Dodsley, I have the pleasure to inform you that we think Mr. Shenstone out of Danger; Dr: Ash who has just left him, hearing me say that I would Write to you this post, desired I would present his Compliments to you & assure you of the same His recovery gives us all good Spirits; though he is yet too weak and low to bear the Light, or the Visits and Messages of his Friends, who send from all Quarters to know how he does. I exclude every thing from him that may cause the least disturbance, & by so doing, and giving him the Bark, we shall be able to prevent a relapse, which might be dangerous, if not fatal. I have not been six Hours from hence, since I last wrote to you for he will not permit me to leave him; indeed I could not, it would have been cruel in me if I had! When he is able to bear it, I will communicate the tender concern you feel for his sufferings to him. - His discourse since his being confined to this Bed, has been only what related to his Affairs, and that I have endeavoured to let be, no more than what was needful; and I dare say you do not doubt my cure of him, as the pleasure & Happiness I enjoy in this part of the world is connected with his Friendship and Affection to me! - I am glad you have not taken Jazzy into the Collection: He probably means to amend it, and if he never had been able so to do; it, and other Things would not have been suppressed. - When you write I beg the Favour of about half a dozn: prints of the Grove, to colour for 2 or 3 Ladies, one of which I mean to send to ire: Cozn: at Duffield. - I am sorry I have no Frank, to enclose my Letter. I thought to have sent this away to the post this Evening, but must defer it now till tomorrow, though I am sorry to think what you must suffer every time the post-man goes by your Door without calling at it. - Mr Inge my Attorney in Brook Street has not sent the Books I ordered from you to be sent thither, but as he is over Powered with Business, and I am an idle Fellow, it is my own fault that I do not send to him. - I mean however to write to him in a week or two, and will desire you to send for them if I do not receive them soon after. - Pray do inform me whether Dr: Smollet's History of England be worth purchasing, the cuts 167 in Number if well engraved must be worth the Money - The Natural History of the County of Kerry excites also my Curiosity - you know my Taste for Curiosities - All this however does not exhibit any Taste in me for poetry, indeed I dare not presume to like or dislike any thing of that kind before I know Mr: Sh-e's Opinion, and though he is so very delicate, I would scorn to be his Echo, because it precludes all Taste of one's own, did I not know him to be as just, and generous, as he is correct and delicate. God preserve his valuable Life, 'till we have had a larger share of the Happiness he confers upon all around him! - if I do not hear from you in a week, I will write again. When will your two Vols: come out? - I am Dear Sir Ire: most Obliged Humb: Servant John Scott Hylton Monday Morning 9 o'clock I am this moment come from him, he has had rather a bad Night, occasioned partly by the weather, which was very stormy 'till after Twelve. I have dressed his Blisters, and the fatigue of that has thrown him into a dose, which I hope may refresh him. - His Head was clearer this Morning, & his Ideas less confused than they have been hitherto. - I will write sooner than a week, should he happen to be worse, which I do not however Apprehend. To Mr: R: Dodsley / in Pall-Mall / London

Sedgefield Feb. 24. 1758. Dear Sr. The sheet preceding these which. I return, yt. is, the Sheet G, I have not seen: I hope you have taken care to correct it well. When you have finished the Life , I wish you with. send it all to me by the Newcastle Coach, directed to me at ye. College Durham, that I may look it over, in order to make an Errata of any material mistakes that may remain. The Appendix I suppose you will print on a less Letter: I think that will be more proper, & besides the Volume is big enough. Remember to send me with ye. proof sheets of it, the Copy of Nos. 5, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14, 15: I shall otherwise have no Copy to correct by. When shall you want the Preface, &c? - My Wife, though better than she has been, yet still continues very ill. - Believe me, Dear Sr. Yours most Affectionately R. Lowth

Pall mall Feby. 27th. Dear Sir I verily think that if you leave off your agreeable Excursions and occasional Criticisms you will rob your work in a great degree of that variety which rendered it so entertaining; you will make it seem not all of a piece and lead your readers to think that the best part of Pope's Works are huddled together in haste, if not slubber'd over and neglected. If you are afraid of any severe or ill-natured remark in the College, might not that be obviated by letting the second volume come out by your Brother? Or might you not say in a prefatory Advertisement, that though you had collected your materials long ago, your present avocations which you thought it your duty not to neglect, had prevented your putting them together sooner? I really think that another volume is as little as can possibly be employed to make the Work at all uniform; but it is certainly of more importance not to risk the censure of neglecting your present Business. Would not an Advertisement prefixed, professing, from your own want of time that you had given up all your materials to your brother, obviate all blame, & save the work? To confess the truth, I am afraid such a hasty jump to the end of the work will look like being in too much haste to be rid of it, and may prejudice the reader against it, as You have led him to expect rather more than a volume than less. I am ever dear Sir Affectionately Yours R. Dodsley If Vernon's poems come to Fletcher push them To the Revd Mr Warton / at the College / Winchester / Hints

Sedgefield March. 5. 1758. Dear Sr. I think Mr. Green has done the Crosier extremely well. I enclose directions for finishing the Plate. It is plainly too large for our Page, especially in the width: & it may be lessen'd without any damage to it. You'll be so good as to give him the proper dimensions. The Engraver would have performed better in the Genealogical Table, if he had not so scrupulously followed the Copy as to the Manner of it, which. was never meant as a Rule for him. Pray see that he makes the Corrections & Alterations given there. And let me have another Proof of Both before they are worked off. The Dean of Winchester tells me, you will see Mr. Taylor. I had desired him to satisfy him for his 2 Drawings. He says, that you will not only have an earlier opportunity, but will know better how to do it. I beg therefore that you will undertake it. Believe me, Dear Sr. Yours most Affectionately R. Lowth

Pall mall Mar. 15th. Dear Mr. Shenstone I have longed to write to You almost as much as to hear from You: I venture at last, & hope this will find you so much recovered, that You may favour me with a line to confirm me in that hope: but I beg, if it still continues to be uneasy to You to write, that you will by no means attempt it. I sent by Frimen's Waggon on Monday, Carriage paid, a complete Set of the Poems, & two or three 5th. and 6th. which beg your acceptance, and which I suppose you will want to give to those who had the former four from You. I have my self sent the two last to Mr Graves, Mr Jago, and Mr. Giles: I have also sent a complete set to Mr Bond and Mr Pixel. I hope You will be able to look into them, and that they will afford you some amusement. I shall be very glad to hear your opinion of them as soon as it shall become not disagreeable to You to take a pen into your hand. Dr. Akenside presents his Compliments, & desires your acceptance of the enclosed which will be published in a day or two. He, and many others very much regret ye loss of your Elegy in the Collections. I will not tire you with a long letter - God bless you, and restore you to perfect health! I know not any thing that will give me so much pleasure as to hear it, being ever most sincerely and affectionately Yours S. Dodsley P.S. I intended to have written to Mr Hylton to night but find I have not time. I beg my compliments, & that he will accept of the two Volumes which are enclosed in your parcel: & if You are not yet well enough to let me hear from You, I hope he will continue his indulgence in letting me hear of You.

Lapel House 22d April 1758 Dear Sir, I have neglected writing to you for a long time, and that upon the Supposition that Mr. Shenstone's Health being in a manner re-established, my Correspondence would not be of so much Consequence as it had been. - I do now, and ought sooner to have returned you my best thanks for your kind present of ire. 4 and 5th: Vols: of the poems, which are more than my little squib of an Epigram could merit by way of return. I think there are many good things in the Collection, and I was in great Hopes of seeing One very good thing there to have rendered the whole more pleasing to your Friends; what I mean is your Melpomene. Perhaps you may publish it with other pieces of your own separate, some time hence: This is a point to be wished for, and I hope not to be despaired off. - Mr: Shenstone is to all appearance as well as ever, he rides, and walks out almost every Day, but he is still weak and low-spirited at times. a journey to London, Bath &c would do him much service; I wish he would accept your kind invitation to meet Mr: and Mrs: Graves at your House in May, and I would very gladly do myself the pleasure to accompany him to such agreeable Company - I am in haste, & hope you will excuse me with an assurance that I am ever dear Sir Ire: most Obliged and Obedt: Servant John Scott Hylton To / Mr. Dodsley / in / Pall-mall / London

Claverton, 25 April 1758 Dear Sr. The great Civility of your Offer deserved my earliest acknowledgment - But when I consider ye particular nature of that offer, I am quite ashamed to have kept you so long in suspense - about my accepting of it - as it may have been highly inconvenient to you on many accounts - You will imagine, that I have been deliberating upon it - or waiting for Mr Shenstone's Resolution - But alas! ye chief Motive for our taking a London Journey is entirely inconsistent with the agreeable Scene you have so kindly decked out for us - You must know then Sr. that I shall be on this occasion a Sort of Bear-leader to a Young Gent - whom I have had for 5 Years under my Care - and who is so destitute of friends amongst his own family - capable of taking care of him, that his Father has requested me to take him with me into Berkshire - & when we are there, to show him London Town for a few days - So that, though we will contrive to be somewhere within Distance of you we cannot make a mere Convenience of your house - as we should be forced to do - if we accepted ire kind Offer - I have not heard yet from Mr Shenstone but am in hopes his Physicians will force him from his beloved Retreat - as a Change of Air must necessarily be of great service to him - . I hope your Person is more at liberty than it was last summer - but perhaps the Public will be the better for ire confinement - as I am sure ire mind is always free - For my part - though I long to be more at Leisure - for Meditation & Recollection - Yet I find my present Connections engage me in a Life of absolute Dissipation - and I never have a moment to myself - Mrs Graves joins in best Respects with sr ire obliged humb Sert Ric. Graves To / Mr Dodsley / in Pall-mall / London

Durham June 9. 1758. Dear Sr. I have recd. your packet. I must beg of You to send two more of Wm. of Wkm to Winchester directed to Dr. Eden, & one to Mr. Prince at Oxford, for presents. To me also two more: & with them be pleased to send, Four Essays upon the English Language, by Professor Ward; An Introduction to Languages &c, by Mr. Bailey; Tragoediarum Graecarum Delectus by Dr. Burton, with. De Greece. Litt. Institution Dissertatio, by the same, bound together: Voltaire's Histoire Universal, the best Edition in French. All bound & Lettered. The first Volume of Duncombe's Horace, which. Mr. Duncombe says he ordered for me, as a Present; & pray enter my name as a Subscriber for the same. Pray send me likewise a Specimen of different sorts of your best Letter writing Paper. And add likewise to the Books above ordered, Theatre des Grecs, par le Pere Brumoy, the very best Edition (in 8vo. or 12mo) handsomely bound. I wish you a good Journey into the North; pray let me know your Route, & when you are to be at Edinburgh I have never a Frank. Believe me, Dear Sr. Yours most affectionately R. Lowth. To Mr. Dodsley / Bookseller in Pall Mall / London.

Pall mall Augst. 22d. Dear Sir I did not finish my long Tour till Saturday last, & this is ye first Letter I sit down to write. I left Mr. Spence in good health at Durham, where he comes into Residence as this day, & will consequently be there for three weeks longer at least. But I suppose you have heard from him before now, & how much he admires your Elegies, &c I have sent them to go by tomorrow's Coach, which will be in Birmingham on Thursday night, where I hope You will receive them safe, & that you will lose no time in putting them to press. The other two Volumes I will send if you desire it, but had rather keep them till You come to Town, which I hope I may now most certainly depend upon. I will not forget the Pigeons as soon as I have an opportunity of enquiring about them. I beg you will send me (and by the return of the Post if you possibly can) ye Letter I left in your hands, with your corrections. You will also let me have as soon as you have opportunity, a Description of ye Leasows, for ye use I mentioned to You. I called at Duffield in my return, & thank you for pointing out to me so agreeable a relation. She is indeed a fine Girl, & desires her Compliments to You & Mr. Hylton; and pray be so good as to give him mine. I hope I am secure of seeing You next Winter, as I know Mr. Spence will very strongly insist on your returning his visit at Byfleet. He is not without hopes of seeing you also at Durham; and indeed you would be pleased with it, as it is one of the most romantic places I ever saw. It is situated on four or five Hills, & the river Wear encompasses almost ye whole of it. On the North of ye Cathedral is an old Castle which is the Bishop's Palace, where ye present Bishop, Dr Trevor, has made very considerable Improvements. On the South is a large Court called the College, round which are the Dean's & Prebends' Houses, which are handsome & convenient. From the upper end of this Court, a short passage leads directly to what they call the Water-Walks, a Scene more delightful than can well be conceived. It consists of a sweet Walk on a large sweep or bend of the River, arched over with wild hanging Woods & intermingled Rocks, on a steep ascent that goes up almost perpendicular from it. There are Seats here and there on the bank of the River, & some interspersed in the retired parts of the woody ascent, affording various and delightful prospects. The whole City is surrounded with hills, not high, but pleasing; & on the other side is Pella Wood, which is a scene of the same kind with ye former, only bolder, wilder, & both more rural & more retired. But amongst all these enchanting Prospects, let me not forget, what is as much so as any of them, the Retirement of our friend at his Abbey of Finculo, about four miles from Durham. It consists of the Ruins of an old Abbey, enough of which is remaining to render it a fine venerable Object. It is situate in a romantic valley, by the side of ye River, which here tumbles along amongst rough Stones & pieces of rock; & on the opposite side is a steep craggy ascent intermingled & overhung with Woods, in a very picturesque manner. Hither we brought a cold Collation, drank your health, & heartily wished for your Company. I must conclude abruptly, for I shall not have time to finish several other letters which must go by this night's Post. I am ever Affectionately Yours R. Dodsley P.S. Pray don't neglect to return me ye Letter. It may be of Consequence. Has Mrs. Gataker yet called on You? If she should, she will well deserve your particular regard. To / William Shenstone Esqr / at the Leasows / near / Birmingham

Lapall-House 14th: Sept: 1758. Dear Sir, I heard some time since by Mr: Shenstone that you were returned from Scotland, and hope you had as much pleasure in your Expedition as you expected, of which I have heard no Acct: more than that Dr: Roebuck informed me that you and Mr: Spence were at Edinburgh when he was at Glascow, which was a little unfortunate, as his Company and Information might have been of service to you in your Tour. - I have been at Worcester Music meeting, and was extremely delighted with every Thing during my stay in that City, from whence I returned last Saturday; I met with several of my Acquaintance at the Oratorios, amongst whom was our Friend Mr: Shenstone, who staid two Days, and seemed very well pleased with the whole - Lady Coventry shone as brilliant as ever, & Mr: Beard & Frasi were the same sweet Singers as they were when I heard them four years ago. - Mr: Wilmot of Worcester desired me when I wrote to you to enquire the prizes, of the two following Books, whether they can be procured, and what Character they bear. you may find them in the list of Foreign Books at the End of the Gentm's: Magazine for December 1757. Collection Academique composer, des Memoirs, Acts, et Journeaux des plus celebres Academies, et Societies Literaries, concernant l'Historie Natural &c. Dijon The 6th: Vol: what is the price of it, and also of the former Volumes? The other Book is, Monnoies en Argent queen composent un des differentes parties du Cabinet des sa Majesty l'Empereur, depuis le plus grandes pieces jusq au Florin inclusivement - Folio Vienna. Containing all the Silver Coins of the European princes &c from 1460 to this time. engraved by M. Winkler. I have not either Time or Materials to make this Letter much longer, but shall just add that I think Mr: Shenstone & you have done me more honour than I have the right to claim, by the Insertion of my Verses upon his place, in the London Chronicle; indeed I was not privy to it, and they are so much improved that I have scarce Vanity enough to think them my own Offspring. Do be so kind to let me hear from you soon, & believe me ever most Affectionately, Dr: Sir Ire: Most Obliged Hble Servant John Scott Hylton Dr: Grainger, and Mr: Those: Warton have been both of them at The Leasows.

Pall mall Sept 19th. Dear Sir I am very glad to hear that you got as far from home as Worcester; I hope it was by way of inuring your self to travel, in order to enable you by degrees to reach London. I shall probably see Mr. Beard & Mr Havard before it is long, & will deliver your Compliments. I do not wonder You was pleased at Worcester Music-meeting, as I am informed there was much more eagerness amongst ye Ladies to see You, than to hear the Music. My reason for sending for the Letter, (which is much improved by your Corrections) was in order to have printed the Play; but my Lord Chesterfield has dissuaded me from it: and thinks it will still at some time or other be acted. A description of the Leasows suitable to our book cannot be very long; however, we are not in haste for it, as ye Work goes on but very slowly. Mr. Hylton's Poem is extremely pretty, and I intend to get it inserted in the London Magazine. I wish we had known You had ye least inclination to have seen Scotland; we should certainly have tried to push it forward into a resolution; and indeed it would have much enlivened those dreary hills. Durham is certainly all and more than I have described; and Mr. Spence I know would be extremely glad to see you there for a month or two; but I hope You will first pay him a visit in this Neighbourhood. I have not yet had an opportunity of seeing Mr. Henly, to know whether he still intends to part with his Pigeons: he has been in the West almost ever since I came home. As to Franks, you could not have asked at a worse time, as I have no body in Town to apply to: however I have enclosed three, & will send You more as soon as I have an opportunity of getting any. But pray never shorten your Letters to me on that account, nor lessen their numbers: do you think I should be sorry to pay double Postage? I heartily congratulate You on your friend Lord Stamford's great acquisition of Fortune. Not a word about the Elegies? I hope you have put them into Mr. Baskerville's hands; or if not, that You will bring them to Town with You. I am ever Dear Sir most sincerely Yours R. Dodsley

Pall mall Octr. 14 Dear Mr. Shenstone! The Gout in my elbow is somewhat abated, and I will try to answer the remainder of your Letter, beginning where I left off. I have spoken to Dr. Akenside: he desires his Compliments, but will not hear of printing the Ode you mention, & says he has told the Doctor his reasons. You have not mentioned your Elegies, but promise that in your next perhaps you may . Very cautiously expressed, and means exactly perhaps you may not . But after what you tell me of your several Avocations, I do not wonder that you seem doubtful whether you shall be able to do any thing else. However, I expect to see you this winter, & after what has past, which I will take no notice of even to your self, I think it probable the Elegies may travel with you in Manuscript up to London. Since I wrote last, I have absolutely fixed with Mr. Rich for the acting of my Play: it is going immediately into Rehearsal, & must be acted the latter end of next Month. And now perhaps you may think me very whimsical should I intimate that upon looking again at the Epilogue, I am not quite satisfied with it; & very unreasonable if I should desire you would try your hand about a new one. But the truth is, I should be proud of the Honour of your Name, & glad that ye Entertainment might at least have ye advantage of ending with spirit. My friend Mr. Hindley is so far from parting with his Pigeons, that he has built them a new house: but he has promised me some young ones in the spring, which he says may be likely to settle more kindly with you than old ones. In the mean time however, I have sent you by Mr Allen's Birmingham Waggon of this day, carriage paid, five pair of old ones. viz: 1 pair Fan tails, 1 Turbots, 1 Barbs, 1 Capuchins, 1 Croppers. I have sent them in a large Cage, sent a peck of Tares along with 'em, gave the Waggoner great charge of them, & hope they will come safe. The Waggon should come into Birmingham on Thursday night; but he says he shall have some repair to make in it on Thursday, so it may be Friday morning before he gets in. You will probably find them, like some other London Beauties, a little dirty and draggletail'd, but they will spruce themselves up at the Leasows: where, if they do not settle very kindly, I shall think them birds of no Taste , whatever may be their Beauty . I am Dear Sir Affectionately Yours R. Dodsley

Sunday Morng. Dear Sir I most sincerely congratuate You upon Your Success last Night - I heard with much concern, that some of ire. Friends, particularly Mr. Melmoth were angry with me for playing the Busy Body against ire. Tragedy. this I think is very hard upon Me, for I am certain that Your house was far from receiving any injury from Ours - however if You will call upon Me, & let me know, how I can support ire. Interest, without absolutely giving up my own, I will do it; for whatever You or ire. Friends may think I am most sincerely Ire. Wellwisher & humble Sert DG.

Decr. 5th. Sir I thank you for your Compliments on the success of Cleone, and could have wished You had thought proper to have put it in my power to have thanked you for contributing towards it: but I think it is not now in your own to redress the injury you have done me. You know full well that profit was but my second motive for bringing this piece on the Stage, and you have taken effectual care to nip its Reputation in the bud, by preventing ye Town, as far as lay in your power, from attending to it. As to my proposing any means in which you can now be of service to me, I hope you do not think that, after what has past, I can possibly bring my self to ask a favour of you. In short, if your behaviour to me has been right, I see no cause you have to be concerned about it; if wrong, why was it so? I am certain I gave you no provocation for it. I therefore leave it on your self to pursue what measure you may think most consistent with your own reputation; as to mine, you have certainly in this instance done all you could to lessen it. However, I beg you will believe it is with some regret I feel I cannot at present subscribe my self, with that cordiality I have always wished to be, Sir Your friend and Servant R Dodsley

Master Robert Dodsley. When I first read Your peevish Answer to my well meant proposal to You, I was much disturbed at it - but when I considered, that some minds cannot bear the smallest portion of Success, I most Sincerely pitied You; and when I found in ye same letter, that You were graciously pleased to dismiss Me from ire. Acquaintance; I could not but confess so apparent an Obligation, & am with. due Acknowledgmts Master Robert Dodsley ire. most obliged D.G

Pall mall Decr 16 Dear Mr. Shenstone I did not think it ever could happen that I should have occasion to make an Apology for not writing to You, as I am never better pleased than when so employed. Yet so it is, and I am afraid You will think me inexcusable: but when You consider the perpetual hurry I have been in for this month past, I know You will forgive me. I have such a chaos of things in my head to say to You, that I feel it will be impossible to reduce them to any order. I must therefore throw them out as they rise, and that with all the rapidity I can, as I am still very much pressed for want of time. This is the 12th. Night of the Play, & it has been received with great Indulgence. It has steamed the Tide of Fashion, which runs very strong against that House; and has supported its self against the strength and popularity of Mr. Garrick, which have been remarkably exerted against it. On its first night he acted the part of Marplot in the Busy body, a Character he had never appeared in before; and this he continued to run against it the 2d 4th 5th & 7th. Nights which at first had the effect he intended, of making the Town, who he knew would follow him, appear to neglect Cleone; and thus he hoped to have justified his former conduct in refusing it. It happened, however, that after ye 3d or 4th Night, it rose in reputation, the audiences increased, and though they have not been crowded, they have been better than have usually appeared at that House, and sufficient to induce the Manager to carry it on for his own advantage. The Epilogue was received with great applause, and I wish, for my own credit, your Letter had come time enough for me to have prefixed your Name to it ye first Edition. However, that Edition, which was 2000, was sold off the first day; and I have printed 2000 more with your Name. But what will you say to me for the alteration I have audaciously ventured to make in the close? What apology can I offer for adulterating your spirited Wine with my flat Cydar? I will make none but the Truth, which is, that I was afraid of offending the Ladies, and desirous of palliating matters with them at taking leave. The whole Town have been unanimous in blaming Mr. Garrick for his behaviour in this affair, and it has occasioned a fresh quarrel between him and me, the particulars of which are too long for a letter, but I will acquaint You with them when I see you, which, as you have got a Chaise & Horses, I hope I shall do soon after Christmas. Mr. Spence will be in Town in February, & will not be happy if he does not see you. I am glad to hear of your application to the correction of your Works: how many days did it last? Do you like the Title of Shenstoniana? Is it not now too trite? At first when I read your Dream I was amazed, and thought some God had been whispering to You in your slumbers; but I soon began to suspect, that your Inspiration was not, as usual, from Apollo, but the Post Office: & was not long ere I discovered that a certain Wren had flown that way, & sung the song of Triumph in your ear. I hope you have before now recd a book for your Self, Mr. Hylton & Mrs. Cutler. I sent them to Mr. Giles, & desired him to forward them directly. The Books you bespoke are all in hand, but Mr Montagu is very slow; however, as it is on so good an occasion, I shall not fail to hasten him all I can. I am ever Dear Sir Affectionately Yours R. Dodsley

Claverton, 20 Dec. 1758 Dear Sr I received ire tragedy of Cleone - which I shall deposit in my Archives with double pleasure - both as a valuable performance, & as a testimony to my descendants, that I was acquainted with so worthy an Author - And what can be more glorious for You, than to have entertained the whole nation in its most rational Amusement - without flattering the bad taste of the multitude or any vicious passion of the great world - ? I drew tears from Mrs Graves even by my reading of your play; so can easily conceive the Effect of it, in Mrs Bellamy's Action - which I find attested by the public Chronicles of the transactions of the town. - I have no idea of any thing more mortifying to a certain M-g-r than to see his rival Theatre crowded by the very performance, which (I'm certain) he refused throe envy to the Author - I hope Sr Mr Shenstone thought my Affairs of importance enough - to explain to you at ye Leasows - our unaccountable Behaviour - when we we were last in London - We took Lodgings for a week - but staid in town only two days - (on acct. of Mrs Graves's illness) one of which was spent in waiting on my late Patron - the other on a gentleman, who is so kind as to act as my Banker - & on whom I depended for money to carry me down again - If we take ye same Journey next Whitsuntide - Mrs Graves has determined to make our first Visit to our worthy friend in Pall-mall - I am Sr Ire affect. humb Sert. Ric. Graves P.S. I have had the Small-pox this Autumn - after escaping it 40 years - which is one reason - why I did not sooner take some notice of our rudeness when in Town -

Pall mall Febry. 20th. Dear Mr. Shenstone! How much am I obliged to you for your kind attention to my affairs? I like your idea for the Title page extremely; a Gentleman of my acquaintance, from the stage Box one night with his pencil made a little sketch of Mrs. Bellamy in the very attitude you mention, and he tells me if he can finish it to his mind, he will also etch it for me for that purpose; Hayman is desiging a frontispiece from the dying Scene, & I hope in a post or two to receive the new Edition of your Grove together with the Epilogue, & then let any Lady say if they dare that the Play is not a fine one. I am obliged to You for your Criticisms on it, & shall avail my self of them; I will consider also every thing that has been said against it in the Reviews & Magazines, & endeavour by this means to make my Enemies do me the Office of Friends. Mr. Deane has done me the favour to drink a dish of Tea with me this afternoon; he sets out for the Country on Monday next, and desire his Compliments to You. I sent you by Trimen's Waggon yesterday two sets of Letters, Burke's new Edition of ye Sublime, with two Quires of blue Paper, & I enclose with this Dr. Grainger's Letter to Smollet. I will not put Cleone to press till I hear from you again, as I am willing to do all I can towards rendering her less unworthy of that indulgence with which the Public overlooked her Imperfections. The last Edition of Sir William Temple is four Vols in Octavo Price 24s. There is a fine Edition of Montaigne in French 3 Volumes Quarto, Price 30s: and in English 3 Vols Octavo, Price 15s. You must perceive in what a hurry I write, & will therefore pardon all imperfections. I hope I shall in a little time contrive to be somewhat more at leisure. I am ever Dear Sir Affectionately Yours R. Dodsley

Lapel House 21 Febry: 1759 Dear Sir, I am so very much your Debtor, that I can scarce think I am able to compound with you if that might set me clear in your Account. - Indeed, I do not know how to exculpate myself for not writing to you long ago; and to offer up my congratulations upon your Success of Cleone, would be paying a Compliment because the rest of the World have paid it. However I was not without my Hopes and Fears for you before Cleone made her Appearance; and I can only truly say that the reputation & Fame you have thereby aquired gave me the Sincerest pleasure. I return you many Thanks for the present you made me of your Play, which, however I did not receive till a Fortnight after it came to Giles's Hands; & hope nothing of mine may ever come into his Hands again. I never liked him in my Life, I know him to be a sycophant, & a peace of mischief he intended me with Mr. Shenstone has rendered him detestable to me! But enough of this - Mr. Shenstone has sent to have an improved drawing of the Grove, I think he said, to decorate ire. intended Edition of Cleone - which when it comes out I wed desire to be set down for one or two. I dare say it will sell. - Mr. Shenstone has put me (by his own Example) upon adding a few more Books to my Collection - can you be so good to send me the following, in a Box, directed for me here, or to Mr: Iris's? Borlace's Not: Histy: of Cornwall, in Sheets, let the Cuts be a good Impression. The Elabratory laid open, Octvo: a new Book last year, bound & lettered. Edward's Canons of Criticism & the last Edition, bound, gilt, & lettered. A set of Dr: Newton's Cuts (if to be purchased) for my Baskerville's Milton. Dr: Grainger's Tibullus, bound, gilt, and lettered. Mrs: Lenox's Female Quixote 2 Vols: - bound & lettered. I want also to know the price, size, & reputation of Oudenhorp's Seutonius. The person who takes this to Birmingham, is in such haste, that I must conclude, but will write a more orderly Letter next time, if you will accept this from Dear Sir Ire: most Obliged & Obedt: Servant John Scott Hylton Poor Thomas at the Leasews, was released from all his Pain & Sufferings last Tuesday Morng: he was sensible 'till abt an Hour before he died. - Mr. Shenstone had long expected it, and therefore bore it better than he otherwise would have done. To / Mr: R: Dodsley / in Pall-mall / London

Pall mall Mar. 15th. Dear Sir I write this not to answer any of your Letters, but merely to tell you that I sent by last Monday's Waggon in a parcel directed to Mr. Hylton, Blackstone's Analysis, Collection of Farces, & a Skin of green Morocco Leather. You will wonder why I am in so much hurry that I cannot write you a Letter; the reason is I am settling my affairs, and leaving off the business to my brother, so that if you write a Letter that will not reach me till after Lady-day, you will be so good as to direct it to me at the Chinese Porter in Cockspur Street near Charing Cross. I hope the Swans came safe; they will change their colour next moulting time, & I am told will be very fine ones. I send you enclosed a proof of the Epilogue; if you have any Corrections to make, You will send them by the return of the post. The drawing of the Grove is very beautiful, vastly improved, & I hope to send you a proof of it by the next Post: The Halcyon is the prettiest thing I ever saw. I hope Grignion will do justice to them both. I have not yet got any ornament for the Title page from the Gentleman I mentioned. But perhaps it is better without, as it might have been thought overadorn'd. Hayman has made I think a very good Drawing for the Frontispiece, it is the Scene of Cleone's Death.
