column46: Oxon~ July 29 1688. Sr We reached this place on ye 11th instant, and tho~ ye weather was excessive hot, yet after ye two first days travelling grew easy and pleasant. On the Friday following (with ye advice of good friends, as Dr Dixon, and some others, and by reason of the Provost's absence, who is yett in Wales) I waited on Dr Mill with your letter, who im~ediately entered my Brother Com~oner of ye Hall: I was much averse to his being entered in that quality, but the Dr laying down the little difference in charge between a Battler and a Com~oner, and weighing that with the many advantages which would necessarily attend such an admission; and with his promises to satisfy you farther in it, I was forced to submit. The Dr professes great kindness to him, and has placed him in a good chamber next to his own: he has a very civil and ingenious chamber-fellow who was lately Batch. of Arts and Demi of Magdalene Coll. His Tutor is one Mr Codrington Viceprincipal of the Hall, a man reputed to be very sober and civil, exceeding industrious, and careful of his Scholars, and I question not but he'll be as careful of him as of any. Last Saturday I had him matriculated, and so just kept that term which ended that day. The University has got time till next Term to put yir answer to ye Quo-warranto sent agst that part of our charter relating to ye Printing and prohibiting books. Last Sunday night an express came from ye Earl of Ossery to the Vice-Chancellour to acquaint him with ye death of ye Duke of Ormond, who was our Chancellor, where upon the Vice-Chan~ called a Convocation on Monday for an election of another, and ye Earl of Ossery was elected to succeed his Grandfather: but on Tuesday a Mandate came to elect ye Chancellor of England Chancellor of ye University, which coming too late we hope it will be of no ill consequence. Bp Gifford President of Mag~. Coll~. confirmed a great many last week in ye Coll~. Chapel where they have Mass daily, and Sermons on Sundays. The report that was about ye breaking of ye brass eagle in that Chapel is false. That Coll~ is pretty full, and all Papists except 2 or 3. The Judges came hither last night, and this morning they were both at Sermon in St Marries Church, but in ye Afternoon Rotherham was at a Presbiterian meeting; and ye Sheriff was at Mass. This City got a new Charter ye other day but with what alterations is not known. This with my duty to you self I am Your very dutiful Son Hen. Fleming. For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal These.

Sr Besides a circular letter whereby I have given notice of Sr G Fc & my standing at ye next election I have also written to my more pticular friends amongst which those of Crostwhait pish are not ye least; and as I am much obliged to you for yt grt assistance I have usually had from them so I pray, to recom~end my acknowledgmts ye more to them, yt you would please to take care of ye conveyance of ye enclosed after you have sealed it. I know not whether Sr George be yet returned out of Yorkshire. I have writ him 2 letters to desire him to give such Orders to my Agents as he thinks fit. I was in hopes to have heard from you after ye Assises & of ye receipt of ye Barometer, which came by Tho: Briggs abt 3 weeks ago. I have had a late letter from Rosecastell, & am well pleased with ye hopes of seeing My Lord here, being much obliged to him for ye Countenance he gives or school at St Bees. The Citadel of Belgrade is taken by storm, ye Garrison 4000 al put to ye sword, ye D of Bavaria wounded in ye Assault & several grt officers slain - Six capts of ye D. of Berwicks Regimt cashiered for refusing to admit some Irish into their Companies. I am Sr Ire most humble Served J. Louder. Lond~ Sep. 11th 88 Sr D. Fleming. For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal Kendal Westmerland

column37: rector of Grasmere 1685, rector of Asby 1694-1728
column39: The Flemings in Oxford Being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Vol. II 1680-1690. Ed. by Magrath, John Richard. Oxford Historical Society 62. 1913.
column46: Oxon~ September. 20 1688. Sr I have here sent you my Brother George's Account, which I am confident is as moderate, as any Battler, for the first quarter. His charges will be little or nothing more then a Battler excepting tutorage, which (if one consider how negligent Tutors generally are of such, by reason of their small allowance) none can think it money ill spent. What books I have bought him are either such as I have not, or such as I cannot want: for I shall be very careful in laying out money for anything whatever, if I can possibly assist him otherwise. By this note you may partly judge what will be convenient to send him by Burnyeat, to supply him with firing, pay Battles, and procure other necessaries for all winter. The Dr and his Tutor are both so careful and kind to him, that I am sure he will never have occasion to repent his being admitted into that house. I must likewise be a humble petitioner for myself, for some money by the carrier; for by that time that he can arrive here, the sum which I brought up with me, by buying clothes, and other conveniences, will be nearly, if not altogether exhausted; and my expenses are like to be such, that less then 20l cannot defray them; yet I leave that to yourself. Our greatest discourse here is about a Parliamt, and we daily expect the writs. We have three candidates already for this University, viz. Mr. Finch who was solicitor, Sr Thomas Clergis, and Dr Masters who was formerly of New College: And if no more appear it's presumed the two first will be elected. One of ye late elected Demise of Mag. Coll~. a papist, hanged himself in his study, ye cause unknown. This day we elect our Vice-Chancellour for the succeeding year, and Dr Ironside of Wadam Coll~, is to be continued. My duty to your self, and love and service to all Brothers and Sisters, I am Your very dutiful Son Hen. Fleming. For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal-hall near Kendal These

column37: rector of Grasmere 1685, rector of Asby 1694-1728
column39: The Flemings in Oxford Being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Vol. II 1680-1690. Ed. by Magrath, John Richard. Oxford Historical Society 62. 1913.
column46: Oxon~ October. ye 21st 1688. Sr Yours by Burnyeat I received yesterday, and am not a little surprised to meet with so small a return of money. You are pleased to say in yours, that you cannot believe me to be so extravagant as to spend a years revenue in one quarter : and very good reason why you cannot, since you well know I did not bring a years revenue up with me. For as I remember you were pleased to lend me £5, which I sent hither by Burnyeat shortly after Candlemas last; and if I be not very much mistaken, it was repaid out of the first money received of Mr Brathwaite after that time, which I take to be no inconsiderable part of this revenue. And moreover all my expenses during my stay in ye country, as in some Pamphlets, linen, shoes, and several journeys (none of which but were more or less chargeable to me) were all defrayed out of this same revenue; and tho~ it went out but in small parcels, yet being many amounted to a considerable sum; and excepting one half crown which you were pleased to give me, for a new years gift, I had no other supply. Now since all yes must needs be known by you, I am jealous of some other design in sending so little then the fear of throwing it away foolishly , for certain it is, if we both stay here till the carrier come again, (which will be near upon half a year) without some further aid, we must live like fools, or worse for want. But if by clipping my allowance from £20 to £15 and from that to £6 of £7 you design to weary me out of a Coll~ life, I must needs declare that it's already done effectually: For tho~ there is no place in ye world that I admire like this, yet I desire to stay no longer, then I can with credit and out of debt. For I am so sensible of the ill effects of ticking, that I'll sooner deny myself such things as I most of all covet, and be confined to any course of life, in wilfully to throw myself into the mercy of a creditor, who may ruin me at pleasure. Therefore to avoid the necessary and natural consequents of living here without a competency, I design (with your leave) to betake myself into the country, betwixt and Christmas, leaving things here as well as my abilities will permit; and so take my leave of Oxon~ till I am in a better capacity of supplying myself with necessaries. To write news were to deceive or impose upon you, since here's nothing now but uncertainties. Great preparations are everywhere against the Dutch, whose landing is daily expected. The Bishop of Winchester came hither last night in order to ye restoring of ye old Fellows of Magd~. College. He was brought into town by about 400 horse, and a considerable number of coaches, most being scholars. Most of ye Popish Fellows are gone already; and it's expected yt tomorrow or next day Dr Hough ye President, and ye other Fellows will take possession of ye College. This with my duty to your self, and love and Service to all Brothers and Sisters I ever remain Your very dutiful son Hen: Fleming. My Brothr Goo. presents his duty to you. For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal-hall near Kendal These

column37: gentry lower: son of Sir Daniel Fleming
column39: The Flemings in Oxford Being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Vol. II 1680-1690. Ed. by Magrath, John Richard. Oxford Historical Society 62. 1913.
column46: Oxon. October 28. 88. Sr The letter you was pleased lately to send me, enclosed in that you writ to my brother, as also the other you sent me by Burnyeat, I received safely; in the latter of which you had enclosed one for the VicePrincipal my Tutor, with a Ginny in it as a token, this letter you commanded me to give him; but Sr I hope you will not take amiss my not giving it to him; for it came at such a time, as we are liker to lose him, then keep him, seeing that he hath gotten a Parsonage in the country, to which I suppose he intends to go; therefore by my brothers advise I kept it and have it by me expecting your further command about it. Sr my brothers kindnesses to me are so very great, as that a separation from him will be to me an exceeding great loss, and the cause of no small grief, now I find how great an happiness it is, to have amongst so many strangers a really affectioned brother. Sr the Fellows of Magdains College are now, to ye unutterable joy of all here, restored again; as the bonfires made upon that account doe plainly show, whose number was such as I suppose none was able to tell; so that all thing here are very well, nothing being wanting, but your blessing to, Sr Your very obedient Son George Fleming. For Sr Daniel Fleming These

column37: rector of Grasmere 1685, rector of Asby 1694-1728
column39: The Flemings in Oxford Being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Vol. II 1680-1690. Ed. by Magrath, John Richard. Oxford Historical Society 62. 1913.
column46: Oxon~ Octobr. 29 88. Sr I writ to you ye 21st instant by the Post, which I hope you have received, and to which I beg an answer as shortly as conveniently you can. My Brother Georges Tutor has had a Parsonage lately proffered him near Bristol, and he's not yet resolved whether to accept it or no; so that, since his staying in the Hall is uncertain, we thought fit not to deliver your letter till further order from you; for we shall be very careful of throwing away money foolishly, tho~ we cannot be trusted with it. As soon as I am satisfied with his resolutions you shall know them; and till then your letter and token shall lay in my Brothers hands to be disposed off as you think fit. Tho~ the Bishop of Winchester came hither on Saturday gone sennet in order to the restoration of Magl~. Coll yet by ye time he got into town, an express came for him to appear in council at Whitehall by ten of ye clock on Monday; in compliance to which he departed hence on Sunday morning early. But on Wednesday following he unexpectedly returned, and the next morning he went down to prayers, being met at ye College gate by Dr Hough and most of the old Members of yt Society: all which being done they went into ye Coll~. Hall, where the Bishp called for the butteryBook and having first struck out all the names of the Popish Fellows and Demise, ordered Dr Hough to be entered President, and the old Fellows, Demise, Chaplins, Clerks and Choristers to be placed as formerly. Two who had been Demise formerly and got Fellowships lately, being Protestants are made Demise again. But Charnock, who was formerly a Fellow, and left his religion is turned out of all and suffers with those of his own persuasion. And tho~ the Coll~ has but been restored these 4 days, yet it is almost in as good order as it was a year ago; few of the house being absent. The City is likewise brought to it Primitive state. With my duty to your self and love to my Brothers and Sisters, I am Your very dutiful Son Hen. Fleming. For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal-hall near Kendal These.

column22: rector of Grasmere 1685, rector of Asby 1694-1728
column39: The Flemings in Oxford Being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Vol. II 1680-1690. Ed. by Magrath, John Richard. Oxford Historical Society 62. 1913.
column46: Rydal, October. 30. 88 Son Henry, I have yours of ye 21th instant; and as you were not a little surprised at my sending up £5 less than you desired, so let me tell you, I am no less surprised to receive such a letter from you, after I had so long a time & at so great a charge maintained you at ye University. You do very kindly & dutifully acquaint me, that you are jealous of my having some other design in sending you so little, then ye Fear of throwing it away Foolishly, And you fairly intimate that I have a design to weary you out of a Coll~. Life. I must tell you, Son, that you are under a great mistake. For I design nothing; save what may be for your good. I know what money Tom Burnyate did carry from home for you; because I have paid him for ye carriage of it, & for your Books, which might have been saved, if you intended so shortly for ye country. Before your last going from home I was told that you should say you would be here again before next Xtmas, which I then could not believe: But now (notwithstand you write there is no place in ye world you admire like Oxford) I have some reasons to give credit unto it. I did not know what money you carried up your self; only I remember, that besides ye money lent you (which you afterwards repaid) I paid money unto you, & for you, more than ye half crown you are pleased to mention. It will be no satisfaction unto me, to have you or your Brother to live otherwise at Oxford than you should do. All necessaries I would have you both to have, & for other things abate what you may; for I have many to maintain, money is scarce, & ye times are very uncertain. Your own is 40li per annum, and I will yearly add 10li thereunto so long as you shall stay at Oxford & have no other Preferment; upon which I presume, a sober man & a close student may make a shift to live without appearing like a Fool or worse. I shall not oblige you to do anything against your will, but what is your Duty. Therefore ye Lord direct you for ye best. Your sister Wilson was last Tuesday brought in Bed of a son; & they intend to christen him upon Thursday come seven-night. My blessing to Goo. & assist him what you may, which will be no loss unto you during ye life of Your loving Father D. F.

column37: rector of Grasmere 1685, rector of Asby 1694-1728
column39: The Flemings in Oxford Being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Vol. II 1680-1690. Ed. by Magrath, John Richard. Oxford Historical Society 62. 1913.
column46: November 17 88. Sr Yours of Octobr ye 30th I meet with the other day, but before it came to me I had made some preparations for a journey; And find no reason yet (if the Wars were at an end and safe travelling) why I should not go on; unless your promise of 10l~ p~ ann~ should stop me: Whereas when you were pleased to allow 20l~, I found it required good manaigmt to keep things straight; and you know 10l~ is no inconsiderable sum in a scholars pocket. I remember I did say that I designed again for ye country about Xtmas, and ye reason was because I could have no security of Mr Brathwait for my money, and moreover about yt time our agreement is at an end. For I am unwilling to venture all I have much longer where it's an accident if ever I receive one penny. I could wish to know whether it's your pleasure I should stay or no, since in your last you mention little or nothing of it; and if I must stay, how I can have ye 40l~ so secured, as to have it duly paid; which if I cannot have done, I shall not be able to come down another time. We hear the P. of Orange's army is very strong, and increases daily. Its reported that they have taken Bristol and 3 regiments of K~gs horse are gone over to them. This day we have a report yt the King has recalled his forces, and designs to have a Parliamt as shortly as may be. So with my duty to your Self, and love and Service to all with you I remain Your very dutiful son Hen. Fleming. My brother Goo. is very well and begs your blessing

column46: Rydal, Nov. 19, 88. Son Henry, Yours of ye 21st of October last I soon after received, and upon ye 30th of ye same month I returned you an Answer by ye Post, wh I presume you have received; if not, upon notice I will write again unto you. I have also received your letter of October. 29 last by Tho. Burnyate, with one enclosed from George. I am glad to hear that you are both well, & I think you have done prudently in not delivering ire Letter & Guinny unto Mr Vice-Principal; which let George keep until I shall order him otherwise. You write, - we shall be very careful of throwing money away foolishly, though we cannot be trusted with it. The former part of this I like very well, & you show a great deal of wisdom in it: But ye latter part thereof I like not so well; & I think you had done as wisely, & as dutifully, if you had omitted it; considering what sum~s of money I have trusted you with, since your first going to Oxford. I was in hope that your having been so long at ye University would have instructed you, to have writ more decently to your Father, who hath been very kind unto you. These Actings comport not either with your Duty, or Interest; and if you know (notwithstanding those Provocations) how solicitous I have been for your good (writing lately a letter unto my Lord Viscount Preston in your behalf) you would behave yourself a little more gratefully, if there were no more in ye case. Huffing & snuffing will not turn to any Account with me therefore I could wish my Friends (especially my children) not to make any use of them. The times are very uncertain, & we know not how long we shall enjoy any thing: which makes me heartily to wish you & your brother, to be sure to Fear God & to keep his Commandments; wh I think is ye whole Duty to man. The Lord bless & direct you both; and whilst you do deport yourselves as you should do you shall not want what is necessary from Your loving Father D. F. Remember me to all good Friends with you.

column37: rector of Grasmere 1685, rector of Asby 1694-1728
column39: The Flemings in Oxford Being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Vol. II 1680-1690. Ed. by Magrath, John Richard. Oxford Historical Society 62. 1913.
column46: Oxon~ Jan~. ye 19 1688/9 Sr Yours of October the 30th, as likewise that of November ye 19th came safe to me, which were the last I received. Not knowing how shortly Burnyeat may return, I have here enclosed my Brother George's accounts, which are so moderate, as I hope will prove beyond exception; whereby you may see (that tho~ I have been kept short my self) I have taken care to supply him with all necessaries. His Tutor is lately gone into ye country to view the Parsonage again, but what his resolves will be, cannot be known till his return which is daily expected. We are now pretty quiet again here, being not so much troubled with the noise of Drums and trumpets, nor with daily false reports of outrages com~itted by the Irish Papists, followed with frequent Alarms, as of late we have been. This place has had its full proportion of soldiers, constantly quartering between 2 and 3000 ever since it was first taken by my Lord Lovelace, who was met at the East Gate of the City by the Major and Aldermen in their formalities, and complemented by the Recorder with a speech. Shortly after his entry he com~anded two bridges to be broke down, viz. on the East and West sides of the town, and secured the north and south sides with strong guards. The Prince of Orange was within 6 miles in his march to this town, where he designed to stay some considerable time, being before invited by the Vice-Chancellour with a promise of all the University plate; but receiving and express of the Kings departure, he took other measures, and went directly with his forces to London. Nevertheless the Prince of Denmark came and stayed 5 or 6 days, where he was met by his Princess, who were both with their retinues during their stay entertained at the University charge, which amounted to 1000l~ at least. Mr Obit. Walkers books which he lately printed are all seized by the soldiers and are to be burned shortly. The Fellows of his College sent to desire him to resign his headship, which he refuses; but what methods will be used to bring him to it, is not known. Mr Massey, the Dean of Christ-Church Coll~ fled upon the Prince of O's landing, and it's said he will be succeeded in that place by Dr Aldridge who is Subteen and Canon, and that Mr Finch Warden of All Souls Coll~ will succeed ye Dr in his Canonry. This with my Duty to your self, and love and service to all my Brothers and Sisters, I am Your most dutiful Son Hen. Fleming.

column46: Rydal, Jan. 25. 88. Son Henry, Although I have not received any letter from you since yours of Oct. 29. 88 yet now I shall acquaint you, that the Lease of your Parsonage being expired ye 6th of this month your Curate spoke to me inquireing what you would do about it; I told him I knew not, having not heard from you of a long time; but I advised him to write unto you, which he said he hath done. You had best, I think, either come down yourself, or give directions unto some to act therein. I hear Tho. Burnyeats will be for Oxford ye 14th of ye next month, & before that time I presume some of us will hear from you. Let me know how your brother Goo. is, & how he follows his studies. Tell him I hope to hear from him. Your sister Wilson's son Thomas dyed yesterday. The Lord bless you & Goo. I am Your loving Father D. F.

column22: rector of Grasmere 1685, rector of Asby 1694-1728
column39: The Flemings in Oxford Being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Vol. II 1680-1690. Ed. by Magrath, John Richard. Oxford Historical Society 62. 1913.
column46: Rydal, Fibre. 15. 88. Son Henry I have received yours of Jan. 19. 88 with your Brother George's Account therein, & you have done very well in supplying him with all necessaries, although it was with money I sent you. That you may not be kept short I have called upon Mr Brathwait, who hath sent you 20£ by this Bearer, & that Goo. may have some money beforehand, I have sent 15£ (by Tho. Burnyate) unto you for his use. I writ not long since unto you, about ye taking care of your business here at Gresmere, by yourself or some other. Your brother & sister Wilson are hugely afflicted for ye Death of their youngest son Thomas. All your other Friends are well save your brother Willia~ whose leg doth somewhat trouble him: But I hope its past ye worst. Remember me to all good Friends with you, & continue your kindness unto your brother Goo. which will be acceptable unto me. The Lord bless you both. I am Your loving Father D. F. I writ then another letter to Goo.

column46: Oxon. February ye 19th. Sr Least my so long silence should have any way though in ye lowest degre been offensive to you, those few lines are to mediate for me, and to desire the continuation of your most paternal affections to me; our news here Sr at present is but small, except that upon the 14th was the solemn thanks giving for our deliverance from the great danger we were in by Popery; upon the 16th was the Prince and Princes of Orange proclaimed at several places of this City King & Queen the Major and all ye chief of the city being mounted upon horseback; both this day and the former was concluded with ringing of Bells, making of Bonfires and with great expressions of joy; the Fellows of University College have now since Obedia Walkers being imprisoned, elected one Mr Farrar ye senior fellow to be their Master; this Sr is the greates news we have here at present; so desiring your blessing I rest Sr Your most obedient son George Fleming. For Sr Daniel Fleming att Rydall-hall ne'er Kendal. These

column37: gentry lower: son of Sir Daniel Fleming
column39: The Flemings in Oxford Being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Vol. II 1680-1690. Ed. by Magrath, John Richard. Oxford Historical Society 62. 1913.
column46: Oxon. March ye 18th 89. Sr Yours of the 15th of February came safely to my hands, as the money did also to my Brother Henry's, which you was pleased to send him for my use; of which your bounty I hope Sr you will never find occasion by my behaviour to repent; I cannot but with shame confess that your so paternal affection doth by much surmount all the returns a filal obedience though unparalleled is able to make, yet I shall endeavour as far as possible to emulat your virtues and excel your love by my obedience; these Sr your kindnesses I hope together with your blessings you will be pleased to continue to me as long as I may justly subscribe myself Sr Your most obedient Son George Fleming. Sr I shall want a new suit before that the Carrier come again to Oxford; therefore I desire you let my Brother know your pleasure in it. For Sr Daniel Foaming att Rydall. These

column46: Oxford May ye 4th 89. Sr The letter which you was pleased to send me by my cousin Wilsons, arrived safe at my hands; in obedience to which I shall acquaint you with my progress as well in my private as public study. At my first arrival my chief studies was Logic, for the obtaining of which my Tutor read unto me Sanderson's and Du Treus Logicks, over & aboue which I myself read Aristotles Organon, and Chrackanthorps Logic with others of the same subject which my Brother furnished me with; but at present my study is Moral Philosophy concerning which I have lecters from my Tutor in Stierius Ethics; along with which I read myself Aristotles Ethics and Curcellaeus; as for exercise we have Disputations, Declamations, Recitations and other exercise very constantly. Our Principal is at present at Lundon. great numbers of solders are daily listed here, my brother and all friends here are very well, as I hope all with you Sr are in the North; Sr I hope you received my letter by Burnyeat in which I desired your pleasure about a new suit of which I stand in great need; this Sr being all at present I stand in need of, hoping you will continue your fatherly affection and blessing to us, I rest as in duty bound Sr Your very obedient Son George Fleming. For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal-Hall near Kendal These

column46: Oxon~. May ye 18th 1689. Sr I received a letter lately from my Brother William which did not a little trouble me, finding in it an account of your displeasure at my last to you, caused by my neglecting to date it, and by not returning an answer to yours in relation to Mr Brathwaite. As to the first, I am generally so very careful, and especially when you are concerned, that I should not have believed it possible for me to be guilty of an error in that kind, had it not come from unquestionable hands. And as to the other I declare that I never received that of yours, and so could not possibly return an answer to it; and moreover not thinking it proper to trouble you with such business, I writ to my Brother William in the beginning of February to desire him to agree with Mr Brathwaite for another year, not in the least questioning but yt he would have acquainted you with it: and least that should have miscarried, I writ to Mr Brathwaite himself by Burnyeat, which I presume he received. This I took to be sufficient, especially when I never heard anything to ye contrary; and if after all offence be taken, for my own justification I can truly and sincerely say, that it was designed for the best, and so may (I hope) be the sooner pardoned. The Act of Parliament for taking the oaths has been published some time ago, and very few here seems to decline the taking of them: and its said that such as doe, must subscribe a declaration in place of ye oaths. Mr Allan Fisher had a Parsonage of about 100£ p~ ann~ given him last week by the College, for which he must quit his Fellowship. A critical history of ye New-testament by Father Simon was published this week. This with my duty to your self, and love to all my Brothers and Sisters, I am Your very obedient Son Hen. Fleming. For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal-hall near Kendal These.

Ever honoured Sr As it is my Ambition to serve you with my utmost industry so I resolve to doe it with ffreedom and sincerity, ffor I look upon it as belonging to my Duty to acquaint Parents with what grounds I have for my ffears as well as hopes of their Sons. Truth is therefore Sr I have had some obscure intimations of your two elder sons under my care to be a little inclined to drink, upon which score I have given them several sharp reproofs and told them how much I abhorrd, and how little I would endure that vice in any of my scholars, especially in them because it would render them so far degenerate from that great example of sobriety as well as Learning from whom they derived their Birth; and to whom I owe all the Honour, and observance I can possibly show. I hope the vice hath yet got but little root, for it hath been practised but seldom, and very privately, and a timely admonition from you may make my reproofs more successful and work a thorough reformation. I have added likewise much towards it I believe by parting with the chief ring-leader since they went home. Sr my own Duty in my calling, and the great Regard I owe unto you, put me upon this discovery which I hope you will not take in ill part. I always praesum'd that it was your mind that your sons should be strictly kept to their work and from all appearance of vice which is one reason of my present ffreedom with you. I humble beg a line from you that I may for the future fully understand your pleasure, which shall very readily be observed by Honoured Sr Your most faithful humble served Posthumus Wharton May 22d 1689. This ffor the Worshipful Sr Daniel ffleming Knight at Rydal with care

column46: Oxon July ye 20, 89 Sr I have received yours by London, yet but very lately; as the other also which you was pleased to send me by this Bearer. I am very glad to hear the account that I gave you of my progress in those sciences which are here to be acquired, is so pleasing to you, the increasing of which is my greatest ambition. Sr since my last I have read over the never too much to be praised Moral Philosophy; which I shall as much as in me lays practice as well as study: now by the directions of my Tutor (who this next week leaves that Hall) I have read most part of Justinians Institutions, being an Epitome of the Civil Law. I having now Sr made this progress, do most humbly desire you would be pleased to acquaint me what particular study you think fitting I should follow, that in it I may fix as yet my wandering thoughts: but if so be you are so graciously pleased as to leave it to my own election, my choice should be the Common Law, as being that which I always, even from my childhood, but now much more admire; this Sr I hope you will let me study, if so be you can find no inconveniences in it, as being most agreeable to my inclinations. Sr my Brother hath got me a new suit and as reasonable as he could; now Sr desiring the continuation of your favours to me, and your blessing; I rest Sr Your very obedient Son and Servant George Fleming. Sr I desire to know what it is your pleasure to do with the Guinny you was pleased to send the late Vice-Principal, wh. I by your orders have by me. For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal These.

column37: rector of Grasmere 1685, rector of Asby 1694-1728

column46: Oxon~ July 22 89. Sr Yours of May the 13 enclosed in one to my Cousin Fletcher I received about three weeks ago; and since by the Bearer hereof Tho. Burnyeat I have received one of June 20th with 20£. By which I understand that mine with my Brother Goo's account bearing the same date with your last, fell short of reaching you before the carriers departure. I am sorry to find Mr Brathwait so backward in performing his conditions; for it cannot be for want of money that 3£. 10s was sent instead of 20£; since ye Easter book itself generally exceeds 20£. But however if you had not been pleased to have given some assistance at this time I had certainly met with an intolerable disappointment. My Brothr Goo. will loose his Tutor very shortly, yet I hope he'll rather get by the change: for he who is to succeed is one Mr Kennet Master of Arts of the same Hall, a very sober, civil and ingenious man. I find my Brother at all times to be very sober and studious, which I think is manifest fro~ his being constantly (but when public exercise in ye Hall or Prayers or suchlike requires his absence) in his chamber; from ye many books he reads, the good account he gives of them, and the collections he makes out of them, and lastly from ye good character the Principal and his Tutor have all along given him. Ever since he came he has had a Catalogue of my Books, whereby he may make choice of such as he has a mind to peruse. On the Seventh of this instant several of our College received ye Sacrament and the day following making use of the certificate you sent we took the Oaths and subscribed ye declaration, ye Quarter Sessions for this City beginning that day; where likewise about 50 or 60 scholars and townsmen did ye like; but since that day I do not hear of any yt receives the Sacrament before ye taking of the Oaths, tho~ the Sessions (which are held twice every week for that purpose) are constantly crowded with Heads and Fellows of Colleges: for as I am informed Lt Ch. Justice Holt said when he was here that it was not at all necessary. I believe ye whole University will not afford above six dissenters. Father Simon's Critical History of New-testament is sold here for 5s bound. This with my duty to your self, and love and service to all with you, I am Your very dutiful Son Hen. Fleming. The President and Fellows of Magdalene College took the Oaths this day in a Body. For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal-hall near Kendal These

column37: gentry lower: son of Sir Daniel Fleming
column39: The Flemings in Oxford Being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Vol. II 1680-1690. Ed. by Magrath, John Richard. Oxford Historical Society 62. 1913.
column46: Oxon August ye 16th, 89. Sr I having now so good an opportunity by this bearer of writing unto you; could not in duty let it pass, though it be only to acquaint you of my brother (whose very loving affection is in no wise by length of time waxed coulder unto me, but rather with time increases) and my good health, hoping, which is my greatest satisfaction, it will find all at Rydal so also: Sr I have now changed my Tutor as I write to you in my last letter; my present Tutors name is White Kennet. Sr here were great expressions of joy upon the news of the Princess of Denmark's being delivered of a Son; as also upon the news of Lundonderry's being relieved; the noise of the oaths is now over, being the general discourse, and only which lately was hear; Sr I desire you to present our service to all my brothers and Sisters; and the continuation of your favours to us, which is the only petition of Sr. Your most obedient Son George Fleming For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal near Kendall These

column22: gentry lower: son of Sir Daniel Fleming
column39: The Flemings in Oxford Being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Vol. II 1680-1690. Ed. by Magrath, John Richard. Oxford Historical Society 62. 1913.
column46: Rydal, Sept. 3. 89. Son George, I have received yours of July 20. and of Aug. 16. last past, and I am very glad to hear of your Health, & of your well doing. Whilst you shall continue in ye University, I would have your chief Study to be Logic, Ethics, Phisicks, Metaphisicks, & Divinity, the last of which will be ye best for body and soul, and wherein you one may meet with ye best encouragements: For if one be a good Divine, he may probably have a good living bestowed upon him, & continue in ye University; whereas no good Lawyer can be made out of ye Inns of Court; and to keep one there above 7 years, will be a greater charge than I shall be able to perform. You do well to let me know your inclination, & I should comply therewith as far as I can: But I know yt Lawyers get little until they be very eminent, & such as shall prove so, must spend much before they be so, As concerning the Guinny, you may keep it for your own use. I am very glad to hear from you, that your brother Henry is so very kind unto you; & I hope you'll make him such returns as you can. It is ye Duty & Interest of Brethren to love another, & I heartily wish that my son Will. did so the same which would be for his credit & my comfort. I hope your new Tutor will read constantly unto you, & that your brother Henry will direct you in your studies. We have been troubled with ye Quartering of soldiers here, at Coniston, & in all this Country, who are now gone for Ireland. All here are, I thank God, very well. Your brother Will. hath lately left us, concerning whom, I shall referr you unto your brother Henry. All your Relations are in good health, & remember you. My service to your Principal & Tutor, & to all my Friends in Queens. The Lord bless you. I am Your very loving Father D. F.

column46: Oxon~ September ye 21st 1689. Sr Yours of the 3 instant I received last Monday, and am not a little concerned at ye ill news in it. As yet I have heard nothing of my brother William, which makes me conclude, that he has either taken another road, and so gone directly to London, or that your letter meeting with him at Ingleton, has put a stop to his journey; the latter of which I could heartily wish. His going away has been a long time designed, for (as I remember) he was once very near it when I was last in the country, and for what reason best known to You and Him; but it being deferred till now, I was in hopes all differences had been composed, and he resolved to stay at home. If he makes Oxford his way, I shall doe my best endeavours to diswaide him from going any further, it being not only my interest, but duty likewise to manaige with all earnestness. I have here sent my Brothr George's account, which I hope will come safe to you before Burnyeat return. If Mr Brathwaite be not more punctual for the future in sending money, I shall be forced to come for it my self, for I am now put to such a strait, upon his neglect, that if I once get free I shall not willingly entangle my self again. I have been confined to my chamber a few days by reason of gripes and sudden pains, occasioned as I presume by a cold; which I hope, by the help of Physic will be shortly removed. This with my duty to your self and love to all my Brothers and Sisters, I am Your very dutiful Son Hen. Fleming. Brother George gives his duty to you. We expect Colonel Walker here next week to take his Doctors degree.

column22: rector of Grasmere 1685, rector of Asby 1694-1728
column39: The Flemings in Oxford Being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Vol. II 1680-1690. Ed. by Magrath, John Richard. Oxford Historical Society 62. 1913.
column46: Rydal Oct. 9, 89 Son Henry, I have yours of Sept. 28 last past, & I am glad to hear yt you are well again. Tho. Burnyates began his journey from Kendal upon Saturday last, & Mr Braithwait hath sent you by him 16£ - 10s - 0d which is, I presume, all ye Rent yet due unto you from him. His next Rent-day will not be, I think, before ye sixth day of January next, & I wish that 20£ may be as well paid you, trading being so very bad. I sent you, for your Brother George, 10£ - 00s - 0d, which I hope Tho. Burnyate will pay unto you. Although Sr. Jo. Louder doth what he can to perswaide your brother William forthwith to return home, & I have writ a very kind Letter to him; yet he is so wilful as I fear he'll sell his horses & make a stay in London, until he shall ruin him self, & do what mischief he can to his Family. Divers of our Country-Sparks have made sad Exits; & I wish he may not do so too. Since you think Returns are so slow from all hands, you may come into ye Country, & manage your own affairs: for I wish all things may be done for ye best. What Books I have I will send you while you shall be here: there fore bring down no more with you than necessary; since I know yt carriage of them is dear. If you shall not leave your Study in charge with your brother George, yet I question not but that you'll continue your kindness unto him in letting him have such Books of yours as shall be convenient for him. My Service unto all good Friends in Oxford, & ye Lord bless you & your brother George. I am Your very loving Father Dan: Fleming.

column37: rector of Grasmere 1685, rector of Asby 1694-1728
column39: The Flemings in Oxford Being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Vol. II 1680-1690. Ed. by Magrath, John Richard. Oxford Historical Society 62. 1913.
column46: Oxon~ Octob~r 15 1689 Sr Since my last to you I have received another letter from my brother William, where-in he shows a great desire of coming to some conditions with you, and return from London: for he says, I am not desirous to take up money upon terms that may be prejudicial to me or those that come after me, if I could avoid it, but I cannot see my Father designs me almost any thing. I shall make him a proposal so fair as will if he agrees to it, let him have 5000£ or 6000£ in his power to dispose of towards providing for his younger children, and if he rejects it, as I fear he will, take up money and go to live at Kendal . How fair this proposal is I shall not pretend to determine; But it's easy to judge, if he takes up money, (which he will certainly doe, if not complied with in his terms) how prejudicial it will be hereafter to himself, or those that come after him, to have an estate laden with debts, which cannot possibly be small, being founded upon such uncertain security. Such proceedings has been the destruction of many great familys and estates, and there is now too much reason to fear, that yours will in no small measure suffer, if not prevented by a timely accom~odation. For he, being gone so far, and having brought himself to this extremity, he must of necessity proceed, unless you interpose. It's a good old maxim, That of two evils the less ought to be chosen ; now whether it is less, and so more eligible, to resign a part of an estate at present to an eldest son, who ought to have a sufficient maintenance out of it; or to keep it all, and by so doing force him to live upon his wits, and so hazard the loosing of it all fro~ ye family hereafter, besides ruining so many children, is no difficult task to decide. For what a miserable and deplorable case it will be at Your death, (which god alone knows when that may be) to have so many in a manner left to the mercy of an offended Brother, a Brother who has for several years believed himself to be in no small measure injured, and if forced to proceed in taking up money, for want of your compliance, will certainly as debts increase think things worse then ever: and moreover a Brother, who being so much dipped in mortgages and engagements cannot be able to be kind and affectionate, if so minded; These things requires more then a slight consideration, and I hope as terms are offered there will be no standing upon punctilios, since the event is like to be so very bad. And besides this, it can be no very indiscreet thing to avoid the scandal of it, since a great part of it (whether deservedly or no) will inevitably fall upon your head. For peoples tongues are not easiely constrained, and those that know the least are generally the most ready in dispensing there own sentiments, and when once a story has got wind, it is not very quickly stifled. I have done my best endeavours to perswaide him to moderate proposals, and I hope they'll be such, as you'll quickly comply withal. If I have been too tedious, or write too much, the great trouble that I am in, that things are so very bad, may I hope in part atone for the fault. This with my duty to your self, and love to all my Brothers and Sisters, I am Your very dutiful Son Hen. Fleming. This night I received Yours by Thomas Burnyeat, and was in hopes to have had some addition to the money Mr Brathwait was to send, but now finding that 10£ p~ ann~ is clearly lost, and that I cannot live here creditably without it, I'll even resign the other 10£, and live as I can on my own in the country; which I'll take care to doe by the year be out with Mr Brathwait, if I borrow money for my journey, which I believe I must; unless I have some further supply this winter. For Sr Daniel Fleming att Rydal-hall near Kendal These By ye way of London.

column46: Oxon~ Octob~r 19 1689 Sr I see my Brother is now resolved to go on; for last post he gave me an account that he despaired of your coming to any conditions, so that he designed to fall to work with all expedition . He is desierous of my joining with him that money may be raised upon more reasonable terms; and I can scarce see how I can civilly deny him, as long as I doe not find that you design him any thing at all. Kind letters will not maintain him, nor pay the debts which he has already contracted; and he is moreover resolved, rather then go home to be worse used then he has been, he will part with half of the estate, nay all . You may easiely stop him yet if you please, but if once he sells any part of ye estate, which he is just upon doing, it will then be too late. Therefore I hope you'll be pleased im~ediately to offer something that may hinder the ruining himself and us all. For sell he must and certainly great pennyworth whether I join with him or no. As I would not willingly have an estate thrown away for a trifle, neither would I him to want, while he may be relieved out of what he has a title too. Therefore I humbly beg that you would suddenly prevent the ruin, which must necessarily follow such proceedings. I have received yours of ye 9th instant; and if I come into the country this winter, I shall scarce think of returning in hast, unless things change. This with my duty to your self, I am Your very obedient Son Hen. Fleming. For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal-hall near Kendal These By the way of London.

column46: Oxon Novemb~: 4. 89. Sr I have received yours of Sept 3 and Octob~ 4. And in answer to the former am resolved, as in duty bound, to make my inclinations howsoever otherwise bend at all times, and in all cases conform to your most just commands; and though I cannot but confess my self always to have been mightily addicted to the Law; and more espetially now of late to have had some objections against that of my being a Divine; as being altogether conscious to my self of my inibilities for so glorious a study, and my not being able to undertake so great a charge as divines, howsoever it is for the most part looked upon, must of necessity be answerable for; yet now these objections howsoever at other times powerful with me, are but as it were trifle when as I perceive it is your pleasure I should be a Divine. But in reference to the latter I was scarce able to keep secret the sorrow I was in, to hear of my Brother Williams so strange departure from Rydal without your private. Sr I hope you will be pleased to continue your kindnesses, and blessings upon us, which is the chiefs wishes of Sr Your very obedient son George Fleming For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal These

column46: Oxon. November: ye 7th or 8th, 89. Sr It would be in a very high degre inconsistent with the most Christian bonds of filliyal obedience; for me who have been in a more spetial manner sensible of your most paternal affection; to let slip any opportunity of returning you my unfeigned thanks for the same; or not to acquaint you with the present conjuncture of my affairs; but at this time more espetially being by all ye laws both of duty and justice more emedietly obliged to let you know, in how high a manner I have here been treated by my most loving Brother, that you may in some kind, as you in your great prudence thinks most fitting, I being altogether unalbe, retaliate those many, those great, and those frequent kindnesses by him conferd upon me. For in a word he hath been a Brother, a Counsoler, and a Tutor, yea even a second Father unto me; so that it is not without cause, that I have with great regret heard of, but with much more shall see this his departure from Oxford; which would yet affict me in a much higher strain, but that I have by long experience found you, o Sr, to have always supplied me with whatever the most affectionate of Fathers, the most loving of Brothers, and the most kind of Friends could be capable to desire, much less perform unto me; whereupon I shall make bold, desiring the continuation of these your favours, to subscribe my self Sr Your most obedient Son George Fleming Sr my Brother hath left me a few of his books; and hath delivered me the remainder of the money you was pleased to send me, the last time Burnyeat was hear; I shall, if you please to let me have the husbanding of it, be as wary in laying it forth, as possible. For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydall These.

column46: Oxon~ Feb: 15, 89/90 Sr I received yours, and according to your orders have sent you a Catalogue of the Books my Brother hath given me since my coming to Oxford. I have here also sent you my Bill, which I hope will please you, judging the length of this quarter. Sr I am in great need of a new gown, this that I have being not at present able to hang to gether upon me; I having gotten it mendid as long as I could possibly. Sr I shall also want a new suit before Burnyeat come the next time, so that unless you be pleased to send me money this time by Burnyeat, I shall not know how to do in it. Sr all friends here are very well, and Dr Mill presents his service to you, he sent for me very lately to his chamber, and told me that there was a custom of the Hall, by which we were all obliged, to give 20 shillings, or Books aequivelant to it, to the Library or the Hall, and so to have a key of it; and this he said he woul see us all perform it, which all now have done except my self; this I hope you will consider of against Burnyeat come; and unless I perform it rather in money or Books the Principle will take it very ill; Sr I desire you would present my service to all my Brothers and Sisters; and that you would be pleased to continue your most fatherly affetion, and blessings to Sr Your most obedient Son & Servant George Fleming. For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal near Kendal. These.

column46: Oxon~. April 2 1690 Sr I have received yours by this Bearer and ye noney you was pleased to send me by him; to wit, 15£, according to your letter; I gave Doctor Mill twenty shillings, according to your command, that he might buy therewith such books as he pleased for our Library; and he there upon gave me a key; he is exceeding kind unto me in a particular manner, and of his own accord reads us a litter every Sunday after sermon in Grotius de Veritate Cristianae Religionis; I desire you Sr to return him thanks for this his care, which will without doubt augment it, for nothing is more prevailent with him then such like returns; he went last Friday for London, not as a Convocation-man, but to preach, it being then his turn. Sr, as I write in my last, I stand in great need of a new suit, it being impossible for this to serve, till Burnyeats come again, neither will thy money suffice for it, I therefore most earnestly expext your pleasure in this case, which togethe with your blessing is all that at present is desired by Sr Your most obedient son George Fleming Sr my most humble service to all at Rydal, Conistone, Parkhouse, Over-hall, and Ingleton For Sr Daniel Fleming att Rydall These

column46: May ye 4. 90. Sr I have received your letter of ye 17 April; & am glad that you are pleased to grant me a new suit, which I shall buy as cheap as I am able; but Sr the greatest want is money, for that you sent by Burnyeat will not do it, I desire you therefore to let me know your pleasure in it, as shortly as you can; Sr I shall also want a new Waistcoat, that which I have now having served me ever since my leaving Rydal. Dr Mill is yet at London; Dr Hough is to be Bishop of Oxford, though there was a strong report that Dr Mill should have had it; there hath been a great fire ne'er this place, at a Town called, to ye best of my memory, Garington, the loss amounting to some thousands of pounds, a man was there taken who was suspected to have set it on fire; Sr fearing to let the post be gone I must in hast conclude, and rest Sr Your most obedient Son George Fleming. For Sr Daniel Fleming att Rydal near Kendal These By the way of London

column46: Oxon June ye 15. 1690 Sr The Time of Tom's coming to Oxon~ being now nigh approaching, I have sent you according to your former orders, a bill of my disbursments; which I must confess amount to a much greater sum than I could heartily wish it would; but howsoever I am fully persuaded, that out of your fatherly affection, you will be pleased to receive it with your wonted candour. This Lent I performed the exercise of Under-Bachelor in the public Schools, being an exercise that is required from one whilst Vunger-graduate; it is to be done upon a several days, as you will find it in my bill, and as my Brother Henry can inform you. Dr Dixon hath been lately at Oxford, and did me the honour to come and visit me at my chamber, and inquired very earnestly after you; he was also very important with me, to come and see him at his personage (which is but a few miles from hence) I told him I should be very ambitious to wate at any time upon him yet, though he was very earnest that I should, I prescribed no set time; but he after this seeing our Principal Dr Mill got leave of him yt I should go after act; and moreover engaged my cousin Wilsons to go also at that time; they are fully purposed to go, and are very importunant with me to resolve to go along with them as the Doctor desired; but for my part Sr I am resolved to do nothing, though at so great distance, without your privety and permition; so that I shall expect your pleasure in it, being contious to my self that you know much better what is convenient and requisite for me then I do my self. Sr if so be you think fitting I should go which in part may be a preservative to my health after having been as it were sifled up so long in a cloister; and may be a refreshment to my studies, I hope you will be pleased to allow me something for it. I shall now make bold to desire you together with the continuance of your blessings & other favours that you would be pleased to give me some directions for my future studies which will be a very great furtherance to them. Sr I am Your most obedient Son George Fleming. For Sr Daniel Fleming att Rydall near Kendal These Westmourland

Wayhill June ye 21 (90) Sr Having had long experience of your kindness to me, & being informed that you have lately given a fresh instance thereof by being instrumental not only in accommodating & putting an end to a troublesome concern betwixt me & the Arch-Deacon, but also in espousing and vindicateing my right, (which every body would not have done so zealously & effectually as I perceive you did) I think myself obliged to thank you for this, as well as former favours, & should be glad of an opportunity of making some requiteall, if it ever lay in my power: but it is like to be your privilege to obleige beyond all possibility of a requiteall. I prsume (Sr) I need not tell you that I have changed my condition lately, & that I hope twill prove for the best: If I have not made a good choice att last, I must blame my self. Both the prsent Burgesses for Bristol are near related to my wife, & her Father, old Sr John Knight (who dyed about 7 years ago) was parliamt man for Bristol several years together: Her Broth is Barrister att Law, & has been so for many years, which may be of some advantage to me, if I should have anothr touch with the Town of Andover about ye ffair, or any others that deny my rights: So that it is well for the Arch-Deacon that you have adjusted matters betwixt us. He now desires that Isle empower Mr Mounsey to receive the money att the day & grant him a discharge, which shall not be refused by Sr your humble Served Tho: Dixon. These To the Right Worpfull Sr Daniel Fleming Knight att Rydall-hall near Kendall in Westmoreland prsent.

column46: Oxon. September: 16: 1690. Sr I have here sent you enclosed a Bill of my Disbursements, & hope you will be pleased to send me a further supply by Tom. Sr I shall want a load of wood, & shall be obliged to do some exercise publicly. I desire you to consider this, and to let me have so much, as yt I shall not be moneyless before another return. The Small-Pox was in the Hall this vacation, which made so many retire into the country, as yt there was none left here but Dr Mill & my self; in which time he took the trouble several times upon him, to come to my Chamber, & to see what I was doing, and to look what sort of books I had gotten, which having seen, he ordered me to buy all means Dr Sandersom de Obligation conscientiae, et juramenti, & the new Philosophy, saying he wondered I should be without them so long, being such books, as without them one could never be a good Philosopher, or capable of appearing in the public schools with any honour; now Sr I hope you will be pleased to let me have these books (without which I shall but be an Ignoramus in Philosophy) though they be of a high price, but above all I desire you to continue your fatherly affection to Sr Your most obedient Son George Fleming Sr If my Battles or expenses be over great it is to be attributed to my Cousin Browham's being here; which I hope you will excuse. For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydall near Kendal Westmourland.

column46: Rose, Dec. 22. 1690. Worthy Sr The Bearer telling me that he intends to wait on you very shortly I could not omit to return you thanks for your kind Lre, and for that notable piece of Wythburne-News you therein sent me. I must also thank you for Mr Ellis's Sermon, which I like extremely well, and have herewth returned you together with three other Observators which will afford you some Diversion being near of Kin to ye 3 former. I hear nothing yet of certainty either of Sr Chr. Musgrave's or of Sr George's Return into ye Country. Mrs Susan Fletcher goes tomorrow for Long-Newton, having obtained her father's Leave for her going. Mr. Fletcher & his Sister Mrs Alice are there yet; and I believe have no thoughts of returning till after Xmas at ye soonest. Last night (I am told) Mr Aglionby returned to Carlisle; but I can~ot hear that he has obtained any thing above, more in that he is put into the Com~ission of Peace again, and (as they say) made one of his Ma~ties learned Counsel, which I think will not signify much here in this Country whatever it may do above. I will say nothing of Public matters because I am sure you will have them at large from other hands. So wishing you a merry Xtmas & happy New-year, with my true respects & service to your self & all yours I remain ever Sr Your most faithful Sert Tho. Carliol. My wife prsents her humble Service to yorself & all her good friends at Ridal. For Sr Daniel Fleming Knight These at Rydal

Jan. 14th 1690/91. Honoured Sr I heartily wish my endeavours for your son had been so successful, that I could thence have advised his going to the University, but I am so well assured, that Learning suits not with his Genius, that I cannot (without doing violence to my own Reason) give any advice yt way; Any other becoming Employment would I believe be of much more advantage to him where Industry could doe the work, for that, I conclude, he would not be deficient in, These three, Sr, you are pleased to continue under my Care, shall certainly have it employed to the utmost, your great ffavours claim from me the best of my endeavours, and no less shall be paid by, Honoured Sr Your most faithful humble Served Posthumus Wharton. This ffor the Worshipful Sr Daniel ffleming at Rydal.

Sedber ye 24. 90. Dear Father I must needs confess that I am infinitely bound to you for your tender care over me, but espetially for one thing (which I must omit being not able to declare without a blush) that you were so pleased to bestoe on me that delightful pardon which I could scharse expect at your hand, seeing I had so much striven to displease you, being not so wise as I ought to have been, was drawn to these expenses (which you wear pleased to pardon me for) by fare promises but deceitful performents of those whom I need not hear to nominate; but I hope I shall be more causious for the futuer in chuseing of my friend. I have hear sent you the mesuers which I should have done before now but being in hast made me forget to send them, for which I hope you will not think much. We are all well this all at present from him who makes it his deli study to become the gratefulest of your sons, Roger Fleming. For Sr Daniel Fleming these at Rydal

Jan: 17th 1690/91. Honoured Sr I am solicited to give you this trouble upon the account of a young man Mr Rich. Holme, yt you'll please to grant him the Liberty of teaching to write at Hauxhead. I was easily induced (Sr) to address you in his behalf, because he is a person of whom I have had a long experience, and have found him very sober and sedulous. He was formerly my Scholar and of late years hath taught my Scholars to write, and in several other schools he hath found employment, and discharged his office with general satisfaction. If you please (Sr) to accept of him, it will be a great encouragement to the young man, and no small addition to the many ffavours already conferred upon Honoured Sr Your most ffaithful humble Served Posthumus Wharton. This ffor the Worshipful Sr Daniell ffleming Knight att Kendale

column46: Oxon. Feb. 2: 90. Sr I hope you received my letter by Tom, as also the Book; I have now sent you my Bill, and do most ardently desire, it may give you full satisfaction; which I am fully convinced it will, if respect be had to the times; in which all things, by reason of the taxes, are at extravagant prices. Sr, as for this time, I shall want a new suit, and a new studying gown; I shall also undergo public examinations in the schools, all which, Sr, I hope you will be pleased to consider at this time; they being of that nature, yt they cannot be any longer prolonged. Dr. Mill continues his kindness to me, and now of late hath mightily augmented; and ye reason as I suppose is, he hath heard my brother Richard is intended for Oxford, whom he expects to enter. Sr my cousin Browham is Chaplin to, and lives with, the Bishop of Lincoln. Sr I hope you will be pleased to present my most humble service to all my Brothers and Sisters, who now after so long a separation I shall be very glad to see, and I hope you will continue your favours to Sr Your most obedient Son George Fleming. Sr I have payed Post to London; for other-wise I cannot send a letter at present to you. Sr I have been very obnoxius all this winter to a pain in ye head, insomuch that it hath been no small affliction to me & a great hindrance to my studies; I have taken some Physic, but it doth nothing avail; I am by all advised to cut of my hair as the only preservative, but nothing without your directions; I fear it will be worse when ye weather grows hotter. For Sr Daniel Fleming att Rydall near Kendal These Westmourland Post Payed to London.

column37: gentry lower: son of Sir Daniel Fleming

column46: Oxon~ March ye 31: 91. Sr I have received your last letter, and am much more sorry to hear that there was anything in mine should give you the least discontent, then I am glad to be authorised the receiving of five pounds more. Sr as for my necessity I do not question in the least but that Dr Mill if desired would give you full satisfaction. I have received according to your letter 5£ of Tom. As for the Books you writ about I spoke to Dr Mill in relation to them; who very kindly desired me not to trouble my self about them, but to leave ye sole care to himself, so I suppose you will hear more of it in his letter. My cousin Browham is now with ye Bishop of Lincoln in the quality, as far as I can hear, of a chaplin, but in prospect of other preferment. Mr Redman & his Sons together with Mr Brow~sword was so kind as to call here in their way to London. Sr I have sent you an Oxford Almanac and desire to be accounted Sr Your most obedient Son & Servant George Fleming. For Sr Daniel Fleming att Rydall These

May 28th 1691 Ever-Honoured Sr I hope your Sons will be Scholars and all my endeavours shall be employed to hasten them to the University. my next shall point (as near as I dare) at the time when I think to have them ready, I always conclude it the most advantageous way to have scholars well furnished with School-Learning before they go to the University and I believe it is your desire that your Sons should be so. I humbly beg (Sr) that you'll please to let them know that it is your intention to send them to the College, that they may have no other thing in their thoughts, and that you'll please to oblige them to a constant diligence, both at home during this short vacation that they may perform the exercise; and read the books I have given them in charge; and also for the future; which will make their time with me shorter and sooner complete them for the Coll: I will give you no further trouble save to subscribe my Self Honoured Sr Your most faithful humble Served Posthumus Wharton This ffor the Worshipful Sr Daniel ffleming Knight at Rydal

column46: Oxon~ June ye 20th, 1691 Sr I have received the first volume of ye Fasti Oxonienses, and accordingly I have payed 15s; 5s in hand at the time of subscription, and 10s at the delivery of this first volume; I should be very glad to hear how you would have it bound. Sr I have here sent you my account, and I hope you will not take it ill, that it is something high, for as much as it is made up of nothing but what was absolutely necessary. I have now performed all pubic exercise for my Bachelors Degree, so that nothing now remains but the taking of it. Sr there is in my account 15s as a present to a Gentleman woh teaches me Mathematics, this Sr I did at the Doctors command who continues his favours to me. The Doctor intends I shall learn Hebrew this quarter, it will be chargeable, and therefore I hope you will be pleased to think upon it. I desire you to allow me something to provide fuel with against winter, for it may now be had at almost half the price, it will then be sold for, but Sr I could wish rather to winter with you at Rydall if it might be lawful; for now I have no public exercise to perform; but after that I have taken a Degree, I shall have many things of that nature to do; the Statutes allows one to be absent 2 Terms; as for Tutors they naiver trouble themselves with one (after that he is 3 years standing) except we may call it a trouble to receive Tutoridge; and I do not question but I shall be able to profit more under your and my Brothers Company, then I shall at Oxford whilst Undergraduate. Sr if I desire what you think inconvenient, I hope you will be pleased to excuse me who am Sr Your most obedient Son George Fleming. For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydall near Kendal Westmourland Theses. Post paid to London

column46: Rydal, July 1. 91 Son George The last week Tho. Burnyate came hither, & I writ unto Dr Mill & unto you by him. I then sent you 10l~i, presuming it (with what you formerly had) would serve until his next journey unto Oxford. Since his leaving this country I received yours of ye 20th of the last month, with an account therein much higher than I expected. You acquaint me, that you have received the First Volume of the Athenae Oxonienses, & Fasti Oxonienses, which I hope you'll take care to be perfect, & to be bound up (without any misplaceing) in a strong plain Bindeing. Let your Book-Binder take notice in writing how he Binds it, that he may ye better remember to bind ye second Volume in ye same manner; which is promised to be delivered this Trinity Term. I doubt not, you have given an Account of my Name, Title, & place of Abode; that it may be printed with other Subscribers; And when this Book is Bound, Let Tho. Burnyate bring it hither safely unto me. I shall be very glad to see you here at Rydal, since you do desire it; and if Tho. Burnyate can now furnish you with an Horse &c. you may come down with him, in case your most worthy Principal shall approve of it. Pray give my best service unto him, to all my good Friends at Queens, & to Mr Todd, if he be be in Town. The Lord bless you in all your undertakeings; & whines you shall come down, take care to leave all your Books, &c. with a Trusty Friend or Relation, Bringing a Catalogue of them with you. I am Your loving Father D. F.

column46: Oxon July 16th 91. Sr I am very sorry my last came not to your hands before this carriers journey for Oxford: and yt upon a twofold account, for ye first place being thereby deprived of having your directions about the binding your Athenae Oxonienses (which at length I venterd upon, & have here sent you, & as well bound as I could possibly have it; But the other is his coming before you understood ye posture of my affairs; & so you have not thereby, (which I do not question but otherwise you so kind a Father would have) sent me a supply proportionable to my necessities; and in relation to this Dr. Mill understanding what you wear pleased to send, ordered me to take up of Tom some more, yt I might thereby be able to defray my just expenses; but I, though reduced to the greatest extremity, being conscious to my self of having offended once before in this nature would not venture upon a second attempt of this kind; but rather lay myself at your mercy, which I knew to be more befitting my condition, & I hope will be more advantage to me. Sr I think I may be so bold as to challenge anyone to show me the least tittle in which I have been wanting in my duty to you (having always esteemed your advice & com~ands so sacred, as yt I took it for granted to be impossible for me to live well & contentedly unless in the highest conformity to them) except in this one thing, expenses, in which in all humility I confess my self to have erred, and God knows how much I have been avers to it. I wish to God you could but see my heart, you would, upon this account, & out of fear to offend you, find it in an agony, & distilling drops of blood; but Sr to come to the point, which I could be glad to have no occasion to do, as I now am sorry for the contrary I do most humbly desire you would be pleased to contribute more to with you have already sent me; for this will not be able to keep me out debt till you receive this letter, and Sr to deal ingeniously with you, as I hope you will pardon with you find amiss; the cause of this my want is so. When my cousin Browham was at Oxford last Act; I was put to greater expenses by much then I gave you an account of, intending to pay the rest out of my own pocket, as also in some expenses in my public exercises, which I did not put to your account; so that it amounting to a sum~ I found my own pocket over shallow to discharge it, so that it always increasing don I what I could to the contrary at last it cast me a full Quarters Battles behindhand; so that what you now have sent me will but just set me streigt with the world; & therefore I shall be 2 Quarters battles behind before Tom come again (which in the house I must not be) unless you will be pleased in the mean space to supply me with with will be needful to defray them; & I hear promise if you will speedily do it, & set me clear; not only for ye future to extenuate my expenses to your full satisfaciton, but also augment my studies of which I will give you a specimen in whatever you shall desire. Sr I desire you to let me hear as soon as you can, for my occasions desire no less, & you shall always find me, as I must confess you have hitherto, one of ye most dear, so Your most obedient son, & devoted servant G. Fleming. Sr I do not question but take up though Tom be not hear with moneys you shall think fit till Tom come again. Sr I hope you will be pleased to let me in a short time se Rydal. For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal These With a Book.

column46: Rydal, Oct. 2. 91. Son George I have received your letters of ye 10th and of ye 17th of ye last month, with enclosed Account; and I am very glad to hear that you are well. Although I should be very well pleased to see you here, according to your desire, yet being disappointed of an Horse, and having advised with your Brothers, Will and Henry, who think it will be much more for your credit and advantage to continue at Oxford until you shall have taken your degree of Bachelor of Arts. I hope you'll be so wise as to submit cheerfully to do what may be best for you. I am in hopes to get shortly some Preferment for you; and if you continue studious, you may with ease much better fit your self for the same where you are then here in ye country. I advise you to look upon Divinity as ye main of your studies; and upon other things only by way of Recreation. Herein if you shall consult my good Friends your Principal and Mr Todd (to whom give my humble service) I doubt not they'll be pleased to direct you. I have paid this Bearer Tho. Burnyates the six pounds you had of his, and I have now sent you fifteen pounds by him, hoping that you'll be as good an Husband thereof as you can possibly: for by reason of Taxes & want of Trade, money grows every day scarcer in this Country. Be sure to loose no time whilst you are in ye University: for God only knows how long I shall live to maintain you there. If I mistake not, Dr Musgrave, ye last Dean of Carlisle, from a Com~oner came to be a Tabiter and afterwards a Fellow of Queens, and I wish you had as good Friends there to do ye like: for where you are your charge will grow daily greater. Your Brother Michael hath been indisposed of late but is now pretty well: many are sick hereabouts,& in other parts of ye country. The Lord bless you and grant that you may ever do what may be best for you, I am Your very loving Father D.F.

October. 20th 1691 Honoured Sr I have endeavoured to serve you since your sons came to Sedbergh, with what care I could, though not always with what effect I wished, I am now sorry that I should have this occasion of writing or sending to you which is to give you an account of your Son Roger's'disobedience, and my resentment of it. I send this Gentleman on purpose to give you a true relation of it, lest it should be misrepresented to you, he is one whose Son is my head-schollar, and was involved in the same circumstances with your son though not so deeply engaged. After an Hearing of the matter I hope you'll be pleased to give your son a sharp letter, and enjoin him obedience to his Master, for without that it is in vain for me to think of teaching School the rest I leave to the Bearer being in some hast and beg leave to subscribe myself Honoured Sr Your most faithful though troubled Served Posthu: Wharton This ffor the Worshipful Sr Daniel ffleming att Rydal

Dec: 18th 1691. Honoured Sr I remember some time ago you were pleased to demand what time would be requisite to make your two elder Sons R. and J. fit for the University, to which I then gave no positive answer but told you my next Letter should make some mention of it, and this is the first I have troubled you with since - which I praesume to send on purpose to answer your former Question, that Spring twelve-months is as soon as possibly wee can tolerably finish that work, and though wee have a great deal of work to doe in that time, yet if their endeavours fail not I doe not doubt but to use those measures that will gain the end; I know some of their class go to the Universe. this year but that is irregular and out of course, for their's being the second class should continue till the next year: Sr I always have and will still use my utmost endeavours to serve you being, Honoured Sr Your most humbly devoted Served Posthumus Wharton. This ffor the Worshipful Sr Daniel ffleming att Ridal with care

Lond~ Jan. 16th. 91. Sr The last Session Sr Goo. Fletcher acquainted me it was ire desire yt two of ire younger sons sld go to Sea, I told him it was very easy to dispose of one or both, understanding them to be within ye Age established for Volunteers; & accordingly I expected them, & spoke to him of them this Session but yrs this Post disappoints my hopes of serving you, if ire Sons Age be twenty four, No one yt I know having been admitted above 18, nor of yt Age unless prpared by ye Theory, ye exact Establishment being sixteen. - I also discoursed Sr George abt ire other son who is a Minister, whether if he sld come to Town it might not be for his advantage to be known to some of ye Comrs of ye Great Seal, for if he be forward and fit for ye World it were not difficult to serve him, but if more p~per for yt Country it will be harder, they having few Livings so far North. I am thus pticular yt you may ye better know if I can be useful to you being ever yrs J. Louder For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydall Kendall Westmrland
