column46: Oxon~ June 15. 97. Sr I should sooner have answered your last letter had I not been desirous at ye same time to give you an account of the receipt of ye Bill you pleased to mention in it; but that being not yet come to my hands makes me now give over all hopes of meeting with it. I am sorry you were not then, but I hope since resolved of sending James up this Act, unless you think fit to bestow him some other way, then you have formerly designed. For not to insist upon his Degree which requires his attendance here, my being now upon the place to have an eye constantly upon him, may possibly be an opportunity not again to be had, & such as may have (after this his being in ye Country) better effects upon him then any other method can be found out. I hope, Sr, you'll be pleased to excuse this my freedom it proceeding from no other then the desire I have to see James do well & if it should fall out otherwise it might not be in his power to blame any other then himself for it. Idleness, Sr, you know has never been though productive of any thing good, but on ye contrary ever pernicious to youth; this consideration, Sr, moves me to be the more earnest in soliciting his return, that he may be employed, & as he has upon your account many willing to oblige him, so he may be in a capacity to receive their favours. Once more give me leave to desire his company, yt it may not be said, yt when he was desirous to remove to a place of better instruction & example, you wear not pleased to consent unto it. What's due here in town from my Brothers seems all very clear except ye Chandlers Bill which Mr Waugh & I'll examine if you'll please to send money by Tom, & send you ye Bills & acquittances. Now after my request for my Brother, be pleased Sr to receive one for my self. What you pleased to order me by Bill, not coming to me makes my necessities the greater, living now upon credit. I must therefore desire you to supply me with what you shall please to think fitting for me, to clear 2 Quarters Battles, my Hebrew Tutor, & Bottanick Professor with both which I shall have concluded in a month or 2, add to these a new suite of clothes & other necessary expenses, to defray all these charges, Sr, will I fear require Twenty Pounds at ye least; this I hope is the last quarter I am to tarry here, & you have been all along so extraordinary kind to me, yt I cannot doubt you'll suffer me to want in this. Mr Waugh has found by my Cos. Browham's Books that Roger & James' Caution was charged to you, but James's never paid to the Bosser, so that my Cos. Browham stands charged with it. Mr Kennet's Book of ye Aniqties of Ambrosden was above my hands to purchase, being a 4o of 14 or 15 shillings price. If you please, Sr, to give orders how you'll have it bound, I shall take care of it. Mr. Terrils Book is in Folo price 20 shillings. Mr Principal is of opinion its well worth your having for as much as ye Author he supposes ye best versed in Engl~. History of any man in the Kingdom. Mr Principle never read the Book. Mr Tanner is very cautious, but told me yt he supposed it would not answer your expectation, & that its doubted by many whether he'll proceed or no any further; its true the Bookseller, after abut half of ye Book was printed off would proceed no further so yt the Author was putt to ye inconvenience of both the Charge of Printing & trouble of compiling ye work. Those who dislike the Book think he does not account right for ye Original of Govmt which is not the least part of this vol. None I meet with but grant it to contain several good things, nor any undertake to vindicate it from a great many faults. So Sr Desiring your Blessing rest Sr Your most obed~t Son to com~and Goo: Fleming For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal near Kendal These

column46: Oxon~ Aug. 13. 97. Sr I received yours of ye 6th together with my Brother Daniels ye last night, & being desirous to give you ye news of this place by ye 1st Post, went directly to enquire for Dyson ye Carrier but found he was not as in come to Oxford. Mr Teasdel one of ye Fellows of Qc Coll: came to town a few days ago not to say weeks (after amost a years being in ye North, & a little at London) & died yesterday in ye afternoon of a Fever. Mr Dale another of ye Fellows is under ye same distemper, & by ye generality given for lost. The former is much lamented by all yt knew him, & this will be by ye admirers of good Discipline to whom Qc was indebted for what it had. These, Sr, had nothing extrordinary in their distemper, but being upon this melancholy subject, I cannot pass by ye death of Mr Harding which had something singurlar in it; he was one of ye senior Fell. of Trin. Coll. Bach. of Divty a Great Tutor & of the 1st rank for Learning, & little inferior in years; this Gent having been too free with a Doctor of Physs reputation of his own Coll. was putt in ye Vice Chanl Court for it, & finding himself in danger of Beggin Pardon was so enraged at it, yt a sickness of 2 or 3 day's put a period to his life. he refused to see ye Gent whom he had wronged, & so became lamented of none but censer'd by most, So, Sr, begging your blessing I rest Sr Your most obedient son to command Goo: Fleming Sr fearing to miss ye Post, I shall answer ye rest of your letter when I have seen Dyson. I desire you would please to consider how I may send my Books ye Best & Cheapest. For Sr Daniel Fleming These.

column46: Rydal, Sept. 17. 97. Son George, I have Received your Letters of Aug. 13 & of Sept. 1. 97; & I am glad to hear that you are well, & that you have Received ye 14l~i from Dyson. The best & cheapest way, I think, to send all your & your Brothers Books & other things hither will be to send them by your Oxford waggon unto London (in Dale-Boxes, or rather made up in a Pack) with this Direction viz. For Mr Thomas Brathwait at Kendal, to be left with Mr John Gowling at the Castle-Inn in Wood-street, London, to be sent by Kendal-Carrier. Do not mention your own name in ye Directions: for then they will come hither, as Merchants Goods, much cheaper. Thomas Brathwait aforesaid hopes to be at London about ye end of the next week, where he intends to stay about a Fourthnight; and if you can get all ye things sent unto London in that time, he will take care of them, pay for their Carriage, & send them hither; otherwise he will speak to Mr Jo. Gowling to do it for him. I hear Tho. Burnyate will begin his Journey for Oxford ye last of this month, by whom I shall write further, & send you more money. As concerning ye Discharging of your Brothers old Ticks, I must refer you to my Letter of ye First of July last. I like Mr Kennets Parochial Antiquities so well, as I should be glad to hear of his Publishing his second Part, & of his improving ye History of ye Baronage of England, or ye Monasticon Anglicanum. My best service to your most Learned & obliging Principal. Enquire what Mr Tanner is doing. The Lord bless you. I am Your loving Father D. F. My Cousin Will Kirkby of Ashslack is lately dead. If you are ye waggoners servant, he'll be more careful of your Goods. column46: The copy of my letter to my son Henry of June 20. 84. Rydal, June 20. 84. Son Henry, I writ unto you not long since, which I enclosed in a Letter unto your Cousin George Fletcher; & I then acquainted you with my having received yours of Mar. 19 & of Apr. 18. last past. I have also received yours of May ye 5th, with ye Logical-Verses therein; which had been a long time in coming hither. I was the other day much surprised when your brother acquainted me with what you had writ unto him; little expecting to have had from you such a return, for my great care & charge in duly supplying you: Although I perceive you take no great pleasure in being advised by me; yet (being your Father) I must again & again acquaint you, that it will be both your Duty & Interest to be very studious & provident, & I think it will be also for your credit amongst all sober & prudent persons. The more you shall spend, ye less I am sure you'll study & Time & Treasure are more precious, than many young men do esteem them, & so long as you shall behave yourself as becomes you, I will endeavour (with Gods assistance) to supply you with what is necessary; and that is as much as, I think, you can reasonably expect from me: For you know how many other children I have, and that I must take care of all them as well as of you. What you propose, will I believe turn to ye advange of neither you nor me: therefore let us think no more of it, but endeavour cheerfully to discharge our several Duties both to God & man. I have here by this Bearer sent you 5l~i for your self with 5s to be spent by ye Fellows, & 2s - 6d by ye Tabiters. My Aunt Anderton is lately dead; but all your other Relations are (I thank God) very well. Remember me to all my Friends with you. The Lord bless you, & direct you in all your ways. I am Your very loving Father D. F.

column46: Son George, Yours I have this day received from Tho. Burnyate; & I am hugely troubled to discover by it, that my last Letter hath miscarried. Having kept a copy of it for my own remembrance, I hereunder written send you what I then writ; but since what is past is not to be recalled, you & I must now look forward. I find your charges do swell much beyond my expectation, much of which I take for granted hath no way advanced your studies, especially such charges as relate to any of ye Female sex. I have spoke to Tho. Burnyate to furnish you with 5 or 6l~i, & he hath promised me to write unto Oxford about it, and when as I shall hear yt you have received it, I will repay it unto him here in ye country. This I hope will put you on until his Return, and if this way fail, you may take up so much as shall be necessary for you of any other, & I shall send ye same up to him. I hope you'll make good your promise, of Extenuating your Expenses & of Augmenting your Studies, according to your Letter; and I shall be glad to see you here so soon as you can come down conveniently. Had my Letter reached you, you might have rid hither upon one of Tho. Burnyates Horses; which I fear cannot now be done until his next Return, & then wee will do what wee can that you may come down with him. I hope this will preserve you from all Extremities and Agonies; and yt you'll take For ye Future care not to do anything imprudent or which may incline me to doubt your Veracity. Be sure to make good use of your time now at Oxford; for God knows how long I shall live to keep you there. My best service unto your most worthy Doctor, & remember me to all my other good Friends in Queens. The Lord bless you, & keep you out of all ill company. I am Your loving Father D. F. Richard (aged about 22 years) is a good scholar & very diligent in writing, taking pleasure therein; And Roger (aged about 21 years) is strong, a good scholar, & hath a good mother wit. They all three are very sober & well disposed, & they do well understand Numeration, Addition, Subtraction, Multiplication & Division; and other parts of Arithmetic they'll soon learn, in case it shall be necessary for them. Some would have them to be soldiers; but I had rather they were placed in some other honest way of living; & if that will not do, they may then turn soldiers at sea; which will probably be ever in vogue for this kingdom. I think my son Michael would be fit for a place in ye Excise, & the other two would be qualified to be Clerks &c. Beggars must be no choosers; therefore we must be content with such honest & reputefull places as will maintain them, if our good Friends can procure any for us in ye Treasury, Navy, Customs, Excise &c. I heartily wish you an Happy New Year. I shall be willing to be at any reasonable charge to help them into a way of living, not knowing how long I shall live to maintain them. My humblest service to your self and ye two Sr Johns. shall ever remain their & Sr Your most obliged Servant D. F. I writ another Letter, not this Dat. Jan. 8. 91.

column46: Sr I return you my hearty thanks for ye Favour of your last kind Letter, and I am very glad to hear that you are well recovered of your late Indisposition. We are in great hopes, that every Post will bring us good News from Namur, & Saint Maloes; & if our Fleet shall be able to give ye French another Root at sea, it will be of great advantage unto us. Mr. Ogle (schoolmaster of Blencow) came lately hither to desire my vote for one of his Sons, a Bachelor of Arts in Scotland, to be schoolmaster of Barton, upon ye Resignation of Mr. William Airay the present Schoolmaster there; who came also hither whilst Mr. Ogle & I were discoursing that business, & who then told me, he had acquainted you, that upon a right Stating of Accounts, & payment of what was due unto him by ye Feoffees, then upon six months notice he would Resign ye school of Barton to ye Feoffees thereof: But they declining to perform ye same, he hath not now (for anything that I can discover) any thoughts of Resigning it, & he hopes that you'll not force him to it. He is generally reported to be very sober, Industrious, & a good Scholar; and for a particular Pique, its pity that yt school should be deprived of so good a Master. I have since received a Letter from Mr. Wharton School-master of Sedbergh, recommending one Sisson, a scholar of his, to be master of Barton School; and what you shall think will be ye best to be done in this case, I shall readily concur with your choosing. We have a Report, that Mr James Graham will be shortly at Levens; but I presume he'll not come thither, until he hath inured himself, & given ye Government satisfaction as to his good deportment. I believe our Barony Gentlemen will appoint July 12. at our next Quarter Sessions at Kendal, according to their Recognizances; and I shall be glad to receive your Orders as to our proceedings against them. He was of Queens College when your sons were there, He is a Master of Arts of above 7 years standing, he doth Preach very well; and if you'll grant him your Presentation to that church, I hope he'll so deport himself towards you & ye Parishioners, as that you both will be well pleased with him. Not knowing how long I may live, I hope my Good Friends will forgive me in being very desirous to have as many of my children well settled as I can in my life time, & that they'll be assisting unto me therein; which will ever oblige Sr Your most obliged humble Servant Dan. Fleming. Rydal, Jun. 29. 92. For the Honble Sr Jo. L. Baronet, a member of Parliamt at his House in Southampton-square these London.

column46: Rydal. July 29. 92 Sr Could I have imagined that you would be prevailed with to spoil a very good school-master by making him a Parson; or to impropriate the Revenue of ye Rectory of Distington, for ye Reading of a Mathematical Lecture in another Parish, I should not have given you the trouble of my last Letter. For divers are of opinion that Tithes &c have been given & consecrated Deo & Sanctae Ecclesiae ; & so being dedicated to God & his service, the taking them away from ye proper use & end, cannot be less sacrilegious, than if they were without dispute jure Divino . I am yet in great hopes, that you will not long hesitate of the granting my desire & Request, & that there is no truth in a late Report at Oxford, of your giving ye nomination of ye Clerk for Distington unto Mr Rook, and that He (with some others) are using their interest to get one Tompson of Queens to be presented by you; one who I think my son may compare with even for Mathematics, & or any other kind of Learning. I know with some to be a Gentleman & a Relation are great prejudices; but I am far from having any such thoughts of you. A living here in ye North is much more to be desired than one in ye South, for a Northern man; and if I had ye least doubted of my own Interest with you, I should have desired Sr Jo. Louder, Sr Goo. Fletcher & some other of my good Friends, to have joined in recommending my son unto you. I have another son, called George, at Oxford, A Bachelor of Arts, a good scholar, very sober & studious, & a great lover of ye Mathematics; & if he had ye encouragemt of such a Living as this of yours, would, I doubt not, in a short time make an Excellent Mathematician. If you have a mind to enquire after him, Doctor Mill can give you an Account of him, who will, I presume do it ingenuously & impartially, notwithstanding he is, as I hear, engaged for Tompson not my son. I give you many thanks for ye favour of your last Letter, & for all your other kindnesses; And having many children, I hope my good Friends & Relations will not think much at me, if I press hard for their assistance, especially in such things as they cannot fairly make any profit of, & as are in their own power to oblige me with; And whatsoever kindness you shall be pleased to do herein with either of my sons, will be ever most thankfully acknowledged by him, & Sr Your most affectionate kinsman & faithful servant D. F. For ye Right Honble. Sr Jo. L. Bar. one of ye Lords of ye Admiralty, at his House in Southampton Square London these

column46: Rydal, Aug. 22. 92. Son George, I have yours of July 16, July 19, & of ye 8th instant; & I am glad to hear that you are well. I writ unto Sr Jo. Louder, both concerning your brother Henry, & you; but I have not yet received so good an Answer from him as I hoped to have done, concerning either of you. When wee meet with disappointments, you & I must take it patiently, & say little, least it turn to our future prejudice. In time, I hope, all will do well; & you may be assured, that I will do what I can for your Preferment, if you'll continue to study closely, & fit your self for it. You do very well to follow ye Advice of ye Bishop of Serum, in his Discourse of ye Pastoral Care; which is, I think, an excellent Book, & which I hope will do much good. The sooner you are in Deacons Orders I think it will be ye better; for then if any Preferment happen you may soon be ordained Priest, & so be capable of having a Living. Fear God, & doubt not, but that all things will prove well in ye conclusion. I have paid Tho. Burnyate all his Disbursements, and I hope you'll get ye 2d Volume of Woods Athenae Oxon. to be bound like ye former, & send it down by him at his next coming from Oxford; not doubting but that you'll give it a Reading over in ye interim. Give my Service unto Mr Provost; your worthy Principal, Mr Todd, my Godson, & unto all ye rest of my good Friends with you, who I doubt not will be ready to advise & assist you, when you shall desire it of any of them. We have here but bad Hay-weather, & the Husbandman meets with Disappointments, as well as others: therefore let us all thank God for what wee enjoy, be patient, & things will prove better. Although you write in one Letter, that your Leg is very well; & in another since that it is almost well, & not troublesome unto you; yet I wish you to take care of it, & to tell me truly how it is. The Lord bless you, & direct you in all your undertakeings. I am Your loving Father D. F.

column46: Rydal, October. 7. 92. Son George, Yours of Sept. 21. 92 I have received, and I hope you'll have many opportunities of showing your self an Obedient Son, & therein never to Repent it. I am sorry to hear of your having a natural Aversion (as you call it) to that which I hope will prove so advantageous both to your Soul & Body, and if I were not in great hopes thereof, I should have saved some money which you have cost me at Oxford. I am much obliged to your most worthy Principal for giving you a Title, & for his other Favours unto you. I hope ere long to congratulate his being a Bishop. The Plasters mentioned in your Account, make me fear that your Leg is not perfectly well. Your Limborch's Theology Christiana I presume is a very good Book, it being of a great price. Let me know why you now buy six chairs; & what ye meaning is of ye Thirds for your Chamber; & what Maresius treats of. That your Determining will run so high as you mention, is much; and though I send you Thirty pounds by this Bearer Tho. Burnyate, yet I hope you'll be as provident thereof, & put it as far, as you can possibly: For you'll not easily believe, how scarce money is with me, & how much I am put to it to maintain you at Oxford. Let this Bearer bring me ye Second Volume of Wood's Athenae Oxonienses; & I am glad to hear that it will be Answered, which will probably discover more Truth unto us, if it be done by a good hand. I would have you study closely, not knowing how long you shall stay in ye University. Your brother William left us ye third day of September last, intending for ye City of Bathe (where he did see Mr Rook & Mr Todd) & to take London in his way home; presuming he is now at London, & will be here before Christmas next. I am sorry to hear of your wearing a Periwig; since it will be inconvenient both unto you & me; & I think there was no great need thereof. My humble service to Mr Principal, my Godson, & all other good Friends in Oxford. I have been some times indisposed of Late; but now, I thank God, I am very well. The Lord bless you, & direct you, in all your ways. All here remember you very kindly. I am Your loving Father D. F.

column46: Rydal, Nov. 29. 92. Sr My son George hath lately wrote unto me, That (although you were pleased to favour him with a Title), he hath missed of being ordained Deacon; which hath put him into such a Ruffle, as to acquaint me, that he never heard of any, who after one Repulse ever made a second Effort as to Holy Orders, that he would now serve Their Majesties in Their Fleet or Army, or in some place at Court. This was a great surprise unto me, having had great hopes of his well doing. I have writ unto him, adviseing him to consult you (his very good Friend) & others, in this great Affair; which may turn to his making or marring. I hope you'll continue your kindness unto him & me, to discourse him freely in this business, to look upon ye Copy of his last Letter unto me if he have one, & upon my Answer thereunto sent him by this Post, & to advise him for ye best. If I knew ye whole of this Affair, I could then better judge thereof. Give me leave to return you my most hearty thanks for your many Favours unto him; and however things shall happen, I will ever remain Sr, your most affectionate & obliged Servant D. F. For Doctor Jo. Mill These.

column46: Rydal, Jan. 27. 92/93. Son George, Having received yours by Tho. Burnyates, I writ unto you Nov 29 last past, hoping to have heard from you, or seen you, soon after. I had an intimation of your being at London, from whence I thought you would have written unto me, & acquainted me with some of your designs in & Remarks of that place. Considering your Carriage when last here in ye Country, & your Letters since, I was fully persuaded that (out of choice) you would have made Divinity your main study; and although I might recommend but never used anything (if you do me right) that looked like compulsion or importunity towards you; yet I own it, it was, & yet is, my opinion, that ye Study of Divinity is ye most honourable, & that it would in all probability prove the best for your Soul, Body, & Estate. Since what I have said, & writ to you, prevails so little, nay, since what your most Real Friend & most obliging & worthy Principal hath advised you to, takes no great place; I shall forbear moving you to any Study that you shall be averse to, nor shall I continue you any longer in Oxford, a Place which you write too rashly & unkindly of, but I shall order you to come hither with Tho. Burnyates, at his next Return from Oxford, & then you & I shall consult to do what may be ye best for us both. Although I told you in my last, yt it would be difficult to procure you a good place at Court, & that every one there could not reasonably expect to prove a Sr Joseph Williamson; yet upon your coming hither I will try what my Friends will, or can, do for you in your own way. I am sorry that I have blaimed ye Bishops Secretary as to your not being Ordained, when it was (as it now plainly appears unto me) your own fault; But of this enough. I design to send up your Brother Roger, by Tho. Burnyates, & that upon his Horse you shall come hither. I intend him to be entered in Queens College as a Battelar, and if my Godson & Cousin Henry Browham will take him for his Pupil, to recomend him to his care. Pray consult him herein, & let me hear from him & you as soon as you can. You shall leave all your Books, Bedding, &c with your Brother Roger, (unless Leyborns Cursus Mathematicus, & such little Books as you would bring hither, which I have not) until you shall settle at London, or elsewhere. I hope you'll comply with what I would have done, & then I shall continue to endeavour your welfair. My Service to all my good Friends. The Lord bless you. I am Your loving Father Dan: Fleming. I have here sent you a copy of Dr Mills letter, which pray consider very well. If you'll come hither sooner than by Tho. Burnyates, & can reasonably hire a good Horse hither, order it so, as your Brother Roger may ride back on your Horse to Oxford, who will begin his journey ye 3d or 4th day of March next.

column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal, Jan. 27. 92/93. Sr I am infinitely obliged unto you for your kind Letter, & for the good advice you were pleased to give my Son George. It is a great trouble unto me, that he will not be advised by his best Friends, & that he should be so unsettled in his Studies. I am clearly of your opinion, expressed in your last Letter; & when as he shall grow older & wiser, I hope he will be so too; but all ye danger is it may then prove full late. I have writ unto him, that I would have him come hither with Tho. Burnyates at his next coming from Oxford, & then he & I shall consult to do what may be ye best for us both. I hope you, & all other my good Friends, will continue your kindness to him & gratify him (so far as it shall be reasonable, & may be conveniently obtained) in his own way. I have usually advised & persuaded my children, as much as I thought was fitting, being not willing to make use of any compulsion or importunity unto any of them, when of ye age of Discretion; and I hope he will say (if he'll do me right) that I have used ye like towards him. Fathers who have many children must sometimes meet with disappointments: for they are certain cares, & uncertain comforts. If a son will not thrive one way, his Father must endeavour another. I am sorry that he hath given you so much trouble, & that he hath not been governed by you, when it was so much for his own honour, & advantage. I hope in time he will be wiser & more settled, & ever acknowledge his many great obligations unto you, which shall be ever most gratefully remembered by Sr Your most affectionate and obliged humble Servant Dan: Fleming. For Dr Mill.

column46: Rydal, Mar. 10. 92. Sr, Letters directed to me at Rydal in Westmerland, are usually sent by ye Yorkshire-Post unto Appleby & Penrith, where they often lye long before I receive them: But Letters directed to me at Kendal, or at Rydal near Kendal, are usually sent from London by ye Lancashire-Post, & such come to my hand much safer, and sooner. Yours of ye 16th of ye last month, being directed to me at Rydal in Westmerland came but lately unto my hand, having stayed a long while at Appleby, or Penrith. Since you are therein pleased to acquaint me, that you will either undertake ye care & Tuition of my Son Roger yourself, o place him where you will take effectual care he shall not be neglected I shall leave ye Election thereof to Mr Provost & yourself, hoping that if you be not his Tutor, such an one may be pitched upon, as will read daily unto him, & will give me a particular Account of his Disbursments, that I may ye better know how to send supplies unto my Son. The Bishop of Carlisle did so for me, & Dr Dixon did so for my son Henry; But I am afraid all others have not done so. I thank you for your kind Letter & I doubt not but that Mr Provost & you will do for my Son Roger for ye best. Upon you two I do rely, taking it for granted that my son George will contribute what lies in his power. I wish that my son Roger may get well to Oxford, ye ill ways & weather considered. My best service to my ancient Friend Mr Provost, & be assured that I am Sr, Your very affectionate God-Father D. F. For Mr Hen. Browham These

column46: Rydal, Sept. 15. 93. Sr. I have received both your kind Letters, & I am much obliged unto you for them. I wish you had given me a more full answer unto mine, that my Son might have known what to have done. I presume He will not deny you any Lawful and Reasonable Conditions; and I cannot think yt you will desire more from any man. I am very glad to hear, that you are concerned in ye Britannia; & if I may be any way serviceable unto you therein, I shall very frankly do it. You have much obliged me in being so kind unto my Son at Queens, & I doubt not of Mr Provosts respects unto him, so long as he shall continue civil and studious. I am glad to hear, that the Britannia advances a pace, & I hope yt it will be well done. My humble service to Mr Provost, Dr Mill, & all my good Friends in Queens. I am Sr Your affectionate & obliged Servant D. F. To Dr Todd these.

column46: Rydal. Oct. 3. 93. Sr Yours of ye 18th of July last came soon after unto my hand, and I gave you many thanks for ye Favour thereof, & for your great kindness unto my son Roger, who hath given me an Account of it. I have looked over your disbursements for him & I shall very willingly allow you for Tuition 20s ye quarter, although he is but a Battler, since I would have my Son well read to. I have sent unto you (by this Bearer Tho. Burnyate) Ten Pounds for ye use of my Son, which, with what he hath in his hand, will I hope serve until this Bearers next Journey. So long as Roger shall continue a good husband of his time & money, you may acquaint him that I will be kind unto him. I hear nothing but that all your Friends in ye Country are well. My service to Mr Provost, & to all other my good Friends in Oxon. I am, Sr, Your obliged & affectionate God-Father D. F. For Mr Hen. Brougham These.

column46: Rydal, Fibre. 16. 93. Sr, Many thanks for yours of Nov. 14 last past, & for your Account of the 6th instant. You are so very kind unto, & careful of my son Roger, as his brother James hath a great desire to be also under your Tuition. I hope you'll be pleased to oblige both him and me therein; and as I would have my two sons to be entered, & to live alike, so will I allow you the like apiece for them. I have sent you for them by this Bearer Tho. Burnyates 20l~i, & I have sent by him to my son Roger 10l~i, desiring that in case of any want, one of you may supply ye other. I have writ unto Mr Provost, who I hope will encourage my sons, so long as they shall act as they ought to do. Your uncle Jo. doth often join with me in remembering you, & we hope to wait upon Mr High Sheriff at Carlisle-Assises, where we fancy you'll give us a Sermon. My service to your self, & to all other my good Friends in ye College. I hope you'll not permit any of my Sons Fellow-Travellers to be Entered before him. I am Sr Your affectionate & obliged Kinsman D. F. For Mr. Henry Brougham These Having seen ye late Bishop of Lincoln's Remains, pray let me know how Genuine they be, & whether any more of them will be shortly published, & by whom.

column46: Rydal, October. 5. 94. Sr My son George having a great desire to visit Oxford again, in order to take his Degree of Master of Arts, & to fit himself for ye Ministry; I am very willing to comply with him therein, hoping that as you have been very oblige unto him, so you'll be pleased to continue your kindness in directing him in his studies, & in assisting him to his Degree. Since his being Ordained Deacon & Priest he hath met with such disappointments from some of his near Relations, as would have discouraged many a young man; but I am in great hopes, that he'll not permit what is bypassed (& out of his power to amend) to trouble him; and that, in hopes of better success hereafter, he'll rigorously follow his studies for ye time to come. He hath not been idle whilst he was here, keeping himself always well employed, & having been very studious. Some of my good Friends, I hope, will be kind unto him in helping him unto some preferment; & I doubt not but that you'll advise him the best way to fit himself for it. He hath a great Honour for you, & will I am confident be directed by you. I will only add, that I am Sr, Your most obliged & faithful Served D. F. For Dr Mill at Oxon.

column46: Rydal, Nov. 10. 94. Sr, I was in great hopes to have seen you & my cousin John, here in your Return, until I received your Letter; which came too late unto my hand for my meeting you at Kendal. I should have had some serious discourse with you concerning my 2 sons, which I forbore at Carlisle, in hopes of doing it here. Your Uncle Jack is disappointed as well as I am, he having prepared both Venison & strong Ale for your entertainment. Since you think, that 10l~i or 15l~i will serve my Sons Roger & James until Tho. Burnyates next journey for Oxford, I hope that my son Goo. will furnish you with so much; and upon your letting me know how Accounts stand with you, I will send money by Burnyates accordingly; only I must desire you, & my son George, to use your interests with Roger and James, that as little be spent foolishly as may be. Had I seen you, I should have acquainted you, that at Appleby my Lord Chief Justice desired that you & Mr Waugh would print your Assise-Sermons, & Mr Waugh in told me that you two would consider of it. I have lately seen your Printed Reflections; & to be free with you and your brother Chaplain, I think Sr P. P. will put you hard to it, unless you shall publish some of ye most useful MS of your late Patrons; which you were not (as you confess) absolutely prohibited to publish, and which some think will be convenient, if not necessary, for you to perform for a general Good. My service to Mr Provost, Mr Waugh, & all my good Friends in Queens. I am Your very affectionate Kinsman & faithful Servant D. F.

column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal, Fibre. 7. 94/95. My Lord Hearing that some of our Country Lawyers & Attorneys are endeavouring to have in every Lent, an Assises at Kendal; ye Judges to take that Town in their way from York to Lancaster; and presumeing that this new Project may give Charge & Trouble to your Lordship's officers, as well as to ye Justices & Jurors of this County; I thought it convenient to give your Lordship an intimation thereof, that you may obstruct, or forward ye same, as you shall think best. I know your Lordship is Patron of divers good Livings in this Country, & I having now three sons (George, Roger & James) at ye University of Oxford, the Eldest of whom is Master of Arts, Deacon, & Priest; I hope you'll give me leave to wish, that you would be pleased to present my son Goo. F. to one of them when as any of them shall become void. I assure your Lordship, that Hee is very sober, ingenious, & studious; & yt he wants nothing but a noble Patron & encouragement to make him considerable. I have received so many Favours from your Lordship, & you taking so much pleasure in doing good, encourage me to make this Address, hoping that you'll pardon ye trouble thereof. I shall ever remain My Lord, Your Lordships most obliged humble & obedient Servant D. F. For the Right Honble. the Earl of Thanet these, at his House in London.

column22: professional: principal of St. Edmund Hall, Oxford; clergy lower
column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal, Fibre. 7. 94. Sr, I am infinitely obliged unto you for your kind Letter, & for your many Favours unto my Son George, who is very sensible of your great kindness unto him, & who will, I hope, be directed by you in his studies, & all things else that shall be of moment unto him. Some of his Relations failing him, it will be his interest to set a greater value upon such good Friends as shall prove so unto him; and I am very hopeful, that, with ye assistance of your good Advice, his disappointments may prove to his advantage. We have had a great Storm of Frost and Snow; but it is now gone off very calmly without a Flood. I hope, yt my son George will shortly be Master of Arts, & that he will closely follow ye Study of Divinity. I heartily wish you much Health & Happiness, & I shall always remain Sr Your very affectionate and Most obliged Servant D. F.

column22: clergy lower: prebendary of Asgarby; professional: fellow of Queen's College, Oxford
column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal, Fibre. 8. 94. Sr, Yours of Dec. 29. last came soon after unto my hand, & I thank you for ye Favour thereof, & for your having so great a care of my two Sons, Roger & James. I am troubled to find their Accounts run so high; taking it for granted, that where there is so great spending there is but little studying. I hope they'll have ye wit & grace to follow your good Advice, & I doubt not but that my Son George will join with you in adviseing them to be good Husbands, & to follow their studies closely. I will allow them only 10s apiece quarterly for unnecessary Expenses, which I hope they'll comply with, otherwise I will make it worse for them: for if I cannot order them, yet I can order my Purse; which if I once shut, I shall not easily open again for them. In ye Foot of your Account you write that there Remains due to you 22l~i - 4s - 3d, which I think should rather be 2l~i - 4s - 3d: for you have omitted 20l~i in your Account, which Sum I sent you in June last, & if you have my Letter of ye 16th of that month, it will show you I then sent 20l~i unto you, for ye use of Roger & James, by Tho. Burneyate. I have now sent 20l~i more unto you, for ye use of my two sons, wh I hope you'll make serve them both, until I shall send you more. Their Battles & Expenses (not to instance in some other particulars) are extravigantly high. I hope it will be amended for ye future. My service to Mr Provost, & to all other my good Friends with you. I shall ever remain Sr, Your very affectionate Cousin & obliged Servant D. F.

column22: clergy lower; graduate student at Oxford
column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal, Fibre. 8. 94. Son Goo. Yours of ye 29th of ye last month, with your Account enclosed, is come unto my hand, and I am very glad to hear that you are well. I have sent you 30l~i by this Bearer Tho. Burnyate, hoping that it will enable you to take your Degree of Master of Arts: I have also sent by him 20l~i unto my cousin Brougham for ye use of my Sons Roger & James; and in case my Godson & you shall judge it best for my Son Roger to come hither with this Bearer, I would have my Son Roger to do it, since he neglects his study so much, as I hear he doth: In his Absence I hope your Brother James will not ruin himself. Pray acquaint my Cousin Brougham with this, having altered my intentions since I writ to him. I am glad to hear, that Camden's Britannia will be soon extant, & that Mr Gibson hath an hand in it. I presume your sister Alice hath answered your desires. I will only trouble you in giving me ye Titles & characters of good new Books; since I can have them as cheap from London, as from Oxford. Your Brother Michael hath been here ever since a little before Xtmas last, who is very much improved; stammering little, swearing nor taking any Tobacco at all, & being very free from Drinking, which are very great Accomplishmts in a Camp, as well as in a College. He hath raised about another Score of able Soldiers, & intends to march them shortly for Flanders. Such of my children as shall live soberly, frugally & dutifully, shall not want what encouragements I can give them. I have writ to ye Earl of Thanet, on your behalf; & I should have done ye like to Sr Joseph W. if I had not heard of his being in Ireland. I have received a very obliging Letter from your most deserving Principal, to whom I pray give my most hearty Service, & to all my good Friends in Queens. Make what hast you can in your Degree & Academical Studies; not knowing how soon you may be called from ye University, by my Death, or by some Prefermt. The Lord bless you & your two Brothers, & grant yt you all may do for ye best; which will be for your Reputations, as well as for ye Satisfaction of Your loving Father D. F.

column22: clergy lower: prebendary of Asgarby; professional: fellow of Queen's College, Oxford
column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal, Jun. 21. 95. Sr, I thank you for yours of ye 25th of May last, & for your honest freedom used therein. I am not a Lover of Flattery, either on my own behalf, or on ye behalf of any of my children; But a true Account of Matter of Fact is that which I like best. My Son George will I hope be with you before this, and upon ye Horse which he Rides unto Oxford, I would have my Son Roger to ride hither. A little Country Air will probably do him no harm, & I have writ to him to come hither either with Tho. Burnyates, or sooner if he hath a desire to travel another Road. When he shall begin his journey hither, pray furnish him with forty shillings to bear his charges, & pay of an Extravagant Reckoning of his of Three Pounds, which he hath desired of me. I have here sent you by Tho. Burnyates Twenty five Pounds, for ye use of my Sons Roger & James; and what it shall fall short of clearing what is due from them, I shall, God willing, send you at Toms next Journey to Oxford. I hope my son James will follow ye good example of his brother George, and not of any who is given to Debauchery, or Idleness. I doubt not you'll be often adviseing of him, & I hope he'll have ye Wit & Grace to do as he should do. My service to Mr Provost, yourself; & to all my other good Friends. I shall ever remain Sr, Your very affectionate God-Father and obliged Servant, D. F. To Mr Hen. Brougham at Oxon These

column22: clergy lower: prebendary of Asgarby; professional: fellow of Queen's College, Oxford
column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal, Oct. 4. 95. Sr, I thank you for yours by Tho. Burnyates, & for ye Account you then sent me, which was much higher than I expected. My son Roger hath so far added to his Extravagances, as he is not yet arrived here, staying with my Cousin Swettenham in Chesshier. I hope that my Son James is more orderly & studious since his Brother hath left him. Such as have given Credit to any of my Sons in their Extravagances I concur with you, that it is very fit they should stay awhile for their money, for ye preventing of ye like for ye Future, I have now sent you Thirty Pounds by this Bearer, for ye Discharge of your Accounts, & for ye use of my Son James, not doubting but that you'll be often adviseing him to be very studious & provident, & that you'll furnish him with all necessaries so long as he shall do well. My humble Service to Mr Provost, your self, & all other my good Friends in Oxford. I am Sr, Your very affectionate kinsman and most obliged Servant D. F. For Mr Henry Brougham at Oxon.

column22: clergy lower (had the living of Aspatria); graduate student at Oxford
column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal, Oct. 4. 95. Son Goo. Yours of July ye 16th last I have, and ye Books you sent me are come unto my hand: I thank you for them. I cannot yet give you any Account how ye Bishop will dispose of his MS. although I writ about them. I am sorry to hear your own money proved so bad, which will caution you in receiving another time. Mr Lawson did not call here although he came near us. Your Brother Roger is not yet come home, staying in Cheshire with my Cousin Swettenham. My son Dan. hath received yours of Aug. 16. 95, and he hath paid Mr Holmes for ye Grates. Your brother Michael, in his second attack of ye Castle of Namur, was shot in his left shoulder, with a Musket Ball, & he writ that he hoped to be well again in a Fourthnights time. We have not heard from him since Aug. 18. 95. I have yours of Sept. 22. 95, & one from your brother James of ye same date. I am glad to hear from you, that He is well & orderly, & he acquaints me that you are always ready to instruct him. It is very well done to be often adviseing him, & I hope he will have ye Wit & Grace to avoid all ill company, & to follow your good Advice & Example. I will order my son Dan. to receive what is due unto you, & to pay what is due from you, whereof he will give you an Account. I have, according to your desire, sent you by this Bearer thirty pounds, which your brother Dan may repay me as he shall receive money of yours. I was afraid that your Curate would have left you, but I now hope he will stay with you. I writ to young Goo. Wilson at London, who hath compounded for your First-Fruits, & hath paid ye First payment thereof. Your uncle Roger hath been indisposed in his Health. Here is like to be great Disputes in most places about Parliament men. All your Relations are, I thank God, pretty well. I have writ to your most worthy Principal, my Godson, & to my son James. Be sure more to fit your self well for Asp. & trifle not away your time in other studies. My humble service to all good Friends in Oxford. The Lord bless you & James. I am Your loving Father D. F.

column22: clergy lower (had the living of Aspatria); graduate student at Oxford
column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Son George I am very glad, to discover by yours of ye 10th instant, that you have found your mistake before it was too late; and I hope this will caution you for the Future not hastily to engage in anything of moment without good advice of those who do really wish you well, & are able to advise you. Upon your writing a Letter unto my Lord Bishop, I hope he will be pleased to give you Leave to be absent from Aspatrick this winter; and yt you'll provide a good Stock of Sermons now whilst you are at ye University, not squandering away your time in other Studies. I shall be glad to hear that you have received the 30l~i I sent you by Tho. Burnyate, & my Cousin Henry Brougham ye like sum for himself & your brother James. My son Roger is not yet come home, & I have not heard Lately from ye Captain. Here is a great Contest between Sr Christo. M. Sr Jo. L. & Sr Rich. S. about being Parliament men for this County. I writ to you unto London as you desired. The Lord bless you & James. My service to all my good Friends. I am Your loving Father D. F. Rydal, October. 25. 95.

column22: clergy lower (had the living of Aspatria); graduate student at Oxford
column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal. Nov. 15. 95. Son George, Tho. Burnyates hath brought me a Letter from you, & another from your Brother James; and I am very glad to hear that you are both well, & do follow your studies closely. Your Brother Michael came Post from London unto Liverpool in Lancashire, having received Orders from his Colonel. He arrived here ye 4th instant, & did go last Monday unto Lancaster to wait there upon his Colonel at his Election, ye next day, for a Parliament man for that County. No more News of your Brother Roger, who is not yet come hither. I am much obliged to Dr Charlotte for his kindness unto you, to whom pray give my service & thanks. I shall not encourage you to endeavour to be Chaplain unto ye House of Commons; that being a place of daily attendance (in reading every morning Prayers yt ye House of Com~ons sit & saying Grace every Dinner at ye Speakers) without any Allowance that I know of. Besides whosoever shall be chosen Speaker usually employs his own Chaplain, or some beneficed Clergyman in London, therein. Sometimes ye House recom~ends their Chaplain unto ye King for some preferment, & sometimes he get it in case he be a very deserving Person. A man is sure to be at a great Charge in Living at London; and it will be very hazardous in getting any Preferment. If ye last Speaker be chosen again, I have no acquaintance with him, and so am not able to help you therein, if it were worth your while to have it. I am sorry to hear that my Godson wants his Health. I have lately sent my son Daniel unto Aspatrick & Rose-Castle concerning your business; and he will give you an Account of his Journey. My Lord Bishop is content with your staying this winter at Oxford; but you must provide sermons against ye Spring: for your Curate will I believe serve but one year. My service to Mr Principal & all other my good Friends. The Lord bless you & James. I am Your loving Father D. F.

column22: clergy lower: prebendary of Asgarby; professional: fellow of Queen's College, Oxford
column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal. Fibre. 6. 95. Sr Having not heard from you this long time, & not knowing how Accounts stand between you and my son James, I have sent unto my Son George six Guineas, which will be nine pounds, & which he will deliver unto you. My fearing that you are either not well, or gone out of Oxford, made me send this money unto him; and I thought it better to send you Gold than Silver, since most all here in ye country is very bad, & little milled money of silver is yet to be got. When I shall know how Accounts do stand, I can ye better know how to make you a Return ye next time. I hope my Son James continues sober & studious & I doubt not you'll be often adviseing him, which I wish he may observe. My humble Service unto Mr Provost, your self, & all my good Friends in your College. I am Your very affectionate & much obliged kinsman & Servant D. F.

column22: clergy lower (had the living of Aspatria); graduate student at Oxford
column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal, Mar. 13. 95. Son George Thomas Burnyate brought me yours this evening, and I am glad to hear that you & James are well. Your other two Letters I have, & you should have had an Answer to them ere this, had I not been commanded into Cumberland upon ye Discovery of ye late Plot. As concerning your staying longer in Oxford, I shall be governed by my Lord Bishop of Carlisle therein, to whom you had best write & know his Lordships pleasure & what your Curate will do. And as to what relates unto your Brother James, I have a Letter from his Tutor, which is not so clear as I could wish it. I would have you to consult your Brother, as to his real Fancy & Fitness to be a Poor Child, this being ye time of making or Ruining of him; and I would have you to advise with my ancient good Friend the Provost, & with such of ye Fellows as you are well acquainted with, concerning this matter. If they shall encourage you, I would have him to try his Fortune in standing; and as concerning his Degree, there is time enough to resolve of that. If my Cousin Brougham be returned to ye College, he will, I doubt not, assist you therein. I fear, that I shall not meet with an opportunity, to send you & my Godson some money, before ye Return of your Carrier. Your Brothers, Will, & Michael, are at London. The Lord bless you all; & let James peruse this Letter. My service to all my good Friends. I am Your loving Father D. F.

column22: clergy lower (had the living of Aspatria); graduate student at Oxford
column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal, Apr. 6. 96. Son George, Having received yours of Mar. 29, 96, I am very sorry to hear of my Godson's Death; both for your sake, & my son James. I presume there will be no difference between his Executor, or Administrator, & me: for I have his Account, under his own hand, of Fibre. 1. 95; & what is since, I hope will not be much. As concerning yourself, you mention not anything whether you have writ unto ye Bishop of Carlisle, & what you have done as to your Curate, whose year will be out in ye beginning of ye next month Let me know your mind, as soon as you can, that your brother Daniel may do therein what he can for you. As to your Brother James, I wish heartily, that he would resolve to follow his Study closely, & that he would use his utmost endeavours to get to be chosen a Poor Child, hoping that then in a short time he will be fit for other preferment: But in case he will not, nor cannot, then I must be forced to take him from ye University, & God knows what will become of him. As to ye choice of a Tutor I must leave it to you & him. Pray let James peruse this Letter, and take a copy of so much as concerns him: for I have not time now to write unto him. He is of such an Age, & hath, I hope, so much Grace & Discretion, as to advise freely with you for his welfare, & to acquaint you with his thoughts. If I can return, you any money, before Burnyates his next Journey, I will. My humble service to your most worthy Principal, & to all my good Friends. Consider my Last Letter, & ye Lord bless & direct you & your Brother James. I am Your loving Father D. F.

column22: clergy lower (had the living of Aspatria); graduate student at Oxford
column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal, May 7. 96. Son George, I have sent your Brother Daniel unto Aspatrick, who hath served you there as well as he could possibly. He found your Curate very unreasonable in his demands; and I am afraid we shall not get him contented to continue another year. I hear, that my Lord Bishop is not well pleased that you come not down according to your promise unto his Lordship. Whosoever dotes upon what they want, & undervalues what they have, will never live contentedly. If you would be advised to come down shortly, & to serve your own cure, at least until you can procure a curate upon reasonable terms; I think it would be much better for you, than any Lecturers place in London that I can be able to procure you. A man who designs to be great, must not neglect little things: for otherwise he often catches at a shadow, and thereby loses ye substance. I should think it would be a recreation for you to be here sometimes, & to be sometimes at Aspatrick; & when you are so near Rose, you may more probably better your preferment. Parents can but advise, & if children will not be ruled by them, they may repent it when it will be too late. Let me soon hear from you in answer, both to this letter, and that I writ to you Apr. 26. 96. My humble service to Mr Principal, & all other my Good Friends. The Lord bless you & your brother James. I am Your loving Father D. F.

column22: professional: fellow of Queen's College, Oxford; clergy lower
column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal, May 30. 96. Sr Hearing lately from my Son George, that you are pleased to accept of his Brother James to be one of your Pupils, I return you many thanks for ye same, not doubting of your care of, and kindness unto him. Although he but a Battler, yet I allowed quarterly 20s unto my Cousin Brougham, for Reading ye more constantly unto him; and I shall be very willing to grant you ye like. I hope you'll be often adviseing him to be studious, & provident; & to have a special care in avoiding of all ill company. My service to Mr Provost & to all other my good Friends with you. I am Sr Your very affectionate Friend & Servant D. F. To Mr John Waugh These.

column22: clergy lower (had the living of Aspatria); graduate student at Oxford
column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal, Aug. 13. 96. Son George, You forgot in yours of July 27. 96. to acquaint me how much you had received of ye 20l~i I returned you by John Harrison of Kendal, for ye use of you & my son James; & you also forgot to take any notice of ye Ten Guineas I sent you by Tho. Burnyates at his last being with you. I have writ ye to Mr Waugh, which I hope will clear that Account. I have repaid unto Tho. Burnyates ye Two Guineas you had last from him. If you knew how difficult it is to receive good money, & to get it returned unto you, you would spare us therein as much as may be. If things do not mend, you will both, I fear, be forced to come into ye Country. I am troubled, that any unkindness shall be between my Ancient Friend ye Provost, & my son Henry, which may prove prejudicial unto your Brother James. The Paper of Reflections you mentioned, you have not yet explained unto me. My service to all my good Friends, & ye Lord bless you & James. I am Your loving Father D. F.

column22: clergy lower (had the living of Aspatria); graduate student at Oxford
column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal, Oct. 2. 96. Son George, Having received yours of Sept. 20, & my son James of Sept. 24. last past, I was much surprised at my Ancient Friend, the Provost, his little kindness towards my son James; and since his countrymen do not esteem him worthy to be of ye Foundation, I must otherwise dispose of him. If James will assure you, to follow his study in good earnest, to be sober, civil, & a good Husband, & to be governed by you; & If your most worthy Principal will be pleased to admit James into his Hall, you may remove him thither as soon as you can conveniently; only I would have you consult Dr Mill & Mr Waugh therein, that your Brother may fairly leave ye College, howsoever he hath been treated by some therein. I would have you to be your Brothers Tutor, if Mr Principal shall approve thereof and I shall not doubt but to receive a good Account of James his well doing, unless it be much his own Fault. Let him be a Battler in your Hall, as he hath been in Queens; & let me know truly, from time to time, how he employs him self, & improves in virtue & knowledge. I hope this unkindness may prove to your Brothers advantage, if he have ye Wit & Grace to make a Right use of it. Give my humble service to my kind & Real Friend Doctor Mill & remember me to Mr Waugh & ye rest of my Friends in Queens College. Let James see this Letter, & I shall comply with you in yours. I have sent by this Bearer, Tho. Burnyates, Twenty Guineas for your self & James. The Lord bless you both. I am, Your loving Father D. F.

column22: clergy lower (had the living of Aspatria); graduate student at Oxford
column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal, Jan. 28. 96/97. Son George I have yours of October. 14 & Nov. 10 last past, & of ye 12 instant, & I should have sooner writ to you concerning my cousin Henry Brougham's Accounts, had I heard who had been his Administrator. Mr Waugh acquaints me, that there is due unto himself upon my son James his Account, six pounds fifteen shillings & eleven pence, besides his Tuition for ye last half quarter; And that there is due, upon my cousin Henry Brougham's Account, in all Twenty three pounds sixteen shillings & three pence; in which should be allowed ye sum of Five pounds, for my sons, Roger & James their Caution-money. Although it be now very difficult to get any Returns, by reason of the great confusion now in this country about paying of money, yet I have prevailed with John Harrison of Kendal to return you another Thirty pounds, which I hope he will perform more punctually than he did ye last time. He is lately gone to London, & hath promised me to write unto you about it, When as you shall receive ye same, pay off Mr Waugh, & ye sum above said due upon my Cousin Hen. Broughams Account; But advise with Mr Waugh to whom it shall be paid, least I pay it twice over, either to some one of ye College, or Town. I have sent you here enclosed a copy of my cousin Henry Brougham's Account, which I hope will clear all disputes, upon Mr Waugh's & your considering ye same. As concerning your Brother James, I find so great charge & so little Improvement, as I cannot yet resolve of sending him again unto Oxford. However I must ever acknowledge a very great obligation unto your most worthy Principal concerning you & him. And as concerning yourself, I would have you provide to come hither with Tho. Burnyates, at his next Return, by whom I shall send you more money. The Bishop, your Parishioners & I will then expect you, & Iv hope you'll not then fail us all. I doubt not but that it will prove for your Health, Wealth & Reputation; and I shall consent to your keeping of a Curate, either Mr Overend or such other Person as you can best agree with. Your sister shall provide what you desire against your coming down. My best service to Doctor Mill, Mr Waugh, & all other my good Friends. I am Your loving Father D. F.

column22: professional: principal of St. Edmund Hall, Oxford; clergy lower
column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal, Fibre. 19. 96/97. Dear Sr, Having received your very kind Letter, I forthwith resolved to grant your Request in case my Lord Bishop would concur with me therein; whereupon I sent an Express to Rose-Castle with your Letter, and his Lordship acquaints me that he had your Letter read over to him with very great satisfaction, being extremely pleased with that very good character you therein was pleased to give of my Son George. My Lord also writes, that being always willing my Son might have time to complete his Studies at Oxford; & upon ye Account which you give he shall much more readily agree to what you requested, hoping that by Michaelmas next wee may see him (as is promised) to all our satisfactions. I heartily wish you many happy New Years, & I shall ever remain Dear Sr Your most obliged & most faithful Servant D. F.

column22: clergy lower (had the living of Aspatria); graduate student at Oxford
column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal. Fibre. 19. 96. Son George, You are, as well as I am, very much obliged unto your most worthy Principal for his very kind Letter unto me on your behalf. My Lord Bishop & I do grant, at his Request, that you may continue with him until Michaelmas next, hoping that then you'll come hither (as is promised) to all our satisfactions. I have sent you by this Bearer Fifteen Guineas, which, with what will Remain of what I last Returned you, will be I hope more than sufficient to supply you until another journey by this Bearer. As to your Curate, there will be no Governing him within any reasonable Bounds: therefore your Brother Daniel will endeavour to provide you another. Be sure you make good ye Doctors Letter; & ye Lord bless you. I have sent a charr-pot for your most Honoured Principal, & I shall pay for ye Carriage of it. I am not yet resolved of sending James. My service to all my good Friends. I am Your loving Father D. F.

column22: clergy lower (had the living of Aspatria); graduate student at Oxford
column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal. Jul. 1. 97. Son George, Your Brother James is much obliged unto you for your great kindness unto him; but I must yet consider of sending him again unto Oxford. What is pretended to be due from your Brothers, I can say nothing thereunto until I shall have a particular account thereof; and until that be done, I shall presume all to be paid. John Harrison hath lately assured your Brother Daniel, that Fourteen Pounds will be paid you by ye Fifth of this Month, to which I have added Ten Guineas sent you by this Bearer. I thank you for your Account of Mr Kennets Book of ye Antiquities of Ambrosden the which being but in 4o is highly Rated. Perhaps ye many Cuts therein occasion ye Dearness of it. If it shall only relate unto Ambrosden & thereabouts I will not buy it, but if there be much general Learning therein, then get it plainly bound, as in Calf's Leather, & send it by this Bearer, & I shall pay him for it. Advise herein with Mr Tanner, whether this Book be worth my buying. As to Mr Terrils Book, you have given me so exact an Account thereof as I will let it alone awhile. Let me know what new Books, of note, you expect shortly to be printed, and whether Sr Henry Chaunceys Antiquities of Hertfordshire be yet extant; and in case it be, then let me know its Volume, Price, & how esteemed by ye learned. Give my humble service to your most worthy Principal, & to Mr Waugh. The Lord bless you. I am Your loving Father D. F.

column22: clergy lower (had the living of Aspatria); graduate student at Oxford
column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal, Aug. 6. 97. Son George, Yours of July 21. 97. I received by ye Post, & soon after I sent your Brother Daniel unto Kendal to acquaint John Harrison with ye effect of your Letter. He was not then in Town, so your Brother lost his journey. Upon Saturday last I caused Daniel to write earnestly unto him, who that day writ an Answer, acquainting your Brother; that Mr Greame was at Kendal ye week before, who told Harrison that he had paid the 14l~i to Mr Dyson a month ago, & that Dyson promised him to pay it a week after unto you, so that Harrison doubts not, but that it will be speedily paid you. I will get Harrison to write again about ye payment thereof. I am sorry that your Oxford carrier had not money enough to pay you for Mr Kennets Book which I must consider at his next Return. He came hither last Monday & delivered me your letter & said that I should receive ye Book within a Fourthnights time. I am sorry to hear of ye failing of Parson Wilsons son, which will be a great Trouble to his Father. I have received one of ye Arch-Deacon's 2d Vol. which I am afraid will not please all persons. As concerning Du Pin, when you shall come hither, you & I will consult about the buying of one of them; & so as I may have ye liberty of Reading it over, I shall probably present you with it; however let me know, in ye mean time, ye price & number of Pages of every Vol. thereof. Let me know when we may hope for something more of Mr Tanners. I am very much obliged unto your most worthy Principal, for his great kindness unto you, to whom give my best service. The Lord bless you. I am Your loving Father D. F. Your brother Michael is well in Flanders.

column22: clergy lower (had the living of Aspatria); graduate student at Oxford
column39: The Flemings in Oxford, being Documents Selected from the Rydal Papers in Illustration of the Lives and Ways of Oxford Men 1650-1700. Edited by John Richard Magrath, D.D. Provost of Queen's College. Vol. III: 1691-1700. Oxford Historical Society 79. (1924)
column46: Rydal, October. 1. Son George, I hope you have Received mine of Sept. 17. 97, wherein I acquainted you how to send hither all your, & your Brothers Books, & other Things, by ye way of London; Such things as are not fit to be brought hither by ye Carrier, you may sell as well as you can. I have Received yours of Sept. 16. 97, and according to your desire, I have sent you by the Bearer, Tho. B. Thirty Pounds (viz. 27 Guineas, & 6s in milled Silver) which I hope will pay for ye Book of Mr Kennets you sent me hither, & will bring you a clear man out of Oxford, so that hereafter I may not hear of any more Duns. This Bearer hath promised me to furnish you with a good Horse to ride on hither: therefore I need not send you one to Oxford. Give unto your most worthy & obliging Principal my most hearty thanks for all his kindnesses unto you, with my best Service. Remember me to all my good Friends in Oxford. The Lord Bless you. I am Your loving Father Dan: Fleming.

column46: Rydal, October. 21. 98. Son William, I have yours of ye 1st, of ye 4th & of ye 11th instant, with ye Papers, & a letter from Fletcher, enclosed; and you should have sooner heard from me had I not been from home at ye Funeral of Mrs Smith, who dyed ye 6th, & was buried ye 11th of this Month. Her Corps was privately conveyed upon ye Monday in ye evening from Rose-castle unto ye Deanery in Carlisle, & ye next day she was very handsomely interred in ye Quire of ye Cathedral, most of ye Gentry & Clergy of Cumberland being there, who had Sack, Burned Claret, Plumb-Cake & cold meat; & who had gloves, ribbons, & mourning Hat-bands, and ye Pall over her Body, was carried by ye Earl of Carlisle & Sir Christ. Musgrave, by Sr Goo. Fletcher & Sr Wilfr. Lawson, & by Sr Rich. Musgrave & my self. Your Bro. Goo. F. did preach her funeral Sermon, upon Rev. 14. 13, and he came off with a general applause. At Louder my Lord, and at Hutton Sr Goo. F. told me you had writ to them, & I think you did well therein. Your Orders concerning Gougers are Notable, & I like your Certificate concerning your taking ye Oaths. I am glad you have gotten an Order for 2 Rooms in ye Excise-office, & I could wish yt you had Fletcher always quartered with you: for then he would bear you company, & you would preserve him from many inconveniences. Mr Swinburne is your kinsman by your Mother, & he is nephew to my Son Bosh. I have signed his, & Goo. Mason's Certificates; but act therein as you please. I am glad to hear of my Nephew Fletchers safe Return, & I heartily wish a good Agreement between his Father & him. Its a long time Since I had a Letter from him. I like my Son Fletchers Letter very well; & he hath already changed his hand for ye better. Every one cannot be a Scholar; for I am sure that I kept him long enough at School to have made him one: In other things he is ingenious enough. Parson Michael continues still very ill, & many think he'll not recover. I am glad to hear, that you have so quiet and orderly a quarter at ye Blew Bell: Sr Christ. P. intends shortly to be with you. The Lord bless you & Fletcher. As for new's, I will allow my Self Sixpence every week; which I hope will weekly buy Two Gazett's & Three Flying Posts, desiring that you will send me every Tuesday (Franked by ye Post) one Gazette & one Flying Post, & every Saturday one Gazette and Two Flying Posts; and I will take care to send you money for them. If you approve of this, then acquaint Mr Sawtel of ye Post Office, that he had best send no more Printed-Newes to Kendal, Mr Brownsword being dead. For other News, I hope you'll intimate them, as they shall happen, unto your loving Father Dan: Fleming. My Letter to my Son Will. F. at London, Oct. 21. 98.

December 4th 1758 Madam I rec'd the linen you sent by the waggon with the three bodice coats, without the two blankets and clouts which I desired for Jho Wigmore, No 6097, above a year old, or any reason for not sending them. The bearer hereof, being come for a child, I take this opportunity of desiring you to send me down by her (if you have them ready) to save carriage, one bodice coat for Those Orange, No 5010, and one for Jho Wigmore, No 6097, also one bodice coat more and two pincloths for Ann Drummond, No 5644, all of them above a year old. If you can't send them by the bearer, please to forward them by the Oakingham Waggon the first opportunity. Ann Lewis, who brought up the poor disturbed baby to the hospital, says you then promised her another dry child when it suited her to take one. And now that unhappy babe is dead, she send her duty to you and desire the favour of another and that you would please to let her know when to come up for one. Please to acquaint the hospital that Mary Blagrove, the nurse of the pocky child, who was thought out of danger, hath of late had very bad symptoms and that Dr Musket hath put her into a course of mercurial physic and saith, if that don't do, she must be salivated; but I hope there will be no occasion for it, as she sent me word a few days ago she thought the physic had done her good. The Hughes

Oakm, January 15th 1759 Sr I am ordered by the Reverend Mr Penington to make up the account relating to the Foundling Hospital and send them which you have herewith, which I hope will be found wright and satisfactory. If any thing be not clear, please to give me an account and I shall endeavour to set it clear. If anything is done contrary to the rules of the hospital, please to inform me. Relating to the expenses of the children, according to your request, have sent Mr Wheeler's bill for the cure of Nurse Deane and attendance of the children under her care. The reason of too apothecaries is Nurse Deane chose Dr Wheeler as being the apothecary she had some times applied to. Please to let me know if I should pay Mr Wheeler's bill or what part of it. If the governors please to allow her something for her loss of time, as I mentioned before, by seeing the bill may judge her case. Inform me what I am to do. Likewise, you have the account from South Morton of the children under Mr Penington's inspection their. Please to send some blank receipts as soon as convenient. The child Constance Jackson, No 10378, died Decr 25th with convulsions and the child Anne Henderson, No 9958, died Decr 9th with convulsions. Have herewith sent their clothes. The shows may be thought dear; the were ordered by Mr Penington to be made at Oakingham, as he thought for the best, to be strong, but I find it will not do for them. The being strong, the childreen outgrow them and are not wore out. That shows at 9d or 10d will answer better, Mr Penington ordered me to inform that, when letters come from the hospital, you'll please to direct to me as Mr Penington is at 25 miles distance from Oakingham and is attended with much trouble sending to and from Morton as it being out of any high road. I am, sr, for the Revd Mr Penington, Your most obdient Humle st J. Buns

Oakm, October 15th 1759 Sr On the other side you have the account relating to the children of the Foundling Hospital under the inspection of the Revd Mr Penington, both at Wokingham and at Morton, Barks. Likewise you have herewith the No 6573. The child died Aug 19th of consumption and No 7896, the child died Augt 26th of consumption. The clothes are kept for others that will want. No 13739, the child died Sept 3rd of fits. You have the clothes herewith. Likewise the clothes which Mr Penington sent me from Morton I have sent to you. Desire to have blank receipts sent by waggon as it is very ilconvenient to pay the nurses without them and causes much trouble. Hope the accts will be found wright. It may be asked why the shows should not be all of a price, to which I answer: them at 12d a pare are which we call homemade for strength, the others were sale shows and did not do but very little service. Likewise why the funeral expenses should be more than last year: to that, the officers of the parish have insisted on my causing an affidavit to be made, which was not done last year. Mr Penington desired me to write my opinion on allowing the nurses 3d per week for clothing as I am much more acquainted with the nurses then him. The are all willing to comply with the rules of the hospital so far as to try what the can do for the money, but I am fearful it will be much more trouble to the inspectors then now. I am doubtful whether many will not neglect to layout the 3d per week for clothes for the pore children, but make them suffer with cold for want of clothes, as many of their own do, whereas the do now keep them warm and clean clothes is allowed them. Which if they should neglect them, it wold cause much more trouble to see the are provided with nessesaryes, and may then be imposed on by their saying shush and shush things belong to the Foundling.
