column46: March 21st, 1752 Dear Peter. I am glad You & Company got safe to Your dear beloved Lichfield, & as glad that You found all well at ye Castle on ye Bridge. You need not have troubled Mr Sharpless to frank Ire Letters, for notwithstanding his Name we were obliged to pay Eight pence for it. I believe he has no right to frank any but his own Letters, and therefore you should Send nothing sent; for ye future trouble not ire Self for such kind of Trifles, will frank and send Any thing of yours for me at a small Sum - I must desire You to Enquire immediately in ye Bishop's Court, what Legacies Lady Avery left & to whom, her Will I suppose is deposited there, & she died about 3 Years ago. these are my Lt Hartington's Com~ands & I beg you'll execute 'Em directly. was it not a £50 Bank Note I gave You? such I intended it; the Reason of my asking is, that I had another in my Pocket Book & am not quite certain if I gave you ye right - must I bottle off ye Ale when it is fine, or what must I do with it besides making myself & friends merry? pray my best Respects to Mr Smart & Mr Seward. pray do not forget Mine & my Wife's Compts to ire Neighbor Mr Fletcher, we talk of him often - our best Loves to Sisters & Ire self & I am most sincerely & Affectionately thine D. Garrick P.S. The felons in Newgate I hear last Night rose against ye Keepers & have murdered some. I don't know ye Particulars.

May ye 12th Dear Peter. My Wife has spoken to Lord Hartington & in ye Strongest Terms upon Your Letter & Recommendation: His Lordship told her that he would certainly write & he should be very glad to serve this Friend of Yours, with several other Compliments too tedious here to mention , as ye Show Bills say. I shall immediately when I have finished our theatrical Campaign, & settled ye Company, determine about ye £400, & send you word - this is our last Night of acting this Season. I have sent you ye Empty Cask, we have not yet tasted our ale, as we imagine it not yet quite fit to make merry with. You promised Me before you left London, to send me My Age as it is written in ye Old Bible, with ye Erasement & interlineation, I shd likewise be glad that Sister Linney would send her Judgment upon ye matter, & as I believe she can have no particular reason to conceal her age no more than Myself, I beg she would Speak without favour to Either. George has had a bad cold, but is better, his wife is well - Draper is returned from Bath as bad as he went, I have lent him a Horse for his last resort, but I think the machine is too far gone to be repaired - My wife sends her Love to you all & I am most Sincerely & affecty yours & their's D: Garrick To Mr Garrick at Lichfield, Staffordshire.

Chiswick June 12th Dear Peter. Had there been any particular Business in ire last Letter to Me, I should certainly have answered it directly; but the finishing of ye Season, ye hurry of New Engagements, & all backed with ye damn'dest Cold that Ever made a poor Mortal Snuffle, have rendered me quite incapable of Every thing, but Signing my Name to Articles, & blowing my Nose; with ye latter of which, I have filled no less than four Hankerchiefs a Day - I am sorry to hear Sister Linney is so bad - I Could have wished that I had known it sooner, for I really think her Health should have been first considered before I have consulted many of my Physical friends about her; have told 'Em of ye Redness of her Face, & that we believe her case to be scorbutic - they think Scarborough would do well - but they think Cheltenham as well, & in some Cases better - & they say Cheltenham Water is so little altered by Carriage that if she liked it she might drink it at home - if you will send me ye Particulars of her case, I will advise with ye best, & send yo their Opinions - she must Eat very little Meat, & no salt Meat; I cannot tell how she lives in general, but I desire you would let me know - if they shd advise ye Cheltenham Waters, let her be regular with them & they must do her good by all acct. If they don't do all we Expect; I shall desire she may go ye Next Season to Scarborough, but I think ye Nearest & Easiest Remedy shd be tried first - write to me directly & you shall receive my answer for I am going to Yorkshire in a fortnight Merrial is with George, so I can give no Account of her, not having seen her for this last Week - I must desire you once more to send a Copy of my age, as it stands exactly in ye Bible with ye razure & interlineation; am not I Seven & thirty, or only Six ye last birth day? - My Love to Sister & believe Me Most affecty Yours & her's D Garrick pray write ye next post

Augt 17th Dear George. I hope before this that You & Spouse are well & quietly settled in Ire new habitation - When ye Dressing Room is finished Send me ye Bills & I'll send you ye Money - let it be pretty & worthy of my reception or tell Siss that I shall throw her & her dressing Room into ye Attorney General's Gardens. What News from ye profound Lacy? I will not give above Seven Pounds p. Week to Bland , & so far You may answer for me, if there is occasion. pray is there any hopes of Draper's recovery? is there any pain in ye Operation of Tapping? does it make ye Patient faint? how does Mrs Draper bear it? - pray remember Me to Kent and tell him that had I any thing to tell him that could divert him, I had written to him before, but what signifies troubling him for Nothing - if this does not satisfy him, let him know I will copy out a Letter from Wit's common wealth & send it to him by ye next post. What say ye Town about Messrs Taaff & Montagu's affair? Lady Burl: is obliged to you for ye Care of her Orders to ye Porter - When does Clutterbuck return to Town, does he know of Lacy's agreement with Maddox - I fancy Lacy will Exhibit him in ye little house in ye Hay market - With all my heart - anywhere so he does not pollute ye purity of Drury Lane - I hope Saunders is getting ye New Entertainment forward, for I would have it ready as soon as possible. is Woodward returned from Birmingham? My Love to him when You see him & thank him for ye Cloak bag - tell him that I hope he will take care to have good houses at ye Opening - till I come - Love to ye Lass with her round Waste, & believe Me Thy most Affect Brothr D: Garrick - pray how does My Wife's Maid Nanny, is She better than when We left her, ask her & Send me Word.

Tuesday Augst 25th Dr George I have Enclosed a Letter for Clutterbuck which I desire You'll let him have immediately, I have left ye Rose Tavern affair to Him & You - do as You think proper & I shall be satisfied. I hope by this You have fathomed ye Dirty Heart of my Partner, I expect to hear Something of Him by ye next post - You mention in ire Lettr to Me the famous Peter Wood , he may be famous for ought I know, but ye Devil take me if Ever I heard his Name before - I hope if ye Rose is taken by Us, that we shall behave handsomely to Miles , for I think he did so by Us - I could wish that You would take a ride to Ealing & inspect ye house & premises You Mention; by ire Description it must fit Me; I hope it wont be gone before I can see it with my Wife; pray send me ye particulars of it, has it any prospect? I desire You will thank Mr Carrington for his kind Care of Me in this affair - Saunders would be a good Man to take with You to see ye house, he will know ye Condition of it at once - I have not answered Leviez's Letter because I imagine he will be in London before one can reach him - Devise I find is coming over, & I hope that he won't bring Pitro too, however we must stand ye Chance; if he shd send a Lettr, open it, & if he sends to know whether we want Pitro with Devise , I think not, our Company is over loaded already, thanks to my Partner Timbertop . I hope Robin will get ready to set out for Us with ye Chariot & four & a Postilion, this Day Sen'night Tuesday ye 1st of Sepbr, he must go to Lincoln & from thence to ye water Side at a place called Wintringham & stay there till we come to him on Friday - He will go there in four Days Easily, pray desire him not to hurry ye horses, & let nobody ride in the Chariot - remember to tell him this - & let him bring with him a Play of Every Man in his Humour & Romeo & Juliet , you may have both from Draper . I shall let You know in my next how You may write to Me on ye Road for I want to know how ye Opening will be & other Matters - I don't think so ill of Moore's play as You do, nor so Well of it as Draper - but mum . I hope when we return that we shall find You & your good wife well - give her a kiss for us both & believe Me Ire most affect Brother D Garrick. The Reason I shall want ye two Plays Every Man , & Romeo , is that I would read 'Em upon ye Road to be ready at a Moment's Warning. Let Cross have ye Enclosed wherever he is, read it & seal it up -

column46: Augst 28th 1752 My Dear George. I hope Robin is set out for Us, & that You have given him directions in writing, If he is not yet gone, for I am not sure whether I ordered him Monday or Tuesday send him forth the Morning after you receive this, which will be Tuesday Sepbr 1st & write the same Night to Me, here as usual, & I shall receive it time enough to go from hence to meet him at ye Water Side Either Friday or Saturday - but I hope Your next Letter will clear up that to Me & then I shall not be kept in Suspense. however George, write me a few Lines on Tuesday, & I shall be more certain, for we receive ye Letters by six in ye Morng & We may set out on our Journey after that - I hope Robin has directions to go to Wintringham by ye Ombre side & wait there for Us - His Journey shd be as follows - from Londn to Biggleswade from Begged to Stamford , from Stamd to Lincoln & from Linn to Wintringham , which last is a very easy day's Journey - however let him do What he will, so he comes safe & well to Wintringham & there wait for Us - If You should write me a Letter ye Night the house Opens Saturdy ye 16th direct it for Me to be left at the Swan at Wellwyn in Hertfordshire where I must stop half a Day to settle Matters with Dr Young - pray write to me there with an acct of ye house, ye Play & other Matters I think you are right to Soften the rough places, which I had put in for Lacy, I want to know much how ye portion works with him - let me know the particulars - Yates is an unaccountable Dog, & I'm afraid has kicked down all ye Milk at Birmingham. My best Services to Woodward & thank him for his News about Theo Cib: but sure it cannot be - pray tell Would I have some News for him too. Miss Auretti, MonSr Pitro, Madme Janeton, ye Father, Mother & all their Generation may Kiss my A-se; I am so sick of their no meaning Messages & Compliments, that Every time I see her Name in a Letter, my Stomach falls a heaving as Yours would do, if You were to sit with Your Nose over a Pot with a Stale Turd in it, & that turd not ire own - No more of ye Aurettis I beg you - heugh - is there any talk of Rich's Opening? when? & who has he got. Say Nothing of Dr Young's play - I have doctored Moore's a little, that is - thickened ye Pudding a little, for indeed as ye Taste of ye Audiences is at present, it was too much upon ye Squatter for 'Em - I can write no more, & I have so laughed with writing this Nonsense that Im but just able to send Love to little Siss Yrs Ever & Ever D G -

column46: Tuesday Sepbr 1st, 1752 Dear George. I received by this Post a Letter from my friend Clutterbuck & You - I find by his, that Lacy has been with him, & is almost dead with ye bloody Flux - He ought to have a thorough Scouring before his inside will be tolerably clear from ye filth & Nastiness that he has been gathering from his Youth upward till now - He desires me to forgive him; that I will with all my heart for I thank my God that I have no Malice in my Nature, but I can't forget him soon, nor will I be upon Brotherly terms with him; there is a rank viciousness in his Disposition that can only be kept under by ye Whip & curb - I suppose Robin Set out for Us this Morng & that he will be at Wintringham on Friday Night - We propose leaving this place Saturday Morng & hope to see You about Wednesday; for as I told You before I must have some Conversation with Dr Young - but say Nothing of this to Lacy, & if he asks when I shall come, say You can't tell - My Service to Cross & let him know I have received his last Lettr & I shall be very well contented with what is Settled, till I see him - Mr Woodward must choose which part he will do in ye Silent Woman & I think Shutter will do Daw as well as any thing - tell him yt I suppose Mr Lacy will Settle ye Parts in ye Double Disappoint - to ye best advantage - I hope he has spoke to Mossop about Subtle - If You write to me a Line about ye house On Saturday Night (ye Opening), direct for Me at ye Bell at Stilton in Huntingtonshire to be left till called for, & for fear of ye worst put in another at ye Same time (two lines will do) directed for Me at ye White Swan at Wellwyn in Hertfordshire to be left till called for, they will neither Miscarry for I know both ye Landlords, & they will carry ye Letter barefoot into Scotland, rather than I should not have it - My Wife thinks ye Maids have Mistook her about cleaning ye windows, She meant that the Glazier was to do 'Em as Usual, & hopes that they have not been showing their Ars-s out of ye windows in Order to clean 'Em - I long to see ye house at Ealing, I am prepossessed that it will do - Mr Carrington is very Obliging, & I shall tell him so when I see him - I am glad to hear that Siss keeps so well, I suppose there will be no Seeing her face for her Belly when I come to Town - give our kindest & best Love to her & both of You believe Me Ire most affect Brother D: Garrick - I have thought better of it, You may if you please only write to Stilton , I have sent you franks. I have Enclosed You half a dozen Lines upon ye affair between Withers & my friend Dr Garnier , if you like 'Em put 'Em into ye Penny post sealed up, the Publisher of ye Whitehall I dare say will put 'Em in, if not there will be no great loss - say Nothing of 'Em to anybody, be sure - Adieu! My Wife desires you'll bid ye Maids dust ye red Room & Pictures, but to care of Gilding & Carving.

Chiswick July ye 4th Dear Peter I have just now heard that there is an Estate belonging to one Mr Boothby (I don't know if it is Ire friend or not) near Ashbourn, of about £300 p ann to be sold, & has been upon Sale near Two Years - Dr Taylor ye Physician tells me that it is one of ye prettiest freehold Estates in ye County of Derby - I wish you would make some Enquiry about it, & let me know ye particulars as soon as You can - pray inform Me if there is ye River Dove near ye house, & what kind of a house, what Wood, what prospect &c &c? - I should be glad to purchase a Good thing in Derbyshire, that I might serve ye Devonshire family upon Occasions. I could be glad that you would get ye best information you can, but not mention my Name Yet, for fear they should rise upon it - Mr Fletcher would perhaps give some account of it - Dr Taylor ye Clergyman who lived once at Ashbourn & belongs now to Westminster told my friend Dr Taylor ye Physician of it - They say it is ye prettiest thing next to Mr Oakover's in ye County - I own I love a good Situation prodigiously, & I think the four great Requisites to make one are, Wood, Water, Extent, & inequality of Ground - I should be glad to know if this place has any, or all - shd you hear of any good thing besides this, that may be had reasonably, & has taste in it, (for do you mind Me, there must be a little Taste for Us), I beg you will let me know - but first Enquire about this Estate of Mr Boothby, I think they say The River Dove washes his Land; which would be a great Inducement to Me, for I must have a River - I am writing now in ye greatest haste, & with ye damndest pen I ever handled; but, you'll decipher me, I don't doubt - I imagine we shall go for Yorkshire on Monday; when You write to me direct for Me under Cover to ye Earl of Burlington in Piccadilly London My wife sends her Love with Mine to you all, & believe Me - Most Affecty & Sincerely Yrs D Garrick how does Linney do? To Mr Garrick in Lichfield, Staffordshire.

Sir. You were most Extremely Welcome to the Ticket or any other assistance in My Power in all your Undertakings, whether Serious or Whimsical - If you choose to relinquish Your right to ye freedom of Drury-Lane Playhouse, you certainly will do as you please - but without ye Ticket, I imagine Mr Murphy will find the Doors open to him as usual - and be it farther known to You Sir, that as I thought You were above an undue Influence, I never meant ye Ticked as ye least Tie upon The Liberty of Your Pen or Conversation. The Mistake between Us about ye Young Apprentice , is indeed most Mysterious & Surprising, & as it was impossible to give you any promise for this Season, on account of my other Engagements with Mr Foot &c, so I most Solemnly declare, that (however You may have mistaken Me) I never hinted or thought of performing it this Winter; nay I imagined You were quite Satisfied with It's appearing next Year, at ye beginning of ye Season, that you approved of It's being left with Me for alterations, (if necessary), & that at ye Same time I told You in what Manner I would Endeavour to Strengthen ye Author's Night. but Supposing this Mistake between Us about ye Time of It's appearing; how could it be insinuated to ire disadvantage that I refused Ire Piece? so far from that - have I not said Every where & to Every body who knew Us both, that ye Subject was well imagined & that I would Act & do Every thing in My Power to make it succeed? - I assure You that I desire no Gentleman to wait upon Me unnecessarily, I hope that I give Myself no Unreasonable Airs to any Author, & however I may have been Misrepresented, I flatter Myself that No Gentleman who has had Dealings with Me, will do me the injustice to charge Me with breach of Promise, false Parade, or the Want of Warmth to Support their Performances, in my double Capacity of Manager & Actor. I am Sr Ire most Obedt hume Served D Garrick. P.S. I was obliged to go from Home Yesterday the moment I had dressed Myself, or I should have sent You an answer before -

Hampton Sepbr 2d Dear Peter I should have answered Yrs sooner, had not George wrote you Word that I agree to ye Gardener's proposals & hope in a Day or two to have notice of his coming, for I shd be glad to see him Settled here, before I repair to London to begin ye Acting Season - I hope he has a good Character in his Neighbourhood, for he will be left in trust of Every thing, house, Garden Workmen &c &c - you must likewise be so good to say what Expenses I am to be at for his Journey, tho as I agree to his wages which are high (I think that he might have bore his own Expenses to Town - however that I leave to you - We shall have no occasion for a Laundry Maid, so we shall spare you that trouble, for my Wife has altered that scheme, at least for a time - but if you shd know of two Maids between this & next Spring, one for Laundry & ye other for a Dairy & the Chickens which are prime in their Way, we shd be greatly obliged to You, if You would give us Notice of them, & secure them for Us - as to Mrs I should be proud & pleased to Serve any of her family, as I did one of her Daughters before - but to obtain a Place yt would be fit for her to accept, would take up Some time & Enquiry, for the People of fashion are all out of Town, & Those I am immediately intimate with are provided with favourites, which I neither can, or indeed would choose to remove - I shall be willing to Say Every thing favourable & kind of ye Young Lady, if I should have an opportunity, or if my good opinion will be Ever Serviceable to her, she may command Me at all times We were indeed most happy at Windham's, all mirth, Joy, Love Elegance & what not. he desired his best wishes to you very affecty - He seems thoughtful at times, greatly so, & I don't absolutely like his Looks & Cough - I write this in great hurry for I have Compy with Me. I have Enclosed (as I have a frank) Some of our periodical Papers - I will not answer for their Superlative Merit, such as they are you are welcome to - We send our Love to you all & I am Yrs Ever D Garrick

Hampton Wednesday Morng After I had wrote to Your Lordp I went to Chiswick to call upon my wife to go to Hampton - Lady Burlington desired to see Me before I set off, I went into her Room, & she told Me with tears, that she had not slept one Wink all Night with reflecting upon our conversation - she then Said, that she must desire me to do for her, what she had several times intended to ask me, which was, to talk with Your Lordp from her, & beg to know, with may have been ye Cause of ire Lordships Coolness & Gravity of late; that she cannot charge herself with ye least Neglect or Unkindness, & that Your Behaviour which is so reserved, afflicts her so sensibly that she must entreat to know ye Reason for it makes her Life miserable - this is ye thing I could have wished, & as she has desired that you may not know of her Ladp's & my conversation, Nothing could have happened so luckily - she says my talking to her has obliged her beyond Measure, & indeed I never saw Such a Change from ye Severe, to ye Good & tender. She is greatly alarmed, & gets me as often as she can into a Corner for advice, & I am to lye there to Night again in order to have my Instructions of What I am to say to Ire Lordship - now indeed is ye time to fix Matters upon such a footing, that No uneasiness shall Enter again into ye family; I cannot say that I have been so pleased & satisfied a long time; & Ire Lordp may be assured that I have acted with all ye Prudence & delicacy, so nice an affair requires, & let me likewise say, with that firmness & regard to both, that unless the Devil steps in between, (and I flatter myself that he is shut out at present) Good, real Good must be ye Consequence. pray let me know when I may see Ire Lordp, for Lie Burlington has desired that I will see You as soon as I can; I suppose Tuesday or Wednesday Morng will be ye farthest. Mrs Garrick sends her Duty & I am as in duty bound Ire Lordship's most faithful & Obedt Sert D Garrick. PS. Ire Lordp must take no Notice of this, till I see you; but this was unnecessary - Ire Lordp has now time to consider what is further to be done.

Novr 2d My Lord. Yesterday, & not before, I had the critical Tete a tete with her almost unintelligible Ladyship: We walked into ye Garden together & she began with asking Me, whether ire Lordship had said anything more of Your Grievances - No Madam (said I) his Lp talked no more of that affair; I indeed Spoke to him & told him I was glad to see that his Lordp seemed to be cheerfuller than Some time ago. Your answer was to Me - While her Ladyp is pleased to be kind I shall return it, & live with her, (if she pleases) as We Used to do before these Bickerings, but I cannot, & ought not, to pass my Life in gloom & with unkind treatment: it is very odd said she; - but I saw her struck & much touched & this Subject dropped - I wanted to introduce the grand affair, which I did by asking her, when you was to return, She said, she did not know, that she had asked Lie Hartn, but she could not tell - I suppose says I, this new Scheme of another house near Uffington is taking place & his Lp is there - oh No Says She, I believe he is still at Chatsworth - then I came in to ye Matter - I could not help laughing at my Lord (said I) for thinking of another house in that cursed Country, & said to Him how can Ire Lordp think of any place when You may have Londesburgh - how so Mr David cried his Lordp? Why I have heard My Lady say that she Wondered how you could go there when you might have Londesburgh; if Lady B - would Choose it to be so (replied ire Lp) she certainly would have Spoke of it - why have I not? (interrupted ye Lady) Several & Several times? you have heard me, have you not? I don't remember Your Saying this to Lt H: Madm, I recollect Something of ire Saying this to Lie Hart. but that was in a careless Way - I mean says she Every thing I say, & I shd think what is said to One is said to Both - I am very sorry (said I) there is is Reserve, for I am Sure Lord Hartn likes Londesburgh so well, that he would have it upon ire own terms - I hope he won't hire this other house, as he talked of, & for a term of Years - here there was a dead Stop, - with only an Ejaculation now & then, of, it is very odd! - I can't make Speeches, - & such kind of no-meaning Words! in short how this will work I can't say - but if she intends as she ought - this will open her Mouth & heart im~ediatly, if Not - I shall be angry, amazed and disappointed - Ire Clothes have been three Days with ye Tailor, I flatter Myself You'll like them; Mrs G- send her Duty & I am My Lord Ire Lordship's Most faithful & most Obedt Served D Garrick. I am going to play Macbeth, & have wrote so unintelligibly that I fear you won't make it out - Ire Lordp will Excuse Me.

column46: Febry 26th 1756 I should not have troubled Your Grace so soon again, had not one part of ye last Letter I had ye honour & pleasure to receive, required an immediate Answer - My Wife had a very good opportunity ye last time she was at Chiswick, of telling her Ladp that I had ventured to write to Ire Grace in favour of Dr Boys, & that I had received an Answer, yt You would not oppose him - I thought this proper to be told as Ire Lordp hinted in ire last; that Letter & one I wrote upon a late melancholy Occasion, (I think) may be all which shd be owned; tho her Ladp will scarcely demand a Confession, but whatever is thought right, We shall acquiesce in - there is such an unaccountable Suspicion & Jealousy in Every Word, Action & Look, that it behoves all Persons concerned to be extremely Wary - Mrs Garrick continues in favour, & was this day honoured with ye Six Duns to Hampton & returns to Chiswick to Dinner - Her Ladp even sent a Slice of Pleasantry to Me with a Loin of Chiswick Pork, which Madam brought home from thence - the Tail of ye Pig was not cut off, but sent with ye Loin, & she desired that I would put it to my Wig, & parade with it in Hyde Park - Her Bosom Friend has left off Tails - I mean to her hair, & now rides out in a Bag - indeed it is time - Poor Miss is much, very Much to be pitied; My Wife is Melancholy about her - a Day or two ago Dr Hoadly (ye Divine) breakfasted with Me, & among other Things I asked whether a piece of News which I had accidentally heard was true, that his Father & ye Duke of Devonshire had some misunderstanding - upon which he told me his Father's Tale, & indeed a most Spiritual one it was, truly Ecclesiastical from top to bottom - I could not help from his own Account to Argue with him, & hint, that ye Arguments were rather those of an Attorney than a Bishop - He likewise seemed to say, that ire Grace was satisfied, which I would not contradict, & that Mr Lowth, was not displeased with his Father's behaviour - this perhaps was only said to soften ye Edges of my impetuosity - I dined Some time ago with Several Gentlemen, among which were no less than Six Members of Parliament, chiefly of ye Minority, & by ye turn of their discourse I could gather, that they have warm Expectations of ire Grace's Sanction, I took no Notice at all, but was somewhat surprised, & thought I with mention it - That ire Grace may still Continue the Darling & Blessing of ye People where You are & that You may soon return safe & well to this Kingdom is ye most Zealous Wish of Ire most devoted D: Garrick My Lord. Since I finished my Letter Mrs G is returned from Chiswick, & had an Opportunity of hearing from poor Miss A- (for she is watched like a Spy) how cruelly she has been Used - indeed so cruelly, that, She cannot bear ye Persecution any longer, & is resolved to leave 'Em Soon - She is denied ye Use of Books, newspapers & Even to speak to ye little ones; They will not suffer her to go into my Lady's Room after Coffee & Tea, but they lock her out, & if by chance she gets in, they return to ye Dining Room; so that now, she is wholly, except at dinner, confined to her own Room - she looks terribly - & is told continually of her being Ugly, & that from her Starring, they are afraid she will be Mad, like Others of ye Family; in Short Every shocking thing that can be conceived is Uttered. this she has opened this Morng to my Wife with floods of Tears; nay her Lp wants to set Mrs G- against her & has told her, that Miss A- rails at her & Me & often abuses Us - their Rancour Even runs into Such foolish improbable Extremes - thus ye Poor Sweet-temper'd Creature scarcely Lives, but can endure it no longer - I make no doubt but Endeavours will be made to Set Ire Grace against her, but be assured she is a most Worthy & truly virtuous Woman & much unfit for her present Society - This I thought not improper to inform Ire Grace of, & indeed my Wife begged that I would - who desires her Duty & respects.

column46: March 20th 1756 My Lord. I had the honour of Ire Grace's last Letter three Days ago; and as her Lp's Health is the subject of one part of it, I would not delay any longer sending the best Intelligence I could about it - Had Mrs Garrick been in ye least apprehensive of Danger from that Quarter, I should have immediately apprised ire Grace of it, but notwithstanding Mr 's Letter, which to be sure was written by her Direction, He must know that it was only a Scene of ye Old Farce: We were alarmed one Morning by Lie Francis sending to my Wife, to go & see her Lp who was taken ill, Mrs G. could not go that Morng; but Lie Rachael & Lie Francis did, & when they had got near Chiswick, behold they met her Lp going to Town, as well as could be Wished; Some little Grumbling's there have been since, & keeping her Bed Chamber, but be assured there is Nothing that ought to alarm Ire Grace - I cannot Express to You, the inward Joy & Satisfaction I feel, at the Unexpected Situation of Affairs in Ireland; It appears to Me (who know the People a little) like a Golden Dream; this Success of Ire Grace is ye Topic & admiration of Every Body, & this alone, all Parties here unite to applaud & rejoice in - may no unlucky Circumstance arise to cloud this delightful prospect! I am not in ye least apprehensive of it, but from my Soul I wish Your Grace in England again, and happy in the Reflection that you have done, what ye Wisest and most Zealous imagined almost an Impossibility. The Politicians & News papers have Settled Matters for Ire Grace already, but as they have joined some improbalities with it, I have not given ye least Credit to it. Miss has left Chiswick & gone to Lady Molineux's - She is to see My Wife on Monday, & I am afraid has a most lamentable Tale to unfold - Mrs Garrick durst not converse with her much at . there were such Jealousies & watchings; - Miss A's Heart was almost broken, & she told Mrs Garrick, that she could Endure it, no longer; my Wife would give no advice, but is very glad that she has left them; Upon my Word the Usage of this good Creature, is not to be believed: Miss endeavoured to quarrel several times with her, in order that some story might be told of her Behaviour to my Lady, to hurt her Elsewhere - This Scheme has been tried with regard to Me, but I am as insensible to her Wickedness, as her heart is to goodness, and did not other Considerations strike upon my Mind, I should absolutely forget that such strange unheard of Creatures were in Being - Your Grace may be Assured that I shall be must punctually discreet about poor Miss A- when I see her, I shall pour some balm upon her Wounds, & desire her not to imagine that any unjust representations of her, will Ever Effect her with Ire Grace - I was frightened most Extremely two Days ago, Mrs Gk was taken ill at Hampton & very much so, I brought her very ill to Town, but Dr Taylor in a few hours set us all to right again. I am Ever & Ever Ire Grace's Most devoted & Obedt D: Garrick

Monday - Sir. I should not have troubled You with this, my last Letter, were it not to Answer that part of Yrs which relates to my Friend Mr Berenger - He might indeed say, that he knew of my good Intentions towards You, but he scarce could tell You that I had intentions to Serve You in ye Orphan of China , as he knew from ye Nature of ye Affair, that it was impossible - Your Warmth, or Quickness to Err , as you are pleased to call it, has hurried You a little too far in that part of ire Lettr, where you talk of Equitable treatment , so I shall leave that to be answered by Ire own Feelings, when The Quickness of Seeing ire Error , returns: I have always declared that my private Resentments shall never interfere with ye Public Entertainments; & Mr Murphy may be assured, tho He should publish twenty Volumes of abuse upon Me, whenever he sends Me a Performance that I think will succeed upon ye Stage, I will certainly perform it in ye best manner I am able, nor will I receive One , on ye Other hand, tho whose only Merit should be, that It's Author has published the same Quantity of Panegyric upon Me - The New Acquisition of Mr Derrick which you are pleased to honour me with, is not ye only Mistake in Ire Letter, but that & Ire mention of Shakespeare - Voltair Hawkesworth &c are visible proofs of Ire anger but surely not of Ire Wit, Ire Judgment, or Ire Justice. I am not in ye least surprised, that Your Letter of Yesterday, should be so totally inconsistent with that I received from You ye Day before - My Acquaintance which You so warmly desired in that, & which I so freely & as Warmly offered to You in my Answer, I now as Willingly take again & assure You that it shall not Ever incommode You for ye future. I am Sr Ire most humle Ser D Garrick

column46: Sepbr 10th 1757 My Lord. Mrs Garrick & I are very happy that You are pleased to Express such confidence of our Taste, but our great desire & Endeavour to do Nothing that shall displease Ire Grace has induced Us to send the Enclosed - which I must beg to have returned to Me by ye next Post, that the Embroiderer may finish his Work in Time. We think that ye two pieces of Velvet yt are pined together will make a most agreeable Mixture; the figured Velvet for ye Sleeves & Waistcoat, & ye plain one, for ye Coat; but then to be complete it must be Embroidered with Silver, for we fear that Gold will be too heavy - the Single pattern of figured Velvet would likewise make waistcoat & Sleeves with ye Plain one, tho not so Gay; or a whole Suit of it Embroidered with Silver or Gold, would look well - We shall wait for Your Grace's Determination & immediately go to work - We would certainly choose ye two pined together with Silver, & if ire Grace pleases, the Embroiderer would make ye Stalks of ye little flowers in Silver, & put a Spangle into ye Middle of Each little Rose, where there is now a small hole - There was a Report at Hampton - Yesterday that there was an insurrection in Derbyshire about ye Militia Act, & that Chatsworth was surrounded by ye Mob - We are in hopes that it is a Mistake, for it would be very hard that Ire Grace should have any uneasiness about an Act, which I am persuaded, You could neither project or approve of. Mrs Garrick joins with Me in Duty and I am My Lord Ire Grace's most humble, faithful and most Obedient Servant D Garrick. PS. pray return ye Patterns.

column46: Hampton Sepbr 14th 1758 My Lord. I received Ire Grace's Letter with the Draught for five hundred pounds. I cannot Express how much I think Myself obliged to Ire Grace for this new Mark of Ire Kindness to Me; I will take care that such confidence & Bounty shall be returned by care & punctuality at least on my part - the Mistake about Ire Grace's being in Town was owing to Mr Martin who told Me that he met You going to Kensington, & when I asked at Devonshire House, the SubPorter's answer to me, that You was gone to Chatsworth, (which might imply Ire being in Town ye Day before,) confirmed Me in it - Nor were Mrs Garrick & I undeceived till the Day before Yesterday, when Mrs Mostyn told my Wife that You had not been in Town at all, but that she had written to desire that Ire Grace would come upon My Lady Burlington's dangerous Relapse - Mrs Garrick attends there Every day, & she assures Me that she never saw so Woeful a Spectacle, & that it is impossible her Ladysp should continue long in her present melancholy, wretched Condition - My Wife was quite in ye vapors at her Return from Chiswick last Night, & still thinks she cannot possibly hold long as She is - She goes again to day & is resolved, if she can, to persuade her to be removed from the filth, she is at present in - It is Exactly, by her Account, Dean Swift's Description of the Yahoos - her looks are dreadful & her Shrieks more so - all is not right within! - at Mrs Garrick's going away Mrs Huet called her into a room & with tears in her Eyes opened her heart to her; she has conceived some terrible Notions of a certain Person, & thinks her Ladyp's Actions wholly influenced by her - My Wife was indeed struck with some things but she rather persuaded Mrs Huet that she might be mistaken - I was desired not to send this to Ire Grace, but I could not forbear it, tho perhaps of very little Consequence - I shall be in London on Monday next & will certainly send the patterns by Tuesday's or Thursday's post to Chatsworth - If any Matter should arise, for Mrs G- is now at , I shall certainly trouble Ire Grace with another Letter on Saturday. I am My Lord Ire Grace's Most humble & most faithful Sert D Garrick

column46: Octr 5th 1758 My Lord. What I have to say to Ire Grace is of little Consequence, & Yet I could not forbear giving You this trouble - Mrs Garrick called Yesterday at Chiswick to see ye Young Lords & Lady Dorothy; but they were with ye Duchess of Devonshire. She saw Mrs Loxley, who entered into some particular conversation with her, which Mrs Garrick thinks Ire Grace shd know - she therefore desires that You will Suspend any Intentions that Your Grace may have, or be Solicited about, with regard to Lady 's Maids till Mrs Garrick has seen Ire Grace - I know that my violence & Suspicions are laughed at, but indeed I am seldom Violent without some foundation, or Suspicious without a Cause: - Foul Deeds will rise! Tho all ye Earth overwhelm them &c. In my return to London last Tuesday, I overtook the shattered remains of the Grenadiers & first Battalion of Guards that were so peppered at our last Enterprise : I had much talk with Coll Cary & a Captn Williams - They speak very plain & to the purpose. My heart danced to hear with what warm praises they Speak of Lord Frederick - He is their Darling - Williams , whom I don't know, swore that if Lord Frederick had commanded the Whole instead of the Company of Grenadiers, they should not have been in such deplorable Circumstances. They don't believe that Lordship was Ever in ye Sea; & likewise Williams protested to Me, that Genl Dury who has been so much blamed, was not ye adviser of what proved so fatal to them, but that he behaved, in ye most Noble & Gallant Manner imaginable. He likewise added that he was little known to Genl Dury, but that he thought it his Duty to tell ye truth & more particularly, as he could not justify himself. Mrs Garrick sends her Duty with mine with our thanks for some very good Venison We received two Days ago. I shall pay my Respects at Devonshire house the Moment that I hear Your Grace is in Town. I am Ever & most faithfully Your Grace's Most dutiful D Garrick.

column46: Hampton Augst 3d Dear Sir. I received Ire last Lettr in Hampshire, the Evening before I left Portsmouth, or I should most certainly have appointed a Day for ye Pleasure of meeting You at Winchester. The Liberty you took with Me, I esteem a favour, & I am sorry that I had it not in my Power to see You & my friend, & Dr Hoadly together - I shall wait with Pleasure Your own, or rather Ire Muse's, time, for favouring Me with a sight of ye desert Island , & the Way to Keep him - follow your amusements, & correct at ire Leisure, & my Life for it, we shall neither of us repent ye Consequences - I think myself much honoured by Mr Domvilles favourable Opinion of Me, I beg that You will pay my Respects to him. If you think that the Salt Water will abate your dramatic inclinations, I must absolutely prohibit Your drinking it - I most willingly consent to ire catching as many Cods , as you please, but I prescribe no other Use of ye Sea Water to You - Were it really a Remedy for Every kind of Cacoethes, I could send You a waggon load of Writers (scurvy ones) to be ducked & drenched for their own & ye Public Benefit - The Public has done You Justice, & you cannot possibly make a more grateful return, (next to writing Yrself), than by doing ire best Endeavours to cure these Gentlemen - The Fracas you mention, was a matter of much Concern to me - I despise the attacks & Misrepresentations of Blockwig, but shall be Ever truly Sorry when I am misunderstood by a Man of Genius. I am Dr Sr Your most Obedt humble Sert D Garrick. PS. I was in London the first of Augst but did not flatter Myself that I shd see You - when you return to London, pray let me have a Line from You - any Parcel sent to my house will be with Me here ye next Day. To Arthur Murphy Esqr to be left with Paul Vaillant Esqr in the Strand, London.

Friday noon Dear Sir, I have done a little with my pencil, but not enough; and I am not certain that I have done it as it ought to be. You will consider my cuttings, and look upon them merely as marks that the scene is too long, and follow your own judgment, which must be the best in omitting and restoring. The scenes with me and Bashful are much too long: I have taken out some speeches of merit, merely because they were rather inclining to tawdry. You will do as you please. - I think that the beginning of the third act, between Mrs. Lovemore and me, had better be spared, for fear it should take from the last act; and there is another reason for rejecting it, and a much stronger one, which is, that I shall never be able to change my dress from top to toe (as I must for Lord Etheridge) while the scene of the Ladies is acting. If I were to dress in the hurry I necessarily must to be ready, I shall be so blown that the following scene will suffer for it. - The fourth act is too long, very near as long as the second by the pages, and with very little curtailing: - I am very much in doubt whether the play would not be better without the circumstances of the buckles; for Sir Brilliant breaks in a little improperly upon Sir Bashful and Lovemore. I think Lady Constant may naturally come upon them after she has torn the letter; and, to me, the scenes will appear more spirited and connected - but this you will determine as you please. I have some little to say upon the fifth act, which will give you no trouble: I must desire to read that with you, when I come to town next Monday, if agreeable to you. I shall be at the house between twelve and one, and should be glad to see you there; - if you will bring the four acts as you settle them, we may go immediately to work. - As the fifth act stands, there are no less than three different letters produced and read upon the stage; - should not that circumstance, if possible, be avoided? I think a very little alteration will remedy that, and give the conclusion more spirit. I will offer it to your consideration next Monday, if I have the pleasure of seeing you. Mignionet is now so good a character that I think Mrs. Kennedy should play it, and Mrs. Bradshaw that of Furnish; but those matters I will settle with you on Monday. If I had been allowed more time, I could have done more; but I was willing to send it, that no time might be lost. I am, dear Sir, Your most obedient servant, and sincere well-wisher, D. Garrick.

Sunday, 12 o'clock at night Dear Sir, I have finished your Comedy this moment, and I must send it away by the coach at six o'clock - so I must be very concise with you. - It is a very pleasant laughing Comedy of business, and will have great effect in the acting, but it must be well taken care of in the getting of it up. My objections are very few and trifling. I do not quite like the manner of Belinda's fainting in the Park - there is not sufficient cause for it, as it is now managed - however, you may justify it by Moliere: it is equally probable with his scene. - Should Belinda so readily come into her father's proposal of marrying Belmont? - she should have more regard for her friend Clarissa. The latter end of the last Act is a little too long bringing matters to bear - however, there is so much to be done that you must not cut too deeply neither. - I am half asleep, or I would say more to you - but I thank you for the pleasure I have had; and I most sincerely assure you, that I have the greatest expectations from it. I am, dear Sir, Your most obliged and obedient servant, D. Garrick. To Arthur Murphy, Esquire.

column46: Sepr 17th 1761 Sir I received Your Letter as I was stepping into the Chariot to go to Hampton. I desired my Brother to call upon You but You was in ye Country - I really cannot answer for any idle Stories that may circulate about this Town. it has been asked Me several times, whether We were to have Your Pieces, & my constant answer has been that I imagined We were, for Mr Lacy told Me, that he had Settled with You upon the Terms, that We two had previously talked of, & agreed to, in Bushy Park - and he farther assured Me that You were well pleased with them - I am much Surprised at his proposal of my playing Yates's Character, for he knew my Sentiments upon that Matter. So it stood between Me & Mr Lacy, and I appeal to You Sir, whether it was not very Natural for Me, to think that We had bargained for Your two Pieces. Nay to convince You that I thought so, & that You knew it, I ordered Johnston to write out some of the Parts, & You forbid him, for some Reason or another - You likewise told Me, that You were preparing a Comedy for Us, The Man does not know his own Mind , & that it should be delivered to Me before ye opening of the house, & You told my Brother that You would write to Me about it - But I have neither Seen You, or heard from You, till the Receipt of ire Letter, but have heard from others, that You are in another Interest, which indeed I could not, nor can I now, account for. I am Sr Your most Obedient Served D: Garrick To Arthur Murphy, Esqr at Lincolns-Inn.

column46: Sept 24, 1761 Sir, To take up as little of your time as I possibly can, I must tell you that Mr. Lacy assured me that he had made a bargain with you for the two pieces, and that he engaged to see it fulfilled on my part, which he could very well do for the reasons which I told you in my last letter. - As to his saying that I should appear in Mr. Yates's character, there must be some mistake between you, for he denies his having said to you that I would play Yates's part : he told you, in conversation, that All in the Wrong ought to have been acted in the winter, originally with us, and that I should have done Yates's part; but that he made no stipulation for my taking the part upon the revival of the Comedy. The affair of your new Comedy is wholly in your own hands, and we must acquiesce: the Managers of Drury Lane Theatre have this to say, that you have always settled your own terms with them, and without a single objection on their part: when they have deviated in their agreements with you from the usual compact with authors, it has been at your own request. What additions you have made to my fortune I am much obliged to you for, and am sorry that you think the Managers have been the only gainers. I am, Sir, Your most obedient humble servant, D. Garrick.

column46: Decr 17th 1761 Dear Colman. I rejoice that you are arrived safe at Bath, but most sincerely wish you as little pleasure there as possible, and You may guess the Reason - Fitzherbert being with You will, I fear, most powerfully counteract my Wishes, however I have some small hopes from his not being under ye same Roof with You - I have this moment seen our Friend Churchill & told him a fine Scheme of Vaughn's in conjunction with the Gang of Pottinger - they are going to publish a Set of Papers called the Genius , in order to forestall Yrs & deceive the Public It is a most infamous design, & I desired Churchill would Let Thornton know of it, which he will do immediately, & prevent their Scoundrillity by some humorous Paragraph - If you with have any thing done, write directly & You shall be obeyed most minutely. I have read ire last, & think it a fine Plan a little too hastily finished. there is Strength, & good Sense, but I want more laugh & pleasantry. our New Tragedy creeps on; We might steal it on to Six Nights with much loss, but, I hope, that the Author will be reasonable, & satisfied with what We have already done, without insisting upon our losing more to force a Reputation - this Entry Nous - You have heard I suppose of a Coll Barry , who has taken ye Lyon by the Beard in ye Parliamt house; made no Reply to it, & lost his Question - the Town in general think that ye Coll was rather too rough - There will be fine Work anon! - Whitehead's Play has been once read, & has a great deal of Merit - Pray let me see you soon with ire Bundle of Excellencies - Mr Murphy has at last declared off with us, & in a Letter to Obrien says, that he has been so great a loser by ye Managers of Drury Lane that he can never more have any dealings with Us - Wish Me joy my dear Friend, but Keep this to yrSelf for Many Weighty reasons - My Love to Fitzherbert & believe Me most Affectionately Yours D Garrick Mrs Garrick prests her Compts to you -

Drury Lane Theatre half an hour past Six My dear Peter. If the Sight of my hand writing would give You the Smallest Satisfaction, You should have so Much of it, that there should not be so Satisfied a Gentleman in the whole County of Stafford - I have so much Writing, & like it so little, that I never think of troubling You with a Voluntary , & more so, as I am conscious, that Mine, like those of poor old Lamb, (ire late Organist), would only give You a Yawn or two, & End with a Nap. last Night I had the honour of Some Litchfieldians to Sup with Me, who stayed till near two this Morning. All good men & true - viz - Levett, Sudall Dick Bailey, the two Robinsons, & two Garricks - to which were joined the facetious Author of the Jealous Wife , (my particular friend Colman) & Dr Douglas Chaplain to the Earl of Bath, & tho I was in some alarm all ye Night on Account of a few Symptomatic Creepings about my Kidneys, yet we were very cheerful, tho not roaring - I have undergone a terrible hour & a half three Weeks ago, & now am taking Soap by ye Pound, & Lime water by ye Gallon by way of prevention. We don't despair of Seeing You here this Season, for ire Partner Dick will return soon Enough to You, to give you time to make Us a Visit - if so be as how, Your Inclination tally with ours, & you can please stop ire Ears against ye Lichfield Sirens, who will hold You, & have held You so fast, that a poor Relation can't have a Slice of You to be plain & Serious - George & I have always open Arms & Hearts to receive You - Not but I must hint to You, by ye bye, that if you won't see us this Year, let me beseech You not to make it so late the Next, for our Benefits begin in a Month, & then adieu to all ye Pleasures of ye Theatre. The King has most graciously renewed ye Patent for Me, & I, as Graciously, have given the Same Advantages to Lacy, as I have Myself, tho I was desired to think how I might be particularly favoured in the Grant - I am now Writing, during the first Act of a New Comedy, called the School for Lovers - I have Spoke the Prologue, & don't appear in ye Play till the beginning of the 2d when Sr John Dorilant (that's ye Name) makes his Entrance - and a fine, polite, Sentimental, Windling Son of a Bitch it is - a great favourite of ye Ladies, & much admired by the Clergy, & the Aldermen & Common Council of the City of London - Humbug for Nine Nights - Your singing Boy is to go into training, & may turn out well - We are much obliged to you for Your attention to us - Dick Bailey has Sent me ye enclosed Letter for You, & my Brother George backed by the Crowing of the Prompter summons me away - So, my dear Brother, I shall quit you in ye Words of Hamlet Your most affect Brother D Garrick

column46: Chatsworth July 7th 1763 Dear Peter We arrived here Monday last; George I suppose gave you an Account of our Setting out from London - His Grace of Devonshire desires Me to tell You that he expects to See You at Chatsworth, I will tell You his own Words - 'let Your Brother know Mr David that he must ride to us, in his worse Coat, put his better into ye Portmanteau & make the best of his way to Chatsworth,' in short You have a warm invitation & will come I suppose if not inconvenient to You, I have some thoughts of seeing You at Lichfield in my return from hence & calling at Lord Vernon's to Dinner only, for I have my Wife, a Friend, (who is acquainted with his Lordp Mr Hubert by name), and my two little Dogs - the Duke will be very glad to See Mr & Mrs Docksey here, if agreeable to them - will You be so good to let 'Em know as much, & that I should have certainly called upon 'Em at Mr Seward's, where I heard they were, but was told by a Mr Simpson, that they went from him, the same day I arrived here - I am Dear Peter most Affecly Yours D: Garrick PS We have much laugh & all kind of Liberty - Mr Queen is here & in full Spirits. To Peter Garrick Esqr at Lichfield (turn at Manchester).

column46: Chatsworth July 9th 1763 Dear Peter. I wrote to you a few Days ago from this place, informing you that the Duke of Devonshire desired to see You here with your better Coat in ire Portmanteau; & I likewise begged of You to let my Brother Docksey know that He & his Wife would be welcome at Chatsworth, without running ye least risque of having his principles debauched - Since I wrote to You my first Letter, I have received a Letter from Brother George, who, I find, intends being with You very soon - if You both can spare a Day or two from your Lichfield Friends, the Duke will be glad to See You, You will be both at your liberty to do what you please, & to go when you please - I must tell You that we shall go to Chesterfield Races next Wednesday Sen'night , & Friday Sen'night , so I hope if you come, it will be before that time, for I don't know how soon after that, I shall be thinking of going towards London; I likewise think to take Lichfield in my way, to see what other Sconces You want in Ire Vicar's Hall, for I am told there is yet a deficiency, which I shall most willingly Supply - I write with his Grace at my Elbow, laughing at Me & jogging me, so excuse my Scrawl - pray come soon, or send me a proper Excuse to Show his Grace - we have with Us Mr Fitzherbert, Mr Hubert, Mr Queen, &c &c - all in Spirits - Mrs Garrick joins with me in love to You & Sister & I am Dear Peter Yrs most affecly D Garrick

column46: July 10th 1763 Dear Colman. Many thanks to you for Tarry filius - it is very lively, & I long to see ye second Number - Pray write to me, & let me know how ye Town speaks of our Friend Churchill's Epistle - it is ye most bloody performance that has been published in my time - I am very desirous to know the opinion of People, for I am really much, very much hurt at it - his description of his Age & infirmities is surely too shocking & barbarous - is Hogarth really ill, or does he meditate revenge? - Every article of news about these matters will be most agreeable to me - pray write me a heap of stuff for I cannot be Easy till I know all about Churchill, Hogarth, &c - how did ye Tarry filius work at Oxford? have you yet received any Letter from Lord Bath? pray be particular in that ; for tho my Curiosity is much concerned in my former Questions, my heart & Soul are interested in ye last - Yrs Ever my Dear Colman D. Garrick Mrs Garrick presents her respects to you - All ye News -

My dear Colman. Tho I have said in George's Letter that I would not write to you till I got to Lyons, yet I can't help scribbling to you, for indeed my dearest friend there is no Love lost between us - I am vastly happy that Powel strikes you so much in the Rehearsal - He will surprise, & I most cordially wish it, for I think him a very worthy man - pray take care that the Play is quite ready before He makes his appearance. You can't imagine, my dear Colman, what honours I have received from all kind of People here - the Nobles & the Litterati have made so much of Me that I am quite ashamed of opening my heart Even to You. Marmontel has wrote me ye most flattering Letter upon our supping together, I was in Spirits & so was the Clairon , who supped with us at Mr Neville's - She got up to set me a going & spoke something in Racine's Athalie most charmingly - upon which I gave them the Dagger Scene in Macbeth, ye Curse in Lear, & the falling asleep in Sr John Brute, the consequence of which is, that I am now stared at ye Playhouse, & talked of by Gentle & Simple as ye most wonderful Wonder of Wonders - the first Person I find going to England shall bring you Marmontel's Letter - D'Alembert was one of ye Company & Sings my praises to all ye Authors of the Encyclopedia . I am glad to hear of ye Prologue, if they love to hear me abused, they will have great Pleasure this winter, for I am told they have begun already, but I am happy & in Spirits, & shall not read any Newspapers on this Side the Alps - in Many thanks to you for ye trouble you take about ye Invasion , cut as you please - I leave it to you - as for Midsummer Nights , &. I think my presence will be necessary to get it up as it ought - however if you want to, do for ye best - & I'll Ensure It's success - Mr Calcraft's behaviour astonishes me, but I hope Lacy will be firm - pray continue in his good Graces for my Sake. I believe I forgot to pay a little bill for ye Gazetteers, owing to one Owen , ye bill lay in my Study window, will you discharge it for me, & pay for a pair of Spectacles I bought & forgot at ye optician's (I forgot his name) at Charing Cross: it is on ye left side going down to Whitehall - I hate to be in debt & if you or George will clear me there I shall thank you most sincerely - I am this moment going to see a New piece at ye Italian Comedy, & last Night I saw a new one at ye french Comedy, taken from our Tancred & Sigismunda, it had very indifferent success, but ye Clairon was great; she has her faults (between you & me) but I don't say so here, for she idolises me - God bless you my dear Colman, & have a corner of ire Eye upon my theatricals, I think you have begun well & may continue it, if my Partner be advised & stick tightly to his Business - he behaves well & I most sincerely wish for all our sakes that he may not want Me - I have desired George to write his next Letter to Florence, pray put in a postscript that I may comfort myself in foreign parts with ye sight of ire most agreeable scrawl - once more my worthy Friend Adieu! - My Wife sends her Love to you de bon Coeur - Ever & Ever Yours & Yours D: Garrick George has my direction to Florence to George Colman, Esqr of Lincolns-Inn, London.

column46: Turin Octr the 18th 1763 My dear Colman. I wrote last to George & now for You - We got to this pretty City (for it is no better) last Friday Night, & are obliged much against our wills to stay here till next Saturday, for the Perch of our carriage was broke upon the top of Mount Cenis, by the carlessness of our Voiturier , who instead of carrying it upon ye backs of Mules (as he ought) had it dragged up that wonderful Mountain by 12 Men, & it is a great Miracle that it was not dashed into ten thousand pieces: however We are well contented, & happy, & are resolved to fret at Nothing - Mr Pitt, & all ye English here, are most particularly kind to Us - this Day a Gentleman showed me two London Chronicles in which they have abused Me most clumsily; I read their Malignity with as much sang froid as Plato himself would have done, tho, Entry Nous , I wish they had not mentioned a certain Duke, but he too is above feeling their Nonsense - I cannot but take Notice that Mr Straughn has twice officously excused himself for the abuse upon Me in his Paper, has sworn as often that there shd be no more of it, & has as often treacherously broke his word - but I am neither amazed or uneasy at it, & so you may tell our Friend Becket. We have nothing here in our way, but a miserable Bouffi Opera, & ye worst dancing I Ever saw - the People in ye Pitt & Boxes talk all ye while as in a Coffee house, & ye Performers are Even with 'Em, for they are very little attentive, laugh & talk to one another, pick their Noses, & while they are unengaged in Singing, they walk up to ye Stage Boxes, (in which the other Actors & dancers sit dressed in Sight of ye Audience) turn their backs, & join in ye laugh & Conversation of their Brethren, without ye least decency or regard to ye Audience; I never was more astonished in my life; their Theatres are very Elegant, the whole is composed of Pit & Boxes (five or six rows of Em) without Galleries - Each Box is like a little room where they receive visitors, & think & talk of Every thing but what passes upon ye Stage - I forgot to tell you that we had the finest day imaginable for passing ye terrible Mount Cenis - I was highly Entertained indeed, & it is much more inconceivable, (I mean the manner of ascending & descending) than it is dangerous or Disagreeable. I long to hear from You or George, I am sorry that I did not desire a Letter to this place, it would have reached me by this time, & I shall not be at Florence this fortnight at least, so You must not be surprised that You have not an Answer to any thing may be sent there. remember that I address myself to both of You - all letters for ye future must be directed for Me to ye Marquis Belloni at Rome , till I send to ye Contrary - the travelling through Savoy & Piedmont to this City is the most romantic & delightful with regard to the Scenery, that can be imagined, but the Nastiness in ye Inns, the peculiarity of Nastiness, is likewise as much above conception - I have taken some Memorandums of the things which I have seen with my own Eyes, that exceed all belief, & which I shall write down very soon, & send to our friend Townley as a Nosegay for You & Schomberg - pray make a Holiday on purpose, & let it be read in full assembly over a bottle of ye Dr's Claret by that aforesaid Arch-Blackguard the revd Mr James Townley. Write to me soon I beg of You - let me know Every thing, but most particularly what concerns Yourself, for yt (if good) will be most welcome to me. I write in haste but from ye heart - My fellow traveller Mence is obliged to go off for Minorca. We shall part in a few days, he to his & I for Florence : My wife has been very ill & frightened us all - but She is now well & herself again - she desires her Love to You & George - pray remember Us to the Huberts, Churchill, Schomberg, Drs Hay & Smalebroke & all whom you know, I with remember, if I could. God bless You my dear dear Friend Ever & most affectionately Yours D Garrick PS. Our duty pray to Lord Bath. To George Colman Esqr in the new Square, Lincolns-Inn at London.

column46: Florence Novr 30th 1763 My Lord I had Your Grace's very flattering Commands to give You some Account of our proceedings when we got into Italy: We have hitherto met with no disagreeable Accident but the breaking the Perch of our Coach upon Mount Cenis; which retarded us some Days at Turin, where Mr Pitt conferred all kind of Favours upon Us: from thence we went to Milan, and should I recount to Your Grace the honour I received from Count Firmian, the first Nobleman in the administration there, You would think, as You Used to say to me, that all my Geese were Swans: I had no Letter of recommendation to him, but his Servants were Enquiring after Me long before I came, & when I was there, there was no Civility that I did not receive from him; I cannot forbear Acquainting Your Grace with this Circumstance, as it made my Stay at Milan so very agreeable to Me: Count Firmian understands English, has read most of our best Authors; has an unaffected regard for the English Nation, and joins the Strongest Sense to the most Elegant Manners. from Milan We went to Genoa, which struck us more from its situation than any place we had seen before, the fine weather and the persuasion of many People, determined Us to sail part of our way to Leghorn in a Felucca; We were two Days and a Night upon the Mediterranean, & Mrs Garrick & Biddy were very much disordered by the Voyage, We rested three Days at Leghorn Were well feasted by ye Merchants, & have been Ever since feasting upon Virtue` in the Gallery & in the Palaces of this Place. I have found great preparations making for the Duke of York at Genoa, Leghorn and Florence, but as yet there is no certainty where he is - We shall set forward for Rome to Morrow; the English here are all agreeable, & hold their Conversations in our Apartment (& we have a most magnificent one upon the banks of ye Arno) almost Every Night; there is one Mr Kaye among them, who is known to ire Grace, & is beat constantly by Mrs Garrick at Chess. Lord Fordwick is still here, but assures Me that he shall soon go to England; I wish that it may be as soon as his Friends desire, & sooner, than his inclinations seem at present willing to agree to - Mrs Garrick presents her Duty to Your Grace & to Lady Dorothy, We have seen a Picture so Exactly like her Ladyship that we have visited it several times - I am astonished at the profusion of fine things We meet with in Every part of this City, & at the poverty of the inhabitants; they are a new Set of beings to Me, & quite a new Study - I shall trouble Your Grace no more at present; before I leave Naples, I shall pay my Duty again, & hope in the mean time, that my Brother will be Able to tell me that Your Grace is quite Established in Your health. I am My Lord Your Grace's Most Obedient & most faithful humble Servant D: Garrick I beg that Your Grace will present our Respects to Lord Frederick, Lord George & My great antagonist Lord John.

column46: Naples Decr 24, 1763 My dear Colman Per various casus we are at last arrived at our Journey's End - and a very long one it has been - I have now time to shake my feathers a little, & open my heart to thee, thou best of friends - ! We got to this place the 17th, after a most disagreeable Journey from Rome, for we were taken in ye midst of ye heavy rains here, and were well soaked with them all the Way - at present the weather is inconceivably fine, & we are basking ourselves in a warm sun with the Mediterranean at our feet, and Mount Vesuvius in our view - tho it is Xmas, we have green Peas Every day, & dine with our Windows open - these are our Pleasures in part, as for our distresses, which have been as ridiculous as unexpected since we left Rome & are the common occurrences upon this Road, I shall reserve them for our social hours at Hampton - We are all at this moment, Biddy not excepted, in the highest Spirits, & I am much ye better for my Expedition: My Lady Orford, who is settled here & has the greatest Interest with ye first People, has been most uncommonly kind to us - I am to have ye honour & Satisfaction of Seeing the King's Italian Actors perform before him in ye Palace, which is a most extraordinary favour; they perform Extempore, & ye Nobleman, who stands in the place of ye Lord Chamberlain, has sent me word, that if I will write down any dramatic Fable & give ye Argument only of ye Scenes, in 24 hours after, they shall play it before Me as ye greatest Count they can pay Me - I shall work at it to morrow - I hear there is one great Genius among the Performers - the Situation and Climate of this place are most extraordinary, & the People are still more so; they are a new race of beings, & I have the highest Entertainment in going amongst them, & observing their Characters from ye highest to ye lowest - I was last Night at their great Theatre, which is a most Magnificent one indeed; I was really astonished at first coming into it - it was quite full, & well lighted up - but it is too great, & the Singers were Scarcely heard - the famous Gabrielli pleased me much; she has a good person, is ye best Actress I ever saw on an Opera Stage, & has ye most agreeable voice I ever heard; she sings more to ye ear, than to ye heart - before I left Florence I had much Conversation with an old Servant of Ire Father's, who lives with Sr Mann - he remembers your being born, & showed me ye house where you first wawl'd & cried , I looked at it for ten minutes with pleasure - I need not tell you how well I am prepared to set you right, if you shd hereafter make any mistakes about your Age, & I fear that we already differ a year or two in our Calculation - I cannot quit you, till I say something about Rome: I hardly slept the night before I arrived there with ye thoughts of seeing it - my heart beat high, my imagination expanded itself, & my Eyes flashed again, as I drew near the Port del Popolo ; but the moment I entered it, I fell at once from my Airy Vision & Utopian Ideas into a very dirty ill looking place , (as they call it) with three crooked streets in front, terminated indeed at this End with two tolerable Churches - with a disappointment! my Spirits sunk & it was with reluctance that I was dragged in the afternoon to see the Pantheon - but my God, with was my Pleasure & Surprise! - I never felt so much in my life as when I Entered that glorious Structure: I gaped, but could not speak for 5 Minutes - It is so very noble, that it has not been in ye Power of Modern Frippery, or Popery (for it is a Church you know) to extinguish Its grandeur & Elegance - Here I began to think myself in Old Rome, & when I saw the ruins of the famous amphitheatre - Omnis Caesareo cedat labour Amphitheatro - I then felt my own littleness - & was convinced that the Romans were as much superior to the Moderns in Every thing, as Vespasian's Amphitheatre was to Broughton's - it is impossible, my dear Colman, to have any Idea of these things from any Prints that have been made of 'Em, - all modern performances look better upon paper, but these Ruins are not to be conceived, but by ye sensible & true Avouch of your own Eyes . Tho I am pleased, much pleased with Naples, I have such a thirst to return to Rome, as cannot possibly be slaked till I have drank up half ye Tiber, which, in it's present state, is but a scurvy draught neither. it is very strange that so much good poetry shd be thrown away upon such a pitiful River; it is no more Comparable to our Thames, than our modern Poets are to their Virgils & Horaces - I was so taken up for ye fortnight I was at Rome in seeing ruins, Statues Pictures & Palaces, that I had not ye least inclination to see his Holiness, & his troop of Cardinals, tho they had two or three public days when I was there - I shall have their blessings in ye holy Week. I attend Lord & Lady Spencer to morrow to Herculaneum , where, I am told, they have dug up Every Utensil that were in use among ye Romans, & have got even a Lady's Toilette Entire - the Lady herself was found dressing herself & in ye act of sticking a bodkin into her hair; which bodkin is of a most Elegant make, not much unlike a Modern one, with ye difference of a Jupiter or Minerva carved at ye End of it: next week we shall mount to see ye top of Vesuvius ; it is a most terrible Object indeed, & ye greatest Natural wonder I Ever yet saw - in short we are Encompassed with classical prodigies & when we shall be able to get out of this Enchanting Circle, I cannot possibly tell - I shall write the next post to Brother George, from whom I expect a letter very soon - tho I received one from him, and another from You at Rome - direct your next, as I desired before, A Monsieur Monsieur Barazzi Banquier a Rome - or rather, to Me chez Monsr Frano Barazzi &c . - I have seen ye St James's : here, & from thence & other papers, I see that the Deuce is in him goes on as my heart could wish - I have seen letters, where King is much praised & Miss Plym - but surely O'Brien & Pope must bear ye belle. the poor Midst. Night's Dream I find has failed by a Letter in ye Chronle: - I know ye Author & love him tho he abuses the Grown Gentlemen & ladies - Mrs Cibber, I find, is still prudent, & will run no risks of reputation to support poor Old Drury, to whom she has many, many obligations - What is become of ye Invasion , ye Dupe , & ye new Entertainment ; I hope I shall have some account of 'Em, & a good one, in your next. how does Powell go on? - does he keep or lose his ground - if he is to be advised don't let him play ye fool, as others have done; remember me to all of them, that you think deserve my remembrance; send me some News dear Colman as soon as you receive this - my Love to George - I have not yet received his letter to Florence: If Clutterbuck is among you my best affections to him too, & thank him for his delightful letter & tell him I hope to have ye solid pudding instead of ye praise - I think hitherto that my Plan of Operations have been as nearly followed, as ye Circumstances with admit of, so that be ye success good or bad, I have my share of ye praise as well as of ye pudding - that for Clutterbuck - pray desire George to let me know how David & all his Children are (particularly) in his next - My Wife sends her Love to Him & You & Clutterbuck ; Your Story of Hubert & his family have not surprised me, as we rec'd a Letter from Mrs Hubert & one from Castlefranc: there never sure was such a mean Scoundrel - He had no way to Excuse the meanness of his behaviour to us by pretending a falsehood - I was an Entire Stranger to ye whole, upon my honour, so that it is impossible my Wife could suspect yt her Jewels were changed without acquainting me with it - proof positive - Mrs Hubert might have spared herself ye trouble of sending such a letter after Mrs Garrick to Florence, & she will be sorry that she writ it when she knows ye truth, as I suppose she may before this - What is become of my friend Garnier? - if he's in London pray my Love to Him, we could wish to meet him in Italy, I fear that he will set out next Spring, & then we shall not see him, as our intentions are to go through Germany from Venice, & so by Brussels, & not return to Paris - pray let me know his Motions - What is become of your Terence? I have not yet wrote a word of ye 4th or 5th of the Clandestine Marriage , but I am thinking much about it - We are made so much of (as Mr Cadwallader) by your Dukes & Earls & Barons & Baronets, that I have not a moment for thinking - Churchill's affair makes me unhappy - what are you doing with Wilkes? - is not he undone? or will they go too far , & give him once again ye advantage? - & with will he do with it when he has it? - My heart overflows to Schomberg, Townley, Hubert & I am Ever & most affecty thine my dear friend D Garrick P.S. I have in my hurry forgot this blank side but you can make it out - my Wife & I desire you'll present our Respects to Lord Bath - I do assure You if the Juice was in him , I should not be so Easy with the flirtation that his Lordship sends, & Mrs Garrick receives so warmly, however I am in a Country yt will teach me how to secure my honour under lock & key, & I hope to return to England with less apprehensions of his Lordship - my best wishes to Mr Burney I shall write soon to him. A Monsieur, Monsieur Colman in Lincolns-Inn a Londres, Ingleterra.

column46: Naples Jany ye 2d My dear George. I wrote last Week to my friend Colman, & since that I have received his most friendly & agreeable packet - I rejoice most sincerely with him at ye Success of the Deuce is in him , & am happy that his benefit turned out so Well without my assistance; had I been in England he should have met with no Obstructions in a certain affair, & I hope that he will have philosophy enough to go through those bad roads patiently for a few Months more, which I have laboured through for so many years - My love to him, & all that belong to him, remember that , for I fear I forgot it in my great hurry, & multiplicity of Matter - I yesterday received a very Entertaining letter from our friend Mrs Hale ; pray let her know as much, & how delightful her Correspondence is to Us, & that Mrs will attack her from this place very soon: We have been here a fortnight, & are as well & as jolly, as a fine Climate, fine things & fine doings can make Us - We dine & sup with Lord Spencer, Lord Exeter, the Minister, Consul, &c &c &c almost Every day & Night, we have balls more than twice a Week & parties innumerable - in short We are made very much of, & I have not once yet (tho we have had crosses upon ye road) wished Myself in Southampton Street - I rejoice much at ye Success of Powell ; I hope his head will not be turned with it, & that he will not cease to labour night & day at his profession - I hope too & believe, that Mr Lacy has rewarded him accordingly, you may Answer for Me , pray let it be done handsomely - he has Merit & a family, & will have occasion, for our benevolence - I guess by Colman's letter that Your Season to the 6th of Decr has been tolerable; I long to know how it goes on, & therefore pray write as soon as You have received this, & I may receive it before I leave Rome, where we expect to be about the latter end of February: I shall write the next post day (this day Sen'night) to Mr Burney, & shall let him know the present State of Music in Italy; pray present my best Compts to him, & tell him that his 3 vols of Cochin have been of more Use to Me than all my other books put together - I have lost a little Memdm he gave me about some Music for him; pray ask him to put it down in ire next letter - I want much to know how You have gone on with my good Partner, let me be satisfied in yt particular in ire next; & don't forget to desire Burton to keep an exact list of ye Plays for Me with ye forces, & all occurrences as may happen in ye Course of ye Season, not forgetting the popularity of ye divine Imogen . Colman will tell you how I have been Entertained at Rome, & with what appetite I shall return to it again - the two Dances (Love's Brothers) were very kind & Obliging to us - they are both very ingenious & agreeable Men: the Painter is a great Genius, & will do with he pleases when he goes to London, which will be ye next Spring, I ought to say this Spring, for it is absolutely more than Spring with us - it is as warm now here, as it is with You in June - it is too hot - nay it is Sultry - My Wife sends her love with mine to You & Your Babes - pray write as soon as You receive this - send me a bit of Every thing - & remember to date Ire letter. Yours Ever & Ever most Affectionately D Garrick PS. Remember me to Love &c What's become of ye New Pantomime? A Monsieur, Monsieur Garrick in Somerset Stable Yard near the Strand, London, Ingleterra .
