column46: Naples Jany ye 31st 1764 My dear George. We have been here six Weeks & intend to stay till about the 23d of next Month; then We shall return to Rome for a Month or more, then We shall set out for Bologna in our way to Venice , & from thence through Germany in our way to England - this is our intended Route, which I will dispatch with all convenient speed, but am afraid that I shall not see Your fat face, or kiss ye brawn of it, till ye middle of June - now I am out of ire Clutches I must make a Meal, & a good one, in Italy; I shall never return to it again, & therefore I will make Good Use of my time - We have been very happy here & have received Every mark of favour from all sorts of People - I Eat & drink too much, & laugh from Morning to Night - our Mirth has been lately damped by my poor Wife's keeping her bed & room for many Days, with a most obstinate Rheumatism in her hip - she has been blistered &c &c & tho she is better, yet still continues lame & Weak. however she hopes to be at A Carnival Masquerade (which begins next Tuesday), in ye Dress of a lame old Woman; I have scolded & phyz'd about it, but if she can wag, she goes - We are continually with Lady Orford, Lady Spencer, Lord Exeter Lord Palmerstn & the Nobility of ye Country, who have descended from their great pride & Magnificence to honour Us with their Smiles - in short we are in great fashion & I have forgot England & all my trumpery at Drury Lane, I am glad you go on so well; I find by Gastrell's Lettr & ye news papers, that ye Rites of Hecute go on well. I hope that you will bring Murphy's play out, that I may not be troubled with it when I come to England: I don't understand ire affair with him - pray explain it a little: I have wrote to You from this place & to Colman ; but as my Neapolitan Servant put ye Letters into ye Post We are afraid that he pocketed ye Money & Wiped his Arse with my Wit & humour - I hope you have seen Mrs Hale's Letter, that ire hard Expressions in ire last , may be somewhat melted down in ire next : I can say Nothing about Powel's Benefit, as I am not able to give my opinion at this distance - I fear for his head , & of course for his heart , if he talks of Consequence , he is undone - What in ye name of Wonder is Hamilton doing in Ireland? - I hear, but can't believe ye strange things they say of him - one word about that pray: - You have said Nothing lately of Covent Garden? - do they beat You soundly, or is it only a gentle trimming: have Lacy & you been content with a hundred quarrels a Week? - Colman has hurt me with an Account of his behaviour to him - I fear he dislikes him as my friend - What a beast, if it is so - ! tell Colman that I love him more & more, & thank him most cordialy for his fairy tale - it puzzled me much, for I saw it in ye Papers before I rec'd his letter about it - I have almost seen Every curiosity of this place - I was very near wet to ye Skin yesterday in ye Elision fields at Bay, & therefore did not Enjoy Julius Casar's Palace, & Tully's Villa so much at my Ease as I could wish - I sent Colman an Acct of his age & ye house he was born in. pray let me know if he has received it - I beg one of you will write ye moment you can after ye receipt of this directed to Barazzi at Rome as usual with a whole packet full of News, & the other may write a fortnight after directed to Me, chez Monsieur Udney, Consul de sa Majesty` Britanique, a Venice : I will let You know here or at Rome where You may Write after to Me, for ire letters will be most Acceptable upon ye Road - Lord Exeter sends me ye St James's Chronicle, & the London twice a Week which Entertains me much. I was very much hurt at ye Nonsense in ye St James's about my dancing with ye Duke of D. pray tell Colman that I think Baldwin used me like a Scoundrel to print such a heap of Stuff - Colman, I hope, will receive my Share of that paper for Me, when he receives his own - I shall write to Mr Burney soon - pray remember me kindly to him - with is become of his Musical Entertainment. don't be angry that I urged ye receiving ye debts I mentioned I thought my absence was ye best time for it, & that you might do then what I could not do when in England: My love to Clutterbuck, Townley & all friends - We send our blessings to ire Children & love to yrself - Most truly Affectionately, & Eternally thine D: Garrick. A Monsieur, Monsieur George Garrick in Somerset Stable Yard near the Strand a Londres, Ingleterra .

column46: Rome March the 24th 1764 My Lord I am now writing in a Room, which was once Your Grace's, & is a proof how much this City has fallen since Your time, for the same apartments are now Occupied by Your humble Servant - I have not troubled Your Grace with our Misfortunes at Naples, & our Accidents in going to it - Mrs Garrick & I, willing to get to Naples before Night, set out before our Coach (Your Grace knows my impatience) in a Chaise of Lord Exeter's, which broke down in ye Middle of ye Post, in ye Severest Storm of thunder Lightning, & rain that I ever saw - as the Servant was gone before to prepare post horses, I was obliged to send my wife in a Calash four Miles with a Strange Man to send me help from ye next town, while I sat cooling my heels in ye Road, & taking Care of the nimble-finger'd Neapolitans - My Philosophy had some trial I must confess - whether my wife by this Accident caught Cold, or was effected by the Climate of Naples, I can't determine, but soon after her Arrival there, she was Seized with a Rheumatism in one of her hips, was obliged to keep her bed for a fortnight, & is not yet quite recovered tho it is three Months since she was first Attacked - this has been a great drawback upon our Pleasures, for tho some Husbands would have rejoiced to have their Wives tyd by ye leg; yet I must confess that I have been fool Enough to wish her Even at ye top of Vesuvius with Me - I have had an opportunity to consider the Characters of the People of Naples in different lights - I have seen them, happy & very Miserable in ye Space of three Months - the Scarcity of Corn produced such dreadful sights, which I would not but have seen for ye world, & yet my heart sinks at ye very remembrance of them - I cannot say which surprised Me most - their natural Curiosities, the People, or the Government - to give Your Grace one trait of their great Minister, & whom they call the Pitt of the two Sicilies; the Marquis Tennuci is so frightened at thunder, that when it begins to grumble, he puts on a Domino, Hood & all, made of raw Silk which, as it will not receive Electrical matter, he thinks will secure him from the Effects of the Lightning - My Lord Spencer was most dangerously ill at Naples, He is now at Rome & in perfect health, his Lordship & my Lady have been most particularly civil to Us - his last letters from England have put him into ye highest Spirits, & one paragraph in a former one gave me infinite Pleasure - Your Grace was most warmly extolled for Ire Speech upon a certain Occasion & as warmly applauded for your whole conduct & candour in that affair - the letter was written by One of the other side, & brought double Weight with it - my theatrical affairs have succeeded so well in my Absence, that I have an opportunity of making more Holidays if I choose it; my health & Spirits have been so much improved by this recess, that I am almost tempted to repent of my Follies, & be a Merry Andrew no longer - I have lost all relish for the Stage both as Manager and Actor - I cannot flatter Myself that Your Grace will send me any Commissions to buy Pictures or Statues, for I fear that You will not think my Taste in these Matters (which you always underrated) so improved by my travels to place any confidence in it, but if I could be of ye least Service in Italy I shall be better able to give an Account of Myself, than I can do at present - Mrs Garrick presents her Duty to Your Grace & Lady Dorothy & If I should not be too impertinent I would present my Respects to her Ladyship & all their Lordships - The Duke of York will be here in ye holy Week - Great preparations for his Reception - and it is confidently affirmed from ye best Authority that he will be presented with some of his Holiness's Virtue`, which occasions much uneasiness. I am Your Grace's most faithful & most Obedient humble Servant D: Garrick. PS We shall go from hence in about 3 weeks to Venice.

column46: Rome April 11th 1764 My dear Colman. Though I resolved in my last letter to George not to trouble You any more till I got to Venice, yet I cannot hold it out so long, but must say a word or two more to You from this Place; which of all Places in the World is the most worth coming to & writing about - to show You, that I think so, You must know that I am antiquityhunting from Morning to Night & my poor wife drags her lame leg after me: by ye bye she is now much better, & we have hopes of her being able to run away again from Me, if she can meet with another Captn Casual; She desires her love to you, & thanks You for writing to Me, as I sure to be always in Spirits for some time after ye receipt of a letter from You: I have not been quite so well here as at Naples, which is rather extraordinary; whether I fatigued myself too much, or whether ye Climate does not suit me so well, I can't say, but I have had some disagreeable nervous fiutterings that made me as grave as an Owl for a few days, but since ye rains have fallen (& they come down here in Pailfuls) & ye Sun is bright upon us, I have been as frisky as ye poor flies, who were woefully damped by ye wet weather, but are now as troublesome & as pert as your humble Servant - His Holiness the Pope is trying by prayers tears & intercessions to avert the Famine which his State is threatened with - He has crept up the holy stairs (santa Scala) which were brought from Jerusalem, he has ordered processions & what not - We are not so bad, as they are at Naples, for there indeed ye Tragedy was deep - I remember some Scenes with horror, & since we came away, many People have dropped down in ye Street, & been taken away dead, from mere want of food - our Prospect at Venice is rather worse, for we hear that ye Plague has spread as far Trieste, & that they begin to talk of Quarantine in ye Neighbouring States, if so, we shall run ye gauntlet terribly, but we are not dismayed, & must go through with it - I must thank you again for the trouble & Care you have had about Count Firmian's books - He is very happy at ye Execution of ye Commission, and was highly pleased with your sending your own matters to him gratis - it pleased me much - I have not seen a St James's Chronicle since ye End of Jany - if I have them I wish you with desire George to keep them for me to rummage over when I come to England - Mr Baldwin I hear is no friend to our house - a propose - I am very angry with Powell for playing that detestable part of Alexander - Every Genius must despise it, because that, & such fustian-like Stuff, is ye bane of true merit - If a Man can act it well, I mean to please ye People, he has something in him that a good actor shd not have - he might have served Mrs Pritchard, & himself too, in some good natural character: I hate your Roarers - Delane was once a fine Alexander - damn ye Part - I fear twill hurt him - but this among ourselves - I was told by a Gentleman who is just come from Sterne , that he is in a very bad way - I hope Becket has stood my Friend in regard to what he ought to have received for me, some time ago - I had a draught upon him from Sterne for 20 pts Ever since he went abroad - pray hint this to him, but let him not be ungentle with Sterne - I have sent the plan of a fine Scene & coloured, among some small things in a little Box of Mr Stanley's of ye Custom-house - it is in several parts & wrote upon ye back which is 1st 2d &c - I will send a further explanation of it, but any Italian & our Sanderson will understand it - they shd go upon it directly, it will have a fine Effect. Many thanks to you for ire attendance on ye Pantomime - I am sure they wanted help - no more humour than Brickbats - I am afraid that Love in humorous matters carries too much Gut to be Spirited - flip flaps, & great changes without meaning may distil from the head, whose Eyes are half asleep; but humour, my dear Coley, & scenes that shall be all alive alive ho, can only proceed from men of small stature, whose Eyes are Either quite asleep, or quite awake - in short, from Men who laugh heartily, & have small scars at ye Ends of their noses - I am surprised about Murphy, & want to know how he from Mr Lacy - poor Lloyd! & yet I was prepared - the death of any one we like don't shock us so much when we have seen them long in a lingering decay - Where is ye bold Churchill? - What a Noble ruin! - when he is quite undone, you shall send him here, & he shall be shown among ye great fragments of Roman Genius - Magnificent in Ruin! - I have wrote this on purpose to tell you that Voltaire in his Additions a l'Histoire General , at page 183 under Usages du Seizieme Siecle , says something about translating Plautus into Verse that will be of use in ire preface to Terence - Speed ire Plow my dr friend. have you thought of the Clandestine Marriage ? I am at it - I must desire you to write to me once more & direct a Monsr Monsr G- Gentilhomme Anglais chez Monsieur Dutens a Turin , & I shall get it by hook or by crook Pray send me all kind of news - a Letter from you will comfort me in bad roads, & throe plague & famine - so write I beg as soon as you receive this - desire George to speak to Mr Stanley about my things in his box - my Love to all the Schombergs, Townleys, Kings, Hogarths, Churchills, Huberts &c. &c Yrs most affectionately Ever D G Davd Garrick Remember me kindly at home - A Monsieur, Monsieur Colman in the new Square Lincolns-Inn, London. Inghilterra.

column46: Venice June 6th 1764 My Dear George Here we are still, and indeed very much against my mind; but that the Physicians here all advise me to return to Padua, in order to try an application of the mud of some Mineral Spring at Abano near that city, which they say is a specific for the Rheumatism and Sciatica: My Wife's lameness has been rather worse here, perhaps owing to the watery situation of this place, but I am much out of spirits about it, and would give the world I was at home - God knows whether she may not be crippled all her life, and therefore nobody must blame me for trying every thing for her cure: we go to Padua in a Day or two and shall see what effect the mud will have in three or four days, if a good one we imagine a fortnight will do, and then we Shall set forward for England as fast as we can, unless I am prevented by a letter from you at Ausburgh, which I hope you have written, and I shall receive very soon - I have prepared a great deal of Music for our Use, I am about engaging some Dancers (a Man and Woman) and will endeavour to send you over a good Violin from Rome, an excellent one - If you should have any thing more to say to me, or if any new occurrence has happened, you may write to me at Messrs Selwyn and Folly at Paris and I will direct them how to send it forward to me: If you write don't be longer than a few days after you have received this - I have drawn upon Clutterbuck this day for one hundred pounds in favour of our consul here Mr Udney - pray my Love to Clutterbuck and tell him this, or my friend Stammer, in his absence. I have had notice of the Florence Wine shipped from Leghorn in the Raven Captn Alexr Scott, and some essences for Mrs Garrick; pray take care when they come, to pay freight and duty and lodge them ready for our arrival - perhaps we may be there as soon as the wine - according to my bills of lading you must pay four shillings sterling for freight - I'll send you the bills by a gentleman next Saturday - Captn Butler is here, and has given me the Ghost and the farces - I think to send a few books by him he sets out from hence next Saturday. My Love to all friends, and let me hear from you to Messrs Selwyn and Folly - I shall not go to Paris unless you have sent me other News to Ausburgh; in the mean time our Love to you and yours and believe me most truly and Affectionately Yours D. Garrick. No News from Cibber? What of Yates? - Last Monday I saw the finest sight my eyes ever beheld, it was the Regatta in honour of the King's birth-day, and appeared to be a dream or a fairy tale realised. I am grown fat, and sleep half the day in a Gondola. A Monsieur, Monsieur George Garrick in Somerset Stable Yard near the Strand, London (Inghilterra) .

column46: Abano near Padua June 25th 1764 My Lord. I had the honour of Ire Grace's letter at Venice, where I was Enjoying the magnificent Entertainments which were given by the State to the Duke of York. The Regatta they gave him was all a Dream & fairy Vision, & more than answered our Expectations, tho they were sufficiently raised by the various reports; & the great preparations: It is said that this visit of his Royal Highness has cost the State & ye four Noble deputed Venetians, more than a hundred & twenty thousand Sequins. They were very solicitous (indeed too solicitous) to entertain him, for they would have overlaid him with ceremony & their great wigs, had not He broke from them sometimes to prevent suffocation - His Royal Highness has been most gracious to Me - I am greatly obliged to Your Grace for the very delicate manner of excusing Yourself about Pictures & Statues, and I am thoroughly convinced that it is owing to Your Grace's want of Money , & not to my want of taste, that I have not an immediate commission. I shall execute that of the Prints to the best of my power. I am at this moment in treaty for no less than two Pictures by Tempesto, two Basins, a Vandyke, a Rubens, a Paul Veronese &c. I have a little money to throw away, & I don't see why I should not be a little ridiculous as well as My betters. Mrs Garrick & I are retired to this Place to try the Mud of ye hot springs upon her very disagreeable & obstinate complaint: She has undergone the operation Eight times, & thinks herself the better for it - the People here give such an Account of Its Efficacy, that I have withstood the urgent calls of my Brother, & my own impatience to go to England, in hopes of finding some relief for her, if not a Cure. Should we fail here too, our Journey to England will be as Melancholy as it is long - We are in a very pleasant house, well situated, & built by Palladio - it belongs to a Count Seco, who has most politely lent it to us with Every Convenience, but that of getting good beef & Mutton, till ye 15th of the next month. the imprudent Step of Lady S. S. has sorely vexed me; I always thought she had a foolish liking for ye Drama, & ye dramatis personae , but I could not have imagined, yt the flesh with have overpowered her Spirit, when there was a good understanding to have helped in the Struggle - it is a most deplorable Business indeed! Lord & Lady Spencer left us more than a fortnight ago, & my Pleasures & Spirits are gone with them, his Lordp has made no great purchases in virtue` - he is in treaty about ye famous Magdalen of Guido in ye Barberini Palace at Rome, & I believe he will succeed. He has bought two very famous pictures of Salvator Rosa at florence, & gave two hundred pounds less than ye late Lord Leicester once offered for them; these & a famous Ring, which was Prince Eugene's, & bought of Count Zanetti at Venice, are all his treasure from Italy: I forgot a woman's head by Raphael, as they say, & a very good Sketch of a Picture by Baroche. We lived in the same house with Mr Howard & Mr Langdale - I think it was lucky they travelled together - the first is a very worthy good natured Young Man, & I don't know a better Sort of Man than the last - He is prudent & sensible & what he wants in learning is better supplied by discretion & an Understanding in Spite of his bigotry - I'll answer for it, that Norfolk House is not mistaken in him. Your Grace's trouble, & my Impertinence is at an End - Mrs Garrick joins with me in Duty to your Grace & in Respects to Lady Dorothy & all the Lords. I am Your Grace's Most faithful humble Servant D Garrick PS. We Expect to be in England ye beginning or rather ye 2d Week in August - we shall go by Ausburgh, Stratsburgh, Nancy &c -

column46: Munich the Capital of Bavaria Augst the 23d My dear George My wife wrote to You when I was upon my sick bed, but recovering, I now write myself, to free You from all fears of Me , as Yours dated the 12th of July has Me, of You - I have had a most violent bout of it indeed, but by Care, I am told my health will be ye better for it - our Disorders are partly of ye same kind, & tho we suffer much in our Sickness (I almost gave myself up for gone) we are ye better for it afterwards - I desire no more of this purification - I had two Physicians - I have often made Myself happy that You could Enjoy Hampton tho I could not, I hope You have had ire family there, sent for the Cows, had the old Mare, rid about, Eat ye best fruit, & got Yrself stout as a Lion again to go ye next Campaign, pray go often to Hampton & do, as if it was your own. I think we had a narrow Escape from ye fire tho Your great & brotherly attention to my Concerns there did You no good. for God's sake, my dear George, why will You say I love to hurt You, whenever I receive a letter from You such Expressions damp ye great pleasure I have in receiving it, & particularly as I am now - You might have seen by my letter yt I wanted to come off my not mentioning Coley's Girl in my Letters, & therefore, if I remember right so foolish a thing, I said I wondered you had not delivered my Compts there, & this was all - but for God's sake my dear George don't let Us be warm upon such Nonsense, we love Each other Much, confide in Each Other, & have so many other things of Consequence to think upon, that I beg you'll never mistake me again & hurt me - by ye bye I don't like ye wench, & never thought of her, & yet I would not offend Colman, who I fear will be much harassed with her - an Idiot - my Friend Colman's Fortune & Expectations have made me happy, what a happy little Rogue it will be! - I am sorry ye trumpery cost duty & surprised about ye few books for they all came from England, & most of 'Em, English - I have hired no dancers, I am in treaty for a pair for next Year, if you had written ire Wants Sooner, I could have got a very active Girl at Padua. I shall certainly follow Your & My Friends Advice about not Acting - ire Judgment coincides so much with my own, that it is resolved - the Music you receive may be kept apart till I come - let Johnson have ye Vols - I am a little at a loss what You will do for a Woman Tragedian to stare & tremble with ire Heroes, if Yates should bitch You - but she must come. I hope that Powel will continue to please - He must have a Master to watch his English which I suppose Coley will do - how do Holland & He (Powel) agree - Jealous - Clive I suppose more Fussocky than Ever, & Pritchard often ailing - Pope I hope flourishes - Pray let me know if You think of ye Invasion next Year - or do you keep it till I can oversee it Myself - What is become of Hardham's Girl? & of Jack himself? I could wish by ye bye that You would Ask Leach if he has paid ye 100 pts to Jack I am security for - I am sure you have looked a little into my affairs at Hampton & that all is round & sound - I wish I could part with ye manor of Hendon . I am afraid Mrs Wyld is asleep - if that Weight was off my heart, it would be lighter - but some lucky time may come - My Love to Clutterbuck & all all friends from one End to the Other - I can scarce hold my pen in my hand - direct to Me a MonSr MonSr G chez Monsieur Sager Munck a Franckfort - write directly, & take care to put it into ye proper post - My dearest Brother, Your most truly & Affectionately D Garrick PS. I have wrote about poor Linney several times. Angleterre , To George Garrick Esqr in Somerset Stable Yard in the Strand, London.

column46: Paris Feby 16th Dear Colman. You see by ye Enclosed that you will have a letter by ye next post - when ye Baronet sends it, I shall direct it only, & put it into ye post - I have desired to see him, for it was much ado that we knew how to send ye letter, but he keeps with ye lady, & sees No body chez lui - I'll go to ye Ambassador's tomorrow in hopes of catching him, & I will call at Mademlle Clair's for that purpose too; but I am sorry that you did not draw upon him in my favour (as ye Trade calls it) & then I shd have had a sort of right to torment him - he has some ready money at present, & I could wish that we had our 150 out of it - Monsr de Beaumont wants to know what Security you have, & he can tell you what is to be done here - tho if you are safe in Ireland what more can be done about ye great debt? My dear Colman you frightened with me ye Extract of a Lettr from Paris - I am very sorry that you mentioned ye woeful want of me as Managr & Actr - they will suspect it came from me, & I have no right to say so much, as I have been taking my pleasures & left ye Theatre for a time - it appears ungenerous & ungrateful in me: which hurt me much - I beg that you will do all you can to make them not think ye paragraph mine, if I am suspected - I never in my life praised myself knowingly except a little matter in ye Fribbleriad , which always pinched me - perhaps I am too sensible about this delicacy, & nobody thinks about me or ye Extract - settle my mind about that matter in ire next - the devil was in you to mention the hoop at Sadler's Wells , for I wrote that very thing to my Friend Arden at Lord Sponsor's - I desired you to say something against me, & you stuck ire Pen in ire heart, & wrote as you felt - I wish from my Soul that you had not - If Becket mentions you to any body, it is just as as bad - Made Riccoboni (a very good Novelist, & a generous Creature,) is very angry with Becket. I took his part - I fear he did not do right, she is much hurt at him - We had a fine laugh at Baron D'Albach's (where you dined once) about the Wicked Compy I keep; I am always with that Set. pray set my Mind at Ease, I hate to be thought malicious - Has George said any thing to you about it - ? pray tell me for I can't know Elsewhere, with is become of Hardham's Girl ? & tell me what Poem is that against Murphy & others - there is likewise a Vole of Poetry with cuts & very pretty head & tail pieces I saw in Suard's hands pray let me know something about these matters Yrs ever & cordially D G. Love to yrs P.S. vive la Clandestine Marriage!

column46: Paris March 10th 1765 My dear Colman. I can very readily believe what You tell me of my Brother Consul - He will never forgive my being the means of his making a figure in the world - but this between Ourselves. I have other matters for You when I see You, & which he does not expect - but Mum - pray does Powell continue to visit you, & get a little Sense from you, or is he topsy turvey like ye rest & thinks like Ricd ye 3d that he is himself alone ? I hope he is wiser - but I'll answer for Nothing or Nobody in a playhouse - the Devil has put his hoof into it, & he was a Deceiver from ye beginning of ye world - tell me really what you think of him - I am told by several that he will bawl & roar - Ross , I hear, has got reputation in Lear - I don't doubt it - the Town is a facetious Gentleman - What do you mean, my good friend, by my being obliged to appear, if I manage? upon looking over ire letter, I find your words are Expected to appear - I must entreat you to be very sincere with me - do the Town in general really wish to see me on ye Stage? or are they (which I rather think ye truth) as cool about it as their humble Servant? - I have no maw for it at all, & yet something must be done to restore our credit: that I may be able to play, & as well as Ever, I will not deny, but that I am able to do as I have done, wear & tear, I neither must or can, or will - the Physicians here, Dr Gem among the rest, advise me, to a man, against appearing again - I had a little nervous attack last week, & the Dr croakt more hoarse than usual against my thinking to do as formerly. Tranquillity & retiremt from business (he says) are the only means to make me Myself again. a Tragedy here called ye Siege of Calais written by a Friend of ye Clairon & also my intimate, has made ye People Mad. The Boxes from top to bottom are all taken for Months to come - they give it gratis next Wednesday to ye People, when ye Doors will be opened at 12 o'Clock at Noon, & the Play will begin at 2. it is ye present Epidemical distemper - The Author has recd many favours from ye King - 3000 livers - a Gold Medal - Liberty to dedicate to him - and with not - the French will hardly bear to hear a Criticism upon it - the following distich is handed about in terrorem . D'un Auteur Citoyen vouloir ternir l'honneur, C'est pretendre a l'Esprit au depens de son Coeur. however there are some objections made by ye cooler few - there is much merit in ye Play, & more luck in ye Choice of the Subject - I rejoice at the success, for Monsr de Belloy the Author of it is a most ingenious Modest & deserving man - his Genius is an honour to his own Country & would be to any other - You may mention something of this in ye St James's but not from Me - now to serious business we'll advance - I cannot get a Meeting with ye Chevalier - he is never at home & has not yet appointed a Meeting with me. I send you the last letter I had from him - I would have you write directly to him & before I set off, I will endeavour to get ye draught accepted, for our Friend de Beaumont advises that - I will certainly have a categorical answer from him, which may force him to acceptance & then I will leave ye Note in good hands to get ye money by force. I had a consultation with Mr Beaumont & another Lawyer, they both thought the getting the bill accepd ye best way - ire Indemnification must pass ire common Pleas (you know how) before we could ask a permission here to execute it upon Sr H. a round about way, but might be done - the method in hand is ye best, cd we but get him to Accept. I have sent you a Copy of my lettr (Copied by my Italian Served) when I sent ye Note (for I could not see him) & his answer - You must press the Acceptance, & say, that you shall make a bad figure with me, that I have laid out money for You, & in my next to him, I shall desire an Answer in a very plain manner & hint that you have not used me well to send me a draught was doubtful of acceptance - if you like this Scheme, let me know directly - for I shall have but just time to do it, as it shd be done - I shall follow ire directions. this is all I can say at present, for ye boy waits to take it to our Ambassador's - it goes by his bag - Yrs Ever & most truly D Garrick Madam sends her best to you mine to yrs A Gentleman Yesterday showed me a letter from England in which was ye follg lines to me have they been in ye Papers? I have not got it right the third line is better in ye Original but I have not time to recollect it -

column46: June 30th 1766 Dear Colman. I rejoice much at your safe arrival at Paris - You set out in Storm & tempest & we were afraid that the Sea would have been rather too frisky for ire Stomachs - but the worst is past, & I hope madam & You are well contented with Leviez & his accommodations. to begin with what you are most interested about, I must tell, that ire sweet boy is at this instant as happy & as well as Ever I knew him - I have made him two visits since ire departure, which he has taken most kindly - the last time his Eyes sparkled when he saw Me - He is greatly to know why I call him Georgy go ging - & has very seriously interrogated his Duenna about it - We have worked very hard in the Garden together, & have played at Ninepins till I was obliged to declare off - He is well taken care of indeed - the old Lady, & the maiden Pierce, are most trusty Guardians, & be assured that you may set ire tender hearts at rest about him - I go to Essex tomorrow, & at my return, We are to have a day at Hampton, & he is to make love to my niece Kitty, & a plumb-pudding - He seems very fond of ye Party, & we will endeavour to make him forget his loving parents - once more my dear friend, Let not a single thought about ire Boy disquiet You - He could not be better if you were with him - so no more of that. Thompson dined with me at Hampton - he spoke very highly & affecty of You - he has no design upon us this next Season, but talks of trying his hand again - he intends writing to you, I believe him to be a very good natured, wellmeaning Man - Steevens has inquired after me to give me some papers from You - what they are I can't tell, but we have missed one another, & I am still in ye Dark; & you don't mention with they are in ire letter - I have had a letter from Bickerstaff, he is at Paris, & is going to give some Account of our Theatre in the Journal Encyclopiq : You will see it I suppose - Sanderson tells Me that they have laid ye timbers for ye first floor of ire house, it rises most magnificently to the Ferry-Passengers; you'll be surprised to find yrself Master of a Chateau at ire return - don't lose the Autumn for planting trees to screen you from timber Yard - my love to Madam & remember me to Leviez - You must not see a single french friend of Mine, but you must tell him, how much I am his humble Servant - God bless you & believe me most affectionately yrs D Garrick George desires his best to you A Monsieur, Monsieur Colman chez Monsr Leviez, Merchant des Estampes, rue des Arcs, Fouxbourgs St Germains A Paris.

Sir. Mr King's Accident & Mrs Yates's Indisposition have distressed our affairs so much, that we shall really want Matter to go on with ye business of ye theatre, if we don't bring out what we have in Rehearsal without them - besides if we defer the Alteration of ye Country Wife, we shall not be able to fulfil our Engagements with other Authors - The parts of our Play were delivered out as fast as they were written, & Mr Dodd & Miss Pope who have long Characters (particularly Dodd) had not theirs till the time You favoured me with ire first letter, so I cannot imagine where the Gentlemen of ye other house got their Intelligence. I am very glad that You have not ye least Care about it, but the Whip-hand must be Yours from the Novelty, & Variety - I cannot say that I agree with You in not caring, whether they are damned, or not, I wish 'Em both Success, & don't doubt but they Will have it. I am Sir your most humble Served D: Garrick

Sunday My dear Coley. Hampton has had a prodigious Effect upon Me: my Cough & hoarseness are 50 p cent better for ye Change of air - instead of coughing all night, I have been disturbed but twice & thrice & that not rudely, & have passed ye rest of ye Night very pleasantly - My Wife has persuad'd Me to stay here till Wadi when I hope to wait upon the English Merchant with all my wits & Spirits about Me - in ye meantime, I could wish, if not disagreeable to You, that You would look in upon them on Wednesday , & I will make my appearance on Thursday Morning: I hope to see You Wadi Evening : my Wife says if you will dine with us on Wadi at four She will present us with a fine haunch of Venison - Say You will , in a Note by ye Bearer to Morrow - You must write to me; & say if I am to furnish an Epilogue for the Merchant - I certainly will do my best if you are not provid'd - If you intend to stand by ye London Journal, I will prepare some comicality for it; I have a hundred thoughts about it, & will be always doing something. I intend Crambo to be ye laughing Rhyming reviewer of Every thing - Mrs Pritchard has sent a most kind Message to Me, & will do anything I desire her - she shall set the Part agoing, & when we are safe landed (tho if Mrs Bennet played it there is not ye least danger) Mrs Hopkins may Relieve her, in case of Indisposition &c &c - Poor Becket is very angry with Baldwin for abusing What we act, & he prints - pray keep up ye Ball, we shall have some sport with him. My Love & Best Services to Madam & kiss to your dear little Boy, & my warmest Affections to Your Self my dear Coley - D: Garrick.

Sunday Apple 5th My dear George. In the first place, I am grown as fat as a Hog & You may measure with Me at my return to London, without tucking in Your Guts, till Your face is as red, as bull-beef. I have had a letter from Never who is at Paris, & offers us his Service, in preference to the Opera , Vienna & other Engagements he may have - if Mr Lacy has altered his Mind, I will write to know his proposals; if Mr Lacy thinks it not right to have him, I will let him know we are Engaged - Send me a line about that on Tuesday Post or Wednesday's at farthest, for I will send you a french letter to be put into ye Post on Tuesday afterwds. Colman & Changuion are arrived - We pulled off our hats, but did not smile - our Friends here will stir heaven & Earth to bring Us together - make ye best of it, it will be but a darn. and does Dido please? Good God! - & will they come twice to see it? - Good God! it is time to leave ye Stage, if such a performance can Stand upon It's legs: - Good God! - I have seen a paragraph for Cautherly but not an Advertisement - I hope ye Lad will get Something - I expect a full Account, (& hope of a full house at King's Benefit), of the New hodge podge of Linco: pray let me know it by ye first post; that will be on Tuesday , ye day you receive this - Have you seen Kelly yet? - do you know any thing of his play? - Is Johnston yet arrived from Ireland? - I believe Arthur would gladly receive Miss Reynolds? - I have told him that I with give Up her Articles to her advantage - he knows what she has, & has dined with Mr Davenport - so that perhaps she with be as willing to part with us, as We with Her. Suppose You were to feel her pulse on this Matter, I have kept up her Importance with Arthur - they ask for her here much, & indeed she would be right to desire her Conge` of Us - I see advertised ye theatrical Campaign price s1-d6 - have you heard of it? - pray let me know what the Subject is, & what they say of it? Love to Your dear little ones - Ever & most affectionately Yours D: Garrick Poor Jacob Tonson - I have not put ye name of ye Inn on Dr Hawkesworth's letter, for I doubt whether it is Lion's or Clement's , I believe it is ye last, if Johnston is returned from Ireland he'll tell You, & carry it, for he has done so by many before

Thursday Dr George. In the first place give my best Wishes, & Services to my Partner, & tell him, that I believe his Suspicions are well founded - He may be well-assur'd that I with not suggest ye Smallest hint of what I know to don't imagine, Mr George, that I am such a booby - Colman has told me that he has an affair to open to Me, but we have always been interrupted by Somebody, or another, so I have not yet had ye Whole, & which he has some qualms in bringing out - however I am prepared, & he will be surprised at my little concern & Ease upon this Occasion - I am sure there is Something in it, & yet ye more I think of it, ye more I am puzzled: Who finds Money? - What is the plan? Who are ye directors? damn me if I comprehend it, but I shall know more - suppose You & Mr Lacy meet me at his house at Isleworth next Wednesday Morning, I will come from Hampton, & be with You at his own time, & he may return to Town again - you may send me a Note by ye Hampton Stage Tuesday Next Which I shall receive at the time I arrive there, & pray send the two Reviews for Becket , or what other things You may have for Me. pray mind that - I think we should meet directly - I am glad Vernon has signed - & I think we shd close with Earn , but let Mr Lacy determine. My Wife desires You to write a Note ye Night you receive this (Saturday) to our Maid at Hampton, Nancy Hetherington to prepare some Mutton , & a pudding with some Asparagus for our dinner on Tuesday about 5 o'Clock - rather Six . pray get me all ye News to send on Tuesday by ye Coach. What, has Holland no hand in this? - is he hummed? - I have not ye least Idea of ye Matter nor have I ye least Notion of them doing any thing to give Us one moment of uneasiness - I hope Mr Lacy thinks so too - God bless You & Yours my wife Sends her Love to You all. D Garrick PS. Remember ye Newspapers for Reading & a Slice of News - I shall let you know with C- Says. -

January 15th Dear Sir, I would not willingly hinder your raising the devil for the Northampton Election; and, therefore, I have avoided breaking in upon you. - If you have dispatched the old gentleman (for Mr. Lane tells me you have been of late much locked up), I should be glad you would come abroad again, and see your earthly friends. - Pray let us settle our Zenobia accounts: we have many pounds of yours in our hands - Have you settled with Davies? Will you have my note, or will you have more money - Speak and have, Master Ford! When shall we talk about certain Dramas, or Drama? will you make me the guardian of your dramatic fame, or will you renounce, at once, the devil and all his works, except those which may call your honour to Westminster-hall, or to the Bar of the House of Commons. - I am almost afraid to speak, and yet I cannot be silent. - I would have been with you to-day, but I am going to take a little air at Hampton. Madame Riccaboni sends you a volume and a note. Ever and truly yours, D. Garrick

column46: July 30th 1770 Dear Madam. You cannot imagine how much I think Myself honoured by Your most flattering, friendly letter - the Moment I received it, at my return from Hampshire this day, I sit down to answer it - You may be assured, that no Care shall be wanting on my part to do Justice to ye Author of the Bon ton : I shall not read it in ye Common way, but think twice, before I speak my Mind - if I can see a Merit in it proper for ye Stage, You may depend upon it, that I will show my regard to You, by my Zeal in promoting Its Success: Should I think Otherwise, I should pay a very ill compliment to your friendship, & my own Sense of it, if I did not speak to You, as Your Shakespeare phrases it, as to my thoughts, as I do ruminate . Sorry, very Sorry am I to hear both for ye Sake of ye Author, Stage, & Manager, that a certain Lady has not had, even ye tip of her Finger in the Dramatic pie - if she had I would have underwritten it unseen, & unheard - You have had such wondrous Success in Smuggling, I could wish that you would try another Venture, & take me into partnership - but what a parcel of stuff I am writing, & in the midst of much Company, without fear, or Wit! - I must tell you, that Mrs Garrick (Who begs her best respects may be presented to You) & I set out immediately for Lincolnshire thence to Cambridgeshire, & shall not return home these three Weeks or a Month - I will not pretend to read ye Play, till my return, & then it shall be ye first thing I will do - the Author should know that We are at this Moment Engaged to more plays, & petites pieces than we can act for the two Winters to come, unless any of the Authors of them should choose to withdraw in performances. Pray, dear Madam, accept of this galloping &, I am afraid you'll say, Stumbling Epistle, as ye mere overflowings of a Warm heart, highly Sensible of Your friendship, & favour - You see, how I can trust Your feelings, while I am afraid of Your Understanding - I am Mrs Montagu's most faithful & Obliged humble Servant D: Garrick. upon reading over my hasty letter, I find I have impertinently offered myself as a partner in Smuggling - that is - wishing You would as secretly write a play, as you did a certain Essay, & that I, as Manager, might partake of ye plot & ye Profits. To Mrs Montagu at Denton near Newcastle upon Tyne.

column46: Hampton Augst 22 1770 My Dear Madam The Day after I returned to this Place, I did the thing the most agreeable to Me - obeyed Your Commands - I read over the Comedy with a most uncommon prejudice in It's favour, & Sorry, very sorry I am to say, that with all the influence Mrs Montagu has, & Ever shall have upon Me, I could not turn, or twist my Mind to approve of the Performance: The Scenes are merely dialogues without the least interest in the fable, or indeed Enough of a Story to carry on ire Attention - I likewise think that the Characters are not Well marked, & that the vis comica is wanting through the Whole - Lady Ethrington bids the fairest for a dramatic personage; but she is not new - the follies of her Ladyship have been so highly & exquisitely exposed in one of the last Dialogues in Lord Littleton's Collection, that I should be afraid of It's Success upon the Stage. there is, notwithstanding all I have said, and I cannot conceal, nor will Ever Endeavour to cloak my opinion from You, there is a certain Merit in the Writing of the dialogue but wholly void of dramatic force & interest to give it Success in the representation - I shall return to London next Sunday Evening, when I will carefully convey the Comedy to your house in Hill Street - It gives me great Uneasiness to send You these, my Sincere Thoughts upon a Work, for the Author of Which You express so great a regard. I flatter Myself that You will trust in my Sincerity, what Ever doubts (& I have many Myself) You may have of my Judgment. I am most truly Ire Obliged & Obedt D Garrick Mrs Garrick presents her Respects, & I beg Mine to Mrs Montagu. To Mrs Montagu at Denton near Newcastle upon Tyne.

column46: Jany 25. 1771 Dear Brother. I sit down at this time to do a most disagreeable thing to me, which is to tax you with Neglect, unkindness, & I will not add injustice to Me - I have Suffered much of late, I have hid my uneasiness as well as I could, I have had Moments of good Spirits, but my Mind has still returned to You, & your behaviour to Me - some late circumstances have brought this letter somewhat forwarder than I intended it, & a Weight upon my thoughts have pressed me to disclose 'Em to You - I shall not Accuse You of being always uneasy when You are with Me, & Your excuse of business to get away as soon as possible, I think that would be Weakness in Me, & ye only Way not to remedy it; but as I imagine such seeming unkindness proceeds from Your unwillingness to hear my complaints, Your visits of hurry are not unnatural - but to ye business - did I Ever keep any Concern of any kind from You, have I not always opened my heart, & designs to You, have You not had permission to open my letters, & know Every thing about me, & my affairs? - have you returned this kindness? - have you not been possessed sometime of a Country house of horses, Chariot &c without so much as in ye least hinting it to Me? - had you been possessed of ye fortune of Lord Clive such a Brother (as (I think) I think I have been to You) should have been in common civility at least acquainted with it - I have never heard of it but from ire Neighbours, to whom I have always expressed my ignorance - an old Clergyman attacked me at Court on ye Birthday as Your Neighbor in ye Country - What is this Mystery? - if I was not kindly to be admitted into ye secret, surely I had a right to be a partaker of it - but let that be passed over - I can have my separate Secrets, if I please, & at least balance that Account with You - I have likewise no right, perhaps I have not, to ask how Your Circumstances can bear this load of Expense, & whether it is not strange with ire family, & complaints of hard times, hard relations &c that you have voluntarily taken a load upon You, which, I fear, you are not able to bear - if it is said, for that has been dropped, (for I hear more than I could wish) that Mr insisted upon ire having it, or taking it - this mends not ye matter with Me - I am still unkindly treated - I must tell You too, that You did not please me by sending ye Receipt to Mr Hoar to get money from my tenant G-f? how could you know in With manner I intended to act by him, & ire not telling me of it, till I had exposed Myself, was a most disagreeable Circumstance: I must for ye future Insist that no Monies of Mine, upon any Account are taken up without my Receipt from any one Person whatsoever - I come now to my request - which is that You make me acquainted with the State of Fermignac's Acct - You know that I had resolved not to pay a Shilling of ye Jubilee business but by ye Money owing to Me then - I now calmly assure You, that I will not: I had (I think generously) determined to pay the debts of ye adventurers of ye Jubilee - I told You I would pay 'Em with ye Legacy-Money - I told You to make a partition of it, & that I was ready to give any Security for paying my portion of any after debts, if they shd come in - if You had consulted the Spirit of ye deed, it shd not have been dragged on to this time, to make what would have been a piece of Generosity quickly done, a flat tame Action so laggingly performed - I must entreat You to lay ye account before Me, that I may Act accordingly - I can have no pleasure in knowing more of your Secrets, than what immediately concern Me, But these I have a right to, & my affairs demand that I be instructed immediately - You have known my Wishes, my uneasiness upon this Matter, & I wish You had done it before & openly from Yourself - I am Dear Brother in expectation of ire Compliance with my request. Yrs Sincerely, D Garrick

Friday Night Dear George To begin with my Wife's business first - she desires you to take notice that Mrs Hale & Mrs Calvert have her Box tomorrow Night - She likewise prays you to send to Mrs Pot to offer her ye Box at some of ye benefits She shall choose: He has been particularly civil & she hopes you will not neglect to send Jim to 'Em in Lincoln's-Inn-fields - We have forgot ye George & Ribbon for ye Picture, my Wife thinks that she put it in a brown glove next drawer to yt where the Keys are, if not there, look into ye door of ye bookcase and under ye books & which is next to ye door as you come in to ye bed chamber - When ye little door is opened, there is a drawer, & she may have put ye George there - If Dance is not gone send that (well packed up) & ye Papers & letters by him, if not by ye Stage - Ire sheme of sealing up the Keys, we desire you will do, as it will be one trouble, Should Mr Wyld send for ye Map of Hendon, (& I am surprised he has not) it lies told up in Common paper upon ye Harpsicord - ye Map may be brought down, & left in ye forroom, but give ye damned maid great cautions about it. Tell Johnston I used but four Tickets for ye Messiah , ye other two are wrapped up in ye little table by ye Settee I generally sit upon. how did Miss Hayward come off? I forgot to speak about it - Pope had a Bargen If the Mayor of Garratt shd be done will make a pretence to get up ye West-Indian - some Eye shd be upon yt - I could be glad to know, when I must write to Dick Burke : the Brothers can inform You, where you give, or send ye warrant. I forgot to speak to Johnston to let Miss Bathurst have a side box, (if one drops) for ye first or 2d time of ye West-Indian - Will not you insinuate that the West Indian will be performed on Thursday in Passion Week? I am very unhappy about Wyld, so connected with him, & he so idle - or (which I can't think) so careless of my Interest - I know not what to do - Clutterbuck has written twice, to rouse him - I speak, entreat & Every thing else, but he does not go on - It is strange he did not send for the map - Suppose you was to send a Card to know, if he wants it, for I had left such a charge about it, & have written to know if Mr Wyld has sent for it - the Bitch of a Maid may be knocking when he sends, & ye Copy-holders may be his foes, because he is my friend - It is hard to know, & yet I am distressed about him - he has all ye Papers & knows ye matters of ye manor so well - I can't help it, & so I'll go sleep, if my foot will let me, for it is very painful indeed. did You speak to Lord Pembroke about David's leave to follow his Military Studies at ye Academy - ? I can no more so adieu till next time - Yrs most affecly D: Garrick I must entreat when you go to my house to do ye above business, that you will see my poor cat fed with ye milk we have sent for her - if you don't see her dip her whiskers in it, that unfeeling devil in ye house, will make up a Sack posit to dip Cautherly's chin in. Should you discover anything - pray put somebody into ye house & turn her out directly . Ask for ye milk, & say you promised Me to see her fed.

Hampton Sunday 15th My dear Madam. We have been very unhappy at Your indisposition, much flattered with Your letters, but at ye same time glad that You have not risked your health to do Us honour, & give Us true pleasure: I am not so Selfish to Wish to Enjoy your Mind without It's being well supported by Your natural Spirits - had I been one of Seneca's Friends, I should have desired to be excused attending ye opening Of his Veins, notwithstanding the wonders they relate of his preaching from ye Bath. your alarm from Mr Montagu I hope will be much abated before You receive this - the fears, & anxieties for these Children; may they repay You in gratitude, tenderness & Affection - ! they are very fortunate, & must if they live (for I cannot suppose your Nephews to want either heads or hearts) be happy in themselves, & comforts to Mr Montagu & Yourself. We have had an Excellent day with ye Prince - he is reserved, but Easy - Says little, but to the purpose - an Old Friend of Mine, MonSr Grimm, a kind of German Frenchman, (no bad Mixture) attended him; he is lively, clever, & honourable - beloved by his friends, & has no Enemies - I told him of ye feast I had Endeavoured to procure for him, & he felt ye loss of it, as if he really knew You. a small Note of one Line & a half, left in Southampton Street Either to morrow, or ye next day will make Us happy, if it assures Us that you are well, & have no more apprehensions about ire Nephew - My Wife sends her most affect respects, & is made not a little proud by ye manner you have Spoken of her - I am Madam most truly Your devoted D: Garrick I am so cramped with writing a hundred letters that I can scarce hold my pen to write legibly.

Novr 18th My dearest Madam. I have indeed of late been balancing the Account of good & Evil, and as I have been a great debtor for the real pleasures of last Summer, I have been called to a Severe payment by a fit of ye Stone - I am at present in Heaven, & resolute enough to fulfil a promise I made to ye Prince of Hesse Darnstadt to play ye part of Lusignan for him to Night, as he must leave London to Morrow - Mrs Garrick, (whose admiration of You exceeds that of Women, & not in ye least lessened by her knowing that You are the Goddess of my Idolatry) would have paid her respects, had not her very affectionate attendance & care of me for some weeks past, employed her Wholly - We shall go to Hampton toMorrow as ordered by ye faculty, & at our return we shall certainly, dead or alive, as an Irish Captain once said to Me, pay our respects in Hill Street. Most unalterably Your faithful & devoted David Garrick I write, or rather scrawl from my Couch. To Mrs Montagu.

Hampton Wednesday night My Dear Sir, I brought The Grecian Daughter with me here, have examined her well, and am wonderfully pleased with the Lady. Mrs. Garrick was more affected than ever I knew her to be with any play: - I will never take your word again in any of your own matters. - I have a few objections; chiefly, I think, in the third act - but they are of no consequence, or rather they may be easily got over, if you agree with me. - The part of the Daughter is one of the finest for an actress in all the dramatic circle. - If Barry will take pains with the Father, it will be of great service to him, though second to the Lady. - I wish you and myself joy - finish the fifth act as fast as you can; and pray let me see you either Friday morning at the house, or in the evening in Southampton-street. I would call upon you, but you know too well my present care and hurry to stand upon ceremony. Yours ever and most truly, D. Garrick. Arthur Murphy, Esq. Lincoln's Inn.

Hampton May 2d My dear Madam You had much better stupefy YourSelf with Adam & Eve here, & breathe the fresh air of May 14 Miles from London than racket about in the Smoky Atmosphere of London - I could wish that Your Supreme Spirit on ye full gallop would but just recollect, that It has a body (alas for us not ye Stoutest) to drag after it - You can never die, but You will hurry off Your flesh by degrees, upon Earth, & then Your Spirit having shaken off encumbrances will mount to It's proper Element & habitation, & repose itself to all Eternity. I shall miss You some fine Morning, & upon Enquiring after You, Some of my astronomical friends will tell Me, that You passed over Saint Pal's about a quarter after Eleven - to be serious, for I am amazed at myself that I can dare to write ye above nonsense to you, as true Christians rest one day in Seven, You who are better than they, ought to rest two - & as I know those days would be the most terrible to you of the whole Week, I could wish You to have a few failings, that You might by way of Penance be Obliged to pass Your black letter days at Hampton - if I run on tormenting You with this ribaldry, I shall not have room for business - Saturday Sen'night & Sunday I am Engaged - Don Felix demands me on ye first, & on ye Second I am Engaged to Lord Shelburne & my french friend - I am at this Moment a most miserable being, Lady Pennyman (whom I don't know, nor ever will) will not give up her side box, & unless you will take possession of your Suspended Handbasket over ye Pit for ye first time, what shall I do for You? - I will stir Heaven & Earth - drink up Eisel, Eat a Crocodile, rather than You shall not have ire will - but perhaps You'll think better of it, & avoid the Theatre this Warm Weather - vain as I am of ire presence when I Enact, I had much rather You would avoid a crowded, hot Steamy theatre, which defies All the Powers of Ventilators - rest rest perturbed Spirit ! that my fidgety Soul should be preaching & giving Advice to Wisdom herself is surely very ridiculous - it puts me in Mind of a Sensible Neighbor of Mine - who with ye gravest Countenance, begged & beseeched me, not to hurry or fret myself about any thing - I heard him, & was much touched with his manner, & affectionate expressions of friendp & concern for Me - & pray Mr Rayner (said I) do You never fret, & hurry Yourself? - O damn it (Swore he) that I do from Morning to Night, & for that reason I am the best able to give you my advice - Mutato Nominee de Me . I know what is best for ye same reason, and therefore can advise it, but I want wisdom for practice - I need say no more, but that I am most devotedly Mrs Montagu's D Garrick. PS. I will stay here till Monday. My Wife presents her respects - I have scribbled so fast I can't read it myself - I was born to torment you -

Adelphi Decr 6 - A thousand thanks, my dear Madam, for your very balsamic Letter. I am this moment arrived & can not Even take my Lixivium till I have shown my gratitude. I am much better in my health since I went out of Town, & quite recovered in Mind since I rec'd Ire Wise, feeling, charming friendly ten-thousand-Epithet-Epistle - I must show it Madam that is pose: Mrs Vezey in Town & my heart have no additional flutter? - I believe if my blood shd freeze in my heart this very cold weather, that it would liquefy, like St Januarius's at ye Sight of ire hand Writing - indeed my good Lady, You have made me quite Easy - I love Lord Lyttelton, & would not lose him for Millions - When I can know that our attendance will not be impertinent, We Shall be as punctual in Hill Street, as the first Lady there (or in any Street), is punctual in making her friends & Admirers happy. Most devotedly Yours D: Garrick. I write with ye Gout in my fingers. To Mrs Montagu, Hill Street.

column46: Adelphi - Sepr 24. 1773 Dear Peter. I must recommend, (not with ye usual form, & Spirit of recommendation), but with all my Power & influence, if it extends so far as the City of Lichfield, my old Friend & Acquaintance Mr George Alexander Stevens , a Name well known, & a Person deservedly applauded, for his Peculiarity of Genius, & Universal Love of Mirth & Letters - He has great Merit, & more than all he is a very honest, liberal-minded Man, & deserves Every Encouragement that has been given to him - As he is travelling Your Way with his heads, I must beg leave to introduce him to You, & ire friends, not my dear Peter, that I think You & Ire friends want the least Amendment of Ire Own, but that You may laugh with my Friend Stevens at ye heads of other People - In short, I have so great a desire that he Should be well received, & approved at my own Native Place, (as I always call it, tho dropped at Hereford) that I beg You will let ye Whole Town know that I beg it, as a particular favour, that they will attend his Lectures - If any should be discontented with his Performance, I beg that I may treat them, & that You will pay for all the Malcontents, & draw upon Me for the Sum total - I need not desire You, to let him taste ire Lichfield Mutton & best Ale, Your Own Heart always prevents my Wishes in these Matters. always in a hurry - Dear Peter If the Ladies expect a Maccaroni Player in Master George, they will be dreadfully disappointed - To Peter Garrick Esq, Lichfield.

Adelphi Friday My Best And Most Amiable Friend - When you called last Night my foot was flanell'd up with ye Gout, and a Sight of you, and ten words from You, would have been a Charm for ye foul Fiend - but I was ordered to see Nobody, & did not know it was my cure till it was gone - I am much better, & so well, that I shall be able to appear in Old Lusignan tonight, & in a better Character tomorrow in Hill Street - in that of the faithful Friend, & admirer of Mrs. Montagu - I was reading, or rather dozing over the cold, Northern Critic when you were at the door - notwithstanding his flattery to me, I can't bear the unfeelingness of his Soul. Shakespeare no Tragic Poet! - Shakespeare not the first Tragic poet! - What insensibility! - but more of this when I have ye honour of seeing you tomorrow, which I most certainly will do, tho I am carried in a Litter & so laid at ire feet. Dear Madam, most unalterably & faithfully yrs, D. Garrick. I am always kissing Miss Gregory's hand & will make her cry if possible tonight.

Drury Lane Theatre Monday Decr 12 My dear George. I was much rejoiced at your letter, & I hope your friend Dr Faulkener will land You safe again amongst Us - I shall always hold him in great Esteem for his Care & attention, & am ready to give him more solid proofs of my Gratitude: I have this moment finished ye long part of Hamlet, & my hand trembles while I am writing with ye worst Pen in ye world - Johnston is in a damned humour, & I dare not ask for a better - We go on well, & shall play the Choleric Man for the first time on Monday Next - I was resolved to have it perfect & to do Every thing in my Power for it - I am surprised that he did not write to me by this post, however I trust I shall have one tomorrow, & then I shall be Easy - Ire Sons are Well & Mr Carrington says when he is better he will come to see Me - What can he have to communicate? The 2d Hospital has never sent for a Bill nor do I know where to go after them - so we shall have only one this Season - Foot is arrived & in great Spirits - he asked much after You - they are now playing Dibdin's Nonsense & as it met with some disapprobation ye first night We wish it well over - There is a good ballad or two, ye rest Washy & Slop Dawdry - I really cannot write any more - they make a great Noise in ye house Yours Ever & truly D Garrick. I believe it will be damned - The Cobbler has met with much Obstruction - To George Garrick esq, three Tuns, Bath.

Adelphi March 27 Dear Madam - A new Footman, who being deaf, is not moved with the concord of sweet Sounds, - & being unmercurial in his heels could not overtake the Coach, prevented us from having the pleasure we devoutly (being Sunday) wished for last night - I could have brained the fellow - a Son of Dr. Robertson was with us, & we talked of Nothing but Mrs. Montagu, & Miss Gregory - Mrs. Garrick was indeed just returned from Hampton & my Elder Brother was screwing up his Features to a parting ditty, which he sighed forth, & left us before 5 this morng. The fool was so deaf he could not tell us where you ordered ire Coachman to drive, so that we could do nothing but fret and scold. I had two great favours to ask: the one was to beseech you not to be impressed by any Acct of a late Separation from the house of Cumberland, till you have heard the calm truth from ire humble Servant - Such ingratitude! but I won't say any more at present, but be assured I will never do anything to any one Creature, that shall make You (& that is my only concern) think less favourably of me. Suspend your Justice till the Cause is heard : Your understanding naturally does this, & I flatter myself that your heart will not easily be misled to condemn me - Something too much of this, - the next favour I had to solicit was Your name, which I more Glory in than if Possessed & to be added to ye most noble list I have got for a very ingenious man who has undertaken 6 etchings from the principal Characters of Shakespeare. I have sent you a Sample of the work, which I must beg you to return to day or tomorrow - without your permission I have placed you at the head of my List, & Everybody agrees to the propriety of having such a Leader - Should you meet with any choice Spirits, whose names may be easily got, they will not discredit themselves, & do great Service to a most ingenious Man. - I am Madam with every Sense of Esteem & affection most devotedly Yours, D. Garrick. Mrs. Garrick presents her respects - I would send more than these to Miss Gregory were I not afraid of Mrs. Garrick's Curiosity wishing to read over this letter. I have had a little pain & worse symptoms this morning.

Almacks Novr 7th Dear George. We rejoice at your visible alteration of health & Spirits - Palmer says, that you begin to pick up, I don't mean at ye Whist Table, but in Your looks - pray keep yrself quiet in Mind & ire Body will get better of course - I beg you will let me know the progress of your health & I likewise must insist that you never think of leaving that fountain of Your health, till you can show us a pair of rosy Cheeks, Spirited eyes, and a Belly out of the perpendicular - the Little Gypsy goes on Hummingly, & rises nightly in repute - there was a little odd talk of some party against us, but to this Minute there has not been one Single disapprobation - Weston is dying, & with him goes a good Actor, & a very bad Man - Mrs King is useful, but not excellent - she stops gaps but will not allure - Ire Son David is not yet arrived, he is they say, at Lichfield with his Uncle - all the rest of ire Olive Branches are well, Mr Carrington is better & worse & will continue so, till he dyes - I shall write to you by Palmer - just let us know that you are better - Ever & affecty Yrs D Garrick G. Garrick Esqr, Bath.

column46: Adelphi March 21st 1776 Dear Peter Your Ale is exquisite & I must reward the Brewer, & pay my debts honestly - I wish from my Soul that I could tell You when I shall be at Lichfield, but till I have given my Successors possession, & received my Money I can't stir from ye Property - the day of payment is the 24 of June, & till that happy day is past, I shall not think myself my own Master - but then, I shall shake off my Chains, & no Culprit at a Jail delivery will be happier - I really feel ye Joy, I used to do, when I was a boy at a breaking up: I receive Every honour that a Man can do from all Sorts of people, & I was yesterday enrolled a member among the first & greatest people in this Kingdom - We have a New house built in the best Taste in ye middle of St James's Street, & it is furnished like a palace - Each Member pays 12 Guineas at Entrance - It is ye first Society for titles & property in the known world - I need not tell You that with all this & 14 Dukes at the head of us, that I never was duller in all my Life. I made my best bows to my Brethren, graces and Royalty, drank a Glass of Lemonade to keep me awake, which grip'd Me, the Effects of which I found burdened me & went home as fast as I could. - Dr Johnson & Mr Boswell will be at Lichfield almost as soon as this - he is coming to take his leave of you all before his departure for Italy - You are Johnson's prime favourite - I was sorry not to see Mr Fletcher, I sent after him, the Moment I got up, to his Hotel, but he was flown, & I could never after catch him - I am angry that Mr Lamb would not call upon me again - pray our Loves to all - My Wife will soon answer her Neice's letter - the Bell rings - Yours most affecty D: Garrick George is again ailing I fear he never will be well. I am better, but not quite well - could I get rid of the pain at ye Neck of my bladder, which is lately much better, I should have no complaint -

Hampton April 12th Dear George. As Mr Linley sets off for Bath on Sunday morning, I chose to write by him rather than the Post: it gave Us great Pleasure that Your Change of Places has made such a Change in Your health - I think that Bath for You, is what the Roman Catholics think of their religion, there is no Salvation out of it - You should absolutely resolved to fix Your Standard there - Your Girls & David are almost well, very little remains of their Cough - I shall transplant them next Sunday to their new apartments which their Grandmother has prepared for them, a fine bed on the first floor, but David's bed is taken down in Nat's room - what meanness! - they have forced the Lad to sell out, which has backened him some Years in Life, & now they turn him out to starve, if some Chapter of Accidents is not turned over in his favour - last Night I played Drugger for ye last time - the Morning Post will tell You ye whole of that Night - I thought ye Audience were Mad, & they almost turned my brain: I must desire that my good friend Mr Squire, to whom I beg my best Wishes, & You would consider what our friend Linley means to give Me as a Security, for part of his Share: he is to raise £10 000 & wishes me to take some houses &c he has in Bath, which you will see, besides his Share, as a Security for the Mortgage - he likewise wants to take 4 & 1/2 Pcent - I demur to that, for as I have 5 from Lacy, will it not appear wrong to take less from a new purchaser, & for a less Sum? - pray both think of that & talk ye whole matter over together, & with Linley, & let me know, what it is, that I may do. He is a very honest man, but I must be secure, or what have I been doing? Love to all friends - Yours Ever & Affecly D Garrick. My Wife sends her Love.

column46: Augst the 19th 1776 Dear Peter. We have at last settled our peregrinations - they stand thus - the Duke of Devonshire meeting me 3 Weeks ago at Lord Sponsor's at Wimbleton, desired me, in so affectionate Manner to go to Chatsworth that I could not resist him - Lady Spencer, the first of Women, hearing what was passing, insisted, as affecty that we should be there at ye Same time with them - which will be in ye first Week of ye next Month September - We have therefore resolved to go ye Second or Third to Chatsworth & after being there four or five days at Most, we will be with You at Lichfield for some days - George's Children are with their Grandfather, who is very ill, & does not care to part with them; so we shall come alone to You, & if You will let us keep house for a Week, with Some assistance to Mrs Betty, we will drink soft ale, & laugh like ten Christ'nings - we had rather live simply, Mutton & Pudding than upon all the dainties in the world - Ben Victor who is at Mr Piggot's will meet Us at Lichfield, & I shall take him up to Town with Us - I wish among You, that you could get him a bed - I will give both him & You notice when I shall beat up ire Quarters - We intend this time, to be like Bobadil, not too popular, or generally visited - private is ye word - If you like our Scheme say the Word, and we will be punctual - Our Loves to all of You. Ever & Affecly Yours D: Garrick Send ye enclosed as soon as You conveniently can -

Octr 26 Dear Madam. I congratulate all Your friends & Myself among that honourable, happy Number for Your safe return to us - Mrs Garrick did herself the honour of calling upon You to return her thanks in Person for the great care you have taken, & the trouble you have had, with the friendly favour of Mrs Necker to her - I heard with pleasure of ire being at the french Academy when Voltaire exhibited his malevolent Nonsense (for which too among other Obligations I thank You) upon our beloved & immortal Shakespeare: could any thing possibly add to my Admiration of Mrs Montagu, it was the Expression of contempt & astonishmt which, I hear You put on, at hearing the Weak and impotent ravings of Age, Envy, hatred & Malice - it rejoices Me much to hear, that this unchristian attack upon Genius had not a favourable reception even from his own friends - I doubt not, but You have converted Numbers to the faith, not with Sword as Mahomet did, but by those emanations of Genius, which You have caught from the divinity You have so powerfully, & justly protected & admired - this Attack of Voltaire, I hope, is not to pass unnoticed - If the Champions will not mount with the regulars, the Light horse, & hussars must begin a Skirmish - I most devoutly wish for the honour of a little conversation, which I should immediately have Endeavoured to enjoy in Hill Street, had not a Small attack of ye Gout obliged me to Stay at home for a day or two. Yet may I not hope for that favour, as soon as the more important Matters have had their first dues, & we with our little demands may present ourselves with all Love, & humility? I am Dr Madm Ire most devoted Served D. Garrick Mrs Garrick presents her respects - I with Send my best Wishes, with my Wife's, to Miss Gregory, but alas, I fear the enchantments of french Everything has destroyed all my hopes - I with not have sent this Scrawl could I have written better, but ye illbred Gout has prevented me

April ye 18 My good Madam. I only requested the gentle Stream of Your Bounty, & you have flowed upon Us with a torrent - I am really ashamed of being ye means of Your abundant kindness to Us - I have a Set of friends, whom I intended to call upon Every year for one pound one - as I cannot return the Overplus, I have set it down in my Book over against Your never to be forgotten Name - par advance 5 Years - 5:5:0 give me leave to let you into a little Secret history of this Charity - a Nobleman in your Street whom I visit & who looks like benevolence itself - had a Ticket from Me at ye same time, that I was impertinent enough to send one to You - Your two Names like A fat & lean rabbit in a poulterer's Shop - stand thus together - Mrs Montagu 5:5:0 - no ticket Rt. Honble Lord: W. de Be 0:5:0 - one ticket. Mrs Garrick presents her Respects, with Mine & I at the feet of Miss Gregory am My dear Madam Most devotedly yrs D Garrick before I went out of Town I sent to Holy, but could not find him then, since my return I have been confined with a Sore throat & hoarseness, & cannot yet Stir out - if You have any orders of any kind for your faithful Servant, you may depend upon my Executing them with care & fidelity. Mrs Montagu, Hill Street.

Wynnstay Denbeighshire Sepr 26 Dear Peter We shall certainly be at Birmingham on Sunday Evening the 5th of October , & shall stay ye Next day till about 12, so we may have a good deal of Gabble; I hope You will bring Cousin Bailey with You, & let us have a Snug party - I send this by the Chester post, & you may Send me an answer by ye Same Way - directed to me at Sr Watkin Williams Wynn's Baronet at Wynnstay near Wrexham, Denbeighshire to tell me if you approve ye Party, & it will be convenient - we are very happy here, & cannot stir till Saturday Sen'night the 4th of October - these Welch scenes are quite New to us, & very well worth anybody's Curiosity - at Shrewsbury the Town was in an Alarm at my Coming, & the Raven-Inn besieged - I little Expected so much honour from Salopian Swains, & Welch Mountaineers - their Observations upon my Person, age &c you shall have at Birmingham on Sunday ye 5th Octr if Nothing prevents your making Us happy - a line by ye return of the Post to Chester will oblige Your most affect Brother D: Garrick The Ladies with Me Send their Love - desires her duty & Love to her Father & Mother - She hopes to see her Brother at Birmingham, who she tells me is gone there to be a Doctor - prays is it a Horse-Doctor? Peter Garrick Esqr, Lichfield, Staffordshire.

Wynnstay Sepr 30th My dear Peter Would it not be a little too much upon St Patrick, to desire You, Honey, to meet me at Birmingham & then return to Lichfield with You, which is much nearer my Dear - In short we beg to see You at Birmingham next Sunday because we cannot Stay at Lichfield so long as we could Wish - Should You arrive Sooner than We - I beg You'll bespeak beds sufficient for Us all There will be two wanted for You & Cousin Dick - one for me & my Wife & one for Fosbroke & My Wife's Niece - I have Six horses for which I must have a good Stable & four Men Servants - Sr Watkin tells me it is a good house - We shall be there before Six in ye Evening - I wish You would Order a good joint of Meat for ye Servants some fish if any, & some Chickens or fowls boiled or roasted as You like best & whatever Else you & Cousin choose to be ready about Seven or Sooner - I am writing in ye Dark & Mr Parry ye famous Harper is playing like an Angel
