column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: It is impossible for me not be be much impressed by whatever you suggest, particularly on legal points. I have therefore fully considered your idea of having a question stated to the Attorney and Solicitor-General whether the intended pension for Lord Auckland can be legally granted. As the measure was proposed by Mr. Pitt I thought it right to communicate your doubt to him, and my idea of refferring it rather to Lord Kenyon, whose legal knowledge is certainly equal and his situation superior to that of the above-mentioned gentlemen; besides he can be applied to in a less public manner. Mr. Pitt felt the propriety of my proposal and assured me he would cordially submit to whatever was the decision of so respectable a person. Having advanced thus far it is now necessary for me to state this proposal to you, who, I am certain, cannot but approve of a reference to Lord Kenyon. For the greater precision I have preferred stating this on paper to a conversation, and shall take no farther step till I hear from you. I also mentioned to Mr. Pitt the industry with which a coolness between you and him is propagated, and how detrimental such an opinion must be to my affairs; he has in the strongest and most explicit terms assured me of his inclination to live on the most cordial terms with you, and for that purpose is desirous of having a thorough explanation with you on all subjects, and more particularly of those that may have occasioned any shyness. I think I am certain your attachment and I may say affection for me will, when apprised how essential I look on a good understanding between you is to the ease of my mind as well as to the prosperity of public affairs, make you equally desirous of having such intercourse as may effect what I have so much at heart.

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: At present all our lectures have begun again. I have now from the morning on till noon continually lessons, so that the afternoon I have for my own work. Major Hogrewe is returned from his tour to Osnabruck; he has begun geometry with us, that is to say, so much as is necessary for us to know in order to survey. This we do one day, and the other we repeat the tactics with him. Mr. Less has just finished the course in religion; he intends to repeat some few chapters and then end, for during the 4 years we have gone through the course four times. I continually work for Martens; he now reads a book through with us which he has lately published, it is a Collection of Treaties, which are compiled in the same manner as Wink compiled his. We have to about an hour ago had a great loss for the University in the death of Professor Brands , who, though a young man, yet was endowed with great talents. He died this afternoon at 4 o'clock of a putrid fever. It is at this instant a greater loss for the University as that part of the law has now no Professor who can read it, for Hofrath Claproth, who used to read has been by the physicians forbid to read this summer... The garrison is now very busy exercising; as often as my hours will permit me I go . The 18th there is the Review of the 1st Regt. of Stockhausen at Mundane. I am invited there to see a new manoeuvre that the old General has invented. The Review is to be on the very spot where in the last War he drove the French away. Lichtenberg has today begun to read again for the first time after an illness of 7 months, where his death was daily expected, I think he will now be quite cured.

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: After the recovery of my health it has always been my wish and desire, with your Majesty's pleasure, to embrace the profession destined for me already from my tender years, and which was always my darling thought, a thought, I may say I ever nourished from my youth, and imbibed with my daily nourishment. Thank God, Sir, I am now perfectly recovered; my late indisposition was only the measles, and from them I am also perfectly reestablished. In all my desires and wants, my duty and wish prompts me to have recourse to your Majesty's goodness. The fine and noble description of the British Fleets which are preparing, have roused in me a double desire to go with them, a desire that haunts me day and night. During the whole day I do nothing but think of them, and at night but dream of them. The blood of a British subject boils within me, and I wish to be a witness at what is going forwards. The family of Brunswick have always been renowned for their courage; I wish also to show mine, but in a manner the most useful for my country, wherefore, with your Majesty's gracious permission, I would wish to become midshipman. I say only with your Majesty's pleasure, for let my desire be ever so warm, should it interfere with your Majesty's plans I shall give it up immediately, and, cost me what it will, shall endeavour to forget it entirely. However, should there be a possibility I humbly entreat your Majesty. It is no whim, Sir, for the moment. It is a desire I have cultivated from my tender years, and which once your Majesty saw with pleasure. I gave it up once, thinking my week state of health would not admit of it. Now, thank God, I am recovered, the desire comes again, and with your Majesty's gracious pleasure I shall go aboard a ship, the sooner the better. I have consulted my physicians on the occasion. Professor Stromeyer, first Physician, assures me it would be of great use to my health. Professor Fisher's answer was that persons labouring under breast complaints had frequently been entirely cured by the sea air, and that the trial might be made. I have now laid my petition before your Majesty. Does it meet with your Majesty's gracious pleasure, so much the better for me; if not I shall however ever remain

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: My principal business consists now in reading the different histories of the 7 Years War; in the view of gaining an accurate knowledge of the different places in Silesia I have made myself an extract out of that description made by Archenholtz who served in the late 7 Years War in the Regiment of Forced. I now read the history of it written by the late King. I have just been busy with Major Hograve in learning what is necessary for an officer when in war how one must reconnoitre a country, the necessary precautions that must be taken to place a camp &c., and now we are going to examine carefully some of the chief battles fought in the 7 Years War, as the Battle of Minden according to the plans published of it. As Hograve served the whole 7 Years War he is able to inform me likewise of such things as are perhaps wanting in the plans. I have just been reading the Memoirs of Count St Germain which General d'Estorff had the goodness to lend to me. It shows very evidently what a continual discord reigned in the French Army during the last war, and proves how prejudicial it is for a country when its commanding Generals sacrifice for their private enmities the good of their country. My cousin Augustus of Brunswic paid me a visit last week; he is I believe the happiest being in the whole Electorate since he has got a Company; he does talk of nothing but his Company. In my idea it seems to be very agreeable to command a Company, but I cannot say I should think myself content in being able to command a Company; all my aim and my desire is to command once an army and have once the character of being as good a General as the present Duke of Brunswic.

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: I have thus long deferred having the honour of addressing your Majesty, as the situation hitherto of the Valiant has not afforded matter worthy of your Majesty's perusal. It would be ridiculous in me to give an account of the Fleet as your Majesty must receive the most authentic particulars from the Commander-in-Chief: indeed the Valiant has hitherto so entirely occupied my time that I could not. I am at present satisfied, and, feeling prepared, wait anxiously for the arrival of Lord Howe. Admiral Barrington ordered the Fleet to exercise without regard to form, but to perfect the men with the guns and sails. He has now reported us fit for service. On board the Valiant I kept everybody employed from five in the morning till nine at night. I should have been remarkably well answered if I had not received a draft from the Scipio of six and thirty men more properly to be called wretches; excepting the gunners and quartermasters I have not a man in the ship either as old as myself or has been as long at sea. Another extraordinary circumstance is that none of the seamen have yet had the honour of serving your Majesty: the landsmen are composed of volunteers I raised at Richmond, Roehampton, and in Cornwall. Certainly I cannot say too much of the attention of the officers, but if the men had not of themselves been well inclined, no discipline in this short time could have effected the good order we are now in. At present they are very healthy; they have been very sickly, but by smoking their health is reestablished and I only lost one man. As I expect three and thirty more from the North, upon their arrival I shall weed and then be very well manned indeed. It is a very great satisfaction to see through the whole Fleet the good humour and happiness of the men. I trust, should your Majesty think a war should be declared, that the Fleet will prove their attachment and fidelity and that among the number the Valiant will do her duty: she is a charming ship and I am more and more pleased with her and every body on board of her. I am afraid I have trespassed too much on your Majesty's time. I refrain saying any thing of your Majesty's health as by all accounts I hear of your Majesty's perfect enjoyment of spirits, which is the strongest indication of what I, together with all my fellow subjects, so ardently wish.

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: Your letter of the 23d of last month arrived on Wednesday, which has greatly relieved the Queen and your sisters as well as me from our anxieties on the return of your complaints, as we trust that now the crisis of the disorder is over and that every subsequent accounts will prove you are recovering. I should not do justice to what ought ever to be uppermost in our thoughts did I did express that thanks to the All-Wise Ruler of the Universe for his having supported you on this occasion, and my joy that you are so well grounded in those principles of religion which alone can enable us to support either prosperity or adversity. The attention of those who surround you must have given pleasure, and the medical gentlemen seem to have shown great skill and now are fully acquainted with the nature of your complaint, and therefore will, I trust, be the better able to keep off returns of it. I shall not add more but that I ever remain

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: I could not suffer General O'Hara to leave us without embracing so favourable an opportunity of writing to your Majesty. At the same time I think myself in duty bound to inform you that ever since I have had the honour of being under his command, if my conduct has merited your approbation, I am indebted for this to his attention & his advice upon every occasion in which my own inexperience might have been the cause of my acting improperly. I hope your Majesty will not consider it as presumption in me, when I mention that I believe hardly ever any Officer who has done his duty with such zeal and activity as General O'Harra has done his, could be more universally and generally regretted on his departure than he will be. Lieutenant Colonel Symes has requested me to inform your Majesty in the most dutiful and respectful manner that some family affairs of the most material consequence to him require unavoidably his presence in Ireland towards the ensuing Spring; though certainly I shall be a most material loser by his not remaining with me, I am not selfish enough to wish to detain him when his affairs would suffer so considerably as they are likely to do by his absence. However, if your Majesty graciously indulges me with the removal of my Regiment in the Spring to Canada, he has promised, at my particular request, if it meets with your approbation and he can possibly arrange his affairs by that time, to return to me there in the Fall. The very great assistance he has given me, and the very marked liberality of principles which have guided all his actions to me, merit more grateful acknowledgments from me than I can find words to express. I hope your Majesty will not forget his services, and I beg of you to consider that any mark of your approbation conferred on him, I shall consider as very flattering to me. If you should, in consequence of Colonel Symes's absence, judge it necessary to appoint any other officer to attend me in his room, I venture to submit to your consideration two officers who, to the best of my knowledge, are both respected and esteemed by all who know them. The one has the honour of being one of your Majesty's attendants, Colonel Greville, your Equerry, the other is Major Villettes of the 12th Regt. of Light Dragoons now Aid de Camp to General Pitt. Should you be pleased to approve of one of these two officers, it would be very flattering to me. Before I conclude, may I presume to recommend to your Majesty's favour and protection, when a proper occasion may present itself, Capt. Green, who was so many years in my family? I should not venture to do this, if I did not know him to be equally respectable as a man & as an officer.

column37: royalty, prince, navy officer, Duke of Clarence
column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: I have received very regularly letters from you and am most thankful to the Almighty that the mild climate of the south of France seems so thoroughly to agree with you, and I trust that the passing the succeeding winter in the same fine climate with spending the summer months in some mild air will completely restore your health. I am happy you are able to resume part of your studies, which employment will make you with more pleasure enjoy those of relaxation; there is no greater wisdom than so to oeconomise amusements that they shall continue such during life, which, if too much sought after, naturally must sooner or later become irksome; besides, if the mind be not constantly in the habit of serious employment it will lose its energy, and those powers a man may have been blessed with will entirely vanish.

The time of my departure for America is approaching so very near, that though with reluctance, I find myself under the necessity of writing to you on a subject which I wish ever to avoid troubling you with. It is the first expense I was obliged to incur on my arrival here. Your Majesty knows how perfectly unprovided I was with every individual article that was indispensably necessary for me to keep house. Being obliged therefore to purchase, when I first came here, everything which I wanted, & having no person to employ in this business who was able to prevent my being egregiously imposed upon, that expense which in England might have been amply supplied with twelve hundred pounds, has been rather more than doubled here. With the best inclination, not to trouble your Majesty to defray this, and with the best intention of supplying the whole of it, by what I could save from the yearly income you was pleased to allot me, I have been totally unable to do it, from the very great expense with which the keeping house has been attended, owing to the scarcity of provisions on one side, & the most infamous impositions of the merchants, to which we were forced to submit, on the other. Circumstanced as I am in consequence of this, may I venture to request that your Majesty will assist me in defraying this first expense, which, if you judge it proper, may be deducted from any allowance you may please to regulate when once you may think proper to establish me. I have now mentioned what I thought it necessary to submit to your judgment, and shall conclude with begging you to be convinced that I trust at no future period shall I have occasion to trouble you again on a subject equally irksome to your Majesty to hear and for me to mention.

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: The hearing the cold you caught by the sudden change of weather has subsided without any visible detriment to your health is the more satisfactory as it gives the best ground for hopes that the excellence of the climate of Hie`res is restoring your lungs to their state, and that another winter in that beautiful island will perfect the cure. I lost no time in authorizing Baron Alvensleben to acquaint Captain Hanstein that I approve of Vevay as your summer residence, agreeable to your wish and the opinion of Doctor Zimmerman, and consequently expect this will reach you there. I am certain you will be cautious during the summer of not overheating yourself, and that you will not take more exercise than may be conducive to enable you to return to Hie`res in perfect health; whatever can give air and avoid fatigue seems to be the mode that should be addopted.

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: Your Majesty will be so gracious as to excuse my not having wrote sooner; my intention in so doing was to give you an account of what I had seen on the journey and thus render my letter somewhat more interesting as it else would be. Thursday the eleventh of this month I left Marseilles and went as far as Aix, which seemed to me vastly altered for the worse. It was always a dull town but since the last riots it looks quite deserted. In the great street not a soul to be seen and every face bears fear and sorrow upon it. My next day's tour was as far as Tarascon but as nothing remarkable was to be seen on that road I shall not mention anything about it. The Saturday I reached Nimes by the way of Arles. As this town was so famous in ancient times and is still so now on account of its antiquities, my curiosity was very great to see it. We began by examining the famous obelisk erected on the Market place in honour of Louis the Great. It is of Egyptian granite, sixty one feet high and at the base a diameter of seven feet. A part of an ancient Capitol is another beautiful remains of the Romans. It is half an arch supported by two pillars of the Mixed Order, beautiful beyond description. I could not help reflecting on the difference of the times compared now with the present. When the Romans undertook any such building they constructed it with the intention of making it last for ever as a proof of their grandeur. At present all our undertakings are guided by the idea how to make the most money, consequently those are preferred which are the soonest finished, whereas much time is required for rendering them solid. From the Capitol we went to the Amphitheatre which is much larger than that of Nimes but not so well preserved. The most interesting for me was what I saw last namely the Elision Fields of Arles so famous in ancient times. This is a very extensive piece of ground entirely covered with sarcophagous's. - There is not one of them shut being all opened either by the curiosity of the inhabitants or some travellers. The most valuable are contained within the walls of the Convent of Minimes. Amongst all the sarcophagous's one is particularly remarkable being very well preserved. It is a pagan one and serves at present for a coffin for a Bishop of Arles. Many people have taken the figures for an Assemblage of the Gods, which it is not. It expresses the life of man from the birth to his death. Having seen Nimes already before, I examined the antiquities there very slightly and set out the following morning for Montpellier. I expected a much finer town as what I found it to be. A place so much frequented by strangers ought to have better accommodations. The great walk is the only thing worth seeing here. As for an account of the Canal I shall defer giving any till when I am come to the end of it. My health is at present pretty good though the weather is very cold here. Forgive me, Sir, for having taken up your Majesty's attention so long.

column46: Though I know how much your Majesty dislikes in general compliments upon your birthday, yet I trust that you will not regard in that light my congratulations upon this day, that Heaven may shower down its choicest blessings upon your Majesty's head, and that your Majesty may enjoy every health and happiness for a very long series of years, are my constant and most ardent prayers. I am returned about three days from the Reviews at Magdeburg, which were wonderfully fine. I think there is no comparison between that inspection and the one here; the troops are infinitely finer in point of men and much more exact in their evolutions. The Duke of Brunswick's Regiment surpasses all the others. There was likewise at Magdeburg four battalions of Fusileers, as they are called here, or rather of Light Infantry, which are really wonderfully good and remarkably well exercised. They are very small men, know perfectly the Light Infantry exercise, and at the same time can act in line as well as any other battalion. The Cavalry likewise at Magdeburg are very good, and I think are very much improved on their horses. This was the first year that the Duke of Weymar appeared as Inspector and he really seemed to have given himself a great deal of trouble. The Duke of Brunswick was not sufficiently recovered to be at the Camp, and therefore General Knobelsdorf as the senior Officer commanded.

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: The most daring outrage to a regular Government committed by the new Society, who yesterday published its manifesto in several of the newspapers, could only be equalled by some of its leaders standing forth the same day to avow their similar sentiments in the House of Commons; and I cannot see any substantial difference in their being joined in debate by Mr. Fox and his not being a member of that Society, but if men are to be found willing to overturn the Constitution of this country, it is most providential they so early cast off the mask, and I am most happy it has given Mr. Pitt so fair an opportunity of avowing sentiments that must endear him to all lovers of good order and our excellent Constitution. It is also very material that many speakers on the side of Opposition have pledged themselves to co-operate in opposing these Reformers as well as so respectable a list of friends of Government. I received last night the enclosed paper from the Duke of Gloucester; it is drawn up by the same pen from which intelligence was sent on Saturday from the same channel by Lord Sydney to Mr. Dundas. It deserves the attention of Administration, and it seems highly worthy of enquiry whether any large sum of money has been procured for France from Ireland, and what Irishmen are connected with the French emissaries in this country. I desire Mr. Pitt will in my name give the paper this day to Mr. Dundas, that he may have the matter attended to, and I should think it might easily be traced whether Mons. de Pe`rigord has been secretly at London the last week and whether he returned to Dover, and has publicly returned within these two days.

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: The war on the Continent appearing now to be sure I cannot help expressing my earnest desire of making a campaign, and thereby enlargen my knowledge in the art of war; I should be very happy if your Majesty would be so gracious and permit my serving as volunteer with the Prussian Army which is just marched. You may be assured I shall not neglect any opportunity wherein I may make some progress, and may perfection myself in my capacity as a good officer who may once be made use of for the defence of his King and country. I took the liberty before I wrote to your Majesty to ask General de Freytag's advice, and he much approves my desire. If you are so gracious and grant this my request, I beg most humbly you may immediately give your orders for my departure to the Prussian Army, and give General de Freytag me necessary instructions to choose me two officers who may accompany me, for my real desire is to perfection myself and not to have a suite which is merely troublesome. Dearest father, this request comes alone from my desire of gaining more experience and knowledge in a service for which I am so passionately fond. I entreat your Majesty to answer me soon, and at the same time either write straight forward to the King of Prussia, or send me the letter that I may take it with me, in order that no time may be lost.

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: Your Majesty will no doubt be surprised to find I have had a small return of my old complaint. Indeed it does not pain me a little, the more so as I foresee no alteration for the better unless a total change in my present situation takes place. It hurts me to write this, as I know beforehand it will be unpleasant to your Majesty but I have accustomed myself to be on a confidential footing with you, Sir, and therefore cannot conceal my feelings on this occasion. You yourself would be with reason displeased with me were I to act the hypocrite. My journey is intended for my health but according to the present situation of things it does me more harm than good. I am unhappy; and that is the cause of my present indisposition. The two gentleman who are with me, though they conceal their illness, are both unwell, nay very seriously indisposed. I have asked my physician his opinion on the subject who assures me the one has a breast complaint, the other an abscess in the lower part of his stomach. To be constantly surrounded with melancholy faces, with people who suffer, whose temper is soured by their sufferings is more than I can support and makes me truly miserable. Their indisposition prevents my enjoying many parties on account of their not being able to accompany me. Whenever I want to go out they constantly make difficulties who is to accompany me and when we are out are so melancholy that we never exchange ten words together. Jonquieres is so unwell that he can scarcely bear the motion of the carriage and is forced often to get out and walk. Your Majesty will easily imagine it is no amusement for me to drive alone step by step. I have always shown them the greatest attention, never going out without having one of them with me because it is your Majesty's pleasure and that I never would act against it. At the same time I cannot but find it hard that they should make any difficulty to my going anywhere when I signify a wish for it and that it is a very harmless thing. Such sort of things hurt me much. I know my situation and the inconveniences attending my rank which I never make any difficulty to submit to, but I think a line may be drawn now, especially as I feel myself of an age to begin to act for myself. My wishes are not unreasonable, Sir. My desire is not to run about the town or any such ideas like these - but to be able to say when I like a society there I will go. Till now my conduct has been approved of and I trust it ever will be so. Your Majesty's wish is an order for me. My whole desire is to act according to your satisfaction. With your Majesty's leave I wish to propose a fixed sum for the expenses of my dress and pocket money, the account of which I will send in to you, Sir. This seems to me a good method to know the value of money. Your Majesty has had my word never to make any debts so that you may faithfully rely upon my contenting myself with whatever you think proper to give me. I will here conclude finding myself too weak to continue.

column46: I think it my duty to acquaint your Majesty with a very shocking and unfortunate affair which has happened and which concerns General Guydickens of the 3d Regiment of Foot Guards, whose character till now has ever stood unimpeached in every light, and whose situation both in the Army and in her Majesty's family renders it still more melancholy. Indeed I should have made my report to your Majesty sooner, if I had not waited to be able to give your Majesty every intelligence possible concerning this dreadful affair. On Friday as soon as I arrived upon the Parade of the 2d Battalion of the Coldstream, a soldier whose name is Cannon brought to me a prisoner whom he had just taken upon the Parade, and whom he said he and a Grenadier of the name of Heywood, had caught the evening before in a very indecent situation with a gentleman in Hyde Park, but who had escaped from him at that time. At the same time Captain Hawgill, the Adjutant in Waiting brought me a report from a Sergeant of the Magazine Guard that Heywood was in confinement there by order of General Guydickens for an assault upon him, and also added that General Guydickens was the person whom the soldiers said they had caught with the other prisoner in the most indecent situation and who after some resistance the Grenadier had carried to the Magazine Guard, but when he had charged the Sergeant with him, the Sergeant, knowing him, would not take charge of him, when the General came forwards and naming himself ordered the Sergeant to confine Heywood and a plasterer who had come up during the scuffle. While Captain Hawgill was making this report to me, a Sergeant of the 3d Regt. brought Heywood to me upon the Parade, and told me that General Guydickens had ordered him to be set at liberty. As this affair however had made so much noise I ordered these different people to be kept separate till after the Parade, and then examined them myself separately, and am sorry to say that I found their different accounts agree perfectly. The only thing therefore that I thought I had to do was to send Captain Hawgill immediately to General Guydickens to acquaint him with what had passed, and to tell him that if he felt himself innocent, it was incumbent upon him to clear his character fully, but if not that the only thing he had to do was to send in his resignation and to fly the country immediately and that in consequence of his unfortunate circumstances and of his former good character that I would apply to your Majesty for leave for him to sell his Company. The General appeared exceedingly shocked, and protested his innocence, but seemed to be so distressed that he did not know what to do. It was not till late on Friday evening that the different evidences were examined before the Justices in Bow Street, and they were again examined Saturday and yesterday, and I am sorry to add that these evidences appeared so clear and connected, that the prisoner was fully committed to take his trial, and General Guydickens has given bail this morning to stand his trial likewise. It is much to be hoped that the poor man is innocent, though unfortunately appearances are strongly against him. I trust however that as this unfortunate case must come to a public trial your Majesty will be graciously pleased to suspend your judgement till that is over. The Regiment has behaved most exceedingly well upon it and have resolved to give the General every assistance in their power to clear himself from this shocking accusation. I am afraid I have already trespassed too long upon your Majesty's leisure, but I thought it my duty to lay the whole affair before Your Majesty on account of the General's situation both as an officer and having the honour to belong to the Queen's family at the same time that I hope that your Majesty will not disapprove of what I have had to do in this very unfortunate affair.

column46: I embrace the very first opportunity which has offered since my return from Upper Canada, to inform your Majesty that after being absent only twenty six days, I arrived here on the 6th of the month, having visited every post occupied by any even the smallest detachment of your troops throughout all Canada, except Michillimakinac, Detroit, and Oswego. This latter place I was prevented from seeing by a violent storm which overtook us in our passage across Lake Ontario, and thus rendered it a matter of utter impossibility for me to reach the fort. I had the satisfaction during my tour of seeing every regiment, except the 24th, now in Canada, having met the Queen's Rangers, and the 5th Regiment at Niagara, and being appointed by Major-General Clarke Reviewing Officer for the Regiments in Lower Canada, in which capacity I saw the 26th, and the first and second Battalions of the 60th. A very large deputation from the Indians of all the neighbouring nations came to Niagara to wait my arrival, as soon as they heard that I was to visit Upper Canada. Their professions of attachment to your Majesty and the British Government were extremely warm, and they would not on any account return home to their tribes till they had made me faithfully promise that in the name of them all I should inform you, in the strongest terms I could find, of their zealous attachment to your person, and of their utmost readiness at all times to obey any commands with which you may at any time choose to honour them. I hope you will pardon my presumption in troubling you with this short recital, but I was anxious for your Majesty to see how I had employed the time of my absence. May I presume now, Sir, to request your permission for me to visit the American States in the winter at the close of 1793 or commencement of 1794, in case it should be your Majesty's intention that I should be at that period in this part of the world. Two months, or ten weeks at the utmost, would enable me to visit any part which it is an object for me to see, either in a military point of view, or as a traveller, according to the best information which I have been able to obtain. Should my request not meet with your Majesty's approbation, I must humbly entreat you to overlook my indiscretion in making it. My anxiety never to omit any of the duties of my profession has made me request your indulgence at a season when the severity of the climate prevents any military pursuit from being attended to, except the common routine of interior economy and daily duty. May I presume to hope that the Queen will, through you, Sir, accept of the assurances of my most devoted attachment, and my sisters of those of my most affectionate love.

Your Majesty has made me inexpressibly happy by your graciousness towards me. I return you my most humble thancks, and I assure you, Sir, I will pay such attention to my duty and to my behaviour as shall deserve your approbation, this being the only means of proving to you my gratitude for your goodness to me. I hope to begin soon to learn the service, and General Freytag has promised he would give his orders for it. I will apply myself as much as I can to render myself capable of fulfilling the post your Majesty has given me. You have rendered me doubly happy in placing me a` la suite of the Guards a Redgment to which I always have wished to belong and which certainly is one of the best in your service. Particularly at this present moment am I glad to be in it, I mean, if your Dominions should be attacked by the French, for then I should perhaps have an opportunity of showing you the ardour I have of fighting for my King and country, which shall always be the desire of him who is for ever

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: Though I had the honour of writing to your Majesty last post, yet as this town has been unquiet again, and that the circumstances are in general exaggerated when at so great a distance, I have taken up my pen in order to give you, Sir, as correct a detail as possible. Ever since the last disturbance that took place in January, the people have been far from being satisfied. Every moment false alarms have been given, letters pretended to have been found encouraging uproars, and every night, one was informed, was to be a new scene of confusion. Last Sunday the common people, who are vastly well informed of everything that is going on here, as Government takes its spies from that class, found out that the Neapolitan Minister had bought to a very large amount of corn not only for the the consumption of Naples but likewise in part for the French. This certainly displeased them, and what added to the discontent was that the Neapolitan Minister had not strictly kept to the agreement he had made. In consequence of this a mob assembled tumultuously about his house, and had not the military force been called in, which is much respected here, he might have fared badly. On the Monday following, a Frenchman belonging to the French Hospital happened to have a dispute with a servant of the Secretary of State. In the heat of the quarrel he drew a knife, and, showing it the footman, swore it should be made use of to dispatch him, his master, and the Pope. Some persons hearing the conversation pursued the man, who found means to escape and conceal himself in the Hospital. It was a good while before he could be found, which gave time to the people to assemble, and their number amounted to about five thousand. They wanted to set fire to the Hospital and burn all the French that were in it, but were prevented by the soldiers, who had great difficulty to convey the criminal to prison, the crowd being so exasperated that they wished to kill him. In the course of the two ensuing nights they visited all the houses inhabited by French and burnt even the furniture of one of them. No lives were lost though. The Pope has had some of the heads of these disturbances put in prison, which it is hoped will quiet everything. He has published a very severe Decree to prevent all strangers from being insulted, and now everything is going on as it ought. Some English were rather ill treated here, but everything has been made up amicably and Government has shown itself particularly attentive to them.

column46: Last night I received your letters of the 28th of the last and 2d of the present month. They gave me thorough satisfaction both as to your manner of conducting yourself at The Hague and as to your opinion of the present situation of things there; but I trust by Lord Auckland's dispatch of the 4th that your arrival has proved of the greatest utility by effecting a more decisive mode of conducting business and more activity in the performance of the orders given. Every step is taking here to add to the aquatic preparations making in Holland for the defence of the Meuse, the good effect of which will soon be found if the present east wind does not prevent the vessels from sailing that are ordered for that service. Major-General Abercrombie has orders to proceed from Scotland with the 37th and 53d Regiments of Foot as a farther reinforcement, and probably the 14th Regiment of Foot from Dover will arrive previously. Lieutenant. Colonel Moncrieff, whose experience in America will render him an useful adviser not only for the defence of the Meuse, but also as to other operations, will embark with this Regiment. You may depend on my sending Colonel Sporken in a few days, but it is thought material he should stay here till the answer arrives from Hanover how soon the first four thousand men can begin their march towards Holland, and as by your letters the Prince of Orange has not yet fixed where they shall enter the Republic, nor what quarters shall be prepared for them, this delay cannot be of much consequence. My accounts from Oatlands are very favourable and I trust I shall see the Duchess on Monday at Windsor.

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: I hope that your Majesty will pardon my presumption in troubling you with these lines at a moment when I am sensible that your time must be taken up with attention to matters of the highest importance; I confess, indeed, that I trust the subject on which I am going to address you will plead my excuse. With these expectations, allow me, Sir, to proceed. The present situation of affairs in Europe is so awful, that I cannot help feeling the greatest anxiety when I reflect at what a distance I am at this period from your person, and I cannot refrain from expressing a most earnest wish to be allowed at this moment to return to England. I hope, Sir, that you are fully persuaded how ready I am to obey with the utmost cheerfulness your commands for my remaining abroad in America or elsewhere for any period or in any manner which you may please to point out. But, at this critical conjuncture I am sure that your Majesty must feel how natural it is for a son, possessed of the most devoted filial attachment to his parents, and for a subject professing the most loyal and dutiful zeal for his Sovereign, to wish that he may be permitted to approach his person, at a time when it becomes the first duty in every one, much more in every branch of his own family, to prove their loyalty and zeal. Perhaps, Sir, in the line of my profession an opportunity may now offer in which my services may be useful to my Sovereign, and to my country. Permit me then, Sir, if this should be the case, by allowing me to return home, to have an opportunity of personally offering my exertions as far as my abilities extend in any situation in which you may think fit to employ me. I am confident that every one of your Majesty's children must at this moment vie with each other in endeavouring, by giving daily proofs of their duty and attachment to your person, to make up to you for that load of cares which the present state of public affairs must have brought upon your mind. Allow me then, Sir, to hope that I am not to be the only one who is to be deprived of the blessing of exerting himself in so dear a cause. I have presumed to write to the Queen also, this day, to request that she will render the humble offer of my services acceptable to you, and obtain your acquiescence to my returning home, that I may have the opportunity of personally proving those sentiments of the most devoted attachment for you, and for her Majesty, which I shall ever be proud to profess.

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: Since the 30th am I arrived here. The Regiment has been exactly six weeks on its march, and this is the very first opportunity I have had of writing since my departure from Hanover. To my greatest joy was I yesterday for the first time present at a skirmish between the Imperial Chevaux Lagers and the French Sans Culottes; I had the happiness of being present from the very beginning, though our Regiment had not the honour of sharing with the Imperialists. I was riding with the Veldmarschall Freytag reconnoitring when at once we met an Imperial Officer with 24 horses who told me a party of French was coming on, I embraced with the greatest eagerness ye opportunity of sharing in the sport. The first shot that the Hanoverian Grenadier battalion fired had effect and a driver of the piece of cannon which afterwards was taken fell dead on the spot, for as we advanced I saw the corpse; the fellow was shot through the nose. The first battalion of Diepenbrocke was present; our 2 Regiments, rather I should say four squadrons laying about two English miles from Tourney could come up quick enough to share in the glory; but today we are advanced and have taken our quarters at Aines about a half hour on the left of the Imperial camp; the 1st and 4th Regiments of Heavy Cavalry are encamped, but we, having no tents with us, are in cantonments. One cannot conceive more brave fellows than the Austrian Chevaux Lagers, they gave quarter to no one except one poor boy, and this seemed to be disagreeable to them. My most sanguine wishes are that we may have very soon an opportunity of showing that we Light Dragoons can also take cannon. It was very curious that it had been almost the case that we on our arrival here should have seen the enemy, for about half an hour from the town I got orders from the Duke to advance with the 2 Squadrons; this was a piece of news which rendered us very happy, but unluckily these hopes were soon lost by a second order to enter our quarters which were at La Tomb. Frederic was yesterday the whole time as well as the Veldmarschall present at this affair; the cannon which we took is a very neat piece, well appointed; we have also got the munition car. Since the day I marched from Hanover I have not seen Dolly, but am told he is very well and is vastly pleased with his march. He is at present not yet here but I hope we shall soon get him again here by us. I cannot enough praise the Regiment which I have the honour of commanding. I have not had any reason to find any fault since the very beginning of our march; even I can give you my word of honour that I have not found a single soldier drunk which is saying much when one comes to consider that on the first day's march through Hanover all the Dragoons' good friends on their taking leave offered them brandy enough, and many Dragoons has spared his money in order to buy some forage for his horse when ours was not arrived; and with such fellows it is a true pleasure to attack the enemy. I shall certainly now take every opportunity of writing to your Majesty as is possible.

I cannot let this messenger go off without wishing your Majesty sincerely joy of this day, and of many many very happy returns of it. This midday I have dined at Frederick's, and I have had the honour and pleasure of drinking your Majesty's health in a very large company, and, I may certainly say, of very loyal subjects. Since I have had the honour of writing to your Majesty nothing of great consequence has happened: we are still always enclosing Valenciennes. Last Sunday night the first parallel was opened at about 400 yards from the fortress without a single shot being fired at us. Last night 1200 Hannoverians marched with almost the same success: at least not a single one has been wounded. And I am very happy to say that Colonel Moncriefe, the Chief Engineer, is extremely well contented with them. The heavy artillery is not yet arrived and I hear that it will last some days before it will arrive quite here. Last Saturday I have had the inspection of the right wing, as Field Officer of the day. I was employed the greatest part of the night with General Hammerstein in placing the piquetes which were very much advanced, and in the morning at three o. clock I went with him to Briquette, a village where there is a battalion always on duty and which is relieved every night, which is only 800 yards from Valenciennes. I was very happy of doing this duty for by that a very clear idea how our chain of posts is placed. I wish nothing more than that Valenciennes may be soon taken; certainly nobody will be more happy than .

column46: I have this instant received Mr. Secretary Dundas's letter enclosing the one Mr. Adam has written to him. I own I had flattered myself that with the unpleasant account there would have been some plan for alleviating my son's affairs; indeed, it seems to me that, after the very creditable part he has acted in the present War it is incumbent on every servant of the Crown to join in finding some means of releaving him. I desire therefore Mr. Dundas will show the whole to Mr. Pitt, who I am certain will see the propriety as well as necessity of having this sum made easy to him; indeed Mr. Dundas must feel that Mr. Adams certainly has informed the Duke of York, in whose hands the business has been put, and consequently the very just ground of disgust that must arise at an interference when not accompanied with remedying the evil.

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your Majesty's most gracious letter of the 12, which Colonel Sporken delivered to me this evening. I most humbly agree with your Majesty in the absolute necessity which there is that a well digested plan for the next campaign should be arranged and settled between the different Allied powers, but particularly between your Majesty and the Emperor, and in the great detriment which the want of such a plan was to the whole of the last campaign. It is to be hoped that when the Emperor arrives he will be equally sensible of this, and I am sure that if he listens in the least to Count Mercy, he will do everything in his power to convince him of the necessity of it. Your Majesty will see by my letter to Sir James Murray that I have obeyed your Majesty's commands in communicating to the Prince of Cobourg and to Prince Hohenlo the dispatch which I received on Friday, and I trust that your Majesty will be pleased with my success. Though I am afraid little or nothing can be done on the side of West Flanders yet your Majesty may depend upon it that no opportunity whatsoever of annoying the enemy shall be missed by me, and in consequence your Majesty will find by the dislocation of the winter quarters that a very considerable body of troops are cantoned within nine miles of Courtrai in order to be ready at all times to take advantage of anything which may arise. Your Majesty will long before this have seen by my letter to Sir James Murray that the Landgrave of Hesse Darmstadt has consented to his troops being employed in the Vende`e, so that I trust and hope that none of the British regiments under my command will now be taken from me. The Hessian regiments which are destined to be embarked are already quartered at Ostend and Nieuport in order to be in readiness the moment the vessels are prepared to receive them. I had intended to have left the Darmstadt troops in cantonments round Courtrai till the Cassel troops were embarked, as there is not room enough near Ostend to place any more troops there, but I am afraid I shall be obliged to remove them to Ipres, as they begin to desert so fast that they must be confined in a fortified place. I have appointed Colonel Sporken to come to me tomorrow morning in order to converse with him upon a number of points. I am exceedingly happy that your Majesty has sent him over as it will save a great deal of time.

I am just arrived from Bruges upon Frederick's having wished that I should remain a few days with him. I therefore shall stay here till next Tuesday when I return to my Regiment. I was yesterday presented to it, but only to the Officers, as my own Company has so many sick that I was obliged to put off my seeing it till another time. In general it is amazing the number of sick the different Regiments have; mine has very near five hundred. It is a kind of a fever which the men get, and which pulls them immediately so down that it is a long time before they can recover their strength again. They are well quartered in barracks which upon the whole are pretty good: there are 18 men in a room, but that cannot be helped for the citizens are all free: wherefore no soldiers can be quartered in their houses. The town is very large and monstrously dirty, the streets very narrow, and no place for people on foot to walk. This renders it very disagreeable. The horses your Majesty was so gracious as to give me arrived last Tuesday, and in perfect health; the groom is to return by the next packet boat which sails on Thursday. The Field Marschal returned last Friday from Mons where he had been to see Prince Coburg. General Mack is expected next weeck at Brussels, from whence he is to come to the Army to take the post of Adjutant-General. Ernest is very well; he is with his Regiment almost every day, but he comes back at night for Bruges where he is quartered. This day is the first day that it has snowed; it is exceedingly cold, but I believe very good, for it will be of great service for the recovery of the men.

column46: As the time approaches when, according to the plan of the campaign, I am to move from here with a part of the troops in order to form the army upon the right of the Prince of Cobourg, I think it my duty to ask your Majesty's orders concerning the Hannoverians. It was your Majesty's intention while I was in England that they should form a part of the corps I am to take with me, but I am sorry to say that the sickness which has prevailed so long in the Infantry continues still in such force that I have thought it expedient to ask Count Walmoden's opinion concerning the possibility of their being immediately employed upon active service. Enclosed I transmit it to your Majesty, by which you will see, Sir, that there is only one Brigade of the Infantry who were able to serve, and that the rest must be left back till such time as they are recovered. The Cavalry are in perfect good order and therefore I mean certainly to take them. It therefore now depends upon your Majesty's orders whether I am to take with me such part of the Infantry as is fit to serve at present, or whether I am to leave the whole of the Infantry back till such time as they are completely recovered and then move them forwards and send the Hessians back. There is another point concerning the Hannoverians upon which I must beg leave to trouble your Majesty, which is, that there may be some arrangement taken about their being obliged to cook, and being supplied regularly with meat. I am sure that the want of these arrangements is one of the principal causes of their sickness; besides that, should we succeed and move forwards into France, it must be considered that the country we are to act in is completely eat up, and that if we do not take the precaution beforehand of supplying ourselves with meat &c. the troops must starve. I have talked these points fully over with Count Walmoden who thoroughly agrees with me, and I have desired him to lay these points more fully before your Majesty. I trust that your Majesty will pardon the liberty I have taken of mentioning these things concerning the Hannoverians, but it is owing to my sincere regard for them and to my zeal for the good of the service.

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: Permit me to take the earliest opportunity of congratulating your Majesty on the entire submission of the Island of Martinico to your arms. I look upon myself as peculiarly fortunate in having been able to reach this before the trenches opened on Fort George (late Fort Bourbon), the principal fortress of this country, having thus been able to follow the progress of the siege from the very commencement of the first battery. I beg to repeat to your Majesty the assurance of my warmest gratitude for the high honour conferred by you upon me in appointing me to a command in the army under Sir Charles Grey. I was fortunate enough to be named by the Commander-in-chief to take possession on the 23d, at the head of the Grenadiers, which brigade I am posted to, of the gates of the fortress, and I am at this moment returned from attending the ceremony of the French Garrison laying down their arms, and their embarkation in consequence. With the most fervent wishes for your Majesty's welfare, and happiness, and the success of your arms, wherever they may go, I have the honour .

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: Here I am still and without any prospect of getting better, for though the arm grows thinner, yet 'till this moment I have no strength or power soever in it. The idea of being in this moment an invalid makes me very low spirited, & yet I am not able to alter it being totally unable to ride. The surgeons tell me daily it will be better, but God knows when this will take place. We have been very unlucky. I am sorry to say many and many of your brave subjects, as well British as Hanoverian, have been sacrificed. Heavens grant things may soon change for we are almost knocked up, at least the Hanoverians. I never was so miserable as the last two days, knowing all my friends were in fire, and I hearing the cannonade & not able to serve; a man must be in my situation to feel this.

Sense I last had the honour of writing to your Majesty the Hannoverians have changed their position. We were forced to retire last Thursday from our position behind the Espierre, on account of a village called Leers, which was in our left flank being taken. By this we were in danger of being cut off from Tournai as the enemy could get sooner on the pave` than we could so that by that we should have lost most probably all our artillery, as the pave` is the only road on which it can be transported. There was a bridge of pontons made in the night before over the Scheldt. This was intended for the transportation of the baggage, which is very much in the way on such occasions. I also received orders to retire with my Regiment and the Horse Guards over the Scheldt. This was effected in good order with the alteration that one Battalion of the Guards remained on the pave` for to cover the retreat of the rear guard: and that when that came up it was also to come over the bridge which then was to be taken up. This however was impossible to be effected, for the French advanced with such force that the Battalion was forced to retire on the chausse`e; & as we had waited to the last moment for it, we could only cut through the pontons to hinder any artillery coming over; & then retired as the enemy already begun firing with grape: however, I was so lucky as not to have a single man of the Battalion wounded; except the first Sergeant of the Artillery who was killed with a rifle. I unluckily lost one of the guns which had been drove into a ditch by the horses taking fright; this broke the axe, & therefore there was no possibility of saving it. The Regiments which passed over the river did not come any more into fire the whole day; but the other column which General Busche commanded remained in it till 9 at night. They continued retreating till before Pont a` Chain, a village on the right of the great camp before Marquain: here they formed & a most violent fire of small arms toock place; they were forced again to retreat behind the village, which post they kept. My regiment, or rather the Battalion which had retreated down the pave`, tried three times to storm the village but without effect: at last the Brigade of the Line commanded by General Fox arrived: and after one general discharge of musquetry stormed the village and toock it. They were supported by the Hannoverians, who were almost knocked up, having been above twelve hours in fire during six of which it was so strong that, according to the opinion of those who have served in the Seven Years War, there was not so heavy a one during the whole last war. The English stormed with their accustomed bravery; this Brigade had particularly distinguished itself in the retreat on the 18th when the 37th attacked a French column & forced its way through it. The loss of the Hannoverians is not very considerable, considering the fire in which they had been. Most of the wounds are not dangerous, as they are from small arms; & these fired at a very great distance. The French must have lost prodigiously; the whole village was full of dead bodies, most of which were killed by our artillery, which has done wonders. According to the report of prisoners we have been attacked by four columns each consisting of about 16000 men; a proof of how very strong they are here. Most of the troops we had against us, were troops of the Line; & I believe this, the more, as they fought with such bravery. Last Friday afternoon the Hannoverians received orders to march off for Oudenarde: we marched the first night to Pots, & the next day toock our camp on the heights behind the town: I hear we are to change it this afternoon; & are to fall back with the camp, as the heights are to be fortified: I hope we shall have here a few days rest, for the men are quite knocked up with the fatigues they have undergone. Certainly the service we have had these last six weeck, surpass by a great deal what we had in the last campaign. I have sent to the Field Marschal the lists of what Captains Wangenheim and Jonquieres have expended in England. I could not trouble your Majesty with this, as I am sure that the Field Marschal will report it to you. I must beg pardon for having written so long a letter; and conclude with .

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: Mr. Dundas yesterday acquainted me that the Duke of Portland, if I had not proposed his acceptance of the Lord Lieutenancy and Custos Rotulorum of Middlesex, would have wished to decline it in favour of the Marquess of Titchfield; this struck me so much as an highly advantageous method of bringing a young man of quality into a line the most useful to himself as well as the public if he zealously turns his attention to the police of the county and capital, that I authorized Mr. Dundas to desire the Duke of Portland to stop the Commission of Lord Lieutenant and have another made out in favour of the Marquess of Titchfield; but least any delicacy should have prevented the Duke from taking any step till he heard personally from me; I take this method of expressing my thorough approbation of the idea of the Marquess of Titchfield's being appointed Lord Lieutenant and Custos Rotulorum of the County of Middlesex, and directing that the instruments for that purpose should be prepared.

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: Understanding your Majesty has expressed a surprise at not having received any letter from me for some time, I hasten to recall myself to your gracious memory and explain to you the cause of my silence. Indeed, was I not assured this from authority should not even now venture to trouble you, Sir, understanding that all correspondence with your Majesty's family was forbid me. However erroneous my conduct may have been, your Majesty will I trust not think my heart so perverse as to be capable of forgetting the various kindnesses you have constantly shown me even during my last stay in England. It was a principle of duty that kept my pen from tracing to you, Sir, my feelings on the occasion. Painful in the extreme was it to me to be left so entirely destitute of any friend or adviser, but as I understood it was your Majesty's wish that none of the family should write to me, it seemed also an order for me to correspond with none, which silently submitted to. Private interests, however they may hurt my feelings and wound my heart, were never such as to make me forget for a moment what I owed to my father and Sovereign. That my situation is pleasant I cannot say. Futurity may perhaps shine more propitious than the present awful moment. My confidence in religion and my firm wish to be an honest man can be my only occupation now. Vivacity of youth may make one commit excesses, which it is, in cooler moments, our duty to repair as much as lays in our power, and I trust too much in your Majesty's good heart to fear a moment you will require of me anything but what is right. Any sacrifice which my conscience and honour allow, I am ready to make. Therefore I hope your Majesty will please to let me know through some channel (if you still intend to debar me the satisfaction of one kind line from your own hand) what your intentions may be. The very retired way in which I now live will I trust convince your Majesty of the sincerity of my sentiments. With the warmest prayers for the continuance of your Majesty's health and happiness, I have the pleasure of subscribing myself once more (if your Majesty forgives me), your fortunate son and dutiful subject.

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: As I perceive by the note from Earl Spencer in answer to mine that he concurs in my opinion as to the safest method of addressing myself to Earl Howe, whose health in the present moment is clearly not such as he could safely undertake a Winter cruise, I shall not fail to form my letter to prevent his retiring at present, and I am certain I can put his continuance at the head of the Channel Fleet in a light that will secure his taking the part which on many accounts I think highly necessary. As soon as I receive his answer I will communicate it to Earl Spencer that he may speak more positively to Lord Bridport, whose conduct will be highly absurd if he refuses to serve, and I confess, however I may think in general well of his nautical abilities, I do not look on them as superior to those of Vice-Admiral Cornwallis. The letters from Vice-Admiral Hotham show the necessity of French ships of the line and frigates when the other services will admit of it . The Lowestoffe and Ballet being safe at Tunis is highly agreeable after the unpromising report of Captain Middleton.

Your Majesty's gracious letter of the 3d of this month I received at Ibbenbuehnen the day before I marched for this village, which prevented me returning you sooner my thancks for it. I certainly should have wrote from Munster, but as everything was quiet I would not trouble you with a letter, particularly as I had just wrote when we retreated from Holland. God knows this campaign has been a sad one, particularly the last 3 months of it. The fatigues we have undergone are very great indeed if one reckons the inclemency of the weather, and the more disagreeable as they have not helped anything. We have enjoyed very little rest this winter. I was exactly with my Regiment four weecks at Munster, & then marched into cantoonments which are very bad in this country. I am at this village since last Friday with my Regiment, & the rest of my Brigade, consisting of 3 Battalions & a Regiment of Cavalry, are cantooned in the villages round this. I am here in the second Line as a soutien for the first in case of an attack of the Embs, but hitherto everything is quiet. I can assure your Majesty that I never can thanck you enough for having let me remain this winter with the Army, as it is the greatest comfort in the world to have shared all hardships with the men; and now they are over I would not have missed them for anything. My Regiment is now beginning to get very sickly; this is the consequence of the severity of the last campaign: however, I hope that in a short time I shall get a great number of the convalescents. The worst is, the Hospital is so far off that it lasts a long time before we can get the men back. The weather has since some days grown milder, but the ice is still not yet gone. The roads here are schocking, much worse even than those in Holland, which is saying a great deal. It is with very great difficulty we can get on our artillery, and if the rainy weather sets in I do not know how we shall get on our guns.

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: I have purposely avoided answering your letters of the 9th of last month delivered to me by the Earl of Jersey, as well as that brought to me by the Duke of York of the 24th till the arrival of the Princess Caroline, whose amiable qualities will, I flatter myself, so fully engage your attention that they will divert it from objects certainly not so pleasing to the nation. There cannot be a doubt that the English do view with a jealous eye any decided predilection in those on or naturaly to mount the Throne to military pursuits, and I certainly feel the force of that opinion as strongly as any one. This for a long time made me decline granting you the Commission of Colonel Commandant of the 10th Regt. of Dragoons, and at last ordered it to be prepared on the solemn assurance of those you had employed to name this request, that no higher rank was meant hereafter to be claimed from it, and that the application arose alone from your desire of being employed in forming that regiment, and in going with it to camp, which you could not do without some military rank. I then declared from real affection for you, knowing that the approbation of the public ought to be your first object, that this Commission should not be the forerunner of a military career, and that I should certainly never grant any further military rank. When you therefore two years ago through Lord Amherst applied to be made a Major General, I declined it and mentioned to him what I had expressed on giving you the Commission of Colonel. I own I am sorry you have again applied, but I cannot depart from what I have uniformly thought right. My younger sons can have no other situations in the State or occupation but what arise from the military lines they have been placed in. You are born to a more difficult one, and which I shall be most happy if I find you seriously turn your thoughts to; the happiness of millions depend on it as well as your own. May the Princess Caroline's character prove so pleasing to you that your mind may be engrossed with domestic felicity, which may establish in you that composure of mind perhaps the most essential qualification in the station you are born to fill, and that a numerous progeny may be the result of this union, which will be a comfort to me in the decline of years, from thinking that both these Kingdoms any my German dominions may for ages continue governed by my lineal successors and on the same liberal sentiments of their ancestors, the intention of rendering their subjects prosperous and happy.

column39: The Later Correspondence of George 3. Ed. by A. Aspinall. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5 vols. 1962-1970.
column46: Having been informed by the goodness of the Queen of Naples that a messenger is going to England, I profit by the occasion for to write to your Majesty, being sure that my letter will neither be lost or opened. Encouraged by the very gracious and friendly letter I received from your Majesty about two months ago I most anxiously look forwards for the termination of an affair which so intimately concerns the future happiness of my life, and which may approach me nearer to you, Sir, than have been for a great while. It would be improper in me to adopt any measure 'till informed of your Majesty's pleasure, therefore most ardently desire to know what plans you would wish me to adopt in order to bring matters to a happy and firm conclusion. Your Majesty's goodness and kindness towards me gives me great hopes of this fortunate event soon taking place. My petition now is that some method may be pointed out to me, for at present am totally at a loss to know how to act. The happy union of the Prince of Wales which is so intimately connected with your Majesty's felicity, and of course that of the country, will I hope plead somewhat in my favour, and in consequence give me more particular reason of rejoicing in the event. What I have suffered has been great indeed, for though imprudent, I trust you do not a moment doubt of the honesty and warmth of my heart. Had other circumstances taken place, my rank and my situation might have made me pretend to higher employments. Now totally without ambition, without any pretension whatever, my desire is to see myself quietly and happily settled, which cannot be the case, as long as do not enjoy the good opinion and protection of your Majesty, as also that of the whole family. Should you ever want my services, as have wrote to you, Sir, before, feeble as they may be, with pleasure will I come forwards in whatever way may be most agreeable to your own intentions, desiring nothing so much as to prove to your Majesty that my attachment to your person must be ever unalterable, both from the ties of consanguinity and gratitude. Before I conclude, Sir, allow me to congratulate you on your late birthday. Though in a foreign country you may be assured no one felt more warmly the day, nor desired more to do honour to it than .
