column46: Jan. 5, . My Lord, I go aboard a Saturday. Its ye general talk of a parlimt to meet some say at Norwich; but most at Oxford, in March or Apple. My Lt Arguile, it's believed, is here; his case is thought very hard, and ye proceedings agst him vigorous; and all imputed to ye Duke's severity, and so made use of by those that don't love him, as an argument wht wee may expect from his governmt here. But Arguile is not much pitied, being looked on generally as a very ill man to ye Crown, and who has made use of ye King's favours heretofore to do very great injustices to others. My Lt Preston was sent by ye Kg to bring in ye Morocco ambassador to-day, and he himself is to go into France suddenly to relieve Harry Saville, and Saville is to be a Comr of ye Admiralty, so is Sr John Chichely, which makes ye number 7. I saw the Moors at their lodging. Ye ambassador is a white man, and his cloths white; ye rest are all in scarlet, I think. I am ire Lps most humble servant.

column46: My Lt, I have only time to tell you I recd yrs ye last night. Besides wht I have told you of ye plot, my Lt Brandon and young Mr Hambden were both sent yesterday to ye Tower, and my Lt Howard of Escrick taken out of his house. He had concealed himself in his chimney. So soon as he came to ye King, he fell a crying bitterly, and desired pen and paper that he might recollect and discover wht he knew; so has bine writing his narrative ever since. Last night my Lt Essex was sent for by a sergeant at arms, Coll: Oglethorp and 30 horse. They met him coming to town. He lay all night in my Lord Fevershams lodging, and this morning, after being examined, was sent by water to ye Tower. The Kg is very displeased with him. He is charged, as I hear, to have signed an association. Mr Forbus has taken last night I desire, my Lt, you will thank ire keeper (for I thanked you in my last) for ye bravest buck yt ever I saw, though I have had many good ones from you. My most humble services to my Lady and Mrs Hattons.

My honoured Lord, The conveyance of letters from you has of late bin very propitious, every week having brought me those assurances which I with all imaginable concern desire to receive. Tic to be doubted, when the autumn gusts and winter long nights come on, there will be a more interrupted correspondence; but, if the execrable design against the King and government be fully discovered and broken, there will probably be such a turn of men's minds as may persuade the calling of parliament before the third year is expired, which will have one desirable effect: the bringing back your Lordship to your friends. The discoveries come on so fast that there will want prisons to secure malefactors, and innocent men begin to fear least the really guilty should atone for treason by perjury and revive the old trade of evidence, laying their plot at their neighbours doors. The King does very advisedly hasten the trials that the jealousy of the people may be removed, who think every thing, however real, to be a trick, and that his person may be in some safety by the terror of severity. We wonderd at the Lord Russell's being engaged in so black a design, a man neither needy in his fortune nor extravagant in his manner; but that wonder is increased since the Earl of Essex is in the Tower. One would have thought it impossible that the son of the Lord Capel, after wealth and honour heaped upon him, should design the subversion of the government. Tic less strange that Lord Howard of Estrick, Lord Brandon, Lord Herbert of Cherbury, Mr Wharton, Mr Hambden, and others of the like form should engage in such an affair. The best ont is, a few days will give us light. May they also give security to the King and government. When your brother Grey is come to you, your Lordship will soon observe what we may expect from him. Mr Pullen's characters are, I doubt, not much to be depended on. There must be a fault somewhere besides in my Lord, if, after so many months stay in France, no progress has bin made in the language. My young Lord of Manchester was expected at London on Wednesday last. For ought I know, it might have been well if my Lord Grey had accompanied my Lord Preston; any thing had bin preferable to loitering in English company at Paris. With my wishes of all health and blessing to your Lordship, I remain, my honoured Lord, your Most humble and affectionate served, Jo. Oxon. I send by this conveyance to Southampton five dozen of bottles of our ale. I wish this hot weather permit it to come in good order to you.

column46: July ye 14th, 1683. My Lt, Yesterday morn: my Lt Essex cut his own throat in ye Tower with a razor which he asked of his man that waited on him, having never a penknife to give him. He had asked for a penknife every day since he came thither. He did it in ye close stool room, while his man was gone down; but his page was in ye room. He eat his breakfast well and was not perceivd to be in any disturbance of mind; but, ye day before, he had sent to desire my Lt Clarendon might speak with him, which he did, and he made protestations that he knew nothing of any design to murder the King, but he said nothing to vindicate himself from being in other designs upon the governmt. The Kg happened to be in ye Tower at ye same time this happened, to view ye new fortifications. The news was presently carried to the Old Bailey, where was upon their trials my Lt Russell, Hone, Rouse, and Capt. Blagge, a seaman, who were all found guilty, and who none of them made but very weak defences. My Lord had nothing but to call some persons to give an account of what they knew of his life, to make him unlikely to bee in such wicked designs he stood charged with. The witnesses agst him were my Lord Howard, Rumsey, and Sheppheard, a merchant, at whose house there was some of their consults, and who was to be the treasurer to receive and pay all money. Mr Booth, my Lds son, was brought to town last night and sent to ye Tower. There has bine a good quantity of arms taken at Chester, in Hodge Whitleys son's house, and this inscription on them: Sultan Bantam; all new arms in chests. My Lt Salisbury was married yesterday to ye younger daughter of rich Bennet sister to Sr George Downings son. Sr John Babor's son has run away with Sr Thomas Draper's daughter. There are a hundred gentlemen of quality, of which my Lt Salisbury is one, who have offered themselves to be put into a troop, under ye command of my Lord Ossory or who his Maty pleases, to attend his Matyes person at their own charge.

7th of Augt, 1683. My Lord, Wee have had a deplorable fire, whereby 2 stair cases were most suddenly burnt in ye Temple, and no deeds, monies, clothes, or anything but ye lives of a few, could bee saved. Sr Thomas Robinson, our treasurer, leaping out of his window one pair of stairs, was bruised, being gross; so yt wthin an hour hee dyed, and was just now buried. Hee had an iron chest now found, and ye gold and silver in it melted thought near 10000l, and his office Lt Pemberton hath 6000l to take for it. One Glide, at whose chamber, a ground room, it is thought to have begun, was burned. Mr Lloyd, ye Bp of Peterborough's brother, in ye next chamber, escaped in his shirt. Mr Williams and one lodging with him for a night are both burnt. This was below ye Kings Bench buildings. Lt Dartmouth is reported gone to visit your island, as also Jersey, &c.; and on his return it's said hee will go out with 13 sail, and towards Tangier most believe. Our plot is nothing more known then it was, unless Mr Charlton have added to it by any discovery, hee being newly taken. The trials are abroad 1st too day, but I have not yett had time to read them. Lt Delamere hath made ye application to ye King most winning on his Maty of any of our great men that I hear of. Lt Suffolk, you hear, hath been humbling himself too, as Earl of Kent, Macclesfield, &c. I hope with your Lop., this mystery of iniquity being well and providentially discovered, wee may have a good government ye better hinged and established. My Lord, I present my humblest duty to my Lady, and wish your Lop. and all your family all happiness, being ever, My Lord, Your Lops. obedient servant, W. L.

Most honoured Madam, Your good Ladyship was so obliging to write two days together, and I am desirous to transcribe that pattern; for, tho I would mortify all other ambitions, I can not quietly permit myself to be outdone in kindness. It is a bold attemt to think to equal my Lady Hatton in the expressions of friendship, but I should deserve to forfeit that relation, did I not endeavour to answer the obligations of it in punctual, tho imperfect, returns. I should be glad to hear that my Lord your brother had left Paris and begun his journey for Italy, while the weather favours travail and the Alps have not the cold of winter added to their snow. Your honour was pleased to enquir of a book called the Beauty of Holiness, pretended to be written by the author of the Whole Duty of Man, whither it were really wrote by him. To satisfy your Ladyship herein, I am to let you know that some artifice has bin used by several writers to make their labours more passable by a pretence to this title; and yet, to justify themselves, if a more strict enquiry be made into it, one of them called his book, The Duty of Man; another, The Whole Duty of Man, Gatherd out of the Scriptures; another, A Supplement to the Whole Duty of Man; so that, when the future writings of the first author which refer to his precedent book are questioned, tic answered that they refer to the book called The Duty of Man, and not The Whole Duty. The second says that he refers to that book of his that gatherd the whole duty of man out of Scripture, and not the other; and the third, if he chance to write a farther supplement, will have to say for himself that he only referd to the former supplement, which he plainly owns not to have bin written by the same hand which wrote the original book. Thus, Madam, you see what little arts there are in the world to deceive without saying downright untruths, to the second of which I think your enquiry refers. Within few weeks all the genuine writings will, I hope, be finished in one volume, that will in some measure for the future supersede the like frauds I must not end till I have wished your dear honour all comfort, health, and blessing, and desired you to present my respects to your good sister and daughter, assuring you that I am and ever shall be, honoured Madam, Your most faithful served in our Lord, Jo. Oxon.

Nov. 27, . Did I not believe, dear Madam, that you have better intelligence of all the news then I can give you, I should oftener venture to trouble your Ladyship with my letters; so that, that being the reason of my silence, I hope your Ladyship will forgive the not writing, since I design it as a greater kindness to you, dear Madam, then the contrary. My Lady and all hear was mighty glad to hear that you was breeding, and shall be very much pleased to have that good news confirmed from your Ladyship, and when we shall have the satisfaction of seeing you all in London again. I see my cousin, Jane Hatton, often, so I know by her how all our friends doe at Guersney. Now as to news: Mr Sydney has been tried and found guilty and condemned, but when he is to be execuetted I know not. The Duke of Monmouth surrenderd himself to the King, and was received by him and Duke as well as he ever was. What he has discovered is not known. The Attorney was ordered to putt a stop to all proceedings against him. He goes to court just as he used to doe. I believe your Ladyship knew my Lady Killdaire, who, pore woman, is dead of the small pox, which she got with being with her Lord who has had it. She is a great lose to her son. The other night Lady Mary Garret and her women and some other of her compainions was at a tavern, where they had music; and after some time they went away and would not pay the music; and so their was a quarrel amongst them, and some of the fiddlers was killed, and thoes that did it was taken, and one of them was the Ladies women in mans clothes, who was a Friench women: and she is much concerned and tells many stories of her lady, who their is a warrant from my Lord Chief Justice to take; but I fancy she will not be easily found, for, if she should, it is believed she will be punished. They say the women will be hanged. My Lady and my brother and all hear gives their humble servies to my Lord and your Ladyship and cousin Hattons. I will now releas you, dear Madam, with the assurance of my being Your Ladyships most humble servant, Elizabeth Mountague.

My honoured Lord, In my last I gave your Lordship notice of the calamity which had befallen me in the loss of my sister, which every day I have new occasions to be sensible of. It will be a relief to me to hear that all is safe with your Lordship and my good Lady and the blessing which she gives you expectation of. The late changes at Court have put all men at gaze. The Duke of Monmouths return and pardon and favour with the King and great applications made to him were the wonder of a week; and, after that, his being forbid the Court and discharged from his lodgings at the Cockpit are as unexpected a turn upon the other side. There are not such tides in the sea wherewith you are encompassed as there is in Court interest and favour. Your Lordship hears that Mr. Sidney died with the same surliness wherewith he lived; and indeed men's deaths are seldom better then their lives. I beseech Almighty God to carry your Lordship with an entire virtue and honour throe this naughty world; and, after all your afflictions, to return to you in mercy and comfort. I remain, my honoured Lord, your Most humble and affectionate served, Jo. Oxon.

8 Jan., . My honoured Lord, The northern parts of England are by God and nature liberally stored with fuel; else, your daughter would have an ill time of it this very cold season in his wintering in the north. Notwithstanding the severity of the last year, it was in no degree so fatal as this has proved already, every day bringing news of persons who in several places have bin overwhelmed in snow or otherwise perished with cold; but tic to be hoped that what is violent will not be of long continuance, and the return of the sun will restore us to more treatable weather. This Christmas has produced an alteration in my family. A little before the holidays, Coloner Macartie, uncle to the Earl of Clancartie, brought a letter from my Lord Sunderland, signifying his Mates pleasure that the young Earl should keep his Christmas at London with his uncle. No sooner the poor creature came up but he was married to my Lord Sunderland's daughter, and is finally removed from hence. Such extraordinary proceedings are not used to be very fortunate. If heirs of families can be thus disposed of, parents have little security either of their children or estates. It seems Sr John Churchill has put an end to the contest about the Mastership of the Rolls. If he can hold it for the same term his predecessor did, twill be a very gainful employment to him. But your Lordship sits by unconcerned and pities those that toil to be miserable and envied. That you may have the blessing of content and self-denial is prayed for in your behalf by, my honoured Lord, your Most humble and affectionate served, Jo. Oxon. I am apt to think that my Lord Prestons journey is only to agitate for supplies of money, which letters are not prevalent enough to procure. Since Sr George Wakeman was my Lord Grey's doctor, tic well his ailing was only the jaundice, which every nurse can prescribe to. The exercise of a journey is the surest remedy for that distemper; and Bruxels will make a more thorough cure then the knight.

25 Jan. . My honoured Lord, The weather is such that there is little likelihood my letters should come to your hands. However, I cannot forbear to write and repeat my wishes of health and comfort to your good Lordship and lady. I do not hear of any likelihood of a parliament to call you over this spring, but you have another occasion which I hope will be successful. Tic said that the misunderstandings of the two great men at Court grow every day higher, and that the Earl of Anglesey has lately bin called before the King and Counsel for charging the Lord Howard for accusing the Duke of Monmouth falsely, the Earl saying that the Lord Russel was murdered. My Lord Anglesey, being required by the King to answer whither he had said such things, desired to be excusd, saying that what was suggested was only private discourse in his own house. There is a subpena issued out against the Duke to summon his appearance, but tic not likely to be served, it being not known where he is. Tic thought that the Lords in the Tower may speedily have their liberty. There is no news yet of the fleet at Tangiers. The charge of their work, its thought, will be double to what it was estimated. Captain Herbert, who was lately admiral against Algiers, is made Rear Admiral of England for his life. Your Lordship hears I presume what executions the French make in the Spanish Netherlands, and how Amsterdam and some other towns belonging to the state oppose the levies for their assistance. Also, how the Electoral College advise the Emperor to a peace with France, and how the King of Poland has bin disobligd by the Emperor designing to make a separate peace with the Turks. The league between the Dane and French is said to be renewed, and how far that may extend is not well known. I pray God bring peace out of this discord and confusion, and give comfort and blessing to your Lordship and family. I remain, my honoured Lord, your Most humble and affectionate served, Jo. Oxon.

25 Jan. . Most honoured Madam, You will allow me to give myself the satisfaction of constant writing, tho I am deprived of that of hearing. The severity of cold continues still upon us; but I look down upon it as one of the worst effects of the rigour of the season that all commerce and intercourse are frozen up. We are told strange stories of several streets built upon the river of Thames that have joined Southwark to London. I should be glad if the practice could be improved to make a road to Guernsay and join it unto our continent, that there might be an easier passage for letters to you and for your honours return to us. In the meantime this new city upon the river is a lively emblem of the designs and business of this world, where the foundation is water and the first thaw drowns the whole fabric. That your honour may build upon the unmovable foundations of piety and virtue, which no change of weather or affairs can undermine, is the prayer of, honoured Madam, Your Most faithful served in our Lord, Jo. Oxon.

Hatton Garden, June 21, . My Lord, The consideration I have had of your Lordps melancholia, together with my own, and illnesses yt had attended me, has often prevented my writing to ire Lordp to ask how you doe, though God knows you have been often in my thoughts on many accts, and perhaps as kind one too as can be conceived in the breast of one in my sphere. My Lord, there is no body shall be glador then my self to hear of your Lordps health; and, if I durst, I would advice you to all things lawful for your health and comfort in this world, which may be so managed as not to hinder those of the next. Your Lordp is certainly to consider some things a little sooner under your circumstances then others of your qualities. Will your Lordp pardon me if my affection outruns my judgment (in your Lordps thoughts), if I deserve yt censure when I shall tell you your Lordp I believe will doe well to have an eye to the support of your family, and look upon ire glass how the sand runs, and give me leave to say I know a Lords granddaughter who is about 19, finely accomplished, bred by the Countess of K-, her grandmother, 5 or 6000li certain, or therabouts. Beauty enough, nay, a large share, virtue, and honour unspotted. Those yt have her in care, I am sure, will be glad a time might be thought fit to be admitted into ire Lordps thoughts. Ill say no more now, till I hear whether your Lordp will bear this hint from him yt has no end but true love for your Lordsp and am certainly your Lordps faithful servant. I am not ashamed of my name, but will not now write it; yet I hope ire Lordp knows my hand, though in this place smaller than usual. My Lord, if I have adventured to be reproved, pray doe it tenderly, or I shall be extremely troubled.

column46: 3 Feb., 1685. Yesterday, as ye King was dressing, he was seized with a convulsion fit and gave a great scream and fell into his chair. Dr King, happening to be present, with great judgment and courage (though he be not his sworn physician), without other advise, immediately let him blood himself. He had 2 terrible fits, and continued very ill all day, and till 1 or 2 a clock at night. He had several hot pans applied to his head, with strong spirits. He had the antimoniall cup, which had no great effect; but they gave him strong purges and glisters, which worked very well; and they cuppd him and put on several blistering plasters of cantharides. It took him abt. 8 a clock, and it was eleven before he came to himself. He was not dead, for he expressed great sense by his groans all ye time. At midnight there was little hopes; but after, he fell a sleep and rested well 3 or 4 hours, and Sr Ch. Scarboro told me he thinks him in a hopeful way to doe well. His plasters were taken of this morning, and the blisters run very well; only one is yet on his leg, which is very painful. He found himself ill when he rose; and those abt. him perceived it (but he sd nothing) by his talking and answering not as he used to doe; and he went into his closet in his gown, and stayed half an hour alone; and Thom Howard desired Will Cheffing to go to him, but he with not let him come in, and as soon as he came out the convulsion seized him, and he fell into his chair. The physicians conclude the sore on his heel was ye gowte, and the applying plasters to it repelled ye humour to his head. Tuesday, 7 at night. - The Kings head is not yet opened, that is, ye plasters of cantharides to raise blisters not yet taken of. His mouth and tongue and throat are inflamed with ye hot medicines, and is ye cause he has bine twice let blood since noon; but the 2d time was because ye 1st was unsuccessful; and he bled not above 2 ounces, which was by Pierce, ye 2d time by Holds, and then he bled 9 ounces. The physicians were with ye Council this afternoon, and told them they believed his Majesty in a condition of safety. My Lt Alington died a Sunday. Sr Thomas Vernon is dead too of ye Kgs distemper. The ports are all stopped, and expresses gone to Scotland and Ireland, as to all the Ltenancies in England. All is very quiet here, which God grant may continue and ye King recover.

3rd of Febry, . My Lt, Yesterday, when ye King was dressed, hee fell very suddenly down of an apoplecticall fit or of convulsions (at our end of ye town I have nothing certain), and Dr King then present and having his lance did presently bleed him, which did much good and caused him to recover somewhat of sense. All the day various reports went of his mending and growing worse, as apprehensions &c. are among us. But this present day began with ye good news of his Matys very good night and amending, as much as in so short a time could be hoped. Ye Lt Allington, Constable of ye Tower, dyed suddenly, and our King was mencioning of it when hee was himself taken. My Lt Keeper on Sunday evening told me that hee was much pleased with your Lops. catalogue, and that hee would ask ye favour of seeing some of them. But (my Lt) you have I think in that neglected study over Easton House door, somewhat more considerable to a law student or judge, if you can find opportunity to look for ye same. Mr. Fanshawe will write your Lop. word how happily things go on still at court; and how considerable Dr King is like to bee, I believe many ways your Lop. will hear, for ye Duke was, and is, fully bent for expressing his thanks to him for the good success he hath had. I am in much hast, but always, My Lt, Your Lops. most obedient servant, W. L.

June 23, . My honoured Lt, We are here full of the good news from Scotland, and hope rebellion is a plant which will not thrive better in England. However, we go on to raise in this place our volunteer militia, consisting of two troops of horse and six companies of foot, which will be settled in very few days, and we shall not be sorry to have put ourselves to needless trouble. My Lord Argile will, I hope, be able to give the King a true account what charitable prince it was that assisted him with such a quantity of arms and money, that just retribution be made for so liberal a benefaction. If it please God that a good account be given of the Duke of Monmouth and his party, tic to be hoped there will be no cause for your Lordships being commanded to Guernesay, but that you may be permitted to stay among your friends in England and attend your own occasions. My Lord Grey, I presume, is in the west, where I heartily wish he may light into a good sort of acquaintance. Some of the young noblemen of the town who are gon down, will, I doubt, be of as little use to the public service as they will be to him. God Almighty give a good issue to this concern of the State, and prosper your Lordship in your private interests, which is heartily prayed by, My Lord, Your Lordships most humble and affectionate served, Jo. Oxon.

My honoured Lord, I hope my Lord Grey, who applies himself to your Lordship to be furnished with money to raise his troop, dos also crave your advice and assistance in the choice of his officers and soldiers, men of such fidelity and courage with whom it may be fit for him to hazard the great state of life and fortune. It is an odd piece of pageantry that the late Duke of Monmouth should assume the stile of King; besides the extravagance of the claim, it is not popular with his party, who are all averse from kingly government. So that I am apt to think tic don upon the notion that there is some legal security to them who fight for a king, however frail his title be. But where the whole transaction is madness, tic a vain thing to seek for the reason of what is don. I pray God as good an end may be put to ours as is to the Scottish rebellion. It is not easy to guess, unless there be great expectations from London, what should encourage such a handful of men to wait till they are overlaid by numbers from all parts of the nation. A foreign aid, tho of our next neighbour, cannot give encouragement of having timely relief. I am very sorry to hear that your daughter is indisposd upon her going abroad, but hope the inconvenience suddenly past over, and has left no other effect behind besides caution for the future. Methinks one of the two holidays which now happen should give a vacancy for a meeting in your Lordship's affair, that you may have the satisfaction of some kind of prospect into what is likely to be don. That all your concerns may have blessing and success is earnestly prayed by, my honoured Lord, Your Lordships Most humble and affectionate served, Jo. Oxon.

June 28, . My honoured Lord, It will be high time that somewhat be attemted upon the rebels by the King's forces, for it is an unaccountable thing that they should be suffered to ramble up and down for several weeks without any notice taken of them, or so much as a single troop falling upon their rear. Whatever bystanders think of it, neighbor princes will imagine that we are a very easy prey to an invading army, who cannot make head, in three weeks time, to a desperate man who landed with only an hundred and fifty with him; but I hope this reproach shall proceed no farther, and that rebellion will be as short livd in England as it has bin in Scotland. I perceive the parliament is not yet adjourned, and your Lordship has not hitherto any instructions whither you are to go to Guernsey or Northamptonshire. It is a great satisfaction when our choices are fixed by our superiors, for then, whatever the event be, we can justify ourselves, as to the world, so also, what is of more moment, to our own consciences. If your Lordship be commanded to your government, you have a sister and daughter who will not regret to bear you company, and, if you think fit to leave your daughter behind, God be thanked she has that virtue and prudence which may supersede your fears of his miscarriage in your absence. Tho, considering the tenderness of a young ladies fame in this malicious world, which no guard of innocence or caution can secure, and also considering how boundless a parents fears will be in the behalf of an only child that is far off, I am apt to think your Lordship may in the close resolve not to part company. Whatever you conclude upon, I beseech Almighty God to give it blessing. I remain, My honoured Lord, Your most humble and affectionate served, Jo. Oxon.

My honoured Lt, I am exceedingly glad that your affair goes on so prosperously with my Lord Nottingham; but it was some surprise to me to be told it by the public news letter. This is a peculiar way of publishing the bans of matrimony and, if it can obtain, will supersede the use of an Act of Parliament against clancular marriages. Your daughter, if she can comport with the temper of a grave husband and deny herself those gaieties which may be decent for the wife of one who is of his age, may promise to herself as much happiness in this disposal as is to be had in this world. But little things lead to great, and, if herein she can comply and render herself a meet helper, she will not want any sober enjoyment or real satisfaction. I wish my Lord Clarendon good luck with his honour, which to me seems sufficiently hazardous. His son's match seems very desirable, but it comes often to pass that rich widows prove poor wives; and I am told there are several pretensions to the personal estate of Mrs Whitmore, which may make a better dividend among the lawyers then the executor of kindred. If the condition of those other officers who are cashiered be no worse then Mr Cook's, they will not be in ill circumstances by the loss of their commands. I pray God fit us for the more necessary duty of obeying, and preserve to us our laws and our religion. I add my heartiest prayers for the continuance of all blessing to your Lordship and family, remaining, My honoured Lord, your most humble and affectionate served, Jo. Oxon.

My honoured Lt, I was in hope that the practice of duelling had bin forgot; but, if it be resumed, tic to be doubted this little interval of late will only give a greater appetite and the recommendation of a fashion newly revived. This instance happening where an example is not likely to be made is the more unfortunate, for without severity a stop will not be put. The age of the young lady whom your Lordship mentions is no objection, unless there have bin some personal obstacle which has kept one from a husband till two or three and twenty years are over when there was a portion of 20000l. Tic easy payment of 1000l to Dr King to quit scores by a knighthood, which in truth is the fining him a hundred pound. In the mean time, tic well that a good officer is remembered at Court after a year is past, and that respit, which by the doctor's means was given, proved of greater importance then could be easily imagind. I am, thank God, still upon my legs, and continue to go to church without inconvenience. I pray God perpetuate the happy opportunity. Adding my prayers for the health and prosperity of your Lordship and family, I remain, My honoured Lord, Your Most humble and affectionate served, Jo. Oxon.

. You had heard from me last post, dearest Brother, but by a mistake my letter was forgot to be sent, which I fretted extremely att, but was born for misfortune of all kinds, and I am sure it would be ye greatest to me in ye world to give ire Ldp the least occasion to believe yt any thing can ever make me omit paying all the duty and respect that is due to ye best of brothers. Lt Nottingham designs to go to on Tuesday next, in order to see Lt Banbery's house, which he has a mind to buy. He was with me yesterday, to settle my answer, which I must, it seems, put in, for they will hear of nothing till that be done; and an inventory of every thing must be set down, with they doe not demand as well as with they doe. When they have had all, I hope theyl be satisfied, and I must bare the loss. Captain Hatton has had an unfortunait accident hapnd at Carlisle. I have not heard a perfect relation how ye quarrel began, but, in short, Lieutenant Gorge Comely has killed Majoer Morgan, that dined with ire Ldp, at his tent, and tic said nobody was by when it was don but Captain H. There are two papist officers put into their places. Lady Manchester and all ye young ladies very well, present theere servis to ire Ldp and my dear sister. She is this day gone to a weding feast. Lt Colrain's son married to a merchants daughter in ye City. Lt Montagu's son, if not dead, is given over by ye drs. The death of ye little Princess, Lady Anne, is a great aflection to ye Princes. Lt Grey has had another loss, besides his plate. His page has picked his pocket of several guineas, but his Ldp has only had him whipped for it and still keeps him. Lt Manchester does not come from Venice till after Easter, and will not be in England so soon as April, as was expected. The Dean of Pal's presents his servis to ire Ldp. I find he is very well inclined to leave St. Andrews, but, so many persuades him against it, he is not yet resolved with to doe. Lady Ann Grimston in town, and her neighbour Wyseman come to her house again. It seems North was concerned in making ye match for Mr Spencer. She invited them both to her house, and when they met she locked them in a rome together. There are many surcomstances too long to trouble your Ldp with from, my dearest Brother, Ire most truly afet sister and most obedient servant, A. H. Lt and La. Nottingham humbly beg ire blessing. My servis to dear pretty Miss Bety. Lt N. will write next post. The little Prences has not ye measells but a fever, and was last night in a great danger.

March 8th, . I am so troubled for ire being ell, my dearest Brother, I don't know with to doe. I have had so many aflictions of this kind, yt I cant but dread this which would, I am sure, be ye greatest yt ever can happen to me in ye world. If it be God's will, as I pray night and day, to restore you to health again, with ever ellse God pleases to lay upon me, I will never rapine, but think myself happy so long as I have my dearest brother Hatton. I am sorry my ugly letter gave you any disturbance. If I doe not hear next post of ire being better I will come down, and please God to see you, with ever becomes of me. Lt Not: is now at Milton, and left this letter to be sent to ire Ldp. Tic a great blessing to us all that ire Ldp will take care of yrselfe. Yt ye remedies you use for ye recovery of ire health may be successful shall be ye daily prayer of, dearest Brother, Ire most aft sister to serve you, A. H. Lady Not begs ire blessing.

Easter Even, . It was ye kindnest thing in the world, dearest Brother, to let me hear from you last post; for, in earnest, I am so concerned for my poor sister 's confinement to his chamber, yt my thoughts are never at rest but when I hear from you. It would be a melancholy thing to be always in a chamber and have nothing to doe, but pretty Miss Betty makes it not so I hope to her dear mama. I am mighty glad she breeds her teeth so well. There was yesterday a vast crowed at Whithall to hear Dr Sharp. Ye Bishop went from thence to ye King's Chaple, and was there till ten a clock at night, and a Maunday Thursday went along with Laban all ye time he washed ye poor men's feet. Tic said Nil Guin is dead. Ye King has seized on his estate and jewles for his son, but, unless he will change his religion, he's not to have any thing, which he is yet very unwilling to. Lady Not. asks ire blessing and my dear's, whose humble servant I am, and, dearest Brother, Ire most affct sister to serve you, A. H.

June 9th . My Lord, Though its near a 11 at night, and I fear the post is going, I cannot forbear to send you a peace of news, odd and unusual. There was a rich Spanish ship coming from the West Indies yt was sunk three score years ago, laden with gold and silver. Duke Albemarle, Sr Narborough, Sr James Hays, and another, got a patent from the late King, on terms to get all the gold and silver they could from the bottom of the sea by any art yt ever they have been 10 years a trying, and got dyvers (men used to it) out of the West Indies, and found this ship, and got her up and safe into the river, worth two hundred and 50 thousand pounds in gold and silver. Duke Albemarle's share, 2 eights, is 40000; Sr James Hays as much, 40000; and others proportionable. The King reserved a 10th for himself. It's certainly true; you'll hear it more at large quickly. Pray excuse Ire humble servant, Ed. King. The news came yesterday morn, at 3 a clock; and I beseech you present my humble service to my Lady Hatton. They are working on another ship.

column46: At ye Camp , July 13th, . My Lord, I recd ye news of my Ladies bringing you a son with all ye joy I cd have done for my heir, and wish you a long and solid comfort in it. I had done it ye last post, but that ye Kg surprised us in drawing us out unexpectedly to our arms; and, indeed, we can, while we stay here, promise little time to ourselves. To morrow, the Kg treats ye 2 Queens here. The Guards will be all drawn into ye field from London, and we shall make 4 lines of horse and foot, and have abundance of firing and fireworks. Wthin 2 or 3 days, I believe, the fort may be finished. It's a curtain of 2 half bastions, abt ye bigness of Sherenesse, with a ravlin before ye curtain; and this is to be attacked in form by ye whole army, and will take up some days. The D. of Albemarle dined here yesterday with ye Kg, and says his ships are now all sailed to Portsmouth, and he will be soon there to embark. My Lt Faversham is gone to Sr John Raisby's, not to Welbeck, in order to a treaty with Lt Newcastle for his daughter. Lt Dumbarton is gentleman of ye bedchamber in Lt Somts place.

March 24, . My Lord, It was this morning before I could prevail with Mr Sadlor to see my Lady Hatton's picture, which is well painted, very fleshey and well coloured, and is a very fine peace and extremely like too. But I found a great fault (as I called it) in a part of the face; which I convinced him of, and he mended it to his own great satisfaction and his wive's as well as mine, whilst I stood by; and I mended another in my Lady's hand of as great a concern, which I am sure your Lordp will be pleased with too; but your dear pretty son with his fine diamond eyes I durst not meddle with, because I have not had him in my sight, in the life, which pray God preserve. We hear the Bishop of Oxford died Tuesday last, not a . The Duke of Barwich has the small pox, this the 5th day. My Lord Peterborough is at Drayton since Monday last. I entreat my humble service to my Lady Hatton, and am Your Lordps most affectionte sert, Ed. King.

column46: Shene, May 15th . My Lord, It's a great while since I heard from you; and ye longer I think, because, when I did so last, you complaind of ill health. I was all the last week and part of that before at Sherenesse and Rochester, to attend his Maty, who went to give order abt ye navy, making several new platforms and batteries upon the Midway, and ye putting out some ships to sea and to get others in a readiness, if there shd be occasion for it, as I hope there will not yet awhile. For, though the Duch are (they say) out with a more considerable fleet then we yet know wht they have to doe with, I can hardly think they will attempt any thing upon us. It will be (though) to insult us, if they come to brave it on our coast. I left riding before Sherenesse our R Ad: Strickland with 3 more men of war, 4th and 5th rates, and 3 or 4 fireships; and, it may be, these, or ye men of war at least, are designed to carry Q. Dowager to Portugal, who, they say, goes in August. My son Harry has a mind to go with her, and from thence into Spain, and then into Italy, if he can get ye Kgs leave.

column46: Letcomb, June 18, . I must, my Lord, in ye first place return you thanks for ire present of opobalsamum, from which I have found more benefit then from any physic I ever took; which I experienced by accident, for, missing ye regimt at Aylsbury, I writ to our colonel for leave to be absent from my command for a fortnight or 3 weeks longer, and, ye waters being out, I wase advised to come hither by Oxford, where, designing to have some pectoral pills and a decoction made up according to a perscription of Dr Fowkes, in which balsum of Tolu wase to be dissolved, which wase not to be had (any thing tolerable good) at Oxford, instead thereof I made use of opobalsamum, by which I have found very great benefit. I met at Oxford with Mabillon his Musaeum Italicum, and a peace of Dr Bernards newly out of ye press, de Ponderibus et Mensuris, a subject I know not displeasing to ire Lop. Therefore I have with Mabillon sent it to ire Lop. These 2 books, with Ford's Psalms, cost a little above with I promised for ire 2 dictionaries. I have like wise sent some seeds I procured from Mr Bobart. Some of them are very curious plants, and I should advise ye sowing of part of each parcel of ye choicest seeds now, and ye rest next spring. For those plants which are annual, being sowed so late, will not I suppose come to perfection this summer, and will therefore continue all winter and flower earlier and more beautifully next year. I have settled a correspondence with Mr Bobart, and he hath, in ye season, promised me some curious plants which I design for ire Lop. Dr Morrison 2d volume is in great forwardness, 120 plates are engraven, and about 40 only wanting to perfect ye work. At ye press at ye Theatre I accidentally met with Dr Mills, whose Greek Testament is advanced as far as ye 16th of ye Acts. I found I had highly recommended myself to him and many in the University by having been instrumental in prevailing with Mr Dodwell to accept ye history lecture, which he hath done to ye great satisfaction of ye University. Dr Mills kept me a day longer at Oxford then I designed, treated me all ye time, and brought me into ye acquaintance of so many persons I had much ado to get from them. Amongst others he carried me to Dr Aldrige and Dr Hammond at Christchurch, who both give you their service and testify a great honour and regard for ire Lop. I went to visit ye 2 black walnuts trees you so much admired, but I could see but one, and yt a most beautiful tree. Ye other is cut down, and I doubt yt I saw will have ye same fate, for it is much slighted and vilified. The Bp of St Asaph his Chronology did, in ye press, advance apace; but, as you have heard, there is an unhappy stop put to it at present. It was printing in Latin and in English, in distinct volumes. If it pleases God he enjoys his liberty, he will very vigorously pursue ye finishing yt so much desired work. I am, my Lt, Ire Lopps very humble servant, C. Hatton.

29 Septr, 1688. My Lt, I wish, in so doleful a case as our country now seems to bee in, that I knew any thing worth writing or of a reviving sort; but so it is (my Lt), the foreign invaders will probably bee landed this next week, if not at ye first of it. His Maty had 6 Bps. to him yesterday morning, and one of them said: omnia been` , as I am told. Too day hath produced a declaration why ye parliament writs are recalled, and a pardon also as I hear. Lt Lovelace is in England, and was at Wickham election of a mayor a day or two since. Whither Lt Shrewsbury bee with ye Prince of O. or here is in uncertain report. And so for other lords. It is sd the Kg will not delay when he hears where the landing is. I wish your Lop. much health, and a quiet world to us all in God's good time. My service humbly presented to my Lady and to Mrs Hatton, I subscribe, with some hast, My Lt, Your Lops. most obedient Wm. L.

column46: Sheernesse, October 2d, . My Lord, I hope you are not in Holland, though I hant had ye honour to hear from you a great while, and that there is so much news from thence. The wind is fair to day to bring ym for England, if they be so resolved, which it has not bine before a good while. We have abundance of materials sent hither, and there are at least 40 carpenters to abt a hundred laborers at work to put this place in a better defence. All ye platforms already repaired. Here is come into ye harbour, wthin 2 days, 7 fireships, where they are to stay for further orders. I had a letter yesterday from a captn in ye Downs, that ye fleet was coming to ye Nor; so I hope we are safe here, but I think this country or place is suspected to be attempted, because there is lately two regimts more come to Rochester. I thank God, I have kept free of ye ague yet, but I have a terrible cold; and every day our people fall down of agues. I have 200 commanded men in constant guarrison of Coll: Hales regimt, and an order to send for ye rest of ye regmt upon ye sight of a foreign fleet. They lye at Canterbury and Sittingburn, but there are 100 of ym commanded away lately, to relieve so many of my regimt who were at Landguard Fort; my regmt being commanded to London from Yarmouth. In easterly winds I am ever troubled with ye hand I write with a cramp, which puts me to so much pain I can scarce hold my pen at present.

October , 1688. My Lt, At such a season as this I hold myself bound to give your Lop. 2 letters for one. Last post I sent your Lop. account where 1000l might bee had, and that if you came up I thought the better. The wind keeping westward, the Dutch fleet is not arrived, as far as I can hear. Yesterday our King had the Bps with him again, and told them of this invasion again and how little concerned his people seemed. He declared Magdalen College should bee restored by the Bp of Winton, the visitor; that a fast should be held; and that prayers for ye occasion should bee penned and presently used. Mr Godwin Wharton is laid in ye Tower, but for what indeed I have not yet heard. Some report goes as if 16 comissions were taken with one -; I forget the man's name. I hear there was a disturbance in Lime street last Sunday, and ye mayor was feign to quiet the same. The friery by the arch in Lincolns-Inn Fields also hath been ill treated. Lt lieutenants of ye Romish profession begin to be removed, for that none care to act under them. I wish your Lop. good health and quiet into your family, being, My Lt, Your Lops. most obedient servant, Wm. L.

Sunday, Nov. 25, . My Lord, I hope ire Lop. will pardon me the misinformations I sent you in my letter on Tuesday last; for in such a conjuncture as this, when every man is greedy of news and talks himself as his interest or inclination leads him, tic not to be wonderd at yt there be many false reports, and tic hard to distinguish ye true; and therefore I will venture again to write you with I hear. Tic said yt Plimouth is surrendered to ye Prince, and yt Briston has declared for him, and yt my Lt of Derby joins with ye other Lords in ye North. But I think I have better assurance of what follows: That our fleet is much shatterd by the late storms. Sr Jo. Berry is come to ye Spithead with 3 or 4 ships which will want considerable repairs, and says he knows not wht is become of ye rest; but I hear and believe yt 7 of ym are gone to ye Dutch. The King has bin very ill at Salisbury, and bled much at ye nose, and has bin twice let blood, and could have no rest but by ye help of opiates. Very few of ye gentlemen of ye country came to him, for indeed most of ym are gone to ye Pr of Or., who is upon his march with his whole army; and ye King has ordered his army to come back, and they are now upon their march, and he himself is expected on Tuesday; so yt it looks as if London was to be ye stage, especially since it cannot be imagined but yt ye army which is forming by ye Lords in ye North will come to London too. But, however, I can't think Kirby a safe place for ire Lops family; for, though tic said yt they were to be at Northampton as last night, yet no doubt some of ym, particularly those of Lincolnshire and ye others in Yorkshire who are not yett got together, will come by Stanford; and though no injury could be apprehended from a disciplind army, yet in so great a number of men so suddenly drawn together there will be stragglers, and ire Lops house is too near ye road (especially if they go cross ye country to Northampton) not to be visited. So yt I have this to say yet for Kensington, yt tic safer then Kirby from ye violence of disorderly soldiers; and besides, by a speedy removal from Kirby, you will avoid ye importunities of some whom you would be unwilling to deny, and yet cannot grant what they will ask; and in such difficulties tic best to prevent ye necessity of answering. I must confess to ire Lop yt difficulties must be expected here too, and I have reason to expect my share in ym; but I hope in God to have an honest issue out of ym, and I shall be ye less concerned whatever it is. My Lt Danby has certainly possessed himself of York for ye Pr. of Orange. Just now I hear yt my Lord Churchill and Duke of Grafton are gone to ye Pr. of Or. with 6000 horse and foot, and many of ye rest of ye English and Scotch are going too, particularly Kirk and Trelawny. The King is in a very ill condition of health by his bleeding, insomuch yt he has wrote to ye Queen she must expect no more letters from him, because he can't hold down his head. Pray let me hear yt you have recd this, and wht your resolutions are about staying at Kirby or leaving it.

Tuesday, Nov. 27, . My Lord, He yt will write news cant want matter, for he will have enought to contradict one post with he wrote by ye former. Bristol has not declared for ye Pr. of Or., but are ready for him; for there are not ten men there yt will oppose him. The gentlemen of Herefordshire and Gloucestershire are in arms, and Sr Edward Harley at ye head of ym; and ye Duke of Norfolk is so in Norfolk. Kirk is not gone to ye Pr. of Or., but is arrested at ye head of his regiment in his march with ye army back; but he certainly intended it, for he stayed 12 hours at Warminster before he marched, after he received orders to doe so. My Lt Churchill and Grafton carried very few men with ym, and not 6000 as I wrote in my last; tho yt was ye news yt my Lt Middleton sent at first to ye Queen. Prince George and ye Duke of Ormond and Lt Drumlanerick are gone to ye Pr. of Or.; and yesterday morning ye Princess of Denmark went away with my Lady Churchill and Mrs Berkley, but none know whither. The King came in ye afternoon, and this afternoon summoned all ye Lds Spirit. and Temporal about ye town to Whitehall to consult about calling a parlt; and he has declared that he resolves to call a parlt, and thought he should not alter it, but would consider of it, and of ye things necessary in order to it which had bin mentioned by ye lords, viz: security for ye lords and now with ye Prince to come to it, and doing several acts of grace to ye people. And I believe there will some of ye lords be sent to ye Prince, to treat about it; and I am told yt some of ye Court lords did declare that ye King could not rely upon his army, tho ye King seemed yet to have confidence in its fidelity. Tic said ye Pr. of Orange was on Sunday at Salisbury, and last night at Andover, where ye Lt Feversham was to be with ye army; and tic concluded yt there has bin action, or else yt many of ym are gone to ye Prince; but just now I hear yt the Prince was last night only at Sherborne.

Tuesday, ye 27th Nov. . I hope, being ire Losp is so unwilling to remove, you will not be obliged to it, and must confess I am something of ire opinion yt where you are is safe from anny yt will hurt you as you can be; for, tho there should be rising northward, which there is reason enough to expect, you wont probablely have anny of the Irish near you, who I find have given every where more terror then anny forrieng forces. The King returned last night to London. He has been much troubled with a bleeding of ye nose, for which he has been twice let blood since he went. My Lt Churchill and the Duke of Grafton and Coll. Berkeley went on Saturday to the Prince of Orange, and on Sunday the Prince of Denmark and the Duke of Ormond. Yesterday morning the Princess went away, were is not yet known, with her only my Lady Churchill and Mrs Berkely. Yesterday my Lt Feversham and my Lt Dumbarton seized on Coll: Kirk, it being suspected he would go over to the Prince. I hear to day of a great tumult at Uxbridge, were the soldiers have been a great while very insolent, and yesterday set the twone on fire in three places, which moved the inhabitants to rise to defend themselves and to quench the fire; whereupon the soldiers fell to blundering, and the inhabitance have killed, they say, 30 soldiers. Ire Losp. saying nothing how all ire family does makes me hope they are all well. I am ire most obedient daughter and humble servant, A. Nottingham.

The 11 of December, . I heard yesterday, by a servant of my Lord Godolphins yt came this way, yt the Lords will be back to day, were they will a clear coast, for yesterday ye Qeueen and Mr Whales went and took watter at Durham Yard, and from thence to Foxhall, were the coaches were ready for them, for Dover; and with them, tic said, my Lord Chancellor, my Lord Peterborough and my Lord Salisberry and my Lord Sunderland are gone, but whether with the Qeueen or no I cant tell; and tic said ye Chief Justice Herbert is gone too. To day the King is gone, as I am told, but I have but an imperfect account of it from some of my own servants yt were in twone. It has been much talked of, and I think not without a cause, of the Qeueen Dowagers going to Eastwell, my Lord Winchelsease; but she has now put yt of for some time. There has been a skirmish at Reading, were the Irish were very insolent and threaten us. There manner is to fire the twone, and thereupon the inhabitants being frightnend run out and meet with some of the Princes forces (they say that regiment that was my Lord Scarsdale, since yt the Duke of St Albaneses), and begged of them to rescue them, as those they looked upon as there deliverers; and so they fell upon the Irish men and killed ten of them and took 30 prisoners, for at first they made some resistance, but then betook themselves to their best weapons, there heels, and, because nothing should hinder these last, threw of their boots and arms and whatever was cumbsersum to them. My Lt Feversham was coming and meet them in this disorder; so he presently ordered Twyford bridge to be broken down, yt they might not be pursued. There was in Reading at yt times my Lord Dunmore regiment, who are Scosh, and some of Sr John Leniers regiment; but they never a man drew a sword, but went of civilly to make room for the Princesses forces. They talk much of my Lt Inchaquen being up in Ireland, and my Lord Tryconnel breeding who wold speak to an Englishman with his hat on. The Duke of Gordon is turn protestant and is up in Scotland with the Duke of Qeueenbourough. They say yt one Tuesday last my Ldy Marie Fenwick declared herself a papist. I beg the favour of ire Lops. to present my humble duty to my Lady and service to my cousin Finch and his lady. I will be sure to let my Lord know, when he comes, what ire Lordsh. says of Mr Pullyn. I am ire Losp. most obedient Dau: Anne Nottingham.

Kensington, Dec. 13, 1688. My Lord, My wife wrote you word by ye last post yt ye King was gone away; and he is now seizd at Feversham by the rabble, who will offer him no violence but will not suffer him to go away without ye consent of ye city of London. In this conjuncture ye Lords meet every day, and this day they have sent ye Lds Aylesbury, Middleton, and Yarmouth, to attend ye King; and ye Lt Feversham is gone by their order with 120 horse and 40 grenadiers to preserve ye King from any violence of ye people, but not to restrain him in ye least from any liberty or resolution yt he pleases to take; and they have wrote to ye Pr. of Or. an account hereof. Tic thought ye Queen and Pr. of W. will be taken too, for some vessels are in pursuit of ym; and Father Petre is in Kent street, and order is sent to apprehend him. My Lt, I will not pretend to advise ire Lop.; but I think it would be very fit for you to be in town at this time, when every day produces such extraordinary things; and, tho you cant remove ire family on a sudden, yet you might immediately come yrselfe, and I should be glad you would come hither yt we might consider of ye present circumstances and how to behave ourselves; and London is not yet a safe place, ye rabble committing every night great disorders; and there is another reason for ire coming, and yt is, ye Pr of Or may be here tomorrow, but there is no doubt but he will be here on Saturday. I came back on Tuesday night; but I have no time to give you a narrative of yt negotiation, most of which is in print already. My most humble service to my Lady and Mrs Hatton. I am, Ire Lops most obedient humble served, Nottingham.

Thursday, 13th of Decr, 1688. My Lord, On Tuesday evening his Maty did leave Whitehall; and, being in Feversham creek retaken, they say here that hoe's come back to Whitehall too night. Sr Ed. Hales and Mr Sheldon were in his company. The Earl of Salsbury and Mr Ch. Hales were taken at Ashford, Mr Obit. Walker and others at Sittingborne, Baron Jennor and others at Feversham. The multitude have done strangely to the Spanish ambassador in burning his books, coach, and spoiling his goods and house and what was there, as in a franchise, laid in. And so have divers lesser things been spoiled and done. Last night all the town were, by false rumours of ye Irish soldiers, kept in fear and up all night. The Duke of Grafton is come to town to day. I wish, my Lt, here may come good out of all this hurly-burly. Had I time, your Lop. should hear oftener; but last post I had none, and not much now, being all ye afternoon taken off by Temple business, which on this present juncture takes up much of one's time. I am, with true respect, My Lt, Your Lop.'s most humble servant, Wm. L.

Thursday night, Dec. 13, . Every day brings new alarms or woonders, nay, almost every hour. I intended to send with papers are out, but I find 2 or 3 of them in the gazett, which cam not out till 7 this night. The mobile have been extremely insolent and ungovernable, and yet are not suppressed. This day, about 1 a clock, we had news that the King was stopped by fisher boats, and that he is now at Feversham in Kent. I went to Whitehall and met my Lord Prestons lady, who said it was true, and so said Lady Peterboro and Lady Clevland and many more; and this night the Duke of Grafton is com to town. I went to great him, but he was with the Lords in counsel to night; and I find this news has shoakt their measurs for the presant, but I believe they must proceed now. The Prince of O. is not com yet. Lt Peterb. is taken too, and his it. Sr Adieu. Hails is said to be with the , and the of Chester (but I doubt yt). We hear 24 priests taken in one vessel, and all wish it true. I was in Cheapside wn the Chancellor was brought to my Lt Mayor. There never was such joy; not a man sorry yt we could see. They longed to have him out of the coach, had he not had a good guard. Dr. Oats, I am told, is dressed in all his Drs robes again, and expects liberty quickly. We had a terrible alarm last night; at 12 a clock in the night cried, "Arm! arm! arm!" 7000 Irish was com from the army, disbanded but in a body, and killing all they met. We was all up in arms till 5 in the morning. It arise from some disorder amongst them in Brainford, and was allayed by telling the Princes van guard of horse pursued them and cut them to pieces. It's a strange thing we have not the truth out yet. We doe not think we are safe till the Prince com's; all the Protestants long for him. Ho! you are happy in your quiet place. God keep it so. Pray pray for us, as my poor wife desires me to tell you with her humble service to ire Lp and to my , and mine too. Just now I am told (just now) that the King is dead 2 hours after he was taken, if I may use yt word. I have also word brought me that there is 4 troops of the P. of O. horse come to town: Coll. Slingsby's regiment. Since I wrote this, the news letter came. I doe not know which is best: to have the news that belongs to the Bill of Mortality true or false, nor, upon the whole, I doe not believe the first, but that he is taken by Admiral Herbert.

Saturday, 15th of Decr, 1688. My Lord, Now it appears here how needful the Prince of Orange his coming to this populous place is; till which, indeed, here is nothing but distraction and danger. The King is at Feversham, as it is said, and pretty well, at the mayor's house. Desirous hee was of being at liberty to bee gone, but most believe the people there will not, unless by the Prce of O. his direccion, leave him to himself and to bee gone. His Maty wrote up to Mr Froude to send him a few servants and some linen and money. Four lords went unto him, vizt the Earl of Ailesbury, Earls of Yarmouth and Feversham, and Lt Middleton. Most of this day his Maty was reported to bee dead; but I hear it was an untruth; although it is by his best friends thought hee cannot but bee heart broken and not long in this life. God look on him for good; however, his happiness for this world seems closed. Majr Wildman and Dr Burnett are in seeming power. Some 50 ladies are now at Windsor with the Pr. of O. Too day a declaration is abroad for recalling the disbanded army to their officers or colours, subscribed by the Prce of Orange and dated at his Court at Henly. I am always, My Lt, Your Lops most faithful humble servant, Wm. L.

Dec. 18, . My Lord, I wrote to ire Lop last night by ye post, and when I came home I found ire served here with a letter, but was unwilling to send him back without adding something to my last nights letter; and I was in hopes ire Lop might have bin here if ire pains had abated, which I am extremely sorry are very grievous and frequent. The King came this night to Whitehall, and had sent before my Lt Feversham to Windsor, to invite ye Pr of Or. to London; and St James's House is to be his court. But ye Prince has made my Lt Feversham prisoner for coming into his quarters without a pass, which seems at present but a pretence, for he is extremely angry with him for dismissing ye army as he did, whereby the country has bin exposed to their ripens and outrages, and ye soldiers dispersed, which, had they bin kept in a body, would have bin more ready for foreign service; and perhaps it is thought t'was done on purpose. Besides, the Prince had sent Monsr Zuylesteyn to ye King upon ye news of his being in ye hands of ye rabble (who declared yt they would not let him go without an order from ye Prince), that his Maty should be at full liberty to doe as he pleased with himself. But, upon ye acct he had of ye Kings design of returning to London, he remanded Zuylesteyn to ye King, to tell him he thought it more expedient for him to stay at Rochester; and I hear yt ye discourse at Windsor is, yt ye King's going away is a cession of his right to ye crown. I shall make no comments, but doe extremely wish for ire Lops company here, if ire health would permit it. In ye mean time I shall follow your directions about ire affair of Guernsey, as well as I can and as I have opportunity; but I hope there can be no need of any solicitation on ire behalf, ire patent being for life, or, if there should be any such need, I am apt to think I shall not be a very proper advocate. But ire Lop may be sure yt I shall always take ye same care of ire concerns as of my own. I am Ire Lops most obedient humble servant, N.

column46: April 9, 1689. This day ye bill for ye coronation oath passed, not with opposition in ye House. The Commons have voted ye calling a Convocation. Yesterday they brought in a Comprehension Bill of their own, if possible, more favourable to ye fanatics then yrs, and more destructive to ye of . After it wase read, several moved for a day to be appointed for a 2d reading. Some mentioned that day seven-night, some yt day fortnight. Sr Edward Chisnal said it wase a bill so destructive to ye Ch. of E. he desired it lie on ye table till Doomsday, which some heats which quickly passed over; and then Sr Henry Capell, with a large preamble, attesting his zeal for ye Ch. of E. as ye promoters of yt bill usually doe, declared it wase of yt consequence he must second those who moved for ye longest day. Then replied Mr Speaker: "You move for Doomsday?" which gave no small diversion to all ye House but Sr Henry. And for ire diversion, if you have not heard it, I shall tell you a pleasanter story. The Countess of Dorchester lately went to visit a certain lady, who received her very coolly; upon which ye Countess told her she wase much surprised: "For," said she, "if I have broke one commandment, you have another; and what I did wase more natural." Here is a report 5000 Swedes are landed at North Yarmouth and 10000 more exspected, to remove grievances and defend our liberty and property. All here are ire Lopps, my sister's, nephew, and nieces humble servants, but more particularly ire truly affectionate brother to serve you, C. Hatton.

column46: London, Apple 9th, . Because I hear nothing of ire Lp, I conclude you are yet at Kirby and dare not venture ire ill health in ye crowd on Thursday. I am yet in suspense how my regimt will be disposed, for we are treated so hardly, both in words and deeds, abt it, that, though we are not broke, I cant think they care to keep us. They will not allow us, wht they doe to others, to make our recruits; and tell us wthall the King is so dissatisfied with ye officers abt ye deserting of ye soldiers, that, as a mark of his displeasure, this hardship is put upon us. I have plainly told my Lt Churchill, who is now Lt Marlborough, we think we deserve better usage, as being the regimt who's officers have stuck best together in ye service of any in ye army, there being none but Lt Coll. and one capt. who have quited it; but I doe so despise the opinion I hear is had of me, that I did privately contrive the meeting and deserting at Brandford, &c. as ye playing such a 2ble game, when I had taken this Kings comn, that I am quite weary of serving any longer and am very willing to resign to those they can be better assured of, and endeavour, as soon as I can, to come to an issue in. Sr George Huet kissed ye Kgs hand to day to be a baron; so is Ad: Herbert. Monsr Bentin is Earl of Portland. My Lt Falkland is out, and Mr Russell in his place. Sr George Lockart, ye Lt Pre: of ye sessions in Scotland, most barbarously murdered, as he lighted from his coach to go into his own house, by one Cheesly, who he had given some judgmt agst in behalf of his own wife and children. He was put to ye torture, had his hand cut of, and hanged up in chains. I hear the Kg and Queen are proclaimed in yt kingdom. The Comns have voted ye Kg thanks for declaring he will maintain ye Church of Eng: established by law, and that his Maty be desired to issue out writs to call a Convocation.

May 23th, . My Lord, Having wrote twice to enquire after ire Lordps health and not hearing, I began to fear I forgot to direct them to the Weldon bag, which might occasion their miscarriage. Pray give me leave to send this on the same arrand. By some I have heard your Lordp and family have continued well, and by others yt your Lordp had some of your old pains again, which I am concerned at, but hope the Tunbridge waters will prove more successful than other methods have done. Twill be a kind of presumption to write your Lordp any news, yet, being yesterday with the Earl of Twedall, who is come lately from Scotland on acct of his health (and under my care), read me his letters from thence; that ye Lord Dundee came to Perth and took away ye Lord Blair and two more Conventionors and part of a troop raising there; that Mackey keeps in those parts, but Dundee skulks about; that the young men of yt kingdom are very unanimous and meet in divers places to exercise; that the new battery against the Castle at Edenbrough is now finished and the mortar pieces are planted, and they expect wthin a day or two to begin to use them. Yesterday and to day the town rings with a report from several letters that those in Londonderry have made another sally and killed several thousands Irish and a great many great officers; and they say the Duke of is killed, and that the siege is raised. Yesterday on told me he heard the say there is now 20 sail of Dutch men of war at the Spitthead; but we are informd the French have taken 7 of the Dutch merchant ships worth 150,000ll or more. Many other discourses make a noise here; but so few reports prove true, yt I rather ask your Lordps pardon for with I have said than report more, and humbly entreat my humble service to my Lady, and always heartily pray for your Lordps health and of all yours.

column46: April 15, . I endeavoured, my Lt, to waite on my Lt Nottingham to day, but could not; and shall try again to morrow, and shall not forget Mr Martin's concern. I have been to day at Chelsey garden, and have made choice of 2 pots of ye passion-flower, and am very confident ire Lop need not fear but they will thrive very well, they are so lusty and strong, and, if ire be careful to lay ym well, by this time 12 month you may have 20. I have sent ire Lop ye protestation of some of ye Lds aged ye Act of Recognition, about which there hath been so many and hot debates. The reasons of ye protest are, by order of ye majority of ye Lords by five, razed out of ye journal; but ye names of ye protesting lords remain, and they have with reason entered their protest aged ye razure of yt reason for their first protest. Last night a fire begun, about 12 at night, at ye coffee house over ye mews gate, which burnt with yt violence yt it wase thought fit to blow up ye adjoining houses on each hand, which put a stop to it. C. Hatton.

column46: April 26, . My Lt, Some of my old botanick acquaintances, having made an appointmt to go yesterday to Hampton Court (to see ye famous collection there of ye rare Indian plants which mine Heer Fagel had gathered together), called on me, and I heartily wished ire Lop had been there, for there is about 400 rare Indian plants which were never seen in England; and there is scarce any desirable Indian plant, but a specimen may be seen there; and some very curious Indian plants are in so great perfection yt it is very wonderful and scarce credible. The stoves in which they are kept are much better contrived and built then any other in England. Wee went by water and called at a Drs house by ye way, where I saw a very pretty flowering shrub in his greenhouse, and I have enclosed 2 or 3 seeds, all I could get; and if carefully sowed on a hotbed, I doubt not but they will come up. The greatest news I can send you from here is yt ye Abjuration Bill is flung out of ye House of Commons, at which, it is said, some are so displeased yt there will be another bill brought in much to ye same effect. My Lt Nottingham's abdication is now contradicted by ye coffeehouse newsmongers. Wee are all here both to ire Lop and all at Kirby most faithful and very humble servants. C. Hatton.
