column46: June 7, . I hope, my Lt, it wase not any increase of ire indisposition which wase ye occasion I heard nothing from Kirby ye last post. And, though I have not much news to acquaint ire Lop, yet I will send with I hear stirring, and in ye first place tell you with will be more surprising then afflicting to you. The famed Ferguson is committed to a messenger's hands on suspicion of treason aged ye present governmt. This day Captn Crone wase ye 3d time tried and found guilty of high treason; but, before ye jury brought him in guilty, they were shut up from 3 of ye clock yesterday in ye afternoon till one this afternoon, after which in arrest of judgmt he pleaded an error in ye indictmt as found by ye grand jury, for they signed it Bill Verra ; and the judges have appointed to have it argued by council before ym next Thursday. It is reported yt ye Queen Dowager is ordered to go either to Windsor or Audle-End, because ye Papists, on pretence of going to her chapel, doe meet and cabal. The truth is, ye popish party are very insolent and impudently give ye lie to all other public news, and, though every public intelligence tells us how ye Highlanders are run down, yt ye popish party give out yt they very strong and have lately received great recruits from Ireland. Wee shall never be happy till all our damnable liars are confounded, which God speedily grant. I and all here are, with great sincerity, to ire Lop and all at Kirby most faithful and humble servants. C. Hatton.

Thursday, ye 26 of June, . I find, when ire Losp. writ yrs, you were ignorant of the expectations we are here in of hearing every moment of some engagement at sea between our fleet and the French, for they have lain in sight of one another this 4 days. With will the consequence be wee are in great impatience to know. I think from the first yt I heard it till to day I have thought of nothing else; but now indeed with my uncle Hatton has by his foolishness brought himself into is some concern to me, and I believe will be so to ire Losp. when you hear. Upon suspicion and some discovery several people have been secured in the Tower: my Lord Clarendon and my Lord Newburgh, Sr John Fenwick, Charles Turner, and several more; and he, by the foolishness of his talk and the company he kept, together with the accusation of one Brown, either a bookseller or printer, who is in custody, who said he delivered him a book, which he published, an Answer to a letter to a Bishop (which was writ by the Bishop of St. Asaph). In ye answer to it there are, it is said, very scurolous things on the Government; so, upon this, by the messenger of the press he was seized on this morning and carried before the Council, were he was so thoroughly bewitched as to own the having writ it, which after all I don't think he did, when, if he had not owned it, there was but one witness against him; but now he dexterously adds himself. Ire Losp. speaking of coming up, tho you seem not to be more inclined to it then business oblige you, may not be improper upon this account. I hope it may be no prejudice to ire health, because you say nothing of it nor my brothers and sisters. I beg my humble duty to my Lady and service to my Aunt. I am ire Losp. most obedient daughter, A. Nottingham.

June ye 28, . I was not capable, my Lord, ye last post of acquainting your Ldpps of ye ill news of Mr Hatton being sent to ye Tower by ye Privy Counsel, for high treason, for writing a book which he owned. He is now a close prisoner. I resolve to go to him next week, and I must be confined. I have endeavoured to a got leve to a gon out and in, but it will not be granted. I am in great hopes ire Ldpps will be in town before I go to ye Tower. He went a Thursday night, which prevented his writing to ire Ldpps. He sent down 2 books by ye carrier. Ye dicktionary, which ire Ldpps sent to know ye price, is seven and twenty shillings. I beg my humble servis to my Lady and my sister Hatton. I hope they will pardon me in not writing, for my sorrows are so great it makes me not able to pay my duty. My most humble servis to ire Ldpps, my Lady, my sister Hatton. I am ire Ldpps Most faithful, Humble served, E. Hatton. I hope ire Ldpps will pardon me, for I doe not know what I say, I am in such amaise.

July ye 3, . I received ire Ldpps kind letter, which at this present time I doe much want. I could wish I wase able to give ire Ldpps a true account of what Mr Hatton is acused of; but I am very ignorant, for I did not in ye least know of anything tell ye messenger came for him, and then I had not time to inquire of him, and I cannot larne of any person that have seen it what is in it, but most doe say there is nothing in that can tush his life. I trust in God tic true; but they have peech him of high treason, which makes a great sound. He is kept a very close prisoner, for wee cannot get leave that any person should be admitted, tho a warder is by. I have don all I can in ye world to get leave to go into ye Tower, tho I am willing to be a close prisenor; for he hath noebody with him, and, should he be sick, it may prove of a very ill consequence. As for getting him bailed, it is impossible to have it don, for there is no hopes of his coming out tell next term, and his close confinement I much fear will much prejudice his health. I beg of ire Ldpps to writ to ye President that he may have ye liberty of ye Tower, and that he may be aloud that sumtimes he may see his friends or those persons which he hath real business with concerning his one affairs. And also I humble beg ire Ldpps will be pleased to writ to some of ye Privy Counsel, that I may have order to go into ye Tower, for I will asure ire Ldpps I am under so much sorrow that tic impossibell to be expressed, or can I support myself, for I can declare I have slept not one hour in a night sense he hath ben there. I have another favour to desire of ire Ldpps, that you would be pleased to consider his condition, and that ye place is very chargeable, and no person that he doe owe but sixpence to but is pressing and rude, which makes me exposed deli to great inconveniences. I am ire Ldpps most faithful, humble servant, E. Hatton.

Thursday, ye 3 of July, My Lord has at this present so little time to himself, he hopes your Lordsp will pardon his not writing to you, but will not be failling to doe what lies in his power to serve him whom ire Losp. recommends to him, whose proceedings as been after his usual method, and would more have surprised had it been from anny other body but himself. We are all in twone full of what concerns the fleet, upon which account my Lord Torrington is very hardly spoke of, whither deservedly or no, I must have a better insight to sea fight then I have at this distance to, to venture to judge whither he deserves it or no; but won thing is certain, yt, after the engagement was begun, he let all lye upon the Dutch squadron and did not engage at all with the French fleet, which squadron had certainly been quite lost, but yt the Duke of Grafton, who in this expedition has got immortal fame, would fight, and won ship more came to there assistance. It pleased God to give yt success to there undertaking yt with twenty ships, which were the number of the Dutch and these two that came to there assistance, they made there party so good with the French fleet, which was of eighty two ships, yt but won Dutch ship was lost. There is eight disabled, but will in a little while be fitted up again; of them, a Dutch Vice Admiral and a Rear Admiral and two captains are killed; and of our, won Captain Botham and Captain Pomeroy. There is a report yt six ships of the French are disabled, and yt they are toing them towards some of there own ports, and yt the Plimouth squardon is gone after them. My Lord Stweard and my Lord Pembroke have been so brave to offer their service to the Queen, and are gone down to Dover. I suppose my Lord Pembroke will command his own Marine regiment, and my Lord Stuart will either be a volontier or have some command. It is past ten a clock. I am afraid the post will be gone. I am ire Losp. most obedient daughter, A. Nottingham.

column46: Shene, July 5th, . My Lord, I was yesterday in town, where I heard such melancholy accts of our fleet that I can't see wht in our time scarce can be hoped will redeem ye honour and the interest we have lost by the late action at sea, nor ye fatal consequence it may be like to be to ye nation and all Xtendom. The best acct of it yt I cd learn is, that our fleet did not fight, while the Duch were torn to pieces, who have lost several of their best men and ships, and yt we retreat toward ye Downs as fast as the wind (which is contrary) and ye tide will bring us, and yt ye French at great rate pursue us. My Lds Devonshire and Pembroke are sent to ye fleet to examine these matters, but with wht powers to mend ym I know not. Lt Torrington is most miserably reproached by ye mobile, and not yt I can find excused by any for his conduct; and ye letters he has sent doe but rather increase in lessen it. We are in huge expectation from Ireland, it being ye general opinion ye armies have fought ere this; but I must confess I doe not believe, for I think, if Kg James can possibly, he will avoid fighting, and you know it is not very easy, and in a country where there are such strong posts, to force an army to fight. I had almost forgot to tell you wht is reported and some suspect to be true, yt ye French have sent several galleys full of landsman, with a fleet of 20 men of war, into St. Georges Channel. I heard it said that ye parliament is like to be adjourned but for a fortnight, and in to meet and sit, there being a necessity for a supply, pour fair roler le monte ; yet I fancy, if you doe at this time press hard for ire guarrison, you may be more likely to get something for ym then in a better time. I am very sorry, my Lord, to find that ire pains have returned so ill on you, but I fancy yt wht you say does add to ye uneasiness will abate. My son I hope does mend. He recovers his appetite and strength, but he coughs no blood.

column46: Shene, July 30th, . My Lord, I assure you I had done yt matter some time since, but yt I waited for a fit pretence and opportunity to doe it, which I now took by my neighbour, Sr Capell; and I think her Matie was not dissatisfied with me in it. She was pleased to tell me, as I thought I wrote to ire Lp, that, being my buisnesse would not give me leave to attend it, I did very well to give it up to her hand; so she took it and put it in her pocket, I mean ye commission. I must needs own yt t'was very inconvenient to my present circumstance to quit or part with 5 or 600li a year; yet I thank God I find so much ease by it, that yet I doe not repent me and hope I never shall. But, if I had not quited, truly I found I cd not keep it but upon such terms as it were not worth ye having, to live, as long as this war last, almost constantly upon it; for so I found it was expected and yt I shd have bine commanded so to do, which, had I neglected, with have suspended me, as it did, or turned me quite out. The suspending I told ire Lp of was but upon a pretence taken, not given, and, to deal more freely with ire Lp, I could not fear ye mean applications I found with be required of me from ye noble peer, my Lt Marlboro, to keep myself in, and ye little affronts I recd every day from ye officers who commanded there, as to one they thought they might presume to deal with for not being in yt favour at Court to support me agst it. But there is another thing behind which weighed as much and more with me in all this, and that was, I began to find myself pressed to sign an address of renouncing my late master, which, however, I had sufficiently done in effect, would have bine so odious an ingratitude I despised any advantage to oblige me to, and, whoever they are that have put that a foot, I am confident have done their present Mates no service in. I don't hear yet who does succeed in ye govmt, but, if the King be returned, who I hear was expected on Tuesday at Chester, we shall soon know. My Lord, if it be not past ye season, I beg you will give me a side of venison, baked in 2 or 3 little pots. I wish your Lordps health.

Augt ye 24, . Last Tuesday, my Lord, I got an order to have ye freedom of ye Tower. I went immediait thither. I thank God I found him very well in health, and I did not return to ye Pell Mell tell this day, which I had not come home so sun but to meet ye Dtrs and sergeant about my son, which is in a very weak condition. Mr Hatton does asure me there was never anything offered in ye least to him or proposed sense his confinemt. He fears he shall not be bailed. He hopes he shall have ye freedom of seeing his friends, which as yet he hath not. If ire Ldpps could obtain that favour, it would be to his satisfaction. As for anything else, he believes it is to no purpose for ire Ldpps to give yrself ye trouble as yet to endeavour. He gives his most humble servis to ire Ldpps, my Lady. Sense I came to ye Tower her hath come to or 3 friends, but I suppose it will be forbid if any more should come, they hearing I had an order, which maid them conclude he had ye freedom of seeing his friends. If I did in ye least know that anything had been propose to Mr Hatton, I doe asure ire Ldpps I would let you know. My humble servis to my Lady and ire Ldpps. I am ire Ldpps most faithful, humble served, E. Hatton. My servis to my sister Hatton.

column37: gentry lower; Lieutenant Governor of Guernsey, Captain
column39: Correspondence of the Family of Hatton Being Chiefly Letters Addressed to Christopher First Viscount Hatton A.D. 1601-1704. Volume II. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden New Series 23. Camden Society. 1878.
column46: Novr 11, . I am very sorry, my dearest, yt ire son Robin continues so very ill. God grant he may receive benefit by the advice of ye new surgeon. But, my dearest, I fear my threats will prove more effectual then I designed; for I told thee in jest if thou did pass Sunday thou should be shut out, which is likely to prove true in earnest, for ye hungry head jailer here is so greedy of his pretended fee he grows every day more and more barbarous and vexatious. Had he been educated at Ambonia, he could not be more merciless. And finding yt no person will take notice of his extravagant usage of me, he is ye more encouraged thereto. Worthy Mr Ennis, who being turned out of his living here for not swearing and therefore not capacitated to exercise his ecclesiastic function in his own country, Scotland, is this week going to try whither he cannot more quietly live among ye heathens in America, and last Sunday in ye afternoon came to take leave of me, and brought with him Mr Sawyer, who came to renew yt 2d time I saw him ye promise he made me ye first time I ever did, which is to be bail for me. But on Monday morning came gingle-key, by his masters order, foaming at ye warder for letting any person come to me, and charged him he should let noebody come at me. Certainly I shall be either tried or bailed. If tried, it is a strange outlandish barbarity not practiced heretofore in England not to have ye advise of counsel to prepare for a defence, and, in order thereto, to advise with ym. I am certain, in ye Popish plot all ye prisoners had, some considerable time before their trial, ye freedom of having their friends and council come to them. If I be bailed, it is very reasonable I should endeavour to find out some persons who are willing to doe me yt kindness, and aged whom there can be no exception; and yt I find very difficult; and prithee, my dearest, doe you endeavour with you can to find out some, for, tho very probably I shall not have occasion for them, yet it would be very vexatious to want them should there be occasion. I am very much concerned my brother Hatton should for his health be forced out of town. Both for his sake and my own, I wish you could contrive some way to acquaint my brother with my distress and prevail with him to endeavour to get his son in law to stop ye mouth of ye hungry cur here, for I cannot doe it with a crust, it would be too costly. My cloak transformed in a coat is too thin for this cold place. Pray let ye lining of ye cloak be sent to ye taylor to interline ye coat. The buttons are as you ordered, and therefore you may be secure they please me, and I assure you they doe without any compliment; but, if they did not, I durst not find fault, which I know you will believe. A dieu, my dearest. If you come alone, you are welcome; but more, if with liberty of my seeing my friends. If that honest Scot, Mr. Ennis (whose integrity is a disgrace to most Englishmen of his coat), comes to bid you farewell, pray acknowledge his kindness to me, yrself, and ire son.

I would have waited on ire Ldshpps, but that I had not ye convenience of a coach. I am heartily sorry to here ye ill news of ire Ldpps ill health. I have received a letter from Mr Hatton to send to ire Ldpps. My Lord Lucus doth use Mr Hatton with great unkindness. A Sunday last one Mr Ennes came to take his leave, for he was going for Barbados, and brought with him Mr Sawyer of Kettering, a barrister of law, who offers himself to be bail. My Lord Lucus, being informed therewith, sent a reprimand to ye warder for letting any person go to him. After he hath petition for a trial, and 5 months close imprisonmet, to be deprived to advise with counsel is very hard and never was done before. I beg ire Ldpps, and so doe Mr H., that you would be pleased to move for more liberty. I suppose ire Ldpps hath herd how angry my Lt Lucus was for my Lt Salsbury coming to dine with Mr Hatton, tho my Lt first went to my Lt Lucus; he not being at home, sent to ye Deputy. He was not at home. He called Major Hally, and he staid with them tell my Lt went away. Yet his Ldpps was in a great raig, and then forbid any to come to Mr Hatton. I beg once more of ire Ldpps that he may not be yoused with this severity. Ye enclosed I desire ire Ldpps to return. Mr H. desires ire Ldpps to send to sound Mr and ye Solicitor, to know there intentions how they will proceed. Ire Ldpps was pleased to promise you would. He shall be in distress of bail. I hope ire Ldpps will be pleased to procure him sum, for now in a few days he will have ocation for them, for there names must be sent to Mr Arosmith, to see how he approves of them. Mr Hatton ordered me to writ to ire Ldpps yesterday, and this morning he hath writ to ire Ldpps. Perhaps he hath writ this to ire Ldpps; but I cannot tell whether he hath or not makes me give ire Ldpps this troubell. My very humble servis to my Lady, my sister Hatton, and pretty Miss. I am ire Ldpps most faithful servant, E. Hatton.

Ye 3d of March, . I am very glad to hear ire Losp. and all ye company got so well to Maidwell, which I was so forgetful not to think you were there but sent my letter to Kirby, which made it longer before it got to you. My Lt Finch has writ a letter to my sister Betty, which I hope she has received. Hear is a most dismal story of my Lt Salisberys two brothers who he sent into France. They were at St. Germains, and lay in a room together and quarrelled, tic not yet known for what, but rise out of bed and took there swords, and fought, tell they both fell dwone, which was heard in room under them. They that were there run up to there chamber door, which they found fastend, but, forcing it open, found them weltering in their blood and craling to ask one another pardon. Tic said there was little hopes that either could recover. Some letters say the eldest was already dead, tho won cannot say this is certain; there are so many letters that speak of it yt there relations are fearful it is too true. Sr Edward Villars is to be a Viscount, but wither English or no I cant tell. I beg the favour of ire Losp. to give my humble duty to my Lady. I am ire Losp. most obedient dutiful daughter, A. Nottingham.

My Lord, My being out of my bed 2 nights together with Mr Boyle, who's death I foretold the first day he complaind of an alteration, which was Tuesday; and that day I told my Lt Rochester and others of his friends and desired an other physician to be sent for, which was yt night; and at 10, as I told your Lp, I was sent for to be in the house all night, but did not let him know it, for fear of surprising him (he was up all Tuesday). Wednesday morn was much better, but exceeding low and faint; would rise in the afternoon, and at 5 we met and desired him to go to bed at 7. Dr Stockholm was to sit up; but at 10 or 11 he grew worse, so that my Lord Ranalough and Lady Thanet Dowager, etc., was sent for, and they sent for me. I was just hot in my bed, after something I had taken for my great cold; and, though I had not a grain of hope he would live till I came, yet, considering it was the last attempt I could make to serve won who for many years past had great affection for me and relied under God, as he often told me, upon my care, I was resolved to go to him. It was one a clock in the night; but he was dead before I cam. His lamp went out for want of oil; so did his sister's too. He was buried last night at St. Martin's, and lies by his sister. The Bishop of Salisbury preachd his funeral sermon, and gave a large and true character becoming so great a man as he was, and whose 2d in universal knowledge, etc., twill be hard to find. The Bishop said he had a conversation with him the better part of 29 years; but mine has been above 30 years, and, the last 10 or 12, not 4 days together from him, if in town. It would make me look vain to relate his affectionate expressions to me. He has been kept alive, by God's blessing, upon the dint of care several years, to a wonder. But I ask your Lordps pardon for being so long upon this subject. Seeing the subject will bear it, I hope you'll excuse it. I suppose your Lordp has heard of the barbarous murder of Dr Clinch. He lived in Browlow street in Holborn. Monday night last about 9 at night, 2 men came in a hacknie coach to call him to won not well; but he was not at home, and they said they'd come again. About 10 the same night they came to the end of the street, and sent the coachman for him. He, poor man, took his cloak and went to them into the coach; they bid the coachman drive to the Pie without Algate. But, as soon as they had him, they began their villainies; for his hat was found in the street near Barnards Inn, and we believe he was soon dead. And there, to blind the coachman, they enquired for a man there near Aldgate noebody knew. By this time the dead man began to be cold and stiffish, yt they was sure he was dead. When they cam back as far as Leaden Hall street, they called the coachman and gave him 3s 6d to buy 2 pullets for supper. The man got them quickly, and, when he cam back, there was only ye Dr dead and almost cold; the murderors gon. About 14 days since, 2 huffing men cam at night for me in a hack; but I was abroad. They came a 2d time and was angry I was not at home. Then my wife sent them word they had best get another Dr, (ther's enough) for she beleivd, if I did com home, I would not go with them, nor should not if she could help it; so they went away much out of humour. But, before this, I escaped an eminent danger of ye kind, I bless God, which has stuck by me ever since. But this of Dr Clinch is a terrible thing. It was reported in the city it was me, to the great concern of many of my friends; but my coach being in ye city yt morning gave them another acct, which was too true. My Falconberge cam to my house himself and several others. Since I writ this, we are informed those taken upon suspicion are the very persons yt murdered him; one Harison especially. Just now the Drs wife and the Vice-president of the College send to me to com in my gown to assist with him at the pall this Saturday night. I am not well, yet intend to go, to pay the last respect to him.

column46: London, Jan. ye 28th, . My good Lord, I acknowledge ye noble kind offer you make me of ire house at Maidwell with all the thanks in ye world, though I am not like to receive the benefit by it you intended me; for I believe I shall have some business will oblige me to stay here some time after I leave Shene, which wont be till ye later end of Apple, and Hagley, I think, is much as it was in repair when you were at it; so yt, after my rate of living is like to be there, there will need little to do but furnish it, which I have but too much of. As to my pictures, I have a good many of Sr Peter Lilies, which I am told will not yield near wht they cost; and I doubt those of more esteem will not be very ready money, unless meetly undersold, at this time, because there are so many auctions, as the Duke of Norfolks and others, of ye best collections. But these are not all he has a mind to part with, for there is scarce anything talked of but his endeavouring to be divorced from his wife, and wht ye witnesses have sworn in ye Lords House abt her amours with Mr Germain. To morrow she is there to make her defence, which she must have a great deal of assurance to be able in person to do, as I hear she intends, and has bine once there already to give em a pretty good essay. She is not over bashful where her honour and innocence are at stake. I don't know if you have heard that Mr Germain is ye supposed bastard of ye Kg William's father, as is Monsr de Lawn another, who is ye Queens secretary. The Kg was all day at ye Lords house a Tuesday to hear ye evidence at ye Lords House; and it is sd ye Kg and Q. have expressed a great deal of warmth for ye Duke. But she has a strong party in ye House however, and yt of ye Court faction to support her. My Lt Nottingham is agst her. We have no news from abroad, and I believe ye ports are froze up. Some thing may be expected, when they are open from this hard frost. My Lt Churchill's disgrace has yet made no great change but in ye disposal of his places; nor has it had any consequence to his brs, but that one of ym who was cornet to ye troop is made 1st Lt.

column46: Shene, March 7th, . My Lord, I have yrs upon ire return from Maidwell, and am glad you have so good reason still to like ire purchase. In a letter I lately had from ire Lp, you said something by way of caution to my dealing with Mr Walton, which pray, my Lord, be a little more plain with me. Have you had any experience of his not dealing fairly with you? For I have bine advised and know not who to trust better in ye disposal of my pictures. Ye method I use with him: I send ym to a house close by him, for he has not room in his own, it is already so full, and there he cleans them and mends wht is worn or torn; and, after, I am to get a couple of painters who, together with himself, appraise ym; which appraisemt the 2 painters set their hands to ye list of; and then they will be exposed in an auction, but such as will be privately bought. And one I sold so here a Saturday, which was a half length of Antonio Mores drawing, for 30li. My ink is so bad I can scarce make it doe. Yt picture was cracked quite through and on ye side of ye face, which made it 10li ye worse. I have a very good copy, which you may remember to have seen upon my stairs, of Ch: ye 1st upon ye white horse. Ye original is Vandike and ye copy Remee. If I had ire hall or a good stair case to put it, I shd not be tempted to sell it. If you know anybody it will fit, pray tell em of it; 50li will be ye lowest price of it.

column46: Shene, May 10th, . I have ire Lps of ye 7th. I went to town yesterday abt some buisnesse, else I had not gon out of my cell; for I am, my Lt, of ire advise in such times. It is best to keep close, yet not lye hid, as I almost think some do that they may be looked after, and who else with not. However it is, it is a very jealous time, but tic wht I wonder at I confess yt people of such different principles, and one with think interests, should be jumbled together under ye same prejudice as papists, Ferguson, and they say Oats too; and yt those noblemen and great officers in ye army as stuck by Kg James shd now join to consult and engage their lives and fortunes with ye Lt Malborough and other officers of ye army, who once so traitorously deserted him, of which there are sd to be a great many of them who are already secured, and warrants out for others; ye Bps of Rochester who is confined to his house with a messenger, Bath and Wells sent for. My Lt Feversham was sent for and told yt, by reason of ye great obligations he had recd from Kg James, ye govmt cd not be satisfied with his conduct, unless he with retire into Holland till ye storm was over. I hear his answer was yt he had given no ground to give ye govmt any real ombrage; yt he had much buisnesse here, both of ye Queens his Mrs and his own; and yt he resolved not to banish himself, but claimed his right of a peer and subject. My Lt Fanshaw brought his habeas corpus yesterday and had it; but, when he came to ye Hall, the judge told him he was charged with high treason and he cd not be bailed, so went back to ye Tower. I heard yesterday my Lt Exeter is sent for in custody. I have but one little horse, but if I had 2, and I dare not buy one for fear of being thought to do so for wht I little think of, I with go near to be with you for a few days at Kirby, and so slip down to Hagley, to put matters a little to rights there before I remove with my little family, which I design to do as soon as we can dispose of wht we have yet left here. But I have some doubt, if I were there now, I might be more unquiet in I am here. Our fleets and ye Duch are joined, and a great fleet it is; and probably, if the French will venture it, there may be a battle in few days. It is a strong east wind to keep ym back and to carry us on their coast. I heard ye Kg will be here in a few days. I wish ire Lp health and ye nation peace and ye protestant religion. I heard Lds Macklesfield and Mountague refused to sign Lt Mallbo: warrant for his commitment. He is sd to be kept close prisoner, but his lady has got leave to be locked up with him, tho it's sd he sent to her not to ask it, but to stay with the Psse and take her fortune. Her Higss has but a melancholy court at Zion.

Sept. 8, . My Lord, I cannot be satisfied but to send this to enquire how your Lordp and your family does, and how Mr Hatton is since my last to your Lordp yt I writ in answer to your Lordps concerning his illness, and to enquire if you have felt anything of a frightful earthquake we have had here this Thursday, about 2 a clock. I had been out of town, just come home; and, as I was at dinour in my dining room (one pair of stairs), on a sudden the table and room shook, put us all into a strange confusion. My wife said: "Mr King, wts this?" Her woman yt was at diner with us started from the table, as pale as death, and cried: "Oh! An earthquake!" I rise from the table too in the universal motion I saw and felt; it lasted about a minute and half. Whilst we was talking of it, a neighbour cam in and asked if we perceivd anything of an earthquake, for a great many gentlemen came running into the coffee house, pale and frighted, out of their houses, and the women and children in great numbers cam running out of their houses too into the street in great amazement; and it's the whole talk now all the town over; much more frightful than wht we felt. Some say the Exchange in Cornhill was heard to crack; and the people cam running down from thence, for fear it should fall. I have been since at Westminster where was the same alarm; and a message from Kensington about the same thing there. You'll here more of with is past. I pray God we may have no 2d part of it. But all pray God to keep off the judgments we have deserved. This is a serious thing, and so thought of by your Lordps faithful humble servant, Edm. King.

column37: gentry lower; Lieutenant Governor of Guernsey, Captain

column46: September 10, . We had here, my Lt, last Thursday, at 55 minutes past 2 of ye clock in ye afternoon, an earth-quake, ye effects of which were more or less felt, not only over all London and Westminster but, it is reported, as far as Canterbury and Cambridge. I hope ire Lop wase free from it at Kirby. I wase at home; but none in my little house were sensible of it, which occasioned my not mentioning it to your Lppe. In all places those who were highest were most sensible of it. A person of very great truth and sincerity assured me his books, which were on shelves in his chamber, were flung down. Mr Lownds in ye Pell-Mell, a watch maker and very honest man, did aver to me yt all his clocks did so shake he thought they would have fallen down. In several places all ye people ran into ye streets out of their houses in great distraction, and in many places ye corner houses in ye streets were separated from ye adjacent houses. Last Thursday Admiral Russell came to town, but very privately, to avoid ye triumphal reception he much feared would have been made for him, and for ye like reason chose to come by Hampton rather then Portsmouth. But I doe not hear of any triumphant arches which were making for him, neither for routing 44 French ships with 90 sail, nor for saving ye fleet by disobeying his orders by refusing to comply with ym, which his friends ye commonwealth men say wase ye most meritorious and deserved better to have a marble statue erected for him then his first, tho upon yt account his relations had agreed for one. But it's thought his humility will not let him comply with their desires; for he is so humble he declares he will resign up all his public employments, and not yield, as he did this last summer, to any pressing importunity to take any public employment upon him, till he can better doe service for ye good of ye commons of England then he finds in this juncture of afaires he can. The next week ye Lt Brudnells daughter is to be married to my Lt Newborough. The act of parlt for staving French wines is expired, and several privateers are gone out in hopes of meeting with some ne'er ye coasts of Bordeaux. Captne Cotton writes to me very pressingly to move ire Lop to endeavour to obtain for him a ship to cruise in this winter, which if he can obtain he engages to furnish ire Lop with some tunns of French wines. Those are his words, and I verily believe he doth not doubt but to be enabled to perform his promise. I am Ire Lopps very humble servant, C. Hatton.

June 27, . My Lord, I never write news, because I know your Lordp always has it from better hands. But we are all in great pain about the Turkey fleet still, and the more because the Tholoon fleet is joined Destre. But I shall not forget a story my Lt Cuts told me, 3 days ago, of the Duke of Brandenburg just going to fight against 60 thousand with 50 thousand, and all just ready, a great officer comes in mighty haste, told him he feared it impossible to succeed in such a place, and asked with he should doe. His answer was, in as great haste: "Go on, go on; you must always leave something for God Almighty to doe." So they went on, and killed 10 thousand upon the place and routed the whole army. I am sure we have a great deal for God Almighty to doe for us. At this rate I wish your Lordsp will not fear letters from, My Lord, Your Lordps most humble and faithful servant, Edm. King.

column46: Feb. 6, . My Lord, We have little news, only yt last Sunday morning ye Lord Mordant had intimation by mine Here Benting that he wase dismissed from all his commands and public employments. The common discourse is yt his disgrace proceeded from his bringing in ye bill for a triennial parliament. This day is observed in our quarters with illuminations and other rejoicings, suitable to ye solemnity thereof. The Princess Anne her son came to Berkeley House with a guard of young youths about 10 or 12 years of age, all armed and clothed alike, marching rank and file with their captain, lt, and ensign, and ye insignia belli , which how ne'er it approaches to high treason, not being commissionated by ye King, ye judges (if they please) may determine. I am Ire Lopps very humble servant, C. Hatton.

column46: April 10, . My Lord, All our neighbourhood hereabouts are in great lamentation for ye death of Wilson, by some called Beau Wilson, by others Wonder Wilson, who wase yesterday morning killed in a duel by one Laws, a Scotsmen. Mr Wilson, when he came last out of ye country, brought up his sister with him and took lodgings for her in Berkley street, where lodged a gentlewoman who pretended to great devotion and much frequented ye churches, and thereby recommended herself to Mis Wilson, who took notice to her brother how happy she was to be lodged in ye same house with so religious a person; of which Mr Wilson making mention to some of his acquaintance, they informed him yt ye pretended devot wase a wench kept by one Laws, which as soon as Mr Wilson knew, he presently removed his sister to her aunts house, ye Lady Ash at Twitnam; and publicly taking notice of ye occasion, Laws, instigated by his wench, came last Saturday night and challenged Wilson, who, having long lain under ye imputation of being a coward, desired one of his acquaintance to be his second, declaring yt, to save his reputation, he must and would fight. And, accordingly, yesterday morning he took a hackney coach and met about 11 of ye clock in ye morning with Laws in Southampton Square. And it is generally reported yt Laws gave Wilson his mortal wound before he had drawn his sword; and ye wound which wase in his breast had so large an orifice yt many think it wase made with a bayonett. Wilson instantly dropped down dead, and Laws, who was making his escape in a hackney coach, was pursued by ye boys who were playing in ye Square and seized, and is now in Newgate. It is reported yt ye morning before he fought he made his will, and just as he was going to fight he took out of his pocket about 50 guineas and gave ym to his friend with him; and if he was killed he told him he should keep ym as legacy withal, giving him ye key of his escritoire; and engaged him to promise him, if he then dyed, to take out all ye papers he should find, in ye presence of his brother, in a drawer he described to him, and without looking into ym burn ym. Mr Wilson lived very generously and payed very punctually all personns he had any dealing with, and is generally very well spoken of and much lamented. But how he was enabled to live at such a rate as he did is as great a mystery as ever. The Lord Newbury is dead and left his lady with child, and hath given all his estate to her. His brother who killed Hayward dyed in Nougat. The enclosed will give you all ye public news I hear. My wife and self give our most humble service to Lady Hatton and all at Kirby; and we both are ire Loppes very humble servants. C. Hatton.

column46: Augt 2, . There happened, my Lt, lately a difference betwixt my wives son at Oxford and his tutor, to accommodate which I was obliged to go to Oxford, where ye Vice Chancellor and ye Master of University College did with all due respect mention ire Lop. They are printing catalogues of all ye manuscripts in all ye public and all ye private libraries in England, and if you please to send them a catalogue of ire mssts they will own it as a favour. They are prosecuting very earnestly ye finishing and publication of Dr Morisons Herbal, and beautifying their physic garden. Here is at Vesprit's garden an aloes in flower, which is much admired. I am glad ire Lop likes ye Heleborus Albus Floreatrorubeate . You laughed at me when I wase at Kirby for liking it. We have little news stirring, only that ye French privateers have in St George's channel taken ye Scarborough frigate, ye Irish paquet boat, and 12 ships coming from Virginia, Barbados and Jamaica full laden. I am Ire Lopps very humble servant, C. Hatton.

column46: October 13, . My Lord, Here are some narcissus of Japan come, but ye flowers are all quite whithred, and therefore I desire ire orders whither I shall send them down to Kirby. They came but yesterday morning. We have little news stirring. There is much discourse about ye trials of ye prisoners of state, who were lately brought up out of Lancashire and Cheshire and returned back again there to be tried. They were sent down in great parade, the gentleman porter and jailer of ye Tower attending them, and two wardours on each prisoner. The old decrepit Lord Mollineux, who 86 years of age and very infirm, is, with ye rest of ye Roman Catholics, to be tried at Manchester, in Lancashire. Sr Thomas Stanley and Mr Legh of Lime, our kinsman, are to be tried at Chester. The chief evidence aged them is one Lunt, who was coachman to my Lt Carrington, and, ye last session a bill of felony for having two wives being found aged him, he was not long since by a warrant from ye Lord Mayor taken up, but bailed out, Iron Smith and one Culliford entering into a recognisance of a hundred pounds each for his appearance at ye Old Bailey ye first day of this present session. But he never appeared. His recognisance is forfeited, and a bench warrant granted to seize him wherever found. But, he being now on their Mates service, it is to be presumed no person will be so audacious as to execute ye warrant on him, either in Cheshire or Lancashire, whither he is gone to give evidence aged ye state prisoners, especially when it is known yt very lately ne'er twenty personns, who talking of his having two wives and mentioning some other such like transgressions of his, were taken up by messengers upon warrants for conspiring aged ye lives and reputation of their Mates evidencers. A most wicked and horrid conspiracy aged ye personns of such note and deserved fame. God Almighty defend us aged all traitors. I am Ire Lopps very humble servant, C. Hatton.

column37: gentry lower; Lieutenant Governor of Guernsey, Captain

column46: Jan. 10, . I am much concerned, my Lord, to hear ye pain in ire arm continues. I hope, when ye sharpe weather alters, ire pain will abate. I cannot fully inform you of with sort of ye papers are which will be published in ye 2d vol of Ab. Lauds vindication; but I will endeavour by my next to doe it, and then send you ye prices of ye books you enquire after. The just detestation of ye barbarous proceedings aged yt great and good man must occasion an abhorrence of all parallel procedures. It was to have been wished ye Abps character of K. Char. ye 1st, p. 178, had not been too true, but it must be confessed he was good even to a vice in a prince. What may be a virtue in a private person may be a vice in a public magistrate. Meekness in some personns is a desirable and admirable quality; but old Ale's meekness brought down a heavy judgment from Heaven upon him. The sylogisme, p. 35, is not true in form, but ye sense in which alone it can be understood is very rational. The religion of ye papists is rebellion. But ye religion of ye papists is a branch of ye Christian religion. Therefore a branch of ye Christian is rebellion. Which I think is very false doctrine; for, tho both papists and protestants have turned religion into rebellion, they have thereby departed from Christian principles, which can never favour rebellion. It cannot be supposed ye Abp could say and mean ye religion of ye papists to be more then a branch of ye Christian religion. This day ye Princess Anne of Denmark had a guard sent to doe duty, as formerly, at her door; and it is exspected yt ye Lt Churchill and his lady will be advanced, as in favour, so to a higher degree. He was very zealous for passing ye Treason Bill; but last Tuesday he absented himself from ye committy, where it was carried by 7 votes that ye Treason Bill should not commence till 1698. My Lord Nottingam hath made himself very popular by arguing so zealously for Treason Bill. I am Ire Lopps very humble servant, C. Hatton.

column37: gentry lower; Lieutenant Governor of Guernsey, Captain

column46: Aug. 7, . I am very glad, my Lord, to hear ire eyes are better, and yt my Lady Hatton and all at Kirby are well. I have been very much indisposed, either continually tormented with gripes or, when yt humour is stopped, with an intolerable headache. I was this afternoon to see ye few best plants yet remaining of ye noble collection of plants at Hampton very well painted by one Bugdan, a Hungarian and excellent painter of fruits and flowers. I saw a cereus or sort of prickly Indian fig with a most wonderful flower, differing from all ye flowers I ever saw; the lilium superbum in flower, as also ye coral tree, and one of ye small sorts of aloes with a scarlet flower, and several very fine tulipps, painted from tulipps growing in my Lord Dovers garden at his house in ye country, for whom Bugdan hath painted several very large and curious pictures of flowers for my Lords house here in town. But having lately, with old Mr Evelyn, seen Montague House, I doe not think my Lord of Dovers pictures of flowers comparable to ye flower pictures in Montague House. Having given you an account of some pictures I have seen, I shall tell you of a very large rattle-snake I saw alive, lately brought over from Virginia. It is very curiously coloured and stripped. We looked on him till, by rattling his tail much louder then I could have imagined he could, he gave notice yt he was angry and ready to fly at us; to prevent which, ye lid of ye chest he was in was clapped down. Mr Evelyn is putting forth a book in folo of English medallions, in imitatation of ye Histoire Metallique du Holland. But he can hear of so few yt, instead of medailles with ye inscriptions and reverses, he is forced to make up his book with several discourses relating to yt subject. His book hath been long in ye press and is not yet ready to come out, ye medailles being not yet all engraven. If ire Lop hath any or could procure any relating to any eminent English person or any action done in England, if ire Lop would please either to send a design of ye meddail or lend ye meddail to be here designed, it should carefully be restored with thanks. Mr Evelyn desired me and all his acquaintances here in town to try with medailes they can procure to illustrate his work. I choose rather to entertain ire Lop with these things then public news which is very fabulous. I remember Johannes della Case in his book De Officiis sath: Impudence in courtesans is no fault, for it is absolutely necessary for their carrying on their trade, which he justly condemns. The like apology is ye best can be made for our public newsmongers. I am Ire Lopps very humble servant, C. Hatton.

column37: gentry lower; Lieutenant Governor of Guernsey, Captain

column46: September 2, . I have this day, my Lord, been at Hampton Court, with Dr Udall, to see all ye fine plants there, but, tho I saw several very curious ones, yet ye pleasure was much abated by ye regret for ye loss of a great many choice plants, which I saw when I was formerly there. But ye sight best pleased me was ye cartoons by Raphael, which are far beyond all ye paintings I ever saw. They are brought from ye Tower and hung up there, and are copying for my Lord Sunderland. I am invited to go, this day senight, to Dr Udalls at Enfeild, and, if ire Lop would be pleased to favour me with a peace of venison to present him with, it would be a very great favour, and I should not doubt to procure you, next spring, some choice plants from him. Of all ye hardy plants I saw at Hampton Court, I saw none I liked better then ye Swedish juniper they had from Dr Udall. I hope ire Lopps thrive with you. I am &c. C. Hatton

column37: gentry lower; Lieutenant Governor of Guernsey, Captain

column46: December 4, . My wife, my Lord, did last Thursday return her most humble thanks to ire Lop and my Lady Hatton for ire obliging present of excellent venison, and gave an account how she had disposed of it. To hers I now, my Lord, add mine, being prevented writing then by going to see ye fireworks, for which there had been so long and costly preparations. I was very desirous to see ym, but, not knowing whither conveniently to go, I had given over all thoughts of seeing them, and my curiosity was quite abated; but ye day they were to be I had 3 or 4 tickets sent me, and by my wives earnest persuasion I went; but my curiosity was as little satisfied as any person's there. It is generally reported ye expense for them amounted to 12000ll. There was in St James's Square a sort of triumphal arch built, but very ill designed, on ye top of which were 4 figures made of wood and painted, one at each corner, and, had there not been ye names of with they were designed for, no person could have guessed what they were meant for. Peace out of a cornucopeia flung out rockets of wild fire. Conduct had a death's head in one of her hands. Concord held in a dish a flaming heart; and Valour had by it a ravenous lyon. The whole was an emblem. There was a great unnecessary expense of treasure; several killed; a vast number of crackers; and all ended in smoke and stink. Sr Martin Beckman hath got ye curses of a great many, ye praises of noebody. There was only a vast number of chambers shot of, and a prodigious number of serpents and large rockets, the cases and sticks of which were so large that, when they fell down, killed assuredly 3 or 4 persons, hurt many more. One falling upon ye Lord Hallifaxes his house broke quite throe ye roof, but hurt noebody. Mr Portman and his lady were there. My Lord denied no person who asked leave to come into his house. Mr Secretary Trumball hath resigned ye seals, and is succeeded by Mr James Vernon. The House of Commons are adjourned till Tuesday. Upon a motion of ye Lord Mulgrave, ye lords have voted an address to his Sacred Majesty. I am ire Lopps very humble servant, C. Hatton.

column37: gentry lower; Lieutenant Governor of Guernsey, Captain

column46: Jan. 6, 1697/8. My Lord, Last Tuesday I acquainted you yt Whitehall was then in flames, which burnt till six of ye clock next morning, and by yt time had consumed or ruined all ye buildings except ye Banqueting House; ye row of buildings from thence eastward towards ye street; the Jewell-House and Scotland Yards; the Signet Office, and all ye buildings from thence in a direct line towards ye water; the butteries, sellers, kitchings, ye Comptrolers lodgins, ye chapel, guard chamber, ye King and Queens lodgings; all ye whole pile of buildings towards ye water side, from yt which was Mr Clement his lodgings to ye end of ye stone gallery; and from thence, all ye long gallery, ye Secretary's office, ye Treasury office, ye Council chamber, ye Queens chapel, are all burnt down. Only some few lodgings ne'er ye stone gallery, yt which was Bab Mays lodgings towards ye water side, and ye next lodgings to yt, and some part of lodgings which I was told was ye Lord Portlands, are left standing, but terribly schattered. The house in Scotland yard built by Sr Alexander Fraisier, and Mr Windham's next to it, are standing but much schattered. All ye rest of ye buildings in both Scotland Yards are not at al prejudiced. Next ye water side there are no buildings standing, except from Sr Stephen Fox his house to ye Lt Godolphins lodgings, inclusive, which are not prejudiced. The Lt Montague lodgings are burnt down, but his fine pictures and furniture saved. The fire broke out betwixt 3 and 4 of ye clock in a garret in ye lodgings, as some say, of Colonel Stanley, next to ye Lord Portland, occasioned by a Dutch serving maid laying a sack of charcoal so ne'er ye fire it all took fire, and ye servants hoped to quench it without any help from others, but it increased so violently it occasioned ye ruin of ye whole palace. All persons were intent to save their goods, and all ye gates were locked up to prevent ye mob coming in; and, when ye houses were blown up, most of which were blown up very high, ye timber and rafters lay bare, and there wanted hands to remove ym, so yt, instead of stopping ye fire, it helped to increase it. All ye buildings westward, joining to ye Banqueting House, by being blown up about six of ye clock on Wedensday morning, saved that which remains, as monument where the Blessed Martyr, Kg Charles ye First, was murdered by his rebellious subjects. God divert his just judgments! I am ire Lopps very humble servant, C. Hatton.

My Lord, I return my most humble thanks for ye honour of ire Lordps letter. I have not yet bin any were, but at shopes and a veseting; but I believe shall be on Monday at a ball at St. Jeames, where, as they tell me, there is a famose new danser to apere, which is to charm us all, but not make amends for ye loss of Mrs Ibbings who danced at Lincolns Inn Field and is lately dead. But as ye quality of ye Ladies that dance at Court is not to be compared with so mean a person as a player, so I am sure most of there indiferent dancing is not to be mentioned with her good. There is one Mr Colson I am sure my Lady has seen at diner with my Uncle is going to be married, which one would wonder at, there being nothing to be liked in him but his fin diamond ring. I beg humble duty to my Lady. I will write to her next post. I am, my Lord, Ire obedient daughter, A. E. H.

My Lord, I am so overjoyed when I hear from ire Lordsp, its not to be expressed. I desire you will beg pardon for me to my Lady for writing such a short letter to her, and tell her I was last night at St Jeames, and yt there was but a few dancers. Ye best were Lady Hartington, Lady Betty Candish, Mrs Lutteril, Mrs Godfery, and Lady Essex, and Mrs Roper who was ye new dancer. Indeed she did it very well, but had too much endeavoured to imitate Lady Hartingtons noding her head, which is only becoming to herself. Ye best of ye men was Lord Interim, Lord Anglese, and Lord Essex. But my Lord Interim has cut of his hear, and got one of ye new fassioned perewks, which have so much hear in them yt a good one cant cost les then 60 pound, and yt monstros bigness with his little face did not look so well. I hear Lady Banbery is dead, and ye Wardon of All Souls. Next week Lady Ann Churchil is to be married to Lord Spenser. My Aunt Portman desires you to write to my Aunt Mary, to by her a set of ye French baskets they use for a desert, and ye colour are to be white and gold and grean, and, when you get hers, Nevil desires a set too, and if you will take care to bay my Aunt Mary for them, and they'll bay you again. My Aunt says yt, if you will give me leave to learn to draw, Mrs Tollett shall teach me. I desire my duty to my Lady and service to all my friends at Kirby. I am, my Lord, Ire dutiful daughter, A. E. H.

column46: September 28, . I shall endeavour to procure you from Paris some acorns of ye Ilexs you desire. Mr Evelyn hath been with me, and tells me he hath a new book of sallating just finished at ye press, and will be published ye next week. He sets up for a great virtuoso in sallating. In his book he takes notice yt juice of oranges in salats is preferable in vinegar. But ye oranges must be cut with a silver knife, for a steel blade will give a tincture of steel to ye juice. Last Saturday ye Lt Ferrers came to town with his new lady, with a very great equipage. Mr Cooke and his lady carried her mother in their coach to Barnet to meet them, and they came directly to her mothers house in Dover Street, where they had a supper which is said to have cost 50 pound. The discourse thereof ever since serves to entertain ye gosseping neighbours, for at present we are here very barren of news. I am Ire Lopps very humble servant, C. Hatton.

I take it, my Lt, as very great honour yt you will trouble yrself to write to me, but when I consider how weak ire eyes are I had rather be without ye happynys of ire Ldsps letters then have you in ye lest hurt ire eyes. I was last night (with Lady Longuevil and Lady Arundel) at ye Princess's, and Lady Long: was so kind to offer to carry me to ye Oppera to day with her and Lady Portland; but I was so unfortunate as to be engaged to go to Lady Denbighs to see ye famous Mrs Binges dance, or else I should have bin glad to have waited on Lady Long:, tho I had seen it before and think it very silly. Mr Abel is to have a fine music meeting to morrow, and ye tickets are guineas a piece, which is a little to much for me to throw away; so I shall not be there, and I find so many yt can afford it better of my mind, yt I fancy, if he had had lower rates, he would have got more. They say here yt Mrs Reves is to have my Lord Leicesters second son, whom Lt Romney designs to make his heir. Tic to be hoped he will use her better then his Bro did her sister; for, as the town says, he beat her wthin a week after she was married, which I think should make this young lady afraid. I have so much buisness here yt I hope my Lady will excuse me till next post. I beg my duty to her, and I am, my Lt, Ire Ldsp most obedient and dutiful daughter, A. E. H.

column46: Feb. 6, 1699/1700. No body doth more detest than I doe printing books with fictitious cuts, such as are in Knocks his History of ye Island of Ceylon and many such other books. But yet I should be very well pleased to see Caesars Commentaries, illustrated (as they design at Oxford) with cuts well designed of all ye Roman military instruments, their habits, their manner of encamping, their warlike engines, their manner of sacrificing, and things of this nature, which may be much better described by cuts designed from Antiques than is possible to be done by words. And was it possible to have true designs rightly adapted to Vitruvius his architecture, I verily believe your Lop would prefer an edition of Vitruvius adorned with such cuts before ye commentaries of Philander, Leo Albertus, Perrault, or Huzout. Propose to any of our English booksellers proper and useful cuts to illustrate any author they are printing, they cannot be prevailed with to have them engraven. But, on ye contrary, give them any fictitious or fabulous design, they will be very ready to have them printed. They printed Wafers voyage with fictitious cuts very readily; but Dampier would have given them a true draught of Guam prows, which are ye swiftest vessels in ye world, but they would not engrave ym nor several other curious draughts which might have been useful. But they would not be prevailed upon to cause them to be engraven. If ire Lop desires any more mellonn seeds from Italy, I can furnish you with some which I have lately received. I saw a letter this day which came from Rome, which sath my Lady Salisbury is recovered, but my Lord of Exeter indisposed, but making a very fine equipage to appear with as soon as he is recovred. I am Ire Lopps very humble servant, C. Hatton.

column46: Hagley, 21 Sep. 1702. I think I have since seen what you tell me of Mr Metwin's letter. I think ye Portugal interest not much to be depended on either way, being obliged to follow ye success of the Spd and confederates; and yt of Cales will most concern them, except when it comes nearer em. I had a letter last post from Sr J. at Bath, of ye 12th, and, having made his court, he says he would return yt night to Laycock. He says he went to Bath from thence in ye stage coach, wherein were 3 women, 2 of which were set down at an inn in Cosham, which was but 2 miles from Laycock. One of em was, as much as she could, disguised, as with not let him alight to help her out of ye coach. He suspected something extraordinary, and by her books of devotion, which she left in ye coach and sent her footman for with other things, which he looked in and perceived her religion and confirmed him in his guess, it was my Lady Tirconnell in her way to Ireland; and he says Lady Malborogh went yt same day to see her and returned that night.
