column46: Lincoln's Inn, April 14, 1773 Dear Mr. Mason Don't imagine I should have neglected you so long, if I had had a word to say to you worth making the subject of a Letter. My health, since I wrote last, has been tolerable; but that is all I have to boast of; for the town has afforded me little or no amusement. I have long since lost my relish for what are called diversions , & have little left even for books , even if the dullness of the present times could supply me with any, that were readible. Yes, I beg your friend Sir Dalrymple's pardon: his appendix is really entertaining: And, if it were not for the petulant satyr on la te`te couronne`e , I might perhaps allow that the Epistle to Sir W. Chambers has its merits. As to the tragical outcry of A. Stuart on a good friend of mine, I must positively aver that it is very ill, as well as passionately written. To tell you the truth, the pleasantest part of my time this winter, has been spent among your Dowagers, to whom our good friend of did me the honour to introduce me. My chief objection to them is, that, as I find from their conversation, they spoil you terribly. Out of pure kindness to you, I do what I can to lessen you in their esteem; but, to say the truth, to small purpose. I even saw in the hands of one of them, the etching of your Head, in an elegant purple frame, sprinkled with bay leaves (of her own workmanship) and inscribed with this motto - As worthy of the Purple as the Bays . Think how a Churchman & Critic, like myself, must have been shocked with this adulation! But now, to be very serious. I believe, your advice about Thurcaston may be good: And yet, If I knew how to provide for poor Ball, I should not hesitate a moment about resigning it. It with. do no good to increase his salary, unless I could ensure it to him for life. ... I have been looking out for a house, but have not sped yet, & I think shall not, the price of houses in a situation, which. I like, being more than I ought to give. But enough of this project. Dr. Balguy has carried a town cold with him to Bath, & our friend the Bp is where he has been all the winter, at Gloucester. I am to go to him at the end of June, to attend him on his visitation - What I shall do with myself afterwards, I no more know, than how the Bishops will get out of the scrape, they have brought themselves into with the Dissenters. But what care you about Bishops, when you can get your purple better cheap from Mrs. Delaney! - As to your Whitsunday sermon, why did not you send it me, for my revisal. You had no opportunity, I warrant; as if I had not seen, &, to my shame, without remembering, & knowing again, the good & amiable countenance of your relative, & my quondam Host, Mrs Dodsworth. Adieu, my dear Sir! - though I should have taken my leave of you, before I had turned a new leaf, as, upon recollection, I now find that my loquacity will put you to the expense of four pence extraordinary, that is, eight pence more than twenty such sheets as this are worth. Who knows but this Letter may get in to some future collection of a Sir J. Dalrymple (for assuredly you will preserve it in your strong box at Aston) &, therefore to balk the curiosity of malignant readers, I will conclude it without the name of your assured friend & Servant.

column46: Aston July 19 1788 My dear Lord I have sent the Picture this day to Sheffield according to your Lordships directions & I hope it will be forwarded to Hartlebury from Birmingham safely. It may not be amiss to give you with it some Notices as Old Pig and his brother antiquarians call them of the Original. which. is painted down to the knees on a three-quarter Canvas. The right hand holds a letter superscribed To Joseph Add (the rest of the word is hid by the thumb) one of his Majestys Principle Secretaries of State. on the side is a table on which. are two volumes of Rymers Foedera. As the Picture belongs now to the family of the late Governor Verelst, who when living could give me no other account of it than that it had been long an heirloom, I suspect it to be painted by Cornelius Verelst, the son of Harman who was brother of Simon the famous Flower Painter whom Prior has complimented. Harman who was a Portrait Painter died 1700 & left a Son Cornelius of the same Profession (see Mr. Walpoles Catalogue vol. 3, p. 34) who I believe was the Governors Grandfather . Mr. Addison sat to Jervas for his picture in 1715 as appears from a joint Letter of Popes & Gays (see Warburtons Edition vol. 7. P. 307.) two years before he was made Secretary of State. This is one Reason why I do not think Jervas Painted the Picture in question. Another is that Jervas was a Scholar & would not have written principle . However this be, as Mr. Addison died in 1719 & was born in 1672, He must have been 45 or 46 when he sat for this Picture, and the Countenance of it agrees with that Age. I think that which. your Lordship has appears much older. so much for my notices. I must however set you right in one thing that the Copy was not painted by myself, but by a Friend of mine Mr. Holland who was of Peterhouse. I don't know whether you recollect him. I think it a very accurate Copy but you must hang it on a side light on acct of some small defect in the Canvas, which. a front light only renders Visible. I wish your Lordship may get as easily through the fatigues I find brewing for you, as you did through the Trial. For my Part I know not which. I should hold the more penible . Mrs. Abigail says in your favourite comedy "now the Coast is clear I may call in my Drummer". & so say I "that the Coast must be clear before your Lordship must call in Your very faithful & affectionate humble Servant W. Mason

column39: The Correspondence of Richard Hurd & William Mason And Letters of Richard Hurd to Thomas Gray. Intr. & notes by Ernest Harold Pearce. Ed. with notes by Leonard Whibley. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1932.
column46: York Nov. 26 1791 My Dear Lord, I don't write to your Lordship so often as I think of you, & wish to enquire after your health, because I know that answering Letters is troublesome to you. and although I send you at present a short letter of my own, in order to enclose a very long one, I shall not expect an answer relative to either, for a reason which. will hereafter appear in the course of my Epistle. First let me assure you that the Person who writ the Letter gave me the copy of it, without the least guess concerning the use I meant to make of it. I only told him I thought it was well written contained many right sentiments, & that I wished to communicate it to a friend. The writer is the Son of a Parochial Clergyman in this City, who died young, & left a wife & four or five children absolutely unprovided for. I remember (about 20 years ago) that I contributed a few guineas to a subscription here, which. proved ample enough to enable his Widow to open a linnen-drapers shop, where as occasion offered I bought my family linen. This Son was of a studious turn, & my friend Dr. Burgh took a good deal of pains in preparing him for admittance into Clare Hall, but where he did not stay long enough to become a graduate, probably on acct. of his finances. He has been four or five years in Priest's orders, has a small Curacy with two Churches near York, which. he expects to lose soon on the Death of his Rector who is very old & infirm. He has lately had the offer of a preachership in Scotland near Montrose, the profits of which are not by any means considerable & I believe depend on contribution. He had reason to believe from the Letter of Mr. R., who advised him to come to the Place by way of probation, that Socinianism and free thinking were very fashionable in that quarter, & the Letter, which. I saw, was a very scotch one & led to that Idea. All this told, your Lordship will have all the Data necessary previous to your Perusal of this his answer. His going into Scotland is still in suspense & he need not determine on the journey till next March. In the interim, I own I am wishing (so much has the Letter prejudiced me in his favour) that some good Curacy if not some small living might be procured him in England; and I fancy that your Lordship when you have red it may wish so too, &, if you wish, you may perhaps find opportunity to fulfil our joint wish. But observe me, my dear Lord! I make no personal request. I only throw the Letter, like a Lottery ticket into a wheel, where it may possibly turn up a small prize; or from a possibility you may transfer it into some other ecclesiastical Wheel, where small prizes may bear a greater proportion to blanks than in your own. What may procure him, as a single man, a mere maintenance is all I aspire at for him. In vindication of my own impartiality in attempting to do him service, I will add that he is a descendant of that rank Tory Bishop Watson in James the 2d's time, and the first things that brought him into my notice, were a couple of well written Letters about a year ago in the Gentleman's Magazine which. he had published in vindication of his ancestor's character against some person who had attacked it. My Whigism was not strong enough to refuse giving him credit for the attempt. I remember Mr. Pope in one of his Letters to Dean Swift solicits him to subscribe to Old Sam Westley's comment on Job because he was a staunch Tory, & I quote his authority for my example in the present case for troubling your Lordship with a Letter, which. has run out to a much greater Length than I intended, when I sat down to write it. I am now in the first Month of a second residence which. I have had resolution to take with the hope that next summer (if not for the whole of my Life) I may have more time to visit my friends, and amongst these to visit your Lordship at Hartlebury. I am with my kind Compliments to your Nephew (who I could wish would give me a single line with regard to your Lordship's health) My Dear Lord Your very sincere & devoted Servant W. Mason

column39: The Correspondence of Richard Hurd & William Mason And Letters of Richard Hurd to Thomas Gray. Intr. & notes by Ernest Harold Pearce. Ed. with notes by Leonard Whibley. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1932.
column46: Dear Mr. Mason My nephew encloses to you some seeds of our oriental plant (whether rightly named by my Gardiner, I cannot say) & I take the opportunity to write one word to you. You will see that what you said to me, when you was here, had it's proper weight with me, when I tell you that I have sent the Bp's Life to the press. Only so many copies will be worked off as will satisfy the demands of the Purchasers of the 4th. edition, which. I think are not more than 200. So bounded is my ambition both for my friend, & for myself! I have lately amused myself with reading again your agreeable life of Mr. Gray. His Letters paint his character to the life. If he had been more at ease in his circumstances, & a little higher in rank, he would have been, not more estimable, but more happy. It will always give me a pleasure to hear from you, though I write but few, & short Letters myself. With all affection, Dear Sir Your faithful humble servant R. Worcester

column39: The Correspondence of Richard Hurd & William Mason And Letters of Richard Hurd to Thomas Gray. Intr. & notes by Ernest Harold Pearce. Ed. with notes by Leonard Whibley. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1932.
column46: Aston March 26 1795 My dear Lord, It was but four days ago, that I recd. your preliminary Discourse; for wishing to receive it safer than by common conveyance, I desired a Gentleman in this neighbourhood to bring it down from Mr. Stonhewer, who had before procured it for me from Robson the bookseller, & this Gentleman instead of staying in London a week did not return of three: otherwise I should have written to your Lordship sooner, as I had promised. I have red it, according to Bp Horsley's, but not your Orthography, with much care, & yet to me, whatever it may have to your Lordship, It has no faults, or I no faults can spy. I mean with respect to style, manner, and all that relates to the Bps own character; with respect to the Character of others incidentally drawn I also agree with you more than the present race of Readers will: & I admire evry part of the work, in which. you have shown the least degree of Prudence, & consequently the highest degree of downright declaration of your own Sentiments. This became the Biographer of Warburton, & in this you have answered my Expectation to the full. Your Lordship knows I always differd with you with respect to a favourite Hypothesis of yours, that Genius has a precise time for coming to its acme , or at least decreases sooner than the corporeal faculties, & this, I know, you imputed long ago to our excellent friend & have now publicly avowed it. For my own part, I think his unfinished ninth book is an instance to the contrary; for there is more of original, I will not say uncontrovertible, thinking in that Book than in almost any thing he has written, & expressed with as much force. The most paradoxical part of it, respecting the fall, is surely ingenious in the highest degree. But that it is more than ingenious I say not. However such original thought could not have entered into any Man's brain, whose imagination & Fancy had been by Time impaired. I know your Lordship & I shall never agree on this point, yet as I have been so long in the habit of speaking my mind to you as well (to my own detriment perhaps) as to all the world, I trust you will forgive me. I have done so lately to a very learned Chaplain of my Lord of Durham's, a Mr. Burgess, who sent me a private printed copy of the Epistola ad Pisones, every sentence of which was most licentiously transposed, because, Forsooth!, he & his brother Chaplain had agreed that "in its first form it was more immethodical than the Epistolary style permitted". But I gave him a Rowland for his Oliver, as our good Bishop would have said & done, & hope on this acct to be set down as a true Pupil of the Warburtonian School by the Prelate himself. But to return to a better subject. I am heartily rejoiced that your Lordship has given this finish to an Edition, which. would have been imperfect without it, & that you have finished it in a way, which., when Prejudice has had its day, will be as honourable to your own memory as that of our illustrious friend. Believe me to be with compliments to your Nephew and with the sincerest Respects to yourself My dear Lord, Your very affectionate Served. W Mason I have a great mind to fill up the remainder of this Paper with a Septuagenarian-Petrarchian Sonnett, which. I wrote last month on my Birthday, though I know you will condemn it, because it was written full thirty years after a Poet should have left off writing.

column39: The Correspondence of Richard Hurd & William Mason And Letters of Richard Hurd to Thomas Gray. Intr. & notes by Ernest Harold Pearce. Ed. with notes by Leonard Whibley. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1932.
column46: My dear Sir Your Letter of the 26th. past, crossed one of mine to you - I cannot but be much pleased with your approbation of the Life , because I know you always tell me your real sentiments. I have reason to believe that the characters of Sicker & Lowth are not relished by your friend the Bp. of London, and by the family, or schools rather, of W. of Wickham. Nor could anything else be expected from either quarter. Your account of the Durham critics is pleasant enough. Who is this Sturges ? He must be a poor creature to have recourse to such licentious transpositions for the vindication of his author. His patron, I believe, means well; but so much vanity is never attended by true judgment. I rejoice to hear that you have no complaints to make of old age. To me, it's depredations are very sensible. As to the general question, I perceive, we are not likely to agree. But in the particular case of the ixth. book, we differ less than you imagine. The matter of that book is, as you observe, as original & ingenious, as anything he ever wrote. But then you are to reflect, that the matter had been laid in and digested, in his better days. The composition , though of wonderful merit, as I observe, all circumstances considered, is yet inferior to that of the other books; such notes & passages only excepted as he had written long before. On the whole, there are exceptions to the general Rule, but it holds good for the most part. At least, I think so. But now for the Septuagenarian Sonnet. I like it extremely well, both sentiment & expression. The only criticisms I have to make upon it, are 1. that reign in v. 8 does not rhyme well with men . 2 That silent lay, That musing gratitude v. 11 & 12. The second that , should be which . 3. I have fancied that in the last line And praise with more than tongue - might be expressed more happily. Take notice, I do not forbid your writing a sonnet, now & then, or any short poem. But a long work of invention, another Georges, for instance, or dramatic poem, I shall not allow you to undertake at 70. This deanery yet hangs. I know not why unless these stirs in Ireland have occasioned any delay. Dr. Evans' dependence, if he thinks of it at all, can only be on the Duke of Portland. With my nephew's best respects, & my fervent wishes that you may live to write many more birth-day Sonnets, I am ever, Dear Sir, Your affectionate humble servant R. Worcester

My dear Lord, I have been most shamefully remiss in not writing to you of so many months, but the truth is I have for many months been much indisposed with indigestion, flatulence, & nervous feelings which. have depressed my spirits extremely, so that I have written no Letters except on immediate business. I have however lately began with an infusion of Quasi, a strong bitter, which. from the good effect I have already experienced seems to promise, under providence, a cure of my complaint. I believe I promised your Lordship a present of my slight Musical Essays, & that afterwards, when I had resolved on making no present on acct of my numerous acquaintance, I forgot to apologize for having withdrawn my Promise. So that probably you have never seen them. If so there is little harm done, for by what I find they are mighty likely to pass through the world unnoticed. I have been two months residing in this dullest of all dull places, & have lost the comfort of the late uncommonly fine Autumn, with nothing to do (as the ceiling of our Cathedral is stuccoing) but to chant the second Service on a Sunday; The want of a proper substitute obliges me to this. Your Lordship disliked the last line of my Sonnet. Pray substitute this in its place - shall Faith convey And Hope the Cherub of unwearied Wing. By which. I mean to express, in the Sonnet style, what Pope has in the Didactic Hope travels throe nor quits us when we die. This Letter, short as it is, is the longest I have written of some time for in a morning my hand has been hardly able to direct a pen tho now much better. It is written merely to hope for a line from your good Nephew (for I feel as if I was unworthy to receive one from yourself) to know si valeas that I may say from my heart Been est in hope that I may finish the Sentence in my next Letter, from My Dear Lord Yours truly and affectionately W. Mason

column39: The Correspondence of Richard Hurd & William Mason And Letters of Richard Hurd to Thomas Gray. Intr. & notes by Ernest Harold Pearce. Ed. with notes by Leonard Whibley. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1932.
column46: Aston Jan. 25 1796 My dear Lord, I am conscious that I have deferred answering your Lordship's last very obliging Letter much longer than I ought to have done, but instead of making apologies, which. are always tedious both to the writer & the reader, I shall only say, what I trust you will candidly admit, - better late than never. Your defence of Musical Creeds is ingenious, but it rather comes ill from a Clerk of his Majesty's Closet, & which. I should not admit even from a Dean of his Chapel. the Truth is, that the Apostle's Creed, I believe, never was set to Music, tho the Nicene has, & is so performed in many Cathedrals, but not in the Chapel of the supreme head of the Church of England. When I had the honour to be a Chaplain, I noted this & approvd it, having always found that the Harmonical Music it was set to rendered it absolutely unintelligible; on this acct, when I was well with the Dean of York & a kind of Prime Minister to him, I persuaded him, quoting my regal Authority for it, to have it simply red & instead of two unmeaning Voluntaries a fine Sanctus of Dr. Boyce's performed going & coming from the communion Table, for which. also I had the same Authority: and so in our Minster it continues still to be. But indeed, my good Lord, you seem to carry your cautious & temperate Ideas of reform almost as far as your Old Brother Beveridge, who writ a tract, which. I once saw, against Tate & Brady's new version of the Psalms, because it was too refined & Poetical, & most manfully and Episcopally & Orthodoxly defended Old Thomas Sternhold. I remember, when the Nicene Creed was sung at York, It was usual for the Dean or Officiating Residentiary to chant audibly "I believe in one God" - & then the Organ & Choir took up in their Counterpoint & Canon the rest of it. On which. some wag, who I suppose, suspected the Chanter to be a Socinian, said "& I fancy you believe no more" & if the said Officiating Prebend, as I think he was, was a relation of Archbishop Herring's he perhaps made a good guess. So much then for the subject of Musical Credos , for that is the musical term. A very excellent Woman with whom I had long been acquainted died last Month, after suffering more than fourteen years in a peculiar species of Atrophy attended with much pain & an entire loss of strength in evry limb, but retained her Memory & intellects, which. were great, even to the last. I had promised her many years ago to write her Epitaph, which. I have lately done, though from a much earlier Idea, & your Lordship will oblige me much if you will give me your Critique upon it, as I wish to make it as perfect as I am able. As besides her moral & truly Christian Character, she was eminent in copying Pictures with her needle, this Talent, which. was at the time almost new and singular, required to be noticed. Therefore I thought it necessary to borrow aid from Scripture & the design of the Monument, which. is of the kind they call Mural, is to be an antique female figure working on a frame, & an Easel before her with an original Canvas on a painter's Easel under this Alto Releivo on the front of a Cinerary Vase the following inscription on a plain marble tablet. Every body that knew her will say nothing here is exaggerated, Particularly her uncommon soundness of Judgment, which. was of the masculine cast. I wish much to have your Lordship's early opinion of these lines, because I know not how soon I may be called upon for them. My friend Dixon has left me for Buxton by the advice of a physician in this neighbourhood, in order to fix a flying Gout, which. has of late attacked his Bowels. I hope to see him again on his return, & I hope with improvd Health. for myself, God be thanked, I never was better, I went through a course of Quasi for six weeks, which. I was ordered to repeat after a month, The interval I filled up with a daily pint of Tar Water, and am now in my second Course of Quasi, tho hardly necessary. I wish Dr. Johnson, who I find has edited his ganglions afresh, may put your Lordship in the same regimen, & this the rather because Quasi is incapable of Adulteration. Whereas I am told by the Faculty that Bark is now seldom to be met with genuine. I enclose a line to my good friend your Nephew on a very different subject concerning which. I doubt not he will give me his best advice & assistance. Hoping that this wonderfully mild, tho somewhat boisterous, Winter, if the two terms be not incongruous, has agreed with you. I conclude with perfect respect Your Lordships truly affectionate, W. Mason

column39: The Correspondence of Richard Hurd & William Mason And Letters of Richard Hurd to Thomas Gray. Intr. & notes by Ernest Harold Pearce. Ed. with notes by Leonard Whibley. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1932.
column46: Aston July 9th. 96 My dear Lord, I am sorry the proof of my R. C. came to your Lordship so inopportunely but am therefore the more obliged to you for examining it & transmitting it to me again so speedily. After having recd. your imprimatur , I employed a morning in rectifying most of the Passages you had so justly objected to, some lines seemed to me not to have appeared clear to you from false punctuation only, others from perhaps your not knowing to what I precisely alluded therefore these latter I suffered to remain. I then sent my Alterations to York and ordered my Printer (who I can safely confide in) to take off a dozen copies, very few of which. I shall at present communicate to any person besides your Lordship to whom I now send one under a separate cover. The notes many of which. are now written are not merely textual, nor are they intended to load the page. But (should ever the Poem be made public juris ) are illustrative & to be placed at the End. Notes of this kind I think will be useful if not even absolutely necessary to such Readers as I have said I write for, and as I shall treat certain Socinian arguments in them as detected Falsehoods I shall venture to make them a butt for Wit ; some of Lindsey's particularly, who has much offended me by his dull pertness respecting your Lordship in a preface which. he lately writ to usher in some trash of Priestley's imported from America, & which. I take for granted you never saw. I will not be hasty in expecting a further Critique from you, tho I shall wish to know that the Packet is rec'd safe. For as I mean to make you a visit this summer (when Summer is actually set in, which. with us is not yet the case) I shall wait for your further strictures viva` voce . Believe me My Dear Lord, Yours most respectfully & cordially W. Mason My kind Compts. to your Nephew. I hear poor Mainwaring is, or has been dangerously ill at Stratton.

My dear Lord You will find by the next page that I go scribbling on to the end of the Chapter. But you must forgive me, it is my principal Amusement. The 28th. Chapter of Job appears to me to be quite a purpureus pannus totally unconnected with all of Job's final defence, which. either went before or follows it. Yet, when considered in this detatchd Light, it also appears to be a Complete Ode, & of the very first & most perfect Lyrical form when somewhat cleared from its oriental redundancies, which. in my Version is here done. Our Bible Version of this Chapter is peculiarly obscure &, I suspect, Faulty. Yet if, according to a conjecture of Albert Schultens, we insert in the beginning of the third verse Man for he , much of the obscurity will be removed. Schultens however had no idea that it was a Lyrical composition, for he only calls it Peroratio magnifica pro Coronide imposita universes disputationibus , which. it is so far from being, that Job continues his speech in the very next Chapter, taking up a quite different subject, a narrative of his former state of prosperity. But all this is of that species of Lauda Been Criticism, which. men, conversant with words more than sentiments, must necessarily make, & if they are able to express themselves in what is called Classical Latinity they will obtain that degree of celebrity, which. the Lecturer of Job got, who, I dare say, never knew the merit of this peculiar Chapter which., had he known it, & in consequence versified it in Alcaics or otherwise, He would have done more than he has done by his Versions of what all the world before knew were either pathetic or sublime. What I wish from your Lordship is merely this, that you would note what you think requires emendation in this Copy, provided you think it deserves such pains, & if you do, I mean to print it in a private way, with a short address to you, explanatory, like this Letter of the Idea I have conceived of the Original. I shall put down a few references at the Bottom of this page to Lessen your trouble. My third Volume I find is published, & the Booksellers to whom the 500 Copies were sold, have put a Lying Advertisement to it, viz. that the Book consists wholly of things not before published. But the Best of Booksellers (& I believe they who have it are the best) are what our good Bp W. would have called Scounderels . I have not yet heard a syllable about it from any of my Correspondents. I wish your Lordship & Nephew all good and seasonable wishes, hoping that your health has not been affected by the hitherto severe winter. Believe me to be with all sincerity Your Lordship's truly respectful Served. W. Mason

column39: The Correspondence of Richard Hurd & William Mason And Letters of Richard Hurd to Thomas Gray. Intr. & notes by Ernest Harold Pearce. Ed. with notes by Leonard Whibley. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1932.
column46: H.C. Jan. 24, 1797 Dear Sir I have your Letter without date, & your Ode on Wisdom . You have picked some gold out of Schultens dunghill. But these dull interpreters are not much worth your notice. You may venture without scruple on man for he . Houbigant translates v. 3 thus - Nihil jam tenebris opertum; nihil rarum et pretiosum. Reperit homo gemmas abditissimas - and in a note, ille est homo, de quo in fine capitis superioris . v. 19. You may make use of Schultens' vase , though Houbigant translates, as our bible does, - euro non compensabitur defaecato - v. 21 celestial intelligences seems nobler than the fowls of the air . But I doubt it's truth. The former may be supposed to know that obedience is true wisdom; not so, blind mortals, or even the eagle-eyed inhabitants of air. Houbigant's version is, Ea mortalium omnium latet aspectibus; ea coeli volucribus abscondita . But the authority of Schultens will justify you, if you prefer his comment. And now to your questions. I not only approve your Ode but think it excellent. Nor do I find a single verse, or word to alter. As soon as I saw your new volume advertised, I ordered our Worcester bookseller to send for it. But it is not yet arrived. - Our booksellers are grown rich & great, & therefore inattentive. I don't wonder they blundered in the advertisement; if it be a blunder, for it makes for them, though not for the author. Your report of Roscoe's book made me send for it. He seems well versed in the Tuscan history & literature. He, also, writes an easier style (though not without affectation) & is more decent than Gibbon. But he is of that school in religion, & in politics, a Jacobin. So fine a thing it seems to our modern historians & Virtuosi to have, & to profess to have, no religion. I scribble this in haste on that day, on which. I enter by God's great mercy on my 78th. year. Yet here I am, reading and criticizing your poetry. But it is divine poetry, & not unworthy it's subject. May you live long to amuse yourself in this way, & to oblige & entertain your old friend & affectionate servant R. Worcester P.S. My nephew is much yours. If anything more occurs to me on the subject of your Ode, you shall hear again from me.

column39: The Correspondence of Richard Hurd & William Mason And Letters of Richard Hurd to Thomas Gray. Intr. & notes by Ernest Harold Pearce. Ed. with notes by Leonard Whibley. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1932.
column46: Aston Jan: 31st. 1797 My dear Lord, I am highly gratified by the Approbation you have given to me of my Ode. I own I rather thought well of it myself, but I writ it with so much greater facility than I did that from Isaiah forty years ago, that I suspected I had only acquired by habit a quickness of execution, but might have lost a strength of colouring and expression. I am afraid Scultens, of whom I have as mean an opinion as your Lordship, will not either authorize the Sculptured Vase or the Celestial Intelligences. the Truth is, I took them from a French Version of Schultens translated by Messrs. Joncourt Sacretaire & Allemand printed at Leiden 1748 The latter of whom Allemand came over with the Dutch Ambassador on the King's Accession &, on seeing me at Lord Holdernesse's, sent it me when he returned. This version is said in the preface to have been revised & approved by Schultens himself. But on consulting his wretched Latin in Dr. R Gray's edition (the only Hebrew Book in my Possession) I find no Authority for either of the Passages, one of which according to Schultens is The other But I will keep the thing by me a little while, & then make the Lines in question more germane to the Hebrew Verity. Houbigant, for the extracts from whom I am much obliged to Your Lordship, is, I fancy an Hebraist of a better form, but how strange it is that one Word can mean either flame or Bread ? I cannot however see the Connection, which. your Lordship calls so close, in the Original. You must know, that ten or twelve years ago I versified the whole Poetical part of Job into dramatic Verse. But it appeared Prolix, & I threw it aside. This Winter I happened to find it amongst other Ebauche`es , and have since returned it to the anvil, versified the Prose Introduction & conclusion, so that it appears a sort of Epo-dramatic Composition similar as to manner with Paradise Regained. I give your Lordship this information merely to add that this Chapter puzzled me so much, that I could not possibly connect it with what proceeded it. I found it so perfectly Lyrical, & breaking off so abruptly, therefore I versified it in unequal Couplets of two tens & two eights like Milton's version of Quis multi Graceless &c, but as I knew you did not like Blank Verse (neither do I the unequal Blank Verse) I tried my hand at it again in Strophe &c Rhymed, in the way in which. I sent it for Your Lordship's amusement. As to Houbigant's Dictum that it refers to Men in the last verse of the preceding Chapter, My Bible prints the word in Italics , which. indicates it not to be in the original, so this necessary word is omitted in each place. For myself I am not displeased with the Pains I have taken with the whole Book, as I think it has given me a clearer insight into what you call this Mysterious Composition, & convinced me that Our friend's Conjecture, though certainly only a conjecture, is the best & only clue to direct one through the Labyrinth. Believe me to be, My Dear Lord Your obligd & affectionate Served. W. Mason

column39: The Correspondence of Richard Hurd & William Mason And Letters of Richard Hurd to Thomas Gray. Intr. & notes by Ernest Harold Pearce. Ed. with notes by Leonard Whibley. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1932.
column46: Aston Ap. 3 -97 My dear Lord, I enclose, as you desire, another Copy of the Ode. My Curate who is at once my Orthographer & Punctuator, vindicates himself from your Lordship's criticisms by saying that the distinction between Ever & Eer is now little regarded, but I kiss the rod; there is certainly too many ears of one sort or other in the Ode, as it now stands, but at present it can't be helped. I am a little, though not much, curious to know whether His Grace of Grafton has made a present to Your Lordship & consequently to Hartlebury Library of a New Edition of Professor Greisbatch first Vol: of his Greek Testament. I have had that inexpressible Honour. If you have not, you will perhaps smile to know that this Celsissimus Dux bonarum Literarum patronus Egregius has had a certain number of Copies printed at Halle in Saxony on fine English paper, which. he makes presents of, & for which. the Learned Professor gives him due Encomiums in his Prefatio . With kind compts. to your Nephew I remain My Dear Lord Yours most truly W. Mason

column39: The Early Letters of Bishop Richard Hurd 1739-1762. Ed. by Sarah Brewer. Church of England Record Society, Volume 3. Woodbridge: Boydell Press. 1995.
column46: To / the Revd. Mr. Potter at / Batcombe near Brewton / in Somersetshire / By London. Comb: Novr. 11th. 1739. Dear Sir I am now sate down to answer your two Letters. And as to ye. first, I cannot but observe yt. ire. passion for the happy Lady, you mentioned, is perfectly honourable, & altogether worthy a Gentleman, & a Clergyman. There is certainly something in love of a very refined, & delicate nature, when founded upon virtue, & good sense, & under the guidance of reason. And I can't but rejoice to find yours of yt. kind; a remarkable instance of which. you have given in being so exact in a point, in which. it had been excusable to have offended. As warm a lover with a less share of good sense would hardly have prevailed upon himself to neglect the completion of his happiness, for the distant, possible difficulties, yt. might arise in the remainder of his life. But you have judged better, & given the Lady at once a convincing proof of your affection & prudence. Pecuniam in loco negligere, maximum interdum est lucrum , says Master Terence, & to neglect happiness in it's proper place is sometimes the best way of increasing it. The case before us is, I think, one of yt. nature, & I don't in the least doubt but Providence will hereafter make up your loss with ample Interest. And that she may do this by bestowing upon you as large a living, as you can desire, in a short time is the sincere wish of one, who at present lies under the disgrace of a suspected friend. By the conclusion of this last sentence you'll easily perceive I am passing from your former, to your late letter. And of which. give me leave to say, yt. it is ye. only disagreeable one, I ever received from Mr. Potter. To suspect my friendship, & sincerity, to accuse me of coolness & indifference, & to represent me either as forgetful, or designedly negligent of a friend, for whom I have often professed great esteem, & respect, these, Sir, are particulars that bear so hard upon my reputation, yt. I could not peruse your letter with that pleasure, & satisfaction, I was wont to do. It would be easy to enlarge upon this subject but as it is in itself very disagreeable I shall leave it; after having first observed to you, yt. you have prevented me in making any Apologies for my long Silence, by mentioning the fifth of November. Nor will you be surprised at it's engrossing the greatest part of my Time, if you consider the niceness of Ears, & the slow Invention of their Orator. But of this enough; proceed we now to answer the remaining part of your letter. And here, if it had not the appearance of flattery, I should immediately say, you might have spared yourself the trouble of proving to me, yt. the Country had not yet vitiated your taste of polite learning. The Style & manner in which your letters are wrote, abundantly convince me, yt. the Revd. Mr. Potter of Batcombe is not changed from Ds. Potter of Em~anuel, & yt. Pope, Prior, & Addison are not less your Favourites in Somersetshire, than formerly they were in the Seat of the Muses. The Pierian Spring has too delicate a flavour, ever to be exchanged by any thinking man for a more ignoble liquor; & though his health, or some other extraordinary cause may oblige him to draw from a common, or insipid stream, yet his taste can never so far degenerate as to forget the delightful relish of the one, & prefer a less pure draught of the other. This, Sir, is the case of all those, who have ever tasted that sacred Spring; but you who have drunk largely of it, & whose Brain has been sobered by copious draughts, can never forget the richness of it's flavour, or drink with pleasure of any other Stream. If you will excuse the coarseness of the Comparison, I would venture to say, yt. the Mental Taste, I have hitherto been speaking of, is not very unlike the corporeal Taste of those good Wives, who by degrees contract so great a love for Gin, yt. it is not in their power to lay it aside, & betake themselves to any other liquor. I have indeed begged pardon for the meanness of my Allusion; but upon a review it is so nauseous upon so delicate a Subject as that of Taste, yt. I am very sensible, if it meets with pardon, it deserves none. I have run directly counter to the practice of all polite writers, & instead of discovering a fineness of taste in my manner of talking upon that subject, have only convinced you, yt. I want that Taste I commend, & am entirely ignorant of the Elegancies of a genteel Style. We are told of Longinus, yt. "His own Example strengthens all his Law" And yt. "He is himself the great Sublime he draws." But it may be said as truly to my honour, yt. my own Example weakens my observations, & yt. I am just the reverse of that polite Taste I would describe. From what has been said it appears a dubious case, whether I am a proper judge of a fine taste, or no, or rather it evidently appears, I am not. The consequence of which. is, yt. I pay no great complement to your letters, when I affirm them to be written in an elegant taste. But whatever may be determined of that point, this I can affirm, yt. they are always particularly agreeable to me, and always discover that taste which. I have ever looked upon to be a fine one. And therefore give me leave to say further, yt. you cannot oblige me more, than by writing very frequently; and (if I thought my letters could be as agreeable to you), I would faithfully promise, they should be as frequently answered by, Sir, your unjustly suspected Friend, & Humble Served. R. Hurd. P.S. I need say nothing of your Brother, because he writes by this post.

column46: To / the Revd. Mr. Potter at Batcombe / near Brewton / in / Somersetshire. / By London. Comb: Decr. 14th. 1740. Dear Sir I am at last at leisure to answer your very obliging Letter, and shall begin with thanking you for the Speech, you sent me by ire. Brother. It was indeed, as you foretold, of no great Service to me, & therefore I cannot easily admit your Excuse for not sending your own. "But it was incorrect, it seems, & therefore you would not let me see it". Surely my friend has no great opinion of my Candour & sincerity to make such an Apology. Incorrectness I could have pardoned, nay perhaps should have admired. For there is something beautiful in the negligent, careless strokes of a Master hand. As to your Brother's Affair, it was a great to me to find it so soon, & so happily composed. I suppose, He has wrote you an acct. of Particulars, & therefore you'll not expect me to enlarge upon it. Only this I must add by way of reply to your request, yt. had there been any occasion for my advice in the Affair, he should not have wanted it. Sometime ago he favoured me with the sight of a small paper of verses, written upon Dr. Bowden, that showed a truer spirit, & a more masterly turn of Expression, in. I had before observed in his Compositions. Upon a perusal of them, I gave him the commendation, he deserved, & encouraged him to employ his more vacant hours in amusements of that kind. In doing which I had this double view; 1st. by putting him upon composition to improve his taste in polite learning; & in the next place, to draw him off by that means from some little indiscretions to which. the fire & vivacity of his youth & temper are in his more disengaged moments apt to subject him. For the same reason I have sometimes recommended to him books of polite Amusement, yt. were new to him, & have endeavoured to mix 'em so with his other Studies, as to give no interruption to them. If you think me right in this, I shall receive some pleasure, as I have contributed something to his instruction & interest, and as it may serve to show my respect for you both. The Amatorial Differences, you mentioned, surprised me a good deal, & are a fresh instance of the hypocrisy, & falseness, of that Sex, we call fair. I faithfully believe an Elegant, but idle Writer of the Augustine Age, when he tells us from his own Experience, Catullus. But at the same time I don't doubt but my friend will remember, that to conquer such difficulties is the business, & province of noble & exalted Spirits. The Occasion must necessarily suggest to you the first Scene of Terence's Eunuch, & perhaps some other passages of the like Nature in Heathen Literature. And indeed such helps may be of no inconsiderable Service to a delicate, & refined Imagination. But besides these, I doubt not but Mr. Potter will draw such assistances from Religion (for the importance of the Occasion will, I think, justify so serious a thought) and Philosophy, as will enable him to bear up against all the Attacks of love, & Beauty, of faithlessness & Woman. Methinks I see you after a certain intermediate Space, post aliquod spatium requiemque furoris , look back with transport upon the dangers, & difficulties, you've past. Twill be something like a review of the many hazards, & fortunate escapes, which. an old traveller entertains himself with, upon retiring to a calm retreat, far from the uncertain & delusive Deep, that had once tempted him to leave the Shore, & had been the Scene of his former disquietudes, & misfortunes. It were easy to carry on this Allusion much further, had not Horace already done it with infinitely greater beauty in one of his Odes. All yt. I shall add is an hearty wish, yt. you may happily escape the present Shipwreck; & may soon be in a condition to testify your happiness, not by suspending, but sending a votive Table to your well-Wisher. In short, you must give me leave once more to press you to undertake your promised work. And this I am the more inclined to do at present, as it will serve for an agreeable amusement in your present troubles, &, I hope, call your thoughts from yt. Object, that had hitherto engrossed but too many of them. What you mention about coming to Comb: next Summer gives me great pleasure, & I will, if possible, contrive to meet you there. Hudson has not wrote to me since April; & Go~ld has been silent a long time. Whether I am to be favoured with a continuance of their correspondence, is a secret, which. my Eyes cannot at present pry into. But however that be, it will be some comfort to me, yt. I have not yet lost the regard, & correspondence of my good friend of Somerset. From the whole tenor of this Epistle you'll easily perceive I am in a very idle humour, & have wrote with Ease. This indeed generally passes for a complement, but then it must be such ease, as proceeds from art, not Chance: The latter of which. has been the chief governess in this Scroll. Notwithstanding which. believe me to be (what I am not the less on acct. of my present disposition) your most Sincere Friend, & Served. R. Hurd. P.S. Your B: is yours: write very soon.

column46: To / the Revd. Mr. Potter at Batcombe / near Brewton in / Somersetshire / By London. Comb. April 19th. 1741. Dear Sr, Your last very handsome & obliging letter gave me that pleasure, I always receive from the correspondence of a sincere & ingenious Friend. As the contents of it were elegant, I was entertained; as they were friendly, I was delighted. For both I am obliged to you. Only one part has thrown me into a Dilemma, yt. I hardly know how to get over. Your manner of expression in some places carries in it so great an Air of complement, yt. it must infer no small degree of vanity to believe you; & yet there is something so truly cordial, & affectionate runs through the whole; yt. I cannot disbelieve you. The most prudent way perhaps is to moderate the affair a little: I hope, I believe, I know you respect me; that respect might carry you too far in your profession of it, & heighten your colouring too much. However it be, I am determined rather to be thought vain, than suspicious; the one indeed implies a weakness, but such a one as is pardonable; whereas the other has something criminal in it's nature, & betrays a darkness of Soul, I should be sorry to be charged with. Should I enlarge upon the ease, & beauty of your Poetry at this time, it would look too much like an exchange of complement, & a mere return of words. I cannot however omit saying, lines pleased me; & if there be any fault in them, it is that they are too much in the taste, & manner of Prior's. A little paradoxical this, you'll think, yt. to be very like one of the best of Poets, is to be faulty! But it is easily explained: our taste for poetry in this age is founded entirely upon the practice, & manner of Mr. Pope, & as Prior happens to differ from him in the turn, & run of his versification, he is not looked upon as an exact model. This indeed seems to be his only fault; he is rather loose & careless in his numbers, & often so, as to take off from the delicacy & beauty of a Sentiment. I ascribe not this to negligence, or the want of a discerning Ear; Mr. Prior is well known to have excelled in the later, &, I believe, he used much care. It was perhaps rather owing to too great an affectation of ease in writing, which., though justly admired in this poet, & indeed the greatest perfection in works of Genius, should never be aimed at, & observed at the expense of Strength, harmony, & beauty. But I ask pardon for the freedom I have taken both with your (justly) favourite Poet, & with you. Sincerity is one of the first qualifications you require in ire. Ideal friend, & if I could be vain enough to think any part of so amiable a character belonged to me, it is that. The other eminent virtues, required in your piece, I presume not to lay any claim to, but this I arrogate to myself with so much confidence, yt. I shall venture to assert in the following couplet, "My tongue impartial never will commend The slightest Errors even in a Friend." It gives me some pain to observe, yt. the word Pen with. suit this place, much better than Tongue. A length of days has passed, since it was in my power to use is. member in your Service. Too many mountains rise between us to suffer any sounds to reach your ears, from this quarter, except what are made visible upon paper. And this way (thank Heaven) we can converse. Nor Seas, nor deserts can prevent this kind of Intercourse; but our thoughts, fleeting & transient, as they are, become permanent & lasting, & take a secure flight to whatever part of the Globe, it may please their master to send them. It is for this reason, yt. the absence of friends becomes tolerable, & it is from this expedient, if anything should hinder our meeting at Cambridge this year, that I promise myself some comfort. Believe me, Sr., to see you here with. be the greatest pleasure, & if it can be done with any sort of convenience, you may be sure, I shall endeavour to do it. But Cambridge is not at present so agreeable to me, as once it was, & whether other reasons may not conspire to hurry me away before the commencement, is what I cannot now promise. In the mean time be assured of my affection for you, & doubt not of my sincere endeavours to see you, & to serve you. Your Brother the other day recd. a very handsome letter from the Author of the late English Aeneid. It was occasioned by a complement he made him upon his Translation; a pretty Poem, but not quite so correct, as it is wished it had been. I had seen it some time before, but as ire. Brother never gave me the least hint of his design, I did not pass so severe a judgment upon it, as otherwise I should have done. However Mr. Pitt seems to like it very much: the complement he has recd. upon this occasion, & indeed the whole letter, do him more honour, than it is proper any other person should mention to him. I am glad to find, you have read Dr. Delany's life of David; I am certain it pleased you. There is an uncommon Spirit runs through the whole performance, & something so ingenious in the digressions, disquisitions, &c that, I think, I never met with anything more entertaining. In his remarks on the 18th. Psalm, the Dr. observes (if I remember right, for I have not the book by me) that the word Temple is used by the inspired Author to signify the Heavens with great beauty in the following Passage. "In my distress I called upon the Lord, & cried unto my God: heard my voice out of his Temple &c." Ps. 18. v. 6. I was pleased the other day to find it used exactly in the same by the Sublime Lucretius: L. 2. v. 1037. It occurs also in a passage of the first Book, where the Epithet Tonitralia, to which. it is joined, with. not improperly mark the Idea, we have of that Temple, when "the Lord thunders in it, & the Highest gives his voice." Ibid: v:13. L. 1. v. 1098. I don't recollect, that this form of Expression is ever used by Virgil. An excellent paragraph in ire. last letter to ire. Brother has prevented my saying anything upon the Subject of ire. Love. Keep to your resolution, & ell's well. You see I did a politic thing in my last to explode method, since I should have found it a very difficult task to have connected so many different Scraps, as this letter consists of, in any tolerable form & order. It has been of vast Service to me through the whole, & gives me an opportunity even at the last of letting you know, without any form, yt. the polite Scheme, I hinted to you, was learning French. And to show you I have made some progress in the language, give me leave to subscribe myself, but with the sincerity of an Englishman, Vo`tree tree`s humble Servitor R. Hurd. P.S. Ire. Bro: is all but Bachelor, & at ire. Service.

column46: To / Mr. Edward Macro at the Revd. Dr. / Macro's in Norton near St. Edmunds Bury / Suffolk. / By London Brewood Jan: 1st. 1741-2 Dear Sir, Your last found me in the middle of a Sermon; and as that kind of business does not love Interruption, you'll forgive my deferring to answer it, till I had in some sort brought it to a conclusion. I thank you, Sir, for that regard, I might almost say, zeal, you show for my Interest: it discovers a Sincerity and warmth of friendship, and therefore lays me under the most agreeable Obligation. As to the Curacy, you mention, I am not in a capacity to take it at present; I am not, nor can be in orders till Lent, and the Gentleman, I suppose, cannot wait till then. Thirty five pts. a year is indeed but a small thing; however, as I have a desire to settle in that part of the world, if that difficulty could be got over, I should incline to accept it. I do not conceive, of what use the house, you speak of, can be to me, since my income would hardly enable me to set up for an Housekeeper. I should like too to know the distance of the place from Bury, and whether the Rector resides at it. If Mr. Lyne writes, I shall take care to send letters of thanks both to him and Mr. Elliot: till then I dare say you'll think it more prudent in me to omit them. An obligation I am as ready to acknowledge as any man, but am afraid, that to be forward in this case would have too much the Air of Solicitation, and Assiduity; things of which. you know I am not very fond. In the mean time it is a very sensible pleasure to me to find Mr. Elliot interesting himself in my behalf; as the worthiness of his character had always attracted my esteem, and as the many valuable qualities, he possesses, makes it an honour to be regarded by him. To say the truth, he is almost the only Man of fortune, whose acquaintance I have ever had the honour of, to whom I could have been pleased to have recommended myself. - The favour of Mr. Lyne you may imagine I take kindly, as it comes from one, whose kindness I had no reason to expect. But as I consider Mr. Macro, as the primum mobile , or the Spring, that has set even these in action, it is to him I can't but think myself more particularly obliged. - I need not apologize for leaving a Subject with some abruptness, which., if continued, would displease you. Let me therefore choose a less offensive Topic. Mr. Cox, I remember, mentioned an Emendation Dr. Macro had made in I Ep. Cor c. 14. v. 6, where, instead of I would read , or , or something like it. The alteration I let great light in upon a passage, as it now stands, sufficiently obscure. But he seemed at the same time to doubt, if was ever used in that sense in good Greek. I happened the other day to meet with it used in the new Testament exactly in the same manner, in which. the Dr. would use it there. It is in the 13. c. of the Acts of Ap: and the 41st. verse, where is to be construed etiamsi , and has the same force, as . The remark, I am afraid, will be but of little Service: however I could not help just taking notice of it. What luck had I to mention the Muses in my last? Or if I must mention them, why was it done in the sneering and disrespectful form of, si Muses placate ? The jades have been even with me for it: they have plaug'd me with rhyme, & it's attendant, Head-ach, pretty heartily since that time; and as if versifying of any kind were not punishment enough, they have put me upon the most painful and laborious part of it. To speak plain English, in the frost, that happened about a fortnight ago, and which. hung the hedges with a Snowy kind of Substance, in forms the most lovely I remember to have seen, the thought struck me, that a description of it would be no disagreeable amusement at a time, when I found myself confined to the House. But a second thought convinced me of the rashness of my design, by putting me in mind of the fine description of winter in Virgil's Georgics, and that after him an attempt of that kind must be most impertinent. However not being willing to be entirely balked of my aim, I resolved to attempt a translation of that famous Episode, and apply in some sort the Scythian-winterpiece to our own condition in Staffordshire. The inimitable beauty of the Original, when I came to look into it, somewhat discouraged me; however I went through it, and shall here send you a copy for your amusement. It is usual with tenants to make little presents at this Season to their Landlords; a goose, or Turkey is carried with great form to the Squire, and though he wants them not, & has much better of his own, yet he never fails to accept them, and, if he happens to be, what they call, a well-spoken man, with expressions of great civility and respect. Permit me, Sir, to imitate this laudable custom, and though there is no want of amusements at Norton, please to accept this, as my Xstmas Offering. A friend, I think, has a greater right to them, than a Landlord; and as this is the only one in my power to make, let not the meanness of it be any Objection. Upon comparing it with the Original you'll perceive I have taken some liberty in two or three places, but it is in such, as I must confess to you I was not able to turn more literally with any tolerable grace. The line, that describes Icicles hanging at the beards of the Scythians, is extremely beautiful in the Latin; but I could not cloth the Image in any English words, that did not evidently turn it into burlesque. Dr. Trap, I remember, says there is fire in this description of Virgil, but I wish my copy be not too cold and have any degree of heat in it. All I shall say further upon it this weather lasts, my complement will not be ill-tim'd; since Nature will afford you a pretty exact Image of that, which. is the Subject of it. The Scythian Winter-piece from Virgil's George: L. 3. 1. 349. After this tedious letter, I shall not detain you long. It would however be unpardonable in me to omit the complements of the Season, and my Service to Mr. Cox. The usual mirth and good-humour of this part of the year will furnish you with abundant matter to write upon. I shall therefore expect, you'll keep me in countenance, by sending me an answer very soon, that shall bear some proportion to the length of this. I am, dear Sir, your most obliged Friend & Served. R. Hurd.

column46: To / the Revd. Mr. Potter at Batcombe / near Brewton in / Somersetshire. / By London. Dear Sir, Your last opens with such tenderness of Sentiment and Expression, that I could not help concluding at first, you had forgot yourself, and directed a letter to me, that was intended only for Hetty. Indeed the profession you make of your regard for me, and my letters, is so much above anything, either I, or they, can pretend to, that I could not well give it any other turn. At least I am to resolve it into that habitual complaisance, which. grows upon a man in Love, and by degrees wears him, like the Air and converse of a Court, into a degree of Politeness, unknown to the rest of the world. In one point however I am willing to think my comparison fails; for though I have charged you with a Courtier's politeness, yet you have not, I am sure, his Insincerity; and that is an Idea, which. the word Courtier has been usually made to convey. In short, I believe you to be, though a Lover, that is half a Courtier, a very honest man; and that your letter, however extravagant in point of language, at least means this, that you have a real respect for me. I would willingly show you the same in my turn, and by some act or other convince you, if it should seem necessary, of a mutual, and, I hope, equal respect from me. This I am now about to attempt by writing you, what I have not done to any one a long time, a whole Sheet. The Subject may indeed chance to want an Apology, for it is of myself. Yet the making one would have in it an air of greater distance, and form than ought to be observed between Friends. Take then the following Impertinence, and treat it as you please. About a Month ago I received a very obliging Offer, from a friend at Cambridge (whom, I believe, you don't know, and therefore I need not mention) of a little Living in Norfolk, about 70, or 80 pts. a year, and a neat house upon it. As my Inclination leads me to settle somewhere in that part of the Kingdom, and as the Thing itself was not of a contemptible value, you'll imagine I was not backward to accept it. Some small difficulty however arising about it, my Friend advised me by the next Post to appear upon the Spot, and settle matters myself. Immediately upon this I went for Cambridge, and got there last Sunday Fortnight. From thence I rode to my Friend's Father, whose Interest it was, that procured me this living, and who was the chief Manager in the affair. Upon consulting him the great Difficulty, I found, was my not being in Orders, and under Age. This made it necessary to choose a Person to hold it for me; but who that Person, was the Task. Considering however that Hudson was very near, within about 16 miles, and that "Honest" was the Epithet we used to give him, I resolved to ask the Favour of him. With this design the next Day brought me to Ipswich, or rather Wherestead. I was riding by the house, and was just going to enquire where he lived, when Bob came running out, broad awake, you may be sure, and marvelling much to see me there. His Eyes indeed, as well as his words, witnessed his Surprise; but glad he was to see me, and, my horse committed to the care of a Served., in we went. Osculation, and a Commerce of hands, you'll imagine, passed between us. This over, down we sat, and began to chatter. But not to tire you with a Detail of particulars, after Dinner, and over a glass of wine, I told him the design of my coming, and, in short, begged him to hold a Living for me. After a few questions about Residence &c he told me, he would; and it was presently agreed, that he should enter upon it by Trinity Sunday, (for it with. not lapse till after) and that I should be Curate. In order to this I intend at that time, for I am yet a lay-man, to take Orders. The remaining part of the Evening we spent very cheerfully, and among our friends and acquaintance did not forget those in Somersetshire. The next morning I took leave, and returned to my new Friend, or rather Patron, with whom I passed two or three Days most agreeably. He was, I found, a very polite, and learned man, well versed in most Sciences, but particularly curious in Manuscripts, Medals, and painting. He has an collection in each of these ways, and very obliging in giving me a Sight of 'em. From his conversation I with pleasure observed an extreme candour, in his judgment both of men, and books. He seems a most generous friend; particularly his civilities to me were beyond anything, I ever met with. On Saturday I returned to Cambridge, dined on Sunday with the Master of Emm:, and was the other part of the Day with my Friends. On Monday I set out for Shropshire, met with bad weather by the way, but reached Hatton by the Thursday following, which., to be exact in the chronology of my Expedition, was April 8th. 1742. As I rode through the open fields in Northamptonshire, I could not but observe with pity the sad State of modern Shepherds: ah! how unlike the golden dreams I had formed to myself in considering the Ancient. Instead of a lovely Antrum, so much talked of in Virgil, a thin, leafless Thom was all the Shelter; and so far from piping it, like their old Brethren, were they, that not a single note was heard throughout the doleful Region. Their condition seemed to me the more miserable, from their being exposed at that time to some heavy Showers; and from thence instead of regarding them, as I had used to do, as the favourites, I now began to look upon 'em as Objects of the peculiar wrath, of Heaven. But to amuse myself in that disagreeable Situation, I attempted to throw a few thoughts of this kind, which. the melancholy Scene suggested, into Rhyme, and as Pack Horses may be 'd to do with their Bells, divert myself on the road with a little Jingling. What a kind of Sound they may make in your Ears I know not; it is a comfort however, that if you do not like, you may refuse to hear, 'em. To be read, or thrown by therefore, just as you please, I have wrote you a Copy of them. I call it, for I know not what other name to give it, a Soliloquy. Now I am got upon Poetry, pray have you seen the new Dunciad? It is believed to be, and certainly is, Mr. Pope's. No one, that I know of, but himself could finish a piece with such exactness. Yet there are some reasons, might tempt one to think otherwise. Pray give me your Opinion in your next. If you have not seen it, it will entertain you; for though some other studies may not, yet Poetry is, I think, allowed to consist with Love. Haec been conveniunt, et in una sede morantur. (To a Scholar and a Friend I never apologize for a Scrap of a Latin.) Though I must own I could wish the latter were expelled it's Seat; I should then hope for more of the former from you. I should then too hope, you'd be at leisure to give me now and then a thought upon my favourite Subject, Pastoral. For, though I do nothing this way at present, I don't forget it. I have lately applied to a Gentleman, that is going to make the Tour of Italy, to inform me in some things relating to Mantua, particularly what is the present face of the Country, and whether it answers in any degree to the description, Virgil has left of it. But this, with ev'rything that concerns this whimsical Design, I beg may be a Secret. Will your Brother do anything tow'rds it? Tell him I wish to see his thoughts. He might in the compass of a few letters write me many valuable hints. Let me hear from both of you very soon; twill be a pleasure to be detained by each of you, as long as I have detained you. I am, dear Sir, your most faithful Friend and Served. R. Hurd. Hatton-Grange: April 15th. 1742.

column46: To / Mrs. Macro at Norton to be left / at Mr. Haywood's in the Cook-row / in Bury St. Edmunds. / Suffolk. Sunday Night Reymerston. Madam, An ugly, vexatious business of a Sermon denied me the pleasure of answering your last favour sooner. I have been sacrificing it to day to the people of Reymerston, (or rather to the winds, for they, I believe, had the greatest Share of it.) & now I am retired to my peaceful solitary cell, there to indulge a happy hour in writing to Mrs. Macro. To begin with some appearance of Order I thank you, Madam, for your last two Sides, & am only sorry that paper is so scarce at Norton as not to afford you three. Neither Horace nor the Doctor shall intimidate me, so long as the threatened verbosity comes from such a Correspondent. The Dr. calls it impetuous, & would thereby intimate it's Allusion to a torrent, but with submission he had been more exact, & kept nearer to the truth, had he compared it, as Homer does Ulysse's Eloquence, to the soft fleeces of descending Snows. For like them, were I addressing any but yourself, I should not scruple to say, Your copious Accents fall with easy art, Melting they fall, & sink into the heart. If anything in such a couplet could be objected to, it would be the term copious ; for as yet I have not been so happy to find that epithet applicable to you. But, Madam, how could you be so cruel as not to administer a little comfort to one on so sad an occasion as that of the Gardinerian Affair. You are so good to take some friendly notice of the Shixworthian, which. yet I never regarded; but here, when consolation had been so kind, you quite desert me. Though upon second thoughts (for I've learned from the Dr. that every thing has two handles) I believe you did right. You could not well reconcile me to myself without some sort of praise, or Encomium, & I know my weakness too well to think I could stand your praises without Vanity. My modesty indeed you're pleased to say would secure me there; & it is true I believe it would, were the praises to come from some mouths I could mention, as for instance were Mrs. Gardener's inclined, as I am inclined to think it is not, to heap 'em upon me - but then, Madam, when - but hold I am got into a Sentence that I am sensible I cannot finish without offending, & rather than do that, I'll even leave it abruptly, & begin a second. My new Neighbours Dr. Sharpen & his Lady are come. This afternoon a civil Invitation carried me to drink Tea there. I find him a good genteel sensible Man: as he had no company the conversation soon turned on literary Subjects. I encouraged it's tendency yt. way, & had the Satisfaction of reading a considerable Scholar in him. On my leaving him betwixt Six & Seven (which. I did to give myself the greater pleasure of writing this) he asked me to stay Supper, & on my refusal, attended, as you'll imagine, with an Excuse, added that he was in hopes of seeing me often, & that we should be good Neighbours. My answer to this you'll guess, & therefore I shall not encumber my paper with it. In short his whole behaviour had so much of the Gentleman in it, & his conversation of the man of Sense, that I rejoice extremely at his arrival, & promise myself, what I did not expect to find, good company in Reymerston. As I know your goodness leads you to rejoice with your friends on every instance of their good fortune, I could not help mentioning this to you. Mrs. Sharpen is really a well-behav'd woman. Pray my Service to your Majestic Son. The grandeur of his Person has charmed all the Eyes of Reymerston. One of my neighbours says he's a mighty well-look'd Gentleman, a second calls him a brave young man, & a third, Mary Cocker the Blacksmith's Wife, is of opinion that he has the very presence of a Prince. You'll guess after this how their poor puny parson goes down with 'em. In short I am so alarmed on this occasion, & am in such a dread lest the admired majesticality of his Appearance should alienate the good folks affections from their lawful Pastor, that I could almost wish his last year's consumption had thinned him a little more, & sunk his personableness into a narrower dimension. Pray tell him I think myself obliged for the good of the public to admonish him, either to make his appearance for the future like other folks, or not to appear at all at Reymerston. Well! it is growing late, & yet I don't perceive myself at all drowsy. How you may be indeed by this time I will not take upon me to say; but if you have any Inclination for a nap, there's no likelihood of your taking it yet quietly. Like Mrs. G's, my Larum is still upon the run, though every soul chance to be fast asleep round me. In this indeed she has the Advantage: I have no right honourable to ennoble a Sentence with, no high-sounding Titles to swell my Style , & thunder in the Ear's of my Auditors. That, if anything, might bid fair to keep folks awake; but as for my uniform, humble prate, how is it possible that should have any wakeful Effect, or keep a single Eye from closing? But hold, you'll say, what! always upon Mrs. G-r? Why no truly, I'll even leave that to my Lt - & since you must by this time be weary of the Subject, I'll promise for your ease not to mention it any more. You say, you mentioned every particular of the Shixworth Treatment to Mr. Lunge. I wish he would not take it ill from me that I should send you so particular an Account of it. I did not indeed intend it should go any farther. I regarded it not myself, & imagining you would know that, designed it rather for your Amusement. The account indeed was punctually, literally true; but would it not appear to him like carrying tales, & complaining idly? However I am sensible your Intention was, as in ev'rything else, extremely kind; & after all you would judge much better, than I can, whether it would give Offence. What I am concerned for is to preserve such a decorum in my behaviour tow'rds Mr. Lunge & his family, as not to incur their just censure or Exception, since that would be to bare a more valued friend's Side & make their passes at him more easy & successful. In short it is, as you observe, through me the malheureux Guardian is to be wounded, & if a passage be once made through my spare ribs, the Dr. has not long to survive me. It is on this account I have ventured to propose the foregoing Scruple; & if it seems to express any sort of dissatisfaction about what two of my best friends have meant in my favour, they will please to consider it, as it really is, as a sincere & unfeigned proof of my being their Obliged, Humble Served. R: Hurd. 3 Octr. 1742. Reymerston. I beg my Service to Dr. Macro and Miss. I hope I need not say how agreeable a letter with. be on ire. first leisure.

column46: To / the reverend Mr. Potter / at near / Somersetshire. / by London. Dear Sir, I thank you for the Sermons & Alphabet. I am glad you had not the trouble of transcribing, for as I have now time to learn the characters, they will do full as well. Your last was just what I expected, & shows me how well you can still rally a College life. All I have to say for myself is, that it at present favours some designs, which I am willing to pursue, & is otherwise agreeable in a good measure to my Inclination & Taste. The suddenness of the change after a seeming Resolution to the contrary was what, I can readily imagine, most surprised you. But I had apprehended through mistake that Dr. Macro was agst. it; whereas upon my mentioning the affair to him he entirely advised it. To lay the whole proceeding on this occasion before you in as short a compass as I can, Smelly married: the College wrote to me: Dr. Macro advised: I went to College; learned Hebrew in four days, & was chose Fellow. It was a real pleasure to me yt. by this means a way was opened for a little thing for your Brother; especially as that, I knew, would further introduce him to the Acquaintance of Dr. Macro. There are some few difficulties, or more properly Impositions, which I am sorry to find he must submit to in regard of his board. But notwithstanding these the thing, I hope, will turn out tolerably to his Satisfaction. I had a letter from him yesterday, in which. he seems to be in spirits, & not displeased with his Neighbours. Our visit to Norton I guess you must have heard of: the Dr. has a very favourable opinion of your Brother & will be always glad to see him. The talk of the University at present is about the late Election of a Provost at King's. Dr. George is the man chose by the Society, but the Bishop of Lincoln, who is Visitor of the College disputes the validity of their proceedings on account of there being improper Officers employed in them. All that can be yet concluded about the issue of this Dispute, is that the Lawyers are likely to get handsomely by it. The controversy betwixt Middleton & our Public Orator grows very warm. The Orator is a good deal galled with Middleton's Sneers, & is sending in all haste to the press a voluminous Answer. His friends are under pretty great Apprehensions of the ill Success of this attempt on the Epistles of the Old, & the History of the Modern, Cicero. It was indeed pretty daring in our new-made Orator to attack the most acute controvertist of the Age, especially on a Subject, which., if any man, the Author of the L. of Cicero ought to understand. But it seems a little fatal to the Orators to fall under the correction of Middleton; & if this comes off no better than the last, I would advise the next, should Middleton be then alive, to learn from their Example. Pray give me your thoughts of Dr. Young's Muse, when you write next. I should wish you to be particular because the Critics, I find, are very much divided. In answer to your next, which. I beg may be very quick, I shall say a great deal. At this time you must excuse me, if a number of letters, which. through a late neglect of all my friends, pours in upon me, obliges me sooner, than I could wish, to write myself, dear Sir, your most faithful Friend & S: R. Hurd. Cambridge: 27. Jan. 1742-3.
