I am of opinion they can, and even to a degree bring us into confusion and a breaking among our selves, by giving an extravagant preference in price to one or two concerns. We must consider that we sell for 11s, that is about 9s 4d neat, and can't be imagined this price can be upheld but by our unanimous among ourselves and a friendly correspondence with those necessary evils att the Gate. This ought to be well weighed and an answer must be given the dealors without loss of time. Twixt you and me, they told me that Mr agent had promised that his share should be paid them though others did not. Don't take direct notice of this but by way of supposition the question may be put. I think the dealors in strictness merit a - but the only quaery is if we can subsist and keep together without their assistance. My father approves in everything of what you have wrote concerning the future management of and has signified as much to the by this post, whom he desires you will assist with your advice. He thinks Clark may as well be left out and be no undertaker but may be made useful as a check upon them. More needs not on this head, he having wrote word formerly that Grayson would be better outed than continue, but it must be don with as good a grace as can be. Now about the 2 manors. Mr Sanderson was here and designs to write to you shortly; in the mean time am to acquaint you that this very day Mr Gibson bid anew £5000 for them and the freehold and pressed to be reported the best bidder. Your agent offered £4000 for the manors and Mr Manlove att the same time £1500 for the freehold. An arose for not separating the purchase, but it was carried that they might go to the best purchaser either by the lump or distinctly. Then it was pressed to have part of the money paid into court which was agreed to and time given till this day 3 weeks for making the report. would be glad to know the utmost you would go and he will menage as warily as he can; there will be bidding one above another to be sure till the very day of report, so that you may send him full instructions. He thinks or 300 ought to be returned him in case he be approved the best purchaser, to deposit in court. And as we agree that Mr Willson's name would be the properest to be made use off, he must be wrote to by the to desire or the attorney thinks fit to employ in his behalf to act for him. You will hear further particulars shortly to which I referr and am ...

8th 1710/1 By last post you would have mine att large in answer I think to all former particulars as far as I could. Have since made further inquiry of some Members about the taking place of the additional duty on candles, but they tell me that the bill is not yet brought into the House and when it is a blank is left for the time. However one has promised me to ask Mr Lownds that question and if he will resolve I shall know it and then you may depend it shall be communicated. I referred you to for particulars of the business in his hands; I think it remains as when he wrote, Mr Wilson the best bidder att £6400. As there will be occasion to advance att least a brace of hundred pounds in court and money being very difficult to be had, my father has promised to go to his goldsmith, examine his cash and if he finds sufficient will advance for the present; but care must be taken to remitt it him speedily, least his occasions should require. Both my father and I made an exception against my uncle's letter and therefore stopped it a post; we represented to him the jealousy it might give our partners as then expressed but he said there was no harm in it. You will guess in the main the scope of the letter and what is meant by it, and it would not doe amiss if you should by word of mouth discourse the substance so as not to give offence. You know every additional duty is a burden upon a trade and this lately laid on will contribute to make it go heavily this next year. This will make the dealors more absolutely necessary to us than otherwise, who must exert themselves in the Regulation and for that service only to make things go smoothly on; the only way to free us from general complaints which the last year had like to have brought us into troubles, which where they would have ended God knows. Should you quarrel with the dealors att this time, you may guess att the disturbance and interruption they would unanimously give to the trade. And though you were to engage all the other dealors in your interest, yet they are most of them people of little or no substance for which reason they can't force a trade; if they doe it must be by the creditt you give them and what sort of reckoning you will have with them att the making up your accounts you may judge. When an answer is given to the dealors it must be don with great caution, least if they be discarded their natural malice and spirit of revenge will readily prompt them to produce the letter and probably may bring us into trouble. For instance were it expressed that some of the Ten had received £50 for sale of Fieldhouse coals contrary to the stipulation , if this letter were exposed, as certainly it would be by them if disobliged, the Review would lay hold of it and handle us as last year, that it was a plain proof of a designed monopoly; so that what now seems to sleep would be raised up against us and a prosecution would certainly be set on foot. What then you will say can be don? We think a cautious letter to them must be framed, but particular instances of their false dealing should be represented to my uncle in a letter to him and that he may charge them with by word of mouth. I think it would not be improper if the general answer to the dealors be first enclosed to him that we may peruse and alter if thought necessary. Believe me we can't be too cautious as the world seems disposed. My father writes on this head to the by this night's post, by the help of which the meaning of this may be explained where it wants. I doubt the proposal of £2000 att next and £1000 after will scarce go down, but when the 5 have come to a general result let it be dispatched as above. As to an interest for your own concerns att Gate, it is time it should be looked after and you must employ some friend of yours to transact for I must not appear nor can be of any service. It seems necessary Mr Ord must keep back his leadings whether we keep up our interest with dealors or not. The sexton's adventure made me smile and reflections upon it are such as I should guess att. I have now tired myself sufficiently and the more because this weather does indeed sensibly affect me who am ... P.S. I desire you will send me an account of what money I advanced on the upper seam service. I remember not perfectly well now Brainslope concern was to be divided; as I take it I was to advance the charge of half that concern for the use as we agreed att Percivall's. If I be wrong set me to rights and direct your answer to this postscript enclosed to Mrs in Bedford Row. Adieu I am ...

14th I have often since the receipt of one of your letters some time since reflected upon the contents and now by experience find them true. There are some people in the world endeavouring to trip up my heels or rather to cut my throat with a feather, how justly I know not. I thought I might have deserved better att their hands when I formerly stood in steed of a father, but it is likely former kindnesses are effaced and forgot. It is with very great grief I must tell you that I am suspected, att least to me it seems so, of having raised a considerable sum out of the colliery more than was fitting for my own use and therefore I am refused a request of working 50 tenns for the supplying the quantity allotted me by the Regulation. A small favour demanded God knows to be rejected; and methinks the gain of about £2000 in twelve years service is no very extravagant allowance for one's service and pains, not to mention the entire ruin of a man's health, which att this time is a savage rent charge. But all this I am resolved to bear with patience. The lossess att Bensham are all attributed to my neglect; all losses by fitters or others in the way of trade in my time are not directly but by a side wind levelled in some measure att me. If I have bin guilty of any advantageous thing to the family, that is not noticed or looked upon to be an incumbent duty. My friend we live in an age of generosity; little did I expect such usage, but since I am deprived in effect of being a collier att home, I shall take leave of trade and desire not to be concerned any way relating to it. My service has bin pernicious, therefore I will prevent it for the future; I desire if you have any thing to recommend or propose, let it be don directly by letter to my father. Then you may have an answer but I may sollicitt weeks without before a resolution can be taken on which a certainty may be relied on. Witness this business of Fenham; I have formerly discoursed that point over and over, yet I believe you may have thought my answers very superficial because I could send you no other. Indeed my father is so ill now that he can't think of business, but depend upon it when he is better I durst venture a wager he will have so many objections that before they be answered a vast time will be spent. Therefore herafter when you have any thing to communicate do it directly to himself. Pray enclose your answer to this to Mrs in the Row under a cover and I conjure you not to signify the least of the above mentioned to any person living. I foresee in a little time as things are managed there will be great feuds among us, which I can't but bewail. Pardon the freedom I take but since it is to so particular a friend as yourself I venture to doe it. My father is something better, returns you his thanks; he apprehends the length of the way, the trouble of securing way leaves through so many different proprietors and the uncertainty of the lease makes him wave thinking of it. Doe you think might not be willing to admit of a partner or two and let the come down his way? You may if you think fit try his pulse, suppose Jimmy, you and myself should stand to a half. This I only recommend to your thoughts. To the rest of your letter I must give an answer when my father is in better plight and myself too, for what with these northerly winds and vexations of one sort or other I am almost off my legs. This day I a letter from the 4 directed to Mr Wortley and me desiring we will employ Nevill Ridley as a solicitor to watch the bill and receive instructions from us. Don't you think him so great a friend to Wrightson as to communicate anything we shall entrust him with to that gentleman and that will be informed from time to time? Doubtless they will. Adieu my good friend and let me be in favour or out you shall always find me according to former professions ... Was not the to have had a share in Brainslope after won, as we agreed att Percivall's; was not I to be att a partcharge in winning and what might she cost? Your answer to these. I almost think it would be worth your while to come up on your own account to settle your own private concerns as well as those att the Gate for yourself. I shall be willing to contribute out of our joint concern att towards the charge and right glad should bee to see you.

June 14th I am favored with both yours. The latter was the most acceptable since it brought an account of your safe landing att Gateshead, though you had suffered in the journey by the loss of the Red Lyon juices, but as crabs and lobsters are so easily come att with you I doubt not your speedy recruiting. I have drank the German spew and you know writing makes it fly into the head, therefore must be short and so shall fall to business. Mrs Smith is uneasy till Mrs Barnes's business be concluded, she having obliged her friend to fit up an for her on purpose. You will discourse and let that matter be made an end off one way or other speedily. Mrs Smith is a woman of experience and doubtless if she will be free in giving advice in any sort, she wants not capacity. We are both of opinion that the overplus sum remaining in the hands of your dear Peggy belongs to herself, and should you contest it, Mrs Smith would comb your head for such a presumption were you within her reach. As the world goes I don't admire people's being called strictly to account. I think your vend is extraordinary considering how the season has bin for leading; if you can add 2 keels more to your number, it can't fail of doing well for there are no stocks att steaths, as the masters inform, even Stella was grounded. I believe you will find the trade grow worse every year after this therefore receive the advice you formerly gave to another person, make hay while the sun shine. Get what carriadge you can and lead what is possible; both ships and pans will swallow what ever are brought down. This day I was att Gate and see Oldner, who told me the town was more than half supplied. He had sent up the river Lord 's coals this day. Price is Team from 25 1/2 to , and . My father desires Baker, Bullock and Hutchinsons might take a view of Fenham, that their thoughts might be imparted to the and yourself and that you would send him an account what steaths they might be brought to and about what charge; and if not to advantage but through Mr Montagu, by what means could that be compassed. You and the must draw up a scheme and that will give us an insight. Bowman is here and presses an end of that lease to be made. I have not heard a syllable of the project of widening of our way but what yours mentions. I could not get a penny of money att the Gate this . Oldner was wishing that he had had a list of the ships that loaded of your coals sent him, meaning that he would have bin serviceable to you. I am rather better than when you left me though not much; this hot and sultry weather is burdensome to me and were I not refreshed with some cool breezes in the Row, I fancy I should cease to be. My father desires your acceptance of his best services and so does Mr Honywood who is by. Hugh has bin almost every day att the custom house without effect; he grows very peevish on it. I have wrote a letter and sent it to Lord to sign to Sir Matthew Dudly, one of the commissioners, by which hope for some success. Did you borrow a blue coat from the master of the Gun Tavern and if you did, where was it left? Oldner was making enquiry after it. Mrs makes a tender of her devoirs to her beau, who she says writes such plain lines as she can't venture to read unless in a corner by herself. Pray pay my to the cash keeper and the honest Alderman. I remain ... When will they begin to lead from the new work att Whitefield Stella?

10th Methinks the time of my very tedious, both as to the length of it (which is now near 5 weeks and may be as much longer for ought I know) as also being debarred the use of my penn, which was wont to be a diversion to me though perhaps a nuisance to those I corresponded with. However I would venture that with my friend, as I do att present to transgress my rules by stealing a few short lines in part answer to your last favour of the 28th ult. First then, I find that some people with you are masters of the secret off getting off bad coals in quantities, and it is certain that there has seldom come up more trash to a markett than by this last fleet. I freely own I could have wished that our Stella fitters had not bin so much strangers to that mystery. I think their commodity was not inferior to the Burn or some others, which have disposed of a considerable quantity while our people stood with their arms cross and seemed like Solomon's sluggard; they apprehended a lyon to be upon your key, so durst not venture abroad to sollicitt. Strange perverseness in mankind. The distemper is visible and deeply rooted; we have sufficiently suffered this year but there it is not likely to end. Pray good friend turn your thoughts as my does in the case of my body politic; when an application has bin once tried (which he hoped would have succeeded) and that failed, he rested not till he tried another. And as I have the greatest opinion of his physical performances, so I justly entertain the like of yours in this business. You are upon the spott and know the several parts of the trade that are affected and can give the best guess att the cause, and when that is known pray who can prescribe better. I must own I doe expect no redress but from your endeavours, yet even those can avail little unless the chiefs concerned, that is the 5, should cotton better together than att present they seem to doe; and doubtless the dealers are not unacquainted with the divisions and will improve them by setting distinguishing marks upon some particular concerns. As to the upper seams, spare no industry to get off in this last fleet, though att a less price; they will be infinitely worse for lying over year, increase your dead stock and ten to one but after Christmas 2 or 3 in the will open the trade. I see no help for it. Sunderland grows upon us while we lessen, yet every Tine owner is not I suppose willing to abate one chalder of what his vend has bin for years bypassed and this must needs occasion strange distraction. Would it not be worth your while to postpone the raising of a trunk till we see what turn both the trade and the owners of that concern think to take? has bin out of town near a month and not yet returned, which occasions his silence in your regard; when I see him shall acquaint him etc. My father's offer of taking the tickett was with no other design than hopes of serving you without prejudicing himself. I paid uncle the two £25 for the first . Mrs Smith has writ to Peggy which she says quits scores with you; sends her services, as I do mine also to her and the honest . Kind friend, we are now busy furnishing our little house from top to bottom; and let us contrive as well as we can, will cost us new beginning housekeepers a handsome sum of money, which will drain more than I am att present master off. And as you intimated in one of your former that you would remitt me some towards the latter end of the year, I desire it might be sometime next month if you can , for it will be then that we shall enter upon our new quarters and I shall have several bills to discharge. I must further beg of you to watch John Linskill and desire him to deliver you for my use the bill of sale of a 1/16th of his ship, which belongs to me and the man has never had the manners to do it as yet. If he be not in the ship, pray desire Frank Rudston to write to him for it was partly att your instance that I adventured with him. Pray likewise acquaint honest Jimmy that considering the circumstances of our Stella trade, it seems absolutely necessary that we should have orders from the court how to proceed and then we act securely. To this end a state of the colliery as it is att present with all its difficulties must be drawn up and represented, as also a prospect of gift this next year; and of another hand if that colliery should not be carried on, the inconveniences that would ensue as first the decrease of rents for want of , the loss off the way which would in a manner be entire by rotting upon the ground, the certainty of steath rents etc. to which we are confined by lease. After this the court must judge what is fitting for us to doe and we must pursue the directions given, and then come on it what will, we shall be kept indemnified and blameless in the eye of the world. This must be thought of and returned me up so as to be presented this next term, so pray lay your heads together. I have no more to add, being in an uneasy posture with my 2 legs on a stool almost as highly elevated as my rump. I can't give you authority to drink any new health; I know nothing of the matter further than that the means is frequently made use off for obtaining the end. No more but due respects to friends in your neighbourhood ... My has ordered me to drink punch in moderation, a pint a day. I want some good brandy; pray use your endeavours to procure me some and may disperse 3 or 4 bottles with one master and as many with another. Let them be sealed and tied down. You must also get my madam a table suit of huckaback from Darlington, which I remember is very fine and good of the sort. Adieu. Harry Waters has some money in his hands of mine, £6 14s 6d, the balance of Tom Walker's profitt which you will receive for me and reimburse yourself for these commissions as far as will go.

4th I don't know if I am indebted to my kind friend or no but be that as it will it is no matter; I don't stand upon ceremony, which always ought to give way to business. And as this is the critical time for deciding the fate of the trade and on the resolutions taken depends welfare or ruin, I long to know what steps have bin taken on that head. I have repeatedly recommended both to Jimmy and the to have an understanding in this weighty matter and though either party should suffer a little, better so than the whole go to distraction. Two posts ago I had a letter from the latter, who gives me an account of his installation, thanks me for my thoughts of the renewal of the Regulation, which to him seem the most natural. He adds a computation of charges laying a way from Urpeth to join our own way, as also those of working, and so draws it into a scheme of profit and loss. The quaerys I desire to be satisfied off are whether the lease is to commence att present or after old Tom 's death; whether there be a possibility of obtaining way leaves through grounds and through town fields where are so many different properties? The rent is easy enough. And wain trunk might be converted into a waggon on that occasion very conveniently. He leaves it to me to communicate to my father if I think proper. Accordingly I did in the gross; had I not, perhaps some exception might be taken which I will industriously avoid. I can't yet have his answer. But if the concern were actually taken, she would fall most naturally both for working and leading down Mr way, if he could be prevailed to be content with a share of her and contribute to part of the laying charges through his own ground. This would certainly turn to best account. But of that you can best judge and inform. This fleet is come up. Att their arrival coals were the best, but then the markett was att a stand and since that I hear occasioned by the men refusing to sell but att 29s. I must own I think them in the right. I have wrote to the this post who will discourse you on the points above. I heard you were out of order; pray write particularly to the or send it to me, for without particulars the will not prescribe. I hope Mrs Ramsay (to whom my humble service) will oblige you; there is nothing like taking things in time. The youngest of I doubt will scarce hold out 3 days a violent feavor in her head; poor creature, she has no less than 9 blisters on att this time and is not sensible. If our recovers her he may work miracles. Poor Mrs Smith has likewise bin much out of order for a week by past. She keeps a foot and is to begin to morrow to take some of our sweetmeats. Adieu I am ... Just now the is come in, who in his travels this day hears that our Council disapprove of the peace as proposed. How true this is time will discover.

10th Perhaps my longing desire of hearing frequently from you made me complain without a cause, but I can assure you yours directed to Mr Ashley both came safe and sooner by many hours than if addressed to our own habitation, since in the winter season the post does not deliver our letters till the next . I should in short postscript have advised you of the receipt of yours but he was hurrying me to save a penny so that in all probability I forgot. I have no objection to Johnson's coming, save that by his cunning he may give the dealers a great insight into the foible as the French call it of the coal trade, which they understand too much of already. In the next place you will see they will never treat with us for Stella without the praemiums for the year before as well as this last; both which will to above £200, and perhaps should this be granted I question whether they can doe us or at least will doe us any great service. This is my positive opinion before he arrives, which you will communicate to my good friend of Lamesly and let me know his if we ought to comply provided we have some assurances, which by the by will not be better performed than former ones. But when we have made trial, more cannot be don for the Infant. Our Bucksnook must be wrought to supply the markett with good , nay choice good, the beginning of the year or otherwise the laboring oar will lye dreadfully heavy upon us all the year and that can't be born. Pray therefore send us word if we can propose to work a quantity of right good for this ensuing year. I foresee that concern can't be supported but while the coals are extraordinary, Contract or none. Once a fortnight there ought constantly to be a clear pay att pits and in part for carriadge; the oppression is prodigious by longer delays and gives and others an opportunity of feathering his nest. Recommend this heartily to our friend, who I am sorry is engaged in the black trade if the concern be from Tanfield side. I was sensible from your first undertaking the waggon way you would meet with difficulties and crosses in abundance. There was such a confederated tribe of nested together and each plaid into the other's hand, that I could but admire you could make that impression that has bin made. I believe you will find the same game playing in Richmondshire among the miners and the quondam agents. I am att a loss what to fix you for your pains and trouble; if it should be answerable to either, I know the sum would be very considerable. But att this distance must leave it to Jimmy and your self. You will see what the concern has saved by the alterations and accordingly proportion the reward. I am satisfied £150 is the least that can be made you by the public for your signal services this last year: were they as sensible of it as we that were eye witnesses, they would make it att least a brace. These are my thoughts and pray communicate them to the honest gentleman of Lamesly, who I know will press as much as possible this affair in your favour. My father had last night a large account of the last meeting from the . I have but barely read it over. His quaery to me was what character those fitters have that are appointed for Bensham. They are all set up for themselves since I left you, att least were not of my acquaintance, so was obliged to answer by silence. This good effect the will have, that I hope it will keep both fitters and dealers in a better decorum. Waters's impudence ought to be corrected by the united body. We hear that Biker coal is got: what is your opinion? If the coal be tolerable, that concern may be a thorn in our side and may encourage the fitters to keep up their heads. We leave all of Stella to the honest Vaudois with your assistance and he may depend the dealers will never treat about that concern without the full satisfaction for the 2 last years. But you shall hear more of this shortly for my head and stomach are much disordered and increased by the badness of the weather. The enclosed is my uncle's account of the disposal of your tickett by which you will perceive he has paid me on your account £45 4d for which you have creditt. Yesterday noon dyed old Mrs Blakiston of the gout in her stomach, which had bin there near a month before she sent for our honest but he came too late. The is to the 27th. Next post my wife designs Jimmy a long epistle. Our young pupil has behaved himself not so civilly as he should to his Lady , which has given great offence and makes me sick of my charge. Did you put on board Ableson the wine he presented me? Pray remember me kindly to my factoress. My wife and Mr Genuine present to you their respects and I remain ... I hear by the by that Brummell pretends to lay his way in spite of mankind. My hearty respects to my honest Alderman.

23th Yours enclosed to Mr Ashly came to hand this minute and have sent it to my father to peruse and give him time to consider of it. Therefore am now answering off book, having an hour of leisure and free from company. You desire to know my thoughts of a certain concern but I must first tell you my father's. He you know is very difficult to enter upon any new project which is attended with a present considerable outlay. He is very cautious, which none can blame him for. He sent for me and asked my thoughts. I told him that if way leaves could be had upon tolerable terms and the colliery wrought on such as yours and the represented, I looked upon it as a concern that ought not to be slipped by any means. After a few days he repeated the question; I continued of the same mind. Well, says he, will you go shares? Yes sir, said I, my present opinion is such that I will venture 1/4, nay to share 1/3 if you please. You are welcome, said he. Not long after he produces the several charges of laying the way and working, which he looked upon as too small considerably as well as the rent too great. As to the first I agreed with him that to win and lay the way, £1160 would not doe it. To that of working I told him I thought I could satisfy him to a nicety in that point, for among some of my papers I was sure of finding a project with the exact charges of Mr 's att the time that had taken this, and should look out for it. He was delighted with this. I brought it to him. And where the makes £1 15s the 22 , the other made £1 13s the 42 fother 7 bolls each, so that the tenn would be near upon 50s , water etc. Well, says he, proceed and set down every article what you think may doe. Accordingly I promised I would doe it very liberally, so set down 20d a gate and twice a day made 4d for man and horse, which was as much as his own waggon men could addle. I reckond the way longer by a good mile than Norbanks, however set down 18s a tenn while Mr paid but 12s, yet I would not be positive but that had but 20 to the tenn. I charged 5s tenn for all charges att steath, which is more than will doe it, perhaps pay the and wages into the bargain. The way leaves, steath rents, viewers and all salaries I think £250 yearly, including satisfaction for the liberty of his steath and of the way from the Cowclose to the steath. £2000 for winning the colliery and laying the way and . All these sums except the last I thought would each overdo; and allowing 16 1/2 making out and double coal att 11s, fittage, ' wages and dealers at 6d , there would remain £600 neat upon 600 pitt tenns. The chief dispute with me was whether the way over dean could be effected without casting the way so much to the east as that it would be of the utmost difficulty to bring the up to . As to the rent he was of opinion that 10s was full much. I told him that it was not above 7s for a wain tenn and I thought not att all unreasonable. All this he desired me to draw out in a scheme and send it the which I did above a week ago, and on his answer he will take his final resolution. I would not be over forward in pressing and had rather that things could be brought to bear under the proposal than upon a trial to exceed, for that would make him exceeding uneasy. The next thing that makes the case disputable is the apprehension that it will lessen Team vend and that I doubt is but reasonable to expect. But of another hand I represented that if these coals went unmixed, might probably yield 11s 6d so consequently £250 more yearly profitt; if mixed with Team, would help off with many of his small workings. was with us this day and will wait till we receive the answer. Just now our parcels of wine and ale came home safe. We drank all your healths att supper. The former is very good and the latter we hope, though a little down, will recover with time. The brandy is safe and measure. My good friend will accept of my best thanks for his very kind remembrance. The huckaback 2 pieces of 16d and 14d are with us and well approved off; that of 10 1/2d came not to our hands. I have bin large and particular on the first article of this letter, which you will keep to yourself; if hear further shall be sure to advise. The dealers were with my father 3 days ago. They eat so heartily that poor Mrs Smith could not forbear lifting up her hands, yet would not conclude absolutely for Team the next year though my proposed doing by them as Mr did for and . For they would not engage for 2s 6d if the coals were such as last summer. And if they were assured that they were never so good this next, they would not touch a coal of them unless first satisfied for the year 1710/1711. What ever you doe be sure not to work any but what is choice good and little of Coalburn, as Jimmy and you shall agree, for retrieving the lost reputation. I wish Johnson does not give us the slip, as I have advised the Vaudois. I have wearied my self and my head is confused, but yours is so clear that you will be able I hope to hammer out my meaning. Adieu then and rest assured that I am ... My wife salutes you. My respects to the honest and Mrs .

25th past 7 att night It is of a long standing that I am indebted to you and since you are pleased to allow me that liberty now and then, I doubt I shall be apt to call custom. Your account of the last was the most entertaining of any I have met with. I find your interest helped to strengthen that of the church by which you have curried with the diocesan, and though our friend Jimmy is now allowed to be a white boy, yet I think you stand fairer for while most of your former acquaintance lye under a black censure; how reasonably I can't say but shall leave you to judge. My father being never desired to give the little interest he had, resolved between the two late candidates to stand neuter and leave every one to dispose of their votes as they thought most suitable to their inclinations, but it seems the doctrine is this, those that are not for us are against us. This interpretation I suppose is putt upon it and so he is deemed an enemy to the person elected and the interest that brought him in, by which you see how the cloud still hangs over his head while you are so happy as to enjoy the brightness of the sun in its full meridian. Long may it continue to you in that perfection and answerable to your deserts, still hoping that you will not entirely forget your quondam friends, though now in affliction. But I must drop this subject and proceed to another, which to me seems more material. I must tell you that I had the honour to dine with your honest att my father's last Friday, who entertained me with your nice of his sister's concerns in protecting them against a certain person that formerly by force had got a good yard within them. We drank the champion's health but alas! I was mightily dejected when I heard from that he was confined to his bed. He executed his commission by showing the letters wrote by your ; and as for your project of communicating to Mr Pitts, I could not but approve off and the rather since I find Mr Gibson is so far led by your friend that he will receive no other impression than what he has from him, especially when so backed as by the insinuations and representations of another gentleman, who threatens publicly to tear up all ways that cross a high way or street and so putt the trade upon a level. I won't trouble with a repetition of particulars since I know , who was an ear witness, has given you them att large. Only excuse my adding to your proposal to Sir (for whom assured Mr that he would engage the should let way leave through his grounds upon reasonable terms) that you insist that he grant liberty for a number of years certain, not for his own life, which considering how free he makes with it may not spin out the length of your lease, though you should not renew. I have not seen nor heard from honest since my last to the on that score; my father went about a fortnight since to wait upon him but mistook the coffee house that he frequents, so lost his labour. That concern of his is the only one unopened in all your river that I should covet to be engaged in. Pray how goes on Mr way? Mr would inform what past twixt him and two of the dealers in relation to your concern. They will not undertake for a quantity and indeed there are so many of them in such mean circumstances that you would not desire they should. I doe believe these two are the best of that set but if they will not undertake, I don't see but that if the master undertook for himself, it would be the safest way. But expects your further orders and a ship of the coals for a sample. I am summoned to meet Mr Freak all my father's. Therefore must conclude with hearty wishes for your speedy recovery and the continuance of a health so useful to all your friends. Adieu honest , I remain ... A peace very speedily is expected.

5th I think I must not begin a letter without acknowledging double obligations, but if you had such disturbing weather as we have had of late, you would guess by your own constitution how much a far weaker is influenced by it; and in such circumstances writing is not allowed. It has affected my father not a little, who had begun a letter to you two posts ago but not yet able to finish. Indeed what chiefly disturbed him was his anxious solicitude about poor Kitt Stockdale, who being att diner 3 or 4 days since att Tom Gibson's, was taken so ill with a sort of convulsion that they were obliged to send three people in a coach home with him to support him, and it was so late before he could be removed that the news of his illness came not to my father till near 9 a clock, when good Mrs Smith was detached. She sat up with him as long as she could, being obliged to return to give an account. I can assure you it was a melancholy one since she never expected to see him more. Poor man he lay in such agonys till the next day that he came to himself, that you would admire he should ever get abroad; however his heart was good, and with some cordials (whereof a bottle of your brandy was one) he was brought in a chair to Red Lyon Street day before yesterday where he began again to relapse, but God be thanked, though extremely weak he is got abroad again. You may imagine considering the dearness there is twixt the two what a confusion my father was in, who gave due attendance to his even to the last extremity. This he desired me to acquaint you with and hopes for your pardon to his silence till next post. I gave the a full account of what passed twixt honest and me the day after I received his and your letter, which doubt not he has communicated. promised that when ever he received any account from the north about Urpeth (the letting of which he did not in the least expect) that he would call upon me in his way to his and give me an account, but I have not seen or heard from him since. The loss of poor is not easily to be repaired. My wife and I went last Sunday night to sup att Mrs Wait's, where we found poor Mrs Betty Barnes melancholy to a degree and not without reason. I sent your last enclosed immediately away to . It is a complete answer to such allegations as one would not admire to see subscribe too, but for a person of the other rank methinks tic unaccountable; but one plainly sees that he pins his faith upon some people's sleevs. and I had talked over the matter in my parlour and I gave him such reasons for your conduct as I was capable off and convinced uncle fully, who is a person that is as well heard by as any. But Jackson has laid such a foundation in his opinion as nothing but time and experience can root it out. Therefore I think you are to blame if you concern yourself further. You have don handsomely and friendlily by Mr ; if he will still be led by the nose, much good may doe him. He may smart att long run. I am sensible the weather must have distressed your vend, as also that a trunk though never so small would have bin of singular service. You are left to act as you think fit in relation to that, whose all ways sways with me. Get a ship for a sample as soon as you can when the weather is dry; if the coals be roundy, I hope Projector may be of service, and be sure not to send the worst. Mr has bin sadly plagued with your carrier about a box Jimmy sent up before he came to town, directed to Mr in . sends a letter for the box, which was with a demand of 16s after the rate of 3d pound; the was offered if he would give an acquittance, but that being refused, the money was detained. Now you must know he wrote twice to you about it to know if his paying 3d for a box so directed would not be to your prejudice and that you would discourse the carrier, but you never took the least notice, so that his back is up and what adds to it is since he had like to have bin arrested for the money. He has wrote I suppose an angry letter to Jimmy this post, I suppose on the same subject. Pray if this day's Medley come to your town, read it; you will think the time well spent. I have nothing to add further save my respects to the honest and all friends that wish me well. I am ...

May 13th I am entirely unfitt for this employ therefore must be short, especially since I write by stealth and I know of my being here, who will certainly catechise me if he finds the pen in my hand. What I wrote to the last was by my father's directions and am sorry it should have given any offence. The chief objection he has a mind to have removed was about the validity of the lease let by Jackson to Sir and , for as I take it he had let everything that was in his power, and if that stand good what will a new lease avail us? If it would answer the ends proposed he would be willing to contribute his share among the rest of our brethren, nay even for Bensham it self rather than fail. But we would be glad to be first satisfied what are each man's proportions and to have that objection as above cleared. In the next place as to Stella, we that transact have our hands tied up and can't act with safety but by order of court. I have consulted a great person on this head, who tells me that before we were called to account before the court, we were att liberty to act according to the best of our , but now that we are before our Master nothing can be don with safety for the trustees but by an order. However I doubt not you might menage the matter well enough if you would indulge honest Jimmy a little, but I beg of you not to mention a syllable of this to any person. As to the charges that may accrue by endeavouring to stop the proceedings through what you took off Tom Shaftoe, as it was don by order of the 5 so it must and shall be repaid and that punctually too, though I were to do it out of my own pocket for our share of . Don't take any thing by a wrong handle I beseech you; that you should imagine that we should either call your in question, or your integrity, is all wrong my good friend. I could heartily wish that my head and hands would allow me so much liberty of thought as formerly. I would convince you that we are the same as usual. But by the by let me advise you to state the case plainly and send us up the particulars in a letter to my father, after which you shall have I doubt not a satisfactory account to your mind. Now friend my is come and along with him; there is so much noise I can't tell what I write, excuse therefore all faults and believe me to be with a cordial sincerity and true affection ... I have charged Charles this day with your complaints. Excuse faults.

July 3d 1712 Yours of the 27th ult. lies now before me. It came but to hand late on Monday evening so that I could not send to Mr Sanderson, but on Tuesday I wrote a line to him to entreat him to come to my house any time that day which suited most with his convenience and bring along with him your two letters of the date yours mentions. He returned for answer by word of mouth that he would wait on me; accordingly I stayed below stairs till after 10 att night, att which despaired of seeing him, but just as I was undressing for bed some body rattled att the door and it proved to be my gentleman. I buttoned on my cloths and down I went. I told him I had a budgett off complaints to produce against him for his slowness in proceeding in your business. I read to him part of yours. He told me that he had all along told you the reason of his delay was that he could not proceed till he had got Jackson's answer, a copy of which he had got out of court that very afternoon and not before, and that now he was prepared to go thorough stitch and apprise the court all att once; that as success hitherto constantly attended him, he did not doubt but in less than a fortnight's time to give you an account that would be to your satisfaction, and that he would shortly go to Sir Joseph Jekyll one of your council to give him full instructions and desired I would accompany him. I told him that if he thought I could be any ways serviceable, on notice I would attend. He showed me the 2 letters of the 26th and the other. I explained it to him as I had don some time before so that he owned he thought himself perfectly master of it. Before our conversation ended it struck 11 a clock, which was the reason why I could not write by last post, and before we parted made him promise me he would write att large to you by this post and give you a particular account. As for the ship off Cliffton's I can't tell what will be don. has bin twice down about him but can't get a coal off: they offer him but a guinea a . I went down on Tuesday last to the Gate where I see Cliffton, who told me he had bin near a month att the markett. I inquired what praemium he had to give, the master; he told me 9d . If I mistake not, said I, Mr wrote me word he did allow you 12d. No indeed sir, not one farthing more than 9d. Upon this I sent for Watts and told him that he would oblige me if he would help off with that bulk of upper seams and should receive 4 1/2d provided he would give 22s, which was the lowest price that any of the 11s coals passed att. He would not engage further than a promise to help off with 3 or 4 score att the latter end off the ship. I then sent for Arlington, Hartley and Wren; promised them the same but first of all desired the master not to mention whose coals they were, because you had a little difference with the two latter, but only should call his coals upper seames, which he did. They likewise promised a little assistance; as for the other dealers not one would touch a coal. In short the master does not I find understand the Gate and he will meet with much difficulty. I told him that I hoped to be down once more this week and then shall inquire how those that have promised doe perform, though I own I expect little from either the great or small dealers. I am going to make a visit to our honest Durham Recorder who leaves us to morrow. Wishing you all health and happiness concludes me ... P.S. I went down to the Temple where I see who will give you a full account this post. He likes the affidavits wonderfully you gave him; was asking me if it would not be a prejudice to the lord's colliery if that way was suffered. I told him that it would doubtless; for this reason, that the other coals were a much more vendible commodity which would be led down by that way att a much cheaper rate than usual and in vast quantities, and consequently must lessen the vend of those that had a meaner sort, much as the lessees generally had, and so must throw up their leases etc. He told me it was a very material point and wished you could send up an affidavit to that effect which would be of very singular service. Adieu, excuse errors, I have not time to peruse.

26th 1712 Your very entertaining letter by yesterday's post has revived a little my low pulse, which any that feels it would fancy I was expiring. For this ten days past I have not bin able to set pen to paper but once to Jimmy , and that was a work of necessity that engaged me to give him an account of the insolent behaviour of those vile wretches att the Gate, who though they knew I was so ill as not to receive company yet forced themselves upon me. You will think it strange how they could doe so, but it was by a mistake in my man who told me they were some masters of ships who desired to speak with me, and accordingly were admitted. The first that offered himself was fat , then his , Blunkett and Coltman. We battl'd it for 3 hours till diner parted us: I neither offered them to eat nor drink with us. They insisted upon full pay but I would not part with a farthing till I had Jimmy's order. I told them that they had almost every fleet bought att 6d below the markett, and I could prove it upon them by several of our Team ships as well as others, and that Robinson's and Weatherley's coals which were bought for 10s got the same price with generally speaking; that as they had not performed their part, I hope they would not blame me for keeping such a part of the praemium in hand to make satisfaction to our masters that were sufferers, etc. They stomached this extremely but I stood to my tackle. Indeed some must be thought of to break into the measures of these great men, otherwise we shall be slaves with a witness, and this without loss of time. I am turning my head upon a project for which considering the smallness of the hope may succeed; it is among the petty dealers but where there is a that will not doe. However I want such a headpiece as my friend to assist me or rather to correct my rude notions of trade, whose I set no greater value upon than it deserves. I congratulate you sincerely upon your late but signal victory but be sure not to trust to their . is att Richmond, however I am preparing a note to your namesake the 's son to dispatch yours away to his master. I am satisfied in conscience that what you have so earnestly and hazardously espoused and att long run carried, will prove the saving of the trade from ruin, nay beyond all retrieve, and doe you think or can anybody think it that an answerable return be made you for your pains? I don't mean what was proposed formerly, because that was only for your friend and mine the honest but particularly appropriated to yourself. You have bin a considerable sufferer in your own private concerns to my knowledge and might have had terms such as you pleased to have insisted on from those you have now laid upon their backs, provided you would have given no obstruction to their destructive career. Sure then there is not a coal owner of any consideration in your river but that will make an offering to your self either in one respect or other that should be in some measure adequate to your sufferings and desert. Were I in the country, should be the first that should propose something of this nature and shall in the mean time recommend it as far as I am capable. Considering that no real misfortune befell the judges, it was as lucky and pleasant hit as could have befallen your antagonists. It is so remarkable that in an age it can't be forgot. You can't imagine how crest fallen are those mighty dealers upon these tidings. They used to threaten me with Bucks Nook, that the next year we should go a begging with our Team, and for those and and would be able to supply the chief of the trade to this port with the best of commodity, and I should then plainly see the difference in price which should be 6d . Oh this is a bitter pill to them. I must now beg excuse for breaking of abruptly. My head is sadly disturbed, and I wish I be able to write a few lines to my father; though have no novels of any sort, yet would not be wanting in paying my dutiful respects to him by inquiry after his health, now that the fatigue of the assizes is over. Howere least I have not time, desire you will plead my pardon. My best respects to all friends. I am ... You must make excuses till next post to my father, for I am not in a condition to write. I see Sanderson who promises to write to you but least he should fail, tells me that no affidavits can be preferred before next term. Adieu.

13th 1712 I had yours with the affidavit and enclosed answer to it in course. As luck would have it was come to town 2 or 3 days before, and happened to dine att my cosen's in Bedford Row that very day and was engaged to spend his afternoon there. Upon this notice I wrote a note to him and dispatched it away. I told him that I had by that post a packet with some matter of importance to be communicated to him, that I promised he should be dismissed in half an hour. Upon the of mine the ladies who were att cards with him were very unwilling to part with him, but upon the promise that he should not be detained long they consented. I waited att home all the afternoon and about 8 a clock my gentleman made his appearance. I first produced the affidavit which he had seen before, then I read to him deliberately the answer to every particular of it, with which he was extremely pleased. I asked if any explanation was wanted, he told me no; that it was couched in such plain, easy and express terms that he could make your counsel as much masters of it as I was my self. He told me he had bin att the Lord Keeper's several times to inquire how matters stood, but he was in the country and not expected back for several weeks. Then he went to his secretary on the same inquisitive errand; he was upon his diversions in Kent, which is generally practised by the gentlemen of business during the vacation. So that is positive nothing can be don till next term and is satisfied no alteration of the order will be made, being there has bin no of such a practice in that court. However as was going out of town to visit some of his wife's relations for a week or ten days, I charged that he would call again the last thing he did both at the Keeper's and his secretary's to get information and give you an account, and att his return I shall take care to remind him. All this he gave me his word and hand should be don and every thing else that was necessary. I read him over the letter and desired of him to consider in time what further affidavits were necessary, so that timely notice might be given you. I gave him the answer to the affidavit. I received half a crown for postage, after which we parted. You have now I perceive drawn your sword and thrown away the scabbard. My best wishes attend you. And doubt not of your success, depending on the righteousness of your cause. In the next place, I must most earnestly recommend to you the giving in your account of the Chopwell way without loss of time, though it were but in gross for timber so much, workmanship in another article, so that four or five heads will suffice; and give it into Mr for our accounts must be made up off hand and without that of yours they can't close that year's book. I therefore earnestly entreat you will doe it and I shall reckon it a particular obligation laid upon ...

1st 1712 You have obliged me extremely by your two last. Just now I am sent for to meet Jack att the Tavern to drink a token from Jimmy , a place I have scarce troubled since you left the town. This will oblige me to cut short. Therefore you will excuse if I write as a late author does, by sentences. No longer than yesterday's post, I had in a postscript to the an under my father's own hand for taking upon the best terms. So shall meet Tom and both att the Tavern on Monday or Tuesday next in order to conclude if possible. I thank you for your kind offer in relation the of my 1/4. I acquiesce in what you judge most necessary about working or lying in the upper seams, about which you have a vast of trouble and scurvy usage. I could have wished that the terms for Ramsay's way, as also through Team had bin thoroughly adjusted, for I shall find a tedious business off it if left to me to transact with him. It is not becoming one in my circumstances to object any thing he may think reasonable etc. I am concerned that the number 5 should not as yet have rewarded you for your journey. I was an eye witness to the indefatigable pains you took in a service for which you did deserve a generous recompense and even without a demurr. Methinks it is copying after the public. I am sorry that my interest should be off disservice rather than otherwise to you att this time: and that a suspicion should be raised that I am playing into your hand when I only recommend to them to be mindful and not to neglect a person so capable of serving or otherwise distressing them in their business according as he is used. But a word to the wise is enough. Your scheme seems justly calculated about way and steath rooms. No objection have I to it but this; when it is known that you have taken all those and on supposition that you should even lay the on his back (which I hope you will be able to effect), yet say I, will not that give a colourable handle for bringing in and obtaining an Act for giving a reasonable compensation for all manner off way ? I don't infer from thence that there is any just grounds to be given for so doing, yet reason does not att all times prevail, nay the best are but indifferently heard in a crowd. I give only this touch for you to improve. I am glad to hear you have had the offer of ; it is a certain sign they grow sick of their undertaking. You would doe well to know the real terms on which she will be let, as also the party or parties that will join in the letting, for I am satisfied has the least share and that she is like a bastard whose mother can't give an account off the real father. In the next place you must be satisfied on what terms Sir and others will let way leaves and att what price the way as it now lies. They will certainly endeavour to deny you as much as possible. It is worth while likewise to consider if feasible to lay a from the pitts to the mount, for as it is their coals don't entirely answer the expectations off the markett by reason that they don't come as round as formerly. I thank you for your kind offer off letting me be concerned as a in whatever offers. You lay me under deep obligations, which under present circumstances I cannot tell how to rubb out. My time off draws near. Have but time to thank you for the d's comical adventure; to request secrecy in this as far as you think necessary, and therefore get Mr Ashley to frank for me; and so wish you success in your cause which is putt off till Tuesday or Thursday next and to all your family welfare and happiness. I remain ... Read this if you can.

20th 1712 These great and lasting falls of snow will not allow me to alter my tone in regard to health and what discourages me much is it has affected our honest to that degree that he is confined to his bed, and none allowed to see him but the apothecary. However I can't forbear writing a line to my good friend, notwithstanding these afflictions, and inform him a little of what passes in relation to the matter on the anvil. It is near a week since young Whitfield delivered a paper book off a lease in form, which I read cursorily over and sent it to my father, whose indisposition would not allow him to look it over till the day before yesterday, with which he was not well pleased. The rent is there to commence from Candlemas. The lands he will not on any advanced rent let to us. Therefore we shall have a troublesome matter to adjust about damages. By this lease we are to pay 40s damage for heap room, with the addition of the word yearly; that we are to make ample satisfaction besides for way leaves and all spoil off ground for building hovels, stables, cottages and all other necessaries for the colliery, the like I believe was never heard off. In the next place they foist in a new that we shall not let or assign any part off the colliery to any without the privity and consent of the lessor first obtained in writing, on penalty of forfeiture of the lease; and several other strange unheard off clauses. On this my father called a council, whereof Dan was one and I the other. The question being putt what was most fitting to be done in this emergency, I proposed to send their paper book as also your instructions and lease to John Ord, with yours and the last remarks copied, and those heads that we had agreed to before and was to be the true foundation for a lease, and see if he could hammer out of both a lease that would be most to mutual advantage of both parties; that the harsh part of their paper book should be softened so as it may be advisable for the lessees to comply with. This was resolved upon nominee contradicent and accordingly the whole was putt yesterday into Mr Ord's hands, who promised to bring us a copy of such a lease he shall think proper we should insist on by Tuesday next. He says that several of the lands, as the Riding and others, are copyhold and consequently the bishop's royalty. By all which you may guess that our trouble is not ended, nay far from it, for I doe assure you that Tom is so positive that I doubt he will not relinquish a tittle; therefore must beg your further advice how we should act in this matter and how far. I don't know but that my father writes to the by this post, but if he does not I desire you will communicate to the honest the contents of this letter. In the next place I must acquaint you that we had several meetings with the Billingsgate people but nothing is yet fixed upon with those vermin. They hang in a clan much firmer than the coal owners and are truer to each other; I doubt the harmony among the Gentlemen will not be long lived. My head and from thence to foot are full of pain, therefore excuse faults and hast from ...

1st 1712/13 Yours of the 23th ult. lies before me. Have weighed the account you give about wining off . I must readily concur with you that the best method will be off attempting to get her to the dipp as far as you can, but with this caution that you be sure off a good roof (which may be easily discovered by the boring); otherwise you may depend that where there is but little roof and even that tender, the coal will prove mean and chargeable working, by reason you can't drive the bords to any breadth, and the insett into a colliery is much the same as the outburst off the seam, both being fagg ends and of no intrinsic value. But I know you have the ablest off heads to determine, to whose I perfectly submit, as also to yours about building the steath dyke with stone, and if you get that done for £15 a keel birth it will be a penny well bestowed. has bin with me and informed me off some of the particulars off that letter he last from the honest . You must know that on Saturday I got Mr to step with our rough draught to Tom who had bin in a high wrath att us for keeping his fowl copy till Wednesday; he said it was only tricking him and delaying of time. when I sent him ours last Saturday he was in better temper, all which I attribute to the absence off who was gon into the country for a few days. He promised to peruse and give notice when we should have a meeting, but not the least as yet is come. I must not omit acquainting you that Tromantal called here on Tuesday as he went to visit Tom. I desired he would make this his way home and give an account if any new discovery could be made. He accordingly came and told me that all was broke off; that we had endeavoured to foist in the Riding and collieries which are neither or parcel of and that his had nothing to doe with either, and since we designed to impose upon him we should find our selves mistaken. And further he added that he did apprehend that Ord was employed in drawing our lease, and if that was we should never have any thing to do with the colliery. To this replied that he knew Mr Gowland was our country attorney and that did the family's business in town, and so forth. This is the substance of what past, since which we have not had the least summons. I communicated this to who seemed surprised and would be willing to serve us to the utmost, but it is not in his power att present. He thinks the damages but att the same time joins in opinion with me that his will never sign unless we first comply with that and all other though never so unreasonable. In short I apprehend he will raise new difficulties. It is an easy matter to find a stone to throw att a dog. We must expect all the hardships to be putt upon us, however we must dispense with them as well as we can in hopes that will be kind, and I would willingly part with Riding and if Tom would sign our lease when those two are scratched out. For Mr Ord assures me that the Riding is copy hold and he thinks also that of , and as our landlord is extremely touchy we must not give him the least ground for it. Another he has, as told me, was that some body had wrote his word that you were a party concerned. To which I answered that considering the difficulties we laboured under, I thought we were much obliged to you or any body that would embark along with the and me; that we needed the best off heads as well as purses. I assured him that the and I proposed to have att least each 1/4; that my father had not yet fixed upon his share; sometimes he talked of having the other 1/2 for and the but of what signification will it be to the lessor to know what we admitted? I have read that part of the 's letter to my father ofter than once which related to the settling his demands for way leave, but never found him in an humour disposed to talk off it. You know it must come naturally and without force, therefore must wait a season. Perhaps it might not doe amiss if the did write a line or two to and desire that he would put my father in mind of adjusting that matter speedily. I am heartily sorry to hear your complaints; hope that when is once a going it will afford you some diverting exercise, which may not a little contribute to the health of one of the usefullest friends the world. I wish it may prove such, as also that this ensuing year may be successful to you without limitation. I am ... I am far from well, nay very far, yet jog on. My father is rather better than when I wrote last to the poor .

24th 1712/13 Betwixt you and me, I have scarce ever bin more out of order than for these 3 weeks last past, which still hangs upon me. My complaint chiefly is off a pain between my stomach and bowels. It is constant without cease and from whence this should proceed I know not, unless it be that the humour from my legs be reverted to the stomach and so gets into my head. My appetite is so far gon that an ounce will serve me more than a day. And my head is almost constantly dizzy; this redoubles my complaints to my who has altered his medicines several times without success. I leave you to judge of my circumstances, when a bottle off true and sound clarett does not relish in the least but every glass goes grain. I have bin vomited and purged times without number; nothing remains but patiently to submit. Sure I am that every letter I receive from you affords me more relief than the richest cordial from the apothecary's shop. But a word of business in the next place. I am fully convinced that is endeavouring all he can to undermine us; which after so many assurances that were not extorted from him, when last in town, that he would not be concerned att present with her scarce on any terms since he had won his own anew. Nay had he known that my father had any thoughts that way, he would never have interfered in the least and was sorry that by his means we were screwed up to such high terms. But I find this is all Team talk, as Kitt Stockdale phrases it. He plays his game by who has got the length of old Tom's foot, who has wrought him up to have a perfect aversion to us. I need not represent to you again the violent passion he was in that we did not dispatch the lease quicker. He said that was a plain indication that we did not design to take her att all, but only to prolong a treaty so as to exclude others. When we sent back his own lease with some few he had 3 or 4 days to consider, after which he scratches out the most of ours and sends back word by that if we did not comply, we should never have his consent. Then we detached who talked a little to Tom and told him there was very little difference 'tween us, that he durst affirm that if we had a meeting for one hour, matters in dispute would soon be adjusted. The next day I went to wait on him to desire he would appoint a time and place. But that very day he was taken ill and continued invisible ever since, save that had once or twice and found him so ill that he durst not mention a word of business, except that he promised to send word to and us when he found himself fit for discourse. Since that he has bin removed to Kensington, and when my father very civilly sent his on Tuesday last to inquire after his health, the answer was that he was better but not a syllable of his hopes of seeing us shortly. This came here, brought no tidings from Russell Street but that his did recover. He seems to be very firm and steady to us. He told Mr this that Jack should never have her as long as he lived, though he should offer never so much; that he hoped in a short time all would be concluded with us. Now my good friend time spends apace and these delays off Tom's are purely to make a hard bargain harden, thinking thereby we shall grow sick off waiting, and after all I durst venture a wager that he will not recede in the least from his demands. As to Mrs 's joining, I will be bold to say that she will never be prevailed with to doe . If therefore there be no absolute occasion for her doing, it is better not to mention; it will raise some new scruples before the old ones are removed. For further particulars referr you to Mr Ord who knows all the objections that were last made by and . I must own I can but pity the circumstances of that young gentleman which seem to tend apace to ruin. I did communicate to what you had bin doing for his service and to Mrs what related to her; she wishes all lovers success. is in much wrath with the fitters. Pray what steps are most advisable to be pursued in relation to ; the will inform you of a letter that my pappa wrote to Sir Middleton on that head. Vane will never let his to any of the family. There is a share off Mrs Midford's, 1/24; I should think that Jimmy could be the best transacter there. For we shall find him as averse to treat as in any former ; could you think of any 3d person who might unsuspectedly treat with him? But can you think that any of these will be willing to part with any of their shares att a less price than they have att present? I fancy not till they have bit upon the bridle. However your thoughts are always very acceptable to ... Pray what of gallons go to a bowl: it was inserted by 35 and 3 pints, which I altered to 35 3/4 with a reasonable streak. I am heartily concerned att your illness, which hangs long upon you. Poor Lord sent to inquire when I had heard from his friend , if dead or alive, for he heard not from you above a fortnight since. Besides says my lord, does he write you ever a smotty story; yes I replied. Oh then he will doe well says my lord, but why does he never write me such? I made answer that I apprehended you were in mighty with my lady att present and had no mind to be outed by a fat story. Oh says he, she likes it as well as I.

May 8th 1713 I have bin under great tribulation for several weeks by past, out off which I have no present prospect off deliverance or relief. My legs are more inflamed than off late and the same humour has struck up into my body, stomach and head, which affects me not a little as you may imagine. My has tried several new by altering off his prescriptions but without the least success. All which have weakened me extremely; besides want off appetite and rest have perfectly confounded me. My wife would have the sent for last night after 11 to take a perfect view off my legs, who gave me a dose off opium immediately, but alas I waked att one and never slept till 7 this after which I slumbered till 9. Indeed my good friend I am in a bad condition, but conceal it as much as I can from my hands to avoid trouble. Your silence has a little added to my affliction, though I partly guess att the meaning. You have taken the right method off writing to my father directly upon business, and if you don't receive an immediate and direct answer, yet now and then att some distance off time reminding him or getting to doe it will have the desired effect. I wrote to him by yesterday's post, with a desire to show you the letter; it was in the nature off a begging letter for a little off your assistance, if suited with your convenience. Must likewise desire the favour of you when att leisure to draw a short account off our partnership, that we may see how matters stand between us; and in the next place that you would lessen your stock as much as possible. I dare not venture to give you the reason att this distance, but it is what is practised by the most judicious and most substantial people off this town, and you may depend you will find your advantage in so doing. You see how I make free with my old friend, yet I have not don with my supplications. You must know that our friend Jimmy was so kind as to send me up 4 off good clarett. I got it but into my cellar on Saturday last. My father heard a character, came and tasted and highly approved, upon which could not doe less than make him a present of a ; and Lord having some top company, begged a bottle of north country bear which I readily supplied him with as also half a off the clarett, which was not ill bestowed. In short I am reduced to my primitive half or therabouts, therefore if you could procure me 2 off that which is right good I desire you would doe it and send it ship. Let it be entered, otherwise we shall be putt to trouble. Sometimes perhaps you may meet with a taste of good white; there is no such thing to be had here, none but ports. If such a thing should fall in your way, I would be very thankful for a or so. Be pleased to place to my account what you disburse. There were two complaints one Allatson, master, who sold his coal as : the people att Gate that had some off them make a demand off off my father and no such ship was reported, whence I conclude they came from our . However it would please my father much if we gave ours the name off Redhugh or any other, purely to prevent confusion at the latter end off the year. I had a letter from last post, wherein he tells me that he has or will send up our coals from Chopwell that will prove good in nature, though will perhaps be small. Pray acquaint him that for a little they might be taken off, but he may depend that unless they doe come roundy we shall be dropped as heretofore. And when we were upon a project off retrieving the lost reputation off our coals, that the method is it not by sending up small coal though never so good in nature; no that will not doe. I requested him to give us a taste off the best att first that the dealers may experimentally find their amends, but now we loose time, which is very precious ... must first caution you not to show this to any. Poor Lord has lost his only son by this lady, since which he has bin seized with a sort off an aguish fever has bin vomited once or twice. I saw Tom Day yesterday who tells me his is better. I wish you joy off our peace with France; about middle of next week we expect another day of rejoicing for that with Spain. So I hope we shall be a happy people, and remain ... I hear that the number Ten are publicly soliciting masters to load att the Grand Lease, with large assurances that they shall be within 6d off and price. By this you may judge how natural it is for some people to meet with favours. Pray my humble service to honest Ramsay, whose bill of £100 I have just now paid. .S. I have just now an account that designs to import some good wine. If so it will ease you off the commission, which I discharge, as also off the white wine; but must desire you to inform yourself of himself or and desire if they could get a piece off good white that they would order it accordingly. Adieu.

June 13th 1713 I had yours some time ago, for which I am indebted to you. Your bill was punctually paid and I have given you creditt in my account as I formerly hinted to . This sort off employ is very irksome to me on account off the bad off health and indeed my complaints increase with the heat off the weather; however to hear off the welfare off my friends (amongst which you will give me leave to style Mr none off the least) would be a cordial and not inferior to any I receive from my . Let me therefore have a line or two att a leisure minute, if such a one be to be had, for I know you have bin and I doubt are still upon double duty; I heartily wish that the same success as hitherto has attended you may accompany you to the end off the chapter. Pray let me have your thoughts a little in relation to trade; it is in great confusion beyond all dispute but as it appears to me it is not yet arrived to its full perfection. I draw my inference chiefly from the great number off large ships that are taken up by the att this juncture for transporting our forces from Ostend to Ireland, att least 40 sail, some say 50, which one can't expect to return into the coal trade again before . Again, I apprehend that our oversee trade is knocked on the head, if true what I heard this day, that the have stopped 15 off our ships in Roan river; will not suffer them to unload nor return, it is supposed till such time as they know the fate off the trade bill here in England. Besides I doubt a unanimity off the number 5, who were they actually all off a piece yet I don't see how they can preserve the trade from ruin. These are melancholy circumstances, off which I can't foresee any precaution that will effect a cure. Here I conclude must acquaint my good friend that Mr and mother have both refused absolutely to join with my father in his bill off interpleader and answer unless you be brought in as well as Trumball, which if they persist in will occasion a great delay as well as charge. Further that my father is very unwilling to comply till he had first obtained your permission. He was pleased to ask my opinion: I told him without hesitation that since it appeared to be a point off consequence, I could parole you would not oppose, nor entertain the worse thought off him for so doing. I desired he would write to the to wait on you as soon as his came to hand, that you would lay your heads together, and if you had not leisure to write, that he would by the very return off the post, otherwise it will be too late. He had the account off Mr from Hebdon by last post. Now my good friend I have finished my paper, and have left room only to assure you that I am ...

June 20th 1713 Though I have wrote 4 letters att least to you without any answer to them, save a line or two about a month ago, yet I can't forbear you see giving the trouble of this and taking the opportunity off lamenting my misfortune off having forfeited the of a friend whose correspondence I so much valued; especially att a juncture when I stood most in need off his assistance and advice. You don't know in what perplexity I have bin in off late about my or rather of . In short I have the following account in relation to the upper seams as nicely as I could. That during my uncle Tom's life, Johnson and Ned Carr were the acting for that concern, att which time those upper seams were wrought by W.
