I don't know if the had got any Lisbon or if he had only the prospect off getting.

East Street, 2d 1716 For this fortnight or longer I have bin extremely bad; a constant dizziness in my head, sick att stomach and am apprehensive off a touch off the palsy, being held much after the same manner I was 3 years ago. This makes me wish Sir John 's return. The other day I took away 21 ounces; the blood had not bin out off the vein 2 minutes till it turned all blew and yellow. I took here picra every day but gave no relief. Yesterday T. Wakelin sent me a potion which had no great effect. To morrow he has ordered to drink purging waters with manna or some other equivalent. Believe me my good friend I have had much ado to keep afoot the latter part off the summer. I wish I be able to doe the like this fall. I am now sensible that a constitution when once broke thoroughly, as mine has bin, can never be united again. The learned with all their skill can but make patched work on it. Within this fortnight I wrote twice to you and transcribed in each a long paragraph from a quondam friend off yours; since which I have not had a line from you, which makes me apprehensive one or both might have miscarried. By the same post I wrote to Peter to let you have the off your account but before he did it, that he should advise with the Guardian and have his approbation, without which, as he is on the spott, I know it would be reckoned a presumption off the highest nature. I happened to fall in with Jimmy att the coffee house last Sunday; he told me that he had heard that Mr Pitt and the Lady were upon a close treaty with you, which he hoped would succeed. I replied that if they did not stand in their own light, I doubted not off your inclinations and ability to serve both the and lady. I hear is upon his return, re infect . However his project has obliged the Sunderland owners to admeasure, whereas if I mistake not that was in a great measure disused off last year. I wrote lately to the about Farnacres and desired him to consider, now that he has a fair prospect off getting down a pitt about , if some provision should not be made out off Whickham top coal to help off with those stone coal, without which depend upon it they will not be marketable. I hope your Park water catchers have no diffidence off compassing what they proposed in relation to that concern. I again must repeat my thankfulness to you for all kind offers. What provocation was given the knight, att a late sitting, to the honest to that degree? Has there bin any old grudge lying latent twixt them? No coals go off so currently all this year as Mr . The dealers say that Bucks Nook comes fowl, which is occasioned by mixture; and much crestfallen; Team not much to be complained off; in worse repute than ever, seldom comes within 13d off Team; the Grand Lease abominable; and Felon att a low ebb; and Elswick not so much as once named. Our friends are still in Hertfordshire and don't return till middle off this month; I hear nothing off the motion of those from your quarters, they like their . But if the weather be the same with you as it is here, they will have reason to repent they did not move sooner. I always forget my self when I converse with you; I find no end till I come to that off my paper, which now calls on me to conclude ... The Regent seems very desirous off cultivating a strict friendship with us and there looks to be a good disposition towards peace in the north. When I can learn the certainty you shall hear further. However these have off a sudden raised stocks very high.

27th 1716 I have bin confined to my house ever since my last to you, which was Saturday's post, and very ill I have bin and att present my spirits so sunk that I can scarce speak to be heard. Yet am sensible that a man off industry ought not to be balked. In relation to the affair off and misapplication off the moneys for charitable uses, some honest gentlemen in the neighbourhood or substantial or inhabitant I believe might file a short bill off complaint against the managers, and if they can make out their allegations that very charitable gift may be obliged to make good the charge off the suit. You know that my Lord can't be advised with because it may come before him; but I know a parallel case in some measure to this where the parties prosecuting succeeded. I was directed as most proper to take the opinion off some learned counsel, which is the best way off proceeding if as above or by information in the Bench. If you think proper, draw up the state off the case as full yet as brief as you can and I shall lay it before some able off the learned. To have his opinion will not cost above 2 . As to your former enclosed I can't yet come att it to gratify your desire off having it returned, neither can I give you a farther insight than what has bin hitherto done. If you will take my notion tic this. Suppose you should get the who is willing to signify the substance off what he knows, without any name, transmitt it and I will lay it before you know , who will be better able to judge off the merit. You know we are cautious how we promise, but when we have done, a punctual performance may be expected and above all a secrecy from that quarter may be depended upon. I need not enlarge. Pray is not a new undertaking near bottomed? Tic about the time proposed. Adieu ...

20th 1716 I am obliged by your the last post, which had it brought better tidings off your health would have bin much more acceptable, though I think towards the end off the first paragraph you seem to prick up. Alas , I am pestered with an old humour which haunts a great toe. I have bin in Small's hands almost every day this fortnight; you can't readily imagine the pain I undergo by having the nail even to the very root forced out, and the surgeon's design seems to leave me none. Besides his cutting and slashing, he never leaves me without an application off precipitate corrosive powders which keep me warm day and night: this last I did not sleep an hour from the time I went to bed till I rose this , and that is a melancholy ditty. The wrote me word off the coaling Farnacres and promised a further account in a post or two; nevertheless should be glad from time to time to hear from you the cracks off her. In answer to his I told him I expected to have a for a trial gratis (save I would pay freight) as soon as he had got well into her. In the next place must tell you that neither my father nor I ever heard a syllable from on the subject; we had bin att his door two or 3 times, insomuch that I advised my father to send this to know what he had done in the matter. The answer was that he was wrote to to sue out the patent, for Mr I presume, but when he applied he found some other person had bin employed in that affair and that they had sent it down by Tuesday's post; by which I apprehend that Mr must have miscarried. Had I not bin confined in a manner to the house by this toe I would have had from his own mouth the particulars. Mr Roper was the person sent, and he can neither receive nor bring an answer to satisfaction. No more on this till I am better informed from himself, save that I am given to understand that the Gatekeeper corrected the mistake by inserting Wolsington instead off Elswick, but these matters for your self. I delayed answering your quondam 's for a fortnight att least and then did it in a few lines. The 4 names I sent to my friend this afternoon in a letter, since which have had no account than that it was to his own hand and that is enough. One would think that an evil spirit was got into a off mine. My father had an account off it before but chose to conceal it. You have business enough for a off tolerable heads on your hands besides that off the public. We are all mortal and suppose you should drop, would not your family be strangely bewildered? Could Mr entail on his posterity his head and genius in business well and good, but when all is don experience is a great matter. Excuse this freedom, which comes from him that is not capable off advising, yet is a perfect well wisher to you and yours. Adieu ... We don't know what to think off the dismission off Lord Townsend. The Torys crow. Mrs having obtained a commission off lunacy her husband, the met this day. I heard her council. By what passed it is guessd'd she will prove him such.

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: London Nov 11 1731 Dear Momma We take this opportunity to return you thanks for your kind letter, and are very glad to hear that sister July is so well recovered. Our cloths are very threadbare and look very shabby. We should be very glad to make them last till we come down to you at Christmas but they are worn out so already that we cannot. We have took several chances in the Lottery, and return you thanks for the money. I am, by one of the boys going away, now the eighth boy in the election, and shall, if I keep my place, I believe get into College, which I do not only hope to do, but also to get up higher. We have no particular news here. I hope you and sister Chichester and my sisters and little Miss Kitty are all very well. My brothers and I join in duty to you and love to sisters This is all at present from Your dutiful & affectionate son Roger Newdigate Mrs Webber gives her service to you and sisters.

Westminster March 11 Dear Momma I received & would have answered yours before but being pretty much pressed in time & knowing your goodness would excuse me I deferred it till this opportunity. Mr Kollogrew sent an invitation to me & accordingly I waited on him on Tuesday last, He joins with his sister in service to you and all friends. I have according to your orders enquired about the Salmons & find that there are six parts in every volume, each part at one shilling a piece, & the binding will come to about one £ at least if you care to have them, Mr Barker desires one of the other volumes that they may be matched in the binding, & I dare say he won't impose on me. My Lady Sadly & Sir Charles desires their services, I was at her house to dinner on Saturday last when she took me to the Opera, where I heard the famous Fannello, who I think (& you know I'm a great judge of music & a perfect master in the art of whistling) very well deserves his character & is the most extraordinary person I ever heard. You may think after the charms of his voice, how I shall bear the noise of rooks and the quawking of your Ladyship ducks, & the solitary walks near purling rills, with what you country ladies think so charming, the pleasing sonnets of the airy choir, which will appear to me, worse than the shrieking of a violin ill played on. I shall die to befoul my fingers with a filthy hoe & shall address your Ladyship in nothing but Italian now & Fannello's praises. I hope you will excuse these airy flights which may seem odd to you but are common & fashionable and therefore necessary to us town gentlemen. I am Dear Momma Your dutiful & affectionate son R. Newdigate Mrs Webber desires her service, I was going to thank you for the ale, but upon recollection I won't thank you till I have it.

Westminster November 15 Honoured Madam I received yours & beg you would return Mr Bromley my acknowledgements of the favour he does me. I did not at first comprehend who was included in the name of Mr B... but having met with a clergyman who has for many years enjoyed the living of Buckington & has just got from our Chapter that of Hinckly (I have forgot his name). I was informed of the happy news of the visit intended to me & have been perplexing myself ever since to find some way of avoiding it. I'm glad to hear Mr Chichester and my sister are safe arrived. I received on Wednesday last the Epitaph for my poor brother & think Mr Walwyn has with a great deal of elegance done justice to his character. I have just wrote to him to return him thanks. Imagining that you would have a curiosity to see it I have attempted it in English. I will send a copy of the Latin one next week when I hear if you have any objections to it or not. I'll send it to Mr Rysbrack. I hope you'll excuse the hurry of this & I remain Your most affectionate & dutiful son R Newdigate For the Lady Newdigate, near Coventry, Warwickshire.

Calais August 21 New Stile We set out from London, dear Madam, as we proposed, on Monday at two o'clock in a sloop of Mr Bonnets, and lay at anchor that night before Gravesend. Our cabins were very convenient and we slept as heartily, most of us, as if we were upon land. The next day we fell down to the Nor and saw 3 men of war riding there at anchor. From thence we came to the downs, leaving Goodwin Sands to the left hand. There were 3 more men of war there. We cast anchor here and lay that night, the wind for this part of the voyage being South East which was directly in our teeth. The second morning we sailed within a league of Dover Castle, where we were becalmed and were obliged to cast anchor. The castle and cliff made a very beautiful appearance at that distance. Here we waited for the tide 3 hours. We were very fortunate in having a brisk gale upon weighing anchor which carried us in between 3 & 4 hours into this harbour, with the English and French coasts in our view all the way. We had a very agreeable voyage though not a very short one. We were 49 hours or thereabouts from the time we sat out. The voyage is sometimes performed in 24. There were none of the company at all sea sick. Calais is a very neat, clean town, but nothing extraordinary. I think it exceeds all our seaports I have seen in the neatness of the streets, which is a sure sign of our exceeding them in our trade, for it is that which dirties our streets. The vast difference in the people, buildings, as well as the language makes it impossible for one to hesitate a minute whether we are in England, besides the crucifixes, one of which is stuck up in every opening about the town. We went to see the church, which is a good old gothic building and was built by the English when they were masters of the town. The pictures are but indifferent and some of the altars most tawdrily dressed up with made flowers and garlands. We are got in a very good inn here. The butler is exceeding bad but the Burgundy makes up for it. It is a very ridiculous sight to us that are not used to it to see the lowest of the workmen in their bags, solitares, and pig-tails. Here is a carpenter working at a chaise in the yard at this instant with a tail tied up in coarse brown tape that reaches several inches below his - . Since I began we have agreed for our chaises at 19 guineas each. We have nothing now to do but to buy saddles and jack boots for the servants. We set out to morrow for Bologna in our way to Paris, which we hope to reach in three days. Lord Litchfield, Sir Francis Dashwood and Jack go to morrow to see Dunkirk and on Saturday set sail from thence for England. We are just come from seeing a monastery of Poor Clares, and a House of the Capuchins who are the dirtiest fellows I ever yet saw. They never touch money, but without any hindrance conducted us to a sister who received the money for them that we gave. You may give them as much money as you please, though they themselves are so scrupulous they won't handle a farthing of it from you. This is certainly a very ridiculous piece of form. I have sent you a small piece of work of the Poor Clares to wear in your watch. You may see I have sent you a very particular account of our voyage, with many trifling circumstances that attend it, which I know you will receive with greater regard to the sender than the things themselves, or I should not have troubled you with this long detail. I shall be very glad to hear from you, Dear Madam, as soon as you please, to know how things go on in old England. Daniel, as we imagined, is very awkward here, neither understands nor is understood, he will be still worse when he gets further, but I fancy he will do pretty well. My duty attends you and my best respects Mr Ludford and family and all friends & Mr Chichester etc A. Palmer etc etc. I shall receive your letter as soon as it arrives there from Paris. Jack desires his service, and the rest of our company. I have nothing to add but that I continue with the greatest affection Your most dutiful son R. Newdigate. Direct A Monsieur le Chevalier Newdigate recommend a Monsieur Waters Banquier a Paris .

Angers Sept. 8th N.S. Dear Madam I have been for some time in hopes of receiving letters from England, but have yet received none. I am in expectation of them every day. In my last I gave you an account of our journey to Paris. We stayed there a week & left it on Monday the 1st New Style. We were almost entirely taken up with fitting ourselves out with necessaries and conveniences, & found it much of the same nature with London, a perfect vuide bourse as the French call it. I had the satisfaction of finding my clothes in the top of the fashion, so saved the expenses of making any alterations. Mr Waters came to wait upon us, to give us the form of drawing upon him when we have occasion. We went to wait upon Lord Waldegrave. He was exceeding civil, sent his Gentleman of the Horse with us to show us Versailles, Marli etc and invited us to dinner. We dined then and met a great many English, but none of distinction, except the illustrious , Poet Laureate. The day before we came away we were at his chapel, Lady Vane was there. She looked very gay, was very gently dressed, and painted a la mode francoise , the purest vermilion. I was surprised to find young Massingberd there & had only time to ask him how he did. We saw no other English there that we knew. The town itself has a quite different air from London. The buildings are entirely stone & most of the houses of a prodigious height & all the streets extremely narrow. The River Seine very little exceeds our Fleet Ditch, though of infinite advantage to the town. The streets are all finely paved, like Whitehall, & the manner of hanging the lamps in the middle of the street by ropes from house to house, has a very pretty effect, though we did not see them lighted. The Berlin coaches are very easy and calculated for the narrowness of the streets, for they turned in a very small compass. We saw the Palace of Luxembourg & the Gallery of Rubens, the History of Mary de Medicis. The prints I have at Arbury are extremely well taken and all the likenesses of the faces well preserved. The Dowager Queen of Spain at present inhabits it. The Tuilleries is a very old building and the Louvre not finished. We were at an opera. I had bad taste enough to think it the greatest jumble of noise and jargon that I ever yet heard, though they are certainly to be commended in one thing; that it is all their own manufacture without any foreign importation. We had only time to run over Versailles It is certainly the greatest piece of magnificence since the time of Solomon, and all its grandeur owing to itself without any advantage of situation. The apartments lye all open to the meanest peasant, though the dirt they bring with them does not add much to the beauty of the place. The Great Gallery is the finest room I ever saw. It's entirely wainscoated with marble of different kinds, and adorned with antique statues set in niches. The ceiling is the history of the grand Monarch painted by Le Brun. In one of the rooms I saw the original picture of Darius's tent by the same hand. You have Lens's copy of it by you which wants only the colouring, which is indeed the chief part. The gardens are one vast profusion of expense. The quantity of marble in the fountains, statues and buildings, is immense. One would think there was no other stone in the country. We had not time to see half the garden & what we did see was to great disadvantage, the king being at Marli & none of the water works playing. From hence we went to Trianon, a little palace just by Versailles where the king used to retire from his grand apartments at that place. The apartments are very pretty but all unfurnished. We came from thence to Marli, which is a most delightful place, as pretty as the other is magnificent. The ordinary waterworks all played. The whole scene put me in mind of the enchanted palaces of Romance. The account we have heard of it and used to mention agrees in every particular. We arrived at Orleans on Tuesday night, and embarked our chaises there & fell down the river Loire to Blois. It is reckoned the finest river in France and is navigable for 440 miles, from Nantes to Roan. For the whole summer it is but just passable with the lightest boats, full of sand banks and very little water. In winter it is very large & troublesome. There is a prodigious bank raised all along the side to preserve the country from being ruined by it. It's a continual expense to keep it in repair and there is a fund set apart for that purpose. At Blois we disembarked, heartily tired with the tediousness of our voyage, there being no other method of getting down but being pushed with poles. We lay the next night at Tours & the next arrived at this place. The whole road was very pleasant lying all along the raised bank of the river. The town of Angers is very indifferent. We are got into a very good house, at the rate of about £3.10.0 per month apiece for our board, which is dear but the usual price. We have the house to ourselves. We came here on Saturday and yesterday received the visits of most of the English in the place. Lord Charles Manners, Lord Fitzwilliams, Mr Foster, Mr Read, Mr Wright & others that I knew nothing of. I fancy we shall find the place agreeable when we come to be acqainted with it. We took a walk into the Manege yesterday. I saw Mr Bromley's and Sir Thomas Twysden arms up there which is the custom when people go away. I hope you'll excuse the hurry of my letters. I am willing to send as much as I can, which makes me take no pains about the correctness of the stile. I long very much to hear from you, which is the greatest pleasure I can receive at this distance. Till then I must content myself with the thoughts of old England and those I left in it, & believe my affection will grow, if possible, more strong by absence. I have seen nothing hitherto, I assure you, but what has increased my esteem for my own country, nor one particular in which my judgement will give the preference to France. The misery of the poor & the extravagant profusion of the rich, for whom they labour is prodigious, though they are still happy for they think themselves so & know no better. For the last hundred miles we came even wooden shoes were finery, and most of the peasants we saw, men, women & children, had neither shoes nor stockings of any kind. In my next I will send you an account of our sojournment here where we are encamped for the winter in very comfortable lodgings. I am dearest Madam Your most dutiful & most affectionate son R Newdigate A` Monsieur le Chevalier Newdigate a`Angers par Paris

I need not tell you, Dearest Madam, that I have succeeded, for you have on the outside the visible marks. This has been a day of considerable fatigue, but I have mended so much ever since I came here, & my spirits have been so well supported, that I do not find myself in the least the worse. There was an appearance for me (I am assured, for I could not see) of 1500 freeholders, & not one voice against me. To see myself at once established in so creditable a manner you will easily imagine gives me very great pleasure; & the expense which is very considerable may, I hope, be made up before long by a prudent management. Dick has been very obliging, but I should be glad if Clarke could send muster me up fifty or more & send a note payable at a short date to me at Mr Cooks, for I believe I must make a few visits before I see you. I am, dearest Madam Your affectionate & most dutiful Son R N
