column46: December 22nd 1745 I was very much mortified... to break off my last like the Bear & the Fiddle, but the Fates & the Bellman would have it so. My hurry was so great that I don't know what I wrote, or where to begin. We thought it fair to give Mrs Barradel notice of our journey & she accordingly sent to us Mr Nichols, of Hillingdon, who is her first cousin & heir, to accompany us. I set out at eleven from your brother's (on Sunday) in a chariot & four but when I came to L...s we sent it back for a coach & six, in which we left Town before two & got last night to Godstone. Our company L..., myself, Mr , & poor old Thomas, who moves me very much. At five this morning we set out & bated at Grinstead & Uckfield, the roads very bad but much worse from thence, about twice as deep as the deepest slough to Cotton Church, but no ways dangerous. We were at a non plus at Lord Gage's park gate, no keeper to be found & our daylight near spent & the common road impossible. But under the sanction of my privilege we broke the chain & went through a charming park, a winding pool of a very great length, loosing itself in several branches amongst fine young woods. The soil however is bad & the park too flat. From hence we came into a chase of the Duke of Dorset's called the Broil, where we were really embroiled, for nothing could be deeper except a farm which we were so happy as to obtain leave to trespass over. But they had not the conscience to wait for our money. From hence we mounted the Downs, where we were not so unreasonable as to load our horses but trudged to the top of them, & so far outstep'd them that we got to Lewes before them, above two miles & half. From the top of the Cliff Hill we saw the whole beautiful vale you admired all under water, & entered the town the opposite side, to what you did. We called upon Trayton, whom we had given the trouble of sealing up everything. He is positive there is no will, for before Dick's last journey to Town he asked him if he had one, to which he answered he had not, but believed he must make one when he was in Town .. There has been no will found in Town, though not absolutely certain there is none. It was a little melancholy to come to this desolate house, to be welcomed with mourning faces, as coming to put an end to a scene of comfort & tranquillity which all enjoyed before, & in a place where I was so lately & so cheerfully entertained. We are to do nothing to night but to morrow, between nine & ten, we are to make a general search. Mr Trayton, Mr Ridout & Mr Gilbert, a person engaged for Mr Bromfield, are to be with us. If I find upon the estimate any part of the goods, linen etc, are bargains I will endeavour to get them as part of my debt to Harefield from him, but if I am administrator I shall be able to choose upon those conditions. I have now a writing table in my view, which puts me in mind of your closet, but I don't want any ...

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: Spring Gardens 10 O'clock May the 9th 1747 Dear Sir Enclosed I have sent you the daily Advertiser in which Sir Hugh avows your meeting, as this may occasion difference of sentiments in gentlemen. I will endeavour to fix the meeting we proposd as soon as possible & will make it my business today to find them out. As the advertisement carries an insinuation that we have jointly asked votes, I believe you will think I ought to set that clear by declaring in answer that I never thought of addressing myself to anybody till Sir Hugh declared (as you heard) that he had asked the gentlemen and 5 or 600 freeholders. That even then I had not asked for myself or one else but only desired they would reserve themselves to the sense of a meeting. That I then assured Sir Hugh that as I would not join him so I would not join any one else, nor even think of standing myself without their concurrence, having been chosen myself upon the resolution of such a meeting & being desirous to support & keep undivided the old institutions of the County in the old way. If something to this purpose meets with their approbation, or you think anything more should be added, pray let me know. Who am Your etc etc R N You will see Mr Cooke today

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: May 26th 1747 Spring Gardens Dear Sir The contents of your letter gave us great pleasure as a strong conviction of what before we only hoped. I can't yet find that any considerable ground is got by the positive solicitations carried on, most people are well upon their guard & refuse to engage. In the Chancery Office I am told not above three would promise which is a particular instance, as we have no reason to expect much more than a majority there for the County Interest. Mr Child's advertisement gives great satisfaction & will make many easy. I should have wrote before but intended to wait upon you, which cant be now till Thursday or Friday but as I cant fix either till I know when the Scotch bill return to us with the Lords amendments. I hope it will be no confirmation to you I am Your most obliged humble servant R N

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: Harefield Place February 12th 1747 Dearest Madam I need not say it is a great concern to us not to meet you here, but when we consider what your employment is, that you are paying the last kind office to a child you loved & who loved you, we are better pleased that you are absent. I am no ways surprised to find by yours that your present melancholy situation affects your spirits & we both most heartily wish it was in our power to endeavour to administer comfort where you are, but that is impossible yet, my affairs here & in Town being fixed so as they can't be altered. And indeed I cannot write myself without feeling for her, for you & all her family, though the difference in our ages & the distance of our lives gave less opportunity, yet I never met with anything from her, but an obliging behaviour & a sisterly affection, which I hope I shall always be so sensible of as not to omit any opportunity of doing service to those she leaves. But the affection of all who love her must make them wish her pains at an end, her life has long been tiresome & without comfort, her situation full of danger & misery, which indeed she herself was least sensible of since the loss of him who occasioned it. In the sight of her friends no great one, but perhaps in some degree shortened her life. But from whencesoever it arose her strength has been impaired, her constitution broke, her spirits worn out, and the greatest blessing we can wish for her is the last, a contented & resigned end to a life which she has rather suffered than enjoyed. Our comfort is, & her happiness will be, that she meant well & lived well, her children nearly come to that age when a mother's tenderness is often prejudicial, but never necessary as their proper education must be at a distance, & as to their affairs she was never capable of them. They were always, and will be, left in hands which she believes, & I hope, never will betray that trust. She will at once be free from pain and anguish, no longer tortured with physic & physicians, no longer a gaolkeeper trembling at every alarm; there the wicked cease from troubling, there the weary are at rest. In every light we see this change, it is for her advantage, & can anyone that loves wish her to return to misery & sorrow. I know you don't wish it for her. You are too well acquainted with her situation & constitution, & yet I do not wonder that your fortitude of mind is overcome & shaken in the tender office you are now performing, but I know you never forget that tears, like leaves which winter or tempest forces from the tree & scatters through the air, may flow at liberty over the tombs of the dead, but the stock & branches still remain firm & uninjurde & time again heals every wound. But though we don't complain at your concern we are too much interested in your welfare not to wish it may be moderate, not too great nor too lasting. Your health is not established to bear it & when we think of you we should be happier if it was not necessary for you to be present, but this is unreasonable since in that hour such a friend is the greatest of blessings. The subject is to melancholy to dwell longer on & I should not have done it so long, but where you are I know it is unavoidable to you. If nothing alters our route we propose to be in Town on Sunday night, to stay there till Thursday & on Friday, if you are still at Abinger to come there, if not to Harefield, but our purpose may be changed as there is occasion, except only that I must be in Town till Tuesday noon. If any alteration should be, as it is impossible for me to send either servant or horse, I beg you will send back to us here the messenger you have now sent. We shall not set out for Town till after dinner & shall be very anxious to know how you are. My wife is writing for herself so I shall only add that I am Dearest Madam Your most affectionate, most dutiful son R Newdigate

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: April 25 1748 Dear Sir I am always glad when it is in my power to contribute to your pleasure, & happy in an opportunity of showing how much it is my wish to continue the union & friendship between our familys, which becomes relations & neighbours. As to your accounts between us they will be easily settled if I have the good luck to meet you at Harefield the week after next, As to the disappointments you mention I assure you I hardly ever had your success in life from which I have reaped so entire satisfaction, without my public employment. I have got rid of all the fatigue, all the mortification that attends the fruitless endeavours to serve ones country & can now enjoy my self without anyone's having a right to reproach me, & find so many sweets in that enjoyment that it will be no common temptation in my present way of thinking that will draw me out to sea again. My wife etc etc R N

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: Oxford Investiture 1749 My dearest Child I am just stolen away from the side table where Thomas Rowney presides to give you an account of myself. I got to Ladbrook sooner than expected, found Charles Palmer but indifferent, drank tea with Miss Betty, set out at 7 next morning, got to Great Tu, within five miles of Ditchley, where I luckily dined, for Lord was gone 3 hours before I came there, so I was forced to come on. At Thomas Rowney's found him, the Duke of Beauford etc talking over degrees. They determined that I should be a Doctor, which is to be performed tomorrow. This day I am only a Master & a nobleman. Lord Harley, Sir J Phillips, Sir J Shaw, Mr Drake, Mr Powney, Mr Wills, Mr Palmer Mr Norb Berkely were dubbed Doctors of Civil Law; Mr Bagot, the old gentleman, & Mr Gibbs, architect, Masters of Arts. This was all we did today. We are now going to the Oratorio of Esther, which will cut this short. Tomorrow Lord Westmoreland, Sir Francis Dashwood, Sir L Holte, Lord Burleigh, myself & others are to have the honour. The Orator is hard drove for speeches. The chief matter he takes from the Baronetage & Peerage . Tomorrow is the grand solemnity. Sir Watkin Win & Sir Wat B... are not yet come. Bagot tells me there is a scheme for his travelling with Lord Bruce, who is here, & his tutor, a gentleman who has been abroad. This gives me great joy. Lord , who is the same boy in his robes, Doctor's gown or anything else, always jolly & good humoured, talks of going home on Friday. If so I shall go with him & stay part of the day. When I shall see thy dear face again I can't positively say. If I can get to Ladbrook on Saturday you will see me on Sunday, but I don't believe Lord will go on Friday as he says. If so I shall not get home till Monday or Tuesday. You see, you must not expect me ... I begin already to think it long since I saw you. I begin already to think it long since I saw you. Every body thinks this affair ill concerted. It would have been put off a month, but for Lady Williams, so that has turned out just wrong. God Almighty bless & keep you, dear child ... I have stolen a minute & must return, so good night. Think of me all day long & dream of me all night. Yours most entirely R N Wednesday. 2 minutes before the Oratorio begins, 4 o'clock. I have not time to read what I have wrote.

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: Arbury April 26th 1749 Dear Sir I thank you for the obliging manner in which you have taken the preference I have given you. I thought it due to so good a neighbour to give him an oppurtunity to make a situation which he likes still more agreeable, & it is very fortunate that the very lands which he would choose are those which are most to my purpose to part with. I am very glad my convenience, my motive for the offers, falls in so luckily with yours. The complaint is very trifling & you are very good to consider as an obligation what is really my interest. To your objections I must answer, as Mr Eyre probably has, by my direction, that Mat Fields Farm may, as you say, very probably be untenanted. It was once so within the last 30 years for 3 years together which has indeed bust its reputation, but when the number of acres is considered must be worth the rent which has never been raised since I have an account of it. You are misinformed as to Bayhurst grounds. They always went at £15 & might still have been let at the same rent if I had chose to add them to the distant farm which they lay to before. Fr. Trevor, I believe, will be glad to continue the tenant. The other two, as you say, will probably be empty, & I have no objection to making a reasonable deduction for that hazard. You have not yet gone through half the falls of the old Park Wood and they all very unequal. The Mayhurst is as big again. I find a deduction of half the profits of the woods since I let it to you. Mr Ware's farm was, as you say, advanced upon the building the house etc. It is now in very good repair & well tenanted, 7 or 8 years of a lease remaining, and a new lease desired at the same rent for as many years as I will grant it. You will not wonder, then, that I refuse to make any abatement with this particular. I will rather except it from the proposal than submit to any. The present tenant of the Chalk Dell will, I believe, take a lease at the rent. The part of widow Townleys which I propose to sell is - 30 acres 3 roods 37 perches . The remainder, without house barns, stables, hovels etc is - 44.3.4. The yearly rent £55. I should not think the house an encumbrance if it stood on my part, & while you consider what you make of the tithe barn I believe you will allow the division pretty equal. I am more unwilling to part with this than any of the land proposed, so can't think of selling the whole, & indeed our lands will be better divided thus than as now, or if you had the whole. One great end I propose is to prevent our tenants interfering. The meadows which I reserve are the inlet of water to all my floated meadows & the rest lies convenient for my other farms. I tell you my reasons, without reserve, for the division as in the particular which I hope you will be satisfied with as you say it is not very material to you. I never heard of any repairs wanting, having laid out a considerable sum upon the farm within these 4 years. In asking only 12 years purchase I think I have made considerable allowances for Dobyns house, which is now in good repair. The valuation of the timber, I am assured, is made as usual in these cases but I don't understand it myself. There is no mistake in the valuation of the lands in the woods, - I mean the reserved right of the growth of timber. You now pay £20 for the underwood of the old Park Wood only, the tenants with their farms have the privilege of that of the little woods & shows the whole amounting to near 70 acres, one half of the value of which at least is, & has been always, in my own hands, & is worth more than a farm of £30 a year. Were the old Park Wood only stripped of the timber would you let it for £20 a year? & the young timber continuing to grow is worth a great deal more than the underwood would advance - more than no timber. Whatever reason there may be for disputing the valuation there can be none for setting it aside. I have now examined all the objections & pointed out such parts as may admit of some abatement, but I am sorry to find we so widely differ that I can't venture to propose any, as there is only room for an inconsiderable one. For taking away that part of widow Townleys which you have added, & in the room of it adding the article which you have omitted, there is still near a £1000 difference between us. I am not willing to leave out the lands you mention. My reason for offering them is that they are outskirts & lie more inconveniently to me than they do to you. I will give you no more trouble than only to take notice that this estate for above 40 years has held up its head under a greater burden than which now lies upon it. My predecessors submitted to receive nothing from it rather than dismember it & I thank God none of them had less reason to sell them than I have, & am therefore determined to sell it well or not at all. You are very welcome to see any of the particulars, & if you desire further satisfaction in any particular I shall be very glad to wait upon at the Courts on the 12th or after. The Ladies all join in compliments to you & Mrs Cooke, my mother in part for thinking of her love I have ordered R Miles to fell what elms you desire And am, Dear Sir Etc

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: Arbury June 15th 1749 Dear Sir I am sorry I did not express myself clearly enough to you at Harfield, to leave no doubt of my resolution as to the parcels which I shall sell, but hope you will not take it ill that after having reconsidered what I had before, upon full consideration, determined, I must repeat to you that I cannot think of parting with more of Trenleys Farm than what is already in the particular. Upon weighing the objections which you make to that particular I am convinced that they ought to have some force, and in consideration of some articles which do now appear to me overstraind, in consideration of your advanced offer and to show that I scorn to make an unreasonable advantage, I will abate £500 of my demand and am willing to take £9500 for the whole as in the particular given in. As it is now time to enter upon the management of the lands which will be upon my hands in case we should not agree, I must beg the favour of an answer as soon as conveniently may be, I am, Dear Sir Your most faithful & obliged Cousin & humble servant R N

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: Arbury February 12th 1749 Dear Sir I have indeed neither thoughts nor desires to enter again into public life, and most heartily wish you success in your present undertaking. It is impossible for me to attend the meeting on Thursday at so short a warning but I will certainly wait upon you at Brentford in case of an opposition, and in the meantime, as you desire, will make applications to my friends in your favour, though I think it unnecessary as all those are, I am convinced, already prejudiced in your favour, who are capable of concern to see the County of Middlesex degraded into a mere Court Borough. I am sorry that this reproach could ever have been laid upon it, but flatter myself, from the late exertion of liberty in Westminster, that you have reason to entertain better hopes, and that the eyes of men are open to distinguish between those who court their favours, with design to sell them for honours & profit, and those who desire no other reward for their time, labour & expense than the satisfaction of having served them diligently, faithfully and disinterestedly. I speak with a freedom that my present situation allows, and heartily wish every freeholder may be of the same sentiment with me, that in choosing you we lay an honourable burden upon you only to serve ourselves. The ladies join me in compliments to yourself and Mrs Cooke, and in wishing you success without trouble. I am, Dear Sir Your affectionate cousin etc R N

Dear Sir I give you many thanks for your most obliging letter but indeed no fresh instance was necessary to convince me of your friendship. I must also beg you to express my gratitude to Dr Blackstone & Mrs Clitherow for their good opinion of me & endeavours to serve me. When the County of Middlesex did me the honour to elect me, in which I hope I shall never forget my obligations to you, I was glad to know Parliament & ambitious to serve them. When they rejected me my concern was for the old County Interest which I at once broken & ruined. Since that I have lived in more ease & tranquillity than ever I knew before, & it must be a great temptation indeed, no less an honour, that which you & my friends are now troubling yourselves to advance me to, which would prevail with me, circumstanced as I am, to enter again in public life. If that honour can admit of any advancement it is the manner in which my friends endeavour to obtain it for me, for which they have my acknowledgements, & I assure them that as I have been ignorant hitherto of every circumstance relative to this affair I will still continue so, & shall not presume to hear any overtures whatsoever for I have no pretensions, no determination whatever but to be sensible of the honour they have done me in their thoughts of me, & to be very well satisfied whatever is their conclusion. I must only beg that... I must repeat my obligations to Dr Blackstone for his friendship to me, who have no title to it, & to yourself & Mrs Clitherow for your congratulations upon the appearance of success, so far beyond my expectations or desires, Also for your account of what is going forward & I hope you will continue your correspondence. What is the inducem't for moving a certain person into the upper house before his time? They will not upon my account run the hazard of dividing the Interest. I am ambitious of the honour of serving them but more so of the continuing that impregnable unanimity which has hitherto distinguished that University upon these occasions. Mrs Clitherow & all your family have all our best wishes at all seasons I am Dear Sir Your most faithful & obliged humble servant R N

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: Epping Place March 18th 1750 Dear Madam I have very little to say in my defence for not writing to you sooner but as I know Sophie communicates to you the contents of my letters I hope you excuse it. I received the enclosed yesterday by an express to Epping Place. I was not surprised at the contents of which I had heard a report, & well knew that whenever they were in a situation to want my assistance their pride would stoop to ask it. I have sent you my sister's letter & Mr Craven's with the answers &, as much as I can recollect of the contents of Mr Ludford's to Mr Craven. The effects of a Commission taken out against Lord Donegall I have long ago considered. My sentiments upon that head stirred up the wrath of Mr Ludford long ago, as you may remember in one of his letters which I have at Arbury. I believe it to be the only certain method to secure to the children a vast inheritance in future & the share they are by law entitled to of the profits of the estate in the meantime, to be the only sure guard against the plundering them (if he should fall into bad hands) of the last, & against the marrying to some person who would take care to produce children to strip them of the first. The effects of such a Commission with a Retrospect I have also considered & must confess that, notwithstanding the resentment which I can't deny the usage I have met with raises in me, I cannot consider it without concern & uneasiness. Mr Ludford must produce an account not only of what has come into his hands but of what Mr Chichester squandered, & answer it as far as the Executorship of the last will do so, & as far as his own abilities. Should it turn out that £2000 only, more than he can show to be laid up for the children, should be required of him, where will he go for that sum only? His estate is settled, he can't touch it, his personal estate though he strips to his shirt will not answer it. What then must be consequence? Instead of 2000 perhaps he may have ten times that sum to answer for. How can he stand it? If this is the case, as it appears to me to be, should a Commission be obtained in an hostile manner. It is not a time to think of past injuries, nor even whether the sums which disappeared have been squandered in riot, extravagance & ambitious views, whether I have really known affectionate sisters, or any other tie but that of blood, but to consider that tie only, to consider two innocent nephews on one side, two helpless nieces on the other & as far as their interests are compatible to serve them all as well as I can. In this view I have talked with all the gentlemen mentioned who will, I dare say, cooperate with me in any scheme that will prevent what Mr Ludford (inconsiderately if he really means it) says he does not fear, a Retrospect, but to make any proposals of accommodation to Lady Barrimore to stop the issuing of the Commission, or to do anything whatever to that end, I absolutely refuse, for the reasons above. For I can never consent to leave the inheritance of those nephews one moment in hazard, such as they are now in, & I have above represented. I have desired F. Newdigate, if he finds by Lady Barrymore's Agent, whom he is to meet today, that I can be of any service as to the preventing the Retrospect, to give me notice, otherwise that it is better for Mr Ludford not to call me in, for if I am asked my sentiments as to the good of the family by Lady Barrimore I should not choose to answer, which would be enough to make her guess the reason & summon me before the Chancellor where I could not refuse to do so. Tuesday the 19th. I have not seen Francis Newdigate but hear that Lady Barrimore is willing to treat but insists upon their producing his Lordship. It is upon Deal's affidavit that the Petition is founded. Mr Ludford now feels the imprudence of following the dictates of revenge & malice. I apprehend too he will suffer for his last folly at Warwick, which I fear has made him many powerful enemies who will push him to the utmost. Mr Stratford, who called upon me this morning, says the Attorney General, whom they understood to be retained in general for them, declares himself for Lady Barrimore. Wilbraham, too, is engaged on her side & a Mr Dickson is her Agent. No one but Mr Ludford seems to believe Lord Donegall can go through an examination & that a Commission will not pass. For my part I think & hope it will not fail, & only wish Mr Ludford may be wise enough to throw no difficulties in the way in case they can be prevailed upon to give up the Retrospect, which I should think they will, as Lord Barrimore himself had once the plucking of this pullet. I propose to go to Harfield on Saturday in order to settle yours as well as my own affairs of which I will, at my return, give you an account. I rejoice to hear you are all well & am Dearest Madam Your most dutiful & affectionate son R Newdigate

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: Park Place February 2nd 1752 Dear Madam, I sent you an account last post which I doubt not will make you anxious to hear further. This morning I received a letter from Mr Dixon to desire me to meet him at Mr Wilbraham's who had much to say to me. I declined this, being really engaged, but if I had gone, Mr Wilbraham's arguments, I knew, could only regard his client, Lady Barrimore, for whom I am not concerned. Mr Dixon, by my appointment, however, has just brought me his sentiments which, he says, are that the method proposed & insisted upon by the Lord Chief Justice, to draw the bill simply and purely to give a power to let leases for 99 years, which is the end proposed, will not do, for that method will condemn the Deed of Trust, the Decree, the Council that advised it & all their proceedings upon it. This I told him is of no concern to me. If they think proper to act under it, they do it at their peril, but for my part I will never consent to a confirmation of them. He added that uses must be appointed for the money arising, & there never was a case giving the surplus to the next of kin during a man's life, nor could be. My proposal was to give a power to Trustees to let leases, & to apply the money arising from the estate, first, to the maintenance of Lord Donegall, secondly, to the payments of the debts, thirdly to be placed in Funds, to be distributed after the death of Lord Donegall to the next of kin by name, to Lady Barrimore, Lord Mazarine, & Arthur & John Chichester by name, or their legal representatives. This is necessary in the last case particularly, for otherwise Miss Chichester will have a share. He could not pretend this was not such a disposition as any man might legally make, and resorted at last to his directions which, he said, were very different, & he must have fresh instructions, which would make it impossible to obtain an account this Sessions. I told him I should not object to such a bill as above, nor should object to a confirmation by Act of Parliament of such a deed as I could consent to, & that such a deed might have been drawn last year if others of the children's friends had been consulted. He said he understood I had refused to act or interfere. I told him my reason for it, that my sister's will had put it out of my power to act with Mr Ludford upon an equal footing but that I never had nor would refuse it where I could do them service. The result of our conference was to let alone the Act of Parliament this Sessions & to endeavour to settle the whole in such a manner as I & my Council can approve, in order to have it confirmed by Parliament afterwards. Thus ended the affair, & I am excused waiting upon the Lord Chancellor tomorrow. Mr Dixon owned the deed was drawn in too much haste but that Ludford had done such things & had such influence that it was not proper Lord Donegall should continue a minute in his hands. He could not say he had done & undone for his own interest, by which I perceived he meant the wills which had been made. That Ludford was exceedingly frightened, begged him not to be hard upon him & that he could have had him upon his knees if he pleased, the night before the inspection. But after that, in Court, his looks were changed & he would hardly pull his hat to him. But that at last he pressed hard to kept Lord Donegall, offered to keep him for a thousand a year only for, says Dixon, he had great schemes in his head. He was to oppose Lord B at Warwick! The consequences of this whole, I hope & expect, will be greatly for the advantage of the children. This affair having been canvassed thus, they will probably not venture to act under a deed so impeached - if not, another must be drawn which I shall not approve unless the interest of the children is fully provided for & all the savings possible made. Thus, probably, Mr Ludford's Castle in the Air' will vanish, his £2000 is not paid, & perhaps never will, his accounts will be examined for the whole time Lord Donegall was with him, & the balance exacted. It is but justice it should be so, & if that is not done they are liable to be called to a strict account. A Commission may still pass, & all their deeds voided, & payments to be refunded. We were in hopes of a letter from you last post but conclude you are well as we have nothing to the contrary from Arbury. Sir Walter Bagot is come, so is Lord Guernsey, but I have not seen Sir John Cotton. I fear he's at the point of death in our neighbourhood. Our street is littered of & noises kept out as much as possible. He came out of the country two days ago & has been worse ever since. W. Palmer & the two dined with us on Sunday. I think I never saw boys more improved than the two last, the eldest quite sensible, ready & entertaining, & Dr Nichols says great things of his improvements. We could not but be pleased that notwithstanding all they must be sure to have heard all day long to our disadvantage they seemed highly pleased & glad to see us. James has just brought word that Sir John Cotton is dead, between 5 & 6 this evening. We have lost the best piece of the old Patriot Rock. I am Dearest Madam Your most dutiful & affectionate son R N

Dear Madam Macartney is returned from Guildford & has brought five affidavits to support our Petition proving Lord incapacity. We find every day more people willing to prove it. I am to go tomorrow morning to settle the Petition with Council which, I hope, will be delivered to the Lord Chancellor before night. I waited on Lady Tyrawley today as she is a near relation of the family & have the satisfaction to find that she, as well as all mankind besides, thinks I am doing an act of justice, & for the service of the children. I hear not a word on their side, only Lady Barrimore's people seem not so much against the Commission though I believe it is only outside, for all their schemes are already blown up by the impeaching the credit of the Deed, & the Commission will put it out of the power of anyone to impose upon Lord Donegall. If the Chancellor approves we shall have him up in less than a fortnight. Our facts are very strong & can be well proved, though no other evidence of Lord 's incapacity is necessary than the very deed they would confirm; if there was Lady Barrimore's custody for his life without a possibility leaving her, let her use him never so ill, & besides up his whole fortune to Trustees without leaving himself a single shilling for his pocket, & even under his hardest masters he used to be allowed a guinea per month. Lady Primson I saw the day before yesterday. She is a zealous advocate for , who was with her in Town. I hear a reason suggested, that some of her relations will suffer by a retrospect, which makes the matter clear. Mrs Drelincourt is very stout & well in appearance. The bell waits... I am, dearest Madam, Your most dutiful & affectionate son, R Newdigate

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: Lincoln's Inn Fields April 14th 1752 Dear Madam I am just come from Lincoln's Inn Hall where our cause has been opened but the Chancellor, being obliged to go to Council, we could not proceed, but are to do so on Friday evening at 6 o'clock. Mr Ludford put in an affidavit on Saturday accusing me & my wife both of an inclination to have Lord Donegall ourselves, and some some other dirty insinuations which I was, much against my will, obliged to answer, & think I have done it fully & with candour & truth, having left out several strong things which I well remember, & put in nothing but what I was assured was absolutely necessary. I have the satisfaction to find my conduct impeached by none but the contrary party, all others rather blaming me for not applying sooner rather than for this application. Mr Ludford came in a great passion, would not return my bow but belched forth to me, Baronet! Things are very bad between you and me'. I replied I was sorry for it, or to that effect. He said he could prove that I & my wife had consulted together about having my Lord, & he would prove it so that I could not deny it. I answered I had denied it & had sworn to that denial & that I defied his proofs. What will become of the noble peer no one can say, but Mr Ludford's conduct appears in such a light that no one, not his own council, can defend him. I am going to Copt Hall tonight & cannot, I fear, see you so soon as we proposed, but we must go through with it now we are engaged. I am Dearest Madam Your most dutiful son R Newdigate Ebdell has put in a mean dirty affidavit to support Ludford.

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: Friday April 17th 1752 My Dearest We are put off again to Wednesday evening which mortifies me exceedingly. It is now ten o'clock. The Chancellor begun before 7, Forester spoke and Blackstone, very short but well enough. The Solicitor General then opened on the other side & spoke very little, I thought, to the purpose. Their affidavits were then read, then Mr Clarke spoke for them, then Wilbraham, who fairly owned the whole transaction & insisted that it was the best agreement could be made for the family. Mr York followed. Their arguments were chiefly, that a Commission would have, no one knows, what end consequences, would destroy all my Lords acts, from his coming of age. Then my affidavit was read, & Mr Ludfords answer, which I found on my coming here but which contradicts not one fact which I have advanced except that of the staircase, which he swears was not making, I think, till April. But I never said 'making', but 'altering', which was doing as I have sworn, & you must well remember. Afterwards Mr Henley was going to reply when Lord Chancellor broke up the Court & fixed Wednesday. He took away Ludfords letter, which I annexed to my affidavit, with him. He said the surplus was not provided for as it ought, & that was a fault in their deed, & on going wished the parties could agree on some method to settle that. To which the Solicitor General answered that it had been considered as well as possible & nothing more could be done. My Council all agree that there can be no agreement so we must wait the issue on Wednesday, which cannot fail to conclude, so consider before you come down what you will do. I think you had better set out on Monday & leave me, but you shall decide as you please, I am tired so Adieu My Dearest Sophie Your most affectionate R N

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: April 18th 1752 Lincoln's Inn Fields Dear Madam I have little more to say yet, our Affair not being concluded last night as I expected, but we are to have another hearing on Wednesday. The Chancellor sat upon us from before seven till past ten, heard all the affidavits & all the Council except Mr Henley, upon the reply for us. Their chief arguments against us were that, I was a stranger in blood to Lord Donegall, that all his relations were agreed, that Macartney had contradicted his evidence (for my Lord) of last year, that he was the instigator of this & was turned out because he could not account. One of their Council, Wilbraham, confessed my lord's weakness as fully as could be wished, & said that all had been done that could be in such a case by the Deed, to which the Chancellor himself answered that there was a flaw in the distribution of the surplus which is a declaration that gives one great satisfaction, as he has already shown by it that he thinks my application neither improper nor frivolous. He added that something must be done in it & advised all parties to consider of it against the next day. I am going to Epping again and have some thoughts of sending the coach off on Monday but shall leave the ladies to their choice. It is a great mortification to be kept from Arbury but I must content myself. I am, dearest Madam Your most affectionate & dutiful son R Newdigate

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: Lincolns Inn April 23 1752 Dearest Madam We have lost our cause, very much contrary to the expectation of every body that knew anything of it. The Chancellor spoke an hour & half & always mentioned me with honour, that I had applied properly, that I had applied worthily & honourably, but that Lord Donegall, being confessedly no idiot nor lunatic, it was in the sound discretion of the Court whether they would grant a Commission or not, & that no line being drawn, no time of commencement of insanity, a jury might find back to Lord Donegall's birth, which would set aside the marriage settlement of Lord Donegall, & that upon Mr Chichester, & therefore the infants would be in greater danger under a Commission than at present under the Deed. Therefore dismissed the Petition. He said it might be proper still to enquire about £3720 which Mr Ludford released, & that belongs to little Jack, but I don't know how far I may think proper to proceed in this affair again. I am very easy under this disappointment, having followed the opinion of Mr Fazakerley & the other Councils in the discharging what I thought my duty in order to save a great sum of money & a great inheritance to the two poor orphans, who are now liable not only to loose that whole sum but loose Lord Donegall's inheritance, & the inheritance even to Mr Chichester's estate too, if Lord Donegall is married & a child produced & a Lunacy should be obtained afterwards which nothing but a Commission, now granted, can effectually prevent. I have not totally lost my time or trouble or expense, for everyone is convinced my application was well grounded & disinterested, which is a very great satisfaction, for everyone agrees that I have acted the part I ought. I shall return to Epping tomorrow & propose to set out for Arbury on Friday morning early, & hope to be there on Saturday night, & that we shall see you soon after, I am Dearest Madam Your most affectionate & dutiful son R Newdigate

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: Thursday February 15th 1753 Dear Madam I have only time to tell you I am just come from the Judges where I met Ludford & the rest. He seemed very quietly disposed & the rest rather fond than otherwise. By consent we put it off to try if anything can be done by the reference before Monday next. Last Monday I myself proposed to Mr Barry, by a friend, to refer to Mr Fazakerley the whole matter, which Mr Barry accepted, & on Tuesday evening Mr Fazakerley expected Mr Wilbraham, their referee to meet him, but with him came the whole crew, which, not a little, nettled Fazakerley, who expected Wilbraham alone, & made him interrogate Ludford upon the deed which he destroyed till he looked as if he was ready to sink into the earth. He said the deed of 1746 which he burnt would have destroyed the family. Fazakerley took him up. 'And did you make such a deed, Sir?' Mr Dixon came to me at the Coffee House, where I told him he deserved to be pulled by the nose for the letter he wrote about me. Some few words more passed but he was all along rather fond & fawning. What will be the issue? I cannot yet tell if they will leave their own referee & mine to themselves. It will be fairly & easily settled, & if they don't all mankind say it is impossible their bill, as it is, should pass either House. Besides, I had an hint yesterday that their great friend, Lord Brooke, was concerned to have it thought he made a party matter of it. Said he should be glad to talk with me, & I shall go accordingly tomorrow or next day. There seems to me great appearance of success but one way to be sure of it is to be in the right & then one can never want it I am Dearest Madam Your most dutiful & affectionate son R N

Dear Madam Going yesterday morning to Mr Eyre's to consider of the hearing before the Lords on Friday, I found a letter from their Agent that as I had signified my intention to petition for a Commission he would not give the Lords any further trouble about the Bill but would put it off till that affair is determined. This he did for a fortnight, which is in effect dropping the Bill. Thus I have obtained a complete victory in the first attack, which I was always of opinion I should, for what I had to produce at the Bar is a deep laid dark scene of iniquity, which they contrived to shuffle off at the Committee but which would have hurt them much more at the Bar where the Chancellor is present, & for that reason they did not care to face us. As they have not totally dropped the Bill the Chancellor, I'm afraid, will not let me petition whilst the affair is in the of , which will put me to this inconvenience, that I cannot proceed till the Session is at an end. But as it is more for their interest than mine that the affair should be determined soon I hope something will be contrived to go on immediately & I have no more doubts of succeeding in the Commission than I had in putting an end to their Bill in the House of . Mr Ludford was with Mr Fazakerly on Monday & talked of referring the matter to him & Wilbraham. But I have nothing to refer. All mankind agree that a Commission is the only desirable thing. All mankind call upon me to do my utmost to obtain it. My honour is engaged for it, & justice requires that Lord affairs should continue no longer in such hands. Though is not the object of my concern yet his family is, & I am ready to save them where I can, consistently with honour & justice, but they have tried every art & the utmost their Court Friends could do for them, their new allies, Lords Brook & Archer, but thank God justice has prevailed there, & I doubt not will in the other, though Mr has declared he will oppose the Commission while I have it twenty times under his head is the best thing for the family. If he alone could suffer by a retrospect it is no more than he well deserves. From the proofs he has with him, & his behaviour since his breach with them last year, which he insists was only because the interests of the children were neglected, Macartney rises every day in our opinion & I greatly hope his future conduct will be agreeable to it. Deal, & a Mr Hill, who lived with Donegall, & many others, are ready to make affidavits or do anything to assist the children. We want no evidence, nor anything but a speedy hearing. I am, dearest Madam Your most dutiful & affectionate son R Newdigate

Dear Madam We had a meeting today at the Judges Chambers where they have positively refused (notwithstanding what they wrote as in the last), to submit to the award of Mr Fazakerley & Wilbraham, who fully agreed & called the attorneys to tell them the result as you heard before. They carried their assurance so far as to deny the fact, as you will soon be told in Warwickshire by one of the archcontrivers, though Mr Wilbraham their own referee declaring the clauses they refuse are the best thing that can be for the good of the family. So we are all at sea again & the opposition in the House of Lords must go on. I am sorry for it, but the further they go the deeper they plunge, & the advantages I have obtained by the reference are very considerable, as all men must acknowledge that malice has nothing to do in my prosecution & that I have no other object but what I declare. I suppose their bill will be in the House of Lords to morrow where my Petition shall directly follow, I am, Dear Madam In great haste Yours most dutifully R N

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: Park Place March 17th 1753 Dear Madam Just come from the Play & have not time to send you a long letter but only in short to say that I have great hopes that my Council in the Committee of Lords today have given their Bill a fatal stroke, at least that side wind confirmation of their proceedings, which was the reason of their bringing the Bill, for the leasing the Town of Belfast. I don't object. The Committee came to no determination today but are to do so on Tuesday next, but by the looks of the Committee, & the long faces of my adversaries, I venture to promise myself success. They have chose to expose themselves, & they have had it to day strongly, particularly Mr Ludford. They would not agree to make an amicable end before, & they deserved it, & now they have put the affair on such a footing that it is impossible for me to let the confirmation of the deed pass with any modification they may offer, if the Lords should, as I persuade myself they will, strike out the deed from the Bill. The whole scene of iniquity has been displayed, but it is so deep it requires much enquiry to know all its secret recesses, & that enquiry will come in the Court of Chancery. They may thank themselves for that too. The Bell will not stay I am Dearest Madam, Your most dutiful & affectionate son R Newdigate

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: Park Place March 22nd 1753 Dear Madam I have nothing more to send you in relation to the Donegall affair but that in order to clear myself from the imputation of having obstructed a public as well as a private benefit by the throwing out the Bill for leasing the town of Belfast, as in the Committee I had consented to their powers of leasing as fully as they asked them, if they would take them simply & without a confirmation of the Deed of 1751, but they refused unless upon their own conditions. I contrived yesterday to speak to the Lord Chancellor myself & to let him know I was willing & desirous the Bill might go on for the leasing the town, & if it was possible without Lord Donegall's assent, which I could not procure, would carry it on myself. He answered that I could not without his consent. Do they then obstruct the rebuilding the town or do I? The list sent you last post I find was faulty. Their 7 Lords were Lord Sandys, who alone spoke for them, Lords Brooke, Archer, Hertford, Warwick (but I am not quite sure he voted), Duke of Dorset & Lord Kildare. The 14 that voted for me were Lord Oxford, Lords Raymond, Marchmont, Finlater, who spoke, Lords Shaftesbury, Litchfield, Ward, Northampton, Folly, Aberdeen, Folkestone, Willoughby of Parham, Feversham & the Duke of Portland. , I hear, says the Scotch Lords came down & that it was a contest between the Scotch & English linen manufacturers. That that is false appears from their being 3 Scotch Lords on one side & 3 Irish on the other, so that it was not carried by them. Those whom people call Court Lords on both sides were equal too, & all the Patriot Lords, thank God, were on mine. The House of Lords have gained reputation by rejecting a Bill which, upon the face of it, is a job. I will not say a W...k job as some lords have done, but all do me the honour to clear me from all imputations, & truth breaks out in spite of all the fogs that the Devil & his abettors have raised. , I find, is endeavouring to stir something against upon G.N's account but thank God the parties concerned are so satisfied that I will do them justice that he stands alone. I wish he could fall alone too, as by the answer he has put into my Bill he is likely to fall, & that his family may not suffer for him, I am, Dearest Madam Your most dutiful & affectionate son R Newdigate

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: November 13th 1760 Spring Gardens My best & Dearest On the other side I send you the great news of the day, for which the Park guns were fired this morning. The Guard fired volleys tonight & all the Town is bonfire & illumination. I foolishly swore at the Post last night for not bringing me a letter from my Dear Sophie, but I was sure it had miscarried & that I shall hear tomorrow, which upon recollection is as soon as I can possibly , but my life has been so very rapid & contained such variety since I left you that I have fancied much more time than 3 days has past. In my last I told you I was to be presented the next morning. I was so, & we were all most graciously received & afterwards saw the University of Cambridge present their their Address. Today I was at the Drawing Room which was also much crowded. I never saw a greater propriety of behaviour upon all these occasions than in the young monarch, so obliging, so free, so easy, yet preserving a proper dignity throughout. At the Leve`e yesterday he spoke to all that were introduced, & today in the Drawing Room of some hundreds of ladies I believe he omitted none, & all with an ease & readiness as if he had been King all his life. Yesterday the Vice Chancellor came up. We expect to be nobly attended tomorrow. I have been all day upon the prance in Lockwoods Coach to great men's doors to desire their attendance; Lord Granville's, Mr Pitts, Mr Legge's the Speaker etc. At all was very graciously received. Mr Pitt, as Secretary of State, will attend in his Office. Mr Leg will put on the Doctor's gown. We are to walk in procession from St James's Coffee House & afterwards to go to the Princess. The Duke of Beauford, Lord Abingdon, Suffolk, etc, are come up. The archbishops, Bishop of Durham, Duke of Leeds etc etc. Lord Litchfield is in Town but, alas, our Chancellor will not. Writes from Bath he can't bear a sudden journey & if he could, could not go through the fatigue. Tic a pity but we must make the best of it. P. Palmer is just come. He will go but dares not attempt to kneel. Mrs Prows is better. Lady Williams is come up in a great fright. Sir Watkyn has had a milliary fever but they say is safe. I can see nobody but at Court where I pass all my time. Yesterday indeed I condescended to dine at Lockwoods. Your brother I have not seen, nor heard if he will come. I had letters yesterday from Winchester. The 1st Division of L... come in today. Our first march tomorrow to Newbury in a day. On Wednesday I apprehend they will be at Shipston & Chipping Norton & halt Thursday. On one of those of days, I flatter myself, I shall join them & still march one division into the County. When I know more you shall hear it. The copy of a letter from the King of Prussia to his Queen at Magdebourg, Marshal Dan, with his left, occupied the strong camp near Torgau which Prince Henry, sometime since, held out against him. His right was covered with an abattoir de bois - trees felled, with cannon placed among them. The King ordered General Ziethen to attack the Marshal's left at eleven of clock which, after some resistance, he forced, upon which the King attacked the right & carried it. The action was very bloody, there and in the trenches, but at last the rout was general. The King took all their cannon & turned it upon them, & made great slaughter of the enemy, who never fired again afterwards. The action lasted till 7 & the Prussians continud under arms upon the bridges till 10. Marshal Dan escaped over the Alb in a boat.

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: House of Commons January 25th 1761 I have just seen a Petition which Sergeant Hewitt will present tomorrow from the inhabitants of Coventry for a road from thence through Caresley, Corley, Fillongley, Slolely Hill, Whitacre, Bentley to Baddesley Coalpits & so to Tamworth. I have wrote to Mr Baxter to acquaint my neighbours of Atherstone, & desire you will do so to those at Nuneaton & the neighbourhood, particularly Mr Busleton, Mr Vincent & Mr Barber. Some of the principal inhabitants of Corley & Fillongley declared to me their intention to oppose any such attempt, and if they will all agree to sign a Petition as oppressive to them, without hopes of any emolument, and the inhabitants of Atherstone & Nuneaton will sign another, as it must greatly affect both towns, and the present as well as the intended turnpike roads through them, and the mortgagees of the Hinkley Road & acting Commissioners will sign another (or, if thought more expedient all may join in one) to show that this new project is for a road parallel through out to one or the other of those roads, and if ever effected must hurt their tolls, and if measured cannot be more than one mile nearer to Baddesley & Birch Coppice pits than the road through Nuneaton & Atherstone I am well assured the project will, without difficulty, be brought to an end. I desire you will also give notice of this to Mr Lines & Roger Roe, to acquaint the inhabitants of Corley & Fillongley. Give my compliments to all and let them know I desire to have their opinions upon the subject, & if they think proper to oppose I am ready to give them my assistance, & desire to have an answer as soon as possible. I send you enclosed a Petition which I received from Mr Baxter for the addition to be made to the new intended road from Atherstone etc which I think, with the amendments which I have made, will do very well if they think proper to approve and sign it, & let Mr Baxter or Mr Fowler send it to me. I will put it into Sir Charles Mordaunt's care.

I do not find my opinion altered by the argument which you are told to send me against an opposition to the Badgley bill, nor by what I have in letters, nor can I see the Justice of the people of Atherstone or Nuneaton who, for their convenience, would load the people of Corley, Fillongley, my own tenants at Astley with a unprofitable & intolerable burden, but I have not yet seen Mr Baxter, so can't yet say what I shall think necessary to be done. You must take what the Astley tenants will pay you for Dr Winchester, & pay it Mr Fletcher when you get it, for I cannot get at the book, if I haven't , but I think I left it you out . If he has anything to say to the Doctor let him write, himself, don't you do it. I am glad to hear you are at work in the garden again, for I will have no more carting after this spring. Do you keep the stag out still? I don't propose to quick any part of Thomas Jelliff's this year, but don't forget the nursery in New Orchard. Tell Roger Roe I think he had better cover his sashes with oild paper till the inside is done, or, if not, all the lower panes as I don't choose to hazard the plate glass. Have you received the panes I ordered in lieu of the broken ones? You give me no answer whether Cooper will be a Sergeant which I desired you to ask him? I am sorry for poor Uxbridge. I am afraid they use the horses very ill in taking them back, for I commonly now lose an horse or two by the journey. I am sorry for your colds. As to cash to Mr Vincent it is so convenient a way of having my returns by taking the pay here in Town that you must contrive to supply him with pay for the men for the next month, let whatever will be the consequence. The whole pay, if the Company was complete, is about £50, which you may pay by 10 or £20, as he wants it, from this time to the 20th of March, & if you put off all other payments for that time. The men must be supplied, but I hope you will not be put to those difficulties. My new tenants for Lord Coventry's you should press, as well as all the rest in arrears. May I hope in that time not put you to distress. Sell the hogs you propose ... Keep the poles a little longer.

I am obliged to you all for your care & diligence in my cause, & very happy in the success of it, which I hope will tend to keep the rest of my neighbours from running to that vile shop of Law which can only conduct them to ruin. Preach this doctrine amongst them & let them know that it is not out of wrath to White but for the sake of example to others that I have given orders to proceed against him for the last penny, & I hope they will never forget this remarkable instance, that it is not out of goodwill or compassion to themselves but merely from the desire to injure me that they & their complaints are so well received there. I think you will do well to get in some cattle to eat the grass but whether to buy them or to joist some in will turn to most advantage I am a little doubtful, but this I leave to your judgement, which must be directed by the price of the cattle. I hope you have gone on peaceably & quickly with the tithe & that John Pain in particular has not been troublesome. I wrote to you last post & shall be glad to hear a particular account of your goings on. I hope Francis is careful of his cellars & that you take care they are not always open, as when I am at home, for treating & junketing at this time are out of season, & I hope, & don't doubt, you will maintain the family at as little expense as possible. My service to Mr Preston & all friends I have received of Robert Haymes, of Hurly 5 6 for his wife. So you must pay it to Jee at the Swan at Atherstone, where her husband orders her to go for it.

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: Arbury May 9th 1761 Dear Sir I have given Mr Truesdales proposal the fullest consideration & shall send you my deliberate answer to every particular. Though there are same lands which I should have been as well pleased if he had left yet I have no objection to those he has chosen for himself, & am willing to let him have the whole particular, in all £355 per annum as proposd & at the price proposd. I shall only observe that a considerable concession is made in allowing 20 shillings per acre for the meadows in Goodchilds Farm, which I reserve, when his whole farm is let, one with another, at 14 shillings only per acre, and that the meadows which I give up at his desire from Wingroves Farm, which he values at 20 shillings, is fairly worth 30 shillings per acre. I cannot understand why Norris's is to be valud only at 14 years purchase, which I cannot submit to, as his orchard & garden are worth full two thirds of what the whole is valued at. I must therefore desire they may be reserved out of the sale. In the room of Goodchilds Barn, which I reserve, I have given up that which is in my own hands & lies more convenient, which is used as a workshop. John Iv has barns enough without that at Moorhall, but if Mr Truesdale is of another opinion he shall have liberty to remove it, but I will not be at one shilling charge on that head. I am willing to make the usual allowance in the timber & in short to take £1000 for all that is growing on the premises. Whether the purchase is concluded or not before the 1st of July I must desire £2000, in case we should agree, may be advanced to be made up to £7000 on the conclusion, & will submit to take 4 only, though I pay at this time 5, & wait a reasonable time for the remainder. I have now gone through the particulars of your letter & shall only observe that I am surprised to find no mention made of the Place house itself. Does Mr Truesdale mean that I shall pull it down & convert the materials myself? For I cannot believe he can expect that such an house, the materials of which alone were valued by your brother at £800, exclusive of half a mile of lead pipes from the conduit & ponds, should pass in silence in so trifling a sale as this, of £350 per annum . If he means the first I am ready to agree to it. If the last I must beg you will inform him that I look upon it as no favour done me in giving 30 years purchase for old rents, nor £1000 for £1350 worth of timbers; for what then am I to make such a concession or improve upon myself in thinking I get 30 years purchase when I give back above two years purchase in the value of the mansion, which alone was let within these 20 years at £70 per annum . Mr Wight has just left me & I desire you will inform Mr Palmer that I shall pay in £500 more to Lord Coventry the beginning of next week. I have then but a small sum unprovided, which he assures me I may depend upon before the time, & having thus provided for my new purchase I am very easy whether I immediately dispose of Harefield or wait till a Peace, when I am sure to have no dispute for 30 years purchase, nor a considerable sum for an house capable of great improvement & whose situation & other conveniences will not fail to give them due value. I know as well as Mr Truesdale that this is a bad time to sell, & the worst consequence to me will be the continuing to pay for a short time 5 for the money. But as in the beginning of our treaty I declared myself ready to abate something of my demand for the house, & that it may not go off, as from your letter I conclude it will, with the reputation of invincible obstinancy on my side, I desire you will tell him, as my last word, that I am ready to take for the whole £12 000, & nothing under. This is my fixed resolution. I send you back the copy of your letter which came to me from Leicester (where I shall not return till Monday night) fearing you may not have a copy. Did you receive mine on the death of Mrs Jones? I am much obligd to you for the great pains you have taken, & I am, Dear Sir Your most sincere friend & humble servant R N

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: Arbury June 6th 1761 Dear Sir I am very sensible that you are in the right & that I can afford to sell for at least £200 less this year than the next, & though in case of a Peace I might expect much more yet as that is uncertain I would not let Mr Truesdale go for a trifle. But he is surely the hardest man to deal with that ever was. He now offers £11,550. Before, it was £11,542, a very great condescension! But does he mean it upon the terms of my letter & Norris's house & orchards, or will he let me carry away the worthless materials of the place? I have no answer to these. As to the barns at Moorhall I do absolutely insist upon their being reserved, & will not conclude without. The Church (all but the pew below the Chancel & the gentlemens' seats), & churchyard must be specially excepted. The water must run as at present, & my tenants for Cositas & Venables must have their turns of the water. The timber we valued at £1350 when the stockings etc were excepted, which amounts to £173, so conclude cannot be overvalued, & I have a right to insist upon that addition. But this you will represent, & do what you can. If the rest is agreed to I have only to put my proposal also in form which, if he rejects, - Farewell, Mr Truesdale. I will then take the 11,000 guineas which he offers upon these conditions: - 1st. That upon my mother's signing the deeds he shall present her with one hundred guineas, which she insists upon for her right in the placehouse, 2nd. That he shall receive the rents from Lady Day last, & pay 4 for the purchase money from thence. 3rd. That he shall pay the arrears of rent due at Lady Day last on the 1st of July in the enclosed rent roll, 4th. That he shall also advance the £1500 on the first of July. The payment of the remainder may be left to his & my convenience. Those sums for which I pay 5 cannot be repaid till the year is out; which will be in March - £4000, in April 1500, & if they will lower their interest may not be wanted then. Only he must undertake to enable me to give them notice. The sums of £1000 & £400, for which I pay the same, may be repaid as soon as I can receive them. But in those also I will allow some time if he requires it. Mr Hoare's mortgage, I apprehend, must be paid on the exchange of the deeds. But if an article is signed, that may be put off till it suits him. As this will be much within the terms of payment which he himself offers I hope he will consider & make the rest easy to me. And particularly if it shall appear that there is such an error as above in calculating the timber, that he will make an addition for it which is but just. But in this, & what remains, I leave myself to your discretion, being well assured you will do all you can for me. But pray do not forget that nothing but this encumbrance, brought on me by my new purchase, could make me consent to anything like the terms contained in this, & but for that Mr Truesdale or somebody else should pay for an hundred pleasures & conveniences that that place will afford to such a purchaser. I will add no more but to desire that if he boggles at these I may hear no more of him. I am, Yours most sincerely R N Time is so short that I must have an immediate answer, & pray do what you can to secure me part of the £1500 (if he refuses this) elsewhere on any terms, for fear Mr Wright should fail.

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: Arbury July 4th 1761 Dear Sir I should have been very glad to have known upon what terms you have the money which you have paid for me, as it would be a real satisfaction to me to be assured you have put yourself to no inconvenience & I should better have known how to deal with that B... Mr . But no situation of my assessment shall bring me to submit to his new articles which, dictatorlike, he produces without scruple when he himself will not give way in one tittle. I will therefore be positive on my side. First, I peremtorily declare I will not convey on any terms one inch of the Chancel or of Brackenbury Chapel, nor one yard of the churchyard. Before, he only desired the use of them, which I am ready to agree to, as in my last. 2nd, I will not convey to him Goodchilds Barn, nor anything at Moorhall but the materials of J Eve's Barn. As I retain above 20 acres of Goodchilds Farm I will have that barn with them, as I give up a barn (the Workhouse) that lies more convenient for Goodchilds use. 3rd If by fixtures are meant marble tables in the Hall, brewing vessels, cooler, boilers etc, grates or such like, they all belong to my mother, & he will not have them unless he pays for them. I would not have stood on little things but he shows me the way. As to the rest, the pipes, cisterns & the sole use of the conduit, & liberty to mend the pipes, doing no wilful damage to Richard Hills farm I agree to. The great Pond near Ashleys. I will not on any terms convey the use of the water as far as the arch will carry it, for the use of the Place; & liberty to fix & repair sluices for that purpose he may have. The rest, with fish & fishing, I reserve to be let with the manors, & will not separate them. I am in no hurry for the arrears, for all I desire is to have them secured, & as the tenants, however poor, are responsible I will stay as long as he pleases if he will covenant that they shall pay me in the first place & his growing rent after I am served. I don't choose to discount being unwilling, as he wont let me have another shilling from him, that he should ever get another from me. Pray tell him it is too late now July 1st is over to enhance upon his demands, & if he does not choose the purchase under the terms above I desire neither you nor I may have further trouble. I can depend upon Mr Wright in a short time, & if any particular day is necessary to refund you by I may know it that I may press him farther. You are all my concern on this occasion. As he does not pay till Michaelmas the receiving the rents till then is only of course & not to my advantage at all. Prompt payment is certainly so. I should have added that he is welcome to use the house as he pleases, even before the articles signed. The crop & the grass of orchard etc till Michaelmas I must have or be paid for. I send you the inventory. They are all of small value. If you agree they shall all go to Brackenbury unless he will pay for what he wants. On Monday I go to to Leicester & propose to be back on Saturday. I forgot to thank you for your last which gave me great satisfaction & will send you some franks the first opportunity &am etc You still say nothing whether he expects interest for the £1500 till Michaelmas. From his other exactness I conclude he does, & if so must pay it.

column39: The Correspondence of Sir Roger Newdigate of Arbury Warwickshire. Ed. by A. W. A. White. The Dugdale Society: Hertford. 1995.
column46: Arbury July 17th 1761 To Mr Eyre, Attorney Etc Dear Sir I have executed & return enclosed the Article with some small alterations, the first in relation to moving J. Eves Barn. I have given to Lady Day, but if he desires to Midsummer I have no objection, but a time must be fixed, & Lady Day is long enough for pulling down & removing, as he re-erects upon his own premises. Goodchild, having the lease from me may, if he pleases, keep Venables & Costars till the end of his term, so I will not object to his having the barn, provided he gives it up with those meadows which, as it must be by an agreement with him, cannot hurt his landlord. I did not understand he was to have the oak that is felled this spring. It should in reason have been excepted as he has more timber already than he pays for. I don't understand the words 'free use in common'. As to the pews they must be better explained in the deed, & I desire you will now explain my sense of them to Mr Truesdale to prevent mistakes. That I mean only to allow himself & family, servants excepted, to sit in Church times in the Chancel, & the same for his servants in the Brackenbury Chapel, but nothing there mentioned is to give him a power to alter, repair or strike a nail in any part of either, or any other power or liberty whatsoever. This I desire you will take particular case of, & if the words can be explained to give further liberty send me another article, properly worded, to execute, & cancel this, for in this point I will run no hazard. Having had so much trouble already to bring this to bear I beg it may stand clear of any new Treaty, & that he may execute as I have done, after which if he desires a new agreement for the rest he shall have them altogether: Remainder of Trenleys, as you set it, at £16.0.0 Hovels at £20.0.0 Hills at £30.0.0 £66.0.0 The timber to be valued by one or two persons to be named, the price 30 years purchase, but pray let him sign & seal before a word is said of this. I mentioned before the goods I mean to reserve. He is to have only what is, strictly speaking, fixtures. Thank you for writing about Brentwood. I must send you the paper next letter about fishery. I have no time, being now on the point of setting out for Leicester, to say more than Yours R N

column46: Plymouth October 17th 1762 My Dearest Sophie I was going as I promised to attempt to describe to you Mount Edgecombe but as I can always speak best with my pencil I have scratched out a map of the situation, which is one of the most magnificent I ever beheld, as you may judge by the sketch I send you, & I assure you I have introduced very little more than what you command from the Park & House. Palmer & I took our horses on Friday & rode to the Town of Dock, 2 miles, & to the passage which I have marked. From thence we sailed to Lord Edgcombes gates & walked over a fine lawn to the house, which is about halfway up the hill. The stone of this country is too hard & rough to work to a truth, as we masons say. Its colour too, which is a reddish black. being all really marble mixed with a very white lime, is not agreeable to the eye, & the house being old, with 4 octagons newly added to the angles, makes a better appearance at a distance than near. The inside too is very indifferent, & has nothing worth seeing but some fine marble pillars in the hall, which are cut out of the hill itself, & take a fine polish. The gardener not being in the way we scrambled up to the highest part of the park, which is full of plantations but too bleak for them to prosper. We went near Maker Church & then turned south, down the hill to a stile which introduced us into the plantation, along the cliff & to one of the most agreeable walks I ever saw. The sun shone upon the unbounded ocean which lay under us, chequerd with the shadows of the clouds as they passed, & we seemed as far from the resort of Man as if the country was desert, till two large vessels came in full sail from the East Point, under the new house, & drew us on to the busy scene which this town of war & trade exhibits on every side. Everything on that side seemed in motion. In one part of the cliff walk an awkward arch is built, throe which you see the Eddistone as a termination. The garden disappointed me, a few scattered myrtles grow bushwise about but look very unthriving. There are two hedges of the same, about two feet high, some magnolias, one lemon & an orange or two not much higher look miserably, & I could discover the marks of shelter applied to them in the winter. The winds are very bleak & I was surprised to find all the oranges housed. They are in tubs &, I think, the finest plants I ever saw, brought from Genoa a few years ago, the stems eight feet high, clear & beautiful, the heads not 4 feet round, but if they ever grow in proportion to the stems they will be very extraordinary. The taste of gardening as well as building here runs very low. Nature has left no room for improvement here, planting excepted, which is well done. I will now leave you to my drawing, only add the colouring which the sun gave it, & I can't. But remember the verdure of the hills & enclosures. Park & lawns very fine, the tops of the cliffs & quarries red, their feet black with the beating of the waves, the houses rough stone, much limed, whitish, their roofs of slate, blue, the ships some with flags out, some in full sail, the water everywhere chequered with little boats & sloops, & varying its colours to the sun & clouds. Nothing could be more beautiful. I longed for you to see it. All I can do is to describe it. Now I must tell you, Madam, this is the last letter I shall honour you with. Perhaps, please God, I may be with you before this . Hard luck indeed if I am not before another could. Tomorrow for the first time I am Field Officer of the Day. At noon I take a walk & visit the prisons. That's all my business except wearing a sash & gorget. Whaler is gone to day to Bath. His uncle there is dead & has left him all he has. You may see my walk for tomorrow in the Plan, where I have marked all the prisons. Hay has resigned upon a bullying letter of the Colonel. Says his Commission is taken from him. He paid Dadley for doing his duty. Now the Corps must suffer for the vacancy. This is all.
