column46: November 25th 1762 Spring Garden I kiss my dearest Sophys pale... I came safe & without the least accident at 10 o'clock this morning, & immediately marched to Cocoa to breakfast to learn news. As I came back to dress looked into the Mews where were more than 200 people, I believe, gathered round the Coachhouse doors to have the first sight of the State Coach. It was then 11 o'clock & they were to wait till near one. At half past 12 I went in a chair with great difficulty to the House, for such was the eagerness of all ranks to see the show that every street & alley was full, & though they permitted his Majesty to go down, they made him wait above an hour in Palace Yard, & at last were forced to drive all the coaches that filled the streets into the Park to make room for him to return, which was not accomplished till past 4. Many of the Members, amongst them Bagot, Sir etc could not get down to the House. Lord , some say, was mob'd & insulted, & some incivilities went higher, No Scotchm-n, Newcastle for ever' etc. That noble began with a mob & seems determined to end with one, for they say it was not only curiosity to see the Coach that drew together such a concourse. I send you the Speech; the Address is the echo to it. It was moved by Lord Carysford, seconded by Lord Charles Spencer. There was a peculiar gravity & piety in the Motion that moved up Mr Calvert who said he could make the House laugh, & he did so by accusing the noble lord of having stole his speech from the Preface to 4 Sermons published by Fleetwood, Bishop of St Asaph at the time of making the Peace of Utrecht, but said he had misquoted & repeated the passage. The truth is his Lordship had altered the passage which you will find in Boyer's Oueen Anne, 1713. The Prelate set up the Whigs' standard & his sermons were burnt by the Hangman, by order of her last Parliament. He displayed the wonderful successes of that war to the period of the Treaty, then stops & adds, Our enemies will tell the rest with pleasure'. Lord stole the first part, the last would not fit him, so he altered it. A thorough . He stood for it for a considerable time. Nothing was said in opposition. The Lord Mayor called it an innocent address & said if the Preliminaries are as they were printed in the papers he would undertake to prove them inadequate to our victories, insecure & inglorious. Charles Townsend answered him with spirit; said he had the honour to descend from a person whose glory it was to have been voted an enemy to his country by that Parliament that made the Treaty of Utrecht, & if this was like that he would showed his blood was genuine, but believed it very different. This was all we had of consequence. The Address passed name con . In the Lords Lord Egmont & - I forget who -, moved the Address. Lord Aylesford & Lord Northumberland moved an Address to the Queen on the birth. We have lumped that in ours... Now for conjectures. The struggle, they say, is whether or Newcastle shall be . Both master the Houses. The last, they say themselves, have 120. Mr Fox, who is very gracious to us, says only 75 Commons & 42 Lords, 8 of whom are . They are not to oppose the Preliminaries, which are expected in the next week, but to attack Lord in every shape. 8 of them were to have thrown up yesterday when they went in a body to the Leve`e , but thought better of it, the having declared that no man that gives up now shall ever come in again, & they say they would not give his the uneasiness to break his word as they are sure he must take them again. So resignations are stopped & I conclude from thence their opposition will be shortlived. The Country Gentlemen, I believe, will be unanimous. That is a blow they will feel, & if they let the Preliminaries be approved by Parliament, if I was the Minister, I should care little for them afterwards. There is great confusion but Lord seems to be very firm, goes on his way & keeps his object steadily in view & probably, I think, will attain it. The speech promises reductions. Denbigh says the Militia will be immediately in part disembodied after the ratifications come over, those who are in their Counties & not on duty first, others not till the Peace is concluded amongst which he reckons ours, which will stay perhaps 2 months more where they are. For this he quotes Lord Ligonier. The papers say Miss Pakington is dead. How sudden & surprising! I shall consult Telly about mourning. The Bell will not let me read nor finish my letter...

column46: House of Commons April 24th 1766 Sir I hope you will excuse the hurry in which I wrote on Friday but I have much more to ask forgiveness for, having, upon the receipt of your last, taken into consideration the difficulties & delays which must necessarily proceed from the uncertainty of procuring the whole sum, from which Mr Keen will not depart, & the reasonable objections you & the society may have to engaging yourselves for it. I have taken the liberty to agree with Mr Keen myself & to sign the agreement in my own name, & you may expect to see him next week to make a beginning. The plans & the particulars which he has signed I shall send by the Machine. They are complete except in some trifling articles to which he agrees. I have just had the pleasure of communicating this to Mr Chambers, who flatters me you will excuse me. I have mentioned his name to our Chancellor & am in hopes he will succeed in his application. I am, with great respect, Your most obliged, humble servant R N

column46: Spring Gardens December 11th 1767 Dear Sir The instant of your friends now before me deserves my utmost gratitude & the fullest answer in my power to give. I know of no intention to extend the Botly Turnpike Bill beyond the limits of the Petition, which I observe was signed by the Vice Chancellor himself, nor will the rules of the House suffer it. I had no intimation of that Bill, nor was it recommended to my care. On Monday next the Committee is to sit upon it, when I shall certainly attend it. If anything like what you mention should be happening, which I think cannot be done, will certainly follow your friendly advice. As to the Bill to allow collegiate bodies etc to exchange, I cannot, upon memory, say whether I sent it to the Vice Chancellor or not. I rather believe I did, but sure I am that I had neither letter nor instructions from him about it, nor took any part in it. So much for my Parliamentary conduct, which I doubt not from inability or ignorance deserves much reprehension, but want of regard for that venerable body for which I serve, or want of integrity or zeal for my country, I defy the purest malice to show in the course of upwards of twenty years which I have sat there, most of them in your service. Excuse a little honest indignation which the reception of Mr Walter's obloquy has met with draws me into. If the University expects perfection in Man I pretend not to it, & I think I could make a very good defence if I knew what he has charged me with. If I am examined about a transaction in my private family, why I discharged Mr Walters, I answer, - Because by an arrogant, disobliging ill-bred behaviour in my house, & at my table, he had made himself disagreeable to me & all my family. Had I not a right to do so, & without giving a reason? But to your friendship I will go further. because he often neglected the duty of his office, & more immediately because after taking the Curacy of my church at Astley, under the express condition of doing duty there on Saints days & Holy days, he suffered the Holy Week to pass without prayers, even on Good Friday, as I remarked, & when I justly told him that before he entered upon it Dr had made it the condition of his doing so, & that & I both expected it from him, he flatly & rudely told me I might expect what I pleased he would not do it. When I told him I hoped he would resign, he told me he would not do that neither, & kept the Curacy 2 months after without weekly duty. And can my good constituents at Oxford think or expect, highly as I esteem their favour, & I do esteem it as the greatest honour & ornament of my life, that I could sit quietly down with such a person as my table companion after this, longer than a reasonable notice which was given him. If he had been poor distressed he should still have had my pity but he was above me &, I believe, took two or three journeys to Oxford, chiefly to vent his spleen. But I trusted & do trust that my character is better established than to be the victim to his slanderous tongue. This is as far as I can recollect the whole of the story. He had afterwards a controversy with Dr upon it who, I doubt not, keeps his letters & will be glad to produce them in his our vindication. But is there not something of envy to him that helps to set about these malicious rumours. Trace them perhaps. My conjecture may be right. I have seen enough of Parliament & of the miserable state of this country to be without concern whether I ever sit there again. Retirement I love & know how to enjoy. I despise idle slanders & do not fear their consequences. Conscious that I have done my duty I know they cannot embitter that retirement which, in five years more perhaps, may be my choice. There I hope & trust your good opinion & that of many more good friends will follow bear me company. I am, dear Sir Your much obliged, humble servant R N

column46: February 18th 1768 Dear Sir I was favored with your letter & don't know how to express my gratitude to you for the obliging expressions of your regard for me. I have already repeatedly received from the University of Oxford the highest honour that I think can be conferred upon a subject. No other seat ever could or ever will draw me again into public life when they are pleased to give me a dismission. I have therefore no concern for myself, but most heartily & anxiously wish for the prosperity, peace & unanimity, for the honour & independence, of that venerable body which has hitherto held forth the brightest example to the electors of Great Britain in the free, unsolicited & disinterested manner of their choice. I have enclosed the letter as it has passed Debate last night till 12 on etc, etc, and am Dear Sir Your most obliged & most obedient Servant R N

column46: Arbury March 28th 1770 Sir As I could not see the Archbishop I have wrote to him, & beg you will give him the letter of which I send you a copy, & one I received from Mr Chester with my answer. If the Archbishop is not there, desire the Bishop who presides to open my letter, which is to the Governors. If Mr Chester comes or sends to you pray enter into no treaty with him, but only tell him I have laid the whole before the Governors, when I beg you will attend with Maberley to prove what I allege. Lay the whole before them, & if they approve of the proceedings of their servants I must apply elsewhere. I have been so lucky to find the letter in which you first hinted anything of expense to me, with a copy of my answer, which is full enough to the point, which I send you. Pray keep these papers & return them when all is over. If any of the matters I have asserted is controverted I have the papers to prove them, but have not sent them as I don't expect they will. It will be necessary now to show them Mr Chester's bill. I have not said it but I think they will be at no loss to see the collusion between the Office & him in this affair. Without his bill I dare say there would have been no refusal of the payment of the £200, & if you have an opportunity to throw it out to them pray don't lose it. I beg you will be so good to rouse your spirit a little upon this occasion. I sent a draft to Cousins the day I received yours. I am, Dear Sir, Your affectionate, humble servant R Newdigate The ladies send compliments

column46: January 11th 1771 Dear Sir The severity and uncertainty of weather now beginning to thaw, the snow, of which a good deal fell last night, the encumbrance of a house not yet cleared of my Churchman friends, the short time left me for the settling my affairs & the necessary preparations for removing my family to Town, the number of workmen in my house & many more out of it, will all I hope plead in my excuse for not obeying your commands in two letters which came together to me this day. But neither the short notice nor any of the reasons above should have prevented my waiting upon you & accepting your obliging invitation to the Lodgings, was I not fully persuaded that I am too little acquainted with the subject in question to venture to give advice upon it. I have read several attacks upon the Bill intended, in the papers, & have no doubt they will incite proper answers, but if there is any foundation for them perhaps it would be more prudent to try some means of accommodation than to drive them into opposition by hurrying the Bill. I am afraid it will be impossible for me to be in Town till a few days after the meeting, but from my arrival there shall devote my whole time & application to the carrying it through the House, & in every thing obeying your commands, & have no doubt we shall find friends to support us in a matter so highly concerning the University. My wife & Miss Conyers... I am, Sir, with utmost respect Your most obliged, humble servant, R N

column46: February 14th 1771 Mr Vice Chancellor In obedience to your command & by desire of Mr Page I trouble you with our sentiments upon the Bill now before the Commons. We have made it our business to learn what impression the objections so strongly thrown out in the House have made, & are of opinion that the best way to silence our enemies & keep our friends firm will be to submit to alter the plan in a few particulars ... a tax is to be laid upon the buildings to keep the pavements etc clean & lighten the streets, to take place after the first expense of putting them in order. We are accused of the highest injustice in laying the load upon the traveller & farmer, & the examination of our sister, Cambridge, is set up against us, who, with the Town, agreed to do the whole by a tax on the buildings. The Bill was printed but a dispute about the Company put an end to it. We have reason to believe the whole opposition will fall to the ground if the same tax, which is intended to be levied after the first expense, was to be levied immediately. And to go in aid of it, which would only anticipate the charge upon the building for a year or two, & as the sum so raised must be very insufficient, the remainder to be charged upon the tolls which should be the fund to borrow what is wanted upon, as now intended. This would remove the objection of injustice. We shall take our share of the load & only ask for what we are not able to supply ourselves. Another advantage will be that no part of the City or suburbs need then to be left out of the Bill, which they now insist shall only take in the streets through which the great road lies. To relieve the farmers in general we would propose a diminution of the tolls upon their animals etc brought to market to one half of the proposed toll or otherwise, as you think proper. The clause for pulling down obstructions is much too large & must be narrowed by particularising the buildings needing to be removed. We propose the Committee to be adjourned to Monday seven-night & to wait upon Lord to talk over these amendments, if we have your command to do so. Mr Page desires me to add that he will wait upon you with Mr Walker if you desire a farther explication. Have talked with Walker about the objections to the Bill. Seen Stacey again who says if the University & City will pay the intended levies from the beginning, will not object to their taking the tolls to make it out, & if the market people & waggons pay half toll thinks perhaps all opposition may be laid aside. Proposes, if Mr Page approves, to write to the Vice Chancellor tonight & recommend it from both & also from Lord North, with whom Sir Roger is to dine today, to follow this plan as sure to keep our friends firm at least if not silence our enemies. Also to narrow the clause for pulling down what is too extensive & may easily be particularised. Other advantages from laying the levy in the first instance will be that no part of the City or suburbs could then be left out of the Bill, which will be complete & have nothing of Job in it. Mr Page & Mr Walker will come down if desired. If you give us authority we will talk with Lord Macklesfield an immediate answer when to adjourn Committee.

column46: House of Commons 8 o'clock Thursday Set out early & got to Town, time enough to take place & ... & dressed, perfectly well & without accident. Sir Meredith has moved the Petition, seconded by Pitt. I called upon him to open the Petition & purported prayer of it & what the people are who signed it. It is only strictly against the Articles, not the Liturgy, but in consequence goes to both. The subscribers about 250, near 200 clergy. I then opposed the bringing it up & have been very fully supported on both sides of the House, though the intent of seemed to have been to let it be brought up & lie upon the Table. But they have given it up & are for rejecting it at once. Mr Page seconded me. Keep the particulars till you hear from others the part I have taken, for though I cant keep it from you I would not have you the teller of it. 10 o'clock The debate goes on & I shall not have time to send you the result, but I have no doubt of a great majority to refuse the Petition to be brought up. I can tell you no more. I must send my letter. God bless you Near 11

column46: Spring Gardens Saturday February 8th 1772 A letter from my dearest Sophie yesterday recruited my spirits, which were not a little affected by the whirlwind of mind & body in which I had existed for three days past. I set out with concern. I cannot help it when I turn my back on my dearest Ba but it was no small addition that she is a convalescent & her delicate feelings can at anytime tear her slender frame to pieces. The drifting snow, the length & fatigue of the journey, & the anxiety of mind which the momentous business I went upon must occasion I know would distress you more than myself, & had no comfort in the very difficult & dangerous journey (from Devises to Marlborough especially, where the snow had actually filled up the road so as to stop all passage, & I was forced to quit it & drive over the untrack'd Down, but Providence sent us a guide - one of the turnpike laborers sent to dig out the road, who ran all the way before the chaise, the snow & sleet driving all the while that neither man nor horse could hold up its head), but that my dearest Sophie could not conceive our situation to be one half so bad as it was. Thank God we got safe here. I dressed & went to the House & stirred not from thence till 11, & dined at home at midnight. Exceedingly fatigued I was, but Telly recruited me with a good dinner on Friday & I have been perfectly well ever since. Everything relating to the debate has turned out beyond my wish or expectation, & I had the good fortune of dragging the M-n-y - to do what every one agrees they ought but did not intend to do. I learn besides today that there was a meeting of Lord , the Archbishop & others to which I was to have been sent for, who agreed to let the Petition be brought up. If I had been here I should have found it difficult to resist such authority. I was absent, & luckily by my standing saved them & myself from the reproach of lukewarmness, at least in such a cause, for I soon found reason to suspect that the m-n-y having so resolved had determined the faction to lug them into the very step which I actually did. The M-n-y must have followed them instead of me, & I should perhaps have born reproach along with them. As it is, they have a better excuse. I have the satisfaction to find my conduct has been much approved. It is awkward to talk of oneself, but to you it is only like thinking, & you are too much concerned to withhold from you the satisfaction I feel in having done my duty in the manner & with success beyond even my most sanguine hopes. The evening papers contain a fair summary of the debate & the petitions ... ... ... Moysey for their care. I have great confidence in both. God send I may soon see thy own hand again. I thought it altered & fear you suffered by writing your last. Don't put yourself in pain. If you want me I will come directly, but Mr Secmore, coxcomb! has given notice he will attack... ...

column46: Past 8 Tuesday 25th A rap at the door so loud! It can be no less than the Knight of the Shire for Essex. Here he is, jolly & happy, a numerous creditable meeting, everything answering to his wishes. Frank for yourself now, Sir. At 10 minutes after 5 came his express & I packed it off directly. It will be with Lady H... I expect by 8 o'clock tomorrow, & you will not have this till past noon on Thursday. What does the rascally postman mean? It is not dull Tuesday here. But it has been with me, for not a scrap have I from Bath this day. I slept tolerably well last night, but waking in the morning & lying so, a good while tumbling about, some unlucky dust of the warming pan, I believe, for it felt hard & sharp, fell into my eye. I could sleep no more, & all morning was almost wild with pain. I sent for Wood. He came at noon & God be praised took it out, but my eye is still swelled & sore. So, with half an eye, to the House I went, & there had an Herculean labour on my hands & good Sir . Our good Doctor was again attacked. Mr Walsingham moved to expunge the Thanks & we fought to our stumps. The indecency, inconsistency, of first deputing to ask a man to preach, hearing his sermon (16 members were present), not a word said against it, moving & ordering Thanks & desiring to print. Then, in a pet, rubbing them out & expunging from the journals. On it went, till at last Mr Montague gave notice he would move to abolish the observation of the day. Much more consistent, sure, than to reflect on a man for preaching the doctrines of it. I moved the Order of the day & was beat 152 to 101. I think we have gained by this loss. The Vote will not hurt our friend more than the reflections did, & we have showed that we thought his cause defensible & were not afraid to defend it, & the principles advanced to abuse him go as directly to condemn the Service of the Church which they now threaten to abolish also. Such are the principles of these times! You will see me trimmed for this again in the papers but I care not. I will defend the good old Lady & her sons as long as I can stand. Yesterday I sent you the particulars of the Ledbrook melancholy Express. Before that you will have a hint of it from Lady H... to prepare you. This will be a day after. I cannot guess what turn it will take with his successor. How he can go on! ...

column46: Spring Gardens Tuesday March 2nd 1773 I am come at last to my Dear Sophie after dispatching many letters & parcels. I have writ to Moysey, to Page, to Mr Cobb. What a most delicious piece you have sent today; sleep, stomach all well & the doctor writes confirming it, all but my poor dear dextra . I cannot part with that. I have a partiality to it. It gave me yourself. No, I forget, both hands did that. But it has always been my best friend in absence, though sinistra has always done its best too. In short I had rather all was well & no complaints, & the doctor promises well. God send success. Keep the inside safe. We must submit. Lady B... was mighty well yesterday. I have not heard today. Never mind the papers. They misrepresent all they give & make most of it. I said a vast many good things that they don't give you out of envy. This day have I been making Sir eat up his words relating to Tottie. They are in the enclosed. The words the articles taken in their litteral sense' are not in his book, Honour & Blasphemy , are not applied to the articles but Tottie says the Doctrines (that are not there) of absolute decrees & reprobation are horror & blasphemy. Sir 's Bill was read this day 1st time & I took the opportunity to set right this that passed on Tuesday. I had the satisfaction to find everybody thought I did right. Sir looked small. Owned the words were not there in fact but contended the sense was. I replied he might comment as he pleased on the book if he did misrepresent the words. Your brother came again yesterday; came from the House today & dined with me & Charles on turkey, mutton & roast fowls - rare prog from Arbury. I have looked into Venner & like him. But Sir did side the government & nobody thinks it wrong. We are all very silly indeed. Poor Crook! All the neighbours are to be sure the finest assortment that ever was. Sorry for Midge's headache. Glad her cough is over - but sweet chocolate is a very good thing, let me tell you. Keep your house to yourself. I send you Cob's letter & my answer. My budget is out, & here's the bill. God preserve & keep you!

column46: Spring Gardens Wednesday March 10th 1773 Late am I come to my most agreeable sport, having travelled through much labour this day. In the morning petitioning Dissenters to consult & followed them to Sir W Bagot. Saw Lady B... weak abbattue , but for the time of the month better than usual & better upon the whole. Then to battle in the . They had given the Council so little time to prepare that last night he, Mr Perrin, a very eminent man, gave up his brief declaring he could not prepare himself so as to do credit to himself or justice to his clients. Upon this Sir W moved for farther time & we gave them a trimming for the indecency of refusing a few days to petitioners on so important an occasion. Sir W Dolben, Page, Cavendish etc supported, & Mr Tudway, who presented the petition. Tell his manner through the floor. He is a very good boy. We divided for Monday and lost it, 34 to 87. We are grown on the subject since last year when 9 and 75 were the most on any division. We have done with it now till Wednesday. Upon the reading we were tired & had tired the House, so only Mr Tudway made a very good speech against it & was answered by T Townsend, but no division. So till Wednesday. I shall frisk & be jolly. I have no time to say a word how glad I am you go on well, sleep well & are easy & want nothing. No more I hope of the return of pain at night. Do you do as I bid about flannen. Tell Ornament absence does not abate my love but rather increases it. I had rather have all my troop in the morning than that tiresome Midge playing the chimes on a guittair. I can bear Dr Togg Simkin, anything, rather than these. The Bell is come back. God love you both.

column46: Spring Gardens March 17th 1773 I am tired, my Dearest Ba, but must satisfy your curiosity by copying what I have writ to old Winchester at Christchurch. Sir H. Houghton moved to leave the chair. Sir W. Bagot in a very able & ingenious speech opposed. He was supported by Mr Page & answered by Mr Ed Burgh with affected wit as usual but without argument, an eulogium upon Toleration in general, which nobody had said a word against, & ended with a fine Floreat to the Church of England. (This for Ba's private ear I took courage finding him beside the mark & answered him. Spoke long & much tired myself). On one side were Mr Tudway, Sir W Dolben & R N. On the other Mr Dyson, Duntze, Sir W Meredith, G Onslow Mr Graves & Harris. Eyes 69, Nos 16. The then went through the Bill. The arguments were against the particular mode of toleration by the Bill, which is in fact an establishment of every sect under heaven: we allowed the principle of toleration in its largest extent, but insisted that Establishment (as in the Act commonly called the Toleration), though right & proper for those Dissenters who agree in the doctrines of Christianity & principles of civil government with the Church, could not be given to the rabble of Sectarians but that they should be allowed only toleration that is indulgence under the control of Government & only during good behaviour, as is the Constitution of Holland. I flatter myself we had the argument fairly with us - so far to old Now my Ba, I am not the person to say so but it will give satisfaction to my Ba to hear me say I am not dissatisfied with myself nor believe the fair hearers were so with me. I spoke longer than I ever did before & was well heard throughout. Bagot really did admirably & so did Dolben. Naming him puts me in mind to say Keen tolls me today that the Radcliffe trust is filled up with him & Lord North. Your brother was with us - Sir Watkin but I don't know whether he staid the division - Curzon, Lord Guernsey etc. On Friday the report & then only one day more the 3rd Reading when Blackstone's successor, Mr Chambers, is engaged as Council for the petitioning Dissenters. Is not that droll enough. Harris made fun of me for being the intimate friend of them. I have hardly yet read a short piece from Ba. I told you something from Copped about offering them your house, but I learn they bring all the family so it would not hold them. But B... will not the worse for the Abbey full of...

column46: Spring Gardens Lady Day 1773 My best Ba will have a short come off tonight but I will not retaliate - though I can't tell why I should have no letter from Bath today. Not Ba ill, that I wont believe - not Midge ill. I must have had a word then. No - it is the Post failed, it is the footman failed, some nonsense or other that vexes Ba too for my disappointment. Well, we have had it out. The Dissenters Bill is passed - many petitions against it, 5 or 6 today. Mr Chambers, Vinerian Professor spoke admirably 3/4 of an hour for his clients. The debate began at 4, in which we all took our share - lasted till near 7, when on the division 65 for, 14 against. We have made a stout battle for our numbers & have, I believe, blasted the Bill so that I think they will never move it in the same form again. I eat half my dinner before I went & Sir W has carried me to the Board where I eat t'other half, & it was near 10 before I got home. Lady Bagot continues surprisingly well. Lord Chesterfield dead. The Lord Mayor goes up to St James's tomorrow. They say Lord Chamberlain that he likes it not but goes up only officially. I long to hear poor Midge is better - long to see you both - happy that I have but one more letter to write to you. I feel much lighter now the load of Presbytery is off my stomach, & you may expect a very gallant Macaroni ready to take you out of your coach. I have nothing to add to the direction for your journey. Good night. God bless you & send it may be prosperous

column46: Florence December 6th 1774 Dear Sir I am very happy to receive a letter from your hand though the contents are not what I had flattered myself I should have received. That the County of Warwick should run mad with Folly & Wilkism when ever the great patriots of Newcastle, the apes of the enthusiasm of London & Middlesex, come back to their sober senses, though I saw strong symptoms of it before I left you, I could not have believed. I trusted that a great Neptune would have arisen with a Quos ego! to still the madness of the people by taking at least one wise and prudent step in his life, by declaring boldly for the admirable measures of our ancestors which have kept the County for half a century in peace, & setting his face against the disturbers of its peace. I doubted at the time, & it is now too evident I leaned upon a broken reed. How can a person of such weight suffer all his importance to be picked out of his pocket by petty thieves & pilferers. I am mortified for the whole, to see freeholders who should be the bulwarks of the Constitution so easily led by the nose, but my indignation rises at my neighbours, who are the objects of my lowest contempt, & so I shall let them know if I live to come amongst them again. They have done me the favour, I suppose an election tale, to say I don't intend to return, & I fear it has served their purpose; but indeed I intend just the contrary, & I hope & trust I shall have fortitude enough to do so before the end of another year. The step I have taken has, I thank God, turned out very happily hitherto, both to myself & my good companions. We find our time too short, constantly employed & engaged with objects that engage our attention & amuse & please us. Every day of six weeks which we have resided here has produced something new & worthy of notice, & the remainder of our destination, which is till the end of next week, will not be enough to satisfy our curiosity. Our mornings are spent amongst the statues. paintings, intaglios & cameos, medals, antiquities Roman & Etruscan, of the immense collection called the Gallery . We have operas, comedies, balls, all masked, till Advent, since that only serious performances are allowed, tragedies out of Scripture & grave moral stories, amongst them our Elfrida, very well translated, is permitted, with chorus's set very prettily. Sir Horace Mann, our old resident, who was here when I was in Italy before, continues in the most obliging manner to make the place agreeable to all his countrymen. There are few left now, many are gone to Rome & Naples. Lady Orford, now an old woman, all her vivacity, wit & learning sunk in a pack of cards. The Duchess of K..., whom we hear you will soon undutchess, stayed but a few days. General Honeywood, wife & son for his health - Lady Broughton & her husband - Mr Errington - Lord Tylney, Lady Carlisle & a German baron, Lord Haddo - Lord Monson & many more gone or going. Lord Cowper has been settled here long & has with him Mr Seymour, his brother in law, with two pretty daughters - Mr Dashwood, Sir James's second son settles in a house here. But I must not forget the Count of Albany, with his fair young wife, the daughter of the Princess Holberg, who was daughter of the old Earl of Aylsbury, who lived long at Brussels. She is the admiration of all our young men. He is, they say, every day drunk & extremely jealous. Two or three times in the masking season he let himself much down by talking in his cups with some of our young men, of hardship, of suffering for his fathers faults, asking if they were not for justice etc. Poor man. I never see him but with compassion. No prince, not even the Pope, will acknowledge him. His friends would have him no longer assume the title. But can he do otherwise? Would he not confess himself to be the son of the supposititious child he is said to be? He has no attendants here but Lord & Lady Carey ... a family of about 30 & goes about with 2 coaches & running footmen. The Grand Duke does not receive him ... He left Rome because, in the sede vacant , they will ... not pay him the usual honours, so will not return till a Pope is made. They say one is elected but not declared till the arrival of a Spanish Cardinal, who is detained by bad weather. We have frost, snow & continual rains. The mountains, the Appennines all round white with snow, yet so temperate is the climate in all the gardens. There are standard oranges, & walks of them that are never covered, tho the citroncedrate & lemons have been so far more than a month. I am pleased Hutchins has so well executed the general orders I left, the only man in the County I would strenuously support, & the one I would oppose. I could have wished to be able to give you more particular ones. Lord Cowper in the spring is to marry Miss Gore who, with her father etc, is gone to Naples for Mrs Gore's health. This minute I learn for the first time your numbers, & am sorry for the first time I was not then at Arbury. I shall wish to be in the house too if you petition. Present our good wishes to Sir Charles, Mrs Mordant & all your family, & let me hear again from you. In hopes of it I will send my direction; Signor Cavalier Newdigate, dal Marchese Belloni, Rome, Italia . Zofani has almost finished a fine picture for our King, a view of the Tribune of the gallery into which he has introduced the most capital pictures. They are finely copied, but the whole is faulty & I'm afraid can't be mended. The streets are covered with snow & the frost more severe than ever known so early. I saw many orange trees yesterday with their leaves covered with snow. Pray ask our naturalists, how that can be, & whether it is possible for frost at the same degree of the thermometer to kill vegetables, as we know it will do in England, in one climate, & not do so in another? This doubt, I believe, will soon be resolved. The frost continues this December 10th as severe as I ever remember in before Christmas. Miss Conyers & Mr Parker join in compliments. On Monday, se'night, we set off for Rome. Can we do anything for you in this country - Books, Music, Perfumes, Sculpture, painting. Send your orders we shall execute them with pleasure. I am, Dear Sir Yours most affectionately R Newdigate The Spanish Cardinal is gone by, so we shall soon have a Pope.

column46: Rome April 28th 1775 Dear Sir I have been long your debtor, for which I have only to plead the constant business of our mornings in running about this city after sights of one sort or another, & the interruptions of our evenings by the visits of the flights of English returned from Naples. They are now, most of them, gone off again for the Ascension at Venice, & we are preparing for our journey to Naples for which we propose to set out on Monday se'night. We shall leave behind us here the Lady Carlisle, Mr Gore & wife & 3 daughters, the youngest the sposa of Lord Cowper, who is returned to Florence. The eldest has had the misfortune to fall down stairs & break her leg, which has detained them. She was lame before. Mr & Mrs Upton, who is in a way to lie in at Rome a 2nd time. Lady Mary Duncan & Mrs Pitt Lord Ch...ns sister. Lord Balgony, Mrs Crosbie, Mrs Barry, Miss Kerr's, Gray, Sir Charles Watson etc talk of moving soon. The ceremonies of Holy Week a little interrupted our regular Course but are not worth a description. How the Pope washed & kissed the pilgrims feet, waited on them at dinner, walked barefoot or without shoes to kiss a wooden cross etc etc. The Miserere you have often heard of seemed to disappoint most of the English. It is performed on Wednesday & Good Friday, that of Allegri & that of Bari (I think is his name, on Thursday) in the Pope's Chapel by 100 voices without instruments. That of Allegri is more simple & in truth nothing more than an old chant of the 50th Psalm. One verse is sung by the first Masters as the Choir & the next repeated by the whole band as the congregation, much in the manner of our cathedrals, with as much hurry & indecent confusion. Every other verse thus chanted you may imagine makes a strange interruption but serves at the same time very much to enhance the value of the others, which are sung by the first masters & best voices, with a plaintive simplicity & elegance that is wonderful. It is not surprising that it has never pleased any where else, as the whole you perceive depends on the skill & taste of the performers, or perhaps still more, on the traditional manner of performing, which is delivered down for ages & cannot be written. The other Miserere , which was sung on Thursday, is less like a chant & has more variety. It is also very fine, but the simplicity of the other has more admirers. To give you some idea of the solid good sense of this religion I must mention a little of the ceremonial on these days. The Pope on his throne, the cardinals below - 15 candles in a row before them represent the 12 apostles & 3 Maries. But you know they forsook him & fled. So at the end of each psalm one candle is put out by a priest, who first kneels to the Pope & then applies the extinguisher. Thus they are reduced to one - the Virgin Mary. It is not known, & they will not suppose, that she forsook him. So after kneeling as before, instead of extinguishing they take down her candle & hide it behind the altar. Then all the other candles are put out & the Miserere begins, which ends the Service. You know it was the hour of darkness. On Easter Sunday after high Mass the Pope gives the Benediction. No prince on earth ever appeared in such state. He is seen on his throne in the middle arch over the portico of St Peters with his robes & tiara, or triregno as they call it, by many thousands who filled the Piazza & fall on their knees at his appearance. On his throwing out his arms, which he does like the Vrughel man of a regiment in order to be seen at so great a distance, the cannon of the Castle of St Angelo were fired. All the coaches in Rome were there. Such a throne as that noble church. Such a theatre for the spectators, & such humble adoration can no where else be found. We are very happy in the good accounts from Walton wish you joy of Charles's becoming a father. I am pleased with my neighbours of Birmingham. Their petition was well timed & has had its effect. Warwickshire is far from a pleasing subject. We live here in the Empire of Amusement, & after 4 months employed about 4 hours a day, find there is still much to see & more that deserves repetition. But in a few weeks we shall turn our faces to England & be nearer you every day. 3 weeks at Naples, then Rome for a few days; Venice, Verona, Brescia, Bergamo, Turin, Genoa, Nice & the South of France before the winter begins. Paris & London about Christmas next is our present plan. We are all well & join in good wishes to you at Walton. I am, Dear Sir Your very affectionate & obliged humble servant R Newdigate

column46: Bogliaco August 16th 1775 Dear Sir I must begin this as I ended my last, with numberless thanks to you & Mrs Strange for all your favours at Venice & for those that attended our departure from thence. We drank your health's in excellent Hock & English brown beer all the way to Verona, & diligently obeyed our Cicerone's orders at both, as well as at Padua. Mr Parker teased us to death to examine the pavement of the last, & would not be easy till he had begged us into the hot sun to see a bit of cinder of an inch wide in the flags before San Antonio, but at Vicenza he was much worse & almost made us count & measure the rocks all the way up Monte Berice. He is a worthy disciple of yours & will I am sure be much disappointed if he does not find out a volcano on the top of Monte Baldo, who looks down at us with surprising majesty from the other side of this beautiful lake. At Verona your obliging letter brought us a very agreeable acquaintance, Signor Borelli, whom we only saw long enough to regret. We staid only one night at Padua, two at Vicenza & two at Verona, & arrived at Salo' on Saturday. From a most wretched inn we were charitably removed by Signor Gargnani to where Mr Masters recommended us, to a very excellent house of Signor Marchetti, & staid till this day. We are now in a large convenient house swept & furnished since our arrival this morning, not very elegant but, situation thrown in the scale, has charms enough to determine us to stay 3 weeks or a month in it. If in that time we could be so happy as by your instructions to make any discoveries to promote your researches, or to be otherwise useful to you or Mrs Strange farther than in gratitude & good wishes we should be very happy. The weather is still warm though it rains at this instant, & yesterday we had thunder & much lightening. Desire Mrs Strange to figure to herself the scene of last night at Salo' - ourselves with two grave priests in a pretty balcony overlooking this charming lake by the help of the lightening which was incessant & opened the whole scene with all the mountains round. In the midst of the storm a bark landing in our garden a large company who placed themselves round a ombrella which being supported by a man sitting on the ground, served as a table & the top of it as a candlestick for several lights, & formed at once an orchestra for a full concert who struck up at once, the lightening beating exact time as their Maestro di Capella , & the thunder as double base. At Verona Mr Consul Udney joined us & we were all much surprised & mortified with the news of the death of Mr Murray of which there seems too much reason to expect a confirmation. We sincerely feel & lament the situation of poor Mr Smith & Miss Murray & beg our compliments to them on this sad occasion. We have little chance of knowing anything of the world in this retirement but beg your charity if you hear anything new from America. Miss Conyers begs me to tell you she was so lucky to supply herself with hydropales at Vicenza, for the apothecary at Verona had none. From the monks of Berico & the last she has loaded my poor coach with fishes of stone. It has ground all the way since. All join most sincerely in good wishes to you both. I am, Dear Sir Your most obliged, humble servant R Newdigate Alla sua Eccellenza Il Signor Strange Residento Britannico a` Venetia

column46: Bogliaco September 13th 1775 Dear Sir Many more thanks are due to you for your goodness in sending us newspapers, for we have no communication with the world in this retreat where we have now completed a very agreeable month & have all along found a most cordial reception from all degrees of people on this beautiful lake. The weather so seasonably hot that we have passed most of our time in our boat, & have seen all its beauties, gardens, villas, castles & most amazing rocks, & your majestic old friend Baldo, in all their picturesque appearances with the greatest ease & pleasure, by the light of both sun & moon. On Wednesday we depart from Desensano in our boat & shall take Sirmione Catullus's residence in our way, & endeavour to find out the only curiosity in the way that we have heard of, which is a boiling in the lake near that place which throws out a noisome sulphurous smell. At Malsesina too, at the foot of Baldo, are two small islands that they say are of a rock that has a lava appearance but I have not had opportunity to examine them, but cannot omit mentioning them to you. After this I must add, from the partiality I have for my friends here, that I wish this place was better known to the English who wish for a cool month or two in the summer. A very good house, the Case Parcatini here, & our very obliging friends Signory Andrea & Battista Giacomini, who have furnished it, & supplied us with everything wanting, deserve our gratitude, not forgetting Signor Gargnano of Salo, who loaded our coach with provisions when we left that place. Signor Conte Abbito Bettoni Signor Conte & Countess Bernini have been particularly obliging, & we have had all sorts of civilities from the Capitano del Logo, Conte Monterari, Conte Morani, Marchese Archetti etc. In short we depart with regret. The weather has been too hot for expeditions on Monte Baldo or we should certainly have obeyed your commands, & Charles Parker would have undoubtedly found you out a volcano. Most of our time has been spent on the water. My companions desire to join with me in thanks & good wishes to yourself & Mrs Strange, & in desiring you will lay your commands on us at Paris, London or elsewhere, where we shall esteem an honour. The boat jaggles me so I can hardly write, so pray excuse, Dear Sir Your most obliged, humble servant R Newdigate Give me leave to trouble you to inform Mrs Smith that I have ordered the powder to her direction, & with it have taken the liberty to order a parcel of James's Powders to be enclosed, which I beg she will send to Mr Conrad Martens, to be forwarded to Signor Carlo Elena, Chirurgo at Bagliaco by some safe hand. Old Baldo has this morning put on his winter night cap.

Dear Sir I have long intended to throw off that appearance of ingratitude & forgetfulness of my good friends at Venice which I fear has long hung lowering over your idea of me whenever you have turned your thoughts to England. My apology shall be the truth & very short. A very polite message communicated to me by my good friend Lord Decree from the Society of Antiquaries, that they had received from your hands a print of the Arch of the Cite` d'Aoste & hearing that I had more drawings of the antiquities of that place they wished for a farther communication from me on that head, & that Mr de Salis would wait upon me on my arrival in Town at the meeting of Parliament made me defer my answer ... & since that time I did not write, expecting Mr de Salis every day, having determined, as you had done me the honour to introduce my trifling performance to the notice of the Society, that if I had any thing further worthy of their acceptance, it should not be communicated but through your hands. But as Mr de Salis never came near me during the Session, & this affair of course is at an end, I have only to regret that it has induced me to postpone my letter to you & consequently the pleasure of hearing of you & Mrs Strange. This is my best reason. My others are that I every day expected public news worth sending you, & was fully engaged in the business of my constituents or my own private affairs whilst I continued in Town. The Sessions are at an end. No news of importance from America. Nothing here but what your papers tell you, & what is it they do not tell you? According to the complexion of the paper the nation is ruined or triumphant. I believe it is neither. The rebels, it is the general opinion, cannot face the power sent against them. They will retire to their lurking holes & when winter comes again will harass your outposts & continue a running war, perhaps for years. They are enthusiasts that will not be convinced. You may beat them but they will not yield, nor ever be your friends or quiet subjects. They hate your government because they hate your religion. They may injure you but will never serve you, nor be at rest but whilst the sword hangs over their heads. The war can neither be continued nor ended by you unless some means can be found to make themselves pay the army that subdues & restrains them, and even then though they will no longer waste your treasures they will waste your people. The new taxes lie heavy on property but with as much equality as is possible - on money as well as land, on the easy, not oppressive; on the luxurious, heavy; but not felt by the poor. Upon the whole Lord North has well supported his character throughout. The hearts of the nation are with him as far as they can be on anyone that lays heavy burdens. They see thay are necessary & submit. The worst & least reasonable when the calls on the subject are so great, flagrant bello , is one which I will not mention, necessary too I believe, but which he himself would have wished to avoid, or by proper economy to have prevented, but the rapine & avarice of those round him in the House, with the clamorous yellings of the dogs that are shut out of the door, require the force of Hercules to withstand, or his industry to cleanse, the mountain of filth. Upon the whole he is a good man & does all he can to do right. May we not hope to see you & Mrs Strange sometime. Other Ministers can come now & then. I wish to introduce you to a new acquaintance, & to your old one, Mrs Mary Conyers, who is settled near me in an old castle worthy the acquaintance of an Antiquary. She & Mr Parker wish to be remembered by you & join in good wishes to you both. I am, Dear Sir Your much obliged, humble servant R Newdigate PS I can't help sending you a quotation from Bryant, Analysis of Ancient Mythology , Volume I, p.211. The name of the mountain, 'Pyrene', signifies a fountain of fire & that the mountain had once flamed. There was a 'Pyrene' among the Alps Tridentini (note Pliny's Paneg. & in Seneca, Console. Ad Helviam . lib 8 - Aristotle In Meteoric ) and at the foot of it a city of the same name which one would infer to have been so denominated from the like circumstance. Beatus Rhenanus, in his account of these parts, says that there was a tradition of this mountain 'Pyrene' once burning (in Rerum Germanic ... lib.3) & conformably to this notion it is still distinguished by the name of the great Brenner (it is called by the Swiss le Grand Brenner - by the other Germans Der Gross Verner . You may probably have met with the above notation. It seems to confirm your system of fire in the mountains of your neighbourhood. Perhaps a closer examination would produce many instances of the same as it seems to be almost the regular course of Nature that the great ranges of mountains all over the globe are attended with volcanos.

column46: Spring Gardens April 27th 1782 Dear Sir Continual business here & at Harfield, & the usual distractions of the place, have made impossible to answer sooner. I am not at all surprised that the dull & dreary season, & the solitary life you lead, should affect your spirits & make you see things in a different light from what they really are. With one more in family, & when necessaries are at a double expense, & with a less income you contrived to go on comfortably before your removal from Chilvers Cotton; your friends assisted you in settling them, & the charge of a long illness was added to that of necessaries before your unhappy loss. Your income is the same, your expenses much less. Nothing but a change of your own opinions or inclinations can have produced the resolutions you mention. As to Astley, you must recall that before I presented you I told you what duty the parishioners had a right to expect from you; that they had for many years been reduced to a morning Service during winter, & prayers on all the principal Holy days. You made no objection, & I concluded that if any part of that duty was more than you could perform you would provide some person in your stead. I did not expect after this to hear that Mr Liptrott did not do so much duty, nor indeed Mr Howlette after he had the Curacy of Bedworth. The duty they did, circumstances obliged me to submit to, but I was by no means satisfied. The last, Mr Howlette, will tell you that when he resided at Temple House & did duty in my family, he actually peformed the whole. I told you would be expected. So did Mr Cobb, & Mr Walter who left me in a huff because I presumed to tell him I thought it indecent for any parish to be deprived of the duty of Holy Week. These were curates only to Dr Winchester; the flock was his, not theirs, but he insisted it should be done though they received only a salary of £25 & £30 yearly. You will recollect also that I was surprised at your resolution to undertake the second Service at Chilvers Cotton, believing it more than you could perform. Yet though I cannot think you have done justice to Astley your meritorious case of Chilvers Cotton, my own Parish, & the probability of an event which cannot be far off, induced me to acqiesce, & you would have heard nothing from me had the of been served at the late solemn time as your own mind must tell you it ought to have been! Is the weekday Service so fatiguing that you could not have performed it twice in the day at that time at least, you who every Sunday have been able to do so much more? I cannot believe that was the real cause. For a disregard of your duty I have too good an opinion of you to suspect. I rather believe some person desirous to flatter or injure you has misinformed you, & represented me as a person rigid & impertinent who expect unreasonable things from your cloth! And yet, Sir, I am Patron of the living, & as having twice out of my own pocket (for my father's agreement I was not by law bound to perform) advanced the salary I have some right to stipulate a better performance of duty than was actually when the salary was only ten pounds yearly. I have advanced it to near £50, & yet the duty you have performed is not so much as before I came of age. Mr Ebdell, to his death, performed weekly duty there, whilst my mother lived at the castle generally. After his death my chaplains had it in succession & performed as I have told you. I could not avoid this recapitulation, which is unnecessary as you have acknowledged the complaint was founded in reason, & further, you, a little jocosely, compare yourself to a great minister. You have lost confidence. It is your duty to resign. I am very serious upon the subject & shall be very sorry to have you do so. Your general behaviour has been, & I have told you so, very conscienscious & deserving; I wish you to deserve as well of Astley which is properly yours as of Chilvers Cotton. I have required nothing but what is in your power, & have been, & am, contented with an imperfect performance where it is not. As to your future plans, whether more profitable or more agreeable, concerns your alone. When I opened my intentions towards you I told you I would promise nothing, nor will I engage myself at any time to future events which, as you say, perhaps I may never see. You do me honour in desiring my approbation may attend your future plan, & I am glad to observe the inconsistency of your having lost my confidence & yet asking a promise from one which could not be made to one who had done so, as that inconsistency convinces me that all you have written is only as I have said, in the beginning, the effect of low spirits & resentment upon very slight grounds. But if I may advise you it will be to stay patiently where you are & events, however distant they may appear. Do your endeavour & leave the rest to Providence. I am, Dear Sir, Your sincere friend R N

column46: Arbury January 19th 1784 Dear Sir Business & company have hitherto prevented my answering your letter. I am sorry to say I cannot approve your conduct. In every light it appears wrong towards me, towards your parishes & yourself. I had surely some reason to expect to have been consulted before you had taken this hasty step, which I have for sometime heard you intended, but disbelieved, for you had not told me of it: nor to this minute are your reasons come from Mr . In truth you know it was impossible for me to approve it. Your behaviour on the death of an injured orphan was highly laudable & I have often acknowledged it, & whatever was wrong in the prosecution, injurious to myself or to the parish I have always imputed to imposition upon your ignorance of legal proceedings by an interested person & cleared you of blame. I have done more. I have endeavoured at my own cost to take away the object of contention between you & your parishioners & should have succeeded ... ; if your attachment to the cause of one so undeserving had not barred my proceedings & put an end to my mediation. General abuse, harsh language & threats of actions at law against your parishioners have alienated from you the minds of the better part of them who had never offended you & were at that time disposed to settle matters with a due concern to their own property. To your extreme irritability only is owing that your situation has been uneasy; if you had thought it worth while to conciliate the minds of the better sort, you would have had nothing to apprehend from the worst. Guilt is always a coward & shrinks from the steady eye of worth & innocence. With what pleasure did I see my endeavours succeed in placing you in a situation of affluence & comfort. How strangely are my hopes overthrown. With what strange insensibility are you destroying your own happiness? I will still flatter myself your resolution is not unchangeable. Return again to your parishes & your friends, conquer yourself first & follow the example of our great master, the meek & humble Jesus! Believe it possible you are in the wrong. Return, & by a kind & Christian behaviour bring back your flock. You have it still in your power. They will answer every act of kindness with affection. But if you cannot bring yourself to this, you have no choice. Resign your livings. Neither they nor I can sit contented under your non-residence or bear, as they have done too long, to be served by curates picked up at random & changed within the hour. Yesterday your Church was not served as usual, nor do we know what we are to depend upon. Lady desires her compliments. As soon as the boys are returned to school she will send for Elise. She does not think it proper before; she will then take care of her as you desire; but I hope much sooner your calm & serious reflexions will bring you back again to Him & to your parishes, & to Your much disappointed friend & humble, affectionate servant R N

column46: Arbury Wednesday 29th April 1795 My dear Jose I would have written to you sooner but could not! I wanted to hear of you again, & your worthy brother has given me all the comfort he could, but from this delay, I fear, this will find you in a most trying situation; will, I fear, add to the load of your affliction, already too heavy for you to support. But let your tears flow, stop them not! I will add mine to them, & tell you how great is my loss, how vain my hopes, how amazing my disappointment! How aimiable when only a child, how improved by education, how good, how grateful, how pious! As a husband, as a father! But what avails all this? We must go to him, we cannot bring him back again, & all that is left us is, submission to the will of the great Almighty, Ruler of the world, who has placed us here, not to take up our rest here, or sport like the Leviathan; but in patient humility to enjoy the good he bestows, conscious how frail humanity is, & ready to resign into his hands again, to whom it belongs, every blessing we are permitted to enjoy upon that condition only. He takes those we love away, to him, to that place of never fading bliss, to help direct our aim, our wishes to follow after & be with them for ever! But we must wait his will; & you have a sweet inducement to drag you back from these sublime contemplations, your little smiling brood, whom you now hang over with tears, but with tears of joy. They will every day add more & more joy and comfort, & be not in concern for their future prospects, a good Providence watches over them & they will be happy. Mr Anstruther's letter this morning has given us much satisfaction in the hopes of seeing you & your dear babes at Arbury very soon, and in his promise to come with you; indeed I shall want his assistance & advice & it is no small part of your happiness to have a brother so able & so affectionate. But do not linger at your sweet Lodge. Leave it as you used to do to come here, make Trumper your Agent & Steward in your absence; but stay no longer now, than is necessary to pack up for Warwickshire. You will I doubt not see Sir John & Lady Anstruther first, but pray go to them, & come from London directly here. If anything remains undone, you may rely upon Trumper, & the future will be settled, when we are together here. God Almighty give you health, and fortitude of mind to go through the task he has assigned you, in which you may depend upon me to be a father to the sweet orphans & Lady Newdigate to be another nursing mother, & to yourself the minister of every comfort in our power. But I repeat my injunction: stay no longer, where you are, than is unavoidably necessary. The sooner we see you, the better! Adieu, my dear Jazzy, you do not want, I hope, to be told that I am Your most affectionate & faithful friend & humble servant R Newdigate My sincere respects & condolence wait upon Sir John & Lady Anstruther & the dear Jessichine. I expect no answer to this but in person

Arbury Wednesday 30th September My dear Jazzy A thousand thanks to you for your invaluable present, which I shall keep as one of my choicest treasures, and often contemplate with pleasure, not unmixed with pain. But it is what we are born to, as the sparks fly upwards! Submission is our Duty & our Happiness! That all our pleasing hopes of life should fade, Was His Almighty will, and be that Will obeyed! I am concerned to find how difficult is still is for you to turn your thoughts from that object; look round you, on your sweet little flock & think only how greatly incumbent it is to look to your own health, & to make that your first care; the account of you, from your late visitors, does not remove my solicitude upon this point, though your late painful attendance upon a revered parent was the immediate cause, & gives good cause to hope it was only accidental, that your looks did not please them. I hope this expectation may soon be confirmed from your own pen. I wrote you a long letter in a hurry on Monday upon the Grand Junction invasion. I hope all will be made easy there. I forgot to tell you Cooper has sent your lease, which I have not had time to read; when executed I will send you or keep till I see you. Talk your brother & desire his instruction on what is to be done before you surrender the old one. Lady & Mrs came as you promised. Thank God her amendment is wonderful, exceeding all expectation! All here send their love to you. God bless & support you! Good night. Yours most affectionately R N

column46: Arbury 16th February 1797 To Mrs Jane Parker, Widow Harefield Lodge Dear Madam When I granted you a lease for the term of your life, of my house, Harefield Lodge and appurtenances, together with the farm annexed, my sole object was to improve your situation by securing to you a fixed habitation for yourself & your children; but I confess it never entered into my head that such grant could ever affect the lease of the farm for 21 years, which I had before granted to your husband. But as, I am now informed, it may be doubted whether the two aforesaid leases are meant to be concurrent leases, or not, I declare that I mean them so to be; & bind my heirs and executors to do any act which may be necessary to confirm both, or either of them, if any such act should be required by you or your assigns. I am, Dear Madam Your most obedient servant R Newdigate
