column46: Arbury 30 May 1797 Sent to the meeting at Warwick by GT My dear Sir I cannot hear without indignation that any persons should have the presumption to disturb the peace of a County so eminently distinguished for loyalty to our King & zeal for our ancient constitution by an attempt at this critical moment to introduce French principles & mob government. A fabric so ancient may want some repair, but this audacious endeavour to level it to the ground & replace it with the flimsy edifices of anarchy & atheism will, I am confident, be reprobated by the sober voice of your Meeting, as it will by the subscription of Justices who, like myself, are unable to declare their abhorrence of it in person. I shall be happy to hear you do not suffer by your incessant labours to serve your Country, for which we are all deeply indebted to you. I am, dear Sir J... Your affectionate & obedient servant R N

Windsor April 23. 1682 I have received the Letter you wrote lately to me, and am very glad to find by one I had at the same time from my cousin the Princess Louise, that you behave yourself so well, and that she gives you so good a character. I hope you will do nothing to give her reason to alter her opinion of you, and that you will do nothing to make me less kind to you then I am, and you shall upon all occasions find me as kind to you as you can desire. James. For Mrs Henrietta Fits James at Maubuison.

Windsor, May 29. 1683. You have now been long enough where you are, and are of an age proper to know whether that kind of life will agree with you or no; to know which, and the desire I have to see you, has made me desire this bearer, Sir Henry Tichburne, to bring you over into England, along with his Wife, to his own house; where I shall have the opportunity of seeing you when we go to Winchester this summer, and letting you see that I shall always be very kind to you. James.

Windsor, June 9. 1684 Till the Duchess came to this place, I did not know that Sir Charles Waldgrave was dead, or else I had written sooner to you to have told you I was sorry to hear of it; and now that Sir Henry is come to the estate I must recommend to you both to be good managers, and to be sure to live within what you have, and be sure to have a care not to run out at first. Now that the Duchess is here, I shall seldom go to London; when I do, I shall be sure to let you know it, that you may meet me there. Tomorrow I am to go a hunting; and on Friday to Hampton Court: and at any time when you do come hither, take care that it be not when I am abroad, that you may not mise me. Let me hear from you, and be assured I shall always be very kind to you. For the young Lady Waldgrave.

Windsor Saturday Morning I was very sorry to hear this morning of the accident which happened to your brother Harry, and send these foottman on purpose to you, to have an account from you how he do's. They tell me his face will not be marked with it. Pray let me know the truth out, and how soon they think he may be well enough to go. Remember me to your Brother James, and tell him I am sorry his journey should be stopped for some days, especially by such an accident; and tell Harry I hope he will be carefuller for the time to come; and now, that he do what the Surgeons will have him, which is all I shall say now, but to assure you of the continuance of my kindness J. R. For the Lady Waldgrave.

Coventry Sept. 1. 1687 Two days since I was very much allarumd by the Letters which came from France about your brother Berwick, but now, God be thanked, I am at ease concerning him, for by Letters I have had this day from several parts, and from the Army, I find he was very well recovered though still a little weak; and I believe the Earl of Kennole who died at Mohas, near the Army, was the occasion of that report. I believe by that time this gets to you, I shall have letters from him or Sir Ed. Vandery. I have not time to say more, but that you shall still find me very kind to you. For the Lady Waldgrave.

My Lord Whereas we are credibly informed that there are some horse and foot in arms under your command for James Duke of York, which are purposely raised in opposition to us and our royal authority. We thought fit to signify to you our resentment thereof, and do promise ourself that what you have transacted therein is through inadvertence and mistake; and that your Grace will take other means, when you have received information of our being proclaimed King to succeed our royal father lately deceased. We have therefore sent this messenger on purpose to intimate the same unto you; and it is our royal will and pleasure, and we do hereby strictly charge and command you upon notice and receipt hereof, to cease all hostility, and force, and arms, against us and all our loving subjects; and that your Grace would immediately repair to our Camp where you shall not fail of a very kind reception by us. Or in default of the premises, we shall be obliged to proclaim you, and all those in arms under your command, rebels and traitors; and shall proceed against them and you accordingly. Yet we assure ourself that your Grace will pay ready obedience to our command; wherefore we bid you heartily farewell. James R. To our trusty and welbeloved Cousin and Councellor Christopher Lord Duke of Albemarle.

From Ringwood the 9th. Madam Being in this unfortunate condition, and having none left but your Majesty that I think may have some compassion of me, and that for the last King's sake, makes me take this boldness to beg of you to intercede for me. I would not desire your Majesty to doe it, if I wear not from the bottom of my hart convinced how I have bine disceaved in to it, and how angry God Almighty is with me for it: but I hope, Madam, your intersesion will give me life to repent of it, and to show the King how really and truly I will serve him hereafter. And I hope, Madam, your Majesty will be convinced that the Life you save shall ever be devoted to your service: for I have been and ever shall be Your Majesty's most dutiful and obedient servant Monmouth.

Tuesday. Sir I have received your Majesty's order this day that I am to dye tomorrow. I was in hopes Sir by what your Majesty said to me yesterday, of taking care of my Soul, that I should have had some little more time; for truly, Sir, this is very short. I do beg of your Majesty, if it be possible to let me have one day more, that I may go out of the world as a christian ought. I had desired several times to speak with my Lord Arundel of Wardour, which I do desire still. I hope your Majesty will grant it me; and I do beg of your Majesty to let me know by him if there is nothing in this world that can recall your sentence, or, at least reprieve me for some time. I was in hopes I should have lived to have served you, which I think I could have done to a great degree; but your Majesty does not think it fit. Therefore, Sir, I shall end my days with being satisfied that I had all the good intentions imaginable for it, and should have done it, being that I am your Majesty's most dutiful Monmouth. I hope your Majesty will give Doctor Tennison leave to come to me, or any other that your Majesty will be pleased to grant me. To the King.

St. James's Jan. the 22d 1703/4 You having represented that the King of Spain seemed desirous upon the first turn of the wind to make the best of his way to Lisbon with such clean Ships as shall be in readiness for that service, and this matter requireing the greatest secrecy, I think it proper to give you Orders in my own hand to pay the same obedience to the King of Spain, as to the time and manner of his setting sail, and as to the number of Ships which shall be in a readiness to attend him, as you would do to my self, I am Your very affectionett friend Anne R. For Sr. George Rook.

Rose, Sept. 13. 1716. My very good lord In my last I acquainted your Grace that we were in daily expectance of a good number of Northern captives; and that we look for their being followed by several Lords of Session. The prisoners are arrived, and as we hope in salva` custody` . But we are now assured that our Judges are to come from another quarter. It is confidently said that none durst try them at Edinburgh; nor will any that tries them here dare to return thither. Notwithstanding the fair Account which your Grace has had of the present peaceable disposition of the good folks of that country, if we believe the officers who brought the rebels hither, they are very ripe for another Insurrection. I heartily wish that we may have a gaol-delivery here as soon as possible. Not that I have any jealousy that the prisoners are like to make their escape, but because I apprehend, that (if justice be not executed speedily) many of them will leave the world in a less exemplary way than they ought to do. The Castle (where they are lodged) is a moist and unwholesome place; and our garrison is so thin, that the Commandant is forced, for security, to crowd them all into three Rooms. Then the greatest part of them sleep upon bare straw. For though they are generally desirous and sufficiently able to hire beds, the townsmen are loath to let their goods be carried into a place where they are sure to rot. In this miserable state have most of these mad creatures been for four or five days past; several roaring in fits of the gout or gravel. Nor can I see any appearance of their being relieved. These complaints are very uneasy to me. My Lord, I am hourly pestered with addresses and solicitations from the friends and advocates of these unhappy wretches; who will not believe me when I tell them, that I have neither power or inclination to do them any service; but renew their suit every morning with as much earnestness as if no denial had been given them. Amongst the rest the bishop of Edinburgh warmly recommends to my counsel, direction, and favour , a son of his who is one of our guests. This youngster was taken in actual rebellion at the battle of Dumblain; and the father does not pretend to say that he repents of that sin. On the contrary he gives broad hints of his being persuaded that his child now suffers for righteousness sake. He will not so much as undertake to keep the boy out of harm's way for the future, should he now be set at liberty; but rather intimates that his present affliction renders him a proper object of all the good offices that I am capable of doing him. I have dealt very plainly with this mischievous prelate; who (by the way) bemoans the completed desolation of the Scottish Church and the insufferable hardships ( unde et a quo? ) of her poor clergy. I have let him know, that I will no more bestir myself for his son, than I would for my own in the like circumstances; but leave him entirely to God's mercy and the King's. I am ever Your Grace's most dutiful Servant W. Carliol.

Rose, Oct. 13th. 1716. My very good lord Your Grace allows me to trouble You upon every Change of the face of our Affairs at Carlisle; and the only ease that I have is in complaining of my afflictions. On Thursday night last a Squadron of High-Land Witnesses (about twenty eight or thirty) were brought in to us, under a strong guard; and they were followed Yesterday morning by a new Detachment of Advocates, and Writers; a generation of learned men who are commonly so obliging as to make directly for my House. I have been honoured with a visit by one of these already; and I despair not of the like favours from the rest. This gentleman seems to be pretty positive, that we shall have no Judges nor Advocates on his Majesty's side of the question, from Edinburgh; and that, because the whole Nation is averse to Trials of Scotch criminals in our English Forms. He objects particularly, on this occasion, against the admission of such evidence as is now preparing. Socii criminis , he says, never were admitted in Scotland (he will needs say, never ought to be admitted any where else,) as proper witnesses in a Cause of Blood. Such discourse as this I foresee will raise new speculations amongst those of us who are already too much inclined to grumble. Notwithstanding all which, I have yet so much courage as to hope (and it is but just so much) that we shall acquit ourselves like men. The only damping consideration, is, the longer time that's allowed us for cool thinking, the more cowardly we are apt to grow. This was our case twelve months' ago. It may be so again. For my own part, I do seriously protest to your Grace, that I am under deeper apprehensions of mischief to myself and family from the partisans of these Men, now they are in hold, than I was when I saw them in a full march and battle array. I have procured for them daily prayers, and weekly sermons; and have contributed towards the conveniences of their lodgings, which are now (as far as their numbers will admit) sufficiently easy. Yet all these services are spilt upon the ground; because I will not personally preach up their innocence. This is the present state of Carlisle, and of Your Grace's most obedient Servant W. Carliol.

Rose Dec. 17th. 1716. My very good lord My Saturday's Postscript was written in such haste, that I had not time to acquaint your Grace, that the honour of your Letter came to my hand when I was with Mr. Justice Tracy; who had acquainted me with a like application, in favour of the bishop of Edinburgh's son, made to himself by the Earl of Caernarvon. Two such Advocates were soon agreed to be worth a whole Threeve of them from the North; and thereupon I had leave to send for the young fellow to the bar; where he presently appeared; desired to be immediately arraigned; and (that being granted) pleaded Guilty. This he did in so becoming a manner, and so good an appearance of a true penitent heart, that the Judge promised to represent his case favourably to his Majesty; whose mercy he confidently relies upon. I had never seen the young man's face before; but was not a little pleased with his modest behaviour. The Scottish Counsel are very impatient, for want of an opportunity to open their portmanteaus; wherein they are said to have brought many and large volumes of Records, for the ascertaining of the legal privileges and immunities of the ancient Kingdom. Several of them open very loud on this occasion: but the most obstreperous is reported to be one Mr. Graham a person of great learning and eminence. He is the Kings Judge of the Admiralty in Edinburgh; and in the warmth of his zeal has procured leave to be of Counsel for the Prisoners, on purpose to dispute this point: which he declares he'll maintain to the hazard of his very life, as well as his fortunes. The Judges seem to hope that they shall be able to ward off this Argument. And indeed the Solicitor General and the rest of our English Counsel, on the crown side, appear as loath to engage in it. Mr. Mackenzie of Frazerdale (against whom an Indictment was found by the Grand Jury on Saturday last) seems to be the likeliest person to bring on the debate. This Gentleman's case has been so variously represented, that (without a formal Trial) nobody can tell what to make of it. Some stoutly affirm, as himself does, that he never bore arms in the Pretender's camp; that he was carried prisoner into Perth; and thence made his escape before the battle of Dumblain. Others say, that (upon a family disgust) he did freakishly join the Rebels at first; but saw his error pretty early, and stole off to the Duke of Idol. His Grace strongly avows his just claim to remission, or rather an acquittal; and has sent Lord James, now Lord Tullibardin to solicit his cause. On the other hand, Lord Loveit has seized the life-rent of his estate, and will probably be desirous to continue in possession. I have enclosed a List of all that had Bills found against them by the Grand Jury, when I came away on Saturday in the evening; to which I believe I may add Brigadier Campbell, a Bill being preferred against him that day. This unfortunate man was in no engagement; and had not been four days in Scotland, when he was taken in one of the Western Islands. He has been in Foreign Service (under the Czar, the Venetians, &c.) from his youth; and I dare parole for him, if the Government sends him back to the Adriatic coast, he'll never petition for another return into his native country. I am Your Grace's most obedient servant W. Carliol.

London. September 11th. My dear Cousin, Will it not surprise you to hear that the last month, from this very day, has been passed in real affliction without my giving you a line? I wished to spare you pain on my account and I hoped long before this to have written to you from my own comfortable House. I knew I must afflict you write when I would and I staid in hopes of being myself rather more equal to the task than I have lately been. You never imagined your Cousin would have addressed you from a Jail, and although I do not absolutely do that now , being in London in order to give Bail for my appearance at the Spring Assizes, yet my dearest Husband is not now my only Protector as I have the Ilchester Jailor in my suite - though to do him justice he has such a reliance on my honour, in spite of my appearances, that I scarcely ever see him, and since I have had the Honour of his acquaintance nothing can have been more respectful than his behaviour - Indeed we have every alleviation to our Misfortune that People can experience from the kindest Sympathy of Friends, and from the universal detestation the Authors of my troubles are held in by all ranks of People. I must enter into a few particulars, my dear Cos, though you must have heard enough to make you in part acquainted with our situation. It is now five Weeks since I went into Smith's , a Haberdashers in Bath St; to buy some black Lace to trim a Cloak; when I had bought it the Shopman took it to the further part of the shop to put it up - this might have struck me as something particular had I not given the Man a £5 note to pay himself and bring me the difference - when he left me I turned from the counter to the door to catch my Goodman who in going to drink his Water generally passed that way. When the Man brought me my Change and the Parcel I left the Shop carrying the Parcel in my hand. I went homewards the same way that Parrot usually came and had not gone far before I met him, we went together to the Cross Bath, stopped to pay a tradesman's bill, and as we had a letter to put into the Post Office were going through Bath St; where I had an hour before bought my Lace, and when we came opposite the Shop the Woman who had sold me the Lace came across the Street and accosted me with these words, 'I beg pardon, Madam, but was there by mistake a card of white lace put up with the black you bought,' I answered I could not tell as I had not been home but she might satisfy herself as the parcel had never been out of my hand - on saying which I gave it to her. She opened it, and there was a Card of White Edging which She took out saying Oh here it is,' and returned to the Shop. This did not surprise me as I thought it might have proceeded from Shop hurry or Negligence, but before we had got to the Abbey Church Yard the Man who had taken my Lace away to fold up, came after us to desire to know my Name and place of Abode as he had never put up that card of White Edging. This alarmed me a good deal because I had neither asked for White Lace nor had I seen any such thing in the Shop. Never hearing a syllable on the subject from the Thursday till the Monday Night I concluded they had discovered how their Mistake had originated, but on our return from passing Monday evening with some Friends the servant brought me a letter left by the penny post - without name or date, directed to Mrs. Leigh Parrot Lace dealer, No. 1. par. containing these lines "Your many visiting Acquaintance, before they again admit you into their houses, will think it right to know how you came by the piece of Lace stolen from Bath St; a few days ago. Your husband is said to be privy to it." On Wednesday following (the 14th) I was sitting up in my dear Parrot's Bed Chamber when my Maid came up and said a Gentleman in the Parlour wanted to speak to me. Judge of my horror upon going down to find he was a Constable with a Warrant from the Mayor for my immediate appearance. I went up to Parrot sick in Bed, and in profuse perspiration, who forgetting everything but my danger got up and attended me to the Mayor where we found these two Wretches who had sworn solemnly the One to seeing me take the Lace the Other to finding her Lace to the value of 20/s., in my possession - this she certainly did, but how it came there they best can tell as the first I ever saw of it was on the Woman's unfolding the paper with my black Lace. The Mayor and Magistrates, to whom we were well known, lamented their being obliged to commit me to prison on oaths of these People - they could only act in the capacity of Magistrates whatever their own private opinions might be - to prison I was sent - my dearest affectionate Husband ill as he was never left me - his tenderness has been beyond description. After above 17 Weeks confinement, with his large Shoe, and unable to move but with two Sticks, he has never seemed to have a thought but for me. We have had some unavoidable delays which have added to the painfulness of our situation - the Application for Bail could not be made because at this Season the Judges were only occasionally in London; - when we came to London we found no Person of our acquaintance here and though the four Sureties who were to join Parrot in bailing me were found ready and happy to show their best services, and though substantial People (Worth and his Partners our Grocers) yet it was suggested that these malicious People might object to our Tradesmen, and therefore the Lawyer was sent to our own Parish and on his return assured us had fifty been required he could instantly have had them as everybody seemed eager to be the first in our Cause - this is pleasant my dear Cos: - We shall be detained till after Monday as that is the first day the Judge can settle our business - I dread this close air more for Parrot than anything else - the House the Person who is with us uses is the Angel behind St. Clements. We did not care thinking we should be gone by this very day, and as we do not stir out nobody knows anything of us. My paper is full. Accept our love and believe us dear Cos, Your affectionate, J. L. P.

October 10th. . Ilchester, My dear Cousin, Had I not been sure that your good sister would have told you all about us, I would have written to you long ago to have thanked you most cordially for your Affectionate Letter, and to have given you every information concerning my cruel disappointment after having like a School Girl told the intervening days between my imprisonment and my return to the Comforts of a home, which I have not now been at for 7 weeks. Indeed had it been possible for me to have painted the Scenes I have gone through during that period, and to have been certain of its continuance for so long a time, I verily believe every struggle would have proved ineffectual but I was flattered with the Idea of being only ten days here; so my trials have come on gradually but, God knows, I am so far from feeling inured to all I see and hear that, had the choice of Death or such a 7 weeks as the last been left to me (and no dearer object in view to stimulate my wish to live) I should not have hesitated one moment in determining on the first. Whether I may not have to pass the whole of the Winter here is at present uncertain - for after one Judge chose to refuse bailing me, whether from inexperience or profound Wisdom others must determine, why may it not be my Cruel fate to be remanded to Ilchester again? And was this to be the Case, I think I could not stand it - to be the wanton Sport of Malice and Villainy in every shape is too much to endure much longer - and although the Newspapers have only reached as yet the Initials of my Name, they consider me now as fair game, and I shall travel for the future at full length I daresay. Oh, my Good Cousin, it may be to answer some wise purpose that such an atrocious Act, has gone so far, and I hope the Merciful disposer of Events will enable me to bear up in spite of such Affliction, but indeed I am not so far a good Christian as to refrain from wishing they may suffer all the horrors of a worse situation even than mine: Worse indeed it must be now, for their Conscience must be their most terrible accusers. I hear that several similar Attempts have been made by the same Villain, and at the same Shop but none I fear with success enough to set the Wretch in his proper place . You cannot imagine how great a Comfort my old Friend Pen was to us. She was very kind, and in every respect what you would have wished her to be - her Humanity and Good Nature quite won her the Heart of my Jailor , or, as he is styled in Ilchester, the Governor , - (what would my poor Sister say to this) who declares he would go to London to fetch her if I was ill whilst here. This, if She knew the Man, is doing as much as the famous Lyre of Orpheus, for Stones and Savages would dance to Music as soon as he would hold Money cheap. I must keep very fair with him because I hear, and indeed sometimes from his own Mouth, that he has a number of Relatives and dependents who are always on the petty Jury and may do me favour or otherwise if he pleases. Good God! and am I to depend on so many People's good Opinion! Thank that God who lets me feel at peace with myself. I will enjoy that Idea let what may happen - this cannot be taken from me by a Malicious World. One of my greatest Miseries here (indeed my very first) is the seeing what my dearest Husband is daily going through Vulgarity, Dirt, Noise from Morning till Night. The People, not conscious that this can be objectionable to anybody, fancy we are very happy, and to do them justice they mean to make us quite so; but all happiness is only comparative, and it is very fortunate that they are satisfied with their Life - to me a Day Labourer's lot with health and Bread and Cheese would be preferable to the Money they tell me this Governor acquires by His most honourable Employment . I had a long letter from my poor Sister the other day who seems to suffer sadly on our accounts. How many Worthy People have I caused distress to! how shall I ever feel grateful enough for the many real Friendships I have received! When I write, I paint my situation here in as fair a way as I can to her - she has few Comforts: I would not take from them, though I cannot add at present to her happiness. I have a thousand Comforts in one - When I look upon the Man who seems to me from his Fortitude , his sweet serenity, and his Affectionate behaviour to have been sent as my Guardian Angel, my true Support under every Affliction, I am all Gratitude to the Almighty. After all, I would not change my situation, wretched as it appears to the World, for that Woman's whose Husband (if she loves as I do) happens to be out of the Kingdom, in the thickest of dangers, although She may be surrounded by everything the Gay World calls Happiness. What a letter I have written and all about this sad self - I think of you all my dear Cos; I rejoice in everything that tends to your Happiness, and wish you all a continuance of every earthly Comfort. I had an Account of each dear Relative from Pen: and the Account coming from her gave me true pleasure - pray tell her I shall write to her soon, but to you my dear Cousin I wished to write well knowing how anxiously you must feel for me. We are much better in health than I expected we should be - a Head Ache plagues me frequently, but my Heart aches so much oftener that I must not mention this lesser ill. My dear Parrot desires his Affectionate Regards and wishes to yourself, Mrs. C... and our young Cousins - not forgetting dear Pen; believe me ever most sincerely yours, J. Leigh Parrot.

Ilchester, Nov. 10th, 1799. My dear Cousin, I fear my large sheet of paper will fright you, but I feel as if I had a vast deal to say and you have my leave when you have read till you are tired to lay my letter safe in Spider Hole and begin again at your leisure. I had scarcely read your Letter (so long and so kind) when your Friend Maria and her Mother came into my Room - they were indeed most friendly in their behaviour and made me offer of Books, the produce of their Garden, or anything they could at any time contribute to our Comfort - but in truth, my dear Cousin, it is not in the power of anyone, let their benevolence be ever so great, to lessen materially the Many Evils we must unavoidably endure in this House of Misery. To say I thank you for your friendship in this introduction is not saying half enough - you must know what my grateful heart feels and therefore I shall not distress you more with Acknowledgements. I find Mrs. Goodford's Father, and family have conferred favours on this Man, and in some degree he is obliged to them for this place which, though a very shocking one to a Man of feeling must be a very lucrative one to such a Man as the one I now write of. Mrs. G. took him out and told him that, as She should be coming two or three times a week and should probably bring other friends with her, it would be absolutely necessary that we should have a room to ourselves - this the Man seemed to take as a reproof and said he had on my first coming told me that the Dining Room I was to consider as my own whenever I choose to be alone - and so it was till Fires began; but this Room joins to a Room where the Children all lie, and not Bedlam itself can be half so noisy, besides which, as not one particle of Smoke goes up the Chimney, except you leave the door or window open, I leave you to judge of the Comfort I can enjoy in such a Room. I have preferred sitting in our Bed Chamber and, as the Weather hitherto has not been very Cold, by keeping the doors shut I think it full as warm as the Dining Room with its open windows and doors; but as this would not be the proper Room to receive Company in for more reason than one (N.B.) we have only one Chair and one Stool (I desired that, at our Expense , a Fire might be kept every day in the dining Room that I might, in spite of smoke, see Mrs. and Miss Goodford alone if they were so kind as to call on us - but even this Comfort I shall not enjoy, as your friend Maria (who kindly paid me a second Visit two days after her first) found me in my dining Room it is true, but the family there too - nor could their Ignorance let them see their impropriety in continuing there. And yet I dread anything that appears like discontent or Complaint made to my friends. Mrs. Goodford wonders at our not sending for our Servants, or at least for my own Maid - I could not tell her before these people that, though we were bearing a thousand disgusting Matters as to our Accommodations, Food, &c., my Servants would not, and I should have their murmurs added to our other troubles. My Maid is a Welsh Woman with all the honesty and Passion of her Country - she would lay down her life to see me happy when she was not in one of her fits of passion ; but I am certain before she was in this house one week she would fight this swearing Vulgar Man and his Companions, nor could I, even knowing her to be right take her part in any contest - had my poor old quiet Chambers been living she would have been a real Comfort to me here ; but she never could have shown me more true affectionate duty and Respect than my present set of servants have done - indeed they are all highly spoken of by my numerous friends who write constantly from Bath. No! my Good Cousin, I cannot subject even a Servant to the sufferings we daily experience. We have rubbed through three Months and, though the next four may be more trying as the time of the year will be more against us, yet I put my trust in God and as Sterne makes his Maria say - "He will temper the Wind to the shorn Lamb" I hope. My dearest Parrot with his sweet composure adds to my Philosophy; to be sure he bids fair to have his patience tried in every way he can. Cleanliness has ever been his greatest delight and yet he sees the greasy toast laid by the dirty Children on his Knees, and feels the small Beer trikle down his sleeves on its way across the table unmoved. Your old guest Alderman Stonier was a Prince of Elegance to what we meet here. Mrs. Scadding's knife well licked to clean it from fried onions helps me now and then - you may believe how the Mess I am helped to is disposed of - here are two dogs and three Cats always full as hungry as myself. You advise us to procure Bail, and who can doubt our wish of doing this if it could be done with thorough safety at my future trial - but in order to procure Bail (after having been refused it) we have not only to produce the proofs we have of this Man's Negligence in Business, and some appearance of intended Frauds but copies of everything produced in Westminster Hall must be given to these Vile people - of course their counsel will have four Months to endeavour at counteracting all our evidence against him, - and should we not succeed I know I could never support being remanded here again - besides this, our Friend Mr. Hill advises that we should procure all our most Respectable Relations on each side to answer for me, as it would have a wonderful good effect on the Bench - but for what am I to draw all our happy Friends from their Familys? - Why! to save me the inconvenience of passing the next four months where we have passed the last three - Surely my dear Cousin this would be selfishness with a witness - If I was sure that my being so long imprisoned would prejudice a future Jury against me, I should certainly be sorry to lose any chance of an Honourable Acquittal; but I hope that there is more honour left than such prejudice would bespeak. I am more inclined to stay where I am than to run the risk of not succeeding - indeed I could not be happy anywhere whilst this thing hangs on my Mind. A public Court, and my appearance for a Capital Offence, you will allow are quite Antidotes to happiness. You will not my good Cousin like this letter one bit better than my last two - but I cannot dissemble with anyone much less with you - if I am angry all must know it - if I am miserable I cannot hide it. Mrs. Goodford was so good as to say I must come and see her, and she had enquired of the Man if he had any objection - the Answer - None at all - but I am resolved not to stir from this place as a Prisoner except by legal means. I have made my dear Husband promise me that, should she invite him , he will go - indeed I have a pride in letting the World see, and know the Man who thinks me deserving so much affection - besides which I think it may be of considerable advantage to him to get acquainted with some of the leading People in this Neighbourhood before the Assizes come on. I like your Friend Maria much - she seems sensible and feeling - as well as her Mother - we talked you all over at Easton - it happened odd enough but the day before your letter reached her Mrs. Philips (her Brother's Wife) had received a letter from Lady Napier at Bath to enquire whether there was not a Mrs. Leigh Parrot in this prison for the imputed crime of secreting Lace , begging to know how we were, and if we were well accommodated - as we deserved every attention. Mrs. P. could give no answer then, now she knows who this Thief is, and may say something of me. Parrot joins me in kindest Love to Yourself and our circle of Cousins at Easton. I shall write by the next post, or this if I have time, to my Sister, but I fear Pen: will have left Carlton before the letter reaches it. I hear a most pleasant account of you all - but this Gest comes too frequently on you. I really think Steer's Opodeldock has strengthened Parrot's Sprained Ankle; he walks stouter - and is upon the whole better than I could have expected him to be. I have not been quite the thing this last week - anxiety of Mind is not good for Bowels naturally tender, I must not expect to be free from pains of the Body as well as mind - but I am ever most sincerely Your affectionate Cousin, J. Leigh Parrot. P.S. Dallas, Jedge , and Bond are all retained as my counsel.

Ilchester, Jan., 1800. My dearest Cousin, That your Letters afford me real Comfort nobody that knows us both can doubt - Why then, say you, have I not sooner thanked you for your last truly kind one? At a Season too when everyone's good wishes are posting from Friend to Friend. That you have not one Relation or Friend in the World who more sincerely rejoices at your Happiness than myself is most true. I heard of your being surrounded by all your young Props , and in the most fervent prayer did I beg a Continuance of every blessing to you and them, but as my letter could not add one Moment to your Comfort I could not O my kind Cousin! Why should I pain you by telling you of my Griefs! and yet I could not with truth write pleasantly of my dearest Parrot for some time past; I thank God he is now better but for one whole Night, and all the Next day, did he lie in such an Agony of Pain, that my distress was cutting indeed. I was desirous of having the Medical Man of Ilchester, though my Heart ached at the Alternative, (as his trades are Apothecary, Surgeon, Coal dealer, Brick and Tile Maker, &c. , which seemed to bespeak his being good at None) but the dread of his mistaking the Constitution, so naturally full of Gout and the Assurance from my poor Sufferer that he knew it was a severe fit of Gravel, or something like it, (I hope not Gall Stones by the acuteness of pain) made us give this Assistance up, and as he has been better for the last two or three days my mind is a little easier on his Account. I had a Comfortable kind Letter from Good Pen, yesterday. She writes in good spirits, but talks of London being visited by terrible Colds and Coughs - I think One I have got would match any she writes of. - My Sister is writing to inform me of the Addition to her Carlton Comforts - in her last letter she informs me of my having a powerful Champion in your dear John at some Meeting where a Mr. Casamajor chose to tell my strange story - and adding that he had heard particulars from his Relation by Marriage , Sir William East, who was much shocked at it. If he had heard from Sir W. E. I will answer for it he never heard anything said unhandsome of us, for Sir W. on hearing from Payne of Maidenhead how I had been used lamented his being obliged to leave Berkshire the next day for Lady East's health which prevented his offering himself as one of my bail and wished it lay in his power to be of any service as well through the Regard he felt for us as to show his detestation of so much Villainy, for almost a similar Case had nearly involved Lady East in the distress that I was thrown into. Miss Molly Casamajor may love Scandal as well as other Creatures of his description. - Pray thank my Cousin John and tell him I trust I shall never make him blush at having taken up my defence. I find Miss Goodford is coming to visit your Young Married Woman - She is very friendly to us indeed, and if dreadful Roads were not between us I know she would be a very great Comfort to me. Mrs. G. and her friend Mrs. Daniell a most interesting pleasant Woman, made us a long Morning Visit a few days ago. She seems as warm and friendly in her Attentions as if I were her near Relation. You mistake the Matter my dear Cousin when you fancy my Servants have objections to coming here - they wished to come - but one of my Comforts is that I am so truly independent now (suffering so much when poor old Chambers died) that I want no Attendant - when my dear Parrot is ill in Bath, my only pleasure is to attend him myself - besides here is a very respectable Servant in this Family who has attached herself so much to us, that I should have nothing for my Servants to do and I am sure I could not improve them in any one instance here. I hear from them every Week. and they are of some use there, as my old Friends are very frequent in their Enquiries and Messages. I should like to see you hobbling about though I confess two sticks are not advantageous to the Gait. - We have not left off our two yet, though I think our Ankle gains considerable Strength, more owing to keeping it uncommonly warm than to any Medical Applications. I see Mrs. Blundels name amongst those friends who called on me in Bath last week. I suppose she is full of talk of her Brother's gay Choice. I do not think he will dislike a Card playing, Rout going Wife at all - if I was his Lady I should like distraction a little more than I now do. You will not expect any amusing Anecdotes from hence - in truth I never yet have seen so truly miserable a place as this same Ilchester - I make up however in Affection what I may want as to Life or Spirit for I can truly subscribe myself. Your Sincere and Affectionate J. Leigh Parrot. P.S. Pray remember to circulate our kindest Love and Good Wishes to your Fire Side and to Mrs. Johnstone's if they have left Easton.

Ilchester, March 6th, 1800. My dearest Cousin, You have heard from your good Sister some account of my sufferings within the last three weeks; I shall not pain you by the repetition but tell you that I am now comparatively happy in seeing this Treasure of my Life in a Convalescent State. I hope he will leave off the use of James' Powder tomorrow, and, if this sad Cold weather does not prevent him get about in the Air again. I received your Letter, my dear Cousin, when he was in his worst state, for indeed he was very ill; much more so than I have ever seen him. It was a great Comfort to me to hear from yourself that you were so much better. I began to think this World would soon lose every charm for me. You cannot imagine anything more truly Sisterly than Mrs. Goodford's attention to us. She seemed to bring Comfort whenever I saw her and her very sensible feeling. Elizabeth was with us on Sunday Afternoon, though I much fear her Visit was shorter than she had kindly intended it should be, as she found Mr. Watts our Solicitor from Bath with us. He had just returned from London (where Mr. Hill had thought it necessary he should attend the Consultation of my Counsel) and brought the Brief with the Counsel's remarks for Parrot's perusal. This hour's attention to Business gave me a painful Proof of my dear Invalid's inability just now for things of this Nature; he had no rest, although the Opiate which he had been obliged to take every Night never failed before to compose him. Thank God he was next day much better than I had imagined he would have been and has seemed gaining Strength every day since. From our very kind Friend Mr. Hill we understand Mr. Jekyll is very warm in the Business. So very black a Character as the Villain bears who is the Witness against me, one can only wonder at his Courage in exposing himself to the examination of a public Court and yet there seems to be so great a Combination of deep laid schemes, that I can only think with additional horror of what Art may do against Innocence . That the Set (for such I believe I may properly term them) have been thoroughly disappointed in not having a Sum of Money offered is most certain. Nay, I verily believe that even now they flatter themselves that my dear Husband's illness, and possible inability to attend me through such a scene may at the last oblige him to make proposals to them, but little do they know of either himself or me who could fancy such an Idea would ever arise in our breasts. I think I could die before I could do this. I confess I feel more shaken when I think how much this dear Invalid may suffer from the Trial, of fatigue incident to it, than I have ever done for myself, however that merciful God, who has supported us hitherto, will I trust not let us be overturned now. You were very good to say you wish to Attend me, had not your ill health prevented you. I can never doubt your Friendship for a Moment. Mr. Watts informed us that the Counsel wished to have Four of our Country Neighbours, and four of our Bath Acquaintances, to answer for me at Taunton. Relations would not be called upon for this Purpose. I should grieve to give any additional trouble to my kind Friends. One Lady, or at most two with me in Court would be all I ought to have. Your good Sister offered to come to me but it is a long Journey, and in her lame State, with the certainty of unavoidable inconveniences at Taunton, I cannot think of her coming. I have been disappointed in another quarter. My dear Affectionate Sister Austen, though in a state of health not equal to trials of any kind, has been with the greatest difficulty kept from me. In a letter from her a few days ago I had the pain to hear that her Valuable Son James having had his Horse fall with him by which his leg was broken. This is a loss indeed because he had been a perfect Son to me in Affection and his firm Friendship all through this trying Business had taught me to look to him and his Wife (a Relation of Lord Craven's well bred and sensible) to have come to us at the Assizes. Now I can neither ask Mother or Wife to leave him nor could I accept the Offer of my Nieces - to have two Young Creatures gazed at in a public Court would cut one to the very heart. Some of my kind Friends were early in their offers of attending us from Bath . It is a favour I never will first propose to anyone. If the kindness of nearer Friends than Berkshire ones is offered I shall with gratitude accept it. You see, my dear Cousin, this is the only Subject I can now write upon. Though I am highly pleased at our Friend Maria Goodford's account of the Connection and Establishment of your handsome Mary , yet I have never said one word on the subject. I love you all to much not to be deeply interested in every Circumstance contributing to your Happiness, believe me. Pray remember us affectionately to Mrs. Cholmeley and those of my Young Cousins now at Easton. I had a letter from Carlton a little time ago with very kind offers from Mr. Welby of coming to Taunton if he could be of the least Service , but we declined the offer - indeed I know no use he could be of to answer so long a journey. If it had been within a very short distance the sight of Friends must have been Cheering at such a time - but Parrot thinks he shall have no time but for Lawyers. I am sure I shall have no thought but for him. Mr. Watts has taken a House for our Witnesses at Taunton, and says he thinks he shall have to procure 10 or 12 more beds as fresh People were coming forward every day to offer their services - even the very day before he was here he had a Gentleman called to say he would step forward to prove a similar trick in his family at the Shop . This ruinous Expense is what we shall long feel - but we are not expensive People and believe me, Lace is not necessary to my happiness. Adieu my dear Cousin. Accept Parrot's and my most affectionate wishes and ever believe me Your sincere J. L. P.

Bath, April 1st, 1800. My dearest Cousin, Once more I address you unprison'd , but oh! how I have been wrung! - to the very quick believe me. You will rejoice to hear that I was most honourably acquitted - but you will grieve with me that we cannot punish my Vile Antagonists. Let it however comfort us that, if his own Conscience acquits him, he is in the high Road to punishment, most likely to the Gallows. The Circumstances, which my Trial brought out, are sufficient Grounds against him on his Perjured Bankruptcy Business; and some of the Persons then present have promised to do for him. I own what partly consoled me for what I had undergone was the delightful Idea of the Pillory Exhibition for my pretty pair of Lovers - but my Solicitor says nothing can be done. You heard from your Friendly Sister what a Scene of Hurry and Confusion we lived in. ... I fear She was most uncomfortable and I wished her not to be out of the House - bad as it was, it would have been as well as a Lodging out - but She would not have a Bed such as we could offer - indeed I felt myself greatly obliged to her for her kind Appearance. From her you heard how many Witnesses we had taken down. Three out of three and twenty I believe were examined, and were sufficient to prove Mr. Filby Rogue enough in all conscience. I never heard of so vile a Character but I fear he had so many nearly as bad as himself, that swearing black was white seemed nothing to them. Mr. Justice Laurence behaved handsomely, he wished me seated, and sent several times to signify such wishes - and he sent Mr. Jekyl to repeat (in a louder Voice than my Agitation would allow of) any Observations I wished to make to the Judge after the Evidence Against me had been examined; but I must at the same time confess that (unless I was partial to my own Cause) he did not let enough be said of Filby's Villainy - he thought enough had been said to fully clear me, and was pretty sure that the winding up of his Charge to the Jury would put every doubt respecting my Innocence out of the Question; but I think it was a dangerous Experiment. My oath was not betaken; my Husband's Evidence in my favour was nothing - else I could have disproved my having on any Cloak, though the Villain swore he saw the Lace under my black Cloak - several similar Perjuries (had we not been Man and Wife ) might have been proved. The Judge, after he had said everything respecting Filby's Deposition as well as the others, added "And now you have heard all this, if you can believe Filby's Evidence, if you should be inclined to believe His Evidence, I have only to desire you to consider the Attestations of those Gentlemen who have attended on behalf of Mrs. Leigh Parrot's Character." He then repeated each kind Friend's testimony, and their knowledge of me for many years in their own words, which were all as highly gratifying as possible. The Jurymen, who seemed much more enlightened than Petty Jurors generally are took Notes many of them and were 7 Minutes and half studying to explain those Notes to their less intelligent companions, before they brought me in not Guilty - a clapping of hands to show Approbation and Joy immediately began, which the Judge hushed as not being allowable - so this Vile Matter rests. Lord Braybrook, Vansittart, Annesley and Grant, with four Bath Friends kindly attended us. Never tell me of Erskine, Garrow , or any of your Popular Counsellors; my Friend Bond was animation all over - and preserved the Gentleman at the same time, which some of your great Men cannot always support. I was disappointed in Jekyll - Dallas was very well. Pell had little to say but he showed vast feeling by perfectly sobbing whilst my Observations were repeated. Indeed I never saw so many Men weep. I have taken a large sheet thinking to transcribe them for your entertainment - you were with me in thought the whole time I know. The frightful Expense I cannot Estimate. I am told it will be nearer two than one thousand pounds and from the large demands already made only for conveying the Witnesses (and the two days Expenses for the House and Eating at Taunton which alone amounted to £93; odd money), I can easily suppose it will be full that sum. What a comfort that we have no Children! My Lord and Gentlemen of the Jury, I am told that my Counsel cannot be permitted to address to you any remarks on my Case. The Circumstances of it do not render it necessary to detain you long, but as my Counsel are prevented I cannot (although nearly unequal to the speaking in such an Assembly) help taking advantage of this Opportunity. Placed in a Situation in every respect the most Enviable - blessed with a Tender and most Affectionate Husband who is ever anxious to indulge my Wants and anticipate my Wishes and whose Supply of Money is so ample as to leave me rich after every desire is gratified what inducement could I have to commit this offence? Depraved indeed must have been my Mind if with these Comforts I could have been tempted to this Crime. You will hear from my Noble and highly respectable Friends what has been my conduct, and what has been, and still is their opinion of me. Can you think it possible they have been so many years deceived? Is it possible that at this time of Life my disposition should so suddenly change and that I should foolishly hazard the well earned reputation of a whole Life by such Conduct, or endanger the Peace of Mind of a Husband for whom I would willingly lay down that Life? You have heard their Evidence: I shall not, nor indeed can I make any comments upon it: I leave that where I am satisfied it will be used with Justice and Mercy. I will only ask you whether to be found opposite to the Shop within the space of little more than half an hour, and with the Lace in my Hand is like the conduct of a Guilty Person. My Oath is on this occasion inadmissible; but I most solemnly assure you and I call on that God, whom we all acknowledge and adore, to reward or punish me as I now speak true or false and to witness my Assertion, that I did not take the White Lace knowingly from Smith's Shop, nor had I any reason to suspect or believe that the same was in my Parcel when accosted by my Prosecutrix." As soon as the Trial was over, the Adversaries hastened to Bath that they might circulate the story they had fabricated. The Paragraph inserted in the Paper was "that after a long trial and the clearest and most Satisfactory Evidence from the Prosecutrix and Witnesses the Jury were more than half an hour out of Court when they brought the Verdict in not Guilty." It was reported too that I had fainted and was carried out of Court - that another Trial was carried on, and then I was brought in again, tried by a fresh Jury which had all been bribed with a guinea each and they acquitted me. You see my dear Cousin how fertile a Spot Bath is. The Author of the Erroneous Paragraph was made to own it erroneous and, in handbills distributed about, to promise the true statement. We did not reach Bath till 12 o'Clock on Sunday Night and before 10 on Monday Morning our anxious Friends began coming in so that till Bed time I could not get a Moment to write you this Account. I thought I would be early enough to-day, but no such thing, my whole time has been taken up in kissing and Crying. The post is now gone and I could cry to think you should be so many days in hearing from us. May I soon hear that you are quite well, and that dear Mary has made you a Grand-papa . Give our kind love to Mrs. Cholmeley and my Young Cousins. I have written you a monstrous long letter and yet I feel as if I had not said half I meant to say. I have written to Pen: at Yeovil - She will tell you a great deal about us I daresay. Accept our best love, and believe me Your Affectionate J. L. P.

Bath. April 8th, 1800. My Dear Cousin, To be sure (as a kind Friend told me) I stand some chance of being killed by Popularity - though I have escaped from Villainy. The more I reflect on the diabolical Set that swore such abominable Falsehoods the less I wonder at the Numbers that swing every Year - indeed I am almost led to fear that many Innocent People suffer from false Oaths. That these Wretches had marked me for somebody timid enough to be Scared, and Rich enough to pay handsomely rather than go through the terrible Proceedings of a public Trial nobody doubts; and by timing it when I had only my Husband with me there were sure that I could have no Evidence against them. Surely our boasted Laws are strangely defective - owing to this Circumstance I find no Punishment from me can attach to this Villain - and had he gone off the very day before the Trial, we should have lain under the Stigma of having bought him off without a possibility of Clearing ourselves. We had been put to a very great Expense in collecting Witnesses from London to prove frauds in his Bankruptcy Business - from Birmingham to bring out Circumstances which the Judge stopped proceeding on or it might have hanged him. Query did he not richly deserve the Gallows? A fine sum it will cost, and all that we have for it is that the Solicitor for the Bankruptcy assured us he should lay hold of him, and from what he had on my Trial discovered made no doubt of his meeting the fate his Villainy to me deserved without any other Crimes. I think we have left so many Friends at the Castle that if our Debts - or another Filby , should drive us there we shall stand a good chance, nay it was told Parrot by a Person of some Shrewdness that he would stand a very good Chance if he would offer for Ilchester at the ensuing Election. What a noble finish this would be to our Jail Adventures would it not? J. L. P

Bath. April 14th, 1800. My dearest Cousin, Thank you, my good Cousin, for your Letter. We begin to feel more Calm - but the more Calm I feel (though perhaps a a contradiction) the more ruffled I am with all the People principally concerned in this most infamous Transaction. I agree with you about not being quite satisfied with any but Bond; and he would, I am convinced, if the Judge had not stopped him have made that Villain Filby squeak pretty loud. I cannot help thinking (and I suppose this must be quite entry nous ) that the Judge acted very wrong. I may lean too much on my own Side because I know my Innocence and the horrid Roguery of this Set of Perjured People - but I think Judge Laurence leant as much on the other side. He, it is alleged, knew he could in drawing up his Charge show his opinion of my Innocence in his last three or four lines - but to 9 out of ten Petty Jurors this was a dangerous Experiment. Such a Set of Jurors were hardly ever known - they even took Notes - and this accounts for their being above a quarter of an hour in explaining those Notes to those amongst them who were more unenlightened. Why the Judge should stop Mr. Bond when he was showing to the whole Court that Filby was the greatest Villain that ever existed - and not only Perjury but other matters of ye most serious consequences could be brought against him I know not - but this I do know that, if I had been allowed to speak and had been equal to the Exertion, I should have proposed a few questions which would have been I think unanswerable - first why, if the Man saw Lace secreted under my Cloak, did he let me, a perfect Stranger, quit the Shop? That I had no Cloak on was only to affirm what I could bring only my Husband to prove - so that is nothing. I confess when I came into Court and found that the Perjury seemed deeply connected and that not only the Prosecutrix and Filby (her sole Witness as I thought) but the very Shop Girl was in the same strange Story, I was struck with horror to see how far Wickedness might proceed. Yet for myself I felt no ill consequence. I find now that the greatest censure is thrown on the Mayor - and in my opinion he deserves it. It appeared to us unaccountable that we should never have heard anything for a whole week after this Transaction. The Prosecutrix swears that, on her seeing me pass on the opposite side of ye Street in half an hour afterwards, She went out, and upon my giving her the Parcel and saying, if there was white Lace put up with the black I had bought, it must be through the Negligence of her Shop Man. She answered "It is no such thing, it is no such thing you stole it" - Can anyone believe that all this could have been said to me in one of the most public streets in Bath - at two o'Clock when everybody was passing to the Cross Bath to drink the Water and that no person should have heard it which she says was the Case? Can anyone believe that if She had dared to have said this to me My Husband (whom She says answered only "No she did not") would not have taken some legal steps against such defamation of a Wife's Character? Her words were so very different to what She swears , that I could not even suppose it an Accusation - though She says it made me turn Scarlet . When the Man came after me to know our Name: I own then a presentiment of intended Villainy flashed on me, and then I should not have wondered at turning Scarlet or any Colour of the rainbow. We wondered that some Knavish Attorney had not made his Appearance next Morning to have frighted me, but never could I suspect that they were so deep in their Scheme as to have gone to the Mayor; however they swear they did - and they were put off on various Excuses. We have heard that the Mayor knowing our Mode of Living, and our respectable Characters, did full as much as he ought to prevent their proceeding in the Business - but why did he not through some Friend let us know the premeditated Perjury and give us an opportunity of consulting our Lawyer? And another Query of the greatest Consequence is why did he on asking the People at the Town Hall who were in the Shop and hearing that there were two Shop Girls at work which two Girls he sent for immediately, but discharged them in five minutes on one saying She was quite out of hearing, and the other (Rains) saying She only heard me ask for the Lace I had cheapened the Day before, and nothing more, why I say did he not take this in writing or why (now that he finds these Girls both Called upon, and Rains swears to every Particular in which She has been tutoring these 7 Months) does he not state everything as it happened in the Town Hall before him? As to our wish of punishing the Man, who can doubt it! but your Idea of the Case being the same as if I had been called a Thief in a public Paper is I am told by Lawyers quite wrong. - then I could only get redress by proceeding against him, and the King's Bench with ample damages might have been the Consequence. But now a public Court and an honourable Acquittal is much more satisfactory to the whole World - and how can we blacken those People more than they have blackened themselves - the Man is off and the Shop I hear must be ruined. All this my dear Cousin I could not help writing you, though I greatly fear it will make your Head ache to read it. You can have no Idea how very warm and Friendly everybody seems to us. Everyone of our old and our new Acquaintance are coming to us continually - by sitting for seven hours in the Court with wet feet I brought a very bad cold to Bath - attended with one of my bad Coughs. Bath is not the place to lose these disorders in - my dear and Affectionate Sister Austen is impatient for our getting into Hampshire, but I cannot go just yet. I shall not feel quite easy till our heavy Charges are known and paid . I think by the time they are paid, my dear Husband may assert with truth that he is not worth one penny in right of his Wife - I wish I may be mistaken. I find the Carlton Family set forward on their London expedition on the 21st; Pray my dear Cousin do not fancy that I am ever too deeply engaged in any Business or pleasure not to write to you. Never can I forget your warm and Affectionate Zeal. I could not regard you more than I did before, but little did I think to have proved your Friendship in so trying a Cause. God bless you all. Our kind love to you and yours. Believe me Your sincere and faithful friend J. Leigh Parrot.

Kingsweston, 28 Augt 1682 Dear Cousin I have been Rouleing of late between this and Bath, and am tomorrow carrying my little fry to compliment the Company there, of which I had a coachfull of the Ladies here on Wenesday last. So I come slow to the acknowledging yours of the 17th, which came with a valuable Cargo to me. For tho I had no concern in the subject matter of any paper you wrote, yet all of them are to me as so many modells to work by, and of like force as the five Powers in the meckanicks. Wherefore let me not want copies of what you can spare, for they shall not dye, if I or Neddy can help it. The Prints doe constitute you one of the 3 Governors of his Majesty's Irish Revenue, but a word from your self would be more authentic. I wish for his Majesty's sake it were the worst news I could have concerning Ireland. Rejoice at the happy arrival of your two brave Boys. Neddy will be at leisure ere long to try his cousin's patience. Happiness to all is the constant wish of Yours R. Southwell

London, ye 5o Sepbr 1682 Dear Cousin Yesterday came to Town what was declared on Sunday night at Windsor, vizt, That the Revenue of Ireland is to bee managed by the Lt Longford, Lem Kingdon, one Mr Strong of the Excise, Mr Dixon of the Customs of London, and Captain Bridges of Dublin, who as tic thought did but represent Mr Trant. By good Luck I never sollicitated any body in the Case, I only putt in 3 several papers of proposals before you went hence, which I think did the service no harm. As for my self, my work hath ever been my wages in this world. My own buisnesse sticks in the Bog where you left it. I have much to say, but I have nobody to hear me. I will review the specimen of Logic , and perhaps send it inlargd as well as explained. Wee are all in health here. Charles and his sister are in daily emulation about Arithmetic; That spirit doth begin to rise and appear in Charles upon the Charms and Conjurations of his sister. The Latin also joggs on, so as I hope you shall ere long bee ready to receive Cousin Noddy's Arrows. As for news: it is said that the Duke of Hanover is to have my Lt Lowtherdell's Garter. I have writ 3 sheets in answer to 31 questions concerning money. If it take (for I renounce all Judgement of my own) you shall have a Copy. But laying all these things aside, let me here that you and your family are well, for that will best please Yors W. P.

Kingsweston, 11 Sepr 1682 Dear Cousin By yours of the 5th Instant I see the 5 Commissioners of the Revenue of Ireland. The first I easily guess at, but who launched the other 4 into this Bethesda I want to know? You say nothing of their Salary; nor of their subordination to the Treasury here; nor if those 2 points (which so endeared the former prosecution) doe still subsist, as to Tangiers and the Ships, wherein as a Kingsale man I am a little concerned. But I confess I am much more, to see that when the City is delivered, yett noebody reguards the wise man. I will believe that your papers had more effect than you are told of; and seeing they turn you no better to Account, let me at least have the Transcript of what you gave in. For I shrine all up, and fancy that in after times I shall be resorted too for your works, as Mr Hedges is for the true Opo-balsamum. I see also as to your particular affair, that you stick fast as before, and scarce know where with benefit to expose your doleance. I would advise better if I knew how; but surely it can do no hurt if you take Sir Edward Dering fresh at his arrival from Kent and explain to him that by him alone you can hope to be understood. The proposal which by my Lord Hyde's encouragement he so laboured in, being quite laid by, and new things done (wherein as being absent he has no share), I am apt to think he will not be unwilling to learn and know the extent of your case, and afterwards to act as fair opportunities shall be offered him. I take notice that all your clouds are only without doors, for at the same time you can think and turn your mind to the instruction of the unkind world. Your 3 sheets about money shall be much more welcome to me than money itself. And then to have the specimen of Logic enlarged, as well as explained, is a matter I really take to heart. For my chief business is now grown a solicitude for my son's education, and so I am chawing over every thing that I judge useful in order to his easier digestion. Neddy remembers you advised him to gather Tools, as Hammer, saw, pincers, gimblett &c; and he calls the arts and sciences already by these nick-names, and means to value them no more than as they really prove such. And as he passes for the top-artisan that invents a new Tool, so Neddy means to throng in among your admirers; not only for this Logic , but for all other Tools, which either for the Sake of his cousin Charles or the Public you shall vouchsafe to frame or invent. He hopes also you will cause the 104th Psalm to be printed anew. You have also within doors the sunshine of this new and profitable emulation between Charles and his sister. I see that tic she ferments Arithmetic in him, but how you levened her (unless ex traduce ) pray let us know. I have got Dr Wallis by the end touching this subject; for I would fine by comprehending the reason retain the practice, which else vanishes as I have found for want of frequent use. All my young ones are well and afford me much content; tic the most sensible share of worldly happiness we can have. I doe heartily congratulate your part, and am ever Yours R. Southwell

Kingsweston, 28 Nobr 1682. Dear Cousin When by yours of the 24th past I understood your putting off the evil day of a dirty and dangerous Journey, I became much more sedate than before; but when you concluded your letter with an Interdiction to your self, and such a Reverse as to say 'lett there be darknesse', I fell into grief and you may think stupidity (by my long silence); and this for many Accounts. First that the world should be so wicked as to give you provocation, but chiefly that you should take it. For has Sir Walter Raleigh added to his character by burning half the World? Had he not been even more revenged, in heaping up coals and obleiging the ungrateful age? Besides how preposterous is it for the Iniquity of the present bystanders (which are but a handful) to bespite the inoffensive generations that are to come? And how well did Ben Johnson defy their hissings when he declared that what he had written was for Posterity. A prophet has no honour in his own time. I have now the favour of yours of the 25th Instant, and in it some of the Rich Ore of the same old mine. Herein I first congratulate that you take home the prodigal son (I should indeed have said it of the Father) and that you let the world see plain, what they still suspected, that the spirit of Sir William Petty and not of John Grant presided in those Bills of Mortality. Poor John, tho in his purgatory, can hardly drive such points as (by your allowance) he ventured on while here, in his State of fuddling and of frailty. The good man was herein like a dwarf mounted on an Elephant. But although, to keep gravity, you will needs excuse this new eruption and that still you are for unthinking and unobleiging too; I can but smile, as I would doe to hear natural agents such as the sun, moon, and stars talk at the same rate. Wherefore tic but weakly done to say you will not think; and tho you must think, to say you will not Ratiocinate, is to sever heate from Light, which will not doe - or to say again that though you do Ratiocinate we shall no more hear on it. You may better say so much touching Gunpowder, for tic a child when borne that cannot be murdered. Light when generated will shine out and wisdom must still cry aloud in the streets. Wherefore, dear Cousin, make a virtue of Necessity, and what you cannot Resist or suppress, let us have it with a good Grace, and as it were, have amongst you blind Harpers. While I was too credulous of your first anger (which yett I congratulate), I went to ransack all my papers, and have putt together in one Treasure all that ever I had from you, and which shall lye together an Heire-loom not only for this Neddy, but all the Neddyes that may come hereafter. As to your present work; the very Pattern is Admirable - to teach men how to present to the World with vitals, and not with long Hair and Nails which commonly make up the bulk. But Cousin, this Herb is a peculiar of your own Garden, and be not angry if it springs not up in every soil. For me to attempt to propagate This method in my Neighbourhood as you propose, would be to destroy it. I am not their favourite, which I really congratulate, as much as I prefer Philosophy before drinking. I can truly tell you that tic near a month that I wrote to Mr Dickinson and Mr John Ellis in terms of as much concern for you as I could express. My small puggs are all well and very Jovial, for I have got them a blind Harper. I hope the like with my Godson and all his good company, being ever Sr Your most affect Kinsman & most humble servant Robert Southwell I am glad you have speeded orders about our old friend Wm Fitzgerald.

Kingsweston, 16 April 1683 Dear Cousin Your last demonstration was so killing, and in a matter of that bulk and importance, that I have remained ever since as one that had seen a miracle. My Lord Weymouth, who is in the Role of your admirers, was lately here with me. We shall both meet by the end of this month in London, and are not to be long from your House. He was wishing he had your thoughts on the great catastrophe of Banquers; whether land will Rise, or what may be the most probable consequences thereof. But, dear cousin, must you have a fortunate hearing in the Treasury upon Saturday last, and must I owe the glad tidings rather to one of your Judges than your self? Well! Laus Deo , which I heartily pronounced first in consideration of Kerry, and then of nature and Philosophy. For if the World will but give you Rest, I am sure you will be Teeming. My 3 Girls have been coughing till quite tyred out, but the approach of a London Journey seems very restorative. With true Service to my lady, my godson, and the Rest I am ever, Sr Your most affect Cousin & most humble servant Robert Southwell

London, ye 19o April 1683 Dr Cousin To yours of the 16o. I say nothing of my Demonstrations about the Growth of London. When you come, in reference to my Lord Waymouth's questions concerning Bankrupts, I will show you a scheme of a Bankrupt wherein the Lamb may wade, and the Elephant may swim &c. I had a little opium given me on Saturday last, of which I said nothing, as doubting it might be corrected with Castorium and other strong Ingredients, - as it hath been. But I being dosd and Stupefied, can make no Judgement of it, but am sqird back like the weavers shuttle into Ireland, there to endure time and chance. The fits of the Double-Bottome do return very fiercely upon me. I cannot bee dissuaded but that it contains most glorious, useful and pleasant things. My happiness lies in being mad. I wish I were grown up to that Degree as to believe I were fairly dealt with. I doe not attribute my wrongs to much hatred of my Person, as to other internal motions within the lucky Men of Power. Wee long here to see how wan the 3 girls will bee when they come to their cousins hither. I am Yors W. P. I desire you to get me an Account of some Parishes according to the Method enclosed.

Kingsweston, 20 Sept. 1684 Dear Cousin I had not till the last night yours of the 31st past, which I have read over and over, for the great kindness as well as variety of it. I see the Vulture is still knowing in Kerry, when at the same time a man child is borne to make you forget that sorrow. Surely this new ship has stupefied that other anguish; and you might be exalted too much, but for that other dead weight that keeps your life in balance. In the Life of Paulus Emilius by Plutark there are these words: "It seems the province of some God to lessen that happiness which is too great and inordinate, and so mingle the affairs of human life that no one should be entirely free and exempt from Calamities, but (as it is in Homer) that those should think themselves truly blessed to whom fortune has given an equal share of good and evil." But as to the ship, you forget to enclose the Catalogue of wagers, which I lament. If she take into Kingrode on her way about, I will be answerable for her good reception here. As to Kerry, I now write and lend your letter to Mr Poppies, not only for his Entertainment, but that he excite Mr Guy to all that is friendly; and in particular that Mr Dickinson may be called upon, not only to ease the Patient, but the Doctors also, who confess they know not what to make of the Case. But I am at some stand how to think of all that is past, and what the Reports now depending may signify, if you are (as you say) beginning all anew under the new Commission. Nor doe I hear you press on Judgment for the Reduced Column, or whether it be already done or not, whereas in this great point seemed formerly to consist your antidote the Thunderbolt. I would have repeated my visit to my dear Cousins in London, but that I hurried away on the sickness of my 2 eldest Daughters, who attending their Grandmother at Bath, met with this new fever which hath humbled them; For they are still but creeping towards the health and vigour which they formerly had. And this also makes our resolution of a quiet wintering in the Country the more needful, while between the Apple Roaster and the Blind Harper (who is sent for), we shall forget the long and blustering nights. I rejoice exceedingly that my Cousin Charles is in the Career you like, and tic enough to make my Grum~ett proud that you enquire how he climbs his ropes. He is very strong; a stout rider - 110 in 2 days and 1/2 - going 46 the first day (when I lately sent him home from Peterbrough) all on the trott, and one day thunder and rain to the skin. He will Learn anything on Horseback, and if repeated by his Tutor, in half the time he can doe it from the book. Formerly his work was to get many of the finest passages that lay about in verse and Prose, which I reckon he will never forget, but serve hereafter as good materials when he has judgment to spinn them out. He is now chiefly intent to be absolute master of Caesar's Com~entarys, and is learning his Greek Grammar, in order to some sprinkling only of that tongue. There are Virgill's Georgics, Plutark's Lives (as newly translated) and other like things for the by. But wee are now going seriously into Arithmetic, Geometry, Astronomy and Cosmography, or some tincture or Instruction towards them, by the help of one Ferfaix who is coming down and to stay this winter at Least amongst us. I have never pressed or Strained on the Boy to his book, being content to let him grow att the same time in other things; which his going about with me does bring in, As an acquaintance with all my friends and the Business that is depending between us. He reads all my Letters and all the Answers I make, and sometimes he answers some for me, and will write a Letter passing well. He designs and has a Musical Voice; but when all is done, he loves play in his Heart. I have here said enough for 7 years; with all duty to my Lady and love to Charles I am ever

Dublin, 23o Xbr. 1684 Dear Cousin Tho I am not upon my oath, yet for the Honour of Eternal Truth, whom I have ever sought and adoard, I will tell you the whole Truth, and nothing but the Truth, concerning our Naval Experiments. Upon the 15th and 16th of this month, wee got her out, to try her sailing & c, which did not answer expectac~on. The main fault (unto which all the rest were Consequences) was not bearing sufficient Sail, which the Careening I menc~oned in my last seemed to secure our Gravest Shipwrights and Sea-men against; and is a fault the more easily remedied upon our Principle, which all our Modells do still justify. But what is all that? - Wee have suffered a Publiq disappointment! Just now I received a joint Letter from Mr Poppies and Sir Anthony Deane, containing several wagers, with a proposal That I must bee personally a board upon all their trials; with a proposal a little before that if wee did excel all the King's yachts, that then the Charge of our Rigging should be boaren. The Considerac~on of all which doth lessen my trouble concerning this matter.
