I will calmly and gravely spend the remainder of my days in diging for Truth in this matter; and being conscious of no wilful miscarriage therein, will courageously endure the Reproaches and derisions of the Vulgar; remaining with my service to all of your family. Yors most entirely Wm Petty

London, 29th August 1685 Dre Cos To yours of the 25th. As to my wife's perfect Recovery, wee must have patience, but do not doubt it. I agree with you in Hopes that the Duke of Lorraine may bee able to take down the great Troubler of the World, of whom Ireland ought to be jealous. I am also clear that if men will but consider, our terrors concerning Ireland are not well grounded. I only fear what men drunk with Rage and Revenge may doe of harm to Themselves and others. I congratulate what you say of the pretty Spinsters and the Rest of your Rural Gazette. I hope wee may answer your desires in the 2 Barony Maps of land near Kingsale when you come to Town. I think there needs be no formal Essay about what I hinted for reading the Scriptures, for (1st) We hold all equally canonised. (2) Tic Manifest that St Luke and the Acts are the best History of Christ and the Apostles. (3) The Epistles of Peter, James, John and Jude, are stiled Catholiq or General Epistles, directed to the whole world, and not to Particular Churches upon special occasions. (4) They do manifestly contain the whole Christian Doctrine. I only add that the 2 Books of the Chronicles is the like Epitome of the History of the Jewish nation and Church. What you say of My Lord Treasurer pleases me well, and I hope tic not an Embryon, but a foetus prop partum . Get but into that organ loft and I will blow your bellows, having wind enough for all your Pipes - I say Wind. For further impositions about Neddy, I think them needless. You have planted all necessaries in his ground, you have led him through all the shops and warehouses of other things. Let nature now work. See what he will choose and learn of himself. What is cram~ed in by much teaching will never come to much, but parch away when the Teachers are gone. Within a year or two you will have a crisis on him; - let's mark that. I am contented you will be here about the Parliament's sitting. What shall We say more, but the old assertion that I am Yours Wm P. Tell the spinsters what fine wool and flax I wish them to work upon, and how good a market for their wears. I am angry that you did not speak a word, neither of Reason or Ridicule, upon the Paper for the Multiplication of Mankind ; as if that Desideratum were frivolous which I take to be equal to all the Projects which have been these many years for the advantage of the World. Pray send it back with an affidavit on the back of it That you have neither shown it to any fortunate fop, nor taken any copy of it. In dudgeon: Adieu.

Kingsweston, 5 Sept 1685 Dear Cousin I have yours in your own ill hand of the 29th past, but what you say of my Lady's Recovery makes ample compensation. So also does your kind mention of the Spinsters, and the fair opinion of their Brother Neddy, and your Inculcateing the Method of reading the Holy Wrote, which are all favours of Weight. But you come off at last with a Biting Postscript. You chide that I say nothing of your Calculation, as if it were so small a matter to speak Skilfully of Mankind, and to discourse in this Great Case (of) the Effects and power of Generation, as it were the putting of a dozen of Eggs under a Henn! Your Great Demonstration is first the Defect, then the Art, and lastly the value of Multiplication . And since you will force me to object, pray answer me this: Mankind must by your method become at last as thick as grass - not 3 acres to a man, but 3 men to an acre, and what not! Nay the Sea also must be covered as far as timber can be gotten for stages and ships. And now that I speak of a Ship, What if your proposal had been made to those on the Arck, and the Deluge were to have lasted? If getting children had not been restrained, the Ship at last must have sunk or the Surplus gone over-board. Wherefore if the Tower you build, - how beautiful soever in the progress - must by its own height or weight fall at last, what need we raise it higher then it is? Then your Great art cannot remain a Secret, as the Philosopher's Stone, or be monopolised by Letters Patent; for all Men are become Philosophers in this Science. And if the noise that one Kingdom (by adding a Law to Generation) is likely to Infect and devour his neighbour, be but heard, that Neighbour will presently make Resistance by the same Engine; and it will soon go about, since the practice will be more easy to the Latter than it was to the first. Yett they surely who begin with the greatest numbers will have the greatest advantage in this Experiment, tho at the last a superfetation of mankind, since our Space is Limited, must produce either Laws or Bloodshed for their necessary Reducing. So I have seen in Germany most Stately Trees for a great space Burnt down, to get a little Arable to live by. So you knew the Hebrew Children were drowned on account of Multiplication, and somewhere in Greece the old men were by Law to be tumbled over a Bridge. Now if the Success of the Project be Ruinous, what need I speak of the Means towards it - as to putt a Girl at 16 and a Lad at 18 to get Children, before they know how to maintain them, or have served out half their Apprentiseshipps? If a whole Country of poor Labourers should have more Children than honest labour can maintain (as may presently bee, if one may have 25 children, and the first 12 be helpless), it follows that they must be maintained by the State. And consequently the State will be owners and disposers of the Children begotten, and so introduce a vasilage which leaves the Parents no other Right to their Children than the Earth hath to its Plants. How to get new Laws and fit Judges for such a Constitution will in this our Climate be somewhat hard. Then whereas you fix the value of a man's Labour at 83£, and so multiply the value with the increase of men, this my thinks would have a quite Contrary Effect; for if Diamonds grew as com~on as pebbles, they would be but of the same account. So in the case of mortality, if in London it exceed that in the Country, the multiplication of other Cities will doe the like. For if there be more men, there will be and must be more communities; and the more London is populous the more will the Rule of Mortality increase. And so the future Throngs will somewhat impair the numbers you impute to the career of generac~on. But why do I meddle in these matters? You know Calculation is not a Herb of my Garden - tic a peculiar of your own. I can only write captiously and, as they say turn the Tables', because you will have me write. However to make you some amends. I will conclude with a story: There is a Province in China where by the constitution, all of the com~on sort who desired to marry, were twice a year to send up their names to the Capital City and to some Senators who presided for That End. Six of these took Care of the Males, and six more of the Females, and at the day of appearance each of the numbers were marshalled into 3 Squadrons. The men into the most Rich, the most Poor, and those who were indifferent. Also the women into the most Fair, the most ugly, and those also who were indifferent. These indifferents were matched up on equal terms. The most beautiful were at high and valuable rates paid for by the most Rich; and at last the most Poor married the most Ugly. Yett they had this satisfaction: to have all the money divided among them which the most rich had given for the most fair. After this the magistrates lead them to the Nuptial House, where at the public charges they had fiddles and sack possett for that night, and the next morning they had leave to depart. I have shown your Paper to Mr Poppies, who is but one of all mankind who are concerned in it; And I doe hereby make affidavit that I have taken a copy of it. Yrs R. S.

Kingsweston, 24 Sept 1685 Dear Cousin The Enclosed is to one part of your kind letter of the 19th. As to the other, about the Irish Settlement, I must have a little time to ruminate on those master Strokes you give, which in the mean time I very heartily thank you for. I use my servant's hand in the Enclosed, because you have complained that my own is not always current. I hope my lady and the little ones are as I wish them. Mine here I thank God are so. Neddy briggs of your Favours and the fine Maps he has in custody. My 2 daughters think they have got all the mathematics because they can demonstrate an equilateral Triangle. Neddy has got from Caspar a clear plain Stile in all his Letters, so that I never have one hard word from him, which I am pleased with. I have nothing more to add concerning Hobby Horses, and therefore remain Sr, Your most affect Kinsman & humble served Robert Southwell

London, 10 October 1685 Dear Cousin Let me tack on a tip to the tail of our Multiplication business. I have yours of the 24th past. I have out of it and all your other letters picked out what properly belongs to that matter. I have out of my first garble again picked out what was wit, ornament, and Raillery, from the rest. In which finding (tho good) objections against what was not in my first essay, I have added such matter to the Essay as is a fit anvil for your heavy homers. That what you have ingeniously written may not bee lost, I have made men to bee kilt by your Arms. And all this I am importuned to print, wherefore make hast up hither. To conclude (Cousin), If I find that you have done me or my Essay any harm, I will satisfy my Justice upon you only by telling all the women of between 16 and 41 years old that you hinder their having husbands &c. Concerning the Quaeries , Let the Devil take them for me. In consequence of what I said to Monsr Paschall's paper, you would have me do by dear Neddye's head as my Lady Duchess of Ormond did to the round tower in Kilkenny; that is make his wall thiner, break out Lights, make partitions, set up Shelves, bring in furniture, new Frame the stairs, make new passages &c. To all which I will make no answer till you come. I see tic better and easier to bee banged or beaten by you, than to write anything that pleases you. Nevertheless to begin the furnishing of Neddyes Tower, I send you the shortest Catechism I can frame, and suitable to our Com~on prayer Catechism. I call it Religio Christiana puerilis - I might ad Et quae etiam est mea senilis . Here is come out a book of note A Papist misrepresented and represented written by J. L. I object that Hee ought to have put nothing in his Column of 'Misrepresented', but what is found in authentic non-papist authors; and nothing into his Column of 'Represented' but the very words of the Council of Trent. So have you this mighty book answered. When you come up, I will show you 2 sheets written by W P. to the said purpose. I do not know what you meant by 'Brewing' - Explain it, and your operations upon Kings-Weston. Adieu W. P.

Kingsweston, 31 Oct. 1685 Dear Cousin Although I am preparing by this day Seven-night to kiss your hand, yett in the mean time I will thank you for your last, and the Character therein of your short Cathechisme, which I annex also to the Text and send it now to our Neddy to doe the like. Whatever enemy you think me to Multiplication , I have this day planted above 40 fair Trees, and I hope they will produce their like, and so on in Secula Seculorum . O that I could but help to plant one Cedar in Kerry, and have the same prospect of duration! But how my Charity or Courage shall avail herein, unless you have some white powder or other, that can putt any man forward like a Prince Credential! Doe but you take care of this part and I'll warrant you for following Instructions. I long to see the pretty Governante and our Fingallian upon the Stage. My 3 Spinsters charge me strictly to bring them down an exact account of all performance therein. I see you allow me when I come up to talk of stuffing out our puccane I mean Neddy. One point I resolve shall be to know whether you ever wrote down a Set of Cases in the way of Political Arithmetic, in order to instruct and settle the present Age in the method, for this you once did Intend. I hope my lady is in perfect health and all the little ones. Mine are merry and content, which is as good as being wise. I am ever, Sr, Your most affect & most humble servant Robert Southwell

Kingsweston, 23. Dec 1685 Dear Cousin Our Neddy is come, and what between him and Christmas, the Girls think they may be romps by authority. Tic only Mr Kneller that keeps them to any rules of proportion. Your 3 Papers that he brought me, and your letter - the mother that wrapped them all - are welcome more than Christmas it self. I must say as old Dr Clayton, that you brought 3 quarters of these things into the world with you. Non vox hominum sonat. Your Branches of Regal authority show all the extent of that magnificent Palace at once. Your judgment about the Art of Sweetening Sea Water makes me but wish that I had a list of all those thoughts and estimates which produced those few but effectual and mighty determinations. The Epigrams and Mottoes on that Subject show what numberless thoughts you have had, and a method how to employ the Chipps, after you have hewed out the Mayne Timbers and beams for use. The two stratagems of Arithmetic in your letter are very pleasing to us. We admire at the hidden affinity that lies in numbers, and breaks out as water that runs sometimes underground and sometimes above. This I say in reference to the second trick about scattered numbers and their Totals. As to the first, by placing the digits 15 just is made in 6 places, but more in the other 2 places. These matters were the more seasonable for that we had already plungd into a french book of Mathematical Revelations, and poor Noddy's head was almost cloven by hard questions which the girls had prepared for him. They are now reconciled, and all of them your votaries; and doe pay all duty to my Lady, and wish all manner of happiness to their Cousins. I have my share in all these things, and will, as the time requires, conclude with a happy Christmas to you; and am ever with great acknowledgements Your most affect kinsman & most humble servant Robert Southwell

Kingsweston, 28 April 1686 Dear Cousin It is strange I should be so long in acknowledging yours of the 8th, but there are things to tell you of. I was since then at Badminton to meet my Lord of Ormonde - I was at Bathe to compliment my Lord Tirconnell - and at Longleat to bid farewell to my Lord Weymouth, who goes not so soon as he pretended. I have had also some ill tricks of my sore throat: and even your letter was sick, for all of that post fell into the River and yours was tattered and torn, and it was almost Algebra to find it out. After this sincere preamble, I will as sincerely answer you as I can, for what you write concerns your self and 3 cousins whom I have reason to esteem. I say your self, because you mention the Explanation of 12 Theological Words . I am afraid you may herein Quiet mover , and so blister your fingers; and if you show them at all to any, I wish you would let me have the first sight. You know I am your Saucy friend, and adventer to chide while others choose to accuse. As to Cousin Charles, I like extremely the Scope of his Travel. You point at several useful enterprises, but say all in saying he is to shift among the dangerous men. For his mimicall faculty I am as much at a plunge as if my son were a great dancer on the High Rope. If there were no falling in the case, the vigour and activity would be pleasing enough! You handle the matter so as to disown and applaud it at once. You think it is a good offensive weapon and yett such an one as may need a sword to defend It. You think it will allure women, although it terrify men. And so you pass to say that his sister hath a dash of the same. Now I should be sorry to pervert the Observation; and that any she-friend of mine should either terrify women or allure men - Nor can there be a sword in this case to defend it! Can you not remember a certain lady of the Land, who for acting others in her Chamber was brought upon the public Stage, and Sempronia punished more at once than all the Secret farces were worth. Tic true, in mere Children any Simptome of Wit is welcome; but as to my cousin Ann that is now taking her ply, root this weed out I conjure you, as you would a piece of Witch Craft! I have been told of a Marshall of France, Monsr Clerambaut, who was wont to say "Queen est maestro du Ridicule est maestro du monte" ; and that the Duke of Buckingham was so in Love with this saying and that man's example, that he resolved to build upon the same foundation. Build he did (as you very well know), but the foundation being nought, the Storms and tempests beat down his House and great was the fall thereof. As to my Cousin Harry, I am extremely in Love with his faculty of Pro and Con , for that will certainly bring in guinyes at Westminster Hall, tho he should never comprehend whether Pro or Con were most in the Right. This I say because I knew a great man that fulfilled It. I will advise our Neddy to strict in with Cousin Harry betimes, and to Steal a Sight of all the little and great Instructions you give to become picklock of the Law. We have no other engine at present but the demonstrations of Euclide. I pay all service to my lady and kindness to the little ones, being ever Sr, Yrs RS.

Kingsweston, 29 May 1686 Dear Cousin I had your condoling Letter of the 22nd, and pray allow me to tell you what my Little daughter said, being a while ago full of mirth and good humour at the Discourse that was between us: "Truly father", said she, "If a dog should come into the Room, you doe say such play things, that I believe you would make him Laugh." Cousin, you doe wipe off Tears at a very strange rate, but why did nature furnish Them if there must be no Sorrow? Can you, by pointing at what is contemptible in a noble object, Establish your maxim in this also: That nothing is Stronger than its weakest part? I should rather say it is unnatural to lessen any thing that is either anihilated, or must rise glorious. For tho your friends in Eutopia triumph and sing Hymns at a Funeral, tic but to fortify those that must Dye, and by this disguise fling sugar into the bitter Cup. If you would know nature's mind, see what is done even by the men of Leest Humanity. The Cafras and Hattintoes never loose a Friend or Relation but they cut off a Joint from one of their Fingers - so much they scorn the acquisition of Mourning Rings. The Indian women burn with their dead Husbands, And the Husbands of Angola appoint when they dye who shall for 8 days Console the afflicted Widow, and it falls to their next of kin thus to cohabit with Her if they dye Intestate. Funus justa petit and Sal liquefied ut condiat . Tears are the true and natural balsam, and they who refuse Them rob the Dead. But what Art - I was going to say play-words - does your kindness find out to stifle my resentments? You tell me of Empire, and how much I assend by the desolations that are past. If by loosing one wife I have Title to the million that are unmarried, by the same right your million have Title to me; which would prove but a hard Chapter. And how can you magnify my Headship over Infants by the loose of Sir John Percivale? Is not this to magnify the Rolling of Sysiphus's stone - to begin again at the Bottom when I was at the Mountain's top, and thought I had nursed up those who in reason should turn nurses to mine? Thus you see, Cousin, I will not be comforted. For while your good nature finds Arts to divert Sorrow, It discovers there is some sorrow due; and it being as debt, the soonest payment will be the best. As to the Ship, you have already had my wandering thoughts. I doe for Consolation sometimes read the Chapter, how there arose a tempestuous wind called "Euroclidon"; yett after all, how some by swimming, others on Boards and broken planks, got all to Land, so as not a soul was lost. In the next place, when I am more shaken, and think where Neddy (The Pinnace) may have surest anchorage in omne eventum , I start up and shape his Course, blow high, blow low, towards Westminster Hall; for whatever happens Crafty Knaves will Live. I am Yrs R. S.

Kingsweston, 7 June 1686 Dear Cousin I have the favour of 2 of yours of the 5th and the 'State of a Case' Enclosed. One of your Letters is upon Death without Mourning , and seeing it is hard to defend passion against Reason, I will acquiesce in your Arguments and read them upon ill accidents, in hopes they will support me. As to the State of the Case you send now, and the State you sent before, I cannot think how any Cases can be more strong that are not of Mathematical Demonstration. Nor did I tell you what I happened to over hear, but with most friendly Intention - that you might look early out. I have known you formerly to mind your Cylinders, while your Acres were Tearing from you; and you would not desist from Philosophy, as long as it was not in the power of a Decree to forbid Rubarb and Cena from purging. But since the discovery of my own fears hath exceeded all due proportion and that you send "Hulchy Pulchy" to defy It; I will take heart also, as did your Boy Thom, who was sorely affrighted at the roaring of the Sea and the trembling of the Vessel, till he heard the seamen swear. I am glad you expect better things from the new, than you felt from the old Council, and I had no meaning in that phrase of "Land in the Moon" but to excite you as aforesaid. For mariners doe usually cry 'all hands Aboard' when there is thoughts of any danger. I hope, Cousin, in the mean time it will be no false Latin to look well after my Hay, or if I go on with my new Invention of an Oxe-House, where the Cattle are both to eat and drink in the same Crib, and not to stir till they be fitted for the Slaughter. Magister Arts Venture I am ever yrs R. S.

Piccadilly, 12 Junii 1686 Dre Cozn To yours of the 7th I return this humble long answer. I beg your pardon (1o) for comparing your friendly warnings to Goblins and Devils, (2o) for seeming to defy them all with the spell of 'hulchi' &c, wherein I did not doe well. Pray doe not punish me by supposing the like hereafter, for I took all very kindly and thankfully. Nevertheless what shall a man say who hath been used like me ( e.g. in Kerry), but at some times and to an Intimate friend use some words of contempt and desperation when Right and Reason will doe no good? What I said to you was but like that of Rhubarb &c. to the Court of Claims. And I am glad that my spell 'Hulchi' gave you the same comfort that the Seaman's swearing did to Tom. Among other weapons that I am scouring up, I have drawn out a paper showing what money I had at Xmas 1636 - which was 1s. How it rise to 4s 6d, then to 24s, then to 4£. Then to 70. Next how it fell to 26, then rise to £480 at my Landing in Ireland. Next to 13,060£ at finishing the Survey. And how after I got my Land in Ireland and Estate in England &c, it was 3200£ at the King's Restoration &c. And so all along to this very day. Perhaps the like hath not been seen. This and the like gave me courage wherewith I fought Zanchy. Whatever becomes of me I can leave such arguments of 50 years art and Industry as will be a credit to my children and friends. And now instead of Hulchi Pulchi I say God's Will be done - Naked came I into the World and naked must go out of it.' I did, Dear Cozen, obtrude upon you the Case with Lord Dunsany and obeyed you in sending that of Tegrohan. I take my turn to obtrude again upon you that of Macgillicuddy which I think must needs come upon the Stage. And then you shall command another, and so as long as you please, but no longer. Enlarge a little upon the Meat and Drink Cribs which you have for your Oxen. I envy you rural contentments - give me an alms out of your abundance. Fear not Neddy; Isle warrant hee will live, your Godson is short of him in that faculty, Adieu

Kingsweston, 10 July 1686 Dear Cousin Here has been a great Irish wedding in our neighbourhood, and by the title I took share in it, and part of the dinn has even reached this poor place. And these are the causes why I come thus slow to acknowledge yours of the 12th past. I am now returning to the care of Hay Harvest and of my Oxe-House. In this there is nothing new, but that a Stream of Water is to run under the Crib, so they drink where they stand and when they please; and this want of Liberty is to hasten them for the Slaughter. If Irish Rents come in no better, I must invent something more - either the art of fasting or Monsr Payim's Invention to soften beans. I perceive you are scouring old papers, and your short hint of Meliorations from the year 1636 is so entertaining that I wish I had more of It. I thank you for the State of McGillocuddy's business which I have now read again, and I think your measure is very hard, but the time now to redress it much harder. For who can mind right or wrong touching Ham~ocks and Cabins when the whole Ship is in danger, or lies at Hull? And yett I am told (tho you say nothing of It) that Sir William had great access to the Great Man before his going over; that he gave him in several Schemes as to Adventurers and Soldiers, and urged so well the preference of Money to any disturbance of the present Settlement, that the Great Man himself seems to have a Bias that way; that he has been heard to say how his own Fortune was settled by the Acts, and that His Majesty has no thought of parting with a foot of his estate in that Country. And this is all I can say as to the Mayne. I am glad you fancy that Neddy will find out the way of shifting among dangerous men. It will import him both for his own sake and his sisters too. I hope my good lady and all yours are well. We have lost in Sir William Coventry a great man of our nation. I am ever ire R. S.

Piccadilly, 13 July 1686 Dr Cozen I will now answer but a small part of yours of the 10th Instant, and divide even that small part into the 3 partites following (1) Concerning myself. (2) Neddy. (3) The great man you mention. Concerning Myself, I say that I had 13,060£ in cash anno 1656, which at 10 per cent (above 12 being then justly taken) would anno 1666 have been 26,120£, and anno 1676 52,240£, and in this year 1686 104 thousand 480£. I further say that, without meddling with forfeited lands, I could Anno 1656 have returned into England and been at the top of practice in Oliver's Court, when Dr Willis was casting waters at Abington Markett and the Cock Lower but an Egg. And what the superlucration thereof (besides the 104m £) might have been in 30 years, I leave to your judgment. I say the profitt of these 2 funds, would have exceeded my present State by . As to Neddy, I say that this present great and early acquaintance, with the easy access to great Men, will give him bread and cheese by the Law before he bee ripe; whereas my Harry may be an able man 7 years before he gets bread only. As to the Great man, I had indeed strange access and acceptance. I spake unto him as one having authority and not as the Scribes and Pharisees. I said several sour things which he took as Juice of Orange Squeezed into his Mince meat, and not as Vitriol. For some of the things he told me were these: 1o. That all the Lands which the Irish lost as forfeited were not worth Anno 1653, when they left them, near 300m pounds. 2o. That the 34,000 men which the heads of the Irish were permitted and assisted to carry to foreign States, at 10£ per head, were worth more than the said Lands; but 10£ is not 1/2 the value of negroes nor 1/5 of Algier slaves, nor 1/7 of their real value in Ireland. 3o. I said that what the Irish got restored Anno 1663, more then what belonged to them Anno 1641, is now worth much more than all they ever lost. 4o. That they got 1100m Acres of Land by Innocence, making 7 of 8 Innocent. Whereas it appears by the arrears allowed to the 49 officers, that there was a Protestant Army of 20m men from 1641 to 1649, which army together with the 7/8 of the Irish that were Innocent, could not beat 1/8 nocent part of the Irish, but necessitated my Lord of Ormond to make the Peace of 1648 - vide the Articles. This (as Sir Jerome said) "was not half". He heard me with trouble and admiration. He pressed me to speak of the Settlement. I told him there were things in it against the light of Nature and the current Equity of the World, but whether it was worth the breaking I doubted; but if It were broken by Parliament I offered things to be mixed with those Acts as should mend the Condition of all men. Thus much for the present from him who is Yours W-P. The next shall be how I got the shilling at Xmas 1636. How I came by 4s 6d when I went to sea and how I advanced the same to 24s when I went to the Jesuits College. What the setting of my Broken Leg cost to the farrier's wife, what for Crutches &c.

Kingsweston, 11 Augt 1686 Dear Cousin I have yours of the 7th and am so conscious of my late silence, that you deal hardly with me to reproach it. You have sung so many new and surprising Tunes that I am just like the Cobbler's Daw - struck mute on the Caesurean Triumph. But, as in a month he burst out with all the music he had heard, so I wish I may prove like that Daw in this part. We have been of late wholly Intent on our friends from Ireland, and on Sunday the last parcel arrived. And I have frequent returns of a Scurvy Soar Throat, so that, unless I would only admire , I am not in a condition to speak to you at large. Tic almost 20 years past that I have desired the explanation of Ut Apes Geometriam , and you may judge if I am not exalted now to see so many master strokes thereon, and more perhaps than ever you thought at First. But tic now a cloudy and a rainy day, and I will not risk or execute what Tully says on such occasions - periclitandae sunt verse ingenii, et ista mantis interna comentatio proferenda est - for I cannot yett think as I ought or utter what I think. So this is only to bespeak your patience and to advise you to look well after your flock, since already your spinster is called upon. I expect no such humours till Irish Rents are better paid, or to pay Goats Hair instead of wool. My Lady Percivale does most thankfully acknowledge yours and my ladies kind remembrances. She has here 2 brave brawny boys as loud as bedlams and the Girl is of the same Tribe; and in November we expect an other of the same Scantling. I am ever Yrs R. S.

Kingsweston, 13 Sept 1686 Dear Cousin I have yours of the 9th and the Essay Enclosed therein. If admiration could please you I can afford very good measure, but if you love Victory more than submission, I must displease you for I am not able to contend. I have read the paper with strange delight, and doubtless so will the Pope, for my thinks that King should hold none of his Councils secret while a blind man in London can describe more of his Condition that he knew himself. In the mean time you have done our King great Honour to show the world that he Governs the greatest City that is in it. When I consider this discourse and your others of like Nature, let me putt you in mind how you have formerly promised a Sort of Gram~ar or Instruction whereby this Age may be enabled to calculate as you have done, and which assuredly was never done before. Our Neddyes head might in time take this Bias, for he is Inclined to Numbers. What shall I add more at present save my thanks for your great favour in this precious Token, and to one who is already so much in arreare to you upon other Accounts. I still beg for time. And if in the mean time you know what the great Lord is doing, and to what end Mr Nagle, the great Surveyor of Ireland, is come over with him, you will be so kind as to impart a word unto Yrs R. S. All services from herein to the Lady and the little ones.

23 Oct 1686 Dear Cousin We stand in need of your Judgment in a material point. A certain wayfaring man called the other day, and taking notice that one of the 3 spinsters had a very browne neck, "Child" said he "you will not get a Husband unless your neck look whiter" - "Sir" said she "by the time I need a Husband, Browne Necks may come into fashion" - "No" said he "I will here present you with an Amber Neck-lace which will gain you favour immediately; but once that it is on, you must never take it off" - "No Sir" said she "perhaps I may live so long as that such a neck lace may come to throttle me at last." Now what think you of the Girle's Answer? I read lately a melancholy prophesy, and the contents were much to my own sense, and the prophet was a Great Caldean, and had long conversed with Men and Stars; so as I was much disquieted thereat. But when I considered that these things were not wrote either in Serious Prose or in broken ejaculations or distracted words, but in smooth and flowing numbers - then said I, "the bitterness is over past, for who can utter Melody in his sadness, or sing tunably when he is in a Strange land?" Since therefore the matter and the manner doe not agree, I also will sing: "As men by storms may to their Haven Sail, So let your Numbers, not your Sense prevail."

London, 25th X br 1686. Dear Cousin Wee have not seen Neddy these 3 weeks and therefore suppose him to bee with you. If hee had called here, I would have given him the hints you desired; although in truth it is not necessary, for I do not know what is what, and my own cake, whereof I thought to have given you a Bit, may prove dough. I have had a letter from Sir George Curtis, but can say to you little about it as yet. My observing the wind too much, makes me not sow. But Cousin, the Bombs against my Essays are feared, one by La Republiq de Letters , and the other from the great Monsr Auzout from Rome. More are daily expected from Paris and particularly from the famous Abbot Bernou. I received Monsr Auzout's on Wensday last between 9 and 10, and carried the King an Answer before 12, made before all the White Staves in the Bed Chamber. The chief objection was, that the out-Parishes which have stood these 50 years in the Bills of Mortality, should not be accounted London. His paper did fall most upon what Captain Grant and myself had ever writ upon these matters. I promised the King my speedy remarks upon all hee said, which I have since done and I hope pretty well. And afterwards I made 2 new Essays in one, where I proved over again all that I had said before of London, Rome, Roan and Dublin, even allowing Monsr Auzout all his Demands; even those for which hee had offered no manner of proof. In the other Essays, wherein I deal with less favour and more Justice towards the Interest of Paris and Monsr Auzout, I show London to bee equal to Paris, Rome, and Roan, from their own sayings, although I do not believe it myself; which things I intend to show the King tomorrow if I can. I also, in answer to their objecting a City in Persia to bee greater than London, that (by their own sayings) the said Persian City had 44000 Moschees in it before Mahomet was come. This do they get who wrong your poor Cousin, who wishes you a Merry Christmas, and that the next year may bee no worse than the past, and who is your good Company's and Kings-Weston and your own honest servant.

6 Jan 1686/7 Dear Cousin Yours of the 25th past made our Christmas here look like it self, and we were all rejoycd to hear how you repelld the Roman Giant and got his Majesty of your side. When all is settled that relates to this predicament, I hope I shall not be the last to solemnise your fame, if you will but give me the means. Neddy is with us and preparing his mind to pass a little time in Oxford. My Lady Percivale lately lost her only daughter by convultion fits, but the 3 boys doe bravely. I see how cautious you are in Joining issue with Sir G. Curtis, and who can blame you? We are stunt on account of the same motives. What you think fit to spare as news or Information shall be looked on as from the hand it comes. Doe you still think that the Parliament will here meet? I suppose their will soon be one in Ireland. My Lady Dering prepares to be going up on Monday, and my Lady Percivale goes after, and they needs will have two of my girls of the party. I wish a happy year to my lady and to all yours, and am ever, Yrs

7 March. 1686/7 Dear Cousin I have yours of the 5th and thank you for the honour of It. All you write is to me a matter of Record. I could not conceal it from the Lord I am with, nor he forbear to desire an extract of it, so authentic it was in matter of moment and so entertaining in all the Rest. I deplore the ejectments you mention and it drives me to remember a dirty rime imputed to Cromwell when they told him of Magna Charta. My lady has my best wishes whether she goes or stays, and to make them stick I would fasten them with golden pins if I had them. My daughters brag of her ladyships favour towards them, and if my God-son take a stride into the world to enable him (in your own phrase) to 'live among dangerous men', may he prosper like his father's Bee Hive and return home again Crura thymo Plane . You have so anatomized the wooden head, that I shall never mind it more, but for an echo, I wish you had heard one which the Lord Carlinford cairyed me to see within a mile of Milan. We stood in the gallery of a Gentleman's House, one story high, and in his garden (where were Trenches and I think some standing water), the echo repeated after me the word "Home" 21 times distinctly. I thank you for all the proportions of Land you mention. The reason of my enquiry herein was to enable me to Answer those who rashly affirm (and that in print) that the Irish had nothing by the Settlement; that if by the Usurper they were whipped with Iron, it has been since the Restoration with Scorpions. What you add beyond what I requested, which is the Compromise of the 6 July 1665, is what I have long had in my Head, which you now diffinitly explain. I doe believe, and I think remember, that this Agreement was signed at my Lord Anglesey's House in Drury Lane, where the Lord Clancarty, Sir Nicholas Plunkett and the Heads of the Party did meet and agree thereto. I cannot say I saw the Paper, but I remember it was reported in Council that all was Agreed. And when in 1672 the Commission of Enquiry was on foot and Sir Henage Finch acted his part as a Champion for the Settlement, He so vigorously insisted on this Agreement that I remember the good King said in Council, "Nay I doe well remember there was some kind of agreement in this matter". It seems this Paper is now lost or buried with these proceedings - which I once received from Sir James Shaen all in a deal Box; and for want of other Room, they were placed under the great Table in the Council Chamber and I believe remained there till the Chamber was lately altered. And who knows but it may still be found in the same box - if it be not a crime to look for it. As to my having Studied the several Peaces, it was purely to find by those Sibill's Books what might now ensue (at the least). For that which was once contended for with sword in hand, will now certainly be taken when it may be had without contention. And what the moddell will be, is now I think the expectation of every Post. I see how you have laid by the mala stamina of a History that was Intended, and what you say of Sir John Davys his Essays, and the misfortune of his Law and learning, which only enabled him to putt the Patch beside the Hole. If I live to see you I hope to be happier than the world, and see those treasures De Jure Belli, Jure Nature and Jure Gentium . I return home in 3 days.

Piccadilly, 7 April 1687 Dr Cozn The book (which you say might have been a Cartload) had 2 points in it: the one about the Plague, the other about the new Wall propounded for London. Nobody but yourself hath taken notice of the former, and nobody at all of the latter - So deaf are the Adders wee charm unto! As for the Settlement, Let us fancy it to bee a Ship and to be repaired and made better. 1o. The Coventry letter' propounds to break it up, burn most of the materials, and build some other Thing (not another Ship) with the rest. 2o. I meet with another who advises the sawing of it in 2 and making it longer, as also taking down her Upper-workes wherewith she is top-heavy, "for so" saith Hee "She will be a bigger and a better ship" - but Wee have not Carpenters to do it. 3o. The letter of the 15 November (which I praise and admire) thinks That calking it anew, and phay-goodling it almost, may serve turn. 4o. But I lately met with an old Carpenter sitting upon a Log of Timber, smoking his short pipe, to whom I said: "Do ye see that Ship yonder in the road?" - "See her" said hee, "A pox on her! I remember when she was built, and wrought myself for a while upon her, till I found knavery among the Chief owners and the workmen too, by Gad." - "Well" said I, "What do ye think of her?" - "Shoe's a rotten Toad" quoth hee, "There was a Cousin of the owner's that served us in rotten Timber and plank, which as it was laid was tarred over and looked like sufficient stuff, and the Devil and all." - "But do ye think she may bee mended?" - "Never" says hee, "without bringing her into a dry dock and taking out these planks and some of her principal timbers. Nay, a piece of her keel, by Gad." I intended to talk on with this Waspish Nimps but were interrupted &c. Within 2 days I met with Mr Houblon of whom I inquired concerning this Choleric old Coxcomb. But Mr Houblon said: "Hee is not so choleric as one would think, but having been horribly abused in and about that very ship. If you name 3 or 4 words ('Column' is one, the other 2 I can send you) Hee will, like Dol Common in the 'Alchemist', fall into Extravagances. Otherwise he is sober enough." "May be so", quoth I, "for though I got into the 'Anchor' I could not make him drink above a glass or 2." - Thus ends the parable &c. To conclude. I find That if wee had a dry dock, These few timbers might bee mended without prejudice even to the mold of the present Hull.

20 april 1687 Dear Cousin I had the honour of yours of the 7th and have much considerd the Parable of the Ship and your wishes for a dry dock. If a new draft were made, and every one certainly knew what would be done in this dock, and that the majority saw hopes of a Saving Voyage, the thoughts and votes and wishes of the powerful might run one way. But if a Chipp be touched without some such preamble, every plank will groan and expect to be flung into the fire. The Coventry letter' runs now about in every hand on the other side, and gives terror as I am told; tho the Proclamation there, and the later declaration here, seem (as to Property) to Speak better things. I am glad I animadverted on that piece of Angelic virtue in your Essay of limiting the Plague . It was new to me, and a blessing to mankind which I could not but admire. But for the other point of the London Wall , I had heard you speak of it before, so it was not altogether new. Nor am I martial man enough to take all things in that appertain to such a proposal. But we have a Martial King, who hears you patiently, and might putt you to It. And I wonder He or his Lieutenant Generals doe not discuss this great point; as also an other you have in store, touching a defence by wool packs, applicable to land and sea. My friend Monsieur Renaudot is ambitious to wait upon you. He is, among other Ingredients of ability, a good Geometrician; therefore pray smile upon him. To my lady and the little ones all happiness. Yrs

Kingsweston - 21 May 1687 Dear Cousin The last post brought me, in yours of the 17th, a most unwelcome account of damage to your nephew and of approaching danger to your self. I see the Juries are set upon it, and every man must look about; since in this trial there was no defect in any circumstance or essential thing, but singly in the verdict. As for the scramble in Kerry, I see and admire your philosophy that you name it with patience. Before, you were lancd and scarified; but this is plain fleeing off the whole skin. But have the philosophy, and the same patience must also take place. My present care is to save my stake at Kinsale by getting (if I can) a proviso in the new Charter that must follow the destruction of the old, and in which tic expected that all old members may be laid by. I am herein solicitous for the future, since at present I can get no rent from thence. The town is become a poor skeleton, for all the trade is now centred in Cork - and tic high time that your friend Neddy doe hasten to the Law. We are well in this place, as I hope it is with my lady and the little ones. I have been writing a close sheet to Peter Welch in which you are often named. Tic on that part of his letter to the Bishop of Lincoln (p. 224) where he speaks of the Irish Rebellion and extenuates the first Massacre, and I think by the headings of your calculations I have the better of him. Our Neddy is now got into Ethics. I am ever Yrs. R. S. I rejoice however that your nephew Nipper did behave himself so like a man in the day of battle. I remember well since his Father sweat for it in the Court of Claims, till all his hand was wet.

11 June 1687 Dear Cousin This being the longest day in the year, I could wish it were Employed from morning to night in reading or writing like orders in your favour with what you had on the 2nd from the Treasury; And tic most kindly done to send me the Copy of it. If my Lord Godolphin would now take consideration of what Sir Edward Dering Intended, I am able to give a large Testimonial of his being strangely convinced of your hard usage; and that he resolved to intercede not only for a full settlement in your affairs, but to the abating one hundred pounds per annum of the Quit Rents which you submitted unto - which in truth you did at his persuasion - I mean as regards concerns in Kerry. What you apprehend of Shocks and disorders in other parts, I can but deplore, and employ wishes that it were otherwise than you find. I have a great share of disappointment in my own small concerns, scarce getting any Rent at all, and I am menaced by the Courcys with trouble and law suites for having what their Ancestors, they say, had no right to dispose of. And this is the gratitude I find for respects to that poor family for near 40, or rather 50 years past, from my Father and my self. I suppose tic because they think witnesses and Juries can now doe any thing! I see my Godson is going to the Academy, which I very well approve of, as also the disposal of my Cousin Harry. If you can lend the answer of ten Sheets to Phillip Madox, he will presently get it copied out for me, and sent by a safe hand. I see you expect a broadside from Holland, but you have 18 Cities already for you, and so need not tremble before the Thunderbolt falls. I am apt to think they will consider well before they shoot, or repent their shooting. I perceive you have been hearing of exercises at a School, which you think to be a sort of Music meeting, and that there may be Euphoniacall Nonsense. I confess tic happiest when there is more care for the matter than the manner, tho this last is much easier sought for. As to the other it is Donum Dei , and you know to whom it was said at Merton College "Young man you were borne with 3 quarters of what you know". Having named this college, I must not omit to tell you that Neddy does well according to the discipline of the place. He is already turned disputant in the Hall. As you thrive by the order of the 2nd (that seems to show a certainty made in the present Rent, and in the Arrears) pray let me know it, as of all other things whether to profitt or loss - for when I cannot rejoice with you I will morn. Yrs

8 July 1687 Dear Cousin Since my acknowledgement of yours of the 16th past I have received and Read the papers, and doe think I never was better entertained in my life. I could say many things of so excellent a discourse, but will Comprise all in the words of Seneca, speaking of the Law: Non Irascitur sed Castigate . The 4th point which you thought wanting (being part of the Journal of the Supreme Council) is there as well as the rest, and serves as voucher in some particulars of the preceding discourse. I am told from an Intelligent hand, as if there were hopes the Settlement would not be shaken, what ever is done with the Charters. And surely if those who have power, and no passion, did but read and consider your discourse (as perhaps they have done), they must be convinced that the Settlement cannot be broken without strange confusion in all his Majesty's affairs in the Kingdom. But I hear of 11 Lords whose Outlawryes are discharged, and surely this looks not only as the forerunner of a Parlyment, but as some assurance to them of having estates to support the dignity of Peerage. You say nothing as yett of what has happened about Tecrohan, and your silence is a very good sign. The late dissolution makes my hopes of seeing you very remote, and this not only in love to the Country, but as being on ground; for of ten letters from the other side, there is not one Bill. My most humble service to my lady and the little ones. I have been reading this day "the Hind and Panther Transversed" and doe fancy none could make more of it than my Cousin Charles, for he would reach all the good humours that are in it. I am always Yrs

Piccadilly, 4o Aug 1687 Dre Cozn Charles was well at Rotterdam the 29th, but was 4 times 24 hours at sea. I send you the Contents of the discourse I mentioned. I intend it to bee The Bible for Ireland. I have shown it in parts to some great Men, but not yet to the King; but will shortly. The Customs of Dublin have, in this last quarter, fallen from 4 to 3, and the Excise from 7 to 6. Now although it hath been said with a loud voice That the people of Dublin are half run away (and by good observers that 1100 houses are void) Yet your Cousin assures you that in the last quarters hee finds more burials and Christnings than in any of the 10 quarters before. And therefore says that The people do retrench their expense in strong drink by 1/6 part and also in their housing, by crowding 7 families into 6 houses; for 1100 is the 1/6 part of the houses in Dublin. The fall of lands appears to me by the fall of the Price of butter, Cheese, Milk, eggs, flesh, &c. Adieu

Kingsweston, 13 Augt 1687 Dear Cousin I have yours of the 4th and have read the papers enclosed, which are either for transplanting or Propagation. The things are mighty, and call unto my mind that when Paul reasoned of Righteousness, Temperance, and Judgement to come, Felix trembled. You know Columbus made the first offer to us of his Golden World, and was rejected; That the Sybill's Books, tho never so true, were undervalued; and Mr Newton's demonstrations will hardly be understood. The market rule goes fair in everything else, Tantum valet quantum vent potest . So as tho I doe not suspect you can be mistaken in what you assert, since you enumerate so many solid as well as bitter objections thereunto; yett the dullness of the world is such, the opposers so many, your fellow labourers so few, and your Age so advanced, that I reckon the work Insuperable. However I am glad that your thoughts are all written down, for Posterity, as favoured by great Accidents, may cultivate what the present Age neglects. And in the mean time since you propose to entertain the King on these subjects, let me advertise you what his good Brother once said at The Council Board - That he thought you one of the best Commissioners of the Navy that ever was; That you had vast knowledge in many things - "But" said he "the man will not be contented to be excellent, but is still Aiming at Impossible Things". You know I am possession of saying any thing to you that comes in my head; but this I say for your service, that being already advanced in his Majesty's opinion for things that he Comprehends, you doe not grow less by going beyond his Reach. I rejoice to hear that Cousin Charles got safe, tho after good tossing, to the other side. Your letters will not be less welcome if you sprinkle them with a little good tidings of him and of his Improvements. I say the same for the rest, and am ever Yrs Pray Cousin, did you ever use any Art to Improve your memory? Tully De oratore uses many words to show how it may be Improved by Images, but I desire your saying.

Kingsweston, 28 Sept. 1687 Dear Cousin Upon a fresh Review of your letter of the 16th past, the particulars are of that Bulk and importance and my digestion so incompetent, that I must swear, as the honest Recusant did of Queen Elizabeth, That 'if she was not the Head of the Church, he wished she were soe'. But first as to my Cousin Charles. I see you resign him to the impression of his Stars. And as one Tree will not become another, or oaks and Cedars much alter their Shape, so you will allow that withyes are to be twisted towards what one would have them to be, and dead wood must by Carving be brought into Figure. And, it standing thus between your son and mine, perhaps we are both in the right! I perceive you have tried the Artificial Memory and undervalue It. If the Ancient Orators had it with advantage and for use, It seems their method is Lost. The Chief Rule we now have left is only exercise and conning of things overnight. But if you know better, I will ask questions herein at your coming down. You must then also expect I shall be very importunate to see the 20 Articles which contain the Weight of the Crown , which you presented his Majesty - and certainly with the most peculiar Test I ever heard, viz: to pick out any one He wished to be true, and any other He suspected to be false, and that in 24 hours He should have demonstration. But tho you complain after all that you got neither Butter or Hobb-nayles hereby, yett you fare much better than He who found out the Malleable Glass. You doubtless touch a very sore place when you suspect the surviving malice of the Double ship. Your fate compared herein to that of Action's goes very far, as having courted the 's Mysteries. Yett I may say that if this last word should be mistaken for 'Mistresses', then to have had a fresh one and of your procurement, as well as of any others, sounds not as a matter that should have turned to your disadvantage! Your observation of the Poverty that is already grown, and must ensue while mouths increase and yett eating grows less, is so much more a valuable stroke in your Art of Calculation as it is seen felt and understood by all. And doubtelesse the other great things you mention may be as Rationally founded, though unequally comprehended. And I confess unto you that, tho the world should never be wise enough to wed what you propose in the Multiplication of Men and the benefits flowing from it, yett if you have as strong motives for the Truth of these matters as usually convince men from the Pulpit or at the Barr, I cannot wonder that you are Ravished with the harmony and charms of Ratiocination. You very well call it a Labour of Pleasure', but not so properly 'Angelicall', since tic perhaps the only pleasure the angels want. For Intuition of truth may not Relish so much as Truth that is hunted down. But if you intend Pyramids out of these materials to bear testimony of your good will to mankind, when you pass to a better life, you should take care while you are among us to explain all and leave as few Hieroglyphics as is possible. And I, if I live, will not fail to assist my Godson to hand them to the Press. Tho doubtless it were better done while you are yett on this side the pitt. You see how little I can say to those mighty things you honour me withal; But I keep them Charily together, and my son may find Charms where I now Languish. He is now with me and to stay all the winter; since Oxford is already, and is growing more, an unquiet place. I am ever Yrs R. S.

Kingsweston, 10 Oct 1687 Dear Cousin Yours of the 4th came to me the next day after I had sent you some lincks of very Saucy but friendly thoughts. As to your Purchase, I here send you what the Surveyor answers. He is a plain frugal man. And as to instructing Mr Plumbly, I think what you said goes through the whole Alphabet, nor doe I think that ever such a Scheme was made before. I cannot yett find where to wedge in a word, but I will try when tic fair weather, for now I am very dull. If you lay out but 2500£, it must be in Revertions for your Grandson and when the Tenements are full Stated. Our Neddy read these Instructions with marvellous relish, which is some sign he may get them into his head; but he is just now as hot as mustard upon Logic and proposed to me to write his thoughts to Cousin Charles on that dry Subject. I told him Charles might show it his father, and so he might burn his fingers. At last being earnest I let him take his cource, for the exercise may doe him good though Charles has better things to mind. I wish however that Charles would urge him to write 20 letters more on the several parts of this doctrine, for perhaps the being made accountable may doe him some good. The ill weather putts me out of humour to write more at present, than that I am Yrs R. S.

Kingsweston, 16th December 1687 Dear Cousin I was yesterday in some fright upon reading from Phillip Madox the report of your sickness, but the favour of yours of the 13th dispelld the cloud, as making slight of the matter. However it will be very welcome to me to hear that you walk again as you did before. I see and congratulate that you have been able to lay so great a Tanto at the Farmours doors, and that you are hastening to make even with all others. As for the demand of 7774£ 10s-, which yett (as you say) is not half the wrong you have suffered, and of which you shall never willingly abate - the figure I hold between my Friend and Patron, as well as ignorance in the particular merits of the case, makes it fit for me above all other to be silent; and I can assure you that if the old Gentleman had half such a demand from you, I would not be his Herald tho he should desire it. Things of anger and the prospect of war (in a warm attic and as warm a defence) drives the Common friend into a corner; and he steps not out till he finds both convinced in their Hearts that it were their Common Interest to be quiet. From these Motives, and because you also leave me to do what I will with the paper, I will keep it to myself; and the rather because I rarely hear from him since the gout has disabled him, and as seldom write. Even you who are the Claymer, seem tenderly to wish that you had nothing but poses to toss against him, and I am sure I do as cordially wish that at this time of day, and while both are in the storm, there were nothing but sweet odours, as the tossing of Incense, between you. With all true service to my Lady and little ones, I am ever yrs R. S.

column46: Thursday 20: May 1784. When I came home I found a letter from Mrs. Parker, setting forth that Mrs. or Miss Delane was not to be found, and leaving me free to make another Choice - and now where shall I choose Dearest Burney? For the Times come on apace, or shall I accompany my Misses to Brighton myself, settle them there, and return back hither to receive my Husband. - I shall not speak to them about it till I have your Answer, for I know not that this Scheme will succeed; as it may not peradventure so loudly notify to the World that Dislike of my Conduct which their quitting my house on Piozzi's Approach would more particularly testify! - Tell me your Mind as quick as possible, and give me a Hint where to look for a Lady if this Notion don't answer - it would save me a World of Expense - that it would - and the Journey to Sussex would be of Service to my Health: I am all the better for the sweet Visit I paid my Burney in London, and Dr. Dobson says so himself. Miss Thrale says the Lady will not be wanted for a Month, as She will go to some of these famous Matrons who take grown Ladies under their care. Shall I escort them to Brighthelmstone, leave them there with their old Friends and their old Nurse and return? - or shall I let them leave me ? God knows they are the fittest Women in the World to act for themselves. Queeney's whole Diversion was saving my Money in my Absence, with an Activity that warm Friendship seldom inspires: Dear Tit! and she brought me the Bills, and told me with such Triumph that they were only 4£.3s. My Love's Letter was a tender one, he had got three of mine that pleased him, and he thinks I do love him now . What hopes and Fears had the Signor Abate, as Pacchierotti calls him, after the evening spent at Le Texier's. And what says my charming Friend to the World about her zealous Visitor from Bath, about the Meat Breakfasts she made in her Company so kindly? - and with a tender Sweetness unknown to any but herself. It was a pretty Meeting after all was it not? And I had a very good Journey home, with a Dissenting Teacher and his humble Obadiah in the Stage: what one liked least was the Companies of the two Stage Coaches joining at the Dinner, but there was no harm in it; I sate at the head of the Table and Carved for the Men, who absolutely would treat Johnson and I for Love of her Beauty and my Wit, I trow. The Misses were at the Play - since I begun this Letter I have repented on it, and will not have you give me any advice about the Trip to Sussex: My dearest and most delicate-minded Friend shall not be pained by her own Virtue as far as I can defend her; You never have given me any Advice in this Matter, except to let it alone! - and you never shall : I will get through it how I can, if dishonour should come near the transaction, how should I deserve a Man whose Soul is Susceptible of the nicest Sensibility, and whose Rest is broken by Scruples of Refinement. I have resolved in Consequence of this Reflection, and told Queeney, before her Sisters, ten Minutes ago, my Purpose of accompanying 'em - at the same time saying that I might have the Appearance of Collusion to the Town most certainly, and if She thought public disclaiming of my behaviour the best way to keep peace with that World she preferred to me - I would still look for a Lady. I told her also, and I told her truly, that though I resolved to prefer Piozzi to the good will of all Mankind, I never should blame her for giving me the second place to so respectable an Aggregate; that it was fit She should esteem the World, and very fit I should despise it; that it was natural for me to wish She would shake hands with him on his Arrival; but that if She would not do so, for fear People should blame her; I thought the way to show those People her Disapprobation, was to leave me on his Approach: if however she had a mind to part good Friends, and let all see that she did so, I would go with her to Brighthelmston, and leaving her in her own House, as I left her the other Day in mine here, return back to Bath and wait for my Husband, leaving my Maid (whom you like so) to hold him fast if he should come before I can get hither again. Now make me no Answer at all to all this Rodomontade, but tell how much you love me, and that shall content your H: L: T.

column46: written in the Night at Bath 1: of July 1784. I cannot sleep - how should I! my Piozzi is come home; he lives, he loves me, he sleeps tonight at Harford's on the North Parade, in the Bed you slept in there. I have seen him, I have rejoiced over him: I have cried, and prayed, and thanked God - and cried again for Joy, a whole Day, and almost a whole Night. Let me now write to my Burney; She will forgive and soothe my Frenzy, think, my dear Creature! Seventeen Months of Absence, and no Alteration but what Kindness for me has caused: Can I love him too well? has he not cost me my life almost? have I not purchased him with my very Vitals? Oh! we will part no more though,- per non separarti piu as he says. Tell Mrs. Philips my Happiness - she will not laugh much at me, She has been in Love herself, and I hope will continue so to her Life's end. Piozzi says Mr. Locke has written to him - how sweet that was of Mr. Locke! but Norbury Park is the Place for Agree`men's - and it now contains my Burney. This Letter goes to Town, they will send it forward from thence: my Nerves are cruelly agitated, who can wonder? but Dr. Dobson says we shall both recover, as our Disorder is of the same Kind exactly. I hope we shall recover - To live and love so true &c. The separated Ladies write constantly, but the eldest writes very coldly , and though I sent 'em a fond open-hearted Letter, expressing my Agitation of Mind on Piozzis expected Arrival, they none of them name his Name, nor take the smallest Notice, just as if such a Creature had never existed! - You know how to do so to be sure, and yet show affectionate Regard all the Time; but it amazes me to see their Proficiency in such a Power. God bless you sweet Soul, and love me in any way you will , and in every you can : for in all ways of true Friendship and unalterable Esteem will I be ever yours . I have written to the Misses just as they do to me - taking their Ton exactly - cold and kind - They shall begin first I assure you in all that relates to him whom I have chosen to be my Husband with the most constant and deliberate Esteem. Miss Burney.

column46: Berners Street 12: July 1784. I received your Letter here my Love, it was transmitted me from Bath: I cannot get married yet, here are so many delays and Difficulties, for I will settle my Affairs first; and have no one to assist me in so doing, but new Friends - the old ones are so angry: in good Time! being angry is so easy a way to show Kindness. Dr. Johnson wrote me a most ferocious Letter in answer to that you saw the Copy of, but when he read my Reply to it, he softened at once; has sent Prayers and Wishes for mine and my Piozzi's happiness - and behaved with all the Tenderness you can imagine. Lord Dudley has given me Letters to Dr. Harris, to smooth our road through the Ecclesiastical Courts; The Bishop of Durham has interested himself warmly in our Cause - his Lady hearing Piozzi sing, cried out She wondered no longer and good old Lord Conyngham promised for his Lady that She should be the first to wait on us after our Marriage. - so the Last shall be first, and the first last as the Scripture says. In the mean Time our charming Sir Lucas Poppies has offered me every Service, every Civility in his Power - so perhaps We may yet be fashionable and then the People so justly called People of Fashion will be all on our Side; and I shall know what their Tenderness amounts to. Dr. Johnson is going to Derbies - and in very good humour with me I am sure: This Moment I write again to him with Piozzi's Compliments &c. I went to Portland Chapel yesterday, and heard Mr. George Cambridge read prayers and preach; he did both very well, and saved me by Attention from fainting away with the Heat. Bath and London are indeed so hot this Weather that I may defy Naples itself: it will take us a week to stay in Town I dare say, before the Writings are completed; we are then to be married here in the Romish Chapel, and return to my Parish Church at Bath to be married there again as the Law directs. Mean Time I am ill enough and so is my Caro Sposo : but we must get well when we can, and how we can; we shall at least be sick or well together and to us that is no small Consideration. / Ever yours my dear / sweet Friend Ever Yours / Adieu! Miss Burney / at Norbury Park, The Seat of / Locke Esq. / near Dorking / Surrey.

Saturday Indeed my dearest you can scarce imagine how very little I think about what the Guardians say; they none of them say any thing to me good or bad, except Dr. Johnson, who wrote me an affectionate Letter: Miss Thrale complains that they use her very roughly, and I should be sorry beyond endurance, but that I may be sure she may leave their Tyranny when she chooses. Mr. Cator and I must have some Money settling - The other Gentleman's Approbation of my Conduct is of little Consequence to my Happiness, which depends wholly on the health and continued Attachment of my Husband. He is however very far from well, I recover faster by far; and with regard to Reputation, mine can be no better protected than by his Honour; which has I believe no equal. The newspapers say not a Syllable about us, We wait for Mr. Greenland to finish our Parchments, and then shall be married in every requisite Form. The dear Bath Folks long for us back again - Lord Dudley sends me a Thousand Compliments and Love as he calls it to the Angel Gabriel . Lord Conyngharn was Mr. Burton when you and I were at Bath together, and we often met him at Mrs. Lambert. I live here quite for the Purposes of Business, and see no Company of Course but my Piozzi and his Friends; who will I hope always be mine. Mr. Borghi is a Man of very extraordinary Accomplishments, very considerable Understanding, and very pleasing Conversation: his Wife is pretty, and modest, and gentle in her Manners. Young Bartolozzi who lives with 'em is uncommonly agreeable, and I should be strangely fastidious indeed, if I did not take unaffected Delight in the Company of my new Associates. We dined at Mr. Greenland's the other Day - why not? he gave me a gallant Dinner and a private Concert where Piozzi sung with the young Ladies, and all went sweetly and smoothly - or I thought so. The Storms are past I hope, but if more are gathering - let them spare his Head, whom I prefer so much to my own, and take or leave us together , at least. To those who have experienced like me the pangs of Separation, few things are difficult to endure, when assisted by mutual Support. Let me always have your Kindness, and believe me ever / I most tenderly yours / H: L: T. To / Miss Burney / at William Lockes' Esq: / Norbury Park / near Leatherhead / Surrey.

July 1784 My dear Friend Mrs. Thrales marriage has taken such horrible possession of my mind I cannot advert to any other subject. I am sorry and feel the worst kind of sorrow that which is blinded with shame. Sorrow lies in state on the Tomb of the Dead, in the regions of melancholy, it preserves a certain dignity and fears not to meet the eye which casts a look of pity on it, but when one laments and weeps over the disgrace of a Friend bitter are the sensations and as the cause of ones grief is an object of contempt and scorn one cannot disburden the heart by communicating its sufferings but shuts it up with all its poisonous and baleful qualities. I am myself convinced that the poor Woman is mad and indeed have long suspected her mind was disordered. She was the best Mother, the best Wife, the best friend, the most amiable member of Society. She gave the most prudent attentions to her Husbands business during his long state of imbecility and after his death, till she had an opportunity of disposing well of the great Brewery. I bring in my verdict lunacy in this affair. I am heartily grieved for Miss Burney, and Doctor Johnson, female delicacy, and male wisdom, will be much shocked, and they have both a very sincere attachment to their friends, and a delicate sense of honour. I respected Mrs. Thrale, and was proud of the honour she did to the human and female character in fulfilling all the domestic duties and cultivating her mind with whatever might adorn it, I would give much to make every one think of her as mad, the best and wisest are liable to lunacy. If she is not considered in that light she must throw a disgrace of her sex. My spirits are so sunk by all this I must have recourse to a noble subject to raise them. I set before my imagination our Queen coming into the drawing room attended by Lady Harcourt, Thank me my dear Friend for offering to your contemplation what will reinstate your ideas of female purity dignity and excellence: and drive away the Marmiton Cupids, the base plebeian loves, which wait on some soft hearted Dames to the great debasement of their character and the honour of the Sex. ... I am ever most affectionately / Yours / E. M.

column46: Bath Friday 6: August 1784. Dear Miss Burney I not only thought you unkind, but I think so still: True Tenderness does not express herself ambiguously: If I have, as you say, deserved my Husband's Affection, I will take Care not to rely on past Merits , as many Women are apt to do; but will make myself a pleasing Companion if possible, and so sincere a Friend that every Action of my Life shall convince him that my Heart holds no Fellowship with those who refuse him the Esteem due to his Character and Conduct. I am sorry for Mrs. Phillips's bad State of Health, She is in the right to try Continental Air: - Your kind Father has written very sweetly to his ever Affectionate / H: L: Piozzi. Miss Burney at Norbury Park / near Leatherhead / Surrey.

column46: Paris Friday 17: September 1784. Dear Mr. Lysons Though I hear by our Friend Mr. James that you are still at Bath, yet I make use of your own Direction, as it is always safest to follow Rules exactly, when people are very distant from each other. Was I writing to a Person who I thought regardless of me , and only desirous of my Letters , I would not begin by saying how well and how happy I find myself, but if that were not the first thing you wished to hear, I would not write to you at all. The second is how, and what, and where, &c: and what do you see with most Pleasure? and so forth. Why then absolutely I think the Prince of Bourbon's Cabinet afforded me as much Pleasure as anything; and that because it put us in Mind of you , and we cried out Lord! if Mr. Lysons did but see these beautiful Butterflies! and here's Hector I remember him I'm sure - and Achilles with the broad blue Stripe down his Wing - and Beau Paris and all! Mr. James will tell you that all this is at Chantilly, where the Waterfalls are so fine, and the Fish so tame. Well! but this Moment brings me your kind Letter, and assures me I am not forgotten. Mercy on me! What Wonders Mrs. James has written: God bless you speak to every body you know, and protest that I owe nothing; as for the Debts incurred by Johnson, her Husband must see to them - Let us however get rid of the dirty House in Duke Street: I had no Letters from Phillips or Coward while at London, but whoever writes now I shall get the Intelligence safe enough. I'm glad you are sitting for your Picture - The Portrait of Lysons Earl of Tetbury High Chancellor of England in his Youth will be of amazing Value two hundred Years hence. Mean Time tell me some News do of what you hear and see, and do, and study: We find it so very hot we dare not venture the Suffocation of a Theatre: but out-door Diversions so swarm about this gay Town, that there is no need except to put your Head out of Doors, and you see every thing queen respire le Plaisir a Paris, comme l'Opulence a Londres . Assure yourself my dear Sir, and assure my Bath Friends, that it is equally out of the Power of both to drive from my Mind those who have so long and kindly contributed to its Relief: I shall be very studious to execute all your Commissions, but that odious Custom-house! that Foe to friendly Intercourse! how shall we charm or stupefy that ever wakeful Dragon! - Tell Mrs. James that they seized my Flannel Petticoats (although made up) which I had provided for Winter Wear - and upon Muslins and Dimitties - no nuns dimitties said they, but detained all they could find. Well! now am I a professed Traveller, and what shall I tell to divert you of my Travels: Dr. Johnson says (you know) that whoever would entertain another by his Remarks - must make the subject of them Human Life . Mr. Wholly would with equal Confidence assert no doubt, that the Voyager should be particularly attentive to the Scenery of the places he passes through: for both speak of what would most entertain them . I think you would wish to hear a little of each; to be told that the Vines clustering up the Apple Trees and mingling their Fruits, fill one's Eye with Elegance and one's heart with Comfort as one drives along the splendid Avenues which constitute the Approach to this prodigious City, and are called the high Road to it for ten or twenty miles - that your Friends Io and Brassica flutter about the Tuillerie Gardens among the Two legged and less simply coloured Butterflies, every Evening; that though this Town seems in some Respects bigger than London; ill built and crowded to a most disagreeable Excess, the Air seems always fresh, and the Bats fly about the Streets as if we all lived in the Fields. Nothing indeed is a greater proof of the purity of the Air here, than the healthiness of the Inhabitants; in Spite of Dirt, Poverty, and Pressure of one Family against another, in Houses eight Story high, and Streets so narrow that every Noise is echoed and detained below, in such a manner as to stun a Person who has lived 15 Months in the tranquil City of Bath: which is to our Town here, like a new Shilling shining from the Mint, compared to a Hundred Pounds worth of old - but good Half Pence, with here and there a bright Broad Piece of Portugal Gold among them: for you have heard with Truth that the Palaces at Paris are magnificent: - and for the rest I refer you to every penny Book, which can tell you better than I, all that I have to tell; except that I am with unalterable Regard and real Esteem / Dear Mr. Lysons's / Faithful and Affectionate Servant / H: L: Piozzi. My Husband sends you a thousand Compliments - You must now direct to Lyons but write soon - or if you write late - direct to Turin . A Monsieur / Monsieur Samuel Lysons / John Jeffries's Esqr. / Bath.
