column46: 18: August 1792. My dear Mrs. Lewis - wants a Letter to amuse her in a sick Room, and I shall write from one that was sick enough too the other Day, when I was violently seized with that furious Agony in my Stomach and Bowels which now and then attacks me as you know; and leaves a Languor that I trust this Letter will fully evince. I shall dine below for the first Time this Day; and wish it were cheerfuller Weather for the Sake of a Harvest which if not well got in, can scarce afford Corn for the numberless Mouths flocking in daily from the Continent, where I believe Things do go on very dreadfully indeed. Marquis Trot and Mr. Davies; are at Paris shut fast within the Gates, and cannot get out - Their Accounts of the Massacre are very exact I dare say, because they had no motives but Curiosity to be there; and they say 2000 dead Bodies lye unburied in the Streets now, which I fancy must soon produce a Pestilence among the Living. Meantime our Ambassador it seems lent the little Dauphin some of his own Boy's Shirts, for which the Mob will very likely (if they find it out) tear my Lord Gower and his Family to pieces; for I trust these Sons of Freedom will scorn the Law of Nations as well as every other Law made by God or Man. Never were such Blasphemies heard as are uttered in the National Assembly: a Gentleman lately come from thence repeated a Sentence so impious I cannot write it down, - and one Man in Contempt of Christianity has renounced the Name given him by Baptism, taking a Greek one from the Records of Antiquity and Paganism. These are horrible Truths from which one cannot fly - nor from their Evidence. Our Camps are as you say merely Playthings - when the Duke of Brunswic reaches Paris - What scenes will there be? Yet I long for the Time. Miss Lewis was amused I hope - if well enough to take Amusement so dearly bought too, as I am told this was with want of Accommodations &c. Her health is not very bad. Our Neighbours Sir Henry and Lady Martin with their Family are just gone to Whiteknights on a Visit to his Brother I find - They are exceeding amiable People and make us very pleasing Acquaintance - You remember Hunters house the Bottom of our Common, and it is there they reside, on Account I suppose of his Attendance on his Post as Commissioner of the Navy. We like them very much. I had many Congratulations from Friends or Foes or funny Folks or some What, all last Week because of Cecilia's invented Marriage with a Man She never saw; it was a Newspaper Joke I suppose, but am surprised you did not mention it. Letters came even from Wales upon the Subject, but poor Cecy was soon robbed of her Husband by a contradictory Article put in by Mr. Lysons at our Request. She has never seen the Gentleman, and I thought there was no such Man; till somebody told me he was affronted too . Mr. Piozzi has had his half-yearly Visit of the Gout and when I am got better and the Weather settled, I fancy we shall make a Journey to Wales. Till then and ever I remain Dear Mrs. Lewis's / Ever Affectionate and Obedient / H: L: Piozzi. Accept and dispose of Compliments. Mrs. Lewis / London Street / Reading / Barks.

Crown Inn, Denbigh 15: September Saturday I make haste to assure my kind Friend that all Apprehensions for Cecilia are at an end: the Change of Air relieved her Oppression the first day, and carried off what remained of Cold or Cough, or whatever it was, the Second . But soon as arrived here after the rainiest Journey ever seen I suppose, poor Sally Siddons was taken ill of an excessive Sickness and Pain in her Bowels, and our whole Night has been spent as Yours was when I was just as ill at Streatham Park. Dr. Moore exhibited the Ipecacuanha however, and when all the Agony was over - a light Opiate: She is now risen and better, and eating Chicken Broth. I am very sorry to think You have been suffering the same Torture, but do make haste and get well, and take Bark; it is the best thing after all for you who have I think few Complaints except what proceed from irritated Nerves and perpetual Anxiety of Heart. A Decided Situation will tranquillize every Sensation, and calm the tossing of the Waves, which keep on their turbulent Motion very often long after the Storm is over. Yours is surely past, and so Dear Cos, as Celia says to Rosalind - sweet Cos be merry. Your Mother is right I dare say about going to London, Lewisham is a dull place, it were better live here at Denbigh - We have Coals at 10d per C - and they say how dear it all is! and Chickens 1s a couple - and such a Prospect! Well! I do think my own poor Country a very pretty one - that I do: and cheap - for though we are called the Squire and His Lady who live upon the best and pay for the best : they cannot for Shame ask more than seven Guineas of Week for our Lodging and Boarding and Linen and China and all included - four People and three Servants, and we have one very long Room and clean Beds. So much for Wales, meantime our Letters from France will come slowly, though they boast their brisk intelligence, I believe the Duke of Brunswick may be in quiet possession of Paris - or beaten back to Coblentz before we shall hear a Bit about the matter, as this Town lies in the high Road to no Town, and smaller Events than the Deposition or Restoration of Sovereigns make much ado here. We shall be quiet tomorrow and go to Funnen Vaino on Monday if Sally recovers quite well, and I doubt not her doing so, - Our Medical Man here is very kind and comfortable. Helena Williams should mind who she keeps Company with - so indeed should Hector Piozzi: that fine Man She brought to our house lives in no Emigrant's Hotel at Paris but a common Lodging, in a Place where Numbers lodge: he carried no Wife over with him, nor no Children, they are left at Hackney I am told - her Mother and Sister are at Montreuil. Take care of your Mother, and assure her of our true Regard for all that belongs to her Daughter to whom I will be ever a / true and faithful / H: L: P. Miss Weston / at Mr. Charles Playter's / near the Church / Lewisham / Kent.

Crown Inn, Denbigh 1st: October Monday I write myself now, kindest Miss Weston - and I write with steadier Fingers. The Cough has yielded to repeated Bleedings, and She mends as rapidly as She grew ill - Doctor Haygarth it was who threw me in that Agony, by pronouncing Cecilia in serious Danger from the Blood spit up, which He said came from the Lungs: and never did Twenty Guineas purchase as much Affliction at one Dose I do believe, as those we gave to him. Dear Mr. Moore an agreeable Practitioner settled here as Accoucheur, Surgeon &c. who cured Sally Siddons had repeatedly assured me that it was not from the Lungs, and that an obstruction only caused every Alarming Symptom - her quick Recovery gives great Reason to think him right; and he so smiles and so rejoices; yet insists on my telling nobody that He differs from Dr. Haygarth, who is a Man of very high Reputation: and in earnest a very pleasing Physician - skilful too I dare say - and fully persuaded of his own Opinion which is supported by science, as the other's by Experience. Dear Cecy's Recovery will if complete, prove the old Adage that an Ounce of Mother is worth a Pound of Clergy. Meaning that Good Common Sense or Mother Wit as we call it beats Learning out of Doors - So may it prove! - I will now pluck up Courage and write to Sir Lucas myself. Doctor Haygarth recommended us to take Cecilia to a warmer Climate, and that - instantly : at the same Time that he said She must not be hurried , or even suffered to talk much or moved - Naples was the first Place that occurred: but how should we get to Naples ? Through France? they would refuse passports, perhaps hurry her into worse Apartments than these we are in: a Prison, and present her with the Sight of Heads streaming with Blood - Through Germany? through marching Armies into miserable Towns, where want of horses to get forward would detain us in a Climate worse than that of Great Britain: a German Inn to escape catching Cold at, is a good Joke to be sure. Tic a Residence for Pigs only, not delicate Damsels sure. Let it be Lisbon then! very well Lisbon be it - but now do not you open your Lips or black one bit of Paper with this Intelligence, for if She really ails nothing - which Mr. Moore says will very soon appear to be the Case - all these Phantoms vanish, and poor Mr. Piozzi and I are not to be driven forcibly, expensively, dangerously and suddenly from all our Comforts, all our Friends: present Enjoyments, and future Projects. The little Belvedere may yet go forward at Funnen Vaino, and we may yet be merry with you in amany abeautiful Spot, but none like the Vale of Llwydd . My Health though horribly shaken, may tie up again; and I may kiss my pretty black Cock and Hen (that I forgot to thank you for) at poor old Streatham Park. They are of the Polish Breed. We will call them King and Queen of Poland - there will never be any other I fancy. Write to me soon - the moment Cecilia can be moved with Safety we crawl to Chester, and remain under Dr. Haygarth's Care till he consigns us to Sir Lucas - from him I have no Reserves - show him this Letter and Adieu. Jacob's dangerous Sore Throat and Fever has been a great Addition to my Agony - but he will live poor Fellow I thank God; and so the favourite Horses got lamed with neglect while he was sick - and Phillis came to Evil, and all went consistently . I expect My poor Husband to get a Fit of the Gout every day and that would do for me. I should remind myself of the Welch Parson's Letter saying Dear Sir As I was passing the Heights of Snowdon last Week with Mrs. Jones behind me, I got in much Distress - for Night came on, My Horse tired, and my Wife fell in Labour. Adieu dear Friend / believe me ever yours while / H: L: P. Of Sally Siddons I say like as Imogen says of Pisanio - "thour't all the Comfort the Gods will diet me with." Her Mother's Recovery is however one solid and certain Felicity to us all - I do thank God for that She is an invaluable Creature. Miss Weston at / Miss Rathbone's No. 14 / James Street / Westminster.

Thursday 4: October Denbigh. Well my dearest Miss Weston - you are a true Friend if ever any one had a true Friend - and you will think of nobody but me, and of nothing but my Miseries: from some part of which however, charming Sir Lucas's Letter and yours together have relieved me. I write to him today - and I begged Dr. Haygarth to write - his will doubtless be a despairing Letter, he despaired even of Jacob who Mr. Moore protested was never in actual Danger - no matter now though, for he certainly is recovering; and I earnestly hope I did not neglect my Duty to him, while my Heart was full of everything else in the World. Indeed, Indeed, Cecilia has between her Lovers and her Illness worked my poor heart very hard this Year. I marvel Drummond is not come down yet, for he knows all that happened - but the same Avarice which prompted his original Pursuit of her restrains him from spending seven Guineas to follow her , and fret me. - Some certain Comfort every State affords - you know. Cecilia does mend to be sure as fast as ever anybody did mend: ay, and as fast as She grew worse, which was with a rapidity I never before was witness to - nothing new occurring, we shall be at Chester under Dr. Haygarth's immediate Eye on Monday next, you must write thither . Dear Piozzi does not get the Gout, so we shall surely move hence of Monday, but Haygarth is very good that he is and comes at a Call, very quickly too - he has made two Visits, and kind Mr. Moore nurses, and sends his Wife to nurse, and help sit up, and every thing - that is he did do so when wanted - as if he were one's oldest and sincerest Friend. - He never thought her in Danger, and is now the happiest Person except myself in the Town of Denbigh. The Neighbouring Gentlemen send in Baskets of Fruit and Salads and all they think She can want - so if She does hate Wales which I do believe She does most heartily - the People could do no more to make her love if. Remember that though the Dr. came twice - She spit Blood but once; remember too that I did not wait till She spit Blood before I sent for him - that Agony was while He was coming hither - this day seven-night, and Mr. Moore had just bled her as he walked in - the State of her Blood however and of her Case, made Haygarth order the Operation to be repeated - and tic to Bleeding alone that I impute the Cure. Her Bowels are kept open though. She was as well, as lively and as handsome as ever you saw her just before this Attack. She lost the Cold you had observed by the Time she reached Meriden. I remember her running up and down the Garden Slopes like a School-Girl, so She ran up and down the Castle hill here, to fright me and Sally Siddons at the heights She showed herself from - for mere sport and frolic. The Disease was sudden and violent - she had conquered the Cold when Jacob caught his riding in the rain to the Belvedere, and then coming home in the Chaise with us - her Habit wet through. - She would ride that Day though it was show'ry when She set out, - but the roads are so bad for a Carriage that every body will ride that can ; and She is not used to mind a Cold poor soul - but that vile Period being near , the Obstruction and short breathing came on very hastily and terribly indeed. This is I think my most rational Letter yet; show this to Sir Lucas, and he will still form a closer Judgement. Sally Siddons is my darling Daughter, and so affectionate. Farewell - beg dear Mr. Whalley's Prayers for me, and write to Chester to yours / Gratefully / H: L: P. Miss Weston / at Mrs. Rathbone's No. 14 / James Street / Westminster.

Easter Tuesday My dear Mrs. Pennington has often seen People talked into Misery - it is the way now to talk me into happiness; but I am content to be happy the way other people please, and am sure they are right . I returned the Visit I told you of next Day, and they all dined and supped here last Monday . - Oh Yesterday! after an Interval of 14 Days, in which I saw nothing of them. However all is vastly well. They are contented to take me up, as they set me down without alleging a Reason - and I am contented to be taken and left by them without reasoning on the Matter at all. We had a Brilliant Day with Tea and a Dance and Song, and broke not up till four o'clock in the Morning - Our Elastic House pulled out to embrace them and the Hamilton kind and sweet, the Greatheeds - Miss Owen, dear old Mr. Jones, and all the Siddons Family. One of my Delights was to see Cecilia dancing with Mr. Richard Greatheed who when he felt her Pulse at Guy's Cliff I feared would never have made Allemande with her. Every body seemed pleased however, and we all were pleased; our Acquaintance will henceforth be theirs, and Things will Shake naturally into their proper Place so nothing could exceed the Kindness of our common Friends except my Sensibility of it. The Girls seem less shy of Mr. Piozzi than of me, Comical enough! but he is so good, and so attentive to them! How you would love him!! and Public Concerns were prohibited the Conversation, so Mr. Greatheed was quite charming. The dear Broadheads could not come, their Uncle is dead and has disinherited them leaving 50,000£ to a little Currier's Boy who as I say will jump out of his Skin for Joy I suppose, while they fret as I once did on a like Occasion. Know you where Colonel Barry is? I cannot guess, or would have called him to partake our festivity. He is a good Aristocrat by now. I dare say, that the French are forced to bend and suffer Austria, Holland, &c. to resume their old Possessions and enjoy them peaceably. Adieu! tell me you are well and your good Husband better, and do write / Soon to your H: L: P. Mrs. Pennington / Dowry Square / Hot Wells / Bristol.

column46: Streatham Park 16: June 1793. Every Letter I receive from you my dear Friend not only convinces me most unnecessarily of the Loss I sustain in wanting your Conversation - but shows me that we do not understand each other half as well at a Distance. What could I ever have hinted to make you Suppose I considered the diminution of your just Dislike of Mr. Drummond - as possible? He looked like a baffled Blockhead at Yaniewitz's Concert; and if he had any Memory might recollect what I said to him early in the Business - when my Tongue pronounced his Fate precisely as it happened that Night. Sir said I, the Child is but a Child and knows not what Love is: She may be amused with having a Lover for ought I can tell, but in two Years I shall see you pass each other in a Public Place, She - saying to her Friends - That's the Man that was troublesome to me: - you saying to yours, - that's the Girl that jilted me. And so the matter ended. My Prediction concerning Perry will likewise come true: Erskine the worthy counsellor of Tom Payne and Co. has undertaken his Cause, and when I read in the papers that Miss Clerk has had a Child by the Man, and lives with him now in Prison - being again pregnant - her Mother keeping them Company - how can I suppose otherwise? Miss Mills is a Maiden Lady, but dear Mrs. Pennington knows better now sure than to dream of a Woman's bastardising her own Babies, and hanging the Father , who could scarcely have been so; had not there been some Consent on her Side I trust. That the Man is a Rascal and got her at first against her Will, has little Chance of saving her Fortune or a Share of it from him - and after all what must the Girl do? ruin her own Children and write herself up a - for the patriotic Desire of saving future Heiresses! I have no Notion that such a Girl can be found - Bristol however does always produce some staring Wonder, and may produce this. - The dear Siddons left me Yesterday, She has charming Daughters now, and so have I; so we can see little of each other. The Currents of Life draw those who delight in mutual and friendly chat apart from one another - without fault or Blame of anyone's: But busy, busy still art Thou To join the joyless, luckless Vow; The Heart from Pleasure to exclude, And join the gentle to the rude. as in poor Clementina Clerke's Case. Sally is exceedingly well, and just as pretty as every pretty Girl of the same age, and prettier than Maria because her Face looks cleaner. You are lucky in Lady Asgill's Friendship, The Miss I count little upon: a conversible Companion of six and Thirty Years old is a good Thing, and an Infant under seven a delightful thing - but a Miss of 17 can charm nothing as I should think but a Master of 27. I grow too old for either, but the last is far most agreeable. Mrs. Mackay is coming home but her Letters which were so entertaining, now breath nothing but the loveliness of her Titmouse - now that too is right and ought to be so; but I am losing my Friends all away the while. Do not you enjoy the thoughts of our late Discovery that this famous Anacharsis Clouts so well known in the National Convention for forwarding the Cause of Apostasy and Rebellion is no greater nor no less a Man at last than Dignum our Thief; who worked on the Justitia Hall about 15 years ago, and people used to go and see how daintily he fingered the Wheelbarrow I remember. - Well! this is the Hero of modern Democracy, the Legislator of France, the Renouncer of his Baptismal Vow - the Champion of Atheism and Orator of the Human Race . Mr. Lysons came over from Putney late one Evening o'purpose to tell it me, and is it not a capital Anecdote? My dear Master sends you a thousand kind Words - he is very well and busy in his farm and Garden - he joins with me in sincere Concern for the kind, the elegant the friendly Whalleys: Their Misfortunes will end only in Vexation I hope - not Calamity. I shall have the Comfort of our estimable Harriet's Conversation tomorrow, and much shall we talk about you. Indeed I do love your sweet-hearted husband very truly; Mrs. Weston will at last finish her cloudy Day with a bright setting Sun. Colonel Barry and Mr. Dowdeswell are valuable friends and seem to behave most Manly. - Not a Word of poor Helena in all this long Letter; that's a Shame, yet I think her much more sincere than Dr. More, who while he condemns every Fact - justifies - (you may observe) every Principle on which the Facts were committed. Write soon again to / Yours faithfully / H: L: P. Cecilia sends her Compliments. - Mrs. Pennington / Hope Square / Hot Wells / Bristol.

column46: Streatham Park 1st: August 1793. My Dear Girl You said I should copy out my own Book - my own self: so I this Morning set about it, and hope I shall have no evil Cause to remember the first of August as our old Song has it. Mr. Piozzi's going down for a fortnight to Brinbella will give me time to work hard, but my best Friends say tic not big enough, so I must enlarge as well as Copy - Comfort me meanwhile with long Letters. I shall have Time to read nothing else; and shall certainly never read anything with so much pleasure. This day we dine in London at Mrs. Mackay's and look for Servants - our old Housekeeper cannot live or keep her Wits, What ails her I know not, but since that night dear Suzette undertook her Cure She has never been well a day - always in Convulsions somehow, and Charles, the second Gardener has fallen down Stairs upon a Pail at the Bottom, and dislocated his Thigh: so we shall be Streatham Infirmary now and considered by our Neighbour as a mere Sick and hurt Office . Worse than all this, Jacob and I have quarrelled, and I am so sorry! for these five Years has he been uncontrolled Master of our Domestics and domestic Affairs - during which Time (knowing his Power over me through the Horses, Dogs, and Cats) he has given Warning which we would not take about five Times - living on with every Indulgence one could bestow on him and his peevish Wife, for whose Sakes numberless Servants have been parted with - yet yesterday - only because I presumed to ask who were those little Boys, - of two Children whose Attendant said She came to see Mrs. Weston - her Husband flew out and said I sent his Wife's Friends away like Thieves in good Time ! when I had just stuffed the Brats with Gooseberries and Currants - As ill Luck would have it Mr. Piozzi heard his Insolence, and insisted on my bearing it no longer; so now my Parrot and Ponies and all will suffer perhaps for this Foolery - and we shall have a new Coachman, and I shall scream every Step. Cecilia too will have a Maid to seek, and if we get a fine Hairdressing Lady - She will not let her touch her Head, any more than She will endure my Woman about her perhaps - or perhaps such a one may comb her Lady's Head out of her Secrets, or insert some of her own to hatch there - or dress up Twenty Tales, or carry Love Letters - She was at least safe with that spiteful little Weston, and Jacob knew I thought her so. - Shall we get your Protege` Jenny Norton's Daughter? Or can She wash small Linen, do you think, or darne a torn Handkerchief? - Or bind a Petticoat if Allen cuts it out - or hem a Bottom - without turning down yet - or sew on an Edging or such like? I should think her Mother might have taught Her that much, and would keep a hand upon her, and make her honest and humble; for I'll be subservient to no more Abigails or Andrews either. It is a dangerous Post for the Wench that it is, among all our Fellows - but we must get an old Woman for House-keeper that may look to her - My Maid is rather young for a Chaperon , but eminent for Prudence and Steadiness as it is called; and has lived with me three Years. Our Butler is a comfortable Creature and so is the Gardener - the rest are worse than Egyptian Torments - and so I'll plague you no more about them. Here is Rain to allay the Dust on the Road at your Door, pray how many Angles has your Polygon? for I never saw it, nor Neatly Abbey neither. A Man who builds Houses for Noblemen, and has a very good Taste I think, having resided long in Italy, Mr. Brettingham by name - says that of all England he would choose for his Residence the Vicinage of Southampton, with its fine River, and beautiful Ruins, Rides in the New Forest &c. I have been in that Country however twice in my Life; once with you, and once with Count Martenengo as Cicerone - and always missed by some perverseness of Fortune the seeing this Neatly Abbey. The Polygon was not built six Years ago - when we showed off the Place to our Venetian Friends, and Sir Roger Curtis entertained us o'Board the Ganges, and rowed us about in his own Barge through and over the remains of the Royal George - I recollect that the Inn was dearer than any where else, and that they charged for Beds, although we had a magnificent Supper. I think such long Lettere as these seccare buono Nettunno as the Italian says. May he however inspire you to send one no less long in return - to your Affectionate Mother / H: L: Piozzi. Mr. Piozzi and Cecilia send Loves and Compliments - and so I am sure do I. Miss Thrale / Cumberland Place, / Polygon / Southampton / Hints.

Streatham Park Tuesday Morning. 29. My dearest Girl may believe that Mr. Piozzi and I are only too happy that our little Things could be of any use to you. He calls them Suppelletile : it is an excellent Word for such a Heap of Household Stuff. You will wonder what's become of the Slopbason to your best China, but the Blockheads brought it hither parted from all its natural Friends, like an Emigrant. If Sophie is not better even by now , it will vex me cruelly: too many Things do happen to vex one every Day I think: Cecilia alarmed us with a sore Throat last Tuesday and the Moment I had sent for Sir Lucas Poppies, She found out that She would go out next Day to dinner, and I expected more Cold would be caught - but that Experiment failed - her fine Mare which cost 40 Guineas this Spring is expiring this moment of a putrid Complaint, already communicated to old Grey Forester who must be shot, or all our Horses and Cattle will catch the Distemper, and make a complete Undoing of us. Meanwhile this vexacious Finale to the Campaign in Flanders gives me serious Uneasiness - The poor Queen's Murder too, and the Imprisonment, of my once intimate Acquaintance Helen Maria Williams, shock one's Nerves no little. I am sincerely persuaded that when the Convention have done diverting their savage Populace with the Butchery of those remaining to the Blood Royal at Paris - and Famine or Insurrection or whatever Judgment God Almighty will be pleased to send them - comes closer: - they will pull the English out of Prison and massacre them to take off the Attention from themselves; - I'm sure they will. You are in the Place of all this great World that Has come within my Knowledge - most my favourite; and I would it with Vivacity as poor Count Manucci used to say, that We were there too: but It don't suit - and so. Let me hear however of or from dear Sophia, who will perhaps hate Bath, because She was sick there once before, but I hope not. No.2 in the Circus is one of Gibbons's Houses I think, and very pleasant: seven Guineas or eight o'Week I forget which. - Little Floe knows his Way about there as well as I do, and would soon show you the Gate to go in at the Crescent Fields. Here is lovely Weather for walking down to the Pump; and I hope our pretty Sophie will be an early riser, this getting Sick is a vile Thing. I am about disposing of my Synonyms which are at last nearly copied out: every Expense doubles, every Thing purchased at least doubles in price, and my Master has nothing to sell but Hay; and I - nothing but Books - they ought to fetch double what they used to do. You will be disappointed of Miss Wallis the pretty actress, I'm told She is at Bristol dying of The Gout in her Stomach - whilst old Miss Holman of the Crescent is going to be married: so if the World does not come to an End, tic at least turned upside down. Apropos - Do you remember a Print so called? when you were a child - Kitchens &c. with Compartments: in one The Baby beating the Nurse, in another the Fowl roasting the Cook &c. but particularly Peasants sitting with their Hats on, and the King bowing before them and pulling off his Crown. Two Footmen riding in a Chariot and the Noblemen stuck up behind. If I could find that foolish old Thing I'd give a new Edition of it with proper Comments - that I would. One might make good Sport out of it these Democratic Days. Bath used to be a Loyal Place, tell if tic so still: and do dear Love write now and then to yours, and Susannas, and poor Sophy's truly Affectionate Mother / H: L: P. Accept Mr. Piozzi's and Cecilia's best regards. Miss Thrale / No. 2 / Circus Bath.

Streatham Park Tuesday 14. January Dear Mrs. Pennington asks what is become of Mrs. Mackay? Why She is married and settled you know, and is thinking of her Husband and her Children, and her Money and her Mops; and has no Time for Correspondences and Visits of Friendship - She is doing her Duty like you, but cannot like you find a Moment for the recollection of old Acquaintance: We never meet now, unless for five Minutes in a Year. You ask too who is Cecy's new Flirt - I answer, every Man who to the House; he who franks this Letter is the Gentleman I alluded to, but he makes no Proposal of Marriage - because he has no Pretensions in point of Fortune: Mr. Rogers whose Father's Death has left him in the City Phrase a warm man; does make Proposals, and Cecy makes of him, Caricatures. So we go on, and I am almost weary of keeping an expensive House and Table to entertain Lovers who glide by like Figures in a Magic Lantern. Mr. Murphy - having found his Way to the old House, likes it; and comes often and stays long. Dear Siddons is yet in Ireland, Miss Foreign was here last Week - sadly altered. Poor Mr. Chappelow was Ill when we heard last of him, Mr. Jones has the Gout. Davies has taken a Trip to Bath, and expected some Attention from my fair Daughters there, who I fancy shut the Door in his face: Doctor Perney supplied his Place here, read and preached and played on his Long Neck - Young Bartolozzi and Cimad'oro too made us some sweet Music for two or three Days, but Mr. Piozzi said no young Men of his Country should have the Entry`e here, for obvious Reasons: so there's an End of them . So much for Domestic Felicity and the Happiness of Individuals in this workyday World, as Rosalind calls it: Public Affairs go on much worse than they, and the Fog thickens round us both literally and figuratively. Beating the French is kicking at a Woolsack; it is elastic and rises against every Pressure, but perhaps emptying the Bag may cure it of this Elasticity - the Captures of St. Domingo and Pondicherry are the only real Advantages the Allies have had yet. Lord Moyra and Colonel Barry get no Opportunity of showing their Prowess, on which I should however make no small Reliance, could they once get footing in the Country, but seeing how hard it is to effect an Invasion with Ships, should cure us of fearing one from the French who have no Ships: although I am persuaded that the hand of God is in all, and that these People come forth to scourge all Europe with his Permission - Why does nobody quote a more immediate Prophecy, and less equivocal than any which have been mentioned - at least which you have mentioned? "And the second Angel sounded and as it were a great Mountain burning with Fire was cast into the Sea , and the third Part of the Sea became Blood : &c. &c. &c." This Prophecy is to be found in three Passages of the Holy Scripture but I can recollect only that in the 8th Chapter of St. John's Apocalypse. Mr. Gray showed it me in the Old Testament, I have forgot where: but every one seems to think strange Times are coming. There is a Report of the Jews in Holland having sent Circular Letters to the learned of their Nation in every Country to collate the Evidences of our Saviour's Mission, and to examine them against the Prophecies contained in the Bible spoken by his acknowledged Precursors. - Such a Measure would prepare them for Conversion, the Moment God shall be pleased to remove the Film which has been so long before their Eyes. Meantime Miss Hamilton writes willingly to your friends at Bristol, where I hope all good will befall you. Mr. Pennington is well again and that is the best Thing. My Husband has a Cold and Cough and sore Throat which torment him and vex me; he has really lost much Health since You and He parted. Farewell my good / and Dear Friend and forget not your / H: L: P.

column46: Streatham Park Sunday 23: February 1794. My dearest Girl Your kind Letter which I expected in Hanover Square, followed and found me here. We come home every Saturday to Dinner, the London house is a Scene of Confusion and Sackage, but it serves Cecilia to dress in - our Friends keep us from any necessity to dine there: but poor Mr. Piozzi has been forced to spend many Hours without our Company in it - while Sir Lucas Poppies in order to remove the low Fever and Flying Pains which had tormented him so long, insisted on a mere Mutton Broth and Macaroni Regimen sans Wine or Beer too. The Day I wrote to Suzanne was the last he stirred out, and I never shall forget his sufferings that Night at Mr. Chappelow's. Since then things have mended, and we came home at one or two o'Clock after the Eclipse Evening - and gave him an Account how we had seen it plainly, though there were Clouds about too; but between Portman Square and Dover Street, there was Time for Observation - as much as any one now observes such Trifles I believe. Your Intelligence concerning the Jews (at first so disbelieved I was half scorned for mentioning it) is now confirmed and acknowledged; yet who wonders, or cares? or has the slightest Idea regarding it as an Event of any Consequence? Nobody. Of an Invasion there has been much Talk, and of Count Zenobio more: his Countrymen are greatly disgusted with his Conduct, and the Venetian Nobleman you met at our House Excellenza Pisani particularly so; - they are first Cousins, and he offered ten Thousand Pounds immediately, thinking the Exigence a real one: when he discovered it to be fictitious, and the Arrest procured to serve a political purpose, - he refused to see him. What says Hannah More to the present State of Things? Suzanne tells me you visit her. Mr. Leo is a Man eminently qualified for President of a Catch Club, but Mr. Piozzi will be very ill qualified for his Company in Wales I fear - where Drinking is probably more in fashion than at Bath or London. Lady Deerhurst told me at Church to Day that I killed my Husband with racketing him about so, and making him dress and squeeze his Feet into tight Shoes. She did not know I trust, that when we left Mrs. Greatheed's Dinner Table at ten o'Clock last Friday for Lady Martin's Ball, Mr. Piozzi went to Bed, and I staid till Miss Miller - (Daughter of the Batheaston Villa) - begged me to come away, so Cecilia could not complain , though I believe She did regret not dancing the Boulanger at three in the Morning - of two Hundred and thirty People however we left only fifty - so that was fair, and next Friday I will not stay in London at any rate because it is the fast Day. Doctor Bullock has this moment preached us a Sermon your Doctor Randolph could not have exceeded, and that is very high praise. I have just corrected the finishing Sheet of my first Volume, and finding Printing a very tedious Operation indeed; but one need not wish for the Day: twill come time enough I doubt not. Here is a vast heap of Stuff, but I cannot write you a short Letter. Come home when you are got well do Dear Love, that we may meet sometimes; it would exceedingly sweeten my Pleasure in these Assembly Rooms which I frequent so - Theatres I dread worse than Death, - and go I must soon that's certain, or be given up for a Chaperon queen no vaut rein du tout . Adieu and believe me ever / most Affectionately yours / H: L: Piozzi. Give my true Love to Dear Susan and Sophie. Miss Thrale / Milsom Street / Bath.

column46: Denbigh Friday August 22: 1794. I think this Letter will reach my dearest Girl at East Bourne, to thank her even for the kind and friendly Intention of bringing to Denbigh so agreeable a Surprise . We are all quite mortified at the Disappointment, for here is a clean Room and neat hard Bed ready, and the Sweetest Rides in the World - and like as Mr. Poppies did when he had a Villa called Belsize in the Hampstead Road, we see our Country House from our Town House. Indeed Brinbella is not only visible from these upper Windows, but from every body's Windows and every Body's Grounds about this pretty Vale. Yesterday carried us to Downing, Seat of Pennant the famous Naturalist; it was a very entertaining Visit, and he immediately showed us the Animal mentioned as a new Creature with many marvellous Circumstances in a late Daily Paper - but even He has the Grace to think more just now of Roberspierre and his horrible Coadjutors, than of any Caterpillars however hateful and devouring in their Nature. It is a thousand Pities as he said, that the Party gave up their Principals with so little Resistance; had they drawn out Force against Force, some Good might have resulted from the Contest: - as Matters stand - I see nothing better arising than Conviction to all Europe that no Peace can be made with a Country which like France changes its Tyrants so often: and Persuasion to the French that any Government must be preferable to such decided Anarchy. Madame de Tourzel was at Richmond after her Escape on the 2d: of September. What Infatuation was it that prompted her Return? If Princes look melancholy at present it is a good Sign of their good Sense I think: - surely our Heir Apparent has more Wit than to be fretting after Mrs. Fitzherbert; who I hear is very happy, and will I hope soon be married - to some Man of Delicacy, and nice Sense of Honour. Margate is a gay Place it seems, so is Weymouth now : I remember thinking the last a very dull one twice in my Life, I won't try a third: Make haste to Plymouth - Devonshire alone is more beautiful than North Wales, and it is not half as Sublime, or as variegated. But we have Spots here, and I recollect none between Exmouth and Mount Edgecumbe which in Time of War is doubly interesting: if you do not go there - fly hither, and accept me - or my Substitute Mr. Piozzi - for Cicerone. Would you believe that that intelligent Creature Phyllis, whom we unjustly call Fool and pretty Idiot - has taken such a well-founded Terror of Brinbella since her Accident, there is no getting her to endure the Place - except in Company of my Maid or Sam - who both nursed her, and brought her through the dreadful Illness it occasioned - I shall love her the better for showing such proofs of Understanding. Meantime as I told Susan I am really not well; Nervous perhaps, - but my Head and Ears strangely confused somehow - as Sir John Falstaff Says - a whoreson Tingling which arises from much Study and Perturbation of the Brain - it is a kind of Deafness - as he tells Lord Chief Justice: Would it were gone! Mr. Moore says an Emetic would cure me, but my troublesome husband and Daughter have some strange Horror of the Operation, and being aware that I put very little into my Stomach, have a settled Resolution that I shall cast nothing out. Suzette's Table is the prettiest Play thing I ever was Mistress of; - whenever Conversation flags, praise it for me; and add my Thanks betweeen every pause of Extolment : - it is excessively elegant. Mrs. David Pennant, Wife to the Author's eldest Son knows you all, and says how like I am to dear Sophie. Divide my best Love amongst you, and take a large Share for yourself; and accept Mr. Piozzi's true Regards and Cecy's - from the hand of your ever most Affectionate Mother / H: L: Piozzi. Let us hear of you at least if we can't see you. Miss Thrale / Brighton / Sussex.

column46: Denbigh Saturday 23: August 1794. Dear Mr. Chappelow I received your kind Letter, and direct the Answer to Norfolk because I trust you will remain there some Months. How nicely timed was your Notion of the French having too many Blots at home, while their Men filled the Antagonists' Tables! one would have thought you knew what was going forward. Yet I really see small Advantage gained to the general Cause, except Conviction that no Peace can be made with such Mad Men, who idolise a Demagogue one Day, and tear him in Pieces the next. It seems to me that the French are like a Pack of Mongrel Foxhounds, who having once dipped their Jaws in Lamb's Blood - remain incorrigible Sheepkillers for the rest of their Existence, which must be terminated by Hanging - Beating will never cure them. And so poor Astley's pretty Theatre where we met when we met last, is all demolished; - I am really very sorry; And my Lady Bradford wakes from a temporary Suspension of her Faculties to all the Felicity this World can offer - I really am very glad, because you love her. Did you read a staring Tale of some new-discovered Animal in the Newspaper? I asked Pennant our great Naturalist about it, and he showed us a little Drawing of it directly - there was one found near Denbigh many years ago - a Coccus, not a Colossus - but very curious sure enough, and fearfully ugly. Here are fine Rides, and fine Prospects, and a glorious Harvest, and heavenly Weather, but too dry surely; for Jacob writes word that no Rain falls at Streatham Park - I hope our Master will sell his Hay at a fine Price. He was right enough to build in this Country, for never did any Country so agree with him : poor Cecy detests it heartily - who can wonder? here are no Balls, no Beaux, no Spectacles : Make us amends Dear Sir do, and write to us now and then. Your Doctor Thackeray has a great Share of every body's Esteem here, we have not seen him yet, but if my Head Ache and Tinnitus in the Ear continues, which has plagued me cruelly this last Week, I'll consult him; for my Master scorns poor dear Mr. Moore's prescription of an Emetic, though I really believe nothing is better; even though the Complaint should be merely on the Nerves as I partly suspect - the heat is so very relaxing. Adieu! and let's have a Letter from Time to Time from kind Mr. Chappelow, for that will do us all good. So Adieu! and believe / me ever Sir / Your most faithful and Obedient / Servant / H: L: Piozzi. Accept Compliments from my Husband and Daughter.

column46: Denbigh 5: September 1794. Dear Mr. Lysons You are very cruel never to write to us and tell a little news; conscious as you must needs be how welcome a Letter of Chat would be to People in a State of Banishment from the talking World; and shut within these beautiful Mountains with little Idea of any Changes except in the Sky . That has till very lately been sweetly favourable to our Building and our Prospects, but now we fear it is closing in for Rain, to the great Comfort of the few Partridges undestroyed by our Squires within these last four Days. Did Mr. Farringdon ever see this country? I think he would be fond of our View from Brinbella: Mr. Piozzi furnishes his Dining Parlour with Pictures by Cannaletti; we have eight very fine ones: All as you know representing Architecture and Water, a matter of good taste I think - to bring forward in a solitary and distant Retreat some remote Idea of Populous Cities and the busy Hum of Men . But what shall we do with the Places over the Doors - four of them in Fan Mount Shape? What will look well, and look right among our fine Cannalettis? - Nothing on Earth but four original Coloured Drawings of Mr. Farringdon's, representing Old London: - fair August and Father Thames. What Money would pay him I wonder or what Friend persuade him to make us such? - if we should send Measure of the Places they are to fit? You could tell one presently; and now do ask him, and tell us the Result of your Enquiries. Mr. Pennant speaks of you and your Brother with great Regard. He showed me the Drawing from Nature of the nondescript Animal mentioned in the news Papers some Weeks ago - There was one seen at Denbigh. How goes on the Book - and how forward are the Roman Pavements? My Letter can contain nothing but Questions; to which a set of kind Answers will much delight and console / Dear Sir / Yours Sincerely / H: L: Piozzi. My Master and Cecilia are in high Health, and ride out every day. Samuel Lysons Esq. / Temple / London.

column46: Denbigh Friday 19: December 1794. My dearest Girl Che tutto'l Mondo e Paese , is a Truth Mr. Piozzi tells me perpetually, and which your kind Letter of this Morning confirms with particular Exactness - as in those Lines you describe our Life while telling of your own , so that although 300 Miles separate us, we are doing precisely the same things every day, each as the other. A Ride in the fore-part of these fine bright December Afternoons , a Dinner at the End on it: a Game at Casino or Pool at Commerce with Chat among half a Dozen Friends filling up the Evening, and the alternate Sandwiches at Night - is our Course of Existence at Denbigh: and we should vary it a little by dining in Parties when the Moon is good: two, three, and four miles out of Town - was my poor Husband in a Situation to partake such Societies: but Nemesis watched writing that Letter to Sophie, and sent him back to Bed next Day with a complete Relapse; - he is in Bed still: but has done screaming out, and throwing his Cap in the Fire, as Cecy and I say he does always when just at the worst. We are in Mourning for Admiral Cotton now; and shall be whilst we stay here: long and deep Mornings are still indispensable in these remote Regions, where Aristocratic Ideas yet linger in the Minds of Inhabitants who talk much of themselves, and very much of one another: I thought he had contracted his Disorder in Africa, but am persuaded that Dr. Johnson died of repelled Gout - you may remember the Trick he played at Sunninghill, putting his Feet in Cold Water, he never was well after. The Reviewers though lavish in their Praises, do me much wrong in supposing I had any Fragments of his upon Synonymy to consult - the Public has been denied nothing written by him which I possessed, and I never had a Moment's Talk with him on the Subject. You may perhaps recollect Your Father's partiality for Abbey` Girard's Work, when it was in one Volume only; and his tormenting me to read, and commend, and recommend it to you , I have thought a Thousand Times how he would have been pleased with the Performance, but Johnson had never one Thought upon it I'm very sure. Some of my Friends, particularly Mr. Chappelow work themselves up to fancy a new Edition with added Words will be called for; but politics must take a different Turn, if anything but Politics are read this Year I think; and by this Year I mean 1795. Meanwhile I dread nothing so much as Peace with these Enemies of Humankind, while the War - though ruinous - goes forward. We can at least keep them out of our Island by Alien Bills &c. but soon as Hostilities have ceased, we shall have them come up like the Frogs at Touch of Aaron's Wand, into our Houses and the Houses of our Servants ; into our Bed Chambers, into our Ovens, and into our Kneading-Troughs - then for one State Trial you may have forty, and for one Traitor 500 at least. Oh! when our Antagonist is covered with the Itch , let us rather choose to play Quarter Staff with him though stronger; than shake him in a friendly Manner by the Hand . Mean Time you see the Slaves at last are liberated, so the End cannot be very far distant; Lord Moyra will do what Mortal can I am sure; for though little disposed to put my Trust in Armies of late, I do sincerely think that in his Hands the best Cause is in the best Condition; There lives no single Individual in this Land whose Conduct has been so uniformly excellent, or who so entirely possesses the Nation's Confidence - or mine . A matter of exceeding Moment truly. You mention nothing of your Weather at Brighthelmstone, ours has been so generally warm, though turbulent and noisy; that Cecy brought me home a full blown White Rose the last Day She rode to Brinbella, gathered in open Air; rich as to Scent, and bright enough as to Colour. Mrs. Griffithe's Carnations over the way are trained up to Her House Wall indeed, but finer can not be seen even at Florence I am sure in this cold Season of the Year. Count Grimani liked Denbigh Society so well that he has now made us a longer Visit than before, but I cannot get him to admire the Prospect, which I think rather more remarkable than the Company - he says however he never laughed so much in England as he has done since he came into Wales - though I find him a very willing Listener to my Croaking Conversation too. He has seen much of Europe, and has nearly the same Idea of its Duration as myself; but Spain certainly is the next Bubble that breaks. I suppose their King and Queen will run to Naples, when they do run, but where will Marie Caroline go? to escape from that popular fury which was very near setting her on board a Vessel in the Bay and sinking her, had not Miser Fernandino interposed - You should read les Memoirs des Cour D'Italie , you should indeed, Adieu. I am yours / most Affectionately H: L: P. Here's Piozzi writing a long Letter all about himself I doubt not. And the Bishop gone, and no Frank to be had for Love and Money. We all send true Love and Compliments to the Dears. Miss Thrale / Brighthelmstone / Sussex.

column46: Denbigh 14: March 1795. A Thousand Thanks Dear Mr. Lysons for your kind and speedy Execution of my saucy Commands to your Brother: The packet lay at Liverpool by Accident or Neglect, so that I have but just got and read it. Oh Heavens! what a Hash it is of Folly, Blasphemy, and Treason! My very Blood rises at the Thoughts of a Member in the House of Commons abetting so horrible a Performance - and I really do think that if Opposition scruples not to support its Cause by means so criminally desperate - it is the most abandoned of all Oppositions whatever. Mr. Daniel Lysons told me that Brothers rested the Truth of his Mission upon the coming of the Princess Caroline, yet can I not find her Name - perhaps it was in his first Publication. Do me the favour to write word what they do with the Man, and whether he is to baffle them as Mess: Hardy and Joyce did. I expect so. The Rumour of Peace reaches even this distant Region - is there any Ground for it? I have been reading Darwin's Zoonomia and very entertaining it is; but his Notion of the Plants possessing not only Sensation, but Sensibility seems more fanciful than Philosophical. - He says they have sometimes sad, sometimes agreeable Dreams ; our poor Rosebushes at Streatham Park though, never dreamt of such a Winter as they have been enduring. I wonder if they ever dream of Mr. Buchetti who used to follow my Master's Scissors with a Basket: he writes us word from Milan that Italy is metamorphosed into Siberia this Year, but if tic Anno Mundi 1914, we will not wonder at the Surprising Things exhibited. Tell me what they mean by saying so, it is a new Idea of Calculation, and forwards Matters very strangely: Old Isaacson's Chronology though faulty, is surely nearer than this . Apropo`s if you ever see that Book upon a Stall, do buy it me. I think little of the Shakespeare MS. and believe that Jest will be dead before we get home, where I really hope to find myself and you about the 20th of next Month. Dear Sweet Siddons will be going to Scotland by that Time I suppose, or going somewhere, and I shall have scarce any of her Company. Keep well yourself my good Sir, and give my truest Thanks and Compliments to your Brother, and which ever of you have least upon your hands - write the next Letter to her who is very sincerely both His and your / faithful Humble Servant / H: L: Piozzi. Our Friend and Philosopher Mr. Lloyd of Wygfair - pronounce Wickwor , always enquires very kindly after you; he is a very learned and a very pleasing Man. If you see Miss Thrales, tell them we are alive, and coming to Streatham after Easter. Here is Snow again, but it will not lie long as the Sun has too much power now. Surely Things will grow less unseasonably dear round London in April - sure they will - but I fear short Harvests must follow the Frosts and the Floods, and if they do - it will be a dismal Business - Adieu! Samuel Lysons Esq / Temple / No. 2 / London.

column46: Denbigh Monday 30: March 1795. My dear Mr. Chappelow's costly Correspondence with Mrs. Piozzi is not yet near an End - here is another Letter; I am so afraid that you should hear from anybody but ourselves - that Cecy has a Mind to be married. It is so however, the Gentleman's Character, Family, and Person unexceptionable, but his Fortune as certainly below what She might reasonably expect, and below what the Chancellor will insist upon for her I suppose. For what care professional Men about maternal Feelings you know? and why should Lord Loughborough be influenced in Favour of Mr. Mostyn as I am influenced? because he is handsome, or because he is good, or because he is Grandson to my Father's particular Friend, and last of an honourable ancient and Aristocrat Family! All these Reasons are prettier in Wales than London , where a Title , a Wit , or a Beau alone attract Notice, and where a good old Estate of two Thousand Pounds o'Year, may be easily disposed of in a Winter's - nay in an Evening's Frolic. You have however added to my conviction that a good Husband is a Woman's best Friend, by your Account of charming Lady Bradford: it is a very interesting one: I hope She gains ground upon her Illness every day, and what She does gain now , She will lose no more. Let us see you to Dinner on Tuesday the 14th of April, pray do ; and let me tell you some of my Hopes and Fears for a Boy and Girl just beginning the World when that World is in a most terrifying Situation indeed. Will the Prince marry? And must we pay his Debts? Or what is to be done? Things grow tremendously dear in every Place, and the Smithfield Butchers have found the Way down hither and buy up our Bullocks alive. How are we to get out of these Difficulties? Tell us what you know, and tell what you hear of my fair Damsels in Portman Street, and how they will like Dancing Barefoot &c. Mean time and ever believe me Dear Sir most faithfully Yours / H: L: Piozzi. Our Master is as much delighted I think as if he were the Missey's Papa. He is gone to settle the Building of six little Almshouses for turned out Cottagers. Adieu! Let's hear how Lord Fitzwilliams is received in London - and say nothing of Edwy and Elgiva - I have heard how that went. Kemble is restored to the favour of your virtuous Town I hear, and in Cumberlands new Comedy has learned like the fallen Angels in Milton - To take with Ravishment The thronging Audience. Rev: Mr. Chappelow / No. 12 / Hill Street / Berkeley Square / London.

Denbigh - 3: April Good Friday Night. After our Morning's Devotions, Maigre Dinner &c. I was just sitting down to write my dearest Girl a long Letter, while Cecilia fulfilled her Promise of drinking Tea with the Miss Moors at our next door; but going upstairs for this large Paper, my Maid met me with a domestic Distress about the Groom's being Suddenly carried to Prison in our virtuous City of Denbigh for having committed Claudio's Offence in Shakespear's Measure for Measure - before I began then to chat with you, I prefaced a Tale to Mr. Piozzi - with "Bad News to hear" - and whilst the Words were in my Lips, In burst Cecilia, crying "Don't be too much frightened - the House is on Fire:" seeing me sit still and look astonished I suppose - She repeated - " this House, this House"; run, run, and escaped into the Street, whither I followed her , and my Dogs followed me . The Crowd parted us instantly however; and I, snatching Floe and Phillis one under each Arm, took refuge with the agreeable Widow Lady Mrs. - whom I have mentioned to you before, and Disturbed her Te`te a Te`te with L'Amant Favori . From her Back Windows I saw our Flames blazing away, and certain that Mr. Piozzi would save all he could for us, I took Doctor Thackeray's Advice, and a Glass of Cold Water, and sate still ; while my active Titmouse was out and in forty Times I believe - all is extinguished now thanks be to God, and our dear good natured Neighbours, who were literally willing to go through Fire for us, it is plain. So here is an Incident ay and a bright one too, as you would have said had you seen the illumination it made; but though they threw the Things about so, nothing has been lost or spoiled; and the Sun was scarce down when our Uproar commenced, So that Help came immediately. Enough of this Vexation . The Day before Yesterday, Wednesday the 1st: of April, we made a little party to take leave of Brinbella for the Spring and Summer Months - and as we returned home in the Evening found that it had been really all Fools day at Denbigh, where my Friend the Philosopher - as we call Mr. Lloyd of Wickwor, was disturbed and impeded in his Duty as a Magistrate, by the Sudden Entrance of 300 Men armed with Bludgeons into the Town; - a Mob collected from many Miles distance: and headed by a Fellow who in their own Language echoed the Sentiments of Payne and his Jacobin Crew, holding the Horse all the Time, and threatening Death to whoever dared levy Seamen or Militia Men here . Mrs. Clough - Sister to the Surrounded Gentleman - seeing his Distress - sent a Boy for her Husband and her Husband's Brother, but he - delivering his Message awkwardly, then came unarmed, and undefended; and were two more Justices disgraced baffled and insulted in the grossest Manner - whilst our too peaceful Neighbours only wrung their Hands, and cried in their pathetic Welch Way Alas! Alas! our own dear Masters! Alas! Alas! the Esquire of Eriviatte! - meaning Mr. Butler Clough who is almost adored here - and though the Rascals who had excited these Madmen from the Mountains tried to instigate them also to affront the three imprisoned Gentlemen, nothing could they persuade them to join in any such Cause: and happy was it that the Insults were confined to Words only; had one Blow been struck, the Town would have risen on the Rioters, and God only knows how many Lives would have been lost. The Ringleader is marked, and I hear is well known as a Correspondent of Thelwall's who figured away among the seditious Fools in London; He talked the true Language of Democracy - said much to Mr. Lloyd: You have worn Boots and we have worn wooden Shoes long enough now - try how you like the Exchange: and they had Women amongst them with long Knives, with which one of them attempted to cut off the Tail of a beautiful Horse rode by the Philosopher, which nothing but his Coolness and Intrepidity could have prevented. We are now to have Soldiers in the Town, and it is the best way; for these Fellows threatened to go and stop the Corn Ships at Rhydlan, but either repented or thought they had done enough. We think there were not above a Dozen Agitators in the whole - most of them when asked what they came here for? could give no Account at all, only said - "We come o'Mobbing:" or "These honest Men advised us to come along with them." and such Stuff Here is the real and true and exact History of our Denbigh Riot, of which you will hear a hundred false Narrations - but this is Sure to be Authentic. They had the regular Cant of abusing the Clergy - and said to Mr. Mostyn - (not Cecy's Mr. Mostyn - He was with us at Brinbella -) "You Parsons take all from us Poor." They paid some little Respect however to Mr. Clough of Eriviatte, though he is in Orders: but his Brother Mr. Thomas Clough, they threated to broil upon the Coals, and even talked of pulling his Country Seat to the Ground. - On Wednesday it is supposed there will be another Trial of Skill between Law and Licentiousness - between Decency and Delirium - on that Day however we beat our March towards Streatham Park, where I hope soon Personally to tell all my dear Girls that I am their ever / Affectionate Mother H: L: Piozzi. Proper Loves, Compliments &c. Miss Thrale / No. 22. Portman Street / Portman Square / London / Single Sheet.

column46: Streatham Park Monday 18: May 1795. My very kind and wise and worthy Friend Mr. Ray will be less Surprised than another Man would be, to hear that our dear Cecilia and her amiable Sweetheart are the very Plagues of my Life. They will be married, Yes - Oh yes, they will be married before he comes of Age now , they protest they will: and for an admirable Reason; just because Mr. Mostyn can't make Settlement when he is of Age they have found out - till his Estate now entailed on Children, has suffered a Recovery, and this will take up I know not how much Time, and our Lovers are impatient. This however is not all, they will have my Consent, or they will marry without it they say, - and so I lead a sad Life, for no Consent shall they have from me, till You say I had better do so then Suffer worse : and till Mr. Mostyn has signed an Instrument of Honour, declaring his solemn and sacred Intentions to fulfil the Engagement we require, when he comes of Age; faithfully promising to make such provision for my Child as we agreed on, and which must be specified in the Agreement drawn up and signed by Him. If after these Precautions You will say - not as a Lawyer, but as a Friend, that you advise me to tease them and myself no longer; - I will consent ; the more readily if Mr. Mostyn can prevail on his Mother and Mr. Wynn her Husband, just to sign their Names also to the Promise as Guarantees - a Suggestion of Mr. Piozzi's on hearing I believe that some Blame, from some Quarter would follow my consenting to a Marriage with a Young Gentleman however graced with good Qualities - if he were under Age. When my Heart is however strengthened by the non professional but friendly Advice of Mr. Vandercom, whose Honour and Abilities you have heard me speak highly of - and above all, Your own : They shall have no more Torment from their truly Affectionate Mother, and from Dear Mr. Ray's / ever Obliged and Faithful Servant / H: L: Piozzi.

column46: Streatham Park 22: June 1795. My dear Mr. Mostyn will easily imagine with what pleasure I read Mr. Wine's Obliging letter, and the charming account of your Denbigh Frolics to Maria Siddons. Everybody seems happy in our Cecilia's open and decided choice: even Mr. Cator said somewhere he was heartily glad that the young lady had disposed of herself as well. Mr. Piozzi is obliged by your polite remembrances and wishes you would be kind enough to beg Shackfield to undertake the pacifying Mr. Pennant, and the transacting our Exchange of Property with Sir Edward Lloyd; likewise the hastening of Mr. Thomas Lloyd's Accounts hither as early as possible. We cannot get Mead away from London or its Environs, though he is eternally at the Eve of his departure. I wish we knew how far Brynbella was advanced. It must have made a pretty show illuminated. Poor John Mostyn durst not be merry I suppose for fear of disobliging his Uncle and Aunt. Somebody told me there were in a Chester paper lately very rough Censures of their behaviour towards him , which possibly have contributed to sour the Rector's temper but it was his Play to have given money to the Ringers himself , and have appeared at least to approve what he could not prevent - They will make everybody hate them this way. - Did Squire Jones behave good-naturedly? I dare say he did. Give my love to your Wife and tell her that Lord and Lady W's Divorce Papers had passed through the first Court but are now called in, the Reconciliation has completely taken place, and we are to say , it was all a Lye : Nobody is sorry for this but the Civilians. Jacob carried a World of things for Mrs. Mostyn and you to London in the cart this morning. Ask her if you please what she would have done with her few Books ? And let her know that Charlotte Hughes has written very kindly. I see no Summer yet but we live in hopes; The immense quantity of Corn captured will however keep Famine at a distance this year; what becomes of your Regiment I wonder? My Daughters were very jealous about your going that Day you took a longer Journey I remember, but we have never talked on it since. It is Sophia's Birthday but I warrant her Sister will forget that among her Felicities at home. Assure yourself my Dear Sir and convince Cecilia, that home is the only seat of true Happiness. The Duke of York has found that out at last, and leaving his Clubs and riotous Companions, now sits whole Days with his amiable Duchess reading to her or playing small games in her little Societies to amuse her when indisposed and unable to go out upon her charitable visits in the neighbourhood. Make our best Loves and Compliments my dear Sir, where they will be best accepted; and thank your Mama and Sister a thousand times for their kindness to my sweet Cecilia and their politeness / to your ever Affectionate and Obliged / H: L: Piozzi. John Meredith Mostyn Esq. / Llewesog Lodge / near Denbigh / N. Wales.

column46: Streatham Park 24: July 1795. Why do you never write Dear Mr. Chappelow? I have a sad Loss in not receiving your cheerful charming Letters. Cecilia has been married and gone from Us these six Weeks - I think She ran away the very Night I wrote last, but her Husband is very good, and She is very happy, and What more can be wished? It is to Individuals one must look for Felicity, public Matters have I think a melancholy Aspect while we live only by rapine like the wild Arabs, and subsist but on the Corn which being strongest at Sea we seize from our hungry Neighbours, and carry home to our own Den - as Beasts and Birds of Prey do. Tell me something consoling from the Country concerning the hopes of a good Harvest after all this Starvation; and tell that the People are in better humour since my Lord Bridport has locked up all the French Ships in L'Orient, and keeps the Key in his Pocket. All our Indiamen arriving Safe is a vast Thing, and the Escape of Cornwallis's Fleet equal in my Mind to the famous Retreat of Xenophon and his Ten Thousand. Let all this comfort us for eating Bread at a Shilling the Quart Loaf. Letters from Wales speak of great Scarcity and advanced Prices there too; we shall see how that Matter stands in six or seven Weeks more, pray write long before then and say You have not forgotten us. Mr. Murphy and Mr. Jones compose our Household, the young Siddonses supply Mrs. Mostyn's Loss with Light hearts and merry Faces, but I hope for a Sight of their dear Mother before we leave Surrey. Some Offers have been made us of taking Streatham Park, and once we thought of bidding it a long Adieu : but Mr. Piozzi cannot bear to sell his Wife's Life somehow; so we shall shut it up, and at least suffer the Gardens to be no Expense. Our poor Park would not pay mowing this year, so we grazed it, and have got a clear 100£ already - The Sheep are yet to turn in: I shall expect to hear from you that next Summer the Crop will be magnificent after such good Farming; One Load of old Hay fetched us six Guineas, the rest was fetched off the Premises without Expense on our Parts, at four pounds six. I make it a Rule to write Sums of Money in Letters when I would be exact, because in Figures Mistakes are much more easily made. Adieu Dear Sir, The Fur Tippets, warm Fires and frosty Nights which lasted till the 15th of July this dismal Sunless Summer of 1795 - are over now - let the Warmth which at last seems in some Measure to affect all Nature a little dispose your ever kind heart to the Recollection of old Friends, and particularly of / Your ever sincerely / Obliged Servant / H: L: Piozzi. -

column46: Streatham Park Tuesday September 8: 1795. I thank you for your Letter dearest Love, and am glad you are got safe and well to Cheltenham after all your Adventures; we set forward on our Journey the Day after tomorrow, and my Master is employed in packing, while Mr. Macnamara invites us to dine at his House every day, and save the Trouble to Servants here at home - where Mr. Murphy helps us off with agreeable Stories in the Evening, but swears - and truly enough - that whether he talks of Business or of Literature, my absent Head is all upon poor Floe. Nothing however subdues his high Sense of Honour, and Austrian steady Courage, though one pretty Eye has been almost laid bare with the Scalding Water on its Lids, and both Ears are in a most putrid Condition now, and far beyond the Power of Steers's Opodeldoc: had that been applied directly, it might have prevented Suppuration, but at present nothing but Ointments can be used I believe. He licks my Hand all Day and acknowledges my Attentions so prettily! If the erecting Muscles of the Ear are not destroyed, some Beauty may be saved, and Jacob assures me that Life is in no immediate Danger, though a Gangrene will be avoided with Difficulty. Lady Tuite has my true Condolence, but her Favourite's Accident being less out of the common Course of Things than ours , Her Risque is less; it is strictly in Nature that such Animals should run their Chance : and I think that little Dear will do well, though Mrs. Siddons lost a small Spaniel the same way two Years ago. I respect Crop's good Sense of all Things. Mrs. Mostyn will probably give us the meeting at Chester and join in Lamentations for Fizz. You really will have seen almost all that our little Island can show, and I hope will like Wales after all, North Wales, - we are very jealous of the Vale of Montgomery. Dear Louis seize ! If you have a Mind to cry any more over his Misfortunes, read the 2d Vol. of the Life of Dumourier. The present King of France wrote his own Proclamation - as like a Statue as we saw that Man look in the Year 1774, there was a great Character under the Block - it has been chizzeled out by the repeated Strokes of Calamity. He behaves with infinite Propriety - and I find his manner of addressing the Passions - incomparable. Chance threw me One Morning lately into Company of the Marquis de Bouilli` . We had a charming Conversation, and parted mutually pleased with each other. Paris is on the Eve of a prodigious Explosion to be sure, if once the Army and the People quarrel. - Hope may again be kindled. - Of this Truth I am perfectly persuaded, that unless Monarchy is restored in France, there will be no Sovereignty or Subordination in any Part of Europe within a Dozen or fifteen Years. My Heart tells me Venice will longest resist the Torrent of Democracy - Noman shall be the last I will devour as Polypheme says; and by playing the part of Noman thus, they possibly may be neglected till other Pictures are shifted off the Magic Lantern - and so be left to the End. Meanwhile mon Parti est pris , I'll put in for one of the earliest Guillotines, and go with my old Acquaintance Burke and Murphy - unless they leave me in the Lurch, which I scarce expect from them : Every day shows that no Death is as pleasant, as easy, or as honourable: among all those who have endured it in France, not one behaved amiss Man or Woman, except Madame du Barry and Custine. Adieu! for a short Time, and we shall all meet soon please God - at pretty Brinbella. How proud will Mr. Piozzi be to show it you! Give true Love to the Lady Birds, and say how happy their Company and yours will make your ever Affectionate Mother / H: L: Piozzi. Miss Thrale / near the Church / Cheltenham / Glocestershire.

Brynbella Wensday Passion Week I was just sitting down to say that I had not read Burke's Book my dearest Girl - nor was likely to read it, because the Parcel from Streatham Park never came - when I received your second Letter with the Account of old Jacob's arbitrary Proceedings. - He is most unseasonably as well as unreasonably Despotic, but I have written to request my Things, and bid him call on you, and tell how I meditate the sending you some Welch Mutton of the Sort you like. Mrs. Broadhead thinks She has got me a Housekeeper, and whatever you send I am sure I shall be pleased with: The true old Rum above all. I hate a fine Book and a famous Edition a little more every Year than other: You would laugh to see my Anguish about Mrs. Heaton's beautiful Infidel Gibbon - lest a Spot of Ink should penetrate the Papers I have wrapped him in, and make him black on the Outside . The Earthquake made no Impression I dare say beyond those who Actually felt it. Political Concussions are so frequent now, and so feared those of the natural World are scarce regarded; but when we meet we will have some Talk of that, and other Matters too, which fill my Head but can not be conveyed in a Letter half as cleverly as were those verses which I'm glad you liked. Lysons used to repeat a droll Dialogue that I did not write, between Mr. Hayley and Miss Seward; ask him for it. His mutilated Statues and tesserated or tessellated Pavements, will at worst be genuine; but Ireland's Forgeries excite the just Contempt of all but Erskine, who I understand is Counsel for the Delinquent as usual. - See what the Jury says at Drury Lane. Poor dear sweet Siddons has neither the Health nor the happiness her Talents and Virtues and Beauty deserve - but Floretta could only be made lovely by the Fountain in Johnson's Tale I remember. - The Fairy could not make her beloved : and the Public is in no fault with respect to Her . It is however a great Proof of dissolute Manners that the Women of Fashion dress in the Way you speak of - They dared not do so twenty years ago. I fancy the Woman Sir William Hamilton married who showed Postures - dressed in two Shoals which She wrapped round her; one Minute like the Niobe of Florence, one Moment like the Vatican Melpomene &c. was the Original Inventress of these Pranks; but cutting the Hair short behind is like nothing but the Ladies who cropped their Heads at the Siege of Aquileia to make Twine &c. and set up a figure of Venus the bald to commemorate their Spirit of Patriotism. - The Story is not in Calvus . Do you hear any Hopes or Fears for a new Tragedy called Almeyda which I see advertised? It is written by Sophia Lee of Bath, not Harriet; who contributes Prologue and Epilogue alone. My heavy Work chains me down from any Frolic of Fancy - Poor Mr. Greatheed's Regent always meets with something to strike it in, whenever it comes out I think; Mrs. Siddons's swelled Face sent it back this year She says. Make Susan tell if Mrs. Greatheed and She meet at the usual Haunts - in a fever of Spirits at four o'Clock in the Morning was her Expression; and pray mention whether the inordinate Price of Provisions &c. has any visible Effect as to thinning the Numbers in London, which Mr. Chappelow represented to us as in real Distress - like a besieged Town he said it looked. Here is the Equinox come without the Storm I predicted, yet a large Halo surrounded the Moon two Nights ago. If the Fleet can get to the West Indies before Change of Wind, Sugars at least must necessarily fall in their Price, but Taxes do increase in a dreadful Manner - Poor little Tommy must be paid for now. I thought dear Floe was taking Leave of his Friends the other Day, he had a terrible Attack indeed - something of a Fit - succeeded by breakings out upon the Back which I think saved his Life - but as Mrs. Mostyn said when She was a Baby - "The Dog never had good Health." I shall advise her to set Tinker at the Tax Collector when he comes into the Country. Her Cold is better I trust, for my Husband met her Husband at a Dinner given yesterday by the Officers at Denbigh; but the Monkey never comes near me: - I fancy you will see her first. - Mr. Piozzi says he is well, and he knows best; but I think He limps a little. Sophia must acknowledge herself behind hand in Correspondence, but I really do not wonder. She has a great deal upon her Hands - and so have I, if you knew all. - It is much my Wonder what you would think of my new Undertaking? I think that Wit's Work done by a Scholar, never pleases the Public; but that Scholar's Work done by a Wit, always pleases. - Farewell Dear Love, and write very often, it is a great Comfort / to Your H: L: P. If I send you some very curious Fish - do you think they will come Sweet? by a Mail Coach - Yes; but how will they get from the Inn to Portman Square? Miss Thrale / 22 Portman Street / Portman Square / London.
