column46: Beaumaris. Sunday. 10 July 1796. My Dearest Girl There is a passionate Love Letter in the Spectator beginning with Madam - I beg leave that my Paper is not finer : I felt myself inclined to make excuses for mine - but thinking of that , stopped my Hand. Last Night came the Valuables; I shall make Mr. Piozzi wear the Stockings for me, and once washed, they will not be too large for me I dare say. Prunes are a most useful Store, there is no living without them. If the Master of the Troop is able to move - we shall transport our Baggage homewards the straightest way , on Friday next, and think no more of Jaunting for this Summer. I never saw so bad a Bathing Place, the Tide recedes so, there is no dipping but just at high Water; the strong Current which sets in to our little Menai Straight, has so much Power you would wonder, it makes quite an Eddy in one Place near Lord Uxbridge's. Sophia loves an Elemental Wonder, has She been to see the Stone which fell from the Atmosphere in the great Storm last Christmas? - It fell in Yorkshire, but may be seen now in Piccadilly, No. 2 opposite to the Gloucester Coffeehouse, with the Attestations and Affidavits of Clergymen and Gentlemen of acknowledged Character and Property who saw it fall at Noon Day as I remember, but if You call at the Place they'll give Your Curiosity Satisfaction - Mr. Topham to whom it belongs is a Man well known in his Circle: do dear Love make me hear all about it for even the Beaumaris People are beforehand with me in Intelligence. We are impatient for News from Italy, and Mr. Piozzi is firmly persuaded that Buonaparte will find his Domus ultima among the Lombard Territories and penetrate no farther. Could one but get a List of the Names he has sent Prisoners to Paris - one should be so glad. I am really apprehensive we have Acquaintance if not Friends among them. And poor Sir Sydney Smith! when will he come back! These are interesting and critical Moments - sure. I dote on the charming Arch Duchess at Inspruck. - She was a Demi Recluse when I was there, and better beloved than any of the hapless house of Austria: they said she was handsome too, but I always thought Marie Christine who governed Brabant then - the most majestic Beauty among them all. When comes out Camilla? I hope my Name is upon the List of the Two Thousand we are told of, but which I think scarce can be true. It is the fashion to lament the Fate of Monsieur de La Fayette - but I suppose he and his friend D'Arblaye are of the same Feather. I am ready to exclaim with poor old King Lear in the Tragedy - "A Plague upon you Traitors all." Our Attorney General however seems to follow up these Disseminators of Blasphemy and Treason pretty well - There is another of them caught now I see, beside the Wretch that compiled that horrid Political Dictionary. Is Merry's new Poem pretty? Cecilia's Mr. Rogers wrote the Pleasures of Memory if you recollect - and very elegant Verses they were too: I should expect some sweet Poetry on this Subject from the Author of Pauline. - It is not exactly what pleases you I know; who have the Vraye and the Solide always before you; and I will confess that Pope's Epistles, Bosh's Lessons, and Vandyke's Portraits do leave a fullness in the Mind as a good Madeira does in the Mouth, while Charlotte Smith's Sonnets, and Giornovichi's Sonatas, and Angelico's Paintings carry off our Admiration for the Moment like Mr. Macnamara's fine French Wines. So Farewell and send me a Budget full of Chat directed to Brinbella where I hope to sleep next Saturday night. Till then and ever / Yours most Affectionately H: L: P. Here comes the Newspaper: why now you see the Things do fall out (as Bottom the Weaver says) pat as I told you . Tom Paine's Book is advertised with Bishop Watson's Candid Opinion about Truth and Reason and I know not what - by way of Justification and Increase of its Sale. Did not I say it was nonsense to strike soft in a Battle? Pray who did Sir Godfrey Webster marry? If ever I knew, I have forgot. Miss Thrale / No. 22. - / Portman Street / Portman Square / London.

My dearest Girl - Enclosed you will have quite an Essay on the present State of Religion and Politics - to which I refer you, and upon this Sheet of Paper, Talk we of young Master Launcelot. I am too sorry for your Misfortunes with the favourite Animals, and most sympathising Sorrow is mine. Jacob lost my poor honest old Browney Fox upon the Road bringing down those Horses which we bought of Mr. Pollard last Summer, and were cheated in: and went to Law about, and were cast, and have all the Costs to pay, and the standing of the Beasts at Living 8 Months, - and now the best of them is expiring - and for about 300£ Money spent, we shall have one unsound Carthorse. And that Dear Dog, that I would trust with nobody but Jacob lost besides. So you have Company in your Quadrupedal Afflictions. There is nobody to blame however, Browney was lost in a Fog one of these misty Mornings which precede unexampled Heat and Prance is only dying of Fever and Weight and Work and long Journey and change of Air all which combine to kill him. There are Numbers of People dying every Day and every where; a handsome Doctor Campbell who I think you must remember - among the rest. - He was a tall stout Scotsman who had lived in Ireland till he had obtained their Accent added to his own; - speaking of some large Man (Bruce of Abyssinia I believe) indeed now Sir and upon my honour - says he to Dr. Johnson - I am but a Twitter to him. Do you remember our laughing? The last time Mr. Piozzi and I were at Bath he visited us, and reminded me of the Story; he was a fine Figure even then , and had engaged to give the Town a Life of Dr. Goldsmith; and asked me for Anecdotes. - Poor Campbell! Another Man too, Mr. Old of Seighford in Staffordshire; Father to the beautiful Miss Old of whom you have often heard me speak: She was out of her Nymph State, no Aurelia , but a full-winged Butterfly - when Lord Ferrers was tried for Murder: her old Pappy is just now dead Aged 92. What a deal he must have seen and heard! But I fancy he looked at scarcely anything except his Daughter Kitty - I hear She is Kitty still. But what are private Deaths? A Report is Come down here among us - that Paris is in an Uproar, and that a grand Massacre is going on there. A City Letter told me so today. Here I break off! Because we have not plagues enough. Dear, kind, sweet Mrs. Bertie sends me in this Minute 9 o'Clock at Night Saturday 23: her Team with our Things from Chester - and at our Door in Manchester Square here, drops me down one of her Horses ; ay, and he will die too, and we are all hands to work between the two dying Beasts. And what shall I do? We are all half frantic. Add to this that Mr. Bertie has taken to his Bed for Grief on account of Dr. Wenman - his Cousin's Death; they were Schoolfellows, and Playfellows, and intimates, and the whole Family as every one knows distressed with irritable Nerves and a too easily-kindled Imagination, and poor Mrs. Bertie has her Hands full. The Things you bought me are not come yet, but they will come; and I am really very sensible of your obliging Care, and Kindness, - but last Night I recollected the Steers' Opadeldoc, how that was always forgotten - which we used to talk of so - and I should have used it to Prance the Paralytic Horse. After Tragedy comes Epilogue however; the Beasts are both alive and mending o'Sunday - and I shall not hang myself in a Rope behind the Stable Door. What the Mare suffered was to me beyond all Things I ever saw; and Mr. Piozzi has this Instant discovered the Cause of Prince's sudden Seizure - we put him (heated with his Journey) into a new Stable unaired, and just plastering - and killed, or nearly killed the poor Creature by our own faults - he is now grazing under my Window, and seems remotely disposed to recover Life and Limbs. Adieu then, and when you can bear to read no more, burn the Letters of your truly Affectionate / H: L: P.

column46: Brynbella. Tuesday. 25: October 1796. My dearest Child Your sweet Letter came a Day or two ago, when I could not keep my Fingers steady to answer it from Indignation, I think more than even Grief. - They are now quieter, and I will answer it; and then tell why, and at whom I am so angry. Peace if a separate one will not be a good but a dreadful Thing; and it is a separate Peace the French are trying for: hoping to make Great Britain desert her Allies, and suffer them , to ravage Italy without molestation. To this Event many Causes seem to cooperate: the Desire of our Merchants and Traders for Peace almost on any Terms; the Terror of Opposition Clamours should a tempting Offer be refused - and the supineness of those Italian States who are as willing to shut their Ports against us who defend, as against the French who attack them. When I asked a Gentleman once for Directions how to avoid sinking in deep Water - Do so , said he, and moved his forefinger only. If either the Venetian or Tuscan Governments could be prevailed on only to Do so - they might even yet swim. Arch Duke Charles who I am proud to say has often pulled off his Hat to me in the Boboli Gardens at Florence, is indeed a Hero; he was you see however just permitted to save hereditary Dominions , not go further. The Old Black Eagle is to be plucked. There will be no more Caesar I believe, no more Pope after the year 1800 - no more King of the Romans - it is over. So much for Politics - if we refuse Peace Invasion is preparing - no matter! I will tell you my Conjectures concerning that Measure, another Day. Your Literary Questions claim a Word before I begin talking on the Only Thing I am thinking about. I really do like Camilla: The whole of Mrs. Berlinton and Mr. Bellamy and his Death, and dear Eugenia's Conduct is incomparable. I fancy You are answerable for the grand Fault in the Book - its Author knew You to be so wise and so good at 15 Years old that She has given her Heroine a Steadiness of Thought and Dignity of Mind wholly different from that of other Children at so early an Age - and the World cries Unnatural Stuff! But it is said justly enough that one Individual is no Pattern of a Species - Madame D'Arblaye should study Linnaeus. The Taste in this Country is altered since She wrote last - People are tired of Figures in just proportion, some going to Court, some crying Fish, moving across a Camera Obscure in St. James's Street; They want Giants again and Dragons, and with Respect for the German Valour, there is stolen in a revived Liking for Runes and Scaldic Imagery, - from the same Country. Have you read Lenore in the Original? It must be very striking in its own Language, I shuddered over a mean Translation of it. There is a mighty impressive Copy of Verses too in the Gentleman's Magazine for last Month, September 1796 - read them to Sophie and see how She will change Colour. It begins thus "A Warrior so brave and a Lady so bright." I have bid Robson send me Doctor Moore's new Novel - which I hope we shall discuss together in or near Town early next Year. God preserve Your Health and Mr. Piozzi's from calling us to the halfway house, Bath. If a smart shock upon the Nerves cannot be cured by Cold Water at home, tic most likely I may want Assistance from Warm , but I know not how long that Spring would be in washing my Welsh Blood from the Choler that is now fermenting in it. Mason - the maid that waits upon Cecilia - is big with Child, and all the Country says it is by her Master; and our unfashionable Neighbours cry Shame - and Cecy laughs and says - it is the Way , and what signifies making a Bustle about nothing? I have however with some Difficulty obtained a Promise from her Lady that She shall be discharged . You will wonder how I dared mention such Matters to a Person who keeps me at such an immeasureable Distance as Mrs. Mostyn has done ever since You left us: but this Neighbourhood is so very unlike the Vicinage of London, and the People's Notions of Right and Wrong so much more narrow as the Phrase is - and so much more Correspondent to my own; that after hearing these Infamita` repeated in my Ears by every Creature round me for a whole fortnight: and after being told that Cecilia - who scarce speaks to me even in a formal Way once a Quarter - proposed taking up her Abode here at Brynbella while her favourite Servant lay in by her Husband - I watched My Opportunity and yesterday She rode up to the Door, her Groom carrying a large Bundle - when She told Mr. Piozzi and I that John was called to Dover by his Mother whose Husband Mr. Wynn of Llewessog lay dying there with his Regiment; and that Mason was going to buy her some little Things at Liverpool - for which Reason She would spend some Time with us if we pleased. "Nothing could be more desirable," was the Reply - and when we were alone I communicated to her the Scandalous Reports of her Maid's Pregnancy, and the Shame of Keeping such a Hussy in her House - She heard me negligently - expressed her Weariness of the Tale - looked into an old Annual Register as we talked, or rather as I talked, for She said little, till I observed that Mr. Mostyn never called here, and I suppose says I he stays away for Shame. She then looked off the Book, and at me, with much Amazement. For Shame! said She - why what is there to be ashamed of? I suppose he is not the first Man who has got a Pretty Girl with Child - and so ran over a String of fashionable People of whom I never heard; that lead the same Lives. But Place makes a great Difference as I had the honour to tell her; for the Man who keeps a Mistress in Titchfield Street unknown to his Wife after a Dozen Years living together, is a far less Impudent Fellow than he who in a quiet-Christian-like Country sets all the Neighbours staring by Proofs of Intimacy with his Lady's Female Attendant, That Lady but 19 years old and but 19 Months married. What a Blessing her Fortune has not been paid into the hands of such a Man!!! The little Power I have shall be exerted he may assure himself, to keep it long out of his Reach. Adieu! Present My Regards with Mr. Piozzi's Baisemains to the Lady-Loves. I hear all good of Sophia's intended Marriage, and wish her all possible happiness, being ever / her's and dear Susette's and Your own / Affectionate Mother / H: L: Piozzi. Miss Thrale / Mount Ephraim / Tunbridge Wells / Kent.

column46: Brynbella 5: November 1796. Dear Mr. Chappelow I am sorry for the Cause of your long Silence - and heartily rejoiced that it is removed at last - Dover's Powders may be called a rough Remedy - I wonder why James's might not have answered as well - the Ipecacuanha triturated with opium is only raising an artificial Contest between Sickness and Sleep; and drives out in Consequence of that Distress, an Immense Dew upon the Surface - He who takes such Medicine deserves to be well. We must all be stung with Nettles in some sense or other: Cecilia and her Husband are My Urticaria; - find Mr. Murphy and tell him I say so, and he will explain all the rest. - "I shall not be surprised" - (say you immediately) "at anything he can tell." Yes, yes, but you will be surprised, and the more for the sparring Scenes you saw. Oh! but you are at Roydon, and he at London; I forgot that. Why then sure enough Cecy's Maid is Mr. Mostyn's Mistress, and is gone away big with Child; and when I inveighed against such Conduct Cecy says it is the Fashion , and the Way , and every body does so in London - and whore's the harm? She don't care a Pin about the matter She told My Servant who waited on her Toilette when Mason went first away - and what does Mrs. Piozzi trouble her Head about such Stuff for? My Caresses and Lamentations only disgusted her, and She is run for Refuge from them to her Husband's Relations, who will be happy to catch her in this Humour, and when they have got all the Money among them - will turn her out to starve. But if I have a Spark of Influence or Authority, I will get all the Money paid into the Accountant General's Hands, put her into Protection of Chancery - and save her from herself if possible. Hers is a generous Affection indeed, Love without Jealousy, and Tranquillity without Reflection; She and the Man between them have persuaded Miss Thrales too to give up their Chance of her 40000£ if She dies under Age - for the sake of throwing all into his Hands, and then they quit Segroid - and enter upon genteel Life . A pretty Scheme for producing Sin and Sorrow; but I will render it abortive if possible, and with Lord Loughboro's Help secure her a good Settlement and separate Maintenance - against her Mind may change . Let us now talk of something else. The Mr. Brand you speak of I suspect to be Author of a Book on popular Superstitions, very entertaining and pretty: his new Treatise on Associations Has not been yet advertised. Burke's Spirit-stirring Pamphlet on the Peace beats the General in our Ears pretty loudly; he was in the Right to compare himself with old Zisca: I wish his Efforts may have a similar Effect, although he fills my Heart with More horror of the Peace than animating Hope from a long Continuance of War. Butcher's Meat which was at 2d. 1/2 o'Pound in Denbigh Market two Winters ago - when the hard Frost was, now sells in the same for 6d. This is Scarcity, if not Famine: and bad Barley must affect us all, those who do not sell Malt Liquor, buy it: and that is now no small Expense. Mr. Piozzi receives dispiriting Letters from Italy, although the public Prints try to revive Hope - but the King of Naples's Defection I consider as a more vexatious Occurrence than Spain's Declaration of War. Lord Malmesbury seems to behave very well, and like a worthy Son of that great Man his Father; whom I was taught to revere in my Infancy by his and my oldest Friend Dr. Collier. And Pitt is preparing for a gallant Defence should he be forced at last to fight it out on our own Ground. How do your Norfolk Men like this new Cavalry Bill? It is a strange World: I wrote Miss Thrales word how matters stood at Segroid, and how oddly Cecy behaved to me when I expressed my Concern at her Husband's Conduct: and Sophia answers me by saying She thinks her Sister behaved perfectly right in making the best of a bad Lot - and then talks of the French and the English - the War and the Peace as if nothing was the matter, - or as if I had nothing to do with it : Those Dear Misses do really all of them use Me exceedingly ill. Write soon and say you are better and have not forgotten us. Poor Mr. Wynn of Llewessog, Mostyn's Father in Law; is dead of a Quinsy; he was a very worthy Gentleman, and is a Loss to us all. Miss Hamilton says that the Moment Mrs. Lewis died her Daughter went to Reading - to her Aunt I suppose. Adieu Dear Sir / believe me ever truly yours / H: L: P. Rev: Leonard Chappelow / Roydon / near Diss / Norfolk.

column39: The Piozzi Letters. Correspondence of Hester Lynch Piozzi, 1784-1821. Vols. 1-2. Edited by Edward A. Bloom and Lillian D. Bloom. Newark: University of Delaware Press. 1989-1991.
column46: Brinbella Tuesday November 7: 1796. I am my sweetest Child, so much and so justly enraged at this late odious Occurrence, - for Accident we cannot call it - that I am half enraged with dear Sophia for saying with such an easy flourish How She thinks her Sister's Conduct perfectly right , whilst every Moment brings me Conviction that it is perfectly wrong . All the Country for Example was on her Side although She had even studied to make them her Enemies; and would have been easily excited by Me to treat Mr. Mostyn as a general Offender against Society, had not She left my House in Disgust merely because I expressed a small part of the Indignation I felt for her Ill-treatment, and had She not run for Refuge from our Caresses to the Bosom of his Family, and to those very Ladies whom you saw her turn her Back upon at Holywell and Brynbella exactly this Time Twelvemonth. When She is contented is now the general Cry - what need Mrs. Piozzi care? But I do, and will care: for no Man shall insult my Child however She may behave towards Me or however She may pretend to like him the better for it, without being made to feel somewhere ; and I trust such Gentlemen are always Vulnerable in the Purse . I have laid aside all Self Resentments and have written to Mr. Crutcheley and Mr. Cator to request that they will cooperate with me in hastening to pay her Money into the Accountant Generals hands, and leave Lord Loughborough to make her Settlement after due Information of her Husbands Baseness. Cecilia will then obtain a very large Separate Maintenance in Case her Mind may change : for Fashions alter, and the Time may come that She may wish without the Power to vary her Situation, if we miss this Opportunity. - Mr. Murphy says She might even now be divorced, and tic but just that She should know , if She would not desire to use her Advantages. Meantime for Heaven's Sake do not consent to relinquish your Claim upon her 40000£ should She die under Age - What good can that do? Throw an immense Sum into Mostyn's Hands, and pay him for his Insult upon us all in the Person of Cecilia! I hope God Almighty will preserve her to make us great Amends by her future Wisdom and Virtue for the Pain She now gives both to you and me by her Grossness, and her Contemptible Preference of the Bon Ton and genteel Life as She calls it, to every thing in this World and the next - but She may be taken from us; and why for Mercy's Sake would you fling away what Providence and your Father put into your Care? Let me beseech you Dear Love think better of the Business, and keep Susan and Sophie from any Such Heroic Follies. Who would thank you for it? Give your Money to Mostyn, that he may keep Harlots with it! - a pretty Reason. More need to put her Fortune irretrievably into the Court of Chancery; and then, There will be no Talk of Extortion to Lord Loughborough: He will be sure to do what's right - because he cannot be tempted nor prevailed on - to do what's wrong . Mostyn is in London at this Moment I believe, soliciting better Terms from Mr. Cator than he could obtain at Streatham Park from Mr. Murphy; If he does really thus unite the Subtlety of Age with the headlong Sensuality of Youth, he is more dangerous than despicable; and I warn you to beware of his Arts. The Attorney whom Susette and Cecy used to call le petit Cochon noir dropped dead at his House last week; that Event opens a Mine of Misery - Debts and Entanglements to the Family; who now look with Avidity to her Dower for the retrieving of all: but there are 15 Months to come Thank God, and much may yet be done - for my own part I will rely on no one but the Chancellor - and dear Murphy says I'm right . Veniamo ad altro - as the Italians say. The Dear Arch Duke Charles was when I saw him every day - an effeminate Boy, tall of his Age and exceeding fair - with a long cold looking Face, like young Strickland if you remember him a Child, wearing a Girl's Night Cap. The Grand Duchess used to cuff her younglings and walk with them herself, and was particularly fond of this Son whom She persecuted - the people said - to make him say his Prayers. Francis was a haughty-looking Sir, with a Scowling Brow; I recollect liking him best - the old Catalonian Duchess was a Devote proud in Spirit but humble in Her Manner, and used to make these Children bow to me so, it was my greatest Study to avoid 'em. I envy your Acquaintance with Keith Elphinstone - and was boasting the other Day that I thought I knew his Dog . He did but cry "Come into the Weasel, I wants you;" - and the Dutch Admiral instantly obeyed. Mr. Fox's last Speech exhibits a Cruelty and determined Desire of doing Mischief beyond all I ever observed: he wants to tear away the Test Act, that there may be no more Established Religion here than in France; but Anagrams are the Mode now and the Anagram of Test is Stet. I had no Notion my Friend Stanley was enrolled parmi nous autres Auteurs - He was the only Man I ever wished for Cecy; but She hooted him , and said he was superannuated. Hurrah! how swiftly ride the Dead - is a strangely impressive Line whoever wrote it - They say now it has been done by many Translators. In the same Gentleman's Magazine for September You will see Some Extracts from Horseley's Charge to his Clergy which I think incomparable. Edward is very elegant indeed, but not original - The Boy in Clara Reeve's Old English Baron was too apparently the Model. Borrow it from a Circulating Library and look though, for I love not to make unsupported Charges; and it is long since I read that Romance. D'Arblaye's Characters are more varied and better shaded than Dr. Moore's, but her Language would disgrace the Precepts of Socrates and the Invention of Ovid. Is Mrs. Burney dead? I hear so. Adieu! and write soon and say whether our senseless and nearly friendless Cecilia has told you how She admires her Husband, and despises hers and / Your Affectionate Mother H: L: P. Mr. Piozzi sends kind Remembrances to the Lady Loves with my true good Wishes for a happy Meeting in the Library at old Streatham Park. Miss Thrale / Mount Ephraim / Tunbridge Wells / Kent.

Brynbella Saturday December 21: My dearest Child Your kind Letter was conveyed to me this Day by Mrs. Bertie. Mr. Murphy might be sure that I would do whatever he advised about Cecilia because I think it Impossible She can have a more disinterested Friend. If your Alarm concerning the Court of Chancery is the same you hinted to us Three or four Years ago, it would be a wise Measure to inform and consult Murphy how far that Alarm was originally founded in Truth. I never told him because I thought it more Your Affair than mine; and because I had no right to confide other Peoples Secrets - but He told me a thing one Evening in Confidence, which though mysterious beyond my Power of guessing at - seems to invalidate and completely nullify all possibility of the Tale you were imbued with. We will speak freely when we meet, and I am sorry it is to be no sooner. If you only mean that rough Measures may drive Cecilia from us, and make Her cling to The Husband and refuse all Settlement whatever - why I am afraid of that myself . She has never sent or called here since we parted, and is wholly given up to his Family. I met her on a Visit once - looking as black as a Crow - for Mr. Win - when She was here and Allen asked if She could be useful to her in making up Mourning or any thing - Mourning for what? (said She.) I shall mourn for no Welsh Folks not I - but all she then said is denied now I understand; Miss Mason has been fortunate and married , and the whole Story treated as a vile Report of my raising. Mr. Mostyn would not speak to me when we met at Llannerch, but I squeezed Cecy by the Hand malgre` lui - and She looked gay and good humoured as ever - and very well Thank God. I am proud of Old London which is a fine Town and a Gallant City as the Old Ballad sets forth: and I do hope the French will be frighted and be humbler and contented to be quiet sometime; they have not swallowed Sir John Jervis, and they have not taken Mantua any more than the Arch Duke has subdued Kehl. The Power which says Hitherto shalt thou go and no further will perhaps stop the Hurricane upon its Course - if the Time is not come that all Things are to be devoured . Taste in Writing appears to have undergone a vast Change; and the Author now "Who peppers the highest is surest to please." Did you ever read a strange thing and a wicked Thing in my Mind - called Vathek? There is a stranger Thing and a wickeder about the World now - called The Monk. Alonzo the Brave made his first Appearance sir ce Theatre d'horreur ; it is written by a forward Baby of nineteen Years old, and the Girls - as old Plumb said by the London Rogue - take to it hugely . - My Ballad is not begun yet but I have a good Plan in my Head. Mr. Piozzi has just brought me a most elaborate Letter to direct for Susan, he pretends to know Cecilia better than any of us do; and he says - More you preach her, more She will not hear . If I ever do preach any more to her it shall be on the following Text: Her whole Destiny dear silly Soul! is in her own hand; the Chancellor of England, nor the King, Lord, and Commons in Parliament assembled cannot make her a Settlement unless She will accept it . Lord Loughboro' can preach her as Mr. Piozzi calls it, and make her a paternal Discourse, advising her not to be a Charity Girl upon the House of Segroid - but he can do no more, he cannot detain the Money an hour after She is of Age; and the Report here goes that Mr. and Mrs. Mostyn both mean to wait till next February Twelvemonth - and then call in her Fortune from whoever is entrusted with it. If She does do so, I shall be inevitably tempted to hang either her, or myself. Mrs. Bertie will put your Letter in a Frame I fancy, and your Present under a Glass Bell: you were A Sweet Creature to send her such a play thing: it has had its full effect, and her Husband who will be stone-blind in about a Quarter of a Year, has seen this Sight before he took Leave of Life and Light and thou blessed Sun serene . Like the Culprit at Lisbon who solicited so hard that he might not be broke upon the Wheel till he had seen the Town lighted up with the new Lamps all Uso di Londra . And so now if I can find the little Epigram about King Williams Horse Sorel when I come to look in the Library at Streatham Park - you shall pay a penny forfeit, and If I made the Distich in my Sleep, and forgot it again and dreamed that it was in Tyndal's Continuation of Rapine - why I must pay a Penny forfeit - and justly. Because I ought to have remembered the only Latin Distich I ever did make in my Life. Adieu Dearest of all Dear Girls, and pray since so many Acquaintance will be glad to see our Return do you be the gladdest to kiss Your ever / Affectionate H: L: P. The Frank of Lord Dawdley saved nothing, the Office charged 3d . Miss Thrale / Tunbridge Wells / Kent.

column46: Wednesday 12: July 1797. Mr. and Mrs. Piozzi present their best Compliments to Mr. Ray and request the honour of his Company to dinner on the 25 of July next, being The 13th Anniversary of their Wedding Day. - Fine News Mr. Vandercom told us yesterday, when having been disappointed of Our Dividends we went to him for Consolation. Fine News indeed! Why he says that Ward has put our Cause against Cator, down for a hearing - upon Bill and Answer only : so that dear Mr. Murphy may look in vain for Schedules and Proofs - and practise Interrogatories in private at his Leisure; Our Antagonist knows his Ground and laughs at us all. My Master has found out Letters beside, and I know not what; but Vandercom tells me that for the Sake of battling this Business through, - (if to battle it Through should be found advisable; -) - We must pay Mr. Cator the Costs for as far as we have gone; and then recommence our Suit ab Ovo . Because no Chancellor however kind or partial to us, or however prejudiced against a Man of his Character, can refuse to believe Oaths solemnly sworn, against vague Complaints, and empty Affirmations positively denied. It appears to me that if Ward has ruined our Suit in this manner, He ought to pay the Costs as far as they are gone, and set us out to fight on fair Ground again; but Mr. Vandercom says it is not from his Papers that he gained the Intelligence; those Papers Ward keeps to make out his own Demands from; Vandercom gathered from Conversation with Stanley that our Cause was rotten and like to end in Disgrace. All this helps to account for Cator's haughty and fearless Carriage throe the whole Business, he was sure of his Ground You see: And when our Young Ladies called here for a few Days in their Way to Brighthelmston exactly a Week ago, they laughed at us for dreaming of a Conquest over Cator , considering it as mere Quixotism , though they used to do all in their power to stop us from going into Chancery as you may perhaps remember. - I think Mr. Murphy will be as much enraged as Mr. Piozzi has reason to be mortified; and very impatient am I to know Your Sentiments : Pray write soon if You cannot call. The Books remain at Mrs. Ray's and wait your Acceptance, they are very prettily dressed to pay their Duty and carry the Compliments of / Your very much Obliged and faithful Servant / H: L: Piozzi. We have found a Letter from Ward - an old one - saying "that since I appeared to think he protracted our Suit against Cator with a View to enhance his own Charges, he should Charge nothing upon that Score " - and now see what Demands he is making. I think we shall get the Maintenance Money soon; it is now before Mr. Wilmot. Robert Ray Esq. / No. 14 Paper Buildings / Temple / London.

Brynbella Monday 18 September I am excessively obliged to you Dear Mr. Chappelow, but I must do without Grey's Hudibras, for I cannot afford to buy it: - a Guinea might have been spared and I would have saved it in Ribbons, - but not 38s. So you never had my long Letter telling how Cecilia barely escaped with Life from those Pains and Perils which you told me were all out of Fashion - She is alive though and recovers, but it is slowly - They lost the little Boy in the Struggle; and I suppose Mostyn's Terror, Anxiety, and Disappointment have been Punishments enough for any Sins that could have been committed in a Life so short as his has been. They kept me away - till the whole Country cried Shame, and they then let me in - for one five Minutes only - The Husband did not appear, and She poor Soul! could hardly speak. Miss Thrale managed everything I believe; Mrs. Win was not admitted anymore than myself as People tell me: Doctor Thackeray, Mr. Nicholls, and Mr. Moral of Chester who delivered her, have been in constant Attendance these three Weeks exactly: but She is pronounced safe and convalescent now, if I am well informed - and all Physicians are dismissed. Miss Thrale rode hither on Saturday last, We had Mrs. Strickland to visit us from Westmoreland - You have heard me speak of her with Esteem. She is a Courageous Lady; for though Lame and Infirm, nothing could keep Her from visiting an Old Friend when just within 100 Miles of her Brother's House, and She would see Bachygraig too, and Llewenney because it did belong to my Family 40 Years ago. She seemed to like us, and our House, and our Neighbours exceedingly. Mr. Piozzi sends you a Thousand Compliments: he has no present and positive Gout, so we say he is very well - he was monstrously enraged at my begging Admittance to poor Cecy's Bedside and begging so long in vain : but how could I hear of such sufferings without feeling for her? How could I? She was Three Days and Nights in Torture. Now She recovers I will think no more about her, but be as indifferent to them as they are to me - The Harvest has fretted us a good deal here, but our Wheat was got in like the Hay at Streatham Park without a Shadow of Misfortune, and some Oats will be housed tonight. I remember Horton full well, the Seat of Lord Halifax; with whose Children my Childhood was past - but they are dead, and I am living; and those Maps that showed us the Kingdom of France, the Papacy of Rome, and the Republics of Genoa and Venice yet stick up against the old Wall perhaps - though Realms and Commonwealths are gone; and the good little Girls that used to learn their Lessons on them are gone too - All but Dear Sir / Your ever faithful &c. / H: L: Piozzi. How does pretty Mrs. Clay? and how do her Babies? She is an amiable and an interesting Lady, and it vexed me to leave Town without knowing the result of her little Son's Sickness.

column46: Brynbella Wednesday 3rd January 1798. My Dear Mr. Ray I have read over your kind Letter, till I have it by heart. The Master saying we ought not to have spent a single Guinea on Cecy beyond the Allowance is a Joke. How could we help spending it? She was seized here at Denbigh with a Cough and spitting of Blood - we had no Physician nearer than Chester and Haygarth's two Visits cost us 20 Guineas - he ordered her to go abroad immediately without Loss of Time to Lisbon or Naples. - Not to Italy for God's Sake cried My Master - one knows not what might happen nor what might be said. - to Lisbon then Sir replied the Doctor - and quickly . When She recovered a little we went to Chester and spent a Week under Haygarth's immediate Care in that Town - then to Sir Lucas Poppies - who said that Bath and Bristol and Horse Exercise and Asses' Milk would restore her without more ado - and so I thank God - they did restore her. Could we have helped these Expenses? Or could the Master suppose them comprised within 150£ o'Year? - She was not then 15. Kind Miss Weston offered to go with her to Lisbon, and some Lady we must have taken: Could these Expenses have been avoided? You know we always had some prudent Lady with us on her Account: Miss Lee or Miss Before or Miss Weston for Months together. Could those Expenses have been helped . Impossible! But we should have applied for further Allowance to Chancery? We dared not go near the Court of Chancery: Miss Thrale had herself with the utmost Energy and Violence stopped Mr. Piozzi from putting that Child under Protection of the Court sometime before, and renewed her Application again when She was going to be married - frighting us with a wild Story of what was, and what was not done even before I was married myself. Mr. Piozzi unacquainted with our Laws and Language could not resist the strong Adjuration of his Wife's Daughters whom he had always respected, and who he naturally concluded knew their own Affairs and their own Interests best . How then could we have applied to Chancery? Mr. Murphy too - who himself made Mr. Thrale's Will; told us (when we spoke to him of Cecilia's expensive Turn) that the Allowance of 150£ and 200£ per Annum lasted but till the Brewhouse should be sold, and that then we were ad Libitum . Why then should we apply to Chancery? - The Disbursements increasing however, We did at length intend to make the Application - and in that Time the Titmouse ran away. On what Side can we be to blame? I see not. That Story or Phantom or whatever it was concerning Miss Thrale's fears of an Extent of the Crown is an incomprehensible Business. Cecilia herself mentioned it to Mrs. Strickland when She was with her in Westmoreland; and asked her concerning the Character of Mr Thrale - and whether or no She used to consider him as an honest man? Mrs. Strickland was quite shocked. I wish to God they would let their poor father rest in his Grave, and content themselves with sending after him Your much worried Friend / H: L: P. Mr. Piozzi continued exceedingly Ill indeed - let me hear from you soon how things are at last determined. The Moment a Journey is practicable , we set out for old Streatham Park. Robed. Ray Esq. / No. 14 / Paper Buildings / Temple / London.

column46: Brynbella 10: January 1798. Before the long-threatened Blister is put upon my right Arm I will use it once more to assure My very tenderly-remembered Friend that She has never been a Moment forgotten . But I wrote so exceeding long a Letter to Harriet Lee a great while ago upon the odious Subject of Self and Family Affairs - and She answered me so coldly and drily, that I thought nobody would like a Correspondence of that Kind, and felt unable to try at others more entertaining. Desire to see our Place and our Acquaintance brought us hither for three Months Amusement on the 10th of October - I mean of August last: and the first Thing we heard was that Mrs. Mostyn had chosen this Country for Lying In - no doubt said I, that She may be attended by Mr. Moore who was so comfortable and attentive when She was in the same Country confined by Illness Seven Years ago, and dear Miss Weston offered to go with us to Lisbon upon Haygarth's saying her Health required Continental Air. - We sent, and went, and were received civilly and not unkindly; so I thought we were upon Terms - as it is called - and a Servant was daily dispatched to know How She went on. Miss Thrale who was with her always returned for Answer that all was going as well as possible - So we went out as usual to visit our Neighbours and at one Lady's House heard Suddenly and accidentally - not only of her Illness but her extreme Danger. Mr. Moore was in the Room where we heard it, She was attended by People from Chester and Ruthyn - whom neither She nor I had ever seen, but though so oddly thrown aside, Mr. Moore to calm my Inquietude ran away to learn Particulars, and I sate in Agony at Bottom of Denbigh Town while the Footman galloped forward to request my Admission - It was refused - Disastrous Scenes, and a dead Boy followed; Mr. Piozzi shed Tears at the Account of her severe sufferings. In due Time I was admitted, and warned to make my visit short and so I did - The Visit was coldly but not uncivilly in Course of 3 Months returned - and all past off quietly. The Litigation for Recovery of Money spent on Cecilia while She remained with us went on of Course; and the other Day almost, The Master made Report against Mr. Piozzi who he said could compel no Payment, but that Mostyn must be a strange Man (was his Expression) to endeavour so at squeezing his Wife's necessary Expenses out of a Father in Law's Pocket; and added I can tell you Gentlemen that had you come to me as John Wilmot not as Master in Chancery - I should have decided very differently indeed. The Counsellors on both Sides begged him even yet to stand between us and the Chancellor, and act as Referee . If your Clients please replied he - So I will. Mr. Piozzi wrote to express his Consent - but when we asked Miss Thrale concerning her Brother and Sister's Determination - She said It was a Subject that had never employed Their Minds even for a Moment . I requested her to remind 'em of it - and that Night came a Billet with " Proper Compliments: Mr. Mostyn will take Time for Deliberation." - and so he does, for that's a fortnight ago. So much for the Superiority with which Your poor mortified and severely-humbled Friend has been treated - now for Domestic Comforts : On the 20th of October My poor Master went to Bed with a raging Fit of Gout in Breast, Side, Back, and Collar Bone - but soon fixing in one Heel and one Toe, - it tore them open into the most frightful Ulcers I or poor Mr. Moore ever did behold. There has the Gout gnawed and bitten for 12 entire Weeks - during which Time has the truly wretched Patient suffered Torments inexpressible, and I believe rarely endured. - His Letters from Italy irritating even that Anguish by Narrations of what Brothers, Sisters, Friends, &c. endure from the Rapacity of these vile French, false as they are cruel, and insolent as they are Successful: His own particular Town has been the Immediate Seat of Distress - and all there are completely and inevitably ruined . Let us Thank God they have not yet been called hither; they will do us no harm till they are called . It is our own traitorous Vipers I am afraid of - not the French and of the Taxes I am not afraid except as it gives a handle for Abuse to those who object to everything proposed - and propose nothing Themselves. We are in a Leaky Ship, We must pump or drown; and those are the greatest Enemies to general Safety: who cry Oh don't fatigue the poor Men at The Pump, with such hard work; See how cruel you are to urge them thus beyond their Strength! Not at all cruel: Let us pump now with Spirit, and the Vessel may yet get into Harbour - but it is no Moment this for general Relaxation. When I was going over the Alps with Mr. Piozzi The Sight of a dreadful Precipice made me afraid and I said I would walk - it was very late in a fine Summer Evening. Sit still , cried my Master. I cannot sit still, replied I. Stop, stop, You disturb the Drivers You will make them overturn us, pray sit still. No, I would not sit still, I would walk : Well walk away then Said Mr. Piozzi if you will walk; There are a Troop of Wolves ranging the Mountain now - I was told so at the last Inn: They will find their Prey out in an Instant. Oh! you can't imagine after That how still and quiet I sate in the Carriage. Britannia in a similar Situation must act like H: L: P. She must let the Driver alone, and he will avoid the Precipice ; She must not expose herself to this Troop of Wolves. But my Rheumatic Arm aches with even thus much Writing, and my Heart aches for my own Mental and my Husbands Corporeal Sufferings: my Loyal Soul too aches for the general Pressure upon our brave King and skilful Minister; but though Cecilia does refuse to repay the 1400£ She owes Mr. Piozzi, I will not grudge the Taxes - nor will he try to evade them. We raised two Puppies I meant to drown, that they likewise might be entered. Mr. Mostyn's Mother not much better treated by our haughty Cecy than I have been, has sold one of her Estates for 10000£ and given the Money to her Daughter . She is gone to live at Bath I'm told - her Name is Win - ask who knows her &c. The Lees can tell. When Mr. Piozzi recovers, our Meaning is to go to Streatham Park, and wind up our Affairs, and come back hither and live snug, and save Money enough to pay our just Debts and bury us. If we could live 3 Years more, We should have our Income clear of every Encumbrance - and I should publish another Jest Book . But both our Healths are visibly declining . Love us, and pray for us - and write again soon to Yours ever equally and faithfully / H: L: P. What a Mercy it was we were not all allowed to go to Lisbon with Mrs. Mostyn 7 years ago - It would have been a pretty additional Expense, and she would have made us pay it. Accept my Masters true Love. And do write again soon. Mrs. Pennington / Dowry Square / Hot Wells / Bristol.

Sunday 2: September Dear Jacob In the first Place my poor Master is laid up fast with the Gout; in the next Place he frets about that Chandelier which never did come from Mayhew and Ince, let them say what they please. All the Warehouses in Chester have been searched, you should speak to the People about it. The Convex Glass is come, and your Letter, and a Thousand Thanks to Mr. Giles about the Money - he is very good indeed, and I hope very happy with Streatham Park. Here is the hottest Summer I ever knew and the longest and no Rain to speak of from March to September. Yet the Corn does not do amiss - but we have no Hay nor no Straw. I have heard but 3 Times from the 4 Ladies since we parted - I hear however that Mrs. Mostyn is exceedingly well and brisk. Pray let me know from you the Moment She is delivered, for it is very possible her Sisters will not write, Though I do depend on Miss Thrale too, to say at least that She is brought to Bed. It is terrible Weather for her . We are sorry for poor little Presto. Our favourites all keep well here. God bless you - Mr. Piozzi is very ill indeed and I can add no more than / that I am &c. H: L: P. Mr. Jacob Weston / Streatham Park / Surrey.

column46: Brynbella 8: September 1798 My dear Girl - I received Your agreeable Letter and wish you Joy of your Nephew who seems to have been born with much Ease into a World full of various and interesting Circumstances, out of which some make Pleasures, some make Pains - and - others - a mere Spectacle, as they choose. Few now think they are sent hither to discharge any Duties, a Sentiment which when I, and even when You were young - was carefully inculcated. Men indeed, are even in these Days of Illumination now and then forced upon feeling that there are such Encumbrances tacked upon Life, but Ladies - like Leviathan apparently rush into the World as he into the Ocean - to take their Pastime therein. - I am glad Mrs. Mostyn's Child was not a Lady. My Dislike of Ton and Ton Folks is in the way to be cured however. I saw lately a Woman of high Fashion and born to a great Fortune too - turned out of her Husband's house and living on her Friends till the Allowance is settled - half hooted by her Companions, and calumniated by her Servants who told mine that She had lost 20000£ at the Gaming Table, a Circumstance not true as I have heard since. And I saw this Lady as tranquil, as cheerful and as easy-Mannered as People of her Rank always are: and I said to the Bishop of St. Asaph that I had now learned how certainly that which Wisdom and Virtue, Religion and Philosophy, all failed to effect - was without difficulty or Embarrassment brought about merely by Ton . I grieve to think that this grand Panacea, this sweetener of Human Calamity had not reached Teneriffe before the Earthquake. When our Country begins to shake in the natural Sense, - (in the Civil and Political it is already shaken) - the Ton Folks will I am sure treat it as an Event Sans Consequence entirely. Our immediate Neighbours are bustling just now, the French having sent Arms and Officers - so our Rebels may join them if they will: but it is said here that the United Irishmen will all agree together - and drive them out. It was supposed that the Letters from Italy mentioning our Victory over Buonaparte were home Fabrications to serve Ministerial Purposes, but Mr. Piozzi's Brother wrote us an Account of it from Venice, so perhaps those mentioned in the Public Prints were genuine , though not authentic , or authorized Accounts. Mr. Piozzi is in Bed with the Gout, and Hodgkins (his Valet) with a broken Leg: - The Dogs coursed a Liveried across our Grounds, and the Man running and reaching after it fell and was brought home fainting half an Hour ago. - Mr. Moore is called, - I think the Bone is not broken. A Thousand Things combine to shorten my Letter, but nothing shall make me forget the drinking your dear Health next Monday seven-night. The 17: of September was once a Day of Gala with the Turks , for on that Day it is said AD. 630 Mahomet published his Alcoran. T'was also a Day of Pomp to the Catholics when Boniface 8th in 1301 set forth his famous Bull claiming Dominion over all the Kings of the Earth on the same Day : and on that Day were Your blue Eyes first opened / on Your Affectionate Mother / H: L: P. Buonaparte has got old Nilus's Statue for his Countrymen I find - Is that ominous of their taking Egypt? This must be pretty hot Weather there I trust - Will he conquer Deserts and defy Plagues? And is He Miss Thrale / Cumberland Street / London.

column46: No. 43 Great Pultney Street, Bath 18: December 1798. Dear Jacob - I am very sorry you should take it into your Head that I should ever say you were not as attentive as you used to be. I said no such Thing and those who told you so did not speak Truth: you should have more Sense than to mind them. We came safe here God be praised but we did but just save our Distance for my Master was taken with the Gout the third Day after our Arrival and he is in Bed now - but Doctor Harington and Mr. Hay are very comfortable People in the physical Way, and they say he is doing quite well: they look just as they used to do; and Bath is very full and very pretty: I always did love it better than London, and so I do still. - I am glad you like our dear little Boy - we are very impatient to see him; He is in the right to say that his Name is John Salusbury, for so he was Christened just five Years ago, and he is my Child now. It is a Blessing that he has had the Smallpox and I am glad he has a good Spirit to get through this Stormy Life - Poor Fellow he has begun Trouble very early to take such a long Journey at his Age. I have got your old Friend Allen with me again - Mrs. Beckwith is married to Thomas Davies the Gardiner at Brynbella and She gave me no Note at all of it till Three days before we set out for Bath. So as Allen had left her Service at that Mr. Erle's, and I had heard from her, and saw plainly She wished to come home to us; I wrote to bid her meet me at Shrewsbury, and so She did, and here we are at Bath just as it used to be; and I hope we shall all live to meet again happy in 1801. Pray give our Compliments to Mr. Giles always, and every civil Wish possible: I believe we must trouble him to pay Twenty Three Pounds for us to Messrs: Barclay, Bevan and Co. upon Account of our dear little Boy who will be happy with Mr. Davies I am sure, and learn to be a great Scholar - for I set my Heart upon his Learning. In the mean Time good natured Mr. Ray promised us kindly to bring him here to Bath for us to see: I wish you would make Enquiry when they set out, for we both want much to see him. Pray write me word. Jacob Weston / at / Streatham Park / Surrey.

My dear child, I am extremely pleased with your translation now it is writ over fair. It is very close to the sense of the original, and done, in many places, with much spirit, as well as the numbers not lame, or rough. However an attention to Mr. Pope's numbers will make you avoid some ill sounds, and hobbling of the verse, by only transposing a word or two, in many instances. I have, upon reading the Eclogue over again, altered the third, fourth, and fifth lines, in order to bring them nearer to the Latin, as well as to render some beauty which is contained in the repetition of words in tender passages; for example, Nos Patriae fines, et dulcia linquimus arva, Nos Patriam fugimus: Tu Tityre lentus in umbra` Formosam resonare doces Amaryllida Sylvas . We leave our native land, these fields so sweet, Our country leave: At ease, in cool retreat, You Thyrsis bid the woods fair Daphne's name repeat. I will desire you to write over another copy with this alteration, and also to write smokes in the plural number, in the last line but one. You give me great pleasure, my dear child, in the progress you have made. I will recommend to Mr. Leech to carry you quite through Virgil's Aeneid from beginning to ending. Pray show him this letter, with my service to him, and thanks for his care of you. For English poetry, I recommend Pope's translation of Homer and Dryden's Fables in particular. I am not sure, if they are not called Tales instead of Fables. Your cousin whom I am sure you can overtake if you will, has read Virgil's Aeneid quite through, and much of Horace's Epistles. Terence's plays I would also desire Mr. Leech to make you perfect master of. Your cousin has read them all. Go on, my dear, and you will at least equal him. You are so good that I have nothing to wish but that you may be directed to proper books; and I trust to your spirit, and desire to be praised for things that deserve praise, for the figure you will hereafter make. God bless you, my dear child. Your most affectionate uncle.

Bath, Oct. 12, 1751. My dear nephew, As I have been moving about from place to place, your letter reached me here, at Bath, but very lately, after making a considerable circuit to find me. I should have otherwise, my dear child, returned you thanks for the very great pleasure you have given me, long before now. The very good account you give me of your studies, and that delivered in very good Latin, for your time, has filled me with the highest expectation of your future improvements: I see the foundations so well laid, that I do not make the least doubt but you will become a perfect good scholar; and have the pleasure and applause that will attend the several advantages hereafter, in the future course of your life, that you can only acquire now by your emulation and noble labours in the pursuit of learning, and of every acquirement that is to make you superior to other gentlemen. I rejoice to hear that you have begun Homer's Iliad; and have made so great a progress in Virgil. I hope you taste and love those authors particularly. You cannot read them too much: they are not only the two greatest poets, but they contain the finest lessons for your age to imbibe: lessons of honour, courage, disinterestedness, love of truth, command of temper, gentleness of behaviour, humanity, and in one word, virtue in its true signification. Go on, my dear nephew, and drink as deep as you can of these divine springs: the pleasure of the draught is equal at least to the prodigious advantages of it to the heart and morals. I hope you will drink them as somebody does in Virgil, of another sort of cup: Ille Impiger hausit spumantem Pateram . I shall be highly pleased to hear from you, and to know what authors give you most pleasure. I desire my service to Mr. Leech: pray tell him I will write to him soon about your studies. I am, with the greatest affection, My dear Child, Your loving uncle.

Bath, Jan. 12, 1754. My dear nephew, Your letter from Cambridge affords me many very sensible pleasures: first, that you are at last in a proper place for study and improvement, instead of losing any more of that most precious thing, time, in London. In the next place that you seem pleased with the particular society you are placed in, and with the gentleman to whose care and instructions you are committed: and above all I applaud the sound, right sense, and love of virtue, which appears through your whole letter. You are already possessed of the true clue to guide you through this dangerous and perplexing part of your life's journey, the years of education; and upon which, the complexion of all the rest of your days will infallibly depend: I say you have the true clue to guide you, in the maxim you lay down in your letter to me, namely that the use of learning is, to render a man more wise and virtuous; not merely to make him more learned. Macte tua` Virtute ; Go on, my dear boy, by this golden rule, and you cannot fail to become every thing your generous heart prompts you to wish to be, and that mine most affectionately wishes for you. There is but one danger in your way; and that is, perhaps, natural enough to your age, the love of pleasure, or the fear of close application and laborious diligence. With the last there is nothing you may not conquer: and the first is sure to conquer and enslave whoever does not strenuously and generously resist the first allurements of it, lest by small indulgences, he fall under the yoke of irresistible habit. Vitanda est Improba Siren, Desidia , I desire may be affixed to the curtains of your bed, and to the walls of your chambers. If you do not rise early, you never can make any progress worth talking of; and another rule is, if you do not set apart your hours of reading, and never suffer yourself or any one else to break in upon them, your days will slip through your hands, unprofitably and frivolously; unpraised by all you wish to please, and really unenjoyable to yourself. Be assured, whatever you take from pleasure, amusements, or indolence, for these first few years of your life, will repay you a hundred fold, in the pleasures, honours and advantages of all the remainder of your days. My heart is so full of the most earnest desire that you should do well, that I find my letter has run into some length, which you will, I know, be so good to excuse. There remains now nothing to trouble you with but a little plan for the beginning of your studies, which I desire, in a particular manner, may be exactly followed in every tittle. You are to qualify yourself for the part in society, to which your birth and estate call you. You are to be a gentleman of such learning and qualifications as may distinguish you in the service of your country hereafter; not a pedant, who reads only to be called learned, instead of considering learning as an instrument only for action. Give me leave therefore, my dear nephew, who have gone before you, to point out to you the dangers in your road; to guard you against such things, as I experience, my own defects to arise from; and at the same time, if I have had any little successes, in the world, to guide you to what I have drawn many helps from. I have not the pleasure of knowing the gentleman who is your tutor, but I dare say he is every way equal to such a charge, which I think no small one. You will communicate this letter to him, and I hope he will be so good to concur with me as to the course of study I desire you may begin with; and that such books, and such only, as I have pointed out, may be read. They are as follows: Euclid; a Course of Logic; a Course of experimental Philosophy; Locke's Conduct of the Understanding; his Treatise also on the Understanding; his treatise on Government, and Letters on Toleration. I desire, for the present, no books of poetry, but Horace and Virgil: of Horace the Odes, but above all, the Epistles and Ars Poetica. These parts, Nocturne` versate menu, versate diurna` . Tully de Officiis, de Amicitia`, de Senectute . His Catilinarian Orations and Philippics. Sallust. At leisure hours an abridgment of the History of England to be run through, in order to settle in the mind a general chronological order and series of principal events, and succession of kings: proper books of English history, on the true principles of our happy constitution, shall be pointed out afterwards. Burnet's History of the Reformation, abridged by himself, to be read with great care. Father Paul on beneficiary Matters, in English. A French master, and only Moliere's Plays to be read with him, or by yourself, till you have gone through them all. Spectators, especially Mr. Addison's papers, to be read very frequently at broken times in your room. I make it my request that you will forbear drawing, totally, while you are at Cambridge: and not meddle with Greek, otherwise than to know a little the etymology of words in Latin, or English, or French: nor to meddle with Italian. I hope this little course will soon be run through: I intend it as a general foundation for many things, of infinite utitility, to come as soon as this is finished. Believe me, With the truest affection, My dear Nephew, Ever yours. Keep this letter and read it again.

Bath, Jan. 14, 1754. My dear nephew, You will hardly have read over one very long letter from me before you are troubled with a second. I intended to have writ soon, but I do it the sooner on account of your letter to your aunt, which she transmitted to me here. If any thing, my dear boy, could have happened, to raise you higher in my esteem, and to endear you more to me, it is the amiable abhorrence you feel for the scene of vice and folly, (and of real misery and perdition, under the false notion of pleasure and spirit,) which has opened to you at your college, and at the same time, the manly, brave, generous, and wise resolution and true spirit, with which you resisted and repulsed the first attempts upon a mind and heart, I thank God, infinitely too firm and noble, as well as too elegant and enlightened, to be in any danger of yielding to such contemptible and wretched corruptions. You charm me with the description of Mr. Whaler, and while you say you could adore him, I could adore you for the natural, genuine love of virtue, which speaks in all you feel, say, or do. As to your companions let this be your rule. Cultivate the acquaintance with Mr. Whaler which you have so fortunately begun: and in general, be sure to associate with men much older than yourself: scholars whenever you can: but always with men of decent and honourable lives. As their age and learning, superior both to your own, must necessarily, in good sense, and in the view of acquiring knowledge from them, entitle them to all deference, and submission of your own lights to theirs, you will particularly practise that first and greatest rule for pleasing in conversation, as well as for drawing instruction and improvement from the company of one's superiors in age and knowledge namely, to be a patient, attentive, and well-bred hearer, and to answer with modesty: to deliver your own opinions sparingly and with proper diffidence; and if you are forced to desire farther information or explanation upon a point, to do it with proper apologies for the trouble you give: or if obliged to differ, to do it with all possible candour, and an unprejudiced desire to find and ascertain truth, with an entire indifference to the side on which that truth is to be found. There is likewise a particular attention required to contradict with good manners; such as, begging pardon, begging leave to doubt, and such like phrases. Pythagoras enjoined his scholars an absolute silence for a long novitiate. I am far from approving such a taciturnity: but I highly recommend the end and intent of Pythagoras's injunction; which is to dedicate the first parts of life more to hear and learn, in order to collect materials, out of which to form opinions founded on proper lights, and well-examined sound principles, than to be presuming, prompt, and flippant in hazarding one's own slight crude notions of things; and thereby exposing the nakedness and emptiness of the mind, like a house opened to company before it is fitted either with necessaries, or any ornaments for their reception and entertainment. And not only will this disgrace follow from such temerity and presumption, but a more serious danger is sure to ensue, that is, the embracing errors for truths, prejudices for principles; and when that is once done, (no matter how vainly and weakly,) the adhering perhaps to false and dangerous notions, only because one has declared for them, and submitting, for life, the understanding and conscience to a yoke of base and servile prejudices, vainly taken up and obstinately retained. This will never be your danger; but I thought it not amiss to offer these reflections to your thoughts. As to your manner of behaving towards these unhappy young gentlemen you describe, let it be manly and easy; decline their parties with civility; retort their raillery with raillery, always tempered with good breeding: if they banter your regularity, order, decency, and love of study, banter in return their neglect of them; and venture to own frankly, that you came to Cambridge to learn what you can, not to follow what they are pleased to call pleasure. In short, let your external behaviour to them be as full of politeness and ease as your inward estimation of them is full of pity, mixed with contempt. I come now to the part of the advice I have to offer to you, which most nearly concerns your welfare, and upon which every good and honourable purpose of your life will assuredly turn; I mean the keeping up in your heart the true sentiments of religion. If you are not right towards God, you can never be so towards man: the noblest sentiment of the human breast is here brought to the test. Is gratitude in the number of a man's virtues? if it be, the highest benefactor demands the warmest returns of gratitude, love, and praise: Ingratum queen dixerit, omnia dixit . If a man wants this virtue where there are infinite obligations to excite and quicken it, he will be likely to want all others towards his fellow-creatures, whose utmost gifts are poor compared to those he daily receives at the hands of his never-failing Almighty Friend. Remember thy Creator in the days of thy youth, is big with the deepest wisdom: The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom; and, an upright heart, that is understanding. This is eternally true, whether the wits and rakes of Cambridge allow it or not: nay, I must add of this religious wisdom, Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace, whatever your young gentlemen of pleasure think of a whore and a bottle, a tainted health and battered constitution. Hold fast therefore by this sheet-anchor of happiness, Religion; you will often want it in the times of most danger; the storms and tempests of life. Cherish true religion as preciously as you will fly with abhorrence and contempt superstition and enthusiasm. The first is the perfection and glory of the human nature; the two last the deprivation and disgrace of it. Remember the essence of religion is, a heart void of offence towards God and man; not subtle speculative opinions, but an active vital principle of faith. The words of a heathen were so fine that I must give them to you: Compositum Jus, Fasque Enemy, Sanctosque Recessus Mantis, et incoctum generoso Pectus Honesto . Go on, my dear child, in the admirable dispositions you have towards all that is right and good, and make yourself the love and admiration of the world! I have neither paper nor words to tell you how tenderly I am yours.

Bath, Jan. 24, 1754. I will lose not a moment before I return my most tender and warm thanks to the most amiable, valuable, and noble minded of youths, for the infinite pleasure his letter gives me. My dear nephew, what a beautiful thing is genuine goodness, and how lovely does the human mind appear, in its native purity, (in a nature as happy as yours,) before the taints of a corrupted world have touched it! To guard you from the fatal effects of all the dangers that surround and beset youth, (and many they are, name vary illudunt Pestes ,) I thank God, is become my pleasing and very important charge; your own choice, and our nearness in blood, and still more, a dearer and nearer relation of hearts, which I feel between us, all concur to make it so. I shall seek then every occasion, my dear young friend, of being useful to you, by offering you those lights, which one must have lived some years in the world to see the full force and extent of, and which the best mind and clearest understanding will suggest imperfectly, in any case, and in the most difficult, delicate, and essential points perhaps not at all, till experience, that dear-bought instructor, comes to our assistance. What I shall therefore make my task, (a happy delightful task, if I prove a safeguard to so much opening virtue,) is to be for some years, what you cannot be to yourself, your experience; experience anticipated, and ready digested for your use. Thus we will endeavour, my dear child, to join the two best seasons of life, to establish your virtue and your happiness upon solid foundations: Miscens Autumn et Veris Honours . So much in general. I will now, my dear nephew, say a few things to you upon a matter where you have surprisingly little to learn, considering you have seen nothing but Boconnock; I mean behaviour. Behaviour is of infinite advantage or prejudice to a man, as he happens to have formed it to a graceful, noble, engaging, and proper manner, or to a vulgar, coarse, ill-bred, or awkward and ungenteel one. Behaviour, though an external thing which seems rather to belong to the body than to the mind, is certainly founded in considerable virtues: though I have known instances of good men, with something very revolting and offensive in their manner of behaviour, especially when they have the misfortune to be naturally very awkward and ungenteel; and which their mistaken friends have helped to confirm them in, by telling them, they were above such trifles, as being genteel, dancing, fencing, riding, and doing all manly exercises, with grace and vigour. As if the body, because inferior, were not a part of the composition of man: and the proper, easy, ready, and graceful use of himself, both in mind and limb, did not go to make up the character of an accomplished man. You are in no danger of falling into this preposterous error: and I had a great pleasure in finding you, when I first saw you in London, so well disposed by nature, and so properly attentive to make yourself genteel in person, and well-bred in behaviour. I am very glad you have taken a fencing-master: that exercise will give you some manly, firm, and graceful attitudes: open your chest, place your head upright, and plant you well upon your legs. As to the use of the sword, it is well to know it: but remember, my dearest nephew, it is a science of defence: and that a sword can never be employed by the hand of a man of virtue, in any other cause. As to the carriage of your person, be particularly careful, as you are tall and thin, not to get a habit of stooping; nothing has so poor a look: above all things avoid contracting any peculiar gesticulations of the body, or movements of the muscles of the face. It is rare to see in any one a graceful laughter; it is generally better to smile than laugh out, especially to contract a habit of laughing at small or no jokes. Sometimes it would be affectation, or worse, mere moroseness, not to laugh heartily, when the truly ridiculous circumstances of an incident, or the true pleasantry and wit of a thing, call for and justify it; but the trick of laughing frivolously is by all means to be avoided: Risu inepto, Res ineptior nulla est . Now as to politeness; many have attempted definitions of it: I believe it is best to be known by description; definition not being able to comprise it. I would however venture to call it, benevolence in trifles, or the preference of others to ourselves in little daily, hourly, occurrence in the commerce of life. A better place, a more commodious seat, priority in being helped at table, &c. what is it, but sacrificing ourselves in such trifles to the convenience and pleasure of others? And this constitutes true politeness. It is a perpetual attention, (by habit it grows easy and natural to us), to the little wants of those we are with, by which we either prevent, or remove them. Bowing, ceremonious, formal compliments, stiff civilities, will never be politeness: that must be easy, natural, unstudied, manly, noble. And what will give this, but a mind benevolent, and perpetually attentive to exert that amiable disposition in trifles towards all you converse and live with? Benevolence in greater matters takes a higher name, and is the queen of virtues. Nothing is so incompatible with politeness as any trick of absence of mind. I would trouble you with a word or two more upon some branches of behaviour, which have a more serious moral obligation in them, than those of mere politeness; which are equally important in the eye of the world. I mean a proper behaviour, adapted to the respective relations we stand in, towards the different ranks of superiors, equals, and inferiors. Let your behaviour towards superiors, in dignity, age, learning, or any distinguished excellence, be full of respect, deference, and modesty. Towards equals, nothing becomes a man so well as well-bread ease, polite freedom, generous frankness, manly spirit, always tempered with gentleness and sweetness of manner, noble sincerity, candour, and openness of heart, qualified and restrained within the bounds of discretion and prudenence, and ever limited by a sacred regard to secrecy, in all things entrusted to it, and an inviolable attachment to your word. To inferiors, gentleness, condescension, and affability, is the only dignity. Towards servants, never accustom yourself to rough and passionate language. When they are good we should consider them as humiles Amici , as fellow Christians, ut Conserve ; and when they are bad, pity, admonish, and part with them if incorrigible. On all occasions beware, my dear child, of Anger, that daemon, that destroyer of our peace. Ira furor braves est, animum rege queen nisi parrot Imperat, hunc fraenis hunc tu compass catenis. Write soon, and tell me of your studies. Your ever affectionate.

Bath, Feb 3, 1754. Nothing can, or ought to give me a higher satisfaction, than the obliging manner in which my dear nephew receives my most sincere and affectionate endeavours to be of use to him. You much overrate the obligation, whatever it be, which youth has to those who have trod the paths of the world before them, for their friendly advice how to avoid the inconveniences, dangers, and evils, which they themselves may have run upon, for want of such timely warnings, and to seize, cultivate, and carry forward towards perfection, those advantages, graces, virtues, and felicities, which they may have totally missed, or stopped short in the generous pursuit. To lend this helping hand to those who are beginning to tread the slippery way, seems, at best, but an office of common humanity to all; but to withhold it, from one we truly love, and whose heart and mind bear every genuine mark of the very soil proper for all the amiable, manly, and generous virtues to take root, and bear their heavenly fruit; inward, conscious peace, fame amongst men, public love, temporal, and eternal happiness; to withhold it, I say, in such an instance, would deserve the worst of names. I am greatly pleased, my dear young friend, that you do me the justice to believe I do not mean to impose any yoke of authority upon your understanding and conviction. I wish to warn, admonish, instruct, enlighten, and convince your reason; and so determine your judgment to right things, when you shall be made to see that they are right; not to overbear, and impel you to adopt any thing before you perceive it to be right or wrong, by the force of authority. I hear with great pleasure, that Locke lay before you, when you writ last to me; and I like the observation that you make from him, that we must use our own reason, not that of another, if we would deal fairly by ourselves, and hope to enjoy a peaceful and contented conscience. This precept is truly worthy of the dignity of rational natures. But here, my dear child, let me offer one distinction to you, and it is of much moment: it is this: Mr. Locke's precept is applicable only to such opinions as regard moral or religious obligations, which as such, our own consciences alone can judge and determine for ourselves: matters of mere expediency, that affect neither honour, morality, or religion, were not in that great and wise man's view: such are the usages, forms, manners, modes, proprieties, decorums, and all those numberless ornamental little acquirements, and genteel well-bred attentions, which constitute a proper graceful, amiable, and noble behaviour. In matters of this kind, I am sure, your own reason, to which I shall always refer you, will at once tell you, that you must, at first, make use of the experience of others; in effect, see with their eyes, or not be able to see at all; for the ways of the world, as to its usages and exterior manners, as well to all things of expediency and prudential considerations, a moment's reflection will convince a mind as right as yours, must necessarily be to inexperienced youth, with ever so fine natural parts, a terra incognito . As you would not therefore attempt to form notions of China or Persia but from those who have travelled those countries, and the fidelity and sagacity of whose relations you can trust; so will you, as little, I trust, prematurely form notions of your own, concerning that usage of the world (as it is called) into which you have not yet travelled, and which must be long studied and practised, before it can be tolerably well known. I can repeat nothing to you of so infinite consequence to your future welfare, as to conjure you not to be hasty in taking up notions and opinions: guard your honest and ingenuous mind against this main danger of youth: with regard to all things, that appear not to your reason, after due examination, evident duties of honour, morality, or religion, (and in all such as do, let your conscience and reason determine your notions and conduct) in all other matters, I say, be slow to form opinions, keep your mind in a candid state of suspense, and open to full conviction when you shall procure it, using in the mean time the experience of a friend you can trust, the sincerity of whose advice you will try and prove by your own experience hereafter, when more years shall have given it to you. I have been longer upon this head, than I hope there was any occasion for: but the great importance of the matter, and my warm wishes for your welfare, figure, and happiness, have drawn it from me.
