We drove about that vast, and, now magnificent, Place, throe winds and Rain; I, with that Sunshine in my Soul, which your tender and sweetest goodness to me throws over all my Thoughts, and which the charming Present, that morning brought me from you, had lighted up, and cheered my whole being with. your letters are marked more and more every day, with the delightful and transporting character of your happiness; and of your full Persuasion of the ardour and devotion of that deep-rooted and most tender Passion, which makes the Sun of my present existence. I reckon my letter of Wednesday last will have reached you at Wotton: this will present itself to my Dearest Life in her Argyle Buildings. shall I then be sure to find the Object of my every sweetest hope and most ardent Expectation when I arrive Saturday ye 2d Novr:? may I tell myself that she will look with joy upon a Being she has made happy, and feel the heavenly pleasure of bestowing felicity? yes, I may, I do tell myself this transporting Truth, which she has so tenderly told me, in all the delightful variety that Delicacy of mind and generous sensibility of Heart can alone suggest. how can even your commands not to precipitate my return keep me from flying to your feet? from seizing the dear spot of Earth you tread, as an Empire I would not change for that of the World! how shall I describe the insufferable Length of this cruel week? let your own tender, pitying, kindest Heart count with me every hour that stands, not moves, between our delightful meeting. Those weeks of years, so disputed in Chronology, I can too well explain. but it will come, I trust in Heaven, that sweet moment will come, when my Eyes shall see my adored Lady Hector. Harry, for I love Him enough to call him so, allows of your messenger, and generously prefers my pleasure to his own. we rid this morning where I saw you so much pleased, Mr Harrington's Farm: the cascade, the river, the wood, all was delightful; for I saw you in them all, this morning. I have notified my felicity to the good Folks at Wickham, but I have yet had no news of Them. I am sure They will truly rejoice for I know They are truly my Friends. I have also notified to Sr Richard Lyttelton who is arrived but not in Town. think I can know no joy till I see you, but in your letters. You can not say too much for me to Lady Blandford. she has mentioned me with advantage to Her, whose Partiality is for ever essential to my Being. how can I feel too much obliged to Her? she loves you; what a merit to me!

Sunday Wotton Octr. 27th- I intend now to repay my self for having been obliged the Last time I writ to you to confine my Letter to such short bounds that I seemed not to have expressed the smallest part of What I had to say. Yet I flatter my self it will have carried some mark of the satisfaction that reigned in my Heart from the repeated Confirmation of your partial fondness for Me. The return which you know it meets from Me must have assured you with how much pleasure the Lively painting of your sentiments convinces me that I do indeed make you happy by the faithful description of my own. How great is the felicity I enjoy from the sweet persuasion of being placed in your Heart with such flattering Ideas as your fond Love bestows upon me! How can you wonder, without being unjust to yourself, or me, at the Impression which your Matchless Merit has made upon Me? Is not that merit graced by every charm that ought to engage & have I not reason then to applaud my self, as I do, for being sensible to it? Never apply the term delusion to the Dear, & just, Idea I have formed of your Excellence, & tell yourself that whilst Life continues I will never part with Them. Judge now if I am not Likely to carry on, in one Instance, the dispute between us of Superiority, & in your own Way. In every Other Sense in which that word is employed it belongs to you, & I have either so much, or so Little, of the Woman in me that it is an opinion I am determined never to recede from. I hold my purpose of going to morrow, & being in Town on Tuesday, & I feel a pleasure in being fixed at a place which gives me the Advantage of hearing from you so much sooner, that the concern which Always accompanies the parting with my Wotton friends is diminished by it. you wont Imagine I believe that I shall seek to Lose your dear Idea in following the Diversions of the Town. your Thoughts may place me in my Little Indian room, Where I have seen you, & generally they will be right. I must Acknowledge my self to L. Ch. Ed. who I take for granted will have settled her Winters residence in Ire. Street by the time of my Arrival. But except Her & the persons I named to you in one of my Letters I shall reveal my self to nobody. We have had rather Stormy weather these Last days, but such however that I think will have Admitted of your taking your rides under the protection of the Hills. Commodore West makes us a visit to day from Stowe, but when he arrived There and what his further Plans are I know not. you have heard certainly the Tragical Event that has happened in the Queensberry family. I supposed it of a Nature to make the happy tremble from the reflection of the various accidents that might rob them of their felicity, but I find there are doubts whether a Will did not attend This, that can belong to the Unhappy Only. Any Way it is to be sincerely Lamented. Our friends Here propose being in Town the seventh. their most affect. Complts. attend you as usual. I am in doubt whether I shall gain any thing by sending this Letter by the Post of to day, but I choose to flatter my self it will continue its road to Bath to morrow night, & so reach you a day earlier than if I had reserved it for the London Post on Tuesday. I believe you will be satisfied that I was sincere in terming my writing to you my favourite employment. I do indeed Love to repeat the Unfeigned Affection with which. I am for ever Devoted to you. Pray tell the Dr. Governor my plan of being in Town & that from thence I will write to Him By London To The Right Honourable William Pitt Esqr. at the Bath Somersetshire

Octr. Sunday 27th 1754 A series of the most delightful letters that ever spoke a happy Heart had dispelled every sentiment from my breast but those of the sweetest kind; the felicity of truly and most tenderly loving, and, (may I utter the word?) that of knowing your tender feelings corresponded to my own. your kind and too flattering letter of Thursday would have heald any wounds a misunderstanding could have given, and been of Power to recall a mind from Desperation itself to Peace, Confidence, and Joy, had not that same tenderness of Heart and Delicacy of Attention, that gave the pain, infinitely overpayed it, whatever it was, with the most exquisite and transporting Joys which your dear letters since have given me. it is over; forever erased out of memory; or if any vestiges remain, tic only the sweet recollection how dearly my Peace of mind touches you, and how flattering a value your sensibility and delicacy give to all that comes to you from me. which, my lovely, adored Lady Hector, shall I thank and love you most for? the Pain you gave me, when I consider the cause, or the delightful and too tenderly condescending explanation of it? Ages of suffering could not merit the smallest part of those kind and touching Declarations you so solemnly and so sweetly make. indeed, my dearest Life, you do too much for me: it is not fit you should carry the Partiality of your Ideas so far: fear mixes itself with my unspeakable Delight, to think how infinitely you over-rate me. I were a thousand times more worthless than I am, if my Heart did not tell me, and still more, if that Heart did not declare to you, that the Thing you have given up your whole mind and Heart to, is not me; (would to Heaven it was!) but an Idea correspondent to your own matchless excellence, and which ought to be the man that is so blessed to call you his. it is an unaffected fear that mingles itself with my happiness: the tender Delusion can not last; nor that discernment, blind to nothing else, forever shut its Eyes in my favour. thus my fears, and but common Modesty, suggest, and while I melt with tenderness and gratitude at your too partial, loving Heart, I adore, and tremble as I read. how sweet is the detail of the furniture of your rooms? how good in you to think of it? my Thoughts, adored Lady Hector, sweet object of my Every wish, had been there long before you. can you wonder ? Mr Hall has had orders to match the Paper and other furniture in colour, and all is promised to be ready the last day of this month. I write this Post to your Brother Grenville, imploring his kind offices for me every where: with Lawyers; at Stow; and above all with You. if the Law's Delay will mend its pace in my favour, may I not implore, may I not hope that every thing else may correspond to my wishes, and feel a part of my tender Impatience? if my good Angel in Argyle Buildings should smile upon my prayers, I propose to beg my Dear Lt Temple to be in Town by ye 6th Novr. Wotton proposes to be there about that day. our dear Harry thinks nothing so reasonable as my supplications. judge how I love Him; and how endearing a mark that he dos not hate me! I leave Bath Friday, early. Thursday's Post will be the last that can find me here. how little could I bear such an interruption of our intercourse, if it was not to change it for one still so much more sweet! to hear from those loved lips the tender sentiments I have read; and to read them again in a yet more touching and transporting character, in sweetest looks of heart-felt, mutual, blissful Love! I can not close this letter without returning again to your last, and reproaching my lovely Lady Hector with an indignity to herself: tic such for you, to disclaim caprice and artifice; Nature must change before you can know either; for if ever Proceeding was stamp't with the most ingenuous and noble frankness, (I adore so much) and invariable goodness of Heart, tic that which I have so delightfully experienced in every word and action of the glorious and perfect Pattern of womanhood. adieu. To The Right Honourable The Lady Hector Grenville in Argyle Buildings London.

Monday Missenden Octr. 28th- It is Perhaps the first Time that the being Alone at an Inn appeared to be an Agreeable thing, but mistress of my self, & given up to your dear Idea, it is to me a happy Situation. I recd. your Wednesdays Letter Last night at Wotton, & one Also dated the 19th. To the Last I hope my former Letter will have been a complete Answer, as Likewise to the first part of that which bears the Latest date. I will therefore pass to the Subject which demands, from the most powerful Controlment, (the Acquiecing to ire. desire) an immediate Answer. What shall I do! I fear my answer will not correspond to your plan - & yet it is impossible for Me to give to your solicitations an earlier Time than the 15th or 16th. of next month. Don't Imagine I seek for reasons to delay your happiness, & in yours, my Own. I never could have given my Heart so absolutely with an Intention to withhold my Hand. A hundred combining Circumstances make it out of my power not to impose that Interval between your wishes & my consent. Lord Temples Intention When I Left Stowe was not to quit it till the 10th., unless summoned, my Br. G. proposes being in Town the 7th. only, & I think it would be too Late for an Earlier Summons, If other Points could be settled, which certainly they cannot. Mr. Nuthall has writ to excuse Himself from sending the Draught of the Papers at the Time Appointed. They wont be at Wotton before sunday, if he keeps his Word. My Money must be vested before they can be signed after they are perfected & my Dear Harry & I have settled no account. My own Little businesses will not be finished. Let me repeat, that sooner than what I have named, it cannot be. Lady Temple mentioned Stowe to Me the Instant I arrived, but I begged I might be excused from accepting it, though every mark of Grace from my Br. & Her were most flattering to me, & in that Light what I should wish to receive, but in this particular case it was an Honour & a pleasure that I must forego. My reasons were easily approved & when I talked with my Br. I told Him upon his questioning me, what I had named to you. He thought it was a right Idea, but seemed to Like Ealing still better if that conveniently could be. I understand they take up their residence in London the 10th., but you are the only & best Judge of the reasons for or against proposing it. I submit it to you & provided I am not exposed to the Embarrassment of having the Honours done to me by either of the Parties, I am Satisfied. The Commodore tells Me the Lodgings are fitting up at Chelsea for the reception of Empress & His Brother, & that they are to be established There this week or the next. I cannot with justice to my Brothers omit to say that they have both declared themselves depending your upon orders: But you see it could not be to any purpose to avail yourself of their kind declarations. But if if it was not too much trouble I wish you would by a few lines to each of them Let them know that I have done truly by Them. After reading This, plead my cause with yourself, & remember how dear you have reason to think your Happiness is to Me from those expressions Which you have Allowed Tenderness alone could Dictate. The same recollection will Leave you in no doubt of my Looking upon the day that brings you to me as the best & most pleasing of any I have seen. I will say that I feel I shall expect it with an Impatience that will affect every Thought. O! may your Journey be prosperous, free from every thing that is disagreeable, & secure from any disastrous accident! You see I grow acquainted with fears, by what I pray to be averted from you. I hope this Letter will find you safe after your Badmington expedition. Without indulging weak terrors, is not travelling by night an Alarming Circumstance? Pray remember how much I am Interested in your care of your Self. I have this Morning writ a few Words in my Sisters Letter to the poor Unhappy Duchess. All we can Learn tends to confirm the doubt I hinted to you in my Last. You may believe none of us particularised the circumstance of her Affliction, but only condoled with her that there was any cause for it. I shall not seal my Letter Here, but Leave it open to add my being arrived happily in Argile Street. - Monday I am indeed happily arrived, but the Welcome I found surpassed every other pleasure. It was yourself that recd. me. Your Own dear Hand writing greeted my first Steps into my Own Argile residence. How many Charms attend my being in it. The uninterrupted Contemplation of my own Happiness. The endearing recommendation that Here my impatient Eyes will first see you Again. The Employment I shall find, which will all tend to the Unquestionable Proof of the Sincerity of my sentiments. You come then Saturday! The most rigid prudence sure will not demand, that from any consideration of your Health, I should n't enjoy in all its extent the Satisfaction of seeing you something Earlier than I had flattered my self. I have been taken from my Letter to you to give Audience to L. Ch. Edwin to whom I verified my arrival in Consequence of a promise Made to my Sister to get all possible information upon the Unhappy Story of poor Lt. Drumlaneriggs death. The Circumstances I have learnt from Her make Me alter my Opinion & think it the effect of a most Unlucky chance.. I am forced to yield to the necessity of concluding my Letter having engaged as I have said to write to Wotton, & having before Me at this time the genteelest & most Obliging Letter possible from your Sister, which I recd. whilst L. Ch. Edwin was with me & which I feel an infinite impatience to make a proper return To. I shd. say Abundance of Civilities from Lady Ch. but I must Leave them to a better Opportunity, which will be the happy day of my seeing you Here, for according to my Calculation I cannot write to you again. Will you Let me trouble you, that I may gain a Little Time, by not writing on purpose to my Br. to tell Him that a Person called Here to night with a bill drawn by Mr. Fairchild, Lund, & some one other, for his acceptance. The Sum 290:17:9. payable at 40 days sight to Mr. Warner Merchant. I promised to Apprise Him of it & that if the Person with. call Monday next He shd. have the governors Answer. Though my paper is full & that I have no Time I am sorry to say Adieu -

Oct Bath Monday 28th 1754 How vast a store of goodness and humanity; and of the most endearing tenderness to me, in your sweet bit of Paper on Friday! your letter to my poor sister is such a one, that it brought tears of gratitude into my eyes when I read it: I am quite ashamed, and at the same time all Pride and Delight, to be employed in transmitting such a flattering Proof of your Partiality and tenderness to me. the style and manner of it, is above all applause: the whole letter is the sweet Representative of my matchless Lady Hector. The Propriety of her just understanding in adapting so exactly the means to the End, (and how generous (and Godlike an End, to carry comfort and joy to the drooping Heart of perhaps an almost expiring poor woman?) The Elegance and nobleness of your manners, the Superiority of Dignity, in humanely departing from the right of receiving the Offers of Friendship you so generously make; and above all, the kindest, sweetest, angel-like goodness that characterises the Sentiments you have given up your virtuous and tender Heart to; all these are stamp't in the liveliest and most amiable Colours upon every word of that adorable letter. This Post will bring you two Packets from me. one was writ, but could not go, last night. will you be troubled with them both at once? I must send them to you. had I as many Hearts, as many thousands rather, They would all fly to my sweetest Love; and She suffers me to think that She would shut the Door against no one of Them. I must return to your Angel-goodness in writing the first letter to my sister; your Superiority every way in so noble a condescension: of you I dared to request a step so out of form. believe me, adored Lady Hector, your Dignity is even in my view, and to a Mind Superior as yours, I knew that a Condescenscion of Humanity (and such this truly is) would appear the only Dignity. what a happy lot is mine to call a Heart, which every Virtue has taken Possession of, my own? suffer me to be vain, and to use this enchanting word: if it be mine, it is, as the Soul is the Bodies; to animate, to inform, to actuate and command its every motion, and to reign supreme over all its little, unworthy Proprietor. I have a letter from J Wests, in answer to my Notification, full of a sincere and Cordial Joy at my Happiness; our happiness, let me say; for so These good People term it. tic happiness indeed: how, my adored, shall I ever deserve you? Adieu. To The Right Honourable The Lady Hector Grenville in Argyle Buildings London.

Octr. Bath Wednesday 30th 1754 This days Post has been most kind to me in all respects but one: it brought me your sweet letter of Sunday, so like to all your others, and so unlike to all those that have ever come from the Pen of the tenderest and most noble Heart. it brought me, too, many Pleasures and satisfactions that grow out of your matchless goodness, and my inexpressible adoration of you: (and from what else can Pleasure or satisfaction to me possibly spring?) I mean seven or eight letters of most warm participations with me in my felicity, and above all, a letter from my dearest Lt Temple, the very twin Brother to your own sweet letters; for it is, in the warmest and most generous friendship what my adored Lady Hester's letters are, in sentiments, tenderly and delightfully transcending all but the effusions of her own noble Heart alone, given up to the Godlike Pleasure of blessing the suppliant she permits to adore Her. Hagley has paid to my loved Lady Hester's excellences the tribute at least of half a dozen Pens. how much sincerity has flowed from some, time will show, but Truth, if perhaps in part, involuntary, has flowed from all. I transmit Sr George's letter, which is kind and has an air of speaking his sentiments. I imparted my happiness to Him through Wm L: not without some expressions of much reserve towards Him. the more the merit of his obliging letter. the reason I send it to you is, that it points to a contingency that may prove agreeable to our dear Harry. Wm L: wishes to go to America: Lt Halifax has answered sr G: and me, favourably upon it. Bewdley, in that case, opens: the rest you see by Sr George's letter. the Intimation from me pointed to, was throe` Wm L: I added that it might come to Lt T: as from Sr G:'s own original motion . So, my Dearest Lady Hector, if you please, let it be: it will have a thousand healing consequences: poor sr G: by this letter, deserves it; I am sure from me. the intimation therefore from me , may rest always with yourself and Harry, who knows it. give me leave, my Sweet Life, to trouble you, too, to read the letter, such as it is, of an unshining, but a most good and honourable and affectionate woman. the mail from Wickham is admirable. Kitty's letter has all the marks of herself, and and for a principal one Consequently, the most cordial, sincere and warm affection. I love Her for it: my dearest Lady Hector too will love her for it, I am sure, and be diverted with it, as well as affected with esteem and good will to the honest writer of it. I could not dwell upon any letters but your own, unless They bear relation to You. all become interesting that carry that merit in them. I have held my sweetest Life too long in suspense what the Post brought me of ill. it is the Laws delay. Nuthall has either misapprehended his orders, or I did not well explain myself to Mr G: the Reversions are like to cause this cruel Protraction. I had understood They were not to be a Part of the settlements, upon which, my too generous Lady Hector was to throw herself away. I hope the mistake will be Nuthall's, not mine. I have ordered Him to repair to Wotton again. may I flatter myself with the charming hope that my tenderest Life would not wish to delay the felicity and glory she deigns to bestow. I am all Submission to her Will; unrepining, however feeling: but may I most respectfully implore that small niceties of Law may be waved? Difficulties arising from M. G: are and ought to be sacred. these, I trust, will, upon explanation, not be found to be of that description. I write in extreme haste to safe the Post. W:m Lyttelton, who arrived this Evening, has taken a good part of it. Saturday, I trust in Heaven, will give the loved Source of all my felicity to my longing Eyes, in perfect health, and happy in the matchless happiness She bestows. Adieu, till that dear Moment. I set out to morrow after the Post arrives. To The Right Honourable The Lady Hector Grenville in Argyle Buildings London.

Novr. 1754. Marlbro`, Thursday night Thank Heaven I am so far in my way towards that Indian Room to which my adored Lady Hector has kindly directed an imagination that paints but one loved Image to me in colours to fix my mind: every other Idea in the World is thrown infinitely behind, to a back-ground hardly perceptible. were all that both the Indian worlds contain the price of the moment I shall set my foot in that sweet Room, how poor, how nothing were all their Treasures? I have lived throe your two-days letter, with the sweetest transports of Love and Gratitude. I figure, I actually see my loveliest Life at her Inn at Missenden, delivered up, as She too kindly expresses it, to an Idea she qualifies so tenderly: would for ever it were a reality! I am with Her at this moment, I am at her loved feet in that room where she can have the goodness to remember She has seen the most passionately devoted of men; and where she can tenderly confess, her dear Eyes will not see Him with pain, Saturday next. how delightful to me is every step I make in my journey, when I can tell my happy Heart I move with the wishes and Prayers of the best and most amiably perfect of women? let me come to what, indeed, I ought to have begun with: a wish, a supplication, I fear too ardently pursued, and yet refused so amiably and so sweetly, that it were a sort of Sin against such a Love as you have given me to have been more touched and delighted with your consent, than with the manner and the dear accompaniments of your refusal. you seem to make me feel, and to wish to do it without giving me pain, that my Impatience gos faster than your Delicacy and Dignity can allow. I am sure it gos faster, infinitely faster than my own Heart can avow, if it but seems to go faster than the Supreme, deep-rooted Respect, which is fixed in my Soul for your Dignity and your Virtue, would justify. if it be so; I implore, with real self-condemnation and penitence, pardon, for an offence, which, to myself, the most favourable cause of offence, were Love itself, would never pass for an Excuse. how many millions of the tenderest, most ardent Thanks dos my Soul pay your Goodness for having thought the 14 or 15th not too early a Day? I were every way of a composition, more unworthy of my bliss, than I am indeed, if I could think of any thing but what your tender Goodness gives; not of what my ardour may have too pressingly implored, and which your Propriety and Delicacy has most gently and sweetly declined. Your Dear Brother Harry may perhaps write to you to night to endeavour to remove any causes of Delay that take their rise from Him. tic infinitely kind to me: but I sincerely and strenuously dissuaded this very obliging office. All I troubled my sweet Life with last night about Mr Nuthall, is out of date, and I wish had not taken up the Place upon a Paper I hate to fill with any thing, not directly you. when Mr G: comes from Wotton I know all will be found just what I wish it, for it will be as he thinks best. acquiescence to the determinations of my lovely Lady Hector is not what I feel upon your letter of Tuesday: acquiescence were a poor effort of the Love and Devotion, I, indeed, feel for you. my every wish, my whole will is changed into Yours, from the moment I know there is difference between them, not arising from want of goodness towards me; which every hour furnishes me with the happy, endearing proofs of. Millions upon millions of Loves and Gratitudes to my adored Lady Hector for the tender sentiments poor Lt Drumlanrig's disastrous fate called up in her mind. I truly felt to my Soul, what you express so finely and so tenderly; it is indeed an Event to make the happy tremble. I have writ to the poor Duke to enquire after the health of the Family which I dread to hear. I will now dismiss this melancholy subject with the beautiful and touching words of your Dear Brother Lt Temple, Why must I blot this happy Paper with the miserable name of Queensberry? I meant this for the Post, but none gos till Sunday. it will come by a Servant; why not by myself? variety of businesses, the more fatiguing, as they interpose between my Thoughts and the only idea they can consider with pleasure, have, for a day or two, a little hurried, not disordered me, so that I have broke my journey by lying here, and shall not reach London till Saturday morning. I hope to be there about eleven; and soon after my loveliest, sweetest Lady Hector, only, not in Heaven. till that blessed moment, adieu my adored; adieu Thou every Perfection of human Nature. Lt Temple's Thought of Ealing is better than Wickham. Wickham I loved enough already. I am happy that my Sister has appeared to you in a light you seem pleased with. I must think of her, only as you will do. I have no other Test. happy, too happy that there is one Exception to this rule which your tender Partiality has made necessary to me. To The Right Honourable The Lady Hector Grenville in Argyle Buildings London.

column46: , Sept 20th, 1681. I had sooner written to you since my return, had I found any thing here worth informeing you. Yesterday was the election of our mayor, and the man choosen is one Alderman Bailey, whom they put up out of his order to be mayor that they might put by Mr. Harris, the only person in the corporation that is for the Kings interest; but this being an unpardonable crime among our Whiggish townsmen, they have set up this old blade, although more then half doted, because somewhat more agreeable to their principles. The old Lady Lovelace is very busy at all businesses in the town to influence them her way, and she is now grown so zealous a Whig that she goes every Sunday to the Lady Angleseys to make one of the holy sisters at her conventicle. By her and some other that come hither our Oxonians are made so courageous that they talk nothing now but of wageing war with ye King, and the resolution is concluded on that Westminster Hall must decide it between the King and them concerneing the town clerk. However, they thought fit first to give his Majesty some warneing, and therefore some of them attended with a petition at Newmarket for Princes admission, but could find no one there that would introduce them to ye King, so that they were forced to wait till the King came forth to walk, and then they delivered it to him in the fields, and he ordered them to attend the Lt. Conway for an answer, which was a very severe reprofe for their ill carriage to his Majesty both in this and many other affairs; which made them so angry, that when they came home they talked of nothing but of admitteing Prince forthwith and defying the King. For they say the charter which obliged them to have the Kings approbation of their town clerk was given them since the Kings return, and if they forfeit that they tell us they are not concerned, they having other charters whereby they hold all their other privileges in more ample manner and without any such reserve. But when the time came they only admitted Prince as deputy, to serve in time of vacancy; but its supposed they will never otherwise supply ye vacancy, thinking by the trick to evade the Kings prerogative. The only man in the town of any note that is true to the Kings interest is Mr Harris, who is a very honest and very understandeing man, and, although son-in-law to Alderman Wright, yet acts so contrary to him that ye alderman is become a violent and irreconcilable enemy to him, and by his contrivance it is that he is put by from being mayor this year. He is one of the most sufficient men among them, being worth above ten thousand pounds. He is a very fit man to be town clerk, having been bred a lawyer, but he is not willing to take ye trouble. Sr Thomas Chamberlain, one of ye Deputy-Lieutenants of this county, now lies at the point of death; he will leave 2 daughters behind him, each of which will be worth 15000l apiece. I shall take care that Mr Guise wait on you before he leave England; he goes from hence on Wednesday; by him you shall again hear from me.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: Our townsmen still continue in the same humour of disputing the Kings prerogative with him. Princes speech was made at the election of ye new mayor. If you can remember our Town Hall, there is a large yard before it, and there the rabble meet while the wiser heads of them, which they call the Common Council, are consulteing within whom they shall bring out to them; for the Common Council choose two and bring them out into a balkony looking into the yard wherein the rabble meet, and of them two he which they choose is mayor of the town. After Bailey had been thus brought and choosen mayor, then Prince came forth and began, "Gentlemen, I have something to say to you. You have choosen me town clerk and I will defend your right," and so proceeded to brag what he would doe against the King (not without some rude reflections) in defence of the town privileges, and then told them how ill they were used at Newmarket, and at last (as his very words were) he told them indeed he thought the King of himself a very honest man, but he was drawn away by evil councillors; and then Necessity Holloway, being pro-Recorder, stopped him from proceedeing any farther, not that he misliked the matter of his speech, but, as he himself told me, because he thought it not so proper that he should speak so much in his own business. The way they are resolved to proceed they tell me is this. Prince is to sue the mayor for admission in the Kings Bench, and then they say an order must of course issue out to cause the mayor to give a reason why he doth not admit him, and then ye mayor will give the Kings refusal of approbation as the reason, and crave the judgement of ye Court upon it; and they say they have it under the hands of the best lawyers in England that the Court must declare in favour of them, for the charter wherein the King hath this prerogative of approveing ye recorder and town clerk reserved to him was granted by this King since his return; and they make count to cancel this charter and stand to that they had before. However, it seems their courage doth somewhat cool, for yesterday they went in a full body to the Earl of Angleseys to crave his assistance in the case; but I suppose all assistance will come to late in behalf of Prince after so seditious a speech. It seems Alderman Wright is turned out of ye Commission of the Peace for the town, as well as for the county, on the account of the story I writ you of in my last. It seems our plenipotentiaries yt went to Newmarket were likewise very coursely treated at Cambridge; for the innkeeper where they lodged swinged them in their reckoneing most abominably, making them pay five times the price for every thing they had; and hireing a chamber there to lay some of their things till their return, which was but 3 days, they made them pay 20s for it, and, when expostulated with, told them it was accordeing to the rate gentlemen paid at Oxford when ye Parliament was here, and therefore they had no reason to complain; and when they scrupled payment they were in danger of being had before the mayor, but to avoid this they were contented to pay what was demanded; but all put together, and Tompsons narrative of their journey in the last Intelligence, is such a heavy grievance unto them that their great hearts can scarce bear up under the affliction of it. I hope this will put them upon such resentments as to make ym loose their charter. Dr Hammond is married and Jack Benson is towards it, being got into as bad an entanglement of love as his brother Sam was. I have nothing more.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: In my last I promised you an account of ye Earl of Angleseys reception. Accordeing to ye appointment, he was conducted into the town last Tuesday by the townsmen in great state, and he and his two sons made freemen of the town. He made a speech to them, wherein he took notice of their disagreeing with the University, and offered his service to reconcile them to us, or doe them any other kindness that lay in his power. It seems they promised him, when they first went to him, that if he would stand their friend at Court, now the Duke of Buckingham their steward hath no access there, they would have a burgesses place always at his service for whomsoever he should recommend; and this it was that made his Ldship so readily comply with them; and now they begin to defy the Lt. Norris, they having gotten as they think so potent a protection against him; but I suppose his Ldship will not think fit to interfere with any one for their sakes. After he was sworn, a dinner was made ready for him at the mayors, where he was splendidly entertained. The townsmen have had a Common Council to consider of ye affront put upon them in Tompsons Intelligence, and have voted it as a scandalous libel against their most honourable Corporation, and an action is ordered to be entered against him next term. But Tompson is not the only man yt makes sport with their voyage to Newmarket. Alderman Wright lately going before Brazen Nose Coll. a fresh man came out, and spying him past by called after him "Run, Alderman, run; the Black guard are coming!" which put the alderman into so violent a passion that he was scarce himself all that day after. Whenever he comes, he speaks scurrulously of the King. It seems, when ye alderman was at Newmarket with his petition, the King walking in ye fields met Nel Gwyn, and Nel called to him, "Charles, I hope I shall have your company at night, shall I not?" With this story the Alderman makes a great deal of work wherever he comes. He says he had often heard bad things of the King, but now his own eyes have seen it. They are mighty at consultation concerneing ye management of their law suit, and doubt mightily how it will be managed against them, whither the Attorney General will plead against the granteing Prince a mandamus , or let that be granted and after proceed against them with a quo warranto . But which way soever it be, they make mighty sure of their cause; and all the rabble of ye town are for living and dying by it. Dr Morton came hither on Tuesday, and on Friday goes for Ireland.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: Nothing happened worth informeing you at our sessions, but only that 2 malefactors were condemned to death (one for killing her bastard and a rogue for cutteing a purse), and the pro-Town Clerk officiated not in his place. It seems ye townsmen doe not keep to their first courage, but begin to be cautious and wary how they give offence, and therefore have thought fit not to let Prince officiate in the place as they first designed, but have appointed another to doe it. The Vice-Chancellor and ye Bp. have had a great consult about the Secretaries letter concerneing ye reneweing our commission, and have agreed to put in Dr Parrot, Dr Levied, Dr Jane, Dr Beson, Warden of New College, Dr Lloyd, and I think Mr Guise. The Bp. is very desirous he should be in, but the Vice-Chancellor made an exception that he was not so proper as being only a Mr of Arts; but when I went to him and told him he was not to be looked on as an ordinary Mr of Arts, but as a gentleman which lives in town upon his estate which is worth 500l per annum, and therefore sufficient to qualify him for such an office in any county in England, he seemed to be as willing as the Bp., but whither they will return his name or no I can not tell. I desire yt you would give me advice from ye Secretaries, where you will certainly know; for, if his name be not put in at ye Secretaries, I will attempt to doe it at the Lord Chancellors, and I hope there I shall not fail; but if that trouble were saved I should be glad, and therefore I beg your assistance in it. I wonder ye Secretary should say he doth not know him. He knew him once to doe him a very great unkindness in making the Archbp. his enemy, although he did not design it. He is a gentleman of as great worth and eminence in that way of learneing he hath addicted himself to as any in England, or, I believe, in any other country in Europe, and on that account is an ornament to the University, and will er long appear so to the whole nation. He is an extraordinary person and I cannot say enough of him, and beside him I believe you will find few of his estate to devote themselves so industriously to their studies, or of his parts to make so good progress in them. And beside, his good inclinations to the Church doth sufficiently appear in that, in his circumstances and in so ill times, he would go into orders to be rendered thereby ye more capable of serving it. I think such a man is not to be affronted, and now his name hath been mentioned on this occasion it would be an affront not to be put in. Pray use your interest to effect it, and if that doth not succeed I will use mine with the Chancellor. He is married and lives here in the town, and therefore considereing all his qualifications I know not who can be fitter. The Secretary having himself mentioned Dr Jane, the Bp. thought not fit to put in either Dr Hammond or Dr Smith, to avoid envy to our college. Sr William Walter already begins to make an interest to be knight of the shire next Parliament, and will I suppose without any great difficulty carry it, he being a person of general good esteem in ye county. Tomorrow I go to the funeral of Sr Thomas Chamberlain, where I suppose I shall meet most of the gentry of ye county, and perchance shall be able to inform you of something worth observation from thence. St Cyprian is now finished, as likewise a book of Dugdales of Heraldry; it contains ye first principles of it, and the catalogue of ye Nobility and Baronets of ye 3 kingdoms.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: , Feb. 23, . I have yours of Tuesday, and know not what to say to your affair. It is better have the employment you mention then have none at all, especially if you are sent so honourably to it as by the King himself and have his promise of a provision, but to be always mereteing and receive no reward is an hard case. This employment is not worth medleing with, in my judgment, without a future prospect of advantage; if you have any such, it is better embark in it then lie idle, but were it my case I would make my market as good as I could and would not ask less then to be Clerk of ye Council, and old Brown will er long make a place vacant there; you can best judge of it. My good wishes I can put it, but my judgment in cases of this nature is not to be relied on, because not versed in ye affairs of Court or acquainted how your circumstances stand there; only this, I would always lay down as a general rule, to accept of that which is beneath a mans expectations rather then have nothing at all. Your chief point will be to secure a friend which will solicit for you in your absence in case an opportunity happen, and next to take care, while in France, yt the faults of the inexperienced ambassador doe not lie at your door, for I perceive, in effect, you are to be sent his governor, and often it happens to such yt they bear the blame for their pupils fault, whither they can help them or no. I wish you all the success you can desire or expect in this affair, and the best prosperity in all other. If it give you not too much trouble, I would desire you to remember your promise of buying me a beaver, such as is proper for a divine, provided not too big; and get it put into a box and sent to the Oxford carriers either at ye Saracens Head in Snow Hill or ye Oxford Arms in Warwic Lane, which ye person of whom you buy it of I suppose will take care. If it be not sent away as soon as bought, there will be danger of a change afterword.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: Oxford, 12 March, . Our assizes are ended without affordeing me anything observable to inform you of. Here was very little business on ye Crown side. Only a poor fellow is condemned to be hanged for breaking prison. He was last Michaelmas condemned at ye town sessions for cutteing a purse, that having it seems been long his trade, for it appeared by his hand he was formerly burnt for it. However, intercession having been made to the King for him, he was repreved in order to transportation; but before orders came concerneing it he broke prison, and, being a while after caught again at his old trade and put into Newgate, our gaylor challenged him as his, and being brought hither hath sentence of death passed upon him again for breaking his prison; and now I suppose, without any further hopes of mercy, he is to prepare for hangeing, he being a most notorious rogue, as it sufficiently appeared at his trial. That which was most observable was a most terrible abhorrence of ye association presented to the bench by the grand jury, and the Lt. Norris being present undertook ye presenteing of it. It is worded at the highest pitch of loyalty and zeal, and in the end of it they promise ye King yt, whenever he shall think fit to call another Parliament, they will choose only such as shall be acceptable to the King, and will be for the preserving the succession of the Crown to the right heir. Levinz sat judge for ye Crown, and Atkings in ye other court. Friday morneing was wholly taken up in giving ye charge, which was very long, and therefore he made this excuse for it, that there being very little business he had nothing else to entertain ye company with. In his charge he insisted against prosecuteing Protestant dissenters on ye Act of 35th of Queen Elizabeth, and urged some arguments to prove that it was not designed it should be put in execution against them, particularly that of inflicteing lesser penalties since, which he looked on as disalloweing of those rigorous ones inflicted by that Act, and told us that it was never but once put in execution, and that was against some of Colchester; which part of his charge gave us here some offence. Aaron Smiths business is put of till the next assize, some punctilio in law being wonteing for bringeing him to his trial this assizes. We had great expectations of a trial at the other court between ye Lt. Norris and Brom Whorwood, about their quarrel in the Town Hall at the election of ye Town Clerk. Broom brought an action of battery against my Lt. for beateing him, and my Lt. an action of scandalum magnatum against Broom for calleing him young fool. But the Bp. of Oxford interposeing spoiled the sport and made up the matter between them; for in truth ye Lt. Norris first began the quarrel, and called Brom old fool before he called him young fool; and beside it was reather hypothetically then categorically said, for my Lt. calleing him old fool, he replied, "If I am an old fool you are a young fool," and therefore I think his Lordship did very wisely to submit it to the Bps. arbitration. Whenever there is a Parliament its certain this old knave will never more be choosen here, by reason of the trick he hath put upon his brother representative; for Alderman Wright taking care of dischargeing the alehouse and paying the bills of their canvas, when he came to Whorwood to be reimbursed his share of it, the old knave told him if he had payed the bills already there was no need for him to concern himself any further, and ye Alderman could not get as much as a fartheing of him for bearing the expenses of three elections for him; and on this account he is out of all expectations here for ye future, and therefore puts in very violently for an interest at Abington. The town are mightily affrighted with the expectation of a quo warranto , for they having reprieved a wench condemned here for killing her bastard 4 months without the Kings autority to warrant their doing of it, they all give their charter for gon if the King should come upon them for the forfeiture. And that they should receive any favour herein is what, considereing their carriage to the King, is what they cannot reasonably expect; and I hope his Majesty will think so too. Dr Elliot, an eminent physician of this place, is lately dead. The Earl of Northampton next week takes his leave of the University and goes to travel. I thank you for ye trouble you are pleased to give your self in buying me an hat, but ye carrier hath not as yet brought him hither. Pray lets know what is like to become of the charter of London, and with use is made of the information I gave concerneing Norwich.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: Oxford, Aug. 6, 1684. I have ye favour of two of yours to acknowledge. Both of them came to my hands at Woodstock, but now I am again at Oxford. Our Act ended here with ye expulsion of both ye Terrefilii , but that hath not put an end to ye bustle which we are now in on two ; ye one is ye concern of ye whole University, ye other of a private college. Ye University concern is about ye town carter. It seems, to induce them to surrender it, ye Earl of Abington promised them ye addition of several new grants, and in order thereto a petition was presented to ye King in council concerneing it, which contained 5 points; but, ye University apprehendeing that ye King by granteing it would prejudice us, they presented a counter petition in answer to it, and upon a full hearing in council ye town petition was rejected in every point. This was about 5 months since. But ye Lord Abington, not acquiesceing in it, hath ever since been employing his interest in ye town behalf to doe us all ye prejudice he can, and acts very vehemently and peevishly in the thing, and so ye business now stands; but we do not doubt our interest herein, and I hope er long I shall be able to give you an account of our good success. The other affair is concerneing Magd. Coll. Ye divinity lecturer being dead, ye college proceeded to an election, and by a great majority choose on Dr Bailey into ye place, at which Dr Smith, formerly Sr Joseph Williamsons chaplain, being ye senr, thinks himself aggrieved, because at ye colleges petition ye Bishop of Winchester made an injunction yt all offices and lectures should be disposed of accordeing to seniority, supposeing ye persons capable. Upon this ye Dr makes his appeal to ye Bishop, and upon a full hearing ye Bp. determines in favour of Smith, and orders ye college to proceed to a new election and make choice of Smith. Ye college refuses to submit to this sentence; hereupon ye 9 seniors are put out of commons; hereupon ye college address to ye D. of Ormond, and by him present a petition to ye King for redress; and ye Bp. hath been served with an order to proceed no further herein, the King having appointed to have ye hearing of it himself, and there it now rests. In ye meantime Dr Smiths party, which are only two, have presented a libel of accusation to ye Bishop against their head. The crimes they accuse him of are chiefly corruption in soloing of places, and knavery in falsifying ye college register in a thing that was entered there by order of King and council on ye decision of a former controversy in Dr Pierces time heard before ye council, while I suppose you were of ye University, which being much to the infamy of Dr Pierce, when he sold his headship to the present man, it seems one part of ye bargain was that he should race all this out of ye register, as he should have an opportunity of so doing; and accordingly, to make good his promise, this honest man, finding ye whole to be contained within two pages, pasts them both together and so made ye whole disappear. They are now at Farnham about it, but what ye result will be I know not. What we have now don at ye press ye Gazette hath er this told you. Dr Brady hath lately published altogether several tracts he formerly published against some antimonarchical antiquaries, and in ye preface promises us ye 1st part of his long talked of History of England to be published in Michaelmas term. He hath been long a searcher after English antiquity and pretends to have made great discoveries. What they are we shall know when his book comes forth. There is a book lately published by some of ye foreign seminaries against ye Bp. of Winchester in answer to his lately put forth against ye papists, in which the old man is dealt very rudely with. Drayden hath published a translation of Maimburgs History of ye League, as he tells us at ye Kings command. Judge Windham being dead, its talked Roger North, ye Keepers brother, will succeed him. But for such sort of news I refer you to ye news papers you have public with you. My house will be coverd by Michaelmas, and when it is habitable I shall fix my residence in it to ye end of my days. I wish you good health and all things that can be good in that country.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: Oxford, July 9th, 1685. I have received yours, and accordeing to your order have paid your brother 5l. Your former making me hope I should speedily see you here made me defer writing, least my letter might come too late to find you in Dublin. Our rebellion is now over, Monmouth and all his party being routed. Instead thereof we have now got a standeing army, a thing the nation hath long been jealous of; but I hope ye King will no otherwise use it then to secure our peace. The war now from ye field I suppose will pass into ye roads, which we must expect will a while be infested with the remainder of those rogues. You will have a more exact account of these transactions from London then I am able to give you from this place. Our good Bp. is fallen very ill, and I fear will not long last. We begin already to be solicitous who may be his successor. I believe it may be your tutor, and I am of an opinion he may not be so unfit a man as some apprehend. The Bp. of Chichester is lately dead and ye sea of Peterborough is vacant by ye translation of Bp. Lloyd to Norwich. Trelawny will be a Bishop somewhere before all those vacancies be supplied, its supposed at Bristol, the Bp. of that place being to be translated to Peterborough. We have no Act this year, although ye greatest number of Doctors that I ever knew in all faculties, especially in divinity. The rebellion hath been ye occasion of this intermission. Dr Stillingfleet hath lately published a book worth your seeing, containeing an historical account of ye British Church before its suppression by ye Saxon invasion. I shall doe your brother all the service I can, but I believe my time in the college will now be short, especially if ye Bp. dyes. I have now been long enough here to begin to be weary of a place where now almost every one is my junior, and therefore have resolved to retire to my living and fix for good and all there; and in order hereto I have hearkened to proposals that have been made to me of marriage, and because they are such as are very advantageous. I have already got so far as ye sealeing of articles, whereby I have secured to myself 3,000l; but after ye death of ye ffather and mother, whose only child ye gentlewoman is, I believe there will be at least 1,500l more. I little thought I should ever come to this; but abundance of motives have overpowered me, and therefore I have yielded to the circumstances of my present condition, which would neither be convenient nor comfortable to me without this resolution. Although they are very few who I have yet communicated this to, I cannot conceal it from yourself. I doe not ask your advice herein, because it is too late for it; neither doe I your opinion, because you cannot judge of it without knoweing all my circumstances, which it would be too long for me now to tell you.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: Norwich, October. 27th, 1686. I am to beg your pardon that it hath been so long since I wrote to you. The truth is, I have been a long while in an unsettled condition, but now have fixed my self and all my concerns in this place, and shall be glad of a line or two to know of your health. Before I left Oxford I think I acquainted you how our accounts stand, and shall be answereable for what remains due unto you as you shall direct. Your brothers interest being so great at court I should think it might be made use of to get you an establishment in England, so that you might be no longer confined to a place where I fear all things may run into confusion. We live here remote from ye center of affairs and in a great deal of quiet; only fears from London sometimes alarm us here, but I still hope it may go much better with us then we think or doe deserve. Our Dean is here with us, and goes not to London because under his Majestys displeasure, but I hope that affair er long may be over. We have got here a very excellent person for our Bishop, which is a great comfort unto us. I shall be glad to know of your health and how affairs stand with you.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: Norwich, July 12th 1688. It hath been so long since I have heard from you that I begin to fear I must loose your correspondence. I confess we are now at a great distance; however I should be loath our old friendship should be forgot. Your brother being now a great man at Court, I have been expecteing that by his interest a translation might be procured for you to some place in the English Court as advantageous to you as that you have in ye Irish, and I hope some time or other it may be don, that I may have my good friend again where I may sometimes have ye happiness of enjoying his conversation. Things look cloudy upon us here, and ye matter of ye Declaration hath, I fear, put us much under the Kings displeasure. However, I thank God we still live in quiet, and, if God continues that, we may be content patiently to bear all things else. At present we are only hurt in imagination, and our greatest torment is our fears of what may after happen; but I hope they will prove to be only fears and nothing else. I hope when you come into England you may think Norwich worth your seeing, when you have a friend here that would so heartily make you welcome. I have now lived here 2 years in great content, it being ye most delightful city of any I have seen in England for a man to live in, especially in our distrinct, which hath all sorts of conveniences to recommend it to our satisfaction. There is still some money due unto you from me, and it hath lain in London for you now near these 2 years, but it being ye last account I am like to make with you I would gladly have your full discharge when it is paid you, and therefore I hope your occasions may er long call you to London, and then all things shall be made even between us. I confess I am ye more cautious because ye last 15l I paid you had like to have been lost through ye death of your kinsman to whom it was to be paid, and I only ow it to Mr Pitts negligence in omitteing to give him ye bill when he ought that it was not. Pray favour me to let me hear from you when you have leisure, and you will very much oblige, etc.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: , June 7th, 1691. I should be glad to hear whether you have taken my advice in applying to Dr Sharpe in reference to your brother, and what success you have had in it. He is a generous, free spirited man, and would deal well with a chaplain, and in his station will be able to advance him. But as to ye other person you mentioned (whom I thoroughly know), all is ye contrary. He hath nothing in his gift fit for your brother to accept, and, if he had, he is a close designeing man that will reguard little but what tends to his own or relations interests, and I would by no means advise any friend of mine to list himself under him. Whatever ye Church may be advantaged by others of ye new promotion, I expect it will be very little by him. He is indeed my old friend and acquaintance; however, it grieves me to se this diocese sacrificed to his secular interest, he being one that will by no means answer its needs, and I think there is no diocese in England needs a good Bishop more then this. You see the London ministers get all ye preferments, and therefore, if possible, fix your brother there, and I assure you, as ye world now goes, a curacy is better then a living, for, all country commodities being so low and taxes so high, all livings that depend upon prediall tiths are fallen more then half in value. I assure you ye living I now live at, although in common reputation 120l per annum, and so it was when I first took it, is not now worth 401 per annum clear of all charges, and therefore, till ye world be better, I would by no means advise you to putt your brother into such a living as would forfeit his fellowship, but reather to begin in some employment that might be consistent with it and make way for further provision; and in order to this I could not direct you better then to ye Archbishop of York, and I should be heartily glad to hear you have had any success with him.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: Saham near Wanton, in Norfolk, October. 12th, 1691. I doe most humbly thank you for ye favour of yours. I have been a while from home, otherwise you had been troubled from me er this. As to Dr Pococks place, it was offered me and I refused it, and that for two reasons: the first is, I nauseate that learning, and am resolved to loose no more time upon it; and the 2d is, I nauseate Christ Church; and, further, if I should go to Oxford again I must quit whatever I have here, and ye advantage would scarce pay for ye remove. But my main argument is, I have an unconquerable aversion to ye place, and will never live more among such people who now have ye prevaileing power there. I should be glad to be assured you are at the same lodgings, for I will send you a bill for ye remainder of your money in my hand, it being now in London for you. I am glad you have placed your brother as you mention; ye Earl of Pembroke hath good livings in his gift, and if they fall he can provide for him. Our Dean tells me that you have got now an employment; I should be glad to wish you joy of it, if I knew what. It seems you had him always with you at your coffee house, and I wish you had him there still for any good he doth at Norwich, for ye truth is, he is good for nothing but his pipe and his pot, and we are wretchedly holpd up with him. Sr Robert Baldoc that was judge in King James's reign is lately dead.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: Norwich, June 13th, 1692. I doe most heartily thank you for ye favour of yours, which were more then ordinarily welcome for ye sake of ye good news they brought. Till this happy turn our Jacobites were come to that height of confidence to talk openly that now all was their own, and some of them suspended their payment of ye taxes; and at ye bishops visitation at Norwich, which was the 3 latter days of Whitsun week, the Jacobite clergy would not own his jurisdiction and refused to appear; but on Sunday night ye news coming to us of ye victory, they came all the next day and made their submission, and I hope now they will have ye wit to carry themselves better, and if they doe not that ye government will have ye courage to call all such to an account. For in the strength of such a victory the King may now begin to act accordeing to his own measures. I remember, when last at London, I was with one of ye deprived Bishops, who seemed as confident of going again very speedily to his bishopric as I was of going home again, but I thank God he is like now to be disappointed. I perceive the French King and our Jacobites deceived each other; he made them believe wonders he would doe for them, and they made him believe as much that they doe for him. I hope they will now be both undeceived, and an end be put to that great confidence which was between them. I have for 3 years been exceedeingly troubled at Ipswich with an untoward clergyman there, one Alexander. He was lecturer of the town, a place very considerable, but, being turned out for his misdemeanour in ye beginneing of the revolution by the town on whom he depended, he got another church in ye town, although of little or no value, and there did nourish such a faction and division in ye place, and was so closely stuck to by ye Jacobites, as being looked on a martyr for that cause, that he had almost undone ye place in setteing the people together by ye ears. I had autority enough of my side to have routed him, and will enough to doe it, but found him backed by men of that power both in church and state that I durst not meddle with him for fear of draweing them upon myself, but reserved the case for ye Bp., his authority better enableing him to encounter him. But the truth is, I found his Lordship as cautious in the matter as myself, and the mischief must have gone on to ye utter undoing of this place, but that this Jacobite design, God be thanked, hath delivered us from him. It seems he, being an agent employed to give ye party warneing to be in readiness, put on a tinkers habit with a snapsack on his back, and so went on foot through all Essex; but in one place being discovered, where he had been too free of his talk as to ye design on foot, he was followed to Ipswich, and there seized on and laid in jail for treason, which putes an end to the whole controversy.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: Saham near Wanton, in Norfolk, June 27th, 1692. I have yours of the 16th, but it came not to my hands till last Friday, for I was absent at Ipswich on a visitation. I there had ye whole of Alexanders affair. He was of that place, but was turned out about 3 years since for several misdemeanours. To revenge himself for this, he hath lived in ye town ever since, made a party there big enough to put the place into a flame ever since. At first I interposed with my autority to quench it, but finding him backed by the then Archbps. of Canterbury and York, whom he had made believe that he suffered for ye cause of the Church, I thought it best to let it alone, and so it hath stood ever since, and the town and he have been at law ever since; but on this advantage I suppose they will be too hard for him, for one of ye main reasons why he was turned out was his busy opposition to ye present Government, especially in one sermon which they say was ye cause of ye mutiny of ye Scotch soldiers that quartered there about 3 years since, which I suppose you may remember; and his present misdemeanour is a grand confirmation of that argument. The true story of his doings in Essex is, he came to Keldane in a gray coat and pair of bags on his back, which it seems by some was improved into a tinkers budgett, and lay there two days to wait for a coach to go for Ipswich. In the interim he makes it his endeavour to make his landlord a Jacobit; tells him King James was a coming; that if he would not declare for him him now he would be glad to doe it two months hence, for he was coming; that they were sure of ye major part of ye fleet; and a great deal more to this purpose; and that he had 3 horses ready to be employed in his service, whereof one was kept in London, and ye others elsewhere. However, it will be that advantage to ye town of Ipswich to get rid of him that, in case he will quit that place and create no more disturbances there, ye Bp. hath undertook to intercede for him; and I should be heartily glad ye cause would fall this way. He is a fellow of parts, but employs them mostly to doe mischief. The Bp. hath finished his visitation and is again gon to London, but it was little more then pro form` , for ye truth is, in our present case of unsettlement the times will not bear doing more. The Act of Toleration hath almost undone us, not in increasing ye number of dissenters but of wicked and profane persons; for it is now difficult almost to get any to church, all pleadeing ye licence, although they make use of it only for ye alehouse. There must be a regulation in these matters, and yet it will be difficult to get a parliament sober enough to doe it. Phanaticisme hath got ye prevalence in corporations, and ye gentlemen must humour them this way or else they will not be chosen.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: , Nov. 27th, 1693. I have two of yours to thank you for, and I had not been so tardy in acknowledging the debt but that I tarried to have wherewith to make a return, which ye country is not so fertile of as ye city. Out of Suffolk I have full assurance that ye recorder of Oxford is sent thither of purpose to promote ye great design in hand. He is a stranger to that country, and on his first coming thither came with ye letter and ye interest of ye Feltons to back it to make him recorder of that town. He calls himself a lawyer, and yet doth not practice; he seems to be a very fair conditioned good-tempered man, and thereby ye better capacitated to wheedle; but those that send me this character of him have not enabled me to tell you his name, but I have expressly wrote to be informed of it. I have been told also of a person of quality that hath made a tour this last summer through that whole country at ye gentlemen's houses for this purpose; so we see they turn every stone for their design, without considereing they serve none by it but the King of France; and indeed I have been lately told by a very intelligent person that he is well assured that abundance of those that seem fierce Republicarians are in reality fierce Jacobites, and that they openly promote this design for no other end but that it is ye likeliest to bring about what they would really have. Whenever there is a new parliament, the knights of ye shire for Norfolk will be Sr Henry Hobart and Sr Roger Pots, and for Suffolk Sr Samuel Bernardiston and Sr Jarvis Always, all stiff Republicarians; but I hope most of ye burroughs will provide better. I am now at Norwich, where ye Dean behaves himself more like a beast then ever, and is so obstinate and perverse in his own humours (which are indeed intolerable) that there is no endureing of him. I find he is much in with the party, without considereing that if they prevail they will take his deanery from him; and indeed, if that were all the hurt they would doe, it would be no great matter. The Lt. being now out, I suppose all that were put into employment by his means will follow ye same risk, which makes me concerned for you. I shall be glad to know what will be ye event in this matter. I confess, were I worthy to advise you, I should be desirous you still keep your place, although it be by temporiseing with them you cannot like. If ye Government stands, things must revert again to ye interest of those that now seem to be undermost, and my Lt. will be in place again; for I look on it only as a trick to suit ye exigencies of ye times that ye King is forced to humour those men, and if once ye cause be removed ye effect of it will be so also.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: , Dec. 11th, . I have ye favour of yours, and by a letter from another friend ye names of all the pensioners. I am of opinion this discovery will so blast that party that we have no need to fear any thing from them this sessions. The Dialogue between Whig and Tory is with great eagerness dispersed here, and all that's said in it goes for gospel amongst too many. The poison is so taking that I think it needs an antidote. We are here at a miserable pass with this horrid sot we have got for our Dean. He cannot sleep at night till dosed with drink, and therefore, when in bed, his mans business is to drink with him till he hath his dose; and it being his way to keep a man only for ye time of his residence and then dismiss him, he hath spread his fame so through ye whole country that nothing is more scandalous; for his servants, whom he thus dismisses, going into other familys, tell all, especially one, a lewd fellow enough, being entertained by one Mr. Earl, a drinkeing lewd gentleman of this country, to be his butler, gives there a most horrid account of his old Mr ye Dean; and when ye lewd ones there meet together to drink, one of their chief entertainments is to have ye butler come in and tell all his stories of ye Dean of N., which represent him one of ye greatest beasts in nature. And indeed his carriage in business represents him as much a brute as his man can a beast, for he acts by no rules of justice, honesty, civility, or good manners towards any one, but after an obstinate, selfe-wild, irrational manner in all sorts of businesses, whereby he disoblidgeth every one that hath any thing to doe with him. He hath after a most unreasonable manner disoblidged every one of the prebendarys except Hodges, and nothing will satisfy him but to be an absolute king over us. He comes little to church and never to ye sacrament, though we have a sacrament every Sunday; and as for a book, he looks not into any from ye beginning of ye year to ye end. His whole life is ye pot and ye pipe, and, go to him when you will, you will find him walking about his room with a pipe in his mouth and a bottle of claret and a bottle of old strong beer (which in this country they call nog) upon ye table, and every other turn he takes a glass of one or ye other of them. If Hodges comes to him (for scarce any other doth), then he reads Don Quixote, while ye other walks about with his pipe as before, and this is noble entertainment between them. Certainly ye preferments of ye Church were never designed for such drones; and yet these two fellows have about 300l per annum each, and never did it a farthings worth of service in their life, professeing nothing else but to live idly and feed their bellies upon what they have. Hodges indeed is no drinker as ye other, for his body cannot bear it; but although nothing is more mean then he, either in his birth or his merit, yet nothing can be more proud and conceited, or possibly can have a more despicable thought then he hath of the business of his profession, and, to tell ye truth, he is not made for it. Once in a year he will offer to preach, but, his sermons being most on end ye translation of his moral philosophy lectures at Oxford, as soon as ye people see him in ye pulpit they all get out of church. Nothing could be more humble and complaisant then this fellow was all the time of ye 2 late Kings, when he was obnoxious on ye account of his Mr, Shaftsbury, or can there be any thing more proud and insolent then he hath appeared ever since this government began. But I hope after all their point will not go. This discovery of pensioners I reckon will break ye reputation of ye party, especially if it be pursued with 2 or 3 pamphlets, which I heartily wish for. The late Archbp. would be buried in ye churchyard and by a Nonjuror. Dr Trumball, his quondam chaplain, performed that office for him. His library he gave to Emmanuel College in Cambridge, whither he sent it before his death. The reason of his being buried in the churchyard, I am told, was no other but to lie among his relations who are buried there. A friend of mine wrote me from London yt ye of may be Secretary again if he will, and of refusal having put ye King out of all his measures and much exasperated him against that party who assured him yt would accept of ye place, several of our members went out of this country prepared to fall upon the church this sessions; but now, I hope, we shall escape their malice this bout. Our Bp. will never accept of Dublin; he acts here as wise and cunning a part as possibly a man can doe, and will make his fortune any where, and therefore you may be assured he will never leave England. I find the Republicarians in these parts openly sedulous to promote atheism, to which end they spread themselves in coffy houses and talk violently for it, and Dr Burnets Archaiologia is much made use of by them to confute ye account ye Scriptures give us of ye creation of ye world, and other books are also dispersed for this purpose, and ye number of their proselytes I am assured is great. You see where licentiousness and confusion at last end.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: , April 15, 1696. The account which is given in one of ye prints, called ye "Post boy," of the Association of this place gives ye governors of this city great disgust; ffor ye truth is, every word of it is false, and it foully reflects upon them. Ye whole spring of that contrivance I told you in my last, and indeed, considereing ye notion which those had of the word "revenge" who were so zealous for it, there was good reason for ye altereing of it. For they declared they meant thereby that, in case ye King was kilt,they would draw their swords and cut ye throats of all ye Jacobites, and that by virtue of the Parliaments Association they were bound thereto; which extravagance deserved to be discountenanced and disowned; for should ever ye case happen, which God forbid, every man shall be a Jacobite whom ye rabble shall think fit to plunder and abuse. Next Friday our seven condemned criminals are to be executed. They are stout fellows all of them, but as hardened villains as ever I heard of in my life. All that those ministers who assist them can doe to make them sensible of their condition avails nothing, those few minutes they have left they spend in the height of lewdness and frolic.
