The Mayor hath ordered ye town clerk of ye city now in London to prosecute ye writer of ye "Post boy" for slandering them in his print, unless he will discover the intelligencer that sent him ye news from hence, and then they will right themselves of him here on the place. The truth is, whoever wrote that account to him was a very impudent lying fellow, and by one passage I perceive intends a reflection on me, as if I influenced the city to ye alteration; whereas nothing is a more constant rule with me then never to meddle with any of their concerns, and indeed I very seldom go among them. Our close is as it were a town of itself apart from ye city, separated from it by walls and gates. I acknowledge I have as great a share of their respects as any of my profession perchance that hath ever lived among them, but I take care to have nothing at any time to doe with them but in my profession, and in this they have my pains constantly gratis. I am afraid we shall have but a lame return from ye clergy to whom we have sent our Association to be subscribed; it is a very moderate form, and I have sent this argument with it into my archdeaconry: that the ready subscribeing of it will be ye surest way to prevent an harder form from being imposed on us. I have taken all ye care I can to induce all, where I am concerned, to comply. I need not trouble you with a copy of ye form; I suppose you have it at London.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: Norwich, April 17th, 1696. This day ye sentence was executed upon those desperate villains who were condemned at ye last assizes; and their last effort had something it more then ordinary. Those that brought them their coffins conveyed to them therein arms, provisions, and other things, in order to an escape; which having got, they knocked of their irons and made an attempt to break out, but, not being able to succeed, they took possession of ye dungeon, into which there was only one narrow passage, and there stood several days upon their guard. But this morneing, by help of ye soldiers that quarter here, they forced ye place and took ye malefactors, whereon one of them immediately took poison, to prevent ye execution, but by poring oil into his mouth they made him cast it up again, so he lived long enough to be hanged with the rest. They were seven desperate sturdy villains, and we are well rid of them. When they came to ye gallows they did lament that they had been deceived by some at London, who fed them with promises of pardon, and so dyed in a manner by surprise without making any use of ye time which they had between sentence and execution. Yesterday ye Thanksgiveing day was kept here in a more then ordinary manner, the Mayor being willeing to doe more then ordinary to relieve himself from ye slur cast upon him about ye Association by ye weavers and their correspondent, ye writer of ye "Post boy." Next May day they choose a new Mayor; ye man next in order, and who will certainly be chosen, is one Mr Bikerdike, who is ye most intelligent person of ye whole body.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: , April 24th, 1696. There is this morneing gon from hence towards London one Dr Bambridge, a physician of this place. His business is to solicit Mr Tasboroughs discharge, in order to which he is to apply to ye of , with whom he is very dear whenever his Grace comes hither. I have many years looked on him as a very dangerous person. His practice cannot be worth him 40l per annum, and yet he lives at ye rate of 400l per annum, without any visible estate. Everybody looks on him here as a great mystery. Most will have it that he lives by ye trade of a stallion; but no one can tell where he should have trade enough this way to maintain him as he lives. For my part I have looked on him for those ten years to have been a spy for ye papists. I am sure he acted for their interest strenuously in ye late reign, and is continually with them now, and is their servant on all occasions. But as to religion, he hath none but that which will best serve his interest. Some one put in an information against him to the Council table since this plot broke out, but ye of got him of. One part of his instructions are, I hear, to know, what informations are against Mr Tasborough, and from whom. If Mr Tasborough be discharged, I wish it may be on condition that he leave this place, where he hath don a great deal of mischief. His business here is looked on to be to manage the correspondence of ye party in receiving and sendeing all letters, for which they have messengers of their own. Two of them were observed to have been here on ye breaking out of ye plot, and, as soon as they had ye news of it, immediately took horse and rod away. Sr Robert Yallup, Sr Christopher Calthrop, and Sr Nicholas Lestrange, yesterday, upon summons, appeared at the sessions and had ye oaths tendered to them; but all refused. Ye latter paid his 5l and found security accordeing to law, but ye other two refused both, and so are committed. Sr Robert Yallup is ye greatest knave in nature, but ye other two very honest gentlemen. Sr Nicholas Lestrange is a man of parts, virtue, and prudence, but cannot at present conform to ye taking of ye oaths; but Sr Christopher Calthrop a man of strong zeal and weak judgement and totally bigoted to Torisme, but one whom I reckon a harmless man and no otherwise inclined to show his affection to ye cause he is in but by suffering for it; and he seems in his present acteings to court suffereing. I am of opinion that ye Government, as to him, would best serve its interest by dischargeing him.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: Norwich, June 1,1696. I am now returned again from my Suffolk journey, where I found all things very quiet. Ye long struggle which hath been between the two parties in yt country is now totally at an end by ye absolute victory which ye Whig party hath got over ye other. For they have not only carried all ye elections from them in ye last Parliament, but have also made them criminals for opposing them, having brought indictments of riot against them at ye last assizes on this account, and by a packd jury (5 of which were ye members chosen, who came down from the Parliament of purpose for this job) caused ye bills to be found against them, which hath sent ye other party to London with a petition for a noli prosequi ; but those persons who were thus used (and some of them are ye worthiest gentlemen of ye country) are exceedeingly soured against ye Government on this account, which by no means tends to ye Kings interest, or doe I find any one pleased with it but Sr Robert Rich and his gang. Our mayor is like again to recover since sequesterd from ye brandy bottle. I find ye difficulties about ye coin to press hard everywhere all ye way I came, but I hope the mint will take care speedily to remedy this inconvenience.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: , July 20th, 1696. I am sorry ye matter of Sr C. C. did raise such a storm; but some men delight in mischief, and such seldom fail at last of having enough of it upon their own heads. Here hath been of late sculkeing in this town the Archbp. of Glasco, to whom ye Jacobites of the place did much resort. I wish here be not more mischief a breweing, for that party begins again to be very confident and insolent. The Archbp. is now at Yarmouth and there much caressed as I hear. Sr John Barker, one of ye burgesses of Ipswich, lys in a very languishing condition, not like to recover. His death, I believe, will reconcile the town and bring them all again to be of a piece, which hath been in perpetual feuds for these seven or 8 years last past. I intend, if I can, to persuade my Lt Huntingtowr to stand there in case of a vacancy, who is a very sensible man, and with great prudence manageth all affairs that he putts his hands unto, only, having come to an incumberd estate, that frugality and spareing way of living which his circumstances at first made necessary hath habituated him to that which,now he is out of those circumstances, is downright stinginess. For he, having now cleared his estate of ye vast debt which he found upon it, may very well afford to live accordeing to his quality. After his mother ye Duchess of Lauderdale, and his mother-in-law ye Lady Wilbraham, he will have better then 3000l per annum. For Sr Thomas Wilbraham had only two daughters to inherit his estate, which was large. Mr Newport married one, and ye Lt Huntingtowr ye other. He lives most on end near Harborough in Northamptonshire; but ye principal seat of his family is at Helmingham, 7 miles from Ipswich. Here hath lately been in this place one that calls himself Archbishop of Glascoe. The papists did not appear at ye sessions; they say they will return them convict at ye next assizes. I should be glad could I see it, for then ye University would have the disposal of their livings, which now they give to ye worst men they can find. The difficulties about money still grow more presseing. Mr Hodges being here hath received an invitation from Mr Lock, to desire a visit from him, in terms that bespeaks him a dying man.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: , Aug. 24, . We have had here a long assizes, it having continued from Saturday last was seven-night till this evening. On ye Crown side there have been two condemned for murder and one for clippeing and coineing. Att ye other bar ye most remarkable cause hath been between two clergymen, Dean and Williams; ye later about 3 years since married a widow whom we reckoned worth 1500l; ye other pretends a contract and sues Williams upon it, and this time twelmonth had a verdict and 200l damage. Hereon Williams pleads Dean to be guilty of forgery in forgoing ye said contract and several other love letters produced to prove that contract, and upon a long trial of 9 hours last assizes Dean was found guilty of ye forgery; but he having obtained another trial, it was this assizes tried over again, and it took up a whole days hearing, and ye jury were locked up a whole night, and at last, through ye obstinacy of one man, the forgerer was acquitted, though his guilt manifestly appeared to every stander-by at ye trial, and ye Judge yesterday at dinner, when I dined with him, fully expressed himself as to Deans guilt; and indeed he is as ill a man as any of his profession in the countey, and the other as honest a man. This affair hath made much noise and is not yet at an end; there will be another trial about it. Sr affair is much talked of. Sr Roger Pots, one concerned against him, would have persuaded a gentleman to have wrote to Sr C. C. to render himself prisoner again at ye assizes, for, said he, this may prevent a great deal of trouble in Parliament; for it seems Sr threatens he will bring this matter into Parliament. However ye Lord Chief Justice Treby at this assizes hath judged in effect his commitment to be illegal, as really it was; ffor he was committed for not finding security on his second refusal of ye oaths, whereas the first was before ye act of pardon and pardond by it, and, if pardond by it, it cannot certainly operate to make a second offence; for, in that it is pardond, it must fall under oblivion and not be any more remembered, and therefore certainly must not be brought into any reckoneing in order to make a second offence; and when this was pleaded this assizes, in behalf of Sr Nicholas Lestrange who had given security in the same case, that he was illegally put upon it because ye first offence was pardoned, the judge allowed the plea and discharged him. However, ye Duke of Norfolk, who is now here, talks that there will be an order of Council again to recommitt Sr C. C.; and if such a thing should be moved, I wish it might be granted, and let those men who trouble themselves so much in this affair take ye shame of it; ffor ye illegality of his commitment will be manifested, whenever an opportunity shall be given for it. The D. of N. brought down one Mrs Lane. his mis, with him, who made a great show here; however he failed of his main purpose, which was to entertain himself with ye ladies; for, when he had made great preparations for a ball, none would come to it, which gave him yt offence that he said he would never make one here more; and I think it is time for him to leave it of, when all that have any reguard to their reputations think it scandalous to accept his invitations. Our mint doth not yet work, and ye difficulties about ye coin grow worse and worse. Sr John Barker dyed Friday last was seven-night. It is not yet known, or as far as I can hear as much as conjectured, who will stand for the place.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: , May 28, 1697. Dr Smith, one of our prebendarys, dyed last Tuesday. He was a very vigorous old man, and, although past 80, had the strength of a man of 40; but, being taken with an inflammation of ye bladder, ye surgeon who searched him gave his judgement positively that he had a very great stone in his bladder, which misguideing his physicians, they gave him over as desperate; but when opend after his death the mistake appeared, and, had it not been for this mistake, he might easily have been cured and lived many years more. I am now come to be ye senior of our church save one, it being ye 17th year that I have been here prebendary. All this country continues very quiet, and money is now as plentiful among us as ever, and trade begins to grow as brisk. My bookseller writes me that he hath already sold of one impression of my book and is now on a second edition. I have by me a system of the Mohammedan divinity, which is ye oddest stuff that I believe you ever saw; but to ad this will double ye bulk of ye book, which will not be for ye booksellers profit now paper is so dear. This would make that book complete. Perchance paper may be cheaper by that time ye 2d edition is of, and then it shall be ready to be inserted into ye 3d. The life of Mahomet I find is a novelty that makes ye book acceptable. The expectation of a peace is in every bodies mouth, and all very greedily run after ye news to se how it proceeds; and indeed ye taxes are now sufficiently heavy to make them weary of ye war.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: , June 4th, 1697. All this country is filled with very melancholy stories in reference to our present circumstances. They represent Jamaica lost, Aeth taken, the King and ye Duke of Bavaria parted in a feud never to be reconciled again, and that King William is deserted by all ye confederates and left to shift for himself, it being certainly agreed by them to make a peace without him; that, unless ye House of Austria doth consent to such a peace, the French are strong enough immediately to possess themselves of all Flanders and Catalonia; and that we are to be sacrificed to prevent it. If this be our case, it is bad enough with a vengeance. I should be very sorry to see cause to believe any of it; but, were our circumstances well, I scarce think men would be thus bold with ye Government in representeing its case in such a manner. However, as far as it is false, I would be glad to have it authentically refuted. Nothing else from hence worth your knowledge.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: , June 14, 1697. I thank you for ye favour of yours. The Jacobites here grow higher than ever; but an accident happened last Thursday which I believe will cut their combs a little. It being the Prince of Wales's birthday, about 16 of them met at a tavern to drink his health, and among others there was one Captain Ogilby, who had formerly been a captain in Dumbartons Regiment, and hath some years skulked here with a certain widow woman of this country that kept him to serve her purposes. He, with one Doedale and Riley, two Irish papists, and one Caps, a papist of this town, were ye last that left ye bottle. At 12 they broke up and went all 4 home together; on ye way, Doedale and Ogilby quarrelleing, ye later was run thorough and is since dead. Doedale is fled, but ye other two are still on ye place, and I think in law must answer for ye fact, for they are proved all 4 to have had their swords drawn, and ye other two fled ye streets as soon as Ogilby fell. I am told an ejectment hath been left at Sr H. Hobarts house for 8000l, which will reach a great part of his estate. I have been informed out of Suffolk that ye dissenters there are busy upon some designs relating to their interest, against ye next Parliament. I have sent to have it sifted into, and, if there be any thing in it, you shall have an account of it. One of our aldermen, a very rude huffeing fellow, was on Saturday condemned by ye Court of Aldermen to ye stool of repentance for abuseing one of his brethren, that is, to beg his pardon publicly before ye Court in a form prescribed him, and subscribe his hand to it in their public register to stand upon record; and next Wednesday is assigned him for ye day, on penalty of being expelled out of his aldermans place. He is a proud insolent fellow and rich, so the city is in expectation what he will doe. If he refuses it, as by his temper I suspect he will, there will be work for ye lawyers.

column37: clergy lower; Prebendary of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: , Sept. 30, 1698. I am now returned from my Suffolk journey. While I was there ye Earl of Orford came to Orford to influence ye election of a mayor there, and was expected at Beccles this week at Sr Robert Riches, who was making preparations for his reception when I was there last Monday. Sr Robert came to my inn to visit me, and overpowered me with his civilities, and of these I find he is very liberal to other people in his good moods; but, when his passion takes its turn, he vents that in so unreasonable a manner, even upon ye same persons, that I find he hath scarce any interest but among ye dissenters, who in that corner have no other support but what they have from him. There is one Le Pell, an officer in the Danish auxiliary that came over here, who hath caught a young heiresse in my archdeaconry worth 15000l, and he not worth 5 groats. Ye young woman indeed was no beauty, but was reckoned to have wit and discretion; but she miserably betrayed ye want of the latter in this particular. Her name was Brookes. Mr Whitacre, Recorder of Ipswich, who served for that place last Parliament, I find hath so far lost himself in that corporation that he will scarce ever recover himself there again. The Lt. Paston is like to be chosen at Thetford in ye place of Sr Joseph Williamson, who hath let that corporation know that he intends to serve for Rochester. His letters to that corporation in ye behalf of Sloane were in a more than ordinary strain in his favour, calleing him in every line his dear Sloane, and telleing them that they could not be kind to him if they were not so to his dear Sloane also. However, that corporation gets but little credit by this choice. The Duchess of Grafton hath been with her son, ye young Duke, at Euston Hall ever since July; but this next week she goes for London.

column37: clergy upper; Dean of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: , May 9, 1705. The Norwich cause is now going up to the Council, the ffreemen having delivered a petition to ye Lord Townshend, to be presented to ye Queen and Council, against the Mayor and Aldermen, for depriving them of their rights; and the Lord Townshend hath undertaken that it shall be delivered. The case is thus. One Mr Briggs, an alderman, dying ye 3rd of August last, there appeared candidates in that ward for his place Mr Dunch and Mr Austin. Mr Dunch being a sturdy Whig and a fellow of notable parts and understandeing, the Mayor, who is a sturdy Tory, resolved to doe all he could to keep him out; and therefore, although the elections in such cases used to be made within 10 or 12 days, the Mayor deferred it till ye middle of ye last month, hoping in all this time to make sure of a party to keep Dunch out; but it hapneing to work ye contrary way, Dunches party grew by ye delay, and he was chosen by a great majority. Whereon ye Mayor and his party in the Court of Aldermen claimed a right of approveing the alderman chosen, and they would not approve the election of Dunch, but rejected him, giving him for their reasons of so doing that he was a turbulent, malicious man, and of uncivil behaviour in conversation; and ordered ye ward to choose again. The ward met and chose Dunch again, but, notwithstandeing, the Mayor hath sworn in Austin, taking, I suppose, all ye votes given for Dunch to go for nothing. Hereon Dunch hath served mandamus upon the Mayor out of the Kings Bench, and there ye point now is. I find none of their charters can justify their claim to an approbation. They have an instance in their books of an alderman once chosen by ye ward and disapproved by ye Court of Aldermen; but all their charters seem to be quite ye contrary, that ye Mayor is to swear in whomsoever the ward chooses. This is like to creat a great ruffle here, and I take it Blofield will certainly be flung out for being of the Mayors party in this matter. I was apprehensive of it some time since,and took notice to Blofield of it; but his over-confidence in his party made him neglect ye advice I gave him.

column37: clergy upper; Dean of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: Norwich, June 25th, 1705. A rumour hath been here for some time that you have of late been under some trouble; although ye experience which now I have had for near 40 years of your untainted integrity doth give me full assurance that nothing of that which is said can stick upon you, yet to be assured from yourself that all is made clear will be a great satisfaction to me. I beg this favour of you.

column37: clergy upper; Dean of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: Norwich, July 11, 1705. I am very sorry you have suffered that trouble and damage which you mention. Whatsoever may have brought this misfortune upon you I can never think otherwise of you than I have always known and experienced for so many years, and I hope you will so clear this matter as to maintain your reputation as fully and as entirely with every body else as you always must with me; for, whatever becomes of your place, I would advise you by no means to give up ye reputation of your integrity, but vindicate that to ye utmost you are able, that, although you are not in ye same post you were, yet still you may be looked on as ye same honest man. There being few I have had more friendship from than from yourself, I cannot but be very much grieved at this misfortune which hath happened to you, and I assure you I bear my share with you in it.

column37: clergy upper; Dean of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: Norwich, Nov. 26, 1707. I acquainted you in my last with ye case of ye Yarmouth petition, which I am much concerned to oppose; because it lays a great encumbrance upon my estate. To hinder its progress, I have drawn the enclosed petition to be subscribed by myself and others who will be damaged by it; but, being ignorant of the stile and usual form in which such petitions are addressed to ye House, the favour which I beg of you is, that you would put it into due form where it defective, and put the stile of address so as it ought to be, and then send it me back again, that I may get it wrote out fair and subscribed, that so it may be lodged ready to be presented, if their shall be an occasion. But I am of opinion that, when it becomes known that a counter petition is ready, the petition will never be at all presented; for I think it cannot stand against the reasons which we offer against it. I humbly beg your pardon for this trouble which I give you.

column37: clergy upper; Dean of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: Norwich, March 31, . I doe very much thank you for ye favour of yours, and am glad that the Scotch plot is over. I reckon ye Court plot for confoundeing the Ministry and the City plot for the breaking of the Bank and ye East Inti Company are all branches of it, which argues it to be a very deep laid design, and I doubt we doe not yet see half way into the bottom of it. I wish it doe not hereafter break out in some other mischief. I am of opinion people will be willing enough to overlook ye Queens mistake in the matter of the Ministry, provided the Admiralty be better provided for; but ye generality are so exceedeingly dissatisfied with ye present management of that, that they will never cease clamoureing till that great trust be in other hands. And, indeed, I wonder at the indiscretion of those counsels which influence the continueing of the Prince in such a post, where he is only to bear ye blame of other men's miscarriages. Had the Bank broke when ye run was made upon it, I must have broke too, for I had then 4000l in it; but I have now disposed of it to ye purpose for which it lay there. I hope I shall never again have the occasion of running such an hazard. I reckon ye matters that have been of late transacted will, on this baffle, have a great influence on this next election. I wish it doe not carry the Whig interest too high, for that is best when well balanced. I durst not trust them when paramount; whenever they are so, I am afraid they will be making dangerous attempts. I pray God all things may go well at last; at present I think we are much unjointed.

column37: clergy upper; Dean of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: Norwich, Sept. 13,1708. All that I can tell you from hence is, that now taxes begin to come very heavy; and the reason is, that rent comes heavier from the tenants; and, when ye land lord receives nothing, how can he pay anything? The failure of the countryman's trade is ye cause of this. We are now upon a very tickelish point abroad. If this campaign doth not succeed so well as to force the French to a peace next winter, I am afraid we shall not be able to find ffunds for another year. The event shows our victory at Oudenard was no great matter, and we are not strong enough to have any prospect of gaining another, and without gaining another I doubt ye campaign may end to our disadvantage. Our new bishop is gon again to London; he hath set himself in here in a very good interest in his diocese, being generally as much in every mans good opinion as his predecessor was in the contrary. He hath been at great expense about his house, which, from a very ugly one, he hath made very convenient and handsome; but it is likely to cost him several hundred of pounds before he hath don. The Earl of Yarmouth is as low as you can imagine; he hath vast debts, and suffers every thing to run to extremity; so his goods have been all seized in execution and his lands extended, so that he hath scarce a servant to attend him or an horse to ride abroad upon, and yett cannot be persuaded to take any method of putteing his affairs into a better posture, which they are still capable of, if he would set about it. But ye Lord Townshend flourished much among us, for ye whole countey is absolutely at his beck, and he hath got such an ascendant here over everybody by his courteous carriage that he may doe anything among us what he will, and that not only in the countey, but also in all the corporations, except at Thetford, where all is sold. Ye election there is among the magistracy, and 50 guineas for a vote is their price. One Mr Boils, a stranger, was their last chapman, to whom they say they have sold themselves much dearer; for it hath cost him 3000l to get a return from thence for the next Parliament, and that is but a litigious one, for Sr John Woodhouse will be a petitioner against him.

column37: clergy upper; Dean of Norwich, scholar
column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: Norwich, July 11, 1709. I thank you for your kindness to my nephew. He did not let me know of this intended ramble till he was ready to be gon, and therefore it was too late for me to dissuade him from it. I know not what advantage it can bring him, and I am afraid it may doe him a great deal of hurt. My opinion hath been that it would be best for him to marry and settle at home upon his estate, which is better than 1000l per annum; but ye young man hath an ambition to make himself somewhat greater than a country gentleman, and, to give him his due, he hath a capacity for any thing, had he had an education suitable to it; and this it is he hopes to mend by travelling. I hope the new commotions in France may make it necessary for that Crown forthwith to make peace upon the preliminaries agreed, and thereby prevent the fatigues, which otherwise our army must be harassed with, in carrying on a siege in a wet season. My Lord of Norwich is now thoroughly recovered and gon into Suffolk to complete his visitation. Mr Clerk is now here and speaks gratefully to me of your respects to him. He is a person of great learneing and integrity, and I hope he will answer in all things else. His greatest preferment, in being made Rector of your parish, is in that hereby he is emancipated from the Bishop of Ely, whose service and ways he was heartily weary of. That man hath lately made one Dr Canon a Prebendary of his church, on contract to marry his daughter; and it is hard to say which is the greatest fool of the two in this matter. Canon is about 50 years and a very infirm man, being exceedingly troubled with ye falleing of ye gut, which usually takes him up all the morneing to get it up; and she is a young sanguine girl of about 24. That he should at all marry in such a case and such an one as will be sure to loath him, or that ye other should marry such a daughter to such a man, is a folly on both sides which is not to be accounted for, and must end ill on both sides. I reckon the wedding is about this time. Canon is a favourite of ye Lord Treasurer, as having been tutor to his son at Cambridge, and, to give him his due, is a man of worth and learneing; and I suppose his father-in-law expects, on this bottom, to raise him in the Church, perchance to a bishopric. He is already Archdeacon of Norfolk, Prebendary of Ely, and Chaplain to Chelsey Hospital. I hear Dr Robinson is sent for over to be Bishop of Chichester, and I hope he will be a very fit man for it; and his interest with the northern protestants may be of great use to unite them with the Church of England. Should ye present Archbp. hold out a year longer, perchance by that time he may be thought of as a fit person to succeed him; and, if he should hold out so long, I would hope by that time ye man now talked of may so truly represented to ye Queen as not to be approved of by her for that station; and I hear there are many at work to convince her of it, and that she is daily told something or other by those about her to this purpose. The Professor of Divinity at Oxford hath lately married a wife out of this country, and it is a very scandalous match; however, he became drawn into it. She is the daughter of one Coll. Venner, son to the famous Venner that was ye head of the Fifth Monarchy men. This man served ye Venetians in the Morea, and was there a Coll. He, being in Holland when K. William came over, engaged with him in that expedition, and had a regiment in Ireland, and was entrusted with ye government of the hospital of ye army; but, being for his falseness in the management of that trust broken and discarded, he hath retired into this country and hath lived here several years, but with ye worst reputation that you can imagine in all respects, and is one of the most ill-looked fellows that ever I saw in my life, for he had occasion once to appear before me when on public business, and this was ye only time I ever saw him. But you cannot be a stranger to this mans character, and such an alliance cannot be to the credit of ye Professor; and they tell me it is as bad on ye mothers side as on ye fathers, who is daughter to one Dr Gardiner (as they call him), one that practises physic in Covent Garden. The Christ Church men, I apprehend, will make work with him upon this marriage.

column46: Norwich, Dec. 26, 1709. I thank you for ye favour of yours and the trouble which you are pleased, on my request, to take on you of disposeing of ye two books I sent you. I beg your pardon that I thus presume on you; your many favours in other matters have encouraged me also in this to rely upon you. I am glad what I have in this book published gives you satisfaction. I doe not expect so to come of with others, because I go not ye usual way in driveing this matter to those heights where it cannot stand, though I hear the Archbp. likes it well. Another part was intended when I begun, which would be much larger than this, but God hath been pleased to disable me from proceedeing any further by ye calamity which is since fallen upon me. I am sorry ye clergy doe so much embrace Sachevarells cause. I wish it may not provoke the Parliament to vigorous methods against the whole body. John Dyer tells me yt ye 54th Psalm was sung in most of the in London on ye Sunday, in which were preached ye sermons which you mention. By ye present proceedeings of the French King, I suspect he depends upon something to be don in favour of his cause, which is as yet in ye dark, perchance some secret plot to be executed between this and the beginneing of the next campaign; otherwise he acts not with his usual wisdom in continueing the war in such circumstances as cannot promise him any success in it. As to the King of Sweden, I reckon it would be to the advantage of Christendom were he dead, for otherwise he will be always disturbeing peace as long as he shall live. I find in ye news papers that ye Earl of Dorset hath married Mrs Collier, who is ye daughter, I am told, of one Coll. Collier, that was killed in King Williams service in ye last wars. I have a curiosity to know who this gentleman was. My reason for it is, one Collier, that had been a page to the Prince of Orange and afterwards one of his guards, came into Cornwall, being then in poor condition, and married a poor kinswoman of mine that had been a servant in my fathers house. This same man came over with King William and was a Coll. in his army, and was afterwards kilt, I think, Steenkirk. He used often to come to my brother in London while he livd. When you favour me with your next pray give me a line about this matter.

column39: Letters of Humphrey Prideaux Sometime Dean of Norwich to John Ellis Sometime Under-Secretary of State 1674-1722. Ed. by Edward Maunde Thompson. Camden Society New Series XV. 1875.
column46: Norwich, July 7, 1710. During these unsteady times I doe not expect any news from you, but as long as I live I should be glad to hear from you. My case grows worse and worse, and there is no remedy for me but by cutteing; and, on full advice had upon my case, I am told I cannot bear that operation, but that in all likelihood I must die under it. If so, to put myself upon it is nothing less than self murder, and for that I cannot answer to God, who gave me my life; and therefore I must be content to bear my burden as it is, and it is heavy enough. We are here in great confusion upon the convulsions that are above, and there is generally a damp upon the spirits of all men that wish well to their country. Our war against France hath been carried on with great success, and, now we are almost come to the harvest when we are to receive ye fruits of it, its now snatched out of our hands by our own madness; and, as far as I see, we are as far from a peace as we were 7 years since, at least such a peace as will be beneficial for England. We have in our contests at home don more for France this year than we have don against them with all our victories; and, if we go on at this rate, they will carry their point at last, and popery and slavery must be our lot. Although I am going out of the world, I cannot but lament the mischiefs that are like speedily to happen to this nation, if we tread on the same measures yt we now seem to be running into. This will be lamented by those who are now its chief instruments, when it will be too late for them to remedy it.
