column46: Norwich, Sept. 29, 1722. I thank you for your last, and am glad to find by it that your case is much better than mine As to Dr John Clark, his case is thus; about 30 years since Dr Fairfax, then Dean of Norwich, put one Mr Richardson to be Minister of the parish of the Close, with a permission to serve it once a fortnight. This I then protested against as contrary both to former usage and to the service of God Almighty, and have ever since many times expressed my dislike of it, and have as often promised that it should be remedied whenever it should fall in my power. About a year since, Richardson dying, Dr Clark applied to me for the place, and would serve it no otherwise than Richardson did. But, not being able to comply with him herein, I did put another in the place. This is the whole reason of his quarrel with me. I told him I denied him nothing but what I would deny to a brother or a son; that I thought the obligation for doing the best for Gods service to be greater than any obligation whatsoever for ye acting contrary thereto, and neither his brother nor his father think I did otherwise than my duty herein. As to puplick affairs, this country is now become the scene of action; this town is in a general mutiny about the election of a sheriff; our two chief Ministers of State are both Norfolk men; and Layer, who is lately sent to ye Tower, is also of this country, and a viler wretch scarce lives in it. No one that knows him will think him fit to be trusted with the secrets of any plot, or to be relied on in any evidence he shall give about it. He went indeed last year into Italy on pretence of transacting some affairs of my Lord londonderry with Mr Knights, and then he saw ye Pretender, and was admitted by him to audience more then once; and of thus much he has several times bragged in company, and said enough hereof to be hanged for it; and, if this comes to be his lot, scarce anyone here will be concerned for it. The time of the setteing of the Parliament now approaching, I wish all things which are for ye honour of ye King and ye good of the country may be transacted in it.

Houndslerdyck June ye 10th . tic so very long since I have heard from my dear Aurelia that I don't know what to think of it, but now I think ont tic my own faut for I have not yett ansered your to letters I had last the first of which was a very long on & full of news for which I give you a thousand thanks ye to there was but short but you tell me on whom I must lay the faut therefore I say nothing to you. but you will find me very lazy & much to blame not having ritt all this while & I confess I am so but if you knew how little time I have had ever since I came from the hummeling you would not wonder, I have bin heer a week to day last sunday I received yesterday I was at the Hage to see a Princese who is there three days before she was to se me & ondly just friday & Saturday there has bin company heer every day, but this time I was resolved not to louse another post therefore I ritt this in the morning for that reason. I hope I have said enough to persuade you tic not want of kindness (for that you may always be sure of) but time which has hinderd me all this while assuring you that nothing is nor can ever be capable of changing me who am & shall be ever the same kind constant clorine I always was. For Mrs. Apsley.

Dieren June ye 17 . You have taken a way of clearing my douts dear husband which would make me your rival if it wear to any but your prince Ziphares but for him you know I have always had a love to great to increase and to natural not to last always & upon to good an account to make you jelouse. but I cant tel wethere the compliments you make your Clorine at the end of your letter are not to great to have so much credit given them but I am good natured enough to believe I have still the greatest shere of your heart & do consent so dear a creature to you & who is so doble dear to me shoud have some part of it, since she has so much of mine. I hope by this time my dear Aurelia is quite well again, & that she does me so much justice to believe my concern was equal to my love which you know is as it ever was & tho you talk at a fine romantic way of your heart I assure you mine will ever be the same & I will hold yours as fast as ever I can for I am resolved if I can keep it I never will part with it while I live & if I die I pretend so much power over it that I would leave it for a legacy to yours and my dear Ziphares. Pray remember me very kindly to your Mother and Sisters. To Mrs. Apsley.

Edinburgh Sep ye 8. My dear Sem;dra I do again beg your pardon for being these too or three posts without writing to you but seriously I could not possible help it but now I must say something in answer to both your letters which I have received since I wrote to you in the first place I must tell you that I forgot to tell you that you should stand for me to Mrs. Doylys child pray remember me to her when you see her & then I must tell you that tho you heard constantly from Pert who had a great many letters to wrote & went often abroad yet she did not go so constantly every day as I did for I rid every day & then I was often with the Duchess & then I took a little time in my closett when I could catch it consider all these things well & forgive your poor Ziphares as to what you desire to know in your other letter I do asure you I do love you dearly & not with that kind of love that I love all others who proffer themselves to be my friends pray therefore dear Sem;dra love me as well as ever be as free with me as ever wrote me all the news you know send me ye Gazett & other printed paypours that are good & forgive & believe your Ziphares. pray remember me very kindly to your Mo & tell I will writ to her next post.

Edinburgh Sep ye 16. My dear Sem dra I have ten thousand millions of pardons to beg of you for mising these too or three last posts & pray forgive me for it was don out of no unkindness to you upon my word, but I asure you I will henceforward wrote every post & I do indeed pity you, for I am very sensible of your great loss my dear Semdra be a little comforted for it may displease God Almighty to see you not submit to his will & who knows but that he may lay some greater afliction on you death is a dept we must all pay when God is pleased to take us out of this wicked world but I hope you will live a great while & yt we shall be happy in seeing one a another tho God & the King only knows when pray remember me kindly to your mother father & brother farewell my dear I love you dearly upon my word & will never change For Mrs. Apsley.

Houndslerdyck June the 13th . I am ashamed dear Lady Apsley to have bin so long without ansereing your letter which I received by Sir G. Silvius but the treuth is that since he came into this country last I have never bin long enough in a place to have time to ritt to any for whilst I was at Bruxells (I spake it to my shame) I never had time to rit neither to the Duke, the Duchess, nor my sister, whom I hope are now with you in England, you may be sure I shoud be very glad your wish could be treu at this time & that I could come to pay my duty to them & at ye same time se the rest of my good friends, but if it cant be presently I hope I shall once find such a time which you may believe will be a very welcome one to me, in the mean time I hope you will believe that as I have bin so I shall endeavour always to show my self to my lives end both to you & all yours for your sake, your very affectionate kind friend Marie.

Windsor, June ye 12th . My dear Semdra. I received yesterday a letter from my Lady Bathurst I do forgive her for not telling me the secret but I asure you I love you as well as ever I did & I am very sorry you think the contrary I am sure I never intended to do anything that should look like unkindness to you or any of your family & I am extremely sorry if ever I have don anything that you take unkindly I asure you I never did it a purpose & therefore pray forgive me & do me the justice to believe what is a very great truth yt I do love you as well as ever.

Dieren Jully the 25th . I have staid all this while in hopes of an ansere to my last letter. but not getting one I sit down now with full intentions to chid you dear Aurelia for I find the changing of your condition has also changed your mind a great deall or else you would have satisfied me before now & all the fine complements in your which letter you rit me since you are married (but before you had mine) will not searve your turn, for you have known this great while or I may better say ever since you knew me that your letters wear always very welcome & never troublesome, & I have told you twenty times that tic impossible for me to rit so often to you as you can do to me for I can never send you news from heance and you can seldom want it where you are so that you have no excuse of your side & I have reason of mine however you se & have bin I hope a great while very well persuaded that nothing can change me but that whether I wright or no I am & shall be to my lives end ever the same. Now I am in a chiding way I must chid it out once for all but I had almost forgot to say that your not having heard from me was no excuse not to tell me your great afaire as you with reason call it for you knew me enough to trust me if you would have used me like a friend.

St. Jameses Aug ye 14th. my dear Semdra I have intended ever since I came hither to wrote to you & I hope you will forgive me for not doing it sooner I thank you for your letter & pray ask me what ever questions you will for upon my word I love my dear Semandra as well as ever: since I came to town I am grown a very good Housewife for I am constantly dressed by prayer time & I have bin very often ready between nine and ten: I wish & yet I know not how to wish you hear because I am sure you had rather be where you are but yet I cant help having a little self interest: all ye news that I know is that Lady Anne Savell was married last thursday to Lt Vaughan: pray remember me very kindly to your Mother & believe me you shall ever find me the same Ziphares I ever was. since I have wrote my letter I have got a little sister.

Hage December ye 29th . your kind letter dear Aurelia puts in a strange impatience to know what it is you dare not writ & I believe it must be of great importance since you ad presently afer that you would put your life into my hands. for god sake put me out of my pain & let me know it, if ever you have loved me, if ever you have loved your prince, if ever you have loved or do eithere father mothere sister brother, & last of all if you love your dear husband I conjure you to let me know it & yt quikly, or I shall conclude you never did care for me nor for any I have named make no beginning nor ending put no name nor no superscription but put it for me in what you writ to my Mam or let my sister her self send it these, or any other way you can think of so I do but know it. adieu my dear Aurelia by this I shall know if you love me. pray remember me very kindly to your mothere & believe no body wishes more for the continuance of both your healths then I do. For the Lady Bathurst.

Hague Feb. ye 23rd I have found to letters of very old date in my standish which makes me believe I have not ansered them for which I ask you a thousand pardons. the first is of the 19th of December I can assure you dear Aurelia I think all you said very well & am very much of your mind concerning that person you there mention & had I known of the friendship at first I shoud have done all I could in the world to have broke it of but I never knew any thing in the world till such time as she was forbid when I heard it from my sister herself & was very much surprised & troubled to find her concern as great. but then I did not say much because I did not think it nessesery another time you will oblige me very much to let me know if there be any new ones in hand that I may endeavour to stop it if it be not to her advantage or at least do my best for I think nothing more prejudicciell to a young woman then ill company & I hope you will continue your good consells to us both & never flatter neither. By ye tother of the 2nd of January you tell me to things which must needs be very pleasing to you & then you may be sure thay are so to me: I received to days ago another by which I find you are quick of which I wish you much joy, & hope you will ever have all the contentment imaginable in all things this world can aford & eternal happiness in that which is to come you never need to make excuses to me for aquianting me with your concerns for I take so much part in all that belongs to you that I look upon it as a peace of kindness in you to do so I have been hindered so long in the writing of this that having more to write I have time to say nothing else ondly assure you of my continueing the same till death - pray remember me as kindly as possible to your Mothere.

Newmarket March ye 21 . I am very sorry Lady Apsley has bin ill again but I hope now ye spring comes on she will soon recover: this place aford no news but of Races & cock matches which you don't care for. Dr. Lake went last night and will be in town much sooner then this: I am sorry I did not know his wife was ill when he first knew it for I would very willingly have let him go on such an ocation I shall now be very quickly with you for the Duchess intends to go to moro seven-night I can say no more at this time to my dear Semandra but yt she shall ever find me ye same I ever was. For the Lady Bathurst.

Windsor June ye 4 . do not acuse your Ziphares without hearing him & indeed you wrong him mightily in saying he is unkind tho what I am going to say may sound like an excuse yet I asure you tic not so: when I was at London ye first time if I had had time I would have made you a visit & ye reason I have not wrote to you all this time was because I was afraid reading might not be good for you & tho you heard not from me yet I enquired of every body how you did & wrote to your mother a purpose therefore do not have so ill opinions of your Ziphares for tho he changes his condition yet nothing shall ever alter him from being ye same to his dear Semandra that he ever was: as to what you say in your last letter about Sr Benjamin I will be sure to speak to the Duke & do all the kindness yt lies in my power but I must needs tell my dear Semandra this that when I first heard this buisnes concerning my self I spoke to ye Duke of my self for Sr Benjamin Bathurst I am very glad you have got so good a friend as my Uncle Rochester for he can do you as much kindness & service as any body & I am sure any thing that I lies in my power shall not be wanting, once more let me beg you not to have any more ill opinions of me but asure yourself yet all ocations I will be ready to show my self your faithful Ziphares: & now I must desire you yt as soon as you have received this you would send for Mr. Oliver & bid him com hither for tell him I want him mightily to mend one of my gounds & bid him bring me a pair of bodies to wear with a manto.

I believe my dear Semandra thinks me a very strange creature for not having answered your letter in all this while but I do asure you it has not bin my fault for yt day I received it it was so soon after diner yt I could not then possible wrote & after prayers till I went to Whithall I had company with me all day: yeaterday I did intend to have wrote but dining with ye Queen made me so late yt I could have no time before prayers & afterwards again I had company till I went out & therefore pray donot have an ill opinion of me for I do really love you very well & will ever do so & as for ye picture you shall have one very soon & pray believe what I say for it is really true & you shall ever find me your faithful Ziphares.

Why would not my dear Semandra wrote to me before but keep herself uneasy all this while and now I must tell you yt I am not nor never was angry with you in all my life & I asure you no body has ever said anything against you to me & ye reason why I said no more to you yt day you spoke to me was because I can never express my self in words & therefore if ever you have more suspicions of me as I hope you will not after reading this letter let me know them by a letter: but I asure you I love you as well as ever tic true I have sometimes when I do not know it a very grave look which has made others as well as you ask me if I was angry with them yt I looked so gravly on them therefore do not mind my looks for I really look grave & angry when I am not so another thing you tax me of is never sending for you which is a thing I have not don I confess this great but has not bin my fault I asure you for the Prince stays with me every day from diner to prayers & by that time I com from prayers tic half an hour after four & on my playing days from yt time I am always in expectation of company on those days yt I donot play I commonly go to whithall at six so yt yt hour an a half which I have from prayers till I go to the Duchess I am glad sometimes to get a little of it alone it being the only time I have to myself and for ye other part of it the Prince ether comes to me or I go to him and we stay with one another till I go out thus you see I have told you very freely how I spend my time so you see yt tic not my fault yt I donot send for you because I have hardly a moment yt I can send for you but yt before you can com ether I have grave company or am gon to Whithall but at any time whenever you will com I will see you & shall be very glad of your company & if you cannot com if you will will wrote I shall be very glad of your letters & will answer them very punctualy therefore let me beg you if you love your Ziphares give way to none of these false suspicions of me for I do asure you upon my word I do love you as well as ever & will do so as long as I live: as for ye paypour I signed an sealed I do remember it very well and will be as good as my word in it tho I cannot yet, ye reason I will tell you when I wrote next as for what you desire to know about Sir Benjamin no body has ever said anything against him to me or if it had bin so you may be sure I would first ask him him about it I will now end hoping you are very well satisfied yt I am ye same I ever was & ever will be to ye last moment of my life.

Windsor Jully ye 1. my dear Semdra not having time last night to wrote to you by your Brother I now send having a purpose a purpose with this that I might not be any longer without telling you yt I do really love you as well as ever I did I will without fail send your letter to my sister to night I am very sorry you could not com yesterday but I hope by Sunday your face will be well again & then that you will com hither to Church dear Semdra I would say more to you but yt tic past ten o'clock & therefore I must go & be dressed but whether my letters be long or short I will ever be the same. pray remember me very kindly to your mother. For the Lady Bathurst.

Dieren August 25th . I write my last in such hast to my dear Aurelia that I had not then time to ansere that I had of yours & now I have received another since so that I have now to of yours to ansere the first of which was write the day before my sister was to be married, you may believe it was no small joy to me to heer she liked him & I hope she will do so every day more & more for else I am sure she cant love him & without that tic impossible to be hapy which I wish her with all my heart as you may easily imagine knowing how much I love her. by the tothere you tell me of the comitions my sister left with you which I shoud at first have desired you to have done but that she had often bid me employ her & would have it so by all means ye which I did the rathere in hopes of having some comition from her for there is nothing pleases me more then to be so employed, but I don't heer of any yet & indeed this place afords so little of anything but what one has much better in England that I fear I shall not get any at all. adieu dear Aurelia I have this day so many letters to write that I have not time to say any more to you ondly assure you of the continuance of my kindness which nothing but death can ever alter. Pray remember me very kindly to Lady Apsley.

Hague Nov ye 5th. I never found it a hard matter to write to my dear Aurelia before, but at present I don't know what to say for your afliction is so just one can hardly go about to comfort you and indeed upon such ocations tic ondly from God it can come whom I beseech to grant you may bear it like a christian & so as it may sum to your good, as for my own part I assure you I am as sorry for your loss as any body can be which I hope you don't dout, knowing how much I love you. I know tic in afliction friends shoud show them selves & I should be very glad if I knew any way to show you I am so more than you can believe.

Hague April ye 4th . I am very sorry to find yt my Lady Apsley has bin so very ill as you say in your letter but I hope it was ondly the cold wethere & yt with the spring she will recover I am sure if my wishes can contribute to her health she will not want it nor them: as for you dear Aurelia you make me mad with asking pardon for writing a long letter since you may believe thay are very welcome to me I having desired it so often of you for I can compliment with nobody much less with my good friends, I wish I could send you news from heance of any kind, but as you know no body heer so tic impossible: we have ye coldest Easter I think that ever was for it freezes every night still which makes the spring very backward, adieu dear Aurelia believe me ever the same.

Honslerdyck June 9th . I have a long while had to of my dear Aurelias leters to ansere which on thing or other has always hindered me doing till this time, on of them is ondly in contradiction of a former letter and the other tells me of your being with child, I wish you better luke then either the Duchess or my dear sister have had you know how dear she is to me and therefore will not dout how much I was troubled for her I am sure if it had bin my self I could not have bin very much more, but I think we have all reason to thank God she is come of as she is which my thinks is almost a miracle to be so well of a dead child. pray remember me very kindly again to my Lady Apsley & believe me as much yours as ever. The Prince is gone into Brabant so yt I am now alone heer when he comes bake is uncertain for which I am sure you will pity me.

Aughton Octr. 1st 1791. Sr., I wrote to you some time since but no answer, the subject of which was as follows viz. to desire to know if you can give me work if it be for 2 or 3 months only, or till May next at which time if it be agreeable I propose coming to Warrington to reside and harden or finish for you if you want one at that time and if you think proper will turn my lads over or if you can give sufficient work in your Shop will keep 'em on their time out, at the rates you give others, they are forwards in their business and works very well. If you can give me work here till May (as I can't leave here before) you may be assured I shall come to Warrington. I shall send 'em if I send any soft 14 to doz., and propose finishing by the doz. which I think is more satisfaction to both sides. I paid the person for the last being a private but I suppose it was not delivered and will pay for this. Beg you'll keep this a profound secret as I've been told in Greens warehouse of alowing you 13 to doz. hard but thought others did the same, and particularly desire you'll send by return of Post as I shall be in Liverpool on Wednesday next and you'll oblige you Hble Served. Carolus Charles. P.S. Direct for me to be left with In. Collins, Brewer at bosom and Shuffle in Cheapside Liverpool.

Aughton 1st Jan. '92. Sr., I hope you'll Excuse this as I did Expect your writing the week after I was with you, but hope there is Nothing amiss. Mr. Green has not been at home some time before I was with you nor is he yet come or I would not have troubled you and beg you'll be kind enough to send me an order and Steel, and if you'll oblige me with 4 or 5 guineas shall forever remember it and send your work in small parcels or by any stated time you choose. I have money to pay to Different people and Can't get it from 'em. Yesterday week I had not my due by near half, yesterday the same. He will pay only 10 s. pound of the Clear neat Cash when all is Deducted, and I can't take truck for the remaider at his price. H. Yond told my wife yesterday that one of the men in your Shop told him you and I had been making an agreement and I was to go to Warrington to work Constantly for you, by which you may se how Dagerous it is to trust Some people, not that I value it if Green know it, but would advise you to take care who you Confide in, but beg and Desire you'll asaist me in the above friendship and I will give Joseph Henshaw meeting on purpose at Liverpool on Thursday next. Pray don't Sr. don't Disappoint your friend. Cs. Charles. I've paid Carriage.

Aughton 18 Jan. '92. Sir, I received the Steel on Saturday last. I have had not any by me Strong Enough for any but the 5 In. Cross which was in hand before I received it, but my son being taken bad of the bloody flux will throw us a little behind but you may Depend we shall do 'em without Omission now he is gotten better. I can't tell how long they will be in executeing being larger than I ever made any in Lancashire. I am sorry you took Umbrage at my Desiring 4 or 5 guineas. I did not expect it from the acquaintance we have had but when a man is Driven to necessity and near to Desperation I hope you'll excuse the attempt. I think I shall send them by another Hand than Henshaw. I was right in my Conjectures about the Combination but no more of that now. I've a Settlement with Mr. Green and if I must leave him would Desire to do it honourably and quietly as we met so. Will let you know a day or two before the files comes. I could be of great utility to you if things would suit but more of that another time. I don't know the price of the large Cross but shall rely on you for that. I am Sr. your Hble Served. Cs. Charles. P.S. I am more free from Mr. Green by either tie or promise than I am from you, but should not like any transactions betwixt you and I ever turned over. I want to get a Settlement without passion.

Aughton July 7th '92. Sr., I've sent you the following files viz, There is 14 Cross in both sizes. I have more but tyd them in dried paper and they've Contracted rust & are spoiled, these was put in Oily paper and are saved. If you please should be glad you'd send 4 guineas by Sherwood on Tuesday made in a parcel, and the box. I should have sent more files but my son was so put out of the way by his bror. Joseph by being struck and shaked in such a manner by him when I was Absent that I thought for 3 days had not ever seen through it, he not being in a Capacity to bear it. Joseph went from here on Saturday last to bring work to Prescot but has not been seen here since. As he has threatened little Cranage I suppose he has been with you, which if he has should be glad you'd let me know and how they've ordered as his Mother says he shall not go to him any more and is quite Inconsolable, have not much time now but think I shall remove from here sooner than thought of. This you'll keep, but think to come over again to Warrington to'ards Michealmas and by then shall be more settled in some points. Am Sr. with Due respect (not forgetting your favours) Subscribe myself your Hble Served. Cs. Charles. I think there is 2 or 3 of 5 In. frame Saw among 4 1/2.

Aughton July 21st. '92. Sr., I am sorry there was any mistake in the 4 In. frame saw files. Was you not mistaken in booking 'em, as I know there was no more than you mentioned, have sent you the following files Desire if you please to remit me 6 guineas. Let me know if you be willing for Sherwood to Carry the files. Hie proposes Carrying them at 6d. a time. Have had another summons from Mr. Green. I believe he is very Ill at want for files and wonders I neglected him so long. If he searches his breast he may soon know, says he will either come or send if I don't send him an Explanation in a little time and heard he is for bringing an Exorbitant bill against me. His way of trading has been very Intricate. When any cash of any Acct. was to paid he neither could nor would he said pay it Stormingly saying I pay you more money than any one, then paying what he thought proper which caused people to take his goods which price it is two to one you could not get and if Importuned for a bill fly in a passion and tell you he had more plague with than any body else after you had travelled ten or 12 Miles in the night and not a dry thread on you & set in his Warehouse for 6 or 7 hours without being asked what you want. I wish I was well out of his Clutches or power for I suppose I must have little Content till I am. Should be glad of your Advice on Tuesday as I think to give him some Sort of an answer and should be glad you'd put the paper into the box & make the Cash into a parcel and you'll oblige Sr. ire. Hble Served Cs. Charles.

Liverpool September 20th , 1795. Dear Sir, I have made bold to write a few lines to you to beg the favour for you to have lent me three or four guineas. At this present time we are rather in distress or else would not have troubled you. It is to pay a few trifling debts with. You may depend upon me paying you every penny again by stopping so much a week. I am now working the last of your work up. I hope you be so good as to send me more work and to have granted me this one favour and you will greatly oblige me. You may stop it as you please. I received your letter and the money with great satisfaction and I hope while I have my health to do my best for you in every point. So no more at present from your obedient servant Thomas Tatlock.

Liverpool, April ye 9th 1796. Sir, I take the liberty to in form you that this day my wife is got to her bed some time before we expected and as my rent is due it has put me to a great street as my landlord cannot do without it. I shall take it as a great favour if you will assist me with 2 pound ten shillings and if you will please to send me word how much you will choose me to pay a week I will pay it with pleasure. I am sorry that you found fault with the work but I altered my swag to your pattern and no one cuts them but my self and the young man but I will do my endeavour to please you and I hope that you will please to send me the sum mentioned which I shall acknolage as a great favour from Your Humble Servant Thomas Tatlock.

Sr., I have sent these five Gross. They all the Heel Blots I could get Readey But will send you more on Tuesday by Nields Cart. I sent you 18 Dozen Heal Blots and 12 Dozen sewing a week before. I sent them 6 Gross. If not Recd. them pleas to enquire at Mr. Bowman's. By those Mis carreing you might think I was serving sumbody else. I do a sure you I do not Receive 1 shilling in all the Town neither will I, so Long as you will employ me. I will serve you in the Best manner I can so I hope this will Suffice you at present. I am yours at Command James Lyon. October 1795.

Stockport Decr. 17 , 1795. Mr. Stubs, Sir, I Rec'd your Letter yesterday. I am in Good Health but have been much uneasy at your silence so Long. I thought I had offended that you would not Employ me any Longer. I have told Mr. Ouldknow and hee will give me work after Christmas. So I intended to a maid you sum work in the Holodays for what I owe you and to a Returned your Tools. But I will never Leave you while you will Employ me. I will never Bastard my Promise to you. Your abstance has been no profit to me though I have sold sum and I have a Quantity under hand of most useful sorts and will Bring you all I can next week's end. I must beg you will send me Letter to Receive 3 Guineas for its a Long time since I Rec'd much. If you will grant my Desire I will bee under a heavy Stopidge that shall suffice you. I will not send any more by any Body for I will Bring them every other Saturday if God Permit. I remain your Hble Srvt. Jose. Lyon.

Dear Father & Mother I received your letter on Monday the 26 of May and am glad to hear you are all well. I was at Mr. Smiths when I received your letter and as been there ever since. Mr. Smith said if I would not come and stop a week or two he would never come to our house again. I hade engaged my self to Mr. Spears but he wode make me come there first so Mr. & Mrs. Smith went to beg me of. Mr. Smith as made me a present of a Silver Fruit knife in a very handsome case. Mrs. Smith and me either go a visiting every day or else we have company. We was at Mr. Cams on day. He is a file maker. He desired me to give is Copts. to you. I have told Mr. Spear you want me to come home at Whitsuntide but he says he will hear nothing of it. Miss Spear is reckoned to be one of the handsomest and Genteelest young Ladies in all Shefeild and keeps the genteelest company. They keep with pople that keeps their own caraige. You will think I have been weary extravagant but I am obleidged to appear as Genteel as ever I can or I should be nothing at all thought on. Mr. Smiths keeps the genteelest of company. I just been having a tooth pulled out & my mouth is so painful I can scare write. It is Bradfeild Feast next Sunday and Mr. Perkins says he will send a horse for me if I will com. Mr. Parkin received the salmon in good orderer and is very much obleidged to you for it. I have Dined at Mr. Harrison lately. The mad very much on me and desired me to come any time. All your Friends at Shefeild send there compts. to Mrs. Allen and love to my Brothers and Sisters I am Dear Father & Mother your Dutiful Daughter Sarah Stubs.

Chester 22 Septr 1793. Dear Father & Mother, I was much surprised that I did not receive my box yesterday am afraid my mother is worse as she did not send it, it put Miss Cole to great trouble for I had not a clean shirt & she was obliged to get one washed for me on yesterday afternoon. I hope you will not omit sending it tomorrow. Miss Cole's Compliments to both of you my duty to both of you & love to all my brothers & Sisters not forgetting little Ellen & Betsey as Sarah calls her & am Dear Father & mother Your dutiful Son J. Stubs. N.B. We hear Miles is come to Warrington pray is it true. P.S. I have begun book keeping.

Chester Octr 27 1793. Honoured Parents, I take this opportunity of writing to let you know I have a shirt missing & would be obliged to you to ask my Aunt if she as got it. On Friday was the Mayor choosing and to day the went to Warbus church with music and the whole Corporation then the 4 Regt. of Royal Irish Dragoons following them and a very pretty sight it was. My love to all my Brothers & Sisters & to Peter tell him a letter will come as soon without putting speed on it as with, should be glad to hear from you & to hear you grant me my request as in my last. I am Honoured parents, Your dutiful Son J. Stubs. Please to excuse haste as it is almost time to shut up the post office.

Chester Novr 20th 1793. Honoured Parents, I take this opportunity of writing to let you know my Quarter is up on the 18th of Decr. & should be glad to whether I must come home on the 19th because if you would not have to go to that School any longer I had better not to enter on a fresh Quarter so please to let me know in your next. I have not begun Mensuration as yet but shall as soon as Mr. Stolterfoth can get me a case of Instruments, please to send me a bit of blue to mend my coat I have not much to say at present but that Miss Cole is very poorly but hope she be better in the Morning, desires to be remembered to you & my Aunts family. My love to Brothers & Sisters & hope you will accept the same yourselves. I am Honoured Parents, Your dutiful Son, J. Stubs.

Newton, July 4. 1794. Honoured Parents, I received a Shirt yesterday but I think I have a pair of blue Stockings you have not sent which I would thank you to send with my small tooth comb and a case for my other comb and a black lead pencil for I had the misfortune to loose my case of Instruments and black lead pencil out of my pocket when I came to Newton but I have found my Instruments again. Should be glad to know when the Bishop comes to Warrington as I am at an age to be confirmed. Mr. Wallworth has given us leave to keep Rabbits & I should be oblige to you if you will send a hung lock and key and staple there is in my brother Potter's drawer & my watch by the bearer. I am Honoured Parents Your dutiful Son J. Stubs.

Hawarden, April 5th 1796. Honoured Parents, We have not yet received our things and have no need to expect we know were they are. We yet want some Tops and string to spin them with, and a few marbles and also my Brother John's Pilgrims Progress, Sparmans Voyages and a Voyage to the Cape of good Hope and my Sister Mary's Speaker and her Fables and my Ovid and any other books beside you please for me and my Brothers to read at a night for we are quite lost for something to do at a night, and also a tooth brush and tell Mr. Bratt to send Robert some tops and marbles and some little books. We want a school box for that as we have is too little, so you may send them in it and you must be sure send us word to what Inn in Chester they will come to. And also send us word when my Mother will come but would rather she would come to Chester races and then we might go and see one days race and return again. Please to tell my Sister Mary and Sarah and my Brother John to write and send it along with our Parcel. The fever is very ripe about half a mile of us but if it worsens any I will let you know. So no more but give our love to Father and Mother Brothers and Sisters, and also Wm & Easter and hope they are all well as we are at present and am Honoured Parents Your dutiful Son Peter Stubs. N.B. Be sure to write by return of Post.

Hawarden February 19th 1797. Dear Father, Mr. Willett desires me to write to You to ask You if it is your Will that any of us should learn to dance as the dancing Master will attend on the 25th of March if He can get a sufficient Quantity to make it worth his while to attend. The Terms are half a Guinea Entrance and 15s per Quarter but he charges Nothing Entrance to those who have been to a dancing School before and I should be glad if You would answer this Letter as soon as ever you can make it convenient. Sorry am I to inform You that Mr. Willett has sent his Man to Day to Liverpool to Mr. Sherwood's to inform them of his Son being at the Brink of Eternity. He was just got well of the Fever and some other Disorder took him which I doubt will be his End. So no more from Yours &c &c Peter Stubs.

Hawarden May 8th 1797. Hond Parents, We only received our Parcel on Wednesday last or should have certainly returned you our grateful Thanks for it before now and are very much obliged to you for it now. We three and P. Johnson went to Chester on Thursday and returned yesterday, Mr. Cole's being unwell the Beginning of the Week prohibited our going before. I hope you will be sure to let us know how poor James Lion goes on in your next and give our best Respects to him if alive and tell him we are very sorry for him. We have writ & writ to know when our Mother comes and are no wiser yet but I hope you will either say Yes or No in your next . We take it very unkind of you not letting us know of our Sister's Neck being broke or Mary's coming from School or anything. We are like so many lost Sheep ignorant of every thing that passes. All our Eyes are well. Love to yourselves, Brothers and Sisters, E. & W. H. and are Your ever dutiful Sons, P. T. & W. Stubs. N B. An Answer by return of Post.

Hawarden May 21st 1797. Dear Father, A Fortnight has now expired. The Vacation begins to draw near. Mr. Cole proposed that We should be at Chester the Morning We break up and breakfast with him and he will have a Chaise ready for Us to go to Preston Brook &c. We had a Letter from our Sister yesterday and She was very well but I suppose you know that better than Us. I beg you will inform Us in your next whether You approve of the above Plan or no, very soon. Pr Johnson, Self & Brothers are to go to Hollywell, this day Fortnight. We are all well and hearty and join in Love to Yourself and Mother, Brothers & Sisters and are Dear Father, Your dutiful Sons P. T. & W. Stubs. God save the King Amen so be it.

Shefeild, April 29 , 1794. Hond Parents, I arrived safe at Shefeild last night and found Mr. Perkins Family very well. We went out to sup last Night and as had company to day. There has a Gentleman dined here to day from London he calls his name Hurst. He enquired very kindly after you he his a File maker he asked if I was your Sister he was quit astonished when I said I was your Daughter. Mr. Perkins came to meet me yesterday and I am going their to day. Mr. and Mrs. Parkin makes very much on me. I donate see anything distressing yet. Mrs. Parkin seems to be a very agreeable good kind of woman. There is good many people that I am got acquainted I can hardly understand they talk so queer. Mr. Alkock gave me a bill for Mr. Harison. I only saw young Mr. Harison and the old woman the old woman did not speak to me she was stood at the entry end in an old stuf gown and an old bonnet you would hardly pick up in the street but the young man asked come and stop awhile but I think I would rather choose to stop where I ham. I was very sick coming in the coach betwixt Manchester and buxton and I doubt you will be as sick as I was when I tell you that I paid 18s. for riding. We changed horses 4 times and every time we had to pay a fresh coach man that made it 20s., we paid 18d. for a very plain dinner indeed as eve I seat down to. I have no more to say at present but will write again after a while. I am Hond Parents Your dutiful Daughter Sarah Stubs.

Liverpool March 5th. 1796. Dear Parents, It is with the greatest pleasure I take up my pen to write to you, to inform you I like the Situation you have had the goodness to place me in, only for one reason which is that all the young Ladies of my Age in the school are Parlour Boarders. I therefore should be much happier if you would have the kindness to let me be one. The Difference the young Ladies tell me is 6 Guineas a year. If you have any objections I will not desire it. I will be obliged to you if you will send me some Towels, as the young Ladies find their own. Inform me if you peas by your next Letter if you paid the Carriage for my Box to Liverpool. give my love to my Brothers and Sisters & accept the same From your Dutiful Daughter Mary Stubs.

Dear Parents, Mr. Hall called on me last week. I was happy to hear you were all well and got the Fair over without much trouble. Mr. Smith is expected home on Wednesday. Miss Sarah Eyre returns with me on Saturday, but Mr. Eyre says I shall not go than you write for me. I am not of so much consequence as I think of or you could not have spared me so long. I am afraid we shall not have a pleasant journey home, the Snow is seven yards deep on the Moors, the Coach does but go twice a week now on Mondays and Fridays. Mr. Eyres and Mr. Smiths Familys make their best respects to you and Sister Whiteley, give my love to Brothers and Sisters my Duty to my Mother and accept the same from your dutiful Daughter Mary Stubs.

July 13, 84. Hond. dear Brother, Mrs Aston is safely arrived, and as kindly welcomed of all, as we can make appear, till longur time furnish us with opportunity of real servis to her. It had been enough for me, to understand her a friend to Bellamore: that alone had commanded all my forces, and employed them to her best advantage, and my singular content. But experience tells me, that thing content is not to be had in this sad world, unmixed with cars and fears. For she brings the unwelcome news of your decaying strength. How can you blame me for desiring to drop away, to spare my eyes there streams? If you dye before me, I shall quickly go after you. But then, alas! what becomes of our dear girls and boys? Theirs my concern, else I could afford you all the great advantages death will bring you. Forgive me, dear brother, that I wish, and pray, that your sojourning may bee prolonged. You end your letter with a riddle I have not wit to find out. You say, you hope to hear I believe better of you then I did: which seems impossible; my faith concerning you cannot bee more strongly kind, no more then can my love increase. I am unchangeably Hod. dear Brother, Your most entirely loving, though most unworthy sister, W. Thim.

These for Mrs Lumly, within tow doors of Great Turn style, in Lincolns-Inn fields, London, May 5, 86. Dearest Niece, Now your coronation joys are past, I expect you should crown me with the comfort of a letter, for tic a tedious time I have suffered by your silence. I confess I speak my shame, by discovering my self love, and car, to purchase my delights in hearing from you, in circumstances that should render me busied with nothing but preparation for death: for age sumons me quickly to my grave, and I thank God, I find no unwillingness to dye. But why lest I live, I must love. What did I say? Why lest I live, I must love. God forbid my love should dye with life. I meant to say, why lest I live, I must love to converse where I love; therefore deny not that loved joy of a line or tow sometimes to Your most entirely loving aunt, W. Thimelby.

column46: Londn. 12th Aprl., 1763. Dear Sir I am favoured with your very agreeable letter, but have it not now before me, however I remember so much of it - relative to Lt. Bute (his dying speech) that I shall certainly believe you possessed of the gift of second sight . My principal motive for writing to you tonight is just to inform you that the Irish Buttr., or rather Grease Bill is this day after some warm debates passed the Ho. of Comns. but it extended to all the ports of England & is upon any dispute arising, betwixt the importer & Custom Ho. officers, to be decided by a Justice of the Peace & two dealers in Butter, whether it shall be deemed Grease or Butter. Lt. Strange exerted his talents greatly, or I believe it had been thrown out for some irregularities in form caused by the alterations & which there wot. not be time this Session to go through the due forms of to make it regular. I spent Sunday evening with. some gentn. who support poor Annett in his confinement and by voluntary contribution which. I find runs rather short & they will be very thankful to any friends of liberty who are disposed to contribute their mite for that purpose. I do believe you with. be against the extension of the excise laws, as they are most certainly calculated in their very nature to abridge the liberty of the subject & I do my dear friend for the first time differ somewhat from you in my sentimts. on that subject. Yours in all the cordiality of friendship.

column46: To Bror. J. Wedgwood. Burslem, 1st Febry., 1765. Dear Bror. It gave me great pleasure to have it under your own hand that your health & spirits are so good & your affairs in so promising a way of being settled agreeably & with dispatch - this gives us some hopes of having the pleasure of your company this spring which I doubt not you will find very salutary, especially as we now have got such pretty employment for you. Sukey is a fine sprightly lass, & will bear a good deal of dandleing & you can sing - lulaby Baby - whilst I rock the Cradle but I shall hardly find time for nursing as we have another Turnpike broke out amongst us here betwixt Leek & Newcastle & they have vi et Arms - mounted me upon my hobby-horse again, & a prancing rouge he is at present, but hope he will not take the route of London again. He carried me yesterday to Leek from whence I am just returned much satisfied with our reception there. Tomorrow I wait upon Dr. Nigel to beg his concurrence & on Monday must attend a meeting to settle the petition, etc., at Money Ash at ire. frd. Isaac Whieldons - We pray to have the Utoxeter & Burslem Turnpikes joined & to have the Road made Turnpike from Buxton & Bakewell to Leek & from Leek to N:castle. Whether or not our good frds. at Newcastle will give us battle on this occasion we do not know, if they do, there will be some probability of my having a commn. & seeing the great City again. - £2000 is wanting for this road. My Uncles Those. & Jno. have - I am quite serious - at the first asking subscribed - I know you will not believe me, but it is a certain fact - five hundred pounds!!! - I have done the like intending 2 or 300 of it for you, and if you choose any more you must let me know in time - it will not be wanted till summer though it must be subscribed now, turn over if you have not had enough. Mr. Willet hath took the Bank and desires you'll come a fishing as soon as your affairs will permit. We have now added another Christian to our family, & her Momma, who is very well - please now to observe that I do let you know by this present writing that she is Bone fide in good health, & as I was saying before is - privately - Churched, but the weather is too bad to carry her to our Abbey at present. Your Lobsters made an elegant dish, were extreme good, pleased my Daddy vastly who stayed with me three days upon the occasion, & was as usual very merry & very good company. - "Tell Jno. Wedgwood," says the old Gentn., "that I drink his health & thank him for his Lobsters, they are very fine, & a creature that I like." Now whether there was any design in this I cannot pretend to say, far be it from me to judge betwixt you on so nice & knotty a subject. Will you have Taffy again this summer, or some better beast? if you do not choose to ride him agn. I intend parting with him as two horses (now I have got an increase of my Family another way) are rather a needless expense to me. - Sally sends her love to you & Tom with Dr. Bror. Your very affect. Bror. All well.

column46: To Mr. John Wedgwood, Cateaton Street, London. Burslem, Feb. 16th, 1765. Dear Bror. In all your letters you do not say a word about coming into Staffordshire again this spring. I hope you will now soon have settled your affairs so as to leave Town, for I do not think that close, smoky place will ever agree with your constitution, & I do very earnestly entreat you to come & take the benefit of your native, salutary, country Air this Spring, even though it shod. be something inconvenient to your affairs in other respects. Mr. Bentley will be in Town on Wednesday Avenge. next. I am just to kiss his hand as he passes through Newcastle in the Coach on Monday next & shall direct him where to find you. Lrs. to him will be directed - at Mr. Wards Haberdasher in Holborn. I hope Mrs. Blake is coming on in the world as the phrase is, my best respects ever wait on that most Agreeable Lady. I hope you will carry Mr. Bentley to Turnham Green & am well assured those two Geniuses will be highly delighted with the interview. I insist when that happens that I am considered as present in spirit though alas absent in body . I can hardly conceive a Scene I shod. be better pleased in partaking of, but I am going to be very busy, having come to a full resolution of attempting in earnest the French ware, & am every night forming schemes for that purpose. I mention nights for whilst Tom is from home I am too closely confined to the Counting house to do anything of that sort in the day. Your next will I hope tell me he is coming home to me. Adieu. Yours affectionately. Sally sends her love to you & best wishes for the continuance of your health & joins me in love to Tom & Compts. to all. I need not say how agreeable the first part of ire. lr. was to us all. Sistr. Byerley's eyes sparkled like - at it the simile is not at hand & I can't wait for it.

column46: To Mr. John Wedgwood. Burslem, 6 March, 1765. Dear Bror. Your last very kind Letter of 12 days long gave us the greatest pleasure as it assured us you were recovered to your former state of health & spirits again, & we pray God to continue you those invaluable Blessings. Though I have time now only to write a few lines it being near post time, I shall be so unreasonable as to expect a very long one in return. You will I doubt not have a Copious subject - the Confabulations of the Triumvirate . - My good frd. Mr. Bentley I know hath given up our liberty as a Chimera - have you convinced him of his error? or hath he brot. you to be of his opinion? Tom arrived here last night & is set in earnest to his business, & I hope will settle again, he was grown really fond of his business, before your giddy Town set his spirits afloat again, but I have great hopes a little encouragemt. - a set of new books, & one months serene air will bring them to subside again. One piece of news Tom brings which I hope is premature, that is your staying in London all summer. I cannot give my consent to this step believing it will endanger your health, which certainly shod. be your first care. I have just begun a Course of experiments for a white body & glaze which promises well hitherto. Sally is my chief helpmate in this as well as other things, & that she may not be hurried by having too many Irons in the fire as the phrase is I have ordd. the spining wheel into the Lumber room. She hath learnt my characters, at least to write them, but can scarcely read them at present. - This business I often think if you could but once enter into the spirit of it, wot. be the prettiest employment for you imaginable. I do not intend to make this ware at Burslem & am therefore laying out for an agreeable & convenient situation elsewhere. Three packets by one post from Sr. Wm.! two of them enclosing birds, insects & flowers. I have since wrote two lrs. to him directed to Sr. Wm. Meredith in London - that direction I suppose will find a Gentn. of his eminence, if you think otherwise as he is removed to Chelsea pray do the needful for me. Accept our best wishes for your health & happiness, present our respects where due & believe us ever Your very affect. Bror. & Sistr. J. & S. Wedgwood.

column46: To Mr. Jno. Wedgwood. Burslem, 11 March, 1765. Thanks to my dear Bror. for his last very agreeable & entertaining epistle, & the kind offers of transacting any business in London I may want to employ such an hand in. I have had too much experience of your affection & partiality towards me to doubt of your regard for my interest & readiness to promote it, & you are too well acquainted with my business & connections in Town to believe I shall let such offers pass with me as mere compliments only, no, I have already some tolerably solid business cut out for you, if I pursue my scheme of white glazed ware, some materials for which must be boat. & disguised in London before they are sent to me - but more of this hereafter. I congratulate you on the offer of so liberal & honourable an appointmt. made you by the Society of Gentn. Merchts. &c. but you are not explicit enough for me to have a tolerable Idea of the plan, or business of this Society, who can afford their Chairman so handsome an appointmt., or what service they expect in return for it. - I can readily conceive this employment would be an honourable one & that the Gentn. concerned must have a great opinion of the abilities, & integrity of any Gentn. they employed in it, but as to the lucrative part that must depend on circumstances I am entirely a stranger to. I hope in your next you will favour me with a farther explanation on this head. Your feast at Turnham Green (mental feast I mean) was just what I expected, from the meeting & collision of such Geniuses as were there assembled, & from your description with a little of the art of designing I could spread a yard of Canvas over with an excellent group of figures. - How happy shod. I have been in partaking of so instructive, & elegant an Entertainmt.! - but alas I must be content with fashioning my clay at an humble distance from such compy. & live, breathe, & dye, amongst animals but one remove above the Earth they are teazeing. I do not envy my friends their more refined enjoyments of life, but I do sometimes wish for a pair of wings, & a learners seat amongst them, & had the good Bishop Wilkins scheme for flying been brot. to any tolerable perfection, you had most certainly seen me fluttering at your Dining room Window at Turnham Green. I shod. be glad to know how my good friend Mr. Bentley's scheme proceeds, & shod. have wrote to him to-day but have half a doz. other lrs. which must be wrote & will prevent me. That accomplished man is sure to make a figure on almost any subject, & in any company capable of doing justice to his eminent talents. Pray what were the Chief subjects of your conversation with Sr. Wm.? I suppose you attended that worthy Gentns. summons along with Mr. Bentley & others - perhaps, & have no doubt of your being elegantly and agreeably entertained. On Friday last I dined with Mr. Brindley the Duke of Bridgwaters engineer, after which we had a meeting at the Leopard on the subject of a Navigation from Hull, or Wilton Ferry to Burslem agreeable to a survey & plan before taken. Our Gentn. seem very warm in setting this matter on foot again, & I could scarcely withstand the pressing solicitations I had from all present, to undertake a journey or two for that purpose. We are to have another meeting at Henley to-morrow & per Wednesdays post you shall know the result. Mother, Bror. & Sistr. Wedgwood are poorly of colds, mine hath quite left me. Sally & Sukey are well & send love & duty. The finest Girl! - So like her father! Yrs. in the truest affectn. My best respects always wait on Mr. Bentley & the triumvirate.

To Mr. John Wedgwood. Dear Brother I'll teach you to find fault, & scold, & grumble at my not writing, I warrant you, & as to your going to France, I do not believe I can spare you out of London this summer, if business comes in for you at this rate, for instance - An ordr. from St. James's for a service of Staffordshire ware, about which I want to ask a hundred questions, & have never a mouth but yours in Town worth opening upon the subject. The ordr. came from Miss Deborah alias Deb. Chetwynd, sempstress, & Laundress to the Queen, to Mr. Smallwd. of Newcastle, who brot. it to me (I believe because nobody else with. undertake it) & is as follows. A complete set of tea things, with a gold ground & raised flowers upon it in green, in the same manner of the green flowers that are raised upon the mehons , so it is wrote but I suppose it shod. be melons - The articles are 12 Cups for Tea, & 12 Saucers, a slop basin, sugar dish with. cover & stand, Teapot & stand, spoon trea, Coffeepot, 12 Coffee cups, 6 pr. of hand candlesticks & 6 Melons with leaves. 6 green fruit baskets & stands edged with gold. I have just begun an Enamel work & am in great want of some gold powder such as is burnt in upon China. It is made by one Mr. Shenton (only) & sold by him at 7 guineas per os. Mr. Giles Enameler in Berwick St. Old Soho, can tell you where Mr. Shenton lives, which is the best direction I can get. I shod. be glad to have a few pennywts. by way of trial, Mr. Shenton may perhaps give you instructions about the best manner of using it & when I have his address will write farther to him & settle him a Crt. in Londn. for with. Gold I order in future. May send this small parcl. along with some leaf gold I have ordd. from Mr. Gifford in Maiden Lane Wood St. unless you find a quicker conveyance. You may conceal a little of it in a frank. Miss Chetwynds ordr. must be done with this gold if burnt in. My post boy waits - adieu. Yours most cordially. Do not waste a frank on a single lr. All well. Pray put on the best suit of Clothes you ever had in your life , & take the first opportunity of going to Court. Miss Chetwynd is Daughter to the Master of the Mint.

To John Wedgwood. Burslem, 3rd Aprl., before breakfast. Dear Brother I find Tom hath made you acquainted with my late Tour, & in part with our success in it. - Mr. Taylor is just entered into partnership with one Mr. Loyd in the Banking business, & Mr. Loyd it seems is one of the Proprietors in the Burton Navigation which will be injured by our intended Canal, as it is proposed to carry it beyond Burton to Wilton in order to keep clear of their Locks and shallows. We made it appear pretty evident to the Gentn. of Birmingham that £10,000 per annm. would be immediately saved to them in the Article of Land Cargo. to and from the River Trent, so soon as the Canal was brot. to their Town which wot. it is apprehended be in less than three years after it is begun upon. We are informed by a very intelligent Gentn. (Mr. Garbitt) of Birmm. that this Navigation would be a great advantage to the Russia Merchants as they wot. then be able to send their Iron & Flax with much greater certainty & at 15s. per Ton less expense to Birmm. Wolverhampton Walsal &c. & between 30 & 40s. per Ton less into these parts. We have not yet been with the Gentn. of Liverpool, but have recd. instructions per last post from Mr. Bentley in with. manner to make our address the most acceptable there. This scheme of a Navigation is undoubtedly the best thing that could possibly be planed for this country & I hope there is a great degree of probability of its being carried into execution. I met our frd. Mr. Bentley at Trentham & spent the evening with him (till 3 o'Clock morng. when he took Coach again) at Talk, & I need not tell you was greatly entertained with his acct. of Men and things in London. The last post brot. me five packets from Sr. Wm. enclosing prints of different sorts which he is so obliging to employ his good taste in picking up for me at the Printshops, he hath likewise sent me some orders from Sr. Goo. Savil & Gentn. of his acquaintance & hath many more he says for me & in order that I may work after the best models he hath sent me a Dessert service of Dresden China to pattern from. How shall I make any return at all adequate to this Generosity? When you see Sr. Wm. you will let him know I am at least sensible of his distinguishing favours. A VOICE this moment breaks in upon me with - NEWS, NEWS, NEWS, & what do you think it is? why truly, the Marriage writings are making between my Uncle Thomas, & my Cousin Molly, both of venerable memory. This may serve as a Choice drop of Comfort to Old Maids, & Bachelors , & I hope it will have its proper effect. It is farther whispered in my ear by a Voice which always gives me pleasure that the chief stumbling-block to this marriage was removed when she secured a third Person for her own. We have no other very particular news with us that I know of. Sukey smiles this morning & sends Duty to her Uncle, & wot. be very glad to see this Uncle John she hears so much of, in Staffordshire, Sally is very well & joins in best wishes for your health & pleasure with Dr. Bror. Your obliged, & very affectionate Bror.

column46: To John Wedgwood. Burslem, May 29, 1765. Dear Bror. You do not say one word about our worthy friend Sr. Wms. illness. I was told last week at Liverpool that he had been seized with an Apoplectic fit & lay a dying but did not give any credit to the report, as I had recd. a letter from you the avenge. before I left home, which was the same post they must have their intelligence by, & you did not mention anything of it, but a report is now current here of his being carried from the House of Commns. in some sort of a fit, & that he now is extremely ill of a fever. Do let me know by return of post how it is with him, whether he is sick or well, & if I may yet expect the honour of waiting upon him at Burslem, & if you wait upon him, pay my humble respects in what manner you shall think proper, but pray let me know how his health is affected, for since the last report I have been much concerned about it. If I had time and room for it you should have a good scolding for beginning your last letter in such a manner. Am not I teazeing you with my scrawls every week? & sometimes every post? & shod. have no sort of objection to writing oftener still if Journeys, Navigations, & other things did not prevent me. You know I do not want inclination, - you know that ever since I have been capable of distinguishing, I have had the truest & most affect. regards for you, & I am sure you have always given me sufficient reason to believe that our affection was mutual; therefore do not talk of my forgetting such a Brother & friend as you have ever been to me, nor of my being forgotton by you. I cannot bear to think or say any more about it. The latter part of your letter delights me greatly as your poetical description of Groves & springs, the feathered Choir &c. &c. indicates the flow of spirits you enjoyed at the time of writing it, & let me tell you that a pint of new milk & a Role & half a Role by way of finishing a breakfast shows a tolerable good natured stomach, at least we should think so in the country. But I am afraid by your acct. of this new chalybeat Inn & the Compy. who resort to it we are not to have the pleasure of your company in Staffordshire this summer, this I can by no means consent to - we have chalybeats with us, & new milk too, for the very day I knew your quantity, we sold our barren Cow in order to buy a new milch one, & now come as soon as you will there will be enough for us all. Sally says your niece Sukey is worth your coming 150 miles to see, but she may see & talk like a mother, however we do expect to see you some part of the summer amongst us, & the sooner the pleasanter. Believe us ever Your truly affect. Bror. & Sr. J. & S. Wedgwood.

column46: To Mr. John Wedgwood. Burslem, July 6th, 1765. My dear Brothers letter of 28 June rejoiced us all very greatly as it left us no room to doubt of the return of his health & spirits again, pray God preserve to you those invaluable blessings. Your mother sends her love to you, with her blessing provided you do not take her son John into France, she is not willing to trust him with that false-hearted People, & hopes he will not be so hardy to venture himself amongst them, but rather come & visit his friends in Staffordshire. - I cannot help thinking the advice is good & hope it will meet with due attention. I should have wrote to you sooner but have been waiting upon his G- the D- of Bridgwater with plans &c. respecting Inland Navigation. Mr. Sparrow went along with me, we were most graciously recd. spent about 8 hours in his G's compy., & had all the assurances of his concurrence with our designs that we could wish. His G- gave me an ordr. for the completest Table service of Cream colour that I could make, showed us a Roman Urn 1500 years old at least, made of red china, & found by his workmen in Castlefield near Manchester. - After his G- had dismissed us we had the honour, & pleasure too of sailing in his Gondola nine miles along his Canal, through a most delightful vale to Manchester, the next day we waited upon the Cheshire Gentn. at a meeting of the Commrs. for the Weaver Navigation at Northwich, who promised likewise to use their interest in favour of our design, provided we fall into their Navigation. But no more of this 'till you are better acquainted with the subject. I am greatly delighted with the picture you give of yourself, & the short journal of your exercise & diet - pray let us as soon as possible be favoured with a sight of the Original, & edify by your example in early rising, & eating of buttermilk. I shall be very proud of the honour of sending a box of patterns to the Queen, amongst which I intend sending two sets of Vases, Creamcolour engine turned, & printed, for which purpose nothing could be more suitable than some copper plates I have by me. I can adapt the Vases so that the designs & they will appear to be made for each other, & intended for Royalty, nor must you hint to the contrary - but I am one group or design short which I have sketched out & enclosed & desire you'll get it done by Wale unless you know a better hand. It must be engraved, any of the print shops, (Mr. Bowls in Cornhill in particular) will direct you to Wale or some other: the sooner I have it done & sent me, the sooner I shall be able to send the patterns.

column46: To Mr. John Wedgwood, Junr. Burslem, 2nd Augt., 1765. Dear Brother Bror. John is here in his way to London so could not miss the opportunity of sending a line by him. On second thoughts it may not be amiss to know all one can about this burning on gold polishing, & burnishing the same - burnishing is a different operation to polishing, & I shd. be glad to know with. instrument they make use of & be furnished with one of them. I wish you wot. buy & send me per Coach Vol. 1st of the Handmaid to the Arts published in 1758 for Nurse in the Strand. And now as to the price of this ware. I foresee that if the gold must be laid on to have a full metalic appearance the price will be very high, whether they may be deemed dear or not I cannot say, but sure the great Personage they are for wot. have them perfect, & can afford to pay for them, but I wot. rather not fix any price at all upon them if that wot. be approved of, but farther on this subject another time. ... Pray how are you for business, or schemes of pleasure? for I wot. by no means break into the latter, but if it wot. be consistent with both & you shod. choose it I wot. send you a pattern or two & a list of my Chaps, & more bills if you choose such employmt. 'till a better place offers. I have this year sent goods to emote. of abot. £1000 to London all of which is owing for & I shod. not care how soon I was counting some of the money. You know I have often mentioned having a man in London the greatest part of the year showing patterns, taking orders, settling accts. &c. &c. & as I increase my work, & throw it still more into the ornamental way I shall have the greater need of such assistance & shod. be glad to have your advice upon it. Wo'd £50 a year keep such a Person in London & pay rent for 2 Rooms (both back rooms & St. Giles's wot. be as good as St. James's) about so much I think it might answer for me to give. If your Clark hath not full employmt. a thing of this sort might make a little appendage to his salary. My father sends his respects service &c. to you by his son, but he is a Leaky vessel to freight with. Compts. I shall expect answers to all my lrs. very soon from your experienced punctuality & am with the truest Affection Dr. Bror. Your greatly obliged Bror.

column46: To Mr. John Wedgwood. Burslem, 7 Augt., 1765. Dear Bror. I have just had the honour of the D. of Marlbo., Lt. Gower, Lt. Spencer & others at my works. - They have boat. some things & seemed much entertained & pleased. Sally & I are taking a ride to look at poor Sr. Nigil's goods &c. which are to be sold in a fortnight, he hath left Knipersley with his family, & it is much feared his affairs will never suffer his return. Our best affection waits on you. Adieu. I have succeeded the first trial in making powder gold which I have always been told one man only in England could make, & desire you'll send me an os. of pure gold either in Ducats or grain or some form, send the powder too. I am just teased of my life with dilatory, drunken, Idle, worthless workmen which prevents my proceeding in the tea service, to which. more sorts of workmen are necessary than one wot. imagine. The Gentn. above mentd. (not the workmen though) wonder I have not a Wareho. in Londn. where pattns. of all the sorts I make may be seen. Our love to another J. W.

column46: To Mr. Those. Bentley. London Lawrence Lane. Messrs. Berries & Coy. Manchester Warehouse. 15 Octr., 1765. Dr. Sir Before you receive this you will see your spirited & manly paper in the St. James's Chronicle, & I wish it may have the desired effect upon the Public. Sr. Wm. read it there last night, at his own house, & I took the liberty of telling him to whom the Public was indebted for it, he said it was very clever &c. & I hope it falls in with his own sentiments. I have not read the Monthly Review for Augt. or Septr. & therefore have not seen the Review of Mr. Priestley's work, indeed the truth is I have scarcely read anything at all, or thought of anything at all but Pottmaking & Navigating, & when it will be otherwise with me I cannot tell. The Booksellers you know how to deal with & deal by, much better than myself & shall leave that business entirely to you. I have mentioned the affair of Dedication to Mr. Griffiths before I was favoured with yours, we had no very deliberate discussion of the matter, but offhand he thought the Legislature if it meant the Power rather than the Persons could not with propriety be Dedicated to, but if as you say it means King, Lds., & Commns. I shod. think that objection entirely took away. I am my good friend very sorry that this Pamphlet turns out so troublesome an affair to you who I am sure have full employmt. for every moment of your time. As to our friend of Lichfields remarks if you can avail yourself of them in the part not yet printd. I know you will, but the condemnation or postponing of the whole I can by no means agree to nor persuade myself that there is any necessity for it. Must the Uniting of Seas & distant countries depend upon the choice of a phrase, or monosyllable? Away with such hypercriticisms, & let the press go on, a Pamphlet we must have, or our design will be defeated, so make the best of the present, & correct, refine, & sublimate, if you please, in the next edition. P.S. - My Bror. is now with me, & is very certain that if you wot. come & fix in London, & enter a second time into the holy estate of Matrimony that you might choose your Lady, have your Chariot, lead the World in a string, and do what seems good in your own eyes. By the same authority that I mention this, - every Wife, maid and Widow that hath seen Mr. Bentley in London join in this opinion. This deponent farther says not. I am only his emanuensis, if you require an explanation write to him.

column46: To Mr. John Wedgwood. Burslem, 11th Novr., 1765. Dear Brother Nothing prevented us having a pleasant journey home but the badness of the roads which were very bad indeed. We spent half a day very agreeably at Blenheim House and in the evening went with the Steward, his Daughter & four sons to see a play at Woodstock, but alas, we had seen the London Theatre too lately to have much enjoymt. from poverty, rags & blunders on the Woodstock stage. As you talk of sending down a box I must just hint to you that Sister Willets little Lasses will go to bed without their nightcaps soon if they do not recve. an old shirt from their uncle. They send love & duty to you from the Bank, your cousin Sally bids me send her best love (next to her husband or so) to you & tell you she was providing same pork pies & will now send the puddings along with them for ire. Xmas fare before the holidays.

column46: To Mr. John Wedgwood. Burslem, 4th June, 1766. Dear Brother Perhaps you will not be angry at paying for the intelligence that we had yesterday a very Noble, Numerous & amicable General assembly of the Commrs. & Proprietors of the Navigation from the Trent to the Mersey . Lt. Gower, Lt. Grey, Mr. Bagot, Mr. Anson, Mr. Gilbert & the Gentn. of the County did us the honour of attending this Assembly which was conducted through the whole of it with the utmost order, Harmony & as far as appeared, to the entire satisfaction of all parties. I have enclosed you an abstract of the business done, by which you will see the honour done me, which was quite unexpected & voluntary, without the least previous solicitation on my part, & without one dissenting voice. The reason I accepted it was that some of our friends suspected a Candidate wot. offer who lived at too great a distance from the Centre of the business, & of the bolk of the subscribers, to be convenient, on which I was urged to accept it & complied. Mr. Smith of Fenton then proposed me to the Assembly, & I was asked if I wot. accept it, & what security I was willing to give. To the former I answered in the affirmative, & referred myself to their pleasure for the latter. The sum fixed upon was £10,000. All this was begun & ended in about quarter of an hour. Immediately after it was over Mr. Sam Robison took me aside and very genteelly offered to join in my security for so much as his bond wot. be took for, which unexpected favour I shall ever remember with gratitude whether I accept it or not. I own I shod. rather have no other name but Wedgwood in the security, & shod. be glad of your advice on this head. The utmost I ever expect to have in my hands at once is 5 or £6000. P.S. - Mr. Steveson of Stafford was the Person expected to be a Candidate for Treasurer, so you will know where not to mention that Circumstance.
