column46: Burslem, 14th Feb., 1767. How much am I indebted to my dear friend for his affectionate & sympathizeing epistles, & the interest I know he takes in all that concerns me, more - much more than I shall ever be able to pay, unless he will, as usual accept of a grateful heart to balance all deficiencies. But notwithstanding I owe so much, would you believe me so void of shame, Grace or discretion that I am every day wishing to owe more. - I wot. scarcely believe it of myself, but the symptoms are too strong upon me to deny the charge, for every post day I catch myself greedily running over the directions of my letters, & if a well known hand does not appear, Sally is ready to ask what has so suddenly altered my countenance. I am too pettish (for you know I am subject to be choleric on a disappointment) to give her any answer, but read my letters, & unless a good order, or some such circumstance intervenes, few things go right with me that day. I recd. some consolation on a disappointment of this sort from a certain article in the Review for Decr. which as I was going through in the common ordr. of reading for the amusement of Deary she observed me to read with more spirit, & emphasis than usual & interrupting me cried out - Why Jose! one wot. think thou wast reading one of B's letters - & so I am I am very certain - but I will give him a triming for keeping me in the dark, & the Alderman too, who I afterwards found was in the secret, as I suspected, but purposely kept me ignorant to try if I could make the discovery myself, which indeed was very easy to do without making any great merit of my penetration, & I shod. not wonder to hear that G- G- had sent to inquire of the Publisher, who it was that wrote that article. Oh my friend! that your time, & station would permit you to set our Great & little folk right. - Those I mean who have a real intention of serving their Country, if they knew how to set about it. Your province should certainly be to guide, & superintend others, rather then to be busied in any little mercantile affairs of your own. - Pardon the epithet little for with the view I have before me, such they must appear be they ever so great. - Nay do not frown, I do not, I will not flatter , but pray for you - And to Mammon shall my prayer be directed, That it may please him to grant, & continue to you, such a portion of his Divine Essence as may qualify you to take a seat in a certain assembly, grant this one petition, oh! thou sovereign disposer of the Honours, & good things of this World, & I ask no more. Join with me my good friend in this Pious prayer, & at the same time remember that prayer as well as Faith without works, is dead, endeavour therefore, not after knowledge, & literary wisdom , of which you have enough, but after the wisdom of the Children of this world , in plain English - get money - you want some such matter as 4 or £500 per annm. in Terra firm (such is the constitution of things in this sublunary Planet) to make the knowledge & abilities you have acquired of the greatest utility to your Countrymen. If I can at any time be of use to you in this pursuit, you know you will oblige me in letting me know it, my mind is ever willing, & my Body is now better able to serve my friends than it has been for some time past, I have pretty well recovered my strength, & my spirits flow again in their usual Channel. Pray what paper is the advertisement in of the Stone Manufactory you mention, I have not seen or heard anything about it, & unless it shod. happen to be in the St. James's Chronicle, it will not fall in my way. I suppose sand to be the Basis of the stone, & to make it extensively useful, a plain & simple method of converting sand into stone should be published. If the secret, & materials for stonemakeing are local it will be rather a matter of curiosity than utility. If the process can be applied to covering buildings with one complete sheet of stone it will be a valuable acquisition indeed, the roofing may be laid so flatt, & will at the same time be so light that a great saving will be made in the article of Timber, & several other advantages wot. arise from such an invention. Yours at all times.

column46: Burslem, 2nd of Aprl., 1767. My dear friend I thank you most sincerely for your last very affectionate letter, & solicitude for my Bro.rs recovery. He is now got pretty well again, & I did not care to mention his illness to you 'till I could at the same time give you the pleasure of assuring you of his recovery which was the principal reason of my silence whilst he was so very Ill, for he hath been much worse this time than I ever knew him before. Poor Mr. Brindley was not well enough to attend the Commit & General Assembly, he has now given up a journey into Scotland & Ireland, which he had promised Mr. Garbett & Lt. Hertford to make this spring, & is going to Buxton for a few weeks, which I hope will have a good effect upon his constitution, as his ailments certainly proceed from a too intense, & constant application to business, both with body & mind. I am going to see him this morning, & shall endeavour to persuade him to be idle for a season that his stay amongst us may be the longer for it. We were honoured at our General assembly at Stone with the Compy. of the D. of Bridgwater & Lt. Gower, who approved much of our proceedings, & Lt. Gower told us pleasantly, he thought we shod. be stiled the Amicable society of Navigators . You know that Mr. Rentals scheme for executing our Canal with ploughs proved abortive, he had therefore no demands upon us, as we were only to pay him so much per yd. as he finished his work. However to comfort him undr. his disapointmt., & encourage any future attempts of ingenuity, the Assembly have ordd. him a present of thirty Guineas. I wish it had been more, though some of our Proprietors think it a work of supererogation that they might very well have excused themselves from performing. Narrow minds have no idea of paying more money than the Laws of the Land oblige them to. I was going to thank you for your remarks upon the plans, but a Gentn. waits for me in the Wareho. however I cannot forbear telling one piece of news I had from a Gentn. who was at the Commit upon the Carron Navigation. You remember what plauge & trouble our good frd. Mr. Garbett gave us with his limitation scheme of 10 P~ Ct. int. on the Navn. Capital. That very plan is now urged upon him & the intended proprietors of the Navigation sorely against their wills, & he is now reduced to the dilemma of proposing & defending a plan which he was before so vigorous in opposing & depreciating. However his efforts avail as little now as they did before. The Parliamt. will not pass the Act without the limitation, & the subscribers will not have it with that clause, so that the Gentn. from whom I have my information believes this bone of Contention will prevent their having any act at all. How justly may we exclaim - The wicked have dug a pitt for us, & are fallen into it themselves! Adieu. P.S. - Our good wives here are informed that Malaga Raisins are extremely cheap, & desire me to ask you what they can be boat. for per hunt.with. at Liverpool, good, rich fruit . They are 18/- at London. We shall be glad to know as soon as possible, that the season may not slip us, for we are to have an inundation of Raisin wine this year.

column46: London, 27 May, 1767. Dear Sir I spent yesterday afternoon & Avenge. with two or three Gentn. who had resided long in South Carolina, one of whom gave me a small sample of the Cherok Earth, by way of Curiosity, not knowing who, or what I was, for I kept in Cog. I find the E. must be carrd. near 300 miles by Land Carre. which will make it come very heavy. I have had a long Conference with Mr. Griffiths, & am inclined to employ him, but shall be glad to contrive some restriction to prevent his doing too much mischief if he shod. be so inclined. I was with Mr. Bagot this morning & we had a good deal of chat upon political affairs, particularly American, in which I told him my sentiments very freely. That our Policy had a tendency to render the Americans independent a Century sooner than they wot. be in the common order of events, if treated agreeable to sound policy. The Ministry were run very hard yesterday in the House of Lords. They Carried their point by a Majority of three only. The Dukes of York & Gloucester came to vote for the Ministry, otherwise they had carried it by one only, so that a Change is looked upon as inevitable. But that is nothing to you & I, for whoever is in they will make the most of us they can, so my friend let us unite our forces, & endeavour to do the same by them but in honester mode . Mr. Pennant has boat. a very full Table service of Cream colour, otherwise I shod. not greatly like him to represent you in Parliamt., merely because he married the Daughter of an Idolater, for I know no other harm by him. He never can be hearty in the Runkhorn Gap scheme, his Father-in-law, General Warburton being one of the most Zealous worshippers of the Goddess Weaverina so that I shall despair almost of that great project being carried into execution, at least in any moderate time. I am glad to hear Crates sell apace with you. I have no reason to complain here. Vases sell, too, even in the rude state they now are, for such they appear when I take a view of what may be done. The Alderman is well & sends his sincere respects to you, so does our frd. Griffiths. Adieu I am called away.

column46: Charles St., Thursday Evening, Mar. 24, 1768. At the Close of the Poll here my attention was so much engaged with other objects that I did not think at all scarcely about Electioneering, & therefore did not send you the first intelligence of who were in, & who were out, at the Hustings, & now it is too late to send you the intelligence as news so shall say no more about it. One of the objects referred to above was seeking after a house, or rather Warehouse in which I have at last succeeded to my wishes, & quite beyond my most sanguine expectations. I have a lease assigned over to me for forty years, of a house near the bottom of St. Martins Lane, Charing Cross, which will be quite convenient for Westminster, & within a 12d. ride from St. Pals Ch.yd. I think of making habitations for a Colony of Artists - Modelers, Carvers &c. I have already agreed with one very useful Tenant, a Master Enameler, & China piecer, - he joins old valuable pieces of China, not with Rivets, but a white glass, & burns them till the glass vitrifys, & they are as sound as ever they were. I have long had connections with this Man, who is sober, & steady, he is just come out of Yorkshire to settle here. He paints flowers, & Landscapes very prettily, prepares a pretty good powder gold, & has a tolerable notion of Colours. He has an apprentice & another hand, I have set him to work upon Table & desert ware, & shall get his rooms ready in St. Martins Lane immediately. The having such a man as this under the same roof with the Warehouse, to do Crests, or any other pattns. by ordr. - to take sketches &c - is the most convenient thing imaginable, & nobody but ourselves will know what he is doing. A Modeler in the same yd. too will be very clever to send to any Ladies favourite Antique for a copy. I have spent several hours with Lt. Cathcart our Ambassador to Russia, & we are to do great things for each other.

Burslem, Wednesday Evening. To-morrow the Liverpool Coach goes through Newcastle, & takes up there two antique Vases, one is of the Holy Door Marble, & the other Jaune Antique , they are both in one box, & directed for your worship, much good may they do you. That is, may they keep up the disorder which it is thought you have lately been a little, or perhaps, not a little, infected with. I confess this is my kind intention in sending them, & if they have not the desired effect, it is no fault of mine. You'll see the polish is not complete, but you will form from them as they are some idea of their capabilities, & I cod. not bear that you shod. wait another day before you feasted your eyes with such fine things . But you'll please to remember that none of them can be made for sale of some time, Ergo , no Man, Woman, or Child, but your own hous-hold, nor scarcely them, shod. see these things at present. Pray return them by Danl., & return yourself as soon as possible to help me get all things ready to proceed with these Vases. It is with the greatest difficulty imaginable that I restrain from indulging my fancy in making more of them, & if I am not endued with the Continence of a Scipio, & you do not come & prevent me in my doings , I shall never hold out another week. Farewell. One of the Fumigations is a most exelent Enamel colour, so fine a yellow that I have some hopes of the GREAT WORK being perfected, & that we shall be able to turn even the dirt under our feet into Gold . I will leave off at a good word so once more good night.

column46: To Mrs. Wedgwood, at the Brickhouse, Burslem, Staffordshire. 15 Feb., 1769. I thank you my good friend for the noble treat I have just been enjoying. They do me good to see 'em, but alas, the whole four packages are not a mouthful, not one days sale, I could sell I am fully persuaded 1000 worth such Vases if I had them before I come home. Large, very large ones are all the cry, & we must endeavour to satisfy them. You shod. set both the mills to work at grinding & with two sets of hands, one for night, & the other for the day. I must thank my dear Sally for her last favour, though she did not conclude it so meekly as one might wish, but with a Toss of her head cries, I shall not trouble my head &c - Oh Fie Sally Fie, wilt thou never mend? you are a naughty Girl, & fill but half a sheet with your letter, whilst I scribble by the Quire. Oh I had quite forgot to send you a copy of the Advertisemt. I intend for next week. Let me have ire. Criticisms by Saturdays post & it may save me some shame perhaps. the manufacture of Josiah Wedgwood Potter &c, &c - are sold at his Ware-house, the Qns. Arms, corner of Great Newport St. Long Acre, & at no other place in Town. Orders are executed on the shortest notice as above, or at his Manufactory at Burslem in Staffordshire. He does not now charge Cargo. to London, sells for ready money only, & the lowest price is marked on each Article. Card for Direction for Queens Ware and ornamental Vases at the Queens Arms the corner of Great Newport St. Long Acre NB. His goods are not sold at any other place in Town. Goodnight love.

column22: professional: wife of Josiah Wedgwood, master potter

column46: To Mrs. Wedgwood, at the Brick-house Burslem, Staffordshire. Feb. 23, 1769. I have settled a plan & method with - to Tinker all the black Vases that are crooked, we knock off the feet & fix wood ones, blacked, to them, those with tops, or snakes wantg., are to be supplied in the same way. I wish you wot. send me a parcl. of these Invalids by Sundays Waggon, as he wishes to have with. we can furnish him with of each sort together. Some of the Ladies say the same thing that occurred to you & me abot. the sugr. dish Vases - that they are like the things on the tops of Clock cases, or Beds heads. They certainly are not Antique, and that is fault enough to D-n them for with most of our customers. My love to you all, share & divide it as you please, you have my heart though my bodily Tabernacel is confined here at present. J. W. It will be of great importance to have the service for my friend Barclay as neat and fine as possible, the Quakers have for some time past been trying my ware, & verily they find it to answer their wishes in every respect, they have now ordd. this full set, & my future recommendation to the brethren must depend upon their usage in their sample. A word to the wise is enough. Pray say Double only , upon ire. double lrs. - we pt. 2s. 8d. for the last double one, thank Morgan for it.

column39: Letters of Josiah Wedgwood, 1762 to 1770 (vol. 1); 1771 to 1780 (vol. 2). Ed. by Katherine Euphemia, Lady Farrer. London: privately printed for private circulation. 1903. Reprinted. Manchester: E. J. Morten, for the Trustees of the Wedgwood Museum. 1973.
column46: To Mr. Bentley at the Queens Arms, Newport St., Longacre, London. Sept. 16, 1769. Trouble me indeed - you cannot think how happy you make me with these Good, long affect. & instructing letters. They inspire me with taste, emulation & everything that is necessary for the production of fine things & I hope in a few weeks to show you some of the effects of your excellent lectures. I go to Etruria every day almost, but it will not be sufficient to spend an hour or two there in a morning as I do at present, I intend to go & live there if you will lend me your house, & take Mr. Denby with me, whom I shall not spare you at present, he will be very useful to me & will help me to keep them in order with respect to forms which I am convinced with you is the principal part. I give you leave my dear friend to find fault with me as fast as you please - The more & the oftener the better - & I will endeavour to proffit by it. Your letters I must own are a little troublesome to me for I cannot read them to my satisfaction without a heap of books by my side - the Etruscan order book - the Burslem order book, & one I have just made for hints, memorandums &c, so that it is the work of an hour or two to read one of your packets a single time over. Indeed they are now become my Magazines, Reviews, Chronicles, & I had almost said my Bible. - But do not let this discourage you my friend, - go on - I will tell you when I have enough. I think we shod. have some of the casts from Antique gems from Rome as well as the figures, I hope by means of the Gentn. you mention that you will be able to settle a correspondence with some of our ingenious Gentn. or Artists at Rome yourself which I think will be very useful to us. There is a book-seller on the left hand side of the Haymarket touts. the bottom as you go from Piccadilly but he does not make any show of his business to the street. He is a foreigner, & was recommended to me by Lt. Clanbrassil, I ordd. from him a book of Lamps published at Rome, & I imagine the same you mention. I wish you could find him out, he has often good things by him in our way. I have sent Boot to Etruria today to begin upon Terra Cotta figures, but I have only a Sphinx, Lyon & a Triton for him to begin with. I have been obliged to threaten to discharge him for being loose & wild, but he promises to be very good, & will bring up hands to figure making or do anything that we please for our advantage. What do you think of Terra Cotta figures of the same composition with the Fox heads? they wot. have the appearance of Models, & make an agreeable variety with the black, both figures and Vases. Oh! what a feast have I by this post, thank you for it my dear & well-beloved friend, I will do everything possible about the orders & will simplify, & hire hands, & send you Vases & - what will I not do for such packets as these? farewell & believe me yrs. evermore J. W.

column46: To Mr. Bentley, at the Queens Arms, Newport St., Longacre, London. Burslem, 20th Septr., 1769. I hope the enclosed will not come too late to go along with the goods to St. Petersburg, indeed I shod. have wrote sooner, but I have had so much business upon my hands, & hate writing to great folks that both together have prevented me till just now. You'll see you are to write with the Vases. There seems to be difficulty how to deliver these Vases to Lady Cathcart. They must not be presented , & we must not pretend to charge them, so that they must neither be given nor sold , - but we must borrow a pair of her Ladyships chimney pieces to show them upon. I think your letter and mine shod. be wrapped up in two separate cases. May not you give Lt. Cathcart a hint that we are preparing to paint the Etruscan Vases after Mr. Hamilton's Book? I have not yet mentioned to Mr. and Mrs. Willcox our intention of having them to Town, but I asked Mrs. Willcox this morning about her living in London &c & how she shod. like to live there again. She sd. she shod. not like it at all, she had much rather live in Staffordshire. I must talk to her again. Boot is making Tritons & Sphinx's, & does them very well, better than I expected. I hired an ingenious Boy last night for Etruria as a Modeler. He has modeled at nights in his way for three years past, has never had the least instructions, which circumstance considered he does things amazingly & will be a valuable acquisition. I have hired him for five years, & with Denby & him I shall not want any other constant modeler at Etruria. Palmer, & several others wot. fain have hired this Boy but he chose to come to me. Medallion to match the Sacrifice - We have none & I am not in the way of getting such things here. If you can send me one I will put it upon the Vases & think it will be a great improvemt. - you have several subjects in ire. books that will do & you are in the only place in the world for artists.

To Mr. Thomas Bentley at the Queens Arms, Newport Street, Long Acre, London. Burslem. My dear friend If you continue to write such letters as your last there is no saying where our improvements will stop. I read it over, & over again, & still proffitt by every repetition of your agreeable Lessons. And do you really think that we may make a complete conquest of France? Conquer France in Burslem? - My blood moves quicker, I feel my strength increase for the contest. Assist me my friend & the victory is our own. We will make them (now I must say Pots , & how vulgar it sounds) I won't though, I say we will fashn. our Porcelain after their own hearts, & captivate them with the Elegance & simplicity of the Ancients. But do they love simplicity? Are you certain the French Nation will be pleased with simplicity in their Vessels? Either I have been greatly deceived, or a wonderful reformation has taken place amongst them. French & Frippery have jingled together so long in my ideas, that I scarcely know how to separate them, & much of their work which I have seen covered over with ornament , had confirmed me in the opinion. I left London with a full resolution to simplify , & you shall soon be convinced I was in earnest, as a first essay I have discarded the twiggen and flowered handles from the Terrines, & everything except the baskets, where I think their apparent lightness, & real strength , & their similarity to the work of the vessels will induce me to retain them but I am not determined, & shod. be glad of your opinion. I have shapen out some models of Cream Ewers which I hope will be thought pretty well of, 'till I can make better. They are simple, convenient, & of an Antique cast. Half pint mugs come in the next. Porphiry Vases will be very Clever; but we must proceed with some method, & Mr. Baumgartners ordrs. with. plain black ones for your finishing stand first on my list. I shall send another Turner to Etruria on Monday & more finishers as they are wanted. A Porter has offered himself who I think is likely, he is abot. 50, can write, is a stern morose or rather resolute Character, & wants a fixed situation for the remaindr. of his days. The worker in Metal I mentioned to you in my last has tried various schemes but never could succeed as a Master , he is pretty well stricken in years & will now be content with a place that will procure food & raiment for life. I shall still want a Book-keeper & head Clerk at Etruria, I wish I may be lucky enough to meet with them both in one Person, but almost despair of it, as he shod. be something of a Potter, though that is not absolutely necessary. Could you get some such body in London think you for me? I hope you will have an opportunity soon of getting some figures from the Cabinets of ire. Noble customers, which have not yet appeared in the shops. Pray make a push for it when & where you can with decency & I will endeavour to execute them in Terra Cotta. We have the best possible patent for Vases if we can hold it, as I hope we shall for a long time to come, & as to the black composition we could not have a patent for it to answer any purpose on several accounts, which I do not care to mention in writing. I have no objection to the Glass cases or sliders you mention, & think they will have a good effect, we are perfectly agreed in our sentiments that much depends upon the mode of showing these articles, & you are quite a Master in that branch of our science, & I beg you will give free scope to your good taste & Genius in this, & every other manoeuvre which has a tendency to sell fine things at good prices . I am very agreeably flattered with Mrs. Chetwynds disappointment in the Herculaneum, but shall not be quite at ease 'till I know how my Royal Mistress approves of the whole, with the price you have fixed upon it, which I think is no more than it ought to be, everything considered, & hope her Majesty will think so too. All frds. are well here, I dare not tell them of their & my loss by your settling in London all at once but let them into it by degrees as they can bear it. I hate the thoughts of it myself, & shall never be thoroly reconciled to such a plan of separation. J. W.

column46: Etruria., 6th Jany., 1770. As I have not for some time past omitted writing to my dear friend by every post I was surprised to find by your last very affect. letter that you recd. no letter from me on monday or Tuesday last. Upon inquiry I find it was not sent off in time to Newcastle which I had entrusted to Mr. Cox & begged the Man might be sent off in time, but he was not. I thank you my dear friend for the share you take in our afflictions. I know your friendly & affectionate heart, & that you do sympathise with us most cordially, & this persuasion is not without its comfort, though the distance at which we are fixed robs us of a great deal more. I often stand in need of your advice, assistance, & consolation. The great variety, & load of business I am at present engaged in with the near prospect of a vast increase if I pursue the plan I am already in a manner involved in, & can scarcely retreat from, without giving up business entirely & at the same time being threatened with a disorder which must totally incapacitate me from doing anything at all, & yet it is absolutely necessary that I shod. resolve upon, & pursue some one plan immediately - These things altogether, with some other Anxieties I have lately felt, have at times brot. on a temporary suppression of spirits which I am not accustomed to & which do not naturally belong to my constitution. If I carry on my works I must build the next year. If I build I must lay in the Timber & other materials, agree with all sorts of workmen &c immediately, & perhaps may lose both my Eyes (for they are equally affected) before the building is completed. Is not this a terrible dilemma - What shall I do my Good frd. But who can advise what is best to be done, when the better or worse , depends upon an event which we can neither foresee nor command. - But let me turn from this dark scene, & tell you that my good Father continues to recover without much interruption & I hope will be able to come down stairs, & spare me my wife again in a short time which will be a great comfort to me for at present I am sadly forlorn indeed. I hope I shall receive a good letter from you by tonights post which will do me much good. God bless you & preserve you from every evil Amen.

column39: Letters of Josiah Wedgwood, 1762 to 1770 (vol. 1); 1771 to 1780 (vol. 2). Ed. by Katherine Euphemia, Lady Farrer. London: privately printed for private circulation. 1903. Reprinted. Manchester: E. J. Morten, for the Trustees of the Wedgwood Museum. 1973.
column46: Etruria, 20th Feb. 1771. Thank my Dear Friend for his final decision respecting Antipuffado. I had no objection to a short answer, something perhaps betwixt what we had each thought of, but as you are of opinion, that it will be best to treat it with silent contempt, I acquiesce, but I cannot help observing, that the first part of your letter describes the situation of my mind so exactly, as well as your own, that I often think we shall spoil each other for ever acting separately again. I feel the same irresolution steal upon me in other matters, & nothing but the distance betwixt us, & my natural aversion to writing prevents your being troubled with many a thing which only requires a moments thought and resolution to determine; for I can scarcely bring myself to think anything finally determined without having your opinion to guide my resolution upon it. In the case now before us, we must again try our united strength, & if matters are as our Antagonists give out, there is occasion for it all. I hope we shall not stand in need of a Master Potter for an Evidence, it will be very expensive, & I do not know who to ask that wot. come freely, & do us any good . Do you think our Antagonists, & their Attorney are weak enough to give out their real, & strongest arguments , or do they mean to throw out a Tub . If our cause has any weak part & we do not hear of there touching upon it, we must nevertheless imagine they know all, & guard ourselves everyway, & even try all the arguments we can think of to find out any flaw which may at present be hid from ourselves, or our Attorney. But I do not care for saying too much by letter, as I do not think our Country post Offices in general are the most sacred places in the world.

column39: Letters of Josiah Wedgwood, 1762 to 1770 (vol. 1); 1771 to 1780 (vol. 2). Ed. by Katherine Euphemia, Lady Farrer. London: privately printed for private circulation. 1903. Reprinted. Manchester: E. J. Morten, for the Trustees of the Wedgwood Museum. 1973.
column46: Etruria, 9th Septr. 1771. I am very happy to know the Fawn coloured articles are agreeable to your wishes. I believe they will sell, for all who have seen them here have fallen in love with them. I wish you had sent me an acct. of the prices you have fixed them at. I have sold one of the least Teapots at 4/- & the Cream bucket & Ladle 2/- to Mrs. Gifford & we have others ordd. by different Persons & are preparing more Clay for this kind of ware. I am glad to hear that you are receiving for Mr. Shoning's adventure, & I wot. advise if it may yet be done to send parcels with all the letters he was so good to write us & for this plain reason that they cannot do much harm & may do a great deal of good , - you'll consider of it but in all your deliberations you'll be pleased to bear in mind, that as our proffits are - & we want nothing but sale for our goods - we may & should adventure boldly & this would naturally lead me to Mr. Brock's proposal, but I must first ask you whilst it is in my head whether you have done anything touts. making the most of our excellent letter from Portugal? - "What would I do with it" - Why I wot. take it in one hand & Kent's Directory in the other & show it to every Portuguese Marched. in London & tell them that we were introduceing a new manufacture at every Court in Europe & when we have done this they wot. be wanting to themselves & to the interests of their Country if they did not do the rest . - You know how to talk them over excellently upon the subject but I hear you at this distance crying out - where the Dl must the time come from. Why here now I apprehend is a finer opening for Mr. Broke than he could have in being nailed down to any one place, & business enough too for any one man to be continually amongst the Merchts. showing them Patterns, bringing them to the Rooms, taking their orders, & receiving their money . This is a first thought just come into my head as I go on writing to you. If you think it worth the pains, mature it & give it existence. I do verily believe that Mr. Broke would in this way sell us five times the goods he could do in any other, & it might be either upon a fixed salary or a small commn. & upon this plan we do not increase our Warehouses, Stock, book keeping, cares & vexations after goods in a strange land &c &c but the whole is still continued under our own eyes & as snug as may be. - A trial an immediate trial of this may be made without either loss or risque. But at all events retain Mr. Broke. For if this hasty thought does not meet your approbation I have no doubt but we can think of something that will be of service to both Parties.

column39: Letters of Josiah Wedgwood, 1762 to 1770 (vol. 1); 1771 to 1780 (vol. 2). Ed. by Katherine Euphemia, Lady Farrer. London: privately printed for private circulation. 1903. Reprinted. Manchester: E. J. Morten, for the Trustees of the Wedgwood Museum. 1973.
column46: Etruria, 22nd of March 1772. The sun shines, & the birds sing so finely, & we have had so little tolerable weather lately, that it goes against the grain to be confined in a room, when every living creature ought to be in the open Air swelling the chorus of universal praise for the cheering influence of the Sun, & the prospect of a returning spring. We have had a vast deal of hard weather as we call it here, & I suppose you have not had much fine weather hitherto, but we have now two summers before us for one winter, & must endeavour to make the most of them. I am glad you have taken Rooms to your liking at Bath & hope they will answer to all the Parties concerned. I should know what time they are intended to be opened as it will require six weeks or two months to prepare a sortment of useful ware here, services &c, & to get them to Bath by water. With respect to Glazed flowerpots, I believe they are worse for plants growing in than soft biscuit, or porous ones, but then the latter will not stand the frost, & the mischief of the Glazed ones does not I believe proceed from any pernicious quality in the Glaze, but from the roots matting to the outside of the soil, & the inside of the pot, where it is worse for them to meet with a polished surface of any sort, than with one approaching nearer to the nature of earth, say a porous, biscuit body. When the plants are in this state therefore they shod. be shifted into larger pots, & the vacancy between the matted root & the inside of the larger pot shod. be filled with fresh soil, which if it was dry they wot. fill it up better than with moist soil, & the plant will then grow & thrive in either a glazed or unglazed pot, however we will make you some of the latter for those who will not take the necessary pains with the others. We will likewise try to make some middle Teapots, both for Bath, Dublin, Liverpool & London, but as to cheap Vases , I am afraid of danger there. Would it not be better to sell our 2nds, I suppose you have some in London & we can furnish you with some from the works but if you think they shod. be of a new colour & make, I can make plenty of new sorts whenever you please to say the word. The greatest difficulty I have ever found is to check & keep my invention under proper subordination, if I was to give it the reins, I should soon become an errant schemer in the common acceptance of that term. Ise make you new Vases like lightning when you think we may do it with safety. 23d of March they tell me it is .

column39: Letters of Josiah Wedgwood, 1762 to 1770 (vol. 1); 1771 to 1780 (vol. 2). Ed. by Katherine Euphemia, Lady Farrer. London: privately printed for private circulation. 1903. Reprinted. Manchester: E. J. Morten, for the Trustees of the Wedgwood Museum. 1973.
column46: Lichfield, 9th Novr. 1772. I thank my Dear Friend for his last kind letter, & the agreeable intelligence that the K: of Denmark, or somebody for him, has paid for his crockery ware, & that our Rooms begin to fill with good Company again. I have some good news too to tell you, in which I know you will rejoice with me - My wife has not had any of her shivering fits since Wednesday last, & as she gets strength very fast in their absence, I am very willing to flatter myself that she will have no more. I brought her to this place yesterday & we were lucky enough to find the good Doctr. at home. He has ordered her to continue taking the bark & hopes it may prevent her fever fits from returning. I shall return home tomorrow & leave Mrs. W. with her Doctr. for a week or ten days, & hope the change of place, Air, & company will have a good effect - In her absence I am to make the revolution in our household, & if I can make so much time, take a trip into Lancashire to see our Children there. Mrs. W. laughed heartily at your droll account of the Italian Merchant, & I thank you as heartily for making the most of the adventure, & for the hopes you give me of its turning to so good an account.

column39: Letters of Josiah Wedgwood, 1762 to 1770 (vol. 1); 1771 to 1780 (vol. 2). Ed. by Katherine Euphemia, Lady Farrer. London: privately printed for private circulation. 1903. Reprinted. Manchester: E. J. Morten, for the Trustees of the Wedgwood Museum. 1973.
column46: March 23 1773. I have a score or two of Executorship letters, to finish & send off today, but I must say a few words to you about this sd. service for my Great Patroness in the North, which the Consul has been so obliging to bring me, be so good to make my best compliments & thanks to him, & in the next place, if you please to accept a moiety of the honour & profit in finishing this very supurb commission, for such I truly esteem it, it is very much at your service. I suppose it must be painted upon the Royal pattern & that there must be a border upon the rims of the dishes & plates &c of some kind, & the buildings &c in the middle only. The Child & Frog, if they are to be all in the same attitudes, may perhaps be printed. I have no idea of this service being got up in less than two or three years if the Landscapes & buildings are to be tolerably done, so as to do any credit to us, & to be copied from pictures of real buildings & situations - nor of its being afforded for less then £1000, or £1500. - Why all the Gardens in England will scarcely furnish subjects sufficient for this set, every piece having a different subject . I think Mr. Baxter shod. be spoke to very particularly to know what expense he thinks it wot. be prudent to lay upon the service, for he cannot but know that any sum almost may be expended upon this commn. After you have settled that point if you could get he old plates, or the use of them for an impression from each of Stow Gardens &c something clever might perhaps be done at a tolerable expense. - What our hands can do in this business I do not know, you will try the likeliest, & get what other help you can, which you think necessary. I suppose this service is ordered upon the idea of the two services getting up by the King of Prussia which I suppose, have taken, or will take many years to complete. One with all the battles between the Russians & the Turks, drawn under his Majestys inspection & intended as a present you know to the Empress - & the other with all the remarkable views & Landscapes in his Dominions, for his own use. Suppose the Empress shod. die, when the service is nearly completed, as it will be a very expensive business, it may not be amiss to mention something of the kind to the Consul. One wot. on the other hand avoid giving offence by overmuch caution. I will ask Mr. Sparrow what is necessary to be done to make an order binding upon the giver, & write you farther. P S. I want no more sd. about the useful ware in the Catalogue but just to let our frds. know that it is continued as usual with various improvments that they may not think our whole attention bestowed upon ornamts. which you know some of 'em are much inclined to do.

column46: Worsley, 30th May 1773. I left home yesterday & got here at night. My Bror. Jack & Nephew Tom accompany me, our errand is to fetch the Children home, & meet Mr. Broke at Manchester, & as I love to give all possible variety to these jants, for the entertainment both of myself & friends, I have sent for the Boys early this morning to meet us here, & have begged the use of his Graces boat to Manchester, & the day being fine, we shall delight the young folks exceedingly with the sail, & it will not displease the older part of the compy. The improvment of my Nephew, & his reformation which is daily confirming gives me a very sensible pleasure, & I have great hopes it will be continued to me. But his poor stepmother is now in so deplorable a situation that her ill treated, & almost ruined stepson cannot refuse a tear to her misery. - She confesses that it was her daily study to set his Father against him, in which, alas, she succeeded too well, that she has wronged him every way & cheated her own Bror. & sisters, & has been the vilest wretch that ever lived. That her Children cannot prosper for her sake, & she has ruined them & herself too. She has returned Tom about £15 in money & many other things which she had secreted upon my Brothers death at some of her good Neighbours houses. She says she never dares see me again after my telling her so plainly that she must deliver all up, & she assuring me she had done it. But I will not blot my paper nor trouble you with a recital of her black misdeeds - she has been a wretch in grain! but it is all come home to her with a vengeance. She is in the very depth of Pool Taro - has really lost her senses, & is quite distracted, & what I shall do with her, & her eldest Son, who is not one remove from an idiot, I do not know - but the poor Boy I am taking home to this melancholy scene, who is a sensible thoughtful Lad, & must in a day or two meet a mother deprived of reason, & overwhelmed with guilt & despair - & a Brother as unwilling, as he is incapable of being taught or managed to any good purpose - My heart bleeds for this poor Boy, & I would rather take him any other way, but his Mother must & will see him.

column39: Letters of Josiah Wedgwood, 1762 to 1770 (vol. 1); 1771 to 1780 (vol. 2). Ed. by Katherine Euphemia, Lady Farrer. London: privately printed for private circulation. 1903. Reprinted. Manchester: E. J. Morten, for the Trustees of the Wedgwood Museum. 1973.
column46: Birmm. 1st Decr. 1773. It is a Pity but we had more large Dishes in the service, as it is, it will seem, & be in reality, too great a partiality for a Country Esqr. though he does happen to be ones Neighbour, & a good man, to occupy so capital a situation as a large Dish when there is but 2 or 3 in the whole service. If we can afford one of them to Lt. Gower will be as much as the bargain, for we have in my opinion been guilty of a capital omission in not waiting upon his Majesty to acquaint him with the Commds. we have recd. from the Empress & to know his Maj-s pleasure if he would permit us to take any views from the R-l Palaces or Gardens - but it is better late than never & I am firmly of opinion it ought to be done, & beg leave to submit it to your consideration. A Guinea & half is too much per View, we can have some hundreds much cheaper - but do not break off with the Gentn. - tell him if you please that I am coming to Town &c.

column39: Letters of Josiah Wedgwood, 1762 to 1770 (vol. 1); 1771 to 1780 (vol. 2). Ed. by Katherine Euphemia, Lady Farrer. London: privately printed for private circulation. 1903. Reprinted. Manchester: E. J. Morten, for the Trustees of the Wedgwood Museum. 1973.
column46: Etruria, 8th July 1774. I agree with you that our show in Greek Street has been continued open a sufficient time, & am glad to hear you are preparing the catalogue, & making the goods ready for packing. I shall congratulate you most heartily when this tedious business is completed. I hope one other trespass upon your patience, & good nature will complete the whole - I mean the settleing the price of this work with our good Patron Mr. Baxter. According to my ideas, there are many extra's to be brought into the account upon our final settlement with Mr. Baxter. Taking original views, copying Pictures, & Drawings - Buying Books, & Prints to a large emote. The compartments to the Landscapes, & the Frogs & shields I believe did not enter into your estimate, - Insurance upon the works at Chelsea - Making, Translating, & Printing the Catalogue, These things, to say nothing of the expenses of my journeys to London, & stay there at different times on account of this service near six months, & what is much more, the taking up so much of your time, & the constant exertion of your taste, & Talents for two years - I say, not to bring these things to any account, this service has cost several hundred pounds in the extra's above recited which were not included in the estimate at all; and you very well know that with this addition, if you call it £500, there will not be near the proffit upon this service that we have upon our commonest painted goods.

column39: Letters of Josiah Wedgwood, 1762 to 1770 (vol. 1); 1771 to 1780 (vol. 2). Ed. by Katherine Euphemia, Lady Farrer. London: privately printed for private circulation. 1903. Reprinted. Manchester: E. J. Morten, for the Trustees of the Wedgwood Museum. 1973.
column46: Etruria, Decr. 12th 1774. The red & white Onyxes, I apprehend, will not part in the operation of polishing. The black & white ones only appear liable to that accident, those two compositions not uniting cordially together at present; but I have no doubt of a union being made, both binding, & lasting between the Parties. It is a pity to sell any of these seals without polishing them all over. With a partial polish they have too much of the remains of Pot about them. When totally polished they are Gems, and should be sold as such. Besides, to show them partially polished is continuing, & making the gradation visible from Pitcher to Onyx over which metamorphosis we should endeavour to throw an impenetrable veil. I would rather sell one half perfect and hide the rest to be disposed of by our Exeors., than make this tell-tale gradation. I thought you would lose Mr. Smith, but we must not lose the business if it be possible to keep it, as we can now certainly make the finest things in the world for Portraits. - Pray try to obtain another modeler if Mr. Smith is gone, & a polisher, or rather a shop of Polishers will be absolutely necessary , & the sooner the better. Many happy years attend you & yours prays your truly office. friend & his Wife.

column39: Letters of Josiah Wedgwood, 1762 to 1770 (vol. 1); 1771 to 1780 (vol. 2). Ed. by Katherine Euphemia, Lady Farrer. London: privately printed for private circulation. 1903. Reprinted. Manchester: E. J. Morten, for the Trustees of the Wedgwood Museum. 1973.
column46: Etruria, 26th Octr. 1775. You have made Mrs. Wedgwood and myself extremely happy by your very kind & friendly letter, & the good history it contains of our dear Girls behaviour upon our departure. It was womanly, affectionate & such as we hoped for from her. We make some little allowances for the kind partiality of her journalist, & the company we had the satisfaction to leave her in, who would support her mind, & administer relief with that delicacy & propriety which would naturally guard her manner of expressing the grief she must feel upon so trying an occasion - However we know our Dear Sukey to be a good & affectionate Girl, & hope, nay, are fully persuaded she will deserve this character as well from her Father & Mother Bentley, as she has done from her Father & Mother Wedgwood; & under this persuasion we with the greater confidence beg you to take her under your care & protection, & to bestow a small place in your affections upon her as she merits it by an affectionate attention, & obedience to you. The parting scene was far from being indifferent to us, but knowing to whom we had resigned our precious charge, we were comforted, & our sorrow gave way to the pleasing effusions of love & gratitude to our dearly beloved Friends. We have since amused ourselves in travelling with you to Town. We have accompanied you in every stage, & spent the evening with you where you put up at night. I hope you kept your time on Sunday, or we have been sorely deluded with Phantoms all the way. We supped with you at Leicester after a pleasant ride & fine weather on Sunday. Sukey went to bed early, but we chatted an hour or two with you afterwards. On Monday we followed you to Newport Pagnel & spent a comfortable evening with you at the Swan where we were stopped a little the next morning by the Rain, & Sukey eating a little toast at breakfast Wooburn Sands did not quite agree with her. However we got to St. Albans though rather too late, & yesterday we dined with you very jovially in Greek Street. We hope to have all this confirmed by Saturdays Gazette, but the weather continuing so fine we are easier about the time of your leaving Derby. Do not talk of thanks to us - When! or how! shall we be out of debt? Never - so we can only continue our acknowledgments, & be grateful & affectionate to our lives end.

column39: Letters of Josiah Wedgwood, 1762 to 1770 (vol. 1); 1771 to 1780 (vol. 2). Ed. by Katherine Euphemia, Lady Farrer. London: privately printed for private circulation. 1903. Reprinted. Manchester: E. J. Morten, for the Trustees of the Wedgwood Museum. 1973.
column46: Etruria, 14th Jany. 1776. Some terrible Gulf is fixed between you & us, for we have had no Post nor communication with the Metropolis for eight Days past, except by way of Oxford. We suppose it is the snow which bars up the passage, but where it is, or when it is likely to be removed we cannot tell. Your favour of the 8th, being sent the bye Post day has found its way hither, by Oxford & Birmingham, but we have no news of an Age, & have now three Papers due. I believe I can now assure you of a conquest, & a very important one to us. No less than the firing our fine Jasper & Onyx with as much certainty as our Basalts or black ware. We had about 8 doz of heads all fired this new way, which I had tried a few times before with so much success that I ventured to put the above quty. to the test all at one firing, & they were every one good, except a few accidents in cracking, & scarcely any of them, but in respect to firing they were perfect , & the two bodies, blue & white agree perfectly together, &, as I manage them now, it cannot be otherwise. So that I am fully persuaded this new Art, which I have more & more reason to believe will be a very capital one to us, is completed, & brought to perfection, & I heartily give you joy of this last discovery which has given the finishing stroke to the Art. We sent you some of the Heads by Saturdays Coach, & the rest by the Waggon, but there is no saying when you will receive them. We are now going on with some larger Bassreliefs, - Those we had from the Genius of Sculpture , & others for Chimney-Pieces &c, all with blue grounds, & hope to send you a Good assortment of these things before your Company returns to Town, or at least in time for your Spring sale. But for useful China , or such a white-ware as you mention I must beg a longer time. My hands, & Head too have been too full of the business immediately before me - especially the completion of the Art of Jasper making which I was determined to conquer or give up before I entered seriously into any other capital improvement, I say I have been too much engaged hitherto to have brought Porcelain making in such forwardness as to admit of having any ready for sale this season. You know very well that from the moment a finer ware than the Cream-color is shown at our Rooms, the sale of the latter will in a great measure be over there. The consequence then of my showing them a little, before I am certain of being able to supply their wants would be a tantalising them, & ruining my own business. This transition is a very serious subject & what I am by no means ready to make at present & I beg you will insense our good customers of the impossibility of bringing about such great events in a little time. One Barrel of Ale & one of Beer is for Mr. Hodgson with my compliments if you please, & the other two, if you have Cellar room for them I will thank you to give them a place, & hope to quaff a little of it with you over a comfortable pipe sometime in the Spring. Pray give our love to your Triumvirate of Females. We are glad to hear they are well, & well employed, & be so good to tell my Sukey that I would have wrote to her, but am afraid she will have such an inundation of letters all at once that she will not know what to do with them. P.S. Shod. not we have Omia's head? Pray let him take Mr. Banks's Islander with him to Otaheita.

column39: Letters of Josiah Wedgwood, 1762 to 1770 (vol. 1); 1771 to 1780 (vol. 2). Ed. by Katherine Euphemia, Lady Farrer. London: privately printed for private circulation. 1903. Reprinted. Manchester: E. J. Morten, for the Trustees of the Wedgwood Museum. 1973.
column46: Etruria, 12 of May 1776. I congratulate my Dear Friend upon having come to a resolution respecting his Tour to France, for I think it a very comfortable circumstance to have brought such a point to a determination any way, as it gives a kind of rest, & satisfaction to the mind, & enables one to settle any little subordinate plans with more ease & certainty. Well then - as you do not go to Paris, & Paris is so condescendingly good natured as to come to you, we must in our turn be grateful, & entertain them in the best manner we are able. For this purpose I will send you as many fine things as you please - you shall only have to tell me when to stop; & even in that case I am not certain that I shall obey orders, 'till I have about some 15 or 20 thousand pounds worth of such things as must sell; that we may have a Jubilee year, & make a pilgrimage to Rome in company & Kiss his Holiness's sacred Toe together. And indeed if all be true that you tell me (for I own my doubts, that part of your letter reads so like Poetry) concerning the Bishops & Eclesiastics of the Romish Church, if my Faith was not very firmly established I could scarcely answer for the consequences, I assure you. But permit me to ask you a few plain questions upon this subject. Have you really & truly, & Bone Fide any fast, & certain orders for Groces, or sets of the Popes, & for what number? Do you mean that we should send you our present stock of Popes as they are , or that we should first make them into sets, and how many sets dare you order us to make? As the odd Popes in Greek St. & Etruria might happen if they were together to make up some complete sets, wot. it not be better to assemble them all together at one of the places? We are about 9 Popes short, which Mr. Cox will give you an account of. You shall have some Tablets soon. We have nine different Tablets which I hope we can make; none of them less than the Birth of Bacchus, & some of them much larger, but most of them want alterations, & repairs, to fit them for our blue & white Jasper. We have many other good things in the same situation. Oh! for a dozen good & humble modelers at Etruria for a couple of months. What creations, renovations, & generations shod. we make! Well - fair & softly, we must proceed with our own natural forces, for I will have no more fine modelers here, though I seem to wish for them, they would corrupt & ruin us all. I have been obliged to part with Radford. The hours he chose to work would, by the example, have ruined ten times better men than himself.

column39: Letters of Josiah Wedgwood, 1762 to 1770 (vol. 1); 1771 to 1780 (vol. 2). Ed. by Katherine Euphemia, Lady Farrer. London: privately printed for private circulation. 1903. Reprinted. Manchester: E. J. Morten, for the Trustees of the Wedgwood Museum. 1973.
column46: Etruria, 11th of Septr. 1776. The Ladies who will have the honour of presenting you with this intend to make some stay in your Metropolis, and having received great pleasure from their company and conversation in the Country I could not refuse myself the additional satisfaction of recommending them to your friendship and good offices, who, all the world knows are a passionate admirer of the good, & good natured amongst the Fair Sex, & that these Ladies may claim your attention under that idea let my grief, mingled with the sorrows of a long Group of Cousins, Aunts & Friends at parting from them testify. One of these Ladies has spent her time amongst us in visiting, nursing, & watching over the Sick, & she may, without vanity, boast of success in her Pious labours, though it must be confessed, she is apt to make People laugh when they are not well , which you know is a sin against all decorum - But age & experience may get the better of that propensity. The other is either a very good Girl, or a great Hypocrite, but as we are taught to err, if we must err, on the charitable side, we all verily believe her to be a good Girl, & as such we with pleasure recommend her to your protection. A certain Gentleman in Drury Lane who shall be nameless, has some acquaintance with, &, I believe, I may say kindness for the Nurse. If you can bring them together it is ten to one but he takes her into keeping, & you may have the thanks of both. But for the other young Lady, she will not be so easily parted with.

column39: Letters of Josiah Wedgwood, 1762 to 1770 (vol. 1); 1771 to 1780 (vol. 2). Ed. by Katherine Euphemia, Lady Farrer. London: privately printed for private circulation. 1903. Reprinted. Manchester: E. J. Morten, for the Trustees of the Wedgwood Museum. 1973.
column46: Etruria, 28th Apr.l 1777. quite dark. I thank my dear Friend for his last good letter of the 25th & can sympathize with him very feelingly in whatever relates to weakness of the brain , for I often feel it very mortifyingly, & to say I know nothing of this complaint! It is the only weak part of your letter, & the only thing tending that way I have seen from you of some time. Your good offices with Dr. Enfield are very acceptable & I heartily wish they may have a proper effect, but I am upon the brink of despair upon that subject. The Revd. Mr. Taylor of Liverpool has had an invitation into Ireland, to supply the place of his father-in-law who has resigned. I suppose it is a better living than Liverpool. His Wife is an Irish woman, & has been in the Kingdom some time, & it is expected that Mr. Taylor will accept the call, the consequence in all probability will be a call to Mr. Yates to Liverpool - a place we are told of £130 a year! - If this should be the case our mouths are stopped, for who could ask a man to forego a Bishopric for a Vicarage. - However, whilst there is life there is hope say the friends of dying mortals & that you may know how the negotiation stands I enclose you copies of two letters, which Mrs. Bentley will be so good to read to you over your bed pipe, & they may save you the trouble of taking a sleeping dose - one of them at least may have that effect. This packet comes by the favour of Miss Allen, a Lady who is going from Newcastle to pay a visit to the Lord Chancellor. I have told her that if she calls at the Rooms you will be civil to her &c. She was the late Lt. Bathursts unartificial daughter. I wish we could hide you a while at Etruria - But I shall talk foolishly, & show my own head to be muddled - you were not made to be hid any where - you must shine out your day, & I hope a long, long summers day awaits you - I shall not allow of more than one being so much interested in this wish as Your truly affect. friend

column39: Letters of Josiah Wedgwood, 1762 to 1770 (vol. 1); 1771 to 1780 (vol. 2). Ed. by Katherine Euphemia, Lady Farrer. London: privately printed for private circulation. 1903. Reprinted. Manchester: E. J. Morten, for the Trustees of the Wedgwood Museum. 1973.
column46: Etruria, 26th July 1777. Must we not then expect the pleasure of seeing you & our dear Mrs. Bentley in Staffordshire this summer? I hope you will if possible make it convenient, & I will endeavour to return with you to Town & partake with you in the sweets of your country retreat. We have such vicissitudes in the weather here that I have almost given up the antiquated idea of any distinct seasons. My Hay Grass is uncut, & the weather is as cold & rainy as winter. I am now going to Newcastle to meet the heads of our congregation to try if we can settle matters, & agree to give an invitation to a minister. We have had several recommended to us, but I apprehend we shall conclude upon attempting to seduce Mr. Lomas from his flock. I have two reasons which will induce me to concur very strongly in this measure. One is my good opinion of, & respect for the Gentleman & the other is the ample ability of the congregation at Derby to provide themselves with another Pastor, which is not the case with another Society whose minister we have had mentioned to us as not being averse to an invitation from Newcastle. You will perhaps say we are ambitious, if not more. I own the charge, & may our success be equal to our ambition. So much for spirituals.

column39: Letters of Josiah Wedgwood, 1762 to 1770 (vol. 1); 1771 to 1780 (vol. 2). Ed. by Katherine Euphemia, Lady Farrer. London: privately printed for private circulation. 1903. Reprinted. Manchester: E. J. Morten, for the Trustees of the Wedgwood Museum. 1973.
column46: Etruria, 29th Decr. 1777. I have my dear friends very kind letter of the 24th & need not tell him how flattering & pleasing it is to have his good opinion of our dear girls disposition & general behaviour. We have recd. a very friendly letter from Mr. Edgeworth wherein he assures us that we may depend upon his sincerity in telling us that our daughter possesses an extremely good solid understanding, & is capable of learning anything we may please to teach her, & so far as he can judge has the strongest desire to improve herself & acquire proper habits, & that her obliging behaviour, & good disposition give much pleasure to himself & Mrs. Edgeworth. I have written this morning to tell Mr. E. that I cannot leave this place before Monday the 5th of Jany. & shall be detained all that day at a navigation meeting at Stone, & stop another day at least at Birmm., I shall not reach North Church before the 9th. You may be a true prophet with respect to my boys being spoiled for the exertion of their own faculties, if they are enabled to purchase the fruit of other men's. But if I continue long enough amongst them I will endeavour, & I am sure you will assist me, to give them so much pride, & unquietness of spirit, that they shall not be content with anything other people can do for them, if they have not a hand in it themselves. They promise well in these respects at present, & I hope the good dispositions will continue & increase. I have more reasons than one why my name should not appear in the list, which I will tell you when I have the pleasure of seeing you, but in the mean time be so good to subscribe 10 guineas for me, or double that sum if you think proper, because I think it is a charity that should not be postponed, & if you afterwards convince me that I ought to give my name, I will do it along with two or three guineas more, which is as much as I would put my name to, if I did it now. Our Anti-Americans now think that the war would be ended in the best manner we could wish, by granting the Americans all they have hitherto asked us for, but acknowledge this is rather to be hoped for than expected. What fools must we have been then to expend so much blood & treasure for something worse than nothing at all.

column39: Letters of Josiah Wedgwood, 1762 to 1770 (vol. 1); 1771 to 1780 (vol. 2). Ed. by Katherine Euphemia, Lady Farrer. London: privately printed for private circulation. 1903. Reprinted. Manchester: E. J. Morten, for the Trustees of the Wedgwood Museum. 1973.
column46: Etruria, 11th Aprl. 1778. I am glad to hear so comfortable an account of your church which I feared was in real danger . I go hand in hand with you & you will please to do the needful for me now or at any other time. Mr. Elers has given me an order for a little service of Dishes & plates & a terrine fit for so small a family as his but as he is unknowing in these things he leaves it to me. But he gives it as a hint for increasing our sale if we were to introduce arms, crests &c upon the ware & he has sent an impression of his own arms to paint this little set for him by. I am as much obliged to the good gentleman as if the thought was original & have written to him a fine letter by this post promising that he should have a few samples of table plates with crests & arms sent by the coach for his choice, & that when he returned the patterns & made his choice known his commands should be executed immediately. P. S. Poor Lt. Chatham! How are the mighty fallen! His body & mind seem to keep pace with each other. It was almost a pity to call him into life again he made his exit so much in his own way. He certainly will never again die so much to his own satisfaction.

column39: Letters of Josiah Wedgwood, 1762 to 1770 (vol. 1); 1771 to 1780 (vol. 2). Ed. by Katherine Euphemia, Lady Farrer. London: privately printed for private circulation. 1903. Reprinted. Manchester: E. J. Morten, for the Trustees of the Wedgwood Museum. 1973.
column46: Etruria, 15th Septr. 1778. Not recollecting where I left off, & feeling just now very chagrinish at being stopped in my career, & not permitted to proceed in the invention of new pots & pipkins for my own amusement first, & afterwards for the emolument, & entertainment of all the world besides, because, for sooth, nobody will part with their money. - this being the case I begin my letter in abusing the world & everybody in it, for a blind, sneaking, paltry, foolish world, & in lamenting my own hard fate in coming into it at a time when people know, or practice no better. Being thus cruelly deprived of all employment in the plastic art, & firmly believing idleness to be one of the seven-teen deadly sins, in turning my back of the pottery, I have got my face over a shell drawer, & find myself in imminent danger of becoming a connoisseur. You can easily conceive the progress I have made in a month or two in the deep & very elaborate science of shell fancying . Having arranged my whole collection in the most systematic manner, & studied them with the nicest attention, I can tell you, at sight, the difference between a Lunar, & a Semi Lunar - a Buccinum, & a Limpet, & many other nice distinctions which you, who are not so learned in these matters as myself, would not understand, & might therefore undervalue. But this study, alas, like every other extention of the human mind, as it multiplies the avenues to our enjoyments discloses new sources of wants & anxieties, & at this present writing I find myself undone for an Echinites Spalagoides Cretaceous . A Gracirrynchus or two would make a fine addition to my class of Glossopetra, & the Pectunculus minimus triquetrus subfuscus would make me the happiest of chonchiologists. But perfection is not to be expected, & I shall make myself as easy as possible in my present situation; for why should I set my friend to diving in the great deep, hunting along the beach, or rummaging the chalk pits for what he may never find, or finding may not know their value. I could give you a lecture upon the subject this morning with great good will, but I fear you might wish me to ride my own hobby horse along the kings highway without attempting to mount you, vi et arms , upon him, I shall therefore wait to know if you are worthy before I do you the favour, & turn to our good friend at your elbow to pay my acknowledgements for the honour he has done me in his last review, in defending my reputation against that saucy fellow the author of The wreath of fashion . It was kindly done, & I thank him heartily, & will defend the Review - The St. James's Chronicle - The B-D-V &c &c with my latest breath. If he stands in need of a champion of any kind, I have thrown down my glove, never to take it up again, & he may at all times call upon the man with the wooden leg. I rejoice to hear that bathing is likely to agree with our dear Mrs. Bentley, & shall be impatient to have it confirmed, & to learn that both she & yourself receive much benefit from your daily ablutions. I should send my best wishes for the rest of your good party if I thought they were not perfectly well & clever, or that dipping & washing could mend them. Pray give my love to Miss Stamford, & tell her that I wish her merry & happy - that she must not believe all the young men may say at these watering places, & to keep her head & heart clear of such dangerous intruders, I would advise her to fill them both with innocent sea weeds, corrallines & cockle shells - From these I will at any time set her at liberty if she desires it, which is more than I durst promise if any of the former should stick to her.

column39: Letters of Josiah Wedgwood, 1762 to 1770 (vol. 1); 1771 to 1780 (vol. 2). Ed. by Katherine Euphemia, Lady Farrer. London: privately printed for private circulation. 1903. Reprinted. Manchester: E. J. Morten, for the Trustees of the Wedgwood Museum. 1973.
column46: Turnham Green, Decr. 18 1778. Thanks to my dear Friend for his very affectionate & cheering Letter of the 14th., which I must reply to briefly, though with a most grateful Heart. My Head is better & worse as I think more properly or weakly about the ill usage that I have met with, or may still meet with from a Man who sets no Bounds to his Malignity when it is once excited; - or rather as my Head is better or worse I think more properly upon the Subject. A full Discussion, or one good Conversation upon it with my dear Friend would probably do me more good than any other Application: for I have not any Friend here by whose side I have been accustomed to engage & conquer; & who has the same Energy that you constantly possess, when there is occasion for it, either to promote the public good, assist your Friends, or support your own rights. I fancy I can do anything with your help; - & I have been so much used to it, that when you are not with me upon these Occasions I seem to have lost my right Arm. Mrs. Bentley & I are much inclined to accept of your kind Invitation; & I want very much to go & examine into & settle my Affairs at Liverpool: but as you will have all your Infantry & Relations about you soon I am afraid the Time would be inconvenient to you; otherwise we should be very glad to see all the Family happy together before the young Gentlemen return to School, & we will keep the Prospect of this Pleasure in our Thoughts till we hear from you, what Time would be most convenient, provided we should resolve to make a winter Flight. If we should undertake this Journey we must also pay our respects to our Friends at Derby, & so make a sort of running Visit of it though these short winter Days will be very much against Us. Mrs. Bentley & Miss Stamford join in Love & respects to all the good Family with ire. truly affectionate & grateful Friend Those. Bentley. I had almost forgot to tell you the Sherry is excellent, & very comforting to the Heart.

column46: Etruria, 8th of March 1779. I thank you for the account of Dr. Priestleys last, & very curious experiments, which Mr. Warltire says are not only quite new, but likewise very interesting. I find he is a warm admirer of the Doctors, & personally acquainted with him. He often mentions him in his lectures with every mark of honour & respect, calling him the Newton of the age, & assuring his audience that the Doctr. will be equally celebrated in future ages. I find to my grief that I cannot make any great improvement in my present body but it will be china though I have endeavoured all in my power to prevent it. However to give the brat a name you may set a cream-color plate & one of the best blue & white ones before you, & suppose the one you are to name another degree whiter & finer still, but not transparent, & consequently not china for transparency will be the general test of china - Under this idea you may give it a name. What we may inadvertently make transparent, & white will not want any new name. It must be neither more nor less than porcelain .

column46: Etruria, 27 Feb: 1780. I have read my dear friends very good letter over & over & thank him for it most cordially. We will endeavour to take ourselves & distribute to the circle of our afflicted friends that comfort & consolation you so affectionately administer to us. Since my last to you I have been talking with Mr. Lomas about a latin Master & in a conversation upon the subject, he told me that he should have no objection to teach my young men nay he should like it much & it would be an improvement to himself as well as them. I closed cordially with this proposal & he has already entered upon his office & gives the boys a good latin lesson every day. They are very fond of their Master & I hope this junction will be of service to all the parties - The boys will have a Master to their wishes & Mr. Lomas will preserve his latin & perhaps his Greek when Jack comes home - Will have some daily bodily exercise which sedentary Gentlemen are apt too much to neglect & a little help to a lean Salary. My french master has promised me to be more regular & at the same time looks so good that I am apt to believe him so that at present I believe we must continue in the train we are & hope we shall do pretty well. The boys are very attentive & regular in their School hours. They make great progress in their french & we have begun that language at table & shall introduce it in a few days at School. We already market in french & we shall certainly be great adepts before Mr. Potet leaves us. I thank you for the copies of your pamphlet upon machines & congratulate you upon the very honourable testimony in its favour of so great a Master in composition as Mr. Mason. I shall be very glad to read it in print & notwithstanding you have such an authority on your side I shall not be deterred from finding every fault I can either in language or matter, nor from laying every fault I find before you, but to keep up your spirits a little under the apprehensions of my criticisms I will frankly tell you that you have little to fear from anybody else either in Lancashire or any other Shire. You know how we felt under the attacks of our Burton & Weaver antagonists upon a certain occasion - you have now equal advantage from your ground - are no novice in the use of literary weapons & I feel myself so far gifted with the second sight of the north that I do not hesitate to congratulate upon a second equally glorious & equally complete victory. How shall I descend from these elevated subjects down to pots & pipkins . I must however just whisper to you to desire you will circulate the whisper to Pollard & Jennings that my first attention has been to furnish polishing for the former & flummery shapes butter prints & Asparagus pans for the latter.

Park Gate Oct. 1782. Jose has been so good to leave me room for a short Postscript, although as I wrote to Mama yesterday & news at Parkgate does not circulate quite so quick as it does at N. Castle I scarcely know how to fill it up. Spring tide begun the morning we came & as that is so much better than the other tides I only drank the salt water one day before I ventured into the open sea which I did this morning & very courageously too considering what a great coward I am - the water is not near so cold as our bath & not very salt although eneough so to make me shut my mouth a little closer tomorrow. The Ladies here set excellent examples as the dance in with the greatest composure imaginable. Farewell love to every body & accept the same from your affectionate & dutiful daughter S. Wedgwood. Jose has dated his letter Wednesday but we are most of us of opinion that it is Friday Those. says it is Thursday - Who will you believe?

Park Gate, Nov. 2, 1782. Dear Mama I shall tell you a good deal about the yacht in which the Duke & Duchess Came who were very odd figures indeed Duchess of Portland changed hats with one of their attendants so the Ducss. had a black hat on with one black feather the other person with a white hat & about 3 lihgt brown feathers in. they got out of the ship about 4 miles from here they were rowed by 6 people in white shirts with black velvet caps & silver lions (the Dukes crest) it was a pretty sight enough. The Duke came in the yacht, he is a plain dressed man with a wig like my papa's riding wig. Their children are the prettiest I ever saw very like their mother. The yacht is a very pretty vessel a deal of carving & gilding & the borders painted. The cabin of the yacht is red velvet with gilt flowers, very grand indeed. Tell Mr. Lomas We like Park Gate very well & have seen Sir Alexander Scomberg (commander of the yacht) I will write to Kitty next post Our parlours love to every body. I have no more to say but that I am your affectionate son Thomas. Wedgwood.

column46: Pak Gate, Decr. 4th 1782. Dear Papa Yesterday Miss Twamley, Miss Wheeley, Mrs. Shaw Miss Mostyn Tom and I went aboard the Yacht which is at last come but did not at all answer our expectations. As soon as we got upon deck we went down a few steps into a cabin where there was two or three nursery beds for the children & their nurses, there was two doors out of this one of which led into a closet where the captain slept & the other into the state cabin which has two beds in it one for the Lord Lieutenant & Lady it is a crimson silk bed & the other for somebody else I don't know who. The Duke & the Duchess of Portland came over from Ireland in the Yacht. When the Yacht was coming in the duchess got into the Yachts boat with 6 rowers in their shirts & black velvet caps with the Dukes crest in silver upon them. There was a gentleman in the boat that had changed hats with the Duchess. When the Duke quited the Dorset for the boat the Yacht fired 16 or 20 swivels & the same for the Duchess. The Yachts name is the Dorset. Each man has a small cabin & bed to himself. The crew is half English & half Irish when she is at Dublin the Irish stay ashore & when she is here the English stay ashore. Give my duty to Mama, love to my sisters and brother John when you write to him. I am dear Papa your dutiful son Jose Wedgwood.
