column46: Liverpool, Octr. 22: 1765. Dr. Sir When I recd. your first Letter I immediately wrote to Mr. Wedgwood, & told him you condemned the Pamplet, in its present State, not to be printed . In Answer, I was desired to go on with it; as a Pamplet was immediately necessary; & he did not apprehend there was any thing materially wrong in this. When it was sent to me from Newcastle I was desired to have it printed with all possible Dispatch; & told that it was returned without Alteration, much approved. So that the Censure of me for haste is misapplied . I always desired the Thing might not be done hastily - & should never have engaged in it at all, but at the earnest Solicitation of my good Friend Mr. Wedgwood. Mr. Bentley is not afraid the Pamphlet should be improved: he heartily wishes it was much more perfect than it is; & doubts not but Dr: Darwin could have finished it in better manner, if he would have taken that Trouble upon himself which Mr: B understood he did not choose to do. All my intimate Friends know how humbly I think of my own trifling Compositions; & how ready I am at all times to receive their Assistance & Corrections. But this Work is not mine. There are hardly two Paragraphs together of my writing in the whole; - & every one knows there is a great deal of difference between writing a Piece , & endeavouring to mend one. You say the Liverpool Liturgy was not read, because it was ill-written . And yet that Book was written by Gentlemen of as much Learning as any we shall find for this Pamphlet; & had all the Advantage of Reviewing (from which you seem to expect too much,) that a Work could have. It received the Corrections of Many Gentlemen who were as well qualified as any in this Kingdom for that Purpose; - & by many good Judges, it is thought to be excellently well written . So much do Men of Learning & Taste differ in their Judgments! "It is no Discredit to Mr. Bentley, that he does not write agreeably & concisely. But it is no Credit to him that he does not know it." - How must a Man know this? It is the first Time he was ever told so: - & it is not a very easy Matter for any one to discover his own Faults. But, as Mr. Bentley does not presume to judge of Dr. Darwin's Manner of Writing from one Part of this Pamplet, so neither can Dr. Darwin judge of Mr. B's manner from the other . If a Pamphlet, that was written by Nobody; but is the joint work of several Persons, who had no opportunities of consulting together, proves, at last but a Piece of Patch-Work; - this Fault is rather to be attributed to the Circumstances , than to any of the Parties concerned in it. I have written again to Mr. Wedgwood; & shall follow his Instructions. Perhaps it will be best to hand this Pamphlet about as an unfinished Copy ; - &, when it has recd. all the Advantages that Criticism can bestow upon it, to publish it. I thank you for transcribing Mr. Garbet's Letter. I do not know an Object more worthy of the Attention of the Society in the Strand; & wish they may take Notice of it. I do not see any thing very material in the Remarks, but what has been attended to in the Pamphlet; though Birmingham might be made a larger Article, without much Impropriety. If the Lichfield Edition be different from the Ground-work of this Pamphlet, which was sent to me, I have never seen it. If there is to be a rivalship between these two Editions, I resign with all humility & Pleasure. I am concerned for nothing but the general design , & am Dr. Darwin's very respectful Frd & hble Served T. Bentley

February 2, 1705. My dearest dear child, I am very sorry you have lost your Queen, for I know you had a very great veneration for her, and I doe very much pety the Poor Princis Sophie, sure her grief must be great, and having so laitly lost a son to. I lament that such a yousles creature as I should outlive so many fine young folks. Cousin Hanburer sent for Betty and I yesterday to meet Bell and her spouse, where we was all very merry and dranck your health in very good wine; we played at cards, I am groan a great gaimster, but when we meet my cossin is denied to all other company. She and her husband came this afternoon to see me, and Bell and hers, and Peter and his boy, it being my veseting day, and I take the same freedum you gave me when you was hear in making a great show with your tea tables and dishes; but you left but one tea-pott, that is, the little blew and white one. The post I fear will be gon if I ad any more then to asure you never mother loved her only child, more then I doe you, that are the best of children to Your most infinite affectionate Mother I. W.

February 13, 1705. My dearest dear child The other day Peter brought his youngest son to se me which is the finest of all his far beyand Will. I fancy it like dear Paul; it has your skin and very brisk gray eye and a luvly culloar, and very plump round faic, its finer much then the girl, who Bell has given a very fine coat to, it being her God Daughter. Its time for you to think of a Wife, for this will be Potter's fifth child. I am very sorry for poor Major Larranc. I hear he is condemned to be shot to death, about a consperecy to deliver up Gibletor, with sixteen more officers all to dye; he was a friend of poor dear Pal's, so I am heartily sorry for him. We have fine summer whether now, its said to be very sickly. I thanck God we are all well. Fubs is in sum trouble, for yesterday she parted with her last little one, but it is as great a trouble to Pug for she was infinite fond of it, and so was the puppy of her.

March 9, 1705. Yesterday thear was great rejoicing, all the Ladies and Gentlemen in thear Birthday clothes. But the Queen would not give them a Bale nor Play. Betty was in the Drawing room and loocked very handsome. I wish she had a good husband, for she is now in her Pryme and she affects to be afraid of the small pox, and therefore I fear would be pepered with them should she get them, and then her market would be spoiled as sister Skinner ses. We shall go in a fortnight to Twittingham, where I hope to have many a happy day with you. I pray God send Piece, and then I shall long for that happy time; but whilst the war lasts, its my earnest prayers that you may continue where you are and that your days may be long and prosperus. I pray God grant thees blessings to, dearest dear child, your most infinite affectionate mother. Fubs, Pug and Pus presents their duty to Folly and Baden.

Twickenham, March 30, 1705. My dearest dear child, we came hear last Tewsday, which hendred me from writing. Indeed your gardens are very fine, and in very great order. We drink your health every meal. I wish you could be hear with out danger, but when I consedder how many hazards you must run in coming hear I then heartily thanck God for your absence, and beg he of his mercy will continue you in health and prosperity, but that you may still stay where you are tell the war is over, for I can not bair the thoughts of seeing you hear before. Our Bedstids being old and craysy just as Betty stepped into bed broke all to pieces; it can not be mended, I hope you will order Mr. Elleson to get a new one. I will try to patch this up as well as we can, or to Borroe one tell we can get one. Mr. Elleson ses you ordered the Dogs alowanc to be stopped, you know you always allowed a lever, and sheeps head, when your self and all your family was hear, and my nieces family is not so large as yours, she keeps a very good house but thear is Fubs, so I hope you will allow as you did.

Twickenham, April 2, 1705. My dearist and best child, A lyne from you givs me more true comfort and joy then anything hear can doe, although we live very pleasantly hear, eat and drink very plentifully, fynly and neatly, our cook goes far beyond Margett for coocking, and both fish and flesh is very reasonable, and fowl very plentiful, chickens, pigeons, and rabbits, and very reasonable raits all. We have changed only the Butcher upon Pages request, we by of Moar, and have as good meet as ever was eat. We have cider and wine and strong ail every meal, and your Brewer sent such Bitter Bear that none can drink it, so we have it from one at Wesminstor. This day we have been to se Secretary Johnson's gardens, which is much admired, and from thenc we went upon the water, it being a fine warm day. We drink your health every meal. My neic and Mr. Hanburer are very kind to me, and Fubs is a mighty favorett; at first my neic was afraid of her jumping upon her, but Fubs is so subtle as to fawn upon her, and kiss her, and coms gently to her, that she cannot ster without her; and last Sunday would have her go with her to church, and I will asure you, Fubs sat very orderly; and Pug is very kindly treeted but at great distance, for my neic is very much afraid of her. I have got my bedstead mended, in my last I was afraid it could not be dun.

Twickenham, April 3, 1705. My dearest and Best of children, I wish you a happy Easter and many more. The Wedoe Bromly writ me word of is married, I wish you a good Wife before next Eastor. I have found out a match that will plees you I am sure very much; she has four thousand a year and ver pretty, but what will plees you most is - she is but four year old. If you are not married by this next Easter com twelve month, I have promised to take and keep one of Potter's children. Mrs. Wentworth is not married yett, which I wunder at; why would you not take my sister Batthurst offer, for she by me offered to try her Retorick with her and none in the world could doe it better then she, and she assured me she would not doe it for any in the world but you, and she has a great deal of Eloquence, and can doe Better then any. I wish I had but half as much and then this would be les troublesome to you but baer with it and consider it coms from a most vehement lover of you, and can never exspres how much she is, &c. Its not a flurrish but a most sincere truith, and to the utmost of my power I will in al things prove it.

Twickenham, April 12, 1705. My dearest and best of children, I wish you joy, for I hear you are a step higher in the Army, that you are Major-General. In peec I should like it, but O that I had money enough to by it Quite of, and to oblige you to set quiet at home diverting yourself in your gardens, and Boocks, and being happy in a good wife and children - even to think of this is a pleasure to me. The young Lady Blunt told it me. Hear will be a great plenty of fruit this year, al things are very forward and your Gardens are in very good order and charmingly pretty. What I like worse hear is the staying so long for our letters, that is for yours, the rest I can bair with patience. All your dums are very well, Fubs never was a greater darling to you then she is to Cousin Hanburers, to both of them. This town is but emty yett, for thear is but few come down yett. The old Lady Blunt and all her Daughters are gon from henc and live hard by your Aunt Skinner in town; the young Lady lives in that house that Mrs. Clark had next to your little house by the Common. Mrs. Lo contenews yett very ill, I fancy she will hardly climb up May hill. I pray God send you all the Blessings this world can afford it is the sincere and hearty prayers of, &c. My nephew Batthurst showed me a letter of yours which pleesed him very much, and my sister to - it had verses in it. Its said hear your King and his son is going to be married.

Twickenham, June 5, 1705. My dearist and best of children, I give you ten thousand thancks for your two letters, May the 16 & 26, indeed I began to be very much in the spleen having not hard of a great while before. Your brother Arrundell and Mr. Hanburer have both got thear elections. Peter tells me very good news but I want to have it confirmed by you. Its not possible for anybody to be kinder to me then Mr. and Mrs. Hanburer. I am yoused with great respect both by themselves and servants, if I was her mother she could not yous me Better, and Betty is as her sister to them both. Peter his Wife and little Willy coms hear next thursday and stays hear a week or as much longer as they plees. Yesterday Lady Brook Brought her Granddaughter, Lady Rachel Novel to see me. I wish you had her, they say she has at least thirty thousand pt. My sister Skinner is just come, this was to go by the Waterman, but now by her man. She tells me great news, I wish it was treble as much. She ses thear is ten thousand pt coming from Ireland to be put into the Bank of England. I sopose you are assured of the safety of it or else you would not place it thear. I told her the sincere truith that I did know nothing of it. Pray tell me if I may wish you joy or not of being Ambassador, your Brother Peter asures me it is so. If you be yourself cannot be half so much rejoiced at it as I am, my joy is upon what you think not of, for mine is chiefly upon your being out of danger, and I trust in God the wars will be ended before your time will be out. I hear my nephew Batthurst has carried his election. Fubs is fonder of my neic Hanburer than ever she was of you. She can not move out of one room to a another, with out her following; and is very still tell the water is put upon the table, then she jumps up and drincks out of a glass. She will bight her friend Betty if she offers to meddle with my neic, and I could fill a hole sheet of paper, should I tell you all her subtle tricks.

Twickenham, June 12, 1705. In my last I told you Sir John Stanly brought Secretary Hedges to se your lodgins and if he had liked them he had been to have had them. I wrote to my sister Battherst, who was so very oblidging that she wrote emedgetly to the Dutchis, and urged that I had not my health in the country in the winter: and yesterday she sent the Dutchis letter in answer to it, which was that it was to be feared that I could not keep my lodgins long, for sooner or later I must expect to loos them, for it was but reasonable that the Queen's own family should be provided for before strangers. My sister wrote a very kind letter to me and with concern and mighty exprestions of lov to you, and tells me of a kind letter you wrote her, which pleases her very much, and she would advise you to take sum speedy cair to prevent the loosing them, she ses she doubts not but you may prevent it. She sent a man an horse yesterday o purpose, because I should loos no time to tell it you. My chief concern is for you, though I doe confess they are very pretty in my eyes to; and it will be a great charge to remove all the goods, and hear is not room for them; besides nothing can be more convenyent to you, it being so near the Parliament house and the Court. Mrs. Dauson and Mother Harrison and Bridget Harrison all had lodgins in St. Jaimsis upon King Jamsis account, and why not I? my father and mother was servants to the Queen's own mother as well as they; and the two old once kept thears tell they died, and Bridget after, tell the great wind blew them down. I wish you could get money enough to bygh a good house of your own in town, you would soon save it in house keeping, for those lodgins are very chargeable, and all things in public, nothing spoke ore dun but known to all the town and parrafraised upon; but tell your return I wish you might keep them, for the good of all your goods in them, which will be duble charge, not to remove them where thay are to fix. When the Queen Dowager caime over, one of her chief officers, Lord Desilvis, brought his mother over, which was as old and ugly as myself; she never appeared but to me, he being your father's friend. So I cannot help wishing myself in cogneto with you, who is the Darling of my soul, and the delight of my eyes, and dearer to me then any words can exspres, nether is it possible for me to tell you, how much I am, my dearest dear, your most infinite affectionate mother.

September 4, 1705. My dearist and best of children, I think its a long time senc I hard from you. I forgot in my last to tell you Fubs has five of the prettiest puppies that ever you se; she is very fond of them. Four of them are promised already. They are all her colour I hear your master is going to be married, if so pray get Betty to be made of honour, she is very handsome and will soon get her a good husband. Hall ses thear is a niece of Lord Portland's in Holland, a handsome young woman worth thirty or more thousand pound, I wish you had her. If you was married although I leved twenty mylse of of you yet it would be an unspeakable happiness to poor me, for certainly I should never desire to live with a daughter in law, for although themselves are never so good, yet sum tattling servants or aquantenc will put jealosees in thear head, to breed discontents. I fear I should lov her better then any of your sisters; being yours, she must have a greater shair in me then any other, you being more dear to me then all the world beside.

September 18, 1705. My dearist dear and best of children, I am much rejoiced at your fine present, I wish you may often have such and better, tell you are as rich as the Duke of Molberry who is billding the finest house at Woodstock that ever was seen; thear is threscore rooms of a flower, no stairs, only a little pair that goes to the upper rooms, which are only for servants, and staitly wood, which he cuts out walks in, and fine gardens that are four miles about. It is believed furniture and al cannot cost les than three hundred thousand pt, the house will cost above a hundred thousand pt. Why should you not be as fortunate as he? I hard a strange od story the other day of Lord Bradford, you know thear is Prayers at Twitnam wensdays and fridays. Sir William Humble was Buiryed either of Saturday or sunday and the scutyons was upon the reeding desk, and the wensday following, after prayers was up, Lord Bradford tore them down, and stamped them under his feet. Lady Humble's Aunt was thear, and told him his devotion was great that could put himself into so unusyell a potion, without any provocation; and Mr. Lastrang told him this was what did not become a man of his age, honour, and Quality. My Lord sternly asked him who he was, he told him he was a gentleman. Sum say it put him in mind of death, and that was what vexed him, others say it was sumthing in the arms that offended him, thear being more in them then did belong to Sir William, and others that they should not have hung there so long. This is as Mrs. Isbell tells me. All our dums are well, Pug and Fubs are the pretiest of thear kind, sure.

December 14, 1705. My dearist and best of children, - I long to hear you have made your entry. I wish Mr. Powell would give the description of it to your brother, then I should have the pleasure of hearing it. My sister Batthurst has been with the Queen and goes abroad again. My nephew asked me whether any body gave you an account of the Parliament affairs for he sad if you had it not from better hands he should be glad to have so good an opportunity of keeping a constant correspondence without having his letters a trouble to you, and abundance of kind exsprestions. Last night Lord Wesmeath was to see me; it is in the newspapers now that Lord Bellew is turned protestant, and the old Bow Fielding is married to the Dutchis of Cleevland, and she owns it and has kissed the Queen's hand senc; and the young Bow Fielding, he that was king William's page, the Lady Deana Howard, Lord Bradford's Daughter, I think she is; her Daughter married Lord Dudly and has a son. This old lady, for she is near fifty if not quite, is fallen in love with this young Fielding, and ses she only begs he will be sevell to her, she fears he cannot lov her, though she dus him so much, and her Weding clothes are making.

December 20, 1705. My dearist and best of children, - I made as great a mistake about Feelding's weding, as you did about your sister Bellew's coming, for it was not the King's Fielding but my Lord Denby's brother. Now your Crismas is over, and all the trouble of it, which I think great, but I intend to pas by al the good cheer, at leest at home. I am anger with all your sneaking tenants, that never send the leest thing up, nether at Crismas nor no time; all else doe but ours. Little Willy was with me yesterday, he is a fine boy full of mettle; he talks much of you, but remembers your spetting in his face, he flatters me mightily and makes me believe he lovs me mightily. This is a day sooner for the Office is shut up tomorrow being St. Tomassis day, so pray excuse this scroll, I being in great hast this morning, who no pen can exspres how much I am my dearist dear your most infinite affectionate Mother.

January 19, 1706. My dearest dear child, I have not been so long without writing to you, as now that I have mist this two last post, being invited to meet my hole family at Cousin Hanburer's at dinner, where we stayed tell near twelve at night, having a very good dinner and super, and in the afternoon tea and coffy. I have spent two of my days so with her this last week, besides dining thear on Sunday, and two days more at Arrundels; thear I did not dine, the Doctor having so much company, so I went as soon as I had dined, and played att cards al day, and had tea and coffy and cake and wine in the afternoon, and at Mr. Arrundel's cost, but a good supper at night at the Dockter's; so you see I lead a merry life. Lord Sandwidg was ill of a fever, his Lady reported he was mad and would never be fit for buisnes, so would have beged his place for his son and that was not approved of, but it had like to have been given away from both. But a good friend of my Lords has told him of it, and brought him a coach and six horses and carried him away from the place and servants where she left him; he is at Dr. Montegues.

January 30, 1706. My dearest and best of children, I doe agree with you in the advyse you give me in yours of the 24th of this instant, and will endeavour al I can to keep out of debt, for I will make no entertainments that I can avoid. I like being at Twittingham much better than hear, if I considered my own pleasure most, only in spite of all the art mankind can find out thear is several reasons for that to be dearer then hear, and also although all playsis are alike to me for health, mine consisting only in my mind, but Betty never has her health so well thear, ether very early in the spring or very laid in the year, nor many more are so that dwell in Twittingham. To live at Ashby would be chargeable then hear amongst such a next of Begers, and your grandmother was an exsterordenary woman, she had skill in surgery and also in Physic - God knows I am ignorant in both; and at Waikfield I think it not proper having formerly leved thear, and thear being a great deal of gentry thear, and the Oglethorps are very poor. Lord and Lady Eglinton boarded a great while at Doncaster. I know two or three plasis I could be in cogneto att; but poor Mrs. Lake, senc the Dockter dyed, is a boarder herself. Believe me, my dear creature, if you consider it, you will find it much more credible then levin ether hear or at Twittingham, without a footman and other servants, and leving sneekingly and petefully. I know sum makes a great show with as little, but they are in many traydspeople's boocks, and it will light heavy one them at last. If it plees God I never will live with any child but yourself, who is the best of children.

February 23, 1706. My dearist and very best of children, Mr. Elleson sent me word this morning that you could not write this post, but I should be sure to hear once a week from you, dear creature, doe not obridg me of the chiefest happiness this world can aford me, but let me have but three liens at a time, just to shoe me you are well. You have hitherto been exssteem kind in never failing me that delight. Lord Huntington is dead and Lady Harryot Godolfin has bairryed her youngest son, for which she and Lord Godolfin, his son and the Duke of Molberry are in very great affliction for. In my last I wrote you word Mr. Hanburer was ill, but, thank God, he is now pretty well again. They both design to go to Twittingham next month and carry all thear own servants, and all things for thear kitchen; and Betty and I and Sue are to have our board for nothing, only we put out our washing. I offered to pey, but nether of them would hear of it; I never hard him swear before, but when I did pres him, he swore I should not. You said in one of yours, that you thought Twittingham house would be spoiled for want of leving in, so I thought you would be pleesed att thear going thear; therefore I made them the complement to offer it to them, thay having a mind to go, when the Permed was up into the country Mrs. Hill fetched Betty yesterday to the play, and also her sister Arrundell and treated them both. Mr. Elleson and I had yesterday sum discourse about my boarding with him, he ses it can not be pryvet thear, because Lord Garsy and Mrs. Varnum both coms in the somer thear, and we meet hear at Whithall Chapel; Varnum and her daughter sets in the seem pew with me, the other has both his wife and self forgot me, I believe. thears not a thought in my hart that I would hyde from the Darling of my eyes as you are to, Dearest creature, Your most infinite affectionate mother. Mis Overkirk was married to Lord Bellemount last Sunday at St. Martains church.

February 29, 1706. My dearest dear and best child, - a thousan thancks to you for yours of the 28 of this instant, short as it was, it was most heartily welcome; if but one lyne its much better then none. I will promise you to breack none of your chyney; for fear of your sconces I bought a small pair of black stands, for fear the chyney once should be broack, and cousin Hanburer has bought a pretty set to carry to Twittingham; and sister Bathurst designs to go to Riskins this summer, and Mr. Batthurst and his Lady. I wish you had Lady Mary Haystins, she for certain has twelve hundred a year inherretanc and ten thousand pound. Her brother Lord Huntingdon is very much lamented his death, and he has left Mr. Stanup four hundred a year rentcharge. Lady Harryot Godolfin greeved so much for the death of her youngest son which was the age of Bel's child, that she has throne herself into the smallpox by her exses of grief. The Duke and Dutchis of Molberry went last Monday to Woodstock, which you know is given to my Lord.

March 5, 1706. My dearist and best of children, - I heartily thanck you for your last kind letter the third of March. I think five ginneys is enough, it is what your sister Bellew sent to Peters Nurses, and I sent so much for I am Godmother, pray be not angree, I could doe no less and it is but to each child once, and I am very proud of Kelly's, I being thear great Grandmother. But Lord Rockingham gave three ginneys each, which was nyne in all; and so did the great Lord Halifax, he was Godfather to your sister Bellew; but Lord Strafford gave but five. Lady Suffolk and Lord Clarranden gave to Molly each of them ten ginneys; but they stud with King William's Queen. I think six would be very Noble for you, But less than five you cannot give. I fear you'll think me mad by my last letter, I wrote in hast and dated it the 29 of Febuary and thear is but 28 days in that month. It should have been the second of March. What shall I doe to find words to express how dearly I lov you, or to show you how most sincerely I am Dearist Creature ire, &c.

March 12, 1706. My dearist and best of children, - We want four packets, and I hope I shall have four letters in them, for in your absence nothing is so welcome to me as your letters are. Lady Katthereen Grinvell is married to Mr. Bainton, so poor Mrs. Jeferus must look out a new spark to keep her; al people laughs at her, who set up for wit and discretion, and thincks she has showed nether in this choice. Mr. Charls Arundell has got a munckey, he got it on shipborde, and it is exactly like my Pug, only mine is very pert, and full of devertin tricks, and the other is so kept under it doers not ster but just as they bid it; the eyes of mine sparkles like two dyomons, and is perter then ever you see her, and fuller of tricks, but it must be when she has a mind to it, not else. Betty presents her duty to you; I hear often from her and my neic, they are extremely kind to her. I wish she had a good husband, now is the best time for to get her well off, now she is in her pryme, I think her the hansomist of all her sisters. Indeed Mr. Arundell is an extreme kind husband, as ever I see, to his power. He has a pair of the pretyist coach horses I ever did see; they are very dark, almost like black, with white mains and long white tailse, and they go bridling and prancin along, that al people from the highest to the lowist stairs after them. Several has inquiered of the coachman whether his master will part with them. I wish you had six of them, I am sure you would be in lov with them, did you see them. My dear creature, I will relees you this post, without saying any more then to asure you, no pen can exspres how sincerely I am your most infinite affectionate mother.

April 16, 1706. My dearist and best of children, - I long to have the description of your entry. Hear is a Morockoe Ambassador, he is in his own habbitt, and thear is fain to be a strong guard set att his doar to keep the mob of. I wish Betty could be got in made of Honour, thear are lykly very soon to be room for two or three, as its said. Your sister W. father has settled sumthing upon the eldest girl, and upon Willy for thear life has given two Boocks to the girl to ground her in the true religion, and has wrote one leef to tell her he is her grandfather and godfather, and many good wishis for her and prayers. Dear soul could my wishis and prayers prevail you would be the happiest man in this world, for never did any son deserve it more or was more beloved by a mother then you are by yours.

December 20, 1706. My dearist and best of children, your sister Doneland has been very kindly yoused by the Dutchis of Molberry; her greece came hear to se her, and sent three days after to invite her to dinner, and all this day we have had mantoe women, tierwemen, and al sorts of traits, and to morro she goes as fine as the son to kiss the Queen's hand at Kensington. I am very anger with al your tenants; al others sends fowls, braun, and several things, but yours sends nothing. My neic Hanbury has buried her last son, but her eldist is very well. Betty givs her duty to you, so dus Arundell and her spouse, who are gon to thear new house, but I have not yett seen it; it is amongst the great people in Arllington Street, and I must go in splender when I go thear. The Duke of Buckingham has buried his girl, for which he and his Dutchis is in great trouble. My dear dear soul, I am more then tongue can tell your most infinite affectionate mother.

July 8, 1707. My dearist and best of children, I fear the sight of this large sheet of paper will fright you indeed I always stint my self in my paper, not having power to leev of whilst any room left. First I give a thoussan thancks for your picture, by Mr. Coape; sure not only that but any thing you liked should then be yours. My daughter Wentworth carried me yesterday to Chelcy to see Mrs. Skinner, who is with Lord Shasbary not as a servant but but as a friend. She was to see me and invited us to walk in the Gardens, prommisseing me I should not see my Lord, but he sent to her to know who we wear, and came to us and showed us his gardens and all his ingenious contrivances in his house, gave us fruit and french wine and sack, and Tea, and spoke very handsomely of you, and hee is com to see me att Twittnam. I am in lov with him, and also with his way of living, it is very delightful; he is very obliging and has a mighty ingagin way, but he loocks as if he was very short lived, which is pety. Was he twenty years older and I as many years younger, I would lay al the traps I could to get him, his youmore and mine are so alike, and he has many contrivances in his house that is just to my fancy. I wish Betty had him, he would be next to you in my affection; he is one that I could sooner be in lov with then anybody I ever yett see, he managis his house, and many of his affairs very like you, and is neet in his person like you. I wunder my sister Batthurst got him not for neic Batthurst; she is this day married to Mr. Pie.

November 14, 1707. Mrs. Hill now owns her marriage to Coll. Massum; its much pety Betty can not get to be made of honour. She would soon get a good husband, she is now hansom, but will soon fayde, she is not a lasting buity. Pray what is become of the lady you told me of a month ago, I fancy it was only a dream or will prove no better. I hear Sir Clously Shovel has left a daughter that will be a vast fortune; pray make inqr after her, his son was drowned with him. I am sure, could you but see my fire side, you would laugh heartily to se Fubs upon a cushin, the cat of another, and Pug of another lapped up al but her face in a blanckitt. I have not left room to asure you I am, dear, dear creature your most infinite affectionate mother J. W.

December 23, 1707. My dearist and best of children, I thanck you for yours of the 24 of this instint, although it was short it was heartily welcome to me as al yours are. Last Sunday I was godmother to Mr. Hanbury's boy, they refewsed the Countess of Winchelsee for me, for she offered herself to ether boy or girl; two rich sittissons stud with me, on Sir Ambrose Croly, the other Merchant Morgin, each are worth above a hundred thousand poun a peic. A Bishop crisned it, but what I forgot Sir Clowsly Shovel was buried last night at Wesminstor, and it was very fine and must needs cost a great deal of money.

My dearist and best of children Nephew Batthurst was to see me this morning and made many speeches of his great affection to you; indeed I believe him very sincere. I wish your grant was secured by Act of Permed, and your money and all you have put in sum other bodies name that has nothing to doe with Court nor Army, for I hear its in the Gazette that the Prince of Wails is going towards Dunkirk; then he may soon be hear. Hear is a great deal of grumbling about. All my news I hard just now from Sue, who has been to se some friends in the city, and they are full of such news. I wonder my nephew said nothing of it, but I made him sing all the while he was with me, for he sings charmingly. Coals are above fifty shilling a children to my grief, and coffy ten shilling a pt. I will leev it of if possible, I have for a long time dranck it, twice and some timse three timse a day. The Duke of Newcastle's daughter is violent il of a fever, the Doctors thincks her in great danger; they pray it may prove the small pox, nothing else can save her, as I am told.

Twickenham, September 6, 1708. My dearist and best of children, I long to hear you are safe att Berlin. I have had a great deal of company with me to day, and blind Mrs. Ash who commends the great room for a handsome room. I was in hops she would have commended the picturs to, and Mrs. Windom was hear who leved in this house before, and much admiers the great alteration you have made. Poor Mr. Boucher went to the Bath presently after you went, and dyed the week after he went. He made a great dinner for Sir John Garmain and some others, and finding himself very ill sent for Gath ; but when he came he told him - Dockter you can doe me no good, for I am just a dying, and so dyed. He was brought to this church and buirryed very privately under the Communion table laid at night; thear was a paper put upon the church door in verse about his many wivs, they say he has four. Its not known yett what he has left; two old women was over hard to be very witty saying, why had he no scutchyons, for he might have good arms, a pack of cards, a dyse box, and quarter a pair of sissors. His death is now all the discourse. I hope and wish that you may be in as great favour with this Queen of Prushee as you was with the last.

November 16, 1708. My dearist and best of children I have a most dismal story to tell you, God forgive me for it. I cannot help being more then I ought concerned. I shall never lov anything of that kind a quarter so well again. I had rether lost a hundred pt., nay all the rest of my doms I would have given to have saved poor charming Fubs, never poor wretch had a harder death. As it leved so it dyed, full of lov leaning its head in my bosom, never offered to snap at any body in its horrid torter but nuzzle its head to us and look earnestly upon me and Sue, who cried for three days as if it had been for a child or husband, Sure of all its kind thear never was such a one nor never can be, so many good qualities, so much senc and good nature and cleanly and not one fault; but few human creeturs had more senc then that had. I could write a queer of paper in her commendations. I have buiryed her in this garden, and thear is a stoan laid at her head. I leiv all news and the description of the Prince his buirying to your brother.

November 23, 1708. My dearist and best of children, I have been to see a very good house in St. Jamsis Squire. It has three large rooms forward and two little once backward, closets and marble chimney pieces, and harths to al the best rooms, and iron backs to the chimneys. Thear is two pretty closets with chimneys and glass over them, and picturs in the wenscoat over most of the chimneys, bras locks to al the doars, wenscoat at bottom and top and slips of boards for the hangings. Thear will want little to be dun to it. Thear is back stairs, two coach housis, and stable for ii horses, rooms over for servants, very good offices, a yard for the drying of clothes, and leds for that purpose, a stable yard and a horse pond and back gate, which I forgot the street's name it goes into. Thear is a handsome room al wenscoated for the steward to dine in, and another good room for the other servants to dine in even with the kitchen below stairs under the hall and parlors. It was my Lord Sunderland's, it was to little for them. They sold it to a merchant, who sent his foolish nephew who could not tell me the prise. It is free ground rent, and all is in herretanc. To morrow the man coms to tell me the prise.

November 26, 1708. My dearist and best of children, I have sent you the exact account under the gentleman's own hand; the man that showed me the house was a fool, he did not show me all the stables nor coach housis. Indeed it is a noble house, you may build a gallery over the offices; they say this house is so strong it will last for ever, and all the new buildings are very slight. My old Lady Bristo gave it her daughter Sunderlin, then she let this young Lord and his Lady live some years in it, and after she had sold it they heered it for a year of him. He asurse me none of the chimneys smoke and thear is New Rever water in all the offices and great led sesterns in two or three playsis, the kitchen is one, and the brewhous and wash house. Thear is a large chimney and great and oven and five stoavs in the kitchen. He ses the locks are worth 30 l. , then thear is picturs over the chimneys. Doe you know my Lady Oogla's, her house in the Pelmell is to be sold for two thousand pound. It has a fine prospeck in the Park, but not half so good as that in the Square, nor so convenyent; I believe that can have no stables. I have promised Mr. Stracy his answer in three weeks. I wish and hope you will have that in the square, it is a noble house and fit for you, and strong, no danger of its falling by great winds; abundance of the new buildings fall. It must be very warm having those brick walls. It is a great frost, my hands are so cold I can hardly hold my pen.

December 10, 1708. My dearist and best of children Yesterday I had like to have been caught in a trap, your Brother Wentworth had almost persuaded me to have gon last night to hear the fine muisick, the famous Etallion sing att the rehearsal of the Operer, which he assured me it was so dark none could see me. Indeed music was the greatist temtation I could have, but I was afraid he deceived me, so Betty only went with his wife and him; and I rejoiced I did not, for thear was a vast deal of company and good light - but the Dutchis of Molbery had got the Italian to sing and he sent an excuse, but the Dutchis of Shrosberry made him com, brought him in her coach but Mrs. Taufs hurt and would not sing because he had first put it of; though she was thear yet she would not, but went away. I wish the house would al join to humble her and not receive her again. This man out dus Sefachoe, they say that has hard both.

December 21, 1708. My dearist and best of children, - Now I hope all your troublesome time is over, but now mine is aproachin, for Crismass brings abundance of troublesome gess. I design to be as sneaking as I can, and doe no works of suparflewety, only what just nessessety foarsis. This time of mirth the greatist I shall have will be your dear letters, which are always a joy unexspresable to me. Thear is a story goes for truith that Lady Harryot Veer shows a contract of Mr. Anslow's under his hand and seal; its said he has offered her five thousand pt. or an enewety of five hundred a year for her life, but she can recover half his wiv's fortune, he has laitly married a great fortune Mrs. Knight.

column46: London, December 28, 1708. Dear Brother, I find the Torys design as soon as the house meets again to be very strict in the examination of those that were concern in the late intended invasion, and they talk that they shall be able to bring strange things to light. Mr. Addisson is certain of going over Secretary to Lord Wharton, and Mr. Steel put in for his place, but Lord Sunderland has put him off with a promise to get him the next place he shall ask that may be keep with his Gazette. I hear it is one of the Scotch members that is to come into Mr. Addisson place, but I don't know his name yet. To-day we had the news that Bruges and Placental had surrendered, but yet it is said the Duke of Marlborough won't come over till the middle of February. We have no other manner of news which I am sorry for, for if I knew any I have time enough to writ it; all the world is at the Opera where I can't go. When one does not know what to say they talk of the weather, the sudden change will give me an opportunity to make my letter a little longer; it is now a very hard frost and as great a snow as we have had for many years in England.

column46: London, January 25, 1709. Dear Brother, I have sent you a copy of a letter I writ to my Lord Treasurer, and sent it to him last night, I shall have no opportunity of seeing him till Thursday morning at his Levee, so by the next post I shall be able to tell you how he takes it, but I can't be so soon out of my pains as to what you think on it, I mean well, tho I have not the best way of expressing myself. I could not determine to imitate your stile and hand, because I could not tell how to bring in your knowledge of Lord Herbert's death, who died suddenly last Saturday night which I did not hear till Monday - and then I fell a beating my brains to produce this poor letter, which I almost despair of, for since I have been told Mr. Dolbin, a great stickle for Lord Treasurer in the house of Commons has the fairest prospect of it, Lord Delawar I know asked for it, and my Lord Effingham trusted me with the secret that he intended to ask, and told me that last week he had spoke to Lord T- in general to do something for him, who had promised him to take care of him, and asked him if there was anything in particular he would have, and when he could hear of anything he like to be sure to let him know it. I said not a word of my design to him, nor of my thoughts of Lord T- funning speech that was intended to make him leave the Whigs in the votes of the Duke of Queen's Borrow, which took, but the Court lost it by seven votes; it is said the Whigs bestirred themselves the more about this because the Duke of Monross was not made Secretary of State for Scotland, who is to come in for an equal share of all the profits of our two, but is to transact no affairs but those of Scotland. It is talked as if the Duke of Somerset was not so well with the juncto as usual, and that Duke Hambleton is reckon as a very stanch Whig, and that he's to be made Master of the Horse. I sent you word in my last how gentlemen bestirred themselves to throw out Sir Simon Harcourt who they tell me for his dieing speech made a very bitter one against a great man who commands all the money in the nation, and Mr. Jennins a member died suddenly and Sir Simon is gone down to make an interest there, but let him be choose never so, it is resolved to throw him out; it was the fate of Tony Roe to be served so for a jest, but this is in very great earness. It is said Sir Simmon will print his speech, which they tell me is more artfully worded then Lord Haversham's. There's a dream from Harwich which sells well, and is reckoned a very cunning and insinuating paper, it is too scurrilous and I think a little too big to be put in a letter; most people I have talked with of it will have it Harley's stile, by that you will see it is reckoned no foolish thing. There was an advantage taken on Saturday when the house was thin to desire that an account might be laid before the house of what is done with the contribution money; those that spoke against gave an account that it was an agreement that the Dutch should have it for furnishing the necessaries for sieges, and that the inquiring into that matter might raise jealousy in our best ally, the Dutch; it was answered, they only desired to have that agreement laid before them wherein it was stipulated, and they would be satisfied without any further inquiry, and then it was said there was nothing in writing, but only a tacit consent of the Duke of M-, but of the safe gaurd money some people that love to exaggerate things pretent to say the D. of M. for a 100 days this campaign received each day two thousand pounds.

March 29, 1709. Lady Wharten is very ill of the colic, which has put her in convention fits; the world is so mallistious as to say its only because she has no mind to go to Ireland. Poor Mr. Tilson's brother last Saturday in the morning bought a pair of pistols and half a dozen pistol bullets, and powder; he charged each pistol with a brace of bullets, set himself in a cheer in his chamber and shot both thees pistols into his head, which split his scull in pieces. He left a paper upon his table by him "Let none be surprised att my death, my time was come, and I have freed myself from a melancholy world." He buried his wife two year ago, and has three children; he was in a very plentiful condition. It's in print, and thear they commend him for a very good man, but say it was for a young gentlewoman in Wesminstor he was in lov with. Your Mr. Tilson is very melancholy, I hope he will not doe so.

column46: London, 10 June , 1709. Dear Brother, By this post our Politians of this side the water expected to hear the French were come to, and that they would yield to sign the prelimarys of Peace, but by all that appears in prints it looks to them as if they were determine to stand the fate of another campaign. Monsr Shamirards being turn out, and Madam Mentenon's going into a covent is interpreted as the Old King's resigning in a manner the Government in his life time to the Dauphin. But a Gentleman told me that Sir Harry Furnace told him he read a letter of the Duke of Marlborough's which had these words, that if they did not hear from the French in a day or two, they would then begin again, from whence some people will still conclude that the Peace will still be this Summer, and that the delay the French has made is concerted and is only to save appearance to the Spainers, and a little to the Elector of Bavarior. At our coffee houses we are very angry that the news talks of our beseigeing Douay; for their opinion is that we ought not to amuse ourselves in taking towns, but march directly to Paris. When they are told that an army can't march without having before provided magasins, or at least to have such a train of provisions with them as will subsist an army that is to burn and destroy all before them, they give no answer to this but - How did Prince Eugene march his army over the mountains without such a train or money, and his march to the relief of Turin was in like manner; it is but to employ him and the business is done. Or - why not go on with the scheme that was talked of before the Peace was thought so near a conclusion, that an army should march from Flanders into Pickardy, and that a fleet from hence should land upon the coast, with all necessary to support such an army. - If they are told it is too late to provide such provision, then they fall upon the credulity of those that gave so much into the faith of the French King's sincerity to peace. I have given you a strange medley of discourse, but there nothing else talk of, and I hold myself oblige to writ to you every post.

1709. My dearist and best of children, I hope I have laid a good foundaytion for you with your ingenious headpeec to finish. It would be to tedious to trouble you with all my inventions to bring this to pas, but in short I found none seemed so secure as this. Hall who is very dexterus at all things he wrote a letter wherein he aquanted Lady Brownloe that he was sent by a parson of quality about a buisnes that might be a great satisfaction to each family, and beged the favour he might speak a word in pryvitt with her ladyship. So he stayed tell she was up, and she came to him, but brought her steward who stood at a distance while he told her that he was sent by a parson of qallety which had seen her youngest daughter and was very much in lov with her, which if she pleesed to give leev she should have a parteculor of his estate, and then know his name. So she said she could say nothing without knowing the name. So he told her it was you. She said she had hard a very good corrector of you, but she was not willing to marry the youngest before the elder; She smiled when he said you was in lov with her. She said she would consider of it; he asked her if she would give him leeve to wait of her again, She said by no means - or if she would give me leev to wait upon her, she said no, she would not have me give my self that trouble, but she presented her service to me. He told her I sent him, and you had wrote two or three letters to me about it. So Ellison, Hall, and I think that you should write immediately to my Lady and another enclosed to the young one, and not to let it get wind. I am possetivly sure it will doe if you will go one with it, and yet no creature hear knows it but Hall and Ellison; for I shall despair if any of Potter's family know it, not but he and his wife are both to good to hinder it, but she has many relations to my knowledge would leeve no stoan, as the saying is, unturned to hinder it. You know this Lady Brownloe has five daughters, the eldest married to Lord Exetor, the second to Lord Gilford, the third is going but not yet married, but al things conclewded one with Lord Sherwood, who I hear has no very great estate but they say the Earl of Exetor lovs drincking and so dus this Lord Sherwood, and that he has made the match up. This is what Hall tells me. Peter told me he was to be married to this lady, for your sister Wentworth is very great with Lord Sherwood's mother and sister. He nor Lord Gilford are what I like. Lord Gilford loocks not at all like quality but a little ugly man. I think Lord Sherwood is proper and tall, but loocks heavy and dull. As much as I see of them, the youngest will be envied by all her sisters, if it be her happy fate to get you. Elleson sess Mrs. Reevsis mother is dead and that she has undeniable twenty four thousand pound, and he thought you had liked her. Lady Gilford lives over against your sister Arundell; I think her very pretty, but I know the youngest is thought by all the pretyist of them all. Dear soul, loos no time, but write, and if you would att the same time indite one for me, I may enclose yours and give it ether to Elleson or Hall to carry; it will not be proper for me to carry it, because he ask leev for me to wait of her and she refewsed it, and I am so dashed to a stranger that I shall spoil the cause quite. God derect you and prosper you, and make you in this and in al things throughout happy, to the great comfort of, Dearist, dear creature Your most infinite affectionate Mother.

column46: London, 21 February , 1710. Dear Brother, Saturday last I sent your two letters to Mr. Bromley and frank't them as you ordered, and yesterday I received another which I send away by this post, and find by your last resolve of having it like brick and stone twill be like the Duchess of M- house she has built in the Queen's Guarden, which is said to be one of the most perfect Models thats in England. There's no news, but all the Ladies are making their advances to the Lords, to get tickets from them to see and be seen at the Trial, for that reason the Young Lords make a bustle to have their full number of ticket, 8 a peace, though they know there is not room for half that number. They have made an order of the house that no absent lords shall have any, and so all that will have any must be at the call of the house the day before. Here's a supposed letter to a friend sent me by the Penny Post, which the Tories would have believed to be more then a jest in it. It was talked by some as if there was a design to stir up the house of Commons to impeach Mr. Harley for writing his thoughts so freely, as they say he did, to one of the States General, laying open the vast need England had of Peace, our debts being so great, and the Reasons the Queen had, not to have such favourable thoughts as formerly of the Duke of M-; but of his writing such a letter it is thought they wanted sufficient proof, or when proved they doubted whether they could carry the matter so high as to bring it to an impeachment to do Mr. Harley any harm. It seems we are not the only Court that discards old favourites for new ones, for it is said there's a new one sprung up at Berlin.

March 18, 1710. My dearist and best of children, I hear the Duke of Molbery is going over to treat about a peec, I pray heartily for his good suckses, and then as heartily for your return. I hope you will not let one post slip without a letter to Lady B. and her daughter; in my own imagination I doe conclewd it dun, if it be not your fault, delay in such afairs loocks ill and seldom prospers. I went the other day to see your great wulf dogs. I think them very handsome, but they are very poor; they eat bread very gently out of my hand, but you must take cair they hurt not Folly nor Dorrendor. Just now the Lady Raby that would be so was to see me, she goes to morroe into the country, but I own I like this last much better. God grant this last may be so and make you as happy as ever man upon earth was, or can be, in a wife. I am sure it must be her own fault if she be not so, for so good a son can not but be a good husband. One great happiness, they are all modest virtuous young women. I hear send you a paper to make you laugh. Dear Dear Creature I am your most infinite affectionate mother J. W.

Twickenham, June 29, 1710. My dearist and best of children, in my last I told you all my news, and have only one dismal story to tell you now, which is that most of the young men in this town are in Newgate. It seems its a custum in thees country towns for the young men to steel the Maypoale from one to the other, so all the young men of Twitnam went to Whitton and they it seems had notis of it, so was upon thear guard and fought for it. It was in the dark, and they had not been known only one of them to save himself told of the rest, and one of the Whiten men is dead, and another very ill, but he its thought will recover. Sir Charls Duncome lives at Whiten, so he must be for his own towns men. One of thees poor wretches was brought home hear last night dead of the small pox, his mother ready to run mad for him, as good a young man as ever leved. Lady Mary Chambers promised he should com to no hurt, for she loved him very much, he having been a servant of hers, he is much lamented. Mr. Elleson has been hear to look after the affairs hear, so Pall, Pug, and the rest of thear train went with him in to the charming garden. Hear is Lady Grenvill with her two grandsons the Duke of Buford's sons, lovely boys, I wish you had two such. Lady Clarck has beged me to give her most humble service to you and ses she lovs you dearly. She is so fond of me, that if she dyse before me I am sure she will make me her air, or at leest leev me a good legacy. I wish I could find out a cheap and good picture drawer and I would send you Gallant his wife and daughter and beloved al thear picturs, and Pug in the middle. I see one of Willy Wentworth dun in black, very like him, and for five shilling. I fear my little sun at Ritchmon is quite vanished, and no more thought of; I should rether have the Duke of Buforde, for all he has two sons. My letter is called for, so I must only asure you I am, my dearist dear creature Your most infinite affectionate mother.

Twickenham, July 7, 1710. My dearist and best of children, I never remember such cold whether at this time of the year, which I fear will make corn grow dear; it is risen a little. I told you a great lye in a former letter, that thear was a great many of the young men of this town in Newgate, but thear was but two, most of the rest run away; one of those two dyed thear, and yesterday the other was quited, which was your poor glazier's son, who is grown very poor, being laime this great while. Its said Sir Charls Dunckom made the jury at Tedinton bring it in murder, but the jury at London brought it in but chance medley. Al this town hate Dunckome and Secretary Johnson, for he said he would have them all hanged. Just now I hear Dunckom is so much concerned for the death of that poor good young man that dyed in Newgate, that he has been a friend to this and bailed him his own self.

Twickenham, July 22, 1710. My dearist and best of children, ten thousand thancks to you for all your kindness, whatever coms from you will be highly valued by me. I hope you will bring the little dog yourself, but I doe not wish for your coming tell the timse are more settled, sure amongst all thees changes it will be hard if you get not a good one. I thought it had been a brag, but is certainly true, Lord Paulett, Secretary Johnson nephew, who has a vast estate, was offered to be secretary of state, and he refused it; and now he has excepted of the preveseel, I think it is, or some such great place. Certain those that has no dependence upon the Court are much happier, but few are of that mind. Last Sunday, thear could not be a more dismal melancholy sight then poor Lady Tufton led by her eldist son, the eldist daughter following led by the other, and the other four daughters following one after the other, al in long scarfs, and allamode huods over thear faicis, not a bit to be seen of them. So they sat al church-time, and a very hot day, I wonder they was not smothered. The young lady you ask after was one Mrs. Cornish the shreevs grand daughter that was hanged a little before King Charls dyed or not long after, I forget which, he was in some plot; I think your sister Wentworth got aquanted with them at the Bath. This young women is very handsome, but not so handsome nether. Indeed you have set me a task, its what is so conterary to me I know not how to effect it but one moment, I wish the poor man be safe, for we have had terrible storms hear. Coll. St. Peer and his lady was hear and lodge at Ritchmon. I have a coach att my doar so must conclewd Dearist dear Soul Your most affectionate Mother.

Twickenham, July 28, 1710. My dearist dear, yesterday morning came your gentleman of the horse and brought me, what was most welcome to me, the good news of your health and good loocks, and al the pretty things, and the water, which next post I will tell you how I like it; I cannot se so soon. Your box of essins is very pretty, so is the shoe you sent me, and the prints. He has ten for Yorkshire, your brother six, and the box of treeckle she is to have when she coms hear, which will be next week; the rest shall be disposed as you ordered, and the arms I will keep tell your closet flower is finished, it must lye awhile because else the boards may shrink - a million of thancks to you for all thees pretty things. The gentleman would not dine hear, he said he had abundance of business and was to return back presently again to London. I would by no meens have you part with your pretty Pearl tell you come yourself, and then you will see my Gallant and the rest are as well loosed to as your Perle, and Sue is as fond of them as myself. It has been a very sickly time at London and every where, I thanck God I am very well now but my head has been much out of order, but it went of only with a vapor fit. I did fear convulsions, but it did not com to that. I was blooded and toock abundance of slops; my blood had no fault but being to good and to much, the finest colour you ever see; and Jackson hear blooded me, and I bled presently very freely; and at London just before you came I had Missis Dockter, and a famous sirgion and nether could bleed me but at my wrist and keeping my hand in hot water. Your sister Betty has won a pair of silk stockings at the half crown lottry, I wish I could give you joy of the thousand a year for your lot.

Twickenham, October 3, 1710. My dearist and best of children, the Queen is com to Hampton Court, sure she will not stay long, it is so very cooled. Its said she designs to stay six weeks. Thees three nights I have been much happier then in the days, for I have dreamed I have been with you. I had a very comickal letter the other day from Miss Bellew, where she dossiers me to let all her relations know she is in the land of the leving yett, and is in better health then she has been of some years, and has worked me a very pretty black and white purse, and sent me. Flert has a another lettor of pretty puppies, she has five now, but never had but four before. The man stays, so you will be rely this time when I have assured you that I am more then I can tel you, my dearest dear soul, your most infinite affectionate mother.

column46: London, 31st November , 1710. Dear Brother, What past remarkable in the house of Lords Tuesday I did not hear till next morning or else I should have sent it you by that Mail. When they had drawn up or resolved upon their address of thanks to the Queen for her Speech My Lord Scarborough made a motion as if he thought it then a proper time for that house to thank his Grace, and was seconded by the Duke of Richmond. The Duke of Argile rise up and desired the Noble Lord that spoke first would explain himself, for he did not know who he meant by his Grace; Lord Scarborough answered he could mean nobody but his Grace the Duke of M- who has made such a Glorious campaign. Then the Duke of A- made a speech against the thanks of the house being given to the D. of M-; all I could hear of his Speech was that he said it was true there was four towns taken this Campaign, and but one of those four was of any use or advantage to the allies, the other three having cost more blood then it was worth, and before the house thought of giving him any thanks they should have an account of the business he was chiefly sent over for. A Plenipotentionar for a Peace, when that matter was heard it would be time enough to consider whether thanks should be given him. Lord North rise up and second the Duke of Argile. Then Lord Ferrers rise up, and they say, said a great many handsome things in the praise of the Duke of M- but concluded as he was not here it would be more proper to defer the thanks of the house till he came over, which was a motion the Duke of M- friends were glad to close in with that it might never come to a question to have the house divide about it, for they saw they should lose it. Lord Wharton they tell me made a very confused speech, which seemed not to be acted but real; he said he was a mased that such a motion should now have been made, but more a mased that being moved it should meet with any opposition, and after repeating some of the great services the Duke of M- had done the Nation, which was not spoke with his usual briskness, he joined in with lord Ferrers to have the matter dropped till the arrival of the Duke of M-. It is doubt'd whether Lord Scarborough designed this motion as a service or a disservice to the Duke, it was plain he did it with out consulting any of the great men of that side for they all seemed to be surprised and unprepared for it. In the house of Commons the Whigs, the Tories say, have begun to show their teeth before they can bite. Mr. Walpool, at the committee that was appointed to draw up their Address of thanks for the Queens speech, Sr Thomas Hanmore was in the chair, took notes and writ down what he seemed not to like; they there told him it was unparliamentary to writ so before the thing was finished. But he maintained it to be the right of every member to writ what he pleased or why had they pen and ink allowed. After some squabling they yield him the point, but when it was finished they desire to have his notes, but he made no answer but took his paper and lapped it up very deliberately and went away with it into the house, and showed it to Letchmore and some more who set there heads together how they would desire to have it amended when it came into the house. The Tories tell me as they had cooked it they made arrant nonsense on it and there was an hour debate about the words which and and , who was for the Which and who for the And I know not, after that Mr. Walpool would have the Pretender mentioned, which accation'd some debate, but Mr. Harley's speech yield up that matter. He said their mentioning the house of Hanover implied they had not thoughts of the Pretender, without naming him, which seemed to be all together needless, but since he had been named he knew what use would be made of it without doors if now refused. So it was agreed to but they amended to that amendment, so that the Tories say the Whigs did but make a rod for their own breech. It was presented to the Queen to day about three a clock, since I shall see it in Print to morrow I thought it was not worth making my dinner stay to hear it. I must confess I long till it comes out because I have heard all this talk about it, though I believe 'twon't be so well as the Lords for I hear it is three times as long.

December 29, 1710. My dearist and best of children, hear are choice of good housis to be had. My Lord Broocks is as I told you of in my last, which stands in the midst of good company. Thear is five years to com of my Lords Lees which is to be sold, and I sent to inquire what they ask for thear time, and who the land lord is, and his rait to sell it. Thear is a pretty garden and a doar into St. James Park. The next house is Lord Litchfeild's, Lady Overkirk designs to leev it and take a les; you know thear is a pretty garden and a charming prospect, and the most convenyents in the world for thees lodgins. Thear is a doar at the foot of the stairs that coms in to thear eating room, the worst is the coming to it in a coach is not handsome; the coach way is in Downing Street. It belongs to the Crown and is granted by three lives and one of these three lives is out, so the life you may beg of the Queen that is out, and the other two I hope you may beg as they fall. Therefore this house may be a great peneworth to you, and it is as noble a house as you can have. And thear is a third which is a very good one, and very convenient and well built, my father had the building of it, and it cost ten thousand pt. The walls are of a great height, because none should over look them, a pretty little garden and coach house and stables for more then oaght horses. Its the strongest built of all the housis in the Squar; its next doar to my nephew Batthurst. The prise is six thousand pt. My father built it by the order of King Jaims for Lady Dorchester. The ground rent is very small, not above 15 pt. a year. Moonsear Spannyor leved thear. In the worst of thees housis one mey be very esy and happy. Nether of the other two have coach housis or stables belongin to them. My nephews house has six rooms of a flower, besides closets and very good sailors and offesis and good rooms over the stables. Lady Dorchisters is much better, its the best in the squar. Pray tell me which of them you like. Dear soul my paper is al filled with thees housis, I wish the best of them were filled with you and all your goods, with the adetion of a good, buitefull, virtuous wife, to the great comfort of, my dearist dear, your most infinite affectionate mother. Thear is a vollery of birds to Lord Litchfields.

column46: London, February 20, 1711. Dear Brother, This loyal country club is a great disturbance to Mr. Harley, who finds they are past his governing; their Number is increased to a 150. They are most of them young gentlemen of estates that has never been in Parliament before, and are not very close, but declare to every body what they design, to have every Whig turned out, and not to suffer that the new Ministry should shake hands as they see they do with old. I was told by two or three of this club last Sunday, that they begin to send the old Fellows among them, but damn they won't be bite so, and that neither their weadles nor threats shall bring them under government, what has once been carried by the majority of their club they will stand to to a man in the house; they don't care for their telling 'em they will be dissolved for it is what they know they dare not do, for they will be all choose again. Mr. Bathurst who is of this club, tells me they talk of examining into the grants, and he asked me the nature of yours which I told him, and he said as it was a lease there was no danger and he would give me timly notice if there was any occasion to make friends about it. I spoke afterword to Lord Windsor about it and he said there was some such talk but it would come to nothing, for the talk was of ordering a committee to inspect into the exobitant Grants, and he did not see that would reach any body but Lord Portland's; yours was so inconsiderable and judged so by the house when jack How mentioned the exorbitant grants in King W- time, that there would be no occasion to make friends about it, if there was he himself would be your Solicitor. It is talk now by every body that the Duke of Argile won't go into Spain, that last week he was very plain with persons at the helm, and told them if they did not support him so and so he would not go, for if they designed Spain should be lost by degrees, he had rather any body went then he. They say this has so much offended that the 3000 a year pension that was said to have been granted him is not yet past nor will not pass, but he goes on with the resolution of selling his regiment for 7,000 to Coll. Selwine if he can raise the money. Frank Godfrey is to sell for the same sum to Coll. Dunn who it seems pretents to sell out of Pique that Britain and Sutton has their commission of Brigadier antedated to his, and it has been decided that it shall stand good against him. Old regiments become now the fashion to be sold makes Coll. Cornwall very fond of buying one, and has said often to me he wished you would talk with him in earness about selling yours to him as you did in jest when here in England, for he had rather have yours then any Regiment in the Service, and would give what any body would give. I don't hear there's any alteration in the resolutions concerning you, I am told of it by every but I still say I know nothing.
